0.name: Mosquito jscript backdoor
0.uncertain_mes: [Mosquito](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0256) is a Win32 backdoor that has been used by [Turla](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0010). [Mosquito](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0256) is made up of three parts: the installer, the launcher, and the backdoor. The main backdoor is called CommanderDLL and is launched by the loader program. (Citation: ESET Turla Mosquito Jan 2018)
0.profile: [profile]Mosquito JScript Backdoor, also known as Mosquito, is a Win32 backdoor attributed to the Turla group. It consists of three components: an installer, a launcher, and the main backdoor module called CommanderDLL. A key technical behavior is its use of Google Apps Script as its command and control (C&C) server. It targets Windows platforms and has been observed using privilege escalation via the Metasploit module ext_server_priv.x86.dll.
0.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Mosquito JScript Backdoor, also known as Mosquito, is a backdoor attributed to the Turla group. It uses Google Apps Script as its command and control (C&C) server. Its key behaviors include collecting system information, uploading and executing files, and executing shell commands. It targets web servers, functioning as a proxy to relay HTTP requests from other compromised hosts and can perform SEO fraud by manipulating responses to search engine crawlers. It has been used in operations against diplomats in Eastern Europe.[/profile]

2.name: custom metasploit shellcode executable
2.profile: [profile]Custom Metasploit Shellcode Executable, also referred to in Turla operations as 'mosquito', is a custom executable containing Metasploit shellcode used to maintain Meterpreter sessions. It achieves persistence by saving to the Windows Startup directory as 'msupdateconf.exe'. The malware is attributed to the Turla intrusion set and is designed for the Windows platform.
2.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The malware "custom metasploit shellcode executable" is a generic executable containing Metasploit shellcode, used to maintain access via a Meterpreter session. It is attributed to the Turla group in the context of the Mosquito toolset. A key technical behavior is achieving persistence by saving itself to the Windows Startup directory, specifically as "C:\Users\<username>\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\msupdateconf.exe". Its target platform is Windows.

3.name: persistence
3.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may clear artifacts associated with previously established persistence on a host system to remove evidence of their activity. This may involve various actions, such as removing services, deleting executables, [Modify Registry](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1112), [Plist File Modification](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1647), or other methods of cleanup to prevent defenders from collecting evidence of their persistent presence.(Citation: Cylance Dust Storm) Adversaries may also delete accounts previously created to maintain persistence (i.e. [Create Account](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1136)).(Citation: Talos - Cisco Attack 2022)

In some instances, artifacts of persistence may also be removed once an adversary’s persistence is executed in order to prevent errors with the new instance of the malware.(Citation: NCC Group Team9 June 2020)
3.profile: [profile]Clear Persistence, designated as T1070.009 under the Defense Evasion tactic, is a technique where adversaries remove artifacts of previously established persistence on a host to conceal their activity. This cleanup can involve actions like deleting services, executables, modifying the Windows Registry or macOS Plist files, and removing accounts created for persistence, as observed in campaigns by groups like APT28, APT17, and FIN7. The technique is also used to prevent errors when deploying new malware instances.
3.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "persistence" is a high-level tactic within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, not a specific technique, and therefore lacks a T-ID. It encompasses the adversary's objective to maintain their foothold on systems across restarts, changed credentials, or other interruptions. Specific techniques for achieving this include abusing Microsoft Office application startup mechanisms like add-ins (T1137.006) and templates, which execute code when Office applications launch. Adversaries may also later clear these persistence artifacts (T1070.009) to remove evidence of their activity.

5.name: metasploit module
5.profile: [profile]The entity "metasploit module" is a tool or framework component, not a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique, so no standard ID, Tactic, or Platform is assigned. It is directly connected to the "privilege escalation" attack pattern. Retrieved information indicates Metasploit modules can be used to exploit default accounts for initial access, persistence, and privilege escalation, and to abuse stolen private keys for remote service access, as referenced in a Metasploit SSH module.
5.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "metasploit module" is not a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique but a tool or framework used to execute various techniques. It is commonly associated with the tactic of Privilege Escalation. The Metasploit framework contains modules that automate the exploitation of software vulnerabilities, such as those in default accounts (T1078.001), to execute code and elevate permissions from user to SYSTEM/root. It is also utilized for techniques like Dynamic-link Library Injection (T1055.001) to run arbitrary code within the address space of legitimate processes for evasion and potential privilege escalation.

6.name: privilege escalation
6.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may exploit software vulnerabilities in an attempt to elevate privileges. Exploitation of a software vulnerability occurs when an adversary takes advantage of a programming error in a program, service, or within the operating system software or kernel itself to execute adversary-controlled code. Security constructs such as permission levels will often hinder access to information and use of certain techniques, so adversaries will likely need to perform privilege escalation to include use of software exploitation to circumvent those restrictions.

When initially gaining access to a system, an adversary may be operating within a lower privileged process which will prevent them from accessing certain resources on the system. Vulnerabilities may exist, usually in operating system components and software commonly running at higher permissions, that can be exploited to gain higher levels of access on the system. This could enable someone to move from unprivileged or user level permissions to SYSTEM or root permissions depending on the component that is vulnerable. This could also enable an adversary to move from a virtualized environment, such as within a virtual machine or container, onto the underlying host. This may be a necessary step for an adversary compromising an endpoint system that has been properly configured and limits other privilege escalation methods.

Adversaries may bring a signed vulnerable driver onto a compromised machine so that they can exploit the vulnerability to execute code in kernel mode. This process is sometimes referred to as Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver (BYOVD).(Citation: ESET InvisiMole June 2020)(Citation: Unit42 AcidBox June 2020) Adversaries may include the vulnerable driver with files delivered during Initial Access or download it to a compromised system via [Ingress Tool Transfer](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1105) or [Lateral Tool Transfer](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1570).
6.profile: [profile]Exploitation for Privilege Escalation is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1068 under the Privilege Escalation tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It involves exploiting software vulnerabilities, such as programming errors in OS components or high-privilege software, to execute adversary-controlled code and elevate permissions from user to SYSTEM/root or escape virtualized environments. A specific method is Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver (BYOVD), where a signed vulnerable driver is introduced to exploit a kernel vulnerability. This technique is used by groups like APT28, APT29, and FIN6.
6.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Privilege Escalation" is a core adversarial objective, not a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique with a single ID. It is the tactic of gaining higher-level permissions on a system or network. Technical mechanics involve exploiting software vulnerabilities (T1068) to execute code from a lower to a higher privilege context, including kernel mode via vulnerable drivers (BYOVD), and abusing credentials from local (T1078.003) or domain accounts (T1078.002) to bypass security restrictions. It is performed on various platforms and is associated with groups like APT29 and Turla.[/profile]

7.name: mosquitto backdoor
7.profile: [profile]Mosquitto Backdoor, also known as Outlook Backdoor, is attributed to the Turla intrusion set. It leverages the Metasploit framework and uses the MQTT protocol for command and control, specifically communicating with the broker.emqx.io server by publishing Base64-encoded shellcode payloads to client-specific topics. It primarily targets Windows platforms as a backdoor.
7.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Mosquitto backdoor is a malware that uses the MQTT protocol for command and control, specifically publishing and subscribing to topics on brokers like broker.emqx.io to transmit base64-encoded shellcode payloads. It is related to or shares infrastructure with the Wikiloader malware. There is no specific attributed group or target platform information available in the provided context.[/profile]

8.name: Metasploit
8.profile: [profile]Metasploit is a penetration testing framework used for security assessments and by threat actors for malicious purposes. It is not malware itself but a tool leveraged by intrusion sets like Turla, RocketKitten, FIN7, and Kimsuky. It generates various payloads and shellcode, including Meterpreter and SMB backdoors like SWRORT, to facilitate initial infection, credential theft, lateral movement, and system control, primarily targeting Windows platforms. Its open-source nature makes it widely accessible for exploitation.[/profile]
8.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Metasploit is a penetration testing framework used for security assessments and by threat actors for malicious purposes. It is not a single malware but a toolset that can generate and deliver various payloads, including Meterpreter shellcode and backdoors like SWRORT.SMB. It is used by multiple threat groups, including Kimsuky, APT33, Lazarus Group, and Operation C-Major, for initial infection, credential theft, lateral movement, and system control. It primarily targets Windows systems and is associated with delivering other malware, such as the Mosquitto backdoor used by Turla.[/profile]

11.name: Gazer
11.uncertain_mes: [Gazer](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0168) is a backdoor used by [Turla](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0010) since at least 2016. (Citation: ESET Gazer Aug 2017)
11.profile: [profile]Gazer, also known as Crutch, is a backdoor attributed to the Turla APT group, used from at least 2015-2016 through early 2020. Its key technical behaviors include acting as a document stealer, employing evasion techniques like changing internal strings and randomizing markers, and securely wiping files. It is associated with components like WhiteBear and utilizes specific resources for C&C communication and RSA encryption keys for its operations.[/profile]
11.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Gazer is a backdoor and document stealer malware attributed to the Turla APT group, used since at least 2016. Key technical behaviors include using RSA encryption for its components, employing a C&C communication DLL for transport, and evading detection by modifying strings, randomizing tags, and performing secure file erasure. It targets Windows systems and utilizes compromised legitimate websites and specific registry paths for persistence and operation.[/profile]

16.name: RSA
16.profile: [profile]RSA is a widely used asymmetric encryption algorithm (public key cryptography) that employs a keypair: a public key for encryption and a private key for decryption. It is formally identified as a component of MITRE ATT&CK technique T1573.002 (Asymmetric Cryptography) under the Command and Control tactic. The algorithm is used to establish secure channels, often to conceal C2 traffic or for exfiltration over encrypted non-C2 protocols. Adversaries, including groups like Turla, may target systems using RSA SecurID tokens to intercept multi-factor authentication codes and bypass security mechanisms.[/profile]
16.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "RSA" refers to the widely used RSA public-key encryption algorithm, a specific implementation of the MITRE ATT&CK technique Asymmetric Cryptography (T1573.002) under the Command and Control tactic. It operates across multiple platforms. Technically, it uses a public-private key pair where data encrypted with a recipient's public key can only be decrypted with the corresponding private key, ensuring confidentiality for C2 or data exfiltration channels. It is also referenced as a target for interception in multi-factor authentication bypass techniques, where adversaries may capture RSA SecurID token codes.

17.name: 3DES
17.profile: [profile]3DES is the Triple Data Encryption Algorithm, a symmetric block cipher used to encrypt C2 traffic, as seen in malware like Gazer. It functions by applying the DES cipher three times to each data block, increasing security compared to single DES. This technique falls under the MITRE ATT&CK sub-technique T1573.001 (Symmetric Cryptography) within the Command and Control tactic, and is employed by groups such as Turla to obfuscate network communications.[/profile]
17.profile_without_enhance: [profile]3DES is a symmetric encryption algorithm used by adversaries to conceal command and control traffic, referenced under the technique Standard Cryptographic Protocol (T1032). It uses the same key for encryption and decryption and is commonly employed alongside other algorithms like AES and DES by groups such as APT28 and Lazarus Group to obfuscate network communications.

18.name: Process Injection
18.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may inject code into processes in order to evade process-based defenses as well as possibly elevate privileges. Process injection is a method of executing arbitrary code in the address space of a separate live process. Running code in the context of another process may allow access to the process's memory, system/network resources, and possibly elevated privileges. Execution via process injection may also evade detection from security products since the execution is masked under a legitimate process. 

There are many different ways to inject code into a process, many of which abuse legitimate functionalities. These implementations exist for every major OS but are typically platform specific. 

More sophisticated samples may perform multiple process injections to segment modules and further evade detection, utilizing named pipes or other inter-process communication (IPC) mechanisms as a communication channel.
18.profile: [profile]Process Injection, identified as T1055, is a Defense Evasion and Privilege Escalation technique applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS. It involves executing arbitrary code within the address space of a legitimate live process to evade detection and potentially gain elevated privileges. Specific implementations include DLL injection using APIs like `VirtualAllocEx` and `CreateRemoteThread`, PE injection, and proc memory injection via the `/proc` filesystem on Linux. More sophisticated variants use process hollowing or segment modules across multiple injections, utilizing inter-process communication like named pipes. Associated malware includes Gazer and Carbon orchestrator, and it is used by groups like APT28 and Turla.
18.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Process Injection is identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1055, primarily within the Execution tactic and applicable to multiple platforms. It involves executing arbitrary code within the address space of a separate live process to evade detection and potentially gain elevated privileges. Common methods include DLL injection using APIs like VirtualAllocEx and CreateRemoteThread, Portable Executable (PE) injection, and platform-specific variants like proc memory injection via the /proc filesystem on Linux. This technique is widely used by threat actors such as APT41, Lazarus Group, and Wizard Spider.

19.name: Alternate Data Streams (ADS)
19.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may use alternate authentication material, such as password hashes, Kerberos tickets, and application access tokens, in order to move laterally within an environment and bypass normal system access controls. 

Authentication processes generally require a valid identity (e.g., username) along with one or more authentication factors (e.g., password, pin, physical smart card, token generator, etc.). Alternate authentication material is legitimately generated by systems after a user or application successfully authenticates by providing a valid identity and the required authentication factor(s). Alternate authentication material may also be generated during the identity creation process.(Citation: NIST Authentication)(Citation: NIST MFA)

Caching alternate authentication material allows the system to verify an identity has successfully authenticated without asking the user to reenter authentication factor(s). Because the alternate authentication must be maintained by the system—either in memory or on disk—it may be at risk of being stolen through [Credential Access](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0006) techniques. By stealing alternate authentication material, adversaries are able to bypass system access controls and authenticate to systems without knowing the plaintext password or any additional authentication factors.
19.profile: [profile]Alternate Data Streams (ADS) is a technique for hiding data, identified as NTFS File Attributes (T1096) and a sub-technique of Hide Artifacts (T1564.004). It operates on the Windows platform as part of the Defense Evasion tactic. The technique exploits the NTFS file system's ability to store arbitrary data or complete files within additional file attributes, known as Alternate Data Streams, attached to a Master File Table (MFT) entry. This allows adversaries to conceal malicious payloads within metadata to evade static detection tools. It is also used to bypass Mark-of-the-Web (MOTW) security controls, as the Zone.Identifier stream is itself an ADS. The malware Gazer is associated with this technique.
19.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Alternate Data Streams (ADS) is a sub-technique of NTFS File Attributes (T1564.004) under the Defense Evasion tactic on Windows platforms. It exploits the NTFS file system's ability to store multiple data streams within a single file, allowing adversaries to hide malicious payloads or data in a secondary stream (e.g., `file.txt:malicious.exe`) that is not visible through standard directory listings. This method evades static detection tools. ADS is also used to bypass Mark-of-the-Web security by manipulating the `Zone.Identifier` stream.

21.name: Persistence
21.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may clear artifacts associated with previously established persistence on a host system to remove evidence of their activity. This may involve various actions, such as removing services, deleting executables, [Modify Registry](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1112), [Plist File Modification](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1647), or other methods of cleanup to prevent defenders from collecting evidence of their persistent presence.(Citation: Cylance Dust Storm) Adversaries may also delete accounts previously created to maintain persistence (i.e. [Create Account](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1136)).(Citation: Talos - Cisco Attack 2022)

In some instances, artifacts of persistence may also be removed once an adversary’s persistence is executed in order to prevent errors with the new instance of the malware.(Citation: NCC Group Team9 June 2020)
21.profile: [profile]The entity is mapped to MITRE ATT&CK technique T1070.009: Indicator Removal: Clear Persistence, under the Defense Evasion tactic for Windows platforms. It involves adversaries removing artifacts of previously established persistence mechanisms to eliminate evidence, including actions like deleting services, executables, modifying the Windows Registry or Plist files, and removing created accounts. This cleanup prevents defenders from detecting the persistent presence and can also avoid errors with new malware instances. Associated threat groups include APT28, Turla, and Lazarus, with malware like Gazer and Bateleur utilizing this technique.
21.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Persistence, designated as a high-level tactic rather than a specific technique ID, is a core adversary objective to maintain long-term access to a system, often following initial compromise. It is executed across multiple platforms, primarily Windows, through various mechanisms. A key technical method involves modifying system configuration, such as Windows Registry keys, to execute malicious code automatically, as exemplified by the specific technique COM Object Hijacking (T1546.015) which hijacks legitimate Component Object Model references. Persistence can also be achieved by abusing application startup features, like Microsoft Office add-ins (T1137.006), to run code when those applications launch.[/profile]

23.name: File Upload
23.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may upload malware to third-party or adversary controlled infrastructure to make it accessible during targeting. Malicious software can include payloads, droppers, post-compromise tools, backdoors, and a variety of other malicious content. Adversaries may upload malware to support their operations, such as making a payload available to a victim network to enable [Ingress Tool Transfer](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1105) by placing it on an Internet accessible web server.

Malware may be placed on infrastructure that was previously purchased/rented by the adversary ([Acquire Infrastructure](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1583)) or was otherwise compromised by them ([Compromise Infrastructure](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1584)). Malware can also be staged on web services, such as GitHub or Pastebin; hosted on the InterPlanetary File System (IPFS), where decentralized content storage makes the removal of malicious files difficult; or saved on the blockchain as smart contracts, which are resilient against takedowns that would affect traditional infrastructure.(Citation: Volexity Ocean Lotus November 2020)(Citation: Talos IPFS 2022)(Citation: Guardio Etherhiding 2023)(Citation: Bleeping Computer Binance Smart Chain 2023)

Adversaries may upload backdoored files, such as software packages, application binaries, virtual machine images, or container images, to third-party software stores, package libraries, extension marketplaces, or repositories (ex: GitHub, CNET, AWS Community AMIs, Docker Hub, PyPi, NPM).(Citation: Datadog Security Labs Malicious PyPi Packages 2024) By chance encounter, victims may directly download/install these backdoored files via [User Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204). Masquerading, including typo-squatting legitimate software, may increase the chance of users mistakenly executing these files.
23.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique Upload Malware (T1608.001), a sub-technique of Stage Capabilities under the Resource Development tactic. It operates across multiple platforms and involves adversaries placing malicious software—including payloads, droppers, backdoors, and backdoored files like software packages or container images—on internet-accessible infrastructure. This infrastructure can be adversary-controlled, compromised, or legitimate third-party services such as web servers, GitHub, Pastebin, decentralized storage like IPFS, blockchain smart contracts, and software repositories (e.g., PyPi, Docker Hub, NPM) to enable subsequent operations like Ingress Tool Transfer or to trick users into direct download and execution.[/profile]
23.profile_without_enhance: [profile]File Upload is a technique where adversaries transfer malicious files to a victim system, often to a web-accessible directory like a shared webroot, to enable subsequent execution. This can facilitate lateral movement by allowing the adversary to browse to and trigger the malicious content, which then runs under the context of the web server process, potentially with elevated privileges. The uploaded files can include backdoors, payloads, or tools, and may be staged on compromised or purchased infrastructure, including third-party services like GitHub or Pastebin.

24.name: Resource 101 (RSA Private Key)
24.uncertain_mes: [Skeleton Key](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0007) is malware used to inject false credentials into domain controllers with the intent of creating a backdoor password. (Citation: Dell Skeleton) Functionality similar to [Skeleton Key](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0007) is included as a module in [Mimikatz](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0002).
24.profile: [profile]Skeleton Key, also known as Resource 101 (RSA Private Key), is malware attributed to APT5. It functions by injecting false credentials into domain controllers to create a persistent backdoor password, with similar functionality available as a module within Mimikatz. Its primary target platform is Windows domain controllers. The malware is related to the Gazer malware family, where a specific RSA private key (resource 101) is used to encrypt and decrypt other resources, which are compressed with bzip2.4 and stored in a format similar to Microsoft's PVK key.[/profile]
24.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Resource 101 (RSA Private Key) is a cryptographic resource used by the Gazer (Crutch) malware, attributed to the Turla APT group. It functions as an RSA private key stored in a format similar to a Microsoft PVK file, with its header stripped and later appended by the loader. This key is used to encrypt and decrypt other resources (specifically values 104–111) within Gazer, which are also compressed with bzip2.4. The key is stored in a specific Windows Registry subkey ({629336E3-58D6-633B-5182-576588CF702A}) as part of Gazer's operational infrastructure.[/profile]

27.name: Configuration Update
27.profile: [profile]Configuration Update is a technique where adversaries modify network device configurations to weaken defenses or enable persistence. This can involve altering files that determine device operation, often using management tools like SNMP or Smart Install. The technique is linked to malware such as Gazer and Orchestrator, and is related to broader tactics like compromising software supply chains and dumping network configurations for data collection.
27.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Configuration Update is a technique where adversaries modify settings on systems or network devices to weaken security, enable persistence, or facilitate further malicious actions. This can involve altering network device configurations via management protocols like SNMP or CLI commands, or modifying system files such as shell configuration scripts (e.g., /etc/profile, ~/.bashrc) to execute malicious code automatically. It is associated with groups like Salt Typhoon and Contagious Interview.

28.name: File Download
28.profile: [profile]File Download is a technique, likely corresponding to MITRE ATT&CK T1105 (Ingress Tool Transfer), under the Command and Control tactic. It involves transferring files from an external system into a compromised environment using utilities like `certutil`, PowerShell commands (e.g., `IEX(New-Object Net.WebClient).downloadString()`), `curl`, `wget`, or `scp`. Adversaries, such as APT17, use this to introduce tools like the Gazer backdoor, often verifying file integrity with checks like `certutil -hashfile`. The technique can also abuse services like Dropbox for automated syncing.[profile]
28.profile_without_enhance: [profile]File Download is a technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, identified as T1105 (Ingress Tool Transfer), under the Command and Control tactic. It involves adversaries transferring tools or files into a compromised environment using utilities like `certutil`, PowerShell commands such as `IEX(New-Object Net.WebClient).downloadString()`, or tools like `curl`, `wget`, and `scp`. This method is often used to deliver additional payloads after initial access, with adversaries potentially abusing services like Dropbox for automated syncing or using LNK files to smuggle download commands past filters.

29.name: Command Execution
29.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may abuse utilities that allow for command execution to bypass security restrictions that limit the use of command-line interpreters. Various Windows utilities may be used to execute commands, possibly without invoking [cmd](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0106). For example, [Forfiles](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0193), the Program Compatibility Assistant (`pcalua.exe`), components of the Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL), `Scriptrunner.exe`, as well as other utilities may invoke the execution of programs and commands from a [Command and Scripting Interpreter](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059), Run window, or via scripts.(Citation: VectorSec ForFiles Aug 2017)(Citation: Evi1cg Forfiles Nov 2017)(Citation: Secure Team - Scriptrunner.exe)(Citation: SS64)(Citation: Bleeping Computer - Scriptrunner.exe) Adversaries may also abuse the `ssh.exe` binary to execute malicious commands via the `ProxyCommand` and `LocalCommand` options, which can be invoked via the `-o` flag or by modifying the SSH config file.(Citation: Threat Actor Targets the Manufacturing industry with Lumma Stealer and Amadey Bot)

Adversaries may abuse these features for [Defense Evasion](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0005), specifically to perform arbitrary execution while subverting detections and/or mitigation controls (such as Group Policy) that limit/prevent the usage of [cmd](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0106) or file extensions more commonly associated with malicious payloads.
29.profile: [profile]Indirect Command Execution is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1202 under the Defense Evasion tactic, primarily for Windows. It involves abusing trusted system utilities like Forfiles, pcalua.exe, Windows Subsystem for Linux components, or Scriptrunner.exe to execute commands without invoking the standard cmd interpreter, thereby bypassing security restrictions. Adversaries may also misuse ssh.exe via its ProxyCommand or LocalCommand options. This technique is associated with groups like Lazarus Group and Redcurl, and malware such as Gazer and Bateleur.[/profile]

Adversaries may compromise a network device’s encryption capability in order to bypass encryption that would otherwise protect data communications. (Citation: Cisco Synful Knock Evolution)

Encryption can be used to protect transmitted network traffic to maintain its confidentiality (protect against unauthorized disclosure) and integrity (protect against unauthorized changes). Encryption ciphers are used to convert a plaintext message to ciphertext and can be computationally intensive to decipher without the associated decryption key. Typically, longer keys increase the cost of cryptanalysis, or decryption without the key.

Adversaries can compromise and manipulate devices that perform encryption of network traffic. For example, through behaviors such as [Modify System Image](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1601), [Reduce Key Space](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1600/001), and [Disable Crypto Hardware](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1600/002), an adversary can negatively effect and/or eliminate a device’s ability to securely encrypt network traffic. This poses a greater risk of unauthorized disclosure and may help facilitate data manipulation, Credential Access, or Collection efforts. (Citation: Cisco Blog Legacy Device Attacks)

74.name: Exfiltration
74.profile: [profile]Exfiltration is the adversary technique of stealing data from a victim network. It is a core tactic within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, encompassing numerous sub-techniques like T1041 (Exfiltration Over C2 Channel) and T1048 (Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol). This technique is employed by groups such as Turla, APT28, and OilRig, and can involve malware like Crutch. Specific methods include automated data transfer, using physical media like USB devices, or leveraging common web services and webhooks to blend exfiltration traffic with normal network activity.[/profile]

It encompasses various specific techniques for transferring stolen data, such as using automated processes (T1020), scheduling transfers (T1029), or leveraging specific channels like USB (T1052.001), Bluetooth (T1011.001), web services (T1567), or webhooks (T1567.004). These methods often aim to blend with normal traffic, use encrypted channels like HTTPS, or bypass network controls, particularly in air-gapped environments.

87.name: HTTP API
87.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may interact with the native OS application programming interface (API) to execute behaviors. Native APIs provide a controlled means of calling low-level OS services within the kernel, such as those involving hardware/devices, memory, and processes.(Citation: NT API Windows)(Citation: Linux Kernel API) These native APIs are leveraged by the OS during system boot (when other system components are not yet initialized) as well as carrying out tasks and requests during routine operations. Adversaries may abuse these OS API functions as a means of executing behaviors. Similar to [Command and Scripting Interpreter](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059), the native API and its hierarchy of interfaces provide mechanisms to interact with and utilize various components of a victimized system. Native API functions (such as NtCreateProcess) may be directed invoked via system calls / syscalls, but these features are also often exposed to user-mode applications via interfaces and libraries.(Citation: OutFlank System Calls)(Citation: CyberBit System Calls)(Citation: MDSec System Calls) For example, functions such as the Windows API CreateProcess() or GNU fork() will allow programs and scripts to start other processes.(Citation: Microsoft CreateProcess)(Citation: GNU Fork) This may allow API callers to execute a binary, run a CLI command, load modules, etc. as thousands of similar API functions exist for various system operations.(Citation: Microsoft Win32)(Citation: LIBC)(Citation: GLIBC) Higher level software frameworks, such as Microsoft .NET and macOS Cocoa, are also available to interact with native APIs. These frameworks typically provide language wrappers/abstractions to API functionalities and are designed for ease-of-use/portability of code.(Citation: Microsoft NET)(Citation: Apple Core Services)(Citation: MACOS Cocoa)(Citation: macOS Foundation) Adversaries may use assembly to directly or in-directly invoke syscalls in an attempt to subvert defensive sensors and detection signatures such as user mode API-hooks.(Citation: Redops Syscalls) Adversaries may also attempt to tamper with sensors and defensive tools associated with API monitoring, such as unhooking monitored functions via [Disable or Modify Tools](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1562/001).
87.profile: [profile]Native API, designated as T1106 under the Execution tactic, operates across Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. Adversaries directly invoke low-level OS kernel services via system calls (syscalls) or through user-mode interfaces and libraries, using functions like NtCreateProcess, CreateProcess(), or fork() to execute binaries, commands, or load modules. This technique provides a controlled mechanism to interact with system components and is often leveraged to subvert user-mode API hooks and defensive monitoring. Associated malware includes Backdoor, and it has been used by groups such as Lazarus Group, Mustang Panda, and Sandworm Team.[/profile]

This activity is often a component of broader techniques like Application Layer Protocol (T1071.001) for communication or Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol (T1048). The technical mechanics involve embedding commands and data within standard HTTP/S request and response traffic to blend with normal web activity and avoid detection.

88.name: DLL Hijacking
88.uncertain_mes:
Windows systems use a common method to look for required DLLs to load into a program. (Citation: Microsoft DLL Search) Adversaries may take advantage of the Windows DLL search order and programs that ambiguously specify DLLs to gain privilege escalation and persistence. 

Adversaries may perform DLL preloading, also called binary planting attacks, (Citation: OWASP Binary Planting) by placing a malicious DLL with the same name as an ambiguously specified DLL in a location that Windows searches before the legitimate DLL. Often this location is the current working directory of the program. Remote DLL preloading attacks occur when a program sets its current directory to a remote location such as a Web share before loading a DLL. (Citation: Microsoft 2269637) Adversaries may use this behavior to cause the program to load a malicious DLL. 

Adversaries may also directly modify the way a program loads DLLs by replacing an existing DLL or modifying a .manifest or .local redirection file, directory, or junction to cause the program to load a different DLL to maintain persistence or privilege escalation. (Citation: Microsoft DLL Redirection) (Citation: Microsoft Manifests) (Citation: Mandiant Search Order)

If a search order-vulnerable program is configured to run at a higher privilege level, then the adversary-controlled DLL that is loaded will also be executed at the higher level. In this case, the technique could be used for privilege escalation from user to administrator or SYSTEM or from administrator to SYSTEM, depending on the program.

Programs that fall victim to path hijacking may appear to behave normally because malicious DLLs may be configured to also load the legitimate DLLs they were meant to replace.
88.profile: [profile]DLL Search Order Hijacking (T1574.001) is a Defense Evasion and Persistence technique for Windows. It exploits the standard Windows DLL search order by placing a malicious DLL with the same name as a required library in a directory searched before the legitimate location, such as the program's current working directory. This can also be performed remotely via Web shares. Adversaries may further modify .manifest or .local redirection files to control loading. If the vulnerable program runs with elevated privileges, this technique enables privilege escalation. Associated threat groups include APT17, APT29, Winnti, and menuPass.[/profile]
88.profile_without_enhance: [profile]DLL Hijacking, also known as DLL Search Order Hijacking (T1574.001), is a Defense Evasion and Persistence technique primarily for Windows. It exploits the Windows DLL search order by placing a malicious DLL with the same name as a required library in a directory searched before the legitimate location, such as the application's current working directory. This causes the vulnerable program to load and execute the adversary's code, which can be used for privilege escalation if the host process runs at a higher privilege level. Attackers may also use .manifest or .local files for redirection or perform remote hijacking via Web shares.

89.name: Write Files
89.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may attempt to steal Kerberos tickets stored in credential cache files (or ccache). These files are used for short term storage of a user's active session credentials. The ccache file is created upon user authentication and allows for access to multiple services without the user having to re-enter credentials. The /etc/krb5.conf configuration file and the KRB5CCNAME environment variable are used to set the storage location for ccache entries. On Linux, credentials are typically stored in the `/tmp` directory with a naming format of `krb5cc_%UID%` or `krb5.ccache`. On macOS, ccache entries are stored by default in memory with an `API:{uuid}` naming scheme. Typically, users interact with ticket storage using kinit, which obtains a Ticket-Granting-Ticket (TGT) for the principal; klist, which lists obtained tickets currently held in the credentials cache; and other built-in binaries.(Citation: Kerberos GNU/Linux)(Citation: Binary Defense Kerberos Linux) Adversaries can collect tickets from ccache files stored on disk and authenticate as the current user without their password to perform [Pass the Ticket](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1550/003) attacks. Adversaries can also use these tickets to impersonate legitimate users with elevated privileges to perform [Privilege Escalation](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0004). Tools like Kekeo can also be used by adversaries to convert ccache files to Windows format for further [Lateral Movement](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0008). On macOS, adversaries may use open-source tools or the Kerberos framework to interact with ccache files and extract TGTs or Service Tickets via lower-level APIs.(Citation: SpectorOps Bifrost Kerberos macOS 2019)(Citation: Linux Kerberos Tickets)(Citation: Brining MimiKatz to Unix)(Citation: Kekeo)
89.profile: [profile]Steal Kerberos Ticket Granting Tickets (T1558.005) is a Credential Access technique targeting Linux and macOS platforms. Adversaries steal Kerberos tickets from credential cache (ccache) files, which are created upon user authentication and stored in locations like `/tmp/krb5cc_%UID%` on Linux or in memory on macOS. The stolen tickets enable Pass the Ticket attacks for lateral movement and privilege escalation without requiring the user's password, and tools like Kekeo can convert these files for use on Windows systems.[/profile]

This action is often a prerequisite or component of more specific techniques like Obfuscated Files or Information (T1027) or Hidden Files and Directories (T1158).

92.name: Execute Additional Processes
92.profile: [profile]Execute Additional Processes is a technique where adversaries launch extra processes from a compromised or legitimate parent process to execute malicious payloads, often for defense evasion or privilege escalation. This behavior is commonly observed in malware like backdoors, where it facilitates lateral movement, persistence, or the execution of secondary payloads without direct user interaction, blending malicious activity with normal system operations.

93.name: Search for Files with Specific Extensions
93.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may abuse internet browser extensions to establish persistent access to victim systems. Browser extensions or plugins are small programs that can add functionality to and customize aspects of internet browsers. They can be installed directly via a local file or custom URL or through a browser's app store - an official online platform where users can browse, install, and manage extensions for a specific web browser. Extensions generally inherit the web browser's permissions previously granted.(Citation: Wikipedia Browser Extension)(Citation: Chrome Extensions Definition) Malicious extensions can be installed into a browser through malicious app store downloads masquerading as legitimate extensions, through social engineering, or by an adversary that has already compromised a system. Security can be limited on browser app stores, so it may not be difficult for malicious extensions to defeat automated scanners.(Citation: Malicious Chrome Extension Numbers) Depending on the browser, adversaries may also manipulate an extension's update url to install updates from an adversary-controlled server or manipulate the mobile configuration file to silently install additional extensions. Adversaries may abuse how chromium-based browsers load extensions by modifying or replacing the Preferences and/or Secure Preferences files to silently install malicious extensions. When the browser is not running, adversaries can alter these files, ensuring the extension is loaded, granted desired permissions, and will persist in browser sessions. This method does not require user consent and extensions are silently loaded in the background from disk or from the browser's trusted store.(Citation: Pulsedive) Previous to macOS 11, adversaries could silently install browser extensions via the command line using the profiles tool to install malicious .mobileconfig files. In macOS 11+, the use of the profiles tool can no longer install configuration profiles; however, .mobileconfig files can be planted and installed with user interaction.(Citation: xorrior chrome extensions macOS) Once the extension is installed, it can browse to websites in the background, steal all information that a user enters into a browser (including credentials), and be used as an installer for a RAT for persistence.(Citation: Chrome Extension Crypto Miner)(Citation: ICEBRG Chrome Extensions)(Citation: Banker Google Chrome Extension Steals Creds)(Citation: Catch All Chrome Extension) There have also been instances of botnets using a persistent backdoor through malicious Chrome extensions for [Command and Control](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0011).(Citation: Stantinko Botnet)(Citation: Chrome Extension C2 Malware) Adversaries may also use browser extensions to modify browser permissions and components, privacy settings, and other security controls for [Defense Evasion](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0005).(Citation: Browers FriarFox)(Citation: Browser Adrozek)
93.profile: [profile]The entity "Search for Files with Specific Extensions" is a Discovery technique. It involves adversaries enumerating files and directories, often using command shell utilities like `dir`, `tree`, `ls`, `find`, or `locate` to search for files with particular extensions. This information gathering shapes follow-on actions, such as data theft or lateral movement, and may be performed via a Network Device CLI on network devices. The technique is associated with numerous threat groups including Kimsuky, APT28, and MuddyWater.

This automated search helps identify specific data of interest, such as documents or credentials, to shape subsequent actions like data collection or exfiltration.

94.name: Encrypt Files
94.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may attempt to steal Kerberos tickets stored in credential cache files (or ccache). These files are used for short term storage of a user's active session credentials. The ccache file is created upon user authentication and allows for access to multiple services without the user having to re-enter credentials. The /etc/krb5.conf configuration file and the KRB5CCNAME environment variable are used to set the storage location for ccache entries. On Linux, credentials are typically stored in the `/tmp` directory with a naming format of `krb5cc_%UID%` or `krb5.ccache`. On macOS, ccache entries are stored by default in memory with an `API:{uuid}` naming scheme. Typically, users interact with ticket storage using kinit, which obtains a Ticket-Granting-Ticket (TGT) for the principal; klist, which lists obtained tickets currently held in the credentials cache; and other built-in binaries.(Citation: Kerberos GNU/Linux)(Citation: Binary Defense Kerberos Linux) Adversaries can collect tickets from ccache files stored on disk and authenticate as the current user without their password to perform [Pass the Ticket](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1550/003) attacks. Adversaries can also use these tickets to impersonate legitimate users with elevated privileges to perform [Privilege Escalation](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0004). Tools like Kekeo can also be used by adversaries to convert ccache files to Windows format for further [Lateral Movement](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0008). On macOS, adversaries may use open-source tools or the Kerberos framework to interact with ccache files and extract TGTs or Service Tickets via lower-level APIs.(Citation: SpectorOps Bifrost Kerberos macOS 2019)(Citation: Linux Kerberos Tickets)(Citation: Brining MimiKatz to Unix)(Citation: Kekeo)
94.profile: [profile]The entity "Encrypt Files" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the provided context, the input data primarily describes the MITRE technique "Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets: Kerberos Credential Cache (T1558.005)", which involves stealing Kerberos tickets from credential cache (ccache) files. The technique falls under the Credential Access tactic and targets Linux and macOS platforms. Adversaries locate these files via the `/etc/krb5.conf` configuration or `KRB5CCNAME` environment variable, with typical Linux file paths like `/tmp/krb5cc_%UID%`. Stolen tickets enable Pass the Ticket attacks for lateral movement and privilege escalation without requiring the user's password, and tools like Kekeo can convert these files for use on Windows systems.[/profile]
94.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Encrypt Files is a technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, primarily associated with the Impact tactic (TA0040) and applicable across multiple platforms. It involves adversaries using encryption to render files inaccessible, often as part of ransomware attacks to extort payment for decryption keys. Common targets include user documents, PDFs, images, and critical system files. The technique may be combined with other behaviors like modifying file permissions or using worm-like propagation via network shares to maximize disruption.

113.name: AcidBox
113.uncertain_mes:
By Martin Lee, Paul Rascagneres and Vitor Ventura.
Introduction
The attribution of cyber attacks is hard. It requires collecting diverse intelligence, analyzing it and deciding who is responsible. Rarely does the evidence available to researchers reach a level of proof that would be acceptable in a court of law.

114.name: Appending Data in Icon Resources
114.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may smuggle commands to download malicious payloads past content filters by hiding them within otherwise seemingly benign windows shortcut files. Windows shortcut files (.LNK) include many metadata fields, including an icon location field (also known as the `IconEnvironmentDataBlock`) designed to specify the path to an icon file that is to be displayed for the LNK file within a host directory. 

Adversaries may abuse this LNK metadata to download malicious payloads. For example, adversaries have been observed using LNK files as phishing payloads to deliver malware. Once invoked (e.g., [Malicious File](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002)), payloads referenced via external URLs within the LNK icon location field may be downloaded. These files may also then be invoked by [Command and Scripting Interpreter](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059)/[System Binary Proxy Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1218) arguments within the target path field of the LNK.(Citation: Unprotect Shortcut)(Citation: Booby Trap Shortcut 2017)

LNK Icon Smuggling may also be utilized post compromise, such as malicious scripts executing an LNK on an infected host to download additional malicious payloads.
114.profile: [profile]Appending Data in Icon Resources, also known as LNK Icon Smuggling (T1027.012), is a Defense Evasion technique for Windows. It abuses the IconEnvironmentDataBlock metadata field within Windows shortcut (.LNK) files to embed external URLs pointing to malicious payloads. When the LNK file is executed, it can download and invoke the remote payload, often used in phishing or for post-compromise downloaders. This method has been associated with groups like Mustang Panda, Gamaredon Group, and Kimsuky.[/profile]
114.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Appending Data in Icon Resources is a technique where adversaries hide malicious code by appending it to the icon resources of legitimate files, such as executables, to evade detection. This method leverages the structure of file resources to conceal payloads.

115.name: SSP Abuse for Persistence
115.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may clear artifacts associated with previously established persistence on a host system to remove evidence of their activity. This may involve various actions, such as removing services, deleting executables, [Modify Registry](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1112), [Plist File Modification](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1647), or other methods of cleanup to prevent defenders from collecting evidence of their persistent presence.(Citation: Cylance Dust Storm) Adversaries may also delete accounts previously created to maintain persistence (i.e. [Create Account](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1136)).(Citation: Talos - Cisco Attack 2022)

In some instances, artifacts of persistence may also be removed once an adversary’s persistence is executed in order to prevent errors with the new instance of the malware.(Citation: NCC Group Team9 June 2020)
115.profile: [profile]SSP Abuse for Persistence, identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1547.005, is a persistence tactic executed on the Windows platform. It involves adversaries modifying specific Windows Registry keys, such as HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa\Security Packages, to add a malicious Security Support Provider (SSP) Dynamic Link Library (DLL). This DLL is then loaded into the Local Security Authority (LSA) process during system boot, granting it access to stored credentials like domain passwords and smart card PINs. The technique has been associated with the Turla intrusion set and the AcidBox malware.
115.profile_without_enhance: [profile]SSP Abuse for Persistence is a persistence technique, likely mapped to MITRE ATT&CK ID T1547.005, under the Persistence tactic for Windows platforms. It involves adversaries modifying specific Windows Registry keys, such as HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa\Security Packages, to add a malicious Security Support Provider (SSP) DLL. This DLL is then loaded into the Local Security Authority (LSA) process at system boot, granting it access to stored credentials like domain passwords and enabling persistent execution.

116.name: Registry Payload Storage
116.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may store data in "fileless" formats to conceal malicious activity from defenses. Fileless storage can be broadly defined as any format other than a file. Common examples of non-volatile fileless storage in Windows systems include the Windows Registry, event logs, or WMI repository.(Citation: Microsoft Fileless)(Citation: SecureList Fileless) Shared memory directories on Linux systems (`/dev/shm`, `/run/shm`, `/var/run`, and `/var/lock`) and volatile directories on Network Devices (`/tmp` and `/volatile`) may also be considered fileless storage, as files written to these directories are mapped directly to RAM and not stored on the disk.(Citation: Elastic Binary Executed from Shared Memory Directory)(Citation: Akami Frog4Shell 2024)(Citation: Aquasec Muhstik Malware 2024)(Citation: Bitsight 7777 Botnet)(Citation: CISCO Nexus 900 Config).

Similar to fileless in-memory behaviors such as [Reflective Code Loading](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1620) and [Process Injection](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1055), fileless data storage may remain undetected by anti-virus and other endpoint security tools that can only access specific file formats from disk storage. Leveraging fileless storage may also allow adversaries to bypass the protections offered by read-only file systems in Linux.(Citation: Sysdig Fileless Malware 23022)

Adversaries may use fileless storage to conceal various types of stored data, including payloads/shellcode (potentially being used as part of [Persistence](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0003)) and collected data not yet exfiltrated from the victim (e.g., [Local Data Staging](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1074/001)). Adversaries also often encrypt, encode, splice, or otherwise obfuscate this fileless data when stored. 

Some forms of fileless storage activity may indirectly create artifacts in the file system, but in central and otherwise difficult to inspect formats such as the WMI (e.g., `%SystemRoot%\System32\Wbem\Repository`) or Registry (e.g., `%SystemRoot%\System32\Config`) physical files.(Citation: Microsoft Fileless)
116.profile: [profile]Registry Payload Storage, also known as fileless storage (T1027.011) under the Defense Evasion tactic, operates on Windows, Linux, and Network Device platforms. This technique conceals malicious payloads or data by storing them in non-file system locations like the Windows Registry, WMI repository, event logs, or shared memory directories (e.g., `/dev/shm`), which map directly to RAM to avoid disk-based detection. Adversaries, including groups like APT32 and Turla, often encrypt or obfuscate this stored data. The technique can bypass antivirus tools and read-only file system protections, though it may leave indirect artifacts in central system files.
116.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Registry Payload Storage is a technique where adversaries conceal malicious payloads within the Windows Registry to evade file-based detection. This method, a form of fileless storage, involves writing data to registry keys, which can be encrypted or encoded to further hide the activity. The stored payloads are often used for persistence or as staged data, and their execution may be triggered by manipulating registry entries, such as service configurations or autodial DLL paths.

118.name: MSVC/C++ Compiler
118.profile: [profile]MSVC/C++ Compiler is a native utility used for the compilation of source code into executable binaries, as referenced in MITRE ATT&CK sub-technique T1027.004 (Obfuscated Files or Information: Compile After Delivery). This technique falls under the Defense Evasion tactic and is applicable to Windows platforms. Adversaries deliver payloads as uncompiled C++ source code to evade detection targeting binaries, then use the MSVC compiler (cl.exe) or related tools like MSBuild to compile the code locally on the victim system, enabling execution while bypassing application controls that trust these signed Microsoft utilities. It has been associated with malware like AcidBox.
118.profile_without_enhance: [profile]MSVC/C++ Compiler is a technique adversaries use to compile malicious source code into executables on a victim system, often to evade detection targeting pre-built binaries. This involves using the native Microsoft Visual C++ compiler tools (like cl.exe) or other compilers such as GCC. The method is closely related to the MITRE technique Compile After Delivery (T1027.004), where payloads are delivered as text-based source code and then compiled locally. This allows execution of arbitrary code while potentially bypassing application controls that trust signed or standard development utilities.

121.name: Zlib Compression
121.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may use compression to obfuscate their payloads or files. Compressed file formats such as ZIP, gzip, 7z, and RAR can compress and archive multiple files together to make it easier and faster to transfer files. In addition to compressing files, adversaries may also compress shellcode directly - for example, in order to store it in a Windows Registry key (i.e., [Fileless Storage](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/011)).(Citation: Trustwave Pillowmint June 2020)

In order to further evade detection, adversaries may combine multiple ZIP files into one archive. This process of concatenation creates an archive that appears to be a single archive but in fact contains the central directories of the embedded archives. Some ZIP readers, such as 7zip, may not be able to identify concatenated ZIP files and miss the presence of the malicious payload.(Citation: Perception Point)

File archives may be sent as one [Spearphishing Attachment](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001) through email. Adversaries have sent malicious payloads as archived files to encourage the user to interact with and extract the malicious payload onto their system (i.e., [Malicious File](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002)).(Citation: NTT Security Flagpro new December 2021) However, some file compression tools, such as 7zip, can be used to produce self-extracting archives. Adversaries may send self-extracting archives to hide the functionality of their payload and launch it without requiring multiple actions from the user.(Citation: The Hacker News)

[Compression](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/015) may be used in combination with [Encrypted/Encoded File](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/013) where compressed files are encrypted and password-protected.
121.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique Compression, identified as T1027.015 under the Defense Evasion tactic and applicable to multiple platforms. It involves using compression utilities or libraries like ZIP, gzip, 7z, RAR, or zlib to obfuscate payloads and files. Specific mechanics include compressing shellcode for fileless storage in the Windows Registry, creating concatenated ZIP archives to evade detection by some readers, and distributing malicious payloads via spearphishing attachments or self-extracting archives. It is often combined with encryption and has been used by groups including Gamaredon Group, Leviathan, and Threat Group-3390.[/profile]
121.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Zlib Compression is a sub-technique of Obfuscated Files or Information (T1027) under the Defense Evasion tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It involves using the zlib library to compress data, such as payloads or collected files, to obfuscate content, reduce size for exfiltration, or evade detection. This method is distinct from using standalone utilities and is often implemented by linking against the library during compilation, as seen in custom programs or malware. It is associated with threat groups like Lazarus Group and Threat Group-3390.[profile]

124.name: Kernelmode Driver
124.profile: [profile]Kernelmode Driver is a malicious driver component associated with the Turla intrusion set. For Trickbot, it is implemented as the 'RwDrv.sys' kernel driver. In AcidBox, the driver is delivered as an encrypted, unsigned kernelmode DLL payload with exports named InitEntry and InitExit. Its primary function is to operate at the kernel level to evade detection and establish persistence on compromised Windows systems.

It is associated with malware families like Rovnix, TrickBot (via the RwDrv.sys driver), and AcidBox. The driver is loaded into kernelmode memory, often from an encrypted resource, and may be structured as a kernelmode DLL with export functions like InitEntry and InitExit. Its primary function is to operate at the kernel level to evade detection and maintain system control.

129.name: Data Exfiltration
129.profile: [profile]Data Exfiltration is a high-level objective rather than a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique, encompassing the unauthorized transfer of data from a target network. It is associated with the Exfiltration tactic and various platforms. The process often involves specific methods such as using automated processing, scheduling transfers to blend with normal activity, and compressing or encrypting data prior to transfer using utilities or custom methods to avoid detection. It is linked to malware like Kopiluwak and Hammertoss and groups including OilRig, APT28, and FIN7.
129.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Data Exfiltration is a technique for stealing information from a network. It is often a follow-on step after data collection. Adversaries use various methods to transfer stolen data, including automated processes (T1020), scheduling transfers at specific times (T1029), and using different channels like webhooks (T1567.004), Bluetooth (T1011.001), or USB devices (T1052.001). Prior to transfer, data is often compressed or encrypted (T1560) to avoid detection. This technique is associated with threat groups like Gamaredon Group, Tropic Trooper, and Lazarus Group.

130.name: C2 Communication Encryption
130.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may compromise a network device’s encryption capability in order to bypass encryption that would otherwise protect data communications. (Citation: Cisco Synful Knock Evolution)

Encryption can be used to protect transmitted network traffic to maintain its confidentiality (protect against unauthorized disclosure) and integrity (protect against unauthorized changes). Encryption ciphers are used to convert a plaintext message to ciphertext and can be computationally intensive to decipher without the associated decryption key. Typically, longer keys increase the cost of cryptanalysis, or decryption without the key.

Adversaries can compromise and manipulate devices that perform encryption of network traffic. For example, through behaviors such as [Modify System Image](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1601), [Reduce Key Space](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1600/001), and [Disable Crypto Hardware](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1600/002), an adversary can negatively effect and/or eliminate a device’s ability to securely encrypt network traffic. This poses a greater risk of unauthorized disclosure and may help facilitate data manipulation, Credential Access, or Collection efforts. (Citation: Cisco Blog Legacy Device Attacks)
130.profile: [profile]This entity is mapped to MITRE ATT&CK technique T1600, named Weaken Encryption, under the Defense Evasion tactic for Network Devices. Adversaries compromise a network device's encryption capability to bypass protections for data communications, using specific sub-techniques like Reduce Key Space (T1600.001) and Disable Crypto Hardware (T1600.002) to negatively affect or eliminate secure encryption, increasing the risk of unauthorized disclosure and facilitating data manipulation or credential access. The intrusion-set Turla has been associated with related activities.[/profile]
130.profile_without_enhance: [profile]C2 Communication Encryption is a technique where adversaries encrypt command and control traffic to conceal it. This typically involves using standard symmetric encryption algorithms like AES, DES, or RC4, or implementing custom encryption schemes. Often, multiple layers of encryption are employed, such as tunneling a custom encryption protocol within an existing encrypted protocol like HTTPS, to further obfuscate the communications and evade detection.

131.name: Witchcoven
131.profile: [profile]Witchcoven, also known as SparklingGoblin, is a malware entity attributed to the intrusion set Turla. Its key technical behaviors include leveraging the PlugX malware framework, which is associated with numerous groups including APT 22, APT 26, APT31, APT41, Aurora Panda, Calypso Group, Dragonok, Emissary Panda, Hellsing, Hurricane Panda, Leviathan, Mirage, Mustang Panda, Nettraveler, Nightshade Panda, Slime29, Samurai Panda, Stone Panda, UPS, and Violin Panda. It also utilizes the FlowCloud infrastructure, further linking it to Stone Panda. The primary target platform is Windows, as indicated by its association with Winnti and the PlugX framework.
131.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Witchcoven is a malware entity. It is associated with the SparklingGoblin threat group and is related to or shares context with other malware families including Winnti, PlugX, and FlowCloud. Its known infrastructure involves compromised websites, and it utilizes tracking cookies as an indicator of its activity.

134.name: Whiteatlas
134.profile: [profile]WhiteAtlas, also known as Skipper, is a malware attributed to the Turla group. It is delivered via .JS attachments, often alongside the related malware WhiteBear, and is used for malicious activities such as data exfiltration and system compromise. 139.name: ComRAT
139.uncertain_mes: [ComRAT](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0126) is a second stage implant suspected of being a descendant of [Agent.btz](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0092) and used by [Turla](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0010). The first version of [ComRAT](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0126) was identified in 2007, but the tool has undergone substantial development for many years since.(Citation: Symantec Waterbug)(Citation: NorthSec 2015 GData Uroburos Tools)(Citation: ESET ComRAT May 2020)
139.profile: [profile]ComRAT, also known as comrat, is a second-stage implant malware attributed to the Turla group and is a suspected descendant of Agent.btz. Its key technical behaviors include using a Virtual FAT16 File System, being deployed via existing access methods like the PowerStallion PowerShell backdoor, and featuring two command and control channels: HTTP (using the same protocol as ComRAT v3) and email via the Gmail web interface for receiving commands and exfiltrating data. The malware's orchestrator component is injected into explorer.exe to control functions and execute backdoor commands. It primarily targets Windows platforms, with its installer being a PowerShell script that creates a scheduled task and stores an encrypted payload in the Registry.

Its key technical behaviors include operating with two command and control channels: an HTTP protocol identical to its v3 variant and an email channel using the Gmail web interface to receive commands and exfiltrate data. Associated C2 domains include crusider.tk, duke6.tk, and sanitar.ml. It is delivered via IronPython scripts that decrypt and inject the ComRAT DLL.[/profile]

Specific associated file hashes include b641687696b66e6e820618acc4765162298ba3e9106df4ef44b2218086ce8040 (prophile.py) and c430ebab4bf827303bc4ad95d40eecc7988bdc17cc139c8f88466bc536755d4e (profilec.py). It operates by loading into the IronPython interpreter to decode and decrypt embedded payloads, specifically a .NET injector and the ComRAT DLL payload. Key techniques include using .NET Framework APIs, loading additional assemblies, and potentially causing sandbox interpreter crashes to evade detection. Its primary target platform is Windows, and it serves as a delivery mechanism for second-stage implants like ComRAT (Agent.btz).[/profile]

147.name: 使用 .NET Framework API
147.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may interact with the native OS application programming interface (API) to execute behaviors. Native APIs provide a controlled means of calling low-level OS services within the kernel, such as those involving hardware/devices, memory, and processes.(Citation: NT API Windows)(Citation: Linux Kernel API) These native APIs are leveraged by the OS during system boot (when other system components are not yet initialized) as well as carrying out tasks and requests during routine operations. Adversaries may abuse these OS API functions as a means of executing behaviors. Similar to [Command and Scripting Interpreter](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059), the native API and its hierarchy of interfaces provide mechanisms to interact with and utilize various components of a victimized system. Native API functions (such as NtCreateProcess) may be directed invoked via system calls / syscalls, but these features are also often exposed to user-mode applications via interfaces and libraries.(Citation: OutFlank System Calls)(Citation: CyberBit System Calls)(Citation: MDSec System Calls) For example, functions such as the Windows API CreateProcess() or GNU fork() will allow programs and scripts to start other processes.(Citation: Microsoft CreateProcess)(Citation: GNU Fork) This may allow API callers to execute a binary, run a CLI command, load modules, etc. as thousands of similar API functions exist for various system operations.(Citation: Microsoft Win32)(Citation: LIBC)(Citation: GLIBC) Higher level software frameworks, such as Microsoft .NET and macOS Cocoa, are also available to interact with native APIs. These frameworks typically provide language wrappers/abstractions to API functionalities and are designed for ease-of-use/portability of code.(Citation: Microsoft NET)(Citation: Apple Core Services)(Citation: MACOS Cocoa)(Citation: macOS Foundation) Adversaries may use assembly to directly or in-directly invoke syscalls in an attempt to subvert defensive sensors and detection signatures such as user mode API-hooks.(Citation: Redops Syscalls) Adversaries may also attempt to tamper with sensors and defensive tools associated with API monitoring, such as unhooking monitored functions via [Disable or Modify Tools](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1562/001).
147.profile: [profile]The entity "使用 .NET Framework API" corresponds to the MITRE ATT&CK technique Native API (T1106) under the Execution tactic, applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves adversaries directly or indirectly calling low-level OS functions, such as via system calls or through higher-level frameworks like .NET, to perform actions like process creation (e.g., using CreateProcess() or NtCreateProcess) and to potentially bypass defensive hooks. This method provides a controlled interface to kernel services for executing binaries, commands, or loading modules. Associated threat groups include APT37, Lazarus Group, and Turla.
147.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "使用 .NET Framework API" corresponds to the MITRE ATT&CK technique Native API (T1106) under the Execution tactic, primarily on Windows platforms. It involves adversaries interacting with the native OS application programming interface to execute behaviors, with higher-level frameworks like Microsoft .NET providing language wrappers for these API functionalities to enable ease-of-use and code portability. This technique is utilized by various threat groups including Lazarus Group, Mustang Panda, and Turla.

148.name: 无需编译 .NET 程序集
148.profile: [profile]The entity "无需编译 .NET 程序集" aligns with the MITRE ATT&CK technique AppDomain Manager Injection, identified as T1574.014 under the Persistence and Privilege Escalation tactics for Windows. This technique hijacks the .NET AppDomainManager to load and execute malicious .NET assemblies without requiring them to be compiled on the target. Attackers achieve this by tampering with .NET configuration files or process environment variables to instruct a benign .NET application to load a specified malicious assembly, or by creating a custom application domain within a target process to host the execution of the arbitrary code. It is associated with malware like IronPython script and shares a conceptual relationship with other .NET hijacking techniques such as COR_PROFILER (T1574.012) and trusted utility abuse via Regsvcs/Regasm (T1218.009).
148.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The technique "无需编译 .NET 程序集" aligns with MITRE ATT&CK ID T1574.014, named "Hijack Execution Flow: AppDomainManager", under the Persistence tactic for Windows platforms. It involves adversaries hijacking the .NET `AppDomainManager` class to load and execute malicious .NET assemblies without requiring compilation. This can be achieved by creating a custom application domain within a target process or by tampering with .NET configuration files or process environment variables to force a benign application to load a specified malicious assembly.

149.name: 加载附加程序集
149.profile: [profile]The entity "加载附加程序集" (Load Additional Assembly) aligns with the MITRE ATT&CK technique AppDomainManager Injection (T1574.014) under the Persistence tactic, targeting the Windows platform. This technique involves hijacking the .NET AppDomainManager to load and execute malicious assemblies within a target process. Attackers achieve this by tampering with .NET configuration files or process environment variables to instruct a legitimate .NET application to load a specified malicious assembly, such as an IronPython script, thereby executing arbitrary code under the guise of a trusted process.
149.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "加载附加程序集" (Load Additional Assemblies) is a technique for executing code by loading .NET assemblies into a process. This is analogous to MITRE ATT&CK technique T1574.014 (AppDomainManager Injection) under the Persistence and Privilege Escalation tactics. It operates on the Windows platform by hijacking the .NET runtime's assembly loading process. Adversaries may tamper with configuration files or environment variables to force a legitimate .NET application to load a specified malicious assembly, or they may create a custom application domain within a target process to host and execute the payload.

151.name: 沙箱解释器崩溃
151.profile: [profile]沙箱解释器崩溃 is a technique where adversaries cause a sandbox interpreter to crash, potentially to evade analysis. This is linked to the IronPython script malware. The technique involves exploiting vulnerabilities or feeding malformed data to the interpreter, leading to a denial-of-service condition within the sandbox environment, which can disrupt security analysis and detection processes.

153.name: MSIL Implant
153.profile: [profile]MSIL Implant, also known as MSIL/Agent, MSIL/Kryptik, MSIL/Injector, MSIL/ClipBanker, and MSIL/Keylogger, is a family of .NET-based malware. It is attributed to the Turla intrusion set. Key behaviors include acting as a backdoor, data theft (clipboard and keystroke logging), and injection. It targets the Windows platform and is often distributed via malicious Microsoft Office documents. It is related to the Kopiluwak backdoor and is part of broader campaigns like OriginBotnet and Predator the Thief.

It is associated with the Kopiluwak Backdoor used by the Turla intrusion set. 154.name: Kopiluwak Backdoor
154.uncertain_mes: [KOPILUWAK](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S1075) is a JavaScript-based reconnaissance tool that has been used for victim profiling and C2 since at least 2017.(Citation: Mandiant Suspected Turla Campaign February 2023)

It is deployed by a JavaScript dropper that profiles the victim system and establishes persistence. The backdoor is a robust tool capable of exfiltrating data, downloading additional payloads, and executing arbitrary commands. The malware primarily targets the Microsoft .NET (MSIL) platform and uses techniques like Base64 encoding and RC4 encryption for its operations.[/profile]

155.name: JavaScript Dropper

Its technical behaviors include being an obfuscated, memory-only JavaScript dropper, often embedded within HTML files and delivered via CDNs. It functions as a dropper for other malware families such as Vultur and GrimPlant. Its target platform is primarily Windows systems.[/profile]
