Infrastructure and supplementary information note its use in G20-themed attacks and its presence in obfuscated memory-only JavaScript stages within cached HTML files on CDNs.

156.name: Base64
156.profile: [profile]Base64 is a standard binary-to-text encoding scheme used by adversaries to obfuscate command and control (C2) traffic, making it more difficult to detect. It is formally identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1132.001 (Data Encoding: Standard Encoding) under the Command and Control tactic. This technique is platform-agnostic and involves converting binary data into a radix-64 ASCII string format, which adheres to common protocol specifications. It is employed by threat groups such as Lazarus Group and MuddyWater to encode malicious payloads within network communications.
156.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Base64 is a standard data encoding technique (T1132.001) used by adversaries within the Command and Control tactic to obfuscate C2 traffic, making it more difficult to detect. It functions as a binary-to-text encoding scheme that adheres to existing protocol specifications, converting binary data into an ASCII string format. This technique is commonly employed by groups like APT33, Lazarus Group, and Sandworm Team to encode payloads or communications within network protocols.

157.name: RC4
157.profile: [profile]RC4, identified as a symmetric encryption algorithm, is referenced in MITRE ATT&CK techniques T1573.001 (Encrypted Channel: Symmetric Cryptography) and T1048.001 (Exfiltration Over Symmetric Encrypted Non-C2 Protocol), primarily under the Command and Control and Exfiltration tactics. It operates across multiple platforms. The algorithm uses a single shared key for both encryption and decryption of data. Adversaries employ it to manually encrypt command and control or exfiltration traffic, potentially adding a layer of obfuscation on top of or within standard network protocols. It has been associated with malware like Kopiluwak and Kiloalfa and intrusion sets including APT29.
157.profile_without_enhance: [profile]RC4 is a symmetric encryption algorithm referenced in MITRE ATT&CK techniques T1573.001 (Encrypted Channel: Symmetric Cryptography) and T1048.001 (Exfiltration Over Symmetric Encrypted Non-C2 Protocol), primarily under the Command and Control and Exfiltration tactics. It is used by adversaries to conceal C2 traffic and exfiltrated data by applying the same key for both encryption and decryption, often implemented manually within protocols like HTTP or FTP, potentially creating multiple encryption layers.

161.name: Download Payloads
161.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may embed payloads within other files to conceal malicious content from defenses. Otherwise seemingly benign files (such as scripts and executables) may be abused to carry and obfuscate malicious payloads and content. In some cases, embedded payloads may also enable adversaries to [Subvert Trust Controls](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1553) by not impacting execution controls such as digital signatures and notarization tickets.(Citation: Sentinel Labs) 

Adversaries may embed payloads in various file formats to hide payloads.(Citation: Microsoft Learn) This is similar to [Steganography](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/003), though does not involve weaving malicious content into specific bytes and patterns related to legitimate digital media formats.(Citation: GitHub PSImage) 

For example, adversaries have been observed embedding payloads within or as an overlay of an otherwise benign binary.(Citation: Securelist Dtrack2) Adversaries have also been observed nesting payloads (such as executables and run-only scripts) inside a file of the same format.(Citation: SentinelLabs reversing run-only applescripts 2021) 

Embedded content may also be used as [Process Injection](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1055) payloads used to infect benign system processes.(Citation: Trend Micro) These embedded then injected payloads may be used as part of the modules of malware designed to provide specific features such as encrypting C2 communications in support of an orchestrator module. For example, an embedded module may be injected into default browsers, allowing adversaries to then communicate via the network.(Citation: Malware Analysis Report ComRAT)
161.profile: [profile]Embedded Payloads, identified as T1027.009, is an obfuscation technique under the Defense Evasion tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. It involves concealing malicious code within otherwise benign files like scripts, executables, or binaries, including as overlays or nested within files of the same format, to bypass detection and potentially subvert trust controls without altering digital signatures. This embedded content can later be extracted and injected into processes. The technique has been associated with groups like Lazarus Group, TA577, and Moonstone Sleet, and is used by malware such as the Kopiluwak Backdoor.[/profile]
161.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Download Payloads" is a technique where adversaries retrieve malicious code from remote locations to support operations. This action typically occurs during the Execution tactic, often following initial access, to transfer tools like backdoors or post-compromise utilities onto a compromised system. The technique involves using commands or scripts within the victim's command-line interface or through malicious files, such as LNK files that smuggle download commands in their icon metadata, to fetch payloads from adversary-controlled web servers, cloud storage, or software repositories. It is commonly observed across Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms and is associated with groups like Mustang Panda and Kimsuky.

163.name: Fingerprinting
163.profile: [profile]Fingerprinting is a reconnaissance technique where adversaries actively probe victim infrastructure via network traffic to gather information for targeting, such as identifying open ports, services, or system attributes. This can involve using native network protocols like ICMP or crafting web traffic with spoofed browser attributes (e.g., user-agent strings) to blend in and evade defenses. It is associated with the APT28 intrusion set and the MSIL Implant malware, and it supports initial access and capability development.[/profile]
163.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Fingerprinting is a reconnaissance technique (T1595) within the Discovery tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. It involves adversaries actively probing victim infrastructure via network traffic to gather information for targeting. This can include using native network protocol features like ICMP. The gathered intelligence may reveal opportunities for further reconnaissance, establishing operational resources, or achieving initial access.

166.name: HTTPS encrypted channel
166.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may employ an encryption algorithm to conceal command and control traffic rather than relying on any inherent protections provided by a communication protocol. Despite the use of a secure algorithm, these implementations may be vulnerable to reverse engineering if secret keys are encoded and/or generated within malware samples/configuration files.
166.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique Encrypted Channel (T1573), which falls under the Command and Control tactic and applies to multiple platforms. It involves adversaries employing a separate encryption algorithm to conceal command and control traffic, rather than relying on a protocol's inherent encryption. This implementation can be vulnerable to reverse engineering if secret keys are embedded within malware samples or configuration files. The technique has been associated with groups including APT29, Bitter, Tropic Trooper, and Magic Hound.[/profile]
166.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "HTTPS encrypted channel" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the retrieved context, it likely refers to the use of the HTTPS protocol to establish an encrypted command and control or exfiltration channel. This technique leverages the inherent Transport Layer Security (TLS) of HTTPS to conceal malicious traffic, making detection more difficult. It is commonly associated with exfiltration sub-techniques like T1048.001 (symmetric) and T1048.002 (asymmetric), where data is stolen over an encrypted protocol separate from the primary C2 channel.

167.name: Upload files
167.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may upload malware to third-party or adversary controlled infrastructure to make it accessible during targeting. Malicious software can include payloads, droppers, post-compromise tools, backdoors, and a variety of other malicious content. Adversaries may upload malware to support their operations, such as making a payload available to a victim network to enable [Ingress Tool Transfer](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1105) by placing it on an Internet accessible web server.

Malware may be placed on infrastructure that was previously purchased/rented by the adversary ([Acquire Infrastructure](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1583)) or was otherwise compromised by them ([Compromise Infrastructure](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1584)). Malware can also be staged on web services, such as GitHub or Pastebin; hosted on the InterPlanetary File System (IPFS), where decentralized content storage makes the removal of malicious files difficult; or saved on the blockchain as smart contracts, which are resilient against takedowns that would affect traditional infrastructure.(Citation: Volexity Ocean Lotus November 2020)(Citation: Talos IPFS 2022)(Citation: Guardio Etherhiding 2023)(Citation: Bleeping Computer Binance Smart Chain 2023)

Adversaries may upload backdoored files, such as software packages, application binaries, virtual machine images, or container images, to third-party software stores, package libraries, extension marketplaces, or repositories (ex: GitHub, CNET, AWS Community AMIs, Docker Hub, PyPi, NPM).(Citation: Datadog Security Labs Malicious PyPi Packages 2024) By chance encounter, victims may directly download/install these backdoored files via [User Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204). Masquerading, including typo-squatting legitimate software, may increase the chance of users mistakenly executing these files.
167.profile: [profile]Upload Malware, designated as T1608.001 under the Resource Development tactic, is a technique where adversaries stage malicious content on accessible infrastructure. This involves placing payloads, droppers, or backdoors on adversary-controlled or compromised web servers, cloud storage, or third-party services like GitHub, Pastebin, or package repositories (e.g., PyPI, Docker Hub). The malware can also be hosted on decentralized systems like IPFS or blockchains to resist takedown. This staging enables subsequent operations such as Ingress Tool Transfer (T1105) and can leverage masquerading tactics like typo-squatting to facilitate user execution.[/profile]
167.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Upload files is a foundational action rather than a distinct MITRE ATT&CK technique. It is a common step enabling other techniques, such as Ingress Tool Transfer (T1105), by placing malicious or benign files on adversary-controlled or third-party infrastructure like web servers, cloud storage (e.g., AWS S3, Dropbox), or code repositories (e.g., GitHub, PyPi). This action supports operations like staging malware (T1608.001) or tools (T1608.002) for download and execution on victim networks.

168.name: Execute files
168.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may attempt to steal Kerberos tickets stored in credential cache files (or ccache). These files are used for short term storage of a user's active session credentials. The ccache file is created upon user authentication and allows for access to multiple services without the user having to re-enter credentials. The /etc/krb5.conf configuration file and the KRB5CCNAME environment variable are used to set the storage location for ccache entries. On Linux, credentials are typically stored in the `/tmp` directory with a naming format of `krb5cc_%UID%` or `krb5.ccache`. On macOS, ccache entries are stored by default in memory with an `API:{uuid}` naming scheme. Typically, users interact with ticket storage using kinit, which obtains a Ticket-Granting-Ticket (TGT) for the principal; klist, which lists obtained tickets currently held in the credentials cache; and other built-in binaries.(Citation: Kerberos GNU/Linux)(Citation: Binary Defense Kerberos Linux) Adversaries can collect tickets from ccache files stored on disk and authenticate as the current user without their password to perform [Pass the Ticket](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1550/003) attacks. Adversaries can also use these tickets to impersonate legitimate users with elevated privileges to perform [Privilege Escalation](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0004). Tools like Kekeo can also be used by adversaries to convert ccache files to Windows format for further [Lateral Movement](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0008). On macOS, adversaries may use open-source tools or the Kerberos framework to interact with ccache files and extract TGTs or Service Tickets via lower-level APIs.(Citation: SpectorOps Bifrost Kerberos macOS 2019)(Citation: Linux Kerberos Tickets)(Citation: Brining MimiKatz to Unix)(Citation: Kekeo)

183.name: Set Host(s)
183.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may break out of a container or virtualized environment to gain access to the underlying host. This can allow an adversary access to other containerized or virtualized resources from the host level or to the host itself. In principle, containerized / virtualized resources should provide a clear separation of application functionality and be isolated from the host environment.(Citation: Docker Overview)

There are multiple ways an adversary may escape from a container to a host environment. Examples include creating a container configured to mount the host’s filesystem using the bind parameter, which allows the adversary to drop payloads and execute control utilities such as cron on the host; utilizing a privileged container to run commands or load a malicious kernel module on the underlying host; or abusing system calls such as `unshare` and `keyctl` to escalate privileges and steal secrets.(Citation: Docker Bind Mounts)(Citation: Trend Micro Privileged Container)(Citation: Intezer Doki July 20)(Citation: Container Escape)(Citation: Crowdstrike Kubernetes Container Escape)(Citation: Keyctl-unmask)

Additionally, an adversary may be able to exploit a compromised container with a mounted container management socket, such as `docker.sock`, to break out of the container via a [Container Administration Command](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1609).(Citation: Container Escape) Adversaries may also escape via [Exploitation for Privilege Escalation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1068), such as exploiting vulnerabilities in global symbolic links in order to access the root directory of a host machine.(Citation: Windows Server Containers Are Open)

In ESXi environments, an adversary may exploit a vulnerability in order to escape from a virtual machine into the hypervisor.(Citation: Broadcom VMSA-2025-004)

Gaining access to the host may provide the adversary with the opportunity to achieve follow-on objectives, such as establishing persistence, moving laterally within the environment, accessing other containers or virtual machines running on the host, or setting up a command and control channel on the host.

198.name: Task Orchestration
198.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may abuse the Windows Task Scheduler to perform task scheduling for initial or recurring execution of malicious code. There are multiple ways to access the Task Scheduler in Windows. The [schtasks](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0111) utility can be run directly on the command line, or the Task Scheduler can be opened through the GUI within the Administrator Tools section of the Control Panel.(Citation: Stack Overflow) In some cases, adversaries have used a .NET wrapper for the Windows Task Scheduler, and alternatively, adversaries have used the Windows netapi32 library and [Windows Management Instrumentation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1047) (WMI) to create a scheduled task. Adversaries may also utilize the Powershell Cmdlet `Invoke-CimMethod`, which leverages WMI class `PS_ScheduledTask` to create a scheduled task via an XML path.(Citation: Red Canary - Atomic Red Team)

An adversary may use Windows Task Scheduler to execute programs at system startup or on a scheduled basis for persistence. The Windows Task Scheduler can also be abused to conduct remote Execution as part of Lateral Movement and/or to run a process under the context of a specified account (such as SYSTEM). Similar to [System Binary Proxy Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1218), adversaries have also abused the Windows Task Scheduler to potentially mask one-time execution under signed/trusted system processes.(Citation: ProofPoint Serpent)

Adversaries may also create "hidden" scheduled tasks (i.e. [Hide Artifacts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1564)) that may not be visible to defender tools and manual queries used to enumerate tasks. Specifically, an adversary may hide a task from `schtasks /query` and the Task Scheduler by deleting the associated Security Descriptor (SD) registry value (where deletion of this value must be completed using SYSTEM permissions).(Citation: SigmaHQ)(Citation: Tarrask scheduled task) Adversaries may also employ alternate methods to hide tasks, such as altering the metadata (e.g., `Index` value) within associated registry keys.(Citation: Defending Against Scheduled Task Attacks in Windows Environments)
198.profile: [profile]Scheduled Task/Job (T1053.005) is a Windows-specific Execution and Persistence technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework. It involves abusing the Windows Task Scheduler via utilities like `schtasks`, .NET wrappers, WMI, or PowerShell's `Invoke-CimMethod` to schedule malicious code for initial or recurring execution. Adversaries use it for persistence, lateral movement, and to run processes under privileged contexts like SYSTEM, and may hide tasks by deleting the associated Security Descriptor registry value or altering registry key metadata.
198.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Task Orchestration is a technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework under ID T1053, primarily supporting the Execution and Persistence tactics across Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves abusing system or container orchestration utilities like the Windows Task Scheduler (via schtasks, WMI, or PowerShell), cron, or Kubernetes CronJobs to schedule and automate the execution of malicious code. This can facilitate initial access, persistence, lateral movement, and can be combined with masquerading to hide tasks by manipulating registry metadata or security descriptors.

199.name: Code Injection
199.profile: [profile]Code Injection is a technique where adversaries execute arbitrary code within a target process to evade defenses and potentially gain elevated privileges. This is often achieved through process injection methods like DLL injection, which uses Windows API calls such as VirtualAllocEx and WriteProcessMemory to write a malicious DLL path into a process's memory, then loads it via CreateRemoteThread. It is associated with groups like Turla and APT28 and malware such as Carbon orchestrator, operating primarily on Windows platforms under the tactic of Defense Evasion.[/profile]
199.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Code Injection is a technique where adversaries introduce and execute arbitrary code within a target application or process to bypass defenses or gain control. It is a broad concept that encompasses specific sub-techniques like Process Injection (T1055), which includes methods such as Portable Executable Injection (T1055.002), Asynchronous Procedure Call injection (T1055.004), and Dynamic-link Library Injection (T1055.001). These methods often use Windows API calls like `VirtualAllocEx`, `WriteProcessMemory`, and `CreateRemoteThread` to write code into a legitimate process's memory space and then execute it, masking malicious activity under a trusted process.

200.name: Named Pipe/TCP Communication
200.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may use an existing, legitimate external Web service as a means for sending commands to and receiving output from a compromised system over the Web service channel. Compromised systems may leverage popular websites and social media to host command and control (C2) instructions. Those infected systems can then send the output from those commands back over that Web service channel. The return traffic may occur in a variety of ways, depending on the Web service being utilized. For example, the return traffic may take the form of the compromised system posting a comment on a forum, issuing a pull request to development project, updating a document hosted on a Web service, or by sending a Tweet. 

Popular websites and social media acting as a mechanism for C2 may give a significant amount of cover due to the likelihood that hosts within a network are already communicating with them prior to a compromise. Using common services, such as those offered by Google or Twitter, makes it easier for adversaries to hide in expected noise. Web service providers commonly use SSL/TLS encryption, giving adversaries an added level of protection.
200.profile: [profile]Named Pipe/TCP Communication is a technique for command and control (T1102.002) under the Command and Control tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It involves using legitimate external web services like social media or popular sites (e.g., Google, Twitter) as a bidirectional communication channel. Commands are sent to a compromised system and output is received back over the same service, often via methods such as posting forum comments, issuing pull requests, updating web documents, or sending Tweets. This traffic blends with normal, encrypted HTTPS activity to evade detection. Associated threat groups include Turla, APT28, and Lazarus Group, and it has been linked to malware like Carbon orchestrator.[/profile]
200.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Named Pipe/TCP Communication is a technique for command and control. It involves adversaries using named pipes or raw TCP sockets to establish communication channels between compromised systems, allowing for the execution of commands and data exfiltration while potentially evading detection by blending with legitimate inter-process or network traffic.

201.name: Configuration Acquisition
201.profile: [profile]Configuration Acquisition is a technique for collecting sensitive system and network administration data from configuration repositories or directly from devices. It aligns with the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1602 (Data from Configuration Repository) under the Collection tactic, targeting multiple platforms. Adversaries use protocols like SNMP and SMI to query repositories or dump device configurations, revealing network layouts, device software details, and credentials for later use. The intrusion-set Turla and malware Carbon orchestrator are associated with this activity.
201.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Configuration Acquisition is a technique aligned with MITRE ATT&CK ID T1602 under the Collection tactic, targeting multiple platforms. It involves adversaries collecting sensitive system administration data from configuration repositories used to manage remote devices. This data, which can include network layouts, device software details, and legitimate credentials, is often accessed using common management tools and protocols like Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) or Smart Install (SMI) to query repositories or export configuration files for later analysis.

202.name: Storage Folder Monitoring
202.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may store data in "fileless" formats to conceal malicious activity from defenses. Fileless storage can be broadly defined as any format other than a file. Common examples of non-volatile fileless storage in Windows systems include the Windows Registry, event logs, or WMI repository.(Citation: Microsoft Fileless)(Citation: SecureList Fileless) Shared memory directories on Linux systems (`/dev/shm`, `/run/shm`, `/var/run`, and `/var/lock`) and volatile directories on Network Devices (`/tmp` and `/volatile`) may also be considered fileless storage, as files written to these directories are mapped directly to RAM and not stored on the disk.(Citation: Elastic Binary Executed from Shared Memory Directory)(Citation: Akami Frog4Shell 2024)(Citation: Aquasec Muhstik Malware 2024)(Citation: Bitsight 7777 Botnet)(Citation: CISCO Nexus 900 Config).

Similar to fileless in-memory behaviors such as [Reflective Code Loading](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1620) and [Process Injection](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1055), fileless data storage may remain undetected by anti-virus and other endpoint security tools that can only access specific file formats from disk storage. Leveraging fileless storage may also allow adversaries to bypass the protections offered by read-only file systems in Linux.(Citation: Sysdig Fileless Malware 23022)

Adversaries may use fileless storage to conceal various types of stored data, including payloads/shellcode (potentially being used as part of [Persistence](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0003)) and collected data not yet exfiltrated from the victim (e.g., [Local Data Staging](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1074/001)). Adversaries also often encrypt, encode, splice, or otherwise obfuscate this fileless data when stored. 

Some forms of fileless storage activity may indirectly create artifacts in the file system, but in central and otherwise difficult to inspect formats such as the WMI (e.g., `%SystemRoot%\System32\Wbem\Repository`) or Registry (e.g., `%SystemRoot%\System32\Config`) physical files.(Citation: Microsoft Fileless)
202.profile: [profile]Storage Folder Monitoring is a technique for fileless data storage, likely aligned with MITRE ATT&CK ID T1027.011 under the Defense Evasion tactic, targeting Windows, Linux, and Network Device platforms. It involves storing payloads or staged data in non-file system locations like the Windows Registry, WMI repository, or Linux shared memory directories (e.g., /dev/shm) to evade disk-based security tools. Data is often obfuscated, and activity has been associated with groups like Turla.
202.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Storage Folder Monitoring is a technique where adversaries monitor specific folders, like the Windows Startup folder (e.g., C:\Users\[Username]\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup), to detect file additions or modifications. This activity is often part of the Persistence tactic, as monitoring startup locations allows adversaries to ensure their malicious payloads execute upon user login. The technique leverages file system events on platforms like Windows to maintain covert access.

211.name: just-in-time disassembly
211.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may abuse time providers to execute DLLs when the system boots. The Windows Time service (W32Time) enables time synchronization across and within domains.(Citation: Microsoft W32Time Feb 2018) W32Time time providers are responsible for retrieving time stamps from hardware/network resources and outputting these values to other network clients.(Citation: Microsoft TimeProvider)

Time providers are implemented as dynamic-link libraries (DLLs) that are registered in the subkeys of `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\System\CurrentControlSet\Services\W32Time\TimeProviders\`.(Citation: Microsoft TimeProvider) The time provider manager, directed by the service control manager, loads and starts time providers listed and enabled under this key at system startup and/or whenever parameters are changed.(Citation: Microsoft TimeProvider)

Adversaries may abuse this architecture to establish persistence, specifically by creating a new arbitrarily named subkey  pointing to a malicious DLL in the `DllName` value. Administrator privileges are required for time provider registration, though execution will run in context of the Local Service account.(Citation: Github W32Time Oct 2017)
211.profile: [profile]The entity "just-in-time disassembly" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the provided input, the relevant technique is "Time Providers" (T1547.003), a Persistence tactic for Windows. It works by registering a malicious DLL as a time provider in the Windows Registry key `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\System\CurrentControlSet\Services\W32Time\TimeProviders\`. The Windows Time service loads and executes this DLL at system startup, requiring administrator privileges for registration but running in the Local Service account context. This technique has been associated with the Turla intrusion set and Uroboros malware.
211.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity 'just-in-time disassembly' is a technique for evading analysis, likely categorized under Defense Evasion. It functions by delaying the disassembly of malicious code until the moment of execution, preventing static analysis tools from examining the complete payload beforehand. This method is often combined with other obfuscation techniques like junk code insertion to further hinder detection and reverse engineering efforts.

212.name: bypassing patch protectors
212.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may modify the operating system of a network device to introduce new capabilities or weaken existing defenses.(Citation: Killing the myth of Cisco IOS rootkits) (Citation: Killing IOS diversity myth) (Citation: Cisco IOS Shellcode) (Citation: Cisco IOS Forensics Developments) (Citation: Juniper Netscreen of the Dead) Some network devices are built with a monolithic architecture, where the entire operating system and most of the functionality of the device is contained within a single file.  Adversaries may change this file in storage, to be loaded in a future boot, or in memory during runtime.

To change the operating system in storage, the adversary will typically use the standard procedures available to device operators. This may involve downloading a new file via typical protocols used on network devices, such as TFTP, FTP, SCP, or a console connection.  The original file may be overwritten, or a new file may be written alongside of it and the device reconfigured to boot to the compromised image.

To change the operating system in memory, the adversary typically can use one of two methods. In the first, the adversary would make use of native debug commands in the original, unaltered running operating system that allow them to directly modify the relevant memory addresses containing the running operating system.  This method typically requires administrative level access to the device.

In the second method for changing the operating system in memory, the adversary would make use of the boot loader. The boot loader is the first piece of software that loads when the device starts that, in turn, will launch the operating system.  Adversaries may use malicious code previously implanted in the boot loader, such as through the [ROMMONkit](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1542/004) method, to directly manipulate running operating system code in memory.  This malicious code in the bootloader provides the capability of direct memory manipulation to the adversary, allowing them to patch the live operating system during runtime.

By modifying the instructions stored in the system image file, adversaries may either weaken existing defenses or provision new capabilities that the device did not have before. Examples of existing defenses that can be impeded include encryption, via [Weaken Encryption](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1600), authentication, via [Network Device Authentication](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1556/004), and perimeter defenses, via [Network Boundary Bridging](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1599).  Adding new capabilities for the adversary’s purpose include [Keylogging](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1056/001), [Multi-hop Proxy](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1090/003), and [Port Knocking](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1205/001).

Adversaries may also compromise existing commands in the operating system to produce false output to mislead defenders.   When this method is used in conjunction with [Downgrade System Image](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1601/002), one example of a compromised system command may include changing the output of the command that shows the version of the currently running operating system.  By patching the operating system, the adversary can change this command to instead display the original, higher revision number that they replaced through the system downgrade. 

When the operating system is patched in storage, this can be achieved in either the resident storage (typically a form of flash memory, which is non-volatile) or via [TFTP Boot](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1542/005). 

When the technique is performed on the running operating system in memory and not on the stored copy, this technique will not survive across reboots.  However, live memory modification of the operating system can be combined with [ROMMONkit](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1542/004) to achieve persistence.
212.profile: [profile]Patch System Image, identified as T1601.001 under the Defense Evasion tactic, targets network device platforms. This technique involves modifying the operating system image file, either in storage via protocols like TFTP, FTP, or SCP, or in runtime memory using native debug commands or a compromised bootloader like ROMMONkit. The modifications can weaken defenses such as encryption or authentication, add capabilities like keylogging, and alter system commands to produce false output, such as hiding a system downgrade. It has been associated with the Turla intrusion set and Uroboros malware.[/profile]
212.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "bypassing patch protectors" is a technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, identified as T1601.001 under the tactic Defense Evasion, primarily targeting Network Devices. This can be achieved through native debug commands with administrative access or via a compromised bootloader, such as through a ROMMONkit, allowing runtime patching to implant backdoor passwords or weaken existing defenses.

246.name: DPC (Deferred Procedure Call)
246.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may inject malicious code into processes via the asynchronous procedure call (APC) queue in order to evade process-based defenses as well as possibly elevate privileges. APC injection is a method of executing arbitrary code in the address space of a separate live process. APC injection is commonly performed by attaching malicious code to the APC Queue (Citation: Microsoft APC) of a process's thread. Queued APC functions are executed when the thread enters an alterable state.(Citation: Microsoft APC) A handle to an existing victim process is first created with native Windows API calls such as OpenThread. At this point QueueUserAPC can be used to invoke a function (such as LoadLibrayA pointing to a malicious DLL). A variation of APC injection, dubbed "Early Bird injection", involves creating a suspended process in which malicious code can be written and executed before the process' entry point (and potentially subsequent anti-malware hooks) via an APC. (Citation: CyberBit Early Bird Apr 2018) AtomBombing (Citation: ENSIL AtomBombing Oct 2016) is another variation that utilizes APCs to invoke malicious code previously written to the global atom table.(Citation: Microsoft Atom Table) Running code in the context of another process may allow access to the process's memory, system/network resources, and possibly elevated privileges. Execution via APC injection may also evade detection from security products since the execution is masked under a legitimate process.

Variations include Early Bird injection, which runs code in a suspended process before its entry point, and AtomBombing, which uses the global atom table. This grants access to the host process's memory and resources while evading detection by masking execution within a legitimate process. It has been associated with groups like FIN8 and Turla, and malware such as rootkits.[/profile]

249.name: Bidirectional Communication
249.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may use an existing, legitimate external Web service as a means for sending commands to and receiving output from a compromised system over the Web service channel. Compromised systems may leverage popular websites and social media to host command and control (C2) instructions. Those infected systems can then send the output from those commands back over that Web service channel. The return traffic may occur in a variety of ways, depending on the Web service being utilized. For example, the return traffic may take the form of the compromised system posting a comment on a forum, issuing a pull request to development project, updating a document hosted on a Web service, or by sending a Tweet. 

Popular websites and social media acting as a mechanism for C2 may give a significant amount of cover due to the likelihood that hosts within a network are already communicating with them prior to a compromise. Using common services, such as those offered by Google or Twitter, makes it easier for adversaries to hide in expected noise. Web service providers commonly use SSL/TLS encryption, giving adversaries an added level of protection.

254.name: Encryption
254.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may compromise a network device’s encryption capability in order to bypass encryption that would otherwise protect data communications. (Citation: Cisco Synful Knock Evolution)

Encryption can be used to protect transmitted network traffic to maintain its confidentiality (protect against unauthorized disclosure) and integrity (protect against unauthorized changes). Encryption ciphers are used to convert a plaintext message to ciphertext and can be computationally intensive to decipher without the associated decryption key. Typically, longer keys increase the cost of cryptanalysis, or decryption without the key.

Adversaries can compromise and manipulate devices that perform encryption of network traffic. For example, through behaviors such as [Modify System Image](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1601), [Reduce Key Space](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1600/001), and [Disable Crypto Hardware](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1600/002), an adversary can negatively effect and/or eliminate a device’s ability to securely encrypt network traffic. This poses a greater risk of unauthorized disclosure and may help facilitate data manipulation, Credential Access, or Collection efforts. (Citation: Cisco Blog Legacy Device Attacks)

The primary backdoor component in these attacks is Tavdig, also known as WorldCupSec or TadjMakhal. Epic Turla is associated with other tools like Custom Backdoor and Trojan.Wipbot, and its infrastructure has been referenced in reports on related malware such as Mosquito.

262.name: Comrat
262.uncertain_mes: [ComRAT](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0126) is a second stage implant suspected of being a descendant of [Agent.btz](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0092) and used by [Turla](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0010). The first version of [ComRAT](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0126) was identified in 2007, but the tool has undergone substantial development for many years since.(Citation: Symantec Waterbug)(Citation: NorthSec 2015 GData Uroburos Tools)(Citation: ESET ComRAT May 2020)
262.profile: [profile]ComRAT, also known as Comrat, is a second-stage implant attributed to the Turla intrusion set. It is a descendant of Agent.btz, first identified in 2007 and substantially developed since. Its key technical behaviors include using a Virtual FAT16 file system, being deployed via existing access like the PowerStallion backdoor, and employing two command and control channels: an HTTP protocol identical to its v3 variant and the Gmail web interface for receiving commands and exfiltrating data. The malware's orchestrator component is injected into explorer.exe to control functions and execute backdoor commands. It targets the Windows platform.
262.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Comrat, also known as ComRAT, is a second-stage implant and backdoor attributed to the Turla intrusion set, suspected of being a descendant of the Agent.btz worm. Its key technical behaviors include employing dual command and control channels via HTTP (using the same protocol as ComRAT v3) and email through the Gmail web interface for receiving commands and exfiltrating data. It is deployed using existing access like the PowerStallion PowerShell backdoor, utilizes a Virtual FAT16 File System, and its installer is a PowerShell script that creates a Windows scheduled task and registry entry for an encrypted payload. The orchestrator component is injected into explorer.exe. The target platform is Windows-based systems.[/profile]

264.name: Snake
264.uncertain_mes: Since January 2020, the CrowdStrike® Falcon OverWatchTM managed threat hunting team has observed an escalation in hands-on-keyboard activity. The COVID-19 pandemic has fundamentally shifted the way businesses are working, and adversaries are taking full advantage of businesses that fail to adapt their security postures in response.
264.profile: [profile]Snake, also known as Uroburos and Carbon System, is attributed to the Turla intrusion set. It operates as an implant, communicating via HTTP, HTTP2, and TCP protocols, with its network traffic often encrypted. The operators can easily modify its network-based signatures to evade detection. The malware is associated with hands-on-keyboard activity, particularly exploiting shifts in business security postures, as observed since early 2020.
264.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Snake, also known as Uroburos and Cobra, is a sophisticated rootkit malware attributed to the Turla intrusion set. It is designed for stealthy, long-term espionage, using complex encryption and a modular architecture to exfiltrate sensitive data. It primarily targets Windows platforms and is part of a broader ecosystem including the Carbon System backdoor. Its infrastructure involves HTTP, HTTP2, and TCP communications for data exfiltration, with operators capable of changing network signatures to evade detection.[/profile]

265.name: Trojan.Wipbot
265.profile: [profile]Trojan.Wipbot, also known as Tavdig, is attributed to the Turla intrusion set and exploits CVE-2013-5065 for privilege escalation on unpatched Windows XP systems. A related wiper variant sends reconnaissance data to a specified Telegram channel using a consistent Bot ID and Channel ID across Windows and Linux platforms.
265.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Trojan.Wipbot, also known as Tavdig, WorldCupSec, or TadjMakhal, is a backdoor malware attributed to the Turla intrusion set. It is used as the primary backdoor in Epic Turla attacks, which involve exploits against patched vulnerabilities, social engineering, and watering hole strategies. It is associated with the CVE-2013-5065 exploit to achieve administrator privileges on unpatched Microsoft Windows XP systems. The malware is also linked to infrastructure sending reconnaissance to a Telegram channel and is associated with other tools like Custom Backdoor.

266.name: Trojan.Turla
266.profile: [profile]Trojan.Turla, also known as Carbon, Comrat, and FA, is attributed to the Turla intrusion set. It functions as a backdoor, with a specific variant known as the Turla Outlook Backdoor. Its key technical behaviors include establishing persistence and command-and-control, often leveraging Microsoft Outlook as a vector for its operations, and it primarily targets Windows-based platforms. Its infrastructure is associated with the broader Turla malware ecosystem.[profile]
266.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Trojan.Turla is a malware entity associated with the Turla intrusion set. It is related to other Turla malware such as Carbon, Comrat, and FA. Specific technical behaviors include the use of an Outlook backdoor for persistence and command and control. The malware targets Windows platforms, leveraging components like PowerShell scripts for deployment and employing methods such as storing encrypted payloads in the Windows Registry.[/profile]

267.name: FA
267.profile: [profile]FA is a malware entity associated with the Turla intrusion set. It is directly linked to the Trojan.Turla malware. The retrieved information, while not providing direct technical details on FA itself, includes references to other malware families (LatentBot, Remcos, Hemigate) and their associated groups (APT33, The Gorgon Group, UAC-0050, Earth Estries), but these connections are not explicitly established for FA within the provided context. 268.name: Custom Communication Module
268.profile: [profile]Custom Communication Module, also known as vncDll or tvncDll, is a malware module attributed to the intrusion set Turla and used by groups like Wizard Spider (TA505/UNC1878). Its key technical behavior is implementing a custom communication protocol to interact with command-and-control servers, complicating traffic analysis. This module is associated with malware families such as TrickBot, Carbon, and Sav, indicating its deployment on the Windows platform as part of broader banking trojan or backdoor operations.
268.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Custom Communication Module is a malware component used by the Turla intrusion set within its Carbon and Sav malware families. It facilitates custom command-and-control (C&C) communications, as seen in Carbon's framework and Sav's botnet operations. The module is designed for Windows systems, enabling data exfiltration and persistence mechanisms.[/profile]

269.name: Sav
269.profile: [profile]Sav is a malware entity attributed to the Turla intrusion set and utilizes a Custom Communication Module. It has been associated with botnet command-and-control (C&C) infrastructure, with domains historically registered through the US-based registrar Sav. Its technical behavior involves establishing persistence via registry keys for automatic execution on system startup. The malware targets Windows platforms and its C&C activity has been observed to decline significantly over time.[/profile]
269.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Sav is a malware family. It is associated with the Turla intrusion set and uses a Custom Communication Module that implements a custom, obfuscated protocol for command-and-control traffic, primarily targeting Windows systems.

270.name: Rootkit
270.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may use rootkits to hide the presence of programs, files, network connections, services, drivers, and other system components. Rootkits are programs that hide the existence of malware by intercepting/hooking and modifying operating system API calls that supply system information. (Citation: Symantec Windows Rootkits) 

Rootkits or rootkit enabling functionality may reside at the user or kernel level in the operating system or lower, to include a hypervisor or [System Firmware](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1542/001). (Citation: Wikipedia Rootkit) Rootkits have been seen for Windows, Linux, and Mac OS X systems. (Citation: CrowdStrike Linux Rootkit) (Citation: BlackHat Mac OSX Rootkit)

Rootkits that reside or modify boot sectors are known as [Bootkit](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1542/003)s and specifically target the boot process of the operating system.
270.profile: [profile]Rootkit is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1014 under the Defense Evasion tactic, applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS. It operates by intercepting and modifying operating system API calls to hide malware, files, network connections, and other components. Rootkit functionality can reside at the user or kernel level, or within a hypervisor or system firmware. A specific variant known as a Bootkit (T1542.003) modifies boot sectors like the MBR or VBR to achieve persistence below the OS. Associated malware includes Carbon, and it has been used by intrusion sets like Turla, APT41, and APT28.[profile]
270.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Rootkit is identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1014 under the Defense Evasion tactic, applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It works by hiding malware presence through intercepting and modifying operating system API calls that supply system information, operating at user or kernel levels, or lower in hypervisors or firmware. Related groups include APT41 and APT28, and it is implemented via malicious kernel modules or extensions to conceal files and processes.

277.name: Hide Itself on Infected Machines
277.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may manipulate network traffic in order to hide and evade detection of their C2 infrastructure. This can be accomplished by identifying and filtering traffic from defensive tools,(Citation: TA571) masking malicious domains to obfuscate the true destination from both automated scanning tools and security researchers,(Citation: Schema-abuse)(Citation: Facad1ng)(Citation: Browser-updates) and otherwise hiding malicious artifacts to delay discovery and prolong the effectiveness of adversary infrastructure that could otherwise be identified, blocked, or taken down entirely.

C2 networks may include the use of [Proxy](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1090) or VPNs to disguise IP addresses, which can allow adversaries to blend in with normal network traffic and bypass conditional access policies or anti-abuse protections. For example, an adversary may use a virtual private cloud to spoof their IP address to closer align with a victim's IP address ranges. This may also bypass security measures relying on geolocation of the source IP address.(Citation: sysdig)(Citation: Orange Residential Proxies)

Adversaries may also attempt to filter network traffic in order to evade defensive tools in numerous ways, including blocking/redirecting common incident responder or security appliance user agents.(Citation: mod_rewrite)(Citation: SocGholish-update) Filtering traffic based on IP and geo-fencing may also avoid automated sandboxing or researcher activity (i.e., [Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1497)).(Citation: TA571)(Citation: mod_rewrite)

Hiding C2 infrastructure may also be supported by [Resource Development](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0042) activities such as [Acquire Infrastructure](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1583) and [Compromise Infrastructure](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1584). For example, using widely trusted hosting services or domains such as prominent URL shortening providers or marketing services for C2 networks may enable adversaries to present benign content that later redirects victims to malicious web pages or infrastructure once specific conditions are met.(Citation: StarBlizzard)(Citation: QR-cofense)
277.profile: [profile]The technique is formally known as Hide Infrastructure (T1665) under the Command and Control tactic. It involves manipulating network traffic to conceal C2 infrastructure by filtering out traffic from defensive tools and blocking common incident responder user agents. Adversaries use proxies or VPNs to disguise IP addresses, enabling them to blend with normal traffic and bypass geo-fencing protections. Infrastructure is further hidden by using trusted services like URL shorteners for benign-looking redirects to malicious pages. This activity is associated with groups like APT29 and Zirconium.[/profile]
277.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Hide Itself on Infected Machines" is a technique where adversaries conceal malicious artifacts on compromised systems to evade detection. This involves abusing operating system features to hide files, directories, or user accounts, and may include creating isolated computing regions using virtualization. The activity is closely related to the MITRE ATT&CK technique Hide Artifacts (T1564) under the Defense Evasion tactic, applicable across multiple platforms.

278.name: Block Incoming Email Notifications
278.profile: [profile]Block Incoming Email Notifications is a sub-technique (T1564.008) within the Defense Evasion tactic, targeting Windows and cloud email platforms. Adversaries create or modify inbox rules, often via PowerShell cmdlets like `New-InboxRule` or `Set-InboxRule`, to automatically move or delete incoming emails. This is used to hide security alerts, command and control communications, or responses to internal phishing emails by filtering messages containing keywords like "malware" or "suspicious". It has been observed in use by groups such as FIN4 and Scattered Spider.
278.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Block Incoming Email Notifications is a sub-technique of Email Hiding Rules (T1564.008) within the Defense Evasion tactic. It operates on email client and server platforms, where adversaries create or modify inbox rules to automatically move, delete, or mark as read incoming emails containing specific keywords (e.g., "malware," "suspicious," "phish"). This is done to hide security alerts, command and control communications, or responses to internal spearphishing emails, thereby delaying detection. Techniques include using PowerShell cmdlets like `New-InboxRule` or `Set-InboxRule` on Windows systems or abusing organization-wide transport rules in Microsoft Exchange.

279.name: Execute Commands
279.profile: [profile]Execute Commands is a foundational adversary behavior, formally mapped to MITRE ATT&CK technique T1059 (Command and Scripting Interpreter) under the Execution tactic. It operates across Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms by abusing built-in or cross-platform interpreters like cmd, PowerShell, Unix shells, Python, JavaScript, and Visual Basic to run arbitrary commands. This can be achieved through interactive shells, script execution, or by embedding commands in initial access payloads. Related activity includes adversaries like Lazarus using backdoors and web shells to facilitate command execution, and the abuse of cloud management services (e.g., AWS Systems Manager, Azure RunCommand) to run commands remotely in virtual machines.
279.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Execute Commands is a foundational technique (T1059) under the Execution tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. It involves adversaries abusing command-line interfaces and scripting interpreters, such as the Windows Command Shell (cmd), PowerShell, Unix shells, Python, or JavaScript, to run arbitrary commands and payloads. These commands can be executed directly, via batch files, or through remote services and are commonly delivered through initial access payloads or interactive remote shells.

280.name: Dynamic Link Library (DLL) Module
280.profile: [profile]Dynamic Link Library (DLL) Module is a malicious component, specifically a 64-bit Windows DLL. It is associated with the Backdoor malware family and is used as a RAT module, installed as a service. It has been linked to groups including Lazarus Group, APT28, and Stone Panda. Key technical behaviors include DLL side-loading. Its target platform is Windows. It is also known by the file names dwnhost.dll and DLL64.dll, and is related to the file laxhost.dll.
280.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Dynamic Link Library (DLL) Module is a backdoor malware component. It is associated with intrusion sets including Turla, Winnti, DeepPanda, APT17, Lazarus, OilRig, and FIN7. Key technical behaviors include being installed as a service and utilizing DLL side-loading (e.g., XXXModule_dlcore0). It primarily targets the Windows platform.

281.name: COM Object Hijacking
281.uncertain_name: component object model and distributed com
281.uncertain_mes:
**This technique has been deprecated. Please use [Distributed Component Object Model](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/003) and [Component Object Model](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1559/001).**

Adversaries may use the Windows Component Object Model (COM) and Distributed Component Object Model (DCOM) for local code execution or to execute on remote systems as part of lateral movement. 

COM is a component of the native Windows application programming interface (API) that enables interaction between software objects, or executable code that implements one or more interfaces.(Citation: Fireeye Hunting COM June 2019) Through COM, a client object can call methods of server objects, which are typically Dynamic Link Libraries (DLL) or executables (EXE).(Citation: Microsoft COM) DCOM is transparent middleware that extends the functionality of Component Object Model (COM) (Citation: Microsoft COM) beyond a local computer using remote procedure call (RPC) technology.(Citation: Fireeye Hunting COM June 2019)

Permissions to interact with local and remote server COM objects are specified by access control lists (ACL) in the Registry. (Citation: Microsoft COM ACL)(Citation: Microsoft Process Wide Com Keys)(Citation: Microsoft System Wide Com Keys) By default, only Administrators may remotely activate and launch COM objects through DCOM.

Adversaries may abuse COM for local command and/or payload execution. Various COM interfaces are exposed that can be abused to invoke arbitrary execution via a variety of programming languages such as C, C++, Java, and VBScript.(Citation: Microsoft COM) Specific COM objects also exists to directly perform functions beyond code execution, such as creating a [Scheduled Task/Job](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1053), fileless download/execution, and other adversary behaviors such as Privilege Escalation and Persistence.(Citation: Fireeye Hunting COM June 2019)(Citation: ProjectZero File Write EoP Apr 2018)

Adversaries may use DCOM for lateral movement. Through DCOM, adversaries operating in the context of an appropriately privileged user can remotely obtain arbitrary and even direct shellcode execution through Office applications (Citation: Enigma Outlook DCOM Lateral Movement Nov 2017) as well as other Windows objects that contain insecure methods.(Citation: Enigma MMC20 COM Jan 2017)(Citation: Enigma DCOM Lateral Movement Jan 2017) DCOM can also execute macros in existing documents (Citation: Enigma Excel DCOM Sept 2017) and may also invoke [Dynamic Data Exchange](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1173) (DDE) execution directly through a COM created instance of a Microsoft Office application (Citation: Cyberreason DCOM DDE Lateral Movement Nov 2017), bypassing the need for a malicious document.
281.profile: [profile]COM Object Hijacking is a deprecated technique. The current MITRE ATT&CK technique for this behavior is Component Object Model Hijacking (T1546.015) under the Persistence tactic for Windows. It involves adversaries establishing persistence by modifying Windows Registry keys to replace references to legitimate COM objects with malicious code, which is then executed when the hijacked system component is invoked through normal operation. This can include abusing Type Libraries to redirect to remote scripts. The intrusion-set Turla has been associated with this technique.
281.profile_without_enhance: [profile]COM Object Hijacking is a persistence technique (T1546.015) within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, executed on the Windows platform. It involves adversaries modifying Windows Registry keys to replace references to legitimate Component Object Model (COM) system components with malicious code, ensuring the malicious payload is executed whenever the hijacked component is invoked through normal system operations, often targeting frequently used objects to avoid detection.[/profile]

283.name: Carbon System
283.uncertain_mes: The Turla espionage group has been targeting various institutions for many years. Recently, we found several new versions of Carbon, a second stage backdoor in the Turla group arsenal. Last year, a technical analysis of this component was made by Swiss GovCERT.ch as part of their report detailing the attack that a defense firm owned by the Swiss government, RUAG, suffered in the past.
283.profile: [profile]Carbon System, also known as cobra carbon system, is a second-stage backdoor attributed to the Turla intrusion-set. It functions as a plugin-based system, with several Epic backdoors designed to operate as its plugins requiring a specialized loader. It has been used in attacks against institutions, including the Swiss defense firm RUAG. Its target platforms are not specified in the provided data.
283.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Carbon System, also known as Cobra Carbon System and Uroburos, is a second-stage backdoor malware attributed to the Turla intrusion set. It functions as an implant for data exfiltration, using encrypted communication via HTTP, HTTP2, and TCP protocols. The malware can operate as a platform, with plugins like the Epic Backdoor designed to work with it, requiring a specialized loader for deployment on victim systems.

284.name: Cobra
284.profile: [profile]Cobra is a malware entity associated with the Turla intrusion set, as indicated by its connection to the Uroburos malware. It is referenced in the context of the Turla group's second-stage backdoor known as Carbon. The profile also notes a potential link to the Lazarus Group through a related entity tagged as HIDDEN-COBRA, and it is mentioned in operations such as Cobra Venom, Kitty Phishing, and Kabar Cobra, which are associated with the Kimsuky group.
284.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Cobra, also known as Snake, is a sophisticated rootkit malware attributed to the Turla intrusion set, designed for stealthy, long-term espionage and data exfiltration. Its key technical behaviors include the use of complex encryption and a modular architecture for flexibility. It primarily targets Windows platforms and is part of a broader malware ecosystem that includes related components like Carbon, with infrastructure managed by the Turla group for intelligence gathering.[/profile]

285.name: Dropper
285.uncertain_mes: [SplatDropper](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S1232) is a loader that utilizes native windows API to deliver its payload to the victim environment.  [SplatDropper](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S1232) has been delivered through RAR archives and used legitimate executable for DLL side-loading.  [SplatDropper](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S1232) is known to be leveraged by [Mustang Panda](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0129) and was first observed utilized in 2025.
285.profile: [profile]The malware is known as SplatDropper, a loader that uses native Windows API to deliver its payload, is delivered via RAR archives, and employs legitimate executables for DLL side-loading. It is attributed to the Mustang Panda group and was first observed in 2025. Its key technical behaviors include delivering subsequent stages like Stage 1, Stage 2, and Stage 3, and it targets Windows platforms.
285.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Dropper is a generic malware component type, not a specific family. It functions as a delivery mechanism, deploying subsequent payloads like Stage 1, Stage 2, and Stage 3 in multi-stage infection chains. It is associated with various threat groups, including pinchy spider (via REvil), and is referenced in malware families such as Vultur, Brunhilda, and Chinoxy. Its technical behaviors involve delivering and executing encoded or non-persistent payloads to establish further compromise.[/profile]

286.name: Stage 1
286.profile: [profile]Stage 1 is a malware component, specifically the initial stage of the NosyDoor downloader, also referenced in the execution chains of InvisiMole and MatanBuchus. It is delivered by a Dropper and is classified as MSIL/TrojanDropper. Its key technical behavior is to serve as the first phase in multi-stage infection chains, leading to subsequent payloads like stage 2 components (e.g., SharedReg.dll). The target platform is Windows, indicated by its use of files like Registry.pol and Registry.plo.[/profile]
286.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Stage 1 is a malware component, also referenced as NosyDoor stage 1, and is delivered by the Dropper malware associated with groups like Lazarus, Turla, and Winnti. It functions as an initial payload in multi-stage attack chains, such as those used by InvisiMole, and is often deployed via document lures like COVID-19 alerts to install subsequent stages like Stage 2 or backdoors such as Chinoxy. Its key technical behavior is to install further malicious payloads onto a target system, and it is associated with campaigns by REvil and Brunhilda.[/profile]

287.name: Stage 2
287.profile: [profile]Stage 2 is a malware component, specifically a payload or shellcode stage. It is delivered by a Dropper. Its technical behavior involves being deployed as XOR-encoded shellcode and configuration data, which is decoded and executed by a malicious DLL upon activation, as observed in related payloads like pipesnoop and httpsnoop. Its target platform is Windows.[/profile]
287.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Stage 2 is a malware component that follows an initial dropper in multi-stage attacks. It is referenced as encoded shellcode and configuration, which a malicious DLL decodes via XOR before execution. It is associated with subsequent stages like Stage 3 and is delivered by droppers attributed to groups including Lazarus, Turla, Winnti, Hellsing, Ice Fog, Pirate Panda, Rancor, TA428, Tick, Tonto Team, Karma Panda, and Pinchy Spider.[/profile]

288.name: Stage 3
288.profile: [profile]Stage 3 is a malware stage associated with the Turla intrusion set. It is deployed by a Dropper. It is referenced as a component in other malware families including WhisperGate, CCleaner Backdoor, and VPNFilter, where it serves as a non-persistent payload or a critical execution phase. Its specific technical behaviors and target platforms are not detailed in the provided context.[/profile]
288.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Stage 3 is a malware payload referenced in multi-stage attack chains, following initial stages like Stage 1 and Stage 2. It is specifically named as a component in the WhisperGate wiper attack and is also mentioned in the context of the CCleaner backdoor and VPNFilter campaigns. Its role is typically as a subsequent, more advanced payload deployed after initial compromise.[/profile]

289.name: Implant
289.profile: [profile]Implant is a malware entity, also known as Backdoor.Turlacarbon.A and Win32.Trojan.Cobra.A, with Backdoor Functionality. It is associated with intrusion sets including Lazarus, Turla, and APT28. Its technical behaviors involve mutual TLS authentication using an implant certificate (imcrt) and private key (imkey), and it communicates with a C2 server over encrypted HTTPS for task synchronization, status processing, file transfer via specific endpoints (e.g., /implant/task_created_events, /implant/files/), and heartbeat checks. The target platform is Windows.[/profile]
289.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Implant, also known as Backdoor.Turlacarbon.A and Win32.Trojan.Cobra.A, is attributed to the Turla intrusion set. Its key technical behaviors include a modular architecture with a library named CARBON.dll, deployment as a module like msi32.dll with dual standard/backdoor functionality, and operation as part of the multi-stage Cobra Carbon System. It targets the Windows platform, uses HTTPS for encrypted C2 communication, and employs random file names for defense evasion.[/profile]

290.name: Random File Names
290.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may gather employee names that can be used during targeting. Employee names be used to derive email addresses as well as to help guide other reconnaissance efforts and/or craft more-believable lures.

Adversaries may easily gather employee names, since they may be readily available and exposed via online or other accessible data sets (ex: [Social Media](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1593/001) or [Search Victim-Owned Websites](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1594)).(Citation: OPM Leak) Gathering this information may reveal opportunities for other forms of reconnaissance (ex: [Search Open Websites/Domains](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1593) or [Phishing for Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1598)), establishing operational resources (ex: [Compromise Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1586)), and/or initial access (ex: [Phishing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566) or [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078)).
290.profile: [profile]The entity "Random File Names" is a technique for defense evasion, identified as T1036.005 within the MITRE ATT&CK framework under the Masquerading tactic, applicable to multiple platforms including Windows, Linux, and macOS. It involves adversaries naming malicious files with common, benign, or random strings to avoid detection by security tools and users. This obfuscation can include using names similar to legitimate system files or generating random alphanumeric strings to blend in with normal directory listings and bypass static analysis.
290.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Random File Names is a technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, categorized under Defense Evasion. It involves adversaries naming malicious files with random or seemingly benign strings to bypass static signature-based detection and avoid alerting users. This obfuscation makes it harder for security tools to identify the file based on its name alone and can be used in conjunction with other techniques like Masquerading to increase the likelihood of successful execution.

293.name: Backdoor.Turlacarbon.A
293.profile: [profile]Backdoor.Turlacarbon.A, also known as Win32.Trojan.Cobra, is a backdoor attributed to the Turla intrusion set. Its technical behaviors include a modular architecture with a library internally named CARBON.dll, and it operates in stages, with one stage referred to as "user" by its authors. The malware targets the Windows platform and is distributed as part of the Cobra Carbon System.
293.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Backdoor.Turlacarbon.A, also known as Win32.Trojan.Cobra.A, is a backdoor malware attributed to the Turla intrusion set. Its key technical behaviors involve using a configuration file with an implant certificate (imcrt) and private key (imkey) for mutual TLS authentication, and it communicates with its command and control (C2) server over encrypted HTTPS to specific endpoints for tasking, file transfer, and heartbeat checks. It primarily targets the Windows platform.[/profile]

294.name: Win32.Trojan.Cobra.A
294.profile: [profile]Win32.Trojan.Cobra.A, also known as Backdoor.TurlaCarbon.A, is a malware implant attributed to the Turla group. It is a backdoor and part of the Cobra Carbon system, with a known sample MD5 hash of 43e896ede6fe025ee90f7f27c6d376a4. Its key technical behavior is functioning as an implant, and it targets the Windows (Win32) platform.

297.name: Named Pipe Communication
297.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may use an existing, legitimate external Web service as a means for sending commands to and receiving output from a compromised system over the Web service channel. Compromised systems may leverage popular websites and social media to host command and control (C2) instructions. Those infected systems can then send the output from those commands back over that Web service channel. The return traffic may occur in a variety of ways, depending on the Web service being utilized. For example, the return traffic may take the form of the compromised system posting a comment on a forum, issuing a pull request to development project, updating a document hosted on a Web service, or by sending a Tweet. 

Popular websites and social media acting as a mechanism for C2 may give a significant amount of cover due to the likelihood that hosts within a network are already communicating with them prior to a compromise. Using common services, such as those offered by Google or Twitter, makes it easier for adversaries to hide in expected noise. Web service providers commonly use SSL/TLS encryption, giving adversaries an added level of protection.
297.profile: [profile]Named Pipe Communication is a technique for inter-process communication (IPC) where adversaries use named pipes to transfer data or commands between processes, often to evade detection by segmenting malicious modules. This method is associated with the Turla intrusion set and is referenced in techniques like Process Injection (T1055), where it serves as a covert channel for more sophisticated attacks. The core mechanic involves leveraging legitimate OS IPC mechanisms to establish stealthy communication channels between separate processes.
297.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Named Pipe Communication is a technique for Inter-Process Communication (IPC) within the same host, allowing processes to share data and synchronize execution. It is commonly used as a covert communication channel to evade detection, particularly in sophisticated attacks like process injection where it can segment modules. This technique is platform-specific, with named pipes being a primary implementation in Windows environments for local data exchange between processes.

298.name: Thread Execution
298.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may inject malicious code into hijacked processes in order to evade process-based defenses as well as possibly elevate privileges. Thread Execution Hijacking is a method of executing arbitrary code in the address space of a separate live process. Thread Execution Hijacking is commonly performed by suspending an existing process then unmapping/hollowing its memory, which can then be replaced with malicious code or the path to a DLL. A handle to an existing victim process is first created with native Windows API calls such as OpenThread. At this point the process can be suspended then written to, realigned to the injected code, and resumed via SuspendThread , VirtualAllocEx, WriteProcessMemory, SetThreadContext, then ResumeThread respectively.(Citation: Elastic Process Injection July 2017) This is very similar to [Process Hollowing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1055/012) but targets an existing process rather than creating a process in a suspended state. Running code in the context of another process may allow access to the process's memory, system/network resources, and possibly elevated privileges. Execution via Thread Execution Hijacking may also evade detection from security products since the execution is masked under a legitimate process.
298.profile: [profile]Thread Execution, also known as Thread Execution Hijacking (MITRE ATT&CK T1055.003), is a Defense Evasion and Privilege Escalation technique for Windows. It works by suspending an existing live process thread, hollowing its memory, and writing malicious code into it using API calls like OpenThread, VirtualAllocEx, WriteProcessMemory, and SetThreadContext before resuming the thread. This allows execution within a legitimate process to evade detection and potentially access system resources. It is distinct from Process Hollowing as it targets an already running process and has been associated with threat actors like Turla.[/profile]
298.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Thread Execution is a technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, specifically identified as sub-technique T1055.003 (Thread Execution Hijacking) under the Defense Evasion and Privilege Escalation tactics, primarily targeting Windows platforms. It works by suspending an existing process thread, hollowing its memory, and writing malicious code or a DLL path into it using API calls like OpenThread, SuspendThread, VirtualAllocEx, WriteProcessMemory, and SetThreadContext before resuming the thread with ResumeThread to mask execution under a legitimate process. This method provides access to the host process's resources and evades detection.

It targets unspecified platforms and is related to the Carbon/Cobra malware family.

303.name: Module Control
303.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may abuse control.exe to proxy execution of malicious payloads. The Windows Control Panel process binary (control.exe) handles execution of Control Panel items, which are utilities that allow users to view and adjust computer settings. Control Panel items are registered executable (.exe) or Control Panel (.cpl) files, the latter are actually renamed dynamic-link library (.dll) files that export a CPlApplet function.(Citation: Microsoft Implementing CPL)(Citation: TrendMicro CPL Malware Jan 2014) For ease of use, Control Panel items typically include graphical menus available to users after being registered and loaded into the Control Panel.(Citation: Microsoft Implementing CPL) Control Panel items can be executed directly from the command line, programmatically via an application programming interface (API) call, or by simply double-clicking the file.(Citation: Microsoft Implementing CPL) (Citation: TrendMicro CPL Malware Jan 2014)(Citation: TrendMicro CPL Malware Dec 2013) Malicious Control Panel items can be delivered via [Phishing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566) campaigns(Citation: TrendMicro CPL Malware Jan 2014)(Citation: TrendMicro CPL Malware Dec 2013) or executed as part of multi-stage malware.(Citation: Palo Alto Reaver Nov 2017) Control Panel items, specifically CPL files, may also bypass application and/or file extension allow lists. Adversaries may also rename malicious DLL files (.dll) with Control Panel file extensions (.cpl) and register them to HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Control Panel\Cpls. Even when these registered DLLs do not comply with the CPL file specification and do not export CPlApplet functions, they are loaded and executed through its DllEntryPoint when Control Panel is executed. CPL files not exporting CPlApplet are not directly executable.(Citation: ESET InvisiMole June 2020)
303.profile: [profile]Module Control is the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1218.002, a Defense Evasion and Execution tactic for Windows. It involves abusing the legitimate control.exe binary or malicious Control Panel (.cpl) files, which are renamed DLLs, to proxy execution. Adversaries can execute these items via command line or API calls, and they may register malicious DLLs with a .cpl extension in the HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Control Panel\Cpls registry key to be loaded through the DllEntryPoint when Control Panel runs, potentially bypassing allow lists. The intrusion-set Turla has been associated with this technique.[/profile]
303.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Module Control is a technique used by adversaries to manage malicious modules or components within compromised systems, such as IIS web servers, to maintain persistence and control. It involves installing and manipulating components like ISAPI extensions, filters, or IIS modules, which are deployed as DLL files to intercept and modify web traffic, execute commands, or proxy communications. This allows adversaries to extend their access and evade detection by leveraging legitimate server functionalities for malicious purposes.
