Its key behaviors involve cryptographic operations and network communication using libraries like sails.io and socket.io-client, targeting systems for data exfiltration.[/profile]

392.name: VBA Macros
392.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may hide malicious Visual Basic for Applications (VBA) payloads embedded within MS Office documents by replacing the VBA source code with benign data.(Citation: FireEye VBA stomp Feb 2020) MS Office documents with embedded VBA content store source code inside of module streams. Each module stream has a PerformanceCache that stores a separate compiled version of the VBA source code known as p-code. The p-code is executed when the MS Office version specified in the _VBA_PROJECT stream (which contains the version-dependent description of the VBA project) matches the version of the host MS Office application.(Citation: Evil Clippy May 2019)(Citation: Microsoft _VBA_PROJECT Stream) An adversary may hide malicious VBA code by overwriting the VBA source code location with zero’s, benign code, or random bytes while leaving the previously compiled malicious p-code. Tools that scan for malicious VBA source code may be bypassed as the unwanted code is hidden in the compiled p-code. If the VBA source code is removed, some tools might even think that there are no macros present. If there is a version match between the _VBA_PROJECT stream and host MS Office application, the p-code will be executed, otherwise the benign VBA source code will be decompressed and recompiled to p-code, thus removing malicious p-code and potentially bypassing dynamic analysis.(Citation: Walmart Roberts Oct 2018)(Citation: FireEye VBA stomp Feb 2020)(Citation: pcodedmp Bontchev)
392.profile: [profile]VBA Stomping, identified as T1564.007 under the Defense Evasion tactic for Windows, is a technique where adversaries hide malicious VBA payloads in Office documents. They overwrite the visible VBA source code in module streams with benign data or zeros while preserving the compiled malicious p-code in the PerformanceCache. If the Office version matches the _VBA_PROJECT stream, the malicious p-code executes directly, bypassing static analysis tools that scan source code and potentially evading dynamic analysis when versions mismatch and benign code is recompiled.[/profile]
392.profile_without_enhance: [profile]VBA Macros is a technique where adversaries embed and execute malicious Visual Basic for Applications code within Microsoft Office documents, often delivered via spearphishing attachments. The macros automate tasks to run malicious commands on the host. Related evasion methods include VBA stomping, which hides malicious compiled p-code by overwriting the source code, and persistence mechanisms like Office template macros that modify base templates (e.g., Normal.dotm) to execute code on application startup.

393.name: Job Description Lures
393.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may abuse task scheduling functionality to facilitate initial or recurring execution of malicious code. Utilities exist within all major operating systems to schedule programs or scripts to be executed at a specified date and time. A task can also be scheduled on a remote system, provided the proper authentication is met (ex: RPC and file and printer sharing in Windows environments). Scheduling a task on a remote system typically may require being a member of an admin or otherwise privileged group on the remote system.(Citation: TechNet Task Scheduler Security)

Adversaries may use task scheduling to execute programs at system startup or on a scheduled basis for persistence. These mechanisms can also be abused to run a process under the context of a specified account (such as one with elevated permissions/privileges). Similar to [System Binary Proxy Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1218), adversaries have also abused task scheduling to potentially mask one-time execution under a trusted system process.(Citation: ProofPoint Serpent)
393.profile: [profile]Job Description Lures is a social engineering technique used in the reconnaissance phase of an attack, where adversaries gather information about job roles and employee names to craft believable phishing lures. This information is typically collected from open sources like social media or victim-owned websites. By understanding organizational roles, attackers can tailor spearphishing messages, often sent via third-party services, to appear as legitimate job opportunities or other credible requests, increasing the likelihood of eliciting sensitive information or gaining initial access.[/profile]
393.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Job Description Lures is a technique within the Reconnaissance tactic, likely on multiple platforms, where adversaries craft fake job postings or recruitment messages to elicit sensitive information or establish rapport with targets. This method leverages social engineering, often using information gathered from prior reconnaissance to create believable lures, such as posing as a recruiter to ask about organizational policies, services, or technical details. It is related to spearphishing for information and gathering employee names and roles to enhance the effectiveness of the social engineering attempt.

394.name: Impersonation
394.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may impersonate a trusted person or organization in order to persuade and trick a target into performing some action on their behalf. For example, adversaries may communicate with victims (via [Phishing for Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1598), [Phishing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566), or [Internal Spearphishing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1534)) while impersonating a known sender such as an executive, colleague, or third-party vendor. Established trust can then be leveraged to accomplish an adversary’s ultimate goals, possibly against multiple victims. 
 
In many cases of business email compromise or email fraud campaigns, adversaries use impersonation to defraud victims -- deceiving them into sending money or divulging information that ultimately enables [Financial Theft](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1657).

Adversaries will often also use social engineering techniques such as manipulative and persuasive language in email subject lines and body text such as `payment`, `request`, or `urgent` to push the victim to act quickly before malicious activity is detected. These campaigns are often specifically targeted against people who, due to job roles and/or accesses, can carry out the adversary’s goal.   
 
Impersonation is typically preceded by reconnaissance techniques such as [Gather Victim Identity Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1589) and [Gather Victim Org Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1591) as well as acquiring infrastructure such as email domains (i.e. [Domains](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1583/001)) to substantiate their false identity.(Citation: CrowdStrike-BEC)
 
There is the potential for multiple victims in campaigns involving impersonation. For example, an adversary may [Compromise Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1586) targeting one organization which can then be used to support impersonation against other entities.(Citation: VEC)
394.profile: [profile]Impersonation is a social engineering technique (ID T1656) under the Initial Access tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. It involves adversaries posing as trusted persons or organizations, such as executives or vendors, to deceive targets into actions like sending money or divulging information. This is often executed via phishing emails using urgent language like "payment" or "request" and is typically preceded by reconnaissance to gather victim identity and organizational details to substantiate the false persona.
394.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Impersonation, identified as T1656, is a social engineering technique within the Initial Access tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. It involves adversaries masquerading as trusted individuals or organizations, such as executives or vendors, to deceive targets into performing actions like sending money or divulging credentials. This is often executed via phishing communications using manipulative language (e.g., "urgent" or "payment") and is typically preceded by reconnaissance to gather victim identity and organizational information to substantiate the false persona.

395.name: Code Reuse
395.profile: [profile]Code Reuse is a technique where adversaries leverage legitimate, pre-existing code from software libraries, frameworks, or system binaries to perform malicious actions, thereby blending their activity with normal operations to evade detection. This approach can involve calling trusted system functions or incorporating open-source offensive security tools into their own malware. The intrusion-set Lazarus has been associated with this practice.
395.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Code Reuse" is an attack-pattern. Based on the retrieved information, it is most closely related to the technique of Reflective Code Loading (T1620). This technique falls under the Defense Evasion tactic and operates across multiple platforms. It involves adversaries loading and executing payloads directly within a process's own memory, bypassing the need for files on disk. This method conceals execution, evades process-based detection, and can keep payloads encrypted until runtime.

396.name: Obfuscation (XOR Encryption)
396.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may obfuscate command and control traffic to make it more difficult to detect.(Citation: Bitdefender FunnyDream Campaign November 2020) Command and control (C2) communications are hidden (but not necessarily encrypted) in an attempt to make the content more difficult to discover or decipher and to make the communication less conspicuous and hide commands from being seen. This encompasses many methods, such as adding junk data to protocol traffic, using steganography, or impersonating legitimate protocols.
396.profile: [profile]Obfuscation (XOR Encryption) is a specific data obfuscation technique for Command and Control traffic, aligning with MITRE ATT&CK T1001 under Command and Control. It works by applying a simple XOR cipher to encrypt C2 communications, which is a weak, custom cryptographic method that can be implemented without external libraries to hide command patterns. This technique is distinct from general command obfuscation and has been used by groups like Lazarus for custom archival and encryption in operations.
396.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Obfuscation (XOR Encryption) is a sub-technique of Data Obfuscation (T1001) under the Command and Control tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. It involves using the XOR (exclusive OR) logical operation with a fixed or generated key to encrypt data, creating a weak ciphertext that can conceal payloads, configuration files, or command and control traffic. This method is a form of custom cryptographic protocol (T1024) and can be used for archiving data via custom methods (T1560.003), often implemented without external libraries to avoid detection.

397.name: API Hiding (GetProcAddress)
397.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may use email rules to hide inbound emails in a compromised user's mailbox. Many email clients allow users to create inbox rules for various email functions, including moving emails to other folders, marking emails as read, or deleting emails. Rules may be created or modified within email clients or through external features such as the New-InboxRule or Set-InboxRule [PowerShell](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001) cmdlets on Windows systems.(Citation: Microsoft Inbox Rules)(Citation: MacOS Email Rules)(Citation: Microsoft New-InboxRule)(Citation: Microsoft Set-InboxRule) Adversaries may utilize email rules within a compromised user's mailbox to delete and/or move emails to less noticeable folders. Adversaries may do this to hide security alerts, C2 communication, or responses to [Internal Spearphishing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1534) emails sent from the compromised account. Any user or administrator within the organization (or adversary with valid credentials) may be able to create rules to automatically move or delete emails. These rules can be abused to impair/delay detection had the email content been immediately seen by a user or defender. Malicious rules commonly filter out emails based on key words (such as malware, suspicious, phish, and hack) found in message bodies and subject lines. (Citation: Microsoft Cloud App Security) In some environments, administrators may be able to enable email rules that operate organization-wide rather than on individual inboxes. For example, Microsoft Exchange supports transport rules that evaluate all mail an organization receives against user-specified conditions, then performs a user-specified action on mail that adheres to those conditions.(Citation: Microsoft Mail Flow Rules 2023) Adversaries that abuse such features may be able to automatically modify or delete all emails related to specific topics (such as internal security incident notifications).
397.profile: [profile]API Hiding (GetProcAddress) is a technique for evading detection by dynamically resolving Windows API function addresses at runtime, often using functions like GetProcAddress() and LoadLibrary() to load hashed or obfuscated function names, thereby concealing malicious API calls from static analysis and import address table inspection. It is associated with groups like Lazarus and Mustang Panda.[/profile]
397.profile_without_enhance: [profile]API Hiding (GetProcAddress) is a sub-technique of Obfuscated Files or Information, identified as T1027.007, under the Defense Evasion tactic primarily for Windows. It involves malware using dynamic API resolution to conceal its function calls, specifically by storing hashes of API function names instead of literal strings and then using functions like GetProcAddress() and LoadLibrary() to resolve and load these functions at runtime, thereby obfuscating the import address table and evading static analysis. This technique is used by groups like Lazarus Group and Mustang Panda.

398.name: Shortcut Modification
398.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may create or modify shortcuts that can execute a program during system boot or user login. Shortcuts or symbolic links are used to reference other files or programs that will be opened or executed when the shortcut is clicked or executed by a system startup process.

Adversaries may abuse shortcuts in the startup folder to execute their tools and achieve persistence.(Citation: Shortcut for Persistence ) Although often used as payloads in an infection chain (e.g. [Spearphishing Attachment](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001)), adversaries may also create a new shortcut as a means of indirection, while also abusing [Masquerading](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1036) to make the malicious shortcut appear as a legitimate program. Adversaries can also edit the target path or entirely replace an existing shortcut so their malware will be executed instead of the intended legitimate program.

Shortcuts can also be abused to establish persistence by implementing other methods. For example, LNK browser extensions may be modified (e.g. [Browser Extensions](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1176/001)) to persistently launch malware.
398.profile: [profile]Shortcut Modification (T1547.009) is a Persistence tactic technique for Windows platforms. Adversaries create or modify shortcuts (LNK files) to execute malicious programs during system boot or user login, often by placing them in startup folders. They may edit a shortcut's target path, replace a legitimate shortcut entirely, or create a new one while using Masquerading to appear benign. This method can also involve modifying LNK browser extensions for persistent execution. Associated threat groups include Lazarus Group, Gorgon Group, APT39, and Leviathan.[/profile]
398.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Shortcut Modification (T1547.009) is a Persistence tactic technique used on Windows platforms. It involves creating or modifying shortcuts, often in startup folders, to execute malicious programs during system boot or user login. Adversaries may edit the shortcut's target path or replace a legitimate shortcut entirely, and can combine this with Masquerading to disguise the malicious file. This technique has been used by groups like Lazarus Group and APT39.

399.name: File Attribute Modification
399.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may modify property list files (plist files) to enable other malicious activity, while also potentially evading and bypassing system defenses. macOS applications use plist files, such as the info.plist file, to store properties and configuration settings that inform the operating system how to handle the application at runtime. Plist files are structured metadata in key-value pairs formatted in XML based on Apple's Core Foundation DTD. Plist files can be saved in text or binary format.(Citation: fileinfo plist file description) Adversaries can modify key-value pairs in plist files to influence system behaviors, such as hiding the execution of an application (i.e. [Hidden Window](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1564/003)) or running additional commands for persistence (ex: [Launch Agent](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1543/001)/[Launch Daemon](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1543/004) or [Re-opened Applications](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1547/007)). For example, adversaries can add a malicious application path to the `~/Library/Preferences/com.apple.dock.plist` file, which controls apps that appear in the Dock. Adversaries can also modify the LSUIElement key in an application’s info.plist file to run the app in the background. Adversaries can also insert key-value pairs to insert environment variables, such as LSEnvironment, to enable persistence via [Dynamic Linker Hijacking](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1574/006).(Citation: wardle chp2 persistence)(Citation: eset_osx_flashback)
399.profile: [profile]File Attribute Modification, identified as T1647, is a Defense Evasion technique primarily targeting macOS. It involves adversaries modifying key-value pairs in property list (plist) files, such as `info.plist` or `~/Library/Preferences/com.apple.dock.plist`, to alter system behavior. Specific technical mechanics include adding malicious application paths to the Dock plist, setting the `LSUIElement` key to run applications in the background, or inserting environment variables like `LSEnvironment` to enable persistence through methods like Dynamic Linker Hijacking. The intrusion-set Lazarus has been associated with this activity.[/profile]
399.profile_without_enhance: [profile]File Attribute Modification is a technique where adversaries alter file timestamps or other metadata to hide malicious activity. This is often done to evade forensic detection by making files appear legitimate. Specific methods include modifying the $STANDARD_INFORMATION attribute in Windows NTFS using API calls or using the `touch` command in Linux to set access and modification times. This technique is associated with the timestomp sub-technique (T1070.006) under the Defense Evasion tactic and is applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms.

400.name: Decryption Routine
400.profile: [profile]Decryption Routine is a technique used by adversaries to reverse encryption or obfuscation applied to files or data, often as part of Command and Control or Defense Evasion. It is commonly associated with groups like Lazarus. The technical mechanics involve using built-in malware functionality or system utilities, such as `certutil` or the Windows `copy /b` command, to decode or reassemble payloads. This process may require a user action or a specific key to execute the deobfuscation or decryption.
400.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Decryption Routine" is a core component of adversarial tradecraft, specifically aligning with MITRE ATT&CK technique T1140, "Deobfuscate/Decode Files or Information," under the Defense Evasion tactic. It operates across common platforms like Windows and Linux. This technique involves using built-in malware functionality or system utilities, such as `certutil` or the Windows `copy /b` command, to decode or decrypt obfuscated payloads. It is frequently employed by groups like Lazarus Group, APT28, and MuddyWater to reveal hidden malicious code for execution or data exfiltration.

401.name: Anti-VM Techniques
401.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may leverage [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078) to log directly into accessible cloud hosted compute infrastructure through cloud native methods. Many cloud providers offer interactive connections to virtual infrastructure that can be accessed through the [Cloud API](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/009), such as Azure Serial Console(Citation: Azure Serial Console), AWS EC2 Instance Connect(Citation: EC2 Instance Connect)(Citation: lucr-3: Getting SaaS-y in the cloud), and AWS System Manager.(Citation: AWS System Manager).

Methods of authentication for these connections can include passwords, application access tokens, or SSH keys. These cloud native methods may, by default, allow for privileged access on the host with SYSTEM or root level access. 

Adversaries may utilize these cloud native methods to directly access virtual infrastructure and pivot through an environment.(Citation: SIM Swapping and Abuse of the Microsoft Azure Serial Console) These connections typically provide direct console access to the VM rather than the execution of scripts (i.e., [Cloud Administration Command](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1651)).
401.profile: [profile]The entity "direct cloud vm connections" is identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1021.008 under the Defense Evasion tactic, targeting IaaS platforms. It involves adversaries using valid accounts to gain direct console access to cloud-hosted virtual machines via native provider methods like Azure Serial Console, AWS EC2 Instance Connect, or AWS System Manager, authenticating with passwords, tokens, or SSH keys. This method often grants privileged SYSTEM or root access, enabling environment pivoting without executing scripts. The intrusion-set Lazarus is associated with this technique.
401.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Anti-VM Techniques" is a defensive evasion tactic where adversaries detect and evade virtualized environments to hinder analysis. This involves checking for artifacts like specific processes, registry keys, hardware components, or network configurations indicative of virtual machines, sandboxes, or debuggers. If such an environment is detected, the malicious code may alter its behavior, delay execution, or terminate to avoid detection by automated security tools.

402.name: Backdoor Functionality
402.profile: [profile]Backdoor Functionality is a technique where adversaries insert malicious access points into systems, often through supply chain compromise (T1195.003) by modifying hardware or firmware in devices like servers or network infrastructure. It is also implemented by implanting backdoors into cloud or container images (T1525) within a victim's environment, such as AWS AMIs or Docker containers, to establish persistence. The intrusion-set Lazarus is associated with employing such backdoor techniques.[/profile]
402.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Backdoor Functionality is a general concept rather than a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique ID. It involves adversaries inserting hidden access mechanisms into systems, as seen in techniques like Supply Chain Compromise: Compromise Hardware Supply Chain (T1195.003), where hardware or firmware is modified to insert a backdoor into devices like servers or network infrastructure. Similarly, Implant Internal Image (T1525) describes implanting backdoors within cloud or container images, such as AWS AMIs or Docker containers, to establish persistence. This functionality provides adversaries with covert, high-degree control over compromised systems, making detection difficult.[/profile]

403.name: Encrypted Network Traffic
403.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may use traffic signaling to hide open ports or other malicious functionality used for persistence or command and control. Traffic signaling involves the use of a magic value or sequence that must be sent to a system to trigger a special response, such as opening a closed port or executing a malicious task. This may take the form of sending a series of packets with certain characteristics before a port will be opened that the adversary can use for command and control. Usually this series of packets consists of attempted connections to a predefined sequence of closed ports (i.e. [Port Knocking](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1205/001)), but can involve unusual flags, specific strings, or other unique characteristics. After the sequence is completed, opening a port may be accomplished by the host-based firewall, but could also be implemented by custom software.

Adversaries may also communicate with an already open port, but the service listening on that port will only respond to commands or trigger other malicious functionality if passed the appropriate magic value(s).

The observation of the signal packets to trigger the communication can be conducted through different methods. One means, originally implemented by Cd00r (Citation: Hartrell cd00r 2002), is to use the libpcap libraries to sniff for the packets in question. Another method leverages raw sockets, which enables the malware to use ports that are already open for use by other programs.

On network devices, adversaries may use crafted packets to enable [Network Device Authentication](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1556/004) for standard services offered by the device such as telnet.  Such signaling may also be used to open a closed service port such as telnet, or to trigger module modification of malware implants on the device, adding, removing, or changing malicious capabilities.  Adversaries may use crafted packets to attempt to connect to one or more (open or closed) ports, but may also attempt to connect to a router interface, broadcast, and network address IP on the same port in order to achieve their goals and objectives.(Citation: Cisco Synful Knock Evolution)(Citation: Mandiant - Synful Knock)(Citation: Cisco Blog Legacy Device Attacks)  To enable this traffic signaling on embedded devices, adversaries must first achieve and leverage [Patch System Image](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1601/001) due to the monolithic nature of the architecture.

Adversaries may also use the Wake-on-LAN feature to turn on powered off systems. Wake-on-LAN is a hardware feature that allows a powered down system to be powered on, or woken up, by sending a magic packet to it. Once the system is powered on, it may become a target for lateral movement.(Citation: Bleeping Computer - Ryuk WoL)(Citation: AMD Magic Packet)
403.profile: [profile]The entity "Encrypted Network Traffic" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the provided context, it likely refers to the obfuscation of malicious network communications. This involves using encryption algorithms (like AES or RC4) or standard cryptographic protocols (such as TLS) to conceal command and control (C2) traffic, making it blend with legitimate encrypted traffic to evade detection. Adversaries may implement this by embedding encryption keys within malware or using it in conjunction with other techniques like traffic signaling to hide malicious ports and data exfiltration. Groups like Lazarus and Winnti are associated with such practices.
403.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Encrypted Network Traffic is a technique used by adversaries to conceal command and control (C2) communications and exfiltrated data from detection by employing encryption. This involves using standard cryptographic algorithms like AES or RC4 to obfuscate network traffic, which can be applied to both C2 channels and data exfiltration over alternative protocols. The implementation aims to hide malicious activity within normal-looking encrypted streams, though it may be vulnerable if encryption keys are embedded within the malware.

404.name: Operation Blockbuster
404.profile: [profile]Operation Blockbuster is a destructive disk-wiping campaign attributed to the Lazarus intrusion set. It employs malware that directly accesses and overwrites arbitrary portions of storage devices with random data, often using third-party drivers like RawDisk to bypass the operating system. To maximize impact, the malware can propagate across networks using worm-like features, leveraging techniques such as Valid Accounts and Windows Admin Shares to interrupt availability on a wide scale.[profile]
404.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Operation Blockbuster is a destructive malware campaign, not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. It is associated with the Lazarus Group and employs disk content wiping (T1488) to disrupt availability. The malware overwrites arbitrary portions of disk drives with random data, often using direct disk access via tools like RawDisk. It can propagate across networks using worm-like features, leveraging techniques such as Valid Accounts (T1078) and Windows Admin Shares (T1077) to maximize impact.

407.name: APK Samples
407.uncertain_mes:
Introduction:
Earlier today, IDF’s spokesperson revealed that IDF (Israel Defense Force) and ISA (Israel Security Agency AKA “Shin Bet”) conducted a joint operation to take down a Hamas operation targeting IDF soldiers, dubbed ‘Rebound’.

It is attributed to the AridViper group and is associated with the 'Rebound' campaign targeting IDF soldiers. Key technical behavior involves the use of an embedded APK named HenBox. The target platform is Android mobile devices.[/profile]

It may be used in operations like 'Rebound' targeting IDF soldiers and can be embedded within other malware like HenBox, Poison Ivy, PlugX, and Farseer. Its primary target platform is Android.

408.name: Macro Payload
408.profile: [profile]Macro Payload is a generic term for malicious code delivered via macros. It is attributed to the Lazarus intrusion set. Key technical behaviors include being embedded within documents like Excel files, using obfuscated Excel 4.0 macro formulas, and leveraging Windows API calls such as URLDownloadToFile to download and execute secondary payloads like IcedID, QBot, or Emotet. The primary target platform is Windows, exploiting its macro execution environment to initiate infection chains.
408.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Macro Payload is a generic term for malicious code delivered via documents, often Excel files, using obfuscated Excel 4.0 macro formulas. It is associated with downloaders for specific malware families like IcedID and QBot, and is used by groups including Gold Cabin and Lunar Spider. The typical execution chain involves macros using WinAPI functions like URLDownloadToFile to fetch a payload from a generated URL, which is then executed in-memory, often via rundll32. It primarily targets Windows systems through weaponized Office documents.

409.name: PE文件
409.profile: [profile]PE文件 is a file format used by malware families like PlugX and Hidden Bee, and is associated with groups including Lazarus, APT32, and Leviathan. PlugX variants may lack or contain standard PE signatures. Hidden Bee uses a mutated PE format stripped of DOS/NT headers and section names, requiring repair to become a standard PE. CACTUSTORCH can decrypt and load a PE file in memory from shellcode. The format is targeted at Windows platforms and is often involved in memory-based loading and execution techniques.[/profile]
409.profile_without_enhance: [profile]PE文件 is a generic term for the Portable Executable file format used in Windows operating systems, which is often leveraged as a container or delivery mechanism for malicious code. It is referenced in the context of specific malware families like PlugX, which uses PE files both with and without standard signatures, and Hidden Bee, which employs a mutated variant of the PE format by stripping headers and section names to evade detection. The format is also utilized by Cactustorch, where a decrypted shellcode writes and loads a PE file in memory. These instances highlight its role as a fundamental target platform for malware execution and a common element in technical behaviors involving fileless execution, obfuscation, and dynamic loading.

410.name: ELF文件
410.profile: [profile]ELF文件 is a malware entity targeting Linux systems (ELF format). It is attributed to the Lazarus intrusion set. Key technical behaviors include using peer-to-peer serverless communication for C2 (similar to Tox backdoor), employing encryption via NaCl, and utilizing UDP with DHT for peer discovery. Infrastructure and supplementary info indicate potential variants or related components like SSHdoor and Manjusaka, which share the ELF file type and may represent different versions or tools within the same ecosystem.[/profile]

Its attributed groups remain unknown.

411.name: ELF Arm
411.profile: [profile]ELF Arm is a malware variant targeting ARM-based systems. It is associated with the Lazarus intrusion set and is related to other malware families like ManusCrypt, Clevore, and Cruprox. Its technical behaviors include functioning as a backdoor, potentially using peer-to-peer communication and encryption methods similar to the Tox protocol, and it can act as a downloader or loader for other payloads. It is associated with or considered part of the ManusCrypt malware family, which is a Remote Access Trojan (RAT) attributed to the Lazarus group and part of the TraderTraitor cluster focused on cryptocurrency theft. ELF Arm is directly related to other malware such as Clevore and Cruprox, which exhibit behaviors like creating registry keys for persistence to launch on system startup, monitoring specific applications, and engaging in network interactions. Target platforms are not explicitly specified, but the association with ELF and ARM suggests potential targeting of Linux-based systems or embedded devices using ARM processors.[/profile]

412.name: TLS Spoofing
412.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may redirect network traffic to adversary-owned systems by spoofing Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) traffic and acting as a malicious DHCP server on the victim network. By achieving the adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) position, adversaries may collect network communications, including passed credentials, especially those sent over insecure, unencrypted protocols. This may also enable follow-on behaviors such as [Network Sniffing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1040) or [Transmitted Data Manipulation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1565/002). DHCP is based on a client-server model and has two functionalities: a protocol for providing network configuration settings from a DHCP server to a client and a mechanism for allocating network addresses to clients.(Citation: rfc2131) The typical server-client interaction is as follows: 1. The client broadcasts a `DISCOVER` message. 2. The server responds with an `OFFER` message, which includes an available network address. 3. The client broadcasts a `REQUEST` message, which includes the network address offered. 4. The server acknowledges with an `ACK` message and the client receives the network configuration parameters. Adversaries may spoof as a rogue DHCP server on the victim network, from which legitimate hosts may receive malicious network configurations. For example, malware can act as a DHCP server and provide adversary-owned DNS servers to the victimized computers.(Citation: new_rogue_DHCP_serv_malware)(Citation: w32.tidserv.g) Through the malicious network configurations, an adversary may achieve the AiTM position, route client traffic through adversary-controlled systems, and collect information from the client network. DHCPv6 clients can receive network configuration information without being assigned an IP address by sending a INFORMATION-REQUEST (code 11) message to the All_DHCP_Relay_Agents_and_Servers multicast address.(Citation: rfc3315) Adversaries may use their rogue DHCP server to respond to this request message with malicious network configurations. Rather than establishing an AiTM position, adversaries may also abuse DHCP spoofing to perform a DHCP exhaustion attack (i.e, [Service Exhaustion Flood](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1499/002)) by generating many broadcast DISCOVER messages to exhaust a network’s DHCP allocation pool.
412.profile: [profile]The entity "TLS Spoofing" is a misnomer in the provided data; the actual technique described is DHCP Spoofing, which maps to MITRE ATT&CK ID T1557.003 under the Collection tactic for Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. This technique involves an adversary deploying a rogue DHCP server on a victim network to intercept and redirect traffic, achieving an adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) position. The rogue server responds to client DHCP DISCOVER or DHCPv6 INFORMATION-REQUEST messages with malicious network configurations, such as adversary-controlled DNS servers, to route and potentially collect client communications, including unencrypted credentials. The intrusion-set Lazarus has been associated with this activity.
412.profile_without_enhance: [profile]TLS Spoofing is a technique where adversaries impersonate legitimate TLS servers by presenting fraudulent certificates or manipulating the TLS handshake to intercept, decrypt, or manipulate encrypted communications. This attack, which operates across network platforms, falls under the tactic of Credential Access or Collection, enabling man-in-the-middle positions to capture sensitive data like login credentials transmitted over what appears to be a secure channel.

413.name: SNI Field Manipulation
413.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may manipulate accounts to maintain and/or elevate access to victim systems. Account manipulation may consist of any action that preserves or modifies adversary access to a compromised account, such as modifying credentials or permission groups.(Citation: FireEye SMOKEDHAM June 2021) These actions could also include account activity designed to subvert security policies, such as performing iterative password updates to bypass password duration policies and preserve the life of compromised credentials. 

In order to create or manipulate accounts, the adversary must already have sufficient permissions on systems or the domain. However, account manipulation may also lead to privilege escalation where modifications grant access to additional roles, permissions, or higher-privileged [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078).
413.profile: [profile]SNI Field Manipulation is a technique used within the broader Tactic of Defense Evasion (specifically T1090.004, Domain Fronting) to obfuscate network traffic. It operates by exploiting Content Delivery Networks (CDNs) that host multiple domains. The technical mechanic involves deliberately mismatching the domain name in the TLS header's Server Name Indication (SNI) field with the domain in the HTTP Host header, or leaving the SNI field blank in a "domainless" variation. This causes the CDN to route encrypted HTTPS traffic based on the HTTP header, making it appear to be going to an innocuous front domain while actually communicating with a different, adversarial-controlled domain. The Lazarus Group has been associated with related obfuscation techniques.[/profile]
413.profile_without_enhance: [profile]SNI Field Manipulation is a technique within MITRE ATT&CK, likely associated with Tactic T1090.004 (Domain Fronting) under Command and Control. It operates across network platforms by altering the Server Name Indication (SNI) field in the TLS handshake to obfuscate the true destination of HTTPS traffic. Specifically, adversaries may set the SNI field to a different domain or leave it blank while the HTTP Host header contains the actual target domain, exploiting Content Delivery Networks that route based on the Host header after TLS decryption to hide malicious communications.

416.name: Record Microphone
416.profile: [profile]Record Microphone, also known as Audio Capture (T1123), is a collection technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework. It involves adversaries using malware or scripts to interact with a computer's microphone or audio-enabled applications via operating system or application APIs to capture audio recordings. Captured audio files are typically written to disk for later exfiltrated. This technique is employed by groups like APT37 and can be used to listen into sensitive conversations for intelligence gathering.

418.name: Upload Local Files
418.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may upload malware to third-party or adversary controlled infrastructure to make it accessible during targeting. Malicious software can include payloads, droppers, post-compromise tools, backdoors, and a variety of other malicious content. Adversaries may upload malware to support their operations, such as making a payload available to a victim network to enable [Ingress Tool Transfer](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1105) by placing it on an Internet accessible web server.

Malware may be placed on infrastructure that was previously purchased/rented by the adversary ([Acquire Infrastructure](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1583)) or was otherwise compromised by them ([Compromise Infrastructure](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1584)). Malware can also be staged on web services, such as GitHub or Pastebin; hosted on the InterPlanetary File System (IPFS), where decentralized content storage makes the removal of malicious files difficult; or saved on the blockchain as smart contracts, which are resilient against takedowns that would affect traditional infrastructure.(Citation: Volexity Ocean Lotus November 2020)(Citation: Talos IPFS 2022)(Citation: Guardio Etherhiding 2023)(Citation: Bleeping Computer Binance Smart Chain 2023)

Adversaries may upload backdoored files, such as software packages, application binaries, virtual machine images, or container images, to third-party software stores, package libraries, extension marketplaces, or repositories (ex: GitHub, CNET, AWS Community AMIs, Docker Hub, PyPi, NPM).(Citation: Datadog Security Labs Malicious PyPi Packages 2024) By chance encounter, victims may directly download/install these backdoored files via [User Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204). Masquerading, including typo-squatting legitimate software, may increase the chance of users mistakenly executing these files.

The uploaded malware is then made available for operations like Ingress Tool Transfer or to trick users into downloading it via User Execution, often using masquerading tactics like typo-squatting.

419.name: Execute Local Files
419.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may attempt to steal Kerberos tickets stored in credential cache files (or ccache). These files are used for short term storage of a user's active session credentials. The ccache file is created upon user authentication and allows for access to multiple services without the user having to re-enter credentials. The /etc/krb5.conf configuration file and the KRB5CCNAME environment variable are used to set the storage location for ccache entries. On Linux, credentials are typically stored in the `/tmp` directory with a naming format of `krb5cc_%UID%` or `krb5.ccache`. On macOS, ccache entries are stored by default in memory with an `API:{uuid}` naming scheme. Typically, users interact with ticket storage using kinit, which obtains a Ticket-Granting-Ticket (TGT) for the principal; klist, which lists obtained tickets currently held in the credentials cache; and other built-in binaries.(Citation: Kerberos GNU/Linux)(Citation: Binary Defense Kerberos Linux) Adversaries can collect tickets from ccache files stored on disk and authenticate as the current user without their password to perform [Pass the Ticket](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1550/003) attacks. Adversaries can also use these tickets to impersonate legitimate users with elevated privileges to perform [Privilege Escalation](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0004). Tools like Kekeo can also be used by adversaries to convert ccache files to Windows format for further [Lateral Movement](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0008). On macOS, adversaries may use open-source tools or the Kerberos framework to interact with ccache files and extract TGTs or Service Tickets via lower-level APIs.(Citation: SpectorOps Bifrost Kerberos macOS 2019)(Citation: Linux Kerberos Tickets)(Citation: Brining MimiKatz to Unix)(Citation: Kekeo)
419.profile: [profile]Execute Local Files is a technique with uncertain mapping to the MITRE ATT&CK framework. The provided data strongly describes the theft of Kerberos tickets from credential cache (ccache) files, which is formally known as "Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets: Kerberos Credential Cache" under ID T1558.005, falling under the Credential Access tactic for Linux and macOS platforms. The technical mechanics involve locating ccache files via the `/etc/krb5.conf` configuration, the `KRB5CCNAME` environment variable, or default paths like `/tmp/krb5cc_%UID%` on Linux, then extracting tickets to perform Pass-the-Ticket attacks for lateral movement and privilege escalation, potentially using tools like Kekeo for format conversion. The intrusion-set Lazarus is a known user of related TTPs.

This can involve using command interpreters or system APIs to load and execute these files, bypassing the need for external downloads. The technique is associated with the Execution tactic and is applicable across multiple platforms including Windows, Linux, and macOS.

424.name: Observe SMS/MMS
424.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may leverage messaging services for SMS pumping, which may impact system and/or hosted service availability.(Citation: Twilio SMS Pumping) SMS pumping is a type of telecommunications fraud whereby a threat actor first obtains a set of phone numbers from a telecommunications provider, then leverages a victim’s messaging infrastructure to send large amounts of SMS messages to numbers in that set. By generating SMS traffic to their phone number set, a threat actor may earn payments from the telecommunications provider.(Citation: Twilio SMS Pumping Fraud)

Threat actors often use publicly available web forms, such as one-time password (OTP) or account verification fields, in order to generate SMS traffic. These fields may leverage services such as Twilio, AWS SNS, and Amazon Cognito in the background.(Citation: Twilio SMS Pumping)(Citation: AWS RE:Inforce Threat Detection 2024) In response to the large quantity of requests, SMS costs may increase and communication channels may become overwhelmed.(Citation: Twilio SMS Pumping)

It involves a threat actor obtaining phone numbers from a telecom provider and then abusing a victim's messaging infrastructure, often via public web forms for OTP or verification that use services like Twilio or AWS SNS, to send a high volume of SMS messages. This generates fraudulent traffic to the actor's number set for financial gain, potentially overwhelming communication channels and increasing costs for the victim. The intrusion-set Lazarus has been associated with this activity.[/profile]

425.name: Record Web History
425.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may search the command history on compromised systems for insecurely stored credentials.

On Linux and macOS systems, shells such as Bash and Zsh keep track of the commands users type on the command-line with the "history" utility. Once a user logs out, the history is flushed to the user's history file. For each user, this file resides at the same location: for example, `~/.bash_history` or `~/.zsh_history`. Typically, these files keeps track of the user's last 1000 commands.

On Windows, PowerShell has both a command history that is wiped after the session ends, and one that contains commands used in all sessions and is persistent. The default location for persistent history can be found in `%userprofile%\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\PSReadline\ConsoleHost_history.txt`, but command history can also be accessed with `Get-History`. Command Prompt (CMD) on Windows does not have persistent history.(Citation: Microsoft about_History)(Citation: Medium)

Users often type usernames and passwords on the command-line as parameters to programs, which then get saved to this file when they log out. Adversaries can abuse this by looking through the file for potential credentials.(Citation: External to DA, the OS X Way)
425.profile: [profile]Record Web History is a credential access technique, identified as T1552.003, under the Credential Access tactic. It operates across Linux, macOS, and Windows platforms by searching shell command history files for insecurely stored credentials. Adversaries examine files like ~/.bash_history, ~/.zsh_history, or the PowerShell persistent history file at %userprofile%\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\PSReadline\ConsoleHost_history.txt to find usernames and passwords typed as command-line parameters. The intrusion-set Lazarus has been associated with this behavior.[/profile]
425.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Record Web History is a technique where adversaries collect a user's web browsing history to gather intelligence. This falls under the Collection tactic and typically targets multiple platforms including Windows, macOS, and Linux. The technical mechanics involve accessing and exfiltrating data from local browser history files or databases, such as those for Chrome, Firefox, or Safari, which contain visited URLs, timestamps, and often cached data. This information can reveal user habits, accessed resources, and potential authentication tokens.

Adversaries may search scan databases to gather actionable information. Threat actors can use online resources and lookup tools to harvest information from these services. Adversaries may seek information about their already identified targets, or use these datasets to discover opportunities for successful breaches. Information from these sources may reveal opportunities for other forms of reconnaissance (ex: [Active Scanning](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1595) or [Search Open Websites/Domains](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1593)), establishing operational resources (ex: [Develop Capabilities](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1587) or [Obtain Capabilities](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1588)), and/or initial access (ex: [External Remote Services](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1133) or [Exploit Public-Facing Application](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1190)).

On Linux, information can be gathered from files under `/etc/NetworkManager/system-connections/`, while on macOS, the `security find-generic-password` command can be used. This activity supports discovery and credential access for ongoing campaigns.

448.name: Encryption Algorithms
448.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may compromise a network device’s encryption capability in order to bypass encryption that would otherwise protect data communications. (Citation: Cisco Synful Knock Evolution)

Encryption can be used to protect transmitted network traffic to maintain its confidentiality (protect against unauthorized disclosure) and integrity (protect against unauthorized changes). Encryption ciphers are used to convert a plaintext message to ciphertext and can be computationally intensive to decipher without the associated decryption key. Typically, longer keys increase the cost of cryptanalysis, or decryption without the key.

Adversaries can compromise and manipulate devices that perform encryption of network traffic. For example, through behaviors such as [Modify System Image](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1601), [Reduce Key Space](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1600/001), and [Disable Crypto Hardware](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1600/002), an adversary can negatively effect and/or eliminate a device’s ability to securely encrypt network traffic. This poses a greater risk of unauthorized disclosure and may help facilitate data manipulation, Credential Access, or Collection efforts. (Citation: Cisco Blog Legacy Device Attacks)
448.profile: [profile]This entity aligns with MITRE ATT&CK technique T1600, named Weaken Encryption, under the Defense Evasion tactic for Network Devices. Adversaries compromise a device's encryption capability to bypass protections for network traffic. This is achieved by manipulating the device through specific sub-techniques: modifying the system image, reducing the cryptographic key space, or disabling dedicated cryptographic hardware to degrade or eliminate secure encryption.

It refers to the use of cryptographic ciphers like AES, DES, 3DES, Blowfish, and RC4 to protect data confidentiality and integrity. Adversaries employ these algorithms to encrypt command and control traffic, conceal collected data prior to exfiltration, and implement custom encryption schemes, often using symmetric keys where the same key is used for both encryption and decryption.

449.name: Data Deletion Methods
449.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may delete files left behind by the actions of their intrusion activity. Malware, tools, or other non-native files dropped or created on a system by an adversary (ex: [Ingress Tool Transfer](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1105)) may leave traces to indicate to what was done within a network and how. Removal of these files can occur during an intrusion, or as part of a post-intrusion process to minimize the adversary's footprint. There are tools available from the host operating system to perform cleanup, but adversaries may use other tools as well.(Citation: Microsoft SDelete July 2016) Examples of built-in [Command and Scripting Interpreter](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059) functions include del on Windows, rm or unlink on Linux and macOS, and `rm` on ESXi.
449.profile: [profile]Data Deletion Methods is a technique aligned with MITRE ATT&CK ID T1070.004 under the Defense Evasion tactic, applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. It involves adversaries deleting files like malware or tools to remove forensic traces, using native OS commands such as `del` on Windows or `rm` and `unlink` on Linux/macOS, or specialized utilities like Windows Sysinternals SDelete. This action is distinct from destructive data wipes and is employed by numerous threat groups including APT28, Lazarus Group, and Volt Typhoon to minimize their operational footprint.[/profile]
449.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Data Deletion Methods is a technique for destroying files to hinder recovery, often for sabotage or covering tracks. It uses commands like `del` or `rm` to remove file pointers, but adversaries may overwrite data with random content or use secure deletion tools like SDelete to make files irrecoverable. This can target local files or cloud storage objects via lifecycle policy manipulation.

451.name: WannaCry

452.name: advanced persistent threat
452.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may search private data from threat intelligence vendors for information that can be used during targeting. Threat intelligence vendors may offer paid feeds or portals that offer more data than what is publicly reported. Although sensitive details (such as customer names and other identifiers) may be redacted, this information may contain trends regarding breaches such as target industries, attribution claims, and successful TTPs/countermeasures.(Citation: D3Secutrity CTI Feeds)

Adversaries may search in private threat intelligence vendor data to gather actionable information. If a threat actor is searching for information on their own activities, that falls under [Search Threat Vendor Data](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1681). Information reported by vendors may also reveal opportunities other forms of reconnaissance (ex: [Search Open Websites/Domains](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1593)), establishing operational resources (ex: [Develop Capabilities](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1587) or [Obtain Capabilities](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1588)), and/or initial access (ex: [Exploit Public-Facing Application](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1190) or [External Remote Services](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1133)).

The intrusion-set Lazarus has been associated with this behavior.

These methods highlight the advanced, multi-stage nature of such threats, focusing on persistent, evasive access across platforms like ESXi and various hardware components.

461.name: Server Message Block (SMB)
461.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may buy, lease, rent, or obtain physical servers that can be used during targeting. Use of servers allows an adversary to stage, launch, and execute an operation. During post-compromise activity, adversaries may utilize servers for various tasks, such as watering hole operations in [Drive-by Compromise](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1189), enabling [Phishing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566) operations, or facilitating [Command and Control](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0011). Instead of compromising a third-party [Server](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1584/004) or renting a [Virtual Private Server](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1583/003), adversaries may opt to configure and run their own servers in support of operations. Free trial periods of cloud servers may also be abused.(Citation: Free Trial PurpleUrchin)(Citation: Freejacked) 

Adversaries may only need a lightweight setup if most of their activities will take place using online infrastructure. Or, they may need to build extensive infrastructure if they want to test, communicate, and control other aspects of their activities on their own systems.(Citation: NYTStuxnet)
461.profile: [profile]Server Message Block (SMB) is a network file, printer, and serial port sharing protocol primarily for Windows, with implementations like Samba for Linux and macOS. Adversaries use SMB with Valid Accounts to access remote shares, including hidden administrative shares (e.g., C$, ADMIN$, IPC$), for lateral movement, file transfer, and remote execution via techniques like Scheduled Tasks or WMI. It can also be abused in forced authentication attacks to harvest credential hashes when a system connects to an adversary-controlled SMB resource.[/profile]
461.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Server Message Block (SMB)" is a network file, printer, and serial port sharing protocol primarily for Windows, with implementations like Samba for Linux and macOS. Adversaries abuse SMB for lateral movement by interacting with remote file shares, including hidden administrative shares (e.g., C$, ADMIN$, IPC$), using valid accounts or Pass-the-Hash. It facilitates remote execution via associated protocols like RPC for techniques such as Scheduled Task, Service Execution, and WMI. SMB is also exploited in credential theft through forced authentication attacks, where systems automatically send user hashes when connecting to adversary-controlled resources.

462.name: Ransomware attack
462.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may downgrade or use a version of system features that may be outdated, vulnerable, and/or does not support updated security controls. Downgrade attacks typically take advantage of a system’s backward compatibility to force it into less secure modes of operation. 

Adversaries may downgrade and use various less-secure versions of features of a system, such as [Command and Scripting Interpreter](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059)s or even network protocols that can be abused to enable [Adversary-in-the-Middle](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1557) or [Network Sniffing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1040).(Citation: Praetorian TLS Downgrade Attack 2014) For example, [PowerShell](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001) versions 5+ includes Script Block Logging (SBL), which can record executed script content. However, adversaries may attempt to execute a previous version of PowerShell that does not support SBL with the intent to [Impair Defenses](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1562) while running malicious scripts that may have otherwise been detected.(Citation: CrowdStrike BGH Ransomware 2021)(Citation: Mandiant BYOL 2018)(Citation: att_def_ps_logging)

Adversaries may similarly target network traffic to downgrade from an encrypted HTTPS connection to an unsecured HTTP connection that exposes network data in clear text.(Citation: Targeted SSL Stripping Attacks Are Real)(Citation: Crowdstrike Downgrade) On Windows systems, adversaries may downgrade the boot manager to a vulnerable version that bypasses Secure Boot, granting the ability to disable various operating system security mechanisms.(Citation: SafeBreach)
462.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique Downgrade Attack, ID T1562.010, under the Defense Evasion tactic and applicable to Windows and potentially other platforms. It involves forcing systems into less secure modes by exploiting backward compatibility, such as executing older PowerShell versions to bypass Script Block Logging or downgrading HTTPS connections to unencrypted HTTP to facilitate sniffing. The intrusion-set Lazarus has been associated with this technique, and it is conceptually related to ransomware operations where impairing defenses precedes encryption for impact.[/profile]

To maximize impact, it may propagate via worm-like features using techniques like Valid Accounts and SMB shares, and may exclude critical system files (e.g., .dll, .exe) to maintain system operability for ransom delivery.

477.name: Phishing Emails
477.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may send phishing messages to gain access to victim systems. All forms of phishing are electronically delivered social engineering. Phishing can be targeted, known as spearphishing. In spearphishing, a specific individual, company, or industry will be targeted by the adversary. More generally, adversaries can conduct non-targeted phishing, such as in mass malware spam campaigns.

Adversaries may send victims emails containing malicious attachments or links, typically to execute malicious code on victim systems. Phishing may also be conducted via third-party services, like social media platforms. Phishing may also involve social engineering techniques, such as posing as a trusted source, as well as evasive techniques such as removing or manipulating emails or metadata/headers from compromised accounts being abused to send messages (e.g., [Email Hiding Rules](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1564/008)).(Citation: Microsoft OAuth Spam 2022)(Citation: Palo Alto Unit 42 VBA Infostealer 2014) Another way to accomplish this is by [Email Spoofing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1672)(Citation: Proofpoint-spoof) the identity of the sender, which can be used to fool both the human recipient as well as automated security tools,(Citation: cyberproof-double-bounce) or by including the intended target as a party to an existing email thread that includes malicious files or links (i.e., "thread hijacking").(Citation: phishing-krebs)

Victims may also receive phishing messages that instruct them to call a phone number where they are directed to visit a malicious URL, download malware,(Citation: sygnia Luna Month)(Citation: CISA Remote Monitoring and Management Software) or install adversary-accessible remote management tools onto their computer (i.e., [User Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204)).(Citation: Unit42 Luna Moth)
477.profile: [profile]Phishing, identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1566 under the Initial Access tactic, is an electronically delivered social engineering attack targeting various platforms. It involves sending messages, primarily emails, containing malicious attachments or links to execute code, often leveraging email spoofing, thread hijacking, or directing victims to call numbers for malware download. Associated groups include Sea Turtle, Kimsuky, and Axiom, and it is distinct from T1598 (Phishing for Information) which focuses on credential harvesting.[/profile]
477.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Phishing Emails is a technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, aligning with ID T1566 under the Initial Access tactic and applicable to multiple platforms. It involves adversaries sending emails containing malicious attachments or links to execute code, often using social engineering by posing as a trusted source. Evasive methods include email spoofing, manipulating email headers, and hijacking existing email threads to enhance credibility.

481.name: Ransomware
481.profile: [profile]Ransomware is a malicious software technique that encrypts data on target systems to interrupt availability and extort monetary compensation. It typically targets common user files like Office documents, PDFs, and images, and may also encrypt critical system files, disk partitions, or virtual machines. To maximize impact, ransomware often employs worm-like features for network propagation using techniques like Valid Accounts and SMB/Windows Admin Shares, and may use tactics such as Internal Defacement or "print bombing" to intimidate victims. Adversaries may selectively exclude certain system files to avoid detection and ensure the system remains operational to display ransom demands.
481.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Ransomware" is a malware attack pattern, not a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique. It is a primary method for the technique Data Encrypted for Impact (T1486) under the Impact tactic. Ransomware operates by encrypting files, disk partitions, or virtual machines to render data inaccessible, demanding payment for decryption. To maximize impact, it may propagate via worm-like features using techniques like Valid Accounts and SMB shares, and may avoid encrypting critical system files (e.g., .dll, .exe) to maintain system operation for ransom delivery.

482.name: Network Scanning
482.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may scan victims for vulnerabilities that can be used during targeting. Vulnerability scans typically check if the configuration of a target host/application (ex: software and version) potentially aligns with the target of a specific exploit the adversary may seek to use.

These scans may also include more broad attempts to [Gather Victim Host Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1592) that can be used to identify more commonly known, exploitable vulnerabilities. Vulnerability scans typically harvest running software and version numbers via server banners, listening ports, or other network artifacts.(Citation: OWASP Vuln Scanning) Information from these scans may reveal opportunities for other forms of reconnaissance (ex: [Search Open Websites/Domains](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1593) or [Search Open Technical Databases](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1596)), establishing operational resources (ex: [Develop Capabilities](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1587) or [Obtain Capabilities](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1588)), and/or initial access (ex: [Exploit Public-Facing Application](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1190)).
482.profile: [profile]Vulnerability Scanning, identified as T1595.002, is a Reconnaissance technique used across multiple platforms. It involves probing target hosts and applications to harvest configuration details like software versions and listening ports from server banners and network artifacts, aiming to identify exploitable vulnerabilities that align with specific exploits. This activity is associated with groups such as APT41, Sandworm Team, and Lazarus, and the information gathered can enable further reconnaissance, capability development, or initial access via exploits.
482.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Network Scanning, identified as T1595.001 "Scanning IP Blocks" within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, is a reconnaissance tactic conducted on the pre-attack platform. This technique involves adversaries probing victim IP address blocks to gather network information, ranging from simple ICMP ping sweeps to identify active hosts to more detailed scans that harvest software versions from server banners and listening ports. The gathered intelligence on network topology and services is used to inform subsequent targeting, reconnaissance, and initial access operations.

501.name: Dynamic API Loading
501.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may obfuscate then dynamically resolve API functions called by their malware in order to conceal malicious functionalities and impair defensive analysis. Malware commonly uses various [Native API](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1106) functions provided by the OS to perform various tasks such as those involving processes, files, and other system artifacts.

API functions called by malware may leave static artifacts such as strings in payload files. Defensive analysts may also uncover which functions a binary file may execute via an import address table (IAT) or other structures that help dynamically link calling code to the shared modules that provide functions.(Citation: Huntress API Hash)(Citation: IRED API Hashing)

To avoid static or other defensive analysis, adversaries may use dynamic API resolution to conceal malware characteristics and functionalities. Similar to [Software Packing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/002), dynamic API resolution may change file signatures and obfuscate malicious API function calls until they are resolved and invoked during runtime.

Various methods may be used to obfuscate malware calls to API functions. For example, hashes of function names are commonly stored in malware in lieu of literal strings. Malware can use these hashes (or other identifiers) to manually reproduce the linking and loading process using functions such as `GetProcAddress()` and `LoadLibrary()`. These hashes/identifiers can also be further obfuscated using encryption or other string manipulation tricks (requiring various forms of [Deobfuscate/Decode Files or Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1140) during execution).(Citation: BlackHat API Packers)(Citation: Drakonia HInvoke)(Citation: Huntress API Hash)
501.profile: [profile]Dynamic API Resolution is a Defense Evasion technique with MITRE ATT&CK ID T1027.007, operating on Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It conceals malware by obfuscating API calls, typically storing hashes of function names instead of literal strings. During runtime, malware manually resolves these hashes using functions like `GetProcAddress()` and `LoadLibrary()` to load necessary libraries and retrieve function addresses, thereby avoiding static artifacts in the import address table (IAT) and impairing defensive analysis. This technique is associated with threat groups like Lazarus Group and Mustang Panda.[/profile]
501.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Dynamic API Loading is a technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, aligning with the concept of Obfuscated Files or Information: Dynamic API Resolution (T1027.007) under the Defense Evasion tactic, primarily for Windows platforms. It works by malware storing hashes or encrypted identifiers of API function names instead of literal strings, then using functions like `GetProcAddress()` and `LoadLibrary()` to manually resolve and load those functions at runtime, thereby concealing malicious calls from static analysis and altering file signatures.

502.name: Port Listening
502.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may use port knocking to hide open ports used for persistence or command and control. To enable a port, an adversary sends a series of attempted connections to a predefined sequence of closed ports. After the sequence is completed, opening a port is often accomplished by the host based firewall, but could also be implemented by custom software.

This technique has been observed both for the dynamic opening of a listening port as well as the initiating of a connection to a listening server on a different system.

The observation of the signal packets to trigger the communication can be conducted through different methods. One means, originally implemented by Cd00r (Citation: Hartrell cd00r 2002), is to use the libpcap libraries to sniff for the packets in question. Another method leverages raw sockets, which enables the malware to use ports that are already open for use by other programs.
502.profile: [profile]Port Knocking, identified as T1205.001 within the Defense Evasion tactic, operates on Linux, Windows, and macOS. The technique hides open ports by sending a sequence of connection attempts to predefined closed ports; after the correct sequence, a host-based firewall or custom software opens a specific port for adversary use. Implementation methods include using libpcap libraries to sniff for the trigger packets or leveraging raw sockets. It has been associated with threat groups like UNC3886 and Promethium.[/profile]
502.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Port Listening is not a distinct MITRE ATT&CK technique. The retrieved information describes related concepts like port knocking (T1205.001), which dynamically opens a listening port after a sequence of connection attempts to closed ports, and the use of non-standard (T1571) or commonly used ports (T1043) for command and control to bypass network defenses. The core technical mechanic involves a service or malware binding to a network port to await incoming connections, which is a fundamental step for establishing persistence and C2 channels.

503.name: Firewall Hole Creation
503.profile: [profile]Firewall Hole Creation is a technique for bypassing network controls by adding, deleting, or modifying firewall rules to allow unauthorized traffic. It aligns with the MITRE ATT&CK technique Disable or Modify System Firewall (T1562.004) under the Defense Evasion tactic, primarily for Windows and ESXi platforms. Technical execution includes using command-line tools like `esxcli network firewall set`, editing Windows Registry keys, or the Control Panel to create rules for protocols like RDP on non-standard ports. The intrusion-set Lazarus and malware TangoAlfa are associated with this activity, which facilitates C2, lateral movement, and data exfiltration.
503.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Firewall Hole Creation is a technique aligned with MITRE ATT&CK sub-technique T1562.004 (Disable or Modify System Firewall) under the Defense Evasion tactic, applicable to Windows, Linux, and ESXi platforms. It involves adversaries adding, deleting, or modifying specific firewall rules to bypass network controls, which can be executed via command-line (e.g., `esxcli network firewall set` in ESXi), editing Windows Registry keys, or using the Windows Control Panel. This action enables unauthorized command and control communications, lateral movement, and data exfiltration, such as creating a rule for RDP on a non-standard port.

504.name: Netsh Firewall Command
504.uncertain_mes: Netsh.exe (also referred to as Netshell) is a command-line scripting utility used to interact with the network configuration of a system. It contains functionality to add helper DLLs for extending functionality of the utility. (Citation: TechNet Netsh) The paths to registered netsh.exe helper DLLs are entered into the Windows Registry at HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Netsh. Adversaries can use netsh.exe with helper DLLs to proxy execution of arbitrary code in a persistent manner when netsh.exe is executed automatically with another Persistence technique or if other persistent software is present on the system that executes netsh.exe as part of its normal functionality. Examples include some VPN software that invoke netsh.exe. (Citation: Demaske Netsh Persistence) Proof of concept code exists to load Cobalt Strike's payload using netsh.exe helper DLLs. (Citation: Github Netsh Helper CS Beacon)
504.profile: [profile]Netsh Helper DLL is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1546.007 under the Persistence tactic for Windows. It works by registering a malicious DLL in the Windows Registry at HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Netsh, which is then executed whenever the legitimate netsh.exe utility runs, such as automatically by other persistence methods or by software like VPN clients. This allows adversaries to proxy execution of arbitrary code, including loading payloads like Cobalt Strike beacons, to maintain access. The Lazarus group has been associated with this technique.[/profile]
504.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Netsh Firewall Command is a technique for Defense Evasion (T1562.004) on Windows platforms, where adversaries abuse the netsh.exe command-line utility to disable or modify the system firewall. This is executed via commands like `netsh advfirewall set allprofiles state off` to turn off the firewall entirely or by adding, deleting, or modifying specific rules to allow unauthorized network traffic, such as opening non-standard ports for C2 or lateral movement, thereby bypassing network security controls.

505.name: Antivirus Feature Targeting
505.profile: [profile]Antivirus Feature Targeting is a technique where adversaries exploit specific antivirus (AV) software features or configurations to evade detection. This can involve writing malicious files to folders or using file names that are excluded from AV scanning by default to hide artifacts. Adversaries may also discover and verify existing AV exclusions in a victim environment through reconnaissance. 509.name: System Tray Icon Management
509.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may smuggle commands to download malicious payloads past content filters by hiding them within otherwise seemingly benign windows shortcut files. Windows shortcut files (.LNK) include many metadata fields, including an icon location field (also known as the `IconEnvironmentDataBlock`) designed to specify the path to an icon file that is to be displayed for the LNK file within a host directory. 

Adversaries may abuse this LNK metadata to download malicious payloads. For example, adversaries have been observed using LNK files as phishing payloads to deliver malware. Once invoked (e.g., [Malicious File](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002)), payloads referenced via external URLs within the LNK icon location field may be downloaded. These files may also then be invoked by [Command and Scripting Interpreter](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059)/[System Binary Proxy Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1218) arguments within the target path field of the LNK.(Citation: Unprotect Shortcut)(Citation: Booby Trap Shortcut 2017)

LNK Icon Smuggling may also be utilized post compromise, such as malicious scripts executing an LNK on an infected host to download additional malicious payloads.
509.profile: [profile]System Tray Icon Management is a technique, likely aligned with MITRE ATT&CK ID T1027.012 (LNK Icon Smuggling) under Defense Evasion, targeting Windows. It involves abusing the IconEnvironmentDataBlock metadata field within Windows shortcut (.LNK) files to embed and execute commands that download malicious payloads from external URLs, often delivered via phishing or executed post-compromise. This method bypasses content filters and has been associated with groups like Mustang Panda, Gamaredon Group, and Kimsuky.[/profile]
