This involves hiding or spoofing the icon to avoid detection, such as showing a fake "healthy" status after disabling security tools like Windows Defender. It is associated with the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1564.003 (Hidden Window) under the Defense Evasion tactic, primarily on Windows platforms, and has been used by groups like BlackBasta to delay defender responses.

517.name: Keylogging
517.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may log user keystrokes to intercept credentials as the user types them. Keylogging is likely to be used to acquire credentials for new access opportunities when [OS Credential Dumping](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003) efforts are not effective, and may require an adversary to intercept keystrokes on a system for a substantial period of time before credentials can be successfully captured. In order to increase the likelihood of capturing credentials quickly, an adversary may also perform actions such as clearing browser cookies to force users to reauthenticate to systems.(Citation: Talos Kimsuky Nov 2021)

Keylogging is the most prevalent type of input capture, with many different ways of intercepting keystrokes.(Citation: Adventures of a Keystroke) Some methods include:

* Hooking API callbacks used for processing keystrokes. Unlike [Credential API Hooking](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1056/004), this focuses solely on API functions intended for processing keystroke data.
* Reading raw keystroke data from the hardware buffer.
* Windows Registry modifications.
* Custom drivers.
* [Modify System Image](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1601) may provide adversaries with hooks into the operating system of network devices to read raw keystrokes for login sessions.(Citation: Cisco Blog Legacy Device Attacks)
517.profile: [profile]Keylogging, identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1056.001 under the Credential Access tactic for Windows, macOS, and Linux platforms, involves intercepting user keystrokes to capture credentials. Specific technical mechanics include hooking keyboard API callbacks, reading raw data from the hardware buffer, modifying the Windows Registry, and deploying custom drivers. It is commonly used by groups like APT28, Lazarus Group, and Kimsuky, and has been associated with malware such as Carbanak and XAgent. This technique is often employed when credential dumping is ineffective and may be combined with actions like clearing browser cookies to force re-authentication.[profile]

This technique is notably employed by groups like APT28, Lazarus Group, and Kimsuky.

518.name: DNSCalc-style Encoding
518.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may encode data with a standard data encoding system to make the content of command and control traffic more difficult to detect. Command and control (C2) information can be encoded using a standard data encoding system that adheres to existing protocol specifications. Common data encoding schemes include ASCII, Unicode, hexadecimal, Base64, and MIME.(Citation: Wikipedia Binary-to-text Encoding)(Citation: Wikipedia Character Encoding) Some data encoding systems may also result in data compression, such as gzip.
518.profile: [profile]DNSCalc-style Encoding is a specific implementation of the standard encoding technique (T1132.001) under the Command and Control tactic. It operates by encoding command and control data using a system that adheres to standard protocol specifications, such as Base64 or hexadecimal, to obfuscate traffic. This technique is associated with malware like Kiloalfa and has been used by threat actors including Lazarus Group and MuddyWater to make C2 communications more difficult to detect.

The specific mechanics involve using a custom encoding scheme, named after the DNSCalc tool, to transform data within network communications, making detection and analysis more difficult. This method is distinct from standard encoding systems like Base64 or ASCII.

532.name: Hosts File Manipulation
532.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may manipulate accounts to maintain and/or elevate access to victim systems. Account manipulation may consist of any action that preserves or modifies adversary access to a compromised account, such as modifying credentials or permission groups.(Citation: FireEye SMOKEDHAM June 2021) These actions could also include account activity designed to subvert security policies, such as performing iterative password updates to bypass password duration policies and preserve the life of compromised credentials. 

In order to create or manipulate accounts, the adversary must already have sufficient permissions on systems or the domain. However, account manipulation may also lead to privilege escalation where modifications grant access to additional roles, permissions, or higher-privileged [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078).
532.profile: [profile]Hosts File Manipulation is a technique used in the Defense Evasion tactic, primarily on Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves adversaries modifying the system's hosts file (e.g., C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts) to redirect network traffic from legitimate domains to malicious IP addresses under their control, thereby bypassing DNS resolution and facilitating phishing, malware delivery, or command and control communication redirection.
532.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Hosts File Manipulation is a technique where adversaries modify the local hosts file to redirect network traffic, typically for defense evasion and initial access. It operates on Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. The technical mechanics involve editing the hosts file (e.g., C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts on Windows) to map legitimate domain names to malicious IP addresses, thereby bypassing DNS resolution and enabling traffic interception, phishing, or blocking access to security sites. This method is often used to facilitate other malicious activities like credential theft or malware delivery.

533.name: Suicide Script Execution
533.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may use trusted scripts, often signed with certificates, to proxy the execution of malicious files. Several Microsoft signed scripts that have been downloaded from Microsoft or are default on Windows installations can be used to proxy execution of other files.(Citation: LOLBAS Project) This behavior may be abused by adversaries to execute malicious files that could bypass application control and signature validation on systems.(Citation: GitHub Ultimate AppLocker Bypass List)
533.profile: [profile]Suicide Script Execution is a technique aligned with MITRE ATT&CK T1216 (System Script Proxy Execution) under the Defense Evasion tactic for Windows. It involves abusing trusted, often Microsoft-signed, system scripts to proxy the execution of malicious files, thereby bypassing application control and signature validation. The malware Tangobravo and IndiaCharlie have been associated with this method.
533.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Suicide Script Execution is a technique where a script, after performing its malicious task, deletes itself to remove forensic evidence. This self-deletion mechanism is a form of defense evasion, commonly executed on Windows platforms via command-line operations like `del %0` or by spawning a separate process to delete the primary script file, hindering post-incident analysis.

551.name: Sector Overwrite Attack
551.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may downgrade or use a version of system features that may be outdated, vulnerable, and/or does not support updated security controls. Downgrade attacks typically take advantage of a system’s backward compatibility to force it into less secure modes of operation. 

Adversaries may downgrade and use various less-secure versions of features of a system, such as [Command and Scripting Interpreter](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059)s or even network protocols that can be abused to enable [Adversary-in-the-Middle](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1557) or [Network Sniffing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1040).(Citation: Praetorian TLS Downgrade Attack 2014) For example, [PowerShell](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001) versions 5+ includes Script Block Logging (SBL), which can record executed script content. However, adversaries may attempt to execute a previous version of PowerShell that does not support SBL with the intent to [Impair Defenses](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1562) while running malicious scripts that may have otherwise been detected.(Citation: CrowdStrike BGH Ransomware 2021)(Citation: Mandiant BYOL 2018)(Citation: att_def_ps_logging)

Adversaries may similarly target network traffic to downgrade from an encrypted HTTPS connection to an unsecured HTTP connection that exposes network data in clear text.(Citation: Targeted SSL Stripping Attacks Are Real)(Citation: Crowdstrike Downgrade) On Windows systems, adversaries may downgrade the boot manager to a vulnerable version that bypasses Secure Boot, granting the ability to disable various operating system security mechanisms.(Citation: SafeBreach)
551.profile: [profile]Sector Overwrite Attack, also known as downgrade attack, maps to MITRE ATT&CK ID T1562.010 under the Impair Defenses tactic and applies to Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. This technique exploits system backward compatibility to force operation into less secure modes, such as executing older PowerShell versions to bypass Script Block Logging or downgrading HTTPS connections to unencrypted HTTP to enable network sniffing. It has been associated with the Lazarus intrusion set and WhiskeyAlfa malware.[/profile]
551.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Sector Overwrite Attack" is a technique where adversaries directly overwrite specific sectors on a storage device, such as the Master Boot Record (MBR) or Volume Boot Record (VBR), to divert system execution during startup to malicious code. This allows for persistence at a layer below the operating system, making remediation difficult. The technique is related to bootkits and firmware corruption, as it involves manipulating low-level system components to compromise boot integrity and potentially deny system availability.

553.profile: [profile]The entity "DDoS Attack" is a network-based denial-of-service technique, distinct from the MITRE technique "Downgrade Attack" (T1562.010) provided in the input. A DDoS attack aims to exhaust the bandwidth or resources of a target network or service by flooding it with high-volume traffic from multiple systems, often using a botnet. Attackers may spoof source IP addresses to obscure the origin of the traffic. This technique is associated with groups like APT28 and Sandworm Team and is used for purposes such as extortion, hacktivism, or distraction.[/profile]

It can utilize various protocols like UDP, ICMP, or TCP and may involve IP spoofing to obscure the attack source. This technique is associated with groups like Sandworm Team and APT28, and relates to MITRE techniques such as Network Denial of Service (T1498) and Endpoint Denial of Service (T1499).

554.name: Windows Service API
554.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may create or modify Windows services to repeatedly execute malicious payloads as part of persistence. When Windows boots up, it starts programs or applications called services that perform background system functions.(Citation: TechNet Services) Windows service configuration information, including the file path to the service's executable or recovery programs/commands, is stored in the Windows Registry.

Adversaries may install a new service or modify an existing service to execute at startup in order to persist on a system. Service configurations can be set or modified using system utilities (such as sc.exe), by directly modifying the Registry, or by interacting directly with the Windows API. 

Adversaries may also use services to install and execute malicious drivers. For example, after dropping a driver file (ex: `.sys`) to disk, the payload can be loaded and registered via [Native API](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1106) functions such as `CreateServiceW()` (or manually via functions such as `ZwLoadDriver()` and `ZwSetValueKey()`), by creating the required service Registry values (i.e. [Modify Registry](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1112)), or by using command-line utilities such as `PnPUtil.exe`.(Citation: Symantec W.32 Stuxnet Dossier)(Citation: Crowdstrike DriveSlayer February 2022)(Citation: Unit42 AcidBox June 2020) Adversaries may leverage these drivers as [Rootkit](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1014)s to hide the presence of malicious activity on a system. Adversaries may also load a signed yet vulnerable driver onto a compromised machine (known as "Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver" (BYOVD)) as part of [Exploitation for Privilege Escalation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1068).(Citation: ESET InvisiMole June 2020)(Citation: Unit42 AcidBox June 2020)

Services may be created with administrator privileges but are executed under SYSTEM privileges, so an adversary may also use a service to escalate privileges. Adversaries may also directly start services through [Service Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1569/002).

To make detection analysis more challenging, malicious services may also incorporate [Masquerade Task or Service](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1036/004) (ex: using a service and/or payload name related to a legitimate OS or benign software component). Adversaries may also create ‘hidden’ services (i.e., [Hide Artifacts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1564)), for example by using the `sc sdset` command to set service permissions via the Service Descriptor Definition Language (SDDL). This may hide a Windows service from the view of standard service enumeration methods such as `Get-Service`, `sc query`, and `services.exe`.(Citation: SANS 1)(Citation: SANS 2)
554.profile: [profile]Windows Service, identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1543.003 under the Persistence tactic for Windows platforms, involves creating or modifying system services to execute malicious payloads at startup. Adversaries configure services using utilities like sc.exe, direct Registry edits, or Windows API calls such as CreateServiceW(), and may install drivers via PnPUtil.exe. This technique can enable privilege escalation to SYSTEM, hide services using SDDL permissions with sc sdset, and is used by groups like Lazarus for persistence and evasion.
554.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Windows Service API is a method adversaries use to interact with the Windows service control manager for persistence and execution. It maps to MITRE ATT&CK technique T1543.003 (Windows Service) under the Persistence tactic for Windows platforms. Technical mechanics involve using native API functions like `CreateServiceW()` to create or modify services, often via utilities like `sc.exe` or direct Registry manipulation, enabling malicious payloads to run with SYSTEM privileges at startup or to load drivers for rootkit functionality.

556.name: CreateService
556.profile: [profile]CreateService is a method within MITRE ATT&CK technique T1050 (New Service) under the Persistence tactic for Windows. It involves creating a new Windows service, with its executable path stored in the Registry, to execute adversary-controlled code. This service can be configured to run at system startup for persistence and may execute with SYSTEM-level privileges, enabling privilege escalation from an administrator account. The intrusion-set Lazarus has been associated with this technique.
556.profile_without_enhance: [profile]CreateService is a technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, operating under the Persistence tactic on Windows platforms. It involves adversaries creating a new Windows service to execute malicious binaries or commands, often configured to run at system startup for persistence. The service's executable path is stored in the Windows Registry, and services execute with SYSTEM-level privileges, enabling privilege escalation from an administrator account. This method is directly associated with techniques like New Service (T1050) and Service Execution (T1035).

557.name: Service Name Conflict Resolution
557.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may dynamically establish connections to command and control infrastructure to evade common detections and remediations. This may be achieved by using malware that shares a common algorithm with the infrastructure the adversary uses to receive the malware's communications. These calculations can be used to dynamically adjust parameters such as the domain name, IP address, or port number the malware uses for command and control.

Adversaries may use dynamic resolution for the purpose of [Fallback Channels](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1008). When contact is lost with the primary command and control server malware may employ dynamic resolution as a means to reestablishing command and control.(Citation: Talos CCleanup 2017)(Citation: FireEye POSHSPY April 2017)(Citation: ESET Sednit 2017 Activity)
557.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique "Dynamic Resolution" (T1568) under the Command and Control tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It involves malware using a shared algorithm with adversary infrastructure to dynamically adjust C2 parameters like domain names, IP addresses, or port numbers to evade detection. This technique can also serve as a mechanism for establishing Fallback Channels to reestablish lost C2 connections. Associated threat groups include APT29, Gamaredon Group, and Lazarus.
557.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Service Name Conflict Resolution is a technique where adversaries exploit the operating system's service name resolution process to execute malicious code. This can involve creating or modifying a service with a name that conflicts with or closely resembles a legitimate system service, potentially causing the system to load the adversary's malicious binary instead of the intended one during the resolution process. This method is used for persistence and defense evasion, primarily on Windows platforms.

558.name: License Key Exploitation
558.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may reduce the level of effort required to decrypt data transmitted over the network by reducing the cipher strength of encrypted communications.(Citation: Cisco Synful Knock Evolution)

Adversaries can weaken the encryption software on a compromised network device by reducing the key size used by the software to convert plaintext to ciphertext (e.g., from hundreds or thousands of bytes to just a couple of bytes). As a result, adversaries dramatically reduce the amount of effort needed to decrypt the protected information without the key.

Adversaries may modify the key size used and other encryption parameters using specialized commands in a [Network Device CLI](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/008) introduced to the system through [Modify System Image](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1601) to change the configuration of the device. (Citation: Cisco Blog Legacy Device Attacks)
558.profile: [profile]The entity is a MITRE ATT&CK technique named Reduce Key Space with ID T1600.001 under the Defense Evasion tactic, targeting Network Devices. It involves weakening encryption on compromised network devices by reducing the cryptographic key size, for example from hundreds of bytes to just a couple, dramatically lowering the effort needed for decryption. This modification is typically performed using specialized commands in a Network Device CLI, often introduced via a modified system image. The technique has been associated with intrusion sets like Lazarus and malware such as WhiskeyAlfa and Shamoon.[/profile]
558.profile_without_enhance: [profile]License Key Exploitation is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the retrieved context, it likely refers to adversaries exploiting vulnerabilities in software licensing mechanisms, such as using stolen or forged license keys to bypass authentication, gain unauthorized access, or escalate privileges within an application or system. This method can be a vector for initial access or persistence.

560.name: Compromised Infrastructure
560.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may manipulate network traffic in order to hide and evade detection of their C2 infrastructure. This can be accomplished by identifying and filtering traffic from defensive tools,(Citation: TA571) masking malicious domains to obfuscate the true destination from both automated scanning tools and security researchers,(Citation: Schema-abuse)(Citation: Facad1ng)(Citation: Browser-updates) and otherwise hiding malicious artifacts to delay discovery and prolong the effectiveness of adversary infrastructure that could otherwise be identified, blocked, or taken down entirely.

C2 networks may include the use of [Proxy](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1090) or VPNs to disguise IP addresses, which can allow adversaries to blend in with normal network traffic and bypass conditional access policies or anti-abuse protections. For example, an adversary may use a virtual private cloud to spoof their IP address to closer align with a victim's IP address ranges. This may also bypass security measures relying on geolocation of the source IP address.(Citation: sysdig)(Citation: Orange Residential Proxies)

Adversaries may also attempt to filter network traffic in order to evade defensive tools in numerous ways, including blocking/redirecting common incident responder or security appliance user agents.(Citation: mod_rewrite)(Citation: SocGholish-update) Filtering traffic based on IP and geo-fencing may also avoid automated sandboxing or researcher activity (i.e., [Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1497)).(Citation: TA571)(Citation: mod_rewrite)

Hiding C2 infrastructure may also be supported by [Resource Development](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0042) activities such as [Acquire Infrastructure](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1583) and [Compromise Infrastructure](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1584). For example, using widely trusted hosting services or domains such as prominent URL shortening providers or marketing services for C2 networks may enable adversaries to present benign content that later redirects victims to malicious web pages or infrastructure once specific conditions are met.(Citation: StarBlizzard)(Citation: QR-cofense)
560.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique "Hide Infrastructure" (T1665) under the Resource Development tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. It involves manipulating network traffic to conceal command and control (C2) infrastructure through specific methods such as using proxies or VPNs to disguise IP addresses, filtering traffic to block or redirect common security tool user agents, and implementing IP or geo-fencing to evade automated sandboxes. This activity is often supported by related techniques like Acquire Infrastructure (T1583) and Compromise Infrastructure (T1584), and has been associated with groups like APT29 and Zirconium.
560.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Compromised Infrastructure" aligns with the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1584, categorized under the Resource Development tactic and applicable across multiple platforms. This technique involves adversaries taking over third-party infrastructure—such as physical or cloud servers, domains, network devices, and web services—instead of acquiring it legitimately. The compromised assets are then used to stage, launch, and execute operations, helping malicious activities blend with normal traffic, support phishing campaigns, or form botnets for proxy services.

561.name: Stolen License Keys
561.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may search for private key certificate files on compromised systems for insecurely stored credentials. Private cryptographic keys and certificates are used for authentication, encryption/decryption, and digital signatures.(Citation: Wikipedia Public Key Crypto) Common key and certificate file extensions include: .key, .pgp, .gpg, .ppk., .p12, .pem, .pfx, .cer, .p7b, .asc. Adversaries may also look in common key directories, such as ~/.ssh for SSH keys on * nix-based systems or C:\Users\(username)\.ssh\ on Windows. Adversary tools may also search compromised systems for file extensions relating to cryptographic keys and certificates.(Citation: Kaspersky Careto)(Citation: Palo Alto Prince of Persia) When a device is registered to Entra ID, a device key and a transport key are generated and used to verify the device’s identity.(Citation: Microsoft Primary Refresh Token) An adversary with access to the device may be able to export the keys in order to impersonate the device.(Citation: AADInternals Azure AD Device Identities) On network devices, private keys may be exported via [Network Device CLI](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/008) commands such as `crypto pki export`.(Citation: cisco_deploy_rsa_keys) Some private keys require a password or passphrase for operation, so an adversary may also use [Input Capture](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1056) for keylogging or attempt to [Brute Force](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1110) the passphrase off-line. These private keys can be used to authenticate to [Remote Services](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021) like SSH or for use in decrypting other collected files such as email.
561.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique "Unsecured Credentials: Private Keys" (T1552.004) under the Credential Access tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. Adversaries search for private key files (e.g., .key, .pem, .pfx) in common directories like `~/.ssh` or via specific CLI commands like `crypto pki export` on network devices. These stolen keys are used to authenticate to remote services like SSH or decrypt files. Attackers may use keylogging or brute force to obtain required passphrases. Associated groups include TeamTNT, Scattered Spider, and Volt Typhoon.[profile]
561.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Stolen License Keys" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on retrieved information, it describes an adversary behavior of acquiring software license keys, often through theft or cracking trial versions, to illegitimately enable or use commercial software tools for malicious operations. This activity supports the acquisition of tools (T1588.002) and may involve exfiltration over a command and control channel (T1041). The technical mechanics involve obtaining keys to activate software, bypassing legitimate licensing controls.

562.name: Multi-threaded Attack
562.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may downgrade or use a version of system features that may be outdated, vulnerable, and/or does not support updated security controls. Downgrade attacks typically take advantage of a system’s backward compatibility to force it into less secure modes of operation. 

Adversaries may downgrade and use various less-secure versions of features of a system, such as [Command and Scripting Interpreter](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059)s or even network protocols that can be abused to enable [Adversary-in-the-Middle](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1557) or [Network Sniffing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1040).(Citation: Praetorian TLS Downgrade Attack 2014) For example, [PowerShell](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001) versions 5+ includes Script Block Logging (SBL), which can record executed script content. However, adversaries may attempt to execute a previous version of PowerShell that does not support SBL with the intent to [Impair Defenses](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1562) while running malicious scripts that may have otherwise been detected.(Citation: CrowdStrike BGH Ransomware 2021)(Citation: Mandiant BYOL 2018)(Citation: att_def_ps_logging)

Adversaries may similarly target network traffic to downgrade from an encrypted HTTPS connection to an unsecured HTTP connection that exposes network data in clear text.(Citation: Targeted SSL Stripping Attacks Are Real)(Citation: Crowdstrike Downgrade) On Windows systems, adversaries may downgrade the boot manager to a vulnerable version that bypasses Secure Boot, granting the ability to disable various operating system security mechanisms.(Citation: SafeBreach)
562.profile: [profile]The entity "Multi-threaded Attack" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the provided data, the core concept aligns with the MITRE technique "Downgrade Attack" (ID: T1562.010), a sub-technique of Impair Defenses. It operates by exploiting a system's backward compatibility to force the use of less secure, outdated versions of software or protocols to bypass security controls. Specific mechanics include executing older versions of PowerShell to evade Script Block Logging or downgrading HTTPS connections to unencrypted HTTP to facilitate traffic interception. The Lazarus group has been associated with related multi-stage command and control activities.[/profile]
562.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Multi-threaded Attack" is not a formally defined technique in the MITRE ATT&CK framework. Based on the provided context, it is a method used to enhance Denial of Service (DoS) attacks. The technique operates by employing multiple concurrent threads or processes to generate and direct a high volume of malicious traffic toward a target system or network. This multi-threaded approach aims to maximize resource consumption and traffic throughput, thereby increasing the scale and effectiveness of the DoS attack to more effectively overwhelm and degrade the availability of the targeted service.

563.name: GetDiskFreeSpaceEx
563.profile: [profile]GetDiskFreeSpaceEx is a Windows API function used within the broader technique of Local Storage Discovery (T1082). This technique falls under the Discovery tactic and targets the Windows platform. The function is specifically employed to enumerate local drives and disks, retrieving their attributes such as total and available free space. This reconnaissance activity is often a precursor to ransomware encryption or lateral movement, as observed in campaigns linked to groups like Lazarus.

It is employed by threat actors including Lazarus Group and Volt Typhoon as part of their system reconnaissance activities.

564.name: Sleep API
564.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may interact with the native OS application programming interface (API) to execute behaviors. Native APIs provide a controlled means of calling low-level OS services within the kernel, such as those involving hardware/devices, memory, and processes.(Citation: NT API Windows)(Citation: Linux Kernel API) These native APIs are leveraged by the OS during system boot (when other system components are not yet initialized) as well as carrying out tasks and requests during routine operations. Adversaries may abuse these OS API functions as a means of executing behaviors. Similar to [Command and Scripting Interpreter](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059), the native API and its hierarchy of interfaces provide mechanisms to interact with and utilize various components of a victimized system. Native API functions (such as NtCreateProcess) may be directed invoked via system calls / syscalls, but these features are also often exposed to user-mode applications via interfaces and libraries.(Citation: OutFlank System Calls)(Citation: CyberBit System Calls)(Citation: MDSec System Calls) For example, functions such as the Windows API CreateProcess() or GNU fork() will allow programs and scripts to start other processes.(Citation: Microsoft CreateProcess)(Citation: GNU Fork) This may allow API callers to execute a binary, run a CLI command, load modules, etc. as thousands of similar API functions exist for various system operations.(Citation: Microsoft Win32)(Citation: LIBC)(Citation: GLIBC) Higher level software frameworks, such as Microsoft .NET and macOS Cocoa, are also available to interact with native APIs. These frameworks typically provide language wrappers/abstractions to API functionalities and are designed for ease-of-use/portability of code.(Citation: Microsoft NET)(Citation: Apple Core Services)(Citation: MACOS Cocoa)(Citation: macOS Foundation) Adversaries may use assembly to directly or in-directly invoke syscalls in an attempt to subvert defensive sensors and detection signatures such as user mode API-hooks.(Citation: Redops Syscalls) Adversaries may also attempt to tamper with sensors and defensive tools associated with API monitoring, such as unhooking monitored functions via [Disable or Modify Tools](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1562/001).
564.profile: [profile]Native API, designated as T1106 under Execution, operates across Windows, Linux, and macOS. Adversaries directly invoke low-level OS kernel services through system calls or user-mode libraries like Windows API CreateProcess() or GNU fork() to execute binaries, run commands, or load modules. This technique is used to subvert user-mode API-hooking sensors, often by using assembly to invoke syscalls directly, and is associated with groups like Lazarus.
564.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Sleep API" is a technique where adversaries use programmatic sleep commands or native system scheduling functions to delay malware execution. This method, aligned with the Delay Execution tactic (T1678), operates across multiple platforms to evade detection by exceeding time thresholds of automated analysis environments. It involves calling API functions like sleep() to introduce pauses, sometimes combined with loops of benign commands (e.g., ping) or API hammering to overload sandboxes with junk data.

565.name: EvtClearLog
565.profile: [profile]EvtClearLog is a technique for clearing Windows Event Logs to hide intrusion activity, corresponding to MITRE ATT&CK ID T1070.001 under the Defense Evasion tactic for Windows platforms. This is executed with administrator privileges using utility commands like `wevtutil cl system`, `wevtutil cl application`, and `wevtutil cl security`, or via PowerShell with commands such as `Remove-EventLog -LogName Security`. Adversaries may also directly delete log files from `C:\Windows\System32\winevt\logs\`. The intrusion-set Lazarus is associated with this technique.
565.profile_without_enhance: [profile]EvtClearLog is a technique for Defense Evasion, identified as T1070.001, targeting Windows systems. It involves clearing Windows Event Logs to erase evidence of intrusion. Adversaries with administrator privileges typically use commands like `wevtutil cl security` or PowerShell's `Clear-EventLog` and `Remove-EventLog` to delete logs from the System, Application, and Security channels. They may also directly delete the log files located in `C:\Windows\System32\winevt\logs\`. This activity is associated with threat groups including APT28, APT29, and Volt Typhoon.

595.name: Spear Phishing
595.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may send phishing messages to gain access to victim systems. All forms of phishing are electronically delivered social engineering. Phishing can be targeted, known as spearphishing. In spearphishing, a specific individual, company, or industry will be targeted by the adversary. More generally, adversaries can conduct non-targeted phishing, such as in mass malware spam campaigns.

Adversaries may send victims emails containing malicious attachments or links, typically to execute malicious code on victim systems. Phishing may also be conducted via third-party services, like social media platforms. Phishing may also involve social engineering techniques, such as posing as a trusted source, as well as evasive techniques such as removing or manipulating emails or metadata/headers from compromised accounts being abused to send messages (e.g., [Email Hiding Rules](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1564/008)).(Citation: Microsoft OAuth Spam 2022)(Citation: Palo Alto Unit 42 VBA Infostealer 2014) Another way to accomplish this is by [Email Spoofing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1672)(Citation: Proofpoint-spoof) the identity of the sender, which can be used to fool both the human recipient as well as automated security tools,(Citation: cyberproof-double-bounce) or by including the intended target as a party to an existing email thread that includes malicious files or links (i.e., "thread hijacking").(Citation: phishing-krebs)

Victims may also receive phishing messages that instruct them to call a phone number where they are directed to visit a malicious URL, download malware,(Citation: sygnia Luna Month)(Citation: CISA Remote Monitoring and Management Software) or install adversary-accessible remote management tools onto their computer (i.e., [User Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204)).(Citation: Unit42 Luna Moth)
595.profile: [profile]Spear Phishing, identified as T1566, is a targeted Initial Access technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework applicable to multiple platforms. It involves sending tailored electronic messages, such as emails with malicious attachments or links, to specific individuals or organizations to execute code. Technical mechanics include using social engineering to pose as a trusted source, employing email spoofing, thread hijacking, and evasive tactics like manipulating email headers or using compromised accounts. It is distinct from credential harvesting (T1598) and is commonly used by groups like APT28, APT29, and Lazarus.[/profile]
595.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Spear Phishing is a targeted social engineering technique, identified as a sub-technique within MITRE ATT&CK's Initial Access tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. It involves sending tailored electronic messages, such as emails, to specific individuals, companies, or industries. The messages often contain malicious attachments or links to execute code, or they may direct victims to call phone numbers for further social engineering. This method frequently employs evasion tactics like email spoofing, thread hijacking, or the use of tracking pixels to increase credibility and bypass security measures.[/profile]

596.name: Watering Hole Attacks
596.profile: [profile]Watering Hole Attacks, known as T1189 in the MITRE ATT&CK framework, fall under the Initial Access tactic and target multiple platforms. This technique involves compromising websites frequently visited by a target group to stage malicious resources, enabling drive-by compromise when users browse to the site. It is commonly employed by threat actors like APT29, Turla, and Lazarus.
596.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Watering Hole Attacks, known as T1189 in the MITRE ATT&CK framework, is an Initial Access technique primarily targeting web platforms. It involves compromising websites frequented by a target demographic and staging malicious web resources on them. When a user visits the compromised site, the attack exploits client-side software to execute drive-by compromise, allowing adversaries to gain access to the victim's system. This method is often used to support other malicious activities, such as spearphishing campaigns.

597.name: PowerShell-based Attacks
597.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may abuse PowerShell commands and scripts for execution. PowerShell is a powerful interactive command-line interface and scripting environment included in the Windows operating system.(Citation: TechNet PowerShell) Adversaries can use PowerShell to perform a number of actions, including discovery of information and execution of code. Examples include the Start-Process cmdlet which can be used to run an executable and the Invoke-Command cmdlet which runs a command locally or on a remote computer (though administrator permissions are required to use PowerShell to connect to remote systems). PowerShell may also be used to download and run executables from the Internet, which can be executed from disk or in memory without touching disk. A number of PowerShell-based offensive testing tools are available, including [Empire](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0363), [PowerSploit](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0194), [PoshC2](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0378), and PSAttack.(Citation: Github PSAttack) PowerShell commands/scripts can also be executed without directly invoking the powershell.exe binary through interfaces to PowerShell's underlying System.Management.Automation assembly DLL exposed through the .NET framework and Windows Common Language Interface (CLI).(Citation: Sixdub PowerPick Jan 2016)(Citation: SilentBreak Offensive PS Dec 2015)(Citation: Microsoft PSfromCsharp APR 2014)
597.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique "PowerShell" (T1059.001), a Command and Scripting Interpreter sub-technique under the Execution tactic for Windows. It involves abusing the PowerShell environment to execute commands and scripts, using cmdlets like `Start-Process` and `Invoke-Command` for local or remote code execution. Adversaries can download and run executables from the internet, executing them directly in memory, and can bypass the `powershell.exe` binary by leveraging the underlying `System.Management.Automation` assembly DLL through the .NET framework. This technique is widely used by numerous threat groups, including Lazarus.[/profile]
597.profile_without_enhance: [profile]PowerShell-based Attacks correspond to the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1059.001 (Command and Scripting Interpreter: PowerShell) under the Execution tactic for Windows platforms. This technique involves abusing the built-in PowerShell environment to execute commands and scripts, including using cmdlets like Start-Process and Invoke-Command to run executables or commands locally and remotely. It enables downloading and executing payloads from the internet directly in memory to avoid disk, and execution can occur without invoking powershell.exe by leveraging the underlying System.Management.Automation assembly. Numerous threat groups and tools like Empire and PowerSploit utilize this method.

598.name: AppLocker Bypass
598.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may modify file attributes and subvert Gatekeeper functionality to evade user prompts and execute untrusted programs. Gatekeeper is a set of technologies that act as layer of Apple’s security model to ensure only trusted applications are executed on a host. Gatekeeper was built on top of File Quarantine in Snow Leopard (10.6, 2009) and has grown to include Code Signing, security policy compliance, Notarization, and more. Gatekeeper also treats applications running for the first time differently than reopened applications.(Citation: TheEclecticLightCompany Quarantine and the flag)(Citation: TheEclecticLightCompany apple notarization )

Based on an opt-in system, when files are downloaded an extended attribute (xattr) called `com.apple.quarantine` (also known as a quarantine flag) can be set on the file by the application performing the download. Launch Services opens the application in a suspended state. For first run applications with the quarantine flag set, Gatekeeper executes the following functions:

1. Checks extended attribute – Gatekeeper checks for the quarantine flag, then provides an alert prompt to the user to allow or deny execution.(Citation: OceanLotus for OS X)(Citation: 20 macOS Common Tools and Techniques)

2. Checks System Policies - Gatekeeper checks the system security policy, allowing execution of apps downloaded from either just the App Store or the App Store and identified developers.

3. Code Signing – Gatekeeper checks for a valid code signature from an Apple Developer ID.

4. Notarization - Using the `api.apple-cloudkit.com` API, Gatekeeper reaches out to Apple servers to verify or pull down the notarization ticket and ensure the ticket is not revoked. Users can override notarization, which will result in a prompt of executing an “unauthorized app” and the security policy will be modified.

Adversaries can subvert one or multiple security controls within Gatekeeper checks through logic errors (e.g. [Exploitation for Defense Evasion](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1211)), unchecked file types, and external libraries. For example, prior to macOS 13 Ventura, code signing and notarization checks were only conducted on first launch, allowing adversaries to write malicious executables to previously opened applications in order to bypass Gatekeeper security checks.(Citation: theevilbit gatekeeper bypass 2021)(Citation: Application Bundle Manipulation Brandon Dalton)

Applications and files loaded onto the system from a USB flash drive, optical disk, external hard drive, from a drive shared over the local network, or using the curl command may not set the quarantine flag. Additionally, it is possible to avoid setting the quarantine flag using [Drive-by Compromise](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1189).
598.profile: [profile]The entity is a macOS-specific defense evasion technique known as Gatekeeper Bypass, which corresponds to MITRE ATT&CK ID T1553.001 under the Defense Evasion tactic. It involves subverting Apple's Gatekeeper security controls, which verify applications via quarantine flags, code signing, and notarization. Adversaries exploit logic errors or unchecked file types; for example, prior to macOS 13, they could write malicious code into previously opened applications to bypass checks on subsequent launches. Additionally, files from external media or using specific commands like curl may not trigger the quarantine flag, allowing execution without prompts. The intrusion-set Lazarus has been associated with this technique.[/profile]
598.profile_without_enhance: [profile]AppLocker Bypass is a defense evasion technique for Windows platforms where adversaries circumvent application whitelisting controls. Methods include abusing trusted, signed Microsoft binaries like CMSTP.exe with malicious INF files or using trusted scripts to proxy execution of malicious payloads, thereby evading signature validation and policy enforcement.

599.name: Decoy Document (Coinbase Lure)
599.profile: [profile]Decoy Document (Coinbase Lure) is a technique used for Initial Access, primarily on Windows platforms. It involves creating or modifying malicious document templates, such as Office Open XML (OOXML) or RTF files, to conceal and fetch malicious payloads when the document is opened. This method can evade static detection as no typical indicators like macros are present initially. The Lazarus group has been associated with using this technique, which is often delivered via phishing to force authentication or execute code.
599.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Decoy Document (Coinbase Lure)" is a specific instance of the MITRE ATT&CK technique Template Injection (T1221), falling under the Initial Access tactic. It operates on the Windows platform. This technique involves adversaries creating or modifying references in Office document templates (like .docx or .rtf files) to conceal and fetch malicious payloads when the document is opened, often delivered via phishing. In this specific case, the decoy document is crafted to impersonate a legitimate Coinbase communication to lure the victim.

600.name: Memory Injection
600.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may inject malicious code into process via Extra Window Memory (EWM) in order to evade process-based defenses as well as possibly elevate privileges. EWM injection is a method of executing arbitrary code in the address space of a separate live process. Before creating a window, graphical Windows-based processes must prescribe to or register a windows class, which stipulate appearance and behavior (via windows procedures, which are functions that handle input/output of data).(Citation: Microsoft Window Classes) Registration of new windows classes can include a request for up to 40 bytes of EWM to be appended to the allocated memory of each instance of that class. This EWM is intended to store data specific to that window and has specific application programming interface (API) functions to set and get its value. (Citation: Microsoft GetWindowLong function) (Citation: Microsoft SetWindowLong function) Although small, the EWM is large enough to store a 32-bit pointer and is often used to point to a windows procedure. Malware may possibly utilize this memory location in part of an attack chain that includes writing code to shared sections of the process’s memory, placing a pointer to the code in EWM, then invoking execution by returning execution control to the address in the process’s EWM. Execution granted through EWM injection may allow access to both the target process's memory and possibly elevated privileges. Writing payloads to shared sections also avoids the use of highly monitored API calls such as WriteProcessMemory and CreateRemoteThread.(Citation: Elastic Process Injection July 2017) More sophisticated malware samples may also potentially bypass protection mechanisms such as data execution prevention (DEP) by triggering a combination of windows procedures and other system functions that will rewrite the malicious payload inside an executable portion of the target process. (Citation: MalwareTech Power Loader Aug 2013) (Citation: WeLiveSecurity Gapz and Redyms Mar 2013) Running code in the context of another process may allow access to the process's memory, system/network resources, and possibly elevated privileges. Execution via EWM injection may also evade detection from security products since the execution is masked under a legitimate process.
600.profile: [profile]Extra Window Memory Injection, designated as T1055.011 under the Defense Evasion and Privilege Escalation tactics, targets the Windows platform. This technique involves injecting malicious code into a process by abusing the Extra Window Memory (EWM) allocated for a window class. Attackers write code to shared memory sections, place a pointer to it in the EWM, and then redirect execution control to that address, thereby evading monitoring of common APIs like WriteProcessMemory and potentially bypassing defenses like Data Execution Prevention (DEP). The intrusion-set Lazarus has been associated with this method.[/profile]
600.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Memory Injection is a general technique for executing arbitrary code within the address space of a separate live process to evade defenses and potentially gain elevated privileges. It encompasses several sub-techniques, including Portable Executable (PE) injection using Windows APIs like `VirtualAllocEx`, `WriteProcessMemory`, and `CreateRemoteThread`, and Dynamic-link Library (DLL) injection which similarly writes a DLL path and invokes `LoadLibrary` via `CreateRemoteThread`. Other variants involve injecting code via the `/proc` filesystem on Linux by overwriting a process's memory map using tools like `dd`, or using Extra Window Memory (EWM) in Windows to store a pointer to malicious code. The execution is masked under a legitimate process, allowing access to its memory and resources while evading detection.

601.name: AES Encryption
601.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may compromise a network device’s encryption capability in order to bypass encryption that would otherwise protect data communications. (Citation: Cisco Synful Knock Evolution)

Encryption can be used to protect transmitted network traffic to maintain its confidentiality (protect against unauthorized disclosure) and integrity (protect against unauthorized changes). Encryption ciphers are used to convert a plaintext message to ciphertext and can be computationally intensive to decipher without the associated decryption key. Typically, longer keys increase the cost of cryptanalysis, or decryption without the key.

Adversaries can compromise and manipulate devices that perform encryption of network traffic. For example, through behaviors such as [Modify System Image](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1601), [Reduce Key Space](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1600/001), and [Disable Crypto Hardware](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1600/002), an adversary can negatively effect and/or eliminate a device’s ability to securely encrypt network traffic. This poses a greater risk of unauthorized disclosure and may help facilitate data manipulation, Credential Access, or Collection efforts. (Citation: Cisco Blog Legacy Device Attacks)
601.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique "Weaken Encryption" (ID: T1600) under the Defense Evasion tactic, targeting network platforms. It involves compromising network devices to degrade or disable their encryption capabilities, thereby bypassing data-in-transit protection. Specific methods include modifying the system image, reducing the cryptographic key space, or disabling dedicated crypto hardware. This facilitates unauthorized data access and manipulation. The intrusion sets Lazarus and OilRig are associated with this technique. AES is a common symmetric encryption algorithm referenced in related techniques for command and control or exfiltration.[/profile]
601.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "AES Encryption" is a symmetric encryption algorithm used to conceal command and control traffic and data exfiltration, often implemented within other encrypted protocols like HTTPS. It is referenced in MITRE ATT&CK techniques T1573.001 (Symmetric Cryptography) and T1048.001 (Exfiltration Over Symmetric Encrypted Non-C2 Protocol). Adversaries employ AES to manually encrypt communications, potentially creating multiple encryption layers to evade detection.

602.uncertain_mes:

602.profile: [profile]Spritz Encryption Algorithm is a custom cryptographic algorithm that adversaries may use to conceal command and control traffic, falling under the technique of Custom Cryptographic Protocol (T1024). It is a symmetric stream cipher designed for resource-constrained environments. While specific technical mechanics from the provided data are limited, its use indicates an attempt to implement a non-standard encryption scheme to obfuscate communications, which may be vulnerable to analysis if the algorithm is poorly implemented or the key is embedded within the malware. The Lazarus group has been associated with the use of symmetric cryptography for C2.[/profile]
602.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Spritz Encryption Algorithm is a symmetric stream cipher algorithm that adversaries may employ to conceal command and control traffic, falling under the general technique of symmetric cryptography (T1573.001). It operates as a custom cryptographic protocol where the algorithm itself, rather than a standard like AES, is used to encrypt communications. This implementation can vary in sophistication and, if poorly implemented or with keys embedded in malware, may be vulnerable to analysis and reverse engineering to discover the encryption mechanism.

603.name: Shortcut Object Creation
603.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may create or modify shortcuts that can execute a program during system boot or user login. Shortcuts or symbolic links are used to reference other files or programs that will be opened or executed when the shortcut is clicked or executed by a system startup process.

Adversaries may abuse shortcuts in the startup folder to execute their tools and achieve persistence.(Citation: Shortcut for Persistence ) Although often used as payloads in an infection chain (e.g. [Spearphishing Attachment](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001)), adversaries may also create a new shortcut as a means of indirection, while also abusing [Masquerading](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1036) to make the malicious shortcut appear as a legitimate program. Adversaries can also edit the target path or entirely replace an existing shortcut so their malware will be executed instead of the intended legitimate program.

Shortcuts can also be abused to establish persistence by implementing other methods. For example, LNK browser extensions may be modified (e.g. [Browser Extensions](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1176/001)) to persistently launch malware.
603.profile: [profile]Shortcut Modification, identified as MITRE ATT&CK T1547.009 under the Persistence tactic for Windows, involves adversaries creating or modifying shortcuts to execute malicious programs during system boot or user login. This is achieved by placing shortcuts in startup folders, editing the target path of existing shortcuts, or replacing legitimate shortcuts entirely. Techniques include masquerading shortcuts as legitimate programs and modifying LNK browser extensions to persistently launch malware, as observed with groups like Lazarus.
603.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Shortcut Object Creation is a technique for establishing persistence, likely aligning with MITRE ATT&CK ID T1547.009 under the Persistence tactic on Windows platforms. It involves creating or modifying Windows shortcut (.LNK) files to execute malicious programs during system boot or user login, often by placing them in startup folders. Adversaries may edit the target path of a shortcut or replace an existing one to redirect execution to their malware, sometimes using masquerading to appear legitimate. This method can be used in infection chains, such as through spearphishing attachments, to maintain access.

604.name: VBScript Execution
604.profile: [profile]VBScript Execution is a sub-technique (T1059.005) under the Execution tactic, targeting the Windows platform. It involves adversaries using the VBScript language to execute malicious commands, often by embedding scripts into files like HTML Applications (HTAs) or Office documents to automate tasks. Groups like FIN7 and Lazarus have employed this method, leveraging tools like mshta.exe to proxy execution of VBScript payloads, bypassing application controls and browser security settings.[/profile]
604.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "VBScript Execution" is a sub-technique of Visual Basic (T1059.005) within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, falling under the Execution tactic and targeting the Windows platform. It involves adversaries using VBScript, a legacy Windows scripting language, to run malicious commands. This is commonly achieved by embedding scripts in files like HTML Applications (HTAs) executed via tools like `mshta.exe`, or within documents to automate tasks. The technique is frequently associated with spearphishing campaigns and is used by numerous threat groups, including FIN7, Gamaredon Group, and Lazarus Group, to bypass controls and execute payloads.

605.name: Download via Bitsadmin
605.profile: [profile]Download via Bitsadmin is a technique (T1197) within the Execution tactic for Windows. It involves abusing the Background Intelligent Transfer Service (BITS) to download files, often using the BITSAdmin tool or PowerShell to create jobs. This method is favored for its low network visibility, ability to operate over idle bandwidth, and persistence, as jobs can be configured to execute code upon completion or survive reboots. The Lazarus group has been associated with this activity.
605.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Download via Bitsadmin is a technique (T1197) under the Defense Evasion and Persistence tactics, primarily on Windows. It involves abusing the Background Intelligent Transfer Service (BITS) to asynchronously download files using tools like BITSAdmin or PowerShell. This method is low-bandwidth, often firewall-permitted, and can create persistent jobs that execute code upon completion or after a reboot, also enabling file exfiltration.

606.name: Internationalized Domain Name (IDN)
606.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may match or approximate the names of legitimate accounts to make newly created ones appear benign. This will typically occur during [Create Account](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1136), although accounts may also be renamed at a later date. This may also coincide with [Account Access Removal](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1531) if the actor first deletes an account before re-creating one with the same name.(Citation: Huntress MOVEit 2023)

Often, adversaries will attempt to masquerade as service accounts, such as those associated with legitimate software, data backups, or container cluster management.(Citation: Elastic CUBA Ransomware 2022)(Citation: Aquasec Kubernetes Attack 2023) They may also give accounts generic, trustworthy names, such as “admin”, “help”, or “root.”(Citation: Invictus IR Cloud Ransomware 2024) Sometimes adversaries may model account names off of those already existing in the system, as a follow-on behavior to [Account Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1087).  

Note that this is distinct from [Impersonation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1656), which describes impersonating specific trusted individuals or organizations, rather than user or service account names.
606.profile: [profile]Internationalized Domain Name (IDN) is a sub-technique of T1583.001 (Acquire Infrastructure: Domains) within the Resource Development tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. Adversaries use IDNs and different character sets (e.g., Cyrillic, Greek) to create visually similar lookalike domains, known as IDN homograph attacks, which are used to deliver malware via techniques like Phishing and Drive-by Compromise. This technique is distinct from masquerading account names (T1036.010) and has been used by groups including Lazarus.
606.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Internationalized Domain Name (IDN) is a technique used within the Resource Development tactic for adversary infrastructure. It operates by registering domain names using internationalized character sets (e.g., Cyrillic, Greek) to create visually similar lookalikes of legitimate domains. This enables IDN homograph attacks, where these deceptive domains are used to deliver malware via phishing or drive-by compromise, exploiting visual spoofing to trick victims.

607.name: Execution via PowerShell
607.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may abuse PowerShell commands and scripts for execution. PowerShell is a powerful interactive command-line interface and scripting environment included in the Windows operating system.(Citation: TechNet PowerShell) Adversaries can use PowerShell to perform a number of actions, including discovery of information and execution of code. Examples include the Start-Process cmdlet which can be used to run an executable and the Invoke-Command cmdlet which runs a command locally or on a remote computer (though administrator permissions are required to use PowerShell to connect to remote systems). PowerShell may also be used to download and run executables from the Internet, which can be executed from disk or in memory without touching disk. A number of PowerShell-based offensive testing tools are available, including [Empire](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0363), [PowerSploit](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0194), [PoshC2](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0378), and PSAttack.(Citation: Github PSAttack) PowerShell commands/scripts can also be executed without directly invoking the powershell.exe binary through interfaces to PowerShell's underlying System.Management.Automation assembly DLL exposed through the .NET framework and Windows Common Language Interface (CLI).(Citation: Sixdub PowerPick Jan 2016)(Citation: SilentBreak Offensive PS Dec 2015)(Citation: Microsoft PSfromCsharp APR 2014)
607.profile: [profile]Execution via PowerShell is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1059.001 under the Execution tactic, targeting Windows. It abuses the PowerShell CLI and scripting environment to run code, using cmdlets like Start-Process and Invoke-Command for local or remote execution. It can download and run executables from the internet, executing them from disk or directly in memory. Execution can also occur without invoking powershell.exe by leveraging the underlying System.Management.Automation assembly via .NET. Numerous threat groups, including Lazarus, use this technique.[/profile]

Execution can bypass direct invocation of powershell.exe by leveraging the underlying System.Management.Automation assembly, and is associated with tools like Empire and PowerSploit.

608.name: javascript obfuscator
608.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may abuse various implementations of JavaScript for execution. JavaScript (JS) is a platform-independent scripting language (compiled just-in-time at runtime) commonly associated with scripts in webpages, though JS can be executed in runtime environments outside the browser.(Citation: NodeJS) JScript is the Microsoft implementation of the same scripting standard. JScript is interpreted via the Windows Script engine and thus integrated with many components of Windows such as the [Component Object Model](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1559/001) and Internet Explorer HTML Application (HTA) pages.(Citation: JScrip May 2018)(Citation: Microsoft JScript 2007)(Citation: Microsoft Windows Scripts) JavaScript for Automation (JXA) is a macOS scripting language based on JavaScript, included as part of Apple’s Open Scripting Architecture (OSA), that was introduced in OSX 10.10. Apple’s OSA provides scripting capabilities to control applications, interface with the operating system, and bridge access into the rest of Apple’s internal APIs. As of OSX 10.10, OSA only supports two languages, JXA and [AppleScript](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/002). Scripts can be executed via the command line utility osascript, they can be compiled into applications or script files via osacompile, and they can be compiled and executed in memory of other programs by leveraging the OSAKit Framework.(Citation: Apple About Mac Scripting 2016)(Citation: SpecterOps JXA 2020)(Citation: SentinelOne macOS Red Team)(Citation: Red Canary Silver Sparrow Feb2021)(Citation: MDSec macOS JXA and VSCode) Adversaries may abuse various implementations of JavaScript to execute various behaviors. Common uses include hosting malicious scripts on websites as part of a [Drive-by Compromise](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1189) or downloading and executing these script files as secondary payloads. Since these payloads are text-based, it is also very common for adversaries to obfuscate their content as part of [Obfuscated Files or Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027).
608.profile: [profile]The entity "JavaScript Obfuscator" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique; it is a specific application of the technique Obfuscated Files or Information (T1027). This technique falls under the Defense Evasion tactic and is platform-agnostic. It involves adversaries encrypting, encoding, or otherwise obfuscating JavaScript payloads to avoid detection by security controls. This is commonly done because JavaScript is text-based, making obfuscation straightforward. The obfuscated scripts are often delivered via methods like drive-by compromises or HTML smuggling, where they may be hidden in blobs or data URLs, and are subsequently deobfuscated and executed on the victim's system. The intrusion-set Lazarus is a known user of this practice.[/profile]
608.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "javascript obfuscator" is a sub-technique of Obfuscated Files or Information (T1027). It falls under the Defense Evasion tactic and is applicable to multiple platforms. This technique involves adversaries obfuscating malicious JavaScript payloads, which are text-based, to avoid detection by security controls. Common obfuscation methods include encoding, compression, or splitting the script content, often used in conjunction with delivery mechanisms like drive-by compromises or HTML smuggling to conceal the malicious intent until execution.

622.name: WCRY
622.profile: [profile]WCRY, also known as WannaCry Ransomware, is attributed to the Lazarus Group. Its key technical behaviors include spreading via the leaked NSA ETERNALBLUE exploit and encrypting victim data using a combination of RSA (via Windows CryptoAPI) and a custom implementation of AES-128-CBC. The malware targets Windows systems and creates persistence through registry keys for automatic execution.
622.profile_without_enhance: [profile]WCRY, also known as WannaCry Ransomware, Wannacrypt, Wanna Decryptor, or Wannacryptor, is attributed to the Lazarus intrusion set. It is a worm-like ransomware that spreads by exploiting the SMBv1 vulnerability EternalBlue, primarily targeting Windows systems to encrypt files. It uses a combination of RSA and AES-128-CBC for encryption, with a custom implementation for AES. Its infrastructure and campaigns have been associated with global attacks since May 2017.

623.name: Ransomware Campaign
623.profile: [profile]Ransomware Campaign is a type of cyber operation primarily associated with the Impact tactic (T1486) and Financial Theft objective (T1657), targeting multiple platforms. It involves encrypting data on target systems to render it inaccessible, demanding a ransom for decryption. Common files like documents, PDFs, and images are typically encrypted, and the malware may employ worm-like propagation using techniques like Valid Accounts or SMB shares. Associated groups include Lazarus, and campaigns often involve data exfiltration and threats to leak data to increase extortion pressure.
623.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Ransomware Campaign" is a broad attack pattern, not a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique. It is described as a campaign type where adversaries encrypt data on target systems to interrupt availability and extort monetary compensation, often by encrypting common user files, critical system files, or cloud storage objects. This activity typically involves the technique Data Encrypted for Impact (T1486) under the Impact tactic. Campaigns may employ worm-like propagation using techniques like Valid Accounts and SMB shares, and often involve data exfiltration and threats of public data leaks to pressure victims for payment.

The malware's infrastructure involves a downloadable decryptor from a specific website.

626.name: SMBv1.0
626.profile: [profile]SMBv1.0 is a deprecated version of the Server Message Block (SMB) protocol. It is a file, printer, and serial port sharing protocol for Windows machines on the same network or domain. Adversaries may use SMB to interact with remote network shares, such as hidden Windows admin shares (e.g., C$, ADMIN$), to move laterally, transfer files, and execute binaries through techniques like Scheduled Tasks or Service Execution. The Lazarus intrusion-set has been associated with using SMB for lateral movement.

Attackers use it to transfer files, execute binaries remotely via methods like Scheduled Tasks, and interact with systems using remote procedure calls. Its use is commonly associated with threat groups like APT28, Lazarus Group, and Wizard Spider.

627.name: Cryptominer Plugin
627.profile: [profile]Cryptominer Plugin is a malicious component attributed to the Lazarus intrusion set. It functions as an orchestrator for cryptocurrency miners, specifically embedding and managing the XMRig miner for Monero and the NBMiner for Ethereum. The malware drops these miners to disk and executes them during periods of user inactivity (after 30 seconds), but terminates the mining processes if system-monitoring tools are detected or user activity resumes, demonstrating stealthy resource theft behavior primarily targeting Windows systems.
