It has been associated with groups including emissary panda, hurricane panda, lazarus group, leviathan, red menshen, and stone panda. Its key technical behavior involves orchestrating and executing embedded miners like XMRig for Monero and NBMiner for Ethereum, which are triggered during periods of user inactivity and terminated upon detection of monitoring tools or resumed user activity. It targets general computing platforms to perform unauthorized cryptomining operations.

629.name: Service Execution
629.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may abuse the Windows service control manager to execute malicious commands or payloads. The Windows service control manager (services.exe) is an interface to manage and manipulate services.(Citation: Microsoft Service Control Manager) The service control manager is accessible to users via GUI components as well as system utilities such as sc.exe and [Net](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0039). [PsExec](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0029) can also be used to execute commands or payloads via a temporary Windows service created through the service control manager API.(Citation: Russinovich Sysinternals) Tools such as [PsExec](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0029) and sc.exe can accept remote servers as arguments and may be used to conduct remote execution. Adversaries may leverage these mechanisms to execute malicious content. This can be done by either executing a new or modified service. This technique is the execution used in conjunction with [Windows Service](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1543/003) during service persistence or privilege escalation.
629.profile: [profile]Service Execution, identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1569.002, falls under the Execution tactic on Windows platforms. It involves abusing the Windows Service Control Manager (services.exe) to run malicious commands or payloads by creating or modifying services, using utilities like sc.exe, Net, or PsExec which can facilitate remote execution. This technique is commonly employed by groups such as APT41, FIN7, and Wizard Spider for persistence or privilege escalation.
629.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Service Execution, identified as T1035, is an Execution tactic technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework for the Windows platform. It involves executing malicious commands or payloads by interacting with the Windows Service Control Manager (services.exe). This can be achieved using native utilities like sc.exe or Net, or tools like PsExec, which create a temporary service via the service control manager API to run code, and can be used for both local and remote execution.

630.name: Network Service Scanning
630.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may attempt to get a listing of services running on remote hosts and local network infrastructure devices, including those that may be vulnerable to remote software exploitation. Common methods to acquire this information include port, vulnerability, and/or wordlist scans using tools that are brought onto a system.(Citation: CISA AR21-126A FIVEHANDS May 2021) Within cloud environments, adversaries may attempt to discover services running on other cloud hosts. Additionally, if the cloud environment is connected to a on-premises environment, adversaries may be able to identify services running on non-cloud systems as well. Within macOS environments, adversaries may use the native Bonjour application to discover services running on other macOS hosts within a network. The Bonjour mDNSResponder daemon automatically registers and advertises a host’s registered services on the network. For example, adversaries can use a mDNS query (such as dns-sd -B _ssh._tcp .) to find other systems broadcasting the ssh service.(Citation: apple doco bonjour description)(Citation: macOS APT Activity Bradley)
630.profile: [profile]Network Service Scanning, identified as T1046, is a Discovery technique used across multiple platforms. It involves actively probing remote hosts and network devices to enumerate running services, often through port scans, vulnerability scans, or wordlist scans. Specific methods include using tools brought onto a system or leveraging native network protocols; for example, in macOS environments, adversaries can use mDNS queries like `dns-sd -B _ssh._tcp .` via the Bonjour service. This reconnaissance aids in identifying potential targets for subsequent exploitation. The technique is associated with numerous threat groups, including Lazarus, APT41, and Volt Typhoon.[/profile]
630.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Network Service Scanning, identified as T1046 within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, is a Discovery tactic conducted across multiple platforms. It involves adversaries probing remote hosts and local network devices to enumerate running services, often using port scans and tools brought onto a system. In cloud environments, this can extend to discovering services on other cloud hosts and connected on-premises systems. Specific methods include using native applications like macOS's Bonjour mDNSResponder daemon, with commands such as `dns-sd -B _ssh._tcp .` to find systems advertising services like SSH.

631.name: Exploit Public-Facing Application
631.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may attempt to exploit a weakness in an Internet-facing host or system to initially access a network. The weakness in the system can be a software bug, a temporary glitch, or a misconfiguration.

Exploited applications are often websites/web servers, but can also include databases (like SQL), standard services (like SMB or SSH), network device administration and management protocols (like SNMP and Smart Install), and any other system with Internet-accessible open sockets.(Citation: NVD CVE-2016-6662)(Citation: CIS Multiple SMB Vulnerabilities)(Citation: US-CERT TA18-106A Network Infrastructure Devices 2018)(Citation: Cisco Blog Legacy Device Attacks)(Citation: NVD CVE-2014-7169) On ESXi infrastructure, adversaries may exploit exposed OpenSLP services; they may alternatively exploit exposed VMware vCenter servers.(Citation: Recorded Future ESXiArgs Ransomware 2023)(Citation: Ars Technica VMWare Code Execution Vulnerability 2021) Depending on the flaw being exploited, this may also involve [Exploitation for Defense Evasion](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1211) or [Exploitation for Client Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1203).

If an application is hosted on cloud-based infrastructure and/or is containerized, then exploiting it may lead to compromise of the underlying instance or container. This can allow an adversary a path to access the cloud or container APIs (e.g., via the [Cloud Instance Metadata API](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1552/005)), exploit container host access via [Escape to Host](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1611), or take advantage of weak identity and access management policies.

Adversaries may also exploit edge network infrastructure and related appliances, specifically targeting devices that do not support robust host-based defenses.(Citation: Mandiant Fortinet Zero Day)(Citation: Wired Russia Cyberwar)

For websites and databases, the OWASP top 10 and CWE top 25 highlight the most common web-based vulnerabilities.(Citation: OWASP Top 10)(Citation: CWE top 25)
631.profile: [profile]Exploit Public-Facing Application is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1190 under the Initial Access tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It involves exploiting software bugs, glitches, or misconfigurations in internet-facing systems like web servers, databases (SQL), services (SMB, SSH), network device protocols (SNMP, Smart Install), and cloud or container instances to gain initial network access. This can provide a path to cloud APIs or allow escape from containers. Groups such as APT28 and Lazarus have been associated with this technique.
631.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Exploit Public-Facing Application (T1190) is an Initial Access tactic targeting multiple platforms, including Windows, Linux, macOS, and cloud. Adversaries exploit weaknesses like software bugs, misconfigurations, or temporary glitches in internet-facing systems to gain initial network access. Commonly targeted applications include websites/web servers, databases (e.g., SQL), standard services (e.g., SMB, SSH), network device management protocols (e.g., SNMP), and exposed cloud or container APIs. Exploitation can provide a path to underlying infrastructure, potentially leading to further compromise via cloud metadata APIs or container escape.

632.name: UDP Port 137
632.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may use port knocking to hide open ports used for persistence or command and control. To enable a port, an adversary sends a series of attempted connections to a predefined sequence of closed ports. After the sequence is completed, opening a port is often accomplished by the host based firewall, but could also be implemented by custom software.

This technique has been observed both for the dynamic opening of a listening port as well as the initiating of a connection to a listening server on a different system.

The observation of the signal packets to trigger the communication can be conducted through different methods. One means, originally implemented by Cd00r (Citation: Hartrell cd00r 2002), is to use the libpcap libraries to sniff for the packets in question. Another method leverages raw sockets, which enables the malware to use ports that are already open for use by other programs.
632.profile: [profile]The entity "UDP Port 137" is a specific network port used for NetBIOS Name Service (NBT-NS). This port is a component within the MITRE ATT&CK technique LLMNR/NBT-NS Poisoning and Relay (T1171) under the Credential Access tactic. Adversaries exploit this UDP port to spoof responses and poison name resolution services on a local network, intercepting authentication traffic like NTLMv2 hashes from victims attempting to connect. This traffic can then be relayed or cracked offline to gain unauthorized access. The technique is platform-agnostic but primarily targets Windows environments where these legacy protocols are enabled.[/profile]
632.profile_without_enhance: [profile]UDP Port 137 is the standard port for the NetBIOS Name Service (NBT-NS), a Windows protocol for local network host identification. Adversaries can exploit this service through techniques like LLMNR/NBT-NS Poisoning and Relay (T1171), where they spoof responses to network traffic to intercept authentication attempts, capturing hashed credentials that can be relayed or cracked offline. This port is also listed as an example of a commonly used port (T1043, deprecated) that attackers may leverage to blend with normal activity, though its primary relevance is as a specific vector for network poisoning attacks within the Discovery and Credential Access tactics.

637.name: Ransomware Infection
637.profile: [profile]Ransomware Infection is a technique (T1486) under the Impact tactic, targeting Windows, Linux, and macOS systems. It involves encrypting files on target systems to render data inaccessible, demanding a ransom for decryption. Common user files like documents, PDFs, and images are typically encrypted, often requiring preparatory steps like File and Directory Permissions Modification. To maximize impact, ransomware may propagate via network shares or valid accounts and can exclude critical system files (e.g., .dll, .exe) to maintain system operability for ransom delivery. Groups like Lazarus employ this technique.[/profile]
637.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Ransomware Infection" is a broad attack pattern that maps to the MITRE ATT&CK technique Data Encrypted for Impact (T1486) under the Impact tactic, targeting Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves encrypting files on target systems to render data inaccessible, demanding a ransom for decryption. Common technical mechanics include encrypting user documents, images, and source code files, often renaming them or using specific file markers. To maximize impact, ransomware may propagate via worm-like features using techniques like Valid Accounts and SMB shares, and may avoid encrypting critical system files (e.g., .dll, .exe) to maintain system operability for ransom delivery.

638.name: Impact Ransomware

Its key technical behaviors include file encryption for ransom and data theft for extortion (doxware). It targets Windows platforms, with detections by major antivirus vendors like DrWeb (Trojan.Encoder.35760), ESET-NOD32 (MSIL/Filecoder.Hamster.A), and Kaspersky (HEUR:Trojan-Ransom.MSIL.Crypmod.gen).[/profile]

642.profile: [profile]Ransomware, also known as Ransomexx, is attributed to the intrusion set Gold Dupont. It is associated with the groups Lazarus and FIN7, and shares connections with the Shamoon malware. Key technical behaviors include file encryption for extortion, with variants like Moisha Ransomware detected under multiple signatures including Trojan.Encoder.35760 and Ransom:Win32/Moisha!MSR. 643.name: File Encryption
643.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may compromise a network device’s encryption capability in order to bypass encryption that would otherwise protect data communications. (Citation: Cisco Synful Knock Evolution)

Encryption can be used to protect transmitted network traffic to maintain its confidentiality (protect against unauthorized disclosure) and integrity (protect against unauthorized changes). Encryption ciphers are used to convert a plaintext message to ciphertext and can be computationally intensive to decipher without the associated decryption key. Typically, longer keys increase the cost of cryptanalysis, or decryption without the key.

Adversaries can compromise and manipulate devices that perform encryption of network traffic. For example, through behaviors such as [Modify System Image](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1601), [Reduce Key Space](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1600/001), and [Disable Crypto Hardware](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1600/002), an adversary can negatively effect and/or eliminate a device’s ability to securely encrypt network traffic. This poses a greater risk of unauthorized disclosure and may help facilitate data manipulation, Credential Access, or Collection efforts. (Citation: Cisco Blog Legacy Device Attacks)
643.profile: [profile]The entity "File Encryption" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. The provided input primarily describes the technique "Weaken Encryption" (T1600) under the Impact tactic, targeting network devices. This technique involves compromising a device's encryption capability to bypass protections, for example by modifying its system image, reducing the cryptographic key space, or disabling dedicated crypto hardware, thereby weakening or eliminating secure traffic encryption. The malware WannaCry is associated with this behavior. Information about general file encryption for obfuscation or exfiltration is contextually related but describes distinct techniques like T1022 or T1027.013.[/profile]
643.profile_without_enhance: [profile]File Encryption is a technique where adversaries encrypt files to obfuscate their content, impeding detection and analysis. This is often used to conceal malicious artifacts within payloads, configuration files, or data targeted for exfiltration. Encryption can be applied using standard algorithms like AES or through common archive formats like RAR and zip, sometimes with hardcoded or user-supplied keys. The obfuscated content is typically revealed only upon execution or decryption.

646.name: Extortion Tactics
646.profile: [profile]The entity "Extortion Tactics" is a technique aligned with the Financial Theft tactic (T1657). It involves coercing victims into paying a ransom, often following data encryption and exfiltration, as seen in ransomware campaigns like WannaCry. Threat actors may threaten to leak stolen data via dedicated leak sites unless payment is made, and they may use this financial motive to mask other disruptive goals like data destruction.
646.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Extortion Tactics is a technique within the Financial Theft (T1657) objective, falling under the Impact tactic. It is executed across multiple platforms. The technique involves demanding payment from a victim, often following data encryption and exfiltration, with threats to publicly leak sensitive data unless a ransom is paid. Adversaries may use dedicated leak sites to distribute victim data and may also abuse the threat of financial theft to mask other goals like data destruction.

652.name: Fancy Bear
652.uncertain_mes:
[APT28](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0007) is a threat group that has been attributed to Russia's General Staff Main Intelligence Directorate (GRU) 85th Main Special Service Center (GTsSS) military unit 26165.(Citation: NSA/FBI Drovorub August 2020)(Citation: Cybersecurity Advisory GRU Brute Force Campaign July 2021) This group has been active since at least 2004.(Citation: DOJ GRU Indictment Jul 2018)(Citation: Ars Technica GRU indictment Jul 2018)(Citation: Crowdstrike DNC June 2016)(Citation: FireEye APT28)(Citation: SecureWorks TG-4127)(Citation: FireEye APT28 January 2017)(Citation: GRIZZLY STEPPE JAR)(Citation: Sofacy DealersChoice)(Citation: Palo Alto Sofacy 06-2018)(Citation: Symantec APT28 Oct 2018)(Citation: ESET Zebrocy May 2019)

[APT28](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0007) reportedly compromised the Hillary Clinton campaign, the Democratic National Committee, and the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee in 2016 in an attempt to interfere with the U.S. presidential election.(Citation: Crowdstrike DNC June 2016) In 2018, the US indicted five GRU Unit 26165 officers associated with [APT28](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0007) for cyber operations (including close-access operations) conducted between 2014 and 2018 against the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA), the US Anti-Doping Agency, a US nuclear facility, the Organization for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons (OPCW), the Spiez Swiss Chemicals Laboratory, and other organizations.(Citation: US District Court Indictment GRU Oct 2018) Some of these were conducted with the assistance of GRU Unit 74455, which is also referred to as [Sandworm Team](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0034).
652.profile: [profile]Fancy Bear, also known as APT28, Sofacy, Sednit, and Pawn Storm, is a Russian state-sponsored cyber espionage group attributed to the GRU's 85th Main Special Service Center (military unit 26165). It has employed tools like DownRage and is known for sophisticated spear-phishing and credential-harvesting campaigns. The group primarily targets government, political, and defense sectors in North America and Europe, including entities like the U.S. Democratic National Committee and the Romanian Ministry of Foreign Affairs, with motivations centered on espionage and geopolitical influence operations.

Its key custom malware includes Zebrocy, Komplex, XAgent, CHOPSTICK, and the Calypso RAT. Characteristic TTPs involve sophisticated spear-phishing with spoofed messages and malicious Office documents, exploitation of zero-day vulnerabilities (notably in Adobe Flash), and specific anti-forensics techniques like using the WinRAR GUI for archiving and the cipher.exe utility for secure file deletion. The group is widely attributed to Russia's GRU military intelligence, specifically Unit 26165. It primarily targets government, military, diplomatic, and media organizations in North America and Europe, with motivations centered on state-sponsored espionage and influence operations.[/profile]

663.name: targeted attacks
663.profile: [profile]The entity "targeted attacks" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique but a general concept. Based on the retrieved information, it is associated with Denial of Service (DoS) techniques, specifically Endpoint Denial of Service (T1499) and its sub-techniques like Application Exhaustion Flood (T1499.003). These techniques involve exhausting system resources or exploiting applications to crash services, often using botnets or IP spoofing. The intrusion sets APT17 and Lazarus are linked to this concept, indicating its use by advanced threat actors.[/profile]
663.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "targeted attacks" is a generic term not corresponding to a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique ID. Based on retrieved information, it is contextually associated with Denial-of-Service (DoS) techniques. These techniques involve exhausting system or network resources to degrade or block service availability, using methods such as direct network floods with high-volume traffic (often via botnets using UDP, ICMP, or TCP) or application-layer attacks that target resource-intensive features. The Sandworm Team has been associated with related endpoint DoS activities.

664.name: cyber espionage
664.profile: [profile]The entity 'cyber espionage' is a high-level adversarial goal, not a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique, and therefore lacks a standard T-ID, Tactic, or Platform. It is a primary objective for advanced persistent threat (APT) groups like APT28, APT17, and Lazarus. The goal involves the clandestine theft of sensitive information, often facilitated by techniques such as obtaining capabilities (T1588) like malware and exploits, and monitoring threat intelligence reports (T1681) to adapt operations and evade detection.[/profile]

It encompasses the overarching goal of illicitly accessing and exfiltrating sensitive information for strategic advantage. Based on related content, this activity can involve preparatory steps like obtaining malware or exploits (T1588) and monitoring threat intelligence reports about their own operations to adapt and evade detection (T1681). It may also use disruptive actions, such as external website defacement (T1491.002), to deliver messages or create distrust as part of a larger influence campaign.

666.name: cryptocurrency mining
666.profile: [profile]Cryptocurrency mining is a resource hijacking technique (T1496) under the Impact tactic, targeting cloud, server, and endpoint platforms. It works by adversaries leveraging compromised system compute resources to validate cryptocurrency transactions and earn currency, often degrading system performance. This activity is commonly associated with groups like Lazarus and may involve killing competing mining processes to monopolize resources. It can be deployed via malicious cloud images or containers.
666.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Cryptocurrency mining is a resource hijacking technique where adversaries leverage compromised system compute resources to validate cryptocurrency transactions and earn virtual currency, often impacting system availability. This activity, which can target servers, cloud systems, endpoints, and containerized environments, is formally categorized under MITRE ATT&CK as T1496 (Resource Hijacking) within the Impact tactic, applicable to multiple platforms including Linux, Windows, and cloud. A specific implementation is detailed in sub-technique T1496.001 (Compute Hijacking), where malware may also kill competing mining processes to monopolize resources. The technique can be deployed via malicious container images or cloud machine images.

667.name: consumer devices
667.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may compromise third-party network devices that can be used during targeting. Network devices, such as small office/home office (SOHO) routers, may be compromised where the adversary's ultimate goal is not [Initial Access](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0001) to that environment, but rather to leverage these devices to support additional targeting.

Once an adversary has control, compromised network devices can be used to launch additional operations, such as hosting payloads for [Phishing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566) campaigns (i.e., [Link Target](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1608/005)) or enabling the required access to execute [Content Injection](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1659) operations. Adversaries may also be able to harvest reusable credentials (i.e., [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078)) from compromised network devices.

Adversaries often target Internet-facing edge devices and related network appliances that specifically do not support robust host-based defenses.(Citation: Mandiant Fortinet Zero Day)(Citation: Wired Russia Cyberwar)

Compromised network devices may be used to support subsequent [Command and Control](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0011) activity, such as [Hide Infrastructure](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1665) through an established [Proxy](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1090) and/or [Botnet](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1584/005) network.(Citation: Justice GRU 2024)
667.profile: [profile]The entity maps to the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1584.008, named Network Devices, under the tactic Resource Development. It involves adversaries compromising third-party network devices, such as SOHO routers and internet-facing edge appliances lacking robust defenses, not for initial access to that environment but to repurpose them for subsequent operations. Once compromised, these devices can be used to host phishing payloads, harvest reusable credentials, and establish proxy or botnet infrastructure to support command and control activities, as observed in campaigns linked to groups like Volt Typhoon and APT28.[/profile]
667.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Consumer Devices, designated as T1584.009 under Resource Development, involves adversaries compromising or leveraging third-party consumer-grade devices like IoT gadgets, smart home products, or mobile phones to establish infrastructure for attacks. These devices are often targeted due to weaker security and can be used to host phishing payloads, act as proxies for command and control, or harvest credentials, supporting groups like Volt Typhoon and APT28.

668.name: ICS attacks
668.profile: [profile]The entity "ICS attacks" is a broad category of malicious activities targeting Industrial Control Systems (ICS). It is not a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique and therefore lacks a standard ID, Tactic, or Platform. Based on the provided context, it is associated with the intrusion set Lazarus. Technical mechanics for specific ICS attacks can include endpoint denial of service to disrupt critical services, the use of mutexes for process synchronization and to avoid re-infection, and the injection of junk data into C2 protocols to hinder traffic analysis and detection.[/profile]
668.profile_without_enhance: [profile]ICS attacks, identified as a broad category within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, encompass tactics like Impact and Initial Access, targeting Industrial Control System (ICS) platforms. These attacks specifically aim to disrupt critical infrastructure by performing Endpoint Denial of Service (DoS) to degrade or block the availability of essential services, such as those hosted on ICS endpoints. Attackers may exhaust system resources or exploit vulnerabilities to cause persistent crashes, with techniques potentially involving IP address spoofing and the use of botnets to amplify the attack and complicate mitigation efforts.

681.name: IT service providers
681.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may abuse time providers to execute DLLs when the system boots. The Windows Time service (W32Time) enables time synchronization across and within domains.(Citation: Microsoft W32Time Feb 2018) W32Time time providers are responsible for retrieving time stamps from hardware/network resources and outputting these values to other network clients.(Citation: Microsoft TimeProvider)

Time providers are implemented as dynamic-link libraries (DLLs) that are registered in the subkeys of `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\System\CurrentControlSet\Services\W32Time\TimeProviders\`.(Citation: Microsoft TimeProvider) The time provider manager, directed by the service control manager, loads and starts time providers listed and enabled under this key at system startup and/or whenever parameters are changed.(Citation: Microsoft TimeProvider)

Adversaries may abuse this architecture to establish persistence, specifically by creating a new arbitrarily named subkey  pointing to a malicious DLL in the `DllName` value. Administrator privileges are required for time provider registration, though execution will run in context of the Local Service account.(Citation: Github W32Time Oct 2017)
681.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique "Time Providers" (ID: T1547.003), categorized under Persistence for Windows platforms. It involves adversaries abusing the Windows Time service (W32Time) architecture by creating a malicious DLL and registering it as a time provider. This is achieved by creating a new subkey under `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\System\CurrentControlSet\Services\W32Time\TimeProviders\` with the `DllName` value pointing to the malicious DLL, which is then loaded and executed at system startup by the time provider manager running in the Local Service account context, requiring administrator privileges for the initial registration.
681.profile_without_enhance: [profile]IT service providers, as a potential attack vector, are not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the retrieved context, adversaries may compromise or abuse third-party IT service providers, such as Virtual Private Server (VPS) hosts or cloud infrastructure providers, to acquire infrastructure for later stages of an attack like command and control. This allows them to leverage the provider's reputation for stealth and make attribution more difficult.

689.name: Phishing Email
689.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may send phishing messages to gain access to victim systems. All forms of phishing are electronically delivered social engineering. Phishing can be targeted, known as spearphishing. In spearphishing, a specific individual, company, or industry will be targeted by the adversary. More generally, adversaries can conduct non-targeted phishing, such as in mass malware spam campaigns.

Adversaries may send victims emails containing malicious attachments or links, typically to execute malicious code on victim systems. Phishing may also be conducted via third-party services, like social media platforms. Phishing may also involve social engineering techniques, such as posing as a trusted source, as well as evasive techniques such as removing or manipulating emails or metadata/headers from compromised accounts being abused to send messages (e.g., [Email Hiding Rules](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1564/008)).(Citation: Microsoft OAuth Spam 2022)(Citation: Palo Alto Unit 42 VBA Infostealer 2014) Another way to accomplish this is by [Email Spoofing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1672)(Citation: Proofpoint-spoof) the identity of the sender, which can be used to fool both the human recipient as well as automated security tools,(Citation: cyberproof-double-bounce) or by including the intended target as a party to an existing email thread that includes malicious files or links (i.e., "thread hijacking").(Citation: phishing-krebs)

Victims may also receive phishing messages that instruct them to call a phone number where they are directed to visit a malicious URL, download malware,(Citation: sygnia Luna Month)(Citation: CISA Remote Monitoring and Management Software) or install adversary-accessible remote management tools onto their computer (i.e., [User Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204)).(Citation: Unit42 Luna Moth)
689.profile: [profile]Phishing, also known as T1566, is an Initial Access tactic used across multiple platforms. It involves sending emails with malicious attachments or links to execute code, often leveraging social engineering by posing as a trusted source. Techniques include spearphishing specific targets, using compromised accounts for thread hijacking, email spoofing, and employing evasive methods like manipulating email headers or hiding rules. It is distinct from T1598 (Phishing for Information), which aims to gather data rather than deliver payloads.[/profile]
689.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Phishing Email is a specific technique within the broader MITRE ATT&CK Phishing (T1566) technique, falling under the Initial Access tactic and targeting multiple platforms. It involves sending emails containing malicious attachments or links to execute code, often employing social engineering by posing as a trusted source. Evasive methods include using compromised accounts to send messages, manipulating email headers, spoofing sender identities, and hijacking existing email threads to enhance credibility.

690.name: Infiltrate Computer Networks
690.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may gain initial access to target systems by connecting to wireless networks. They may accomplish this by exploiting open Wi-Fi networks used by target devices or by accessing secured Wi-Fi networks — requiring [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078) — belonging to a target organization.(Citation: DOJ GRU Charges 2018)(Citation: Nearest Neighbor Volexity) Establishing a connection to a Wi-Fi access point requires a certain level of proximity to both discover and maintain a stable network connection. 

Adversaries may establish a wireless connection through various methods, such as by physically positioning themselves near a Wi-Fi network to conduct close access operations. To bypass the need for physical proximity, adversaries may attempt to remotely compromise nearby third-party systems that have both wired and wireless network connections available (i.e., dual-homed systems). These third-party compromised devices can then serve as a bridge to connect to a target’s Wi-Fi network.(Citation: Nearest Neighbor Volexity)

Once an initial wireless connection is achieved, adversaries may leverage this access for follow-on activities in the victim network or further targeting of specific devices on the network. Adversaries may perform [Network Sniffing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1040) or [Adversary-in-the-Middle](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1557) activities for [Credential Access](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0006) or [Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0007).
690.profile: [profile]The entity "Infiltrate Computer Networks" aligns with MITRE ATT&CK technique T1669 (Wi-Fi Networks) under the Initial Access tactic, targeting Windows, Linux, and macOS. Adversaries gain access by exploiting open Wi-Fi networks or accessing secured ones, potentially using valid accounts. To bypass physical proximity, they may remotely compromise dual-homed third-party systems to serve as a bridge to the target network. Once connected, this access enables follow-on activities like network sniffing or adversary-in-the-middle attacks for credential access and discovery.
690.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Infiltrate Computer Networks" is a broad adversarial objective, not a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on retrieved context, this objective can be achieved through various technical mechanics. These include connecting to target Wi-Fi networks, either by exploiting open networks, using compromised credentials for secured ones, or bridging through dual-homed systems to bypass proximity requirements. Once initial wireless access is gained, adversaries may perform network sniffing or adversary-in-the-middle attacks for credential access and discovery. The objective may also involve the use of legitimate remote desktop software like VNC or AnyDesk for command and control, or manipulating hardware in the supply chain to insert backdoors.

691.name: Packed using UPX
691.profile: [profile]Packed using UPX is a specific implementation of the Software Packing technique (T1027.002) under the Defense Evasion tactic. It uses the UPX packer utility to compress or encrypt an executable, altering its file signature to evade signature-based detection. The packed code is decompressed in memory during execution. The Lazarus intrusion-set is known to use this technique.
691.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Packed using UPX is a specific implementation of the Software Packing technique (T1027.002) under the Defense Evasion tactic. It uses the UPX packer to compress or encrypt an executable, altering its file signature to evade signature-based detection. The packed executable is decompressed in memory during execution. This technique is commonly used by various threat groups to obfuscate malware payloads.

692.name: Maintain Persistence
692.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may clear artifacts associated with previously established persistence on a host system to remove evidence of their activity. This may involve various actions, such as removing services, deleting executables, [Modify Registry](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1112), [Plist File Modification](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1647), or other methods of cleanup to prevent defenders from collecting evidence of their persistent presence.(Citation: Cylance Dust Storm) Adversaries may also delete accounts previously created to maintain persistence (i.e. [Create Account](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1136)).(Citation: Talos - Cisco Attack 2022)

In some instances, artifacts of persistence may also be removed once an adversary’s persistence is executed in order to prevent errors with the new instance of the malware.(Citation: NCC Group Team9 June 2020)
692.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique "Indicator Removal: Clear Persistence" (T1070.009) under the Defense Evasion tactic, applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. Its technical mechanism involves adversaries removing artifacts of previously established persistence to erase evidence, including actions like deleting services, executables, registry keys, plist files, or user accounts. This cleanup prevents defender detection and can also avoid errors when deploying new malware instances. The intrusion-set Lazarus is associated with this behavior.
692.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Maintain Persistence is a core adversary objective, not a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique ID. It is a tactic within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, encompassing techniques that allow adversaries to retain access across system restarts or credential changes. Specific techniques for achieving this include using network logon scripts (T1037.003) assigned via Active Directory or Group Policy, and Windows logon scripts (T1037.001) configured via the `HKCU\Environment\UserInitMprLogonScript` Registry key. Adversaries may later clear persistence artifacts (T1070.009), such as by deleting services or accounts, to remove evidence of their activity.

693.name: Fake TLS Protocol
693.profile: [profile]Fake TLS Protocol is a sub-technique of Protocol or Service Impersonation (T1001.003) under the Command and Control tactic. It works by adversaries initiating a fake SSL/TLS handshake to make subsequent command and control traffic appear to be legitimately encrypted, which can interfere with security tool detection and blend the traffic with trusted entities. This technique has been associated with the Lazarus intrusion set.[/profile]
693.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Fake TLS Protocol is a technique within Protocol or Service Impersonation (T1001.003) under the Command and Control tactic. It operates by adversaries impersonating a fake SSL/TLS handshake to make subsequent command and control traffic appear to be standard, encrypted TLS communications. This impersonation is designed to blend malicious traffic with legitimate network activity and can interfere with security tooling that relies on protocol identification.

694.name: TLS Handshake
694.profile: [profile]TLS Handshake is a technique used within the Command and Control tactic, primarily on Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. Adversaries may impersonate a fake SSL/TLS handshake to make subsequent traffic appear as legitimate, SSL/TLS-encrypted network communication, which can blend in with normal traffic and potentially interfere with security tooling. This method is associated with groups like Lazarus.
694.profile_without_enhance: [profile]TLS Handshake is a technique within the broader protocol or service impersonation method (T1001.003) under the Command and Control tactic. It involves adversaries impersonating a fake SSL/TLS handshake to make subsequent malicious traffic appear as if it is SSL/TLS encrypted. This impersonation can interfere with security tooling and help the traffic blend in with legitimate network traffic or trusted entities, disguising command and control activity.

695.name: SNI Record Usage
695.profile: [profile]SNI Record Usage is a technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, specifically identified as T1090.004, a sub-technique of Proxy under the Command and Control tactic. It operates on multiple platforms. The core technical mechanic involves manipulating the Server Name Indication (SNI) field in the TLS header to obfuscate network traffic, as seen in domain fronting where a different domain is placed in the SNI field than in the HTTP Host header to misdirect routing through a shared CDN. A variation, "domainless" fronting, uses a blank SNI field to bypass validation. This technique has been associated with groups like APT29 and Lazarus.[/profile]
695.profile_without_enhance: [profile]SNI Record Usage is a technique for network traffic obfuscation, likely aligning with the MITRE ATT&CK framework under a sub-technique of Proxy or Encrypted Channel. It operates by manipulating the Server Name Indication (SNI) field within TLS handshakes. As detailed in the context of domain fronting, adversaries can use a different domain in the SNI field than in the HTTP Host header, or leave the SNI blank ("domainless" fronting), to disguise the true destination of HTTPS traffic when routed through a shared Content Delivery Network (CDN). This allows malicious traffic to appear destined for a benign front domain while being internally routed to a different, controlled endpoint.

696.name: Batch Script
696.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may use Windows logon scripts automatically executed at logon initialization to establish persistence. Windows allows logon scripts to be run whenever a specific user or group of users log into a system.(Citation: TechNet Logon Scripts) This is done via adding a path to a script to the HKCU\Environment\UserInitMprLogonScript Registry key.(Citation: Hexacorn Logon Scripts) Adversaries may use these scripts to maintain persistence on a single system. Depending on the access configuration of the logon scripts, either local credentials or an administrator account may be necessary.
696.profile: [profile]Batch Script, also known as Windows Logon Script (T1037.001), is a Persistence technique for Windows. It works by adding a script path to the HKCU\Environment\UserInitMprLogonScript Registry key, causing the script to execute automatically when a specific user logs into the system. This method is used by groups like Cobalt Group and APT28 to maintain access on a single host, potentially requiring local or administrator credentials for configuration.
696.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Batch Script is a technique within the Command and Scripting Interpreter tactic (T1059.003) for Windows execution. It involves using batch files (.bat or .cmd) to provide the Windows command shell with a list of sequential commands to run, enabling automation of long, repetitive tasks or execution of the same commands across multiple systems. Adversaries leverage this for payload execution and to run commands, often forwarding input and output over command and control channels.

697.name: Decoy Documents
697.profile: [profile]Decoy Documents is a technique used within the Initial Access tactic to deliver malicious payloads. It involves creating and distributing documents, such as Microsoft Office files, that appear legitimate but contain embedded code to execute malware when opened. The Lazarus intrusion-set has been known to employ this method. The technique operates across Windows, macOS, and Linux platforms by exploiting features like macros or embedded objects to gain a foothold on a victim's system.
697.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Decoy Documents is a technique where adversaries create fake documents to mislead defenders or users, often as part of a broader deception strategy. The retrieved information does not provide specific technical mechanics for this technique, but it is contextually linked to data handling and exfiltration stages, such as data compression (T1002) and automated exfiltration (T1020), where sensitive documents are processed.

698.name: Execute Shell Commands
698.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may backdoor web servers with web shells to establish persistent access to systems. A Web shell is a Web script that is placed on an openly accessible Web server to allow an adversary to access the Web server as a gateway into a network. A Web shell may provide a set of functions to execute or a command-line interface on the system that hosts the Web server.(Citation: volexity_0day_sophos_FW)

In addition to a server-side script, a Web shell may have a client interface program that is used to talk to the Web server (e.g. [China Chopper](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0020) Web shell client).(Citation: Lee 2013)
698.profile: [profile]Execute Shell Commands is a technique within the broader Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059) tactic of Execution. It involves adversaries abusing native system shells, such as the Windows Command Shell (cmd) or Unix Shell (e.g., bash, sh), to run arbitrary commands, scripts, or binaries. This provides direct control over a system, often for tasks like payload delivery, lateral movement via remote services like SSH, or persistence through shell scripts. The technique is platform-agnostic, applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS, and is commonly leveraged by groups like Lazarus for direct command execution.[/profile]
698.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Execute Shell Commands is a technique within the Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059) tactic of Execution. It operates across Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. The technique involves adversaries directly invoking system shell interpreters, such as cmd.exe on Windows or sh/bash/zsh on Unix-like systems, to run arbitrary commands. This provides direct control over the system for activities like executing payloads, running scripts, or performing reconnaissance, and can be performed locally, interactively via a C2 channel, or remotely through services like SSH.

699.name: String Interpolation Function
699.profile: [profile]String Interpolation Function is a technique with no official MITRE ATT&CK ID or Tactic classification. Based on provided context, it involves manipulating how strings or file names are displayed to disguise malicious content, similar to the right-to-left override (RTLO) technique (T1036.002). This can be used to trick users into executing malicious files by making them appear as benign documents (e.g., displaying "March 25 rcs.docx" for an executable). The intrusion-set Lazarus has been associated with related obfuscation methods.[/profile]
699.profile_without_enhance: [profile]String Interpolation Function is a deprecated technique. It involves manipulating how strings are constructed or displayed in code to disguise malicious intent, similar to how the right-to-left override (RTLO) character (U+202E) is abused to reverse the display order of subsequent text and hide file extensions, tricking users into executing malicious files. This can be used in conjunction with spearphishing and malicious file delivery.

700.name: Indirect Library Call
700.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may abuse utilities that allow for command execution to bypass security restrictions that limit the use of command-line interpreters. Various Windows utilities may be used to execute commands, possibly without invoking [cmd](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0106). For example, [Forfiles](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0193), the Program Compatibility Assistant (`pcalua.exe`), components of the Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL), `Scriptrunner.exe`, as well as other utilities may invoke the execution of programs and commands from a [Command and Scripting Interpreter](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059), Run window, or via scripts.(Citation: VectorSec ForFiles Aug 2017)(Citation: Evi1cg Forfiles Nov 2017)(Citation: Secure Team - Scriptrunner.exe)(Citation: SS64)(Citation: Bleeping Computer - Scriptrunner.exe) Adversaries may also abuse the `ssh.exe` binary to execute malicious commands via the `ProxyCommand` and `LocalCommand` options, which can be invoked via the `-o` flag or by modifying the SSH config file.(Citation: Threat Actor Targets the Manufacturing industry with Lumma Stealer and Amadey Bot)

Adversaries may abuse these features for [Defense Evasion](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0005), specifically to perform arbitrary execution while subverting detections and/or mitigation controls (such as Group Policy) that limit/prevent the usage of [cmd](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0106) or file extensions more commonly associated with malicious payloads.
700.profile: [profile]Indirect Command Execution, also known as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1202, is a Defense Evasion tactic used on Windows platforms. It involves abusing trusted system utilities like Forfiles, pcalua.exe, Windows Subsystem for Linux components, or Scriptrunner.exe to execute commands without invoking the standard command-line interpreter (cmd.exe), thereby bypassing security controls that restrict cmd usage. Adversaries, including groups like Lazarus and Redcurl, also exploit the ssh.exe binary's ProxyCommand and LocalCommand options via the -o flag or SSH config modifications to run malicious commands. This technique subverts detections and mitigations like Group Policy.[/profile]
700.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Indirect Library Call is a technique where adversaries execute malicious code by calling legitimate library functions indirectly, often to bypass security controls. It operates within the Execution tactic (TA0002) on Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. This is achieved by using intermediary code or system utilities to load and execute a malicious library (like a DLL) without a direct call, leveraging functions such as `LoadLibrary` through vectors like `CreateRemoteThread` or by abusing trusted system processes and scripting interpreters to evade detection.

701.name: Character Replacement Function
701.profile: [profile]Character Replacement Function is a technique used by adversaries like the Lazarus intrusion-set to obfuscate malicious code and evade detection. It operates by substituting characters in strings, commands, or file names with visually similar or functionally equivalent alternatives, such as using homoglyphs, Unicode characters, or case variations. This manipulation can disguise malicious intent in scripts, configuration files, or command-line arguments, complicating static analysis and signature-based defenses. The technique is a sub-technique of Obfuscated Files or Information (T1027) within the Defense Evasion tactic, primarily targeting Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms.
701.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Character Replacement Function is a technique for obfuscating malicious strings or file names, often to evade detection or trick users. A specific application involves abusing the right-to-left override (RTLO) Unicode character (U+202E), which causes subsequent text to display in reverse, making a file like "March 25 \u202Excod.scr" appear as "March 25 rcs.docx". This is commonly leveraged in spearphishing and malware delivery campaigns by groups like Ke3chang and BlackTech to disguise executable files as benign documents.

702.name: Communication Protocol
702.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may use an existing, legitimate external Web service as a means for sending commands to and receiving output from a compromised system over the Web service channel. Compromised systems may leverage popular websites and social media to host command and control (C2) instructions. Those infected systems can then send the output from those commands back over that Web service channel. The return traffic may occur in a variety of ways, depending on the Web service being utilized. For example, the return traffic may take the form of the compromised system posting a comment on a forum, issuing a pull request to development project, updating a document hosted on a Web service, or by sending a Tweet. 

Popular websites and social media acting as a mechanism for C2 may give a significant amount of cover due to the likelihood that hosts within a network are already communicating with them prior to a compromise. Using common services, such as those offered by Google or Twitter, makes it easier for adversaries to hide in expected noise. Web service providers commonly use SSL/TLS encryption, giving adversaries an added level of protection.
702.profile: [profile]Communication Protocol is the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1102.002, categorized under Command and Control. It operates across Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. This technique involves adversaries using legitimate external web services like social media or cloud platforms for bidirectional command and control. Commands are sent to a compromised system via the service, and output is returned through the same channel, for example, by posting a comment, updating a document, or sending a tweet. This traffic blends with normal user activity and often uses SSL/TLS encryption for added stealth. It is associated with groups including Lazarus, APT28, and MuddyWater.[/profile]
702.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Communication Protocol" is a fundamental concept in adversary command and control (C2) infrastructure, not a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique. It serves as the underlying mechanism for data exchange between compromised systems and attacker servers. Adversaries manipulate these protocols to evade detection, using methods like splitting traffic across different protocols to bypass firewalls, tunneling one protocol within another (e.g., SSH or DNS over HTTPS) to conceal traffic, or employing non-application layer protocols like ICMP which are less commonly monitored. They may also use legitimate web services (e.g., social media) or develop entirely custom C2 protocols to blend with normal network noise and avoid security appliances.

703.name: Shared Cleanup Batch Script
703.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may execute malicious payloads via loading shared modules. Shared modules are executable files that are loaded into processes to provide access to reusable code, such as specific custom functions or invoking OS API functions (i.e., [Native API](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1106)).

Adversaries may use this functionality as a way to execute arbitrary payloads on a victim system. For example, adversaries can modularize functionality of their malware into shared objects that perform various functions such as managing C2 network communications or execution of specific actions on objective.

The Linux & macOS module loader can load and execute shared objects from arbitrary local paths. This functionality resides in `dlfcn.h` in functions such as `dlopen` and `dlsym`. Although macOS can execute `.so` files, common practice uses `.dylib` files.(Citation: Apple Dev Dynamic Libraries)(Citation: Linux Shared Libraries)(Citation: RotaJakiro 2021 netlab360 analysis)(Citation: Unit42 OceanLotus 2017)

The Windows module loader can be instructed to load DLLs from arbitrary local paths and arbitrary Universal Naming Convention (UNC) network paths. This functionality resides in `NTDLL.dll` and is part of the Windows [Native API](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1106) which is called from functions like `LoadLibrary` at run time.(Citation: Microsoft DLL)
703.profile: [profile]Shared Modules is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1129 under the Execution tactic for Linux, macOS, and Windows. It involves adversaries executing arbitrary payloads by loading shared modules like DLLs or shared objects. This is achieved using module loader functions such as `dlopen`/`dlsym` on Linux/macOS or `LoadLibrary` via the Windows Native API, allowing execution from arbitrary local or UNC network paths. It has been used by groups like Mustang Panda.
703.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Shared Cleanup Batch Script is a technique where adversaries use batch scripts to delete files and artifacts post-intrusion to remove traces of their activity. This leverages the Windows command shell (T1059.003) for execution, employing native commands like `del` to perform the cleanup, aligning with the File Deletion (T1070.004/T1107) objective of minimizing their forensic footprint.

704.name: Network Protocols
704.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may communicate using application layer protocols associated with electronic mail delivery to avoid detection/network filtering by blending in with existing traffic. Commands to the remote system, and often the results of those commands, will be embedded within the protocol traffic between the client and server. 

Protocols such as SMTP/S, POP3/S, and IMAP that carry electronic mail may be very common in environments.  Packets produced from these protocols may have many fields and headers in which data can be concealed. Data could also be concealed within the email messages themselves. An adversary may abuse these protocols to communicate with systems under their control within a victim network while also mimicking normal, expected traffic.(Citation: FireEye APT28)
704.profile: [profile]Mail Protocols, identified as T1071.003 within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, is a Command and Control technique under the Command and Control tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. It involves adversaries using common email delivery protocols like SMTP/S, POP3/S, and IMAP to conceal command and control traffic by embedding data within standard protocol fields, headers, or the body of email messages to blend with normal network traffic and evade detection. This technique has been associated with groups including APT28, Turla, and Lazarus.[/profile]
704.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Network Protocols is a broad category within adversary command and control, corresponding to MITRE ATT&CK technique T1071 (Application Layer Protocol). It falls under the Command and Control tactic and applies to multiple platforms. Adversaries use common application layer protocols like HTTP/S, SMTP, SMB, FTP, MQTT, and WebSocket to blend malicious traffic with normal network activity, embedding commands and data within standard protocol fields and headers to avoid detection. This technique is widely employed by numerous threat groups including APT28, Lazarus Group, and Turla.

705.name: Library Name Obfuscation
705.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may obfuscate command and control traffic to make it more difficult to detect.(Citation: Bitdefender FunnyDream Campaign November 2020) Command and control (C2) communications are hidden (but not necessarily encrypted) in an attempt to make the content more difficult to discover or decipher and to make the communication less conspicuous and hide commands from being seen. This encompasses many methods, such as adding junk data to protocol traffic, using steganography, or impersonating legitimate protocols.
705.profile: [profile]Library Name Obfuscation is a technique for hiding malicious code by renaming or disguising library files to evade signature-based detection. This method, which aligns with the Defense Evasion tactic, operates across multiple platforms. The technique specifically involves altering the names of dynamic-link libraries (DLLs) or other shared libraries to appear benign, thereby bypassing security controls that rely on known malicious filenames. It is associated with intrusion sets like Lazarus.
705.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Library Name Obfuscation is a technique for Defense Evasion, where adversaries rename or disguise malicious libraries to appear legitimate and avoid detection. This involves altering the library's filename or metadata to mimic trusted system or software libraries, thereby bypassing security tools that rely on naming conventions for identification. The technique is executed on the host system and is related to broader obfuscation methods like Obfuscated Files or Information (T1027).

706.name: Process Creation String Interpolation
706.profile: [profile]Process Creation String Interpolation is a technique where adversaries construct process creation commands by dynamically building strings, often to obfuscate the final executable path or arguments. This method can bypass static command-line analysis by assembling the command from variables, concatenated strings, or environmental values at runtime, making detection more difficult. The intrusion-set Lazarus has been associated with this behavior. It is related to broader execution and defense evasion tactics.[/profile]
706.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Process Creation String Interpolation is a technique where adversaries manipulate command-line arguments stored in a process's memory to disguise malicious activity. On Linux, the `argv[0]` parameter, which typically holds the process name, is stored in user-space memory. Adversaries can overwrite this and other argument strings with null bytes to erase the original launch command, then write a spoofed, benign-looking command (e.g., `cat resolv.conf`) into the `argv[0]` memory location. This manipulation is reflected in `/proc/<PID>/cmdline` and tools like `ps`, effectively hiding the true nature of the process from detection and analysis.

707.name: Dropped Batch File Content
707.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may gain access and continuously communicate with victims by injecting malicious content into systems through online network traffic. Rather than luring victims to malicious payloads hosted on a compromised website (i.e., [Drive-by Target](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1608/004) followed by [Drive-by Compromise](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1189)), adversaries may initially access victims through compromised data-transfer channels where they can manipulate traffic and/or inject their own content. These compromised online network channels may also be used to deliver additional payloads (i.e., [Ingress Tool Transfer](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1105)) and other data to already compromised systems.(Citation: ESET MoustachedBouncer)

Adversaries may inject content to victim systems in various ways, including:

* From the middle, where the adversary is in-between legitimate online client-server communications (**Note:** this is similar but distinct from [Adversary-in-the-Middle](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1557), which describes AiTM activity solely within an enterprise environment) (Citation: Kaspersky Encyclopedia MiTM)
* From the side, where malicious content is injected and races to the client as a fake response to requests of a legitimate online server (Citation: Kaspersky ManOnTheSide)

Content injection is often the result of compromised upstream communication channels, for example at the level of an internet service provider (ISP) as is the case with "lawful interception."(Citation: Kaspersky ManOnTheSide)(Citation: ESET MoustachedBouncer)(Citation: EFF China GitHub Attack)
707.profile: [profile]The entity "Dropped Batch File Content" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the provided context, it appears to be a specific instance of content injection (T1659), a technique used for initial access and command and control. It operates by manipulating compromised network traffic channels, such as at an ISP level, to inject malicious code into data streams destined for a victim. This can be done "from the middle" by intercepting communications or "from the side" by racing malicious responses to the client. The technique has been associated with the Lazarus Group and the MoustachedBouncer campaign.
707.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Dropped Batch File Content" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the provided context, it describes a method where adversaries create and execute malicious batch (.BAT) files on a system. This is a sub-technique of file-based execution, often used for scripting commands to achieve objectives like lateral movement, persistence, or data exfiltration. The batch file content typically contains a sequence of commands interpreted by the Windows command-line interpreter.

712.name: Operation Heavy
712.profile: [profile]Operation Heavy is a campaign attributed to the Lazarus intrusion set. It employs the Screen Capture technique (T1113) to gather information by taking screenshots of the desktop, often using native utilities or API calls like `CopyFromScreen`, `xwd`, or `screencapture`. The campaign also uses Junk Data (T1001.001) in C2 protocols to hinder detection by adding random characters and Multilayer Encryption (T1079), tunneling custom encryption within protocols like HTTPS.
712.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Operation Heavy is a cyber attack pattern. Its technical mechanics involve using multiple layers of encryption for command and control communications, often by tunneling a custom encryption scheme within a standard protocol encryption like HTTPS or SMTPS to obscure malicious traffic.

713.name: wipers
713.uncertain_mes: [Wiper](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0041) is a family of destructive malware used in March 2013 during breaches of South Korean banks and media companies. (Citation: Dell Wiper)
713.profile: [profile]The malware family is named Wiper, also known as wipers, and is attributed to the Lazarus intrusion set. Its key technical behavior involves destructive data wiping, as exemplified by specific variants like HermeticWiper and AcidPour, which share similar destructive capabilities. The primary target platforms are South Korean banks and media companies, with notable activity occurring in March 2013. Supplementary information includes associated file hashes for the HermeticWiper variant.
713.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity 'wipers' refers to a class of destructive malware designed to render systems inoperable by wiping data. Specific examples include HermeticWiper and AcidPour. HermeticWiper is identified by hashes such as 1bc44eef75779e3ca1eefb8ff5a64807dbc942b1e4a2672d77b9f6928d292591. AcidPour is noted as a behavioral successor to the earlier AcidRain wiper. These wipers are characterized by their core function of data destruction, targeting system integrity and availability.

714.name: data theft
714.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may steal monetary resources from targets through extortion, social engineering, technical theft, or other methods aimed at their own financial gain at the expense of the availability of these resources for victims. Financial theft is the ultimate objective of several popular campaign types including extortion by ransomware,(Citation: FBI-ransomware) business email compromise (BEC) and fraud,(Citation: FBI-BEC) "pig butchering,"(Citation: wired-pig butchering) bank hacking,(Citation: DOJ-DPRK Heist) and exploiting cryptocurrency networks.(Citation: BBC-Ronin) 

Adversaries may [Compromise Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1586) to conduct unauthorized transfers of funds.(Citation: Internet crime report 2022) In the case of business email compromise or email fraud, an adversary may utilize [Impersonation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1656) of a trusted entity. Once the social engineering is successful, victims can be deceived into sending money to financial accounts controlled by an adversary.(Citation: FBI-BEC) This creates the potential for multiple victims (i.e., compromised accounts as well as the ultimate monetary loss) in incidents involving financial theft.(Citation: VEC)

Extortion by ransomware may occur, for example, when an adversary demands payment from a victim after [Data Encrypted for Impact](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1486) (Citation: NYT-Colonial) and [Exfiltration](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0010) of data, followed by threatening to leak sensitive data to the public unless payment is made to the adversary.(Citation: Mandiant-leaks) Adversaries may use dedicated leak sites to distribute victim data.(Citation: Crowdstrike-leaks)

Due to the potentially immense business impact of financial theft, an adversary may abuse the possibility of financial theft and seeking monetary gain to divert attention from their true goals such as [Data Destruction](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1485) and business disruption.(Citation: AP-NotPetya)
714.profile: [profile]Financial Theft, designated as T1657, is an adversary objective within the Impact tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. It involves stealing monetary resources through methods like unauthorized fund transfers via compromised accounts, extortion via ransomware that encrypts and exfiltrates data to demand payment, and social engineering schemes such as business email compromise (BEC) where impersonation deceives victims into sending money. This objective is pursued by groups including Lazarus, FIN13, and Scattered Spider, and can also be used as a diversion for other goals like data destruction.[/profile]
714.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Data Theft is a broad adversary objective, not a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique, and falls under the Exfiltration tactic. It involves the unauthorized removal of data from a victim network. This can be achieved through various methods, including exfiltrating data over existing command and control channels or via physical media like USB devices. The stolen data often includes sensitive information such as financial records, intellectual property, or personal data, which adversaries may leverage for extortion, espionage, or direct financial gain.

715.name: dropper
715.uncertain_mes: [SplatDropper](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S1232) is a loader that utilizes native windows API to deliver its payload to the victim environment.  [SplatDropper](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S1232) has been delivered through RAR archives and used legitimate executable for DLL side-loading.  [SplatDropper](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S1232) is known to be leveraged by [Mustang Panda](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0129) and was first observed utilized in 2025.
715.profile: [profile]SplatDropper, also known as dropper, is a loader that utilizes native Windows API to deliver its payload, delivered through RAR archives and using legitimate executables for DLL side-loading. It is attributed to the Mustang Panda group and was first observed in 2025. Key technical behaviors include its delivery method and side-loading technique, targeting Windows environments. Infrastructure or supplementary details include its use in campaigns involving similar dropper variants like those associated with groups such as Hellsing, Ice Fog, and Karma Panda.
715.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Dropper is a malware type, also known as an 8.t dropper variant. It has been used by multiple threat groups including Hellsing, Ice Fog, Pirate Panda, Rancor, TA428, Tick, Tonto Team, and Karma Panda. Its key technical behaviors involve using document lures (like COVID-19 alerts) for initial infection and dropping payloads such as the Chinoxy backdoor. It has been associated with infrastructure and tools used by groups like Pinchy Spider (linked to REvil) and has been observed targeting platforms like Android, as indicated in Brunhilda campaigns. The malware utilizes components like passwords and public keys in its operations.[/profile]

716.name: myres
716.profile: [profile]Myres is a resource name used by the Lazarus intrusion set to store a payload DLL within a loader component, as seen in the Babar malware. The loader extracts the resource named MYRES, writes it as a temporary file, and moves it to the AppData folder as wmimgnt.dll, setting hidden attributes and altering timestamps to appear old. The target platform is Windows.[/profile]
716.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The malware 'myres' is a payload DLL resource embedded within loaders like 'babar'. It is stored in a PE resource named MYRES and is extracted to a temporary file, then moved as 'wmimgnt.dll' to the AppData folder with hidden attributes and altered timestamps. It is associated with the group 'snowglobe'.

717.name: RSA encryption
717.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may compromise a network device’s encryption capability in order to bypass encryption that would otherwise protect data communications. (Citation: Cisco Synful Knock Evolution)

Encryption can be used to protect transmitted network traffic to maintain its confidentiality (protect against unauthorized disclosure) and integrity (protect against unauthorized changes). Encryption ciphers are used to convert a plaintext message to ciphertext and can be computationally intensive to decipher without the associated decryption key. Typically, longer keys increase the cost of cryptanalysis, or decryption without the key.

Adversaries can compromise and manipulate devices that perform encryption of network traffic. For example, through behaviors such as [Modify System Image](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1601), [Reduce Key Space](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1600/001), and [Disable Crypto Hardware](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1600/002), an adversary can negatively effect and/or eliminate a device’s ability to securely encrypt network traffic. This poses a greater risk of unauthorized disclosure and may help facilitate data manipulation, Credential Access, or Collection efforts. (Citation: Cisco Blog Legacy Device Attacks)
717.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique "Weaken Encryption" (ID: T1600) under the Defense Evasion tactic, targeting Network Devices. Adversaries compromise a device's encryption capability to bypass data-in-transit protections, for example by reducing the cryptographic key space or disabling dedicated crypto hardware, as observed in legacy device attacks. The intrusion set Lazarus has been associated with this activity.[/profile]
717.profile_without_enhance: [profile]RSA encryption, formally known as Asymmetric Cryptography (T1573.002), is a technique under the Command and Control tactic. It is a public key encryption algorithm used to conceal C2 traffic, where data is encrypted with a recipient's public key and can only be decrypted with the corresponding private key, ensuring only the intended recipient can read the communications. It is commonly used to establish secure channels, such as in SSL/TLS, before switching to symmetric encryption for efficiency.

720.name: bat files
720.uncertain_mes:
Introduction
Zscaler’s ThreatLabz threat research team recently has spotted a new variant of the emerging X-FILES infostealer attack with enhanced features to exfiltrate sensitive information. X-FILES is a stealer that aims to steal sensitive information, including logins and financial data.
720.profile: [profile]X-FILES Stealer, also known as bat files, is an infostealer attributed to the Lazarus group. It aims to steal sensitive information like logins and financial data, with variants using .bat files for execution. Its target platforms are Windows systems, and related infrastructure involves malicious .bat files found in open directories, as seen in campaigns using tools like AsyncRAT, SystemBC, and GhostSocks.
720.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "bat files" refers to batch script files (.bat) that can be used for malicious purposes, such as in the deployment of malware like AsyncRAT and SystemBC. These files are often found in open directories alongside other executable and script files (.exe, .vbs, .ps1) and are associated with groups like Vanilla Tempest. Specific malicious batch files include "COPY.bat" and "WMI.bat," which are linked to SystemBC infrastructure. The primary target platform is Windows, leveraging its native command-line interpreter for execution.

721.name: Obfuscate API functions
721.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may interact with the native OS application programming interface (API) to execute behaviors. Native APIs provide a controlled means of calling low-level OS services within the kernel, such as those involving hardware/devices, memory, and processes.(Citation: NT API Windows)(Citation: Linux Kernel API) These native APIs are leveraged by the OS during system boot (when other system components are not yet initialized) as well as carrying out tasks and requests during routine operations. Adversaries may abuse these OS API functions as a means of executing behaviors. Similar to [Command and Scripting Interpreter](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059), the native API and its hierarchy of interfaces provide mechanisms to interact with and utilize various components of a victimized system. Native API functions (such as NtCreateProcess) may be directed invoked via system calls / syscalls, but these features are also often exposed to user-mode applications via interfaces and libraries.(Citation: OutFlank System Calls)(Citation: CyberBit System Calls)(Citation: MDSec System Calls) For example, functions such as the Windows API CreateProcess() or GNU fork() will allow programs and scripts to start other processes.(Citation: Microsoft CreateProcess)(Citation: GNU Fork) This may allow API callers to execute a binary, run a CLI command, load modules, etc. as thousands of similar API functions exist for various system operations.(Citation: Microsoft Win32)(Citation: LIBC)(Citation: GLIBC) Higher level software frameworks, such as Microsoft .NET and macOS Cocoa, are also available to interact with native APIs. These frameworks typically provide language wrappers/abstractions to API functionalities and are designed for ease-of-use/portability of code.(Citation: Microsoft NET)(Citation: Apple Core Services)(Citation: MACOS Cocoa)(Citation: macOS Foundation) Adversaries may use assembly to directly or in-directly invoke syscalls in an attempt to subvert defensive sensors and detection signatures such as user mode API-hooks.(Citation: Redops Syscalls) Adversaries may also attempt to tamper with sensors and defensive tools associated with API monitoring, such as unhooking monitored functions via [Disable or Modify Tools](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1562/001).
721.profile: [profile]Native API, designated T1106, is an execution technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves adversaries directly invoking low-level OS system calls or APIs, such as NtCreateProcess or CreateProcess, to perform actions like process creation and file operations. This method can be used to bypass user-mode API hooks by using assembly to invoke syscalls directly. The technique is associated with groups including Lazarus, Mustang Panda, and Sandworm Team.[/profile]
721.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Obfuscate API functions is a technique to conceal malicious functionalities by dynamically resolving API calls during runtime, preventing static analysis. It involves storing hashes of function names instead of literal strings and using functions like GetProcAddress() and LoadLibrary() to resolve and invoke the APIs, often with further obfuscation via encryption. This method helps adversaries evade detection by obscuring API function calls in malware payloads.

722.name: file deletion after infection
