722.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may delete files left behind by the actions of their intrusion activity. Malware, tools, or other non-native files dropped or created on a system by an adversary (ex: [Ingress Tool Transfer](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1105)) may leave traces to indicate to what was done within a network and how. Removal of these files can occur during an intrusion, or as part of a post-intrusion process to minimize the adversary's footprint. There are tools available from the host operating system to perform cleanup, but adversaries may use other tools as well.(Citation: Microsoft SDelete July 2016) Examples of built-in [Command and Scripting Interpreter](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059) functions include del on Windows, rm or unlink on Linux and macOS, and `rm` on ESXi.
722.profile: [profile]file deletion after infection is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1070.004 under the Defense Evasion tactic, applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. It involves adversaries removing non-native files like malware or tools to erase traces of intrusion, using OS-native commands such as `del` on Windows or `rm` and `unlink` on Linux/macOS, or specialized tools like SDelete for secure deletion. This cleanup can occur during or after an operation to minimize forensic evidence and is often linked to groups like Lazarus.[/profile]
722.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "file deletion after infection" is a post-compromise technique for Indicator Removal (T1070). It involves adversaries deleting files like malware, tools, or logs left on a system to erase traces of their intrusion and minimize their forensic footprint. This cleanup can be performed using native OS commands such as `DEL` or dedicated tools like Windows Sysinternals SDelete.

723.name: XOR pattern
723.profile: [profile]XOR pattern, which is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique, is a simple cryptographic method often used by adversaries for data obfuscation. It is commonly implemented as a custom archival method (T1560.003) to compress or encrypt collected data prior to exfiltration, or as part of a custom cryptographic protocol (T1024) to hide command and control traffic. The technique involves XOR-ing plaintext with a fixed key, producing a weak ciphertext that can be reversed through malware analysis. Groups like Lazarus, FIN6, and APT28 have been associated with related obfuscation and custom encryption behaviors.[/profile]
723.profile_without_enhance: [profile]XOR pattern is a custom cryptographic technique used by adversaries to obfuscate data or network traffic. It is associated with the MITRE ATT&CK technique Custom Cryptographic Protocol (T1024) under the Command and Control tactic. The method involves applying an XOR operation to plaintext with a fixed key, producing a weak but simple cipher. This approach is used to hide command and control communications and has been employed in custom data archival, such as by groups like Lazarus Group, to encrypt collected information prior to exfiltration without relying on external libraries.

724.name: Dynamic loading
724.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may dynamically establish connections to command and control infrastructure to evade common detections and remediations. This may be achieved by using malware that shares a common algorithm with the infrastructure the adversary uses to receive the malware's communications. These calculations can be used to dynamically adjust parameters such as the domain name, IP address, or port number the malware uses for command and control.

Adversaries may use dynamic resolution for the purpose of [Fallback Channels](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1008). When contact is lost with the primary command and control server malware may employ dynamic resolution as a means to reestablishing command and control.(Citation: Talos CCleanup 2017)(Citation: FireEye POSHSPY April 2017)(Citation: ESET Sednit 2017 Activity)
724.profile: [profile]Dynamic Resolution, designated T1568 under the Command and Control tactic, operates on Windows, Linux, and macOS. It evades detection by using malware that shares an algorithm with adversary infrastructure to dynamically adjust C2 parameters like domain names, IP addresses, or port numbers. This technique can also serve as a mechanism to reestablish lost C2 connections for Fallback Channels. It has been associated with groups including APT29, Gamaredon Group, and Lazarus.
724.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Dynamic loading is a technique where adversaries execute malicious code by loading shared modules or libraries into a process at runtime, rather than from a persistent file on disk. This is often achieved using system APIs like `LoadLibrary` on Windows or `dlopen` on Linux/macOS to load DLLs or shared objects from arbitrary local or network paths. The technique enables execution of modular payloads, helps evade file-based detection, and can mask malicious activity within legitimate processes. It is related to techniques like Shared Modules (T1129) and DLL side-loading (T1073).

725.name: Malware Families
725.uncertain_mes:
A .NET rat targets Mongolia
A new document royal road v7 installs a backdoor in .NET. a first executable is dropped \os03C2.tmp. This exe has many similarities with older campaigns using by Operation LagTime or Tonto Team.
Document
The decoy document is a document about infection of covid19 in Russia send to the Mongolia Authorities. The document is fake signed A. Amarsaikhan.
725.profile: [profile]The malware, referred to as nmass, is a .NET-based remote access trojan (RAT) targeting entities in Mongolia. It is delivered via a malicious Royal Road v7 document masquerading as a COVID-19 report from Russia, which is fake-signed by "A. Amarsaikhan." The initial payload is dropped as a file named "os03C2.tmp." Its code shares similarities with malware used in campaigns attributed to Operation LagTime or Tonto Team. The intrusion-set Lazarus is a connected entity in its threat graph.
725.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Malware Families is a broad category encompassing multiple distinct malware families. It includes nmass malware, a .NET RAT targeting Mongolia via decoy documents, with similarities to campaigns by Operation LagTime or Tonto Team. It also includes Wroba.g, Wroba.f, Wroba.j, and Fakecop Android malware families used by groups like Roaming Mantis and Yanbian Gang, sharing infrastructure and distribution channels. The category is referenced in contexts involving APT33 and other threat groups.

726.name: fake TLS protocol
726.profile: [profile]The entity "fake TLS protocol" is a technique for command and control obfuscation, aligning with MITRE ATT&CK sub-technique T1001.003, Protocol or Service Impersonation, under the Command and Control tactic. It operates across multiple platforms by impersonating a legitimate SSL/TLS handshake to make subsequent malicious traffic appear to be standard encrypted web traffic, thereby evading detection and analysis. This technique is associated with the Lazarus intrusion set and involves manipulating network traffic to mimic trusted services without necessarily using valid encryption, distinguishing it from standard cryptographic tunneling.
726.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Fake TLS Protocol is a technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, specifically categorized as Protocol or Service Impersonation (T1001.003) under the Command and Control tactic. It operates by adversaries impersonating a fake SSL/TLS handshake to make subsequent command and control traffic appear as if it is legitimately encrypted, which can interfere with security tooling and help the traffic blend in with trusted network entities. This method is often used to disguise malicious communications and evade detection.

728.name: User-Agent Spoofing with Misspelled Mozillar
728.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may create or modify launch agents to repeatedly execute malicious payloads as part of persistence. When a user logs in, a per-user launchd process is started which loads the parameters for each launch-on-demand user agent from the property list (.plist) file found in /System/Library/LaunchAgents, /Library/LaunchAgents, and ~/Library/LaunchAgents.(Citation: AppleDocs Launch Agent Daemons)(Citation: OSX Keydnap malware) (Citation: Antiquated Mac Malware) Property list files use the Label, ProgramArguments , and RunAtLoad keys to identify the Launch Agent's name, executable location, and execution time.(Citation: OSX.Dok Malware) Launch Agents are often installed to perform updates to programs, launch user specified programs at login, or to conduct other developer tasks. Launch Agents can also be executed using the [Launchctl](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1569/001) command. Adversaries may install a new Launch Agent that executes at login by placing a .plist file into the appropriate folders with the RunAtLoad or KeepAlive keys set to true.(Citation: Sofacy Komplex Trojan)(Citation: Methods of Mac Malware Persistence) The Launch Agent name may be disguised by using a name from the related operating system or benign software. Launch Agents are created with user level privileges and execute with user level permissions.(Citation: OSX Malware Detection)(Citation: OceanLotus for OS X)
728.profile: [profile]The entity "User-Agent Spoofing with Misspelled Mozillar" is a technique for defense evasion, likely corresponding to T1036.012 (Browser Fingerprinting). It operates on web platforms by modifying the HTTP User-Agent request header string to spoof browser and system attributes, such as mimicking a legitimate browser like Mozilla with intentional typos (e.g., "Mozillar"). This manipulation helps adversaries blend malicious web traffic with legitimate traffic to evade fingerprinting-based detection systems. The technique is used to avoid identification by network defenses and may be employed following system information discovery to craft convincing spoofed attributes. The intrusion-set Lazarus is associated with this activity.[/profile]
728.profile_without_enhance: [profile]User-Agent Spoofing with Misspelled Mozillar is a technique for evading detection by modifying the HTTP User-Agent request header to mimic legitimate browser attributes. It operates within the Defense Evasion tactic, specifically as a sub-technique of Masquerading (T1036.012). The method involves crafting a spoofed header, such as intentionally misspelling "Mozilla" to appear as "Mozillar," to bypass security controls that rely on fingerprinting for identifying anomalous or malicious web traffic. This allows adversaries to blend their network activity with normal user traffic.

729.name: Hangul HWP Document
729.profile: [profile]Hangul HWP Document is a malicious document file format. It is used as an infection vector by the Lazarus intrusion set and is associated with the APT37 group. It is specifically employed to deliver malware such as ROKRAT. The document is created using the Hangul Word Processor, a popular office software in South Korea, and targets users of that platform.
729.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Hangul HWP Document is a malicious document type exploiting the Hangul Word Processor (HWP) format, a popular South Korean alternative to Microsoft Office. It is used as an infection vector by threat groups including APT37 (as seen in ROKRAT campaigns) and Kimsuky (as seen with BabyShark). It leverages vulnerabilities like CVE-2015-6585 and primarily targets users and organizations in South Korea.[/profile]

734.name: backdoored software
734.profile: [profile]The entity is known as backdoored software, which is a tactic used by threat actors like the Lazarus intrusion set. This involves legitimate software installers or archives, such as vcperf, Zabbix, Webroot AV, TeamViewer, VLC Media Player, and WinRAR, being trojanized with backdoor capabilities like FinSpy to compromise systems, primarily targeting Windows platforms through maliciously modified installation files.[/profile]
734.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Backdoored software is a malware entity that involves the compromise of legitimate software installers or archives to embed malicious backdoor functionality. It is associated with APT29 (as seen in the 'graphdrop' context) and shares a conceptual link with other backdoor-capable malware like 'daxin' and the FinFisher RAT, which also uses trojanized applications such as TeamViewer, VLC Media Player, and WinRAR installers. The key technical behavior is the distribution of backdoored versions of tools like vcperf, Zabbix installation archives, and Webroot AV installation archives to facilitate unauthorized access and control.

735.name: Distribution of Backdoored Software
735.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may gather information about the victim's host software that can be used during targeting. Information about installed software may include a variety of details such as types and versions on specific hosts, as well as the presence of additional components that might be indicative of added defensive protections (ex: antivirus, SIEMs, etc.).

Adversaries may gather this information in various ways, such as direct collection actions via [Active Scanning](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1595) (ex: listening ports, server banners, user agent strings) or [Phishing for Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1598). Adversaries may also compromise sites then include malicious content designed to collect host information from visitors.(Citation: ATT ScanBox) Information about the installed software may also be exposed to adversaries via online or other accessible data sets (ex: job postings, network maps, assessment reports, resumes, or purchase invoices). Additionally, adversaries may analyze metadata from victim-owned files (e.g., PDFs, DOCs, images, and sound files hosted on victim-owned websites) to extract information about the software and hardware used to create or process those files. Metadata may reveal software versions, configurations, or timestamps that indicate outdated or vulnerable software. This information can be cross-referenced with known CVEs to identify potential vectors for exploitation in future operations.(Citation: Outpost24)

Gathering this information may reveal opportunities for other forms of reconnaissance (ex: [Search Open Websites/Domains](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1593) or [Search Open Technical Databases](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1596)), establishing operational resources (ex: [Develop Capabilities](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1587) or [Obtain Capabilities](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1588)), and/or for initial access (ex: [Supply Chain Compromise](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195) or [External Remote Services](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1133)).
735.profile: [profile]The entity is a reconnaissance technique named "Gather Victim Host Information: Software" with the MITRE ATT&CK ID T1592.002, under the Reconnaissance tactic and applicable to multiple platforms. It involves adversaries collecting details about installed software on victim hosts, including types, versions, and security components like antivirus or SIEMs. This information is gathered through methods such as active scanning, phishing, compromising websites to deploy info-stealing content, analyzing public data sets like job postings or network maps, and extracting metadata from victim-hosted files (e.g., PDFs, DOCS) to identify software versions and potential vulnerabilities. The collected data can enable follow-on activities like further reconnaissance, capability development, or initial access via supply chain compromise. The technique has been associated with groups including Andariel, Sandworm Team, and Magic Hound.
735.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Distribution of Backdoored Software" is a software supply chain attack technique where adversaries manipulate legitimate software prior to delivery to a consumer to compromise systems. This technique, mapped to MITRE ATT&CK ID T1195.002 (Compromise Software Supply Chain) under the Initial Access tactic, involves uploading maliciously modified software packages, binaries, or updates to third-party repositories, marketplaces, or distribution channels. The goal is to have victims unknowingly download and execute the backdoored software, often through methods like typo-squatting legitimate packages, to establish initial access or persistence.

736.name: remote desktop client
736.profile: [profile]The entity 'remote desktop client' is a legitimate software tool for remote system access, but it is frequently exploited by threat actors like the Lazarus intrusion set for lateral movement and persistence. It is mentioned in the context of other malware such as Mimikatz, Agent Tesla, and IcedID, where it is used as part of attack chains involving credential theft, data exfiltration, and exploitation of vulnerabilities like Zerologon (CVE-2020-1472). Its misuse is associated with various groups including APT10, APT32, Anunak, Gallium, Sweed, Gold Cabin, and Lunar Spider, primarily targeting Windows environments through protocols like RDP and tools such as AnyDesk, UltraVNC, and TightVNC.
736.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The malware 'remote desktop client' is a tool used by multiple threat groups including APT10, APT32, Anunak, and Gallium, often in conjunction with credential dumping tools like Mimikatz to exploit Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP). It is also associated with other remote access software like AnyDesk, UltraVNC, and TightVNC, as seen in campaigns by groups such as Sweed, Gold Cabin, and Lunar Spider. Its key behavior involves facilitating unauthorized remote access to compromised systems.

740.name: Spear Phishing Campaign
740.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may send phishing messages to gain access to victim systems. All forms of phishing are electronically delivered social engineering. Phishing can be targeted, known as spearphishing. In spearphishing, a specific individual, company, or industry will be targeted by the adversary. More generally, adversaries can conduct non-targeted phishing, such as in mass malware spam campaigns.

Adversaries may send victims emails containing malicious attachments or links, typically to execute malicious code on victim systems. Phishing may also be conducted via third-party services, like social media platforms. Phishing may also involve social engineering techniques, such as posing as a trusted source, as well as evasive techniques such as removing or manipulating emails or metadata/headers from compromised accounts being abused to send messages (e.g., [Email Hiding Rules](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1564/008)).(Citation: Microsoft OAuth Spam 2022)(Citation: Palo Alto Unit 42 VBA Infostealer 2014) Another way to accomplish this is by [Email Spoofing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1672)(Citation: Proofpoint-spoof) the identity of the sender, which can be used to fool both the human recipient as well as automated security tools,(Citation: cyberproof-double-bounce) or by including the intended target as a party to an existing email thread that includes malicious files or links (i.e., "thread hijacking").(Citation: phishing-krebs)

Victims may also receive phishing messages that instruct them to call a phone number where they are directed to visit a malicious URL, download malware,(Citation: sygnia Luna Month)(Citation: CISA Remote Monitoring and Management Software) or install adversary-accessible remote management tools onto their computer (i.e., [User Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204)).(Citation: Unit42 Luna Moth)
740.profile: [profile]Spear Phishing Campaign aligns with MITRE ATT&CK technique T1566 (Phishing) under the Initial Access tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It involves sending targeted electronic messages to specific individuals or organizations, often containing malicious attachments or links to execute code. Adversaries employ social engineering, posing as trusted sources, and use evasive techniques like email spoofing, thread hijacking, or manipulating email headers from compromised accounts. Groups such as APT28, Lazarus, and APT29 are associated with this technique.[/profile]
740.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Spear Phishing Campaign is a targeted social engineering attack, aligning with MITRE ATT&CK technique T1566.001 (Spearphishing Attachment) under the Initial Access tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It involves sending tailored emails to specific individuals or organizations, often using malicious attachments or links disguised as legitimate content to trick recipients into executing code or divulging credentials. The campaign employs sophisticated lures, email spoofing, and thread hijacking to increase credibility and evade detection, frequently conducted by advanced threat groups.

741.name: CFO Job Decoy
741.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may abuse task scheduling functionality to facilitate initial or recurring execution of malicious code. Utilities exist within all major operating systems to schedule programs or scripts to be executed at a specified date and time. A task can also be scheduled on a remote system, provided the proper authentication is met (ex: RPC and file and printer sharing in Windows environments). Scheduling a task on a remote system typically may require being a member of an admin or otherwise privileged group on the remote system.(Citation: TechNet Task Scheduler Security)

Adversaries may use task scheduling to execute programs at system startup or on a scheduled basis for persistence. These mechanisms can also be abused to run a process under the context of a specified account (such as one with elevated permissions/privileges). Similar to [System Binary Proxy Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1218), adversaries have also abused task scheduling to potentially mask one-time execution under a trusted system process.(Citation: ProofPoint Serpent)
741.profile: [profile]Scheduled Task/Job (T1053) is a Persistence and Execution technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS. It involves abusing native OS utilities like Windows Task Scheduler, cron, at, or launchd to schedule the initial or recurring execution of malicious code at specified times or system startup. Tasks can be configured to run under the context of privileged accounts and can also be scheduled on remote systems, such as via RPC in Windows environments, to facilitate lateral movement and mask execution within trusted processes. The intrusion-set Lazarus has been associated with this technique.[/profile]
741.profile_without_enhance: [profile]CFO Job Decoy is a technique for Persistence and Execution, likely on Windows platforms, that involves creating a deceptive scheduled task named to impersonate a legitimate Chief Financial Officer (CFO) role or related process. This decoy task is used to execute malicious code at system startup or on a scheduled basis, leveraging native task scheduling utilities to blend in with normal administrative activity and avoid detection.

742.name: Job Description Lure
742.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may abuse task scheduling functionality to facilitate initial or recurring execution of malicious code. Utilities exist within all major operating systems to schedule programs or scripts to be executed at a specified date and time. A task can also be scheduled on a remote system, provided the proper authentication is met (ex: RPC and file and printer sharing in Windows environments). Scheduling a task on a remote system typically may require being a member of an admin or otherwise privileged group on the remote system.(Citation: TechNet Task Scheduler Security)

Adversaries may use task scheduling to execute programs at system startup or on a scheduled basis for persistence. These mechanisms can also be abused to run a process under the context of a specified account (such as one with elevated permissions/privileges). Similar to [System Binary Proxy Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1218), adversaries have also abused task scheduling to potentially mask one-time execution under a trusted system process.(Citation: ProofPoint Serpent)
742.profile: [profile]Job Description Lure is a specific application of the Scheduled Task/Job technique (T1053) within the Execution and Persistence tactics, targeting Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves creating malicious scheduled tasks or cron jobs that are disguised with legitimate-sounding names and descriptions to appear as benign system or business-related activities, thereby facilitating the initial or recurring execution of malicious code. The Lazarus group has been associated with this technique.[/profile]
742.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Job Description Lure is a social engineering technique used in the Initial Access tactic. It involves creating and distributing fake job postings or descriptions to lure potential victims. These postings are designed to appear legitimate and enticing, often for high-profile or desirable roles, to trick individuals into interacting with malicious content, such as downloading malware-laden documents or revealing sensitive information. This method exploits human curiosity and professional ambition to gain a foothold within a target organization.

743.name: Reconnaissance
743.profile: [profile]Reconnaissance is the initial phase of the Cyber Kill Chain (Tactic: Reconnaissance). It involves gathering information about a target to plan subsequent attacks. This includes active scanning techniques like probing victim infrastructure with network traffic (e.g., ICMP) to identify vulnerabilities, as well as passive methods like collecting employee names from social media or websites to craft targeted lures. Threat groups such as APT28, APT29, Lazarus, and menuPass are known to conduct extensive reconnaissance. The gathered intelligence supports later stages like developing capabilities, obtaining initial access, and executing intrusions.[/profile]
743.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Reconnaissance is a foundational tactic within the Cyber Kill Chain framework, preceding weaponization and delivery. It encompasses the initial phase where adversaries gather information about a target to inform subsequent attack stages. Specific techniques include active scanning (T1595), which involves probing victim infrastructure via network traffic like ICMP, and gathering employee names (T1589.003) from sources like social media to craft lures and derive email addresses. This tactic is platform-agnostic and enables adversaries to identify vulnerabilities and plan their operations.

744.name: Remote Access Trojan (RAT)
744.profile: [profile]Remote Access Trojan (RAT) is a category of malware. It is associated with groups such as Lazarus. Specific variants include AsyncRAT, DCRat, Remcos, AveMaria, and NanoCore. These RATs provide attackers with complete control over compromised systems, typically targeting Windows, Mac OS X, or Linux platforms.
744.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity is a generic classification for Remote Access Trojan (RAT) malware, with specific examples including AsyncRAT, DCRat, Remcos, AveMaria, and NanoCore. It provides attackers with complete control over compromised systems across platforms like Windows, Mac OS X, and Linux. Typical features include backdoor access and remote system management capabilities.

747.name: C2 Protocol
747.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may steal data by exfiltrating it over an un-encrypted network protocol other than that of the existing command and control channel. The data may also be sent to an alternate network location from the main command and control server.(Citation: copy_cmd_cisco)

Adversaries may opt to obfuscate this data, without the use of encryption, within network protocols that are natively unencrypted (such as HTTP, FTP, or DNS). This may include custom or publicly available encoding/compression algorithms (such as base64) as well as embedding data within protocol headers and fields.
747.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique "Exfiltration Over Unencrypted Non-C2 Protocol" (ID: T1048.003) under the Exfiltration tactic. It involves stealing data by sending it over a separate, unencrypted network channel (like HTTP, FTP, or DNS) instead of the primary C2 channel, potentially to an alternate location. To avoid detection, adversaries often obfuscate the data within these protocols using methods like Base64 encoding or by embedding information within protocol headers and fields, all without applying encryption. Associated threat groups include Lazarus, FIN6, and APT32.
747.profile_without_enhance: [profile]C2 Protocol is a foundational technique for Command and Control. It involves establishing a communication channel between an adversary and a compromised system to send commands and receive data. This channel can be implemented using various standard or custom network protocols, often employing obfuscation methods like data encoding (e.g., Base64) or encryption to blend with normal traffic and avoid detection. Adversaries may also use protocol tunneling, encapsulating C2 traffic within another protocol like HTTPS or DNS, to bypass network security controls.

749.name: Duuzer
749.profile: [profile]Duuzer, also known as duuzer, is a malware attributed to the Lazarus group. It utilizes computers infected with the Brambul malware as command-and-control (C&C) servers. Its technical behaviors include establishing persistence through registry key creation for automatic execution on system startup. The primary target platform is Windows systems. This malware family is associated with broader intrusion campaigns conducted by the Lazarus intrusion set.[/profile]
749.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Duuzer is a malware attributed to the Lazarus Group. It uses computers infected with the Brambul malware as command-and-control (C&C) servers, indicating a relationship where Brambul infrastructure is leveraged for Duuzer's operations.

It was created around 2009 and shares behavioral similarities with the later WannaCry ransomware, which is considered a mutation of it. The malware primarily targets computers with vulnerable versions and settings to cause harm. Key indicators of compromise include specific MD5 hashes such as 1c532fad2c60636654d4c778cfe10408.
750.profile_without_enhance: [profile] Brambul is a worm attributed to the Lazarus group, originally created in 2009. It spreads via SMB protocol brute-force attacks using common passwords and targets Windows systems with vulnerable versions and settings. It shares behavioral similarities with and is considered a precursor to the WannaCry ransomware.

751.name: Joanap
751.profile: [profile]Joanap, also known as joanap, is a two-stage malware attributed to the Lazarus Group. It establishes peer-to-peer botnet communications on compromised Windows devices to exfiltrate data, drop and run secondary payloads, initialize proxy communications, and perform file and process management.
751.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Joanap, also known as joanap, is a two-stage malware attributed to the Lazarus Group. It establishes peer-to-peer communications to manage botnets, enabling data exfiltration via HTTP POST, dropping and executing secondary payloads, and initiating proxy communications on compromised Windows systems. Its functions include file and process management. The primary target platform is Windows.

755.name: Backdoor
755.profile: [profile]Backdoor is a broad technique (not a specific MITRE ID) where adversaries establish persistent, unauthorized access to a system. It can be implemented via software, firmware, or hardware, such as by compromising the hardware supply chain (T1195.003) to insert difficult-to-detect access. Backdoors are used by groups like Lazarus and enable follow-on actions like patching domain controller authentication (T1556.001) for credential bypass or using junk data in C2 traffic (T1001.001) to evade detection.
755.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Backdoor is a general technique (T1133) within the Persistence tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. It involves establishing a covert method of maintaining access to a compromised system, bypassing normal authentication. Specific implementations include patching domain controller authentication processes (like with Skeleton Key malware) to accept a universal password, or manipulating hardware components in the supply chain to insert physical backdoors into devices prior to deployment.

756.name: Watering Hole
756.profile: [profile]Watering Hole is a technique where adversaries compromise websites frequented by a target audience to stage malicious resources for drive-by compromises. It is used by intrusion sets like Lazarus and Turla. The technique involves adversaries uploading or installing capabilities on infrastructure they control, such as compromised websites or web services, to serve malicious content when a user visits the site. This staged content is a key mechanism for enabling initial access.[/profile]
756.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Watering Hole is a technique for initial access, where adversaries compromise websites frequented by a target audience to distribute malware. It is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique with a T-ID but is often associated with the tactic of Initial Access. The technical mechanics involve identifying and compromising a legitimate website that the intended victims are likely to visit, then staging malicious web resources or scripts to exploit visitors' browsers and deliver payloads, as referenced in the staging of capabilities for drive-by compromises.

757.name: Collect System Information
757.uncertain_mes: An adversary may attempt to get detailed information about the operating system and hardware, including version, patches, hotfixes, service packs, and architecture. Adversaries may use this information to shape follow-on behaviors, including whether or not the adversary fully infects the target and/or attempts specific actions. This behavior is distinct from [Local Storage Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1680) which is an adversary's discovery of local drive, disks and/or volumes. Tools such as [Systeminfo](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0096) can be used to gather detailed system information. If running with privileged access, a breakdown of system data can be gathered through the systemsetup configuration tool on macOS. Adversaries may leverage a [Network Device CLI](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/008) on network devices to gather detailed system information (e.g. show version).(Citation: US-CERT-TA18-106A) On ESXi servers, threat actors may gather system information from various esxcli utilities, such as `system hostname get` and `system version get`.(Citation: Crowdstrike Hypervisor Jackpotting Pt 2 2021)(Citation: Varonis) Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) cloud providers such as AWS, GCP, and Azure allow access to instance and virtual machine information via APIs. Successful authenticated API calls can return data such as the operating system platform and status of a particular instance or the model view of a virtual machine.(Citation: Amazon Describe Instance)(Citation: Google Instances Resource)(Citation: Microsoft Virutal Machine API) [System Information Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1082) combined with information gathered from other forms of discovery and reconnaissance can drive payload development and concealment.(Citation: OSX.FairyTale)(Citation: 20 macOS Common Tools and Techniques)
757.profile: [profile]System Information Discovery, designated T1082 under the Discovery tactic, operates across Windows, macOS, Linux, and Network and Cloud platforms. Adversaries gather detailed OS and hardware data, including version, architecture, and patch levels, to inform follow-on actions. This is executed using tools like the `systeminfo` command on Windows, the `systemsetup` utility on macOS, CLI commands such as `show version` on network devices, and `esxcli` commands on ESXi servers. Cloud instance metadata is also collected via provider APIs. The technique is distinct from local storage discovery and is used by numerous threat groups, including Lazarus, for reconnaissance and evasion.
757.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Collect System Information is a Discovery technique where adversaries gather detailed OS and hardware data like version, patches, and architecture to inform follow-on actions. Specific mechanics include using tools like `systeminfo` on Windows, the `systemsetup` command on macOS, network device CLI commands (e.g., `show version`), and esxcli utilities (`system hostname get`) on ESXi. It also involves querying cloud provider APIs (AWS, GCP, Azure) for instance metadata. This information aids in payload development and evasion.

758.name: Create Processes
758.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may create an account to maintain access to victim systems.(Citation: Symantec WastedLocker June 2020) With a sufficient level of access, creating such accounts may be used to establish secondary credentialed access that do not require persistent remote access tools to be deployed on the system.

Accounts may be created on the local system or within a domain or cloud tenant. In cloud environments, adversaries may create accounts that only have access to specific services, which can reduce the chance of detection.
758.profile: [profile]Create Account, identified as T1136, is a Persistence technique used on Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves adversaries creating local, domain, or cloud tenant accounts to establish secondary credentialed access, which can bypass the need for persistent remote access tools. In cloud environments, they may create service-specific accounts to reduce detection likelihood. This technique is associated with groups like Scattered Spider, Indrik Spider, and Salt Typhoon.[/profile]
758.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Create Processes" is a foundational attack pattern for execution. It involves adversaries spawning new processes to run malicious code or legitimate system tools for malicious purposes. This technique is platform-agnostic, applying to Windows, Linux, and macOS, and is a core component of the Execution tactic. Specific implementations include using APIs like CreateProcess on Windows or command-line utilities, often to chain with other techniques for privilege escalation or defense evasion.

759.name: Access Files
759.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may attempt to steal Kerberos tickets stored in credential cache files (or ccache). These files are used for short term storage of a user's active session credentials. The ccache file is created upon user authentication and allows for access to multiple services without the user having to re-enter credentials. The /etc/krb5.conf configuration file and the KRB5CCNAME environment variable are used to set the storage location for ccache entries. On Linux, credentials are typically stored in the `/tmp` directory with a naming format of `krb5cc_%UID%` or `krb5.ccache`. On macOS, ccache entries are stored by default in memory with an `API:{uuid}` naming scheme. Typically, users interact with ticket storage using kinit, which obtains a Ticket-Granting-Ticket (TGT) for the principal; klist, which lists obtained tickets currently held in the credentials cache; and other built-in binaries.(Citation: Kerberos GNU/Linux)(Citation: Binary Defense Kerberos Linux) Adversaries can collect tickets from ccache files stored on disk and authenticate as the current user without their password to perform [Pass the Ticket](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1550/003) attacks. Adversaries can also use these tickets to impersonate legitimate users with elevated privileges to perform [Privilege Escalation](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0004). Tools like Kekeo can also be used by adversaries to convert ccache files to Windows format for further [Lateral Movement](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0008). On macOS, adversaries may use open-source tools or the Kerberos framework to interact with ccache files and extract TGTs or Service Tickets via lower-level APIs.(Citation: SpectorOps Bifrost Kerberos macOS 2019)(Citation: Linux Kerberos Tickets)(Citation: Brining MimiKatz to Unix)(Citation: Kekeo)
759.profile: [profile]Access Files, also known as ccache files and identified as T1558.005 under the Credential Access tactic, targets Linux and macOS platforms. This technique involves stealing Kerberos tickets from credential cache files, which store a user's active session credentials. Adversaries locate these files via the /etc/krb5.conf configuration or the KRB5CCNAME environment variable, with common paths including /tmp/krb5cc_%UID% on Linux and in-memory storage on macOS. The stolen tickets enable Pass the Ticket attacks for lateral movement and privilege escalation without requiring the user's password, and tools like Kekeo can convert these files for use on Windows systems.[/profile]
759.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Access Files is a foundational technique for adversaries to read, write, or modify files on a system, often as a prerequisite for data theft, persistence, or privilege escalation. It involves directly interacting with file system objects and can bypass standard access controls using tools like `icacls`, `cacls`, `takeown`, and `attrib` on Windows to modify permissions, or by performing direct volume access to analyze disk data structures. This behavior is instrumental in many attack chains, enabling actions such as planting backdoors, stealing credentials from stored files, or hijacking system binaries.

760.name: End Processes
760.profile: [profile]End Processes is a technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, mapped to T1489 (Service Stop) under the Impact tactic. It operates across Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. Adversaries, such as the Lazarus group, stop or disable system services to render them unavailable, inhibit incident response, or enable follow-on actions like Data Destruction. This can involve targeting critical services like MSExchangeIS or disabling many services to cause system-wide disruption, including in cloud environments via APIs like AWS's DisableAPIServiceAccess.
760.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "End Processes" is a technique where adversaries terminate running processes to disrupt system operations, disable security tools, or enable follow-on actions like data destruction. This can be achieved using commands like `taskkill` on Windows or `kill` and `pkill` on Linux/Unix systems, often targeting critical services such as MSExchangeIS or SQL Server to render applications or the entire system unusable.

761.name: Delete Files
761.uncertain_mes:
An adversary may delete a cloud instance after they have performed malicious activities in an attempt to evade detection and remove evidence of their presence.  Deleting an instance or virtual machine can remove valuable forensic artifacts and other evidence of suspicious behavior if the instance is not recoverable.

An adversary may also [Create Cloud Instance](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1578/002) and later terminate the instance after achieving their objectives.(Citation: Mandiant M-Trends 2020)
761.profile: [profile]The entity "Delete Files" is a technique for defense evasion, primarily used in cloud environments to remove forensic evidence after malicious activities. Adversaries delete cloud instances or virtual machines to eliminate artifacts, often using this in conjunction with creating instances (T1578.002). Groups like LAPSUS$ and Storm-0501 have employed this method. The technique is associated with the MITRE ATT&CK ID T1578.003 under the tactic Defense Evasion, targeting cloud platforms.
761.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Delete Files" aligns with MITRE ATT&CK technique T1070.004, a sub-technique under Defense Evasion. It involves adversaries deleting files left behind by their intrusion activities, such as malware, tools, or other non-native artifacts, to remove forensic evidence and minimize their footprint. This cleanup can occur during or after an intrusion using built-in command interpreters like `del` on Windows or `rm`/`unlink` on Linux and macOS, or specialized tools like SDelete. The technique is widely used by numerous threat groups, including APT29, Lazarus Group, and FIN6.

763.name: Upload Files
763.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may upload malware to third-party or adversary controlled infrastructure to make it accessible during targeting. Malicious software can include payloads, droppers, post-compromise tools, backdoors, and a variety of other malicious content. Adversaries may upload malware to support their operations, such as making a payload available to a victim network to enable [Ingress Tool Transfer](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1105) by placing it on an Internet accessible web server.

Malware may be placed on infrastructure that was previously purchased/rented by the adversary ([Acquire Infrastructure](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1583)) or was otherwise compromised by them ([Compromise Infrastructure](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1584)). Malware can also be staged on web services, such as GitHub or Pastebin; hosted on the InterPlanetary File System (IPFS), where decentralized content storage makes the removal of malicious files difficult; or saved on the blockchain as smart contracts, which are resilient against takedowns that would affect traditional infrastructure.(Citation: Volexity Ocean Lotus November 2020)(Citation: Talos IPFS 2022)(Citation: Guardio Etherhiding 2023)(Citation: Bleeping Computer Binance Smart Chain 2023)

Adversaries may upload backdoored files, such as software packages, application binaries, virtual machine images, or container images, to third-party software stores, package libraries, extension marketplaces, or repositories (ex: GitHub, CNET, AWS Community AMIs, Docker Hub, PyPi, NPM).(Citation: Datadog Security Labs Malicious PyPi Packages 2024) By chance encounter, victims may directly download/install these backdoored files via [User Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204). Masquerading, including typo-squatting legitimate software, may increase the chance of users mistakenly executing these files.
763.profile: [profile]Upload Malware, designated T1608.001 under the Resource Development tactic, is a technique where adversaries stage malicious files on accessible infrastructure. This includes placing payloads, droppers, or backdoored software packages on adversary-controlled web servers, compromised infrastructure, or public services like GitHub, Pastebin, IPFS, blockchain smart contracts, and software repositories (e.g., PyPi, NPM, Docker Hub) to facilitate later stages of attack such as Ingress Tool Transfer or User Execution.
763.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Upload Files" is a general action, not a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on retrieved information, it is contextually related to adversary preparatory procedures like "Upload Malware" (T1608.001) and "Upload Tool" (T1608.002), which are sub-techniques of the "Stage Capabilities" tactic. This involves placing malicious or dual-use files on internet-accessible infrastructure—such as compromised web servers, cloud storage (e.g., AWS S3, Dropbox), code repositories (e.g., GitHub, PyPi), or decentralized networks (e.g., IPFS)—to make them available for subsequent operations like Ingress Tool Transfer (T1105).
