765.name: Change Time Attributes
765.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may abuse extended attributes (xattrs) on macOS and Linux to hide their malicious data in order to evade detection. Extended attributes are key-value pairs of file and directory metadata used by both macOS and Linux. They are not visible through standard tools like `Finder`,  `ls`, or `cat` and require utilities such as `xattr` (macOS) or `getfattr` (Linux) for inspection. Operating systems and applications use xattrs for tagging, integrity checks, and access control. On Linux, xattrs are organized into namespaces such as `user.` (user permissions), `trusted.` (root permissions), `security.`, and `system.`, each with specific permissions. On macOS, xattrs are flat strings without namespace prefixes, commonly prefixed with `com.apple.*` (e.g., `com.apple.quarantine`, `com.apple.metadata:_kMDItemUserTags`) and used by system features like Gatekeeper and Spotlight.(Citation: Establishing persistence using extended attributes on Linux)

An adversary may leverage xattrs by embedding a second-stage payload into the extended attribute of a legitimate file. On macOS, a payload can be embedded into a custom attribute using the `xattr` command. A separate loader can retrieve the attribute with `xattr -p`, decode the content, and execute it using a scripting interpreter. On Linux, an adversary may use `setfattr` to write a payload into the `user.` namespace of a legitimate file. A loader script can later extract the payload with `getfattr --only-values`, decode it, and execute it using bash or another interpreter. In both cases, because the primary file content remains unchanged, security tools and integrity checks that do not inspect extended attributes will observe the original file hash, allowing the malicious payload to evade detection.(Citation: Low GroupIB xattrs nov 2024)
765.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique "Extended Attributes" (ID: T1564.014) under the Defense Evasion tactic, applicable to Linux and macOS platforms. It involves adversaries hiding malicious payloads within extended file attributes (xattrs) to evade detection by tools that only inspect standard file content. On macOS, payloads are embedded using the `xattr` command and retrieved with `xattr -p` for execution via a scripting interpreter; on Linux, `setfattr` writes payloads into the `user.` namespace, and `getfattr --only-values` extracts them for execution. This leaves the original file hash unchanged, bypassing security checks. The intrusion-set Lazarus has been associated with this technique.[/profile]
765.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Change Time Attributes" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the provided context, it refers to the technique of timestomping, which is officially recognized as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1070.006 (Indicator Removal: Timestomp). This technique falls under the Defense Evasion tactic. Adversaries modify file timestamps (like modify, access, create, and change times) to hide new or altered files by making them blend in with legitimate files in the same directory. On Windows, this involves altering the `$STANDARD_INFORMATION` attribute in the Master File Table (MFT), often via user-level API calls, and may include "double timestomping" by also modifying the kernel-managed `$FILE_NAME` attribute to evade forensic detection. On Linux and ESXi systems, commands such as `touch -a -m -t` can be used to set specific timestamps.

766.name: Disguise Malware
766.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may develop malware and malware components that can be used during targeting. Building malicious software can include the development of payloads, droppers, post-compromise tools, backdoors (including backdoored images), packers, C2 protocols, and the creation of infected removable media. Adversaries may develop malware to support their operations, creating a means for maintaining control of remote machines, evading defenses, and executing post-compromise behaviors.(Citation: Mandiant APT1)(Citation: Kaspersky Sofacy)(Citation: ActiveMalwareEnergy)(Citation: FBI Flash FIN7 USB)

During malware development, adversaries may intentionally include indicators aligned with other known actors in order to mislead attribution by defenders.(Citation: Olympic Destroyer)(Citation: Risky Bulletin Threat actor impersonates FSB APT)(Citation: GamaCopy organization)

As with legitimate development efforts, different skill sets may be required for developing malware. The skills needed may be located in-house, or may need to be contracted out. Use of a contractor may be considered an extension of that adversary's malware development capabilities, provided the adversary plays a role in shaping requirements and maintains a degree of exclusivity to the malware.

Some aspects of malware development, such as C2 protocol development, may require adversaries to obtain additional infrastructure. For example, malware developed that will communicate with Twitter for C2, may require use of [Web Services](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1583/006).(Citation: FireEye APT29)
766.profile: [profile]Disguise Malware is a sub-technique of Malware Development (T1587.001) under the Resource Development tactic. It involves adversaries intentionally crafting malware to appear as if it originates from a different threat actor by incorporating false flags, such as code signatures, infrastructure, or behaviors associated with other known groups. This practice is used to mislead attribution efforts by defenders and complicate forensic analysis, as seen in campaigns like Olympic Destroyer. The technique is platform-agnostic and is employed by groups like Lazarus to obscure their involvement in attacks.
766.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Disguise Malware" aligns with MITRE ATT&CK technique T1036, Masquerading, under the Defense Evasion tactic. It operates across Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. This technique involves adversaries altering the appearance of malicious files to evade detection, specifically by changing file signatures, extensions, or icons to mimic legitimate formats like .txt or .jpg. This can include creating polyglot files that function as multiple file types. The goal is to bypass file validation checks and deceive users into executing the payload, often used in conjunction with techniques like Ingress Tool Transfer.

767.name: Registry Key Manipulation
767.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may reduce the level of effort required to decrypt data transmitted over the network by reducing the cipher strength of encrypted communications.(Citation: Cisco Synful Knock Evolution)

Adversaries can weaken the encryption software on a compromised network device by reducing the key size used by the software to convert plaintext to ciphertext (e.g., from hundreds or thousands of bytes to just a couple of bytes). As a result, adversaries dramatically reduce the amount of effort needed to decrypt the protected information without the key.

Adversaries may modify the key size used and other encryption parameters using specialized commands in a [Network Device CLI](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/008) introduced to the system through [Modify System Image](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1601) to change the configuration of the device. (Citation: Cisco Blog Legacy Device Attacks)
767.profile: [profile]Registry Key Manipulation, identified as MITRE ATT&CK T1112, is a Defense Evasion and Persistence technique primarily targeting Windows platforms. It involves adversaries interacting with the Windows Registry using tools like Reg.exe or remote access software to modify keys and values. This manipulation can hide configuration data or malicious payloads, impair defenses by altering security settings, enable lateral movement by modifying remote system registries, and establish persistence by creating or abusing keys, such as prepending names with null characters to hide them from standard utilities. The intrusion-set Lazarus has been associated with this technique.[/profile]
767.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Registry Key Manipulation, identified as MITRE ATT&CK T1112, is a defense evasion and persistence technique within the Windows platform. Adversaries interact with the Windows Registry to hide configuration data or payloads, impair defenses by modifying security settings, and establish persistence by altering service execution paths or abusing features like the Microsoft Office "Office Test" key. This is commonly performed using built-in utilities like Reg.exe or remote access tools, often requiring administrative privileges for key modifications and leveraging weaknesses in Registry key permissions to redirect legitimate processes to malicious executables.

768.name: Network Enumeration Tools
768.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may enumerate system and service logs to find useful data. These logs may highlight various types of valuable insights for an adversary, such as user authentication records ([Account Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1087)), security or vulnerable software ([Software Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1518)), or hosts within a compromised network ([Remote System Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1018)).

Host binaries may be leveraged to collect system logs. Examples include using `wevtutil.exe` or [PowerShell](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001) on Windows to access and/or export security event information.(Citation: WithSecure Lazarus-NoPineapple Threat Intel Report 2023)(Citation: Cadet Blizzard emerges as novel threat actor) In cloud environments, adversaries may leverage utilities such as the Azure VM Agent’s `CollectGuestLogs.exe` to collect security logs from cloud hosted infrastructure.(Citation: SIM Swapping and Abuse of the Microsoft Azure Serial Console)

Adversaries may also target centralized logging infrastructure such as SIEMs. Logs may also be bulk exported and sent to adversary-controlled infrastructure for offline analysis.

In addition to gaining a better understanding of the environment, adversaries may also monitor logs in real time to track incident response procedures. This may allow them to adjust their techniques in order to maintain persistence or evade defenses.(Citation: Permiso GUI-Vil 2023)
768.profile: [profile]Network Enumeration Tools, mapped to the MITRE ATT&CK technique Log Enumeration (T1654) under the Discovery tactic for Windows and Cloud platforms, involves adversaries using built-in system utilities to collect and analyze logs for reconnaissance. Specific technical mechanics include using commands like `wevtutil.exe` or PowerShell on Windows to export security event logs, and leveraging cloud utilities such as Azure VM Agent's `CollectGuestLogs.exe` to harvest logs from cloud infrastructure. Adversaries may also target centralized logging systems like SIEMs, bulk export logs to adversary-controlled infrastructure for offline analysis, and monitor logs in real-time to track incident response and evade defenses. This technique is associated with groups including Volt Typhoon, APT5, Mustang Panda, Ember Bear, and Aquatic Panda.
768.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Network Enumeration Tools is a technique for discovering remote systems and network infrastructure. It maps to MITRE ATT&CK ID T1018 (Remote System Discovery) under the Discovery tactic. Adversaries use tools like ping, net view, or network device CLI commands (e.g., show cdp neighbors, show arp) to identify other hosts by IP, hostname, or logical identifiers for lateral movement. This activity is commonly associated with groups like Volt Typhoon, FIN6, and Sandworm Team.

769.name: Process Termination
769.profile: [profile]Process Termination is a technique used by adversaries to stop running processes, often to disrupt system functionality, evade detection, or remove security software. It is associated with the intrusion set Lazarus. The technique involves using commands or APIs like `taskkill` on Windows or `kill` on Linux/Unix to terminate specific processes by name or PID, which can disable defenses or cover tracks after malicious activity.
769.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Process Termination is a defense evasion technique where adversaries stop security software or forensic analysis processes to avoid detection. It operates across Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. The technical mechanics involve using native system commands or APIs like `taskkill` on Windows or `kill` on Unix-based systems to end specific processes. This action can disable endpoint protection, logging, or other defensive tools, allowing malicious activities to continue unimpeded.

770.name: Brute Force Attack
770.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may use brute force techniques to gain access to accounts when passwords are unknown or when password hashes are obtained.(Citation: TrendMicro Pawn Storm Dec 2020) Without knowledge of the password for an account or set of accounts, an adversary may systematically guess the password using a repetitive or iterative mechanism.(Citation: Dragos Crashoverride 2018) Brute forcing passwords can take place via interaction with a service that will check the validity of those credentials or offline against previously acquired credential data, such as password hashes.

Brute forcing credentials may take place at various points during a breach. For example, adversaries may attempt to brute force access to [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078) within a victim environment leveraging knowledge gathered from other post-compromise behaviors such as [OS Credential Dumping](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003), [Account Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1087), or [Password Policy Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1201). Adversaries may also combine brute forcing activity with behaviors such as [External Remote Services](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1133) as part of Initial Access. 

If an adversary guesses the correct password but fails to login to a compromised account due to location-based conditional access policies, they may change their infrastructure until they match the victim’s location and therefore bypass those policies.(Citation: ReliaQuest Health Care Social Engineering Campaign 2024)
770.profile: [profile]Brute Force Attack is identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1110 under the Credential Access tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. It involves systematically guessing passwords through repetitive mechanisms, either online against authentication services or offline using acquired password hashes. This technique is often combined with other behaviors like OS Credential Dumping for post-compromise access or with External Remote Services for initial access, and adversaries may adjust infrastructure to bypass location-based conditional access policies. It is associated with numerous threat groups including APT28, APT41, and Lazarus.[/profile]
770.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Brute Force Attack is identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1110, primarily within the Credential Access tactic and applicable across multiple platforms. It involves systematically guessing passwords through repetitive mechanisms, either via online interaction with authentication services or offline against acquired credential data like password hashes. This activity is often conducted against services such as SSH, SMB, RDP, and web applications, and may be combined with other techniques like OS Credential Dumping for initial access or to bypass conditional access policies by matching victim infrastructure.

771.name: File Property Spoofing
771.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may redirect network traffic to adversary-owned systems by spoofing Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) traffic and acting as a malicious DHCP server on the victim network. By achieving the adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) position, adversaries may collect network communications, including passed credentials, especially those sent over insecure, unencrypted protocols. This may also enable follow-on behaviors such as [Network Sniffing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1040) or [Transmitted Data Manipulation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1565/002). DHCP is based on a client-server model and has two functionalities: a protocol for providing network configuration settings from a DHCP server to a client and a mechanism for allocating network addresses to clients.(Citation: rfc2131) The typical server-client interaction is as follows: 1. The client broadcasts a `DISCOVER` message. 2. The server responds with an `OFFER` message, which includes an available network address. 3. The client broadcasts a `REQUEST` message, which includes the network address offered. 4. The server acknowledges with an `ACK` message and the client receives the network configuration parameters. Adversaries may spoof as a rogue DHCP server on the victim network, from which legitimate hosts may receive malicious network configurations. For example, malware can act as a DHCP server and provide adversary-owned DNS servers to the victimized computers.(Citation: new_rogue_DHCP_serv_malware)(Citation: w32.tidserv.g) Through the malicious network configurations, an adversary may achieve the AiTM position, route client traffic through adversary-controlled systems, and collect information from the client network. DHCPv6 clients can receive network configuration information without being assigned an IP address by sending a INFORMATION-REQUEST (code 11) message to the All_DHCP_Relay_Agents_and_Servers multicast address.(Citation: rfc3315) Adversaries may use their rogue DHCP server to respond to this request message with malicious network configurations. Rather than establishing an AiTM position, adversaries may also abuse DHCP spoofing to perform a DHCP exhaustion attack (i.e, [Service Exhaustion Flood](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1499/002)) by generating many broadcast DISCOVER messages to exhaust a network’s DHCP allocation pool.
771.profile: [profile]The entity is DHCP Spoofing, identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1557.003 under the Credential Access tactic, applicable to Network platforms. It involves an adversary operating a rogue DHCP server on a victim network to intercept and redirect client traffic. The technique works by responding to client DHCP DISCOVER or DHCPv6 INFORMATION-REQUEST messages with malicious network configurations, such as adversary-controlled DNS servers, to achieve an adversary-in-the-middle position for credential collection or to enable follow-on attacks like network sniffing. It has been associated with the intrusion set Lazarus.[/profile]
771.profile_without_enhance: [profile]File Property Spoofing, known as Masquerade File Type (T1036.008) under the Defense Evasion tactic, primarily targets Windows, Linux, and macOS. This technique involves adversaries disguising malicious payloads by altering file properties such as the file signature (magic bytes), extension, and icon to mimic legitimate file types like text (.txt) or image (.jpg) files. The goal is to bypass file validation checks and input sanitization, often during tool transfer or malware storage, by making the file appear benign to users and automated defenses. Polyglot files, which function as multiple file types, may also be used for this purpose.

772.name: Network Share Creation
772.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may look for folders and drives shared on remote systems as a means of identifying sources of information to gather as a precursor for Collection and to identify potential systems of interest for Lateral Movement. Networks often contain shared network drives and folders that enable users to access file directories on various systems across a network. File sharing over a Windows network occurs over the SMB protocol. (Citation: Wikipedia Shared Resource) (Citation: TechNet Shared Folder) [Net](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0039) can be used to query a remote system for available shared drives using the net view \\\\remotesystem command. It can also be used to query shared drives on the local system using net share. For macOS, the sharing -l command lists all shared points used for smb services.
772.profile: [profile]Network Share Discovery (T1135) is a Discovery technique used to identify shared folders and drives on remote or local systems, primarily on Windows and macOS platforms, as a precursor to data collection or lateral movement. It operates via the SMB protocol using commands like `net view \\\\remotesystem` or `net share` on Windows and `sharing -l` on macOS. This technique is associated with numerous threat groups including APT41, Lazarus, and Wizard Spider.
772.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Network Share Creation, identified as T1135 within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, falls under the Discovery tactic and primarily targets Windows and macOS platforms. This technique involves adversaries creating new shared folders or drives on a compromised system, often using the native `net share` command on Windows to establish a share, which can then be used as a source for information gathering or as a staging point for lateral movement across the network.

773.name: Sending System Details
773.profile: [profile]Sending System Details is a reconnaissance technique where adversaries gather detailed information about a victim's operating system and hardware, including version, patches, architecture, and configuration. This data, collected using tools like `systeminfo` or OS utilities, is used to shape follow-on attack behaviors and tailor payloads. The technique is associated with the Lazarus intrusion-set and numerous other threat groups.
773.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Sending System Details" is a cyber adversary behavior where collected system information is exfiltrated from a compromised host. This technique falls under the Collection tactic, as it involves gathering and transmitting data like OS version, hardware specs, and installed patches. The technical mechanics involve adversaries using commands or scripts to query system details and then sending this data to a remote server, often via standard protocols or encoded within outbound network traffic, to support further stages of an attack.

774.name: RC4 Encrypted Connection
774.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may employ an encryption algorithm to conceal command and control traffic rather than relying on any inherent protections provided by a communication protocol. Despite the use of a secure algorithm, these implementations may be vulnerable to reverse engineering if secret keys are encoded and/or generated within malware samples/configuration files.
774.profile: [profile]RC4 Encrypted Connection is a sub-technique of MITRE ATT&CK T1573.001 (Symmetric Cryptography) under the Command and Control tactic. It operates across Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. This technique uses the RC4 stream cipher to encrypt C2 traffic, providing obfuscation independent of the underlying protocol's security. The implementation's security can be compromised if the symmetric encryption key is hardcoded within the malware or its configuration, making it vulnerable to extraction and traffic decryption. It is associated with groups like Lazarus, Muddywater, and APT28.[/profile]
774.profile_without_enhance: [profile]RC4 Encrypted Connection is a technique for concealing network traffic, likely aligning with MITRE ATT&CK's T1573.001 (Symmetric Cryptography) under the Command and Control tactic. It involves using the RC4 symmetric encryption algorithm to obfuscate data in transit, often for C2 channels or data exfiltration. This method may be implemented manually within malware to encrypt protocol traffic, potentially creating multiple encryption layers when used over protocols like HTTP or HTTPS.

780.name: Volgmer
780.uncertain_mes: [Volgmer](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0180) is a backdoor Trojan designed to provide covert access to a compromised system. It has been used since at least 2013 to target the government, financial, automotive, and media industries. Its primary delivery mechanism is suspected to be spearphishing. (Citation: US-CERT Volgmer Nov 2017)
780.profile: [profile]Volgmer, also known as volgmer, is a backdoor Trojan attributed to the Lazarus Group (also referenced as HIDDEN COBRA). It has been used since at least 2013, primarily delivered via spearphishing, to target government, financial, automotive, and media sectors. Its key function is to provide covert access to compromised systems.[profile]
780.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Volgmer is a backdoor trojan malware, also known as a remote access trojan (RAT). It is attributed to the Lazarus Group, which is also associated with HIDDEN COBRA and TraderTraitor clusters. Key technical behaviors include providing covert access to compromised systems, using SSL encryption for command and control (C2) traffic, potentially employing a custom binary protocol for C2, and establishing persistence through Windows registry modification, such as updating service registry keys. It targets Windows platforms and has been used in campaigns against government, financial, automotive, and media sectors, with infrastructure involving C2 servers and static or dynamic IP addresses.

786.name: Pseudo-Random Naming
786.profile: [profile]Pseudo-Random Naming is a technique used for defense evasion, where adversaries generate file or resource names using algorithms that produce seemingly random or gibberish strings. This method, often implemented via Domain Generation Algorithms (DGAs), makes malicious artifacts appear benign and harder to block or track by defenders. It is commonly employed by groups like Lazarus to name malware or command-and-control infrastructure, complicating detection and analysis efforts.
786.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Pseudo-Random Naming is a sub-technique of Masquerading (T1036) within the Defense Evasion tactic. It operates by generating file or directory names that appear random or benign to blend in with legitimate system files, thereby evading detection. This technique is commonly used by adversaries across various platforms to hide malicious artifacts.

787.name: Trojan Malware
787.uncertain_mes:
A .NET rat targets Mongolia
A new document royal road v7 installs a backdoor in .NET. a first executable is dropped \os03C2.tmp. This exe has many similarities with older campaigns using by Operation LagTime or Tonto Team.
Document
The decoy document is a document about infection of covid19 in Russia send to the Mongolia Authorities. The document is fake signed A. Amarsaikhan.
787.profile: [profile]Name: nmass malware. Aliases: Trojan Malware. Attributed Groups: Operation LagTime, Tonto Team. Key TTPs/Technical Behaviors: A .NET-based remote access trojan (RAT) delivered via a Royal Road v7 document lure, dropping an initial executable (os03C2.tmp). The decoy is a fake document about COVID-19 infections in Russia, falsely signed by A. Amarsaikhan, targeting Mongolian authorities. Target Platforms: Windows. Infrastructure/Supplementary Info: Shares similarities with older campaigns by the attributed groups.
787.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Trojan Malware is a broad family of malicious software that includes backdoors like Volgmer, which is attributed to the Lazarus group (HIDDEN COBRA) and used in campaigns such as TraderTraitor for cryptocurrency theft. It provides covert access to compromised systems, with targeting observed since at least 2013 against government, financial, automotive, and media sectors. Specific variants within this family can include loaders, stealers, and keyloggers, and they are deployed via techniques like phishing and trojanized software infections. The malware primarily targets Windows platforms.

790.name: Collecting System Information
790.uncertain_mes: An adversary may attempt to get detailed information about the operating system and hardware, including version, patches, hotfixes, service packs, and architecture. Adversaries may use this information to shape follow-on behaviors, including whether or not the adversary fully infects the target and/or attempts specific actions. This behavior is distinct from [Local Storage Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1680) which is an adversary's discovery of local drive, disks and/or volumes. Tools such as [Systeminfo](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0096) can be used to gather detailed system information. If running with privileged access, a breakdown of system data can be gathered through the systemsetup configuration tool on macOS. Adversaries may leverage a [Network Device CLI](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/008) on network devices to gather detailed system information (e.g. show version).(Citation: US-CERT-TA18-106A) On ESXi servers, threat actors may gather system information from various esxcli utilities, such as `system hostname get` and `system version get`.(Citation: Crowdstrike Hypervisor Jackpotting Pt 2 2021)(Citation: Varonis) Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) cloud providers such as AWS, GCP, and Azure allow access to instance and virtual machine information via APIs. Successful authenticated API calls can return data such as the operating system platform and status of a particular instance or the model view of a virtual machine.(Citation: Amazon Describe Instance)(Citation: Google Instances Resource)(Citation: Microsoft Virutal Machine API) [System Information Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1082) combined with information gathered from other forms of discovery and reconnaissance can drive payload development and concealment.(Citation: OSX.FairyTale)(Citation: 20 macOS Common Tools and Techniques)
790.profile: [profile]System Information Discovery, identified as T1082, is a Discovery tactic used across Windows, macOS, Linux, Network, and IaaS platforms. It involves gathering detailed OS and hardware data like version, patches, and architecture using tools such as the `systeminfo` command on Windows, the `systemsetup` tool on macOS, CLI commands like `show version` on network devices, and `esxcli` utilities on ESXi servers. In cloud environments, adversaries leverage authenticated APIs (e.g., AWS, GCP, Azure) to query instance metadata. This information is used to shape follow-on attack behaviors and payload development.
790.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Collecting System Information is a technique aligned with MITRE ATT&CK ID T1082 under the Discovery tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It involves adversaries gathering detailed OS and hardware data like version, patches, and architecture to inform follow-on actions. Specific methods include using tools like the `systeminfo` command on Windows, the `systemsetup` tool on macOS with privileges, network device CLI commands (e.g., `show version`), and ESXi CLI utilities such as `system hostname get`. In cloud environments, adversaries may query IaaS APIs (e.g., AWS, GCP, Azure) to retrieve instance metadata. This information is often used for payload development and evasion.

791.name: Updating Service Registry Keys
791.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may achieve persistence by adding a program to a startup folder or referencing it with a Registry run key. Adding an entry to the "run keys" in the Registry or startup folder will cause the program referenced to be executed when a user logs in.(Citation: Microsoft Run Key) These programs will be executed under the context of the user and will have the account's associated permissions level. The following run keys are created by default on Windows systems: * HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run * HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunOnce * HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run * HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunOnce Run keys may exist under multiple hives.(Citation: Microsoft Wow6432Node 2018)(Citation: Malwarebytes Wow6432Node 2016) The HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunOnceEx is also available but is not created by default on Windows Vista and newer. Registry run key entries can reference programs directly or list them as a dependency.(Citation: Microsoft Run Key) For example, it is possible to load a DLL at logon using a "Depend" key with RunOnceEx: reg add HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunOnceEx\0001\Depend /v 1 /d "C:\temp\evil[.]dll" (Citation: Oddvar Moe RunOnceEx Mar 2018) Placing a program within a startup folder will also cause that program to execute when a user logs in. There is a startup folder location for individual user accounts as well as a system-wide startup folder that will be checked regardless of which user account logs in. The startup folder path for the current user is C:\Users\\[Username]\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup. The startup folder path for all users is C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\StartUp. The following Registry keys can be used to set startup folder items for persistence: * HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Explorer\User Shell Folders * HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Explorer\Shell Folders * HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Explorer\Shell Folders * HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Explorer\User Shell Folders The following Registry keys can control automatic startup of services during boot: * HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunServicesOnce * HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunServicesOnce * HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunServices * HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunServices Using policy settings to specify startup programs creates corresponding values in either of two Registry keys: * HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\Explorer\Run * HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\Explorer\Run Programs listed in the load value of the registry key HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Windows run automatically for the currently logged-on user. By default, the multistring BootExecute value of the registry key HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\System\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager is set to autocheck autochk *. This value causes Windows, at startup, to check the file-system integrity of the hard disks if the system has been shut down abnormally. Adversaries can add other programs or processes to this registry value which will automatically launch at boot. Adversaries can use these configuration locations to execute malware, such as remote access tools, to maintain persistence through system reboots. Adversaries may also use [Masquerading](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1036) to make the Registry entries look as if they are associated with legitimate programs.
791.profile: [profile]The entity "Updating Service Registry Keys" is the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1547.001, a Persistence tactic for Windows. It achieves persistence by adding entries to Registry run keys (e.g., HKCU\...\Run, HKLM\...\RunOnceEx) or placing executables in startup folders (e.g., C:\Users\[Username]\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup), causing referenced programs to execute automatically upon user login or system boot. The malware Volgmer is known to use this technique.
791.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Updating Service Registry Keys is a persistence technique where adversaries modify Windows service configuration data stored in the Registry, specifically under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services. By altering keys like binPath/ImagePath, FailureCommand, or Performance, they can redirect service execution to a malicious executable or DLL, enabling persistence and potential privilege escalation when the service starts, fails, or is invoked. This technique is executed using tools like sc.exe, PowerShell, or Reg and primarily targets the Windows platform.

792.name: Downloading/Uploading Files
792.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may attempt to steal Kerberos tickets stored in credential cache files (or ccache). These files are used for short term storage of a user's active session credentials. The ccache file is created upon user authentication and allows for access to multiple services without the user having to re-enter credentials. The /etc/krb5.conf configuration file and the KRB5CCNAME environment variable are used to set the storage location for ccache entries. On Linux, credentials are typically stored in the `/tmp` directory with a naming format of `krb5cc_%UID%` or `krb5.ccache`. On macOS, ccache entries are stored by default in memory with an `API:{uuid}` naming scheme. Typically, users interact with ticket storage using kinit, which obtains a Ticket-Granting-Ticket (TGT) for the principal; klist, which lists obtained tickets currently held in the credentials cache; and other built-in binaries.(Citation: Kerberos GNU/Linux)(Citation: Binary Defense Kerberos Linux) Adversaries can collect tickets from ccache files stored on disk and authenticate as the current user without their password to perform [Pass the Ticket](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1550/003) attacks. Adversaries can also use these tickets to impersonate legitimate users with elevated privileges to perform [Privilege Escalation](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0004). Tools like Kekeo can also be used by adversaries to convert ccache files to Windows format for further [Lateral Movement](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0008). On macOS, adversaries may use open-source tools or the Kerberos framework to interact with ccache files and extract TGTs or Service Tickets via lower-level APIs.(Citation: SpectorOps Bifrost Kerberos macOS 2019)(Citation: Linux Kerberos Tickets)(Citation: Brining MimiKatz to Unix)(Citation: Kekeo)
792.profile: [profile]Steal Kerberos Ticket Granting Tickets, identified as T1558.005, is a Credential Access technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework targeting Linux and macOS platforms. It involves adversaries stealing Kerberos tickets from credential cache (ccache) files, which are stored on disk in locations like `/tmp/krb5cc_%UID%` on Linux or in memory on macOS. The stolen tickets, including Ticket-Granting Tickets (TGTs), enable authentication without a password to perform Pass the Ticket attacks, privilege escalation, and lateral movement, with tools like Kekeo used to convert ccache files for use on Windows systems.[/profile]
792.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Downloading/Uploading Files" is a fundamental action, not a distinct MITRE ATT&CK technique. It is a core component of numerous techniques, primarily facilitating command and control, lateral movement, and exfiltration. Key related techniques include Ingress Tool Transfer (T1105) for bringing tools into a compromised environment, Stage Capabilities (T1608) for setting up infrastructure, and Exfiltration to Cloud Storage (T1567.002) for data theft. Common utilities for execution across Windows, Linux, and macOS include `certutil`, `PowerShell`, `curl`, `wget`, `scp`, and `ftp`. This behavior is foundational to adversary operations across all intrusion phases.

794.name: Executing Commands
794.profile: [profile]Executing Commands is a core technique (T1059: Command and Scripting Interpreter) under the Execution tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. It involves abusing built-in or cross-platform interpreters like Unix Shell, Windows Command Shell, PowerShell, Python, JavaScript, or Visual Basic to run arbitrary commands. This can be achieved by embedding commands in initial access payloads, using interactive shells, or leveraging remote services. The malware Volgmer is known to use this technique.
794.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Executing Commands is a foundational technique (T1059) within the Execution tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. It involves adversaries abusing command-line interfaces and scripting interpreters, such as Unix Shell, Windows Command Shell, PowerShell, Python, or JavaScript, to run arbitrary commands. This can be achieved through interactive shells, scripts embedded in initial access payloads, or via remote services, and is often used to establish persistence by inserting malicious commands into shell configuration files like /etc/profile or ~/.bashrc.

795.name: Terminating Processes
795.profile: [profile]Terminating Processes is a technique where adversaries stop system processes to disrupt operations, evade detection, or enable further malicious actions. It is often used to disable critical services, security tools, or specific applications, as seen with malware like Volgmer. This can facilitate data destruction, encryption, or inhibit incident response by rendering services or security monitoring unavailable.[/profile]
795.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Terminating Processes is a technique adversaries use to stop or disable services and processes on a system, often to inhibit incident response, cause damage, or enable follow-on actions like Data Destruction or Data Encrypted for Impact. This can involve disabling critical individual services, such as MSExchangeIS to make Exchange content inaccessible, or stopping many/all services to render systems unusable. Adversaries may also stop services in cloud environments, for example by using the DisableAPIServiceAccess API in AWS to prevent service-linked role creation.

796.name: Listing Directories
796.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may set files and directories to be hidden to evade detection mechanisms. To prevent normal users from accidentally changing special files on a system, most operating systems have the concept of a ‘hidden’ file. These files don’t show up when a user browses the file system with a GUI or when using normal commands on the command line. Users must explicitly ask to show the hidden files either via a series of Graphical User Interface (GUI) prompts or with command line switches (dir /a for Windows and ls –a for Linux and macOS). On Linux and Mac, users can mark specific files as hidden simply by putting a “.” as the first character in the file or folder name (Citation: Sofacy Komplex Trojan) (Citation: Antiquated Mac Malware). Files and folders that start with a period, ‘.’, are by default hidden from being viewed in the Finder application and standard command-line utilities like “ls”. Users must specifically change settings to have these files viewable. Files on macOS can also be marked with the UF_HIDDEN flag which prevents them from being seen in Finder.app, but still allows them to be seen in Terminal.app (Citation: WireLurker). On Windows, users can mark specific files as hidden by using the attrib.exe binary. Many applications create these hidden files and folders to store information so that it doesn’t clutter up the user’s workspace. For example, SSH utilities create a .ssh folder that’s hidden and contains the user’s known hosts and keys. Additionally, adversaries may name files in a manner that would allow the file to be hidden such as naming a file only a “space” character. Adversaries can use this to their advantage to hide files and folders anywhere on the system and evading a typical user or system analysis that does not incorporate investigation of hidden files.
796.profile: [profile]The entity "Listing Directories" is a technique where adversaries enumerate files and directories to gather system information. Its technical mechanics involve using command-line utilities like `dir` on Windows or `ls` on Linux and macOS to list contents, which aids in discovery for follow-on actions. The malware Volgmer is associated with this behavior. While the provided data suggests a potential link to the MITRE technique "Hidden Files and Directories" (T1564.001), the core activity described is directory listing, not file hiding. Therefore, the primary focus is on the enumeration aspect as a discovery method.
796.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Listing Directories" is a Discovery technique. This activity supports follow-on actions by mapping the file system structure to identify data of interest or other targets.

797.name: Botnet Controller Functionality
797.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may buy, lease, or rent a network of compromised systems that can be used during targeting. A botnet is a network of compromised systems that can be instructed to perform coordinated tasks.(Citation: Norton Botnet) Adversaries may purchase a subscription to use an existing botnet from a booter/stresser service. 

Internet-facing edge devices and related network appliances that are end-of-life (EOL) and unsupported by their manufacturers are commonly acquired for botnet activities. Adversaries may lease operational relay box (ORB) networks – consisting of virtual private servers (VPS), small office/home office (SOHO) routers, or Internet of Things (IoT) devices – to serve as a botnet.(Citation: ORB Mandiant) 

With a botnet at their disposal, adversaries may perform follow-on activity such as large-scale [Phishing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566) or Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS).(Citation: Imperva DDoS for Hire)(Citation: Krebs-Anna)(Citation: Krebs-Bazaar)(Citation: Krebs-Booter) Acquired botnets may also be used to support Command and Control activity, such as [Hide Infrastructure](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1665) through an established [Proxy](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1090) network.
797.profile: [profile]Botnet Controller Functionality is a sub-technique, ID T1583.005, under the Resource Development tactic. It involves adversaries acquiring a pre-existing network of compromised systems (a botnet) by purchasing, leasing, or renting it from services. These botnets are often built from end-of-life internet devices, SOHO routers, IoT devices, or VPS networks. Once acquired, the botnet provides functionality for follow-on attacks like large-scale phishing, DDoS campaigns, or to establish proxy networks for command and control infrastructure.
797.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Botnet Controller Functionality is a technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, specifically identified as sub-technique T1583.005 under the Resource Development tactic. It operates across multiple platforms. The core technical mechanic involves an adversary leasing or renting an existing botnet infrastructure, such as operational relay box (ORB) networks consisting of virtual private servers (VPS), SOHO routers, or IoT devices, from a booter/stresser service. This acquired network of compromised systems provides the controller functionality to perform coordinated follow-on activities like large-scale phishing or distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks, and can also be used to hide command and control infrastructure through proxy networks.

798.name: SSL Encryption
798.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may compromise a network device’s encryption capability in order to bypass encryption that would otherwise protect data communications. (Citation: Cisco Synful Knock Evolution)

Encryption can be used to protect transmitted network traffic to maintain its confidentiality (protect against unauthorized disclosure) and integrity (protect against unauthorized changes). Encryption ciphers are used to convert a plaintext message to ciphertext and can be computationally intensive to decipher without the associated decryption key. Typically, longer keys increase the cost of cryptanalysis, or decryption without the key.

Adversaries can compromise and manipulate devices that perform encryption of network traffic. For example, through behaviors such as [Modify System Image](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1601), [Reduce Key Space](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1600/001), and [Disable Crypto Hardware](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1600/002), an adversary can negatively effect and/or eliminate a device’s ability to securely encrypt network traffic. This poses a greater risk of unauthorized disclosure and may help facilitate data manipulation, Credential Access, or Collection efforts. (Citation: Cisco Blog Legacy Device Attacks)
798.profile: [profile]SSL Encryption, identified as T1600 within the MITRE ATT&CK framework under the Impact tactic, targets network platforms. This technique involves compromising a network device's encryption capability to bypass data protection. Adversaries achieve this through specific sub-techniques like Reduce Key Space (T1600.001) and Disable Crypto Hardware (T1600.002), which manipulate or eliminate the device's ability to securely encrypt traffic, thereby increasing the risk of unauthorized data disclosure and facilitating other malicious efforts such as data manipulation or credential access.[/profile]
798.profile_without_enhance: [profile]SSL Encryption, identified as T1573.002 within the MITRE ATT&CK framework under the Command and Control tactic, is a technique where adversaries use the SSL/TLS protocol to conceal C2 traffic. It employs asymmetric cryptography to establish a secure session, after which symmetric encryption is typically used for efficient data transfer. This method is distinct from general encryption weakening or multilayer encryption and is commonly implemented to obfuscate communications in protocols like HTTPS.

799.name: Custom Binary Protocol
799.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may use a custom cryptographic protocol or algorithm to hide command and control traffic. A simple scheme, such as XOR-ing the plaintext with a fixed key, will produce a very weak ciphertext.

Custom encryption schemes may vary in sophistication. Analysis and reverse engineering of malware samples may be enough to discover the algorithm and encryption key used.

Some adversaries may also attempt to implement their own version of a well-known cryptographic algorithm instead of using a known implementation library, which may lead to unintentional errors. (Citation: F-Secure Cosmicduke)
799.profile: [profile]Named Custom Binary Protocol, this technique corresponds to MITRE ATT&CK ID T1024 under the Command and Control tactic. It involves adversaries designing and implementing a non-standard network protocol for C2 communications to evade detection by blending with or avoiding known protocol patterns. Implementations can range from simple XOR-based encryption with a fixed key, which is cryptographically weak, to more complex custom schemes or flawed re-implementations of standard algorithms, as seen with malware like Volgmer and Carbanak. The custom protocol operates atop standard network stacks like TCP/IP, distinct from protocol tunneling which encapsulates traffic within another protocol's encryption layer.
799.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Custom Binary Protocol is a command and control technique where adversaries implement a non-standard, application-layer communication protocol, often using raw sockets or mimicking legitimate protocols, to evade detection by blending with normal traffic or bypassing filters that rely on known protocol analysis. This method is distinct from simple encryption and involves the design of unique client-server data exchange formats.

800.name: Registry Modification
800.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may interact with the Windows Registry as part of a variety of other techniques to aid in defense evasion, persistence, and execution.

Access to specific areas of the Registry depends on account permissions, with some keys requiring administrator-level access. The built-in Windows command-line utility [Reg](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0075) may be used for local or remote Registry modification.(Citation: Microsoft Reg) Other tools, such as remote access tools, may also contain functionality to interact with the Registry through the Windows API.

The Registry may be modified in order to hide configuration information or malicious payloads via [Obfuscated Files or Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027).(Citation: Unit42 BabyShark Feb 2019)(Citation: Avaddon Ransomware 2021)(Citation: Microsoft BlackCat Jun 2022)(Citation: CISA Russian Gov Critical Infra 2018) The Registry may also be modified to [Impair Defenses](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1562), such as by enabling macros for all Microsoft Office products, allowing privilege escalation without alerting the user, increasing the maximum number of allowed outbound requests, and/or modifying systems to store plaintext credentials in memory.(Citation: CISA LockBit 2023)(Citation: Unit42 BabyShark Feb 2019)

The Registry of a remote system may be modified to aid in execution of files as part of lateral movement. It requires the remote Registry service to be running on the target system.(Citation: Microsoft Remote) Often [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078) are required, along with access to the remote system's [SMB/Windows Admin Shares](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002) for RPC communication.

Finally, Registry modifications may also include actions to hide keys, such as prepending key names with a null character, which will cause an error and/or be ignored when read via [Reg](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0075) or other utilities using the Win32 API.(Citation: Microsoft Reghide NOV 2006) Adversaries may abuse these pseudo-hidden keys to conceal payloads/commands used to maintain persistence.(Citation: TrendMicro POWELIKS AUG 2014)(Citation: SpectorOps Hiding Reg Jul 2017)
800.profile: [profile]Registry Modification, identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1112, is a defense evasion, persistence, and execution technique primarily for Windows. Adversaries use tools like the built-in Reg utility or remote access tools to interact with the Windows Registry. Specific technical mechanics include modifying registry keys to hide configuration or payloads, impair defenses by enabling macros or storing plaintext credentials, and enabling lateral movement by modifying remote registries via SMB/RPC. A notable evasion method involves prepending key names with a null character to create pseudo-hidden keys that conceal persistence mechanisms.
800.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Registry Modification is identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1112, primarily supporting Defense Evasion, Persistence, and Execution tactics on Windows platforms. It involves adversaries interacting with the Windows Registry using tools like the built-in Reg utility or remote access tools via the Windows API to modify keys and values. Specific technical mechanics include hiding configuration or payloads via obfuscation, impairing defenses by enabling macros or modifying credential storage settings, and facilitating lateral movement by modifying remote registries, which often requires valid accounts and SMB admin shares. Attackers may also hide keys by prepending names with null characters to create pseudo-hidden keys for concealing persistence mechanisms.

815.name: Wiper Attack
815.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may downgrade or use a version of system features that may be outdated, vulnerable, and/or does not support updated security controls. Downgrade attacks typically take advantage of a system’s backward compatibility to force it into less secure modes of operation. 

Adversaries may downgrade and use various less-secure versions of features of a system, such as [Command and Scripting Interpreter](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059)s or even network protocols that can be abused to enable [Adversary-in-the-Middle](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1557) or [Network Sniffing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1040).(Citation: Praetorian TLS Downgrade Attack 2014) For example, [PowerShell](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001) versions 5+ includes Script Block Logging (SBL), which can record executed script content. However, adversaries may attempt to execute a previous version of PowerShell that does not support SBL with the intent to [Impair Defenses](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1562) while running malicious scripts that may have otherwise been detected.(Citation: CrowdStrike BGH Ransomware 2021)(Citation: Mandiant BYOL 2018)(Citation: att_def_ps_logging)

Adversaries may similarly target network traffic to downgrade from an encrypted HTTPS connection to an unsecured HTTP connection that exposes network data in clear text.(Citation: Targeted SSL Stripping Attacks Are Real)(Citation: Crowdstrike Downgrade) On Windows systems, adversaries may downgrade the boot manager to a vulnerable version that bypasses Secure Boot, granting the ability to disable various operating system security mechanisms.(Citation: SafeBreach)
815.profile: [profile]The entity is a Downgrade Attack, formally identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1562.010 (Impair Defenses: Downgrade Attack). This technique operates on Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It works by exploiting a system's backward compatibility to force it into less secure modes, such as executing an older version of PowerShell to bypass Script Block Logging, downgrading HTTPS connections to unencrypted HTTP to expose data, or manipulating the Windows boot manager to a vulnerable version that disables Secure Boot and other OS security mechanisms. The intrusion set Lazarus has been associated with this technique.[/profile]
815.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Wiper Attack is a destructive technique aimed at rendering systems inoperable by corrupting or deleting critical data and system files, often to disrupt operations or destroy forensic evidence. It typically aligns with the Impact tactic (T1485) and targets multiple platforms including Windows, Linux, and macOS. Technical mechanics involve overwriting the Master Boot Record (MBR) or specific file systems with random data, using custom malware like Shamoon or NotPetya, and employing commands such as `dd` or `format` to destroy partitions. This attack is distinct from data encryption in ransomware and is frequently associated with hacktivist or state-sponsored campaigns.

816.name: Destructive Malware
816.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may develop malware and malware components that can be used during targeting. Building malicious software can include the development of payloads, droppers, post-compromise tools, backdoors (including backdoored images), packers, C2 protocols, and the creation of infected removable media. Adversaries may develop malware to support their operations, creating a means for maintaining control of remote machines, evading defenses, and executing post-compromise behaviors.(Citation: Mandiant APT1)(Citation: Kaspersky Sofacy)(Citation: ActiveMalwareEnergy)(Citation: FBI Flash FIN7 USB)

During malware development, adversaries may intentionally include indicators aligned with other known actors in order to mislead attribution by defenders.(Citation: Olympic Destroyer)(Citation: Risky Bulletin Threat actor impersonates FSB APT)(Citation: GamaCopy organization)

As with legitimate development efforts, different skill sets may be required for developing malware. The skills needed may be located in-house, or may need to be contracted out. Use of a contractor may be considered an extension of that adversary's malware development capabilities, provided the adversary plays a role in shaping requirements and maintains a degree of exclusivity to the malware.

Some aspects of malware development, such as C2 protocol development, may require adversaries to obtain additional infrastructure. For example, malware developed that will communicate with Twitter for C2, may require use of [Web Services](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1583/006).(Citation: FireEye APT29)
816.profile: [profile]The entity "Destructive Malware" is a type of malware specifically designed to cause irrecoverable damage. It operates under the Impact tactic (T1488) on Windows platforms. Its core technical mechanic involves directly overwriting arbitrary portions of a disk's content with random data, often using third-party drivers like RawDisk for low-level access, to render data unrecoverable and interrupt system availability. This malware may propagate across networks using worm-like features, leveraging techniques such as Valid Accounts and Windows Admin Shares. It is associated with threat groups like Lazarus, as referenced in its destructive operations.
816.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Destructive Malware is a technique where adversaries deploy malware specifically designed to cause widespread damage and disrupt availability. It is mapped to MITRE ATT&CK technique T1485 (Data Destruction) under the Impact tactic, targeting Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. The malware's core technical mechanic is the irreversible overwriting or deletion of data on storage devices, often using direct disk access via tools like RawDisk to bypass the operating system. It can propagate across networks using worm-like capabilities, leveraging credentials and admin shares to maximize destruction, as seen in campaigns like Lazarus Group's attacks.

817.name: Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures (TTPS)
817.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may abuse SQL stored procedures to establish persistent access to systems. SQL Stored Procedures are code that can be saved and reused so that database users do not waste time rewriting frequently used SQL queries. Stored procedures can be invoked via SQL statements to the database using the procedure name or via defined events (e.g. when a SQL server application is started/restarted).

Adversaries may craft malicious stored procedures that can provide a persistence mechanism in SQL database servers.(Citation: NetSPI Startup Stored Procedures)(Citation: Kaspersky MSSQL Aug 2019) To execute operating system commands through SQL syntax the adversary may have to enable additional functionality, such as xp_cmdshell for MSSQL Server.(Citation: NetSPI Startup Stored Procedures)(Citation: Kaspersky MSSQL Aug 2019)(Citation: Microsoft xp_cmdshell 2017) 

Microsoft SQL Server can enable common language runtime (CLR) integration. With CLR integration enabled, application developers can write stored procedures using any .NET framework language (e.g. VB .NET, C#, etc.).(Citation: Microsoft CLR Integration 2017) Adversaries may craft or modify CLR assemblies that are linked to stored procedures since these CLR assemblies can be made to execute arbitrary commands.(Citation: NetSPI SQL Server CLR)
817.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique "SQL Stored Procedures" (ID: T1505.001) under the Persistence tactic, targeting Windows platforms. It involves adversaries creating or modifying SQL stored procedures to maintain persistent access to database servers. This can include enabling and using built-in features like xp_cmdshell to execute operating system commands or leveraging CLR integration to run custom .NET assemblies that execute arbitrary commands, often requiring elevated database permissions to implement.[/profile]
817.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures (TTPs) is a broad concept in threat intelligence, not a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique. It refers to the patterns of behavior, methods, and tools used by adversaries during cyber attacks. The retrieved information illustrates various specific TTPs, such as Environmental Keying (T1480.001) which uses cryptography to constrain malware execution to a specific target environment, and techniques for persistence like abusing SQL stored procedures (T1505.001) or Linux file permissions (T1222.002). These examples demonstrate how TTPs encompass the detailed technical mechanics and procedures that define adversary tradecraft.

It was employed in the 2009 Operation Troy campaign alongside Mydoom to conduct a large-scale DDoS attack against US and South Korean websites, impacting about three dozen targets and placing the text "Memory of Independence Day" in the master boot record (MBR).[/profile]
