It was attributed to the Lazarus Group and was employed to conduct a large-scale, unsophisticated DDoS attack against US and South Korean websites. Its key technical behavior involved overwriting the master boot record (MBR) of infected systems with the text "Memory of Independence Day."

825.name: Mydoom
825.profile: [profile]Mydoom, also known as MyDoom, is a worm attributed to the Lazarus intrusion set. It propagates via email, as evidenced by email screenshots, and has been active since at least 2004 with continued sightings. Its source code has been published online. The primary target platform is Windows systems.
825.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Malware Name: Mydoom. Aliases: None explicitly stated. Attributed Groups: Potentially linked to the Lazarus APT group. Key TTPs/Technical Behaviors: Propagates as a worm, notably via email campaigns, with source code publicly available. Target Platforms: Windows systems. Infrastructure/Supplementary Info: First major activity in 2004, with reports of continued propagation in recent years.

826.name: Massive DDoS Attacks
826.profile: [profile]Massive DDoS Attacks is a distributed denial-of-service technique (aligned with MITRE ATT&CK T1498 - Network Denial of Service, under the Impact tactic) targeting network bandwidth to degrade or block service availability. It typically involves a botnet generating a high-volume flood of network packets, often using stateless protocols like UDP or ICMP, to saturate the target's connection. Attackers may spoof source IP addresses to obscure the traffic origin and complicate defense. This method has been used by groups like Lazarus for purposes including political disruption, hacktivism, and extortion.[/profile]
826.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Massive DDoS Attacks is a distributed denial-of-service technique targeting network or endpoint availability, often categorized under MITRE ATT&CK techniques like T1498 (Network Denial of Service) or T1499 (Endpoint Denial of Service) within the Impact tactic. It typically involves using a botnet to generate a high volume of traffic from many systems to exhaust the target's bandwidth or system resources, frequently employing IP address spoofing to obscure the attack source and complicate defense. These attacks are used for purposes such as extortion, hacktivism, or political disruption, as seen in campaigns by groups like APT28 and Sandworm Team.[/profile]

836.name: Dark Seoul Operation
836.profile: [profile]Dark Seoul Operation is a cyber campaign attributed to the Lazarus intrusion-set. The campaign involved the use of data wiper malware to destroy data on compromised systems, specifically targeting South Korean media and financial institutions in 2013. This disruptive attack caused significant operational damage by erasing hard drives and master boot records of infected computers.
836.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Dark Seoul Operation is a specific cyber attack campaign, not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the retrieved context, it is associated with techniques for gathering victim information from closed or paid sources, such as private databases or dark web markets, to enable further reconnaissance, capability development, or initial access. The campaign's mechanics involve purchasing technical data like employee contacts or infrastructure details to identify and exploit targets.

837.name: Wiper Tools
837.uncertain_mes: [Wiper](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0041) is a family of destructive malware used in March 2013 during breaches of South Korean banks and media companies. (Citation: Dell Wiper)
837.profile: [profile]Wiper Tools, also known as Wiper, is a family of destructive malware attributed to the Lazarus intrusion set. It was used in March 2013 during breaches of South Korean banks and media companies. Its primary function is data wiping, as indicated by related malware components like HermeticWiper and the data wiper component within Industroyer, targeting critical infrastructure and corporate networks.[/profile]
837.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Wiper Tools is a family of destructive malware, also known as wiper, used in targeted attacks such as the March 2013 breaches of South Korean banks and media companies. It functions as a data wiper component designed to destroy information on compromised systems, with related tools potentially including port scanners and denial-of-service (DoS) utilities. Its primary target platforms are Windows-based systems within critical infrastructure sectors like finance and media. Associated infrastructure and supplementary tools may involve components like an OPC DA payload for industrial control system (ICS) targeting.

838.name: Lateral Movement
838.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may transfer tools or other files between systems in a compromised environment. Once brought into the victim environment (i.e., [Ingress Tool Transfer](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1105)) files may then be copied from one system to another to stage adversary tools or other files over the course of an operation.

Adversaries may copy files between internal victim systems to support lateral movement using inherent file sharing protocols such as file sharing over [SMB/Windows Admin Shares](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002) to connected network shares or with authenticated connections via [Remote Desktop Protocol](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/001).(Citation: Unit42 LockerGoga 2019)

Files can also be transferred using native or otherwise present tools on the victim system, such as scp, rsync, curl, sftp, and [ftp](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0095). In some cases, adversaries may be able to leverage [Web Service](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1102)s such as Dropbox or OneDrive to copy files from one machine to another via shared, automatically synced folders.(Citation: Dropbox Malware Sync)
838.profile: [profile]Lateral Tool Transfer is a Lateral Movement technique (MITRE ATT&CK ID T1570) used across Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves transferring files between compromised systems using inherent protocols like SMB/Windows Admin Shares or authenticated RDP sessions. Adversaries also leverage native tools such as scp, rsync, curl, sftp, and FTP, or abuse web services like Dropbox and OneDrive via automatically synced folders to stage tools and facilitate further movement within a network. This technique is associated with groups including APT41, Turla, and Volt Typhoon.[/profile]
838.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Lateral Movement is a high-level tactic (TA0008) within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, representing the adversary's actions to move through a network after initial access. It is not a single technique but a category encompassing various methods like lateral tool transfer (T1570), which involves copying files between systems using protocols like SMB or tools like scp and rsync. Adversaries also abuse local accounts (T1078.003) by reusing passwords to move laterally and elevate privileges across the network.

839.name: Hangman Malware
839.uncertain_mes:
A .NET rat targets Mongolia
A new document royal road v7 installs a backdoor in .NET. a first executable is dropped \os03C2.tmp. This exe has many similarities with older campaigns using by Operation LagTime or Tonto Team.
Document
The decoy document is a document about infection of covid19 in Russia send to the Mongolia Authorities. The document is fake signed A. Amarsaikhan.
839.profile: [profile]Hangman Malware, also known as nmass malware, is a .NET-based remote access trojan (RAT) attributed to the Lazarus intrusion set. It is deployed via spearphishing using a malicious Royal Road v7 document, often a fake COVID-19 report for Mongolia, and drops an initial executable (e.g., \os03C2.tmp). Its technical behavior shows similarities to campaigns by Operation LagTime or Tonto Team, and it primarily targets Windows platforms.
839.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Hangman Malware, attributed to the Lazarus Group, was deployed in spearphishing campaigns from 2014-2015, including attacks using the CVE-2015-6585 zero-day vulnerability. Its activity is associated with broader operations like Operation Troy and DarkSeoul, and it shares a timeline with other Lazarus malware such as Wild Positron/Duuzer.

840.name: Darkseoul
840.profile: [profile]Darkseoul, also known as DarkSeoul, is attributed to the Lazarus intrusion set. It is referenced in the context of other malware like Wannacryptor and Bankshot, with file paths indicating its presence in directories such as './troydarkseoul/DarkSeoul/' and associated with file hashes like 0A8032CD-6B4A710B1771A080FA09FB87, DB4BBD-C36A78A8807AD9B15A562515C4, and F0E045210E3258DAD91D7B6B4D64E7F3.[/profile]
840.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Darkseoul is a malware attributed to the Lazarus Group, with technical indicators including file paths and timestamps such as './troydarkseoul/DarkSeoul/DarkSeoul_0A8032CD-6B4A710B1771A080FA09FB87' from 2013-01-31. It is associated with other malware like Wannacryptor and Bankshot, which share similar file structures and are also linked to the Lazarus Group.

841.name: Spear-Phishing
841.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may send phishing messages to gain access to victim systems. All forms of phishing are electronically delivered social engineering. Phishing can be targeted, known as spearphishing. In spearphishing, a specific individual, company, or industry will be targeted by the adversary. More generally, adversaries can conduct non-targeted phishing, such as in mass malware spam campaigns.

Adversaries may send victims emails containing malicious attachments or links, typically to execute malicious code on victim systems. Phishing may also be conducted via third-party services, like social media platforms. Phishing may also involve social engineering techniques, such as posing as a trusted source, as well as evasive techniques such as removing or manipulating emails or metadata/headers from compromised accounts being abused to send messages (e.g., [Email Hiding Rules](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1564/008)).(Citation: Microsoft OAuth Spam 2022)(Citation: Palo Alto Unit 42 VBA Infostealer 2014) Another way to accomplish this is by [Email Spoofing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1672)(Citation: Proofpoint-spoof) the identity of the sender, which can be used to fool both the human recipient as well as automated security tools,(Citation: cyberproof-double-bounce) or by including the intended target as a party to an existing email thread that includes malicious files or links (i.e., "thread hijacking").(Citation: phishing-krebs)

Victims may also receive phishing messages that instruct them to call a phone number where they are directed to visit a malicious URL, download malware,(Citation: sygnia Luna Month)(Citation: CISA Remote Monitoring and Management Software) or install adversary-accessible remote management tools onto their computer (i.e., [User Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204)).(Citation: Unit42 Luna Moth)
841.profile: [profile]Spear-Phishing, also known as T1566, is an Initial Access tactic used across multiple platforms. It involves sending targeted electronic messages, often emails, to specific individuals or organizations. The messages contain malicious attachments or links designed to trick the recipient into executing code, leveraging social engineering by posing as a trusted source. Evasive techniques include email spoofing, thread hijacking, and manipulating email metadata. Associated threat groups include APT17, Lazarus, and FIN7.[profile]
841.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Spear-Phishing is a targeted social engineering technique, corresponding to MITRE ATT&CK ID T1566 under the Initial Access tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It involves sending tailored electronic messages, such as emails, to specific individuals or organizations to deliver malicious attachments or links that execute code, often employing sender spoofing or thread hijacking to appear legitimate. This method is distinct from broad phishing campaigns due to its precise targeting.

843.name: Positron/Duuzer
843.profile: [profile]Positron/Duuzer, also known as Duuzer and Wild Positron/Duuzer, is attributed to the Lazarus Group. It is associated with spearphishing campaigns exploiting vulnerabilities like CVE-2015-6585 and was deployed around 2015, linked to broader operations such as DarkSeoul.[/profile]
843.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Positron/Duuzer, also known as Duuzer, is attributed to the Lazarus Group. It was deployed in 2015 and is associated with spearphishing attacks leveraging the CVE-2015-6585 zero-day vulnerability. Its technical behaviors include using a dropper for deployment. The target platform is Windows.

844.name: Code Obfuscation Techniques
844.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may obfuscate command and control traffic to make it more difficult to detect.(Citation: Bitdefender FunnyDream Campaign November 2020) Command and control (C2) communications are hidden (but not necessarily encrypted) in an attempt to make the content more difficult to discover or decipher and to make the communication less conspicuous and hide commands from being seen. This encompasses many methods, such as adding junk data to protocol traffic, using steganography, or impersonating legitimate protocols.
844.profile: [profile]The entity aligns with MITRE ATT&CK technique T1001, Data Obfuscation, under the Command and Control tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. This technique involves hiding C2 communications to evade detection, not necessarily through encryption. Specific methods include adding junk data to protocol traffic, using steganography to conceal data within other files, and impersonating legitimate protocols to blend in with normal network activity. It is associated with groups like Gamaredon Group and Lazarus.
844.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Code Obfuscation Techniques" is a general concept for evading detection, aligning with the MITRE ATT&CK technique Obfuscated Files or Information (T1027) under the Defense Evasion tactic. It operates across multiple platforms and involves methods to make code or files difficult to analyze. Specific technical mechanics include encrypting or encoding file content, using polymorphic code that mutates with each execution, and applying command-line obfuscation with special characters, string splitting, or tools like Invoke-Obfuscation. These techniques are used by numerous threat groups to hide malicious functionality from signature-based defenses.

845.name: Commercial Software Protectors
845.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may gather information about the victim's host software that can be used during targeting. Information about installed software may include a variety of details such as types and versions on specific hosts, as well as the presence of additional components that might be indicative of added defensive protections (ex: antivirus, SIEMs, etc.).

Adversaries may gather this information in various ways, such as direct collection actions via [Active Scanning](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1595) (ex: listening ports, server banners, user agent strings) or [Phishing for Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1598). Adversaries may also compromise sites then include malicious content designed to collect host information from visitors.(Citation: ATT ScanBox) Information about the installed software may also be exposed to adversaries via online or other accessible data sets (ex: job postings, network maps, assessment reports, resumes, or purchase invoices). Additionally, adversaries may analyze metadata from victim-owned files (e.g., PDFs, DOCs, images, and sound files hosted on victim-owned websites) to extract information about the software and hardware used to create or process those files. Metadata may reveal software versions, configurations, or timestamps that indicate outdated or vulnerable software. This information can be cross-referenced with known CVEs to identify potential vectors for exploitation in future operations.(Citation: Outpost24)

Gathering this information may reveal opportunities for other forms of reconnaissance (ex: [Search Open Websites/Domains](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1593) or [Search Open Technical Databases](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1596)), establishing operational resources (ex: [Develop Capabilities](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1587) or [Obtain Capabilities](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1588)), and/or for initial access (ex: [Supply Chain Compromise](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195) or [External Remote Services](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1133)).
845.profile: [profile]This entity, "Gather Victim Host Information: Software" (T1592.002), is a reconnaissance technique within the Reconnaissance tactic. It operates across multiple platforms and involves adversaries collecting details about installed software on a target host, including types, versions, and the presence of security components like antivirus or SIEMs. This information is gathered through methods such as active scanning, phishing, analyzing compromised website visitors, examining public data sets like job postings or resumes, and extracting metadata from victim-owned files to identify outdated or vulnerable software for potential exploitation. The technique is associated with groups including Andariel, Sandworm Team, and Magic Hound.
845.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Commercial Software Protectors, also known as software packers or protectors, are a technique (T1045) within the Defense Evasion tactic. Adversaries use these tools to compress or encrypt executable files, altering the file signature to evade signature-based detection. Packers like MPRESS and UPX are common examples, but adversaries may employ custom or virtual machine-based protection to obfuscate their code, making analysis and detection more difficult.

846.name: Rewrite Algorithms
846.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may make use of Domain Generation Algorithms (DGAs) to dynamically identify a destination domain for command and control traffic rather than relying on a list of static IP addresses or domains. This has the advantage of making it much harder for defenders to block, track, or take over the command and control channel, as there potentially could be thousands of domains that malware can check for instructions.(Citation: Cybereason Dissecting DGAs)(Citation: Cisco Umbrella DGA)(Citation: Unit 42 DGA Feb 2019)

DGAs can take the form of apparently random or “gibberish” strings (ex: istgmxdejdnxuyla.ru) when they construct domain names by generating each letter. Alternatively, some DGAs employ whole words as the unit by concatenating words together instead of letters (ex: cityjulydish.net). Many DGAs are time-based, generating a different domain for each time period (hourly, daily, monthly, etc). Others incorporate a seed value as well to make predicting future domains more difficult for defenders.(Citation: Cybereason Dissecting DGAs)(Citation: Cisco Umbrella DGA)(Citation: Talos CCleanup 2017)(Citation: Akamai DGA Mitigation)

Adversaries may use DGAs for the purpose of [Fallback Channels](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1008). When contact is lost with the primary command and control server malware may employ a DGA as a means to reestablishing command and control.(Citation: Talos CCleanup 2017)(Citation: FireEye POSHSPY April 2017)(Citation: ESET Sednit 2017 Activity)
846.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique Domain Generation Algorithms (DGAs), ID T1568.002, under the Command and Control tactic for Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It works by algorithmically generating a large number of potential command and control domains, often using time-based seeds or word lists to create seemingly random strings like "istgmxdejdnxuyla.ru", making blocking and tracking difficult. This technique is used for establishing fallback channels and has been associated with groups like APT41 and TA551.
846.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Rewrite Algorithms" is an attack-pattern technique. It involves adversaries altering or modifying existing algorithms, such as encryption or compression routines, to evade detection or analysis. This can include custom implementations of symmetric cryptography or data archival methods to obfuscate command and control traffic or exfiltrated data, making defensive efforts more difficult.

847.name: Underground Packers
847.profile: [profile]Underground Packers is a term associated with software packing, a technique for evading detection by compressing or encrypting executables to change their file signature, with utilities like MPRESS and UPX being common examples. This aligns with the MITRE ATT&CK technique Software Packing (T1027.002) under the Defense Evasion tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. The technique is used by adversaries, including the Lazarus intrusion-set, to conceal malicious code, where packers decompress the executable in memory to avoid signature-based analysis.
847.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Underground Packers is a technique for software packing, aligning with MITRE ATT&CK ID T1027.002 under Defense Evasion. It involves compressing or encrypting executables to alter their file signatures and evade signature-based detection. Packers like MPRESS and UPX are common, but adversaries may use custom or underground packers to avoid known artifacts. The packed code is typically decompressed in memory during execution.

848.name: DLL Loader
848.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may abuse dynamic-link library files (DLLs) in order to achieve persistence, escalate privileges, and evade defenses. DLLs are libraries that contain code and data that can be simultaneously utilized by multiple programs. While DLLs are not malicious by nature, they can be abused through mechanisms such as side-loading, hijacking search order, and phantom DLL hijacking.(Citation: unit 42)

Specific ways DLLs are abused by adversaries include:

### DLL Sideloading
Adversaries may execute their own malicious payloads by side-loading DLLs. Side-loading involves hijacking which DLL a program loads by planting and then invoking a legitimate application that executes their payload(s).

Side-loading positions both the victim application and malicious payload(s) alongside each other. Adversaries likely use side-loading as a means of masking actions they perform under a legitimate, trusted, and potentially elevated system or software process. Benign executables used to side-load payloads may not be flagged during delivery and/or execution. Adversary payloads may also be encrypted/packed or otherwise obfuscated until loaded into the memory of the trusted process.

Adversaries may also side-load other packages, such as BPLs (Borland Package Library).(Citation: kroll bpl)

Adversaries may chain DLL sideloading multiple times to fragment functionality hindering analysis. Adversaries using multiple DLL files can split the loader functions across different DLLs, with a main DLL loading the separated export functions. (Citation: Virus Bulletin) Spreading loader functions across multiple DLLs makes analysis harder, since all files must be collected to fully understand the malware’s behavior.  Another method implements a “loader-for-a-loader”, where a malicious DLL’s sole role is to load a second DLL (or a chain of DLLs) that contain the real payload. (Citation: Sophos)

### DLL Search Order Hijacking
Adversaries may execute their own malicious payloads by hijacking the search order that Windows uses to load DLLs. This search order is a sequence of special and standard search locations that a program checks when loading a DLL. An adversary can plant a trojan DLL in a directory that will be prioritized by the DLL search order over the location of a legitimate library. This will cause Windows to load the malicious DLL when it is called for by the victim program.(Citation: unit 42)

### DLL Redirection
Adversaries may directly modify the search order via DLL redirection, which after being enabled (in the Registry or via the creation of a redirection file) may cause a program to load a DLL from a different location.(Citation: Microsoft redirection)(Citation: Microsoft - manifests/assembly)

### Phantom DLL Hijacking
Adversaries may leverage phantom DLL hijacking by targeting references to non-existent DLL files. They may be able to load their own malicious DLL by planting it with the correct name in the location of the missing module.(Citation: Hexacorn DLL Hijacking)(Citation: Hijack DLLs CrowdStrike)

### DLL Substitution
Adversaries may target existing, valid DLL files and substitute them with their own malicious DLLs, planting them with the same name and in the same location as the valid DLL file.(Citation: Wietze Beukema DLL Hijacking)

Programs that fall victim to DLL hijacking may appear to behave normally because malicious DLLs may be configured to also load the legitimate DLLs they were meant to replace, evading defenses.

Remote DLL hijacking can occur when a program sets its current directory to a remote location, such as a Web share, before loading a DLL.(Citation: dll pre load owasp)(Citation: microsoft remote preloading)

If a valid DLL is configured to run at a higher privilege level, then the adversary-controlled DLL that is loaded will also be executed at the higher level. In this case, the technique could be used for privilege escalation.
848.profile: [profile]DLL Side-Loading, identified as T1574.002 within the MITRE ATT&CK framework under the Defense Evasion tactic for Windows, involves adversaries executing malicious payloads by hijacking a legitimate application's DLL load process. This is achieved by placing a malicious DLL in a location where the application searches before the legitimate library, such as the same directory, causing the trusted process to load the adversary's code. The malicious DLL may be configured to also load the legitimate library to maintain normal program behavior, evading detection. This technique is used by groups including Lazarus, APT41, and MuddyWater.[/profile]
848.profile_without_enhance: [profile]DLL Loader is a technique for executing malicious code by abusing the Windows dynamic-link library loading mechanism. It operates within the Defense Evasion and Persistence tactics on Windows platforms. The technique involves planting a malicious DLL and then triggering its load by a legitimate process, often through methods like DLL search order hijacking where a trojan DLL is placed in a directory searched before the legitimate library, or through side-loading where a trusted application is invoked to load the adversary's payload. This allows the malicious code to run under the guise of a trusted process, evading detection.

849.name: Encrypted Container
849.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may employ an encryption algorithm to conceal command and control traffic rather than relying on any inherent protections provided by a communication protocol. Despite the use of a secure algorithm, these implementations may be vulnerable to reverse engineering if secret keys are encoded and/or generated within malware samples/configuration files.
849.profile: [profile]Encrypted Container, also known as Encrypted Channel (T1573), is a Command and Control technique under the Exfiltration tactic. It conceals C2 traffic by applying an encryption algorithm directly to the data, independent of the underlying protocol's security. Implementations can be vulnerable if secret keys are embedded within the malware or its configuration files, allowing for potential reverse engineering. The Lazarus intrusion-set has been associated with this technique.
849.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Encrypted Container is a technique where adversaries use encrypted containers to hide malicious activities. It falls under the Defense Evasion tactic. The method involves deploying a container, such as via Docker, configured to use encryption for its data or network traffic, making detection and analysis difficult. This can facilitate activities like data exfiltration or command and control while evading security tools.

850.name: Encrypted Registry Value
850.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may employ an encryption algorithm to conceal command and control traffic rather than relying on any inherent protections provided by a communication protocol. Despite the use of a secure algorithm, these implementations may be vulnerable to reverse engineering if secret keys are encoded and/or generated within malware samples/configuration files.
850.profile: [profile]Encrypted Registry Value is a defense evasion technique where adversaries store malicious configuration data or payloads within the Windows Registry in an encrypted form to avoid detection by security tools. This method involves modifying registry keys to hide obfuscated information, requiring the malware to decrypt the data at runtime. It is associated with groups like Lazarus and is a specific application of general obfuscation principles to the registry subsystem.
850.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Encrypted Registry Value is a defense evasion technique (T1112.001) within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, operating on the Windows platform. It involves adversaries storing malicious payloads or configuration data within Windows Registry values that have been encrypted or encoded to evade detection by security tools. This method is used to hide information, such as commands for persistence or lateral movement, by leveraging the Registry's structure to conceal obfuscated data from plain-text inspection.

851.name: Password-Protect Installer
851.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may establish persistence and elevate privileges by using an installer to trigger the execution of malicious content. Installer packages are OS specific and contain the resources an operating system needs to install applications on a system. Installer packages can include scripts that run prior to installation as well as after installation is complete. Installer scripts may inherit elevated permissions when executed. Developers often use these scripts to prepare the environment for installation, check requirements, download dependencies, and remove files after installation.(Citation: Installer Package Scripting Rich Trouton)

Using legitimate applications, adversaries have distributed applications with modified installer scripts to execute malicious content. When a user installs the application, they may be required to grant administrative permissions to allow the installation. At the end of the installation process of the legitimate application, content such as macOS `postinstall` scripts can be executed with the inherited elevated permissions. Adversaries can use these scripts to execute a malicious executable or install other malicious components (such as a [Launch Daemon](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1543/004)) with the elevated permissions.(Citation: Application Bundle Manipulation Brandon Dalton)(Citation: wardle evilquest parti)(Citation: Windows AppleJeus GReAT)(Citation: Debian Manual Maintainer Scripts)

Depending on the distribution, Linux versions of package installer scripts are sometimes called maintainer scripts or post installation scripts. These scripts can include `preinst`, `postinst`, `prerm`, `postrm` scripts and run as root when executed.

For Windows, the Microsoft Installer services uses `.msi` files to manage the installing, updating, and uninstalling of applications. These installation routines may also include instructions to perform additional actions that may be abused by adversaries.(Citation: Microsoft Installation Procedures)
851.profile: [profile]Password-Protect Installer is a technique where adversaries embed malicious code within legitimate installer packages to gain persistence and privilege escalation. It maps to MITRE ATT&CK ID T1546.016 under the Persistence tactic and affects macOS, Linux, and Windows platforms. The technique works by modifying OS-specific installer scripts, such as macOS `postinstall` or Linux `postinst` scripts, which inherit elevated permissions during application installation to execute malicious payloads or deploy components like Launch Daemons. The intrusion-set Lazarus has been associated with this method.[/profile]
851.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Password-Protect Installer" is a technique where adversaries password-protect malicious installer packages to hinder analysis and evade detection. This method, which falls under the Defense Evasion tactic, operates across multiple platforms. The protection requires a password to execute the installer's contents, which can include malicious scripts that run with elevated permissions during installation, thereby slowing forensic examination.

852.name: Disposable Material
852.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may use alternate authentication material, such as password hashes, Kerberos tickets, and application access tokens, in order to move laterally within an environment and bypass normal system access controls. 

Authentication processes generally require a valid identity (e.g., username) along with one or more authentication factors (e.g., password, pin, physical smart card, token generator, etc.). Alternate authentication material is legitimately generated by systems after a user or application successfully authenticates by providing a valid identity and the required authentication factor(s). Alternate authentication material may also be generated during the identity creation process.(Citation: NIST Authentication)(Citation: NIST MFA)

Caching alternate authentication material allows the system to verify an identity has successfully authenticated without asking the user to reenter authentication factor(s). Because the alternate authentication must be maintained by the system—either in memory or on disk—it may be at risk of being stolen through [Credential Access](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0006) techniques. By stealing alternate authentication material, adversaries are able to bypass system access controls and authenticate to systems without knowing the plaintext password or any additional authentication factors.
852.profile: [profile]Use Alternate Authentication Material (T1550) is a Lateral Movement technique used to bypass access controls. Adversaries steal and reuse cached system authentication material like password hashes, Kerberos tickets, or application tokens, which are generated after successful login and stored in memory or on disk. This allows them to authenticate to systems without needing the plaintext password or additional factors. The technique is associated with the Lazarus intrusion-set.
852.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Disposable Material" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on retrieved context, it likely refers to adversaries using temporary or single-use assets to obscure their operations. This concept is analogous to techniques like "Use Alternate Authentication Material" (T1550) for credential theft and lateral movement, "Junk Data" (T1001.001) for C2 traffic obfuscation, and "Email Accounts" (T1585.002) where disposable email services are used to acquire infrastructure and conduct phishing while reducing attribution risk. The core technical mechanic involves employing transient resources that are discarded after use to evade detection and hinder forensic tracing.

853.name: Newer Versions

862.name: Data-Destructive Cyberattacks
862.profile: [profile]The entity "Data-Destructive Cyberattacks" is a broad category of adversary behavior focused on destroying data to disrupt availability. It is strongly associated with the specific MITRE ATT&CK technique Data Destruction (T1485) under the Impact tactic, applicable across Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. Technical mechanics involve overwriting files with random or specific data (like image files) to render them irrecoverable, often using malware with worm-like propagation capabilities leveraging valid accounts and credential dumping. The intrusion-set Lazarus is a known practitioner. This is distinct from disk wiping techniques that target storage device sections rather than individual files.[profile]
862.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Data-Destructive Cyberattacks is a technique aligned with MITRE ATT&CK Tactic Impact (TA0040) and likely Technique T1485 (Data Destruction). It targets system and network availability by destroying data, often rendering it irrecoverable. This can involve overwriting files or directories with random or specific data (like image files) using methods that bypass simple file deletion. Malware implementing this may have worm-like propagation features, leveraging credentials and network shares. In cloud environments, it can extend to deleting critical storage objects, virtual machines, and database instances.

874.name: RSA-2048 encryption
874.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may compromise a network device’s encryption capability in order to bypass encryption that would otherwise protect data communications. (Citation: Cisco Synful Knock Evolution)

Encryption can be used to protect transmitted network traffic to maintain its confidentiality (protect against unauthorized disclosure) and integrity (protect against unauthorized changes). Encryption ciphers are used to convert a plaintext message to ciphertext and can be computationally intensive to decipher without the associated decryption key. Typically, longer keys increase the cost of cryptanalysis, or decryption without the key.

Adversaries can compromise and manipulate devices that perform encryption of network traffic. For example, through behaviors such as [Modify System Image](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1601), [Reduce Key Space](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1600/001), and [Disable Crypto Hardware](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1600/002), an adversary can negatively effect and/or eliminate a device’s ability to securely encrypt network traffic. This poses a greater risk of unauthorized disclosure and may help facilitate data manipulation, Credential Access, or Collection efforts. (Citation: Cisco Blog Legacy Device Attacks)
874.profile: [profile]The entity "RSA-2048 encryption" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the provided context, it relates to the technique "Weaken Encryption" (T1600) under the Defense Evasion tactic, targeting network devices. Adversaries compromise a device's encryption capability to bypass data protection, for example by performing "Reduce Key Space" (T1600.001) or "Disable Crypto Hardware" (T1600.002) to negatively affect secure network traffic encryption. This facilitates unauthorized data disclosure and manipulation. The malware Wanacrypt0r is associated with this behavior.
874.profile_without_enhance: [profile]RSA-2048 encryption is a specific implementation of the Asymmetric Cryptography technique (T1573.002) under the Command and Control tactic. It operates across multiple platforms, using a public-private key pair where data encrypted with a 2048-bit public key can only be decrypted by the corresponding private key. This method is commonly employed to establish secure channels for C2 communications or to exfiltrate data over encrypted non-C2 protocols like HTTPS, ensuring only the intended recipient can access the transmitted information.

877.name: DDoS Botnets
877.profile: [profile]DDoS Botnets are a common infrastructure for conducting Network Denial of Service attacks, corresponding to MITRE ATT&CK sub-technique T1498.001. They involve using a network of compromised systems (botnets), which can be built, controlled, or rented by adversaries to generate high-volume traffic from globally distributed sources. This traffic, often using stateless protocols like UDP or ICMP, floods a target's network to cause service degradation or outage. In large-scale attacks, each bot may send minimal traffic, making it exceedingly difficult to distinguish the DDoS from legitimate client activity.
877.profile_without_enhance: [profile]DDoS Botnets is a technique for conducting Distributed Denial of Service attacks, aligning with the MITRE ATT&CK tactic Impact (TA0040) and potentially Network Denial of Service (T1498). It operates across multiple platforms. The technique involves using a network of compromised systems (a botnet) to generate a high-volume of network traffic directed at a target service or network to exhaust its resources and cause availability loss. Botnets can be built, controlled, or rented by adversaries, and they often use stateless protocols like UDP or ICMP for flooding, making attack traffic difficult to distinguish from legitimate connections.

878.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may downgrade or use a version of system features that may be outdated, vulnerable, and/or does not support updated security controls. Downgrade attacks typically take advantage of a system’s backward compatibility to force it into less secure modes of operation. 

Adversaries may downgrade and use various less-secure versions of features of a system, such as [Command and Scripting Interpreter](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059)s or even network protocols that can be abused to enable [Adversary-in-the-Middle](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1557) or [Network Sniffing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1040).(Citation: Praetorian TLS Downgrade Attack 2014) For example, [PowerShell](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001) versions 5+ includes Script Block Logging (SBL), which can record executed script content. However, adversaries may attempt to execute a previous version of PowerShell that does not support SBL with the intent to [Impair Defenses](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1562) while running malicious scripts that may have otherwise been detected.(Citation: CrowdStrike BGH Ransomware 2021)(Citation: Mandiant BYOL 2018)(Citation: att_def_ps_logging)

Adversaries may similarly target network traffic to downgrade from an encrypted HTTPS connection to an unsecured HTTP connection that exposes network data in clear text.(Citation: Targeted SSL Stripping Attacks Are Real)(Citation: Crowdstrike Downgrade) On Windows systems, adversaries may downgrade the boot manager to a vulnerable version that bypasses Secure Boot, granting the ability to disable various operating system security mechanisms.(Citation: SafeBreach)
878.profile: [profile]The entity "DNS Attack" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the provided context, it likely refers to Denial-of-Service (DoS) attacks targeting DNS services. These attacks can be executed through methods like reflection amplification, where adversaries spoof a victim's IP address to send high-volume DNS query responses from third-party servers, overwhelming the target. This technique falls under the Impact tactic, specifically Network Denial of Service (T1498), and can be performed on network infrastructure platforms. The intrusion-set Lazarus is a known associated threat actor.[/profile]
878.profile_without_enhance: [profile]DNS Attack is a network-based denial-of-service technique, aligning with MITRE ATT&CK Tactic Impact (TA0040) and Platform Network. It functions by exploiting the Domain Name System protocol, often through reflection amplification where an adversary sends spoofed DNS queries to open resolvers, causing them to send large response traffic to a victim's IP address, overwhelming its resources. This method can generate attack traffic volumes orders of magnitude greater than the initial requests.

However, adversaries may attempt to execute a previous version of PowerShell that does not support SBL with the intent to [Impair Defenses](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1562) while running malicious scripts that may have otherwise been detected.(Citation: CrowdStrike BGH Ransomware 2021)(Citation: Mandiant BYOL 2018)(Citation: att_def_ps_logging)

879.profile: [profile]The entity is a Network Denial of Service (DoS) technique known as an NTP Attack, which leverages the Network Time Protocol (NTP) for reflection amplification. This attack is formally categorized as T1498.002: Reflection Amplification under the Impact tactic and targets network services. Attackers spoof the victim's IP address to send small request packets to NTP servers, which respond with significantly larger data packets directed back to the victim, overwhelming their network bandwidth. This method is part of a broader class of volumetric DDoS attacks that exploit protocol characteristics to amplify traffic, with the Lazarus intrusion-set linked to its use.[/profile]
879.profile_without_enhance: [profile]NTP Attack is a specific technique within the broader MITRE ATT&CK technique T1498.002: Reflection Amplification, falling under the Impact tactic. It operates on network platforms by exploiting the Network Time Protocol (NTP). The technical mechanics involve an adversary sending spoofed request packets to NTP servers (reflectors) with the victim's IP address as the source. The servers then send a high-volume of response traffic back to the victim, amplifying the attack traffic and causing a denial of service by exhausting the target's network resources. This method is a prominent example of a reflection amplification flood.

880.profile: [profile]Downgrade Attack, identified as T1562.010 under the Impair Defenses tactic, targets Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms by exploiting system backward compatibility to force less secure operational modes. This technique specifically involves executing older versions of PowerShell to bypass Script Block Logging, downgrading HTTPS connections to unencrypted HTTP to enable traffic interception, and reverting the Windows boot manager to a vulnerable version to circumvent Secure Boot. The intrusion set Lazarus has been associated with this activity.[/profile]
880.profile_without_enhance: [profile]CGN Attack is a network denial of service technique where adversaries exploit Carrier-Grade Network Address Translation (CGNAT) infrastructure to amplify traffic and exhaust connection state tables, causing service disruption. This attack leverages the high ratio of internal private addresses to a single public IP, allowing a small number of spoofed requests to generate a large volume of traffic that overwhelms the target.

881.name: Svchost-Based Service
881.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may employ various time-based methods to detect virtualization and analysis environments, particularly those that attempt to manipulate time mechanisms to simulate longer elapses of time. This may include enumerating time-based properties, such as uptime or the system clock. 

Adversaries may use calls like `GetTickCount` and `GetSystemTimeAsFileTime` to discover if they are operating within a virtual machine or sandbox, or may be able to identify a sandbox accelerating time by sampling and calculating the expected value for an environment's timestamp before and after execution of a sleep function.(Citation: ISACA Malware Tricks)
881.profile: [profile]The entity "Svchost-Based Service" is a persistence technique where adversaries create or modify Windows services that run under the svchost.exe process to execute malicious payloads repeatedly at system startup. This technique, part of the MITRE ATT&CK framework, is classified under T1543.003 within the Persistence tactic for the Windows platform. It involves configuring service entries in the Windows Registry or using utilities like sc.exe to install services that can execute with SYSTEM privileges, often masquerading as legitimate services to evade detection. The intrusion-set Lazarus has been associated with this method.
881.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Svchost-Based Service is a Windows persistence technique where adversaries abuse the svchost.exe process to host malicious services. This method involves creating or modifying Windows services configured to run within a shared svchost process group, often by manipulating the Registry to add a service to a svchost group via the `ServiceDll` parameter under `HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\[ServiceName]\Parameters`. Executing malicious code within a legitimate svchost instance helps evade detection by blending with normal system activity. This technique is associated with tactics like Persistence and Privilege Escalation and is commonly used by groups such as APT19 and Cobalt Group.
