882.profile: [profile]Keylogger, also known as 404 keylogger, is a piece of malware attributed to groups including Lazarus, RocketKitten, APT3, OilRig, and APT28. It establishes persistence via registry keys such as HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run and HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon. Its key technical behavior is keylogging, capturing user input. The malware is related to or shares code similarities with other keyloggers like Phoenix Keylogger, which is an evolution of the Alpha Keylogger, and entities such as apt3 keylogger and Coper. It targets the Windows platform.
882.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Keylogger is a malware type that functions as a credential access tool, specifically MITRE ATT&CK technique T1056.001 for Windows, capturing keystrokes via API hooking or hardware buffer reads to intercept passwords and bypass multi-factor authentication. It is used by groups like RocketKitten, as seen in the related Tspy_Woolerg malware which ensures persistence via registry keys. Related keyloggers include APT3 keylogger, Coper, and Phoenix keylogger, with Phoenix being an evolution of the Alpha keylogger, sharing similar SMTP configurations and self-termination functions.

883.name: Wild Positron/Duuzer
883.profile: [profile]Wild Positron, also known as Duuzer, is a malware family attributed to the Lazarus Group. It was deployed around 2015, as part of the group's broader operations that included spearphishing attacks exploiting vulnerabilities like CVE-2015-6585. The malware is associated with historical campaigns such as Operation Troy and DarkSeoul.[/profile]
883.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Wild Positron, also known as Duuzer, is a malware family attributed to the Lazarus Group. It was deployed in 2015, often via spearphishing campaigns that leveraged zero-day vulnerabilities such as CVE-2015-6585. This malware is part of a broader set of tools used by the group, which includes families associated with Operation Troy and DarkSeoul.

884.name: Hangman
884.profile: [profile]Hangman is a malware attributed to the Lazarus intrusion set, specifically its Bluenoroff subgroup which targets the financial sector. It is associated with other malware families like PowerRatankba and Positron. The malware establishes persistence by creating a registry key for automatic execution on system startup. Its primary objective is to facilitate large-scale financial theft.
884.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Hangman is a malware associated with the Lazarus Group's Bluenoroff subgroup, which primarily targets the financial sector. It is mentioned alongside other malware families like PowerRatankba and Positron in the context of these financially motivated theft campaigns. The malware is designed to achieve persistence by creating a registry key to automatically launch a copy of itself on system startup. Its key behaviors involve facilitating theft attempts against financial institutions as part of broader Lazarus operations.

885.name: SMB Worm Tool
885.uncertain_mes: During our routine threat hunting exercise, Cyble Research Labs came across a TOR website listing a variety of malware for sale. This includes stealers, clippers, worms, miners, ransomware, and DDoS Bots which the Threat Actors (TAs) have named ‘Eternity Project.’
885.profile: [profile]SMB Worm Tool, also known as eternity worm, is a modular malware attributed to the Lazarus group. Its key technical behaviors include network propagation via SMB, specifically using the EternalBlue exploit and brute-force authentication, and it contains components such as a listening implant, lightweight backdoor, proxy tool, and destructive tools for hard drives and system cleaning. It targets Microsoft Windows systems and connects to a command-and-control infrastructure.
885.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The malware is known as the SMB Worm Tool. It is attributed to the Lazarus Group. Its key behaviors include network propagation via SMB using brute-force authentication and the EternalBlue exploit, and it contains a modular suite of components: a listening implant, a lightweight backdoor, a proxy tool, a destructive hard drive tool, and a destructive cleaning tool. It targets Microsoft Windows systems and connects to command-and-control (C2) infrastructure.

892.name: SQL Injection
892.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may abuse SQL stored procedures to establish persistent access to systems. SQL Stored Procedures are code that can be saved and reused so that database users do not waste time rewriting frequently used SQL queries. Stored procedures can be invoked via SQL statements to the database using the procedure name or via defined events (e.g. when a SQL server application is started/restarted).

Adversaries may craft malicious stored procedures that can provide a persistence mechanism in SQL database servers.(Citation: NetSPI Startup Stored Procedures)(Citation: Kaspersky MSSQL Aug 2019) To execute operating system commands through SQL syntax the adversary may have to enable additional functionality, such as xp_cmdshell for MSSQL Server.(Citation: NetSPI Startup Stored Procedures)(Citation: Kaspersky MSSQL Aug 2019)(Citation: Microsoft xp_cmdshell 2017) 

Microsoft SQL Server can enable common language runtime (CLR) integration. With CLR integration enabled, application developers can write stored procedures using any .NET framework language (e.g. VB .NET, C#, etc.).(Citation: Microsoft CLR Integration 2017) Adversaries may craft or modify CLR assemblies that are linked to stored procedures since these CLR assemblies can be made to execute arbitrary commands.(Citation: NetSPI SQL Server CLR)
892.profile: [profile]SQL Injection is a technique, often mapped to the Initial Access tactic, where adversaries insert malicious SQL commands into application queries to manipulate or access backend databases. It primarily targets web applications and databases. The attack works by exploiting input validation flaws to execute unauthorized SQL statements, which can lead to data theft, authentication bypass, or command execution. Groups like Lazarus, APT17, and APT28 have been associated with its use.[/profile]
892.profile_without_enhance: [profile]SQL Injection, known as T1190 in the MITRE ATT&CK framework, is an Initial Access technique applicable to web servers. It exploits web applications by inserting malicious SQL statements into input fields, such as login forms or search queries, which are then executed by the backend database. This allows adversaries to bypass authentication, extract, modify, or delete data, and potentially execute commands on the underlying operating system.

893.name: Cross-Site Scripting
893.uncertain_mes:
**This technique has been deprecated. Please use [Command and Scripting Interpreter](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059) where appropriate.**

Adversaries may use scripts to aid in operations and perform multiple actions that would otherwise be manual. Scripting is useful for speeding up operational tasks and reducing the time required to gain access to critical resources. Some scripting languages may be used to bypass process monitoring mechanisms by directly interacting with the operating system at an API level instead of calling other programs. Common scripting languages for Windows include VBScript and [PowerShell](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1086) but could also be in the form of command-line batch scripts.

Scripts can be embedded inside Office documents as macros that can be set to execute when files used in [Spearphishing Attachment](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1193) and other types of spearphishing are opened. Malicious embedded macros are an alternative means of execution than software exploitation through [Exploitation for Client Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1203), where adversaries will rely on macros being allowed or that the user will accept to activate them.

Many popular offensive frameworks exist which use forms of scripting for security testers and adversaries alike. Metasploit (Citation: Metasploit_Ref), Veil (Citation: Veil_Ref), and PowerSploit (Citation: Powersploit) are three examples that are popular among penetration testers for exploit and post-compromise operations and include many features for evading defenses. Some adversaries are known to use PowerShell. (Citation: Alperovitch 2014)
893.profile: [profile]Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) is a client-side injection technique where an adversary injects malicious scripts into a trusted website, which are then executed in a victim's browser. This technique, which falls under the Initial Access tactic and targets web platforms, involves embedding scripts in web pages or applications. The injected scripts can be used to steal session cookies, enabling session hijacking and authentication bypass, as referenced in related techniques for stealing web session cookies. The Lazarus intrusion-set has been associated with this method.
893.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Cross-Site Scripting, identified as T1059.007 in the MITRE ATT&CK framework, is an Initial Access technique targeting web platforms. It involves injecting malicious scripts, typically JavaScript, into web pages viewed by other users, which then execute in the victim's browser. This can be leveraged to steal session cookies for authentication bypass, as seen in techniques like Steal Web Session Cookie, and is a common vector in drive-by compromises where malicious scripts are inserted into legitimate sites.

894.name: Command Injection
894.profile: [profile]Command Injection, identified as T1206 within the MITRE ATT&CK framework under the Execution tactic, targets multiple platforms including Linux, macOS, and Windows. This technique involves adversaries exploiting vulnerabilities in applications to execute arbitrary operating system commands by injecting malicious input, often through web interfaces or API calls. The intrusion sets Lazarus and APT29 are known to utilize this method. Technical execution can involve appending commands to legitimate inputs using separators like semicolons or ampersands, and may be combined with obfuscation to evade detection.
894.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Command Injection is a technique where adversaries exploit vulnerable applications to execute arbitrary commands on the underlying operating system. This is achieved by injecting malicious code into legitimate application inputs, such as web forms or API parameters, which the application then passes to a system shell. The technique, identified as T1190 in the MITRE ATT&CK framework, falls under the Initial Access tactic and primarily targets web applications and their hosting platforms. Successful execution allows attackers to gain control of the system, leading to further compromise.

895.name: Server Fingerprinting
895.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may buy, lease, rent, or obtain physical servers that can be used during targeting. Use of servers allows an adversary to stage, launch, and execute an operation. During post-compromise activity, adversaries may utilize servers for various tasks, such as watering hole operations in [Drive-by Compromise](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1189), enabling [Phishing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566) operations, or facilitating [Command and Control](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0011). Instead of compromising a third-party [Server](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1584/004) or renting a [Virtual Private Server](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1583/003), adversaries may opt to configure and run their own servers in support of operations. Free trial periods of cloud servers may also be abused.(Citation: Free Trial PurpleUrchin)(Citation: Freejacked) 

Adversaries may only need a lightweight setup if most of their activities will take place using online infrastructure. Or, they may need to build extensive infrastructure if they want to test, communicate, and control other aspects of their activities on their own systems.(Citation: NYTStuxnet)
895.profile: [profile]Server Fingerprinting is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique; based on the provided data, the entity likely refers to the technique of acquiring and using physical servers for adversarial operations, which aligns with MITRE ATT&CK ID T1583.004 under the Resource Development tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. Adversaries may purchase, lease, or configure their own physical servers to stage attacks, enabling activities like watering hole operations, phishing, or command and control, and may abuse free cloud server trials to establish infrastructure with reduced traceability. Groups such as Earth Lusca, Mustard Tempest, and Lazarus have been associated with this practice.
895.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Server Fingerprinting" is a reconnaissance technique where adversaries actively probe victim infrastructure to gather information about server configurations, software versions, and network services. This is performed through network traffic and protocol interactions, such as using native features like ICMP or analyzing HTTP headers and response behaviors, to identify potential vulnerabilities or misconfigurations for subsequent targeting stages.

896.name: Input Sanitization
896.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may use methods of capturing user input to obtain credentials or collect information. During normal system usage, users often provide credentials to various different locations, such as login pages/portals or system dialog boxes. Input capture mechanisms may be transparent to the user (e.g. [Credential API Hooking](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1056/004)) or rely on deceiving the user into providing input into what they believe to be a genuine service (e.g. [Web Portal Capture](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1056/003)).
896.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique Input Capture, identified as T1056 under the Credential Access tactic for Windows, macOS, and Linux platforms. It involves capturing user input to steal credentials, using methods that are either transparent to the user, such as Credential API Hooking, or deceptive, like simulating legitimate login prompts through Web Portal Capture. Associated intrusion sets include Storm-1811, APT39, and APT42.[/profile]
896.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Input Sanitization is a defensive security practice, not a MITRE ATT&CK attack pattern. The retrieved information contains descriptions of adversary techniques like Input Injection (T1674), Input Prompt (T1141), and Input Capture (T1056), which are unrelated to the defensive concept. The core technical mechanics involve adversaries exploiting poor or absent input validation and sanitization in applications, such as in XPC services on macOS, to inject and execute malicious code or commands, leading to potential privilege escalation or other system compromise.

897.name: Microsoft EMET
897.profile: [profile]Microsoft EMET is a security mitigation tool designed to protect against software vulnerabilities. It is referenced in discussions about specific exploits, such as CVE-2015-2360 and CVE-2014-4148, where it is noted that EMET could not stop these particular attacks. The tool is mentioned in the context of threat actors like Lazarus and in relation to malware families such as Duqu, Emotet, and Matryoshka RAT, where its effectiveness or presence in an environment is discussed. The name 'Emet' also appears as part of an unrelated Hebrew-language Facebook page called 'Emet press'.
897.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Microsoft EMET is a security tool, not malware. It is referenced in discussions about vulnerabilities like CVE-2015-2360 and CVE-2014-4148, where it is noted that EMET cannot stop exploits for these specific flaws. The tool is mentioned in contexts related to threat actors like Unit 8200 and Rocket Kitten, but only as a subject of their bypass efforts or in unrelated decoy infrastructure names like "Emet press." Its primary function is as a mitigation technology for Microsoft applications.

898.name: Microsoft Applocker
898.profile: [profile]Microsoft AppLocker is a Windows security feature, not malware. It is referenced by the Azorult malware, which is linked to The Gorgon Group, in a technique to impair defenses. This technique involves importing a malicious AppLocker policy via PowerShell commands (e.g., 'Import-Module applocker') to deny the execution of antivirus software, thereby disabling security controls on the target Windows platform.
898.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Microsoft AppLocker is a legitimate Windows security feature, not malware. It is referenced by the Azorult malware, attributed to The Gorgon Group, which abuses AppLocker to impair defenses. The malware uses PowerShell commands like "Import-Module applocker" and "Set-AppLockerPolicy" to import a malicious XML policy designed to deny the execution of antivirus and security software on the Windows platform.

903.name: PowerShell Commands
903.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may abuse PowerShell commands and scripts for execution. PowerShell is a powerful interactive command-line interface and scripting environment included in the Windows operating system.(Citation: TechNet PowerShell) Adversaries can use PowerShell to perform a number of actions, including discovery of information and execution of code. Examples include the Start-Process cmdlet which can be used to run an executable and the Invoke-Command cmdlet which runs a command locally or on a remote computer (though administrator permissions are required to use PowerShell to connect to remote systems). PowerShell may also be used to download and run executables from the Internet, which can be executed from disk or in memory without touching disk. A number of PowerShell-based offensive testing tools are available, including [Empire](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0363), [PowerSploit](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0194), [PoshC2](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0378), and PSAttack.(Citation: Github PSAttack) PowerShell commands/scripts can also be executed without directly invoking the powershell.exe binary through interfaces to PowerShell's underlying System.Management.Automation assembly DLL exposed through the .NET framework and Windows Common Language Interface (CLI).(Citation: Sixdub PowerPick Jan 2016)(Citation: SilentBreak Offensive PS Dec 2015)(Citation: Microsoft PSfromCsharp APR 2014)
903.profile: [profile]PowerShell, designated as T1059.001 in the MITRE ATT&CK framework, is a Command and Scripting Interpreter technique within the Execution tactic, primarily targeting the Windows platform. It involves abusing the built-in PowerShell environment to execute malicious commands and scripts, such as using cmdlets like `Start-Process` and `Invoke-Command` to run code locally or remotely. Adversaries can leverage it to download and run executables directly in memory, bypassing disk, and can execute scripts without invoking `powershell.exe` by accessing the underlying `System.Management.Automation` assembly. It is commonly used by numerous threat groups, including Lazarus, and is associated with offensive tools like Empire and PowerSploit.[/profile]
903.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "PowerShell Commands" aligns with MITRE ATT&CK technique T1059.001 "Command and Scripting Interpreter: PowerShell", under the Execution tactic for Windows platforms. It involves abusing the PowerShell environment to execute malicious commands and scripts, including using cmdlets like `Start-Process` and `Invoke-Command` to run executables or commands locally and remotely. Adversaries can download and run code from the internet, execute payloads directly in memory, and leverage tools like Empire or PowerSploit. Execution can also occur without `powershell.exe` by interfacing with the underlying `System.Management.Automation` assembly via .NET.

904.name: Security Properties
904.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may gather information about the victim's network domain(s) that can be used during targeting. Information about domains and their properties may include a variety of details, including what domain(s) the victim owns as well as administrative data (ex: name, registrar, etc.) and more directly actionable information such as contacts (email addresses and phone numbers), business addresses, and name servers.

Adversaries may gather this information in various ways, such as direct collection actions via [Active Scanning](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1595) or [Phishing for Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1598). Information about victim domains and their properties may also be exposed to adversaries via online or other accessible data sets (ex: [WHOIS](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1596/002)).(Citation: WHOIS)(Citation: DNS Dumpster)(Citation: Circl Passive DNS) Where third-party cloud providers are in use, this information may also be exposed through publicly available API endpoints, such as GetUserRealm and autodiscover in Office 365 environments.(Citation: Azure Active Directory Reconnaisance)(Citation: Office 265 Azure Domain Availability) Gathering this information may reveal opportunities for other forms of reconnaissance (ex: [Search Open Technical Databases](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1596), [Search Open Websites/Domains](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1593), or [Phishing for Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1598)), establishing operational resources (ex: [Acquire Infrastructure](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1583) or [Compromise Infrastructure](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1584)), and/or initial access (ex: [Phishing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566)).
904.profile: [profile]The entity "Security Properties" is a reconnaissance technique under MITRE ATT&CK ID T1590.001, categorized under the Reconnaissance tactic and applicable to multiple platforms. It involves gathering actionable information about a victim's network domains, including administrative data, contacts, business addresses, and name servers. This data can be collected through active scanning, phishing, or querying public datasets like WHOIS and DNS records. In cloud environments, adversaries may exploit public API endpoints such as GetUserRealm and autodiscover in Office 365. The gathered intelligence supports follow-on activities like further reconnaissance, infrastructure acquisition, and initial access via phishing. The technique has been associated with the Sandworm Team.[/profile]
904.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Security Properties" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the retrieved context, it likely refers to the reconnaissance of security configurations or encryption settings, such as the Active Directory property `AllowReversiblePasswordEncryption`. This property, when enabled, allows passwords to be stored with reversible encryption, which adversaries can exploit to obtain plaintext credentials using components like the encrypted password value, a random key, the LSA secret, and a static key from `RASSFM.DLL`. This activity supports credential access and is typically relevant to Windows platforms.

905.name: Logon Activity
905.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may employ various user activity checks to detect and avoid virtualization and analysis environments. This may include changing behaviors based on the results of checks for the presence of artifacts indicative of a virtual machine environment (VME) or sandbox. If the adversary detects a VME, they may alter their malware to disengage from the victim or conceal the core functions of the implant. They may also search for VME artifacts before dropping secondary or additional payloads. Adversaries may use the information learned from [Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1497) during automated discovery to shape follow-on behaviors.(Citation: Deloitte Environment Awareness)

Adversaries may search for user activity on the host based on variables such as the speed/frequency of mouse movements and clicks (Citation: Sans Virtual Jan 2016) , browser history, cache, bookmarks, or number of files in common directories such as home or the desktop. Other methods may rely on specific user interaction with the system before the malicious code is activated, such as waiting for a document to close before activating a macro (Citation: Unit 42 Sofacy Nov 2018) or waiting for a user to double click on an embedded image to activate.(Citation: FireEye FIN7 April 2017)
905.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique "User Activity Based Checks" (ID: T1497.002) under the Defense Evasion tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It involves adversaries checking for user activity artifacts like mouse movement speed/frequency, browser history, cache, bookmarks, or file counts in common directories to detect and avoid virtual machine or sandbox analysis environments. The technique may also involve waiting for specific user interactions, such as a document closing or a double-click, before activating malicious code. Groups like DarkHotel and FIN7 have been associated with its use.[profile]
905.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Logon Activity" is not a formally defined MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the retrieved context, it is a general concept related to user authentication events. Adversaries may monitor or trigger actions based on logon events to establish persistence. This can be achieved through mechanisms like Windows logon scripts, which are automatically executed upon user login by modifying the `HKCU\Environment\UserInitMprLogonScript` Registry key, or through network logon scripts deployed via Active Directory Group Policy. These scripts run with the user's privileges and can be used to maintain access on a single system or across a network.

906.name: Temporary Loss of Sensitive Data
906.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may abuse permission configurations that allow them to gain temporarily elevated access to cloud resources. Many cloud environments allow administrators to grant user or service accounts permission to request just-in-time access to roles, impersonate other accounts, pass roles onto resources and services, or otherwise gain short-term access to a set of privileges that may be distinct from their own. 

Just-in-time access is a mechanism for granting additional roles to cloud accounts in a granular, temporary manner. This allows accounts to operate with only the permissions they need on a daily basis, and to request additional permissions as necessary. Sometimes just-in-time access requests are configured to require manual approval, while other times the desired permissions are automatically granted.(Citation: Azure Just in Time Access 2023)

Account impersonation allows user or service accounts to temporarily act with the permissions of another account. For example, in GCP users with the `iam.serviceAccountTokenCreator` role can create temporary access tokens or sign arbitrary payloads with the permissions of a service account, while service accounts with domain-wide delegation permission are permitted to impersonate Google Workspace accounts.(Citation: Google Cloud Service Account Authentication Roles)(Citation: Hunters Domain Wide Delegation Google Workspace 2023)(Citation: Google Cloud Just in Time Access 2023)(Citation: Palo Alto Unit 42 Google Workspace Domain Wide Delegation 2023) In Exchange Online, the `ApplicationImpersonation` role allows a service account to use the permissions associated with specified user accounts.(Citation: Microsoft Impersonation and EWS in Exchange) 

Many cloud environments also include mechanisms for users to pass roles to resources that allow them to perform tasks and authenticate to other services. While the user that creates the resource does not directly assume the role they pass to it, they may still be able to take advantage of the role's access -- for example, by configuring the resource to perform certain actions with the permissions it has been granted. In AWS, users with the `PassRole` permission can allow a service they create to assume a given role, while in GCP, users with the `iam.serviceAccountUser` role can attach a service account to a resource.(Citation: AWS PassRole)(Citation: Google Cloud Service Account Authentication Roles)

While users require specific role assignments in order to use any of these features, cloud administrators may misconfigure permissions. This could result in escalation paths that allow adversaries to gain access to resources beyond what was originally intended.(Citation: Rhino Google Cloud Privilege Escalation)(Citation: Rhino Security Labs AWS Privilege Escalation)

**Note:** this technique is distinct from [Additional Cloud Roles](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1098/003), which involves assigning permanent roles to accounts rather than abusing existing permissions structures to gain temporarily elevated access to resources. However, adversaries that compromise a sufficiently privileged account may grant another account they control [Additional Cloud Roles](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1098/003) that would allow them to also abuse these features. This may also allow for greater stealth than would be had by directly using the highly privileged account, especially when logs do not clarify when role impersonation is taking place.(Citation: CrowdStrike StellarParticle January 2022)
906.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique "temporary elevated cloud access" (ID: T1548.005) under the Privilege Escalation tactic, targeting cloud platforms. It involves abusing misconfigured permissions to gain short-term, elevated privileges through mechanisms like just-in-time access requests, account impersonation (e.g., using the `iam.serviceAccountTokenCreator` role in GCP or `ApplicationImpersonation` in Exchange Online), and role-passing features such as AWS `PassRole`. This allows adversaries to operate with permissions beyond their standard account level, often for stealthier lateral movement or resource access, and has been associated with groups like Lazarus.[/profile]
906.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Temporary Loss of Sensitive Data is a technique where adversaries cause the temporary unavailability of sensitive data, often as a precursor to exfiltration or to create operational disruption. This can be achieved by moving, compressing, or encrypting data in place, rendering it inaccessible to legitimate users for a period. The technique is associated with the Exfiltration tactic and can involve preparatory actions like Data Compressed (T1002) to make data portable before its potential theft or permanent encryption for impact.

907.name: Financial Recovery Losses
907.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may steal monetary resources from targets through extortion, social engineering, technical theft, or other methods aimed at their own financial gain at the expense of the availability of these resources for victims. Financial theft is the ultimate objective of several popular campaign types including extortion by ransomware,(Citation: FBI-ransomware) business email compromise (BEC) and fraud,(Citation: FBI-BEC) "pig butchering,"(Citation: wired-pig butchering) bank hacking,(Citation: DOJ-DPRK Heist) and exploiting cryptocurrency networks.(Citation: BBC-Ronin) 

Adversaries may [Compromise Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1586) to conduct unauthorized transfers of funds.(Citation: Internet crime report 2022) In the case of business email compromise or email fraud, an adversary may utilize [Impersonation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1656) of a trusted entity. Once the social engineering is successful, victims can be deceived into sending money to financial accounts controlled by an adversary.(Citation: FBI-BEC) This creates the potential for multiple victims (i.e., compromised accounts as well as the ultimate monetary loss) in incidents involving financial theft.(Citation: VEC)

Extortion by ransomware may occur, for example, when an adversary demands payment from a victim after [Data Encrypted for Impact](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1486) (Citation: NYT-Colonial) and [Exfiltration](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0010) of data, followed by threatening to leak sensitive data to the public unless payment is made to the adversary.(Citation: Mandiant-leaks) Adversaries may use dedicated leak sites to distribute victim data.(Citation: Crowdstrike-leaks)

Due to the potentially immense business impact of financial theft, an adversary may abuse the possibility of financial theft and seeking monetary gain to divert attention from their true goals such as [Data Destruction](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1485) and business disruption.(Citation: AP-NotPetya)
907.profile: [profile]Financial Theft, identified as T1657, is an adversary objective within the Impact tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. It involves stealing monetary resources through methods like ransomware extortion, business email compromise (BEC), "pig butchering" scams, and direct bank or cryptocurrency theft. This is achieved by compromising accounts for unauthorized fund transfers, using impersonation in social engineering, and demanding payments via dedicated leak sites after data encryption and exfiltration. Groups like Lazarus, FIN13, and Scattered Spider have been associated with this activity, which can also serve as a diversion for other goals like data destruction.[profile]
907.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Financial Recovery Losses is a technique where adversaries aim to inflict monetary damage on victims, often as a primary objective or to mask other goals like data destruction. It is closely associated with techniques like Financial Theft (T1657) and Inhibit System Recovery (T1490). The mechanics involve methods such as extortion via ransomware, business email compromise fraud, and direct theft through compromised accounts to transfer funds, ultimately causing financial impact and hindering victim recovery.

908.name: Reputational Damage
908.profile: [profile]Reputational Damage is a potential impact or consequence of adversarial actions rather than a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique. It can occur when a victim's resources, such as network bandwidth, are co-opted for illegal activities like botnet operations or proxyjacking, as seen in techniques like Bandwidth Hijacking (T1496.002). This impact is associated with groups like Lazarus and can result from various disruptive techniques, including Service Stop (T1489), that cause operational harm and erode trust.
908.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Reputational Damage is a technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework. It is not a standard technique with a T-ID, tactic, or platform. It is described as a potential consequence or impact of other adversarial actions, such as when a victim's compromised network bandwidth is used for illegal activities like proxyjacking or botnet operations, which can harm the victim's reputation.

909.name: Operational Interruption
909.profile: [profile]Operational Interruption is a technique used by adversaries to disrupt system functions and hinder detection. It is associated with the intrusion set Lazarus. This technique involves actions such as blocking or disabling critical services and sensors, including tampering with Event Tracing for Windows (ETW) via PowerShell commands like Set-EtwTraceProvider or altering registry settings to prevent event telemetry collection. Adversaries may also stop services to enable data destruction or encryption and block network traffic to security monitoring systems like SIEMs to avoid central analysis.
909.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Operational Interruption is a technique adversaries use to disrupt system and network functions, aligning with the Impact tactic. It can be executed by disabling critical services like MSExchangeIS to make data stores inaccessible or by stopping host-based sensors such as Event Tracing for Windows (ETW) through PowerShell cmdlets like Set-EtwTraceProvider or direct registry manipulation. Adversaries may also block network telemetry to SIEMs using host firewall rules, and in cloud environments, they can leverage APIs like AWS's DisableAPIServiceAccess to disrupt operations.

913.name: Hidden Cobra
913.uncertain_mes:
[Lazarus Group](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0032) is a North Korean state-sponsored cyber threat group attributed to the Reconnaissance General Bureau (RGB). (Citation: US-CERT HIDDEN COBRA June 2017) (Citation: Treasury North Korean Cyber Groups September 2019) [Lazarus Group](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0032) has been active since at least 2009 and is reportedly responsible for the November 2014 destructive wiper attack on Sony Pictures Entertainment, identified by Novetta as part of Operation Blockbuster. Malware used by [Lazarus Group](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0032) correlates to other reported campaigns, including Operation Flame, Operation 1Mission, Operation Troy, DarkSeoul, and Ten Days of Rain.(Citation: Novetta Blockbuster)

North Korea’s cyber operations have shown a consistent pattern of adaptation, forming and reorganizing units as national priorities shift. These units frequently share personnel, infrastructure, malware, and tradecraft, making it difficult to attribute specific operations with high confidence. Public reporting often uses “Lazarus Group” as an umbrella term for multiple North Korean cyber operators conducting espionage, destructive attacks, and financially motivated campaigns.(Citation: Mandiant DPRK Laz Org Breakdown 2022)(Citation: Mandiant DPRK Groups 2023)(Citation: JPCert Blog Laz Subgroups 2025)
913.profile: [profile]Hidden Cobra, also known as Lazarus Group, APT38, Bureau 121, and Bluenoroff, is a prolific North Korean state-sponsored cyber threat group attributed to the Reconnaissance General Bureau (RGB) and active since at least 2009. Its arsenal is linked to numerous campaigns including Operation Blockbuster, DarkSeoul, and Ten Days of Rain. The group is known for conducting espionage, destructive attacks like the 2014 Sony Pictures wiper attack, and financially motivated operations. It primarily targets the financial, entertainment, and media sectors globally, with a consistent pattern of adaptation and shared infrastructure among North Korean cyber units, making precise attribution challenging.
913.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Hidden Cobra is a primary alias for the Lazarus Group, a cyber espionage and sabotage collective attributed to North Korea's Reconnaissance General Bureau. The group is known for its use of custom malware like Deltacharlie and has been linked to high-profile destructive attacks and financially motivated campaigns. Its operations target the financial, media, and critical infrastructure sectors globally, with motivations encompassing espionage, financial theft, and political disruption.[/profile]
913.profile_without_enhance_0: [profile]Hidden Cobra, also known as APT37, Reaper, and Group123, is a North Korean state-sponsored threat actor attributed to the Reconnaissance General Bureau. It employs custom malware such as ROKRAT, BLINDINGCAN, and HOPLIGHT, and utilizes spear-phishing, watering hole attacks, and exploitation of software vulnerabilities. The group primarily targets government, military, and media sectors in South Korea, Japan, and the United States, with motivations centered on espionage, data theft, and financial gain.
913.profile_without_enhance_0_no_hsage: [profile]Hidden Cobra, also known as APT38, Lazarus Group, and Guardians of Peace, is a North Korean state-sponsored cyber espionage and financial crime group attributed to the Reconnaissance General Bureau. It is distinguished by its extensive use of custom malware families such as KEYMARBLE, Joanap, and Brambul, and its deployment of sophisticated backdoors like Fallchill and Bankshot. The group employs advanced TTPs including supply chain attacks, spear-phishing, and exploitation of zero-day vulnerabilities, primarily targeting financial institutions, cryptocurrency exchanges, and media sectors globally to conduct financial theft, espionage, and disruptive operations in alignment with North Korean state objectives.

915.name: ratankba
915.uncertain_mes: [RATANKBA](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0241) is a remote controller tool used by [Lazarus Group](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0032). [RATANKBA](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0241) has been used in attacks targeting financial institutions in Poland, Mexico, Uruguay, the United Kingdom, and Chile. It was also seen used against organizations related to telecommunications, management consulting, information technology, insurance, aviation, and education. [RATANKBA](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0241) has a graphical user interface to allow the attacker to issue jobs to perform on the infected machines. (Citation: Lazarus RATANKBA) (Citation: RATANKBA)
915.profile: [profile]RATANKBA, also known as the Powershell version PowerRATANKBA, is a remote access tool attributed to the Lazarus Group. It features a graphical user interface for attackers to issue commands and has been used in financial attacks against institutions in Poland, Mexico, Uruguay, the UK, and Chile, as well as against telecommunications, IT, insurance, aviation, and education sectors. Key behaviors include creating registry keys for persistence and existing in both C/C++ and Powershell variants. Its target platform is Windows systems.
915.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The malware is named RATANKBA, with a PowerShell version also known as PowerRATANKBA. It is attributed to the Lazarus Group. This malware is involved in financially motivated attacks, including attempts to steal funds via the SWIFT banking network, as seen in the 2016 Bangladesh Bank heist. Its technical behavior includes creating a registry key for persistence to ensure automatic execution on system startup. The primary target platform is Windows systems.

916.name: Watering Hole Attack
916.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may downgrade or use a version of system features that may be outdated, vulnerable, and/or does not support updated security controls. Downgrade attacks typically take advantage of a system’s backward compatibility to force it into less secure modes of operation. 

Adversaries may downgrade and use various less-secure versions of features of a system, such as [Command and Scripting Interpreter](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059)s or even network protocols that can be abused to enable [Adversary-in-the-Middle](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1557) or [Network Sniffing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1040).(Citation: Praetorian TLS Downgrade Attack 2014) For example, [PowerShell](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001) versions 5+ includes Script Block Logging (SBL), which can record executed script content. However, adversaries may attempt to execute a previous version of PowerShell that does not support SBL with the intent to [Impair Defenses](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1562) while running malicious scripts that may have otherwise been detected.(Citation: CrowdStrike BGH Ransomware 2021)(Citation: Mandiant BYOL 2018)(Citation: att_def_ps_logging)

Adversaries may similarly target network traffic to downgrade from an encrypted HTTPS connection to an unsecured HTTP connection that exposes network data in clear text.(Citation: Targeted SSL Stripping Attacks Are Real)(Citation: Crowdstrike Downgrade) On Windows systems, adversaries may downgrade the boot manager to a vulnerable version that bypasses Secure Boot, granting the ability to disable various operating system security mechanisms.(Citation: SafeBreach)
916.profile: [profile]Watering Hole Attack is a technique where adversaries compromise websites frequented by a specific target group to stage exploits for drive-by compromises, as referenced in MITRE ATT&CK sub-technique T1608.004. This tactic falls under Resource Development. The attack involves injecting malicious scripts like JavaScript into these sites, often through compromised infrastructure or malvertising, to profile and then exploit visitors' web browsers without requiring user interaction. Groups such as APT32 and Dragonfly have been associated with this method.
916.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Watering Hole Attack is a technique aligned with MITRE ATT&CK ID T1608.004 under the tactic Resource Development. It involves adversaries compromising or creating websites frequented by a specific target community, such as a particular industry or government sector, to stage malicious content. The attack typically exploits vulnerabilities in a user's web browser when they visit the site, often without requiring additional interaction. This is achieved by injecting malicious scripts like JavaScript into the site's pages, modifying files from cloud storage, or using malicious advertisements. The goal is to compromise specific users based on their shared interests or browsing habits.

922.name: Malware
922.uncertain_mes:
A .NET rat targets Mongolia
A new document royal road v7 installs a backdoor in .NET. a first executable is dropped \os03C2.tmp. This exe has many similarities with older campaigns using by Operation LagTime or Tonto Team.
Document
The decoy document is a document about infection of covid19 in Russia send to the Mongolia Authorities. The document is fake signed A. Amarsaikhan.
922.profile: [profile]The malware is referred to as 'nmass malware'. It is a .NET-based Remote Access Trojan (RAT) that uses a malicious Royal Road v7 document as a lure to install a backdoor. The decoy document is about COVID-19 infections in Russia and is fake-signed 'A. Amarsaikhan' to target Mongolian authorities. The initial executable is dropped as 'os03C2.tmp'. Attributed groups are not definitively confirmed from the provided data.[/profile]
922.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Malware, also referenced as nmass, is a .NET-based remote access trojan (RAT) that has been used in campaigns such as Operation LagTime or by groups like Tonto Team. It is deployed via malicious decoy documents, such as a fake COVID-19 document targeting Mongolian authorities, and drops an initial executable file named os03C2.tmp. Its configuration uses JSON files and follows specific filename patterns. The malware's attributed groups remain uncertain, and it primarily targets Windows systems.[/profile]

923.name: suspicious crypters/executables
923.profile: [profile]The entity is a cluster of suspicious crypters and executables, attributed to the Lazarus intrusion set. Its key behaviors include creating suspicious connections after image load, generating files from messaging or mail applications, and deploying malicious Office documents. It also involves the creation of executables or scripts in suspicious paths. The activity is linked to malware families such as Bandook, Hatef, and AsyncRAT, with associated groups including Dark Caracal and Handala.
923.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The malware is identified as 'suspicious crypters/executables'. Its key technical behaviors include establishing suspicious connections after image load, creating files from messenger or mail, and being delivered via malicious Office documents. It is also associated with executables or script creation in suspicious paths. The malware is attributed to the groups Dark Caracal and Handala.

924.name: decoy
924.profile: [profile]Decoy is a technique where adversaries may add junk data to command and control protocols to hinder detection, such as by appending random characters. It is mapped to MITRE ATT&CK ID T1001.001, under the Defense Evasion tactic, and is applicable across multiple platforms. The intrusion-set Lazarus is known to use this technique. This manipulation of protocol traffic prevents trivial analysis and decoding methods.
924.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity 'decoy' is a tactic used to mislead defenders by deploying false or misleading artifacts. It is related to techniques like Masquerading (T1036), where adversaries manipulate file names or metadata to appear legitimate, and Junk Data (T1001.001), which involves adding meaningless characters to C2 traffic to hinder analysis. These methods are employed by groups such as APT28 and Fin13 to evade detection and security tools.

933.name: malicious javascript code
933.profile: [profile]The entity is a malicious JavaScript code attributed to the Lazarus intrusion set. It is used in campaigns like GootLoader (associated with Storm-0249), SUPPER (associated with Vanilla Tempest), and FakeUpdates (associated with Gold Prelude). Its key technical behavior involves being embedded in malicious websites or files to trigger the download of further malicious payloads, such as archive files containing additional scripts, often through mechanisms like URL redirection.[/profile]
933.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity is a malicious JavaScript code, also known as gootloader, supper, and fakeupdates. It is attributed to the groups storm-0249, vanilla tempest, and gold prelude. Its key technical behaviors include being delivered via malicious websites that may implement JavaScript code or conduct URL redirections to trigger the download of an archive file containing the malicious script, which then executes to deploy further payloads. The primary target platform is web browsers and Windows systems through these drive-by download campaigns.

937.name: lateral movement
937.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may transfer tools or other files between systems in a compromised environment. Once brought into the victim environment (i.e., [Ingress Tool Transfer](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1105)) files may then be copied from one system to another to stage adversary tools or other files over the course of an operation.

Adversaries may copy files between internal victim systems to support lateral movement using inherent file sharing protocols such as file sharing over [SMB/Windows Admin Shares](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002) to connected network shares or with authenticated connections via [Remote Desktop Protocol](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/001).(Citation: Unit42 LockerGoga 2019)

Files can also be transferred using native or otherwise present tools on the victim system, such as scp, rsync, curl, sftp, and [ftp](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0095). In some cases, adversaries may be able to leverage [Web Service](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1102)s such as Dropbox or OneDrive to copy files from one machine to another via shared, automatically synced folders.(Citation: Dropbox Malware Sync)
937.profile: [profile]Lateral Tool Transfer, identified as T1570 under the Lateral Movement tactic, is a technique used across Windows, Linux, and Mac platforms. It involves adversaries copying tools or files between compromised systems to support operations. This transfer is executed using native file-sharing protocols like SMB/Windows Admin Shares and RDP, or with system utilities such as scp, rsync, curl, sftp, and ftp. In some instances, adversaries leverage synchronized web services like Dropbox or OneDrive for file transfers. The technique is associated with groups including APT41, Volt Typhoon, and Wizard Spider.
937.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Lateral Movement is a high-level tactic (TA0008) within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, representing the adversary's actions to move through a network after initial access. It is not a specific technique with a T-ID but an overarching category that encompasses numerous specific techniques for pivoting between systems. Common methods include using stolen credentials for remote logins via protocols like RDP or SMB, exploiting software vulnerabilities to execute code on remote hosts, and abusing native administrative tools (e.g., PsExec, WMI) for remote command execution. The goal is to access and control additional systems to locate and exfiltrate target data or deploy further payloads.

938.name: reconnaissance
938.profile: [profile]Reconnaissance is a tactic (TA0043) within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, representing the initial phase where adversaries gather information to plan future operations. It involves techniques like active scanning (T1595), which probes victim infrastructure via network traffic such as ICMP, and gathering specific data such as employee names (T1589.003) to craft lures. Associated intrusion sets include Lazarus and menuPass. This foundational activity supports subsequent stages like establishing resources and gaining initial access.[profile]
938.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Reconnaissance" is a foundational MITRE ATT&CK technique (T1595) within the Reconnaissance tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. It involves adversaries actively probing victim infrastructure via network traffic, such as using ICMP or other protocol features, to gather information that can be used for subsequent targeting, including other reconnaissance activities, establishing resources, or gaining initial access. This technique is distinct from passive information gathering methods.

940.name: hktl_nbtscan
940.profile: [profile]hktl_nbtscan, also known as NBTScan, is a network reconnaissance tool used by the Lazarus intrusion set. It is employed alongside other tools like TrochilusRAT, PlugX, Mimikatz, and Quasar RAT. Its primary function is to scan networks, likely for NetBIOS information, to facilitate lateral movement and intelligence gathering within compromised environments.

941.name: NetBIOS scanning
941.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may scan victims for vulnerabilities that can be used during targeting. Vulnerability scans typically check if the configuration of a target host/application (ex: software and version) potentially aligns with the target of a specific exploit the adversary may seek to use.

These scans may also include more broad attempts to [Gather Victim Host Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1592) that can be used to identify more commonly known, exploitable vulnerabilities. Vulnerability scans typically harvest running software and version numbers via server banners, listening ports, or other network artifacts.(Citation: OWASP Vuln Scanning) Information from these scans may reveal opportunities for other forms of reconnaissance (ex: [Search Open Websites/Domains](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1593) or [Search Open Technical Databases](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1596)), establishing operational resources (ex: [Develop Capabilities](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1587) or [Obtain Capabilities](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1588)), and/or initial access (ex: [Exploit Public-Facing Application](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1190)).
941.profile: [profile]NetBIOS scanning is a reconnaissance technique for discovering network shares and services on Windows systems by querying the NetBIOS Name Service (NBT-NS) on UDP port 137. It is a specific method within the broader Active Scanning (T1595) tactic of the MITRE ATT&CK framework, primarily used on the Windows platform. The technique involves using commands like `net view` to enumerate accessible shared drives on remote systems, aiding in network service and share discovery for subsequent lateral movement or data collection. The intrusion set Lazarus has been associated with this activity.[/profile]
941.profile_without_enhance: [profile]NetBIOS scanning is a reconnaissance technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, categorized under Discovery (Tactic) on the Windows platform. It involves probing UDP port 137 to enumerate NetBIOS names, services, and shares on a network, often using commands like `nbtstat` or tools such as `nbtscan`. This activity maps to technique T1046 (Network Service Discovery) and is used to identify accessible systems and shared resources for potential lateral movement or data collection.

942.name: brute force attack
942.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may use brute force techniques to gain access to accounts when passwords are unknown or when password hashes are obtained.(Citation: TrendMicro Pawn Storm Dec 2020) Without knowledge of the password for an account or set of accounts, an adversary may systematically guess the password using a repetitive or iterative mechanism.(Citation: Dragos Crashoverride 2018) Brute forcing passwords can take place via interaction with a service that will check the validity of those credentials or offline against previously acquired credential data, such as password hashes.

Brute forcing credentials may take place at various points during a breach. For example, adversaries may attempt to brute force access to [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078) within a victim environment leveraging knowledge gathered from other post-compromise behaviors such as [OS Credential Dumping](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003), [Account Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1087), or [Password Policy Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1201). Adversaries may also combine brute forcing activity with behaviors such as [External Remote Services](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1133) as part of Initial Access. 

If an adversary guesses the correct password but fails to login to a compromised account due to location-based conditional access policies, they may change their infrastructure until they match the victim’s location and therefore bypass those policies.(Citation: ReliaQuest Health Care Social Engineering Campaign 2024)
942.profile: [profile]Brute Force is technique T1110 under the Credential Access tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. It systematically guesses passwords via repetitive mechanisms, operating either online against authentication services or offline against acquired password hashes. This activity is often integrated with other techniques like OS Credential Dumping for post-compromise access or with External Remote Services for initial access, and adversaries may adjust their infrastructure to bypass location-based conditional access policies after a successful guess. Associated groups include APT28, APT38, and Lazarus.
942.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Brute Force, identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1110, is a Credential Access tactic applicable across multiple platforms. It involves systematically guessing passwords through repetitive interaction with authentication services (like SSH, RDP, or web portals) or offline against acquired password hashes. This technique is often used for initial access or to compromise valid accounts, and adversaries may combine it with intelligence from credential dumping or password policy discovery to improve success rates.

943.name: file propagation via network share
943.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may look for folders and drives shared on remote systems as a means of identifying sources of information to gather as a precursor for Collection and to identify potential systems of interest for Lateral Movement. Networks often contain shared network drives and folders that enable users to access file directories on various systems across a network. File sharing over a Windows network occurs over the SMB protocol. (Citation: Wikipedia Shared Resource) (Citation: TechNet Shared Folder) [Net](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0039) can be used to query a remote system for available shared drives using the net view \\\\remotesystem command. It can also be used to query shared drives on the local system using net share. For macOS, the sharing -l command lists all shared points used for smb services.
943.profile: [profile]Network Share Discovery (T1135) is a Discovery technique used on Windows and macOS platforms. Adversaries search for folders and drives shared on remote systems to identify information sources for Collection or targets for Lateral Movement. This is commonly performed using the SMB protocol with commands like `net view \\remotesystem` on Windows or `sharing -l` on macOS to list available shares. The technique is associated with groups including Lazarus, APT41, and Wizard Spider.
943.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "file propagation via network share" is a technique for lateral movement where adversaries place malicious files on accessible network shares to infect other systems when users or processes interact with them. This often involves tainting legitimate files or directories on shared drives with malware, scripts, or exploit code. Execution can be triggered by users opening the compromised content, or through mechanisms like malicious shortcut (.LNK) files that run hidden malware before opening the intended directory. The technique leverages existing network protocols like SMB for Windows shares to spread across a network.

972.profile: [profile]Russian commands transliterated from Cyrillic to Latin is a technique used by adversaries like Lazarus to obfuscate command-line instructions. 973.name: using verbs as commands
973.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may reveal credentials of accounts that have disabled Kerberos preauthentication by [Password Cracking](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1110/002) Kerberos messages.(Citation: Harmj0y Roasting AS-REPs Jan 2017) 

Preauthentication offers protection against offline [Password Cracking](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1110/002). When enabled, a user requesting access to a resource initiates communication with the Domain Controller (DC) by sending an Authentication Server Request (AS-REQ) message with a timestamp that is encrypted with the hash of their password. If and only if the DC is able to successfully decrypt the timestamp with the hash of the user’s password, it will then send an Authentication Server Response (AS-REP) message that contains the Ticket Granting Ticket (TGT) to the user. Part of the AS-REP message is signed with the user’s password.(Citation: Microsoft Kerberos Preauth 2014)

For each account found without preauthentication, an adversary may send an AS-REQ message without the encrypted timestamp and receive an AS-REP message with TGT data which may be encrypted with an insecure algorithm such as RC4. The recovered encrypted data may be vulnerable to offline [Password Cracking](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1110/002) attacks similarly to [Kerberoasting](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1558/003) and expose plaintext credentials. (Citation: Harmj0y Roasting AS-REPs Jan 2017)(Citation: Stealthbits Cracking AS-REP Roasting Jun 2019) 

An account registered to a domain, with or without special privileges, can be abused to list all domain accounts that have preauthentication disabled by utilizing Windows tools like [PowerShell](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001) with an LDAP filter. Alternatively, the adversary may send an AS-REQ message for each user. If the DC responds without errors, the account does not require preauthentication and the AS-REP message will already contain the encrypted data. (Citation: Harmj0y Roasting AS-REPs Jan 2017)(Citation: Stealthbits Cracking AS-REP Roasting Jun 2019)

Cracked hashes may enable [Persistence](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0003), [Privilege Escalation](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0004), and [Lateral Movement](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0008) via access to [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078).(Citation: SANS Attacking Kerberos Nov 2014)
973.profile: [profile]AS-REP Roasting (T1558.004) is a Credential Access technique for Windows Active Directory. It exploits accounts with Kerberos preauthentication disabled by sending an AS-REQ message without an encrypted timestamp. If the Domain Controller responds with an AS-REP containing a Ticket-Granting Ticket (TGT) encrypted with a weak cipher like RC4, the encrypted data can be captured and cracked offline to reveal plaintext passwords, facilitating lateral movement and privilege escalation. This can be performed using tools like PowerShell with LDAP filters to enumerate vulnerable accounts.
973.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "using verbs as commands" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the retrieved context, this pattern likely refers to a method where adversaries abuse system utilities or built-in shell commands, such as `sc.exe`, `Reg`, or the `source` command, by treating their action-oriented names (verbs) as direct instructions to modify configurations, execute files, or load functions. This behavior can be part of techniques like Modify Existing Service (T1031) or a deprecated command execution method, operating within Windows or Unix-like platforms to achieve persistence or execution while potentially evading detection by blending with legitimate administrative activity.

975.name: obfuscated VBA macro
975.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may hide malicious Visual Basic for Applications (VBA) payloads embedded within MS Office documents by replacing the VBA source code with benign data.(Citation: FireEye VBA stomp Feb 2020) MS Office documents with embedded VBA content store source code inside of module streams. Each module stream has a PerformanceCache that stores a separate compiled version of the VBA source code known as p-code. The p-code is executed when the MS Office version specified in the _VBA_PROJECT stream (which contains the version-dependent description of the VBA project) matches the version of the host MS Office application.(Citation: Evil Clippy May 2019)(Citation: Microsoft _VBA_PROJECT Stream) An adversary may hide malicious VBA code by overwriting the VBA source code location with zero’s, benign code, or random bytes while leaving the previously compiled malicious p-code. Tools that scan for malicious VBA source code may be bypassed as the unwanted code is hidden in the compiled p-code. If the VBA source code is removed, some tools might even think that there are no macros present. If there is a version match between the _VBA_PROJECT stream and host MS Office application, the p-code will be executed, otherwise the benign VBA source code will be decompressed and recompiled to p-code, thus removing malicious p-code and potentially bypassing dynamic analysis.(Citation: Walmart Roberts Oct 2018)(Citation: FireEye VBA stomp Feb 2020)(Citation: pcodedmp Bontchev)
975.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique "VBA Stomping" (ID: T1564.007), a Defense Evasion sub-technique. It operates on the Windows platform. The technique works by hiding malicious VBA macros in Microsoft Office documents; adversaries replace the readable VBA source code in the module stream with benign or null data while leaving the pre-compiled, malicious p-code in the `PerformanceCache`. This allows the malicious p-code to execute if the Office version matches the document's `_VBA_PROJECT` stream, evading static analysis tools that scan source code and potentially bypassing dynamic analysis when a version mismatch causes recompilation of the benign source. The intrusion-set Lazarus has been associated with this technique.[/profile]
975.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Obfuscated VBA Macro is a technique for evading detection by concealing malicious Visual Basic for Applications code within Microsoft Office documents. This is achieved by modifying the VBA source code, such as overwriting it with benign data or random bytes, while leaving the compiled malicious p-code intact. The malicious p-code executes when the Office version matches, allowing the attack to bypass static analysis tools that scan source code. This technique is commonly used on the Windows platform as part of the Defense Evasion tactic.

980.name: Application Control
980.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may abuse control.exe to proxy execution of malicious payloads. The Windows Control Panel process binary (control.exe) handles execution of Control Panel items, which are utilities that allow users to view and adjust computer settings. Control Panel items are registered executable (.exe) or Control Panel (.cpl) files, the latter are actually renamed dynamic-link library (.dll) files that export a CPlApplet function.(Citation: Microsoft Implementing CPL)(Citation: TrendMicro CPL Malware Jan 2014) For ease of use, Control Panel items typically include graphical menus available to users after being registered and loaded into the Control Panel.(Citation: Microsoft Implementing CPL) Control Panel items can be executed directly from the command line, programmatically via an application programming interface (API) call, or by simply double-clicking the file.(Citation: Microsoft Implementing CPL) (Citation: TrendMicro CPL Malware Jan 2014)(Citation: TrendMicro CPL Malware Dec 2013) Malicious Control Panel items can be delivered via [Phishing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566) campaigns(Citation: TrendMicro CPL Malware Jan 2014)(Citation: TrendMicro CPL Malware Dec 2013) or executed as part of multi-stage malware.(Citation: Palo Alto Reaver Nov 2017) Control Panel items, specifically CPL files, may also bypass application and/or file extension allow lists. Adversaries may also rename malicious DLL files (.dll) with Control Panel file extensions (.cpl) and register them to HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Control Panel\Cpls. Even when these registered DLLs do not comply with the CPL file specification and do not export CPlApplet functions, they are loaded and executed through its DllEntryPoint when Control Panel is executed. CPL files not exporting CPlApplet are not directly executable.(Citation: ESET InvisiMole June 2020)
980.profile: [profile]The entity is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1218.002, named Control Panel Items, under the Defense Evasion tactic for Windows platforms. It involves abusing the legitimate control.exe process or .cpl files to proxy malicious execution. Adversaries rename malicious DLLs to .cpl, register them in the HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Control Panel\Cpls registry key, and execute them via the DllEntryPoint when Control Panel runs, which can bypass application allow lists. The intrusion-set Lazarus is associated with this technique.
980.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Application Control is a defense evasion technique, identified as T1497.001, within the MITRE ATT&CK framework targeting Windows, macOS, and Linux platforms. It involves adversaries attempting to bypass or disable security mechanisms that restrict application execution, such as AppLocker, Software Restriction Policies (SRP), or Gatekeeper. This can be achieved through methods like exploiting trusted directories, using digitally signed binaries, or manipulating file extensions and metadata to evade allow-listing rules and execute unauthorized code.

981.name: Network Segmentation
981.profile: [profile]Network Segmentation is a defensive security measure, not a MITRE ATT&CK attack pattern. It involves dividing a network into smaller, isolated segments using devices like routers and firewalls to control traffic and restrict adversary lateral movement. When these boundary devices are compromised, as seen in techniques like Network Boundary Bridging (T1599), adversaries can bypass segmentation policies to route prohibited traffic, enabling further command and control or data exfiltration across trust boundaries.[/profile]
981.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Network Segmentation is a security architecture technique used to isolate network segments and control traffic flow between them. It is not a specific MITRE ATT&CK attack pattern; it is a defensive control. The retrieved information describes adversary techniques that can bypass or exploit network segmentation, such as compromising boundary devices like routers and firewalls to bridge network trust boundaries (as seen in T1599 - Network Boundary Bridging) or using non-application layer protocols like ICMP or VMCI for command and control to evade segmented network monitoring (as seen in T1095 - Non-Application Layer Protocol).

982.name: Endpoint Hardening
982.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may perform Endpoint Denial of Service (DoS) attacks to degrade or block the availability of services to users. Endpoint DoS can be performed by exhausting the system resources those services are hosted on or exploiting the system to cause a persistent crash condition. Example services include websites, email services, DNS, and web-based applications. Adversaries have been observed conducting DoS attacks for political purposes(Citation: FireEye OpPoisonedHandover February 2016) and to support other malicious activities, including distraction(Citation: FSISAC FraudNetDoS September 2012), hacktivism, and extortion.(Citation: Symantec DDoS October 2014)

An Endpoint DoS denies the availability of a service without saturating the network used to provide access to the service. Adversaries can target various layers of the application stack that is hosted on the system used to provide the service. These layers include the Operating Systems (OS), server applications such as web servers, DNS servers, databases, and the (typically web-based) applications that sit on top of them. Attacking each layer requires different techniques that take advantage of bottlenecks that are unique to the respective components. A DoS attack may be generated by a single system or multiple systems spread across the internet, which is commonly referred to as a distributed DoS (DDoS).

To perform DoS attacks against endpoint resources, several aspects apply to multiple methods, including IP address spoofing and botnets.

Adversaries may use the original IP address of an attacking system, or spoof the source IP address to make the attack traffic more difficult to trace back to the attacking system or to enable reflection. This can increase the difficulty defenders have in defending against the attack by reducing or eliminating the effectiveness of filtering by the source address on network defense devices.

Botnets are commonly used to conduct DDoS attacks against networks and services. Large botnets can generate a significant amount of traffic from systems spread across the global internet. Adversaries may have the resources to build out and control their own botnet infrastructure or may rent time on an existing botnet to conduct an attack. In some of the worst cases for DDoS, so many systems are used to generate requests that each one only needs to send out a small amount of traffic to produce enough volume to exhaust the target's resources. In such circumstances, distinguishing DDoS traffic from legitimate clients becomes exceedingly difficult. Botnets have been used in some of the most high-profile DDoS attacks, such as the 2012 series of incidents that targeted major US banks.(Citation: USNYAG IranianBotnet March 2016)

In cases where traffic manipulation is used, there may be points in the global network (such as high traffic gateway routers) where packets can be altered and cause legitimate clients to execute code that directs network packets toward a target in high volume. This type of capability was previously used for the purposes of web censorship where client HTTP traffic was modified to include a reference to JavaScript that generated the DDoS code to overwhelm target web servers.(Citation: ArsTechnica Great Firewall of China)

For attacks attempting to saturate the providing network, see [Network Denial of Service](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1498).
982.profile: [profile]The entity is Endpoint Denial of Service, identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1499 under the Impact tactic, applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. This technique degrades service availability by exhausting host system resources or causing persistent crashes, targeting layers like the OS, web servers, or databases without saturating the network. It can involve IP spoofing to obscure attack sources and the use of botnets for distributed attacks, and is distinct from network-level denial of service. The intrusion-set Lazarus has been associated with this technique.[/profile]
982.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Endpoint Hardening is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK attack pattern; it is a defensive security practice. The retrieved information describes adversarial techniques that circumvent or target endpoints, such as Endpoint Denial of Service (T1499) which exhausts system resources or causes crashes, Safe Mode Boot (T1562.009) used to disable security software by forcing a limited startup, and Exfiltration Over Webhook (T1567.004) which uses HTTP/S endpoints for data theft. These techniques highlight attack vectors that endpoint hardening measures aim to mitigate.

983.name: Least Privilege
983.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may exploit software vulnerabilities in an attempt to elevate privileges. Exploitation of a software vulnerability occurs when an adversary takes advantage of a programming error in a program, service, or within the operating system software or kernel itself to execute adversary-controlled code. Security constructs such as permission levels will often hinder access to information and use of certain techniques, so adversaries will likely need to perform privilege escalation to include use of software exploitation to circumvent those restrictions.

When initially gaining access to a system, an adversary may be operating within a lower privileged process which will prevent them from accessing certain resources on the system. Vulnerabilities may exist, usually in operating system components and software commonly running at higher permissions, that can be exploited to gain higher levels of access on the system. This could enable someone to move from unprivileged or user level permissions to SYSTEM or root permissions depending on the component that is vulnerable. This could also enable an adversary to move from a virtualized environment, such as within a virtual machine or container, onto the underlying host. This may be a necessary step for an adversary compromising an endpoint system that has been properly configured and limits other privilege escalation methods.

Adversaries may bring a signed vulnerable driver onto a compromised machine so that they can exploit the vulnerability to execute code in kernel mode. This process is sometimes referred to as Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver (BYOVD).(Citation: ESET InvisiMole June 2020)(Citation: Unit42 AcidBox June 2020) Adversaries may include the vulnerable driver with files delivered during Initial Access or download it to a compromised system via [Ingress Tool Transfer](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1105) or [Lateral Tool Transfer](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1570).
983.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique Exploitation for Privilege Escalation (T1068) under the Privilege Escalation tactic, applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves exploiting software vulnerabilities, including in OS components or high-privilege software, to execute adversary-controlled code and elevate permissions from user to SYSTEM/root or escape virtualized environments. A specific method is Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver (BYOVD), where a signed vulnerable driver is introduced to the system to enable kernel-mode code execution.
983.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Least Privilege is a security principle, not a specific MITRE ATT&CK attack pattern, and therefore lacks a standard T-ID or Tactic classification.
