The principle dictates that users and processes should operate with the minimum permissions necessary to perform their function, thereby limiting the impact of a compromise. The sudoers file (`/etc/sudoers`) exemplifies this by controlling command execution privileges, though misconfigurations like `NOPASSWD` can be exploited by adversaries for privilege escalation. This concept underpins secure configuration across platforms to constrain lateral movement and limit damage from credential theft or local account abuse.

984.name: Firewall
984.profile: [profile]The entity "Firewall" is not a MITRE ATT&CK attack pattern itself but a defensive mechanism. The retrieved information describes adversary techniques to subvert it. The primary related techniques are Disable or Modify System Firewall (T1562.004), Disable or Modify Cloud Firewall (T1562.007), and Disable or Modify Network Device Firewall (T1562.013), all under the Defense Evasion tactic. Adversaries target firewalls to bypass network controls, enabling malicious C2, lateral movement, and data exfiltration. Specific methods include using command-line tools (e.g., `esxcli network firewall set` on ESXi), editing Windows Registry, modifying security group rules in cloud environments, or exploiting vulnerabilities in network device management interfaces. The intrusion-set Lazarus is associated with these techniques.[/profile]
984.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Firewall" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. The retrieved information describes related adversary techniques for disabling or modifying firewalls. These include Disable or Modify System Firewall (T1562.004) under the Defense Evasion tactic, executed via command-line, registry edits, or control panels to allow unauthorized traffic. Similarly, Disable or Modify Cloud Firewall (T1562.007) involves altering cloud security group rules, while Disable or Modify Network Device Firewall (T1562.013) targets network hardware rules, often via management console access or exploiting vulnerabilities.

985.name: Intrusion Detection Systems
985.profile: [profile]The entity "Intrusion Detection Systems" is a network security appliance, not a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique. It is referenced as a target of adversary reconnaissance, specifically within technique T1590.006 (Gather Victim Network Information: Network Security Appliances). Adversaries may actively scan for or phish for details about deployed NIDS to identify defensive capabilities and plan subsequent actions like capability development or initial access. Groups such as Volt Typhoon have been associated with this reconnaissance activity.
985.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Intrusion Detection Systems" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique but a defensive system. Adversaries may gather information about network-based intrusion detection systems (NIDS) as part of reconnaissance, using techniques like Active Scanning or Phishing for Information to identify these security appliances and potentially reveal opportunities for further attack or initial access.

986.name: Multi-layered Defense
986.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may exploit a system or application vulnerability to bypass security features. Exploitation of a vulnerability occurs when an adversary takes advantage of a programming error in a program, service, or within the operating system software or kernel itself to execute adversary-controlled code. Vulnerabilities may exist in defensive security software that can be used to disable or circumvent them.

Adversaries may have prior knowledge through reconnaissance that security software exists within an environment or they may perform checks during or shortly after the system is compromised for [Security Software Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1518/001). The security software will likely be targeted directly for exploitation. There are examples of antivirus software being targeted by persistent threat groups to avoid detection.

There have also been examples of vulnerabilities in public cloud infrastructure of SaaS applications that may bypass defense boundaries (Citation: Salesforce zero-day in facebook phishing attack), evade security logs (Citation: Bypassing CloudTrail in AWS Service Catalog), or deploy hidden infrastructure.(Citation: GhostToken GCP flaw)
986.profile: [profile]This entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique Exploitation for Defense Evasion (T1211) under the Defense Evasion tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It involves adversaries exploiting vulnerabilities in defensive security software, operating systems, or cloud infrastructure to bypass or disable security features, evade logs, or deploy hidden resources. This has been employed by groups like APT28 and Velvet Ant, targeting antivirus and cloud services to avoid detection.
986.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Multi-layered Defense is a technique where adversaries implement multiple, overlapping security mechanisms or deceptive layers to complicate detection and analysis. This approach can involve stacking encryption methods, using chained proxies, or deploying segmented command and control channels, making it difficult for defenders to trace malicious activity back to its source or to fully understand the attack chain.

987.name: URL Categorization
987.profile: [profile]URL Categorization is a reconnaissance technique used to profile victims by analyzing and classifying the URLs they visit. This information can be used to identify target interests, organizational infrastructure, or potential vulnerabilities for subsequent attacks, such as spearphishing. The Lazarus group has been associated with this activity.[/profile]
987.profile_without_enhance: [profile]URL Categorization is a technique used by adversaries to classify target URLs for malicious purposes, such as identifying sites for credential harvesting or malware delivery. This process supports spearphishing campaigns by enabling the selection of appropriate lures or the creation of convincing fake websites that mimic legitimate categorized domains. It is often a precursor to techniques like Spearphishing Link (T1566.002) and can involve analyzing web protocols (T1071.001) to blend malicious traffic with normal web activity.

988.name: Social Engineering
988.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may search social media for information about victims that can be used during targeting. Social media sites may contain various information about a victim organization, such as business announcements as well as information about the roles, locations, and interests of staff.

Adversaries may search in different social media sites depending on what information they seek to gather. Threat actors may passively harvest data from these sites, as well as use information gathered to create fake profiles/groups to elicit victim’s into revealing specific information (i.e. [Spearphishing Service](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1598/001)).(Citation: Cyware Social Media) Information from these sources may reveal opportunities for other forms of reconnaissance (ex: [Phishing for Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1598) or [Search Open Technical Databases](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1596)), establishing operational resources (ex: [Establish Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1585) or [Compromise Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1586)), and/or initial access (ex: [Spearphishing via Service](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/003)).
988.profile: [profile]Social Engineering is a broad technique, not a single MITRE ID. It underpins many tactics, primarily Initial Access. It involves manipulating individuals to divulge confidential information or perform actions, such as through pretexting or baiting. Information gathered from reconnaissance, like searching social media (T1593.001), is often used to craft convincing lures for subsequent attacks like spearphishing. Threat actors including APT3, APT28, Lazarus, RocketKitten, and FIN7 employ these methods.
988.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Social Engineering is a foundational adversarial tactic, not a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique, that involves manipulating individuals to divulge confidential information or perform actions that compromise security. It is employed across multiple tactics like Reconnaissance and Initial Access and targets any platform involving human interaction. Technical mechanics include creating deceptive online personas via compromised or fake social media accounts, crafting targeted spearphishing lures via email or voice calls (vishing), and impersonating trusted entities to build rapport and elicit credentials or sensitive data. This tactic often leverages information gathered from prior reconnaissance to enhance the believability of the pretext.

990.name: Dark Seoul/Operation Troy toolset
990.uncertain_mes: As we predicted in last week’s post, threat actors continue to utilize new Realtek vulnerabilities disclosed by IoT Inspector Research Lab to distribute malware. Starting on August 19th, Juniper Threat Labs observed a new set of attacks in the wild on IoT firmware built with the Realtek SDK, this time targeting CVE-2021-35395, which was just disclosed on August 16 by IoT Inspector.
990.profile: [profile]Dark Seoul/Operation Troy toolset, also known as Operation DarkSeoul, is a malware toolset attributed to the Lazarus intrusion set. It is associated with operations targeting IoT firmware, specifically exploiting vulnerabilities like CVE-2021-35395 in Realtek SDK. Key technical behaviors include distribution via new Realtek vulnerabilities. The primary target platforms are IoT devices.[/profile]
990.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Dark Seoul/Operation Troy toolset is a malware toolset associated with the Lazarus Group (also known as HIDDEN COBRA, APT38, and Bureau 121). It is part of broader campaigns including Operation DarkSeoul and Operation Troy, and is linked to subgroups such as Andariel and Bluenoroff. The toolset is used in targeted attacks, with infrastructure and campaigns like Operation GhostSecret and Operation AppleJeus also connected to this activity.

991.name: Tdrop2
991.profile: [profile]Tdrop2 is a member of the Tdrop malware family and is attributed to the Lazarus intrusion set. Its key technical behavior involves acting as a dropper, as indicated by the "dropper2" tag found in its code, which is associated with the deployment of other malware payloads like Brunhilda and Vultur. This dropper functionality is also linked to the MAGICHOUND.DROPIT identifier, connecting it to the Magic Hound campaign. The target platform for this malware is mobile systems, specifically indicated by references to mobile banking applications.
991.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Tdrop2, also known as the Tdrop malware family, is a .NET-based Remote Access Trojan (RAT) associated with the Tonto Team and Operation LagTime threat groups. Key behaviors include deployment via a decoy document, such as a fake COVID-19 related document targeting Mongolian authorities, and dropping an initial executable file. It operates on the Windows platform, uses HTTP for command and control communication, and employs a specific post separator string (6n8fad908fe13c) in its operations.[/profile]

999.name: Spear-Phishing Email
999.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may send phishing messages to gain access to victim systems. All forms of phishing are electronically delivered social engineering. Phishing can be targeted, known as spearphishing. In spearphishing, a specific individual, company, or industry will be targeted by the adversary. More generally, adversaries can conduct non-targeted phishing, such as in mass malware spam campaigns.

Adversaries may send victims emails containing malicious attachments or links, typically to execute malicious code on victim systems. Phishing may also be conducted via third-party services, like social media platforms. Phishing may also involve social engineering techniques, such as posing as a trusted source, as well as evasive techniques such as removing or manipulating emails or metadata/headers from compromised accounts being abused to send messages (e.g., [Email Hiding Rules](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1564/008)).(Citation: Microsoft OAuth Spam 2022)(Citation: Palo Alto Unit 42 VBA Infostealer 2014) Another way to accomplish this is by [Email Spoofing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1672)(Citation: Proofpoint-spoof) the identity of the sender, which can be used to fool both the human recipient as well as automated security tools,(Citation: cyberproof-double-bounce) or by including the intended target as a party to an existing email thread that includes malicious files or links (i.e., "thread hijacking").(Citation: phishing-krebs)

Victims may also receive phishing messages that instruct them to call a phone number where they are directed to visit a malicious URL, download malware,(Citation: sygnia Luna Month)(Citation: CISA Remote Monitoring and Management Software) or install adversary-accessible remote management tools onto their computer (i.e., [User Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204)).(Citation: Unit42 Luna Moth)
999.profile: [profile]Spear-Phishing Email is a targeted social engineering technique (T1566) under the Initial Access tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. It involves sending tailored emails to specific individuals or organizations, containing malicious attachments or links designed to execute code upon user interaction. Evasion methods include email spoofing, thread hijacking, and manipulating email headers from compromised accounts. The technique is notably used by groups like Lazarus to gain initial footholds in victim systems.
999.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Spear-Phishing Email is a targeted social engineering technique (T1566.001) under the Initial Access tactic, primarily targeting Windows, macOS, and Linux. It involves sending deceptive emails to specific individuals or organizations, often using compromised or spoofed accounts to appear trustworthy. The emails contain malicious attachments (like documents or executables) or links that, when interacted with, lead to payload execution or credential harvesting. Attackers use thread hijacking and email hiding rules to evade detection and increase success rates.

1000.name: Wiping Hard Drives
1000.profile: [profile]Wiping Hard Drives, corresponding to MITRE ATT&CK technique Disk Content Wipe (T1561.001) under the Impact tactic, targets Windows systems. This technique involves adversaries overwriting arbitrary portions of a hard drive with random data to render it irrecoverable, often by acquiring direct access to the disk, sometimes using third-party drivers like RawDisk. It is distinct from file-level data destruction and has been used by groups like Lazarus to interrupt system availability, with malware potentially incorporating worm-like propagation features.
1000.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Wiping Hard Drives is a technique for data destruction and availability impact, identified as T1561.001 (Disk Content Wipe) under the Impact tactic. It targets Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. The technique involves adversaries acquiring direct access to a hard drive to overwrite arbitrary portions of disk content with random data, rendering it irrecoverable. This is distinct from file-level destruction and may leverage third-party drivers like RawDisk for direct disk access. To maximize disruption, associated malware can propagate across networks using worm-like features and techniques like Valid Accounts and OS Credential Dumping, as observed in campaigns by groups like Lazarus and Gamaredon.

1001.name: Process Hollowing
1001.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may inject malicious code into suspended and hollowed processes in order to evade process-based defenses. Process hollowing is a method of executing arbitrary code in the address space of a separate live process. Process hollowing is commonly performed by creating a process in a suspended state then unmapping/hollowing its memory, which can then be replaced with malicious code. A victim process can be created with native Windows API calls such as CreateProcess, which includes a flag to suspend the processes primary thread. At this point the process can be unmapped using APIs calls such as ZwUnmapViewOfSection or NtUnmapViewOfSection before being written to, realigned to the injected code, and resumed via VirtualAllocEx, WriteProcessMemory, SetThreadContext, then ResumeThread respectively.(Citation: Leitch Hollowing)(Citation: Elastic Process Injection July 2017) This is very similar to [Thread Local Storage](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1055/005) but creates a new process rather than targeting an existing process. This behavior will likely not result in elevated privileges since the injected process was spawned from (and thus inherits the security context) of the injecting process. However, execution via process hollowing may also evade detection from security products since the execution is masked under a legitimate process.
1001.profile: [profile]Process Hollowing, identified as MITRE ATT&CK T1055.012 under the Defense Evasion tactic for Windows, is a process injection technique where a new legitimate process is created in a suspended state. Its memory is then unmapped using APIs like `NtUnmapViewOfSection` and replaced with malicious code via `WriteProcessMemory` before the thread is resumed, masking execution under a benign process to evade detection. It is notably used by groups like Lazarus, Kimsuky, and TA2541, and is distinct from Thread Execution Hijacking as it creates a new process rather than targeting an existing one.[/profile]
1001.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Process Hollowing is a sub-technique of Process Injection (T1055.012) under the Defense Evasion tactic, primarily for Windows. It works by creating a legitimate process in a suspended state, unmapping its memory with APIs like NtUnmapViewOfSection, and replacing it with malicious code via VirtualAllocEx and WriteProcessMemory before resuming execution with SetThreadContext and ResumeThread, thereby masking malicious activity under a benign process to evade detection.

1002.name: Obfuscate Activity
1002.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may employ various user activity checks to detect and avoid virtualization and analysis environments. This may include changing behaviors based on the results of checks for the presence of artifacts indicative of a virtual machine environment (VME) or sandbox. If the adversary detects a VME, they may alter their malware to disengage from the victim or conceal the core functions of the implant. They may also search for VME artifacts before dropping secondary or additional payloads. Adversaries may use the information learned from [Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1497) during automated discovery to shape follow-on behaviors.(Citation: Deloitte Environment Awareness)

Adversaries may search for user activity on the host based on variables such as the speed/frequency of mouse movements and clicks (Citation: Sans Virtual Jan 2016) , browser history, cache, bookmarks, or number of files in common directories such as home or the desktop. Other methods may rely on specific user interaction with the system before the malicious code is activated, such as waiting for a document to close before activating a macro (Citation: Unit 42 Sofacy Nov 2018) or waiting for a user to double click on an embedded image to activate.(Citation: FireEye FIN7 April 2017)
1002.profile: [profile]Obfuscate Activity, also known as user activity based checks and identified as T1497.002 under the Defense Evasion tactic, operates on Windows, Linux, and Mac platforms. It involves malware checking for signs of a virtual machine or sandbox, such as specific artifacts, and altering its behavior or halting execution if detected. It also monitors for genuine user interaction, like mouse movement frequency, browser history, or waiting for a user to close a document or double-click an image, before activating its payload to evade automated analysis. Groups like DarkHotel and FIN7 have employed this technique.[/profile]
1002.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Obfuscate Activity is a technique adversaries use to hide their actions from detection. This involves concealing malicious behaviors within legitimate processes or network traffic, often by blending in with normal user activity or system operations. Methods include using steganography, impersonating legitimate protocols, or adding junk data to communications to avoid raising alarms. This technique is commonly employed by groups like Gamaredon Group and is related to data obfuscation (T1001) and exfiltration over unencrypted non-C2 protocols (T1048.003).

1003.name: Custom Base64 Alphabet
1003.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may use a custom cryptographic protocol or algorithm to hide command and control traffic. A simple scheme, such as XOR-ing the plaintext with a fixed key, will produce a very weak ciphertext.

Custom encryption schemes may vary in sophistication. Analysis and reverse engineering of malware samples may be enough to discover the algorithm and encryption key used.

Some adversaries may also attempt to implement their own version of a well-known cryptographic algorithm instead of using a known implementation library, which may lead to unintentional errors. (Citation: F-Secure Cosmicduke)
1003.profile: [profile]Custom Base64 Alphabet is a sub-technique of Data Encoding (T1132.001) within the Command and Control tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It involves adversaries using a non-standard Base64 character set to obfuscate command and control or exfiltration traffic, making pattern detection more difficult. This method is distinct from standard Base64 encoding and may be implemented in custom cryptographic or archival schemes, as observed in activities linked to groups like Lazarus.
1003.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Custom Base64 Alphabet is a sub-technique of Data Encoding (T1132) within the Command and Control tactic. It involves adversaries modifying the standard Base64 encoding scheme by using a custom alphabet or character set to obfuscate command and control traffic or exfiltrated data. This method aims to bypass signature-based detection that looks for standard Base64 patterns, making the encoded content more difficult to identify and analyze.

1004.name: String Decryption Routine
1004.profile: [profile]String Decryption Routine is a technique used by adversaries to decrypt encoded strings within malware, often as part of command and control or data exfiltration. It is commonly implemented as a custom cryptographic routine, such as a simple XOR operation with a fixed key, rather than using standard symmetric algorithms like AES or DES. This method is employed by groups like Lazarus to conceal malicious traffic, and its analysis requires reverse engineering of the malware sample to discover the specific algorithm and key.
1004.profile_without_enhance: [profile]String Decryption Routine is a sub-technique of T1573.001 (Symmetric Cryptography) under the Command and Control tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. It involves the specific process of decrypting command and control traffic or payloads that have been previously encrypted using a symmetric algorithm like AES, DES, or RC4. The routine requires the same key used for encryption, and adversaries may implement custom or flawed versions of these algorithms, which can be discovered through malware analysis and reverse engineering to extract the decryption key and logic.

1005.name: File Decoding from .gif/.jpg URLs
1005.profile: [profile]File Decoding from .gif/.jpg URLs is a technique where adversaries hide malicious payloads within seemingly benign image files, such as .gif or .jpg, to bypass security filters. The core technical mechanic involves encoding or embedding executable code or data within the standard binary format of these image files. This obfuscated content is then decoded or extracted on the victim's system to deploy malware, often as part of a multi-stage attack chain linked to groups like Lazarus. The technique leverages common, trusted file types to evade detection during transfer or initial access.
1005.profile_without_enhance: [profile]File Decoding from .gif/.jpg URLs is a technique where adversaries embed and conceal malicious payloads within seemingly benign image files, such as .gif or .jpg formats. This method involves encoding the payload into the image data, which is later deobfuscated and executed on the victim's system. It serves as a form of file-based obfuscation to bypass security filters and detection mechanisms, often delivered via methods like HTML smuggling or spearphishing attachments.

1006.name: Basic Reconnaissance
1006.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may abuse Visual Basic (VB) for execution. VB is a programming language created by Microsoft with interoperability with many Windows technologies such as [Component Object Model](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1559/001) and the [Native API](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1106) through the Windows API. Although tagged as legacy with no planned future evolutions, VB is integrated and supported in the .NET Framework and cross-platform .NET Core.(Citation: VB .NET Mar 2020)(Citation: VB Microsoft)

Derivative languages based on VB have also been created, such as Visual Basic for Applications (VBA) and VBScript. VBA is an event-driven programming language built into Microsoft Office, as well as several third-party applications.(Citation: Microsoft VBA)(Citation: Wikipedia VBA) VBA enables documents to contain macros used to automate the execution of tasks and other functionality on the host. VBScript is a default scripting language on Windows hosts and can also be used in place of [JavaScript](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/007) on HTML Application (HTA) webpages served to Internet Explorer (though most modern browsers do not come with VBScript support).(Citation: Microsoft VBScript)

Adversaries may use VB payloads to execute malicious commands. Common malicious usage includes automating execution of behaviors with VBScript or embedding VBA content into [Spearphishing Attachment](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001) payloads (which may also involve [Mark-of-the-Web Bypass](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1553/005) to enable execution).(Citation: Default VBS macros Blocking )
1006.profile: [profile]The entity "Basic Reconnaissance" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. The provided data primarily describes the MITRE technique "Visual Basic" (T1059.005), a sub-technique of Command and Scripting Interpreter under the Execution tactic for Windows. It involves adversaries using Visual Basic, VBA, or VBScript to execute malicious commands, commonly by embedding VBA into spearphishing attachments or using VBScript to automate behaviors. The Lazarus group is associated with its use. The retrieved information on "active scanning" and "internet connection discovery" is not directly relevant to this specific Visual Basic execution technique.
1006.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Basic Reconnaissance is a foundational adversary technique for gathering information about a target. It is a sub-technique of Reconnaissance (TA0043) and involves initial, often low-effort, information collection activities. This can include passive methods like searching open-source websites and domains, or active methods like scanning for internet connectivity on a compromised host using commands like ping or tracert to determine network capability before establishing command and control. The gathered intelligence is used to inform subsequent stages of an attack, such as developing capabilities or identifying initial access vectors.

1007.name: Download Additional Components
1007.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may install malicious components that run on Internet Information Services (IIS) web servers to establish persistence. IIS provides several mechanisms to extend the functionality of the web servers. For example, Internet Server Application Programming Interface (ISAPI) extensions and filters can be installed to examine and/or modify incoming and outgoing IIS web requests. Extensions and filters are deployed as DLL files that export three functions: Get{Extension/Filter}Version, Http{Extension/Filter}Proc, and (optionally) Terminate{Extension/Filter}. IIS modules may also be installed to extend IIS web servers.(Citation: Microsoft ISAPI Extension Overview 2017)(Citation: Microsoft ISAPI Filter Overview 2017)(Citation: IIS Backdoor 2011)(Citation: Trustwave IIS Module 2013) Adversaries may install malicious ISAPI extensions and filters to observe and/or modify traffic, execute commands on compromised machines, or proxy command and control traffic. ISAPI extensions and filters may have access to all IIS web requests and responses. For example, an adversary may abuse these mechanisms to modify HTTP responses in order to distribute malicious commands/content to previously comprised hosts.(Citation: Microsoft ISAPI Filter Overview 2017)(Citation: Microsoft ISAPI Extension Overview 2017)(Citation: Microsoft ISAPI Extension All Incoming 2017)(Citation: Dell TG-3390)(Citation: Trustwave IIS Module 2013)(Citation: MMPC ISAPI Filter 2012) Adversaries may also install malicious IIS modules to observe and/or modify traffic. IIS 7.0 introduced modules that provide the same unrestricted access to HTTP requests and responses as ISAPI extensions and filters. IIS modules can be written as a DLL that exports RegisterModule, or as a .NET application that interfaces with ASP.NET APIs to access IIS HTTP requests.(Citation: Microsoft IIS Modules Overview 2007)(Citation: Trustwave IIS Module 2013)(Citation: ESET IIS Malware 2021)
1007.profile: [profile]Download Additional Components is a sub-technique (T1505.004) under the Server Software Component tactic within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, targeting Windows platforms. It involves adversaries installing malicious components like ISAPI extensions, filters, or IIS modules as DLL files on Internet Information Services (IIS) web servers to establish persistence. These components, which export specific functions such as GetExtensionVersion and HttpExtensionProc, gain unrestricted access to HTTP requests and responses, enabling traffic observation/modification, command execution, and proxying of command and control communications. The intrusion-set Lazarus has been associated with this activity.
1007.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Download Additional Components is a technique used by adversaries to retrieve and install extra malicious software or modules onto a compromised system to extend their capabilities. It operates within the Execution tactic. The technical mechanics involve using command and scripting interpreters to fetch components from remote locations, often via protocols like HTTP or FTP, and then executing them. This can include downloading payloads referenced in LNK file icon metadata or using legitimate system processes to load malicious DLLs.

1009.name: Tdrop malware family
1009.uncertain_mes:
A .NET rat targets Mongolia
A new document royal road v7 installs a backdoor in .NET. a first executable is dropped \os03C2.tmp. This exe has many similarities with older campaigns using by Operation LagTime or Tonto Team.
Document
The decoy document is a document about infection of covid19 in Russia send to the Mongolia Authorities. The document is fake signed A. Amarsaikhan.
1009.profile: [profile]The malware is known as the Tdrop malware family, also referred to as nmass malware. It is a .NET-based remote access trojan (RAT) that targets entities in Mongolia. Its infection chain involves a decoy document, specifically a fake document about COVID-19 infections in Russia sent to Mongolian authorities, which is signed "A. Amarsaikhan." This document uses a Royal Road v7 template to install the backdoor, dropping an initial executable named \os03C2.tmp. The malware shares similarities with campaigns historically associated with Operation LagTime or Tonto Team, though specific attributed groups remain uncertain. Its primary target platform is Windows via .NET execution.
1009.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The Tdrop malware family is attributed to the Lazarus intrusion set and includes members like Tdrop2, which functions as a dropper. Its primary target platform is mobile, specifically mobile applications, and it may share dropper infrastructure or code with entities like leash, associated with the MAGICHOUND.DROPIT identifier and the Magic Hound group.

1014.name: Weaponized Microsoft Office Documents
1014.profile: [profile]Weaponized Microsoft Office Documents are malicious files used to deliver payloads like ransomware, often exploiting vulnerabilities in Microsoft Office or Adobe Reader. They are associated with groups including Lazarus, Lucky Cat, Sandworm, Hellsing, Ice Fog, Pirate Panda, Rancor, TA428, Tick, Tonto Team, and Karma Panda. The technique is also linked to tools like Royal Road, lowzero, BlackEnergy, and 8.t dropper, which utilize these documents for initial access and execution of malicious code on target systems.
1014.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Weaponized Microsoft Office Documents is a malware delivery mechanism. Aliases include Royal Road. It is associated with groups like Lucky Cat, Sandworm, Hellsing, Ice Fog, Pirate Panda, Rancor, TA428, Tick, Tonto Team, and Karma Panda. Key technical behaviors involve exploiting vulnerabilities in Microsoft Office and Adobe Reader to execute payloads, such as ransomware, without user interaction. The primary target platform is Windows systems via malicious Office document files.

1015.name: Malicious Macros
1015.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may abuse Microsoft Office templates to obtain persistence on a compromised system. Microsoft Office contains templates that are part of common Office applications and are used to customize styles. The base templates within the application are used each time an application starts. (Citation: Microsoft Change Normal Template) Office Visual Basic for Applications (VBA) macros (Citation: MSDN VBA in Office) can be inserted into the base template and used to execute code when the respective Office application starts in order to obtain persistence. Examples for both Word and Excel have been discovered and published. By default, Word has a Normal.dotm template created that can be modified to include a malicious macro. Excel does not have a template file created by default, but one can be added that will automatically be loaded.(Citation: enigma0x3 normal.dotm)(Citation: Hexacorn Office Template Macros) Shared templates may also be stored and pulled from remote locations.(Citation: GlobalDotName Jun 2019) Word Normal.dotm location:
C:\Users\<username>\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Templates\Normal.dotm Excel Personal.xlsb location:
C:\Users\<username>\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Excel\XLSTART\PERSONAL.XLSB Adversaries may also change the location of the base template to point to their own by hijacking the application's search order, e.g. Word 2016 will first look for Normal.dotm under C:\Program Files (x86)\Microsoft Office\root\Office16\, or by modifying the GlobalDotName registry key. By modifying the GlobalDotName registry key an adversary can specify an arbitrary location, file name, and file extension to use for the template that will be loaded on application startup. To abuse GlobalDotName, adversaries may first need to register the template as a trusted document or place it in a trusted location.(Citation: GlobalDotName Jun 2019) An adversary may need to enable macros to execute unrestricted depending on the system or enterprise security policy on use of macros.
1015.profile: [profile]Office Template Macros, identified as T1137.001 under the Persistence tactic, targets Windows and macOS. This technique involves inserting malicious VBA macros into base Microsoft Office templates like Word's Normal.dotm or Excel's Personal.xlsb to execute code automatically when the application starts. Adversaries can modify the default template file locations or hijack the search order, including using the GlobalDotName registry key to point to a remote or custom template, often requiring the macro to be in a trusted location or document to bypass security settings.[/profile]
1015.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Malicious Macros is a technique where adversaries embed malicious Visual Basic for Applications (VBA) code within Microsoft Office documents. This technique, often delivered via spearphishing attachments, relies on user interaction to enable macros, which then execute payloads to establish initial access or persistence. Attackers may hide this malicious VBA source code through methods like VBA stomping, overwriting the source with benign data while leaving the compiled p-code intact to evade static analysis. The execution typically occurs on Windows platforms as part of the Initial Access tactic.

1016.name: XOR Encryption
1016.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may compromise a network device’s encryption capability in order to bypass encryption that would otherwise protect data communications. (Citation: Cisco Synful Knock Evolution)

Encryption can be used to protect transmitted network traffic to maintain its confidentiality (protect against unauthorized disclosure) and integrity (protect against unauthorized changes). Encryption ciphers are used to convert a plaintext message to ciphertext and can be computationally intensive to decipher without the associated decryption key. Typically, longer keys increase the cost of cryptanalysis, or decryption without the key.

Adversaries can compromise and manipulate devices that perform encryption of network traffic. For example, through behaviors such as [Modify System Image](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1601), [Reduce Key Space](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1600/001), and [Disable Crypto Hardware](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1600/002), an adversary can negatively effect and/or eliminate a device’s ability to securely encrypt network traffic. This poses a greater risk of unauthorized disclosure and may help facilitate data manipulation, Credential Access, or Collection efforts. (Citation: Cisco Blog Legacy Device Attacks)
1016.profile: [profile]XOR Encryption is a simple, custom cryptographic technique, often implemented in malware for data obfuscation or weak command and control channel encryption. It operates by applying the exclusive-or (XOR) operation to data with a fixed key, producing a very weak ciphertext that is trivial to analyze and break. This method is commonly used for archiving collected data prior to exfiltration or within custom TCP protocols to hide traffic, as seen in malware like Carbanak and activities linked to groups such as Lazarus and APT28. Its simplicity makes it ineffective against proper cryptanalysis.
1016.profile_without_enhance: [profile]XOR Encryption, corresponding to MITRE ATT&CK technique T1024 (Custom Cryptographic Protocol), falls under the Command and Control tactic and applies to multiple platforms. It involves adversaries using the XOR (exclusive OR) operation with a fixed key to obfuscate data, such as command and control traffic or archived files, producing a weak ciphertext that is often implemented in custom code without external libraries. This method is a simple form of symmetric encryption and is frequently associated with other obfuscation techniques like custom archiving.[profile]

1017.name: Payload Delivery
1017.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may attempt to make payloads difficult to discover and analyze by delivering files to victims as uncompiled code. Text-based source code files may subvert analysis and scrutiny from protections targeting executables/binaries. These payloads will need to be compiled before execution; typically via native utilities such as ilasm.exe(Citation: ATTACK IQ), csc.exe, or GCC/MinGW.(Citation: ClearSky MuddyWater Nov 2018)

Source code payloads may also be encrypted, encoded, and/or embedded within other files, such as those delivered as a [Phishing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566). Payloads may also be delivered in formats unrecognizable and inherently benign to the native OS (ex: EXEs on macOS/Linux) before later being (re)compiled into a proper executable binary with a bundled compiler and execution framework.(Citation: TrendMicro WindowsAppMac)
1017.profile: [profile]The entity corresponds to MITRE ATT&CK technique T1027.004, named Obfuscated Files or Information: Compile After Delivery, under the Defense Evasion tactic, primarily for Windows platforms. It involves delivering payloads as uncompiled source code (e.g., C#, C) to evade binary security tools, requiring on-victim compilation using native utilities like csc.exe, ilasm.exe, or GCC. Payloads may be further obfuscated through encryption, embedding in documents like phishing attachments, or using cross-platform file formats to appear benign before compilation. Associated threat groups include Gamaredon Group, MuddyWater, Rocke, and Sea Turtle.
1017.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Payload Delivery is a technique for introducing malicious content into a target environment. It encompasses various methods, such as delivering payloads as uncompiled source code to evade detection, which then requires compilation via native utilities like csc.exe or GCC before execution. These payloads may be further obfuscated through encryption or embedding within other files. The technique is utilized by threat groups including Gamaredon Group, MuddyWater, Rocke, and Sea Turtle.

1018.name: Fake TLS Communication
1018.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may use an existing, legitimate external Web service as a means for sending commands to and receiving output from a compromised system over the Web service channel. Compromised systems may leverage popular websites and social media to host command and control (C2) instructions. Those infected systems can then send the output from those commands back over that Web service channel. The return traffic may occur in a variety of ways, depending on the Web service being utilized. For example, the return traffic may take the form of the compromised system posting a comment on a forum, issuing a pull request to development project, updating a document hosted on a Web service, or by sending a Tweet. 

Popular websites and social media acting as a mechanism for C2 may give a significant amount of cover due to the likelihood that hosts within a network are already communicating with them prior to a compromise. Using common services, such as those offered by Google or Twitter, makes it easier for adversaries to hide in expected noise. Web service providers commonly use SSL/TLS encryption, giving adversaries an added level of protection.
1018.profile: [profile]Fake TLS Communication is a sub-technique of Web Service (T1102.002) under the Command and Control tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It involves adversaries disguising C2 traffic by impersonating a fake SSL/TLS handshake to make subsequent communications appear as legitimate encrypted traffic, potentially bypassing security tools. This technique is used by groups like Lazarus. The related technique of Bidirectional Communication leverages legitimate web services like social media for C2, where return traffic can be posted as comments or updates, often protected by the service's inherent SSL/TLS encryption.[/profile]
1018.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Fake TLS Communication is a sub-technique of Protocol Impersonation (T1001.003) under the Command and Control tactic. It involves adversaries disguising C2 traffic by initiating a fake SSL/TLS handshake, making subsequent malicious communications appear to be standard encrypted web traffic. This impersonation can interfere with security analysis and tooling by blending the traffic with that of trusted entities.

1019.name: Encoded Strings
1019.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may encrypt or encode files to obfuscate strings, bytes, and other specific patterns to impede detection. Encrypting and/or encoding file content aims to conceal malicious artifacts within a file used in an intrusion. Many other techniques, such as [Software Packing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/002), [Steganography](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/003), and [Embedded Payloads](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/009), share this same broad objective. Encrypting and/or encoding files could lead to a lapse in detection of static signatures, only for this malicious content to be revealed (i.e., [Deobfuscate/Decode Files or Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1140)) at the time of execution/use.

This type of file obfuscation can be applied to many file artifacts present on victim hosts, such as malware log/configuration and payload files.(Citation: File obfuscation) Files can be encrypted with a hardcoded or user-supplied key, as well as otherwise obfuscated using standard encoding schemes such as Base64.

The entire content of a file may be obfuscated, or just specific functions or values (such as C2 addresses). Encryption and encoding may also be applied in redundant layers for additional protection.

For example, adversaries may abuse password-protected Word documents or self-extracting (SFX) archives as a method of encrypting/encoding a file such as a [Phishing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566) payload. These files typically function by attaching the intended archived content to a decompressor stub that is executed when the file is invoked (e.g., [User Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204)).(Citation: SFX - Encrypted/Encoded File) 

Adversaries may also abuse file-specific as well as custom encoding schemes. For example, Byte Order Mark (BOM) headers in text files may be abused to manipulate and obfuscate file content until [Command and Scripting Interpreter](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059) execution.
1019.profile: [profile]Encrypted/Encoded File (T1027.013) is a Defense Evasion technique used across multiple platforms. It involves obfuscating file content to conceal malicious artifacts, impeding static signature detection. This is achieved through encryption with hardcoded or user-supplied keys, or via standard encoding like Base64. Specific applications include abusing password-protected Word documents or self-extracting (SFX) archives to hide payloads, and manipulating Byte Order Mark (BOM) headers in text files. The technique is employed by numerous groups, including Lazarus.[/profile]
1019.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Encoded Strings is a sub-technique of Obfuscated Files or Information (T1027) under the Defense Evasion tactic. It involves obfuscating strings, bytes, and other patterns within files or data to impede static detection. This is commonly achieved using standard encoding schemes like Base64, hexadecimal, or ASCII, which can be applied to specific values like command and control addresses or to entire file contents. The encoded data is later deobfuscated during execution. This technique is used by numerous threat groups, including Lazarus Group and APT33.

1020.name: Beaconing Behavior
1020.profile: [profile]Beaconing Behavior is a technique for maintaining command and control (C2) communication, often categorized under the Tactic of Command and Control. It involves infected systems periodically sending outbound signals (beacons) to an adversary-controlled server to check for new commands, often at predetermined intervals to blend with normal traffic and evade detection. This behavior is a core component of C2 channels, including DNS beaconing where queries are used to tunnel commands. The intrusion-set Lazarus has been associated with employing such beaconing behavior in their operations.[/profile]
1020.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Beaconing Behavior is a technique within the Command and Control tactic, applicable across multiple platforms, where adversaries establish periodic, low-frequency network communication from a compromised host to a controller to avoid detection by blending with normal traffic. This behavior often involves DNS tunneling, embedding commands within DNS queries using records like TXT or A, and is employed by groups like OilRig and APT41.

1021.name: Infrastructure Reuse
1021.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may manipulate network traffic in order to hide and evade detection of their C2 infrastructure. This can be accomplished by identifying and filtering traffic from defensive tools,(Citation: TA571) masking malicious domains to obfuscate the true destination from both automated scanning tools and security researchers,(Citation: Schema-abuse)(Citation: Facad1ng)(Citation: Browser-updates) and otherwise hiding malicious artifacts to delay discovery and prolong the effectiveness of adversary infrastructure that could otherwise be identified, blocked, or taken down entirely.

C2 networks may include the use of [Proxy](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1090) or VPNs to disguise IP addresses, which can allow adversaries to blend in with normal network traffic and bypass conditional access policies or anti-abuse protections. For example, an adversary may use a virtual private cloud to spoof their IP address to closer align with a victim's IP address ranges. This may also bypass security measures relying on geolocation of the source IP address.(Citation: sysdig)(Citation: Orange Residential Proxies)

Adversaries may also attempt to filter network traffic in order to evade defensive tools in numerous ways, including blocking/redirecting common incident responder or security appliance user agents.(Citation: mod_rewrite)(Citation: SocGholish-update) Filtering traffic based on IP and geo-fencing may also avoid automated sandboxing or researcher activity (i.e., [Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1497)).(Citation: TA571)(Citation: mod_rewrite)

Hiding C2 infrastructure may also be supported by [Resource Development](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0042) activities such as [Acquire Infrastructure](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1583) and [Compromise Infrastructure](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1584). For example, using widely trusted hosting services or domains such as prominent URL shortening providers or marketing services for C2 networks may enable adversaries to present benign content that later redirects victims to malicious web pages or infrastructure once specific conditions are met.(Citation: StarBlizzard)(Citation: QR-cofense)
1021.profile: [profile]Hide Infrastructure, designated T1665 under the Resource Development tactic, is a technique where adversaries manipulate network traffic to conceal their command and control (C2) infrastructure. This involves using proxies or VPNs to disguise IP addresses, filtering traffic to block defensive tool user agents, and employing geo-fencing to avoid detection. Adversaries may also mask malicious domains and leverage trusted hosting or URL shortening services to redirect victims, thereby blending malicious activity with normal traffic and prolonging the operational life of their infrastructure.
1021.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Infrastructure Reuse is a technique within the Resource Development tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. It involves adversaries leveraging previously established or compromised infrastructure—such as servers, domains, or botnets—for new campaigns or to support other techniques like Proxy. This reuse allows operations to blend with normal traffic, evades attribution by distancing activity from the adversary's core infrastructure, and can accelerate attack deployment by avoiding the need to procure new assets.

1031.name: Scanning TCP 445 (SMB)
1031.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may scan victims for vulnerabilities that can be used during targeting. Vulnerability scans typically check if the configuration of a target host/application (ex: software and version) potentially aligns with the target of a specific exploit the adversary may seek to use.

These scans may also include more broad attempts to [Gather Victim Host Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1592) that can be used to identify more commonly known, exploitable vulnerabilities. Vulnerability scans typically harvest running software and version numbers via server banners, listening ports, or other network artifacts.(Citation: OWASP Vuln Scanning) Information from these scans may reveal opportunities for other forms of reconnaissance (ex: [Search Open Websites/Domains](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1593) or [Search Open Technical Databases](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1596)), establishing operational resources (ex: [Develop Capabilities](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1587) or [Obtain Capabilities](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1588)), and/or initial access (ex: [Exploit Public-Facing Application](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1190)).
1031.profile: [profile]Scanning TCP 445 (SMB) is a specific form of vulnerability scanning (T1595.002) under the Reconnaissance tactic, targeting Windows platforms via the Server Message Block protocol to identify exploitable services, harvest software versions from server banners, and discover open network shares for potential lateral movement or initial access, as used by groups like Lazarus.
1031.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Scanning TCP 445 (SMB) is a reconnaissance technique, likely a sub-technique of Active Scanning (T1595), used to gather victim network information. It involves probing port 445 to identify systems running the Server Message Block protocol, which is commonly used for Windows file and printer sharing. This scan can reveal accessible network shares, host software versions via banners, and potential entry points for lateral movement or initial access, such as exploiting SMB vulnerabilities or accessing administrative shares.

1032.name: Worm Propagation
1032.profile: [profile]Worm Propagation is a technique adversaries use to spread malware across a network, often leveraging other techniques like Valid Accounts, OS Credential Dumping, and SMB/Windows Admin Shares for lateral movement. It is associated with malware such as Shamoon 2 and the Lazarus intrusion set. The technique can be used to maximize impact in operations where network-wide disruption is the goal, enabling the widespread execution of destructive actions like disk wiping.[/profile]
1032.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Worm Propagation is the technique of malicious software self-replicating across a network. It is often used to maximize the impact of other attacks, such as disk wiping, by enabling malware to spread automatically. This propagation can leverage techniques like Valid Accounts, OS Credential Dumping, and SMB/Windows Admin Shares to move laterally from an initial infected system to other machines on the network.

1034.name: Ransomware (Bitcoin)
1034.profile: [profile]Ransomware (Bitcoin) is a specific implementation of the MITRE ATT&CK technique Data Encrypted for Impact (T1486) under the Impact tactic. It operates across Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. This ransomware encrypts user files like documents and images to interrupt availability, demanding a Bitcoin ransom for decryption. It may propagate using worm-like features via techniques like Valid Accounts and SMB shares, and can avoid encrypting critical system files (e.g., .exe, .dll) to maintain system operation for ransom delivery. The Lazarus intrusion-set has been associated with such activity.
1034.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Ransomware (Bitcoin)" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the provided context, it describes a specific application of the technique Data Encrypted for Impact (T1486), which falls under the Impact tactic. The technical mechanics involve encrypting user files (e.g., Office documents, PDFs) and critical system components to render data inaccessible, demanding a Bitcoin ransom for decryption. Adversaries may use worm-like propagation and avoid encrypting system files like .dll or .exe to maintain system operability for ransom delivery.

1035.name: Exploit
1035.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may attempt to exploit a weakness in an Internet-facing host or system to initially access a network. The weakness in the system can be a software bug, a temporary glitch, or a misconfiguration.

Exploited applications are often websites/web servers, but can also include databases (like SQL), standard services (like SMB or SSH), network device administration and management protocols (like SNMP and Smart Install), and any other system with Internet-accessible open sockets.(Citation: NVD CVE-2016-6662)(Citation: CIS Multiple SMB Vulnerabilities)(Citation: US-CERT TA18-106A Network Infrastructure Devices 2018)(Citation: Cisco Blog Legacy Device Attacks)(Citation: NVD CVE-2014-7169) On ESXi infrastructure, adversaries may exploit exposed OpenSLP services; they may alternatively exploit exposed VMware vCenter servers.(Citation: Recorded Future ESXiArgs Ransomware 2023)(Citation: Ars Technica VMWare Code Execution Vulnerability 2021) Depending on the flaw being exploited, this may also involve [Exploitation for Defense Evasion](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1211) or [Exploitation for Client Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1203).

If an application is hosted on cloud-based infrastructure and/or is containerized, then exploiting it may lead to compromise of the underlying instance or container. This can allow an adversary a path to access the cloud or container APIs (e.g., via the [Cloud Instance Metadata API](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1552/005)), exploit container host access via [Escape to Host](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1611), or take advantage of weak identity and access management policies.

Adversaries may also exploit edge network infrastructure and related appliances, specifically targeting devices that do not support robust host-based defenses.(Citation: Mandiant Fortinet Zero Day)(Citation: Wired Russia Cyberwar)

For websites and databases, the OWASP top 10 and CWE top 25 highlight the most common web-based vulnerabilities.(Citation: OWASP Top 10)(Citation: CWE top 25)
1035.profile: [profile]Exploit Public-Facing Application, designated T1190 under the Initial Access tactic, targets multiple platforms including Windows, Linux, and cloud environments. The technique involves exploiting weaknesses like software bugs or misconfigurations in internet-facing systems such as web servers, databases (e.g., SQL), standard services (SMB, SSH), and network device protocols (SNMP) to gain initial network access. It is commonly used by numerous threat groups including APT28, APT29, and Lazarus, and can lead to further compromise of underlying cloud instances or container APIs.
1035.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Exploit is a foundational attack pattern (ID: T1588.005 / T1587.004) for initial access, execution, privilege escalation, and defense evasion across multiple platforms. It involves taking advantage of a software bug or vulnerability to cause unintended behavior, such as arbitrary code execution. Adversaries often acquire exploits by purchasing, stealing, or downloading them from third parties, or by developing their own through methods like fuzzing. Specific applications targeted include web browsers, office suites, and common third-party software like Adobe Reader.

1036.name: Backdoor Implantation
1036.profile: [profile]Backdoor Implantation is a technique where adversaries insert malicious access points into systems, often through supply chain compromise (T1195.003) or by implanting backdoored cloud/container images (T1525). It provides persistent, covert control, enabling further malicious activities. The Lazarus group has been associated with such operations. Technical mechanics include modifying hardware/firmware before delivery or planting backdoors in infrastructure images like AWS AMIs or Docker containers to ensure continued access when these images are deployed.
1036.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Backdoor Implantation is a persistent access technique where adversaries implant malicious code into systems, images, or hardware. In cloud environments, this involves backdooring container images like Docker or cloud service images (AWS AMIs, GCP Images, Azure Images) within a victim's registry to gain persistent access when infrastructure is provisioned. In supply chain attacks, adversaries manipulate hardware components or firmware before consumer receipt to insert difficult-to-detect backdoors into devices such as servers or network infrastructure.

1037.name: Check Disk Drives
1037.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may wipe or corrupt raw disk data on specific systems or in large numbers in a network to interrupt availability to system and network resources. With direct write access to a disk, adversaries may attempt to overwrite portions of disk data. Adversaries may opt to wipe arbitrary portions of disk data and/or wipe disk structures like the master boot record (MBR). A complete wipe of all disk sectors may be attempted.

To maximize impact on the target organization in operations where network-wide availability interruption is the goal, malware used for wiping disks may have worm-like features to propagate across a network by leveraging additional techniques like [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078), [OS Credential Dumping](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003), and [SMB/Windows Admin Shares](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002).(Citation: Novetta Blockbuster Destructive Malware)

On network devices, adversaries may wipe configuration files and other data from the device using [Network Device CLI](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/008) commands such as `erase`.(Citation: erase_cmd_cisco)
1037.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique Disk Wipe (T1561) under the Impact tactic, targeting Windows, Linux, and Network platforms. It involves adversaries overwriting raw disk data or critical structures like the master boot record (MBR) to disrupt system availability. This can be executed via direct disk access or on network devices using CLI commands such as `erase`. The technique is associated with the Lazarus intrusion set and may incorporate worm-like propagation using techniques like Valid Accounts and SMB shares for broader network impact.
1037.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Check Disk Drives is a discovery technique (ID not specified in MITRE ATT&CK) used to enumerate local storage devices. It involves querying system information to identify drives, their attributes like free space and serial numbers, and shared network resources. Common methods include using commands such as `wmic logicaldisk get` and `Get-PSDrive` on Windows, `lsblk` and `df` on Linux, and `diskutil` on macOS. This reconnaissance aids in subsequent actions like data targeting, lateral movement, or ransomware deployment.

1038.name: Encrypt Data for Impact
1038.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may encrypt data on target systems or on large numbers of systems in a network to interrupt availability to system and network resources. They can attempt to render stored data inaccessible by encrypting files or data on local and remote drives and withholding access to a decryption key. This may be done in order to extract monetary compensation from a victim in exchange for decryption or a decryption key (ransomware) or to render data permanently inaccessible in cases where the key is not saved or transmitted.(Citation: US-CERT Ransomware 2016)(Citation: FireEye WannaCry 2017)(Citation: US-CERT NotPetya 2017)(Citation: US-CERT SamSam 2018)

In the case of ransomware, it is typical that common user files like Office documents, PDFs, images, videos, audio, text, and source code files will be encrypted (and often renamed and/or tagged with specific file markers). Adversaries may need to first employ other behaviors, such as [File and Directory Permissions Modification](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1222) or [System Shutdown/Reboot](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1529), in order to unlock and/or gain access to manipulate these files.(Citation: CarbonBlack Conti July 2020) In some cases, adversaries may encrypt critical system files, disk partitions, and the MBR.(Citation: US-CERT NotPetya 2017) Adversaries may also encrypt virtual machines hosted on ESXi or other hypervisors.(Citation: Crowdstrike Hypervisor Jackpotting Pt 2 2021) 

To maximize impact on the target organization, malware designed for encrypting data may have worm-like features to propagate across a network by leveraging other attack techniques like [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078), [OS Credential Dumping](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003), and [SMB/Windows Admin Shares](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002).(Citation: FireEye WannaCry 2017)(Citation: US-CERT NotPetya 2017) Encryption malware may also leverage [Internal Defacement](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1491/001), such as changing victim wallpapers or ESXi server login messages, or otherwise intimidate victims by sending ransom notes or other messages to connected printers (known as "print bombing").(Citation: NHS Digital Egregor Nov 2020)(Citation: Varonis)

In cloud environments, storage objects within compromised accounts may also be encrypted.(Citation: Rhino S3 Ransomware Part 1) For example, in AWS environments, adversaries may leverage services such as AWS’s Server-Side Encryption with Customer Provided Keys (SSE-C) to encrypt data.(Citation: Halcyon AWS Ransomware 2025)
1038.profile: [profile]Encrypt Data for Impact is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1486 under the Impact tactic, targeting Windows, Linux, and cloud platforms. It involves encrypting files on local drives, remote shares, and cloud storage objects to disrupt availability, typically for ransomware. Technical mechanics include encrypting common user files, critical system files, disk partitions, the MBR, and virtual machines on hypervisors like ESXi. Attackers may use worm-like propagation via Valid Accounts and SMB shares, and employ tactics like file permission modification or system shutdown to access files. In AWS, adversaries can leverage native services like Server-Side Encryption with Customer Provided Keys (SSE-C) for encryption.
1038.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Encrypt Data for Impact, identified as MITRE ATT&CK T1486, is an Impact tactic technique used across multiple platforms. It involves adversaries encrypting data on target systems to render it inaccessible, typically to extort ransom payments or cause permanent disruption. The technique targets common user files, critical system files, disk partitions, the MBR, and virtual machines. To maximize impact, malware may propagate via network shares, leverage cloud storage encryption features like AWS SSE-C, and employ worm-like capabilities alongside intimidation tactics such as changing wallpapers or sending ransom notes to printers.

1039.name: Display Ransomware Message
1039.profile: [profile]Display Ransomware Message is a technique used within the Impact tactic, where adversaries present a ransom note or warning message to the victim, typically following data encryption. This is a component of ransomware operations, as referenced in the related technique Data Encrypted for Impact (T1486), which describes adversaries using internal defacement methods like changing wallpapers or login messages to intimidate victims and coerce payment. The technique is associated with groups like Lazarus.
1039.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Display Ransomware Message is a technique within the Impact tactic, used on Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves presenting a ransom note or warning message to the victim, typically after data encryption, to demand payment for decryption. This can be achieved through methods like changing desktop wallpapers, modifying system login messages (e.g., on ESXi servers), or sending messages to connected printers in a "print bombing" attack, thereby intimidating the victim and coercing compliance.

1040.name: Targeting Backup Mechanisms
1040.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may attempt to get a listing of backup software or configurations that are installed on a system. Adversaries may use this information to shape follow-on behaviors, such as [Data Destruction](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1485), [Inhibit System Recovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1490), or [Data Encrypted for Impact](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1486).  

Commands that can be used to obtain security software information are [netsh](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0108), `reg query` with [Reg](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0075), `dir` with [cmd](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0106), and [Tasklist](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0057), but other indicators of discovery behavior may be more specific to the type of software or security system the adversary is looking for, such as Veeam, Acronis, Dropbox, or Paragon.(Citation: Symantec Play Ransomware 2023)
1040.profile: [profile]Targeting Backup Mechanisms, identified as T1518.002 under Discovery, targets Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. This technique involves adversaries enumerating installed backup software like Veeam, Acronis, Dropbox, or Paragon to inform subsequent destructive actions such as data destruction or encryption. Discovery is performed using commands like `reg query`, `dir`, `tasklist`, or `netsh` to locate specific software configurations and binaries. The gathered intelligence is used to shape follow-on attacks that inhibit system recovery, as observed in campaigns by groups like Wizard Spider.
1040.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Targeting Backup Mechanisms is a technique adversaries use to disrupt system recovery by disabling or destroying backup data and mechanisms. It aligns with the Inhibit System Recovery tactic (T1490) on Windows platforms. Technical mechanics include using commands like `vssadmin.exe delete shadows /all /quiet` to delete volume shadow copies, `wbadmin.exe delete catalog -quiet` to remove the Windows Backup Catalog, and `bcdedit.exe` to disable automatic recovery features. Adversaries may also target network device firmware, ESXi server snapshots, and cloud-based backups to prevent restoration. This technique is often employed by groups like Wizard Spider and Sandworm Team in conjunction with data destruction or encryption attacks.

1041.name: Network Propagation
1041.profile: [profile]The entity "Network Propagation" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the provided context, it is a high-level concept describing how adversaries move laterally within a compromised network. This activity is associated with groups like Turla and Lazarus and involves leveraging compromised network devices for operations such as hosting payloads, enabling command and control, and harvesting credentials to support further targeting and lateral movement.[/profile]
1041.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Network Propagation is a technique used by adversaries to spread laterally across a network after gaining initial access. It involves moving from a compromised system to other connected systems and devices, often leveraging legitimate credentials and remote services like SSH, RDP, or SMB. This movement enables further discovery, credential harvesting, and the establishment of persistent footholds on additional hosts to expand control within the target environment.

1042.name: Connections to CNC Infrastructure
1042.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may manipulate network traffic in order to hide and evade detection of their C2 infrastructure. This can be accomplished by identifying and filtering traffic from defensive tools,(Citation: TA571) masking malicious domains to obfuscate the true destination from both automated scanning tools and security researchers,(Citation: Schema-abuse)(Citation: Facad1ng)(Citation: Browser-updates) and otherwise hiding malicious artifacts to delay discovery and prolong the effectiveness of adversary infrastructure that could otherwise be identified, blocked, or taken down entirely.

C2 networks may include the use of [Proxy](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1090) or VPNs to disguise IP addresses, which can allow adversaries to blend in with normal network traffic and bypass conditional access policies or anti-abuse protections. For example, an adversary may use a virtual private cloud to spoof their IP address to closer align with a victim's IP address ranges. This may also bypass security measures relying on geolocation of the source IP address.(Citation: sysdig)(Citation: Orange Residential Proxies)

Adversaries may also attempt to filter network traffic in order to evade defensive tools in numerous ways, including blocking/redirecting common incident responder or security appliance user agents.(Citation: mod_rewrite)(Citation: SocGholish-update) Filtering traffic based on IP and geo-fencing may also avoid automated sandboxing or researcher activity (i.e., [Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1497)).(Citation: TA571)(Citation: mod_rewrite)

Hiding C2 infrastructure may also be supported by [Resource Development](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0042) activities such as [Acquire Infrastructure](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1583) and [Compromise Infrastructure](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1584). For example, using widely trusted hosting services or domains such as prominent URL shortening providers or marketing services for C2 networks may enable adversaries to present benign content that later redirects victims to malicious web pages or infrastructure once specific conditions are met.(Citation: StarBlizzard)(Citation: QR-cofense)
1042.profile: [profile]Hide Infrastructure, designated T1665 under the Resource Development tactic, is a technique for manipulating network traffic to conceal command and control infrastructure. This involves filtering traffic from defensive tools, blocking common security user agents, and using IP-based geo-fencing to evade sandboxes. Adversaries employ proxies or VPNs to disguise IP addresses, potentially using virtual private clouds to spoof addresses aligning with a victim's range to bypass geolocation controls. The technique is supported by acquiring or compromising infrastructure, such as using trusted hosting or URL shortening services that redirect to malicious pages. Associated groups include APT29 and Zirconium.[/profile]
1042.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Connections to CNC Infrastructure is a technique where adversaries establish direct or indirect network links to their command and control servers to maintain control over compromised systems. This involves using protocols like HTTP/S, DNS, or raw sockets to send and receive commands, often employing tools for traffic redirection such as HTRAN, ZXProxy, or ZXPortMap to proxy communications and avoid direct infrastructure links. Adversaries may chain multiple proxies or use compromised infrastructure to blend malicious traffic with normal network activity, enhancing stealth and resilience against takedowns.

1043.name: Kill Switch Domain
1043.profile: [profile]Kill Switch Domain is a defense evasion technique used by adversaries like Lazarus to control malware. It involves a pre-programmed domain that, when contacted by the malware, instructs it to stop execution or self-destruct, thereby preventing analysis and hindering detection. This mechanism allows attackers to remotely deactivate their tools if they suspect discovery.
1043.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Kill Switch Domain is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the provided context, it is a defensive evasion or command and control mechanism where malware contains a hard-coded domain name. If security researchers or defenders can sinkhole or take control of this domain, the malware's malicious functionality is deactivated, effectively serving as a kill switch to halt its operation.

1044.name: Shadow Copies
1044.profile: [profile]Shadow Copies, identified as a component of MITRE ATT&CK technique T1490 (Inhibit System Recovery) under the Impact tactic for Windows, are volume shadow copies used by Windows for system backups and recovery. Adversaries, such as those deploying WannaCry ransomware, abuse this feature by using native utilities like `vssadmin.exe delete shadows /all /quiet` or `wmic shadowcopy delete` to delete these copies. This action prevents system restoration and aids data destruction or encryption attacks by removing available recovery points.
1044.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Shadow Copies" aligns with the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1490: Inhibit System Recovery, under the Impact tactic, targeting the Windows platform. Adversaries abuse this technique to delete Volume Shadow Copy Service (VSS) snapshots, which are critical for system recovery and data restoration, thereby preventing recovery from ransomware or destructive attacks. This is commonly executed using native utilities like `vssadmin.exe delete shadows /all /quiet`, `wmic shadowcopy delete`, or `diskshadow.exe`. The activity is associated with threat groups including Scattered Spider, Sandworm Team, and Wizard Spider.

1045.name: Modifying +h Flag
1045.profile: [profile]The entity "Modifying +h Flag" is a technique for hiding files and directories on Windows systems using the `attrib.exe` command with the `+h` attribute. This action supports the Defense Evasion tactic by concealing adversary data from typical user inspection or system analysis that does not explicitly search for hidden items. The technique is specifically associated with the Windows platform and has been used by malware such as WannaCry for persistence and evasion.
1045.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Modifying +h Flag" is a technique for hiding files and directories on Windows systems using the `attrib.exe` command with the `+h` attribute. This action supports the Defense Evasion tactic by concealing adversary tools and data from typical user inspection and command-line directory listings. The technique specifically involves executing commands like `attrib +h filename` or `attrib +h /S` to apply the hidden attribute recursively to folders and their contents.

1046.name: ICAcls Privilege Escalation
1046.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may exploit software vulnerabilities in an attempt to elevate privileges. Exploitation of a software vulnerability occurs when an adversary takes advantage of a programming error in a program, service, or within the operating system software or kernel itself to execute adversary-controlled code. Security constructs such as permission levels will often hinder access to information and use of certain techniques, so adversaries will likely need to perform privilege escalation to include use of software exploitation to circumvent those restrictions.

When initially gaining access to a system, an adversary may be operating within a lower privileged process which will prevent them from accessing certain resources on the system. Vulnerabilities may exist, usually in operating system components and software commonly running at higher permissions, that can be exploited to gain higher levels of access on the system.
