1147.name: Multi-Platform Attack Strategy
1147.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may downgrade or use a version of system features that may be outdated, vulnerable, and/or does not support updated security controls. Downgrade attacks typically take advantage of a system’s backward compatibility to force it into less secure modes of operation. 

Adversaries may downgrade and use various less-secure versions of features of a system, such as [Command and Scripting Interpreter](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059)s or even network protocols that can be abused to enable [Adversary-in-the-Middle](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1557) or [Network Sniffing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1040).(Citation: Praetorian TLS Downgrade Attack 2014) For example, [PowerShell](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001) versions 5+ includes Script Block Logging (SBL), which can record executed script content. However, adversaries may attempt to execute a previous version of PowerShell that does not support SBL with the intent to [Impair Defenses](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1562) while running malicious scripts that may have otherwise been detected.(Citation: CrowdStrike BGH Ransomware 2021)(Citation: Mandiant BYOL 2018)(Citation: att_def_ps_logging)

Adversaries may similarly target network traffic to downgrade from an encrypted HTTPS connection to an unsecured HTTP connection that exposes network data in clear text.(Citation: Targeted SSL Stripping Attacks Are Real)(Citation: Crowdstrike Downgrade) On Windows systems, adversaries may downgrade the boot manager to a vulnerable version that bypasses Secure Boot, granting the ability to disable various operating system security mechanisms.(Citation: SafeBreach)
1147.profile: [profile]Downgrade Attack (T1562.010) is a Defense Evasion technique that exploits backward compatibility to force systems into less secure modes. It operates by executing outdated, vulnerable versions of system features to bypass security controls. Specific mechanics include running older PowerShell versions (pre-v5) to disable Script Block Logging, downgrading HTTPS connections to unencrypted HTTP to enable traffic interception, and reverting a system's boot manager to bypass Secure Boot on Windows. The intrusion set APT28 has been associated with this activity.[/profile]
1147.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Multi-Platform Attack Strategy is a technique where adversaries design and deploy malicious operations to function across multiple operating systems or environments, such as Windows, Linux, and macOS. This approach involves creating or using tools, scripts, or malware payloads that are compatible with different system architectures and software, allowing for broader target selection and persistent access. The strategy may include employing cross-platform frameworks, using interpreted languages like Python, or compiling malicious code for each specific platform to ensure execution regardless of the victim's environment.

1148.name: SMTP
1148.profile: [profile]The entity 'SMTP' is referenced in the MITRE ATT&CK framework as a sub-technique for Application Layer Protocol (T1071.003) under the Command and Control tactic. It is used by adversaries like APT28 to blend malicious communications within legitimate SMTP, POP3/S, or IMAP traffic to avoid detection. 1163.name: Privilege Escalation
1163.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may exploit software vulnerabilities in an attempt to elevate privileges. Exploitation of a software vulnerability occurs when an adversary takes advantage of a programming error in a program, service, or within the operating system software or kernel itself to execute adversary-controlled code. Security constructs such as permission levels will often hinder access to information and use of certain techniques, so adversaries will likely need to perform privilege escalation to include use of software exploitation to circumvent those restrictions.

When initially gaining access to a system, an adversary may be operating within a lower privileged process which will prevent them from accessing certain resources on the system. Vulnerabilities may exist, usually in operating system components and software commonly running at higher permissions, that can be exploited to gain higher levels of access on the system. This could enable someone to move from unprivileged or user level permissions to SYSTEM or root permissions depending on the component that is vulnerable. This could also enable an adversary to move from a virtualized environment, such as within a virtual machine or container, onto the underlying host. This may be a necessary step for an adversary compromising an endpoint system that has been properly configured and limits other privilege escalation methods.

Adversaries may bring a signed vulnerable driver onto a compromised machine so that they can exploit the vulnerability to execute code in kernel mode. This process is sometimes referred to as Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver (BYOVD).(Citation: ESET InvisiMole June 2020)(Citation: Unit42 AcidBox June 2020) Adversaries may include the vulnerable driver with files delivered during Initial Access or download it to a compromised system via [Ingress Tool Transfer](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1105) or [Lateral Tool Transfer](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1570).
1163.profile: [profile]The technique is formally known as Exploitation for Privilege Escalation with the MITRE ATT&CK ID T1068 under the Privilege Escalation tactic, applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves exploiting software vulnerabilities in OS components or high-privilege services to execute adversary-controlled code and elevate permissions from user to SYSTEM/root or escape virtualized environments. A specific method is Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver (BYOVD), where a signed vulnerable driver is introduced to the system to enable kernel-mode code execution. This technique is used by groups including APT28, APT29, Turla, and OilRig.[/profile]
1163.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Privilege Escalation is a core adversarial objective, not a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique with a single ID. It is a tactic within the MITRE framework, representing the goal of gaining higher-level permissions on a system or network. Common technical mechanics to achieve this include exploiting software vulnerabilities (e.g., using signed vulnerable drivers via BYOVD) to execute code from user to SYSTEM/root level or escape containers, and abusing credentials from local or domain accounts through dumping or password reuse to bypass security restrictions.

1164.name: Pass-the-Hash
1164.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may “pass the hash” using stolen password hashes to move laterally within an environment, bypassing normal system access controls. Pass the hash (PtH) is a method of authenticating as a user without having access to the user's cleartext password. This method bypasses standard authentication steps that require a cleartext password, moving directly into the portion of the authentication that uses the password hash.

When performing PtH, valid password hashes for the account being used are captured using a [Credential Access](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0006) technique. Captured hashes are used with PtH to authenticate as that user. Once authenticated, PtH may be used to perform actions on local or remote systems.

Adversaries may also use stolen password hashes to "overpass the hash." Similar to PtH, this involves using a password hash to authenticate as a user but also uses the password hash to create a valid Kerberos ticket. This ticket can then be used to perform [Pass the Ticket](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1550/003) attacks.(Citation: Stealthbits Overpass-the-Hash)
1164.profile: [profile]Pass the Hash (PtH) is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1550.002 under the Lateral Movement tactic, primarily for Windows. It authenticates as a user using a captured password hash, bypassing the need for the cleartext password. Valid hashes are obtained via Credential Access techniques and used to perform actions on local or remote systems. A related variant, "overpass the hash," uses the hash to create a Kerberos ticket for Pass the Ticket attacks. Groups like APT28, FIN13, and Wizard Spider have employed this technique.[/profile]
1164.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Pass the Hash (PtH), designated as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1550.002, is a Lateral Movement tactic used on Windows platforms. It authenticates as a user without the cleartext password by using a captured password hash, bypassing normal authentication steps. Valid hashes are obtained via credential access techniques like dumping and are then used directly for authentication to perform actions on local or remote systems. A variant known as "overpass the hash" uses the stolen hash to create a Kerberos ticket for Pass the Ticket attacks.

1166.name: credential-stealing spear-phishing attacks
1166.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may send phishing messages to gain access to victim systems. All forms of phishing are electronically delivered social engineering. Phishing can be targeted, known as spearphishing. In spearphishing, a specific individual, company, or industry will be targeted by the adversary. More generally, adversaries can conduct non-targeted phishing, such as in mass malware spam campaigns.

Adversaries may send victims emails containing malicious attachments or links, typically to execute malicious code on victim systems. Phishing may also be conducted via third-party services, like social media platforms. Phishing may also involve social engineering techniques, such as posing as a trusted source, as well as evasive techniques such as removing or manipulating emails or metadata/headers from compromised accounts being abused to send messages (e.g., [Email Hiding Rules](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1564/008)).(Citation: Microsoft OAuth Spam 2022)(Citation: Palo Alto Unit 42 VBA Infostealer 2014) Another way to accomplish this is by [Email Spoofing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1672)(Citation: Proofpoint-spoof) the identity of the sender, which can be used to fool both the human recipient as well as automated security tools,(Citation: cyberproof-double-bounce) or by including the intended target as a party to an existing email thread that includes malicious files or links (i.e., "thread hijacking").(Citation: phishing-krebs)

Victims may also receive phishing messages that instruct them to call a phone number where they are directed to visit a malicious URL, download malware,(Citation: sygnia Luna Month)(Citation: CISA Remote Monitoring and Management Software) or install adversary-accessible remote management tools onto their computer (i.e., [User Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204)).(Citation: Unit42 Luna Moth)

Attack mechanics include embedding malicious links that direct victims to fake login portals, using email spoofing or thread hijacking to enhance legitimacy, and employing adversary-in-the-middle phishing kits like EvilProxy to capture session cookies and bypass multi-factor authentication. Groups such as APT28, Kimsuky, and Scattered Spider are known to use this method.[profile]

1174.name: multi-factor authentication
1174.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may disable or modify multi-factor authentication (MFA) mechanisms to enable persistent access to compromised accounts.

Once adversaries have gained access to a network by either compromising an account lacking MFA or by employing an MFA bypass method such as [Multi-Factor Authentication Request Generation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1621), adversaries may leverage their access to modify or completely disable MFA defenses. This can be accomplished by abusing legitimate features, such as excluding users from Azure AD Conditional Access Policies, registering a new yet vulnerable/adversary-controlled MFA method, or by manually patching MFA programs and configuration files to bypass expected functionality.(Citation: Mandiant APT42)(Citation: Azure AD Conditional Access Exclusions)

For example, modifying the Windows hosts file (`C:\windows\system32\drivers\etc\hosts`) to redirect MFA calls to localhost instead of an MFA server may cause the MFA process to fail. If a "fail open" policy is in place, any otherwise successful authentication attempt may be granted access without enforcing MFA. (Citation: Russians Exploit Default MFA Protocol - CISA March 2022) 

Depending on the scope, goals, and privileges of the adversary, MFA defenses may be disabled for individual accounts or for all accounts tied to a larger group, such as all domain accounts in a victim's network environment.(Citation: Russians Exploit Default MFA Protocol - CISA March 2022)
1174.profile: [profile]Multi-Factor Authentication, identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1556.006, falls under the Credential Access tactic and targets Windows, Azure AD, and other platforms. This technique involves adversaries modifying or disabling MFA mechanisms after initial access to maintain persistence. Specific technical mechanics include abusing legitimate administrative features like excluding users from Azure AD Conditional Access Policies, registering new adversary-controlled MFA methods, or manually patching configuration files. A concrete example is modifying the Windows hosts file to redirect MFA server calls to localhost, potentially triggering a "fail open" policy that grants access without MFA enforcement. The threat group Scattered Spider has been associated with this activity.[/profile]
1174.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Multi-factor Authentication (MFA) is a security control, not a direct adversary technique. However, adversaries target it through specific bypass and modification techniques. These include Multi-Factor Authentication Request Generation (T1621) to spam users with push notifications causing "MFA fatigue," Multi-Factor Authentication Interception (T1111) to capture codes via keyloggers or compromised services, and Modifying Authentication Process: Multi-Factor Authentication (T1556.006) to disable MFA by altering system files like the Windows hosts file or abusing policy exclusions. Groups like Scattered Spider, APT42, and LAPSUS$ are associated with these methods.[/profile]

1192.name: Politically motivated activity
1192.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may employ various user activity checks to detect and avoid virtualization and analysis environments. This may include changing behaviors based on the results of checks for the presence of artifacts indicative of a virtual machine environment (VME) or sandbox. If the adversary detects a VME, they may alter their malware to disengage from the victim or conceal the core functions of the implant. They may also search for VME artifacts before dropping secondary or additional payloads. Adversaries may use the information learned from [Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1497) during automated discovery to shape follow-on behaviors.(Citation: Deloitte Environment Awareness)

Adversaries may search for user activity on the host based on variables such as the speed/frequency of mouse movements and clicks (Citation: Sans Virtual Jan 2016) , browser history, cache, bookmarks, or number of files in common directories such as home or the desktop. Other methods may rely on specific user interaction with the system before the malicious code is activated, such as waiting for a document to close before activating a macro (Citation: Unit 42 Sofacy Nov 2018) or waiting for a user to double click on an embedded image to activate.(Citation: FireEye FIN7 April 2017)
1192.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique "User Activity Based Checks", identified as T1497.002 under the Defense Evasion tactic for Windows systems. It involves malware checking for indicators of human presence or virtualized environments to evade detection. Specific technical mechanics include altering behavior based on the detection of virtual machine artifacts, monitoring mouse movement speed and click frequency, and waiting for specific user interactions—like a document closing or an image being double-clicked—before activating malicious payloads. Groups like DarkHotel and FIN7 have been associated with this technique.
1192.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Politically motivated activity is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique but describes a broad adversarial intent. Based on retrieved context, such activity often manifests through specific techniques like Defacement (T1491) and Data Destruction (T1485). These are used to deliver political messaging, intimidate, or claim credit for intrusions. For example, in data destruction, adversaries may overwrite files with politically oriented images to render data irrecoverable, while external website defacement is commonly used by hacktivist groups to spread propaganda or trigger events.

1193.name: social engineering tricks

Adversaries may search social media for information about victims that can be used during targeting. Social media sites may contain various information about a victim organization, such as business announcements as well as information about the roles, locations, and interests of staff.

Adversaries may search in different social media sites depending on what information they seek to gather. Threat actors may passively harvest data from these sites, as well as use information gathered to create fake profiles/groups to elicit victim’s into revealing specific information (i.e. [Spearphishing Service](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1598/001)).(Citation: Cyware Social Media) Information from these sources may reveal opportunities for other forms of reconnaissance (ex: [Phishing for Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1598) or [Search Open Technical Databases](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1596)), establishing operational resources (ex: [Establish Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1585) or [Compromise Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1586)), and/or initial access (ex: [Spearphishing via Service](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/003)).

1232.name: Data Manipulation
1232.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may insert, delete, or manipulate data in order to influence external outcomes or hide activity, thus threatening the integrity of the data.(Citation: Sygnia Elephant Beetle Jan 2022) By manipulating data, adversaries may attempt to affect a business process, organizational understanding, or decision making.

The type of modification and the impact it will have depends on the target application and process as well as the goals and objectives of the adversary. For complex systems, an adversary would likely need special expertise and possibly access to specialized software related to the system that would typically be gained through a prolonged information gathering campaign in order to have the desired impact.
1232.profile: [profile]Data Manipulation is the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1565 under the Impact tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It involves adversaries inserting, deleting, or altering data to influence external outcomes, hide activity, or compromise data integrity, thereby affecting business processes and decision-making. This often requires specialized expertise and prolonged reconnaissance, particularly for complex systems. Associated groups include FIN13, APT38, and APT29.[/profile]
1232.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Data Manipulation is a technique with the MITRE ATT&CK ID T1565, categorized under the Impact tactic and applicable across multiple platforms. It involves adversaries inserting, deleting, or altering data to influence external outcomes, hide malicious activity, or affect business processes and decision-making. The specific mechanics and impact depend on the target application or system, often requiring specialized adversary expertise and potentially prolonged reconnaissance to execute effectively against complex environments.

1233.name: Spear phishing
1233.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may send phishing messages to gain access to victim systems. All forms of phishing are electronically delivered social engineering. Phishing can be targeted, known as spearphishing. In spearphishing, a specific individual, company, or industry will be targeted by the adversary. More generally, adversaries can conduct non-targeted phishing, such as in mass malware spam campaigns.

Adversaries may send victims emails containing malicious attachments or links, typically to execute malicious code on victim systems. Phishing may also be conducted via third-party services, like social media platforms. Phishing may also involve social engineering techniques, such as posing as a trusted source, as well as evasive techniques such as removing or manipulating emails or metadata/headers from compromised accounts being abused to send messages (e.g., [Email Hiding Rules](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1564/008)).(Citation: Microsoft OAuth Spam 2022)(Citation: Palo Alto Unit 42 VBA Infostealer 2014) Another way to accomplish this is by [Email Spoofing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1672)(Citation: Proofpoint-spoof) the identity of the sender, which can be used to fool both the human recipient as well as automated security tools,(Citation: cyberproof-double-bounce) or by including the intended target as a party to an existing email thread that includes malicious files or links (i.e., "thread hijacking").(Citation: phishing-krebs)

Victims may also receive phishing messages that instruct them to call a phone number where they are directed to visit a malicious URL, download malware,(Citation: sygnia Luna Month)(Citation: CISA Remote Monitoring and Management Software) or install adversary-accessible remote management tools onto their computer (i.e., [User Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204)).(Citation: Unit42 Luna Moth)
1233.profile: [profile]Spear phishing, identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1566, is a targeted Initial Access tactic used across multiple platforms. It involves sending tailored electronic messages, often via email, to specific individuals or organizations to deliver malicious attachments or links that execute code. Techniques include social engineering, email spoofing, and thread hijacking to appear as a trusted source. This method is associated with groups like OilRig and APT28.[/profile]
1233.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Spear phishing, identified as MITRE ATT&CK T1566.001, is an Initial Access tactic executed via Email. It involves sending targeted electronic messages to specific individuals, companies, or industries. The technique employs social engineering, such as posing as a trusted source, and delivers malicious attachments or links to execute code. Evasive methods include email spoofing, thread hijacking, and manipulating email metadata to bypass detection.

1234.name: Influence Operations
1234.profile: [profile]Influence Operations is a strategic adversarial activity aligned with the MITRE ATT&CK tactic of Impact, though it is not a formally defined technique with a specific ID. It involves coordinated efforts to manipulate public perception, decision-making, or behavior through information warfare. This can include the use of social media accounts (T1585.001) to build fictitious personas for social engineering, as employed by groups like APT28, and may involve underlying techniques like Data Manipulation (T1565) to alter information integrity. The goal is to achieve psychological or political effects rather than direct technical compromise.
1234.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Influence Operations is a strategic activity, not a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique, and is not assigned a T ID. It is a broad category encompassing tactics like Psychological Operations (TA0046) and Online Operational Preparation of the Environment (TA0154). Its platform is broadly "PRE". Technical mechanics involve manipulating information ecosystems, which can include creating and cultivating fake social media accounts (T1585.001) to build personas for social engineering, or manipulating stored data (T1565.001) to affect decision-making and business processes. It is associated with groups like APT38 and Lazarus Group.

1235.name: Data Destruction
1235.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may destroy data and files on specific systems or in large numbers on a network to interrupt availability to systems, services, and network resources. Data destruction is likely to render stored data irrecoverable by forensic techniques through overwriting files or data on local and remote drives.(Citation: Symantec Shamoon 2012)(Citation: FireEye Shamoon Nov 2016)(Citation: Palo Alto Shamoon Nov 2016)(Citation: Kaspersky StoneDrill 2017)(Citation: Unit 42 Shamoon3 2018)(Citation: Talos Olympic Destroyer 2018) Common operating system file deletion commands such as del and rm often only remove pointers to files without wiping the contents of the files themselves, making the files recoverable by proper forensic methodology. This behavior is distinct from [Disk Content Wipe](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1561/001) and [Disk Structure Wipe](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1561/002) because individual files are destroyed rather than sections of a storage disk or the disk's logical structure. Adversaries may attempt to overwrite files and directories with randomly generated data to make it irrecoverable.(Citation: Kaspersky StoneDrill 2017)(Citation: Unit 42 Shamoon3 2018) In some cases politically oriented image files have been used to overwrite data.(Citation: FireEye Shamoon Nov 2016)(Citation: Palo Alto Shamoon Nov 2016)(Citation: Kaspersky StoneDrill 2017) To maximize impact on the target organization in operations where network-wide availability interruption is the goal, malware designed for destroying data may have worm-like features to propagate across a network by leveraging additional techniques like [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078), [OS Credential Dumping](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003), and [SMB/Windows Admin Shares](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002).(Citation: Symantec Shamoon 2012)(Citation: FireEye Shamoon Nov 2016)(Citation: Palo Alto Shamoon Nov 2016)(Citation: Kaspersky StoneDrill 2017)(Citation: Talos Olympic Destroyer 2018). In cloud environments, adversaries may leverage access to delete cloud storage objects, machine images, database instances, and other infrastructure crucial to operations to damage an organization or their customers.(Citation: Data Destruction - Threat Post)(Citation: DOJ - Cisco Insider) Similarly, they may delete virtual machines from on-prem virtualized environments.
1235.profile: [profile]Data Destruction, identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1485, is an Impact tactic executed on Windows, Linux, and cloud platforms. It aims to render files irrecoverable by overwriting them with random data or specific image files, moving beyond simple deletion commands like `del` or `rm`. Malware implementing this technique may propagate using worm-like features and can target cloud storage objects, virtual machines, and critical infrastructure to maximize disruption. Associated threat groups include APT38, Sandworm Team, and Lazarus Group.[/profile]
1235.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Data Destruction is a technique identified as MITRE ATT&CK T1485 under the Impact tactic, applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves destroying files to interrupt availability, often by overwriting them with random data or specific files (like political images) to render data irrecoverable by forensic methods, distinguishing it from disk-level wipes. Malware implementing this may propagate using worm-like features via Valid Accounts or SMB shares, and in cloud environments, it targets storage objects and virtual infrastructure. Associated threat groups include APT38, Sandworm Team, and Lazarus Group.

1236.name: DDoS attacks
1236.profile: [profile]DDoS attacks, corresponding to MITRE ATT&CK techniques T1498 (Network Denial of Service) and T1499 (Endpoint Denial of Service) under the Impact tactic, are executed across multiple platforms. These attacks overwhelm target resources by using botnets to generate high-volume traffic, often employing IP spoofing to obscure the source. The intent is to exhaust network bandwidth or system resources, degrading or blocking service availability for purposes such as distraction, hacktivism, or extortion, as observed with groups like APT28.[/profile]
1236.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "DDoS attacks" is a broad category of Distributed Denial of Service attacks, which is a specific implementation of the MITRE ATT&CK technique for Endpoint Denial of Service (T1499) under the Impact tactic. These attacks work by using multiple compromised systems, often forming a botnet, to generate a high volume of network traffic directed at a target to exhaust its resources, such as bandwidth or system capacity, thereby degrading or blocking service availability. Attackers may use IP address spoofing to obscure the source of the attack and leverage protocols like UDP or ICMP for flooding. This technique has been used by groups like Sandworm Team for purposes including political disruption, hacktivism, and extortion.

1237.name: Valid Accounts
1237.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may obtain and abuse credentials of existing accounts as a means of gaining Initial Access, Persistence, Privilege Escalation, or Defense Evasion. Compromised credentials may be used to bypass access controls placed on various resources on systems within the network and may even be used for persistent access to remote systems and externally available services, such as VPNs, Outlook Web Access, network devices, and remote desktop.(Citation: volexity_0day_sophos_FW) Compromised credentials may also grant an adversary increased privilege to specific systems or access to restricted areas of the network. Adversaries may choose not to use malware or tools in conjunction with the legitimate access those credentials provide to make it harder to detect their presence.

In some cases, adversaries may abuse inactive accounts: for example, those belonging to individuals who are no longer part of an organization. Using these accounts may allow the adversary to evade detection, as the original account user will not be present to identify any anomalous activity taking place on their account.(Citation: CISA MFA PrintNightmare)

The overlap of permissions for local, domain, and cloud accounts across a network of systems is of concern because the adversary may be able to pivot across accounts and systems to reach a high level of access (i.e., domain or enterprise administrator) to bypass access controls set within the enterprise.(Citation: TechNet Credential Theft)
1237.profile: [profile]Valid Accounts is a technique identified as T1078 within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, primarily used for Initial Access, Persistence, Privilege Escalation, and Defense Evasion across Windows, Linux, macOS, and cloud platforms. It involves adversaries obtaining and abusing credentials of existing accounts, including inactive ones, to bypass access controls, gain persistent remote access to services like VPNs, and pivot across systems to achieve high-level permissions without deploying malware, making detection difficult. This technique is notably used by groups such as APT28, APT29, and Volt Typhoon.
1237.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Valid Accounts, designated as T1078, is a technique used for Initial Access, Persistence, Privilege Escalation, and Defense Evasion across Windows, Linux, Mac, and cloud platforms. It involves adversaries obtaining and abusing credentials of existing legitimate accounts, including inactive or default accounts, to bypass access controls, access remote services like VPNs, and pivot across systems. This use of legitimate access often avoids malware, making detection harder, and adversaries may target overlapping local, domain, and cloud permissions to achieve high-level access like domain administrator.

1238.name: Network compromise
1238.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may compromise third-party infrastructure that can be used during targeting. Infrastructure solutions include physical or cloud servers, domains, network devices, and third-party web and DNS services. Instead of buying, leasing, or renting infrastructure an adversary may compromise infrastructure and use it during other phases of the adversary lifecycle.(Citation: Mandiant APT1)(Citation: ICANNDomainNameHijacking)(Citation: Talos DNSpionage Nov 2018)(Citation: FireEye EPS Awakens Part 2) Additionally, adversaries may compromise numerous machines to form a botnet they can leverage.

Use of compromised infrastructure allows adversaries to stage, launch, and execute operations. Compromised infrastructure can help adversary operations blend in with traffic that is seen as normal, such as contact with high reputation or trusted sites. For example, adversaries may leverage compromised infrastructure (potentially also in conjunction with [Digital Certificates](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1588/004)) to further blend in and support staged information gathering and/or [Phishing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566) campaigns.(Citation: FireEye DNS Hijack 2019) Adversaries may also compromise numerous machines to support [Proxy](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1090) and/or proxyware services or to form a botnet.(Citation: amnesty_nso_pegasus)(Citation: Sysdig Proxyjacking) Additionally, adversaries may compromise infrastructure residing in close proximity to a target in order to gain [Initial Access](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0001) via [Wi-Fi Networks](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1669).(Citation: Nearest Neighbor Volexity)

By using compromised infrastructure, adversaries may enable follow-on malicious operations. Prior to targeting, adversaries may also compromise the infrastructure of other adversaries.(Citation: NSA NCSC Turla OilRig)
1238.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique "Compromise Infrastructure" (T1584), categorized under Resource Development. It involves adversaries taking over third-party infrastructure like servers, domains, or network devices to use for staging, launching operations, and blending in with normal traffic. This compromised infrastructure can support activities such as phishing campaigns, proxy services, botnet formation, or gaining initial access via nearby Wi-Fi networks. The intrusion-set APT28 has been associated with this behavior.[profile]
1238.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Network compromise is a broad attack pattern not directly mapped to a specific MITRE ATT&CK ID. It involves adversaries gaining unauthorized access to network systems, potentially through methods like exploiting vulnerabilities, using compromised credentials, or deploying malware. This can enable follow-on activities such as data exfiltration, lateral movement, and establishing persistent command and control. The technique is foundational to multiple tactics, including Initial Access and Lateral Movement, and targets various platforms like Windows, Linux, and network appliances.

1239.profile: [profile]NtQuerySystemInformation is a Windows Native API function used for System Information Discovery (T1082). It operates on Windows platforms as part of the Discovery tactic, enabling adversaries to query detailed OS and hardware data. The function can retrieve specific system data structures, which threat actors like APT28 leverage to profile a target environment and inform subsequent attack actions.
1239.profile_without_enhance: [profile]NtQuerySystemInformation is a Windows API function used for System Information Discovery (T1082) on the Windows platform. 1240.name: GetProcAddress
1240.profile: [profile]GetProcAddress is a Windows API function used for Dynamic API Resolution (T1027.007) under the Defense Evasion tactic. It allows malware to manually resolve and load library functions at runtime by using hashes or obfuscated identifiers of function names instead of literal strings, often in conjunction with LoadLibrary(). This technique conceals malicious API calls from static analysis and avoids leaving clear artifacts in the import address table, impairing defensive efforts. It is associated with groups like Lazarus Group and Mustang Panda.
1240.profile_without_enhance: [profile]GetProcAddress is a Windows API function used for dynamic API resolution, a sub-technique of Obfuscated Files or Information (T1027.007) under the Defense Evasion tactic. It operates on Windows platforms by allowing malware to manually resolve and load library functions at runtime, often using hashes of function names instead of literal strings to conceal malicious calls and evade static analysis. This method is employed by groups like Lazarus Group and Mustang Panda to obfuscate payloads and impair defensive detection.

1241.name: Token Stealing
1241.profile: [profile]Token Stealing is a sub-technique of Access Token Manipulation (T1134) within the Privilege Escalation tactic, primarily for Windows. It involves using built-in Windows API functions like `DuplicateToken` or `DuplicateTokenEx` to copy access tokens from existing processes. These stolen tokens can then be applied to an existing process via Token Impersonation/Theft (T1134.001) or used to spawn a new process via Create Process with Token (T1134.002), allowing an adversary to operate under a different user's security context, commonly to escalate from administrator to SYSTEM level privileges. This technique is used by groups like APT28.[/profile]
1241.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Token Stealing is a technique within the broader Access Token Manipulation (T1134) framework, falling under the Privilege Escalation tactic for the Windows platform. It involves using built-in Windows API functions, such as DuplicateToken or DuplicateTokenEx, to copy an existing access token from a process. This stolen token can then be applied to an existing thread using ImpersonateLoggedOnUser or SetThreadToken to impersonate the security context of another user, commonly to escalate from an administrator to SYSTEM level privileges.

1242.name: Hooking
1242.uncertain_mes:
Windows processes often leverage application programming interface (API) functions to perform tasks that require reusable system resources. Windows API functions are typically stored in dynamic-link libraries (DLLs) as exported functions. 

Hooking involves redirecting calls to these functions and can be implemented via:

* **Hooks procedures**, which intercept and execute designated code in response to events such as messages, keystrokes, and mouse inputs. (Citation: Microsoft Hook Overview) (Citation: Elastic Process Injection July 2017)
* **Import address table (IAT) hooking**, which use modifications to a process’s IAT, where pointers to imported API functions are stored. (Citation: Elastic Process Injection July 2017) (Citation: Adlice Software IAT Hooks Oct 2014) (Citation: MWRInfoSecurity Dynamic Hooking 2015)
* **Inline hooking**, which overwrites the first bytes in an API function to redirect code flow. (Citation: Elastic Process Injection July 2017) (Citation: HighTech Bridge Inline Hooking Sept 2011) (Citation: MWRInfoSecurity Dynamic Hooking 2015)

Similar to [Process Injection](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1055), adversaries may use hooking to load and execute malicious code within the context of another process, masking the execution while also allowing access to the process's memory and possibly elevated privileges. Installing hooking mechanisms may also provide Persistence via continuous invocation when the functions are called through normal use.

Malicious hooking mechanisms may also capture API calls that include parameters that reveal user authentication credentials for Credential Access. (Citation: Microsoft TrojanSpy:Win32/Ursnif.gen!I Sept 2017)

Hooking is commonly utilized by [Rootkit](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1014)s to conceal files, processes, Registry keys, and other objects in order to hide malware and associated behaviors. (Citation: Symantec Windows Rootkits)
1242.profile: [profile]Hooking is a technique for intercepting and redirecting API function calls, primarily on Windows, to execute malicious code. It is implemented through hook procedures for system events, Import Address Table (IAT) modifications, or inline hooking that overwrites function bytes. This allows adversaries to mask code execution within a legitimate process's context, enabling persistence, credential theft by capturing API parameters, and concealment of activities, often in support of rootkits. The technique is associated with the APT28 intrusion set.[/profile]
1242.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Hooking, identified as T1179, is a Defense Evasion and Persistence technique primarily targeting Windows. It involves redirecting calls to Windows API functions to intercept and execute malicious code, commonly implemented through hook procedures, Import Address Table (IAT) hooking, or inline hooking. This allows adversaries to mask malicious execution within a legitimate process's context, access its memory, and potentially gain elevated privileges. The technique is also used for Credential Access by capturing API calls containing authentication parameters and by rootkits to conceal malicious artifacts.

1243.name: _ClientCopyImage

Based on the retrieved information, it appears to be related to the malicious use of cloud or container images, such as backdoored Amazon Machine Images (AMIs), Google Cloud Platform Images, or Docker containers, which adversaries upload to public repositories. Users may inadvertently deploy these malicious images, leading to execution of unauthorized code like cryptocurrency miners, bypassing initial access controls. This behavior is associated with groups like TeamTNT.
1243.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity `_ClientCopyImage` is an attack-pattern technique. It operates within the Execution tactic, specifically as a sub-technique (T1204.003) for User Execution: Malicious Image on cloud platforms. This technique involves adversaries relying on users to run a backdoored or malicious virtual machine or container image, such as an AWS AMI, GCP Image, Azure Image, or Docker container, which is often uploaded to a public repository. Execution occurs when a user unknowingly deploys an instance from this image, bypassing initial access controls and leading to the execution of adversary code, such as cryptocurrency miners. The method may use deceptive naming to mimic legitimate resources.

1244.name: 网站破坏
1244.profile: [profile]The entity "网站破坏" aligns with the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1491, Defacement, under the Impact tactic for multiple platforms. This technique involves adversaries modifying visual content on internal or external enterprise networks to compromise integrity, often to deliver messages, intimidate, claim false credit for intrusions, or pressure compliance by using disturbing images to cause user discomfort. It is associated with the intrusion set APT28.[/profile]
1244.profile_without_enhance: [profile]网站破坏 (Website Defacement) is a technique aligned with MITRE ATT&CK T1491 under the Impact tactic, primarily targeting Web Servers. This action directly denies or degrades service to legitimate users by altering the intended content and presentation of the site.

1245.name: SetWindowLongPtr
1245.profile: [profile]SetWindowLongPtr is a Windows API function used within the technique Extra Window Memory (EWM) Injection (T1055.011), which falls under the Defense Evasion and Privilege Escalation tactics on Windows platforms. It is specifically called to set a value in the EWM, which is a small memory region appended to a window class instance. Adversaries, such as APT28, can abuse this by writing a pointer to malicious shellcode into the EWM via SetWindowLongPtr, subsequently triggering execution control to that address to run code within a legitimate process's context, thereby evading monitoring of common APIs like WriteProcessMemory and potentially bypassing data execution prevention.
1245.profile_without_enhance: [profile]SetWindowLongPtr is a Windows API function used within the technique of Extra Window Memory (EWM) Injection (MITRE ATT&CK ID T1055.011, sub-technique of Process Injection, under the Defense Evasion and Privilege Escalation tactics, targeting Windows platforms). It sets a 32-bit pointer in the EWM of a window class instance. Malware uses this to point to malicious code written into shared process memory, enabling execution in the context of a separate legitimate process to evade monitoring of APIs like WriteProcessMemory and potentially bypass defenses like DEP.

1246.name: 虚假旗行动
1246.profile: [profile]The entity "虚假旗行动" (False Flag Operation) is a strategic deception technique where an adversary conducts an attack while disguising their identity to appear as another entity, often to mislead attribution, sow distrust, or provoke conflict. This aligns with the broader MITRE ATT&CK tactic of Impersonation or Resource Development, though it lacks a specific T-ID. The technique involves using forged artifacts, infrastructure, or TTPs associated with the impersonated group, as referenced in relation to APT28. Technical mechanics include manipulating attack signatures, employing malware or tools known to be used by other threat actors, and coordinating public messaging to support the false narrative.
1246.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "虚假旗行动" (False Flag Operation) is a strategic deception technique where an adversary conducts an attack while disguising their identity to appear as another entity, often to mislead attribution, sow distrust, or provoke conflict. This involves manipulating forensic evidence, using tools or infrastructure associated with other threat actors, or mimicking their tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs). It is a high-level operational security measure used to complicate defensive analysis and diplomatic or legal responses.

1247.name: 数据窃取
1247.profile: [profile]数据窃取 (Data Theft) is a core objective rather than a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique. It is commonly executed by groups like APT28 through established ATT&CK methods such as Exfiltration Over C2 Channel (T1041), where stolen data is encoded into normal command and control traffic, and Exfiltration Over Unencrypted Non-C2 Protocol (T1048.003), which uses protocols like HTTP or FTP, often with obfuscation like base64 encoding. Credential dumping (T1003) is a frequent precursor to enable access for data theft.
1247.profile_without_enhance: [profile]数据窃取 (Data Theft) is a high-level adversary objective rather than a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique, so it lacks a standard ID, Tactic, or Platform. It is performed by executing specific exfiltration techniques, such as exfiltrating data over a command and control channel (T1041) or over an unencrypted non-C2 protocol (T1048.003). The technical mechanics involve stealing and encoding stolen data into normal communications channels, potentially using protocols like HTTP, FTP, or DNS, and may employ obfuscation like base64 encoding without encryption.

1248.name: Malicious URLs
1248.uncertain_mes:
An adversary may rely upon a user opening a malicious file in order to gain execution. Users may be subjected to social engineering to get them to open a file that will lead to code execution. This user action will typically be observed as follow-on behavior from [Spearphishing Attachment](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001). Adversaries may use several types of files that require a user to execute them, including .doc, .pdf, .xls, .rtf, .scr, .exe, .lnk, .pif, .cpl, .reg, and .iso.(Citation: Mandiant Trojanized Windows 10)

Adversaries may employ various forms of [Masquerading](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1036) and [Obfuscated Files or Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027) to increase the likelihood that a user will open and successfully execute a malicious file. These methods may include using a familiar naming convention and/or password protecting the file and supplying instructions to a user on how to open it.(Citation: Password Protected Word Docs) 

While [Malicious File](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002) frequently occurs shortly after Initial Access it may occur at other phases of an intrusion, such as when an adversary places a file in a shared directory or on a user's desktop hoping that a user will click on it. This activity may also be seen shortly after [Internal Spearphishing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1534).
1248.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique Malicious File, ID T1204.002, under the Execution tactic primarily for Windows and other user-interactive platforms. It involves an adversary relying on a user to open a malicious file, such as .doc, .pdf, .exe, .lnk, or .iso, often delivered via spearphishing. Execution is achieved through user interaction, with adversaries employing masquerading and obfuscation, like familiar naming or password protection, to increase success. The technique is frequently associated with groups like APT28 and numerous others, and it can occur at various intrusion phases beyond initial access.
1248.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Malicious URLs, corresponding to MITRE ATT&CK technique T1204.001 (User Execution: Malicious Link), fall under the Initial Access tactic and target multiple platforms. This technique relies on a user clicking a malicious hyperlink, often delivered via spearphishing, to trigger execution. The link may lead to the exploitation of a browser vulnerability, the download of a malicious file, or the harvesting of credentials through a cloned login page. Adversaries often use deceptive URL masking, link shortening services, or typosquatted domains to increase effectiveness and bypass security filters.

1249.name: Exploit documents
1249.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may attempt to exploit a weakness in an Internet-facing host or system to initially access a network. The weakness in the system can be a software bug, a temporary glitch, or a misconfiguration.

Exploited applications are often websites/web servers, but can also include databases (like SQL), standard services (like SMB or SSH), network device administration and management protocols (like SNMP and Smart Install), and any other system with Internet-accessible open sockets.(Citation: NVD CVE-2016-6662)(Citation: CIS Multiple SMB Vulnerabilities)(Citation: US-CERT TA18-106A Network Infrastructure Devices 2018)(Citation: Cisco Blog Legacy Device Attacks)(Citation: NVD CVE-2014-7169) On ESXi infrastructure, adversaries may exploit exposed OpenSLP services; they may alternatively exploit exposed VMware vCenter servers.(Citation: Recorded Future ESXiArgs Ransomware 2023)(Citation: Ars Technica VMWare Code Execution Vulnerability 2021) Depending on the flaw being exploited, this may also involve [Exploitation for Defense Evasion](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1211) or [Exploitation for Client Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1203).

If an application is hosted on cloud-based infrastructure and/or is containerized, then exploiting it may lead to compromise of the underlying instance or container. This can allow an adversary a path to access the cloud or container APIs (e.g., via the [Cloud Instance Metadata API](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1552/005)), exploit container host access via [Escape to Host](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1611), or take advantage of weak identity and access management policies.

Adversaries may also exploit edge network infrastructure and related appliances, specifically targeting devices that do not support robust host-based defenses.(Citation: Mandiant Fortinet Zero Day)(Citation: Wired Russia Cyberwar)

For websites and databases, the OWASP top 10 and CWE top 25 highlight the most common web-based vulnerabilities.(Citation: OWASP Top 10)(Citation: CWE top 25)
1249.profile: [profile]Exploit Public-Facing Application (T1190) is an Initial Access tactic targeting internet-facing systems across multiple platforms. It involves exploiting software bugs, glitches, or misconfigurations in services like web servers, databases (e.g., SQL), SMB, SSH, SNMP, and VMware services to gain initial network access. This can lead to cloud API compromise or container escape. APT28 is a known user of this technique.[/profile]
1249.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Exploit documents" is a technique where adversaries use malicious documents to execute code by exploiting vulnerabilities in client applications, particularly office productivity software like Microsoft Office. This technique falls under the MITRE ATT&CK framework as T1203: Exploitation for Client Execution, within the Execution tactic, targeting Windows, macOS, and Linux platforms. The execution typically requires user interaction, such as opening a phishing attachment, to trigger exploits that leverage software bugs or misconfigurations. It is commonly employed by threat groups including APT28, APT29, and MuddyWater to gain initial access.

1250.profile: [profile]Malicious File, designated as T1204.002 under the Execution tactic for the Windows platform, involves an adversary relying on a user to open a malicious file to gain code execution. This is often used in drive-by compromise attacks, leveraging web-based delivery to exploit client-side vulnerabilities or deliver malware. The iframe typically points to an external malicious server and may be obfuscated to evade detection, facilitating initial access or execution through the user's web browser.

1251.name: Network reconnaissance
1251.profile: [profile]The entity "Network reconnaissance" is a broad Reconnaissance tactic, not a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique ID. It involves gathering information about a target's network infrastructure to support subsequent attacks. This can be achieved through methods like active scanning to probe for live hosts and services, network sniffing to capture traffic and credentials, and discovering network shares, topology, and security appliances. Groups like APT28 and APT3 are linked to this activity, which is foundational for planning initial access and lateral movement.
1251.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Network reconnaissance is a technique used during the reconnaissance tactic to gather information about a victim's network. It involves probing victim infrastructure via network traffic to collect details such as network topology, including the arrangement of internal and external environments and specifics of network devices like routers and gateways. This information can be gathered through methods like active scanning or by accessing online data sets, revealing opportunities for further reconnaissance or initial access.

1252.name: Strategic network compromise (SWC)
1252.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may compromise third-party infrastructure that can be used during targeting. Infrastructure solutions include physical or cloud servers, domains, network devices, and third-party web and DNS services. Instead of buying, leasing, or renting infrastructure an adversary may compromise infrastructure and use it during other phases of the adversary lifecycle.(Citation: Mandiant APT1)(Citation: ICANNDomainNameHijacking)(Citation: Talos DNSpionage Nov 2018)(Citation: FireEye EPS Awakens Part 2) Additionally, adversaries may compromise numerous machines to form a botnet they can leverage.

Use of compromised infrastructure allows adversaries to stage, launch, and execute operations. Compromised infrastructure can help adversary operations blend in with traffic that is seen as normal, such as contact with high reputation or trusted sites. For example, adversaries may leverage compromised infrastructure (potentially also in conjunction with [Digital Certificates](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1588/004)) to further blend in and support staged information gathering and/or [Phishing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566) campaigns.(Citation: FireEye DNS Hijack 2019) Adversaries may also compromise numerous machines to support [Proxy](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1090) and/or proxyware services or to form a botnet.(Citation: amnesty_nso_pegasus)(Citation: Sysdig Proxyjacking) Additionally, adversaries may compromise infrastructure residing in close proximity to a target in order to gain [Initial Access](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0001) via [Wi-Fi Networks](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1669).(Citation: Nearest Neighbor Volexity)

By using compromised infrastructure, adversaries may enable follow-on malicious operations. Prior to targeting, adversaries may also compromise the infrastructure of other adversaries.(Citation: NSA NCSC Turla OilRig)
1252.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1584, Compromise Infrastructure, under the Resource Development tactic and applicable across multiple platforms. This technique involves adversaries taking control of third-party infrastructure such as servers, domains, or network devices instead of acquiring them legitimately. The compromised assets are then used to stage and launch operations, including hosting phishing campaigns, forming botnets for proxy services, or gaining initial access via nearby Wi-Fi networks, which helps malicious activity blend in with normal traffic. The intrusion-set APT28 has been associated with this practice.[/profile]
1252.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Strategic network compromise (SWC), also known as a watering hole attack, is a targeted form of drive-by compromise (T1189) within the Initial Access tactic. It operates on client platforms like web browsers. The technique involves compromising a legitimate website frequented by a specific community (e.g., government, industry) and injecting malicious code. When a targeted user visits the site, scripts automatically execute to find and exploit vulnerabilities in the user's browser or plugins, ultimately granting the adversary code execution on the victim's system to gain internal network access.

1254.name: OAuth permissions
1254.profile: [profile]OAuth permissions, also known as T1098.002 - Additional Email Delegate Permissions, is a persistence technique under the tactic Privilege Escalation, primarily targeting cloud platforms like Microsoft 365. Adversaries, such as APT28, abuse OAuth to grant malicious applications long-term access to a user's data, often using stolen application access tokens. This allows them to bypass multi-factor authentication and maintain access even if the original compromised account is disabled, enabling persistent data exfiltration and further malicious actions within the SaaS environment.[/profile]
1254.profile_without_enhance: [profile]OAuth permissions is a technique adversaries use to gain persistent access to cloud environments by abusing OAuth application integrations. This involves creating or co-opting applications within platforms like Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace and obtaining user consent, often through social engineering, to grant the application permissions. Once authorized, the malicious application can maintain access to user data, bypass multi-factor authentication using application access tokens, and enable automated data exfiltration, even if the original user account is later disabled.

1255.uncertain_mes:

By using compromised infrastructure, adversaries may enable follow-on malicious operations. Prior to targeting, adversaries may also compromise the infrastructure of other adversaries.(Citation: NSA NCSC Turla OilRig)
1255.profile: [profile]Webmail Compromise, mapped to MITRE ATT&CK technique T1586.002 "Email Accounts: Compromise Accounts", falls under the Resource Development tactic and is platform-agnostic. This technique involves adversaries gaining unauthorized access to existing email accounts through methods such as credential phishing, purchasing credentials from third-party sites, brute-forcing using breached password dumps, or bribing insiders. Once compromised, these accounts are leveraged to conduct spearphishing campaigns, send malicious spam, hijack existing email threads for social engineering, and acquire other infrastructure like domains, thereby blending malicious activity with trusted communications. The intrusion set APT28 has been associated with this activity.[/profile]
1255.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Webmail compromise is a technique where adversaries gain unauthorized access to web-based email accounts, such as those on Exchange Server, Office 365, or Google Workspace. This is often achieved by gathering credentials through phishing, purchasing credentials, or brute-forcing using breached password dumps. Once compromised, these accounts are leveraged to conduct further phishing campaigns, send malicious spam, or hijack existing email threads to enhance the credibility of social engineering attacks and evade email filtering.

1256.name: Decoy content
1256.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may gain access and continuously communicate with victims by injecting malicious content into systems through online network traffic. Rather than luring victims to malicious payloads hosted on a compromised website (i.e., [Drive-by Target](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1608/004) followed by [Drive-by Compromise](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1189)), adversaries may initially access victims through compromised data-transfer channels where they can manipulate traffic and/or inject their own content. These compromised online network channels may also be used to deliver additional payloads (i.e., [Ingress Tool Transfer](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1105)) and other data to already compromised systems.(Citation: ESET MoustachedBouncer)

Adversaries may inject content to victim systems in various ways, including:

* From the middle, where the adversary is in-between legitimate online client-server communications (**Note:** this is similar but distinct from [Adversary-in-the-Middle](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1557), which describes AiTM activity solely within an enterprise environment) (Citation: Kaspersky Encyclopedia MiTM)
* From the side, where malicious content is injected and races to the client as a fake response to requests of a legitimate online server (Citation: Kaspersky ManOnTheSide)

Content injection is often the result of compromised upstream communication channels, for example at the level of an internet service provider (ISP) as is the case with "lawful interception."(Citation: Kaspersky ManOnTheSide)(Citation: ESET MoustachedBouncer)(Citation: EFF China GitHub Attack)
1256.profile: [profile]The entity is known as "Decoy content" or "content injection," with a potential MITRE ID of T1659. It falls under the Initial Access tactic and targets network platforms. This technique involves adversaries injecting malicious content into online network traffic by compromising upstream communication channels, such as at the ISP level, to manipulate data-transfer streams. This can be executed "from the middle," where the adversary intercepts client-server communications, or "from the side," by racing malicious responses to client requests. It is distinct from Adversary-in-the-Middle (AiTM) within enterprise environments and has been associated with groups like MoustachedBouncer. The method enables continuous victim communication and can facilitate additional payload delivery through compromised channels.[/profile]
1256.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Decoy content is a technique where adversaries create and deploy fake or deceptive data, files, or resources to mislead defenders, researchers, or automated security systems. This tactic is often used to hide malicious activity, waste analyst time, or establish false indicators of compromise. The technique can involve generating bogus documents, fake network traffic, or spoofed system artifacts to blend in with legitimate content and avoid detection.

1258.name: Malicious application
1258.profile: [profile]Malicious application is attributed to APT28 and possibly referenced by Lazarus Group. It is associated with the malware families gplayed, gravity rat, and HeavyLift, where it often masquerades as a legitimate application installer. Its key technical behaviors include deploying a malicious Electron-based desktop application that executes JavaScript code to perform malicious operations on the infected system. The target platform is desktop systems, and its infrastructure involves malicious installers for initial deployment.[/profile]
1258.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Malicious application is an alias for the malware families gplayed and gravity rat. It is attributed to the Lazarus Group. Its key technical behaviors include masquerading as a legitimate application installer, deploying a malicious Electron-based desktop application, and executing malicious JavaScript code on the infected system. The target platform is desktop systems.

1259.name: ak a chopstick
1259.uncertain_mes: [CHOPSTICK](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0023) is a malware family of modular backdoors used by [APT28](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0007). It has been used since at least 2012 and is usually dropped on victims as second-stage malware, though it has been used as first-stage malware in several cases. It has both Windows and Linux variants. (Citation: FireEye APT28) (Citation: ESET Sednit Part 2) (Citation: FireEye APT28 January 2017) (Citation: DOJ GRU Indictment Jul 2018) It is tracked separately from the [X-Agent for Android](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0314).

It has been in use since at least 2012, typically deployed as second-stage malware but also used in first-stage attacks. 1260.name: webhp
1260.profile: [profile]Webhp is a malware attributed to APT28. It communicates via HTTP POST requests to a command and control server, using a specific user-agent string "Mozilla/4.0 (compatible; MSIE 6.0; Windows NT 5.1; SV1)" and a URI path containing "/webhp?source=". It is designed to target Windows systems, leveraging system processes like explorer.exe and shell32.dll for execution. The malware also attempts to gain the SeDebugPrivilege for elevated access and uses temporary directories for file operations.[/profile]
1260.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The malware 'webhp' is a component or variant associated with the 'taleret' malware family, as indicated by shared command-and-control (C2) infrastructure using the specific URI path '/webhp?source='. Its key technical behaviors include attempting to gain the SeDebugPrivilege, executing commands via ShellExecuteA, and communicating with a C2 server using HTTP. The primary target platform is Windows, as evidenced by its interaction with explorer.exe and shell32.dll. No specific APT or criminal groups are definitively attributed to it in the provided data.

1261.name: xagent
1261.profile: [profile]Xagent, also known as X-agent, is a malware attributed to the APT28 intrusion set. Its technical behaviors include the use of obfuscated Run-Time Type Information (RTTI) in its modules. The malware targets Windows and Linux platforms, with specific versions like version 1 for Windows introduced in 2014 and version 3 for Linux and Windows introduced in 2014-2015. It is associated with the related tool Xtunnel.[/profile]
1261.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Xagent is a malware also known as x-agent. It is attributed to the APT28 intrusion set. Key technical behaviors include persistence via reboot (modifying property list files to auto-execute after reboot) and icon hiding (setting the `apple.awt.UIElement` key to conceal its process). It targets iOS, Linux, and Windows platforms. It is related to the Madcap malware and has been developed in multiple versions, including a version for Windows in 2014 and a version 3 for Linux and Windows in 2014/2015, with modules featuring obfuscated Run-Time Type Information (RTTI).

1262.name: splm
1262.profile: [profile]Splm, also known as XAgent, is attributed to the APT28 intrusion set. Its use by Sofacy (another name for APT28) has reportedly declined since 2018, as indicated by a decrease in global detections. This malware is a tool used by the group for its operations.[/profile]
1262.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Splm, also known as XAgent, is a malware attributed to the APT group Sofacy (also known as APT28). Its key technical behavior includes being used for espionage operations, with its global detections having decreased significantly by 2018. The primary target platform for this malware is Windows systems.

1263.name: eviltoss
1263.profile: [profile]Eviltoss, also known as AZZY, ADVSTORESHELL, and NETUI, is attributed to the APT28 intrusion set. It is a backdoor tool that spans multiple generations, indicating iterative development. It is part of a broader arsenal that includes other tools like CORESHELL, SPLM (Xagent/CHOPSTICK), and JHUHUGIT.[/profile]

1265.name: advstoreshell
1265.uncertain_mes: [ADVSTORESHELL](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0045) is a spying backdoor that has been used by [APT28](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0007) from at least 2012 to 2016. 1266.name: azzy

1268.name: gamefish

1269.name: sednit
1269.profile: [profile]Sednit, also known as APT28, Fancy Bear, Sofacy, Pawn Storm, and STRONTIUM, is attributed to the APT28 intrusion set. 1289.name: Exploits
1289.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may develop exploits that can be used during targeting. An exploit takes advantage of a bug or vulnerability in order to cause unintended or unanticipated behavior to occur on computer hardware or software. Rather than finding/modifying exploits from online or purchasing them from exploit vendors, an adversary may develop their own exploits.(Citation: NYTStuxnet) Adversaries may use information acquired via [Vulnerabilities](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1588/006) to focus exploit development efforts. As part of the exploit development process, adversaries may uncover exploitable vulnerabilities through methods such as fuzzing and patch analysis.(Citation: Irongeek Sims BSides 2017)

As with legitimate development efforts, different skill sets may be required for developing exploits. The skills needed may be located in-house, or may need to be contracted out. Use of a contractor may be considered an extension of that adversary's exploit development capabilities, provided the adversary plays a role in shaping requirements and maintains an initial degree of exclusivity to the exploit.

Adversaries may use exploits during various phases of the adversary lifecycle (i.e. [Exploit Public-Facing Application](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1190), [Exploitation for Client Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1203), [Exploitation for Privilege Escalation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1068), [Exploitation for Defense Evasion](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1211), [Exploitation for Credential Access](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1212), [Exploitation of Remote Services](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1210), and [Application or System Exploitation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1499/004)).
1289.profile: [profile]Develop Exploits, identified as T1587.004 under the Resource Development tactic, is a cross-platform technique where adversaries create their own exploits to leverage software or hardware vulnerabilities, rather than acquiring them externally. Development efforts may be informed by vulnerability intelligence and involve methods like fuzzing and patch analysis to discover bugs, with capabilities potentially extended through contracted specialists. These custom exploits are subsequently used across multiple phases of an attack lifecycle.
1289.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Exploits" is a general concept referring to code that leverages software or hardware vulnerabilities to cause unintended behavior, rather than a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique. It is associated with adversary resource development and is used across multiple tactics including initial access, execution, privilege escalation, and lateral movement. Exploits can be developed in-house via methods like fuzzing, purchased from vendors, or obtained from online sources. They are employed in techniques such as Exploit Public-Facing Application (T1190) and Exploitation for Client Execution (T1203) to compromise systems.

1290.name: JavaScript Trick
1290.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may abuse various implementations of JavaScript for execution. JavaScript (JS) is a platform-independent scripting language (compiled just-in-time at runtime) commonly associated with scripts in webpages, though JS can be executed in runtime environments outside the browser.(Citation: NodeJS) JScript is the Microsoft implementation of the same scripting standard. JScript is interpreted via the Windows Script engine and thus integrated with many components of Windows such as the [Component Object Model](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1559/001) and Internet Explorer HTML Application (HTA) pages.(Citation: JScrip May 2018)(Citation: Microsoft JScript 2007)(Citation: Microsoft Windows Scripts) JavaScript for Automation (JXA) is a macOS scripting language based on JavaScript, included as part of Apple’s Open Scripting Architecture (OSA), that was introduced in OSX 10.10. Apple’s OSA provides scripting capabilities to control applications, interface with the operating system, and bridge access into the rest of Apple’s internal APIs. As of OSX 10.10, OSA only supports two languages, JXA and [AppleScript](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/002). Scripts can be executed via the command line utility osascript, they can be compiled into applications or script files via osacompile, and they can be compiled and executed in memory of other programs by leveraging the OSAKit Framework.(Citation: Apple About Mac Scripting 2016)(Citation: SpecterOps JXA 2020)(Citation: SentinelOne macOS Red Team)(Citation: Red Canary Silver Sparrow Feb2021)(Citation: MDSec macOS JXA and VSCode) Adversaries may abuse various implementations of JavaScript to execute various behaviors. Common uses include hosting malicious scripts on websites as part of a [Drive-by Compromise](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1189) or downloading and executing these script files as secondary payloads. Since these payloads are text-based, it is also very common for adversaries to obfuscate their content as part of [Obfuscated Files or Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027).
1290.profile: [profile]JavaScript/JScript/JXA (T1059.007) is a Command and Scripting Interpreter technique within the Execution tactic, applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves abusing the JavaScript, JScript, or JavaScript for Automation (JXA) engines to execute malicious code. Common implementations include using JScript within Windows Script Host or HTML Applications (HTA), JXA via the `osascript` utility on macOS, and hosting scripts in webpages for drive-by compromises. Payloads are often obfuscated as text-based scripts.
1290.profile_without_enhance: [profile]JavaScript Trick is an attack pattern where adversaries use JavaScript to execute malicious code. It is associated with MITRE ATT&CK ID T1059.007 under the Execution tactic and operates across multiple platforms. The technique involves hosting malicious scripts on websites for drive-by compromises or downloading and executing them as secondary payloads. Adversaries often obfuscate these text-based scripts to evade detection. The method is commonly employed by groups like FIN7, Turla, and MuddyWater.

1310.name: Stage 1
1310.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may upload, install, or otherwise set up capabilities that can be used during targeting. To support their operations, an adversary may need to take capabilities they developed ([Develop Capabilities](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1587)) or obtained ([Obtain Capabilities](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1588)) and stage them on infrastructure under their control. These capabilities may be staged on infrastructure that was previously purchased/rented by the adversary ([Acquire Infrastructure](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1583)) or was otherwise compromised by them ([Compromise Infrastructure](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1584)). Capabilities may also be staged on web services, such as GitHub or Pastebin, or on Platform-as-a-Service (PaaS) offerings that enable users to easily provision applications.(Citation: Volexity Ocean Lotus November 2020)(Citation: Dragos Heroku Watering Hole)(Citation: Malwarebytes Heroku Skimmers)(Citation: Netskope GCP Redirection)(Citation: Netskope Cloud Phishing)

Staging of capabilities can aid the adversary in a number of initial access and post-compromise behaviors, including (but not limited to):

* Staging web resources necessary to conduct [Drive-by Compromise](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1189) when a user browses to a site.(Citation: FireEye CFR Watering Hole 2012)(Citation: Gallagher 2015)(Citation: ATT ScanBox)
* Staging web resources for a link target to be used with spearphishing.(Citation: Malwarebytes Silent Librarian October 2020)(Citation: Proofpoint TA407 September 2019)
* Uploading malware or tools to a location accessible to a victim network to enable [Ingress Tool Transfer](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1105).(Citation: Volexity Ocean Lotus November 2020)
* Installing a previously acquired SSL/TLS certificate to use to encrypt command and control traffic (ex: [Asymmetric Cryptography](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1573/002) with [Web Protocols](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1071/001)).(Citation: DigiCert Install SSL Cert)
1310.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique "Stage Capabilities" (ID: T1608) under the Resource Development tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It involves adversaries uploading, installing, or setting up tools and resources on controlled infrastructure—such as purchased, compromised, or public web/PaaS services like GitHub, Pastebin, or Heroku—to enable subsequent attack steps. This staging supports behaviors like hosting web resources for drive-by compromises or spearphishing links, positioning malware for tool transfer, or installing SSL/TLS certificates for encrypted command and control. The technique is associated with groups like Mustang Panda.
1310.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Stage 1 is a conceptual phase within a multi-stage attack framework, not a distinct MITRE ATT&CK technique. It typically involves establishing an initial foothold, such as deploying a first-stage command and control (C2) payload. This initial stage often has automated capabilities to collect basic host information, update tools, and upload additional files or a more fully-featured second-stage remote access tool (RAT) to redirect to a separate C2 server for interactive control, helping to obfuscate the communication channel.
