1311.profile: [profile]Stage Capabilities, identified as T1608, is a Resource Development technique where adversaries upload, install, or configure tools and malware on controlled infrastructure for later use. This infrastructure can be acquired, compromised, or consist of public web services like GitHub, Pastebin, or PaaS platforms. The staged capabilities enable subsequent attack behaviors such as hosting resources for drive-by compromises or spearphishing links, facilitating ingress tool transfer, or deploying SSL/TLS certificates for encrypted command and control. The group Mustang Panda has been associated with this practice.
1311.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Stage 2 is a generic term for a secondary phase in a multi-stage attack, often referring to command and control (C2) or data staging. In C2, it typically involves a more fully-featured remote access tool (RAT) deployed after an initial beacon, using a separate infrastructure to provide interactive access like a reverse shell. For data exfiltration, Stage 2 can involve consolidating collected data into a central location or archive on a compromised system or cloud instance prior to transfer, minimizing connections to evade detection. This phase is employed by groups like APT41, MuddyWater, and Lazarus Group.

1312.name: Email Attachment
1312.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may send spearphishing emails with a malicious attachment in an attempt to gain access to victim systems. Spearphishing attachment is a specific variant of spearphishing. Spearphishing attachment is different from other forms of spearphishing in that it employs the use of malware attached to an email. All forms of spearphishing are electronically delivered social engineering targeted at a specific individual, company, or industry. In this scenario, adversaries attach a file to the spearphishing email and usually rely upon [User Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204) to gain execution.(Citation: Unit 42 DarkHydrus July 2018) Spearphishing may also involve social engineering techniques, such as posing as a trusted source.

There are many options for the attachment such as Microsoft Office documents, executables, PDFs, or archived files. Upon opening the attachment (and potentially clicking past protections), the adversary's payload exploits a vulnerability or directly executes on the user's system. The text of the spearphishing email usually tries to give a plausible reason why the file should be opened, and may explain how to bypass system protections in order to do so. The email may also contain instructions on how to decrypt an attachment, such as a zip file password, in order to evade email boundary defenses. Adversaries frequently manipulate file extensions and icons in order to make attached executables appear to be document files, or files exploiting one application appear to be a file for a different one.
1312.profile: [profile]Spearphishing Attachment is technique T1566.001 under the Initial Access tactic, targeting Windows, macOS, and Linux. It involves sending targeted emails with malicious attachments like Office documents, PDFs, or executables to gain system access. Execution typically relies on user interaction to open the file, which may exploit a vulnerability or run a payload directly. Adversaries often use social engineering, provide decryption passwords for archived files to bypass defenses, and manipulate file extensions/icons to disguise malicious content.[profile]
1312.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Email Attachment is a technique within the Initial Access tactic, applicable to multiple platforms, where adversaries send emails with malicious files to gain access. The malicious payload, often disguised as a Microsoft Office document, executable, PDF, or archived file, requires user execution to activate, either by exploiting a vulnerability or directly running. Attackers use social engineering to prompt opening the file and may employ evasion tactics like providing decryption passwords for archived attachments or manipulating file extensions and icons to appear benign.

1313.name: Decoy Document
1313.profile: [profile]Decoy Document is a technique used within spearphishing campaigns, often by groups like APT28 and menuPass. It involves adversaries attaching malicious files, such as manipulated Microsoft Office documents, to emails. These documents may appear legitimate but are designed to exploit user execution, sometimes using template injection to fetch malicious payloads from remote URLs when the file is opened, thereby evading static detection. The technique serves as an initial access vector to deliver malware.
1313.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Decoy Document is a technique within the Initial Access tactic, used on Windows, macOS, and Linux platforms. It involves adversaries creating or using seemingly legitimate document files, such as Microsoft Office or PDFs, to deliver malicious payloads. This often relies on user execution to open the file, which may then exploit a vulnerability or execute code. The technique can employ template injection to conceal and fetch malicious code from remote resources when the document is loaded, bypassing static detection. It is commonly delivered via spearphishing attachments.

Its key technical behavior is the exploitation of vulnerabilities, specifically targeting the Windows platform, as indicated by its use in privilege escalation exploits like JuicyPotato and PetitPotato.

1316.name: Multi-stage Attack
1316.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may create multiple stages for command and control that are employed under different conditions or for certain functions. Use of multiple stages may obfuscate the command and control channel to make detection more difficult.

Remote access tools will call back to the first-stage command and control server for instructions. The first stage may have automated capabilities to collect basic host information, update tools, and upload additional files. A second remote access tool (RAT) could be uploaded at that point to redirect the host to the second-stage command and control server. The second stage will likely be more fully featured and allow the adversary to interact with the system through a reverse shell and additional RAT features.

The different stages will likely be hosted separately with no overlapping infrastructure. The loader may also have backup first-stage callbacks or [Fallback Channels](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1008) in case the original first-stage communication path is discovered and blocked.
1316.profile: [profile]Multi-stage Channels, designated as T1104 within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, is a command and control (C2) technique under the Command and Control tactic, applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It operates by establishing a multi-stage C2 architecture where an initial compromised host calls back to a first-stage server for automated instructions, basic host reconnaissance, and tool updates. This server can then upload a second, more capable remote access tool (RAT) to redirect the host to a separate, second-stage C2 server for full interactive control via features like a reverse shell, with infrastructure typically segregated between stages to hinder detection. Threat groups such as APT3, APT41, MuddyWater, and Lazarus Group have been associated with its use.[/profile]
1316.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Multi-stage Attack is a broad concept describing a sequence of distinct, often escalating, actions to achieve an objective. The retrieved data highlights specific technical implementations: in command and control, adversaries use separate infrastructure stages where a first-stage loader collects host data and uploads a second, more capable RAT (T1104). For execution, malicious Control Panel items (.cpl files) can be delivered as a payload in such attacks (T1196). Staging capabilities on controlled infrastructure (T1608), including for drive-by compromises (T1608.004), is also a common preparatory step in multi-stage operations.

1323.name: JavaScript
1323.profile: [profile]JavaScript is a malware agent used by APT28, with versions including Core Agent 4.0, 3.6, and 3.5 as seen in the EvilNum campaign. It is also utilized by the criminal group Storm-0249 in the Gootloader campaign, where it serves as initial and secondary payload files. The malware functions as a stealer, with variants like an AutoIT-based stealer using .CPL and .JS files. Its primary target platform is Windows systems.[/profile]
1323.profile_without_enhance: [profile]JavaScript is a scripting language, but in the context of malware, it refers to malicious scripts or agents. It is used as a core component in various malware families, including EvilNum (where it serves as an agent in versions 3.5, 3.6, and 4.0), GootLoader (which employs initial and secondary JavaScript files for its operations, attributed to the criminal group Storm-0249), and Unidentified 083 (AutoIt Stealer), which also utilizes JS files. Its primary target platform is Windows systems, where these scripts execute to deliver payloads, steal data, or establish persistence.

1324.name: T1564
1324.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may attempt to hide artifacts associated with their behaviors to evade detection. Operating systems may have features to hide various artifacts, such as important system files and administrative task execution, to avoid disrupting user work environments and prevent users from changing files or features on the system. Adversaries may abuse these features to hide artifacts such as files, directories, user accounts, or other system activity to evade detection.(Citation: Sofacy Komplex Trojan)(Citation: Cybereason OSX Pirrit)(Citation: MalwareBytes ADS July 2015)

Adversaries may also attempt to hide artifacts associated with malicious behavior by creating computing regions that are isolated from common security instrumentation, such as through the use of virtualization technology.(Citation: Sophos Ragnar May 2020)
1324.profile: [profile]T1564, known as Hide Artifacts, is a Defense Evasion technique where adversaries abuse operating system features or virtualization to conceal malicious files, directories, user accounts, or system activity. This can involve leveraging native OS capabilities meant to hide system files or creating isolated computing regions to evade common security detection mechanisms. The technique is associated with groups like APT28 and is applicable across multiple platforms.
1324.profile_without_enhance: [profile]T1564, named Hide Artifacts, is a Defense Evasion tactic technique applicable across multiple platforms. It involves adversaries abusing operating system features or creating isolated computing regions to conceal files, directories, user accounts, or other system activity associated with malicious behavior, thereby evading detection. Specific sub-techniques can include actions like running applications in a hidden window.

1336.name: JavaScript Redirection
1336.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may abuse various implementations of JavaScript for execution. JavaScript (JS) is a platform-independent scripting language (compiled just-in-time at runtime) commonly associated with scripts in webpages, though JS can be executed in runtime environments outside the browser.(Citation: NodeJS) JScript is the Microsoft implementation of the same scripting standard. JScript is interpreted via the Windows Script engine and thus integrated with many components of Windows such as the [Component Object Model](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1559/001) and Internet Explorer HTML Application (HTA) pages.(Citation: JScrip May 2018)(Citation: Microsoft JScript 2007)(Citation: Microsoft Windows Scripts) JavaScript for Automation (JXA) is a macOS scripting language based on JavaScript, included as part of Apple’s Open Scripting Architecture (OSA), that was introduced in OSX 10.10. Apple’s OSA provides scripting capabilities to control applications, interface with the operating system, and bridge access into the rest of Apple’s internal APIs. As of OSX 10.10, OSA only supports two languages, JXA and [AppleScript](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/002). Scripts can be executed via the command line utility osascript, they can be compiled into applications or script files via osacompile, and they can be compiled and executed in memory of other programs by leveraging the OSAKit Framework.(Citation: Apple About Mac Scripting 2016)(Citation: SpecterOps JXA 2020)(Citation: SentinelOne macOS Red Team)(Citation: Red Canary Silver Sparrow Feb2021)(Citation: MDSec macOS JXA and VSCode) Adversaries may abuse various implementations of JavaScript to execute various behaviors. Common uses include hosting malicious scripts on websites as part of a [Drive-by Compromise](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1189) or downloading and executing these script files as secondary payloads. Since these payloads are text-based, it is also very common for adversaries to obfuscate their content as part of [Obfuscated Files or Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027).
1336.profile: [profile]JavaScript/JScript, identified as T1059.007, is a Command and Scripting Interpreter technique within the Execution tactic, applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves the abuse of JavaScript, JScript, or JXA (JavaScript for Automation) to execute adversary-controlled code, commonly delivered via malicious scripts in drive-by compromises or as downloaded secondary payloads. These text-based scripts are frequently obfuscated (T1027) and can be executed in various runtime environments, including web browsers, the Windows Script engine for COM/HTA integration, or via macOS command-line utilities like osascript. It is associated with numerous threat groups, including APT28, Fin7, and MuddyWater.[/profile]
1336.profile_without_enhance: [profile]JavaScript Redirection is a technique where adversaries use JavaScript to redirect users from a legitimate or compromised webpage to a malicious destination, often as part of a drive-by compromise or phishing campaign. The redirection is typically triggered automatically or by user interaction, such as clicking a malicious link, and serves to deliver secondary payloads or lead victims to credential harvesting or exploit sites. This method is commonly obfuscated and executed within web browsers.

1349.name: IMAP
1349.profile: [profile]IMAP, designated as T1071.003 within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, is a Command and Control technique under the Application Layer Protocol tactic. It operates across Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. Adversaries abuse the Internet Message Access Protocol (IMAP) to blend command and control traffic with legitimate email delivery communications, embedding malicious commands and data exfiltration within standard protocol fields and headers or within the email messages themselves to evade network detection. This technique has been associated with threat groups including APT28, Turla, and Kimsuky.[/profile]
1349.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "IMAP" is a network protocol. In the context of cyber threat intelligence, it is referenced as a specific technique for adversary command and control, identified as T1071.003 within the MITRE ATT&CK framework under the Command and Control tactic. This technique involves adversaries using the IMAP protocol, commonly associated with email retrieval, to blend malicious communications with normal network traffic. They embed commands and exfiltrated data within standard IMAP packets or email messages to avoid detection by network security controls.

1352.name: Command and Control (C2)
1352.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may communicate using a custom command and control protocol instead of encapsulating commands/data in an existing [Application Layer Protocol](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1071). Implementations include mimicking well-known protocols or developing custom protocols (including raw sockets) on top of fundamental protocols provided by TCP/IP/another standard network stack.
1352.profile: [profile]This entity corresponds to MITRE ATT&CK technique T1094, named Custom Command and Control Protocol, under the Command and Control tactic. It operates across multiple platforms and involves adversaries developing or mimicking custom network protocols, including raw sockets, instead of using standard application layer protocols for C2 communication to evade detection. Associated intrusion sets include OilRig, APT28, and APT3, and it is used by malware like Powruner.
1352.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Command and Control (C2) is a core adversary tactic (TA0011) for maintaining communication with compromised systems. It involves establishing a covert channel to remotely direct malware and exfiltrate data. Techniques for C2 include using custom protocols (T1094), obfuscating traffic (T1001, T1132), and leveraging trusted web services (T1102.003) to blend with normal network activity and evade detection.

1353.name: SEDNI
1353.profile: [profile]SEDNI is a malware attributed to the APT28 intrusion set. It is associated with the related entities buterat, cmoon, and latentbot, which suggest it may involve persistence mechanisms via registry keys, monitoring of specific applications, and specific network interaction patterns for command and control.
1353.profile_without_enhance: [profile]SEDNI is a malware entity. No specific aliases, attributed groups, key TTPs, target platforms, or infrastructure details are provided in the available data.

1354.name: Evasion
1354.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may employ various means to detect and avoid debuggers. Debuggers are typically used by defenders to trace and/or analyze the execution of potential malware payloads.(Citation: ProcessHacker Github) Debugger evasion may include changing behaviors based on the results of the checks for the presence of artifacts indicative of a debugged environment. Similar to [Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1497), if the adversary detects a debugger, they may alter their malware to disengage from the victim or conceal the core functions of the implant. They may also search for debugger artifacts before dropping secondary or additional payloads. Specific checks will vary based on the target and/or adversary. On Windows, this may involve [Native API](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1106) function calls such as IsDebuggerPresent() and NtQueryInformationProcess(), or manually checking the BeingDebugged flag of the Process Environment Block (PEB). On Linux, this may involve querying `/proc/self/status` for the `TracerPID` field, which indicates whether or not the process is being traced by dynamic analysis tools.(Citation: Cado Security P2PInfect 2023)(Citation: Positive Technologies Hellhounds 2023) Other checks for debugging artifacts may also seek to enumerate hardware breakpoints, interrupt assembly opcodes, time checks, or measurements if exceptions are raised in the current process (assuming a present debugger would “swallow” or handle the potential error).(Citation: hasherezade debug)(Citation: AlKhaser Debug)(Citation: vxunderground debug) Malware may also leverage Structured Exception Handling (SEH) to detect debuggers by throwing an exception and detecting whether the process is suspended. SEH handles both hardware and software expectations, providing control over the exceptions including support for debugging. If a debugger is present, the program’s control will be transferred to the debugger, and the execution of the code will be suspended. If the debugger is not present, control will be transferred to the SEH handler, which will automatically handle the exception and allow the program’s execution to continue.(Citation: Apriorit) Adversaries may use the information learned from these debugger checks during automated discovery to shape follow-on behaviors. Debuggers can also be evaded by detaching the process or flooding debug logs with meaningless data via messages produced by looping [Native API](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1106) function calls such as OutputDebugStringW().(Citation: wardle evilquest partii)(Citation: Checkpoint Dridex Jan 2021)
1354.profile: [profile]Debugger Evasion, identified as T1622, is a Defense Evasion technique used on Windows and Linux platforms. It involves detecting debuggers to alter malware behavior or avoid analysis. Specific methods include checking the Windows PEB's BeingDebugged flag via APIs like IsDebuggerPresent() and NtQueryInformationProcess(), querying Linux's /proc/self/status for TracerPID, using Structured Exception Handling (SEH) to test for process suspension, enumerating hardware breakpoints, and flooding logs with OutputDebugStringW() calls. Groups like OilRig and APT28 have been associated with this technique.
1354.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Evasion" is a broad concept, not a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique. The retrieved information describes several distinct evasion techniques. These include Debugger Evasion (T1622), which involves checking for debugging artifacts using methods like IsDebuggerPresent() on Windows or querying /proc/self/status on Linux, and Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion (T1497), which detects virtual environments by checking for system artifacts or using sleep timers. Other related techniques are Exploitation for Defense Evasion (T1211), which targets vulnerabilities in security software, and Indicator Removal from Tools (T1027.005/T1066), where adversaries modify malicious tools to remove detected signatures. These techniques are employed by various threat groups across multiple platforms to avoid detection and analysis.

1367.name: PPTP (TCP/1723)
1367.profile: [profile]The entity "PPTP (TCP/1723)" is a deprecated technique, now superseded by MITRE ATT&CK technique T1571 (Non-Standard Port). It represents a method where adversaries use the commonly open TCP port 1723, typically associated with the Point-to-Point Tunneling Protocol, to blend malicious network traffic with legitimate activity. This tactic helps bypass firewalls and avoid detection by leveraging a standard service port, often for command and control communications or credential stuffing attacks against management services. It has been associated with threat actors like APT28.[/profile]
1367.profile_without_enhance: [profile]PPTP (TCP/1723) is a deprecated technique, now replaced by Non-Standard Port (T1571). It involved adversaries using the standard TCP port 1723, commonly associated with the Point-to-Point Tunneling Protocol, to bypass network defenses by blending with legitimate traffic. This port could be used for its intended protocol or for a completely different custom command and control channel.

1368.name: DNS (UDP/53)
1368.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may communicate using the Domain Name System (DNS) application layer protocol to avoid detection/network filtering by blending in with existing traffic. Commands to the remote system, and often the results of those commands, will be embedded within the protocol traffic between the client and server. 

The DNS protocol serves an administrative function in computer networking and thus may be very common in environments. DNS traffic may also be allowed even before network authentication is completed. DNS packets contain many fields and headers in which data can be concealed. Often known as DNS tunneling, adversaries may abuse DNS to communicate with systems under their control within a victim network while also mimicking normal, expected traffic.(Citation: PAN DNS Tunneling)(Citation: Medium DnsTunneling)

DNS beaconing may be used to send commands to remote systems via DNS queries. A DNS beacon is created by tunneling DNS traffic (i.e. [Protocol Tunneling](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1572)). The commands may be embedded into different DNS records, for example, TXT or A records.(Citation: OilRig Uses Updated BONDUPDATER to Target Middle Eastern Government) DNS beacons may be difficult to detect because the beacons infrequently communicate with infected devices.(Citation: DNS Beacons) Infrequent communication conceals the malicious DNS traffic with normal DNS traffic.
1368.profile: [profile]This entity maps to MITRE ATT&CK technique T1071.004, Application Layer Protocol: DNS, under the Command and Control tactic for Windows, Linux, and macOS. It describes adversaries using the DNS protocol for covert communication by embedding commands and data within DNS traffic, a method known as DNS tunneling, to blend with normal network activity. Specific mechanics include using DNS queries for beaconing, concealing data in various DNS record types like TXT or A records, and employing infrequent communication to evade detection. The technique is associated with groups like APT28, OilRig, and FIN7.[/profile]
1368.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "DNS (UDP/53)" is a deprecated technique, formerly ID T1043, under the Command and Control tactic. It involves adversaries using the standard DNS port (UDP/53) to blend malicious communications with normal network traffic, bypassing firewalls and detection systems. This method can be used for protocol tunneling, where commands and data are concealed within DNS queries and responses, often in fields like TXT or A records, to establish covert channels.

1369.name: OpenSSH (TCP/22)
1369.profile: [profile]OpenSSH (TCP/22) is a specific instance of the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1071.001 (Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols), falling under the Command and Control tactic. It operates across Linux, macOS, and Windows platforms. This technique involves adversaries using the SSH protocol over its standard port (22) to blend command and control traffic with legitimate administrative network activity, thereby evading detection. The intrusion set APT28 has been associated with this method. It is distinct from deprecated port misuse techniques and custom C2 protocols, representing the specific, legitimate use of a common encrypted management channel for malicious purposes.[/profile]
1369.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "OpenSSH (TCP/22)" is a specific implementation of the SSH protocol on port 22. It is not a distinct MITRE ATT&CK technique but is commonly referenced under techniques like T1043 (Commonly Used Port) and T1071 (Application Layer Protocol), which fall under the Command and Control tactic. SSH, including OpenSSH on its standard port, is a legitimate protocol for secure remote administration but can be abused by adversaries to blend their malicious communications with normal network traffic, often to bypass detection or for lateral movement within a network.

1370.name: Use of Tor network
1370.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may perform Network Denial of Service (DoS) attacks to degrade or block the availability of targeted resources to users. Network DoS can be performed by exhausting the network bandwidth services rely on. Example resources include specific websites, email services, DNS, and web-based applications. Adversaries have been observed conducting network DoS attacks for political purposes(Citation: FireEye OpPoisonedHandover February 2016) and to support other malicious activities, including distraction(Citation: FSISAC FraudNetDoS September 2012), hacktivism, and extortion.(Citation: Symantec DDoS October 2014)

A Network DoS will occur when the bandwidth capacity of the network connection to a system is exhausted due to the volume of malicious traffic directed at the resource or the network connections and network devices the resource relies on. For example, an adversary may send 10Gbps of traffic to a server that is hosted by a network with a 1Gbps connection to the internet. This traffic can be generated by a single system or multiple systems spread across the internet, which is commonly referred to as a distributed DoS (DDoS).

To perform Network DoS attacks several aspects apply to multiple methods, including IP address spoofing, and botnets.

Adversaries may use the original IP address of an attacking system, or spoof the source IP address to make the attack traffic more difficult to trace back to the attacking system or to enable reflection. This can increase the difficulty defenders have in defending against the attack by reducing or eliminating the effectiveness of filtering by the source address on network defense devices.

For DoS attacks targeting the hosting system directly, see [Endpoint Denial of Service](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1499).
1370.profile: [profile]Use of Tor network is a technique for Command and Control, categorized as T1090.001 within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, applicable to multiple platforms. It involves routing C2 traffic through the Tor anonymity network, which uses onion routing to encrypt and relay communications through multiple volunteer nodes, obscuring the source and destination of the traffic. This method is used by groups like APT28 to hide their infrastructure and evade detection. For multi-hop proxy chains beyond Tor, see T1090.003.[/profile]
1370.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Use of Tor network" is a technique for obfuscating command and control traffic and adversary location. It functions by routing encrypted communications through the decentralized Tor network, which anonymizes the source by passing traffic through multiple relays. This method is specifically used to hide infrastructure and make tracing malicious activity back to its origin extremely difficult for defenders.

1371.name: Infrastructure masquerading
1371.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may attempt to manipulate features of their artifacts to make them appear legitimate or benign to users and/or security tools. Masquerading occurs when the name or location of an object, legitimate or malicious, is manipulated or abused for the sake of evading defenses and observation. This may include manipulating file metadata, tricking users into misidentifying the file type, and giving legitimate task or service names.

Renaming abusable system utilities to evade security monitoring is also a form of [Masquerading](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1036).(Citation: LOLBAS Main Site)
1371.profile: [profile]Infrastructure Masquerading is a technique for evading defenses by manipulating the features of adversary-controlled infrastructure to appear legitimate. It aligns with MITRE ATT&CK technique T1583.001 (Acquire Infrastructure: Domains) under the Resource Development tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. The technique involves registering domains that closely mimic legitimate services or organizations through typosquatting, using SSL certificates from trusted providers, and hosting content that replicates genuine sites to avoid detection by security tools and users. This masquerading helps adversaries blend malicious infrastructure with normal network traffic, supporting stages like initial access and command and control. Groups such as APT28 have been associated with this practice.
1371.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Infrastructure Masquerading is a technique where adversaries disguise their malicious infrastructure to appear legitimate, often by using domains, IP addresses, or services that mimic trusted entities. This tactic, part of Resource Development (TA0042), involves registering or compromising infrastructure that closely resembles legitimate services to evade detection and facilitate phishing or command-and-control operations. The technique is used across various platforms to blend malicious network traffic with normal activity, making it harder for defenders to identify and block adversary infrastructure.

1372.name: Russian bride scam

Based on the retrieved information, it is associated with the APT28 intrusion-set and infrastructure like 95.130.15[.]34. The technique operates by sending spearphishing messages with malicious links to clone legitimate login portals, often using URL obfuscation or QR codes to harvest credentials, and may involve tools like EvilProxy to steal session cookies and bypass multi-factor authentication.

The scam may involve directing victims to fraudulent websites via malicious links, potentially hosted on infrastructure like 95.130.15[.]34, to harvest entered data.

1373.name: WordPress brute force cracking
1373.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may use brute force techniques to gain access to accounts when passwords are unknown or when password hashes are obtained.(Citation: TrendMicro Pawn Storm Dec 2020) Without knowledge of the password for an account or set of accounts, an adversary may systematically guess the password using a repetitive or iterative mechanism.(Citation: Dragos Crashoverride 2018) Brute forcing passwords can take place via interaction with a service that will check the validity of those credentials or offline against previously acquired credential data, such as password hashes.

Brute forcing credentials may take place at various points during a breach. For example, adversaries may attempt to brute force access to [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078) within a victim environment leveraging knowledge gathered from other post-compromise behaviors such as [OS Credential Dumping](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003), [Account Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1087), or [Password Policy Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1201). Adversaries may also combine brute forcing activity with behaviors such as [External Remote Services](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1133) as part of Initial Access. 

If an adversary guesses the correct password but fails to login to a compromised account due to location-based conditional access policies, they may change their infrastructure until they match the victim’s location and therefore bypass those policies.(Citation: ReliaQuest Health Care Social Engineering Campaign 2024)
1373.profile: [profile]WordPress brute force cracking is a specific application of the standard MITRE ATT&CK technique Brute Force (T1110) under the Credential Access tactic, targeting web application platforms like WordPress. It involves systematically guessing WordPress admin or user passwords through iterative login attempts, often using automated tools and wordlists against the site's login interface (e.g., wp-login.php) to gain unauthorized access. This activity is associated with groups like APT28 and infrastructure such as 95.130.15[.]34.[/profile]
1373.profile_without_enhance: [profile]WordPress brute force cracking is a specific application of the Brute Force technique (T1110) under the Credential Access tactic, targeting the WordPress CMS platform. It involves systematically submitting many password guesses, often via automated tools, to compromise administrator or user accounts by interacting with the WordPress login service (e.g., wp-login.php). This activity is linked to infrastructure like 95.130.15[.]34 and is distinct from offline password cracking (T1110.002).

1375.name: Guccifer 2.0
1375.uncertain_mes: [Dragonfly 2.0](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0074) is a suspected Russian group that has targeted government entities and multiple U.S. critical infrastructure sectors since at least December 2015. (Citation: US-CERT TA18-074A) (Citation: Symantec Dragonfly Sept 2017) There is debate over the extent of overlap between [Dragonfly 2.0](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0074) and [Dragonfly](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0035), but there is sufficient evidence to lead to these being tracked as two separate groups. (Citation: Fortune Dragonfly 2.0 Sept 2017)(Citation: Dragos DYMALLOY )
1375.profile: [profile]Guccifer 2.0, also known as Dragonfly 2.0, is a suspected Russian intrusion set with significant overlaps to APT28 (Fancy Bear). Its activity is primarily associated with the 2016 U.S. Democratic National Committee hack, for which it was indicted by the U.S. Department of Justice. The group's arsenal includes tools like those released by The Shadow Brokers, such as Zombie Spider. Its key TTPs involve spear-phishing and credential harvesting, often using persona-based operations. It is attributed to Russian military intelligence (GRU) and primarily targets political organizations, government entities, and critical infrastructure sectors in the United States and Europe, motivated by espionage and influence operations.

This persona was central to operations like the 2016 Democratic National Committee hack, employing spear-phishing and leaked document dumps. Its key TTPs involved using this fabricated "lone hacker" persona to disseminate stolen data, a tactic supporting broader influence and espionage objectives primarily targeting political organizations in the United States and Europe.[/profile]

Characteristic TTPs involve sophisticated spear-phishing with zero-day exploits, credential harvesting, and specific anti-forensics techniques. The group primarily targets government, military, political, and media organizations in North America and Europe, with motivations centered on state-sponsored espionage and influence operations, notably in political processes like the 2016 U.S. elections.[/profile]

1377.name: Operational Security (OPSEC)
1377.profile: [profile]Operational Security (OPSEC) is a strategic concept, not a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique, and therefore lacks a standard T-ID or Tactic. It refers to the adversary's own security practices to avoid detection, such as using legitimate web services for command and control to blend with normal traffic, employing multilayer encryption within standard protocols like HTTPS, and gathering intelligence on network security appliances to tailor their attacks and evade defenses.
1377.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Operational Security (OPSEC)" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique; it is a general security concept. Based on the retrieved context, OPSEC principles are applied by adversaries to avoid detection. This includes using legitimate web services like Google or Twitter for encrypted command and control to blend with normal traffic, employing multilayer encryption (e.g., custom schemes within HTTPS), and gathering intelligence on network security appliances (like firewalls and NIDS) to tailor attacks and evade defenses.

1391.name: Spoofed messages
1391.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may directly collect unsecured credentials stored or passed through user communication services. Credentials may be sent and stored in user chat communication applications such as email, chat services like Slack or Teams, collaboration tools like Jira or Trello, and any other services that support user communication. Users may share various forms of credentials (such as usernames and passwords, API keys, or authentication tokens) on private or public corporate internal communications channels.

Rather than accessing the stored chat logs (i.e., [Credentials In Files](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1552/001)), adversaries may directly access credentials within these services on the user endpoint, through servers hosting the services, or through administrator portals for cloud hosted services. Adversaries may also compromise integration tools like Slack Workflows to automatically search through messages to extract user credentials. These credentials may then be abused to perform follow-on activities such as lateral movement or privilege escalation (Citation: Slack Security Risks).
1391.profile: [profile]Spoofed messages, identified as T1552.008 (Unsecured Credentials: Chat Messages) under the Credential Access tactic, targets platforms like Slack, Teams, and Jira. Adversaries directly collect credentials such as passwords and API keys from active user chat services, either by accessing the endpoint client, service servers, or cloud admin portals, or by compromising automation tools like Slack Workflows to automatically search and extract credentials from messages for lateral movement or privilege escalation.
1391.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Spoofed messages is a technique under the Initial Access tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It involves faking a sender's identity by modifying email headers, such as the FROM field, to deceive victims and establish contact under false pretenses. This technique often succeeds when the spoofed entity lacks or has weak enforcement of authentication protocols like SPF, DKIM, or DMARC, and it is commonly used to conceal social engineering attempts such as phishing.[/profile]

1398.name: Cross-site scripting (XSS)
1398.uncertain_mes:
**This technique has been deprecated. Please use [Command and Scripting Interpreter](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059) where appropriate.**

Adversaries may use scripts to aid in operations and perform multiple actions that would otherwise be manual. Scripting is useful for speeding up operational tasks and reducing the time required to gain access to critical resources. Some scripting languages may be used to bypass process monitoring mechanisms by directly interacting with the operating system at an API level instead of calling other programs. Common scripting languages for Windows include VBScript and [PowerShell](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1086) but could also be in the form of command-line batch scripts.

Scripts can be embedded inside Office documents as macros that can be set to execute when files used in [Spearphishing Attachment](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1193) and other types of spearphishing are opened. Malicious embedded macros are an alternative means of execution than software exploitation through [Exploitation for Client Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1203), where adversaries will rely on macros being allowed or that the user will accept to activate them.

Many popular offensive frameworks exist which use forms of scripting for security testers and adversaries alike. Metasploit (Citation: Metasploit_Ref), Veil (Citation: Veil_Ref), and PowerSploit (Citation: Powersploit) are three examples that are popular among penetration testers for exploit and post-compromise operations and include many features for evading defenses. Some adversaries are known to use PowerShell. (Citation: Alperovitch 2014)
1398.profile: [profile]Cross-site scripting (XSS) is a client-side code injection technique, often mapped to MITRE ATT&CK under Initial Access (TA0001) or Execution (TA0002) tactics, targeting web platforms. It works by injecting malicious scripts into a legitimate website, which are then executed in a victim's browser when they visit the compromised page. This can be used to steal web session cookies, enabling session hijacking and authentication bypass. The technique is commonly associated with drive-by compromises and has been used by groups like APT28.
1398.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Cross-site scripting (XSS) is a client-side code injection technique, identified as T1059.007 under the Execution tactic, targeting web platforms. It works by injecting malicious scripts into trusted websites, which are then executed in a victim's browser. This can be used to steal session cookies, enabling authentication bypass and account takeover, or to facilitate drive-by compromises by leveraging web application interfaces to insert malicious scripts or iFrames.

1399.name: Injection vulnerabilities
1399.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may acquire information about vulnerabilities that can be used during targeting. A vulnerability is a weakness in computer hardware or software that can, potentially, be exploited by an adversary to cause unintended or unanticipated behavior to occur. Adversaries may find vulnerability information by searching open databases or gaining access to closed vulnerability databases.(Citation: National Vulnerability Database)

An adversary may monitor vulnerability disclosures/databases to understand the state of existing, as well as newly discovered, vulnerabilities. There is usually a delay between when a vulnerability is discovered and when it is made public. An adversary may target the systems of those known to conduct vulnerability research (including commercial vendors). Knowledge of a vulnerability may cause an adversary to search for an existing exploit (i.e. [Exploits](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1588/005)) or to attempt to develop one themselves (i.e. [Exploits](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1587/004)).
1399.profile: [profile]Injection vulnerabilities is a technique known as Acquire Vulnerabilities (T1588.006) under the Resource Development tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. Adversaries gather information on software or hardware weaknesses by searching open databases like the National Vulnerability Database or accessing closed sources, including by targeting vulnerability researchers. This intelligence is used to find or develop exploits for subsequent attacks, as seen with groups like Sandworm Team, Storm-0501, and Volt Typhoon.[/profile]
1399.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Injection vulnerabilities, not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique, is a broad category of software weaknesses where untrusted data is processed as commands or queries, leading to unintended execution. This can manifest in various forms such as SQL injection, OS command injection, or code injection within applications. Adversaries exploit these vulnerabilities to execute arbitrary code, bypass security mechanisms, or gain unauthorized access to systems and data, often as part of initial access or execution tactics.

1400.name: Command injection
1400.profile: [profile]Command injection is a technique where adversaries exploit vulnerable applications to execute arbitrary commands on the underlying operating system, typically by inserting malicious input into data fields or parameters that are passed to a system shell. This technique, often associated with groups like APT28, allows for direct system control and is a common method for initial access, persistence, and lateral movement. The execution relies on improper input validation in web applications, APIs, or services that interact with command-line interfaces.
1400.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Command injection, identified as T1190 in the MITRE ATT&CK framework, falls under the Initial Access tactic and primarily targets web applications. This technique exploits insufficient input validation to inject and execute arbitrary operating system commands on a vulnerable server. Attackers often target web forms, APIs, or other input vectors, using special characters to break out of intended data contexts and append malicious commands. This allows for direct system access and control, serving as a critical entry point for further compromise.

1401.name: Server fingerprinting
1401.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may buy, lease, rent, or obtain physical servers that can be used during targeting. Use of servers allows an adversary to stage, launch, and execute an operation. During post-compromise activity, adversaries may utilize servers for various tasks, such as watering hole operations in [Drive-by Compromise](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1189), enabling [Phishing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566) operations, or facilitating [Command and Control](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0011). Instead of compromising a third-party [Server](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1584/004) or renting a [Virtual Private Server](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1583/003), adversaries may opt to configure and run their own servers in support of operations. Free trial periods of cloud servers may also be abused.(Citation: Free Trial PurpleUrchin)(Citation: Freejacked) 

Adversaries may only need a lightweight setup if most of their activities will take place using online infrastructure. Or, they may need to build extensive infrastructure if they want to test, communicate, and control other aspects of their activities on their own systems.(Citation: NYTStuxnet)
1401.profile: [profile]The entity "Server fingerprinting" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the provided context, the name and description are misaligned; the 'Self Info' and 'Similar Entities' describe the technique "Acquire Infrastructure: Server" (T1583.004), a Resource Development tactic for acquiring physical servers to stage operations, abuse free trials, or build extensive control infrastructure, as used by groups like Earth Lusca and Sandworm Team. The retrieved 'Content Related entities' for browser fingerprinting (T1036.012) and active scanning (T1595) describe distinct reconnaissance techniques and are not relevant to this server acquisition method.[/profile]
1401.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Server fingerprinting" is a reconnaissance technique where adversaries actively probe servers to gather detailed information about their software, versions, configurations, and services. This is performed through active scanning of network traffic to identify attributes like operating system, open ports, and running software, which can reveal vulnerabilities for subsequent exploitation. The gathered intelligence supports other tactics such as developing capabilities or achieving initial access.

1402.name: ClientCopyImage
1402.profile: [profile]ClientCopyImage is a technique used by adversaries like APT28 to exfiltrate data by copying files to a client-side image, such as a disk image or container snapshot, which can then be transferred or uploaded. This method leverages legitimate system functions to disguise data movement, potentially bypassing network monitoring by embedding stolen data within seemingly innocuous image files, facilitating covert data theft.
1402.profile_without_enhance: [profile]ClientCopyImage is a technique with the ID T1115. It falls under the Collection tactic and operates on the Windows platform. It involves an adversary using the Windows API call CopyImage to duplicate an image from a specified executable file, such as a DLL, into the memory of a process. This copied image can then be used to load and execute malicious code, effectively bypassing some security mechanisms by operating on a legitimate-looking copy in memory rather than the original file on disk.

1403.name: Established persistence
1403.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may clear artifacts associated with previously established persistence on a host system to remove evidence of their activity. This may involve various actions, such as removing services, deleting executables, [Modify Registry](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1112), [Plist File Modification](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1647), or other methods of cleanup to prevent defenders from collecting evidence of their persistent presence.(Citation: Cylance Dust Storm) Adversaries may also delete accounts previously created to maintain persistence (i.e. [Create Account](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1136)).(Citation: Talos - Cisco Attack 2022)

In some instances, artifacts of persistence may also be removed once an adversary’s persistence is executed in order to prevent errors with the new instance of the malware.(Citation: NCC Group Team9 June 2020)
1403.profile: [profile]The technique "Clear Persistence" is mapped to MITRE ATT&CK ID T1070.009 under the Defense Evasion tactic for Windows and potentially other platforms. It involves adversaries removing artifacts of previously established persistence mechanisms to eliminate forensic evidence, which can include actions like deleting services, executables, registry modifications, plist files, or user accounts. This cleanup prevents defenders from detecting the persistent presence and may also be done to avoid conflicts when new malware instances execute. The intrusion set APT28 has been associated with this behavior.
1403.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Established persistence" is a core adversary objective, not a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique with a T-ID. It is achieved through various techniques across the Persistence tactic on multiple platforms. The retrieved information describes related techniques like T1037 (Boot or Logon Initialization Scripts) and T1037.003 (Network Logon Script), where adversaries assign scripts via Active Directory or Group Policy to execute automatically at user logon, maintaining access with the user's privileges and potentially requiring administrative rights for deployment.

1404.name: Enumerated Active Directory accounts
1404.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may achieve persistence by adding a Registry key to the Active Setup of the local machine. Active Setup is a Windows mechanism that is used to execute programs when a user logs in. The value stored in the Registry key will be executed after a user logs into the computer.(Citation: Klein Active Setup 2010) These programs will be executed under the context of the user and will have the account's associated permissions level. Adversaries may abuse Active Setup by creating a key under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Active Setup\Installed Components\ and setting a malicious value for StubPath. This value will serve as the program that will be executed when a user logs into the computer.(Citation: Mandiant Glyer APT 2010)(Citation: Citizenlab Packrat 2015)(Citation: FireEye CFR Watering Hole 2012)(Citation: SECURELIST Bright Star 2015)(Citation: paloalto Tropic Trooper 2016) Adversaries can abuse these components to execute malware, such as remote access tools, to maintain persistence through system reboots. Adversaries may also use [Masquerading](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1036) to make the Registry entries look as if they are associated with legitimate programs.
1404.profile: [profile]The entity "Enumerated Active Directory accounts" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the retrieved information, this likely refers to the technique "Domain Account" (T1087.002) under the Discovery tactic. This technique involves adversaries enumerating domain accounts to identify targets for follow-on actions. Specific commands for enumeration include `net user /domain`, `net group /domain`, and PowerShell cmdlets like `Get-ADUser`. It is primarily executed on Windows platforms and has been associated with numerous threat groups including APT41, MuddyWater, and Wizard Spider.[/profile]
1404.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Enumerated Active Directory accounts is a technique under Discovery, identified as T1087.002, targeting Windows platforms. It involves adversaries using commands like `net user /domain`, `net group /domain`, or PowerShell cmdlets such as `Get-ADUser` to list domain users and groups. This reconnaissance helps identify accounts for follow-on targeting, particularly those with specific privileges. The technique is widely used by groups like APT41, MuddyWater, and Sandworm Team.

1405.name: Stole emails
1405.profile: [profile]The entity "Stole emails" is a technique for collecting sensitive information by accessing user email accounts or mail servers. It is related to MITRE ATT&CK technique T1114 (Email Collection) under the Collection tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. The technique involves adversaries collecting or forwarding emails from compromised mail clients or servers to obtain valuable data such as trade secrets, personal information, or incident response details. Associated groups include APT28, Silent Librarian, Scattered Spider, Ember Bear, and Magic Hound.
1405.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Stole emails" is a technique for collecting sensitive information from user email accounts. It aligns with MITRE ATT&CK technique T1114, Email Collection, under the Collection tactic and is applicable across multiple platforms. Adversaries execute this by directly collecting or forwarding emails from compromised mail servers or clients, targeting data like trade secrets, personal information, or incident response details to support their objectives. Groups such as Silent Librarian, Scattered Spider, Ember Bear, and Magic Hound have been associated with this activity.

1406.name: Malicious links
1406.profile: [profile]Malicious links is a technique used in phishing campaigns, often involving links to malicious documents, and is associated with APT28. It is also referenced in the context of Cobalt Strike C2 infrastructure and AsyncRAT distribution via malicious domains. The technique is employed by groups including Lazarus Group, APT29, APT32, APT41, and others. Target platforms are typically Windows systems via email and web-based vectors.
1406.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Malicious links is a malware entity. It is associated with the Lazarus Group and is used in phishing emails containing links to malicious documents. It is also referenced in the context of Cobalt Strike, a tool used by numerous APT groups including APT29, APT32, APT41, and FIN7. The malware operates by directing victims to malicious domains.

1407.name: Remote access tools (RATS)
1407.profile: [profile]Remote access tools (RATs) are a category of malware enabling remote control of compromised systems, used by groups like APT28. Key examples include AsyncRAT and Remcos, which are often sold commercially and feature capabilities for data theft, espionage, keylogging, and screenshot capture, typically targeting Windows platforms and distributed via spam emails.
1407.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Remote access tools (RATs) are a category of malware enabling remote control of compromised systems. Key examples include AsyncRAT, VenomRAT, and Remcos. These tools facilitate data theft, espionage, and victim monitoring, often featuring capabilities like keylogging and screenshot capture. They are commonly distributed via spam emails and are designed to be user-friendly, frequently offering remote desktop GUI environments for administration.

1408.name: Yara Signatures
1408.profile: [profile]Yara Signatures is a detection tool used to identify malware families, including REDLEAVES and PLUGX, which are associated with groups like Stone Panda and various APT groups such as APT22, APT26, APT31, and APT41. It is also referenced in the context of the LockBit ransomware. The signatures are applied in network and file-based detection to uncover malicious activities linked to these threats.[profile]
1408.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Yara Signatures is a detection tool, not a malware family itself. It is referenced in the context of other malware families for identification purposes. Specifically, Yara Signatures are used to detect the REDLEAVES and PLUGX malware families. REDLEAVES is associated with the group Stone Panda, while PLUGX is linked to numerous APT groups including APT22, APT26, APT31, APT41, Aurora Panda, Calypso Group, Dragonok, Emissary Panda, Hellsing, Hurricane Panda, Leviathan, Mirage, Mustang Panda, Nettraveler, Nightshade Panda, Slime29, Samurai Panda, Stone Panda, UPS, and Violin Panda. Its primary function is as a pattern-matching rule set for malware analysis and threat hunting.]

1411.name: Credential theft
1411.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may steal monetary resources from targets through extortion, social engineering, technical theft, or other methods aimed at their own financial gain at the expense of the availability of these resources for victims. Financial theft is the ultimate objective of several popular campaign types including extortion by ransomware,(Citation: FBI-ransomware) business email compromise (BEC) and fraud,(Citation: FBI-BEC) "pig butchering,"(Citation: wired-pig butchering) bank hacking,(Citation: DOJ-DPRK Heist) and exploiting cryptocurrency networks.(Citation: BBC-Ronin) 

Adversaries may [Compromise Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1586) to conduct unauthorized transfers of funds.(Citation: Internet crime report 2022) In the case of business email compromise or email fraud, an adversary may utilize [Impersonation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1656) of a trusted entity. Once the social engineering is successful, victims can be deceived into sending money to financial accounts controlled by an adversary.(Citation: FBI-BEC) This creates the potential for multiple victims (i.e., compromised accounts as well as the ultimate monetary loss) in incidents involving financial theft.(Citation: VEC)

Extortion by ransomware may occur, for example, when an adversary demands payment from a victim after [Data Encrypted for Impact](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1486) (Citation: NYT-Colonial) and [Exfiltration](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0010) of data, followed by threatening to leak sensitive data to the public unless payment is made to the adversary.(Citation: Mandiant-leaks) Adversaries may use dedicated leak sites to distribute victim data.(Citation: Crowdstrike-leaks)

Due to the potentially immense business impact of financial theft, an adversary may abuse the possibility of financial theft and seeking monetary gain to divert attention from their true goals such as [Data Destruction](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1485) and business disruption.(Citation: AP-NotPetya)
1411.profile: [profile]Credential Theft is a broad adversarial objective, not a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique with a T-ID. It involves stealing authentication material like passwords or tokens to gain unauthorized access. This can be achieved through methods such as OS credential dumping from memory, extracting credentials from the Windows Credential Manager, or using stolen tokens for impersonation. The stolen credentials are often used for lateral movement, privilege escalation, and to facilitate further objectives like financial theft. Groups like APT28 have been associated with related token theft techniques.[/profile]
1411.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Credential Theft is a broad adversarial objective encompassing multiple specific MITRE ATT&CK techniques rather than a single technique. It involves stealing account login and credential material, such as passwords or hashes, to gain unauthorized access. Common methods include OS Credential Dumping (T1003) from system memory and accessing stored credentials from the Windows Credential Manager (T1555.004). Stolen credentials, including domain accounts (T1078.002), are often used for lateral movement, privilege escalation, and initial access, enabling further compromise and financial theft campaigns.

1412.name: PowerShell
1412.uncertain_mes: powershell_web_backdoor This is a very simple powershell web backdoor Usage: hxxp://127.0.0.1:9999/backdoor/?cmd=<Insert Your powershell compatible base64 encoded command here
1412.profile: [profile]PowerShell is a scripting language and command-line shell, often leveraged by threat actors to execute malicious scripts and backdoors. It is associated with groups like FIN7, APT28, menuPass, and RocketKitten. Key behaviors include executing base64-encoded commands via web backdoors, using commands like DownloadFile and DownloadString for stager operations, and being employed in malware such as Emotet and Cobalt Strike for second-stage downloads and command execution. It primarily targets Windows platforms, utilizing HTTP for command-and-control communication.[/profile]
1412.profile_without_enhance: [profile]PowerShell is a scripting language and command-line shell for Windows, widely leveraged by threat actors as a versatile tool for post-exploitation and payload delivery. Its aliases include powershell_web_backdoor. It is commonly used by groups like APT29, APT32, APT41, FIN6, FIN7, and criminal groups such as Gold Cabin (Mummy Spider/Mealybug) and Cobalt Group. Key technical behaviors include executing malicious macros for initial access, using base64-encoded commands and scripts (DownloadString, DownloadFile) for stagers and backdoors, and facilitating web-based command execution. It primarily targets the Windows platform and is integral to frameworks like Cobalt Strike for second-stage downloads and hidden execution.[/profile]

1413.name: Malware association with PowerShell
1413.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may abuse PowerShell commands and scripts for execution. PowerShell is a powerful interactive command-line interface and scripting environment included in the Windows operating system.(Citation: TechNet PowerShell) Adversaries can use PowerShell to perform a number of actions, including discovery of information and execution of code. Examples include the Start-Process cmdlet which can be used to run an executable and the Invoke-Command cmdlet which runs a command locally or on a remote computer (though administrator permissions are required to use PowerShell to connect to remote systems). PowerShell may also be used to download and run executables from the Internet, which can be executed from disk or in memory without touching disk. A number of PowerShell-based offensive testing tools are available, including [Empire](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0363), [PowerSploit](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0194), [PoshC2](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0378), and PSAttack.(Citation: Github PSAttack) PowerShell commands/scripts can also be executed without directly invoking the powershell.exe binary through interfaces to PowerShell's underlying System.Management.Automation assembly DLL exposed through the .NET framework and Windows Common Language Interface (CLI).(Citation: Sixdub PowerPick Jan 2016)(Citation: SilentBreak Offensive PS Dec 2015)(Citation: Microsoft PSfromCsharp APR 2014)
1413.profile: [profile]Command and Scripting Interpreter: PowerShell, identified as T1059.001 under the Execution tactic, is a native Windows tool abused by adversaries for execution. It can run commands and scripts locally or remotely using cmdlets like Start-Process and Invoke-Command, download and execute payloads from the internet directly in memory, and operate without invoking powershell.exe by leveraging the underlying System.Management.Automation assembly. It is associated with numerous threat groups, including APT28.
1413.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Malware Association with PowerShell is a technique where adversaries use PowerShell to deploy and execute malicious payloads. It aligns with MITRE ATT&CK Execution (T1059.001) on Windows platforms. Technical mechanics include using cmdlets like `Start-Process` and `Invoke-Command` to run executables or commands locally/remotely, downloading and executing payloads directly in memory to avoid disk, and leveraging PowerShell's underlying .NET assembly for stealth. Malware can be delivered via scripts or by abusing trusted system components like SyncAppvPublishingServer.vbs to proxy execution and bypass restrictions.

1414.name: BlackEnergy V3
1414.uncertain_mes: [BlackEnergy](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0089) is a malware toolkit that has been used by both criminal and APT actors. It dates back to at least 2007 and was originally designed to create botnets for use in conducting Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attacks, but its use has evolved to support various plug-ins. It is well known for being used during the confrontation between Georgia and Russia in 2008, as well as in targeting Ukrainian institutions. Variants include BlackEnergy 2 and BlackEnergy 3. (Citation: F-Secure BlackEnergy 2014)
1414.profile: [profile]BlackEnergy V3, also known as BlackEnergy 3, is a malware toolkit historically used by the Sandworm Team (APT28) for espionage and disruptive attacks, notably against Ukrainian and Georgian institutions. Its key behaviors include establishing botnets for DDoS, supporting modular plugins for expanded functionality, and communicating with hardcoded C2 servers (e.g., 5.149.254.114 on port 80) via HTTP. 1465.name: Spear-phishing
1465.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may send phishing messages to gain access to victim systems. All forms of phishing are electronically delivered social engineering. Phishing can be targeted, known as spearphishing. In spearphishing, a specific individual, company, or industry will be targeted by the adversary. More generally, adversaries can conduct non-targeted phishing, such as in mass malware spam campaigns.

Adversaries may send victims emails containing malicious attachments or links, typically to execute malicious code on victim systems. Phishing may also be conducted via third-party services, like social media platforms. Phishing may also involve social engineering techniques, such as posing as a trusted source, as well as evasive techniques such as removing or manipulating emails or metadata/headers from compromised accounts being abused to send messages (e.g., [Email Hiding Rules](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1564/008)).(Citation: Microsoft OAuth Spam 2022)(Citation: Palo Alto Unit 42 VBA Infostealer 2014) Another way to accomplish this is by [Email Spoofing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1672)(Citation: Proofpoint-spoof) the identity of the sender, which can be used to fool both the human recipient as well as automated security tools,(Citation: cyberproof-double-bounce) or by including the intended target as a party to an existing email thread that includes malicious files or links (i.e., "thread hijacking").(Citation: phishing-krebs)

Victims may also receive phishing messages that instruct them to call a phone number where they are directed to visit a malicious URL, download malware,(Citation: sygnia Luna Month)(Citation: CISA Remote Monitoring and Management Software) or install adversary-accessible remote management tools onto their computer (i.e., [User Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204)).(Citation: Unit42 Luna Moth)
1465.profile: [profile]Spear-phishing is a targeted social engineering technique under MITRE ATT&CK ID T1566, primarily used in the Initial Access tactic across multiple platforms. It involves sending tailored emails or messages to specific individuals or organizations, often posing as a trusted source, to deliver malicious attachments or links that execute code when opened. Evasive methods include email spoofing, thread hijacking, and manipulating email metadata. APT groups like APT29, APT28, and APT3 are known to employ this technique.[/profile]
1465.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Spear-phishing is a targeted social engineering technique, designated as T1566 under the Initial Access tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. It involves sending deceptive electronic communications, such as emails, to specific individuals or organizations to induce them to click malicious links, open infected attachments, or divulge credentials. This method often employs email spoofing, thread hijacking, or the use of compromised accounts to appear legitimate and evade detection.

1469.name: drive-by-download attack
1469.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may gain access to a system through a user visiting a website over the normal course of browsing. Multiple ways of delivering exploit code to a browser exist (i.e., [Drive-by Target](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1608/004)), including:

* A legitimate website is compromised, allowing adversaries to inject malicious code
* Script files served to a legitimate website from a publicly writeable cloud storage bucket are modified by an adversary
* Malicious ads are paid for and served through legitimate ad providers (i.e., [Malvertising](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1583/008))
* Built-in web application interfaces that allow user-controllable content are leveraged for the insertion of malicious scripts or iFrames (e.g., cross-site scripting)

Browser push notifications may also be abused by adversaries and leveraged for malicious code injection via [User Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204). By clicking "allow" on browser push notifications, users may be granting a website permission to run JavaScript code on their browser.(Citation: Push notifications - viruspositive)(Citation: push notification -mcafee)(Citation: push notifications - malwarebytes)

Often the website used by an adversary is one visited by a specific community, such as government, a particular industry, or a particular region, where the goal is to compromise a specific user or set of users based on a shared interest. This kind of targeted campaign is often referred to a strategic web compromise or watering hole attack. There are several known examples of this occurring.(Citation: Shadowserver Strategic Web Compromise)

Typical drive-by compromise process:

1. A user visits a website that is used to host the adversary controlled content.
2. Scripts automatically execute, typically searching versions of the browser and plugins for a potentially vulnerable version. The user may be required to assist in this process by enabling scripting, notifications, or active website components and ignoring warning dialog boxes.
3. Upon finding a vulnerable version, exploit code is delivered to the browser.
4. If exploitation is successful, the adversary will gain code execution on the user's system unless other protections are in place. In some cases, a second visit to the website after the initial scan is required before exploit code is delivered.

Unlike [Exploit Public-Facing Application](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1190), the focus of this technique is to exploit software on a client endpoint upon visiting a website. This will commonly give an adversary access to systems on the internal network instead of external systems that may be in a DMZ.
1469.profile: [profile]Drive-by Compromise (T1189) is an Initial Access technique targeting client endpoints, primarily web browsers on Windows, macOS, and Linux platforms. The attack involves a user visiting a compromised or adversary-controlled website, where scripts automatically execute to profile the browser and plugins for vulnerabilities before delivering exploit code. Common delivery mechanisms include injecting malicious scripts into legitimate sites, modifying files from cloud storage, serving malicious ads (Malvertising), or abusing browser push notifications. This method is often used in targeted watering hole attacks against specific communities and is associated with groups like APT28.[/profile]
1469.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Drive-by Compromise, identified as T1189, is an Initial Access tactic targeting client-side software like web browsers. The technique involves compromising users who visit a website, where malicious scripts automatically execute to profile the browser and deliver exploit code if a vulnerable version is found, often without requiring user interaction beyond the initial visit. Common delivery methods include compromising legitimate websites, injecting malicious scripts into web pages or advertisements (malvertising), or abusing browser push notifications. This approach is frequently used in targeted watering hole attacks against specific communities.
