1514.name: XOR-encrypted
1514.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may employ an encryption algorithm to conceal command and control traffic rather than relying on any inherent protections provided by a communication protocol. Despite the use of a secure algorithm, these implementations may be vulnerable to reverse engineering if secret keys are encoded and/or generated within malware samples/configuration files.
1514.profile: [profile]The entity XOR-encrypted is a specific implementation of the MITRE ATT&CK technique Encrypted Channel (T1573) under the Command and Control tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It works by applying the XOR (exclusive OR) logical operation to command and control traffic or data, using a fixed or simple key, to create a weak but obfuscated ciphertext. This custom cryptographic method is often implemented directly within malware without external libraries, making it vulnerable to reverse engineering if the key is embedded. It has been used by groups like APT28 for data archiving prior to exfiltration.
1514.profile_without_enhance: [profile]XOR-encrypted is a sub-technique for obfuscating files or data, T1027.013, under the Defense Evasion tactic. It operates on multiple platforms by applying the XOR (exclusive OR) logical operation with a key to encrypt content, a simple symmetric algorithm often implemented with hardcoded keys within malware. This method is used to conceal command and control traffic or to encrypt data prior to exfiltration or archival, making static analysis more difficult unless the key is discovered.

1515.name: anti-debugging check
1515.profile: [profile]The entity is a sub-technique of Debugger Evasion (T1622) within the Defense Evasion tactic, applicable to Windows and Linux platforms. It involves specific API checks like IsDebuggerPresent() and NtQueryInformationProcess() on Windows, or querying /proc/self/status on Linux, to detect debugging artifacts such as the BeingDebugged flag or a TracerPID. This detection can trigger altered malware behavior, such as disengagement or payload concealment, and is associated with groups like Mustang Panda.
1515.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "anti-debugging check" is a sub-technique under Debugger Evasion (T1622) in the MITRE ATT&CK framework, falling under the Defense Evasion tactic and applicable to Windows and Linux platforms. It involves malware actively probing for the presence of debugging tools to alter its behavior and avoid analysis. Specific technical mechanics include using Windows Native API calls like IsDebuggerPresent() and NtQueryInformationProcess(), checking the BeingDebugged flag in the Process Environment Block (PEB), or on Linux, querying the TracerPID field in /proc/self/status. Other methods involve checking for hardware breakpoints, performing time-based checks, or leveraging Structured Exception Handling (SEH) to detect if an exception is handled by a debugger.

1516.name: anti-analysis/sandbox check
1516.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may employ various means to detect and avoid virtualization and analysis environments. This may include changing behaviors based on the results of checks for the presence of artifacts indicative of a virtual machine environment (VME) or sandbox. If the adversary detects a VME, they may alter their malware to disengage from the victim or conceal the core functions of the implant. They may also search for VME artifacts before dropping secondary or additional payloads. Adversaries may use the information learned from [Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1497) during automated discovery to shape follow-on behaviors.(Citation: Deloitte Environment Awareness)

Adversaries may use several methods to accomplish [Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1497) such as checking for security monitoring tools (e.g., Sysinternals, Wireshark, etc.) or other system artifacts associated with analysis or virtualization. Adversaries may also check for legitimate user activity to help determine if it is in an analysis environment. Additional methods include use of sleep timers or loops within malware code to avoid operating within a temporary sandbox.(Citation: Unit 42 Pirpi July 2015)
1516.profile: [profile]Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion, identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1497 under the Defense Evasion tactic, operates across Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves malware checking for artifacts of virtual machines or sandboxes, such as specific processes, files, hardware attributes, or security tools like Sysinternals and Wireshark. Techniques include using sleep timers to bypass temporary analysis environments and altering or halting malicious behavior upon detection to avoid analysis. This technique is employed by groups like APT28, DarkHotel, and Gamaredon Group.[/profile]
1516.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Anti-analysis/Sandbox Check is a technique within the broader MITRE ATT&CK technique Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion (T1497) under the Defense Evasion tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It involves malware performing checks for artifacts indicative of a virtual machine or sandbox environment, such as specific processes, files, hardware properties, installed programs, or user activity. If these checks are positive, the malware may alter its behavior, disengage, or conceal its core functions to evade detection and analysis.

1520.name: C2 communication
1520.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may use an existing, legitimate external Web service as a means for sending commands to and receiving output from a compromised system over the Web service channel. Compromised systems may leverage popular websites and social media to host command and control (C2) instructions. Those infected systems can then send the output from those commands back over that Web service channel. The return traffic may occur in a variety of ways, depending on the Web service being utilized. For example, the return traffic may take the form of the compromised system posting a comment on a forum, issuing a pull request to development project, updating a document hosted on a Web service, or by sending a Tweet. 

Popular websites and social media acting as a mechanism for C2 may give a significant amount of cover due to the likelihood that hosts within a network are already communicating with them prior to a compromise. Using common services, such as those offered by Google or Twitter, makes it easier for adversaries to hide in expected noise. Web service providers commonly use SSL/TLS encryption, giving adversaries an added level of protection.
1520.profile: [profile]The technique is MITRE ATT&CK T1102.002, Web Service: Bidirectional Communication, under the Command and Control tactic. It operates across Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms by using legitimate external web services like social media or cloud platforms for two-way C2 traffic. Commands are sent to the compromised host via the service, and output is returned through the same channel via methods such as posting comments, updating documents, or sending tweets. This leverages the service's SSL/TLS encryption and common traffic to evade detection. It is notably used by groups including APT28, Lazarus Group, and FIN7.[/profile]
1520.profile_without_enhance: [profile]C2 communication is a core adversary technique for maintaining remote control of compromised systems, typically mapped to the Command and Control tactic. It involves establishing a covert channel to relay instructions and exfiltrate data. Adversaries often leverage legitimate web services like social media or cloud platforms to host commands and blend traffic with normal activity, sometimes using SSL/TLS for encryption. Techniques include using separate protocols for inbound and outbound traffic to bypass restrictions, employing fallback channels if the primary is blocked, and obfuscating C2 traffic to avoid detection.

1521.name: file deletion
1521.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may delete files left behind by the actions of their intrusion activity. Malware, tools, or other non-native files dropped or created on a system by an adversary (ex: [Ingress Tool Transfer](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1105)) may leave traces to indicate to what was done within a network and how. Removal of these files can occur during an intrusion, or as part of a post-intrusion process to minimize the adversary's footprint. There are tools available from the host operating system to perform cleanup, but adversaries may use other tools as well.(Citation: Microsoft SDelete July 2016) Examples of built-in [Command and Scripting Interpreter](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059) functions include del on Windows, rm or unlink on Linux and macOS, and `rm` on ESXi.
1521.profile: [profile]File Deletion, designated as T1070.004, is a Defense Evasion technique used to remove traces of intrusion artifacts like dropped malware or tools. It operates across Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms using native commands such as `del`, `rm`, or `unlink`, or dedicated tools like Windows Sysinternals SDelete. This action minimizes the adversary's forensic footprint during or after an operation and is commonly associated with groups like APT28, Lazarus Group, and Wizard Spider.[/profile]
1521.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique File Deletion, identified as T1070.004 (a sub-technique of Indicator Removal) within the Defense Evasion tactic, applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves adversaries removing files like malware or tools to erase traces of intrusion, using native OS commands such as `del` on Windows or `rm` and `unlink` on Linux/macOS, or specialized utilities like Windows Sysinternals SDelete. This action can occur during or after an operation to minimize their forensic footprint.

1522.name: command execution
1522.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may abuse utilities that allow for command execution to bypass security restrictions that limit the use of command-line interpreters. Various Windows utilities may be used to execute commands, possibly without invoking [cmd](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0106). For example, [Forfiles](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0193), the Program Compatibility Assistant (`pcalua.exe`), components of the Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL), `Scriptrunner.exe`, as well as other utilities may invoke the execution of programs and commands from a [Command and Scripting Interpreter](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059), Run window, or via scripts.(Citation: VectorSec ForFiles Aug 2017)(Citation: Evi1cg Forfiles Nov 2017)(Citation: Secure Team - Scriptrunner.exe)(Citation: SS64)(Citation: Bleeping Computer - Scriptrunner.exe) Adversaries may also abuse the `ssh.exe` binary to execute malicious commands via the `ProxyCommand` and `LocalCommand` options, which can be invoked via the `-o` flag or by modifying the SSH config file.(Citation: Threat Actor Targets the Manufacturing industry with Lumma Stealer and Amadey Bot)

Adversaries may abuse these features for [Defense Evasion](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0005), specifically to perform arbitrary execution while subverting detections and/or mitigation controls (such as Group Policy) that limit/prevent the usage of [cmd](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0106) or file extensions more commonly associated with malicious payloads.
1522.profile: [profile]Indirect Command Execution, designated T1202, is a Defense Evasion technique primarily targeting Windows platforms. It involves abusing legitimate system utilities to execute commands while bypassing restrictions on standard interpreters like cmd.exe. Specific technical mechanics include using Forfiles, pcalua.exe, Windows Subsystem forLinux components, or Scriptrunner.exe to invoke programs. Adversaries may also misuse ssh.exe via its ProxyCommand or LocalCommand options, invoked with the -o flag or through SSH config file modification. This technique is associated with groups like Lazarus Group and Redcurl.[/profile]
1522.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "command execution" is a general concept within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, primarily associated with the Execution tactic. It encompasses the broader action of running adversary-controlled code on a system, often facilitated by command and scripting interpreters like Windows Command Shell (cmd) or PowerShell. 1525.name: URL generation logic
1525.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may make use of Domain Generation Algorithms (DGAs) to dynamically identify a destination domain for command and control traffic rather than relying on a list of static IP addresses or domains. This has the advantage of making it much harder for defenders to block, track, or take over the command and control channel, as there potentially could be thousands of domains that malware can check for instructions.(Citation: Cybereason Dissecting DGAs)(Citation: Cisco Umbrella DGA)(Citation: Unit 42 DGA Feb 2019)

DGAs can take the form of apparently random or “gibberish” strings (ex: istgmxdejdnxuyla.ru) when they construct domain names by generating each letter. Alternatively, some DGAs employ whole words as the unit by concatenating words together instead of letters (ex: cityjulydish.net). Many DGAs are time-based, generating a different domain for each time period (hourly, daily, monthly, etc). Others incorporate a seed value as well to make predicting future domains more difficult for defenders.(Citation: Cybereason Dissecting DGAs)(Citation: Cisco Umbrella DGA)(Citation: Talos CCleanup 2017)(Citation: Akamai DGA Mitigation)

Adversaries may use DGAs for the purpose of [Fallback Channels](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1008). When contact is lost with the primary command and control server malware may employ a DGA as a means to reestablishing command and control.(Citation: Talos CCleanup 2017)(Citation: FireEye POSHSPY April 2017)(Citation: ESET Sednit 2017 Activity)
1525.profile: [profile]Domain Generation Algorithms (DGAs), identified as T1568.002 under the Command and Control tactic, operate on platforms including Windows, Linux, and macOS. They dynamically generate a large number of potential command and control domains to evade static blocking, using algorithms that produce either random character strings or concatenated words, often based on time or a seed value. This technique is employed by malware like Komplex for resilient C2 communication and as a fallback mechanism when primary channels are lost.
1525.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "URL generation logic" is a technique used by adversaries to create deceptive or dynamic URLs for malicious purposes. It aligns with MITRE ATT&CK technique T1608.005 "Link Target" under the Resource Development tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. This involves crafting URLs that mask their true destination, often using URL schema abuse, link shortening services, or typosquatting domains to increase phishing effectiveness and evade detection. Adversaries may generate unique, single-use URLs or host malicious link targets on trusted platforms to facilitate spearphishing and initial access campaigns.

1528.name: HTTP POST data encryption algorithm
1528.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may compromise a network device’s encryption capability in order to bypass encryption that would otherwise protect data communications. (Citation: Cisco Synful Knock Evolution)

Encryption can be used to protect transmitted network traffic to maintain its confidentiality (protect against unauthorized disclosure) and integrity (protect against unauthorized changes). Encryption ciphers are used to convert a plaintext message to ciphertext and can be computationally intensive to decipher without the associated decryption key. Typically, longer keys increase the cost of cryptanalysis, or decryption without the key.

Adversaries can compromise and manipulate devices that perform encryption of network traffic. For example, through behaviors such as [Modify System Image](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1601), [Reduce Key Space](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1600/001), and [Disable Crypto Hardware](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1600/002), an adversary can negatively effect and/or eliminate a device’s ability to securely encrypt network traffic. This poses a greater risk of unauthorized disclosure and may help facilitate data manipulation, Credential Access, or Collection efforts. (Citation: Cisco Blog Legacy Device Attacks)
1528.profile: [profile]The entity is mapped to MITRE ATT&CK technique T1600, "Weaken Encryption", under the Impact tactic, targeting Network devices. Adversaries compromise a device's encryption capability to bypass data protection, for example by reducing the cryptographic key space or disabling dedicated crypto hardware through sub-techniques like T1600.001 and T1600.002. This manipulation increases the risk of data disclosure and can facilitate credential access or data collection. The malware Carberp and Komplex are associated with this behavior.
1528.profile_without_enhance: [profile]HTTP POST data encryption algorithm is a technique where adversaries encrypt data within the HTTP POST request body before exfiltration to avoid detection. This method is distinct from standard HTTPS channel encryption, often involving custom or additional symmetric encryption algorithms (like RC4 or AES) applied directly to the payload. It is related to the exfiltration tactic, operating on network protocols, and serves to obscure stolen data during transfer over protocols such as HTTP.

1548.name: influence public opinion
1548.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may attempt to exploit a weakness in an Internet-facing host or system to initially access a network. The weakness in the system can be a software bug, a temporary glitch, or a misconfiguration.

Exploited applications are often websites/web servers, but can also include databases (like SQL), standard services (like SMB or SSH), network device administration and management protocols (like SNMP and Smart Install), and any other system with Internet-accessible open sockets.(Citation: NVD CVE-2016-6662)(Citation: CIS Multiple SMB Vulnerabilities)(Citation: US-CERT TA18-106A Network Infrastructure Devices 2018)(Citation: Cisco Blog Legacy Device Attacks)(Citation: NVD CVE-2014-7169) On ESXi infrastructure, adversaries may exploit exposed OpenSLP services; they may alternatively exploit exposed VMware vCenter servers.(Citation: Recorded Future ESXiArgs Ransomware 2023)(Citation: Ars Technica VMWare Code Execution Vulnerability 2021) Depending on the flaw being exploited, this may also involve [Exploitation for Defense Evasion](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1211) or [Exploitation for Client Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1203).

If an application is hosted on cloud-based infrastructure and/or is containerized, then exploiting it may lead to compromise of the underlying instance or container. This can allow an adversary a path to access the cloud or container APIs (e.g., via the [Cloud Instance Metadata API](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1552/005)), exploit container host access via [Escape to Host](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1611), or take advantage of weak identity and access management policies.

Adversaries may also exploit edge network infrastructure and related appliances, specifically targeting devices that do not support robust host-based defenses.(Citation: Mandiant Fortinet Zero Day)(Citation: Wired Russia Cyberwar)

For websites and databases, the OWASP top 10 and CWE top 25 highlight the most common web-based vulnerabilities.(Citation: OWASP Top 10)(Citation: CWE top 25)
1548.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique Exploit Public-Facing Application (T1190) under the Initial Access tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It involves exploiting vulnerabilities like software bugs or misconfigurations in internet-exposed services—including web servers, databases (e.g., SQL), standard services (e.g., SMB, SSH), and network management protocols (e.g., SNMP)—to gain initial network access. This can extend to cloud or containerized applications, potentially leading to compromise of underlying instances and access to cloud APIs. The technique is used by numerous threat groups, including APT28.

The retrieved information describes related techniques like data manipulation (T1565) and stored data manipulation (T1565.001), where adversaries insert, delete, or alter data to affect organizational understanding and decision-making. This activity can be part of broader influence operations, potentially using compromised infrastructure like virtual private servers (T1584.003) to host content or conduct attacks that shape public perception.

1550.name: manipulate views on domestic and international affairs
1550.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may build a container image directly on a host to bypass defenses that monitor for the retrieval of malicious images from a public registry. A remote build request may be sent to the Docker API that includes a Dockerfile that pulls a vanilla base image, such as alpine, from a public or local registry and then builds a custom image upon it.(Citation: Docker Build Image) An adversary may take advantage of that build API to build a custom image on the host that includes malware downloaded from their C2 server, and then they may utilize [Deploy Container](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1610) using that custom image.(Citation: Aqua Build Images on Hosts)(Citation: Aqua Security Cloud Native Threat Report June 2021) If the base image is pulled from a public registry, defenses will likely not detect the image as malicious since it’s a vanilla image. If the base image already resides in a local registry, the pull may be considered even less suspicious since the image is already in the environment.
1550.profile: [profile]Build Image on Host (T1612) is a Defense Evasion technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework for Linux, Windows, and macOS platforms. It involves adversaries bypassing image registry monitoring by sending a remote `build` request to the Docker API. This request uses a Dockerfile to pull a benign base image (e.g., alpine) from a public or local registry and then builds a custom malicious image on the host, often incorporating malware from a command and control server, which is subsequently deployed. This method avoids detection as the base image appears legitimate. The intrusion set APT28 has been associated with this activity.
1550.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "manipulate views on domestic and international affairs" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the retrieved context, it is a specific form of data manipulation (T1565) under the Impact tactic. This technique involves adversaries inserting, deleting, or altering stored data to influence public opinion, organizational understanding, or decision-making processes. The manipulation targets data at rest, such as in databases or files, and requires specialized knowledge of the target system to achieve the desired propagandistic or disruptive outcome.

1551.name: Credential Phishing
1551.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may send phishing messages to gain access to victim systems. All forms of phishing are electronically delivered social engineering. Phishing can be targeted, known as spearphishing. In spearphishing, a specific individual, company, or industry will be targeted by the adversary. More generally, adversaries can conduct non-targeted phishing, such as in mass malware spam campaigns.

Adversaries may send victims emails containing malicious attachments or links, typically to execute malicious code on victim systems. Phishing may also be conducted via third-party services, like social media platforms. Phishing may also involve social engineering techniques, such as posing as a trusted source, as well as evasive techniques such as removing or manipulating emails or metadata/headers from compromised accounts being abused to send messages (e.g., [Email Hiding Rules](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1564/008)).(Citation: Microsoft OAuth Spam 2022)(Citation: Palo Alto Unit 42 VBA Infostealer 2014) Another way to accomplish this is by [Email Spoofing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1672)(Citation: Proofpoint-spoof) the identity of the sender, which can be used to fool both the human recipient as well as automated security tools,(Citation: cyberproof-double-bounce) or by including the intended target as a party to an existing email thread that includes malicious files or links (i.e., "thread hijacking").(Citation: phishing-krebs)

Victims may also receive phishing messages that instruct them to call a phone number where they are directed to visit a malicious URL, download malware,(Citation: sygnia Luna Month)(Citation: CISA Remote Monitoring and Management Software) or install adversary-accessible remote management tools onto their computer (i.e., [User Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204)).(Citation: Unit42 Luna Moth)
1551.profile: [profile]Credential Phishing is a technique under MITRE ATT&CK ID T1566, categorized within the Initial Access tactic and applicable to multiple platforms. It involves adversaries sending electronic messages, such as emails with malicious links or attachments, to trick victims into revealing credentials. This can be executed via spearphishing targeting specific individuals or through broad campaigns, often employing social engineering by posing as a trusted source and using evasive methods like email spoofing or thread hijacking to enhance deception and bypass security measures. Associated groups include APT28, Kimsuky, and Axiom.[/profile]
1551.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Credential Phishing is a technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, aligning with the Phishing tactic (T1566) under Initial Access, targeting multiple platforms. It involves sending deceptive electronic messages, such as emails with malicious links or attachments, to trick victims into divulging authentication credentials like usernames and passwords. This is often achieved through social engineering, posing as a trusted source, and directing users to counterfeit login pages that harvest their input. The technique can be broad or highly targeted (spearphishing) and may employ evasive methods like email spoofing or thread hijacking to increase success rates.

It specifically aims to steal multi-factor authentication (MFA) tokens or application access tokens (like OAuth tokens) by sending deceptive messages that trick users into providing these secondary credentials. This allows adversaries to bypass MFA and gain unauthorized, persistent access to accounts and cloud services (e.g., using stolen OAuth tokens for API access to email), with groups like APT28 associated with its use.[/profile]
1567.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Phishing Second Authentication Token is a technique where adversaries use phishing messages to steal secondary authentication tokens, such as OAuth access tokens, to bypass multi-factor authentication (MFA) and gain unauthorized access to accounts and services. This method typically involves sending malicious links or attachments via spearphishing to trick users into granting token permissions to a malicious application, allowing long-term API access that negates the need for passwords and secondary factors.

1568.name: Forwarding Address Setup
1568.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may achieve persistence by adding a Registry key to the Active Setup of the local machine. Active Setup is a Windows mechanism that is used to execute programs when a user logs in. The value stored in the Registry key will be executed after a user logs into the computer.(Citation: Klein Active Setup 2010) These programs will be executed under the context of the user and will have the account's associated permissions level. Adversaries may abuse Active Setup by creating a key under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Active Setup\Installed Components\ and setting a malicious value for StubPath. This value will serve as the program that will be executed when a user logs into the computer.(Citation: Mandiant Glyer APT 2010)(Citation: Citizenlab Packrat 2015)(Citation: FireEye CFR Watering Hole 2012)(Citation: SECURELIST Bright Star 2015)(Citation: paloalto Tropic Trooper 2016) Adversaries can abuse these components to execute malware, such as remote access tools, to maintain persistence through system reboots. Adversaries may also use [Masquerading](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1036) to make the Registry entries look as if they are associated with legitimate programs.
1568.profile: [profile]The entity "Forwarding Address Setup" is likely a misnomer for the MITRE ATT&CK technique "Active Setup" (T1547.014) under the Persistence tactic for Windows. This technique involves adversaries creating a registry key under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Active Setup\Installed Components\ and setting a malicious value for the StubPath entry, which executes a program when a user logs into the computer to maintain persistence. The intrusion-set APT28 has been associated with this behavior.
1568.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Forwarding Address Setup is a technique where adversaries configure email forwarding rules to exfiltrate sensitive information and maintain persistent access to a victim's communications. This is achieved by creating inbox rules, often through a client application, web interface, or command line, to automatically forward received messages to an external recipient controlled by the attacker. Adversaries may further hide these rules using APIs like MAPI to make them invisible from standard email administration tools, allowing continued data collection even after compromised credentials are changed.

1569.name: Third-Party Application Access
1569.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may use stolen application access tokens to bypass the typical authentication process and access restricted accounts, information, or services on remote systems. These tokens are typically stolen from users or services and used in lieu of login credentials.

Application access tokens are used to make authorized API requests on behalf of a user or service and are commonly used to access resources in cloud, container-based applications, and software-as-a-service (SaaS).(Citation: Auth0 - Why You Should Always Use Access Tokens to Secure APIs Sept 2019) 

OAuth is one commonly implemented framework that issues tokens to users for access to systems. These frameworks are used collaboratively to verify the user and determine what actions the user is allowed to perform. Once identity is established, the token allows actions to be authorized, without passing the actual credentials of the user. Therefore, compromise of the token can grant the adversary access to resources of other sites through a malicious application.(Citation: okta)

For example, with a cloud-based email service, once an OAuth access token is granted to a malicious application, it can potentially gain long-term access to features of the user account if a "refresh" token enabling background access is awarded.(Citation: Microsoft Identity Platform Access 2019) With an OAuth access token an adversary can use the user-granted REST API to perform functions such as email searching and contact enumeration.(Citation: Staaldraad Phishing with OAuth 2017)

Compromised access tokens may be used as an initial step in compromising other services. For example, if a token grants access to a victim’s primary email, the adversary may be able to extend access to all other services which the target subscribes by triggering forgotten password routines. In AWS and GCP environments, adversaries can trigger a request for a short-lived access token with the privileges of another user account.(Citation: Google Cloud Service Account Credentials)(Citation: AWS Temporary Security Credentials) The adversary can then use this token to request data or perform actions the original account could not. If permissions for this feature are misconfigured – for example, by allowing all users to request a token for a particular account - an adversary may be able to gain initial access to a Cloud Account or escalate their privileges.(Citation: Rhino Security Labs Enumerating AWS Roles)

Direct API access through a token negates the effectiveness of a second authentication factor and may be immune to intuitive countermeasures like changing passwords.  For example, in AWS environments, an adversary who compromises a user’s AWS API credentials may be able to use the `sts:GetFederationToken` API call to create a federated user session, which will have the same permissions as the original user but may persist even if the original user credentials are deactivated.(Citation: Crowdstrike AWS User Federation Persistence) Additionally, access abuse over an API channel can be difficult to detect even from the service provider end, as the access can still align well with a legitimate workflow.
1569.profile: [profile]Third-Party Application Access is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1550.001 under the Defense Evasion tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It involves using stolen OAuth or other application access tokens to bypass standard authentication and make authorized API requests to cloud, SaaS, or containerized services. This method negates multi-factor authentication and password changes, as seen with AWS `sts:GetFederationToken` calls to create persistent federated sessions. The technique is used by groups like APT28 and can enable long-term account access via refresh tokens and facilitate privilege escalation in misconfigured environments.[/profile]
1569.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Third-Party Application Access is an initial access technique where adversaries compromise or leverage applications that have existing trusted relationships or integration permissions with a target. This can involve abusing delegated administrative permissions in cloud environments like Office 365, where a compromised partner account grants access to a victim tenant, or exploiting the access of compromised third-party virtual private servers (VPS) to host malicious infrastructure. The method bypasses direct network perimeter defenses by exploiting pre-authorized application-to-application or service provider connections.

1570.name: Forced Logins to Corporate VPN
1570.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may gather credential material by invoking or forcing a user to automatically provide authentication information through a mechanism in which they can intercept. The Server Message Block (SMB) protocol is commonly used in Windows networks for authentication and communication between systems for access to resources and file sharing. When a Windows system attempts to connect to an SMB resource it will automatically attempt to authenticate and send credential information for the current user to the remote system.(Citation: Wikipedia Server Message Block) This behavior is typical in enterprise environments so that users do not need to enter credentials to access network resources. Web Distributed Authoring and Versioning (WebDAV) is also typically used by Windows systems as a backup protocol when SMB is blocked or fails. WebDAV is an extension of HTTP and will typically operate over TCP ports 80 and 443.(Citation: Didier Stevens WebDAV Traffic)(Citation: Microsoft Managing WebDAV Security) Adversaries may take advantage of this behavior to gain access to user account hashes through forced SMB/WebDAV authentication. An adversary can send an attachment to a user through spearphishing that contains a resource link to an external server controlled by the adversary (i.e. [Template Injection](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1221)), or place a specially crafted file on navigation path for privileged accounts (e.g. .SCF file placed on desktop) or on a publicly accessible share to be accessed by victim(s). When the user's system accesses the untrusted resource, it will attempt authentication and send information, including the user's hashed credentials, over SMB to the adversary-controlled server.(Citation: GitHub Hashjacking) With access to the credential hash, an adversary can perform off-line [Brute Force](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1110) cracking to gain access to plaintext credentials.(Citation: Cylance Redirect to SMB) There are several different ways this can occur.(Citation: Osanda Stealing NetNTLM Hashes) Some specifics from in-the-wild use include: * A spearphishing attachment containing a document with a resource that is automatically loaded when the document is opened (i.e. [Template Injection](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1221)). The document can include, for example, a request similar to file[:]//[remote address]/Normal.dotm to trigger the SMB request.(Citation: US-CERT APT Energy Oct 2017) * A modified .LNK or .SCF file with the icon filename pointing to an external reference such as \\[remote address]\pic.png that will force the system to load the resource when the icon is rendered to repeatedly gather credentials.(Citation: US-CERT APT Energy Oct 2017) Alternatively, by leveraging the EfsRpcOpenFileRaw function, an adversary can send SMB requests to a remote system's MS-EFSRPC interface and force the victim computer to initiate an authentication procedure and share its authentication details. The Encrypting File System Remote Protocol (EFSRPC) is a protocol used in Windows networks for maintenance and management operations on encrypted data that is stored remotely to be accessed over a network. Utilization of EfsRpcOpenFileRaw function in EFSRPC is used to open an encrypted object on the server for backup or restore. Adversaries can collect this data and abuse it as part of a NTLM relay attack to gain access to remote systems on the same internal network.(Citation: Rapid7)(Citation: GitHub)
1570.profile: [profile]Forced Authentication, identified as MITRE ATT&CK T1187, is a Credential Access technique primarily targeting Windows platforms. It exploits the automatic authentication behavior of protocols like SMB and WebDAV. Adversaries force a victim system to authenticate to a controlled server by tricking it into accessing a malicious resource, such as via a spearphishing document with a remote template link (e.g., `file[:]//[remote address]/Normal.dotm`) or a crafted .SCF/LNK file. This transmits the user's hashed credentials (like NetNTLM), which can be captured for offline cracking or relay attacks. The technique has been used by groups including APT28, Dragonfly, and DarkHydrus.[/profile]
1570.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Forced Logins to Corporate VPN is a technique where adversaries capture credentials by compromising a corporate VPN login portal. They install malicious code on the externally facing VPN login page to intercept and log user credentials as they are entered during authentication attempts. This can be done as part of an initial web service exploitation or as a post-compromise action using legitimate administrative access to maintain network access through valid accounts.

1571.name: Physical Security Key Bypass
1571.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may reduce the level of effort required to decrypt data transmitted over the network by reducing the cipher strength of encrypted communications.(Citation: Cisco Synful Knock Evolution)

Adversaries can weaken the encryption software on a compromised network device by reducing the key size used by the software to convert plaintext to ciphertext (e.g., from hundreds or thousands of bytes to just a couple of bytes). As a result, adversaries dramatically reduce the amount of effort needed to decrypt the protected information without the key.

Adversaries may modify the key size used and other encryption parameters using specialized commands in a [Network Device CLI](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/008) introduced to the system through [Modify System Image](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1601) to change the configuration of the device. (Citation: Cisco Blog Legacy Device Attacks)
1571.profile: [profile]The entity "Physical Security Key Bypass" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the provided input, the self-info and similar entity data strongly correspond to the known MITRE technique "Reduce Key Space" (ID: T1600.001) under the Defense Evasion tactic, targeting Network Devices. The technical mechanics involve an adversary compromising a network device to weaken its encryption by reducing the cryptographic key size, for example from hundreds of bytes to just a couple, dramatically lowering the effort required for decryption. This modification is typically performed using specialized CLI commands introduced via a modified system image. The intrusion set APT28 is a known related group.[/profile]
1571.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Physical Security Key Bypass is a technique where adversaries circumvent physical multi-factor authentication (MFA) tokens. This can be achieved by compromising the hardware supply chain to implant backdoors into security keys before distribution, or by exploiting logical vulnerabilities in the authentication process on a domain controller to accept false credentials, similar to a Skeleton Key attack. The method enables unauthorized access by subverting the physical token verification step.

1572.name: Biometric Authentication Exploitation
1572.profile: [profile]Biometric Authentication Exploitation is a technique where adversaries target biometric authentication mechanisms to bypass security controls or gain unauthorized access. It aligns with the Credential Access tactic, targeting systems that utilize biometric verification. The technique involves exploiting vulnerabilities in biometric sensors, software, or databases to steal, replicate, or manipulate biometric data such as fingerprints, facial recognition, or iris scans. This can enable impersonation or direct system access without legitimate credentials, as seen in activities by groups like APT28.[/profile]
1572.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Biometric Authentication Exploitation is a technique where adversaries target biometric authentication systems to bypass security controls or gain unauthorized access. This involves exploiting vulnerabilities in biometric sensors, software, or the authentication process itself, such as using fake biometric samples (e.g., forged fingerprints or facial images), replaying captured biometric data, or tampering with the authentication database or algorithms. The goal is to impersonate legitimate users, often as part of credential access or initial access tactics, impacting systems that rely on biometric verification for security.

1573.name: Flash zero-day exploit
1573.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may attempt to exploit a weakness in an Internet-facing host or system to initially access a network. The weakness in the system can be a software bug, a temporary glitch, or a misconfiguration.

Exploited applications are often websites/web servers, but can also include databases (like SQL), standard services (like SMB or SSH), network device administration and management protocols (like SNMP and Smart Install), and any other system with Internet-accessible open sockets.(Citation: NVD CVE-2016-6662)(Citation: CIS Multiple SMB Vulnerabilities)(Citation: US-CERT TA18-106A Network Infrastructure Devices 2018)(Citation: Cisco Blog Legacy Device Attacks)(Citation: NVD CVE-2014-7169) On ESXi infrastructure, adversaries may exploit exposed OpenSLP services; they may alternatively exploit exposed VMware vCenter servers.(Citation: Recorded Future ESXiArgs Ransomware 2023)(Citation: Ars Technica VMWare Code Execution Vulnerability 2021) Depending on the flaw being exploited, this may also involve [Exploitation for Defense Evasion](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1211) or [Exploitation for Client Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1203).

If an application is hosted on cloud-based infrastructure and/or is containerized, then exploiting it may lead to compromise of the underlying instance or container. This can allow an adversary a path to access the cloud or container APIs (e.g., via the [Cloud Instance Metadata API](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1552/005)), exploit container host access via [Escape to Host](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1611), or take advantage of weak identity and access management policies.

Adversaries may also exploit edge network infrastructure and related appliances, specifically targeting devices that do not support robust host-based defenses.(Citation: Mandiant Fortinet Zero Day)(Citation: Wired Russia Cyberwar)

For websites and databases, the OWASP top 10 and CWE top 25 highlight the most common web-based vulnerabilities.(Citation: OWASP Top 10)(Citation: CWE top 25)
1573.profile: [profile]Flash zero-day exploit, mapped to MITRE ATT&CK technique Exploit Public-Facing Application (T1190) under the Initial Access tactic, targets multiple platforms including Windows, Linux, and network devices. This technique involves exploiting previously unknown vulnerabilities in internet-facing applications, such as Adobe Flash, to execute arbitrary code and gain initial network access. It is notably used by groups like APT28. The exploit can be delivered via malicious documents or websites, often requiring user interaction to trigger the vulnerability and achieve code execution.[/profile]
1573.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Flash zero-day exploit is a specific instance of the MITRE ATT&CK technique Exploitation for Client Execution (T1203) under the Execution tactic, primarily targeting platforms utilizing Adobe Flash. It involves adversaries exploiting previously unknown vulnerabilities in the Adobe Flash Player, often delivered via malicious documents or web pages, to execute arbitrary code on a victim's system. This technique has been used by numerous threat groups, including APT28, APT29, and Lazarus Group, to gain initial access.

1574.name: Windows privilege escalation
1574.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may exploit software vulnerabilities in an attempt to elevate privileges. Exploitation of a software vulnerability occurs when an adversary takes advantage of a programming error in a program, service, or within the operating system software or kernel itself to execute adversary-controlled code. Security constructs such as permission levels will often hinder access to information and use of certain techniques, so adversaries will likely need to perform privilege escalation to include use of software exploitation to circumvent those restrictions.

When initially gaining access to a system, an adversary may be operating within a lower privileged process which will prevent them from accessing certain resources on the system. Vulnerabilities may exist, usually in operating system components and software commonly running at higher permissions, that can be exploited to gain higher levels of access on the system. This could enable someone to move from unprivileged or user level permissions to SYSTEM or root permissions depending on the component that is vulnerable. This could also enable an adversary to move from a virtualized environment, such as within a virtual machine or container, onto the underlying host. This may be a necessary step for an adversary compromising an endpoint system that has been properly configured and limits other privilege escalation methods.

Adversaries may bring a signed vulnerable driver onto a compromised machine so that they can exploit the vulnerability to execute code in kernel mode. This process is sometimes referred to as Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver (BYOVD).(Citation: ESET InvisiMole June 2020)(Citation: Unit42 AcidBox June 2020) Adversaries may include the vulnerable driver with files delivered during Initial Access or download it to a compromised system via [Ingress Tool Transfer](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1105) or [Lateral Tool Transfer](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1570).
1574.profile: [profile]The entity corresponds to the MITRE ATT&CK technique "Exploitation for Privilege Escalation" (ID: T1068) under the Privilege Escalation tactic, primarily targeting Windows platforms. It involves exploiting software vulnerabilities, including programming errors in OS components or high-privilege software, to execute adversary-controlled code and elevate permissions from user to SYSTEM or root levels. A specific method is Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver (BYOVD), where a signed, vulnerable driver is introduced to the system and exploited to run code in kernel mode. This technique is used by numerous threat groups, including APT28, to bypass security restrictions when other escalation methods are limited.
1574.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Windows privilege escalation is a broad adversarial objective, not a single MITRE ATT&CK technique. It involves methods to elevate access from a lower to a higher privilege level on a Windows system. Specific techniques include exploiting software vulnerabilities (T1068) to execute code as SYSTEM, abusing Windows services (T1543.003) which run with SYSTEM privileges, and hijacking the DLL search order (T1038) to load malicious code in the context of a privileged process. Adversaries may also abuse Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI - T1047) for execution and circumvent User Account Control (UAC - T1548) mechanisms.

1582.name: operational security
1582.profile: [profile]Operational Security is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK attack pattern but a general adversary practice. The provided context from APT28 and similar techniques like Security Software Discovery (T1063), Disabling Security Tools (T1089), and Network Security Appliances Discovery (T1590.006) indicates it involves actions to avoid detection. This includes discovering and disabling security software, firewalls, and intrusion detection systems, and gathering information on network defenses to evade them and maintain covert access.
1582.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "operational security" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the provided context, it refers to adversary behaviors to avoid detection. This includes using legitimate web services (T1102) like Google or Microsoft for encrypted C2 communication, employing multilayer encryption (T1079) such as custom schemes within HTTPS, and utilizing cloud service dashboards (T1538) with stolen credentials to gather information stealthily without generating API logs. These methods help adversaries blend into normal traffic and protect their infrastructure.

1586.name: X-Tunnel
1586.uncertain_mes: X-ZIGZAG is a lightweight and stealthy RAT designed for educational purposes. With a focus on small size and undetectability, X-ZIGZAG operates entirely in RAM, ensuring no traces are left on the target system. This tool is built without relying on any external libraries or third-party dependencies, making it both efficient and versatile.
1586.profile: [profile]X-Tunnel, also known as X-ZIGZAG, is a lightweight and stealthy Remote Access Trojan (RAT) that operates entirely in memory to avoid leaving traces. It is attributed to the APT28 and APT29 intrusion sets. The malware functions as a network tunneling tool for command and control (C2) communication and network pivoting, providing a secure tunnel to an external server. It was first observed in the wild in May 2013 and has been associated with compromises including the 2016 DNC hack. The tool is built to be efficient and versatile, designed without external library dependencies.[/profile]
1586.profile_without_enhance: [profile]X-Tunnel, also known as XTUNNEL, is a network tunneling tool associated with the APT28 group, first observed in 2013 and linked to compromises like the 2016 DNC hack. Its key technical behavior is establishing a secure tunnel to an external command and control server for network traversal and pivoting.

1591.name: 使用缩短的链接
1591.profile: [profile]The entity "使用缩短的链接" (Use of Shortened Links) aligns with MITRE ATT&CK technique T1598.003 (Spearphishing Link) under the Reconnaissance tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. This technique involves adversaries employing shortened URLs from trusted services to mask malicious destinations, increasing phishing effectiveness by evading blocklists and deceiving victims. It is used in spearphishing campaigns, such as by groups like Silent Librarian and FIN7, to redirect users to credential harvesting pages or malware downloads. The shortened links facilitate initial access and information gathering.[/profile]
1591.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "使用缩短的链接" (Use of Shortened Links) is a technique for initial access and execution, where adversaries employ URL shortening services or similar methods to mask malicious destinations. This tactic, often part of spearphishing campaigns, involves creating deceptive links that redirect victims to credential harvesting pages or malware downloads. Adversaries leverage trusted domains from these services to evade security blocks and increase the effectiveness of their phishing attempts.

1592.name: 假Google登录页面
1592.profile: [profile]The entity "假Google登录页面" (Fake Google Login Page) is a technique for credential harvesting, aligning with the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1583.001 (Phishing: Spearphishing Link) under the Initial Access tactic, primarily targeting web platforms. It involves creating a counterfeit Google login interface to deceive users into entering their credentials, which are then captured by the adversary. This method is commonly employed by groups like APT28 to facilitate initial compromise through social engineering, often as part of broader phishing campaigns targeting email and cloud services.
1592.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity '假Google登录页面' (Fake Google Login Page) is a specific implementation of the Credential Access technique GUI Input Capture (T1056.002). It operates by mimicking the legitimate Google login interface to deceive users into entering their credentials. This technique is commonly used in phishing campaigns to harvest authentication details, often paired with user activity monitoring to time the fake prompts when users are likely accessing genuine Google services.

1594.name: registration of fake domains
1594.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may acquire domains that can be used during targeting. Domain names are the human readable names used to represent one or more IP addresses. They can be purchased or, in some cases, acquired for free.

Adversaries may use acquired domains for a variety of purposes, including for [Phishing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566), [Drive-by Compromise](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1189), and Command and Control.(Citation: CISA MSS Sep 2020) Adversaries may choose domains that are similar to legitimate domains, including through use of homoglyphs or use of a different top-level domain (TLD).(Citation: FireEye APT28)(Citation: PaypalScam) Typosquatting may be used to aid in delivery of payloads via [Drive-by Compromise](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1189). Adversaries may also use internationalized domain names (IDNs) and different character sets (e.g. Cyrillic, Greek, etc.) to execute "IDN homograph attacks," creating visually similar lookalike domains used to deliver malware to victim machines.(Citation: CISA IDN ST05-016)(Citation: tt_httrack_fake_domains)(Citation: tt_obliqueRAT)(Citation: httrack_unhcr)(Citation: lazgroup_idn_phishing)

Different URIs/URLs may also be dynamically generated to uniquely serve malicious content to victims (including one-time, single use domain names).(Citation: iOS URL Scheme)(Citation: URI)(Citation: URI Use)(Citation: URI Unique)

Adversaries may also acquire and repurpose expired domains, which may be potentially already allowlisted/trusted by defenders based on an existing reputation/history.(Citation: Categorisation_not_boundary)(Citation: Domain_Steal_CC)(Citation: Redirectors_Domain_Fronting)(Citation: bypass_webproxy_filtering)

Domain registrars each maintain a publicly viewable database that displays contact information for every registered domain. Private WHOIS services display alternative information, such as their own company data, rather than the owner of the domain. Adversaries may use such private WHOIS services to obscure information about who owns a purchased domain. Adversaries may further interrupt efforts to track their infrastructure by using varied registration information and purchasing domains with different domain registrars.(Citation: Mandiant APT1)

In addition to legitimately purchasing a domain, an adversary may register a new domain in a compromised environment. For example, in AWS environments, adversaries may leverage the Route53 domain service to register a domain and create hosted zones pointing to resources of the threat actor’s choosing.(Citation: Invictus IR DangerDev 2024)
1594.profile: [profile]Registration of Fake Domains, identified as T1583.001 within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, falls under the Resource Development tactic and applies to multiple platforms. This technique involves adversaries acquiring domains to establish infrastructure for operations such as phishing, command and control, or drive-by compromises. Key technical mechanics include registering domains that are visually similar to legitimate ones through typosquatting, the use of homoglyphs, different top-level domains (TLDs), or internationalized domain names (IDNs) for homograph attacks. Adversaries also leverage private WHOIS services to obscure ownership, use varied registration information across different registrars to hinder tracking, and may repurpose expired domains to exploit existing trust. In cloud environments like AWS, they can abuse services such as Route53 to register domains directly from a compromised system.[/profile]
1594.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "registration of fake domains" aligns with MITRE ATT&CK technique T1583.001 (Domains) under the Resource Development tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. This technique involves adversaries acquiring domains, often using deceptive methods such as typosquatting, homoglyphs, or different top-level domains to create lookalike domains resembling legitimate ones. These fake domains are used for phishing, drive-by compromises, and command and control infrastructure. Adversaries may also employ private WHOIS services and varied registration information across different registrars to obscure ownership and evade tracking.

1596.name: Social Engineering Campaigns
1596.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may search social media for information about victims that can be used during targeting. Social media sites may contain various information about a victim organization, such as business announcements as well as information about the roles, locations, and interests of staff.

Adversaries may search in different social media sites depending on what information they seek to gather. Threat actors may passively harvest data from these sites, as well as use information gathered to create fake profiles/groups to elicit victim’s into revealing specific information (i.e. [Spearphishing Service](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1598/001)).(Citation: Cyware Social Media) Information from these sources may reveal opportunities for other forms of reconnaissance (ex: [Phishing for Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1598) or [Search Open Technical Databases](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1596)), establishing operational resources (ex: [Establish Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1585) or [Compromise Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1586)), and/or initial access (ex: [Spearphishing via Service](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/003)).
1596.profile: [profile]Social Media, identified as T1593.001, is a reconnaissance technique under the Reconnaissance tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. It involves adversaries passively harvesting victim data from social media sites to gather information on organizational announcements, staff roles, locations, and interests. This collected intelligence is used to craft targeted lures, such as creating fake profiles or groups to elicit further information, and enables follow-on actions like spearphishing, account establishment or compromise, and initial access operations. Groups like Contagious Interview, Exotic Lily, and Kimsuky have employed this method.[/profile]
1596.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Social Engineering Campaigns" is a broad adversarial approach, not a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique. It encompasses the use of psychological manipulation to deceive individuals into divulging confidential information or performing actions. Based on retrieved information, these campaigns often leverage platforms like social media and email, employing specific techniques such as spearphishing via services to gather credentials or establish fake personas. The core technical mechanics involve creating deceptive communications, often using compromised or fabricated accounts to build trust and elicit sensitive data from targeted victims.

1600.name: Cyber Espionage
1600.profile: [profile]Cyber Espionage is a strategic objective, not a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique, and is typically associated with the Collection tactic. It is conducted by advanced persistent threat (APT) groups such as APT28, Winnti, DeepPanda, and RocketKitten. These adversaries employ techniques like obtaining capabilities (T1588) to acquire malware and exploits, and they monitor threat intelligence reports (Search Threat Vendor Data, T1681) to adapt their operations and evade detection.[/profile]
1600.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Cyber Espionage is a broad adversarial objective, not a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique, and therefore lacks a standard T-ID, Tactic, or Platform. It describes the overarching goal of illicitly gathering intelligence from target systems or networks. Related techniques that can facilitate this objective include obtaining capabilities like malware or exploits from third parties (T1588) and monitoring threat intelligence reports about their own campaigns to adapt their operations and avoid detection (T1681).

1601.name: International Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS)

1612.name: Anonymous Poles (@anpoland)
1612.uncertain_mes:
Threat Intelligence Report
What Is Anonymous Sudan?
Truesec exposes a Russian information operation.
Since January 23, 2023, a threat actor identifying as “Anonymous Sudan” has been conducting denial of service (DDoS) attacks against multiple organizations in Sweden. This group claims to be “hacktivists,” politically motivated hackers from Sudan.
1612.profile: [profile]Primary name: Anonymous Poland, also known as Anonymous Sudan and @anpoland. This entity is believed to be a false-flag operation or sockpuppet attributed to the Russian military intelligence (GRU)-linked APT28 (Fancy Bear) group. 1614.name: Spoofing
1614.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may redirect network traffic to adversary-owned systems by spoofing Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) traffic and acting as a malicious DHCP server on the victim network. By achieving the adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) position, adversaries may collect network communications, including passed credentials, especially those sent over insecure, unencrypted protocols. This may also enable follow-on behaviors such as [Network Sniffing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1040) or [Transmitted Data Manipulation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1565/002). DHCP is based on a client-server model and has two functionalities: a protocol for providing network configuration settings from a DHCP server to a client and a mechanism for allocating network addresses to clients.(Citation: rfc2131) The typical server-client interaction is as follows: 1. The client broadcasts a `DISCOVER` message. 2. The server responds with an `OFFER` message, which includes an available network address. 3. The client broadcasts a `REQUEST` message, which includes the network address offered. 4. The server acknowledges with an `ACK` message and the client receives the network configuration parameters. Adversaries may spoof as a rogue DHCP server on the victim network, from which legitimate hosts may receive malicious network configurations. For example, malware can act as a DHCP server and provide adversary-owned DNS servers to the victimized computers.(Citation: new_rogue_DHCP_serv_malware)(Citation: w32.tidserv.g) Through the malicious network configurations, an adversary may achieve the AiTM position, route client traffic through adversary-controlled systems, and collect information from the client network. DHCPv6 clients can receive network configuration information without being assigned an IP address by sending a INFORMATION-REQUEST (code 11) message to the All_DHCP_Relay_Agents_and_Servers multicast address.(Citation: rfc3315) Adversaries may use their rogue DHCP server to respond to this request message with malicious network configurations. Rather than establishing an AiTM position, adversaries may also abuse DHCP spoofing to perform a DHCP exhaustion attack (i.e, [Service Exhaustion Flood](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1499/002)) by generating many broadcast DISCOVER messages to exhaust a network’s DHCP allocation pool.
1614.profile: [profile]DHCP Spoofing is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1557.003 under the Credential Access tactic, applicable to network infrastructure. It involves an adversary deploying a rogue DHCP server on a victim network to intercept DHCP traffic, such as DISCOVER or INFORMATION-REQUEST messages. By providing malicious network configurations like adversary-controlled DNS servers, the attacker achieves an adversary-in-the-middle position to redirect and collect network traffic, including unencrypted credentials. This technique is also associated with groups like APT28 and APT29.[/profile]
1614.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Spoofing is a broad technique (not a specific MITRE ATT&CK ID) where adversaries falsify data or identities to deceive targets or evade detection. It manifests in various forms: network-level spoofing like DHCP spoofing (T1557.003) to act as a rogue server and redirect traffic; email spoofing (T1672) by modifying email headers to fake sender identities; and system-level spoofing like Parent PID Spoofing (T1134.004) using the CreateProcess API to assign a fake parent process, or Process Argument Spoofing (T1564.010) by overwriting the Process Environment Block to hide malicious command-line arguments. These methods enable initial access, privilege escalation, and defense evasion across multiple platforms.[/profile]

1616.name: Data Collection
1616.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may target user email to collect sensitive information. Emails may contain sensitive data, including trade secrets or personal information, that can prove valuable to adversaries. Emails may also contain details of ongoing incident response operations, which may allow adversaries to adjust their techniques in order to maintain persistence or evade defenses.(Citation: TrustedSec OOB Communications)(Citation: CISA AA20-352A 2021) Adversaries can collect or forward email from mail servers or clients.
1616.profile: [profile]This entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1114, Email Collection, under the Collection tactic, applicable to Windows, macOS, and Linux. It involves adversaries targeting user email from mail servers or clients to gather sensitive data like trade secrets or incident response details. Specific sub-techniques include collecting local Outlook data files (.ost, .pst) and remotely accessing services like Exchange, Office 365, or Google Workspace, potentially using automated tools such as MailSniper. Groups like APT28, Silent Librarian, and Scattered Spider have been associated with this method.
1616.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Data Collection is a broad adversary tactic within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, encompassing the systematic gathering of information from a compromised system. It includes specific techniques like automated collection (T1119), which uses scripts or cloud APIs to search for and copy data based on criteria like file type, and email collection (T1114) targeting local OST/PST files or remote servers like Exchange. Other methods involve collecting clipboard data via commands like `clip.exe` or `Get-Clipboard` (T1115) and searching data from removable media (T1025). Collected data is often prepared for automated exfiltration (T1020).

This method is distinct from network-based obfuscation techniques like adding junk data to C2 traffic or using multiband communication.

Specific methods include prepending, appending, or inserting random characters between significant data within the communication stream. This manipulation aims to prevent trivial decoding and traffic analysis.

1620.name: Polish Air Force Flight 101 crash
1620.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may use brute force techniques to gain access to accounts when passwords are unknown or when password hashes are obtained.(Citation: TrendMicro Pawn Storm Dec 2020) Without knowledge of the password for an account or set of accounts, an adversary may systematically guess the password using a repetitive or iterative mechanism.(Citation: Dragos Crashoverride 2018) Brute forcing passwords can take place via interaction with a service that will check the validity of those credentials or offline against previously acquired credential data, such as password hashes.

Brute forcing credentials may take place at various points during a breach. For example, adversaries may attempt to brute force access to [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078) within a victim environment leveraging knowledge gathered from other post-compromise behaviors such as [OS Credential Dumping](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003), [Account Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1087), or [Password Policy Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1201). Adversaries may also combine brute forcing activity with behaviors such as [External Remote Services](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1133) as part of Initial Access. 

If an adversary guesses the correct password but fails to login to a compromised account due to location-based conditional access policies, they may change their infrastructure until they match the victim’s location and therefore bypass those policies.(Citation: ReliaQuest Health Care Social Engineering Campaign 2024)
1620.profile: [profile]Brute Force (T1110) is a Credential Access technique used across multiple platforms. It involves systematically guessing passwords through repetitive interaction with an authentication service or offline against acquired password hashes. This activity can occur during initial access or post-compromise, often combined with techniques like OS Credential Dumping or External Remote Services. Adversaries, including APT28, may also bypass location-based access policies by changing their infrastructure to match the victim's location.
1620.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Polish Air Force Flight 101 crash is not a documented MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on retrieved context, the name refers to a specific historical incident. The related content describes a general technique of exploiting software vulnerabilities to cause application or system crashes, which can lead to a denial of service (DoS) condition, data destruction, or service disruption.

1623.profile: [profile]Tor Browser is a legitimate privacy-focused web browser designed to anonymize user traffic by routing it through the Tor network. It is referenced in the context of threat actor operations, such as by APT28, where it is used to access command and control panels or download infrastructure, indicating its potential misuse for operational security and covert communication by intrusion sets. Its primary platform is desktop operating systems.[/profile]

1636.name: Dealerschoice

1637.name: Variant A
1637.profile: [profile]Variant A is a malware variant associated with the APT28 intrusion set and is related to the Sibot malware. It is a variant of the TONESHELL malware family, where it differs from Variant B in victim ID generation, using the tick count, username, and computer name. It has been linked to Mustang Panda and Boss Spider groups, with potential connections to Exmatter. Its key behaviors include command code execution and targeted data exfiltration, primarily affecting Windows platforms through sophisticated intrusion campaigns.
1637.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Variant A is a variant of the Sibot malware family, also known as SIBOT, a dual-purpose VBScript malware attributed to APT29. Key technical behaviors include achieving persistence via Windows Scheduled Tasks and the Windows Registry, and it is designed to download and execute additional payloads. It primarily targets Windows platforms and was notably used during the SolarWinds compromise campaign. It is associated with the CVE-2015-7645 vulnerability.[/profile]

1638.name: Variant B
1638.profile: [profile]Variant B, also known as Sibot, is attributed to the APT28 intrusion set. It is distributed as a Mach-O executable within a DMG file. The malware's technical behaviors and target platforms are not detailed in the provided context.

1639.name: malicious RTF documents
1639.profile: [profile]The entity is named "malicious RTF documents". It is an attack vector, not a malware family itself, and is directly associated with the intrusion set APT28. It is used to deliver other malware, as indicated by its role in the deployment of payloads like DCRat, Quasar RAT, and Griffon. The related groups leveraging this vector include APT33, Dropping Elephant, Stone Panda, The Gorgon Group, and FIN7. Its primary technical behavior is the reconstruction of document files into malicious RTF format to exploit vulnerabilities and execute embedded payloads. The target platform is Microsoft Windows systems through document processing software.
1639.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity 'malicious RTF documents' is a file format used to deliver malware. It is associated with the deployment of various remote access trojans (RATs) including DCRat, Quasar RAT, and Griffon. These malicious documents have been used by multiple threat groups, including APT33, Dropping Elephant, Stone Panda, The Gorgon Group, and FIN7, as an initial infection vector to compromise target systems.

1640.name: embedded OLE Word documents
1640.profile: [profile]Embedded OLE Word documents are a delivery mechanism, not a malware family itself. They are associated with APT28. Their key technical behavior is relying on user interaction to click embedded OLE objects for execution, as they do not contain exploits; the OLE storage within the document holds the final payload. This technique targets the Microsoft Windows platform via Microsoft Word.
1640.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Embedded OLE Word documents are a delivery mechanism, not a distinct malware family. They are used as malicious lures, relying on user interaction by clicking embedded OLE objects to execute payloads, rather than containing exploits. This technique has been associated with threat groups such as APT-C-34 and the Lazarus Group. The OLE storage within the document is used to hold the final malicious payload for deployment.

The malware is distributed via malicious Adobe Flash (.swf) files, exploiting vulnerabilities like the 'SWF' File Remote Memory Corruption Vulnerability in Adobe Flash Player.
