1651.name: generating malicious RTF documents
1651.uncertain_mes:
An adversary may rely upon a user opening a malicious file in order to gain execution. Users may be subjected to social engineering to get them to open a file that will lead to code execution. This user action will typically be observed as follow-on behavior from [Spearphishing Attachment](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001). Adversaries may use several types of files that require a user to execute them, including .doc, .pdf, .xls, .rtf, .scr, .exe, .lnk, .pif, .cpl, .reg, and .iso.(Citation: Mandiant Trojanized Windows 10)

Adversaries may employ various forms of [Masquerading](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1036) and [Obfuscated Files or Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027) to increase the likelihood that a user will open and successfully execute a malicious file. These methods may include using a familiar naming convention and/or password protecting the file and supplying instructions to a user on how to open it.(Citation: Password Protected Word Docs) 

While [Malicious File](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002) frequently occurs shortly after Initial Access it may occur at other phases of an intrusion, such as when an adversary places a file in a shared directory or on a user's desktop hoping that a user will click on it. This activity may also be seen shortly after [Internal Spearphishing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1534).
1651.profile: [profile]The entity "Generating Malicious RTF Documents" is a specific technique within the broader T1204.002 Malicious File, which falls under the User Execution tactic and targets Windows platforms. It involves adversaries altering the bytes of an RTF file to insert a template control word field containing a URL, which triggers the download and execution of a malicious payload when the document is opened. This method can be used to conceal exploits and has been employed by groups like APT28 and Gamaredon Group.[/profile]
1651.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Generating malicious RTF documents is a sub-technique of Template Injection (T1221) under the Defense Evasion tactic, primarily targeting Windows. The technique involves modifying the legitimate `*\template` control word within an RTF file to insert a URL pointing to a malicious payload. When the document is opened, the application retrieves and executes the code from the injected remote template, which can be used to deliver exploits or force authentication attempts, often evading static analysis.

1652.name: using embedded OLE Word documents
1652.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may embed payloads within other files to conceal malicious content from defenses. Otherwise seemingly benign files (such as scripts and executables) may be abused to carry and obfuscate malicious payloads and content. In some cases, embedded payloads may also enable adversaries to [Subvert Trust Controls](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1553) by not impacting execution controls such as digital signatures and notarization tickets.(Citation: Sentinel Labs) 

Adversaries may embed payloads in various file formats to hide payloads.(Citation: Microsoft Learn) This is similar to [Steganography](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/003), though does not involve weaving malicious content into specific bytes and patterns related to legitimate digital media formats.(Citation: GitHub PSImage) 

For example, adversaries have been observed embedding payloads within or as an overlay of an otherwise benign binary.(Citation: Securelist Dtrack2) Adversaries have also been observed nesting payloads (such as executables and run-only scripts) inside a file of the same format.(Citation: SentinelLabs reversing run-only applescripts 2021) 

Embedded content may also be used as [Process Injection](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1055) payloads used to infect benign system processes.(Citation: Trend Micro) These embedded then injected payloads may be used as part of the modules of malware designed to provide specific features such as encrypting C2 communications in support of an orchestrator module. For example, an embedded module may be injected into default browsers, allowing adversaries to then communicate via the network.(Citation: Malware Analysis Report ComRAT)
1652.profile: [profile]The entity "using embedded OLE Word documents" is a technique for Defense Evasion and Execution, aligning with the broader MITRE ATT&CK sub-technique T1027.009, "Embedded Payloads." It operates on the Windows platform by embedding malicious payloads within otherwise benign OLE (Object Linking and Embedding) Word document files to conceal execution. This method allows adversaries to deliver and execute code while potentially bypassing static analysis and trust controls, as the malicious content is hidden within a legitimate file structure. The intrusion set APT28 has been associated with related template injection techniques.
1652.profile_without_enhance: [profile]This technique, identified as T1204.002 in the MITRE ATT&CK framework under the User Execution tactic for Windows platforms, involves adversaries delivering malicious Microsoft Word documents containing embedded OLE objects. These objects are used to conceal and execute malicious payloads, often leveraging the legitimate OLE functionality to bypass static security controls that may not flag the document as overtly malicious upon initial inspection.

1653.name: exploiting Adobe Flash vulnerability
1653.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may scan victims for vulnerabilities that can be used during targeting. Vulnerability scans typically check if the configuration of a target host/application (ex: software and version) potentially aligns with the target of a specific exploit the adversary may seek to use.

These scans may also include more broad attempts to [Gather Victim Host Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1592) that can be used to identify more commonly known, exploitable vulnerabilities. Vulnerability scans typically harvest running software and version numbers via server banners, listening ports, or other network artifacts.(Citation: OWASP Vuln Scanning) Information from these scans may reveal opportunities for other forms of reconnaissance (ex: [Search Open Websites/Domains](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1593) or [Search Open Technical Databases](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1596)), establishing operational resources (ex: [Develop Capabilities](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1587) or [Obtain Capabilities](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1588)), and/or initial access (ex: [Exploit Public-Facing Application](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1190)).
1653.profile: [profile]The entity is a specific instance of vulnerability scanning (T1595.002) under the Reconnaissance tactic, targeting Adobe Flash to identify exploitable versions. It involves checking software and version configurations via network artifacts like server banners and listening ports to align with known Flash exploits. This activity is associated with groups like APT28 and can inform subsequent exploitation for initial access or client execution.[/profile]
1653.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "exploiting Adobe Flash vulnerability" is a specific instance of the MITRE ATT&CK technique Exploitation for Client Execution (T1203) under the Initial Access tactic, targeting client-side platforms. This technique involves adversaries exploiting vulnerabilities in Adobe Flash Player, often delivered via malicious documents or web content, to execute arbitrary code on a victim's system. It is commonly associated with threat groups like APT28, APT29, and Lazarus Group.

1654.name: token stealing
1654.profile: [profile]Token stealing, also known as Access Token Manipulation (T1134), is a Privilege Escalation tactic for the Windows platform. It involves using built-in Windows API functions like `DuplicateToken` to copy access tokens from existing processes. This stolen token can then be applied to an existing process via Token Impersonation/Theft (T1134.001) or used to spawn a new process, allowing an adversary to operate under a different user's security context, commonly to escalate from administrator to SYSTEM level privileges. This technique is associated with groups like APT28.[/profile]
1654.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Token stealing is a sub-technique of Access Token Manipulation (T1134) within the Privilege Escalation tactic, primarily for Windows. It involves using built-in Windows API functions like DuplicateToken or DuplicateTokenEx to copy access tokens from existing processes. An adversary, already in a privileged context such as administrator, steals a token to elevate to the SYSTEM level. The stolen token can then be applied to an existing process via Token Impersonation/Theft (T1134.001) or used to spawn a new process with Create Process with Token (T1134.002), enabling actions under the stolen security context and bypassing access controls.

1655.name: hooking
1655.uncertain_mes:
Windows processes often leverage application programming interface (API) functions to perform tasks that require reusable system resources. Windows API functions are typically stored in dynamic-link libraries (DLLs) as exported functions. 

Hooking involves redirecting calls to these functions and can be implemented via:

* **Hooks procedures**, which intercept and execute designated code in response to events such as messages, keystrokes, and mouse inputs. (Citation: Microsoft Hook Overview) (Citation: Elastic Process Injection July 2017)
* **Import address table (IAT) hooking**, which use modifications to a process’s IAT, where pointers to imported API functions are stored. (Citation: Elastic Process Injection July 2017) (Citation: Adlice Software IAT Hooks Oct 2014) (Citation: MWRInfoSecurity Dynamic Hooking 2015)
* **Inline hooking**, which overwrites the first bytes in an API function to redirect code flow. (Citation: Elastic Process Injection July 2017) (Citation: HighTech Bridge Inline Hooking Sept 2011) (Citation: MWRInfoSecurity Dynamic Hooking 2015)

Similar to [Process Injection](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1055), adversaries may use hooking to load and execute malicious code within the context of another process, masking the execution while also allowing access to the process's memory and possibly elevated privileges. Installing hooking mechanisms may also provide Persistence via continuous invocation when the functions are called through normal use.

Malicious hooking mechanisms may also capture API calls that include parameters that reveal user authentication credentials for Credential Access. (Citation: Microsoft TrojanSpy:Win32/Ursnif.gen!I Sept 2017)

Hooking is commonly utilized by [Rootkit](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1014)s to conceal files, processes, Registry keys, and other objects in order to hide malware and associated behaviors. (Citation: Symantec Windows Rootkits)
1655.profile: [profile]Hooking (T1179) is a Defense Evasion and Persistence technique for Windows that redirects API function calls to execute malicious code within another process. It is implemented via hook procedures intercepting system events, Import Address Table (IAT) hooking modifying process IATs, or inline hooking overwriting function bytes. This provides access to process memory, masks execution, and can be used for credential access by capturing API parameters or by rootkits to conceal objects. It has been associated with groups like Turla and APT28.[/profile]
1655.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Hooking, identified as T1179, is a Defense Evasion and Persistence technique primarily targeting the Windows platform. It works by redirecting calls to API functions stored in DLLs through methods like hook procedures (intercepting events), IAT hooking (modifying import address tables), or inline hooking (overwriting function code). This allows adversaries to execute malicious code within another process's context, mask execution, access process memory, and potentially gain elevated privileges. It is also used for Credential Access by capturing API calls with authentication parameters and by rootkits to conceal malicious artifacts.

1656.name: geolocation filtering
1656.profile: [profile]Geolocation Filtering (T1564.010) is a Defense Evasion technique. It involves adversaries restricting their malicious traffic to specific geographic locations, such as by using IP address geolocation to block connections from regions not associated with their target. This helps them blend in with expected traffic and avoid detection by security tools that monitor for anomalous foreign connections. The intrusion set APT28 has been associated with this behavior.
1656.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Geolocation Filtering is a technique adversaries use to restrict malicious activity based on the geographic location of a target system. It operates within the Discovery tactic and is applicable across multiple platforms. The technique involves checking system settings like time zone, keyboard layout, or language via Windows API functions such as `GetLocaleInfoW`, or querying cloud instance metadata for availability zones. Adversaries also use IP geolocation lookup services to infer a host's location, enabling them to avoid infecting systems in specific, non-targeted regions.

1677.name: Microsoft Excel
1677.profile: [profile]Microsoft Excel is a legitimate spreadsheet application that is frequently exploited as an initial infection vector by threat actors. It is notably used by groups like APT28 and TA505, who distribute malicious Excel documents as email attachments or via linked URLs. These documents often contain embedded malware, such as the Get2 downloader, which relies on users enabling macros to execute. The platform is targeted to deliver payloads and initiate further malicious activity.

It is used by threat actors, including TA505, to distribute malicious payloads via attachments or links in emails. These malicious documents often contain embedded downloaders, such as Get2, that lure users into enabling macros to execute the malware. The primary target platform is the Windows operating system, where Excel is used to initiate infection chains.

1678.name: Zero-day Threats
1678.profile: [profile]Zero-day Threats are not a formal MITRE ATT&CK technique but a general category of attack vectors. They involve adversaries exploiting previously unknown software vulnerabilities (zero-days) in applications or systems. This exploitation can be used for various purposes, such as causing a denial of service by crashing the target, as referenced in the sub-technique Application or System Exploitation (T1499.004). Threat actors, including groups like APT28, may monitor threat intelligence reports about their own campaigns to adapt their tactics, including the use of such exploits. The core mechanic is the weaponization of undisclosed vulnerabilities to achieve initial access, privilege escalation, or other tactical objectives before a patch is available.[/profile]
1678.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Zero-day Threats" is a broad attack pattern referring to the exploitation of previously unknown software vulnerabilities. While not a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique, it is a core concept underpinning many techniques, such as T1499.004 (Application or System Exploitation), where adversaries exploit zero-day vulnerabilities to crash systems and cause denial of service. The technical mechanics involve weaponizing undisclosed flaws in applications or operating systems to execute unauthorized code, bypass defenses, or disrupt availability before a patch is available.

1679.name: Active Adversary Pursuit (Hunt) Operations
1679.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may achieve persistence by adding a Registry key to the Active Setup of the local machine. Active Setup is a Windows mechanism that is used to execute programs when a user logs in. The value stored in the Registry key will be executed after a user logs into the computer.(Citation: Klein Active Setup 2010) These programs will be executed under the context of the user and will have the account's associated permissions level. Adversaries may abuse Active Setup by creating a key under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Active Setup\Installed Components\ and setting a malicious value for StubPath. This value will serve as the program that will be executed when a user logs into the computer.(Citation: Mandiant Glyer APT 2010)(Citation: Citizenlab Packrat 2015)(Citation: FireEye CFR Watering Hole 2012)(Citation: SECURELIST Bright Star 2015)(Citation: paloalto Tropic Trooper 2016) Adversaries can abuse these components to execute malware, such as remote access tools, to maintain persistence through system reboots. Adversaries may also use [Masquerading](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1036) to make the Registry entries look as if they are associated with legitimate programs.
1679.profile: [profile]Active Setup is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1547.014 under the Persistence tactic for Windows. It works by creating a malicious Registry key under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Active Setup\Installed Components\ and setting a value for StubPath, which causes the referenced program to execute when a user logs in, often used to maintain persistence with remote access tools and potentially masqueraded as legitimate software. The intrusion set APT28 has been associated with this technique.[/profile]
1679.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Active Adversary Pursuit (Hunt) Operations is a defensive technique not currently in the standard MITRE ATT&CK framework. It is a proactive security operation where defenders actively search for threats within their network to identify and mitigate adversary presence, contrasting with passive monitoring. This involves analyzing logs, endpoint data, and network traffic for anomalies and known adversary Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures (TTPs).

1680.name: Security Product Bypasses
1680.profile: [profile]Security Product Bypasses is a technique adversaries use to evade detection by security software. This can involve disabling or killing security processes, deleting related Registry keys to prevent startup, or using trusted system utilities like mshta.exe to proxy malicious script execution outside of browser security contexts, thereby bypassing application control or whitelisting defenses. The intrusion set APT28 has been associated with this behavior.[/profile]
1680.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Security Product Bypasses is a technique adversaries use to evade detection by security software. It falls under the Defense Evasion tactic. The primary technical mechanic involves abusing trusted system utilities, such as mshta.exe, to execute malicious scripts or HTML Applications (HTA) outside of normal security contexts, thereby bypassing application control or whitelisting solutions. This method exploits the inherent trust and different security context of these utilities to run unauthorized code.

1681.name: Domain Spoofing
1681.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may redirect network traffic to adversary-owned systems by spoofing Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) traffic and acting as a malicious DHCP server on the victim network. By achieving the adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) position, adversaries may collect network communications, including passed credentials, especially those sent over insecure, unencrypted protocols. This may also enable follow-on behaviors such as [Network Sniffing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1040) or [Transmitted Data Manipulation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1565/002). DHCP is based on a client-server model and has two functionalities: a protocol for providing network configuration settings from a DHCP server to a client and a mechanism for allocating network addresses to clients.(Citation: rfc2131) The typical server-client interaction is as follows: 1. The client broadcasts a `DISCOVER` message. 2. The server responds with an `OFFER` message, which includes an available network address. 3. The client broadcasts a `REQUEST` message, which includes the network address offered. 4. The server acknowledges with an `ACK` message and the client receives the network configuration parameters. Adversaries may spoof as a rogue DHCP server on the victim network, from which legitimate hosts may receive malicious network configurations. For example, malware can act as a DHCP server and provide adversary-owned DNS servers to the victimized computers.(Citation: new_rogue_DHCP_serv_malware)(Citation: w32.tidserv.g) Through the malicious network configurations, an adversary may achieve the AiTM position, route client traffic through adversary-controlled systems, and collect information from the client network. DHCPv6 clients can receive network configuration information without being assigned an IP address by sending a INFORMATION-REQUEST (code 11) message to the All_DHCP_Relay_Agents_and_Servers multicast address.(Citation: rfc3315) Adversaries may use their rogue DHCP server to respond to this request message with malicious network configurations. Rather than establishing an AiTM position, adversaries may also abuse DHCP spoofing to perform a DHCP exhaustion attack (i.e, [Service Exhaustion Flood](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1499/002)) by generating many broadcast DISCOVER messages to exhaust a network’s DHCP allocation pool.
1681.profile: [profile]Domain Spoofing, formally MITRE ATT&CK ID T1557.003 (DHCP Spoofing), is a technique under the Collection tactic, applicable to Windows, Linux, and Mac platforms. It involves an adversary operating a rogue DHCP server on a victim network to intercept and redirect traffic. By spoofing DHCP messages (like DISCOVER or INFORMATION-REQUEST), the malicious server provides clients with adversary-controlled DNS settings, achieving an adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) position to collect credentials and communications, particularly from unencrypted protocols. The technique has been associated with intrusion sets like APT28.
1681.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Domain Spoofing, identified as T1672 within the Initial Access tactic, primarily targets email platforms. It involves faking a sender's identity by modifying email headers, such as the FROM field, to make messages appear from a trusted domain. This technique succeeds when the targeted domain lacks or has weak enforcement of email authentication protocols like SPF, DKIM, and DMARC, enabling phishing and impersonation attacks.

1682.name: Espionage
1682.profile: [profile]Espionage is not a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique but a high-level adversarial goal. It is associated with groups like APT28, menuPass, RocketKitten, and Turla. These groups employ techniques such as abusing software deployment tools (T1072) for lateral movement and remote execution, exfiltrating data over C2 channels (T1041), and using custom archival methods (T1560.003) to compress or encrypt stolen data prior to exfiltration.[/profile]
1682.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Espionage is a broad adversarial goal, not a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique, and therefore lacks a standard T-ID and Tactic. The retrieved information describes related techniques for achieving espionage objectives: adversaries may use centralized software deployment tools like SCCM or AWS Systems Manager for lateral movement and remote code execution (T1072), exfiltrate stolen data over existing command and control channels (T1041), and compress or encrypt collected data using custom archival methods prior to exfiltration (T1560.003). These technical mechanics are employed by various threat groups including Mustang Panda, Lazarus Group, and Sandworm Team.

1683.name: Tactics
1683.profile: [profile]The entity "Tactics" is a core concept in the MITRE ATT&CK framework, representing the adversary's tactical goal during an operation, such as initial access or exfiltration. It is directly linked to intrusion sets like APT28, which employ these tactics to structure their campaigns. Retrieved information, while referencing specific techniques like database information mining (T1213.006), multilayer encryption (T1079), and multiband communication (T1026), pertains to implementation techniques and procedures, not the tactical goal itself. Therefore, the profile is defined by its role as a high-level objective category within the cyber kill chain.[/profile]
1683.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Tactics" is a high-level concept in the MITRE ATT&CK framework, representing the adversary's tactical goals or objectives during an attack, such as Initial Access, Execution, or Exfiltration. It does not correspond to a specific technique ID like TXXXX. The provided retrieved information describes specific techniques (e.g., T1213.006 for database information collection, T1079 for multilayer encryption, T1026 for multiband communication) but these are distinct from the general "Tactics" entity itself, which serves as an organizational category for these techniques.

1684.name: Create Fictitious Names
1684.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may gather employee names that can be used during targeting. Employee names be used to derive email addresses as well as to help guide other reconnaissance efforts and/or craft more-believable lures.

Adversaries may easily gather employee names, since they may be readily available and exposed via online or other accessible data sets (ex: [Social Media](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1593/001) or [Search Victim-Owned Websites](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1594)).(Citation: OPM Leak) Gathering this information may reveal opportunities for other forms of reconnaissance (ex: [Search Open Websites/Domains](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1593) or [Phishing for Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1598)), establishing operational resources (ex: [Compromise Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1586)), and/or initial access (ex: [Phishing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566) or [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078)).
1684.profile: [profile]The technique "Create Fictitious Names" is likely T1589.003 "Employee Names" under the Reconnaissance tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It involves adversaries gathering employee names from accessible data sets like social media or victim-owned websites. This information is used to derive email addresses, guide further reconnaissance, and craft believable lures for subsequent attacks such as phishing or establishing valid accounts. Groups like Silent Librarian, Sandworm Team, and Kimsuky have been associated with this technique.
1684.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Create Fictitious Names is a technique within the Reconnaissance tactic, used across multiple platforms. Adversaries generate fake identities or personas, distinct from impersonating real individuals, to build credible online presences for social engineering. This involves developing fictitious profiles on social media, email services, or other platforms, complete with fabricated personal details, photos, and social networks, to establish trust and facilitate operations like spearphishing.

1685.name: Subtle Modification of Country Code
1685.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may modify code signing policies to enable execution of unsigned or self-signed code. Code signing provides a level of authenticity on a program from a developer and a guarantee that the program has not been tampered with. Security controls can include enforcement mechanisms to ensure that only valid, signed code can be run on an operating system. Some of these security controls may be enabled by default, such as Driver Signature Enforcement (DSE) on Windows or System Integrity Protection (SIP) on macOS.(Citation: Microsoft DSE June 2017)(Citation: Apple Disable SIP) Other such controls may be disabled by default but are configurable through application controls, such as only allowing signed Dynamic-Link Libraries (DLLs) to execute on a system. Since it can be useful for developers to modify default signature enforcement policies during the development and testing of applications, disabling of these features may be possible with elevated permissions.(Citation: Microsoft Unsigned Driver Apr 2017)(Citation: Apple Disable SIP) Adversaries may modify code signing policies in a number of ways, including through use of command-line or GUI utilities, [Modify Registry](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1112), rebooting the computer in a debug/recovery mode, or by altering the value of variables in kernel memory.(Citation: Microsoft TESTSIGNING Feb 2021)(Citation: Apple Disable SIP)(Citation: FireEye HIKIT Rootkit Part 2)(Citation: GitHub Turla Driver Loader) Examples of commands that can modify the code signing policy of a system include bcdedit.exe -set TESTSIGNING ON on Windows and csrutil disable on macOS.(Citation: Microsoft TESTSIGNING Feb 2021)(Citation: Apple Disable SIP) Depending on the implementation, successful modification of a signing policy may require reboot of the compromised system. Additionally, some implementations can introduce visible artifacts for the user (ex: a watermark in the corner of the screen stating the system is in Test Mode). Adversaries may attempt to remove such artifacts.(Citation: F-Secure BlackEnergy 2014) To gain access to kernel memory to modify variables related to signature checks, such as modifying g_CiOptions to disable Driver Signature Enforcement, adversaries may conduct [Exploitation for Privilege Escalation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1068) using a signed, but vulnerable driver.(Citation: Unit42 AcidBox June 2020)(Citation: GitHub Turla Driver Loader)
1685.profile: [profile]The entity is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1553.006 "Code Signing Policy Modification", a Defense Evasion tactic used on Windows and macOS systems. It involves modifying system policies to allow execution of unsigned or self-signed code. Specific technical mechanics include using commands like `bcdedit.exe -set TESTSIGNING ON` on Windows or `csrutil disable` on macOS, modifying the Windows Registry, booting into debug/recovery modes, or altering kernel memory variables like `g_CiOptions` to disable Driver Signature Enforcement, which may require a system reboot. It has been associated with threat groups like APT39 and Turla.[/profile]
1685.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Subtle Modification of Country Code is a technique for defense evasion. It involves adversaries altering the country code field in system files, registry keys, or other configuration data to misrepresent the geographic origin of malware or malicious infrastructure. This subtle change can bypass security controls that filter or block traffic based on country codes, aiding in the evasion of network-based detection and attribution efforts.

1686.name: Masquerade as Legitimate Infrastructure
1686.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may reveal credentials of accounts that have disabled Kerberos preauthentication by [Password Cracking](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1110/002) Kerberos messages.(Citation: Harmj0y Roasting AS-REPs Jan 2017) 

Preauthentication offers protection against offline [Password Cracking](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1110/002). When enabled, a user requesting access to a resource initiates communication with the Domain Controller (DC) by sending an Authentication Server Request (AS-REQ) message with a timestamp that is encrypted with the hash of their password. If and only if the DC is able to successfully decrypt the timestamp with the hash of the user’s password, it will then send an Authentication Server Response (AS-REP) message that contains the Ticket Granting Ticket (TGT) to the user. Part of the AS-REP message is signed with the user’s password.(Citation: Microsoft Kerberos Preauth 2014)

For each account found without preauthentication, an adversary may send an AS-REQ message without the encrypted timestamp and receive an AS-REP message with TGT data which may be encrypted with an insecure algorithm such as RC4. The recovered encrypted data may be vulnerable to offline [Password Cracking](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1110/002) attacks similarly to [Kerberoasting](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1558/003) and expose plaintext credentials. (Citation: Harmj0y Roasting AS-REPs Jan 2017)(Citation: Stealthbits Cracking AS-REP Roasting Jun 2019) 

An account registered to a domain, with or without special privileges, can be abused to list all domain accounts that have preauthentication disabled by utilizing Windows tools like [PowerShell](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001) with an LDAP filter. Alternatively, the adversary may send an AS-REQ message for each user. If the DC responds without errors, the account does not require preauthentication and the AS-REP message will already contain the encrypted data. (Citation: Harmj0y Roasting AS-REPs Jan 2017)(Citation: Stealthbits Cracking AS-REP Roasting Jun 2019)

Cracked hashes may enable [Persistence](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0003), [Privilege Escalation](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0004), and [Lateral Movement](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0008) via access to [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078).(Citation: SANS Attacking Kerberos Nov 2014)
1686.profile: [profile]The entity "Masquerade as Legitimate Infrastructure" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the input, the provided data describes the technique "AS-REP Roasting" (ID: T1558.004) under the Credential Access tactic, targeting Windows platforms. This technique involves sending Kerberos AS-REQ messages to domain accounts with preauthentication disabled to receive AS-REP responses containing TGT data encrypted with the user's password hash, which can then be cracked offline. The APT28 intrusion-set is associated with this behavior.[/profile]
1686.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Masquerade as Legitimate Infrastructure is a technique within the Resource Development tactic, used across multiple platforms. Adversaries acquire or compromise infrastructure—such as domains, servers, or cloud services—that closely resembles or impersonates trusted entities to stage and launch operations. This masquerading helps malicious activities blend with normal traffic, evading detection by appearing as contact with high-reputation sites or services, and is often used to support phishing campaigns or proxy redirection.

1687.name: Similar Street Address Scheme
1687.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may bridge network boundaries by modifying a network device’s Network Address Translation (NAT) configuration. Malicious modifications to NAT may enable an adversary to bypass restrictions on traffic routing that otherwise separate trusted and untrusted networks.

Network devices such as routers and firewalls that connect multiple networks together may implement NAT during the process of passing packets between networks. When performing NAT, the network device will rewrite the source and/or destination addresses of the IP address header. Some network designs require NAT for the packets to cross the border device.  A typical example of this is environments where internal networks make use of non-Internet routable addresses.(Citation: RFC1918)

When an adversary gains control of a network boundary device, they may modify NAT configurations to send traffic between two separated networks, or to obscure their activities.  In network designs that require NAT to function, such modifications enable the adversary to overcome inherent routing limitations that would normally prevent them from accessing protected systems behind the border device.  In network designs that do not require NAT, adversaries may use address translation to further obscure their activities, as changing the addresses of packets that traverse a network boundary device can make monitoring data transmissions more challenging for defenders.  

Adversaries may use [Patch System Image](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1601/001) to change the operating system of a network device, implementing their own custom NAT mechanisms to further obscure their activities.
1687.profile: [profile]Similar Street Address Scheme, also known as Network Address Translation Traversal and identified as T1599.001, is a Defense Evasion technique used on network devices. It involves an adversary gaining control of a boundary device like a router or firewall to maliciously modify its NAT configuration. This modification allows the adversary to bypass routing restrictions that separate networks, enabling unauthorized traffic flow between them or obscuring their activities by rewriting packet IP headers. The intrusion set APT28 has been associated with this behavior.[/profile]
1687.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Similar Street Address Scheme" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the provided context, it appears to be a reconnaissance method where adversaries gather a victim's IP address information. This data, which can be collected through active scanning or phishing, reveals details like organizational size, physical location, and ISP to enable further targeting, reconnaissance, or initial access operations.

1688.name: Registering Seven Domains
1688.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may acquire domains that can be used during targeting. Domain names are the human readable names used to represent one or more IP addresses. They can be purchased or, in some cases, acquired for free.

Adversaries may use acquired domains for a variety of purposes, including for [Phishing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566), [Drive-by Compromise](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1189), and Command and Control.(Citation: CISA MSS Sep 2020) Adversaries may choose domains that are similar to legitimate domains, including through use of homoglyphs or use of a different top-level domain (TLD).(Citation: FireEye APT28)(Citation: PaypalScam) Typosquatting may be used to aid in delivery of payloads via [Drive-by Compromise](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1189). Adversaries may also use internationalized domain names (IDNs) and different character sets (e.g. Cyrillic, Greek, etc.) to execute "IDN homograph attacks," creating visually similar lookalike domains used to deliver malware to victim machines.(Citation: CISA IDN ST05-016)(Citation: tt_httrack_fake_domains)(Citation: tt_obliqueRAT)(Citation: httrack_unhcr)(Citation: lazgroup_idn_phishing)

Different URIs/URLs may also be dynamically generated to uniquely serve malicious content to victims (including one-time, single use domain names).(Citation: iOS URL Scheme)(Citation: URI)(Citation: URI Use)(Citation: URI Unique)

Adversaries may also acquire and repurpose expired domains, which may be potentially already allowlisted/trusted by defenders based on an existing reputation/history.(Citation: Categorisation_not_boundary)(Citation: Domain_Steal_CC)(Citation: Redirectors_Domain_Fronting)(Citation: bypass_webproxy_filtering)

Domain registrars each maintain a publicly viewable database that displays contact information for every registered domain. Private WHOIS services display alternative information, such as their own company data, rather than the owner of the domain. Adversaries may use such private WHOIS services to obscure information about who owns a purchased domain. Adversaries may further interrupt efforts to track their infrastructure by using varied registration information and purchasing domains with different domain registrars.(Citation: Mandiant APT1)

In addition to legitimately purchasing a domain, an adversary may register a new domain in a compromised environment. For example, in AWS environments, adversaries may leverage the Route53 domain service to register a domain and create hosted zones pointing to resources of the threat actor’s choosing.(Citation: Invictus IR DangerDev 2024)
1688.profile: [profile]The technique "Acquire Infrastructure: Domains" is identified as MITRE ATT&CK ID T1583.001 under the Resource Development tactic. It operates across multiple platforms. Adversaries acquire domains through purchase, free services, or by registering them within compromised environments like AWS Route53. They employ techniques such as typosquatting, homoglyphs, and IDN homograph attacks to create lookalike domains for phishing, drive-by compromises, and command and control. To obscure ownership, they use private WHOIS services, varied registration information, and multiple registrars, and may also repurpose expired domains to leverage existing trust. Groups like APT28 are associated with this technique.[/profile]
1688.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Registering Seven Domains is a technique where adversaries acquire multiple domain names to establish infrastructure for malicious operations. This falls under the Resource Development tactic (ID: T1583.001) and is platform-agnostic. The technical mechanics involve purchasing or registering domains, often using typosquatting, homoglyphs, or different top-level domains to create lookalike domains for phishing, drive-by compromises, or command and control. Adversaries may use private WHOIS services and varied registrars to obscure ownership, and can repurpose expired domains to leverage existing trust.

These attacks are executed by threat actors like APT28, who may use them to crash applications and cause denial of service, or to deploy malware such as the SUNBURST backdoor, which uses junk data in C2 traffic to evade detection. The exploitation can lead to data destruction, firmware corruption, and persistent system compromise.

1725.name: compromised incoming mail DNS settings
1725.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may communicate using application layer protocols associated with electronic mail delivery to avoid detection/network filtering by blending in with existing traffic. Commands to the remote system, and often the results of those commands, will be embedded within the protocol traffic between the client and server. 

Protocols such as SMTP/S, POP3/S, and IMAP that carry electronic mail may be very common in environments.  Packets produced from these protocols may have many fields and headers in which data can be concealed. Data could also be concealed within the email messages themselves. An adversary may abuse these protocols to communicate with systems under their control within a victim network while also mimicking normal, expected traffic.(Citation: FireEye APT28)
1725.profile: [profile]The entity "compromised incoming mail DNS settings" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. The provided information conflates two distinct concepts: the use of mail protocols (SMTP/S, POP3/S, IMAP) for command and control, which aligns with MITRE ID T1071.003 (Application Layer Protocol: Mail Protocols) under the Command and Control tactic, and reconnaissance of DNS records (including MX records for mail servers) as seen in T1590.002 (Gather Victim Host Information: DNS). The technical mechanics involve adversaries abusing common email protocols to embed malicious commands and data within standard traffic fields and headers to blend in and avoid detection. Groups like APT28 have been associated with this mail protocol technique.[/profile]
1725.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The technique "compromised incoming mail DNS settings" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK entry. Based on the retrieved context, it likely involves an adversary gathering or manipulating DNS records, specifically MX (Mail Exchange) records, to understand or potentially redirect a target's incoming email traffic as part of reconnaissance or initial access preparation. This action is a component of broader adversary activities focused on DNS information gathering for targeting.

The malware is linked to broader campaigns like Aurora Panda and APT31, and it shares infrastructure or TTPs with loaders such as Pirpi and AsyncRAT, which are used to deliver remote access trojans like the 9002 RAT. This malware exploits specific vulnerabilities in Adobe Flash Player, including the 'SWF' File Remote Memory Corruption Vulnerability (CVE-2011-0609, CVE-2011-0611). Its primary target platform is systems running Adobe Flash Player.

1727.name: blocking emails
1727.uncertain_mes: An adversary may attempt to block indicators or events typically captured by sensors from being gathered and analyzed. This could include maliciously redirecting(Citation: Microsoft Lamin Sept 2017) or even disabling host-based sensors, such as Event Tracing for Windows (ETW)(Citation: Microsoft About Event Tracing 2018), by tampering settings that control the collection and flow of event telemetry.(Citation: Medium Event Tracing Tampering 2018) These settings may be stored on the system in configuration files and/or in the Registry as well as being accessible via administrative utilities such as [PowerShell](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001) or [Windows Management Instrumentation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1047). For example, adversaries may modify the `File` value in HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\EventLog\Security to hide their malicious actions in a new or different .evtx log file. This action does not require a system reboot and takes effect immediately.(Citation: disable_win_evt_logging) ETW interruption can be achieved multiple ways, however most directly by defining conditions using the [PowerShell](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001) Set-EtwTraceProvider cmdlet or by interfacing directly with the Registry to make alterations. In the case of network-based reporting of indicators, an adversary may block traffic associated with reporting to prevent central analysis. This may be accomplished by many means, such as stopping a local process responsible for forwarding telemetry and/or creating a host-based firewall rule to block traffic to specific hosts responsible for aggregating events, such as security information and event management (SIEM) products. In Linux environments, adversaries may disable or reconfigure log processing tools such as syslog or nxlog to inhibit detection and monitoring capabilities to facilitate follow on behaviors. (Citation: LemonDuck) ESXi also leverages syslog, which can be reconfigured via commands such as `esxcli system syslog config set` and `esxcli system syslog config reload`.(Citation: Google Cloud Threat Intelligence ESXi VIBs 2022)(Citation: Broadcom Configuring syslog on ESXi)
1727.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique "Indicator Blocking" (ID: T1562.006) under the Defense Evasion tactic, applicable to Windows and Linux platforms. It involves tampering with event telemetry settings to prevent sensor data collection, such as modifying Windows Registry keys (e.g., HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\EventLog\Security) to redirect logs, using PowerShell cmdlets like Set-EtwTraceProvider to disrupt Event Tracing for Windows (ETW), or reconfiguring syslog in Linux/ESXi via commands like esxcli system syslog config set. Adversaries may also block network traffic to security information and event management (SIEM) systems using host-based firewall rules. APT28 is associated with this technique.
1727.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "blocking emails" is a technique where adversaries prevent the delivery or visibility of emails, often to hide malicious activity or evade detection. This can be achieved by creating or modifying email inbox rules to automatically move or delete messages based on keywords, or by using organization-wide transport rules in systems like Microsoft Exchange to filter all incoming mail. Adversaries may employ PowerShell cmdlets such as New-InboxRule or Set-InboxRule to implement these rules, targeting emails containing security alerts, phishing responses, or command-and-control communications to impair defensive visibility.

Its infrastructure and technical behaviors are centered around this impersonation and delivery method to compromise victims.

1733.name: Audio Capture
1733.uncertain_mes:
An adversary can leverage a computer's peripheral devices (e.g., microphones and webcams) or applications (e.g., voice and video call services) to capture audio recordings for the purpose of listening into sensitive conversations to gather information.(Citation: ESET Attor Oct 2019)

Malware or scripts may be used to interact with the devices through an available API provided by the operating system or an application to capture audio. Audio files may be written to disk and exfiltrated later.
1733.profile: [profile]Audio Capture is a MITRE ATT&CK technique with ID T1123 under the Collection tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It involves adversaries using malware or scripts to interact with a computer's microphone or voice/video call applications via available operating system or application APIs to record audio. The captured audio files are typically written to disk for later exfiltration, enabling the gathering of information from sensitive conversations. This technique has been associated with threat groups like APT37 and APT28.[/profile]

1735.name: 隐藏图标
1735.profile: [profile]The entity "隐藏图标" (Hide Icon) is a technique for Defense Evasion, aligning with MITRE ATT&CK sub-technique T1564.003 (Hidden Window) under Tactic T1564 (Hide Artifacts), applicable to Windows and macOS platforms. It involves manipulating application properties to prevent icons from appearing in user interfaces like the Dock or taskbar. On macOS, adversaries can set the `apple.awt.UIElement` tag in a plist file for Java applications. On Windows, methods include using PowerShell with the `-WindowStyle Hidden` parameter or editing the Windows Registry to position windows off-screen. This technique is used by groups including APT28, Fin7, and Kimsuky to conceal malicious processes from users.
1735.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "隐藏图标" (Hide Icon) is a technique for defense evasion, identified as T1564.005 in the MITRE ATT&CK framework, applicable to the macOS and Linux platforms. It works by preventing an application's icon from appearing in the user interface, such as the macOS Dock or Linux system tray, to conceal malicious processes. This is often achieved by setting the `apple.awt.UIElement` key to `TRUE` in a property list (plist) configuration file on macOS.

1736.name: 持久化重启
1736.profile: [profile]The entity "持久化重启" aligns with MITRE ATT&CK technique T1164 "Re-opened Applications". It falls under the Persistence tactic and targets the macOS platform. This technique involves adversaries modifying specific property list files, such as ~/Library/Preferences/com.apple.loginwindow.plist, to add malicious executables. 1755.name: Base64 encoded data with random prefix
1755.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may encrypt or encode files to obfuscate strings, bytes, and other specific patterns to impede detection. Encrypting and/or encoding file content aims to conceal malicious artifacts within a file used in an intrusion. Many other techniques, such as [Software Packing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/002), [Steganography](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/003), and [Embedded Payloads](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/009), share this same broad objective. Encrypting and/or encoding files could lead to a lapse in detection of static signatures, only for this malicious content to be revealed (i.e., [Deobfuscate/Decode Files or Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1140)) at the time of execution/use.

This type of file obfuscation can be applied to many file artifacts present on victim hosts, such as malware log/configuration and payload files.(Citation: File obfuscation) Files can be encrypted with a hardcoded or user-supplied key, as well as otherwise obfuscated using standard encoding schemes such as Base64.

The entire content of a file may be obfuscated, or just specific functions or values (such as C2 addresses). Encryption and encoding may also be applied in redundant layers for additional protection.

For example, adversaries may abuse password-protected Word documents or self-extracting (SFX) archives as a method of encrypting/encoding a file such as a [Phishing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566) payload. These files typically function by attaching the intended archived content to a decompressor stub that is executed when the file is invoked (e.g., [User Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204)).(Citation: SFX - Encrypted/Encoded File) 

Adversaries may also abuse file-specific as well as custom encoding schemes. For example, Byte Order Mark (BOM) headers in text files may be abused to manipulate and obfuscate file content until [Command and Scripting Interpreter](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059) execution.

This user action will typically be observed as follow-on behavior from [Spearphishing Attachment](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001). Adversaries may use several types of files that require a user to execute them, including .doc, .pdf, .xls, .rtf, .scr, .exe, .lnk, .pif, .cpl, .reg, and .iso.(Citation: Mandiant Trojanized Windows 10)

Adversaries may employ various forms of [Masquerading](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1036) and [Obfuscated Files or Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027) to increase the likelihood that a user will open and successfully execute a malicious file. These methods may include using a familiar naming convention and/or password protecting the file and supplying instructions to a user on how to open it.(Citation: Password Protected Word Docs) 

While [Malicious File](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002) frequently occurs shortly after Initial Access it may occur at other phases of an intrusion, such as when an adversary places a file in a shared directory or on a user's desktop hoping that a user will click on it. This activity may also be seen shortly after [Internal Spearphishing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1534).
1793.profile: [profile]Malicious File, designated as T1204.002 under the Execution tactic, primarily targets Windows platforms. This technique relies on user interaction to open a malicious file, such as .doc, .pdf, .xls, .rtf, .scr, .exe, .lnk, .pif, .cpl, .reg, or .iso, often delivered via spearphishing attachments. Adversaries increase success by using masquerading, familiar naming conventions, password protection with instructions, or placing files in shared directories. It is frequently employed by numerous threat groups including APT28, APT29, and Lazarus Group.[/profile]
1793.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Malicious Documents is a technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, categorized under the Execution tactic (T1204.002) and applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves adversaries delivering and executing malicious code by tricking users into opening specially crafted document files, such as .doc, .pdf, .xls, and .rtf. These documents often employ social engineering, masquerading, and obfuscation to appear legitimate and may contain embedded exploits or malicious macros to achieve initial access or code execution, frequently following spearphishing campaigns.

1794.name: NetBIOS Name Service (NBT-NS) poisoning
1794.uncertain_mes:
Link-Local Multicast Name Resolution (LLMNR) and NetBIOS Name Service (NBT-NS) are Microsoft Windows components that serve as alternate methods of host identification. LLMNR is based upon the Domain Name System (DNS) format and allows hosts on the same local link to perform name resolution for other hosts. NBT-NS identifies systems on a local network by their NetBIOS name. (Citation: Wikipedia LLMNR) (Citation: TechNet NetBIOS)

Adversaries can spoof an authoritative source for name resolution on a victim network by responding to LLMNR (UDP 5355)/NBT-NS (UDP 137) traffic as if they know the identity of the requested host, effectively poisoning the service so that the victims will communicate with the adversary controlled system. If the requested host belongs to a resource that requires identification/authentication, the username and NTLMv2 hash will then be sent to the adversary controlled system. The adversary can then collect the hash information sent over the wire through tools that monitor the ports for traffic or through [Network Sniffing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1040) and crack the hashes offline through [Brute Force](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1110) to obtain the plaintext passwords. In some cases where an adversary has access to a system that is in the authentication path between systems or when automated scans that use credentials attempt to authenticate to an adversary controlled system, the NTLMv2 hashes can be intercepted and relayed to access and execute code against a target system. The relay step can happen in conjunction with poisoning but may also be independent of it. (Citation: byt3bl33d3r NTLM Relaying)(Citation: Secure Ideas SMB Relay)

Several tools exist that can be used to poison name services within local networks such as NBNSpoof, Metasploit, and [Responder](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0174). (Citation: GitHub NBNSpoof) (Citation: Rapid7 LLMNR Spoofer) (Citation: GitHub Responder)
1794.profile: [profile]NetBIOS Name Service (NBT-NS) poisoning, also known as LLMNR/NBT-NS poisoning and relay (MITRE ID T1557.001), is a Credential Access and Lateral Movement technique on Windows platforms. It works by spoofing responses to LLMNR (UDP 5355) or NBT-NS (UDP 137) broadcast queries, redirecting victims to an adversary-controlled system to capture NTLMv1/v2 authentication hashes. These hashes can be cracked offline or relayed via protocols like SMB or LDAP to authenticate to and execute code on other systems, using tools like Responder, Metasploit, or NBNSpoof. It has been associated with groups like APT28, Lazarus Group, and Wizard Spider.[/profile]
1794.profile_without_enhance: [profile]NetBIOS Name Service (NBT-NS) poisoning, corresponding to MITRE ATT&CK technique T1557.001, is a Credential Access and Collection tactic primarily targeting Windows platforms. It involves an adversary spoofing an authoritative source by responding to NBT-NS (UDP 137) traffic, poisoning the service to redirect victim communication to a controlled system. This technique captures authentication materials, specifically usernames and NTLMv1/v2 hashes, which can be collected via network sniffing and later cracked offline or relayed to other systems to execute code. Tools like Responder, NBNSpoof, and Metasploit are commonly used to perform this poisoning.

1795.name: Privilege escalation
1795.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may exploit software vulnerabilities in an attempt to elevate privileges. Exploitation of a software vulnerability occurs when an adversary takes advantage of a programming error in a program, service, or within the operating system software or kernel itself to execute adversary-controlled code. Security constructs such as permission levels will often hinder access to information and use of certain techniques, so adversaries will likely need to perform privilege escalation to include use of software exploitation to circumvent those restrictions.

When initially gaining access to a system, an adversary may be operating within a lower privileged process which will prevent them from accessing certain resources on the system. Vulnerabilities may exist, usually in operating system components and software commonly running at higher permissions, that can be exploited to gain higher levels of access on the system. This could enable someone to move from unprivileged or user level permissions to SYSTEM or root permissions depending on the component that is vulnerable. This could also enable an adversary to move from a virtualized environment, such as within a virtual machine or container, onto the underlying host. This may be a necessary step for an adversary compromising an endpoint system that has been properly configured and limits other privilege escalation methods.

Adversaries may bring a signed vulnerable driver onto a compromised machine so that they can exploit the vulnerability to execute code in kernel mode. This process is sometimes referred to as Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver (BYOVD).(Citation: ESET InvisiMole June 2020)(Citation: Unit42 AcidBox June 2020) Adversaries may include the vulnerable driver with files delivered during Initial Access or download it to a compromised system via [Ingress Tool Transfer](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1105) or [Lateral Tool Transfer](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1570).
1795.profile: [profile]Exploitation for Privilege Escalation (T1068) is a Privilege Escalation technique used across multiple platforms. It involves exploiting software vulnerabilities, including programming errors in OS components or high-privilege software, to execute adversary-controlled code and elevate permissions from user to SYSTEM/root or escape virtualized environments. A specific sub-technique is Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver (BYOVD), where a signed vulnerable driver is introduced to the system and exploited to achieve kernel-mode execution.
1795.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Privilege Escalation is a core adversarial objective, not a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique with a T-ID. It is a goal achieved through various methods, including exploiting software vulnerabilities (T1068) to execute code from user to SYSTEM/root permissions or from a container to the host, sometimes via Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver (BYOVD). Adversaries also abuse credentials from local (T1078.003) or domain accounts (T1078.002), often obtained via dumping or reuse, to elevate access and bypass security restrictions.

1796.name: Lateral movement
1796.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may transfer tools or other files between systems in a compromised environment. Once brought into the victim environment (i.e., [Ingress Tool Transfer](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1105)) files may then be copied from one system to another to stage adversary tools or other files over the course of an operation.

Adversaries may copy files between internal victim systems to support lateral movement using inherent file sharing protocols such as file sharing over [SMB/Windows Admin Shares](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002) to connected network shares or with authenticated connections via [Remote Desktop Protocol](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/001).(Citation: Unit42 LockerGoga 2019)

Files can also be transferred using native or otherwise present tools on the victim system, such as scp, rsync, curl, sftp, and [ftp](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0095). In some cases, adversaries may be able to leverage [Web Service](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1102)s such as Dropbox or OneDrive to copy files from one machine to another via shared, automatically synced folders.(Citation: Dropbox Malware Sync)
1796.profile: [profile]Lateral Tool Transfer is identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1570 under the Lateral Movement tactic, applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. This technique involves transferring files between compromised systems to stage tools for further operations. Adversaries achieve this by using native file sharing protocols like SMB/Windows Admin Shares and Remote Desktop Protocol, or by leveraging built-in system tools such as scp, rsync, curl, sftp, and ftp. In some instances, web services like Dropbox or OneDrive are abused to synchronize files across machines via shared folders. This activity is associated with numerous threat groups including APT41, Sandworm Team, and Wizard Spider.[profile]
1796.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Lateral movement is a broad adversarial tactic (not a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique ID) used after initial compromise to navigate through a network. It involves techniques like lateral tool transfer (T1570), where adversaries copy files between systems using protocols like SMB or tools like scp and rsync, and abuse of local accounts (T1078.003) via credential reuse to access other machines. This activity supports further exploitation and data exfiltration across the compromised environment.

1797.name: Credential Harvesting
1797.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may use credentials obtained from breach dumps of unrelated accounts to gain access to target accounts through credential overlap. Occasionally, large numbers of username and password pairs are dumped online when a website or service is compromised and the user account credentials accessed. The information may be useful to an adversary attempting to compromise accounts by taking advantage of the tendency for users to use the same passwords across personal and business accounts.

Credential stuffing is a risky option because it could cause numerous authentication failures and account lockouts, depending on the organization's login failure policies.

Typically, management services over commonly used ports are used when stuffing credentials. Commonly targeted services include the following:

* SSH (22/TCP)
* Telnet (23/TCP)
* FTP (21/TCP)
* NetBIOS / SMB / Samba (139/TCP & 445/TCP)
* LDAP (389/TCP)
* Kerberos (88/TCP)
* RDP / Terminal Services (3389/TCP)
* HTTP/HTTP Management Services (80/TCP & 443/TCP)
* MSSQL (1433/TCP)
* Oracle (1521/TCP)
* MySQL (3306/TCP)
* VNC (5900/TCP)

In addition to management services, adversaries may "target single sign-on (SSO) and cloud-based applications utilizing federated authentication protocols," as well as externally facing email applications, such as Office 365.(Citation: US-CERT TA18-068A 2018)
1797.profile: [profile]Credential Harvesting is a technique where adversaries use credentials from unrelated breach dumps to access target accounts by exploiting password reuse across services. It is mapped to MITRE ATT&CK ID T1110.004 under the Credential Access tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. The technique involves automated attempts against management services on common ports like SSH (22/TCP), RDP (3389/TCP), and HTTP/HTTPS (80/TCP, 443/TCP), as well as targeting SSO, cloud applications, and external email services such as Office 365, which risks triggering authentication failures and account lockouts. Groups like APT29, APT28, Greenbug, and OilRig are associated with this activity.[/profile]
1797.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Credential Harvesting, identified as T1587.001 within the MITRE ATT&CK framework under the Resource Development tactic, is a preparatory technique where adversaries create or acquire fake login portals to collect authentication credentials from victims. This is distinct from post-compromise credential dumping. The technique involves deploying deceptive websites or emails that mimic legitimate services, tricking users into submitting their usernames and passwords, which are then captured by the attacker. This stolen information is subsequently used for initial access or further attacks.

1798.name: Cyber espionage
1798.profile: [profile]Cyber espionage is a high-level adversarial goal rather than a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique, and is not assigned a standard T-ID or Tactic. It is the overarching objective of threat groups like APT28 and APT3, who conduct intelligence-gathering operations. The activity involves sustained campaigns to infiltrate networks and exfiltrate sensitive data, often leveraging various subordinate techniques such as obtaining capabilities (T1588) to acquire tools and searching threat vendor data (T1681) to monitor and adapt to public disclosures of their own operations.[/profile]
1798.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Cyber espionage" is not a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique but a broad adversarial objective. Based on the retrieved context, related activities can include obtaining capabilities such as malware or exploits from third parties (T1588) and monitoring threat intelligence reports about their own campaigns to adapt operations and avoid detection (T1681).

1799.name: Gamefish
1799.profile: [profile]Gamefish, also known as GAMEFISH, is a first-stage malware associated with the APT28 intrusion set. It is used in spearphishing campaigns targeting NATO, the Middle East, Central Asia, and regions further east, and it precedes the deployment of second-stage payloads like the X-AGENT RAT. Its operational security is considered good, and it is part of broader activity subsets involving other malware families like Zebrocy and SPLM.
1799.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Gamefish, also known as GAMEFISH, is a first-stage malware associated with APT28. It is used in spearphishing campaigns targeting NATO, the Middle East, Central Asia, and East Asia. Its primary function is to act as an initial access tool, often followed by second-stage payloads like the X-AGENT RAT, which performs keylogging and file extraction. The malware's operational security is noted as good, and it is part of broader campaign subsets that include other malware families like Zebrocy and SPLM.

1801.name: py2exe
1801.profile: [profile]Py2Exe is a tool used to convert Python scripts into standalone Windows executables. It is utilized by threat actors such as APT28 and groups like UPS and Violin Panda to package malware like Xserver and Skygofree. The tool enables Python-based malicious modules, such as those for Skype synchronization, to run on Windows systems without requiring a pre-installed Python environment, facilitating deployment and evasion.

It was deployed between 2013 and 2015, using decoy documents and droppers like serviceinstallx32.exe for initial access, and employs persistence mechanisms such as registry keys. 1813.name: bootkit
1813.profile: [profile]Bootkit is a type of malware that infects the Master Boot Record (MBR). It is associated with APT groups APT17 and APT28. Specific variants include Rovnix and Downdelph. Key technical behaviors involve hooking low-level system interrupts (INT 13h) and system files (bootmgr, ACPI.sys) to decrypt and execute malicious code before the operating system loads, and subsequently injecting a user-mode component into processes like explorer.exe. It primarily targets the Windows platform.
1813.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Bootkit is a type of malware that operates at the boot or kernel level to gain persistence and stealth. It is associated with the Rovnix bootkit variant and the Downdelph bootkit, which is attributed to APT28. Key technical behaviors include hooking low-level system interrupts like INT 13h, decrypting and executing code from the Master Boot Record (MBR) or physical memory addresses (e.g., 0x97C00), hooking critical system components like bootmgr and ACPI.sys, and injecting a user-mode component into processes like explorer.exe to load further payloads such as Downdelph. Its primary target is the Windows platform's boot sequence and system drivers.

1817.name: Windows rootkits
1817.profile: [profile]Windows Rootkits, corresponding to MITRE ATT&CK technique T1014, fall under the Defense Evasion tactic and target Windows platforms. They are programs that hide malware by intercepting and modifying operating system API calls to conceal files, processes, network connections, services, and drivers. Rootkits can operate at the user or kernel level, or even lower in the system firmware or hypervisor. They are sometimes installed via malicious drivers loaded through Windows services or the "Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver" (BYOVD) method, and have been used by groups like APT28 and UNC3886.
1817.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Windows rootkits, corresponding to MITRE ATT&CK technique T1014, fall under the Defense Evasion tactic and target the Windows platform. They are programs that hide malware by intercepting and modifying operating system API calls to conceal files, processes, network connections, and other system components. Rootkits can operate at the user or kernel level, and may even target lower layers like the hypervisor or system firmware.

1818.name: Windows bootkits
1818.profile: [profile]Windows bootkits are a persistence technique (T1542.003) within the Defense Evasion and Persistence tactics, targeting Windows systems. They modify the boot sectors of a hard drive, such as the Master Boot Record (MBR) or Volume Boot Record (VBR), or files in the EFI System Partition (ESP) on UEFI systems. This allows malicious code to execute before the operating system loads, operating at a layer below the OS to evade detection and complicate remediation. Groups like APT28 and APT41 have been associated with this technique.[/profile]
1818.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Windows Bootkits, identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1542.003, fall under the Persistence tactic for Windows platforms. This technique involves adversaries modifying the boot sectors of a hard drive, such as the Master Boot Record (MBR) or Volume Boot Record (VBR), to execute malicious code before the operating system loads, ensuring deep persistence. In UEFI systems, bootkits may create or modify files in the EFI System Partition (ESP) to run malicious kernel code. This method operates below the OS layer, making detection and remediation challenging, and is a specific type of rootkit that targets the boot process.
