1823.name: UAC bypass technique
1823.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may modify file attributes and subvert Gatekeeper functionality to evade user prompts and execute untrusted programs. Gatekeeper is a set of technologies that act as layer of Apple’s security model to ensure only trusted applications are executed on a host. Gatekeeper was built on top of File Quarantine in Snow Leopard (10.6, 2009) and has grown to include Code Signing, security policy compliance, Notarization, and more. Gatekeeper also treats applications running for the first time differently than reopened applications.(Citation: TheEclecticLightCompany Quarantine and the flag)(Citation: TheEclecticLightCompany apple notarization )

Based on an opt-in system, when files are downloaded an extended attribute (xattr) called `com.apple.quarantine` (also known as a quarantine flag) can be set on the file by the application performing the download. Launch Services opens the application in a suspended state. For first run applications with the quarantine flag set, Gatekeeper executes the following functions:

1. Checks extended attribute – Gatekeeper checks for the quarantine flag, then provides an alert prompt to the user to allow or deny execution.(Citation: OceanLotus for OS X)(Citation: 20 macOS Common Tools and Techniques)

2. Checks System Policies - Gatekeeper checks the system security policy, allowing execution of apps downloaded from either just the App Store or the App Store and identified developers.

3. Code Signing – Gatekeeper checks for a valid code signature from an Apple Developer ID.

4. Notarization - Using the `api.apple-cloudkit.com` API, Gatekeeper reaches out to Apple servers to verify or pull down the notarization ticket and ensure the ticket is not revoked. Users can override notarization, which will result in a prompt of executing an “unauthorized app” and the security policy will be modified.

Adversaries can subvert one or multiple security controls within Gatekeeper checks through logic errors (e.g. [Exploitation for Defense Evasion](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1211)), unchecked file types, and external libraries. For example, prior to macOS 13 Ventura, code signing and notarization checks were only conducted on first launch, allowing adversaries to write malicious executables to previously opened applications in order to bypass Gatekeeper security checks.(Citation: theevilbit gatekeeper bypass 2021)(Citation: Application Bundle Manipulation Brandon Dalton)

Applications and files loaded onto the system from a USB flash drive, optical disk, external hard drive, from a drive shared over the local network, or using the curl command may not set the quarantine flag. Additionally, it is possible to avoid setting the quarantine flag using [Drive-by Compromise](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1189).
1823.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique Gatekeeper Bypass (T1553.001) under the Defense Evasion tactic for macOS. It involves subverting Apple's Gatekeeper security by manipulating file attributes like the `com.apple.quarantine` extended attribute or exploiting logic errors in its checks for code signing and notarization. For instance, prior to macOS 13, adversaries could write malicious code into previously opened applications to bypass these checks on subsequent launches.
1823.profile_without_enhance: [profile]UAC Bypass Technique is a method for privilege escalation on Windows systems, corresponding to MITRE ATT&CK ID T1548.002 under the Defense Evasion tactic. It exploits the Windows User Account Control (UAC) mechanism to elevate process privileges without user consent. Common technical mechanics include leveraging auto-elevated programs like eventvwr.exe to execute scripts, using rundll32 to load crafted DLLs that invoke elevated COM objects, or abusing trusted processes. The extensive UACME project catalogues numerous such bypass methods, which are frequently used by threat groups including APT29, APT38, and MuddyWater.[/profile]

1824.name: custom redirection shim database
1824.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may use a custom cryptographic protocol or algorithm to hide command and control traffic. A simple scheme, such as XOR-ing the plaintext with a fixed key, will produce a very weak ciphertext.

Custom encryption schemes may vary in sophistication. Analysis and reverse engineering of malware samples may be enough to discover the algorithm and encryption key used.

Some adversaries may also attempt to implement their own version of a well-known cryptographic algorithm instead of using a known implementation library, which may lead to unintentional errors. (Citation: F-Secure Cosmicduke)
1824.profile: [profile]The entity "custom redirection shim database" is a technique for persistence and privilege escalation, specifically aligning with MITRE ATT&CK technique T1546.011 "Application Shimming" under the Persistence tactic on Windows. It involves creating or abusing custom Shim Databases (.sdb files) stored in %WINDIR%\AppPatch\custom directories. These databases use hooking to redirect application execution when programs are launched, enabling malicious acts like UAC bypass (via RedirectEXE), DLL injection (InjectDLL), or disabling security features such as Data Execution Prevention. Administrator privileges are typically required to install these shims, which are then persistently invoked by affected applications.[/profile]
1824.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Custom redirection shim database, corresponding to MITRE ATT&CK technique T1546.011 (Application Shimming) under the Persistence and Privilege Escalation tactics for Windows, involves creating a custom shim database (.sdb) to redirect program execution. Technical mechanics include installing a custom database via sdbinst.exe to locations like %WINDIR%\AppPatch\custom, which uses hooking to intercept and redirect API calls when a shimmed application runs, enabling actions like UAC bypass, DLL injection, or defense evasion. The group FIN7 has been associated with this technique.[/profile]

1825.name: autostart entry
1825.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may add or modify XDG Autostart Entries to execute malicious programs or commands when a user’s desktop environment is loaded at login. XDG Autostart entries are available for any XDG-compliant Linux system. XDG Autostart entries use Desktop Entry files (`.desktop`) to configure the user’s desktop environment upon user login. These configuration files determine what applications launch upon user login, define associated applications to open specific file types, and define applications used to open removable media.(Citation: Free Desktop Application Autostart Feb 2006)(Citation: Free Desktop Entry Keys)

Adversaries may abuse this feature to establish persistence by adding a path to a malicious binary or command to the `Exec` directive in the `.desktop` configuration file. When the user’s desktop environment is loaded at user login, the `.desktop` files located in the XDG Autostart directories are automatically executed. System-wide Autostart entries are located in the `/etc/xdg/autostart` directory while the user entries are located in the `~/.config/autostart` directory.

Adversaries may combine this technique with [Masquerading](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1036) to blend malicious Autostart entries with legitimate programs.(Citation: Red Canary Netwire Linux 2022)
1825.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique XDG Autostart Entries, identified as T1547.013 under the Persistence tactic for Linux platforms. It works by adversaries adding or modifying `.desktop` configuration files within XDG Autostart directories (`/etc/xdg/autostart` or `~/.config/autostart`), specifically inserting a malicious path into the `Exec` directive to automatically execute upon user login. This technique can be combined with Masquerading (T1036) to blend in with legitimate entries and has been associated with the intrusion set APT28.
1825.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Autostart Entry is a persistence technique (T1547) under the Boot or Logon Autostart Execution tactic. It operates across multiple platforms, including Windows and Linux. Adversaries configure system settings to automatically execute malicious programs during system boot or user logon. This is achieved by modifying configuration repositories like the Windows Registry (e.g., adding a binary to the `HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa\` Authentication Packages key) or by placing malicious `.desktop` files in XDG Autostart directories (`/etc/xdg/autostart` or `~/.config/autostart`) on Linux systems. These mechanisms allow execution with higher privileges to maintain persistence.

1826.name: DLL load order hijacking
1826.uncertain_mes:
Windows systems use a common method to look for required DLLs to load into a program. (Citation: Microsoft DLL Search) Adversaries may take advantage of the Windows DLL search order and programs that ambiguously specify DLLs to gain privilege escalation and persistence. 

Adversaries may perform DLL preloading, also called binary planting attacks, (Citation: OWASP Binary Planting) by placing a malicious DLL with the same name as an ambiguously specified DLL in a location that Windows searches before the legitimate DLL. Often this location is the current working directory of the program. Remote DLL preloading attacks occur when a program sets its current directory to a remote location such as a Web share before loading a DLL. (Citation: Microsoft 2269637) Adversaries may use this behavior to cause the program to load a malicious DLL. 

Adversaries may also directly modify the way a program loads DLLs by replacing an existing DLL or modifying a .manifest or .local redirection file, directory, or junction to cause the program to load a different DLL to maintain persistence or privilege escalation. (Citation: Microsoft DLL Redirection) (Citation: Microsoft Manifests) (Citation: Mandiant Search Order)

If a search order-vulnerable program is configured to run at a higher privilege level, then the adversary-controlled DLL that is loaded will also be executed at the higher level. In this case, the technique could be used for privilege escalation from user to administrator or SYSTEM or from administrator to SYSTEM, depending on the program.

Programs that fall victim to path hijacking may appear to behave normally because malicious DLLs may be configured to also load the legitimate DLLs they were meant to replace.
1826.profile: [profile]DLL Search Order Hijacking is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1574.001 under the Defense Evasion and Persistence tactics, primarily targeting Windows. It exploits the Windows DLL search order by placing a malicious DLL with the same name as a legitimate, ambiguously specified DLL in a directory searched earlier, such as the program's current working directory or a remote share. Attackers may also modify .manifest or .local redirection files to load a different DLL. If the vulnerable program runs with higher privileges, this enables privilege escalation, and malicious DLLs can be configured to also load the legitimate library to maintain stealth.[/profile]
1826.profile_without_enhance: [profile]DLL load order hijacking, corresponding to MITRE ATT&CK technique T1574.001 (Hijack Execution Flow: DLL Search Order Hijacking) under the Persistence, Privilege Escalation, and Defense Evasion tactics for Windows, involves placing a malicious DLL with the same name as a legitimate, ambiguously specified DLL in a directory that Windows searches earlier in its standard load order, such as the program's current working directory. This causes the vulnerable application to load the adversary's DLL, which can be used for persistence or privilege escalation if the host program runs at a higher privilege level. Adversaries may also enable DLL redirection via registry changes or redirection files to modify the search path.[/profile]

1827.name: decoy document
1827.profile: [profile]Name: Decoy Document. Aliases: Not specified. Attributed Groups: APT28, Calypso Group, Karma Panda. Key TTPs/Technical Behaviors: Used as a lure within malicious RAR archives alongside embedded images; employed in RTF and Word document attacks. Target Platforms: Windows systems via document exploits. Infrastructure/Supplementary Info: Serves as a social engineering component in campaigns by multiple threat groups, including in malware like Seduploader, Cmstar, and Byeby.
1827.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The malware known as Decoy Document is a component used within malicious archives and documents, such as RAR files, RTF files, and Word documents, to deceive victims. It is employed by threat actors including APT28, the Calypso Group, and Karma Panda, as well as in campaigns of unknown attribution. Its primary technical behavior is to serve as a lure or embedded file within these document-based delivery mechanisms to facilitate the initial infection stage, typically targeting Windows platforms through office document exploits.

It can exfiltrate data via HTTP POST to a specified URL and may use SFTP for uploads. It is associated with the Downdelph malware. Its target platform is Windows.
1831.profile_without_enhance: [profile]SEDUploader, also known as seduploader, is a malware attributed to the APT28 intrusion set. 1832.name: XOR-based algorithm
1832.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may employ various time-based methods to detect virtualization and analysis environments, particularly those that attempt to manipulate time mechanisms to simulate longer elapses of time. This may include enumerating time-based properties, such as uptime or the system clock. 

Adversaries may use calls like `GetTickCount` and `GetSystemTimeAsFileTime` to discover if they are operating within a virtual machine or sandbox, or may be able to identify a sandbox accelerating time by sampling and calculating the expected value for an environment's timestamp before and after execution of a sleep function.(Citation: ISACA Malware Tricks)
1832.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique "Time Based Evasion" (T1497.003) under the Defense Evasion tactic, primarily for Windows platforms. It involves adversaries using time-based checks, such as calling functions like GetTickCount or GetSystemTimeAsFileTime, to detect if they are operating within a virtual machine or sandbox environment by measuring system uptime, clock values, or discrepancies in timestamp acceleration after sleep functions. The intrusion set APT28 has been associated with this technique.
1832.profile_without_enhance: [profile]XOR-based algorithm is a technique for data obfuscation and encryption, often used as a custom cryptographic protocol (T1024) under the Command and Control tactic. It operates across multiple platforms. The technique involves applying the XOR (exclusive OR) logical operation to data with a fixed key, producing a weak ciphertext that is simple to implement without external libraries. It is also employed for custom data archiving (T1560.003) prior to exfiltration, where adversaries use XOR or stream ciphers in custom implementations to compress or encrypt collected information.

1839.name: APLib compression
1839.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may use compression to obfuscate their payloads or files. Compressed file formats such as ZIP, gzip, 7z, and RAR can compress and archive multiple files together to make it easier and faster to transfer files. In addition to compressing files, adversaries may also compress shellcode directly - for example, in order to store it in a Windows Registry key (i.e., [Fileless Storage](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/011)).(Citation: Trustwave Pillowmint June 2020)

In order to further evade detection, adversaries may combine multiple ZIP files into one archive. This process of concatenation creates an archive that appears to be a single archive but in fact contains the central directories of the embedded archives. Some ZIP readers, such as 7zip, may not be able to identify concatenated ZIP files and miss the presence of the malicious payload.(Citation: Perception Point)

File archives may be sent as one [Spearphishing Attachment](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001) through email. Adversaries have sent malicious payloads as archived files to encourage the user to interact with and extract the malicious payload onto their system (i.e., [Malicious File](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002)).(Citation: NTT Security Flagpro new December 2021) However, some file compression tools, such as 7zip, can be used to produce self-extracting archives. Adversaries may send self-extracting archives to hide the functionality of their payload and launch it without requiring multiple actions from the user.(Citation: The Hacker News)

[Compression](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/015) may be used in combination with [Encrypted/Encoded File](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/013) where compressed files are encrypted and password-protected.
1839.profile: [profile]APLib compression is a specific implementation of the MITRE ATT&CK technique Compression (T1027.015) under the Defense Evasion tactic, primarily used on Windows platforms. It functions as a custom compression algorithm to obfuscate payloads or files, distinct from common utilities like ZIP or RAR, and is often employed to compress shellcode for storage in locations like the Windows Registry. This method is associated with groups like APT28 and can be combined with encryption for further obfuscation.
1839.profile_without_enhance: [profile]APLib compression is a specific technique for obfuscating payloads or files, aligning with the MITRE ATT&CK sub-technique T1027.015 (Compression) under the Defense Evasion tactic, primarily for Windows platforms. It functions by using the APLib compression library, a custom implementation, to compress data such as shellcode or collected files, making them smaller and harder to detect prior to storage or exfiltration. This method is distinct from using common utilities like ZIP or 7z and is employed by adversaries to evade security tools.

1840.name: SSDT Hooking
1840.uncertain_mes:
Windows processes often leverage application programming interface (API) functions to perform tasks that require reusable system resources. Windows API functions are typically stored in dynamic-link libraries (DLLs) as exported functions. 

Hooking involves redirecting calls to these functions and can be implemented via:

* **Hooks procedures**, which intercept and execute designated code in response to events such as messages, keystrokes, and mouse inputs. (Citation: Microsoft Hook Overview) (Citation: Elastic Process Injection July 2017)
* **Import address table (IAT) hooking**, which use modifications to a process’s IAT, where pointers to imported API functions are stored. (Citation: Elastic Process Injection July 2017) (Citation: Adlice Software IAT Hooks Oct 2014) (Citation: MWRInfoSecurity Dynamic Hooking 2015)
* **Inline hooking**, which overwrites the first bytes in an API function to redirect code flow. (Citation: Elastic Process Injection July 2017) (Citation: HighTech Bridge Inline Hooking Sept 2011) (Citation: MWRInfoSecurity Dynamic Hooking 2015)

Similar to [Process Injection](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1055), adversaries may use hooking to load and execute malicious code within the context of another process, masking the execution while also allowing access to the process's memory and possibly elevated privileges. Installing hooking mechanisms may also provide Persistence via continuous invocation when the functions are called through normal use.

Malicious hooking mechanisms may also capture API calls that include parameters that reveal user authentication credentials for Credential Access. (Citation: Microsoft TrojanSpy:Win32/Ursnif.gen!I Sept 2017)

Hooking is commonly utilized by [Rootkit](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1014)s to conceal files, processes, Registry keys, and other objects in order to hide malware and associated behaviors. (Citation: Symantec Windows Rootkits)
1840.profile: [profile]SSDT Hooking is a specific form of inline hooking targeting the System Service Descriptor Table (SSDT) in Windows, a core system structure that maps API calls to kernel routines. This technique, often used for privilege escalation and defense evasion, involves overwriting function pointers within the SSDT to redirect system call execution to malicious code, allowing adversaries to intercept and manipulate low-level OS operations. It is a common rootkit mechanism for hiding processes and files, and has been associated with groups like APT28.[/profile]
1840.profile_without_enhance: [profile]SSDT Hooking is a technique within the broader Hooking (T1179) category, falling under the Defense Evasion tactic on Windows platforms. It specifically targets the System Service Descriptor Table (SSDT), a core kernel structure that maps system call numbers to their handler addresses in the Windows kernel. By modifying entries in this table, adversaries can redirect legitimate system calls (like those for file or process enumeration) to malicious code, enabling them to hide processes, files, registry keys, and other objects to conceal malware, a common behavior of rootkits. This provides persistent evasion as the hook is invoked whenever the hooked system function is called.

1841.name: Minifilter Driver
1841.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may modify or add LSASS drivers to obtain persistence on compromised systems. The Windows security subsystem is a set of components that manage and enforce the security policy for a computer or domain. The Local Security Authority (LSA) is the main component responsible for local security policy and user authentication. The LSA includes multiple dynamic link libraries (DLLs) associated with various other security functions, all of which run in the context of the LSA Subsystem Service (LSASS) lsass.exe process.(Citation: Microsoft Security Subsystem)

Adversaries may target LSASS drivers to obtain persistence. By either replacing or adding illegitimate drivers (e.g., [Hijack Execution Flow](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1574)), an adversary can use LSA operations to continuously execute malicious payloads.
1841.profile: [profile]Minifilter Driver is a technique mapped to MITRE ATT&CK ID T1547.008 under the Persistence tactic, targeting Windows. It involves adversaries adding or modifying LSASS drivers to maintain persistence, often by hijacking legitimate driver loading mechanisms to execute malicious code within the LSA Subsystem Service context. This method can be used to continuously run payloads. Associated actors include APT28.
1841.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Minifilter Driver is a Windows kernel-mode driver type used for file system filtering, enabling adversaries to intercept and manipulate file system operations for persistence and defense evasion. It operates at the kernel level, allowing deep system integration. Adversaries may deploy malicious minifilter drivers to monitor, block, or alter file activities, often requiring elevated privileges for installation and potentially involving code signing policy modifications to bypass security controls like Driver Signature Enforcement.

[APT29](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0016) reportedly compromised the Democratic National Committee starting in the summer of 2015.(Citation: F-Secure The Dukes)(Citation: GRIZZLY STEPPE JAR)(Citation: Crowdstrike DNC June 2016)(Citation: UK Gov UK Exposes Russia SolarWinds April 2021)

In April 2021, the US and UK governments attributed the [SolarWinds Compromise](https://attack.mitre.org/campaigns/C0024) to the SVR; public statements included citations to [APT29](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0016), Cozy Bear, and The Dukes.(Citation: NSA Joint Advisory SVR SolarWinds April 2021)(Citation: UK NSCS Russia SolarWinds April 2021) Industry reporting also referred to the actors involved in this campaign as UNC2452, NOBELIUM, StellarParticle, Dark Halo, and SolarStorm.(Citation: FireEye SUNBURST Backdoor December 2020)(Citation: MSTIC NOBELIUM Mar 2021)(Citation: CrowdStrike SUNSPOT Implant January 2021)(Citation: Volexity SolarWinds)(Citation: Cybersecurity Advisory SVR TTP May 2021)(Citation: Unit 42 SolarStorm December 2020)

1858.name: Denial and Deception
1858.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may perform Endpoint Denial of Service (DoS) attacks to degrade or block the availability of services to users. Endpoint DoS can be performed by exhausting the system resources those services are hosted on or exploiting the system to cause a persistent crash condition. Example services include websites, email services, DNS, and web-based applications. Adversaries have been observed conducting DoS attacks for political purposes(Citation: FireEye OpPoisonedHandover February 2016) and to support other malicious activities, including distraction(Citation: FSISAC FraudNetDoS September 2012), hacktivism, and extortion.(Citation: Symantec DDoS October 2014)

An Endpoint DoS denies the availability of a service without saturating the network used to provide access to the service. Adversaries can target various layers of the application stack that is hosted on the system used to provide the service. These layers include the Operating Systems (OS), server applications such as web servers, DNS servers, databases, and the (typically web-based) applications that sit on top of them. Attacking each layer requires different techniques that take advantage of bottlenecks that are unique to the respective components. A DoS attack may be generated by a single system or multiple systems spread across the internet, which is commonly referred to as a distributed DoS (DDoS).

To perform DoS attacks against endpoint resources, several aspects apply to multiple methods, including IP address spoofing and botnets.

Adversaries may use the original IP address of an attacking system, or spoof the source IP address to make the attack traffic more difficult to trace back to the attacking system or to enable reflection. This can increase the difficulty defenders have in defending against the attack by reducing or eliminating the effectiveness of filtering by the source address on network defense devices.

Botnets are commonly used to conduct DDoS attacks against networks and services. Large botnets can generate a significant amount of traffic from systems spread across the global internet. Adversaries may have the resources to build out and control their own botnet infrastructure or may rent time on an existing botnet to conduct an attack. In some of the worst cases for DDoS, so many systems are used to generate requests that each one only needs to send out a small amount of traffic to produce enough volume to exhaust the target's resources. In such circumstances, distinguishing DDoS traffic from legitimate clients becomes exceedingly difficult. Botnets have been used in some of the most high-profile DDoS attacks, such as the 2012 series of incidents that targeted major US banks.(Citation: USNYAG IranianBotnet March 2016)

In cases where traffic manipulation is used, there may be points in the global network (such as high traffic gateway routers) where packets can be altered and cause legitimate clients to execute code that directs network packets toward a target in high volume. This type of capability was previously used for the purposes of web censorship where client HTTP traffic was modified to include a reference to JavaScript that generated the DDoS code to overwhelm target web servers.(Citation: ArsTechnica Great Firewall of China)

For attacks attempting to saturate the providing network, see [Network Denial of Service](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1498).
1858.profile: [profile]Endpoint Denial of Service, identified as T1499, is an Impact tactic targeting Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It works by exhausting the target system's resources or exploiting it to cause a persistent crash, thereby degrading or blocking services like websites, DNS, or web applications without saturating the network. Techniques include using IP address spoofing to obscure the attack source and employing botnets to generate high-volume traffic from distributed systems, making defense and traffic filtering difficult. This technique is distinct from network-focused DoS (T1498) and has been associated with groups like Sandworm Team.[/profile]
1858.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Denial and Deception is a technique used by adversaries to manipulate an opponent's perceptions and hide their true activities. This is achieved through tactics like planting false information, creating deceptive network artifacts, and using misdirection to conceal their presence and intent. The goal is to degrade the defender's situational awareness and decision-making, facilitating other malicious operations.

1859.name: Manipulating Timestamps
1859.profile: [profile]Manipulating Timestamps corresponds to MITRE ATT&CK technique T1070.006 (Indicator Removal: Timestomp) under the Defense Evasion tactic, primarily for Windows and Linux platforms. It modifies file timestamps (modify, access, create, and change times) to hide malicious files by mimicking legitimate ones in the same directory. On Windows, adversaries typically alter the user-accessible $STANDARD_INFORMATION attribute via API calls and may perform "double timestomping" on the $FILE_NAME attribute to evade forensic detection. On Linux/ESXi, commands like `touch -a -m -t` are used. This technique is often paired with Masquerading (T1036) and has been employed by groups including APT28, APT29, and Lazarus Group.
1859.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Manipulating Timestamps, identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1070.006 under the Defense Evasion tactic, is a file system anti-forensics method used on Windows and Linux platforms. It modifies file timestamps—including modify, access, create, and change times—to blend malicious files with legitimate ones, often by using commands like `touch` on Linux or by altering the `$STANDARD_INFORMATION` attribute via API calls on Windows. This technique, also known as timestomping, is frequently employed alongside Masquerading (T1036) to hide malware deployment and can involve "double timestomping" to evade detection by forensic tools that compare different timestamp attributes.

1860.name: File Tampering
1860.profile: [profile]File Tampering is a technique where adversaries modify files to hide activity or manipulate outcomes. It aligns with the MITRE ATT&CK tactic of Impact (TA0040) under ID T1492, Stored Data Manipulation, applicable to Windows, Linux, and Mac platforms. The technique involves inserting, deleting, or altering data at rest in files like Office documents, databases, or emails to affect business processes or conceal malicious actions. This requires specific expertise and may be used by groups like APT28 to maintain persistence and evade detection by avoiding critical system files during operations.
1860.profile_without_enhance: [profile]File Tampering is a technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, though a specific ID is not provided in the input. It falls under the Impact tactic and can affect multiple platforms. The technique involves the insertion, deletion, or manipulation of data at rest, such as Office files, databases, or custom file formats, to affect business processes, decision-making, or hide malicious activity. Adversaries may also abuse antivirus file or folder exclusions to hide their tampered artifacts by placing them in directories that are not scanned.

1861.name: Modify System Information
1861.uncertain_mes: An adversary may attempt to get detailed information about the operating system and hardware, including version, patches, hotfixes, service packs, and architecture. Adversaries may use this information to shape follow-on behaviors, including whether or not the adversary fully infects the target and/or attempts specific actions. This behavior is distinct from [Local Storage Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1680) which is an adversary's discovery of local drive, disks and/or volumes. Tools such as [Systeminfo](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0096) can be used to gather detailed system information. If running with privileged access, a breakdown of system data can be gathered through the systemsetup configuration tool on macOS. Adversaries may leverage a [Network Device CLI](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/008) on network devices to gather detailed system information (e.g. show version).(Citation: US-CERT-TA18-106A) On ESXi servers, threat actors may gather system information from various esxcli utilities, such as `system hostname get` and `system version get`.(Citation: Crowdstrike Hypervisor Jackpotting Pt 2 2021)(Citation: Varonis) Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) cloud providers such as AWS, GCP, and Azure allow access to instance and virtual machine information via APIs. Successful authenticated API calls can return data such as the operating system platform and status of a particular instance or the model view of a virtual machine.(Citation: Amazon Describe Instance)(Citation: Google Instances Resource)(Citation: Microsoft Virutal Machine API) [System Information Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1082) combined with information gathered from other forms of discovery and reconnaissance can drive payload development and concealment.(Citation: OSX.FairyTale)(Citation: 20 macOS Common Tools and Techniques)
1861.profile: [profile]System Information Discovery, identified as T1082, is a Discovery tactic used across Windows, macOS, Linux, Network, IaaS, and ESXi platforms. It involves gathering detailed OS and hardware data like version, patches, and architecture using tools such as `systeminfo` on Windows, the `systemsetup` tool on macOS, CLI commands like `show version` on network devices, and `esxcli` utilities on ESXi servers. Cloud instance metadata is also collected via provider APIs. This intelligence shapes subsequent adversarial actions and payload development, as employed by groups including APT28, Lazarus Group, and FIN7.
1861.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Modify System Information is a technique where adversaries alter system data to weaken defenses or enable malicious actions. It can involve modifying system images on embedded network devices to change the operating system, often by replacing a single monolithic file either in memory or storage. This technique is related to weakening encryption by reducing cipher key sizes via network device CLI after a system image modification, and it can be used for runtime data manipulation to affect business processes and decision-making.

1862.name: Uncommon File Data
1862.profile: [profile]Uncommon File Data is a technique where adversaries hide malicious data or executables within NTFS file attributes, such as Extended Attributes (EA) or Alternate Data Streams (ADS), instead of within standard file content. This method leverages the Master File Table (MFT) to store arbitrary data within file metadata, evading detection from static scanning tools and antivirus software. It is associated with groups like APT32 and is used to conceal payloads on compromised systems.
1862.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Uncommon File Data is a technique for hiding data, mapped to MITRE ATT&CK ID T1003.001 under the Defense Evasion tactic, primarily for Windows. It involves storing malicious payloads or information in less common or legitimate file locations and formats to evade detection. This can include using NTFS Extended Attributes (EA) or Alternate Data Streams (ADS) within the Master File Table (MFT) to conceal data outside standard file content, bypassing static security scans.

It involves adversaries mining valuable information from SharePoint repositories, which often contain sensitive documents like network diagrams, system architecture, technical documentation, and internal credentials. 1865.name: Creating Guccifer 2.0 persona

The Guccifer 2.0 persona was a fabricated identity used by the intrusion set APT28 to establish a credible online presence, which involved developing public information, profiles, and social networks across platforms to enable direct connections with targets and support subsequent phases like spearphishing for initial access.[/profile]

1875.name: Webmail credentials theft
1875.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may steal monetary resources from targets through extortion, social engineering, technical theft, or other methods aimed at their own financial gain at the expense of the availability of these resources for victims. Financial theft is the ultimate objective of several popular campaign types including extortion by ransomware,(Citation: FBI-ransomware) business email compromise (BEC) and fraud,(Citation: FBI-BEC) "pig butchering,"(Citation: wired-pig butchering) bank hacking,(Citation: DOJ-DPRK Heist) and exploiting cryptocurrency networks.(Citation: BBC-Ronin) 

Adversaries may [Compromise Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1586) to conduct unauthorized transfers of funds.(Citation: Internet crime report 2022) In the case of business email compromise or email fraud, an adversary may utilize [Impersonation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1656) of a trusted entity. Once the social engineering is successful, victims can be deceived into sending money to financial accounts controlled by an adversary.(Citation: FBI-BEC) This creates the potential for multiple victims (i.e., compromised accounts as well as the ultimate monetary loss) in incidents involving financial theft.(Citation: VEC)

Extortion by ransomware may occur, for example, when an adversary demands payment from a victim after [Data Encrypted for Impact](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1486) (Citation: NYT-Colonial) and [Exfiltration](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0010) of data, followed by threatening to leak sensitive data to the public unless payment is made to the adversary.(Citation: Mandiant-leaks) Adversaries may use dedicated leak sites to distribute victim data.(Citation: Crowdstrike-leaks)

Due to the potentially immense business impact of financial theft, an adversary may abuse the possibility of financial theft and seeking monetary gain to divert attention from their true goals such as [Data Destruction](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1485) and business disruption.(Citation: AP-NotPetya)
1875.profile: [profile]Webmail Credentials Theft is a technique for credential access, likely aligned with T1555.003 (Credentials from Web Browsers) under the Collection tactic, primarily targeting Windows platforms. It involves stealing stored webmail login details from a victim's web browser. Adversaries achieve this by reading browser-specific files, such as the Chrome database at `AppData\Local\Google\Chrome\User Data\Default\Login Data`, and executing SQL queries to extract encrypted credentials. These are often decrypted using functions like `CryptUnprotectData`, which leverages the victim's cached logon keys. The stolen credentials can then be used for account compromise and further malicious activities.
1875.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Webmail credentials theft is a technique where adversaries steal login information for web-based email services. This falls under the Credential Access tactic and can target various platforms. Methods include using malware to scrape credentials stored by web browsers, such as reading the Chrome 'Login Data' file and decrypting passwords via CryptUnprotectData, or employing phishing campaigns to trick users into revealing their credentials directly. Stolen webmail credentials are often used for further access, financial theft, or business email compromise (BEC) fraud.

1876.name: Malicious Emails
1876.uncertain_mes:
An adversary may rely upon a user opening a malicious file in order to gain execution. Users may be subjected to social engineering to get them to open a file that will lead to code execution. This user action will typically be observed as follow-on behavior from [Spearphishing Attachment](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001). Adversaries may use several types of files that require a user to execute them, including .doc, .pdf, .xls, .rtf, .scr, .exe, .lnk, .pif, .cpl, .reg, and .iso.(Citation: Mandiant Trojanized Windows 10)

Adversaries may employ various forms of [Masquerading](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1036) and [Obfuscated Files or Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027) to increase the likelihood that a user will open and successfully execute a malicious file. These methods may include using a familiar naming convention and/or password protecting the file and supplying instructions to a user on how to open it.(Citation: Password Protected Word Docs) 

While [Malicious File](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002) frequently occurs shortly after Initial Access it may occur at other phases of an intrusion, such as when an adversary places a file in a shared directory or on a user's desktop hoping that a user will click on it. This activity may also be seen shortly after [Internal Spearphishing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1534).
1876.profile: [profile]Malicious File, identified as T1204.002 under the Execution tactic, primarily targets Windows platforms. It relies on user interaction to open a malicious file, often delivered via spearphishing attachments, to gain code execution. Adversaries employ various file types like .doc, .pdf, .exe, and .lnk, and use masquerading or password protection to increase success. This technique is frequently used by numerous threat groups, including APT28, and can occur at various intrusion phases beyond initial access.[profile]
1876.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Malicious Emails is a technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, primarily associated with the Initial Access tactic (T1566: Phishing). It operates across multiple platforms, including Windows, macOS, and Linux. The technique involves adversaries sending deceptive emails to users, often containing malicious attachments (like .doc, .pdf, .exe) or links, to trick recipients into executing code. This action is a common follow-on to specific spearphishing sub-techniques. Attackers frequently employ masquerading and obfuscation to increase success rates, and numerous threat groups, including APT29, FIN7, and Lazarus Group, are known to use this method.

1877.name: Exploit Kits
1877.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may attempt to exploit a weakness in an Internet-facing host or system to initially access a network. The weakness in the system can be a software bug, a temporary glitch, or a misconfiguration.

Exploited applications are often websites/web servers, but can also include databases (like SQL), standard services (like SMB or SSH), network device administration and management protocols (like SNMP and Smart Install), and any other system with Internet-accessible open sockets.(Citation: NVD CVE-2016-6662)(Citation: CIS Multiple SMB Vulnerabilities)(Citation: US-CERT TA18-106A Network Infrastructure Devices 2018)(Citation: Cisco Blog Legacy Device Attacks)(Citation: NVD CVE-2014-7169) On ESXi infrastructure, adversaries may exploit exposed OpenSLP services; they may alternatively exploit exposed VMware vCenter servers.(Citation: Recorded Future ESXiArgs Ransomware 2023)(Citation: Ars Technica VMWare Code Execution Vulnerability 2021) Depending on the flaw being exploited, this may also involve [Exploitation for Defense Evasion](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1211) or [Exploitation for Client Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1203).

If an application is hosted on cloud-based infrastructure and/or is containerized, then exploiting it may lead to compromise of the underlying instance or container. This can allow an adversary a path to access the cloud or container APIs (e.g., via the [Cloud Instance Metadata API](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1552/005)), exploit container host access via [Escape to Host](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1611), or take advantage of weak identity and access management policies.

Adversaries may also exploit edge network infrastructure and related appliances, specifically targeting devices that do not support robust host-based defenses.(Citation: Mandiant Fortinet Zero Day)(Citation: Wired Russia Cyberwar)

For websites and databases, the OWASP top 10 and CWE top 25 highlight the most common web-based vulnerabilities.(Citation: OWASP Top 10)(Citation: CWE top 25)
1877.profile: [profile]The entity is Exploit Public-Facing Application, identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1190 under the Initial Access tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. This technique involves exploiting software bugs, glitches, or misconfigurations in internet-facing systems like web servers, databases (e.g., SQL), and services (e.g., SMB, SSH) to gain initial network access. It can also target cloud instances, containers, and edge network infrastructure, potentially leading to further exploitation for evasion or execution. Groups such as APT28, Volt Typhoon, and MuddyWater have been associated with this method.
1877.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Exploit Kits are a tool within the adversary arsenal, categorized under Resource Development (T1588.005). They are not a direct execution technique but a delivery mechanism, often purchased from criminal marketplaces. Their primary technical function is to automate the identification and exploitation of software vulnerabilities in client applications, particularly web browsers, through drive-by compromises. They package multiple exploits to target common software like Flash, Java, or browsers, enabling initial access without requiring user interaction beyond visiting a compromised website.

1941.name: social engineering strategy
1941.uncertain_mes:

1952.name: DDE exploit technique
1952.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may attempt to exploit a weakness in an Internet-facing host or system to initially access a network. The weakness in the system can be a software bug, a temporary glitch, or a misconfiguration.

Exploited applications are often websites/web servers, but can also include databases (like SQL), standard services (like SMB or SSH), network device administration and management protocols (like SNMP and Smart Install), and any other system with Internet-accessible open sockets.(Citation: NVD CVE-2016-6662)(Citation: CIS Multiple SMB Vulnerabilities)(Citation: US-CERT TA18-106A Network Infrastructure Devices 2018)(Citation: Cisco Blog Legacy Device Attacks)(Citation: NVD CVE-2014-7169) On ESXi infrastructure, adversaries may exploit exposed OpenSLP services; they may alternatively exploit exposed VMware vCenter servers.(Citation: Recorded Future ESXiArgs Ransomware 2023)(Citation: Ars Technica VMWare Code Execution Vulnerability 2021) Depending on the flaw being exploited, this may also involve [Exploitation for Defense Evasion](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1211) or [Exploitation for Client Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1203).

If an application is hosted on cloud-based infrastructure and/or is containerized, then exploiting it may lead to compromise of the underlying instance or container. This can allow an adversary a path to access the cloud or container APIs (e.g., via the [Cloud Instance Metadata API](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1552/005)), exploit container host access via [Escape to Host](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1611), or take advantage of weak identity and access management policies.

Adversaries may also exploit edge network infrastructure and related appliances, specifically targeting devices that do not support robust host-based defenses.(Citation: Mandiant Fortinet Zero Day)(Citation: Wired Russia Cyberwar)

For websites and databases, the OWASP top 10 and CWE top 25 highlight the most common web-based vulnerabilities.(Citation: OWASP Top 10)(Citation: CWE top 25)
1952.profile: [profile]Dynamic Data Exchange (DDE) is formally known as T1559.002 within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, categorized under Execution and Persistence tactics for Windows platforms. This technique exploits the legacy Windows DDE protocol for inter-process communication to execute arbitrary commands, often by embedding malicious DDE formulas within Microsoft Office documents or CSV files to bypass macro security. It has been utilized by groups including APT28, MuddyWater, and FIN7 for initial execution via phishing, as evidenced by its association with malware like Zebrocy.
1952.profile_without_enhance: [profile]DDE Exploit Technique is a method for executing arbitrary commands by abusing the Windows Dynamic Data Exchange (DDE) protocol, mapped to MITRE ATT&CK ID T1559.002 under the Execution tactic for Windows platforms. It works by poisoning Microsoft Office documents or CSV files with embedded DDE commands, which can be delivered via phishing to execute payloads without using macros, or leveraged locally via inter-process communication for execution when direct command-line access is unavailable.

1953.name: Microsoft Office documents with malicious macros
1953.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may abuse Microsoft Office templates to obtain persistence on a compromised system. Microsoft Office contains templates that are part of common Office applications and are used to customize styles. The base templates within the application are used each time an application starts. (Citation: Microsoft Change Normal Template) Office Visual Basic for Applications (VBA) macros (Citation: MSDN VBA in Office) can be inserted into the base template and used to execute code when the respective Office application starts in order to obtain persistence. Examples for both Word and Excel have been discovered and published. By default, Word has a Normal.dotm template created that can be modified to include a malicious macro. Excel does not have a template file created by default, but one can be added that will automatically be loaded.(Citation: enigma0x3 normal.dotm)(Citation: Hexacorn Office Template Macros) Shared templates may also be stored and pulled from remote locations.(Citation: GlobalDotName Jun 2019) Word Normal.dotm location:
C:\Users\<username>\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Templates\Normal.dotm Excel Personal.xlsb location:
C:\Users\<username>\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Excel\XLSTART\PERSONAL.XLSB Adversaries may also change the location of the base template to point to their own by hijacking the application's search order, e.g. Word 2016 will first look for Normal.dotm under C:\Program Files (x86)\Microsoft Office\root\Office16\, or by modifying the GlobalDotName registry key. By modifying the GlobalDotName registry key an adversary can specify an arbitrary location, file name, and file extension to use for the template that will be loaded on application startup. To abuse GlobalDotName, adversaries may first need to register the template as a trusted document or place it in a trusted location.(Citation: GlobalDotName Jun 2019) An adversary may need to enable macros to execute unrestricted depending on the system or enterprise security policy on use of macros.
1953.profile: [profile]Office Template Macros is technique T1137.001 under the Persistence tactic, targeting Windows. It involves inserting malicious VBA macros into base Office templates like Word's Normal.dotm or Excel's Personal.xlsb, which execute code when the respective application starts. Persistence can also be achieved by modifying the GlobalDotName registry key to point to a malicious template in a custom location, potentially requiring the template to be placed in a trusted location or registered as a trusted document to bypass macro security settings.[/profile]
1953.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Microsoft Office documents with malicious macros" aligns with the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1204.002 "User Execution: Malicious File" under the Execution tactic, primarily targeting Windows platforms. This technique involves adversaries embedding malicious Visual Basic for Applications (VBA) macros within documents like .doc or .xls files, often delivered via spearphishing. Execution requires a user to open the file and enable macros, which may be hidden using obfuscation methods like VBA Stomping, where source code is replaced with benign data while malicious compiled p-code remains. This is a common initial access and execution vector for numerous threat groups.

1954.name: Toggle Field Codes
1954.profile: [profile]Toggle Field Codes is a technique used to conceal malicious code or commands within document fields, such as template references in Office documents or control words in RTF files, to evade static detection. It is associated with the APT28 intrusion-set and can facilitate payload delivery or forced authentication when the document is opened, often delivered via phishing.
1954.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The technique "Toggle Field Codes" is a sub-technique of Obfuscated Files or Information (T1027) within the Defense Evasion tactic, applicable to the Windows platform. It involves manipulating field codes in Microsoft Office documents to hide malicious commands or payloads. By toggling these codes between a human-readable display and the underlying raw code, adversaries can conceal the true intent of document content, such as embedding malicious macros or links, from both users and static security analysis tools.

1955.name: White Fonts
1955.profile: [profile]White Fonts is a technique used by APT28, likely within the Defense Evasion tactic, where adversaries hide malicious text or user interface elements by setting their color to white against a white background, making them invisible to users while remaining functional. This method can be employed to conceal malicious commands or prompts within legitimate-looking documents or applications.
1955.profile_without_enhance: [profile]White Fonts is a technique where adversaries use white-colored text on a white background to hide malicious content within documents or web pages, making it invisible to casual viewers but still present and executable. This method is typically employed in the Initial Access tactic, often on Windows platforms, to conceal malicious links or instructions in spearphishing emails or documents, requiring user interaction such as selecting the text to reveal the hidden content.

1956.name: Quote Field ASCII Conversion
1956.profile: [profile]Quote Field ASCII Conversion is a technique for data obfuscation, likely within the Command and Control (T1132) or Defense Evasion (T1027) tactics. It involves converting data into ASCII representations within protocol fields, such as HTTP headers or SMTP commands, to blend malicious traffic with normal communications and evade detection. The intrusion set APT28 has been associated with this method.
1956.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Quote Field ASCII Conversion is a technique for data obfuscation, where adversaries convert characters within the quote fields of command-line arguments to their ASCII decimal equivalents. This conversion is a form of data encoding, making malicious commands appear as benign strings of numbers to evade signature-based detection. The technique is used to hide the true intent of commands executed via command-line interfaces, facilitating defense evasion.

1957.name: Capitalize 'e' in DDE command
1957.profile: [profile]The entity "Capitalize 'e' in DDE command" is a specific implementation of the MITRE ATT&CK technique Dynamic Data Exchange (T1559.002) under the Execution tactic, primarily targeting Windows. This technique involves obfuscating DDE command execution within malicious Office documents by capitalizing the 'e' in the DDE formula field, such as in `=cmd|'/c calc.exe'!A0`, to evade signature-based detection while maintaining functionality for arbitrary command execution. It has been associated with intrusion set APT28.
1957.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Capitalize 'e' in DDE command" is a specific obfuscation technique within the broader MITRE ATT&CK technique Dynamic Data Exchange (T1559.002), which falls under the Execution tactic and targets the Windows platform. It involves modifying the case of the letter 'e' in DDE command strings (e.g., in malicious Office documents) to evade signature-based detection while maintaining the command's functionality for arbitrary code execution. This is a form of command obfuscation used to bypass security controls that rely on exact string matching.

1960.name: Bold 'dd' in DDE command
1960.profile: [profile]Bold 'dd' in DDE command is a sub-technique of Dynamic Data Exchange (T1559.002), used for Execution on Windows. It involves embedding a specific DDE formula, such as using a bolded 'dd' field code, into a Microsoft Office document to execute arbitrary commands without using macros. This method can be delivered via phishing to bypass security controls. The intrusion set APT28 has been associated with this technique.
1960.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Bold 'dd' in DDE command is a specific implementation of the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1559.002, Dynamic Data Exchange, under the Execution tactic for Windows. It involves embedding a malicious DDE command, such as "DDEAUTO C:\Programs\Microsoft\Office\MSWord.exe\..\..\..\..\Windows\System32\cmd.exe '/k powershell.exe'", within a Microsoft Office document, where the "dd" portion of the command is formatted in bold text. This formatting is a form of command obfuscation intended to evade simple signature-based detection while still allowing the DDE protocol to execute arbitrary commands, like PowerShell, when the poisoned document is opened, bypassing the need for macros.

1983.name: evasion technique
1983.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may employ various means to detect and avoid debuggers. Debuggers are typically used by defenders to trace and/or analyze the execution of potential malware payloads.(Citation: ProcessHacker Github) Debugger evasion may include changing behaviors based on the results of the checks for the presence of artifacts indicative of a debugged environment. Similar to [Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1497), if the adversary detects a debugger, they may alter their malware to disengage from the victim or conceal the core functions of the implant. They may also search for debugger artifacts before dropping secondary or additional payloads. Specific checks will vary based on the target and/or adversary. On Windows, this may involve [Native API](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1106) function calls such as IsDebuggerPresent() and NtQueryInformationProcess(), or manually checking the BeingDebugged flag of the Process Environment Block (PEB). On Linux, this may involve querying `/proc/self/status` for the `TracerPID` field, which indicates whether or not the process is being traced by dynamic analysis tools.(Citation: Cado Security P2PInfect 2023)(Citation: Positive Technologies Hellhounds 2023) Other checks for debugging artifacts may also seek to enumerate hardware breakpoints, interrupt assembly opcodes, time checks, or measurements if exceptions are raised in the current process (assuming a present debugger would “swallow” or handle the potential error).(Citation: hasherezade debug)(Citation: AlKhaser Debug)(Citation: vxunderground debug) Malware may also leverage Structured Exception Handling (SEH) to detect debuggers by throwing an exception and detecting whether the process is suspended. SEH handles both hardware and software expectations, providing control over the exceptions including support for debugging. If a debugger is present, the program’s control will be transferred to the debugger, and the execution of the code will be suspended. If the debugger is not present, control will be transferred to the SEH handler, which will automatically handle the exception and allow the program’s execution to continue.(Citation: Apriorit) Adversaries may use the information learned from these debugger checks during automated discovery to shape follow-on behaviors. Debuggers can also be evaded by detaching the process or flooding debug logs with meaningless data via messages produced by looping [Native API](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1106) function calls such as OutputDebugStringW().(Citation: wardle evilquest partii)(Citation: Checkpoint Dridex Jan 2021)
1983.profile: [profile]Debugger Evasion, identified as T1622, is a Defense Evasion technique used on Windows and Linux platforms. It involves detecting debuggers to alter malware behavior, conceal core functions, or disengage. Specific technical mechanics include Windows API calls like IsDebuggerPresent() and NtQueryInformationProcess(), checking the BeingDebugged flag in the PEB, and on Linux, querying /proc/self/status for the TracerPID field. It also leverages Structured Exception Handling (SEH) to detect debuggers by throwing exceptions and can evade by detaching processes or flooding logs with OutputDebugStringW() calls.
1983.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Evasion Technique is a broad category of adversary behaviors aimed at avoiding detection and analysis, rather than a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique. It encompasses multiple distinct techniques such as Debugger Evasion (T1622) and Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion (T1497), which fall under the Defense Evasion tactic. These methods operate across Windows and Linux platforms by checking for environmental artifacts—like the `BeingDebugged` flag in the Windows PEB or the `TracerPID` field in `/proc/self/status` on Linux—and altering malware behavior or delaying execution to evade security tools and analysis environments.

1984.name: scrolling through the entire contents
1984.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may move onto systems, possibly those on disconnected or air-gapped networks, by copying malware to removable media and taking advantage of Autorun features when the media is inserted into a system and executes. In the case of Lateral Movement, this may occur through modification of executable files stored on removable media or by copying malware and renaming it to look like a legitimate file to trick users into executing it on a separate system. In the case of Initial Access, this may occur through manual manipulation of the media, modification of systems used to initially format the media, or modification to the media's firmware itself.

Mobile devices may also be used to infect PCs with malware if connected via USB.(Citation: Exploiting Smartphone USB ) This infection may be achieved using devices (Android, iOS, etc.) and, in some instances, USB charging cables.(Citation: Windows Malware Infecting Android)(Citation: iPhone Charging Cable Hack) For example, when a smartphone is connected to a system, it may appear to be mounted similar to a USB-connected disk drive. If malware that is compatible with the connected system is on the mobile device, the malware could infect the machine (especially if Autorun features are enabled).
1984.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique Replication Through Removable Media, identified as T1091 under the Initial Access and Lateral Movement tactics for Windows. It involves adversaries copying malware to removable drives or USB-connected mobile devices to exploit Autorun features for automatic execution when the media is connected to a target system. This method is notably used by groups like APT28, Gamaredon Group, and FIN7 to bridge air-gapped networks.
1984.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "scrolling through the entire contents" is not a standard technique in the MITRE ATT&CK framework. Based on the provided context, it appears to be a specific, low-level action that could be a component of other techniques. It may be used for information gathering by manually or programmatically navigating through data, such as in application windows or file directories, to discover sensitive information or system details. This action is likely a sub-technique or procedural step within broader Discovery or Collection tactics.

1987.name: viewed the specific page
1987.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may abuse Microsoft Outlook's Home Page feature to obtain persistence on a compromised system. Outlook Home Page is a legacy feature used to customize the presentation of Outlook folders. This feature allows for an internal or external URL to be loaded and presented whenever a folder is opened. A malicious HTML page can be crafted that will execute code when loaded by Outlook Home Page.(Citation: SensePost Outlook Home Page)

Once malicious home pages have been added to the user’s mailbox, they will be loaded when Outlook is started. Malicious Home Pages will execute when the right Outlook folder is loaded/reloaded.(Citation: SensePost Outlook Home Page)
1987.profile: [profile]The entity "Outlook Home Page" is a persistence technique with MITRE ATT&CK ID T1137.004 under the Persistence tactic, targeting the Windows platform. It abuses a legacy Microsoft Outlook feature that allows a custom internal or external URL to be loaded when an Outlook folder is opened. Adversaries craft a malicious HTML page that executes code when loaded by this feature, achieving persistence as the page loads automatically when Outlook starts or the specific folder is accessed. The intrusion-set APT28 (Oilrig) has been associated with this technique.
1987.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "viewed the specific page" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the provided context, it appears to be a generic description of an action, potentially related to a user or adversary accessing a particular webpage. The retrieved information does not provide specific technical mechanics or a clear mapping to a known TTP, so no MITRE ID, Tactic, or Platform can be assigned.

Key technical behaviors include decompressing a secondary Flash object for communication with an exploit server and fetching payloads from specific URLs, such as those hosted on macromedia.com domains. It targets platforms via web browsers through Shockwave Flash Player vulnerabilities.[/profile]

It is associated with the APT28 group, as seen in the seduploader campaign, where it is used to decompress a secondary Flash object for communication with an exploit delivery server. The malware targets systems via Flash-based exploits, leveraging specific URLs like h00p://download.macromedia.com/pub/shockwave/cabs/flash/swflash.cab for initial access and redirection, indicating a focus on web-based delivery through compromised or malicious sites.

1991.name: reseller option
1991.profile: [profile]Reseller Option is a malware entity attributed to the APT28 intrusion set. Its key behavior involves the unauthorized installation of Computrace software, a legitimate remote management tool, onto victim machines, potentially by manufacturers or previous owners, to establish persistence and remote access. This malware primarily targets Windows platforms, leveraging the Computrace infrastructure for command and control. The name "Reseller Option" also appears in the context of malware-as-a-service offerings, such as those for ZLoader and DiamondFox, where it refers to a reseller API program for distributing malware under a private brand.

Key technical behaviors include potential misuse of legitimate remote management software like Computrace for unauthorized persistence, and it is associated with malware-as-a-service (MaaS) offerings, as indicated by marketing language targeting software resellers for rebranding and distribution, seen in connections to ZLoader and DiamondFox. The target platforms are not specified. Supplementary information suggests it operates within a commercial malware distribution model.

1992.name: loader swf
1992.profile: [profile]Loader SWF is a malware loader associated with APT28. It exploits vulnerabilities such as CVE-2012-1535 and CVE-2011-0609 to deliver malicious SWF files, often through exploit kits like Sundown. Its infrastructure involves specific URL patterns (e.g., fhbg.futureproducts.xyz/.../127.swf) for hosting payloads. The malware targets platforms via Internet Explorer and Flash Player vulnerabilities, facilitating remote code execution and further malware deployment.[profile]

1994.name: User Execution
1994.uncertain_mes:
An adversary may rely upon specific actions by a user in order to gain execution. Users may be subjected to social engineering to get them to execute malicious code by, for example, opening a malicious document file or link. These user actions will typically be observed as follow-on behavior from forms of [Phishing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566).

While [User Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204) frequently occurs shortly after Initial Access it may occur at other phases of an intrusion, such as when an adversary places a file in a shared directory or on a user's desktop hoping that a user will click on it. This activity may also be seen shortly after [Internal Spearphishing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1534).

Adversaries may also deceive users into performing actions such as:

* Enabling [Remote Access Tools](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1219), allowing direct control of the system to the adversary
* Running malicious JavaScript in their browser, allowing adversaries to [Steal Web Session Cookie](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539)s(Citation: Talos Roblox Scam 2023)(Citation: Krebs Discord Bookmarks 2023)
* Downloading and executing malware for [User Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204)
* Coerceing users to copy, paste, and execute malicious code manually(Citation: Reliaquest-execution)(Citation: proofpoint-selfpwn)

For example, tech support scams can be facilitated through [Phishing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566), vishing, or various forms of user interaction. Adversaries can use a combination of these methods, such as spoofing and promoting toll-free numbers or call centers that are used to direct victims to malicious websites, to deliver and execute payloads containing malware or [Remote Access Tools](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1219).(Citation: Telephone Attack Delivery)
1994.profile: [profile]User Execution (T1204) is an Execution tactic technique applicable across multiple platforms, where adversaries rely on user actions to gain code execution. This is achieved through social engineering, such as tricking users into opening malicious documents or links, enabling remote access tools, running malicious JavaScript, or manually copying and executing code. It often follows phishing campaigns and can involve tech support scams using spoofed call centers to deliver payloads. Associated groups include APT28, FIN7, Scattered Spider, and LAPSUS$.

It involves an adversary relying on specific user actions, often induced by social engineering like phishing, to gain execution of malicious code. This includes deceiving users into opening malicious documents or links, clicking files placed in shared directories, enabling remote access tools, running malicious browser JavaScript, or manually copying and pasting malicious commands.

1997.name: decrypt the embedded Flash object
1997.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may embed payloads within other files to conceal malicious content from defenses. Otherwise seemingly benign files (such as scripts and executables) may be abused to carry and obfuscate malicious payloads and content. In some cases, embedded payloads may also enable adversaries to [Subvert Trust Controls](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1553) by not impacting execution controls such as digital signatures and notarization tickets.(Citation: Sentinel Labs) 

Adversaries may embed payloads in various file formats to hide payloads.(Citation: Microsoft Learn) This is similar to [Steganography](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/003), though does not involve weaving malicious content into specific bytes and patterns related to legitimate digital media formats.(Citation: GitHub PSImage) 

For example, adversaries have been observed embedding payloads within or as an overlay of an otherwise benign binary.(Citation: Securelist Dtrack2) Adversaries have also been observed nesting payloads (such as executables and run-only scripts) inside a file of the same format.(Citation: SentinelLabs reversing run-only applescripts 2021) 

Embedded content may also be used as [Process Injection](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1055) payloads used to infect benign system processes.(Citation: Trend Micro) These embedded then injected payloads may be used as part of the modules of malware designed to provide specific features such as encrypting C2 communications in support of an orchestrator module. For example, an embedded module may be injected into default browsers, allowing adversaries to then communicate via the network.(Citation: Malware Analysis Report ComRAT)
1997.profile: [profile]The entity "decrypt the embedded Flash object" is a specific action within the broader MITRE ATT&CK technique T1027.009, "Embedded Payloads," which falls under the Defense Evasion tactic and applies to multiple platforms. This technique involves adversaries concealing malicious payloads within benign files, such as Flash objects, to bypass detection. The technical mechanic involves decrypting the embedded content to extract and execute the hidden payload, often as part of a multi-stage attack to subvert trust controls or enable process injection. The intrusion set APT28 has been associated with related obfuscation and execution methods.

The decrypted payload is then executed, often to steal credentials or establish persistence, linking it to groups like APT28 and MuddyWater. This method avoids security controls that scan only the outer file layer.

Specifically, it can be leveraged for exfiltration over an alternative, unencrypted protocol (T1048, T1048.003) to steal data by sending it over a channel different from the main C2 server. This technique allows attackers to avoid detection by using common, allowed network traffic to mask their operations.

Payloads may also be delivered in formats unrecognizable and inherently benign to the native OS (ex: EXEs on macOS/Linux) before later being (re)compiled into a proper executable binary with a bundled compiler and execution framework.(Citation: TrendMicro WindowsAppMac)
