2024.name: Token Manipulation
2024.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may modify access tokens to operate under a different user or system security context to perform actions and bypass access controls. Windows uses access tokens to determine the ownership of a running process. A user can manipulate access tokens to make a running process appear as though it is the child of a different process or belongs to someone other than the user that started the process. When this occurs, the process also takes on the security context associated with the new token. An adversary can use built-in Windows API functions to copy access tokens from existing processes; this is known as token stealing. These token can then be applied to an existing process (i.e. [Token Impersonation/Theft](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1134/001)) or used to spawn a new process (i.e. [Create Process with Token](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1134/002)). An adversary must already be in a privileged user context (i.e. administrator) to steal a token. However, adversaries commonly use token stealing to elevate their security context from the administrator level to the SYSTEM level. An adversary can then use a token to authenticate to a remote system as the account for that token if the account has appropriate permissions on the remote system.(Citation: Pentestlab Token Manipulation) Any standard user can use the runas command, and the Windows API functions, to create impersonation tokens; it does not require access to an administrator account. There are also other mechanisms, such as Active Directory fields, that can be used to modify access tokens.
2024.profile: [profile]Access Token Manipulation, designated T1134, is a Defense Evasion and Privilege Escalation technique primarily for Windows. It involves using built-in Windows API functions to copy access tokens from existing processes, a method known as token stealing. These stolen tokens can then be applied to an existing process via Token Impersonation/Theft (T1134.001) or used to spawn a new process with Create Process with Token (T1134.002). While token theft requires an initial privileged context (e.g., administrator) to elevate to SYSTEM, standard users can create impersonation tokens using commands like `runas`. Groups like FIN6 and APT28 have been associated with this technique.
2024.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Token Manipulation, identified as T1134 in the MITRE ATT&CK framework, is a Defense Evasion and Privilege Escalation technique primarily for Windows. It involves modifying access tokens to operate under a different user or system security context to bypass access controls. Adversaries use built-in Windows API functions like `DuplicateToken` to copy tokens from existing processes, a method known as token stealing. These stolen tokens can then be applied to an existing process via Token Impersonation/Theft (T1134.001) or used to spawn a new process with Create Process with Token (T1134.002). This allows an adversary, often already in an administrator context, to elevate to SYSTEM level or impersonate users for remote authentication, while standard users can also create impersonation tokens using commands like `runas`.

2025.name: Exploit Kit
2025.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may attempt to exploit a weakness in an Internet-facing host or system to initially access a network. The weakness in the system can be a software bug, a temporary glitch, or a misconfiguration.

Exploited applications are often websites/web servers, but can also include databases (like SQL), standard services (like SMB or SSH), network device administration and management protocols (like SNMP and Smart Install), and any other system with Internet-accessible open sockets.(Citation: NVD CVE-2016-6662)(Citation: CIS Multiple SMB Vulnerabilities)(Citation: US-CERT TA18-106A Network Infrastructure Devices 2018)(Citation: Cisco Blog Legacy Device Attacks)(Citation: NVD CVE-2014-7169) On ESXi infrastructure, adversaries may exploit exposed OpenSLP services; they may alternatively exploit exposed VMware vCenter servers.(Citation: Recorded Future ESXiArgs Ransomware 2023)(Citation: Ars Technica VMWare Code Execution Vulnerability 2021) Depending on the flaw being exploited, this may also involve [Exploitation for Defense Evasion](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1211) or [Exploitation for Client Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1203).

If an application is hosted on cloud-based infrastructure and/or is containerized, then exploiting it may lead to compromise of the underlying instance or container. This can allow an adversary a path to access the cloud or container APIs (e.g., via the [Cloud Instance Metadata API](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1552/005)), exploit container host access via [Escape to Host](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1611), or take advantage of weak identity and access management policies.

Adversaries may also exploit edge network infrastructure and related appliances, specifically targeting devices that do not support robust host-based defenses.(Citation: Mandiant Fortinet Zero Day)(Citation: Wired Russia Cyberwar)

For websites and databases, the OWASP top 10 and CWE top 25 highlight the most common web-based vulnerabilities.(Citation: OWASP Top 10)(Citation: CWE top 25)

2026.name: EPROCESS Structure Modification
2026.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may corrupt or wipe the disk data structures on a hard drive necessary to boot a system; targeting specific critical systems or in large numbers in a network to interrupt availability to system and network resources. 

Adversaries may attempt to render the system unable to boot by overwriting critical data located in structures such as the master boot record (MBR) or partition table.(Citation: Symantec Shamoon 2012)(Citation: FireEye Shamoon Nov 2016)(Citation: Palo Alto Shamoon Nov 2016)(Citation: Kaspersky StoneDrill 2017)(Citation: Unit 42 Shamoon3 2018) The data contained in disk structures may include the initial executable code for loading an operating system or the location of the file system partitions on disk. If this information is not present, the computer will not be able to load an operating system during the boot process, leaving the computer unavailable. [Disk Structure Wipe](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1561/002) may be performed in isolation, or along with [Disk Content Wipe](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1561/001) if all sectors of a disk are wiped.

On a network devices, adversaries may reformat the file system using [Network Device CLI](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/008) commands such as `format`.(Citation: format_cmd_cisco)

To maximize impact on the target organization, malware designed for destroying disk structures may have worm-like features to propagate across a network by leveraging other techniques like [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078), [OS Credential Dumping](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003), and [SMB/Windows Admin Shares](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002).(Citation: Symantec Shamoon 2012)(Citation: FireEye Shamoon Nov 2016)(Citation: Palo Alto Shamoon Nov 2016)(Citation: Kaspersky StoneDrill 2017)

This technique, often associated with APT28, involves directly manipulating kernel memory to modify process attributes, such as process IDs or security tokens, thereby breaking the parent-child relationship in process trees and enabling stealthy execution. It is a low-level system manipulation that requires high privileges and is used to bypass security mechanisms that rely on process enumeration and monitoring.[profile]

This low-level manipulation is a sophisticated method to conceal the execution chain of malware.

2028.name: Callback Execution
2028.profile: [profile]Callback Execution is a technique used by adversaries to hijack a process's execution flow by manipulating its KernelCallbackTable. This table, located in the Process Environment Block (PEB), contains an array of GUI function pointers. Attackers, such as the Lazarus Group, can locate the table via the `NtQueryInformationProcess()` API, duplicate it, and overwrite a callback function pointer (e.g., `fnCOPYDATA`) with the address of a malicious payload using `WriteProcessMemory()`. The hijacked function is then triggered by sending a Windows message to the process, executing the payload under the guise of a legitimate process, which can evade detection. This technique is associated with the APT28 intrusion set.[/profile]

The execution is masked under a legitimate process, potentially evading detection. This behavior is associated with groups like Lazarus Group.

2031.name: RC4 encryption key

Adversaries may compromise a network device’s encryption capability in order to bypass encryption that would otherwise protect data communications. (Citation: Cisco Synful Knock Evolution)

Encryption can be used to protect transmitted network traffic to maintain its confidentiality (protect against unauthorized disclosure) and integrity (protect against unauthorized changes). Encryption ciphers are used to convert a plaintext message to ciphertext and can be computationally intensive to decipher without the associated decryption key. Typically, longer keys increase the cost of cryptanalysis, or decryption without the key.

Adversaries can compromise and manipulate devices that perform encryption of network traffic. For example, through behaviors such as [Modify System Image](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1601), [Reduce Key Space](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1600/001), and [Disable Crypto Hardware](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1600/002), an adversary can negatively effect and/or eliminate a device’s ability to securely encrypt network traffic. This poses a greater risk of unauthorized disclosure and may help facilitate data manipulation, Credential Access, or Collection efforts. (Citation: Cisco Blog Legacy Device Attacks)

2033.name: network beacon traffic
2033.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may use traffic signaling to hide open ports or other malicious functionality used for persistence or command and control. Traffic signaling involves the use of a magic value or sequence that must be sent to a system to trigger a special response, such as opening a closed port or executing a malicious task. This may take the form of sending a series of packets with certain characteristics before a port will be opened that the adversary can use for command and control. Usually this series of packets consists of attempted connections to a predefined sequence of closed ports (i.e. [Port Knocking](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1205/001)), but can involve unusual flags, specific strings, or other unique characteristics. After the sequence is completed, opening a port may be accomplished by the host-based firewall, but could also be implemented by custom software.

Adversaries may also communicate with an already open port, but the service listening on that port will only respond to commands or trigger other malicious functionality if passed the appropriate magic value(s).

The observation of the signal packets to trigger the communication can be conducted through different methods. One means, originally implemented by Cd00r (Citation: Hartrell cd00r 2002), is to use the libpcap libraries to sniff for the packets in question. Another method leverages raw sockets, which enables the malware to use ports that are already open for use by other programs.

On network devices, adversaries may use crafted packets to enable [Network Device Authentication](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1556/004) for standard services offered by the device such as telnet.  Such signaling may also be used to open a closed service port such as telnet, or to trigger module modification of malware implants on the device, adding, removing, or changing malicious capabilities.  Adversaries may use crafted packets to attempt to connect to one or more (open or closed) ports, but may also attempt to connect to a router interface, broadcast, and network address IP on the same port in order to achieve their goals and objectives.(Citation: Cisco Synful Knock Evolution)(Citation: Mandiant - Synful Knock)(Citation: Cisco Blog Legacy Device Attacks)  To enable this traffic signaling on embedded devices, adversaries must first achieve and leverage [Patch System Image](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1601/001) due to the monolithic nature of the architecture.

Adversaries may also use the Wake-on-LAN feature to turn on powered off systems. Wake-on-LAN is a hardware feature that allows a powered down system to be powered on, or woken up, by sending a magic packet to it. Once the system is powered on, it may become a target for lateral movement.(Citation: Bleeping Computer - Ryuk WoL)(Citation: AMD Magic Packet)
2033.profile: [profile]Traffic Signaling, identified as MITRE ATT&CK T1205, is a Defense Evasion technique used across multiple platforms. It involves sending a specific sequence of packets, known as a "magic value," to trigger a hidden response like opening a closed port for command and control. This often manifests as port knocking, where connections to a predefined sequence of closed ports are attempted, but can also use unusual packet flags or strings. The signal can be observed using libpcap or raw sockets, and on network devices, it may require patching the system image to enable crafted packets for authentication or to activate malicious implants. Groups like APT28, Kimsuky, UNC3886, and Mustang Panda have been associated with its use.[/profile]
2033.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Network beacon traffic is a command and control technique where malware sends periodic, often low-frequency, network messages to an adversary's server to maintain persistence and receive instructions. This traffic, which can use common protocols like HTTP/S (T1071.001) or DNS (T1071.004), is designed to blend with normal network activity to evade detection. The beacons facilitate ongoing communication for remote access and task execution.

2034.name: download second-stage executable
2034.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may upload, install, or otherwise set up capabilities that can be used during targeting. To support their operations, an adversary may need to take capabilities they developed ([Develop Capabilities](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1587)) or obtained ([Obtain Capabilities](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1588)) and stage them on infrastructure under their control. These capabilities may be staged on infrastructure that was previously purchased/rented by the adversary ([Acquire Infrastructure](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1583)) or was otherwise compromised by them ([Compromise Infrastructure](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1584)). Capabilities may also be staged on web services, such as GitHub or Pastebin, or on Platform-as-a-Service (PaaS) offerings that enable users to easily provision applications.(Citation: Volexity Ocean Lotus November 2020)(Citation: Dragos Heroku Watering Hole)(Citation: Malwarebytes Heroku Skimmers)(Citation: Netskope GCP Redirection)(Citation: Netskope Cloud Phishing)

Staging of capabilities can aid the adversary in a number of initial access and post-compromise behaviors, including (but not limited to):

* Staging web resources necessary to conduct [Drive-by Compromise](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1189) when a user browses to a site.(Citation: FireEye CFR Watering Hole 2012)(Citation: Gallagher 2015)(Citation: ATT ScanBox)
* Staging web resources for a link target to be used with spearphishing.(Citation: Malwarebytes Silent Librarian October 2020)(Citation: Proofpoint TA407 September 2019)
* Uploading malware or tools to a location accessible to a victim network to enable [Ingress Tool Transfer](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1105).(Citation: Volexity Ocean Lotus November 2020)
* Installing a previously acquired SSL/TLS certificate to use to encrypt command and control traffic (ex: [Asymmetric Cryptography](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1573/002) with [Web Protocols](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1071/001)).(Citation: DigiCert Install SSL Cert)

2062.name: denial and deception (D&D)
2062.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may perform Endpoint Denial of Service (DoS) attacks to degrade or block the availability of services to users. Endpoint DoS can be performed by exhausting the system resources those services are hosted on or exploiting the system to cause a persistent crash condition. Example services include websites, email services, DNS, and web-based applications. Adversaries have been observed conducting DoS attacks for political purposes(Citation: FireEye OpPoisonedHandover February 2016) and to support other malicious activities, including distraction(Citation: FSISAC FraudNetDoS September 2012), hacktivism, and extortion.(Citation: Symantec DDoS October 2014)

An Endpoint DoS denies the availability of a service without saturating the network used to provide access to the service. Adversaries can target various layers of the application stack that is hosted on the system used to provide the service. These layers include the Operating Systems (OS), server applications such as web servers, DNS servers, databases, and the (typically web-based) applications that sit on top of them. Attacking each layer requires different techniques that take advantage of bottlenecks that are unique to the respective components. A DoS attack may be generated by a single system or multiple systems spread across the internet, which is commonly referred to as a distributed DoS (DDoS).

To perform DoS attacks against endpoint resources, several aspects apply to multiple methods, including IP address spoofing and botnets.

Adversaries may use the original IP address of an attacking system, or spoof the source IP address to make the attack traffic more difficult to trace back to the attacking system or to enable reflection. This can increase the difficulty defenders have in defending against the attack by reducing or eliminating the effectiveness of filtering by the source address on network defense devices.

Botnets are commonly used to conduct DDoS attacks against networks and services. Large botnets can generate a significant amount of traffic from systems spread across the global internet. Adversaries may have the resources to build out and control their own botnet infrastructure or may rent time on an existing botnet to conduct an attack. In some of the worst cases for DDoS, so many systems are used to generate requests that each one only needs to send out a small amount of traffic to produce enough volume to exhaust the target's resources. In such circumstances, distinguishing DDoS traffic from legitimate clients becomes exceedingly difficult. Botnets have been used in some of the most high-profile DDoS attacks, such as the 2012 series of incidents that targeted major US banks.(Citation: USNYAG IranianBotnet March 2016)

In cases where traffic manipulation is used, there may be points in the global network (such as high traffic gateway routers) where packets can be altered and cause legitimate clients to execute code that directs network packets toward a target in high volume. This type of capability was previously used for the purposes of web censorship where client HTTP traffic was modified to include a reference to JavaScript that generated the DDoS code to overwhelm target web servers.(Citation: ArsTechnica Great Firewall of China)

For attacks attempting to saturate the providing network, see [Network Denial of Service](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1498).
2062.profile: [profile]This entity, Endpoint Denial of Service (T1499), is an Impact technique targeting Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It degrades or blocks service availability by exhausting host system resources like CPU or memory, or by causing persistent crashes, rather than saturating the network. Common methods include using botnets to generate high-volume traffic and IP address spoofing to obscure the attack source. The Sandworm Team has been associated with this technique.[/profile]
2062.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Denial and Deception (D&D) is a strategic-level technique used to mislead or misdirect defenders and intelligence collection. It is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique with a specific T-ID. It operates across multiple tactics, primarily impacting Defense Evasion and potentially others like Collection or Command and Control. The technical mechanics involve adversaries adding junk data to protocols to obscure C2 traffic, using multiband communication to split traffic across different channels, and manipulating processes like Image File Execution Options injection to hide malicious activity. The goal is to create noise, false leads, and operational security to avoid detection and analysis.

2063.name: watering hole
2063.profile: [profile]Watering Hole is a technique (T1189) in the Initial Access tactic, targeting web browsers. It involves compromising legitimate websites frequented by a target demographic to stage malicious code, enabling drive-by compromise when users visit the site. This technique is associated with groups like APT28 and can be used to stage capabilities for further attacks.[/profile]

They stage malicious code on these sites to exploit visitors' browsers, enabling drive-by compromise. The attack leverages the trust users have in the legitimate website to facilitate initial access to the victim's network.

2064.name: fingerprinting scripts

Its key technical behaviors include performing extensive fingerprinting of a visitor's browser and system, injecting tracking cookies, and scanning website content for other networks and tracking scripts. It is also known to utilize the FingerprintJS2 library to generate an x64hash128 browser and environmental fingerprint (T1082). These scripts are deployed on compromised websites, often by initial access brokers like SocGholish, to profile victims as part of initial access campaigns, with their infrastructure sometimes hosted on specific autonomous systems like Proton66.[/profile]

It is deployed to infect websites, where it can also inject tracking cookies, scan for other network scripts, and facilitate initial access for other malware like Lumma Stealer, Badaudio, and Gootloader. 2077.name: Enable Content
2077.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may gain access and continuously communicate with victims by injecting malicious content into systems through online network traffic. Rather than luring victims to malicious payloads hosted on a compromised website (i.e., [Drive-by Target](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1608/004) followed by [Drive-by Compromise](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1189)), adversaries may initially access victims through compromised data-transfer channels where they can manipulate traffic and/or inject their own content. These compromised online network channels may also be used to deliver additional payloads (i.e., [Ingress Tool Transfer](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1105)) and other data to already compromised systems.(Citation: ESET MoustachedBouncer)

Adversaries may inject content to victim systems in various ways, including:

* From the middle, where the adversary is in-between legitimate online client-server communications (**Note:** this is similar but distinct from [Adversary-in-the-Middle](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1557), which describes AiTM activity solely within an enterprise environment) (Citation: Kaspersky Encyclopedia MiTM)
* From the side, where malicious content is injected and races to the client as a fake response to requests of a legitimate online server (Citation: Kaspersky ManOnTheSide)

Content injection is often the result of compromised upstream communication channels, for example at the level of an internet service provider (ISP) as is the case with "lawful interception."(Citation: Kaspersky ManOnTheSide)(Citation: ESET MoustachedBouncer)(Citation: EFF China GitHub Attack)
2077.profile: [profile]Content Injection, identified as T1659, is a technique within the Initial Access tactic applicable to multiple platforms. It involves adversaries manipulating or injecting malicious data into compromised upstream network channels, such as at an ISP level, to gain initial access to victims. This is executed either from a man-in-the-middle position or from the side, where a malicious response races to beat a legitimate server's reply. The technique is distinct from enterprise-focused Adversary-in-the-Middle and has been associated with groups like MoustachedBouncer.
2077.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Enable Content is a technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, identified as T1204.002 under the User Execution tactic. It operates on Windows, macOS, and Linux platforms. This technique involves an adversary tricking a user into enabling active content, such as macros or scripts, within a seemingly benign document (e.g., a Microsoft Office file) to execute malicious code. The execution typically occurs when the user clicks a button or allows content after seeing a security warning prompt. This method is a common initial infection vector for malware delivery.

2078.name: malicious program
2078.profile: [profile]The malicious program is attributed to the APT28 intrusion set. Its technical behaviors include using a malicious DLL with hidden export functions to evade dynamic detection and avoid forced execution, and it leverages the eBPF framework to execute malicious user-space code by hijacking benign processes. The malware is also referenced in analyses of other entities like latentbot, atlasagent, and triplecross.[/profile]
2078.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The malware, referred to as 'malicious program', is associated with the 'latentbot', 'atlasagent', and 'triplecross' entities. Its key technical behaviors include manipulating system operations through the 'system control' attack pattern, such as abusing control panel items or bypassing User Account Control. It employs techniques to evade detection, such as concealing the main export function of malicious DLLs to prevent dynamic analysis and forcibly starting execution. The malware can also leverage eBPF programs and benign processes to execute malicious user-space code. Its target platforms are systems where these low-level manipulation and execution techniques can be applied.

2079.name: Sofacy attacks
2079.profile: [profile]The entity "Sofacy attacks" is a technique used by the APT28 intrusion set. It aligns with MITRE ATT&CK technique T1564 (Hide Artifacts), falling under the Defense Evasion tactic and applicable to multiple platforms. Specifically, adversaries abuse operating system features to conceal malicious artifacts like files, directories, or user accounts to evade detection, as referenced in the Sofacy Komplex Trojan. This behavior is distinct from Endpoint Denial of Service (T1499) or protocol obfuscation via junk data (T1001.001), which are separate techniques.[/profile]
2079.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Sofacy attacks is a threat group activity associated with APT28, which employs techniques like Endpoint Denial of Service (T1499) to degrade service availability by exhausting system resources, Hide Artifacts (T1564) to abuse OS features for concealing files and activity, and Junk Data (T1001.001) to obfuscate command and control traffic with meaningless characters, complicating detection and analysis.

2080.name: system control
2080.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may abuse control.exe to proxy execution of malicious payloads. The Windows Control Panel process binary (control.exe) handles execution of Control Panel items, which are utilities that allow users to view and adjust computer settings. Control Panel items are registered executable (.exe) or Control Panel (.cpl) files, the latter are actually renamed dynamic-link library (.dll) files that export a CPlApplet function.(Citation: Microsoft Implementing CPL)(Citation: TrendMicro CPL Malware Jan 2014) For ease of use, Control Panel items typically include graphical menus available to users after being registered and loaded into the Control Panel.(Citation: Microsoft Implementing CPL) Control Panel items can be executed directly from the command line, programmatically via an application programming interface (API) call, or by simply double-clicking the file.(Citation: Microsoft Implementing CPL) (Citation: TrendMicro CPL Malware Jan 2014)(Citation: TrendMicro CPL Malware Dec 2013) Malicious Control Panel items can be delivered via [Phishing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566) campaigns(Citation: TrendMicro CPL Malware Jan 2014)(Citation: TrendMicro CPL Malware Dec 2013) or executed as part of multi-stage malware.(Citation: Palo Alto Reaver Nov 2017) Control Panel items, specifically CPL files, may also bypass application and/or file extension allow lists. Adversaries may also rename malicious DLL files (.dll) with Control Panel file extensions (.cpl) and register them to HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Control Panel\Cpls. Even when these registered DLLs do not comply with the CPL file specification and do not export CPlApplet functions, they are loaded and executed through its DllEntryPoint when Control Panel is executed. CPL files not exporting CPlApplet are not directly executable.(Citation: ESET InvisiMole June 2020)
2080.profile: [profile]System Control, also known as Control Panel Items (MITRE ID: T1218.002), is a Defense Evasion technique for Windows. It involves abusing the legitimate control.exe process or .cpl files to proxy execution of malicious payloads. Adversaries rename malicious DLLs with a .cpl extension and register them in the 'HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Control Panel\Cpls' registry key; these DLLs are then loaded and executed via their DllEntryPoint when Control Panel runs, bypassing application allow lists. Malicious items are often delivered via phishing campaigns.
2080.profile_without_enhance: [profile]System Control is a general attack pattern where adversaries manipulate or influence a system's operations, settings, or security mechanisms. This can involve techniques like abusing control panel items (e.g., malicious .cpl files) to execute payloads, bypassing User Account Control (UAC) to elevate privileges, or modifying low-level system components like Security Support Providers (SSP) to harvest credentials. The goal is to gain and maintain unauthorized control over a compromised system.

2083.name: advanced security measures

This includes disabling the Windows EventLog service via commands like `sc config eventlog start=disabled` or `Set-Service -Name EventLog -Status Stopped`, and modifying related registry keys to stop logging. It is associated with the intrusion set APT28.

These actions align with adversary objectives to evade detection and operate stealthily within a compromised environment.

2093.name: spear-phishing
2093.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may send phishing messages to gain access to victim systems. All forms of phishing are electronically delivered social engineering. Phishing can be targeted, known as spearphishing. In spearphishing, a specific individual, company, or industry will be targeted by the adversary. More generally, adversaries can conduct non-targeted phishing, such as in mass malware spam campaigns.

Adversaries may send victims emails containing malicious attachments or links, typically to execute malicious code on victim systems. Phishing may also be conducted via third-party services, like social media platforms. Phishing may also involve social engineering techniques, such as posing as a trusted source, as well as evasive techniques such as removing or manipulating emails or metadata/headers from compromised accounts being abused to send messages (e.g., [Email Hiding Rules](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1564/008)).(Citation: Microsoft OAuth Spam 2022)(Citation: Palo Alto Unit 42 VBA Infostealer 2014) Another way to accomplish this is by [Email Spoofing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1672)(Citation: Proofpoint-spoof) the identity of the sender, which can be used to fool both the human recipient as well as automated security tools,(Citation: cyberproof-double-bounce) or by including the intended target as a party to an existing email thread that includes malicious files or links (i.e., "thread hijacking").(Citation: phishing-krebs)

Victims may also receive phishing messages that instruct them to call a phone number where they are directed to visit a malicious URL, download malware,(Citation: sygnia Luna Month)(Citation: CISA Remote Monitoring and Management Software) or install adversary-accessible remote management tools onto their computer (i.e., [User Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204)).(Citation: Unit42 Luna Moth)
2093.profile: [profile]Spear-phishing is the targeted form of T1566 (Phishing) under the Initial Access tactic, primarily targeting Windows, macOS, and Linux platforms. It involves sending tailored electronic messages, often via email, to specific individuals or organizations, using social engineering to pose as a trusted source and deliver malicious attachments or links that lead to code execution. Evasive techniques include email spoofing, thread hijacking, and manipulating email headers or metadata from compromised accounts. This technique is notably used by groups like FIN7 and APT28.[/profile]
2093.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Spear-phishing is a targeted social engineering technique, identified as a sub-technique of Phishing (T1566) within the Initial Access tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It involves sending deceptive electronic communications, such as emails, to specific individuals, companies, or industries. The mechanics typically include posing as a trusted source, using malicious links or attachments to deliver payloads, and employing evasive methods like email spoofing or thread hijacking to increase credibility and bypass security measures.

2094.name: backdoors
2094.profile: [profile]Backdoors (T1205) are a Persistence technique used across multiple platforms, allowing adversaries to maintain access to compromised systems. They can be implemented via hardware supply chain manipulation (T1195.003) to insert difficult-to-detect components, or through software like malware (T1588.001) acquired from criminal marketplaces. A specific technical method involves using socket filters (T1205.002), where adversaries with elevated permissions attach filters to network sockets using libraries like `libpcap`; these filters monitor for a specific crafted packet and, upon receiving it, trigger actions such as activating a reverse shell or installing an implant, providing a passive and stealthy command channel.[/profile]
2094.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Backdoors is a broad technique (not a specific MITRE ID) where adversaries establish persistent, covert access to compromised systems. Technical mechanics include manipulating hardware supply chains to insert undetectable backdoors into devices, using socket filters with libraries like libpcap to trigger implant activation from specific network packets, and acquiring backdoor malware from criminal marketplaces. This supports persistence and command and control across various platforms.

2095.name: information stealers
2095.profile: [profile]Information stealers is a category of malware designed to illicitly gather and exfiltrate sensitive data from a compromised system. This technique, which aligns with the Credential Access tactic, operates across multiple platforms including Windows, Linux, and macOS. It functions by scanning for and collecting specific data types such as credentials, browser cookies, cryptocurrency wallets, and system information, often using keyloggers or clipboard monitors. The stolen data is typically sent to a command-and-control server, as seen in operations linked to groups like APT28. This activity is distinct from general discovery techniques and focuses on the targeted theft of valuable information for financial gain or espionage.
2095.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "information stealers" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique but describes a class of malware or tools. Based on context, it aligns with the tactic of Collection (TA0009) and operates across multiple platforms. Technical mechanics involve capturing sensitive data like credentials, browser information, and system details from a compromised host, often using keylogging, credential API hooking, or file scraping. This stolen information is frequently exfiltrated over command and control channels for further malicious use.

2123.name: Compromised account
2123.profile: [profile]Compromised Account is a technique within the broader Valid Accounts (T1078) framework, used for Initial Access, Persistence, Privilege Escalation, and Defense Evasion. Adversaries, such as APT28, obtain and abuse credentials from existing user, domain, or cloud accounts to bypass access controls, pivot across networks, and maintain persistent access to systems like VPNs and remote services. They often target inactive user accounts to evade detection and may use these compromised credentials to conduct follow-on activities without deploying malware, making their presence harder to identify. 2155.uncertain_name: component object model and distributed com
2155.uncertain_mes:
**This technique has been deprecated. Please use [Distributed Component Object Model](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/003) and [Component Object Model](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1559/001).**

Adversaries may use the Windows Component Object Model (COM) and Distributed Component Object Model (DCOM) for local code execution or to execute on remote systems as part of lateral movement. 

COM is a component of the native Windows application programming interface (API) that enables interaction between software objects, or executable code that implements one or more interfaces.(Citation: Fireeye Hunting COM June 2019) Through COM, a client object can call methods of server objects, which are typically Dynamic Link Libraries (DLL) or executables (EXE).(Citation: Microsoft COM) DCOM is transparent middleware that extends the functionality of Component Object Model (COM) (Citation: Microsoft COM) beyond a local computer using remote procedure call (RPC) technology.(Citation: Fireeye Hunting COM June 2019)

Permissions to interact with local and remote server COM objects are specified by access control lists (ACL) in the Registry. (Citation: Microsoft COM ACL)(Citation: Microsoft Process Wide Com Keys)(Citation: Microsoft System Wide Com Keys) By default, only Administrators may remotely activate and launch COM objects through DCOM.

Adversaries may abuse COM for local command and/or payload execution. Various COM interfaces are exposed that can be abused to invoke arbitrary execution via a variety of programming languages such as C, C++, Java, and VBScript.(Citation: Microsoft COM) Specific COM objects also exists to directly perform functions beyond code execution, such as creating a [Scheduled Task/Job](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1053), fileless download/execution, and other adversary behaviors such as Privilege Escalation and Persistence.(Citation: Fireeye Hunting COM June 2019)(Citation: ProjectZero File Write EoP Apr 2018)

Adversaries may use DCOM for lateral movement. Through DCOM, adversaries operating in the context of an appropriately privileged user can remotely obtain arbitrary and even direct shellcode execution through Office applications (Citation: Enigma Outlook DCOM Lateral Movement Nov 2017) as well as other Windows objects that contain insecure methods.(Citation: Enigma MMC20 COM Jan 2017)(Citation: Enigma DCOM Lateral Movement Jan 2017) DCOM can also execute macros in existing documents (Citation: Enigma Excel DCOM Sept 2017) and may also invoke [Dynamic Data Exchange](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1173) (DDE) execution directly through a COM created instance of a Microsoft Office application (Citation: Cyberreason DCOM DDE Lateral Movement Nov 2017), bypassing the need for a malicious document.

2156.name: 利用OrderBox DNS服务器
2156.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may communicate using the Domain Name System (DNS) application layer protocol to avoid detection/network filtering by blending in with existing traffic. Commands to the remote system, and often the results of those commands, will be embedded within the protocol traffic between the client and server. 

The DNS protocol serves an administrative function in computer networking and thus may be very common in environments. DNS traffic may also be allowed even before network authentication is completed. DNS packets contain many fields and headers in which data can be concealed. Often known as DNS tunneling, adversaries may abuse DNS to communicate with systems under their control within a victim network while also mimicking normal, expected traffic.(Citation: PAN DNS Tunneling)(Citation: Medium DnsTunneling)

DNS beaconing may be used to send commands to remote systems via DNS queries. A DNS beacon is created by tunneling DNS traffic (i.e. [Protocol Tunneling](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1572)). The commands may be embedded into different DNS records, for example, TXT or A records.(Citation: OilRig Uses Updated BONDUPDATER to Target Middle Eastern Government) DNS beacons may be difficult to detect because the beacons infrequently communicate with infected devices.(Citation: DNS Beacons) Infrequent communication conceals the malicious DNS traffic with normal DNS traffic.
2156.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique Application Layer Protocol: DNS (T1071.004) under the Command and Control tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It involves adversaries using the DNS protocol to covertly communicate with compromised systems, embedding commands and data within DNS query and response traffic to blend with normal administrative traffic and avoid detection. This is often implemented through DNS tunneling or beaconing, where commands are concealed in fields like TXT or A records, and communication can be infrequent to further evade security measures. Associated groups include APT28, OilRig, and FIN7.[/profile]
2156.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "利用OrderBox DNS服务器" (Exploit OrderBox DNS Server) is a technique for establishing command and control infrastructure. It involves adversaries setting up and using their own DNS servers, such as those from the OrderBox service, to gain greater control over DNS-based C2 channels. This allows them to configure conditional responses to malware and provides more flexibility in structuring the covert communication, bypassing reliance on compromised or hijacked existing servers.

2157.name: influence operations

This activity involves coordinated efforts to manipulate public perception or decision-making, often through information warfare. As indicated by its association with APT28 and related techniques like social media account creation (T1585.001) and data manipulation (T1565), these operations leverage compromised or fabricated online personas and the alteration of information to achieve psychological or political effects.
2157.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Influence Operations is a technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, broadly aligned with the collection of tactics known as Influence. These personas are used to establish connections with targets, often as part of a social engineering campaign to enable initial access. The technique is employed by numerous threat groups, including Lazarus Group, APT32, and Scattered Spider.

This stolen data, which can include personally identifiable information and purchase histories, is then used to enable follow-on attacks like personalized phishing campaigns against the organization's customers for financial gain or further compromise.

2169.name: Exploit Vulnerabilities
2169.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may acquire information about vulnerabilities that can be used during targeting. A vulnerability is a weakness in computer hardware or software that can, potentially, be exploited by an adversary to cause unintended or unanticipated behavior to occur. Adversaries may find vulnerability information by searching open databases or gaining access to closed vulnerability databases.(Citation: National Vulnerability Database)

An adversary may monitor vulnerability disclosures/databases to understand the state of existing, as well as newly discovered, vulnerabilities. There is usually a delay between when a vulnerability is discovered and when it is made public. An adversary may target the systems of those known to conduct vulnerability research (including commercial vendors). Knowledge of a vulnerability may cause an adversary to search for an existing exploit (i.e. [Exploits](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1588/005)) or to attempt to develop one themselves (i.e. [Exploits](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1587/004)).
2169.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1588.006, named Acquire Vulnerabilities, under the Reconnaissance tactic for all platforms. It involves adversaries gathering information about software or hardware weaknesses to inform their operations. This is achieved by searching open databases like the National Vulnerability Database, monitoring vulnerability disclosures, or targeting the systems of vulnerability researchers. Acquired vulnerability knowledge is a precursor to obtaining or developing exploits. Associated threat groups include Sandworm Team, Storm-0501, and Volt Typhoon.[profile]
2169.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Exploit Vulnerabilities" is a foundational concept rather than a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique; it describes the core action of leveraging software or hardware weaknesses to cause unintended behavior. This action underpins numerous specific techniques such as Exploit Public-Facing Application (T1190), Exploitation for Client Execution (T1203), and Application or System Exploitation (T1499.004). The process involves adversaries identifying vulnerabilities, often through research or monitoring databases, and then developing or acquiring corresponding exploits to gain initial access, escalate privileges, or execute code on target systems across various platforms.

2170.name: Zero-Day Attacks
2170.profile: [profile]Zero-Day Attacks is a general attack pattern where adversaries exploit previously unknown software vulnerabilities (zero-days). The technique involves leveraging these unpatched flaws to execute unauthorized code, crash applications or systems to cause a denial of service, or achieve other objectives like data destruction or service disruption, as seen in application or system exploitation (T1499.004). It is associated with intrusion sets like APT28.[/profile]
2170.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Zero-Day Attacks are a broad category of adversarial actions leveraging previously unknown software vulnerabilities, not a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique with a designated ID. They are executed across various platforms to achieve objectives like Initial Access or Impact. The core technical mechanic involves exploiting undisclosed flaws in applications or systems, which can cause crashes leading to denial of service, data destruction, or service stoppage. These attacks are distinct from and can enable other specific techniques like application or system exploitation (T1499.004).

2187.name: coordinated attack
2187.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may downgrade or use a version of system features that may be outdated, vulnerable, and/or does not support updated security controls. Downgrade attacks typically take advantage of a system’s backward compatibility to force it into less secure modes of operation. 

Adversaries may downgrade and use various less-secure versions of features of a system, such as [Command and Scripting Interpreter](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059)s or even network protocols that can be abused to enable [Adversary-in-the-Middle](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1557) or [Network Sniffing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1040).(Citation: Praetorian TLS Downgrade Attack 2014) For example, [PowerShell](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001) versions 5+ includes Script Block Logging (SBL), which can record executed script content. However, adversaries may attempt to execute a previous version of PowerShell that does not support SBL with the intent to [Impair Defenses](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1562) while running malicious scripts that may have otherwise been detected.(Citation: CrowdStrike BGH Ransomware 2021)(Citation: Mandiant BYOL 2018)(Citation: att_def_ps_logging)

Adversaries may similarly target network traffic to downgrade from an encrypted HTTPS connection to an unsecured HTTP connection that exposes network data in clear text.(Citation: Targeted SSL Stripping Attacks Are Real)(Citation: Crowdstrike Downgrade) On Windows systems, adversaries may downgrade the boot manager to a vulnerable version that bypasses Secure Boot, granting the ability to disable various operating system security mechanisms.(Citation: SafeBreach)
2187.profile: [profile]Downgrade Attack (T1562.010) is an Impair Defenses technique targeting multiple platforms. It exploits backward compatibility to force systems into less secure modes, such as executing older PowerShell versions lacking Script Block Logging to evade detection, downgrading HTTPS connections to unencrypted HTTP to expose data, or compromising the Windows boot manager to bypass Secure Boot. APT28 has been associated with this method.[/profile]
2187.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Coordinated Attack is a technique where adversaries orchestrate multiple compromised systems to perform synchronized tasks, often forming a botnet. This approach enables large-scale malicious activities such as Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attacks or extensive phishing campaigns. Adversaries may build their own botnet by compromising systems or acquire existing ones through purchase or takeover. The technique leverages the collective power of these systems to execute commands in unison, enhancing the impact and scale of the attack.

2190.name: Unauthorized Access
2190.profile: [profile]Unauthorized Access is a broad, non-standard technique not formally mapped to a specific MITRE ATT&CK ID. It is associated with the intrusion set APT28 and fundamentally involves gaining entry to systems or data without permission. This can be achieved through exploiting software vulnerabilities to steal credentials, using stolen application access tokens to bypass authentication, or acquiring pre-existing compromised access from brokers. The goal is to establish an initial foothold, often followed by deploying persistent remote access tools or web shells to maintain control.
2190.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Unauthorized Access is a broad attack pattern not formally mapped to a specific MITRE ATT&CK ID, tactic, or platform. It fundamentally involves gaining entry to a system, network, or resource without proper permission. This can be achieved through various technical mechanics, including exploiting software vulnerabilities to forge authentication tickets, using stolen application access tokens to bypass standard login processes, or acquiring pre-existing compromised access from broker networks. The goal is to establish an initial foothold, often as a precursor to more specific malicious activities like data exfiltration or deploying persistent remote access tools.

2192.name: Advanced credential attacks
2192.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may use credentials obtained from breach dumps of unrelated accounts to gain access to target accounts through credential overlap. Occasionally, large numbers of username and password pairs are dumped online when a website or service is compromised and the user account credentials accessed. The information may be useful to an adversary attempting to compromise accounts by taking advantage of the tendency for users to use the same passwords across personal and business accounts.

Credential stuffing is a risky option because it could cause numerous authentication failures and account lockouts, depending on the organization's login failure policies.

Typically, management services over commonly used ports are used when stuffing credentials. Commonly targeted services include the following:

* SSH (22/TCP)
* Telnet (23/TCP)
* FTP (21/TCP)
* NetBIOS / SMB / Samba (139/TCP & 445/TCP)
* LDAP (389/TCP)
* Kerberos (88/TCP)
* RDP / Terminal Services (3389/TCP)
* HTTP/HTTP Management Services (80/TCP & 443/TCP)
* MSSQL (1433/TCP)
* Oracle (1521/TCP)
* MySQL (3306/TCP)
* VNC (5900/TCP)

In addition to management services, adversaries may "target single sign-on (SSO) and cloud-based applications utilizing federated authentication protocols," as well as externally facing email applications, such as Office 365.(Citation: US-CERT TA18-068A 2018)
2192.profile: [profile]Credential Stuffing is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1110.004 under the Credential Access tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It involves using credentials from unrelated breach dumps to gain access by exploiting password reuse across accounts. Attackers typically automate login attempts against management services like SSH (22/TCP), RDP (3389/TCP), and HTTP/S (80/443/TCP), as well as cloud applications and SSO systems. This method risks triggering account lockouts due to authentication failures. The intrusion set APT28 has been associated with this technique.[/profile]
2192.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Advanced credential attacks is a broad category within the Credential Access tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. It encompasses sophisticated methods beyond simple credential theft, such as exploiting software vulnerabilities (e.g., Kerberos flaws like MS14-068 for ticket forgery or replay attacks) to bypass authentication mechanisms and obtain privileged access. These attacks can also involve disabling or tampering with cloud logging (e.g., in AWS or Office 365) to obscure malicious credential activity and evade detection.

2199.name: phishing campaigns
2199.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may send phishing messages to gain access to victim systems. All forms of phishing are electronically delivered social engineering. Phishing can be targeted, known as spearphishing. In spearphishing, a specific individual, company, or industry will be targeted by the adversary. More generally, adversaries can conduct non-targeted phishing, such as in mass malware spam campaigns.

Adversaries may send victims emails containing malicious attachments or links, typically to execute malicious code on victim systems. Phishing may also be conducted via third-party services, like social media platforms. Phishing may also involve social engineering techniques, such as posing as a trusted source, as well as evasive techniques such as removing or manipulating emails or metadata/headers from compromised accounts being abused to send messages (e.g., [Email Hiding Rules](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1564/008)).(Citation: Microsoft OAuth Spam 2022)(Citation: Palo Alto Unit 42 VBA Infostealer 2014) Another way to accomplish this is by [Email Spoofing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1672)(Citation: Proofpoint-spoof) the identity of the sender, which can be used to fool both the human recipient as well as automated security tools,(Citation: cyberproof-double-bounce) or by including the intended target as a party to an existing email thread that includes malicious files or links (i.e., "thread hijacking").(Citation: phishing-krebs)

Victims may also receive phishing messages that instruct them to call a phone number where they are directed to visit a malicious URL, download malware,(Citation: sygnia Luna Month)(Citation: CISA Remote Monitoring and Management Software) or install adversary-accessible remote management tools onto their computer (i.e., [User Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204)).(Citation: Unit42 Luna Moth)
2199.profile: [profile]Phishing, identified as T1566, is an Initial Access tactic used across multiple platforms. It involves sending electronic messages, such as emails with malicious attachments or links, to execute code on victim systems. Techniques include spearphishing specific targets, using social media platforms, spoofing sender identities, and hijacking existing email threads. Evasion methods involve manipulating email metadata or using compromised accounts. Groups like APT28, Kimsuky, and Axiom have employed this technique.[/profile]
2199.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Phishing campaigns are a broad operational activity rather than a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique, often encompassing the execution of techniques like Phishing (T1566) and Phishing for Information (T1598). These campaigns involve sending deceptive electronic messages, such as emails with malicious attachments or links, to execute code or harvest credentials. They utilize social engineering, posing as trusted sources, and may employ evasive tactics like email spoofing or thread hijacking to increase success rates across various platforms.

2215.name: bypass controls
2215.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may undermine security controls that will either warn users of untrusted activity or prevent execution of untrusted programs. Operating systems and security products may contain mechanisms to identify programs or websites as possessing some level of trust. Examples of such features would include a program being allowed to run because it is signed by a valid code signing certificate, a program prompting the user with a warning because it has an attribute set from being downloaded from the Internet, or getting an indication that you are about to connect to an untrusted site.

Adversaries may attempt to subvert these trust mechanisms. The method adversaries use will depend on the specific mechanism they seek to subvert. Adversaries may conduct [File and Directory Permissions Modification](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1222) or [Modify Registry](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1112) in support of subverting these controls.(Citation: SpectorOps Subverting Trust Sept 2017) Adversaries may also create or steal code signing certificates to acquire trust on target systems.(Citation: Securelist Digital Certificates)(Citation: Symantec Digital Certificates)
2215.profile: [profile]This entity is mapped to MITRE ATT&CK technique T1553, Subvert Trust Controls, under the Defense Evasion tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It involves undermining security mechanisms that warn users or block untrusted programs, such as code signing certificates or file quarantine attributes. Specific methods include modifying file permissions or registry settings to bypass these controls, and adversaries may create or steal digital certificates to gain system trust. The intrusion set APT28 has been associated with this technique.
2215.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "bypass controls" is a general attack pattern where adversaries evade security mechanisms. It aligns with MITRE ATT&CK Sub-techniques like T1553.001 (Gatekeeper Bypass) and T1548.002 (Bypass User Account Control), falling under the Defense Evasion tactic. Technical methods include modifying file attributes (e.g., the `com.apple.quarantine` flag), exploiting logic errors in code signing checks, using auto-elevated processes like `eventvwr.exe`, and abusing container files to subvert Mark-of-the-Web protections. These actions allow execution of untrusted code by circumventing prompts and trust validation.

It is the goal of techniques like "Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism" (T1548) and "Elevated Execution with Prompt" (T1514/T1548.004). APT28 is a known intrusion set that employs such methods. Technical mechanics involve circumventing native controls like User Account Control (UAC) or abusing APIs such as `AuthorizationExecuteWithPrivileges` on macOS to prompt users for credentials and gain higher-level permissions, often to install malware or establish persistence.[/profile]
2216.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "escalate privileges" is a broad attack pattern, not a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on retrieved information, it encompasses methods like abusing elevation control mechanisms (T1548) to bypass native privilege controls, and specifically on macOS, leveraging the deprecated AuthorizationExecuteWithPrivileges API (T1548.004 / T1514) to prompt users for credentials and execute code with root privileges, often combined with masquerading. These actions are performed to gain higher-level permissions for malicious activities like software installation and persistence.

2228.name: samsam
2228.profile: [profile]SamSam is a ransomware family first observed in early 2016, also known as S0370. It is attributed to the Boss Spider group, with potential links to APT28. Key technical behaviors include requiring manual operator interaction to execute core components and directly infecting internet-facing web servers rather than relying on phishing. 2252.name: 利用域名注册信息进行基础设施隐藏
2252.profile: [profile]The entity "利用域名注册信息进行基础设施隐藏" (Infrastructure Hiding via Domain Registration Information) is a technique for concealing malicious infrastructure. It is associated with the intrusion set APT28. The technique leverages legitimate domain registration services to create or acquire domains that blend in with normal traffic, making it difficult to attribute the infrastructure to the adversary. This method provides operational security by obscuring the true ownership and control of the command and control servers or other malicious online assets.
2252.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "利用域名注册信息进行基础设施隐藏" (Infrastructure Hiding via Domain Registration Information) is a technique for obscuring malicious infrastructure. Based on related MITRE ATT&CK concepts, this likely involves registering domains using false or anonymized WHOIS data to conceal the adversary's identity and ownership of command and control servers. This method, often used in conjunction with techniques like Domain Fronting (T1090.004) or Dead Drop Resolvers (T1102.001), leverages common web services (T1583.006) to blend malicious traffic with legitimate activity, complicating attribution and infrastructure takedown efforts.

2253.name: spoofed
2253.profile: [profile]The entity 'spoofed' is a general concept, not a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the retrieved context, it is a core action used in multiple techniques. In email spoofing (T1566.002), adversaries modify email headers like the FROM field to impersonate a sender, often exploiting weak or absent email authentication policies (SPF, DKIM, DMARC). This is used for social engineering, such as phishing, and has been associated with groups like APT28. The concept also applies to network attacks like reflection amplification (T1498.002), where adversaries spoof a victim's IP address to direct traffic from reflectors, and to command and control, where junk data (T1001.001) can be appended to spoof or obfuscate protocol traffic.[/profile]
2253.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity 'spoofed' is a general attack pattern, not a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on retrieved context, it describes the action of falsifying an identity or source. In email spoofing (T1566.002), adversaries modify email headers like the FROM address to impersonate a sender, often exploiting weak or absent email authentication policies (SPF, DKIM, DMARC). In network attacks like T1498.002, spoofing involves forging a packet's source IP address to reflect traffic toward a victim in denial-of-service attacks. The core mechanic is the deceptive alteration of identifying information in a communication protocol.

2254.name: cybersquatting
2254.profile: [profile]Cybersquatting, also known as typosquatting, is a technique where adversaries acquire domain names that are visually similar to legitimate domains, often through the use of homoglyphs, different top-level domains, or common typos. This technique, often associated with groups like APT28, is primarily used to facilitate initial access tactics such as Phishing and Drive-by Compromise by tricking users into visiting malicious sites that impersonate trusted ones. The acquired domains can be used to host payloads or serve as part of command and control infrastructure, leveraging the deceptive appearance to bypass user vigilance.[/profile]
2254.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Cybersquatting is a technique where adversaries acquire domain names that are visually similar to legitimate ones, often using homoglyphs, different top-level domains (TLDs), or typosquatting to create deceptive lookalikes. These domains are used for malicious purposes such as Phishing, Drive-by Compromise, and Command and Control. Adversaries may also employ internationalized domain names (IDNs) for homograph attacks and use private WHOIS services to obscure ownership. This method allows them to exploit the trust associated with familiar domain names to deliver malware or conduct other attacks.

2255.name: obscuring ownership

It may involve techniques such as using false registration details, intermediary services, or compromised legitimate resources to create layers of separation between the malicious actor and their operational assets, complicating attribution efforts.

It involves adversaries concealing the true ownership of files, directories, or other system resources to hide their presence and activities. This is achieved by manipulating file attributes, access control lists (ACLs), or using tools to change ownership metadata, making malicious artifacts appear legitimate or belonging to a benign user or system process.

2256.name: suspicious name server activity
2256.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may buy, lease, rent, or obtain physical servers that can be used during targeting. Use of servers allows an adversary to stage, launch, and execute an operation. During post-compromise activity, adversaries may utilize servers for various tasks, such as watering hole operations in [Drive-by Compromise](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1189), enabling [Phishing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566) operations, or facilitating [Command and Control](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0011). Instead of compromising a third-party [Server](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1584/004) or renting a [Virtual Private Server](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1583/003), adversaries may opt to configure and run their own servers in support of operations. Free trial periods of cloud servers may also be abused.(Citation: Free Trial PurpleUrchin)(Citation: Freejacked) 

Adversaries may only need a lightweight setup if most of their activities will take place using online infrastructure. Or, they may need to build extensive infrastructure if they want to test, communicate, and control other aspects of their activities on their own systems.(Citation: NYTStuxnet)
2256.profile: [profile]The entity "Server" corresponds to MITRE ATT&CK technique T1583.004 under the Resource Development tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. This technique involves adversaries acquiring physical servers through purchase, lease, or rental to stage and execute operations, including watering holes, phishing, or command and control. They may configure their own servers or abuse free cloud trials for infrastructure, as observed with groups like Earth Lusca and Sandworm Team.

This activity enables adversaries to have greater control over DNS-based C2 channels, allowing them to configure conditional responses and structure the communication to blend with normal traffic or evade detection. It is associated with groups like Sea Turtle, Axiom, and Hexane.

2258.name: Masquerade
2258.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may masquerade malicious payloads as legitimate files through changes to the payload's formatting, including the file’s signature, extension, icon, and contents. Various file types have a typical standard format, including how they are encoded and organized. For example, a file’s signature (also known as header or magic bytes) is the beginning bytes of a file and is often used to identify the file’s type. For example, the header of a JPEG file, is 0xFF 0xD8 and the file extension is either `.JPE`, `.JPEG` or `.JPG`. Adversaries may edit the header’s hex code and/or the file extension of a malicious payload in order to bypass file validation checks and/or input sanitization. This behavior is commonly used when payload files are transferred (e.g., [Ingress Tool Transfer](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1105)) and stored (e.g., [Upload Malware](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1608/001)) so that adversaries may move their malware without triggering detections. Common non-executable file types and extensions, such as text files (`.txt`) and image files (`.jpg`, `.gif`, etc.) may be typically treated as benign. Based on this, adversaries may use a file extension to disguise malware, such as naming a PHP backdoor code with a file name of test.gif. A user may not know that a file is malicious due to the benign appearance and file extension. Polyglot files, which are files that have multiple different file types and that function differently based on the application that will execute them, may also be used to disguise malicious malware and capabilities.(Citation: polygot_icedID)
2258.profile: [profile]Masquerade, identified as T1036.008 "Masquerade File Type," is a Defense Evasion technique. Adversaries disguise malicious payloads as legitimate files by altering file signatures (magic bytes), extensions (e.g., naming a PHP backdoor as `test.gif`), icons, or contents to bypass validation checks. This includes using polyglot files that function as multiple file types. It is commonly associated with groups like BlackByte, Volt Typhoon, and Mustang Panda.
2258.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Masquerade is a technique under the MITRE ATT&CK framework, identified as T1036, primarily used for Defense Evasion. It involves adversaries manipulating the names, locations, or metadata of files, tasks, services, or accounts to appear legitimate and bypass security measures. This includes altering file signatures and extensions to disguise malicious payloads as benign file types like .txt or .jpg, renaming system utilities, and creating or renaming accounts or scheduled tasks with names similar to trusted ones. The technique is applicable across multiple platforms and is employed by various threat groups to evade detection.

2263.name: spear-phishing attacks
2263.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may send phishing messages to gain access to victim systems. All forms of phishing are electronically delivered social engineering. Phishing can be targeted, known as spearphishing. In spearphishing, a specific individual, company, or industry will be targeted by the adversary. More generally, adversaries can conduct non-targeted phishing, such as in mass malware spam campaigns.

Adversaries may send victims emails containing malicious attachments or links, typically to execute malicious code on victim systems. Phishing may also be conducted via third-party services, like social media platforms. Phishing may also involve social engineering techniques, such as posing as a trusted source, as well as evasive techniques such as removing or manipulating emails or metadata/headers from compromised accounts being abused to send messages (e.g., [Email Hiding Rules](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1564/008)).(Citation: Microsoft OAuth Spam 2022)(Citation: Palo Alto Unit 42 VBA Infostealer 2014) Another way to accomplish this is by [Email Spoofing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1672)(Citation: Proofpoint-spoof) the identity of the sender, which can be used to fool both the human recipient as well as automated security tools,(Citation: cyberproof-double-bounce) or by including the intended target as a party to an existing email thread that includes malicious files or links (i.e., "thread hijacking").(Citation: phishing-krebs)

Victims may also receive phishing messages that instruct them to call a phone number where they are directed to visit a malicious URL, download malware,(Citation: sygnia Luna Month)(Citation: CISA Remote Monitoring and Management Software) or install adversary-accessible remote management tools onto their computer (i.e., [User Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204)).(Citation: Unit42 Luna Moth)
2263.profile: [profile]Spear-phishing attacks, identified as MITRE ATT&CK T1566 under the Initial Access tactic, target Windows, macOS, and Linux platforms. This technique involves sending tailored electronic messages, often via email, to specific individuals or organizations to deliver malicious attachments or links that execute code upon user interaction. It employs social engineering by posing as a trusted source and may use evasive methods like email spoofing or thread hijacking. Groups such as APT3 and APT28 are known to utilize this method.[/profile]
2263.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Spear-phishing attacks, corresponding to MITRE ATT&CK technique T1566.001 (Spearphishing Attachment) under the Initial Access tactic, target Windows, macOS, and Linux platforms. This technique involves sending tailored emails to specific individuals or organizations, often containing malicious attachments like Office documents or executables that require user interaction to execute. The emails employ social engineering, such as posing as a trusted source or using thread hijacking, and may use evasive tactics like file extension manipulation or providing decryption passwords to bypass defenses.

2264.name: watering hole attacks
2264.profile: [profile]Watering Hole Attacks, also known as T1189, fall under the Initial Access tactic and target multiple platforms. This technique involves compromising websites frequently visited by a target demographic, then waiting for victims to visit to exploit their systems. It is used by groups like OilRig and APT28. Staging capabilities on controlled infrastructure, such as web resources for drive-by compromises, is a key preparatory step for these attacks.
2264.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Watering hole attacks, known as T1189 in the MITRE ATT&CK framework, fall under the Initial Access tactic and target multiple platforms. This technique involves compromising websites frequented by a target demographic, then staging malicious web resources to exploit visitors' browsers for system access. The attack is often used to support other malicious activities, including as a link target in spearphishing campaigns.

2266.name: YARA

It is referenced in the context of detection rules for other malware, such as Lockbit, Matanbuchus, and DCRat (with a possible family link to QuasarRAT), indicating its application in cybersecurity analysis and threat hunting to define signatures for malicious software across various platforms.

2267.name: rolling double XOR algorithm
2267.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may abuse a double extension in the filename as a means of masquerading the true file type. A file name may include a secondary file type extension that may cause only the first extension to be displayed (ex: File.txt.exe may render in some views as just File.txt). However, the second extension is the true file type that determines how the file is opened and executed. The real file extension may be hidden by the operating system in the file browser (ex: explorer.exe), as well as in any software configured using or similar to the system’s policies.(Citation: PCMag DoubleExtension)(Citation: SOCPrime DoubleExtension) Adversaries may abuse double extensions to attempt to conceal dangerous file types of payloads. A very common usage involves tricking a user into opening what they think is a benign file type but is actually executable code. Such files often pose as email attachments and allow an adversary to gain [Initial Access](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0001) into a user’s system via [Spearphishing Attachment](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001) then [User Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204). For example, an executable file attachment named Evil.txt.exe may display as Evil.txt to a user. The user may then view it as a benign text file and open it, inadvertently executing the hidden malware.(Citation: SOCPrime DoubleExtension) Common file types, such as text files (.txt, .doc, etc.) and image files (.jpg, .gif, etc.) are typically used as the first extension to appear benign. Executable extensions commonly regarded as dangerous, such as .exe, .lnk, .hta, and .scr, often appear as the second extension and true file type.
2267.profile: [profile]The entity "rolling double XOR algorithm" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the provided context, it is likely a custom cryptographic method. The retrieved information describes adversaries using custom encryption schemes, such as XOR-ing plaintext with a fixed key, to obfuscate data for command and control or prior to exfiltration. This weak ciphertext can be implemented without external libraries, and groups like Mustang Panda and Kimsuky have been associated with similar custom archival or cryptographic techniques.
2267.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "rolling double XOR algorithm" is a custom encryption technique used by adversaries to obfuscate data. Based on related MITRE ATT&CK techniques, it functions as a variant of custom cryptographic protocols (T1024) or a method for archiving data (T1560.003). The core technical mechanic involves applying XOR operations with a key that changes or "rolls" during the encryption process, creating a simple but proprietary cipher. This method is implemented without external libraries to avoid detection and has been associated with threat groups like Mustang Panda and Kimsuky for securing command and control traffic or preparing collected data for exfiltration.
