2280.name: Registry Key for Persistence
2280.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may clear artifacts associated with previously established persistence on a host system to remove evidence of their activity. This may involve various actions, such as removing services, deleting executables, [Modify Registry](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1112), [Plist File Modification](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1647), or other methods of cleanup to prevent defenders from collecting evidence of their persistent presence.(Citation: Cylance Dust Storm) Adversaries may also delete accounts previously created to maintain persistence (i.e. [Create Account](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1136)).(Citation: Talos - Cisco Attack 2022)

In some instances, artifacts of persistence may also be removed once an adversary’s persistence is executed in order to prevent errors with the new instance of the malware.(Citation: NCC Group Team9 June 2020)
2280.profile: [profile]Registry Key for Persistence, corresponding to MITRE ATT&CK technique T1547.001 (Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder), is a Persistence tactic for Windows. It involves adding a program path to specific Windows Registry run keys, such as HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run, causing the referenced program to execute automatically upon user login. This method is commonly abused by adversaries, including APT28, to maintain access by ensuring malware is relaunched after system reboots.
2280.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Registry Key for Persistence is a technique where adversaries add or modify Windows Registry keys to automatically execute malicious code during system boot or user logon, achieving persistence. This aligns with the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1547.001 (Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder) under the Persistence tactic for Windows platforms. Specific mechanics include creating entries in common autostart locations like HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run or HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run, which reference malicious executables or DLLs. Adversaries may also abuse keys like HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Active Setup\Installed Components with a malicious StubPath. This method allows malware to survive reboots and maintain access under the context of the logged-in user.

2281.name: User Interaction
2281.uncertain_mes:
An adversary may rely upon specific actions by a user in order to gain execution. Users may be subjected to social engineering to get them to execute malicious code by, for example, opening a malicious document file or link. These user actions will typically be observed as follow-on behavior from forms of [Phishing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566).

While [User Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204) frequently occurs shortly after Initial Access it may occur at other phases of an intrusion, such as when an adversary places a file in a shared directory or on a user's desktop hoping that a user will click on it. This activity may also be seen shortly after [Internal Spearphishing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1534).

Adversaries may also deceive users into performing actions such as:

* Enabling [Remote Access Tools](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1219), allowing direct control of the system to the adversary
* Running malicious JavaScript in their browser, allowing adversaries to [Steal Web Session Cookie](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539)s(Citation: Talos Roblox Scam 2023)(Citation: Krebs Discord Bookmarks 2023)
* Downloading and executing malware for [User Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204)
* Coerceing users to copy, paste, and execute malicious code manually(Citation: Reliaquest-execution)(Citation: proofpoint-selfpwn)

For example, tech support scams can be facilitated through [Phishing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566), vishing, or various forms of user interaction. Adversaries can use a combination of these methods, such as spoofing and promoting toll-free numbers or call centers that are used to direct victims to malicious websites, to deliver and execute payloads containing malware or [Remote Access Tools](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1219).(Citation: Telephone Attack Delivery)
2281.profile: [profile]User Execution, identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1204 under the Execution tactic, targets Windows, macOS, and Linux platforms. It relies on deceiving a user into performing specific actions to execute malicious code, such as opening malicious documents or links delivered via phishing, clicking files placed in shared directories, or manually copying and pasting malicious commands. This technique is also used to trick users into enabling remote access tools or running malicious JavaScript in their browser. Associated threat groups include APT28, FIN7, Scattered Spider, and LAPSUS$.[/profile]
2281.profile_without_enhance: [profile]User Interaction is a technique where adversaries rely on specific actions by a user to achieve their objectives, such as gaining execution. It is often a follow-on behavior from phishing campaigns, where users are deceived into opening malicious documents or links. This interaction can also involve tricking users into enabling remote access tools, running malicious JavaScript, or manually copying and executing code. The technique is not assigned a specific MITRE ATT&CK ID or Tactic in the provided data, but it is a core mechanism for social engineering-based execution across multiple platforms.

2282.name: Web Beacon
2282.profile: [profile]Web Beacon is a technique for command and control, likely corresponding to T1071.001 (Web Protocols) under the Command and Control tactic. It operates by embedding malicious commands and data within standard HTTP/S or WebSocket traffic to blend with normal web activity, often using fields and headers for concealment. This method allows adversaries to mimic expected traffic and avoid network filtering. The intrusion-set APT28 has been associated with this technique.[/profile]
2282.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Web Beacon is a technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, categorized under Command and Control (Tactic) and applicable to multiple platforms. It functions as a low-and-slow communication method where an infected host sends periodic, often infrequent, DNS queries to an adversary-controlled server. Commands and data are concealed within DNS record fields, such as TXT or A records, to blend with legitimate traffic and avoid detection. This technique is a form of protocol tunneling (T1572) used to maintain covert, persistent access.

2291.name: Beaconing
2291.profile: [profile]Beaconing is a command and control technique (T1071) within the Command and Control tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It involves infected systems sending periodic, often infrequent, network requests (beacons) to an adversary-controlled server to receive instructions, blending with normal traffic to avoid detection. This technique is commonly implemented via DNS tunneling (T1071.004), where commands are embedded in DNS query fields like TXT or A records. Associated malware includes Oopsie and Carberp variant, and it is used by intrusion sets like OilRig and APT29.[/profile]
2291.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Beaconing is a command and control technique where malware periodically sends outbound signals to an adversary's server to maintain persistence and receive instructions. It is often implemented via DNS tunneling (T1071.004), embedding commands within DNS queries using records like TXT or A to blend with normal traffic. Adversaries may use junk data (T1001.001) to obfuscate these communications, making detection more difficult by preventing trivial traffic analysis.

2292.name: Exploit Injection
2292.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may attempt to exploit a weakness in an Internet-facing host or system to initially access a network. The weakness in the system can be a software bug, a temporary glitch, or a misconfiguration.

Exploited applications are often websites/web servers, but can also include databases (like SQL), standard services (like SMB or SSH), network device administration and management protocols (like SNMP and Smart Install), and any other system with Internet-accessible open sockets.(Citation: NVD CVE-2016-6662)(Citation: CIS Multiple SMB Vulnerabilities)(Citation: US-CERT TA18-106A Network Infrastructure Devices 2018)(Citation: Cisco Blog Legacy Device Attacks)(Citation: NVD CVE-2014-7169) On ESXi infrastructure, adversaries may exploit exposed OpenSLP services; they may alternatively exploit exposed VMware vCenter servers.(Citation: Recorded Future ESXiArgs Ransomware 2023)(Citation: Ars Technica VMWare Code Execution Vulnerability 2021) Depending on the flaw being exploited, this may also involve [Exploitation for Defense Evasion](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1211) or [Exploitation for Client Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1203).

If an application is hosted on cloud-based infrastructure and/or is containerized, then exploiting it may lead to compromise of the underlying instance or container. This can allow an adversary a path to access the cloud or container APIs (e.g., via the [Cloud Instance Metadata API](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1552/005)), exploit container host access via [Escape to Host](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1611), or take advantage of weak identity and access management policies.

Adversaries may also exploit edge network infrastructure and related appliances, specifically targeting devices that do not support robust host-based defenses.(Citation: Mandiant Fortinet Zero Day)(Citation: Wired Russia Cyberwar)

For websites and databases, the OWASP top 10 and CWE top 25 highlight the most common web-based vulnerabilities.(Citation: OWASP Top 10)(Citation: CWE top 25)
2292.profile: [profile]Exploit Public-Facing Application, identified as T1190, is an Initial Access tactic targeting multiple platforms. It involves exploiting weaknesses like software bugs or misconfigurations in internet-facing systems, including web servers, databases (e.g., SQL), standard services (SMB, SSH), network device protocols (SNMP), and cloud or container instances. This can provide initial network access and may lead to further exploitation of underlying infrastructure or APIs. The technique is associated with numerous threat groups, including APT28.
2292.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Exploit Injection is a generic attack pattern not directly mapped to a standard MITRE ATT&CK ID. It broadly describes the act of inserting and executing malicious code by taking advantage of a software vulnerability or weakness. This technique can target various platforms, including applications, operating systems, or network services, to achieve initial access, privilege escalation, or other adversarial objectives. The specific mechanics depend on the vulnerability being exploited, such as buffer overflows or injection flaws in input fields.

2293.name: Fingerprinting Script
2293.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may use Windows logon scripts automatically executed at logon initialization to establish persistence. Windows allows logon scripts to be run whenever a specific user or group of users log into a system.(Citation: TechNet Logon Scripts) This is done via adding a path to a script to the HKCU\Environment\UserInitMprLogonScript Registry key.(Citation: Hexacorn Logon Scripts) Adversaries may use these scripts to maintain persistence on a single system. Depending on the access configuration of the logon scripts, either local credentials or an administrator account may be necessary.
2293.profile: [profile]Fingerprinting Script is a technique for discovery, likely mapping to MITRE ATT&CK T1592 (Reconnaissance) on multiple platforms. It involves adversaries using scripts to gather detailed system or network configuration data, such as operating system details, installed software, open ports, and user accounts, to profile the target environment. This information is used to tailor subsequent attack stages. The technique is associated with APT28 and Cobalt Group, who employ it to enhance the precision of their operations.
2293.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Fingerprinting Script" is a reconnaissance technique where adversaries execute scripts to gather detailed system and network information. This technique, which can be implemented using languages like JavaScript, involves querying attributes such as the operating system, installed software, network configuration, and hardware details to profile a target environment. The collected data is used to inform subsequent attack stages, such as vulnerability exploitation or lateral movement.

2294.name: Island-Hopping Technique
2294.profile: [profile]Island-Hopping Technique is a command and control tactic where adversaries compromise an intermediate system within a trusted network to stage attacks on a primary target, often to bypass perimeter defenses. The technique involves using the compromised intermediary as a proxy or relay for communications and malware delivery, obscuring the ultimate target and source. APT28 is a known user of this method. The specific technical mechanics involve establishing a foothold on the intermediate host to proxy traffic, which can include using standard protocols to blend in with legitimate network activity.[/profile]
2294.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Island-Hopping Technique is a command and control tactic where adversaries compromise an intermediate system within a trusted network to stage attacks on a primary target, often using it as a proxy. This method helps avoid direct connections to the final victim, blending malicious traffic with legitimate communications to bypass security controls.

2295.name: iOS Spy App
2295.uncertain_mes: Industrial Spy is a relatively new ransomware group that emerged in April 2022. In some instances, the threat group appears to only exfiltrate and ransom data, while in other cases they encrypt, exfiltrate and ransom data.

Its key behaviors include downloading and installing iOS apps in the background, which then steal Apple ID credentials and exfiltrate them to a command-and-control server. It is also suspected of collecting paid iOS tweaks from compromised devices. The malware is associated with the APT28 intrusion set.[/profile]

A key technical behavior is its ability to stealthily prompt for and exfiltrate Apple ID credentials and passwords to a remote server, similar to the AceDeceiver malware. Its infrastructure involves using Telegram bot APIs for data exfiltration, and it is suspected of harvesting paid iOS tweaks from compromised devices.

2321.name: Backdoor using victim’s mail server
2321.uncertain_mes:
Key Findings
- This research focuses on the ‘Mail-O’ malware used against the FSB and other Russian government organizations, detailed in the May 2021 FSB NKTsKI and Rostelecom-Solar report.
- Early armchair commentary presumed that given the targets, this attack would undoubtedly be the work of a Western government, Five Eyes, or the United States.
- Our analysis disproves that hypothesis.
2321.profile: [profile]The malware is known as Mail-O, a backdoor that uses the victim's mail server for command and control. It is attributed to the APT28 intrusion set. Its key technical behavior involves being controlled via emails, with commands hidden in PDF or JPG attachments using steganography, and it operates to hide its activity by deleting all emails sent to or received from the attacker. The primary target platforms are systems running Microsoft Outlook. It was used in campaigns against Russian government organizations like the FSB.
2321.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The malware is a backdoor that leverages a victim's mail server for command and control, with aliases including Mail-O. It is attributed to the Turla group. Its key technical behaviors involve using email-based command channels, where commands are hidden in PDF or JPG attachments via steganography, and it actively deletes attacker-sent emails to hide its activity. The target platform is Microsoft Outlook, indicating a focus on Windows environments. This operational method allows for covert communication through compromised email infrastructure.

2322.name: Russian language settings
2322.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may impair a system's ability to hibernate, reboot, or shut down in order to extend access to infected machines. When a computer enters a dormant state, some or all software and hardware may cease to operate which can disrupt malicious activity.(Citation: Sleep, shut down, hibernate)

Adversaries may abuse system utilities and configuration settings to maintain access by preventing machines from entering a state, such as standby, that can terminate malicious activity.(Citation: Microsoft: Powercfg command-line options)(Citation: systemdsleep Linux)

For example, `powercfg` controls all configurable power system settings on a Windows system and can be abused to prevent an infected host from locking or shutting down.(Citation: Two New Monero Malware Attacks Target Windows and Android Users) Adversaries may also extend system lock screen timeout settings.(Citation: BATLOADER: The Evasive Downloader Malware) Other relevant settings, such as disk and hibernate timeout, can be similarly abused to keep the infected machine running even if no user is active.(Citation: CoinLoader: A Sophisticated Malware Loader Campaign)

Aware that some malware cannot survive system reboots, adversaries may entirely delete files used to invoke system shut down or reboot.(Citation: Condi-Botnet-binaries)
2322.profile: [profile]The entity "Russian language settings" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the provided data, it appears to be a misinterpretation or mislabeling of the technique "System Language Discovery" (T1614.001) under the Discovery tactic. This technique involves adversaries checking a system's language, such as by querying the Windows registry key `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Nls\Language` or using API functions like `GetUserDefaultUILanguage`, to infer the host's geographical location and tailor their follow-on actions. The provided neighbor and retrieved information for "power settings" (T1653) is unrelated and discarded as irrelevant to this specific language discovery behavior.
2322.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Russian language settings" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the retrieved context, it is a specific application of the technique System Language Discovery (T1614.001), which falls under the Discovery tactic. This technique involves querying a system's language configuration, such as by checking Windows registry keys or API functions like GetUserDefaultUILanguage, to infer the geographical location of a host. Adversaries use this information to tailor their operations, for instance, by avoiding infection of systems in specific regions to reduce scrutiny from law enforcement.

2323.name: Local replication to defeat closed/isolated networks
2323.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may search and gather information about victims from closed (e.g., paid, private, or otherwise not freely available) sources that can be used during targeting. Information about victims may be available for purchase from reputable private sources and databases, such as paid subscriptions to feeds of technical/threat intelligence data. Adversaries may also purchase information from less-reputable sources such as dark web or cybercrime blackmarkets.(Citation: ZDNET Selling Data)

Adversaries may search in different closed databases depending on what information they seek to gather. Information from these sources may reveal opportunities for other forms of reconnaissance (ex: [Phishing for Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1598) or [Search Open Websites/Domains](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1593)), establishing operational resources (ex: [Develop Capabilities](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1587) or [Obtain Capabilities](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1588)), and/or initial access (ex: [External Remote Services](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1133) or [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078)).
2323.profile: [profile]The entity name "Local replication to defeat closed/isolated networks" does not correspond to a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the provided context, the core concept is the technique "Replication Through Removable Media" (T1091). This technique, used for Initial Access or Lateral Movement, involves copying malware to removable media like USB drives to infect systems on disconnected or air-gapped networks. Execution can occur via Autorun features, manual user execution, or by compromising the media's firmware. The related group APT28 has been associated with this method. A related technique for command and control in such environments is "Communication Through Removable Media" (T1092).
2323.profile_without_enhance: [profile]This technique, "Local replication to defeat closed/isolated networks," is a method for lateral movement and initial access. It involves copying malware to removable media, such as USB drives, to bridge air-gapped or disconnected networks. The malware may be designed to execute automatically via Autorun features when the media is connected to a new system, or it may be disguised as a legitimate file to trick users into manual execution. This approach allows adversaries to propagate from an internet-connected system to isolated internal networks, enabling follow-on command and control or data exfiltration activities, as referenced in related techniques for communication through removable media.

2324.name: Formal code development environment
2324.profile: [profile]Formal code development environment is a software development setting used by adversaries to create, test, and refine malicious tools and malware, often blending in with legitimate developer activity. This environment is associated with the APT28 intrusion set and can be leveraged for persistence through malicious IDE extensions or for command and control via IDE tunneling, facilitating stealthy operations within a target network.

Based on the retrieved context, it likely refers to the broader environment where legitimate development tools and processes are exploited. Adversaries may compromise this environment by targeting integrated development environments (IDEs) and their extensions, such as Visual Studio Code, to establish persistent access or command and control channels via IDE tunneling. They can also manipulate software dependencies, development tools, and public code repositories within these environments to introduce malicious code or gather targeting information.

2325.name: Various data theft techniques at defense events and exhibitions
2325.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may abuse the [at](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0110) utility to perform task scheduling for initial or recurring execution of malicious code. The [at](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0110) utility exists as an executable within Windows, Linux, and macOS for scheduling tasks at a specified time and date. Although deprecated in favor of [Scheduled Task](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1053/005)'s [schtasks](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0111) in Windows environments, using [at](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0110) requires that the Task Scheduler service be running, and the user to be logged on as a member of the local Administrators group. In addition to explicitly running the `at` command, adversaries may also schedule a task with [at](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0110) by directly leveraging the [Windows Management Instrumentation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1047) `Win32_ScheduledJob` WMI class.(Citation: Malicious Life by Cybereason) On Linux and macOS, [at](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0110) may be invoked by the superuser as well as any users added to the at.allow file. If the at.allow file does not exist, the at.deny file is checked. Every username not listed in at.deny is allowed to invoke [at](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0110). If the at.deny exists and is empty, global use of [at](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0110) is permitted. If neither file exists (which is often the baseline) only the superuser is allowed to use [at](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0110).(Citation: Linux at) Adversaries may use [at](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0110) to execute programs at system startup or on a scheduled basis for [Persistence](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0003). [at](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0110) can also be abused to conduct remote [Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0002) as part of [Lateral Movement](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0008) and/or to run a process under the context of a specified account (such as SYSTEM). In Linux environments, adversaries may also abuse [at](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0110) to break out of restricted environments by using a task to spawn an interactive system shell or to run system commands. Similarly, [at](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0110) may also be used for [Privilege Escalation](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0004) if the binary is allowed to run as superuser via sudo.(Citation: GTFObins at)
2325.profile: [profile]The entity name "Various data theft techniques at defense events and exhibitions" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. The provided Self Info and Similar Entities describe the standard technique "at" (Scheduled Task/Job: At), which is a utility for task scheduling on Windows, Linux, and macOS, identified as T1053.002 under the Execution and Persistence tactics. Its technical mechanics involve using the `at` command or the `Win32_ScheduledJob` WMI class to schedule malicious code execution, requiring the Task Scheduler service and local administrator privileges on Windows, with access controlled by `at.allow` and `at.deny` files on Linux/macOS. It has been used by groups like APT28. The broader theme of data theft at events is not reflected in the core technical definition.[/profile]
2325.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Various data theft techniques at defense events and exhibitions" is a specific attack pattern where adversaries steal data at physical security and defense conferences. This technique falls under the Collection tactic, as adversaries gather sensitive information through on-site methods. The platform is physical systems or devices present at these events. Technical mechanics involve direct, in-person interception or copying of data from displays, devices, or conversations. Supplementary information links it to broader exfiltration methods, indicating stolen data is often later transmitted via command and control channels.

2334.name: DownDelphi Bootkit
2334.profile: [profile]DownDelphi Bootkit, also known as Downdelph, is a bootkit attributed to APT28. It infects the Master Boot Record (MBR) to control the startup process, targeting Windows 7 on 32-bit and 64-bit architectures. Its key behaviors include hooking Interrupt 13h and the boot manager (bootmgr), decrypting and executing its own code from physical address 0x97C00, and ultimately injecting a user-mode component into explorer.exe to load the Downdelph payload. It belongs to the broader category of MBR-infecting bootkits like Rovnix.

2362.uncertain_mes: [FIN7](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0046) is a financially-motivated threat group that has been active since 2013. [FIN7](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0046) has targeted the retail, restaurant, hospitality, software, consulting, financial services, medical equipment, cloud services, media, food and beverage, transportation, pharmaceutical, and utilities industries in the United States. A portion of [FIN7](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0046) was operated out of a front company called Combi Security and often used point-of-sale malware for targeting efforts. Since 2020, [FIN7](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0046) shifted operations to big game hunting (BGH), including use of [REvil](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0496) ransomware and their own Ransomware-as-a-Service (RaaS), Darkside. The group's TTPs involve phishing with malicious documents and point-of-sale malware targeting. It is attributed to Russian-speaking actors and operated through a front company, Combi Security. Since 2020, it has shifted to big game hunting, using REvil and its own Darkside ransomware. Primary targets are U.S. sectors, including retail, hospitality, financial services, and utilities, with a clear motivation for financial theft and extortion.

2367.name: RC4 algorithm encryption
2367.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may compromise a network device’s encryption capability in order to bypass encryption that would otherwise protect data communications. (Citation: Cisco Synful Knock Evolution)

Encryption can be used to protect transmitted network traffic to maintain its confidentiality (protect against unauthorized disclosure) and integrity (protect against unauthorized changes). Encryption ciphers are used to convert a plaintext message to ciphertext and can be computationally intensive to decipher without the associated decryption key. Typically, longer keys increase the cost of cryptanalysis, or decryption without the key.

Adversaries can compromise and manipulate devices that perform encryption of network traffic. For example, through behaviors such as [Modify System Image](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1601), [Reduce Key Space](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1600/001), and [Disable Crypto Hardware](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1600/002), an adversary can negatively effect and/or eliminate a device’s ability to securely encrypt network traffic. This poses a greater risk of unauthorized disclosure and may help facilitate data manipulation, Credential Access, or Collection efforts. (Citation: Cisco Blog Legacy Device Attacks)
2367.profile: [profile]RC4 algorithm encryption is a symmetric encryption technique (T1573.001) under the Command and Control tactic, used across multiple platforms to conceal C2 traffic. It employs a stream cipher with a variable key size, but its use of a weak key-scheduling algorithm can make it vulnerable to cryptanalysis, allowing adversaries to potentially decrypt captured communications without the key. The malware XAgent has been associated with using this method.
2367.profile_without_enhance: [profile]RC4 algorithm encryption is referenced as a symmetric encryption algorithm used to conceal command and control traffic, as seen in the related technique Symmetric Cryptography (T1573.001). It is a known stream cipher that uses the same key for encryption and decryption. This method is employed by various threat groups, including MuddyWater and APT28, to obfuscate network communications, though implementations using static keys within malware can be vulnerable to reverse engineering.

2368.name: HTTP POST requests
2368.profile: [profile]The entity "HTTP POST requests" is a technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, specifically identified as T1071.001 (Web Protocols) under the Command and Control tactic. It operates across multiple platforms, including Windows, Linux, and macOS. Adversaries abuse the HTTP/S protocol to conceal command and control traffic within normal web traffic, often embedding data within POST request fields and headers to blend in and avoid detection. This method is commonly used by malware like XAgent for data exfiltration, including to webhook endpoints, and is associated with numerous threat groups.
2368.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "HTTP POST requests" is a common technique used within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, often as a sub-technique of Application Layer Protocol (T1071.001) for Command and Control, and for Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol (T1048). It operates across Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. Technically, adversaries embed commands and exfiltrated data within the body of HTTP POST requests to blend with normal web traffic, using tools like `curl` to send data to adversary-controlled web servers or webhook endpoints. This method provides a covert channel that can evade detection by mimicking legitimate HTTPS traffic to common services.

2369.name: HTTP requests
2369.profile: [profile]HTTP requests is a technique used within the broader MITRE ATT&CK technique T1071.001 (Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols) under the Command and Control tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. It involves adversaries embedding command and control communications or exfiltrated data within standard HTTP/S traffic to blend with normal web activity and avoid detection. This method is utilized by malware like XAgent and numerous threat groups, including APT28 and Lazarus Group, to conceal data within common protocol fields and headers.
2369.profile_without_enhance: [profile]HTTP requests are a fundamental network activity that adversaries can exploit within various MITRE ATT&CK techniques. They are commonly used for command and control (C2) communication, as seen in T1071.001 (Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols), where attackers embed commands within standard HTTP/S traffic to blend with normal web activity and avoid detection. This method is leveraged by numerous threat groups, including APT28, Lazarus Group, and MuddyWater. HTTP requests also facilitate activities like Internet Connection Discovery (T1016.001) to check for network connectivity and Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol (T1048) for data theft. The technique is platform-agnostic, affecting Windows, Linux, and macOS systems, and often involves tools like `curl` or built-in scripting to generate and conceal malicious traffic within legitimate web protocols.

2375.name: Base64 encoding (custom alphabet)
2375.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may encode data with a standard data encoding system to make the content of command and control traffic more difficult to detect. Command and control (C2) information can be encoded using a standard data encoding system that adheres to existing protocol specifications. Common data encoding schemes include ASCII, Unicode, hexadecimal, Base64, and MIME.(Citation: Wikipedia Binary-to-text Encoding)(Citation: Wikipedia Character Encoding) Some data encoding systems may also result in data compression, such as gzip.
2375.profile: [profile]Base64 encoding (custom alphabet) is a non-standard encoding technique (T1132.002) used in the Command and Control tactic to obfuscate C2 traffic. It operates by modifying the standard Base64 alphabet, altering the character set used for encoding binary data into text to evade signature-based detection. This method is distinct from standard encoding (T1132.001) and has been associated with malware like XAgent.[/profile]
2375.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Base64 encoding (custom alphabet) is a non-standard encoding technique, aligning with MITRE ATT&CK sub-technique T1132.002 under the Command and Control tactic for multiple platforms. It involves modifying the standard Base64 encoding scheme by using a custom character set or alphabet, diverging from the RFC 4648 specification to obfuscate command and control traffic and hinder detection. This method is a specific implementation of non-standard data encoding.

2376.name: Random string generation
2376.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may make use of Domain Generation Algorithms (DGAs) to dynamically identify a destination domain for command and control traffic rather than relying on a list of static IP addresses or domains. This has the advantage of making it much harder for defenders to block, track, or take over the command and control channel, as there potentially could be thousands of domains that malware can check for instructions.(Citation: Cybereason Dissecting DGAs)(Citation: Cisco Umbrella DGA)(Citation: Unit 42 DGA Feb 2019)

DGAs can take the form of apparently random or “gibberish” strings (ex: istgmxdejdnxuyla.ru) when they construct domain names by generating each letter. Alternatively, some DGAs employ whole words as the unit by concatenating words together instead of letters (ex: cityjulydish.net). Many DGAs are time-based, generating a different domain for each time period (hourly, daily, monthly, etc). Others incorporate a seed value as well to make predicting future domains more difficult for defenders.(Citation: Cybereason Dissecting DGAs)(Citation: Cisco Umbrella DGA)(Citation: Talos CCleanup 2017)(Citation: Akamai DGA Mitigation)

Adversaries may use DGAs for the purpose of [Fallback Channels](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1008). When contact is lost with the primary command and control server malware may employ a DGA as a means to reestablishing command and control.(Citation: Talos CCleanup 2017)(Citation: FireEye POSHSPY April 2017)(Citation: ESET Sednit 2017 Activity)
2376.profile: [profile]Domain Generation Algorithms (DGAs) is a command and control technique with MITRE ID T1568.002 under the Command and Control tactic. It operates by algorithmically generating a large number of potential domain names, often using time-based seeds or concatenating random letters or words (e.g., istgmxdejdnxuyla.ru), to dynamically establish resilient and hard-to-block C2 channels or fallback channels. It is associated with groups like APT41 and malware like XAgent.[/profile]
2376.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Random string generation is a technique used by adversaries to evade detection by creating unpredictable identifiers or data. It is commonly applied in obfuscation and command and control, such as generating random or gibberish strings for domain names in Domain Generation Algorithms (DGAs) to hinder blocklisting and tracking. This method can produce time-based or seed-based variations, making defensive prediction difficult, and is utilized by groups like APT41 and TA551.

2383.name: backdoor
2383.profile: [profile]The entity is a backdoor, a persistent malicious access mechanism. It is not a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique but a general concept implemented by various techniques. For example, adversaries can insert hardware backdoors via supply chain compromise (T1195.003) to gain high-degree control over systems like servers and network devices. Groups like FIN7 and APT28 utilize backdoors, with APT28 also employing related techniques like protocol obfuscation with junk data (T1001.001) for command and control. Backdoors can also be established in software, such as by patching domain controller authentication processes (T1556.001) to create credential-based access.[/profile]
2383.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity is a generic attack pattern named "backdoor," which is not a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique but a broad category. It refers to any method that creates a covert means of accessing a system, bypassing normal authentication. Technical mechanics include manipulating hardware or firmware in the supply chain to insert difficult-to-detect backdoors into devices like servers or network infrastructure, as seen in hardware supply chain compromise. Backdoors can also be established by patching authentication processes on domain controllers, such as with Skeleton Key malware, to inject credentials that allow access to any domain account.

2384.name: cgeventtapcreate
2384.profile: [profile]The entity "cgeventtapcreate" is a macOS-specific technique, likely corresponding to MITRE ATT&CK T1056.001 "Input Capture: Keylogging" under the Collection tactic. It functions by creating an Event Tap via the CGEventTapCreate API to monitor and log user keyboard inputs and mouse events system-wide. This allows adversaries like APT28 to capture sensitive data such as credentials. The technique is a low-level, programmatic form of input capture distinct from script-based methods like AppleScript.
2384.profile_without_enhance: [profile]cgeventtapcreate is a macOS-specific technique for establishing persistence and collecting user input. It involves creating an event tap using the CGEventTapCreate API to monitor and intercept system events like keystrokes and mouse clicks. This allows adversaries to capture sensitive data such as passwords and credentials in real-time, often by hooking into the event stream before it reaches applications. The technique is commonly used in conjunction with scripting methods like AppleScript (T1155) for automation and can be part of broader input capture or GUI interaction strategies.

2385.name: _mycgeventtapcallback
2385.profile: [profile]The entity '_mycgeventtapcallback' is a technique for process hijacking, likely mapped to MITRE ATT&CK ID T1574.013 under the Privilege Escalation tactic for Windows platforms. It involves modifying the KernelCallbackTable in a process's PEB, often by locating it via NtQueryInformationProcess, duplicating it, and overwriting a callback function pointer (e.g., fnCOPYDATA) with a malicious payload address using WriteProcessMemory. Execution is triggered by sending a Windows message to invoke the tampered callback, after which the table may be restored to evade detection, as observed in campaigns by groups like APT28 and Lazarus.[/profile]
2385.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity '_mycgeventtapcallback' is a technique for process hijacking, likely mapped to MITRE ATT&CK ID T1574.013 under the Persistence and Privilege Escalation tactics for Windows. It operates by modifying the KernelCallbackTable in a process's Process Environment Block (PEB), replacing a legitimate callback function (such as fnCOPYDATA) with a malicious payload address. This tampered function is then triggered via a Windows message, executing the adversary's code within the context of a legitimate GUI process to evade detection, and the table may be restored post-execution.

2387.name: pressedkeywithkeycode
2387.profile: [profile]PressedKeyWithKeyCode is a technique for simulating keystrokes to perform actions on a victim's computer, aligning with the MITRE ATT&CK Input Injection technique (T1674) under the Execution tactic on Windows. It operates by preprogramming adversary tooling or using physical devices like Human Interface Devices (HIDs) to monitor system events, such as the Windows message loop, and then injecting specific key sequences. For example, it can detect a user visiting a bank URL and simulate keystrokes to open a browser's developer console, paste malicious JavaScript from the clipboard, and execute it to manipulate web content. This method has been used by groups like APT28 and Fin7 in campaigns involving malicious USB devices to launch PowerShell and download malware.
2387.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "pressedkeywithkeycode" is a technique for simulating keystrokes, aligning with MITRE ATT&CK technique T1674 (Input Injection) under the Execution tactic, primarily on Windows platforms. It works by programmatically generating and injecting key press events with specific key codes into a system's input stream, often using APIs like `keybd_event` or `SendInput` in Windows. This allows adversaries to automate interactions, such as executing commands via a command prompt or manipulating GUI applications, without physical keyboard input.

2412.name: phishing attacks
2412.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may send phishing messages to gain access to victim systems. All forms of phishing are electronically delivered social engineering. Phishing can be targeted, known as spearphishing. In spearphishing, a specific individual, company, or industry will be targeted by the adversary. More generally, adversaries can conduct non-targeted phishing, such as in mass malware spam campaigns.

Adversaries may send victims emails containing malicious attachments or links, typically to execute malicious code on victim systems. Phishing may also be conducted via third-party services, like social media platforms. Phishing may also involve social engineering techniques, such as posing as a trusted source, as well as evasive techniques such as removing or manipulating emails or metadata/headers from compromised accounts being abused to send messages (e.g., [Email Hiding Rules](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1564/008)).(Citation: Microsoft OAuth Spam 2022)(Citation: Palo Alto Unit 42 VBA Infostealer 2014) Another way to accomplish this is by [Email Spoofing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1672)(Citation: Proofpoint-spoof) the identity of the sender, which can be used to fool both the human recipient as well as automated security tools,(Citation: cyberproof-double-bounce) or by including the intended target as a party to an existing email thread that includes malicious files or links (i.e., "thread hijacking").(Citation: phishing-krebs)

Victims may also receive phishing messages that instruct them to call a phone number where they are directed to visit a malicious URL, download malware,(Citation: sygnia Luna Month)(Citation: CISA Remote Monitoring and Management Software) or install adversary-accessible remote management tools onto their computer (i.e., [User Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204)).(Citation: Unit42 Luna Moth)
2412.profile: [profile]Phishing, designated as T1566, is an Initial Access tactic used across multiple platforms. It involves sending electronic messages, such as emails with malicious attachments or links, to trick victims into executing code, often via User Execution. The technique employs social engineering by posing as a trusted source and uses evasive methods like email spoofing, thread hijacking, or manipulating email headers from compromised accounts. It is distinct from credential harvesting (T1598) and is associated with groups like APT28, Kimsuky, and Sea Turtle.[/profile]
2412.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Phishing Attacks correspond to MITRE ATT&CK technique T1566, primarily under the Initial Access tactic and applicable across multiple platforms. This technique involves adversaries sending electronic messages, such as emails with malicious attachments or links, to trick victims into executing code, often leveraging social engineering by posing as a trusted source. It can be conducted via email, social media, or third-party services, and employs evasive methods like email spoofing or thread hijacking to enhance credibility and bypass security measures.

2413.name: type squatting
2413.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may masquerade malicious payloads as legitimate files through changes to the payload's formatting, including the file’s signature, extension, icon, and contents. Various file types have a typical standard format, including how they are encoded and organized. For example, a file’s signature (also known as header or magic bytes) is the beginning bytes of a file and is often used to identify the file’s type. For example, the header of a JPEG file, is 0xFF 0xD8 and the file extension is either `.JPE`, `.JPEG` or `.JPG`. Adversaries may edit the header’s hex code and/or the file extension of a malicious payload in order to bypass file validation checks and/or input sanitization. This behavior is commonly used when payload files are transferred (e.g., [Ingress Tool Transfer](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1105)) and stored (e.g., [Upload Malware](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1608/001)) so that adversaries may move their malware without triggering detections. Common non-executable file types and extensions, such as text files (`.txt`) and image files (`.jpg`, `.gif`, etc.) may be typically treated as benign. Based on this, adversaries may use a file extension to disguise malware, such as naming a PHP backdoor code with a file name of test.gif. A user may not know that a file is malicious due to the benign appearance and file extension. Polyglot files, which are files that have multiple different file types and that function differently based on the application that will execute them, may also be used to disguise malicious malware and capabilities.(Citation: polygot_icedID)
2413.profile: [profile]This technique, formally known as Masquerade File Type (T1036.008) under the Defense Evasion tactic, operates across multiple platforms. It involves altering a malicious file's signature (magic bytes) and/or extension to mimic a benign format (e.g., naming a PHP backdoor as `test.gif`), thereby bypassing validation checks. The use of polyglot files, which function as multiple file types, further disguises the payload. This method is commonly associated with groups like BlackByte, Volt Typhoon, and Mustang Panda to facilitate malware transfer and storage without detection.[/profile]
2413.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Type Squatting is a technique within the Defense Evasion tactic, where adversaries mimic legitimate software names with slight misspellings or variations to trick users into downloading and executing malicious files. This often involves uploading backdoored files to third-party repositories or package libraries, increasing the chance of victim compromise through User Execution when users mistakenly install the malicious software.

2417.name: maintain persistence
2417.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may clear artifacts associated with previously established persistence on a host system to remove evidence of their activity. This may involve various actions, such as removing services, deleting executables, [Modify Registry](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1112), [Plist File Modification](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1647), or other methods of cleanup to prevent defenders from collecting evidence of their persistent presence.(Citation: Cylance Dust Storm) Adversaries may also delete accounts previously created to maintain persistence (i.e. [Create Account](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1136)).(Citation: Talos - Cisco Attack 2022)

In some instances, artifacts of persistence may also be removed once an adversary’s persistence is executed in order to prevent errors with the new instance of the malware.(Citation: NCC Group Team9 June 2020)
2417.profile: [profile]The technique is MITRE ATT&CK T1070.009: Clear Persistence, under the Defense Evasion tactic, applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves adversaries removing evidence of their established persistence mechanisms, such as by deleting services, executables, or registry keys, or by removing previously created user accounts. This cleanup prevents defenders from detecting the persistent access and can also prevent errors when new malware instances are deployed. The intrusion set APT28 has been associated with related persistence techniques.[/profile]
2417.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "maintain persistence" is a core adversarial objective, not a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique with a T-ID. It is a high-level goal within the Persistence tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. Adversaries achieve this by deploying mechanisms like logon scripts, which can be set via Windows Registry keys (e.g., HKCU\Environment\UserInitMprLogonScript) or Active Directory Group Policy to execute automatically upon user login, ensuring continued access.

2418.name: SSL/TLS handshake
2418.profile: [profile]SSL/TLS Handshake is a technique (T1001.003) under the Command and Control tactic, used to evade detection. Adversaries impersonate a fake SSL/TLS handshake to make subsequent command and control traffic appear as legitimate, SSL/TLS-encrypted network traffic, which can blend in with trusted entities and potentially interfere with security tooling. This technique is associated with groups like APT28.[/profile]
2418.profile_without_enhance: [profile]SSL/TLS handshake is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on retrieved context, it is referenced as a component of adversary tradecraft. Adversaries may impersonate a fake SSL/TLS handshake to make subsequent command and control traffic appear to be legitimately encrypted, potentially bypassing security tools. This activity is associated with techniques like Protocol Impersonation (T1001.003) and is used by groups including Lazarus Group and Higaisa to disguise malicious traffic within trusted network protocols.

2419.name: command and control
2419.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may communicate using a custom command and control protocol instead of encapsulating commands/data in an existing [Application Layer Protocol](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1071). Implementations include mimicking well-known protocols or developing custom protocols (including raw sockets) on top of fundamental protocols provided by TCP/IP/another standard network stack.
2419.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique "Custom Command and Control Protocol" (ID: T1094) under the Command and Control tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It involves adversaries developing or mimicking custom network protocols, including the use of raw sockets, instead of using standard application layer protocols for C2 communication to evade detection. This technique is used by groups like APT28 and can be supplemented with obfuscation methods like adding junk data to the traffic.
2419.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "command and control" is a core adversarial tactic (TA0011) within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, representing the phase where adversaries communicate with compromised systems to maintain control. It is not a specific technique with a T-ID but encompasses numerous techniques for establishing and obscuring these communication channels. Technical mechanics for obfuscating this traffic, as indicated by related entities, include adding junk data to protocols to hinder analysis and using multi-stage channels where separate infrastructure is employed for different communication functions to increase detection difficulty.

2420.name: Command Execution Utilities
2420.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may abuse utilities that allow for command execution to bypass security restrictions that limit the use of command-line interpreters. Various Windows utilities may be used to execute commands, possibly without invoking [cmd](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0106). For example, [Forfiles](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0193), the Program Compatibility Assistant (`pcalua.exe`), components of the Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL), `Scriptrunner.exe`, as well as other utilities may invoke the execution of programs and commands from a [Command and Scripting Interpreter](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059), Run window, or via scripts.(Citation: VectorSec ForFiles Aug 2017)(Citation: Evi1cg Forfiles Nov 2017)(Citation: Secure Team - Scriptrunner.exe)(Citation: SS64)(Citation: Bleeping Computer - Scriptrunner.exe) Adversaries may also abuse the `ssh.exe` binary to execute malicious commands via the `ProxyCommand` and `LocalCommand` options, which can be invoked via the `-o` flag or by modifying the SSH config file.(Citation: Threat Actor Targets the Manufacturing industry with Lumma Stealer and Amadey Bot)

Adversaries may abuse these features for [Defense Evasion](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0005), specifically to perform arbitrary execution while subverting detections and/or mitigation controls (such as Group Policy) that limit/prevent the usage of [cmd](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0106) or file extensions more commonly associated with malicious payloads.
2420.profile: [profile]Indirect Command Execution, identified as T1202 within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, is a Defense Evasion technique primarily for Windows platforms. It involves abusing trusted system utilities like Forfiles, pcalua.exe, Windows Subsystem for Linux components, or Scriptrunner.exe to execute commands without invoking the standard cmd.exe interpreter, thereby bypassing security controls. Adversaries may also abuse ssh.exe via its ProxyCommand or LocalCommand options. This technique has been associated with groups including Lazarus Group and RedCurl.[/profile]
2420.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Command Execution Utilities is a technique for Defense Evasion (TA0005), specifically T1202, on Windows platforms. It involves abusing legitimate system utilities like Forfiles, pcalua.exe, Windows Subsystem for Linux components, and Scriptrunner.exe to execute commands without invoking the standard command interpreter (cmd.exe), thereby bypassing security restrictions and application controls. Adversaries may also misuse ssh.exe via its ProxyCommand and LocalCommand options to run malicious code.

2421.name: Tunneling
2421.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may tunnel network communications to and from a victim system within a separate protocol to avoid detection/network filtering and/or enable access to otherwise unreachable systems. Tunneling involves explicitly encapsulating a protocol within another. This behavior may conceal malicious traffic by blending in with existing traffic and/or provide an outer layer of encryption (similar to a VPN). Tunneling could also enable routing of network packets that would otherwise not reach their intended destination, such as SMB, RDP, or other traffic that would be filtered by network appliances or not routed over the Internet. 

There are various means to encapsulate a protocol within another protocol. For example, adversaries may perform SSH tunneling (also known as SSH port forwarding), which involves forwarding arbitrary data over an encrypted SSH tunnel.(Citation: SSH Tunneling)(Citation: Sygnia Abyss Locker 2025) 

[Protocol Tunneling](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1572) may also be abused by adversaries during [Dynamic Resolution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1568). Known as DNS over HTTPS (DoH), queries to resolve C2 infrastructure may be encapsulated within encrypted HTTPS packets.(Citation: BleepingComp Godlua JUL19) 

Adversaries may also leverage [Protocol Tunneling](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1572) in conjunction with [Proxy](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1090) and/or [Protocol or Service Impersonation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1001/003) to further conceal C2 communications and infrastructure.
2421.profile: [profile]Protocol Tunneling, identified as T1572, is a Command and Control tactic used across multiple platforms. It works by explicitly encapsulating one network protocol within another, such as performing SSH port forwarding or using DNS over HTTPS (DoH), to conceal malicious traffic, bypass network filtering, and enable access to restricted systems. This technique is often used in conjunction with proxy methods and has been employed by groups like APT28, FIN7, and OilRig.[/profile]

2423.name: maintain a foothold
2423.profile: [profile]The entity "maintain a foothold" is a concept related to adversary persistence, not a formal MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the retrieved context, it describes actions adversaries take to sustain access to a compromised system, such as by patching vulnerabilities, disabling services, or removing competing malware to ensure exclusive control and reduce detection noise. This behavior is associated with groups like APT28 and supports broader persistence tactics.[/profile]
2423.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "maintain a foothold" is a cybersecurity attack pattern. This is achieved by preventing other threat actors from accessing the same system, for example by patching the initial vulnerability used, disabling vulnerable services, stripping account privileges, or removing competing malware. This action secures exclusive control, reduces environmental noise to avoid detection, and ensures the adversary can maintain their presence for follow-on objectives like resource hijacking.

2430.name: PlugX
2430.uncertain_mes: [PlugX](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0013) is a remote access tool (RAT) with modular plugins that has been used by multiple threat groups.(Citation: Lastline PlugX Analysis)(Citation: FireEye Clandestine Fox Part 2)(Citation: New DragonOK)(Citation: Dell TG-3390)
2430.profile: [profile]PlugX, also known as TinyX or Destroy RAT, is a modular remote access trojan (RAT) first identified in 2012 and often attributed to Chinese-speaking threat actors, including groups like APT3, APT41, Mustang Panda, menuPass, and Winnti. Its key technical behaviors include using encrypted payloads with XOR headers or THOR magic bytes, delivered via malicious DLLs or installers that masquerade as non-malicious files. Primarily targeting Windows platforms, PlugX operates through a loader component to deploy its encoded payloads for remote access and data exfiltration.
2430.profile_without_enhance: [profile]PlugX, a remote access trojan (RAT) identified in 2012, is also known as a variant of itself and is related to malware families like TinyX, Destroy RAT, and components like Malicious dll/installer. It is attributed to numerous Chinese-speaking threat actors and groups including menuPass, Stone Panda, Mustang Panda, APT31, and APT41. Its key technical behaviors involve being delivered via spear-phishing and encoded payloads, using loaders and encrypted payloads (including XOR and unknown encryption) to deploy the RAT, and leveraging components like malicious DLLs for installation. The primary target platform is Windows systems, and it is associated with infrastructure and campaigns used by the attributed groups.[/profile]

2435.name: C&C communication channel
2435.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may employ an encryption algorithm to conceal command and control traffic rather than relying on any inherent protections provided by a communication protocol. Despite the use of a secure algorithm, these implementations may be vulnerable to reverse engineering if secret keys are encoded and/or generated within malware samples/configuration files.
2435.profile: [profile]C&C communication channel, also known as Encrypted Channel (T1573) under the Command and Control tactic, is a technique where adversaries use custom encryption algorithms to hide C2 traffic, moving beyond standard protocol protections. This method can be vulnerable if secret keys are embedded within the malware or its configuration files, allowing for potential reverse engineering. The technique is associated with groups like Winnti, Bitter, Tropic Trooper, Magic Hound, and APT29.
2435.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "C&C communication channel" is a core concept in command and control, not a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique. It refers to the network pathway used by adversaries to remotely control compromised systems. The retrieved information describes related techniques for establishing and using these channels, including employing encryption (T1573) to conceal traffic, using legitimate web services (T1102.002, T1102.003) for bidirectional or one-way communication to blend with normal traffic, and even using the same channel for data exfiltration (T1041). Adversaries may also use fallback channels (T1008) to maintain persistence if the primary channel is lost.

2437.name: financial fraud
2437.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may steal monetary resources from targets through extortion, social engineering, technical theft, or other methods aimed at their own financial gain at the expense of the availability of these resources for victims. Financial theft is the ultimate objective of several popular campaign types including extortion by ransomware,(Citation: FBI-ransomware) business email compromise (BEC) and fraud,(Citation: FBI-BEC) "pig butchering,"(Citation: wired-pig butchering) bank hacking,(Citation: DOJ-DPRK Heist) and exploiting cryptocurrency networks.(Citation: BBC-Ronin) 

Adversaries may [Compromise Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1586) to conduct unauthorized transfers of funds.(Citation: Internet crime report 2022) In the case of business email compromise or email fraud, an adversary may utilize [Impersonation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1656) of a trusted entity. Once the social engineering is successful, victims can be deceived into sending money to financial accounts controlled by an adversary.(Citation: FBI-BEC) This creates the potential for multiple victims (i.e., compromised accounts as well as the ultimate monetary loss) in incidents involving financial theft.(Citation: VEC)

Extortion by ransomware may occur, for example, when an adversary demands payment from a victim after [Data Encrypted for Impact](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1486) (Citation: NYT-Colonial) and [Exfiltration](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0010) of data, followed by threatening to leak sensitive data to the public unless payment is made to the adversary.(Citation: Mandiant-leaks) Adversaries may use dedicated leak sites to distribute victim data.(Citation: Crowdstrike-leaks)

Due to the potentially immense business impact of financial theft, an adversary may abuse the possibility of financial theft and seeking monetary gain to divert attention from their true goals such as [Data Destruction](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1485) and business disruption.(Citation: AP-NotPetya)
2437.profile: [profile]Financial Theft, identified as T1657, is an adversary objective within the Impact tactic. It describes the theft of monetary resources through methods like extortion (e.g., ransomware demanding payment after data encryption and exfiltration), social engineering (e.g., Business Email Compromise using Impersonation to deceive victims into sending funds), and technical theft such as bank hacking or cryptocurrency exploits. Associated groups include FIN13, Scattered Spider, and Winnti.[/profile]
2437.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Financial Fraud, identified as T1657 within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, is a technique under the Impact tactic targeting multiple platforms. It involves adversaries using deception to illicitly obtain funds, often through methods like business email compromise (BEC) where they impersonate trusted entities to trick victims into transferring money to controlled accounts. This technique is associated with groups such as FIN13, Scattered Spider, and Kimsuky.

2439.name: base64 encoding
2439.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may encode data with a standard data encoding system to make the content of command and control traffic more difficult to detect. Command and control (C2) information can be encoded using a standard data encoding system that adheres to existing protocol specifications. Common data encoding schemes include ASCII, Unicode, hexadecimal, Base64, and MIME.(Citation: Wikipedia Binary-to-text Encoding)(Citation: Wikipedia Character Encoding) Some data encoding systems may also result in data compression, such as gzip.
2439.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique "Standard Encoding" (ID: T1132.001) under the Command and Control tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It involves adversaries encoding command and control traffic using common, protocol-compliant schemes like Base64, ASCII, Unicode, hexadecimal, or MIME to obfuscate content and evade detection. Associated threat groups include APT29, MuddyWater, and Lazarus Group.
2439.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Base64 Encoding is a sub-technique of Data Encoding (T1132.001) under the Command and Control tactic. It is a standard binary-to-text encoding scheme used to obfuscate command and control traffic by converting binary data into an ASCII string format, adhering to RFC 4648. This technique is employed by groups like Hafnium and Lazarus to make malicious payloads and communications blend with normal network traffic.[/profile]

2443.name: traditional work schedule
2443.profile: [profile]The entity "traditional work schedule" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the provided context, it appears to be a concept related to scheduling malicious activity. The retrieved information describes adversaries scheduling data exfiltration (linked to MITRE technique T1029) to blend with normal traffic patterns, often using other exfiltration techniques like Exfiltration Over C2 Channel. This scheduled activity is conceptually associated with the intrusion set Winnti. The specific technical mechanics involve timing data transfers to coincide with legitimate business hours or intervals to avoid detection.[/profile]
2443.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "traditional work schedule" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the provided context, it appears to be a concept related to scheduling malicious activity. The retrieved information describes adversaries scheduling data exfiltration or malicious container deployments to blend with normal traffic patterns or maintain persistence, using mechanisms like cron jobs or orchestration tools to execute tasks at specific times or intervals.

2444.name: abusing popular platforms
2444.profile: [profile]The entity "abusing popular platforms" is a technique where adversaries misuse widely-used web services like Google, GitHub, or Twitter for malicious activities such as Command and Control, Exfiltration, or Phishing. This abuse leverages the trusted nature and common traffic of these platforms to blend in and evade detection, as seen in operations by groups like APT29. The technique facilitates hiding malicious infrastructure within expected network noise.
2444.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "abusing popular platforms" is a technique where adversaries leverage widely used web services like Google, GitHub, or Twitter to hide malicious activities within expected network traffic. This method facilitates various stages of an attack, including command and control, data exfiltration, and phishing, by making it difficult to distinguish adversary operations from legitimate user traffic.

2445.name: maintain network persistence
2445.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may clear artifacts associated with previously established persistence on a host system to remove evidence of their activity. This may involve various actions, such as removing services, deleting executables, [Modify Registry](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1112), [Plist File Modification](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1647), or other methods of cleanup to prevent defenders from collecting evidence of their persistent presence.(Citation: Cylance Dust Storm) Adversaries may also delete accounts previously created to maintain persistence (i.e. [Create Account](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1136)).(Citation: Talos - Cisco Attack 2022)

In some instances, artifacts of persistence may also be removed once an adversary’s persistence is executed in order to prevent errors with the new instance of the malware.(Citation: NCC Group Team9 June 2020)
2445.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique "Clear Persistence" (ID: T1070.009), categorized under Defense Evasion. It operates across Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. This technique involves adversaries removing artifacts from previously established persistence mechanisms to eliminate evidence of their activity. Specific technical actions include deleting services or executables, modifying the Registry or Plist files, and removing accounts created for persistence, as observed in campaigns by groups like Winnti to prevent defenders from detecting their long-term presence.
2445.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Maintain Network Persistence is a technique within the Persistence tactic (TA0003) for Windows and potentially other platforms. It involves establishing mechanisms to retain access within a network environment after initial compromise. This can be achieved through methods like deploying network logon scripts, which are automatically executed during user logon via Active Directory or Group Policy Objects to run malicious code across multiple systems. Adversaries may also create redundant access points, such as using multiple remote access tools or valid accounts for external services like VPNs, to ensure continued access if one method is discovered and removed.
