2447.name: CryptUnprotectData
2447.profile: [profile]CryptUnprotectData is a Windows API function used in the Credentials from Web Browsers (T1555.003) technique under the Credential Access tactic. It operates on the Windows platform to decrypt data, specifically by using the victim's cached logon credentials as the decryption key. In practice, adversaries obtain encrypted credentials from browsers like Chrome and then pass them to CryptUnprotectData to recover plaintext passwords, enabling credential theft for further access.
2447.profile_without_enhance: [profile]CryptUnprotectData is a Windows API function used to decrypt data. It is referenced in the context of credential access technique T1503 (Credentials from Web Browsers). On Windows, adversaries can use this function to obtain plaintext passwords from encrypted credentials stored by web browsers like Chrome. The decryption is performed using the victim's cached logon credentials as the key, allowing extraction without requiring the user's master password.

2450.name: Surge in Activity
2450.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may employ various user activity checks to detect and avoid virtualization and analysis environments. This may include changing behaviors based on the results of checks for the presence of artifacts indicative of a virtual machine environment (VME) or sandbox. If the adversary detects a VME, they may alter their malware to disengage from the victim or conceal the core functions of the implant. They may also search for VME artifacts before dropping secondary or additional payloads. Adversaries may use the information learned from [Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1497) during automated discovery to shape follow-on behaviors.(Citation: Deloitte Environment Awareness)

Adversaries may search for user activity on the host based on variables such as the speed/frequency of mouse movements and clicks (Citation: Sans Virtual Jan 2016) , browser history, cache, bookmarks, or number of files in common directories such as home or the desktop. Other methods may rely on specific user interaction with the system before the malicious code is activated, such as waiting for a document to close before activating a macro (Citation: Unit 42 Sofacy Nov 2018) or waiting for a user to double click on an embedded image to activate.(Citation: FireEye FIN7 April 2017)
2450.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique "User Activity Based Checks" (ID: T1497.002) under the Defense Evasion tactic, applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves malware checking for indicators of a virtual machine or sandbox environment, such as analyzing mouse movement speed/frequency, browser history, or file counts in common directories. The malware may alter its behavior, disengage, or delay payload activation until specific user interactions occur, like waiting for a document to close or for a user to double-click an image. This technique has been associated with threat groups like FIN7 and DarkHotel.[/profile]
2450.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Surge in Activity" is an attack pattern where adversaries manipulate network traffic volume to obscure malicious communications and evade detection. This technique involves blending command and control (C2) traffic with a high volume of legitimate user or system activity, making it difficult for security tools to distinguish malicious packets. It can be used to hide data exfiltration or malware beaconing within normal network noise.

2451.name: Change in Tactics
2451.profile: [profile]Change in Tactics is a general adversary behavior rather than a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique. It refers to an intrusion set, such as Winnti, altering its operational methods, tools, or targets to evade detection. This can involve modifying malware signatures to bypass antivirus, switching from credential theft from files to targeting databases, or changing network attack vectors like adopting adversary-in-the-middle positions. The core objective is to adapt and persist by avoiding established defensive patterns.
2451.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Change in Tactics" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the retrieved information, it appears to be a general behavioral concept rather than a specific technical procedure. The related content describes adversaries modifying their tools or system components after detection to evade defenses, such as altering malware signatures or system images. This aligns with the general idea of adapting tactics to bypass security measures, but it lacks a defined ID, specific tactic, or unique technical mechanics.

2453.name: Stealing Developers' Certificates
2453.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may buy and/or steal SSL/TLS certificates that can be used during targeting. SSL/TLS certificates are designed to instill trust. They include information about the key, information about its owner's identity, and the digital signature of an entity that has verified the certificate's contents are correct. If the signature is valid, and the person examining the certificate trusts the signer, then they know they can use that key to communicate with its owner.

Adversaries may purchase or steal SSL/TLS certificates to further their operations, such as encrypting C2 traffic (ex: [Asymmetric Cryptography](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1573/002) with [Web Protocols](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1071/001)) or even enabling [Adversary-in-the-Middle](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1557) if the certificate is trusted or otherwise added to the root of trust (i.e. [Install Root Certificate](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1553/004)). The purchase of digital certificates may be done using a front organization or using information stolen from a previously compromised entity that allows the adversary to validate to a certificate provider as that entity. Adversaries may also steal certificate materials directly from a compromised third-party, including from certificate authorities.(Citation: DiginotarCompromise) Adversaries may register or hijack domains that they will later purchase an SSL/TLS certificate for.

Certificate authorities exist that allow adversaries to acquire SSL/TLS certificates, such as domain validation certificates, for free.(Citation: Let's Encrypt FAQ)

After obtaining a digital certificate, an adversary may then install that certificate (see [Install Digital Certificate](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1608/003)) on infrastructure under their control.
2453.profile: [profile]Stealing Developers' Certificates, identified as T1588.004 under the Resource Development tactic, involves adversaries illicitly obtaining SSL/TLS or code signing certificates to enable follow-on attacks. They may purchase certificates using stolen victim identities or front organizations, or directly steal materials from compromised third-parties like certificate authorities. These stolen certificates are then used to encrypt command and control traffic, conduct adversary-in-the-middle attacks, or sign malicious code to appear legitimate, with groups like Lazarus Group and Winnti employing this technique.[/profile]
2453.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Stealing Developers' Certificates is a technique where adversaries target and acquire code signing certificates belonging to software developers. The objective is to sign malicious binaries, making them appear legitimate and bypassing security policies that require valid signatures. This technique is related to the broader MITRE ATT&CK sub-technique Code Signing (T1553.002) under Defense Evasion, primarily affecting Windows and macOS platforms.

2454.name: Stealing Game Currencies
2454.profile: [profile]Stealing Game Currencies is a technique for Credential Access and Theft, likely targeting online gaming platforms. The technique involves adversaries, such as the Winnti intrusion-set, illicitly acquiring in-game currency or virtual assets. This can be achieved by purchasing, stealing, or forging the digital certificates or authentication tokens used to validate these assets within the game's economy, similar to how capabilities like Kerberos tickets or malware are obtained in other attack patterns. The stolen currencies are then typically exfiltrated from the compromised system or account.
2454.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Stealing Game Currencies is an attack pattern where adversaries illicitly acquire in-game virtual currencies, such as coins or gems, to gain an unfair advantage or for financial gain. This technique involves compromising user accounts, exploiting game vulnerabilities, or manipulating in-game transactions to transfer or duplicate currency. The stolen assets are often monetized through secondary markets.

2455.name: Stealing Source Code
2455.uncertain_mes: **This technique has been deprecated and should no longer be used.** The source command loads functions into the current shell or executes files in the current context. This built-in command can be run in two different ways source /path/to/filename [arguments] or .**This technique has been deprecated and should no longer be used.** /path/to/filename [arguments]. Take note of the space after the ".". Without a space, a new shell is created that runs the program instead of running the program within the current context. This is often used to make certain features or functions available to a shell or to update a specific shell's environment.(Citation: Source Manual) Adversaries can abuse this functionality to execute programs. The file executed with this technique does not need to be marked executable beforehand.
2455.profile: [profile]The entity "Stealing Source Code" is a deprecated technique. Based on the provided data, its standard MITRE ATT&CK mapping cannot be definitively confirmed. The retrieved information primarily describes the "source" command (T1153) for execution, which is not directly related to source code theft. A more relevant technique for stealing source code is "Code Repositories" (T1213.003), which involves adversaries accessing private repositories to collect proprietary code and unsecured credentials, as used by groups like APT41. The technical mechanics involve using tools like git to exfiltrate source code, which can then be used to develop exploits or gain further access.
2455.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Stealing Source Code is a technique where adversaries collect proprietary source code from internal or private code repositories, such as those hosted on GitHub or GitLab, after gaining access to a victim network. This activity supports the Collection tactic and can occur on various platforms. The stolen code may contain sensitive information like unsecured credentials, which adversaries can use for further access via Valid Accounts, or the code itself can be analyzed to develop custom exploits. Groups like APT41, Scattered Spider, and LAPSUS$ have been associated with this behavior.

2459.name: Winnti Malware
2459.uncertain_mes:
A .NET rat targets Mongolia
A new document royal road v7 installs a backdoor in .NET. a first executable is dropped \os03C2.tmp. This exe has many similarities with older campaigns using by Operation LagTime or Tonto Team.
Document
The decoy document is a document about infection of covid19 in Russia send to the Mongolia Authorities. The document is fake signed A. Amarsaikhan.
2459.profile: [profile]Winnti Malware, also known as nmass malware, is attributed to the Winnti intrusion set. It is a .NET-based remote access trojan (RAT) that uses decoy documents, such as a fake COVID-19 report for Mongolia, to deploy backdoors. Its technical behavior includes dropping an initial executable (e.g., \os03C2.tmp) and sharing similarities with campaigns linked to Operation LagTime or Tonto Team. The malware targets Windows platforms and is part of a broader arsenal that includes strains like DEPLOYLOG, Spyder Loader, PRIVATELOG, and WINNKIT.
2459.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Winnti Malware, also known as Winnti 3.0, is attributed to the Winnti intrusion set (APT17). Its key technical behaviors include using a dropper as its initial component, employing DES for initial encryption, and utilizing 1-byte XOR and nibble swap for worker encryption. It targets Windows platforms. The malware's arsenal includes strains like DEPLOYLOG, Spyder Loader, PRIVATELOG, and WINNKIT, and its network communication patterns have been detectable since at least 2013.

2460.name: Winnti 3.0
2460.uncertain_mes: [LockBit 3.0](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S1202) is an evolution of the LockBit Ransomware-as-a-Service (RaaS) offering with similarities to BlackMatter and [BlackCat](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S1068) ransomware. [LockBit 3.0](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S1202) has been in use since at least June 2022 and features enhanced defense evasion and exfiltration tactics, robust encryption methods for Windows and VMware ESXi systems, and a more refined RaaS structure over its predecessors such as [LockBit 2.0](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S1199).(Citation: Sentinel Labs LockBit 3.0 JUL 2022)(Citation: Joint Cybersecurity Advisory LockBit JUN 2023)(Citation: Joint Cybersecurity Advisory LockBit 3.0 MAR 2023)(Citation: INCIBE-CERT LockBit MAR 2024)
2460.profile: [profile]Winnti 3.0, also known as a version of the Winnti malware, is attributed to the Winnti intrusion set. Its key technical behaviors include using a dropper as its initial component and employing DES for initial encryption, with worker encryption using 1-byte XOR and nibble swap. It primarily targets Windows systems. This version is distinct from later iterations like Winnti 4.0, which uses different encryption methods.
2460.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Winnti 3.0, a version of the Winnti malware, is attributed to the Winnti intrusion-set/APT group. Key components include DEPLOYLOG, Spyder Loader, PRIVATELOG, and WINNKIT. It uses a dropper as its initial component, employs DES for initial encryption, and uses 1-byte XOR and nibble swap for worker encryption. It exhibits specific network communication patterns and primarily targets Windows systems, with activity noted since at least 2013.

2461.name: Pivy
2461.profile: [profile]Pivy, also known as BPyCode, is a malware attributed to the Winnti intrusion set. It operates by side-loading into legitimate applications, such as a Samsung tool, to execute its payload. The malware achieves persistence by creating a scheduled task and uses command and control servers including dick[.]ccfchrist[.]com, trout[.]belowto[.]com, and sakai[.]unhamj[.]com for communication.
2461.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Pivy is a malware that is side-loaded into a legitimate Samsung application to achieve persistence by creating a rogue scheduled task. It is associated with the groups Stone Panda, Gallium, and UPS. Its command-and-control infrastructure includes domains such as dick[.]ccfchrist[.]com, trout[.]belowto[.]com, and sakai[.]unhamj[.]com.

2462.name: Chopper
2462.uncertain_mes: [China Chopper](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0020) is a [Web Shell](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1505/003) hosted on Web servers to provide access back into an enterprise network that does not rely on an infected system calling back to a remote command and control server.(Citation: Lee 2013) It has been used by several threat groups.(Citation: Dell TG-3390)(Citation: FireEye Periscope March 2018)(Citation: CISA AA21-200A APT40 July 2021)(Citation: Rapid7 HAFNIUM Mar 2021)
2462.profile: [profile]Chopper, also known as China Chopper, is a web shell hosted on web servers to provide backdoor access into enterprise networks without requiring callbacks to a C2 server. It has been used by multiple threat groups including Hafnium, BackdoorDiplomacy, Leviathan, Mustang Panda, Gallium, APT41, Fox Kitten, Threat Group-3390, and Toddycat. Its key technical behavior is operating as a file-based web shell, primarily targeting web servers to enable remote command execution and data exfiltration.
2462.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Chopper, also known as China Chopper, is a web shell malware used by multiple threat groups including HAFNIUM, BackdoorDiplomacy, Leviathan, Mustang Panda, Gallium, APT41, Fox Kitten, Threat Group-3390, and ToddyCat. It provides backdoor access to enterprise networks by being hosted on web servers, enabling remote command execution without requiring infected systems to call back to a command and control server. Its primary target platform is web servers, and it is often associated with other malware families like PlugX and Mimikatz in broader campaigns.

2463.name: ZXShell
2463.uncertain_mes: [ZxShell](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0412) is a remote administration tool and backdoor that can be downloaded from the Internet, particularly from Chinese hacker websites. It has been used since at least 2004.(Citation: FireEye APT41 Aug 2019)(Citation: Talos ZxShell Oct 2014)
2463.profile: [profile]ZXShell, also known as Sensocode, is a remote administration tool (RAT) and backdoor used for cyber-espionage. It has been attributed to groups including APT41, Emissary Panda, Leviathan, Threat Group-3390, Axiom, and Winnti. Its key technical behaviors involve implementing a specific handshake and communication protocol (for versions like 3.10 and 3.20) to establish control, after which it spawns threads for data transfer and can deploy tools like a keylogger. It is used to exfiltrate data and pivot within victim networks. The malware has been in use since at least 2004 and is associated with Chinese APT operations.
2463.profile_without_enhance: [profile]ZXShell, also known as Sensode or Sensocode, is a Remote Administration Tool (RAT) used by groups including APT41, Emissary Panda, and Leviathan for cyber-espionage. It implements a specific handshake and spawns threads for data transfer after connection. Key technical behaviors include client administration, data exfiltration, and leveraging infected hosts as pivots to attack internal infrastructure. Target platforms are not explicitly detailed, but its operation as a RAT suggests Windows systems. Infrastructure involves a server-client model with a custom C++ server implementation for versions like 3.10 and 3.20.

2464.name: Browser Exploitation Framework (BEEF)
2464.uncertain_mes: Lightning Framework is a new undetected Swiss Army Knife-like Linux malware that has modular plugins and the ability to install rootkits.
2464.profile: [profile]The entity is the Browser Exploitation Framework (BEEF), also known as lightning framework. It is a modular, Swiss Army Knife-like exploitation framework for web browsers, not a Linux malware rootkit as some retrieved data incorrectly suggests. It has been used by groups including Winnti, Newscaster, Fancy Bear, and Rocket Kitten, who have employed customized versions in watering hole attacks by injecting malicious JavaScript into compromised websites to load the framework from attacker-controlled domains.[/profile]
2464.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Browser Exploitation Framework (BEEF) is an open-source browser exploitation framework used in watering hole attacks. It is loaded via malicious JavaScript code injected into compromised websites. It has been used by groups including Rocket Kitten, and customized versions have been used by the Iranian group Newscaster and the Russian group Fancy Bear.

2465.name: Metasploit Meterpreter
2465.uncertain_mes: Web servers are vulnerable to attacks because they are publicly accessible to a wide range of users for the purpose of delivering web services. This accessibility makes them a prime target for threat actors. AhnLab Security Emergency response Center (ASEC) is monitoring attacks targeting vulnerable web servers that have not been patched or are poorly managed.
2465.profile: [profile]Metasploit Meterpreter, also known as meterpreter, is a post-exploitation payload and framework. It is used by various threat actors, including the Winnti intrusion set, and is associated with tools like Mimikatz and Bumblebee, which is linked to groups like Exotic Lily, Gold Cabin, TA578, and TA579. Its key technical behaviors involve establishing command and control (C2) channels, often via the Metasploit framework, for activities like credential dumping and remote system control. It primarily targets Windows platforms but can be deployed against various systems, including vulnerable web servers, to facilitate further exploitation and data exfiltration.[/profile]
2465.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Metasploit Meterpreter, also known as meterpreter, is a payload and post-exploitation framework. It is used as a command and control (C2) component by various malware families and threat actors, including Bumblebee (associated with groups like Exotic Lily, Gold Cabin, TA578, and TA579), Mimic ransomware, and Mimikatz (used by groups like APT10, APT32, Anunak, and Gallium). Its key technical behavior is providing a versatile C2 channel for remote access and control after initial compromise. It is often delivered via files like MSI or JAR. It targets multiple platforms and its infrastructure is integrated with the broader Metasploit exploitation framework.[/profile]

2466.name: Jar File
2466.profile: [profile]Jar File is a malware delivery format, with aliases including RCS and Crisis, and is attributed to groups such as Winnti, Hacking Team, and APT-C-34. It is used to deploy malicious payloads, often masquerading as legitimate documents like "SHIPMENT_DOCUMENTS_INV-PLIST01256_BL PDF[.]jar" to trick users. The primary target platforms are systems capable of running Java applications, including macOS, as indicated by its connection to macOS Application malware. Its infrastructure involves JAR file exploitation for initial access and execution.[/profile]

It is associated with malware campaigns such as RCS and Crisis, which are linked to groups like Hacking Team and APT-C-34. The target platforms are systems capable of running Java applications, typically Windows, macOS, or Linux.[/profile]

2467.name: macOS Application
2467.profile: [profile]macOS Application is a generic identifier for malicious software targeting macOS systems, often appearing as a Trojanized application or installer. It is associated with groups such as the Lazarus Group, which has used similar implants like 'OSX.AppleJeus.C' for fileless execution and remote download capabilities. This malware family, which includes variants like Shlayer and IconicStealer, typically involves disguising itself as a legitimate app to bypass security checks and may be distributed via malicious disk image files.[/profile]
2467.profile_without_enhance: [profile]macOS Application is a malware entity targeting macOS systems, with aliases including OSX.AppleJeus.C and references to Trojanized applications like those based on MinaOTP. It is attributed to groups such as the Lazarus Group and possibly others like APT-C-34, as indicated by its association with Jar File malware used in campaigns like StrRat. Key technical behaviors involve remote download and in-memory execution for fileless attacks, deployment via deceptive files such as Apple Disk Images or installers, and potential payload delivery through JAR archives. Target platforms are primarily macOS, with infrastructure involving malicious apps and installers for initial infection.[/profile]

2470.name: Directed to HTML Page with Fake Resume
2470.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may smuggle data and files past content filters by hiding malicious payloads inside of seemingly benign HTML files. HTML documents can store large binary objects known as JavaScript Blobs (immutable data that represents raw bytes) that can later be constructed into file-like objects. Data may also be stored in Data URLs, which enable embedding media type or MIME files inline of HTML documents. HTML5 also introduced a download attribute that may be used to initiate file downloads.(Citation: HTML Smuggling Menlo Security 2020)(Citation: Outlflank HTML Smuggling 2018) Adversaries may deliver payloads to victims that bypass security controls through HTML Smuggling by abusing JavaScript Blobs and/or HTML5 download attributes. Security controls such as web content filters may not identify smuggled malicious files inside of HTML/JS files, as the content may be based on typically benign MIME types such as text/plain and/or text/html. Malicious files or data can be obfuscated and hidden inside of HTML files through Data URLs and/or JavaScript Blobs and can be deobfuscated when they reach the victim (i.e. [Deobfuscate/Decode Files or Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1140)), potentially bypassing content filters. For example, JavaScript Blobs can be abused to dynamically generate malicious files in the victim machine and may be dropped to disk by abusing JavaScript functions such as msSaveBlob.(Citation: HTML Smuggling Menlo Security 2020)(Citation: MSTIC NOBELIUM May 2021)(Citation: Outlflank HTML Smuggling 2018)(Citation: nccgroup Smuggling HTA 2017)
2470.profile: [profile]Directed to HTML Page with Fake Resume is a technique aligned with HTML Smuggling (T1027.006) under the Defense Evasion tactic, targeting Windows platforms. It involves adversaries delivering malicious payloads by embedding them within seemingly benign HTML pages, such as fake resumes, to bypass content filters. This is achieved by hiding obfuscated data or files inside HTML documents using JavaScript Blobs or Data URLs, which are then deobfuscated and executed on the victim's machine, often leveraging functions like `msSaveBlob` to drop files to disk. The intrusion-set Winnti has been associated with this method.[/profile]
2470.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Directed to HTML Page with Fake Resume" is a technique where adversaries send spearphishing messages (T1598.003) containing a link to a malicious HTML page disguised as a fake resume. This page is designed to execute malicious code upon loading, often leveraging mechanisms like JavaScript Blobs or HTML5 download attributes to bypass security filters and deliver payloads. The technique is used for initial access, typically targeting users via email on Windows platforms.

2471.name: Landing Page Downloads Jar File
2471.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may abuse Microsoft Outlook's Home Page feature to obtain persistence on a compromised system. Outlook Home Page is a legacy feature used to customize the presentation of Outlook folders. This feature allows for an internal or external URL to be loaded and presented whenever a folder is opened. A malicious HTML page can be crafted that will execute code when loaded by Outlook Home Page.(Citation: SensePost Outlook Home Page)

Once malicious home pages have been added to the user’s mailbox, they will be loaded when Outlook is started. Malicious Home Pages will execute when the right Outlook folder is loaded/reloaded.(Citation: SensePost Outlook Home Page)
2471.profile: [profile]Landing Page Downloads Jar File is a technique where adversaries use a malicious landing page to deliver a JAR file payload. The technical mechanics involve a crafted HTML page that, when loaded (e.g., by a user visiting the page or through a redirection), initiates the download and execution of a malicious Java Archive (JAR) file, often leveraging the user's web browser and Java runtime environment. This method is commonly associated with initial access or execution tactics.[/profile]
2471.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Landing Page Downloads Jar File is a technique where adversaries use a malicious web page to deliver a Java Archive (JAR) file to a victim's system. This typically occurs during initial access, such as via a spearphishing link, where the victim is lured to the landing page. The page is crafted to automatically or trick the user into downloading the JAR file, which contains executable Java code, enabling subsequent malicious activity like remote access or malware deployment. This method leverages user interaction and web-based delivery to bypass network defenses.

2472.name: Iframe Injection
2472.profile: [profile]Iframe Injection is a web-based attack technique where adversaries inject malicious inline frames (iframes) into legitimate web pages to redirect users to malicious sites or execute drive-by downloads. It is commonly used by groups like Winnti for initial access, leveraging compromised websites to host and deliver payloads through manipulated web traffic. The technique exploits vulnerabilities in web applications to embed hidden iframes, often leading to malware deployment without user interaction.
2472.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Iframe Injection is a web-based attack pattern where adversaries inject malicious inline frames (iframes) into legitimate web pages to redirect users or load malicious content. This technique typically falls under the Initial Access tactic, targeting web platforms. The injection often involves embedding an iframe tag with a `src` attribute pointing to an attacker-controlled server, which can facilitate drive-by compromises, credential theft, or malware delivery by exploiting trust in the compromised site. It is commonly associated with web skimming and phishing campaigns.

2473.name: Beef Hook Script
2473.uncertain_mes: Hook Version 3: The Banking Trojan with The Most Advanced Capabilities
2473.profile: [profile]Beef Hook Script, also known as hook or Hook Version 3, is a banking trojan attributed to the Winnti intrusion set and is related to the Gagahook malware. It is described as having advanced capabilities, and its technical behavior involves a loader module that writes the double-word 0xBEEFBEEF into a designated 'beef file', with further data written by a manager module. The target platform is not specified in the provided data.[/profile]
2473.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Beef Hook Script, also known as Gagahook, is a malware attributed to the Winnti intrusion set. It functions as a hooking script for the BeEF (Browser Exploitation Framework) platform to enable browser-based attacks and client-side exploitation. Its primary target platforms are web browsers compromised through the BeEF framework.[/profile]

2474.name: Infrastructure Rapid Rotation
2474.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may manipulate network traffic in order to hide and evade detection of their C2 infrastructure. This can be accomplished by identifying and filtering traffic from defensive tools,(Citation: TA571) masking malicious domains to obfuscate the true destination from both automated scanning tools and security researchers,(Citation: Schema-abuse)(Citation: Facad1ng)(Citation: Browser-updates) and otherwise hiding malicious artifacts to delay discovery and prolong the effectiveness of adversary infrastructure that could otherwise be identified, blocked, or taken down entirely.

C2 networks may include the use of [Proxy](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1090) or VPNs to disguise IP addresses, which can allow adversaries to blend in with normal network traffic and bypass conditional access policies or anti-abuse protections. For example, an adversary may use a virtual private cloud to spoof their IP address to closer align with a victim's IP address ranges. This may also bypass security measures relying on geolocation of the source IP address.(Citation: sysdig)(Citation: Orange Residential Proxies)

Adversaries may also attempt to filter network traffic in order to evade defensive tools in numerous ways, including blocking/redirecting common incident responder or security appliance user agents.(Citation: mod_rewrite)(Citation: SocGholish-update) Filtering traffic based on IP and geo-fencing may also avoid automated sandboxing or researcher activity (i.e., [Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1497)).(Citation: TA571)(Citation: mod_rewrite)

Hiding C2 infrastructure may also be supported by [Resource Development](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0042) activities such as [Acquire Infrastructure](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1583) and [Compromise Infrastructure](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1584). For example, using widely trusted hosting services or domains such as prominent URL shortening providers or marketing services for C2 networks may enable adversaries to present benign content that later redirects victims to malicious web pages or infrastructure once specific conditions are met.(Citation: StarBlizzard)(Citation: QR-cofense)
2474.profile: [profile]Infrastructure Rapid Rotation is a technique (T1665) under the Resource Development tactic used to hide C2 infrastructure by rapidly provisioning, modifying, and shutting down servers, domains, or cloud services. This involves using disposable infrastructure from providers with minimal registration, leveraging free trials, and employing proxies or VPNs to blend with normal traffic and evade geolocation-based defenses. It is associated with groups like APT29 and Zirconium.[/profile]
2474.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Infrastructure Rapid Rotation is a sub-technique of Acquire Infrastructure (T1583) under the Resource Development tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. It involves adversaries rapidly provisioning, modifying, and shutting down infrastructure—such as cloud servers, domains, or virtual private servers (VPSs)—to make operations difficult to physically trace and to evade detection and takedown by defenders. This rapid cycling helps blend malicious activity with normal traffic and prolong the effectiveness of their operational infrastructure.

2476.name: Real.html
2476.profile: [profile]Real.html is a malware entity associated with the Winnti intrusion set. Its key behaviors include creating a registry key for persistence to automatically launch a copy on system startup, monitoring specific applications, and engaging in defined network interactions for command and control or data exfiltration. The primary target platform is the Windows operating system.
2476.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Real.html is a malware entity. No specific aliases, attributed groups, key TTPs, or target platforms are detailed in the provided data. The retrieved information references other malware (buterat, cmoon, latentbot) but does not contain context specific to Real.html's technical behaviors or infrastructure.

2486.name: Beef Module
2486.profile: [profile]Beef Module is a component of the Winnti malware family. It is referenced as a 'beef file' by the Sinowal malware, which uses it as a structured data container for modules with entry names like 'mini', 'gbcl', and 'snif'. The Dridex botnet also references a 'beef with get_module' message for requesting software modules from its command-and-control infrastructure to manage traffic load. Its attributed group is Winnti.[/profile]
2486.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The malware "Beef Module" is a software component used by other malware families, notably referenced by sinowal in its 'beef file' structure which stores module data and hashes for entries like 'mini', 'mi64', 'gbcl', 'gc64', 'iecl', 'ffcl', 'crcl', and 'snif'. It is associated with the attack pattern of Code Execution, enabling adversaries to run malicious code on a target system. Its technical behavior involves being requested and distributed via beacon messages to avoid excessive C2 load, as seen in dridex's infrastructure. 2487.name: Jenkins Groovy Code Exec

2488.name: Special DNS Resolution Method
2488.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may dynamically establish connections to command and control infrastructure to evade common detections and remediations. This may be achieved by using malware that shares a common algorithm with the infrastructure the adversary uses to receive the malware's communications. These calculations can be used to dynamically adjust parameters such as the domain name, IP address, or port number the malware uses for command and control.

Adversaries may use dynamic resolution for the purpose of [Fallback Channels](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1008). When contact is lost with the primary command and control server malware may employ dynamic resolution as a means to reestablishing command and control.(Citation: Talos CCleanup 2017)(Citation: FireEye POSHSPY April 2017)(Citation: ESET Sednit 2017 Activity)
2488.profile: [profile]The entity "Special DNS Resolution Method" aligns with the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1568 "Dynamic Resolution", categorized under Command and Control. It operates by using malware that shares a common algorithm with adversary infrastructure to dynamically calculate and adjust C2 parameters like domain names, IP addresses, or port numbers, evading static detection. This method can also serve as a fallback mechanism to reestablish lost C2 connections. Associated groups include Bitter, Gamaredon Group, and APT29.[profile]
2488.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Special DNS Resolution Method is a technique where adversaries employ non-standard DNS queries or resolution processes to evade detection and facilitate command and control. This method can involve using DNS tunneling to conceal data within DNS protocol fields like TXT or A records for covert communication, or spoofing authoritative sources via LLMNR/NBT-NS poisoning to redirect victim traffic and capture authentication hashes. It is associated with the Command and Control tactic and primarily targets Windows platforms.

2489.name: C2 Communication via Common Ports
2489.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may use an existing, legitimate external Web service as a means for sending commands to and receiving output from a compromised system over the Web service channel. Compromised systems may leverage popular websites and social media to host command and control (C2) instructions. Those infected systems can then send the output from those commands back over that Web service channel. The return traffic may occur in a variety of ways, depending on the Web service being utilized. For example, the return traffic may take the form of the compromised system posting a comment on a forum, issuing a pull request to development project, updating a document hosted on a Web service, or by sending a Tweet. 

Popular websites and social media acting as a mechanism for C2 may give a significant amount of cover due to the likelihood that hosts within a network are already communicating with them prior to a compromise. Using common services, such as those offered by Google or Twitter, makes it easier for adversaries to hide in expected noise. Web service providers commonly use SSL/TLS encryption, giving adversaries an added level of protection.
2489.profile: [profile]The entity is named "C2 Communication via Common Ports". It aligns with the deprecated MITRE ATT&CK technique T1043, which falls under the Command and Control tactic. This technique involves adversaries using standard, commonly open ports like TCP:80 (HTTP), TCP:443 (HTTPS), TCP:25 (SMTP), or TCP/UDP:53 (DNS) for command and control traffic to bypass firewalls and blend with normal network activity. They may use the expected protocol for the port or an entirely different one. The intrusion-set Winnti is associated with this behavior.
2489.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The technique "C2 Communication via Common Ports" is a deprecated method; refer to MITRE ATT&CK T1571 (Non-Standard Port) for current mapping. Adversaries use commonly open ports like TCP:80 (HTTP), 443 (HTTPS), 25 (SMTP), or 53 (DNS) for command and control to bypass firewalls and network detection by blending with normal traffic, potentially using the expected protocol or a different one entirely.

2490.name: Stolen Code Signing Certificates
2490.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may buy and/or steal code signing certificates that can be used during targeting. Code signing is the process of digitally signing executables and scripts to confirm the software author and guarantee that the code has not been altered or corrupted. Code signing provides a level of authenticity for a program from the developer and a guarantee that the program has not been tampered with.(Citation: Wikipedia Code Signing) Users and/or security tools may trust a signed piece of code more than an unsigned piece of code even if they don't know who issued the certificate or who the author is.

Prior to [Code Signing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1553/002), adversaries may purchase or steal code signing certificates for use in operations. The purchase of code signing certificates may be done using a front organization or using information stolen from a previously compromised entity that allows the adversary to validate to a certificate provider as that entity. Adversaries may also steal code signing materials directly from a compromised third-party.
2490.profile: [profile]Stolen Code Signing Certificates, designated T1588.003 under the Resource Development tactic, involves adversaries acquiring legitimate signing materials to bypass trust mechanisms. Certificates are purchased using front companies or stolen credentials, or directly taken from compromised third parties. This enables malware to appear authentic, increasing its chance of execution by evading security policies that require signed code. Associated threat groups include Kimsuky, Mustang Panda, and FIN8.
2490.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Stolen Code Signing Certificates is a technique (ID: T1588.003) under the Resource Development tactic. It applies to Windows and macOS platforms. Adversaries steal legitimate digital certificates to sign malicious executables and scripts, thereby bypassing security policies that trust signed code and increasing the malware's perceived authenticity to users and security tools. This method is distinct from creating self-signed certificates.

Its key technical behavior involves hooking into system processes, likely for data interception or browser exploitation as suggested by its BeEF association. The target platform is Windows systems, indicated by its registry key creation for persistence and monitoring of specific applications. Its key technical behaviors involve script-based execution and file manipulation for malicious purposes, primarily targeting web-based platforms and systems.[profile]

2506.name: Covert Access Installation
2506.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may abuse vSphere Installation Bundles (VIBs) to establish persistent access to ESXi hypervisors. VIBs are collections of files used for software distribution and virtual system management in VMware environments. Since ESXi uses an in-memory filesystem where changes made to most files are stored in RAM rather than in persistent storage, these modifications are lost after a reboot. However, VIBs can be used to create startup tasks, apply custom firewall rules, or deploy binaries that persist across reboots. Typically, administrators use VIBs for updates and system maintenance. VIBs can be broken down into three components:(Citation: VMware VIBs) * VIB payload: a `.vgz` archive containing the directories and files to be created and executed on boot when the VIBs are loaded. * Signature file: verifies the host acceptance level of a VIB, indicating what testing and validation has been done by VMware or its partners before publication of a VIB. By default, ESXi hosts require a minimum acceptance level of PartnerSupported for VIB installation, meaning the VIB is published by a trusted VMware partner. However, privileged users can change the default acceptance level using the `esxcli` command line interface. Additionally, VIBs are able to be installed regardless of acceptance level by using the esxcli software vib install --force command. * XML descriptor file: a configuration file containing associated VIB metadata, such as the name of the VIB and its dependencies. Adversaries may leverage malicious VIB packages to maintain persistent access to ESXi hypervisors, allowing system changes to be executed upon each bootup of ESXi – such as using `esxcli` to enable firewall rules for backdoor traffic, creating listeners on hard coded ports, and executing backdoors.(Citation: Google Cloud Threat Intelligence ESXi VIBs 2022) Adversaries may also masquerade their malicious VIB files as PartnerSupported by modifying the XML descriptor file.(Citation: Google Cloud Threat Intelligence ESXi VIBs 2022)
2506.profile: [profile]Covert Access Installation, also known as vSphere Installation Bundles (VIBs) and identified as T1505.006 under the Persistence tactic, targets VMware ESXi platforms. The technique involves abusing VIB packages, which are software bundles containing a .vgz payload archive, a signature file, and an XML descriptor. Adversaries install malicious VIBs using commands like `esxcli software vib install --force` to bypass acceptance levels, enabling persistent execution of tasks such as deploying backdoors or custom firewall rules that survive host reboots. This method has been associated with groups like UNC3886.[/profile]
2506.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Covert Access Installation is a persistence technique where adversaries install remote access tools or backdoors on compromised systems to maintain long-term, stealthy control. This often involves deploying legitimate remote administration software, web shells, or custom malware that establishes a command and control channel. The installation may be configured to survive reboots and blend in with normal system processes to evade detection, providing redundant access for follow-on adversary activities.

2509.name: CHM Email Exploitation
2509.profile: [profile]CHM Email Exploitation is a technique for initial access, likely corresponding to MITRE ATT&CK T1566.001 (Spearphishing Attachment) under the Initial Access tactic, targeting Windows platforms. It involves delivering malicious Compiled HTML Help (.chm) files via email. These CHM files contain embedded scripts or payloads that execute when the victim opens the file, often leveraging the HTML Help executable (hh.exe) to potentially bypass application controls. The intrusion-set Winnti has been associated with this method.
2509.profile_without_enhance: [profile]CHM Email Exploitation is a technique where adversaries deliver malicious Compiled HTML Files (.chM) via email to gain initial access. The CHM file, a compressed compilation of HTML and scripts, is executed by the victim, often leveraging the HTML Help executable (hh.exe) to potentially bypass application controls on unpatched systems. This method combines the delivery mechanism of email with the execution of a malicious payload concealed within a help file format.

2510.name: Landing Page
2510.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may abuse Microsoft Outlook's Home Page feature to obtain persistence on a compromised system. Outlook Home Page is a legacy feature used to customize the presentation of Outlook folders. This feature allows for an internal or external URL to be loaded and presented whenever a folder is opened. A malicious HTML page can be crafted that will execute code when loaded by Outlook Home Page.(Citation: SensePost Outlook Home Page)

Once malicious home pages have been added to the user’s mailbox, they will be loaded when Outlook is started. Malicious Home Pages will execute when the right Outlook folder is loaded/reloaded.(Citation: SensePost Outlook Home Page)
2510.profile: [profile]Landing Page, also known as Outlook Home Page (MITRE ATT&CK ID T1137.004), is a persistence technique within the Persistence tactic, targeting the Windows platform. It abuses a legacy Microsoft Outlook feature that loads a specified URL when a folder is opened. Adversaries craft a malicious HTML page; when this page is set as the home page for an Outlook folder and that folder is loaded (e.g., at Outlook startup), the embedded code executes to maintain access. This technique has been associated with the intrusion set Oilrig.[/profile]
2510.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Landing Page is a technique used in initial access, typically on Windows, Linux, or macOS platforms, where adversaries create a webpage to host malicious content. It serves as the initial point of contact in a phishing campaign, designed to trick a user into clicking a link and visiting the site to deliver a payload or harvest credentials. This technique is distinct from Outlook Home Page abuse (T1137.004) for persistence or Web Portal Capture (T1056.003) for credential theft post-compromise.

2511.name: Code Signing
2511.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may create, acquire, or steal code signing materials to sign their malware or tools. Code signing provides a level of authenticity on a binary from the developer and a guarantee that the binary has not been tampered with. (Citation: Wikipedia Code Signing) The certificates used during an operation may be created, acquired, or stolen by the adversary. (Citation: Securelist Digital Certificates) (Citation: Symantec Digital Certificates) Unlike [Invalid Code Signature](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1036/001), this activity will result in a valid signature.

Code signing to verify software on first run can be used on modern Windows and macOS systems. It is not used on Linux due to the decentralized nature of the platform. (Citation: Wikipedia Code Signing)(Citation: EclecticLightChecksonEXECodeSigning)

Code signing certificates may be used to bypass security policies that require signed code to execute on a system.
2511.profile: [profile]Code Signing (T1553.002) is a Defense Evasion technique where adversaries create, acquire, or steal code signing certificates to sign malware, resulting in a valid digital signature. This provides a false level of authenticity and is used to bypass security policies on Windows and macOS systems that require signed code to execute. The technique is distinct from using an invalid signature.
2511.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Code Signing" is a Defense Evasion technique. It is formally identified as MITRE ATT&CK T1553.002 and is applicable to Windows and macOS platforms. The technique involves adversaries creating, acquiring, or stealing digital certificates to sign their malware or tools, thereby generating a valid signature. This process provides a false level of authenticity and is used to bypass security policies that require signed code to execute, helping malicious binaries masquerade as legitimate software from trusted developers.

2512.profile: [profile]Fake Resume is a social engineering technique where adversaries create and distribute fabricated resumes to gain initial access or gather intelligence, often as part of a targeted campaign. It is associated with the intrusion-set Winnti. The technique involves crafting credible professional documents, typically containing malicious links or attachments, to trick individuals in hiring or professional networks into revealing sensitive information or executing malicious code. This method exploits human trust and organizational recruitment processes.

This method aims to deliver malicious content or gain a foothold by posing as a legitimate job applicant, often embedding malware or malicious links within the resume document to compromise systems upon opening.

2514.name: Open Source Tools
2514.uncertain_mes: **This technique has been deprecated and should no longer be used.** The source command loads functions into the current shell or executes files in the current context. This built-in command can be run in two different ways source /path/to/filename [arguments] or .**This technique has been deprecated and should no longer be used.** /path/to/filename [arguments]. Take note of the space after the ".". Without a space, a new shell is created that runs the program instead of running the program within the current context. This is often used to make certain features or functions available to a shell or to update a specific shell's environment.(Citation: Source Manual) Adversaries can abuse this functionality to execute programs. The file executed with this technique does not need to be marked executable beforehand.
2514.profile: [profile]This entity, named "source" (ID: T1153), is a deprecated technique in the MITRE ATT&CK framework. It involves abusing the built-in shell `source` command (or `.` command) to execute files within the current shell context without requiring the target file to have executable permissions. The specific syntax, including the critical space after the dot (`.`), is used to load and run the file in the current environment rather than spawning a new shell. It has been associated with intrusion sets like Winnti and menuPass.[/profile]
2514.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Open Source Tools is a technique where adversaries acquire or utilize publicly available software tools for malicious purposes. These tools, unlike malware, are legitimate but repurposed, such as PsExec for lateral movement or Cobalt Strike for command and control. The technique supports various stages of an attack, including execution, persistence, and defense evasion, by leveraging tools that may be downloaded from repositories like GitHub or purchased. It is associated with numerous threat groups, including APT29, FIN7, and Lazarus Group, across multiple platforms.

2525.uncertain_mes: [APT41](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0096) is a threat group that researchers have assessed as Chinese state-sponsored espionage group that also conducts financially-motivated operations. Active since at least 2012, [APT41](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0096) has been observed targeting various industries, including but not limited to healthcare, telecom, technology, finance, education, retail and video game industries in 14 countries.(Citation: apt41_mandiant) Notable behaviors include using a wide range of malware and tools to complete mission objectives. [APT41](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0096) overlaps at least partially with public reporting on groups including BARIUM and [Winnti Group](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0044).(Citation: FireEye APT41 Aug 2019)(Citation: Group IB APT 41 June 2021)
2525.profile: [profile]Barium, also known as APT41, Winnti, and TA415, among other aliases including Leopard Typhoon and Double Dragon, is a Chinese state-sponsored cyber espionage group active since at least 2012. It is notable for its dual mission of conducting both espionage and financially motivated operations. The group employs a wide range of custom malware and tools, and shows overlaps with other reported clusters like the Winnti Group. Barium targets a broad array of sectors globally, including healthcare, telecommunications, technology, finance, and the video game industry across at least 14 countries.
2525.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The intrusion set is most widely standardized as APT41, also known as Barium, Wicked Panda, and TG-2633, with historical aliases including Winnti, LEAD, and APT17. Its key malware includes the Winnti backdoor family (with variants like WINNKIT and Spyder Loader), ShadowPad, and PlugX. Key TTPs involve supply chain compromises, spearphishing via malicious landing pages, and the use of stolen digital certificates to sign malware. The group is attributed to China's Ministry of State Security and shows overlaps with clusters tracked as Earth Lusca and Gallium. It primarily targets the global gaming, technology, telecommunications, and pharmaceutical sectors, motivated by a blend of state-sponsored espionage and financial gain.[/profile]

2531.name: Kernel Drivers
2531.profile: [profile]Kernel Drivers is a malicious signed kernel driver component, also known as a custom loader, used by threat groups such as Winnti, Turla, and potentially by groups like Alpha Spider, RansomHub, or Vanilla Tempest. It operates as a low-level system component to facilitate stealth and persistence for associated malware payloads. Its primary target platform is the Windows operating system kernel.
2531.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Kernel Drivers is a malicious signed kernel driver used by groups including Alpha Spider, RansomHub, and Vanilla Tempest. It operates by patching specific kernel structures, such as corrupting the double-linked lists for Windows services and drivers in the kernel, to unlink malicious services and drivers and hide them from system enumeration. This malware is associated with the BlackCat ransomware and shares technical characteristics with components like the Cobra Carbon System used by Turla and the DirtyMoe malware family, indicating its role in sophisticated evasion and persistence on Windows systems.

The malware is cross-platform, as indicated by related entities like CrossRAT, which is a cross-platform RAT, and by references to multi-platform capabilities in the context of the Winnti group's activities.

Its target platforms are not explicitly detailed but inferred to include Windows and potentially other systems based on the cross-platform nature of related RATs. 2533.name: Adobe Service Backdoor
2533.profile: [profile]Adobe Service Backdoor, also known as Outlook Backdoor, is attributed to the Winnti intrusion set. It operates by masquerading as legitimate Adobe software and targets e-commerce platforms, specifically Magento and Adobe Commerce, to exploit vulnerabilities such as unauthenticated remote code execution and admin takeover via menu injection. This backdoor is used to compromise stores and deploy further malicious components.[profile]
2533.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Adobe Service Backdoor is a malware that masquerades as legitimate Adobe software. It is associated with the Magecart group and targets e-commerce platforms, particularly those using Magento and Adobe Commerce. Its key behavior involves exploiting vulnerabilities like CVE-2025-54236 for unauthenticated remote code execution and creating backdoors in popular e-commerce components to facilitate admin takeover and data theft.

2539.name: Brute Force SMB Scanner
2539.uncertain_mes:
The Octopus Scanner Malware: Attacking the open source supply chain
This post details how an open source supply chain malware spread through build artifacts. 26 open source projects were backdoored by this malware and were actively serving backdoored code.
Introduction: The open source supply chain under attack
2539.profile: [profile]Brute Force SMB Scanner, also known as Octopus Scanner, is a malware attributed to the Winnti intrusion set. It primarily targets the open-source software supply chain by backdooring build artifacts and has compromised 26 projects. Its key behaviors include scanning for and brute-forcing SMB and SQL Server (port 1433) credentials using extensive wordlists, as observed in related malware families. The malware operates on Windows systems and uses network libraries like mpr.dll and Netapi32.dll for its scanning functions.[profile]
2539.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Brute Force SMB Scanner is a malware tool designed to perform network scanning and credential brute-forcing attacks. It operates by scanning for open Server Message Block (SMB) ports and conducting password brute-force attacks against them, as indicated by its name and corroborated by related descriptions of SMB brute-forcing activity. The tool's functionality is suggested by related strings referencing scanning execution parameters, IP ranges, thread counts, and authentication failure logs. It targets Windows systems and network services utilizing the SMB protocol.

2546.profile: [profile]Suckfly, also known as APT22, Bronze Olive, and Group 46, is a China-based threat group active since at least 2014. Its key malware and tools include a signed credential-dumping tool, and it uses stolen certificates to sign its malware. Key TTPs involve command-line driven tools and scanning victim internal networks for hosts with specific ports (8080, 5900, 40) open. The group is attributed to China. Target sectors and regions are not specified in the provided data. Its motivation appears to be cyber espionage, focusing on credential theft and network reconnaissance.

Its TTPs involve scanning internal networks for hosts with ports 8080, 5900, and 40 open, and notably using stolen or forged code signing certificates to sign its malware. The group is suspected to have overlaps with or be related to clusters tracked as PINCHY SPIDER (which includes aliases like TA2101, Tunnel Spider, and Maze Team). 2569.name: Custom TCP Protocol
2569.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may use a custom cryptographic protocol or algorithm to hide command and control traffic. A simple scheme, such as XOR-ing the plaintext with a fixed key, will produce a very weak ciphertext.

Custom encryption schemes may vary in sophistication. Analysis and reverse engineering of malware samples may be enough to discover the algorithm and encryption key used.

Some adversaries may also attempt to implement their own version of a well-known cryptographic algorithm instead of using a known implementation library, which may lead to unintentional errors. (Citation: F-Secure Cosmicduke)
2569.profile: [profile]Custom TCP Protocol, also known as T1024, is a Command and Control technique used to hide C2 traffic by employing a custom cryptographic protocol or algorithm. This can range from simple schemes like XOR encryption with a fixed key to more sophisticated custom implementations, which may be reverse-engineered from malware. The technique is associated with the Winnti intrusion set and relates to broader methods like custom command and control protocols and data encryption.[/profile]
2569.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Custom TCP Protocol is a technique where adversaries implement a non-standard application-layer protocol over TCP for command and control or data exfiltration, instead of using common protocols like HTTP. This can involve developing a completely custom protocol or mimicking a legitimate one to blend with normal traffic and avoid detection by network security tools. It is often used in conjunction with data obfuscation methods like custom compression or encryption prior to transmission.

2570.name: HTTPS
2570.profile: [profile]The entity is the standard MITRE ATT&CK technique "Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols" with ID T1071.001, under the Command and Control tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It describes adversaries using common web protocols like HTTPS to blend malicious traffic with normal web activity, concealing command and control data within standard HTTP/S packet fields and headers to evade detection. The technique is associated with numerous threat groups, including APT29 and Winnti from the provided context.
2570.profile_without_enhance: [profile]HTTPS is a sub-technique (T1071.001) within the Command and Control tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. It involves adversaries using the HTTPS protocol to blend malicious network traffic with legitimate web traffic, thereby evading detection and network filtering. Communication with compromised systems is achieved by embedding commands and their results within the standard fields and headers of HTTPS packets, mimicking normal, expected data exchanges.

2571.name: Communication Interfaces
2571.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may use an existing, legitimate external Web service as a means for sending commands to and receiving output from a compromised system over the Web service channel. Compromised systems may leverage popular websites and social media to host command and control (C2) instructions. Those infected systems can then send the output from those commands back over that Web service channel. The return traffic may occur in a variety of ways, depending on the Web service being utilized. For example, the return traffic may take the form of the compromised system posting a comment on a forum, issuing a pull request to development project, updating a document hosted on a Web service, or by sending a Tweet. 

Popular websites and social media acting as a mechanism for C2 may give a significant amount of cover due to the likelihood that hosts within a network are already communicating with them prior to a compromise. Using common services, such as those offered by Google or Twitter, makes it easier for adversaries to hide in expected noise. Web service providers commonly use SSL/TLS encryption, giving adversaries an added level of protection.
2571.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique "Bidirectional Communication" (ID: T1102.002) under the Command and Control tactic for Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. This technique involves adversaries using legitimate external web services like social media (e.g., Twitter) or cloud platforms (e.g., Google) to send commands to and receive output from a compromised system. The return traffic is embedded within the normal use of the service, such as posting a forum comment, updating a web document, or sending a tweet, which provides cover by blending with expected encrypted (SSL/TLS) user traffic. It is notably used by groups including APT28, Lazarus Group, and FIN7.
2571.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Communication Interfaces" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the retrieved context, it likely refers to the general concept of adversary communication methods, which encompasses multiple specific techniques. These include splitting communications across different protocols (T1026, deprecated), using legitimate web services for bidirectional (T1102.002) or one-way (T1102.003) command and control, and abusing inter-process communication (IPC) mechanisms like Windows COM (T1559.001) for local code execution. The core technical mechanics involve leveraging various channels—such as social media, encrypted web services, or system IPC—to send commands, exfiltrate data, and maintain control while evading detection by blending with normal traffic or using trusted system components.

This activity is associated with the intrusion set Winnti.
