2572.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Plugin Management is a technique adversaries use to abuse legitimate software deployment and configuration management tools, such as SCCM, Microsoft Intune, or AWS Systems Manager, for remote code execution and lateral movement across enterprise networks. This method, which can be executed via web protocols or cloud administration commands, allows attackers to run scripts and deploy payloads on connected endpoints, often requiring administrative credentials to access the centralized management suite.

2573.name: Data Encryption
2573.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may compromise a network device’s encryption capability in order to bypass encryption that would otherwise protect data communications. (Citation: Cisco Synful Knock Evolution)

Encryption can be used to protect transmitted network traffic to maintain its confidentiality (protect against unauthorized disclosure) and integrity (protect against unauthorized changes). Encryption ciphers are used to convert a plaintext message to ciphertext and can be computationally intensive to decipher without the associated decryption key. Typically, longer keys increase the cost of cryptanalysis, or decryption without the key.

Adversaries can compromise and manipulate devices that perform encryption of network traffic. For example, through behaviors such as [Modify System Image](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1601), [Reduce Key Space](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1600/001), and [Disable Crypto Hardware](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1600/002), an adversary can negatively effect and/or eliminate a device’s ability to securely encrypt network traffic. This poses a greater risk of unauthorized disclosure and may help facilitate data manipulation, Credential Access, or Collection efforts. (Citation: Cisco Blog Legacy Device Attacks)
2573.profile: [profile]Data Encryption, also known as Weaken Encryption (T1600), is an adversary technique under the Impact tactic targeting network platforms. It involves compromising a network device's encryption capability to bypass protections for data communications. Specific technical mechanics include modifying the system image, reducing the cryptographic key space, or disabling dedicated crypto hardware to degrade or eliminate secure traffic encryption, thereby facilitating unauthorized data disclosure or manipulation. This technique is associated with groups like Turla and Winnti.[/profile]
2573.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Data Encryption, corresponding to MITRE ATT&CK technique T1022, falls under the Exfiltration tactic and applies to multiple platforms. It involves adversaries encrypting collected data using utilities, libraries (e.g., for RAR or zip), or custom algorithms prior to exfiltration to conceal the information's content and evade detection. This technique is often used in conjunction with data archiving (T1560) and is associated with groups like APT28 and Lazarus.[/profile]

2574.name: Data Compression (LZMA)
2574.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may use compression to obfuscate their payloads or files. Compressed file formats such as ZIP, gzip, 7z, and RAR can compress and archive multiple files together to make it easier and faster to transfer files. In addition to compressing files, adversaries may also compress shellcode directly - for example, in order to store it in a Windows Registry key (i.e., [Fileless Storage](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/011)).(Citation: Trustwave Pillowmint June 2020)

In order to further evade detection, adversaries may combine multiple ZIP files into one archive. This process of concatenation creates an archive that appears to be a single archive but in fact contains the central directories of the embedded archives. Some ZIP readers, such as 7zip, may not be able to identify concatenated ZIP files and miss the presence of the malicious payload.(Citation: Perception Point)

File archives may be sent as one [Spearphishing Attachment](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001) through email. Adversaries have sent malicious payloads as archived files to encourage the user to interact with and extract the malicious payload onto their system (i.e., [Malicious File](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002)).(Citation: NTT Security Flagpro new December 2021) However, some file compression tools, such as 7zip, can be used to produce self-extracting archives. Adversaries may send self-extracting archives to hide the functionality of their payload and launch it without requiring multiple actions from the user.(Citation: The Hacker News)

[Compression](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/015) may be used in combination with [Encrypted/Encoded File](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/013) where compressed files are encrypted and password-protected.
2574.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK sub-technique T1027.015, named Data Compression (LZMA), under the Defense Evasion tactic. It involves adversaries using compression, including the LZMA algorithm, to obfuscate payloads and files for evasion. Specific mechanics include compressing shellcode for fileless storage in the Windows Registry, creating concatenated or self-extracting archives to bypass detection tools, and combining compression with encryption. It is associated with groups like Gamaredon Group and Winnti.
2574.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Data Compression (LZMA) is a sub-technique of T1560 (Archive Collected Data) under the Collection tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It involves adversaries using the LZMA compression algorithm, often via custom programs or utilities like 7zip, to compress collected data (e.g., sensitive documents) prior to exfiltration. This reduces data size for efficient transfer and aids in obfuscation, and it is commonly associated with threat groups like Dragonfly and APT28.[profile]

2575.name: Installation-to-Execution Cycle
2575.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may abuse vSphere Installation Bundles (VIBs) to establish persistent access to ESXi hypervisors. VIBs are collections of files used for software distribution and virtual system management in VMware environments. Since ESXi uses an in-memory filesystem where changes made to most files are stored in RAM rather than in persistent storage, these modifications are lost after a reboot. However, VIBs can be used to create startup tasks, apply custom firewall rules, or deploy binaries that persist across reboots. Typically, administrators use VIBs for updates and system maintenance. VIBs can be broken down into three components:(Citation: VMware VIBs) * VIB payload: a `.vgz` archive containing the directories and files to be created and executed on boot when the VIBs are loaded. * Signature file: verifies the host acceptance level of a VIB, indicating what testing and validation has been done by VMware or its partners before publication of a VIB. By default, ESXi hosts require a minimum acceptance level of PartnerSupported for VIB installation, meaning the VIB is published by a trusted VMware partner. However, privileged users can change the default acceptance level using the `esxcli` command line interface. Additionally, VIBs are able to be installed regardless of acceptance level by using the esxcli software vib install --force command. * XML descriptor file: a configuration file containing associated VIB metadata, such as the name of the VIB and its dependencies. Adversaries may leverage malicious VIB packages to maintain persistent access to ESXi hypervisors, allowing system changes to be executed upon each bootup of ESXi – such as using `esxcli` to enable firewall rules for backdoor traffic, creating listeners on hard coded ports, and executing backdoors.(Citation: Google Cloud Threat Intelligence ESXi VIBs 2022) Adversaries may also masquerade their malicious VIB files as PartnerSupported by modifying the XML descriptor file.(Citation: Google Cloud Threat Intelligence ESXi VIBs 2022)
2575.profile: [profile]Installation-to-Execution Cycle, also known as vSphere Installation Bundles (VIBs) and mapped to MITRE ATT&CK T1505.006 under Persistence, targets VMware ESXi platforms. This technique abuses VIB packages, which consist of a .vgz payload archive, a signature file, and an XML descriptor, to establish persistent, reboot-resistant access. Adversaries install malicious VIBs using the `esxcli software vib install --force` command, bypassing default acceptance levels. These packages can be configured to execute backdoors, create listeners on specific ports, or apply custom firewall rules on every ESXi boot, often by masquerading as PartnerSupported through XML modification.[/profile]
2575.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Installation-to-Execution Cycle is a technique where adversaries abuse the legitimate installation process of software to trigger the execution of malicious payloads. This often involves hijacking installer packages or exploiting file permission weaknesses in temporary directories used during installation. By leveraging installer scripts that run with elevated permissions, such as macOS `postinstall` or Linux maintainer scripts, adversaries can establish persistence, escalate privileges, and execute their code under the guise of a legitimate software setup.

2576.name: WinnTI Boot Sequence
2576.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may abuse netbooting to load an unauthorized network device operating system from a Trivial File Transfer Protocol (TFTP) server. TFTP boot (netbooting) is commonly used by network administrators to load configuration-controlled network device images from a centralized management server. Netbooting is one option in the boot sequence and can be used to centralize, manage, and control device images.

Adversaries may manipulate the configuration on the network device specifying use of a malicious TFTP server, which may be used in conjunction with [Modify System Image](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1601) to load a modified image on device startup or reset. The unauthorized image allows adversaries to modify device configuration, add malicious capabilities to the device, and introduce backdoors to maintain control of the network device while minimizing detection through use of a standard functionality. This technique is similar to [ROMMONkit](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1542/004) and may result in the network device running a modified image. (Citation: Cisco Blog Legacy Device Attacks)
2576.profile: [profile]WinnTI Boot Sequence, also known as TFTP Boot (T1542.005) under the Persistence tactic, targets network platforms. It involves adversaries manipulating a network device's configuration to specify a malicious Trivial File Transfer Protocol (TFTP) server, enabling the loading of an unauthorized or modified network device operating system image during the netbooting process. This technique centralizes control and can introduce backdoors, similar to the ROMMONkit method, and is associated with the Winnti intrusion set.
2576.profile_without_enhance: [profile]WinnTI Boot Sequence is a technique for establishing persistence by manipulating the Windows boot process, aligning with the Pre-OS Boot (T1542) tactic on Windows systems. It involves modifying the Boot Configuration Data (BCD) store to force the system into Safe Mode on the next reboot, where many security applications do not start. Adversaries can then configure malicious services or COM objects to load in this minimal environment, effectively disabling defenses and maintaining control. This method is similar to other boot manipulation techniques like Bootkit (T1542.003) and Safe Mode Boot (T1562.009).

2577.name: Sysprep UAC Bypass
2577.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may modify file attributes and subvert Gatekeeper functionality to evade user prompts and execute untrusted programs. Gatekeeper is a set of technologies that act as layer of Apple’s security model to ensure only trusted applications are executed on a host. Gatekeeper was built on top of File Quarantine in Snow Leopard (10.6, 2009) and has grown to include Code Signing, security policy compliance, Notarization, and more. Gatekeeper also treats applications running for the first time differently than reopened applications.(Citation: TheEclecticLightCompany Quarantine and the flag)(Citation: TheEclecticLightCompany apple notarization )

Based on an opt-in system, when files are downloaded an extended attribute (xattr) called `com.apple.quarantine` (also known as a quarantine flag) can be set on the file by the application performing the download. Launch Services opens the application in a suspended state. For first run applications with the quarantine flag set, Gatekeeper executes the following functions:

1. Checks extended attribute – Gatekeeper checks for the quarantine flag, then provides an alert prompt to the user to allow or deny execution.(Citation: OceanLotus for OS X)(Citation: 20 macOS Common Tools and Techniques)

2. Checks System Policies - Gatekeeper checks the system security policy, allowing execution of apps downloaded from either just the App Store or the App Store and identified developers.

3. Code Signing – Gatekeeper checks for a valid code signature from an Apple Developer ID.

4. Notarization - Using the `api.apple-cloudkit.com` API, Gatekeeper reaches out to Apple servers to verify or pull down the notarization ticket and ensure the ticket is not revoked. Users can override notarization, which will result in a prompt of executing an “unauthorized app” and the security policy will be modified.

Adversaries can subvert one or multiple security controls within Gatekeeper checks through logic errors (e.g. [Exploitation for Defense Evasion](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1211)), unchecked file types, and external libraries. For example, prior to macOS 13 Ventura, code signing and notarization checks were only conducted on first launch, allowing adversaries to write malicious executables to previously opened applications in order to bypass Gatekeeper security checks.(Citation: theevilbit gatekeeper bypass 2021)(Citation: Application Bundle Manipulation Brandon Dalton)

Applications and files loaded onto the system from a USB flash drive, optical disk, external hard drive, from a drive shared over the local network, or using the curl command may not set the quarantine flag. Additionally, it is possible to avoid setting the quarantine flag using [Drive-by Compromise](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1189).
2577.profile: [profile]Sysprep UAC Bypass is a specific technique for bypassing Windows User Account Control (UAC) to elevate privileges, falling under the Defense Evasion tactic. It operates on Windows platforms by exploiting the Sysprep utility, which runs with elevated permissions, to execute a malicious payload. This method allows adversaries to achieve administrator-level execution without triggering the standard UAC prompt, leveraging a trusted system process for defense evasion. The intrusion-set Winnti has been associated with this technique.[/profile]
2577.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Sysprep UAC Bypass is a technique for bypassing Windows User Account Control (UAC) to elevate privileges. It specifically exploits the Windows System Preparation Tool (sysprep.exe) and its associated `sysprep.dll` or `sysprep.xml` configuration files. By crafting or manipulating these components, adversaries can execute arbitrary code with elevated permissions without triggering the standard UAC prompt, effectively subverting a core Windows security mechanism. This method is part of a broader set of UAC bypass techniques used for privilege escalation.

2578.name: Automated SSL
2578.uncertain_mes:
Once established within a system or network, an adversary may use automated techniques for collecting internal data. Methods for performing this technique could include use of a [Command and Scripting Interpreter](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059) to search for and copy information fitting set criteria such as file type, location, or name at specific time intervals. 

In cloud-based environments, adversaries may also use cloud APIs, data pipelines, command line interfaces, or extract, transform, and load (ETL) services to automatically collect data.(Citation: Mandiant UNC3944 SMS Phishing 2023) 

This functionality could also be built into remote access tools. 

This technique may incorporate use of other techniques such as [File and Directory Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1083) and [Lateral Tool Transfer](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1570) to identify and move files, as well as [Cloud Service Dashboard](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1538) and [Cloud Storage Object Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1619) to identify resources in cloud environments.
2578.profile: [profile]The entity "Automated SSL" appears to be a misinterpretation of the MITRE technique "Automated Collection" (T1119) under the Collection tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. This technique involves using automated scripts or interpreters to search for and copy data based on criteria like file type or name at scheduled intervals. In cloud environments, it extends to using APIs, CLIs, or ETL services. The technique often incorporates discovery methods like File and Directory Discovery (T1083) and may be associated with groups like Winnti. The retrieved information on digital certificates is unrelated to the core automated collection mechanics and is discarded.
2578.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Automated SSL" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the retrieved context, it likely refers to the automated generation, acquisition, or deployment of SSL/TLS certificates to enable encrypted command and control (C2) traffic over web protocols or to facilitate adversary-in-the-middle attacks by establishing trust. This process can involve using free certificate authorities, creating self-signed certificates, or stealing certificates from compromised entities, followed by their automated installation on controlled infrastructure.

2579.name: Persistence Model
2579.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may clear artifacts associated with previously established persistence on a host system to remove evidence of their activity. This may involve various actions, such as removing services, deleting executables, [Modify Registry](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1112), [Plist File Modification](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1647), or other methods of cleanup to prevent defenders from collecting evidence of their persistent presence.(Citation: Cylance Dust Storm) Adversaries may also delete accounts previously created to maintain persistence (i.e. [Create Account](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1136)).(Citation: Talos - Cisco Attack 2022)

In some instances, artifacts of persistence may also be removed once an adversary’s persistence is executed in order to prevent errors with the new instance of the malware.(Citation: NCC Group Team9 June 2020)
2579.profile: [profile]The entity "Persistence Model" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the provided data, the core concept is "Clear Persistence" (T1070.009), a Defense Evasion technique for Windows. It involves adversaries removing artifacts of previously established persistence, such as deleting services, executables, or accounts, to eliminate evidence of their presence or to prevent errors with new malware instances. The intrusion-set Winnti is associated with this behavior.
2579.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Persistence Model is a general concept for maintaining adversary access, not a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on retrieved context, persistence can be achieved through various technical mechanics, including hijacking the Windows Component Object Model (COM) by modifying Registry references to execute malicious code in place of legitimate software, or by abusing Microsoft Office add-ins and startup mechanisms to execute code when Office applications launch. These methods allow adversaries to ensure their presence remains on a compromised system across reboots and logons.

2583.name: WinnTI 3.0
2583.uncertain_mes: [LockBit 3.0](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S1202) is an evolution of the LockBit Ransomware-as-a-Service (RaaS) offering with similarities to BlackMatter and [BlackCat](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S1068) ransomware. 2588.name: Malicious DLL

It is associated with intrusion sets like Winnti and DeepPanda. Specific malicious DLLs are linked to PlugX, Sunburst, and Cobalt Strike malware families, with PlugX attributed to groups such as APT22, APT26, APT31, APT41, Aurora Panda, and Mustang Panda, Sunburst to APT29 and UNC2452, and Cobalt Strike to APT29, APT32, APT41, and others including Mustang Panda and Winnti. 2589.name: Network Connection Hiding
2589.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may remove share connections that are no longer useful in order to clean up traces of their operation. Windows shared drive and [SMB/Windows Admin Shares](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002) connections can be removed when no longer needed. [Net](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0039) is an example utility that can be used to remove network share connections with the net use \\system\share /delete command. (Citation: Technet Net Use)
2589.profile: [profile]Network Connection Hiding, identified as MITRE ATT&CK T1070.005, is a Defense Evasion technique used on Windows platforms. It involves adversaries removing Windows shared drive and SMB/Windows Admin Shares connections to clean up traces of their operation, typically using the `net use \\system\share /delete` command via utilities like Net. The threat group Winnti has been associated with this behavior.
2589.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Network Connection Hiding" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the retrieved context, it is a sub-technique of Defense Evasion, specifically aligned with T1070.007 - Clear Network Connection History and Configurations. This technique involves adversaries removing forensic artifacts of malicious network connections to evade detection. Key actions include deleting or modifying configuration settings and logs, such as Windows Registry entries for RDP history (e.g., `HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Terminal Server Client\Servers`) and related cache files, to conceal their operational footprint.

2590.name: File Deletion
2590.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may delete files left behind by the actions of their intrusion activity. Malware, tools, or other non-native files dropped or created on a system by an adversary (ex: [Ingress Tool Transfer](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1105)) may leave traces to indicate to what was done within a network and how. Removal of these files can occur during an intrusion, or as part of a post-intrusion process to minimize the adversary's footprint. There are tools available from the host operating system to perform cleanup, but adversaries may use other tools as well.(Citation: Microsoft SDelete July 2016) Examples of built-in [Command and Scripting Interpreter](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059) functions include del on Windows, rm or unlink on Linux and macOS, and `rm` on ESXi.
2590.profile: [profile]File Deletion, identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1070.004, is a Defense Evasion tactic used across Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. It involves adversaries removing non-native files like malware or tools to eliminate forensic traces. This is commonly performed using native command interpreters, such as the `del` command on Windows or `rm` and `unlink` on Unix-based systems, and can also utilize third-party utilities like SDelete for secure deletion. The technique is associated with numerous threat groups, including APT29, Lazarus Group, and Wizard Spider, and is directly linked to the Winnti intrusion set.[/profile]
2590.profile_without_enhance: [profile]File Deletion, also known as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1070.004 (Indicator Removal: File Deletion), is a Defense Evasion tactic. It operates on Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. Adversaries use this technique to remove traces of their intrusion, such as dropped malware or tools, to minimize their forensic footprint. Technical execution involves using native OS commands like `del` on Windows or `rm` and `unlink` on Unix-based systems, as well as third-party secure deletion tools like Windows Sysinternals SDelete. This action can occur during or after an intrusion.

2591.name: Rootkit
2591.uncertain_mes: [Hacking Team UEFI Rootkit](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0047) is a rootkit developed by the company Hacking Team as a method of persistence for remote access software. (Citation: TrendMicro Hacking Team UEFI)
2591.profile: [profile]The Hacking Team UEFI Rootkit, also known as the Hacking Team UEFI Rootkit, is a rootkit developed by the company Hacking Team specifically to achieve persistence for remote access software by targeting the UEFI firmware layer. It is associated with the intrusion sets Winnti and DeepPanda. Its key technical behavior involves embedding itself within the system's UEFI firmware to survive operating system reinstallation. The rootkit is designed to target platforms with UEFI firmware, primarily Windows systems, and operates by decrypting and loading its payload in memory to evade detection.
2591.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Rootkit is a broad category of malware designed to conceal its presence and other malicious activities on a system. Specific examples include the Hacking Team UEFI Rootkit, used for persistence by the Hacking Team company, and the Fudmodule rootkit, which is compressed with VMProtect and associated with the Lazarus Group. Other instances like Tollbooth utilize customized hidden kernel drivers (e.g., Wingtb.sys, Winkbj.sys). Rootkits can operate in user mode or kernel mode to achieve stealth and are often deployed as part of multi-stage attacks for initial access or persistence.

2592.name: Obfuscation
2592.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may obfuscate command and control traffic to make it more difficult to detect.(Citation: Bitdefender FunnyDream Campaign November 2020) Command and control (C2) communications are hidden (but not necessarily encrypted) in an attempt to make the content more difficult to discover or decipher and to make the communication less conspicuous and hide commands from being seen. This encompasses many methods, such as adding junk data to protocol traffic, using steganography, or impersonating legitimate protocols.
2592.profile: [profile]Data Obfuscation, identified as T1001, is a Command and Control tactic used across multiple platforms to hide C2 traffic from detection. It works by adding junk data to protocol traffic, employing steganography, or impersonating legitimate protocols to make communications less conspicuous. This technique is associated with groups like Gamaredon Group and is conceptually related to broader obfuscation methods for files and commands.
2592.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Obfuscation is a broad technique for evading detection by making data, commands, or files difficult to analyze. It encompasses specific sub-techniques such as Data Obfuscation (T1001) for hiding C2 traffic via steganography or protocol impersonation, Command Obfuscation (T1027.010) using syntax tricks, encoding, and tools like Invoke-Obfuscation on command lines, and Obfuscated Files or Information (T1027) involving encryption, compression, or splitting of payloads. These methods are employed across multiple platforms by numerous threat groups to bypass signatures and hinder defender analysis.

2593.name: Command and Scripting Interpreter
2593.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may abuse command and script interpreters to execute commands, scripts, or binaries. These interfaces and languages provide ways of interacting with computer systems and are a common feature across many different platforms. Most systems come with some built-in command-line interface and scripting capabilities, for example, macOS and Linux distributions include some flavor of [Unix Shell](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/004) while Windows installations include the [Windows Command Shell](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/003) and [PowerShell](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001).

There are also cross-platform interpreters such as [Python](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/006), as well as those commonly associated with client applications such as [JavaScript](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/007) and [Visual Basic](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/005).

Adversaries may abuse these technologies in various ways as a means of executing arbitrary commands. Commands and scripts can be embedded in [Initial Access](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0001) payloads delivered to victims as lure documents or as secondary payloads downloaded from an existing C2. Adversaries may also execute commands through interactive terminals/shells, as well as utilize various [Remote Services](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021) in order to achieve remote Execution.(Citation: Powershell Remote Commands)(Citation: Cisco IOS Software Integrity Assurance - Command History)(Citation: Remote Shell Execution in Python)
2593.profile: [profile]Command and Scripting Interpreter, identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1059 under the Execution tactic, is a foundational method adversaries use to execute arbitrary commands across multiple platforms including Windows, Linux, and macOS. It involves abusing built-in interpreters like Windows Command Shell, PowerShell, Unix Shell, Python, JavaScript, and Visual Basic. Commands and scripts are often embedded in initial access payloads such as lure documents, delivered via remote services, or executed through interactive shells to achieve remote execution, as leveraged by groups like APT29, OilRig, and Winnti.[/profile]
2593.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Command and Scripting Interpreter, identified as MITRE ATT&CK T1059, is an Execution tactic technique applicable across multiple platforms. It involves adversaries abusing built-in or cross-platform interpreters like Unix Shell, Windows Command Shell, PowerShell, Python, JavaScript, and Visual Basic to execute arbitrary commands. These commands and scripts can be delivered via initial access payloads, interactive terminals, or remote services to achieve execution on a target system.

2594.name: Remote Desktop Protocol
2594.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may use [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078) to log into a computer using the Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP). The adversary may then perform actions as the logged-on user.

Remote desktop is a common feature in operating systems. It allows a user to log into an interactive session with a system desktop graphical user interface on a remote system. Microsoft refers to its implementation of the Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) as Remote Desktop Services (RDS).(Citation: TechNet Remote Desktop Services) 

Adversaries may connect to a remote system over RDP/RDS to expand access if the service is enabled and allows access to accounts with known credentials. Adversaries will likely use Credential Access techniques to acquire credentials to use with RDP. Adversaries may also use RDP in conjunction with the [Accessibility Features](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1546/008) or [Terminal Services DLL](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1505/005) for Persistence.(Citation: Alperovitch Malware)
2594.profile: [profile]Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP), identified as MITRE ATT&CK T1021.001, is a technique under the Lateral Movement tactic primarily for Windows platforms. It enables adversaries with valid credentials to establish an interactive graphical session on a remote system, often using stolen credentials obtained via Credential Access. Attackers may use RDP to expand network access, perform actions as the logged-on user, and can hijack existing sessions using tools like `tscon.exe` with system permissions to steal sessions without user prompts. It is frequently used in conjunction with persistence techniques like Accessibility Features and is associated with numerous threat groups including FIN7, APT41, and Wizard Spider.
2594.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Remote Desktop Protocol, designated as T1021.001, is a sub-technique under the Lateral Movement tactic, primarily used on Windows platforms. It involves adversaries using valid accounts to log into remote computers via RDP/RDS to gain interactive graphical access, enabling them to perform actions as the logged-on user. Attackers often acquire credentials through Credential Access techniques and may use RDP for persistence via methods like Accessibility Features. A specific technical mechanic for session hijacking involves using the Terminal Services Console command `tscon.exe` with system permissions to steal active or disconnected sessions without user prompts, facilitating privilege escalation and lateral movement.

2595.name: File Transfer
2595.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may communicate using application layer protocols associated with transferring files to avoid detection/network filtering by blending in with existing traffic. Commands to the remote system, and often the results of those commands, will be embedded within the protocol traffic between the client and server. 

Protocols such as SMB(Citation: US-CERT TA18-074A), FTP(Citation: ESET Machete July 2019), FTPS, and TFTP that transfer files may be very common in environments.  Packets produced from these protocols may have many fields and headers in which data can be concealed. Data could also be concealed within the transferred files. An adversary may abuse these protocols to communicate with systems under their control within a victim network while also mimicking normal, expected traffic.
2595.profile: [profile]File Transfer Protocols, designated as T1071.002 within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, is a Command and Control technique under the Command and Control tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. Adversaries use common application-layer file transfer protocols like SMB, FTP, FTPS, and TFTP to blend malicious communications with normal network traffic, embedding commands and data within standard protocol fields, headers, or the transferred files themselves to avoid detection. It has been associated with groups like APT41 and Dragonfly, and malware such as SUNBURST and Carbanak have been observed using related mechanisms.[/profile]
2595.profile_without_enhance: [profile]File Transfer is a technique used for data exfiltration or tool movement, often categorized under Exfiltration or Lateral Movement tactics. It involves moving files out of a network or between systems using standard protocols like SMB, FTP, FTPS, or TFTP to blend with normal traffic. Adversaries may also use native utilities such as scp, rsync, curl, sftp, and certutil, or abuse cloud sync services like Dropbox. The technique is platform-agnostic, applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS, and is employed by numerous threat groups including APT41, Wizard Spider, and Volt Typhoon.

2596.name: Process Discovery
2596.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may attempt to get information about running processes on a system. Information obtained could be used to gain an understanding of common software/applications running on systems within the network. Administrator or otherwise elevated access may provide better process details. Adversaries may use the information from [Process Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1057) during automated discovery to shape follow-on behaviors, including whether or not the adversary fully infects the target and/or attempts specific actions. In Windows environments, adversaries could obtain details on running processes using the [Tasklist](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0057) utility via [cmd](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0106) or Get-Process via [PowerShell](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001). Information about processes can also be extracted from the output of [Native API](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1106) calls such as CreateToolhelp32Snapshot. In Mac and Linux, this is accomplished with the ps command. Adversaries may also opt to enumerate processes via `/proc`. ESXi also supports use of the `ps` command, as well as `esxcli system process list`.(Citation: Sygnia ESXi Ransomware 2025)(Citation: Crowdstrike Hypervisor Jackpotting Pt 2 2021) On network devices, [Network Device CLI](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/008) commands such as `show processes` can be used to display current running processes.(Citation: US-CERT-TA18-106A)(Citation: show_processes_cisco_cmd)
2596.profile: [profile]Process Discovery, identified as T1057, is a Discovery tactic technique used across Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. It involves adversaries enumerating running processes to understand system software and guide follow-on actions. Specific technical mechanics include using commands like `tasklist` or `Get-Process` in Windows, `ps` or enumerating `/proc` in Linux/macOS, `esxcli system process list` on ESXi, and `show processes` on network devices. It is associated with numerous threat groups including Winnti, Volt Typhoon, and Lazarus Group.[/profile]
2596.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Process Discovery, identified as T1057, is a Discovery tactic used across Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. It involves adversaries enumerating running processes to understand the software landscape and guide subsequent actions. Technical mechanics include using commands like `tasklist` or `Get-Process` in Windows, `ps` or enumerating `/proc` on Linux/macOS, and `esxcli system process list` on ESXi hypervisors. This technique is widely used by numerous threat groups, including APT28, Lazarus Group, and Volt Typhoon, for initial reconnaissance.

2597.name: Service Discovery
2597.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may try to gather information about registered local system services. Adversaries may obtain information about services using tools as well as OS utility commands such as sc query, tasklist /svc, systemctl --type=service, and net start. Adversaries may also gather information about schedule tasks via commands such as `schtasks` on Windows or `crontab -l` on Linux and macOS.(Citation: Elastic Security Labs GOSAR 2024)(Citation: SentinelLabs macOS Malware 2021)(Citation: Splunk Linux Gormir 2024)(Citation: Aquasec Kinsing 2020) Adversaries may use the information from [System Service Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1007) during automated discovery to shape follow-on behaviors, including whether or not the adversary fully infects the target and/or attempts specific actions.
2597.profile: [profile]System Service Discovery, identified as T1007 under the Discovery tactic, is a technique used across Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. Adversaries gather information about registered local services and scheduled tasks using native OS commands such as `sc query`, `tasklist /svc`, `systemctl --type=service`, `net start`, `schtasks`, and `crontab -l`. This discovered information is used to shape subsequent attack behaviors, including decisions on infection and specific actions. The technique has been associated with groups including Volt Typhoon, Kimsuky, and OilRig.[/profile]
2597.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Service Discovery is a broad information-gathering technique that maps to multiple specific MITRE ATT&CK techniques, including System Service Discovery (T1007), Network Service Discovery (T1046), and Cloud Service Discovery (T1526). It falls under the Discovery tactic and is applicable across Windows, Linux, macOS, and cloud platforms. The technical mechanics involve using native OS commands and APIs, such as `sc query`, `tasklist /svc`, `systemctl`, `net start`, and cloud-specific APIs like AWS's `DescribeInstances`, to enumerate running services, scheduled tasks, and remote network services to inform subsequent attack actions.

2598.name: LZMA Compression
2598.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may use compression to obfuscate their payloads or files. Compressed file formats such as ZIP, gzip, 7z, and RAR can compress and archive multiple files together to make it easier and faster to transfer files. In addition to compressing files, adversaries may also compress shellcode directly - for example, in order to store it in a Windows Registry key (i.e., [Fileless Storage](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/011)).(Citation: Trustwave Pillowmint June 2020)

In order to further evade detection, adversaries may combine multiple ZIP files into one archive. This process of concatenation creates an archive that appears to be a single archive but in fact contains the central directories of the embedded archives. Some ZIP readers, such as 7zip, may not be able to identify concatenated ZIP files and miss the presence of the malicious payload.(Citation: Perception Point)

File archives may be sent as one [Spearphishing Attachment](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001) through email. Adversaries have sent malicious payloads as archived files to encourage the user to interact with and extract the malicious payload onto their system (i.e., [Malicious File](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002)).(Citation: NTT Security Flagpro new December 2021) However, some file compression tools, such as 7zip, can be used to produce self-extracting archives. Adversaries may send self-extracting archives to hide the functionality of their payload and launch it without requiring multiple actions from the user.(Citation: The Hacker News)

[Compression](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/015) may be used in combination with [Encrypted/Encoded File](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/013) where compressed files are encrypted and password-protected.
2598.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique Compression, ID T1027.015, under the Defense Evasion tactic for Windows, Linux, and macOS. It involves using standard formats like ZIP, gzip, 7z, and RAR to obfuscate payloads or files, including compressing shellcode for storage in locations like the Windows Registry. Adversaries may concatenate multiple ZIP archives to evade detection by some readers or create self-extracting archives to simplify execution. It is often combined with encryption and has been used by groups like Gamaredon Group and TA2541.
2598.profile_without_enhance: [profile]LZMA Compression is a sub-technique of Obfuscated Files or Information (T1027.015) under the Defense Evasion tactic, primarily used on Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. Adversaries employ this specific algorithm to compress payloads or collected data, making them more portable and harder to detect. It can be used to obfuscate shellcode for fileless storage or to minimize data size prior to exfiltration, often implemented via custom programs or common utilities.

2599.name: TCP Protocol
2599.profile: [profile]The entity "TCP Protocol" is a core internet transport layer protocol, not a MITRE ATT&CK attack pattern. It provides reliable, ordered, and error-checked delivery of data streams, operating on ports like 80 (HTTP) and 443 (HTTPS). Adversaries, such as the Winnti intrusion set, may abuse it to blend malicious traffic with normal network activity, often tunneling other protocols within it or using it for custom command and control channels to avoid detection.
2599.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "TCP Protocol" is a fundamental network communication protocol, not a specific MITRE ATT&CK attack pattern. It serves as the transport layer for many adversary techniques, enabling reliable, connection-oriented data transmission. Adversaries leverage TCP to encapsulate malicious traffic within legitimate-appearing connections, often using common ports like 80 or 443 to bypass detection. It forms the underlying basis for techniques such as Application Layer Protocol (T1071) and Protocol Tunneling (T1572), where custom command and control or other malicious protocols are layered on top of TCP to facilitate stealthy communication.

2600.name: Stealth Communication via Common Ports
2600.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may use an existing, legitimate external Web service as a means for sending commands to and receiving output from a compromised system over the Web service channel. Compromised systems may leverage popular websites and social media to host command and control (C2) instructions. Those infected systems can then send the output from those commands back over that Web service channel. The return traffic may occur in a variety of ways, depending on the Web service being utilized. For example, the return traffic may take the form of the compromised system posting a comment on a forum, issuing a pull request to development project, updating a document hosted on a Web service, or by sending a Tweet. 

Popular websites and social media acting as a mechanism for C2 may give a significant amount of cover due to the likelihood that hosts within a network are already communicating with them prior to a compromise. Using common services, such as those offered by Google or Twitter, makes it easier for adversaries to hide in expected noise. Web service providers commonly use SSL/TLS encryption, giving adversaries an added level of protection.
2600.profile: [profile]Stealth Communication via Common Ports is a command and control technique where adversaries use legitimate web services (like social media or cloud platforms) over standard ports such as TCP/80 (HTTP) or TCP/443 (HTTPS) to send commands and receive output, blending with normal encrypted traffic to evade detection. It is associated with groups including APT28, Lazarus Group, and MuddyWater.[/profile]
2600.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Stealth Communication via Common Ports is a command and control technique where adversaries use standard, commonly open ports (like TCP:80, 443, 25, or 53) to blend with normal network traffic, bypassing firewalls and avoiding detailed inspection. The communication may use the protocol associated with the port or an entirely different one. This method is distinct from port knocking, which dynamically opens ports, and from web protocol abuse, which specifically conceals data within HTTP/S packets.

2604.name: Asynchronous Data Transmission
2604.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may inject malicious code into processes via the asynchronous procedure call (APC) queue in order to evade process-based defenses as well as possibly elevate privileges. APC injection is a method of executing arbitrary code in the address space of a separate live process. APC injection is commonly performed by attaching malicious code to the APC Queue (Citation: Microsoft APC) of a process's thread. Queued APC functions are executed when the thread enters an alterable state.(Citation: Microsoft APC) A handle to an existing victim process is first created with native Windows API calls such as OpenThread. At this point QueueUserAPC can be used to invoke a function (such as LoadLibrayA pointing to a malicious DLL). A variation of APC injection, dubbed "Early Bird injection", involves creating a suspended process in which malicious code can be written and executed before the process' entry point (and potentially subsequent anti-malware hooks) via an APC. (Citation: CyberBit Early Bird Apr 2018) AtomBombing (Citation: ENSIL AtomBombing Oct 2016) is another variation that utilizes APCs to invoke malicious code previously written to the global atom table.(Citation: Microsoft Atom Table) Running code in the context of another process may allow access to the process's memory, system/network resources, and possibly elevated privileges. Execution via APC injection may also evade detection from security products since the execution is masked under a legitimate process.
2604.profile: [profile]Asynchronous Procedure Call (APC) Injection, identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1055.004 under the Defense Evasion and Privilege Escalation tactics, targets Windows platforms. It involves injecting malicious code into a process's APC queue using Windows API calls like OpenThread and QueueUserAPC to invoke functions such as LoadLibraryA, executing code in a legitimate process's address space to evade detection and potentially gain elevated privileges. Variations include Early Bird injection and AtomBombing. The intrusion-set Winnti is associated with this technique.
2604.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Asynchronous Data Transmission is a technique for data exfiltration where adversaries send stolen data over a network protocol that uses asynchronous (non-real-time) communication, distinct from the primary command and control channel. This method can leverage protocols like SMTP or FTP for data transfer, helping to blend malicious traffic with legitimate network activity and evade detection by separating exfiltration from command traffic.

2605.name: Send Empty Messages
2605.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may directly collect unsecured credentials stored or passed through user communication services. Credentials may be sent and stored in user chat communication applications such as email, chat services like Slack or Teams, collaboration tools like Jira or Trello, and any other services that support user communication. Users may share various forms of credentials (such as usernames and passwords, API keys, or authentication tokens) on private or public corporate internal communications channels.

Rather than accessing the stored chat logs (i.e., [Credentials In Files](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1552/001)), adversaries may directly access credentials within these services on the user endpoint, through servers hosting the services, or through administrator portals for cloud hosted services. Adversaries may also compromise integration tools like Slack Workflows to automatically search through messages to extract user credentials. These credentials may then be abused to perform follow-on activities such as lateral movement or privilege escalation (Citation: Slack Security Risks).
2605.profile: [profile]The entity "Send Empty Messages" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. The provided information primarily describes a technique for credential theft from user communication services, which aligns with MITRE ID T1552.008 (Unsecured Credentials: Chat Messages) under the Credential Access tactic. This technique involves adversaries directly accessing credentials shared within chat applications like Slack, Teams, or email, either on endpoints, servers, or via compromised administrative portals and integration tools (e.g., Slack Workflows) to automate credential extraction from messages, which are then used for lateral movement or privilege escalation. The intrusion-set Winnti is a related threat actor.[/profile]
2605.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Send Empty Messages" is an attack pattern. Based on the retrieved context, this technique likely falls under the Command and Control tactic, where adversaries use legitimate protocols like MQTT, XMPP, AMQP, or STOMP to blend in with normal network traffic. The technical mechanic involves sending messages with empty or minimal payloads through these publish/subscribe protocols to maintain covert communication channels with compromised systems, avoiding detection by mimicking benign, expected data exchanges between clients and a central message broker.

2606.name: Maintain Communication
2606.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may use an existing, legitimate external Web service as a means for sending commands to and receiving output from a compromised system over the Web service channel. Compromised systems may leverage popular websites and social media to host command and control (C2) instructions. Those infected systems can then send the output from those commands back over that Web service channel. The return traffic may occur in a variety of ways, depending on the Web service being utilized. For example, the return traffic may take the form of the compromised system posting a comment on a forum, issuing a pull request to development project, updating a document hosted on a Web service, or by sending a Tweet. 

Popular websites and social media acting as a mechanism for C2 may give a significant amount of cover due to the likelihood that hosts within a network are already communicating with them prior to a compromise. Using common services, such as those offered by Google or Twitter, makes it easier for adversaries to hide in expected noise. Web service providers commonly use SSL/TLS encryption, giving adversaries an added level of protection.
2606.profile: [profile]Maintain Communication is the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1102.002 under the Command and Control tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It involves adversaries using legitimate external web services like social media or cloud platforms for bidirectional command and control. Infected systems send command output by posting comments, issuing pull requests, updating documents, or sending tweets over these encrypted channels to blend with normal traffic. The technique is used by groups including APT28, Lazarus Group, and MuddyWater.[/profile]
2606.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Maintain Communication" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the retrieved context, it is a high-level concept describing an adversary's objective to sustain command and control (C2) channels. This is achieved through specific techniques like using fallback channels (T1008) if the primary is compromised, employing redundant access methods (T1108) such as alternate remote access tools or web shells, and splitting communications across multiple protocols (T1026) to bypass detection. The core technical mechanics involve ensuring persistent, resilient C2 to avoid disruption and maintain reliable data exfiltration.

2608.name: Hide Real Addresses
2608.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may manipulate network traffic in order to hide and evade detection of their C2 infrastructure. This can be accomplished by identifying and filtering traffic from defensive tools,(Citation: TA571) masking malicious domains to obfuscate the true destination from both automated scanning tools and security researchers,(Citation: Schema-abuse)(Citation: Facad1ng)(Citation: Browser-updates) and otherwise hiding malicious artifacts to delay discovery and prolong the effectiveness of adversary infrastructure that could otherwise be identified, blocked, or taken down entirely.

C2 networks may include the use of [Proxy](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1090) or VPNs to disguise IP addresses, which can allow adversaries to blend in with normal network traffic and bypass conditional access policies or anti-abuse protections. For example, an adversary may use a virtual private cloud to spoof their IP address to closer align with a victim's IP address ranges. This may also bypass security measures relying on geolocation of the source IP address.(Citation: sysdig)(Citation: Orange Residential Proxies)

Adversaries may also attempt to filter network traffic in order to evade defensive tools in numerous ways, including blocking/redirecting common incident responder or security appliance user agents.(Citation: mod_rewrite)(Citation: SocGholish-update) Filtering traffic based on IP and geo-fencing may also avoid automated sandboxing or researcher activity (i.e., [Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1497)).(Citation: TA571)(Citation: mod_rewrite)

Hiding C2 infrastructure may also be supported by [Resource Development](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0042) activities such as [Acquire Infrastructure](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1583) and [Compromise Infrastructure](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1584). For example, using widely trusted hosting services or domains such as prominent URL shortening providers or marketing services for C2 networks may enable adversaries to present benign content that later redirects victims to malicious web pages or infrastructure once specific conditions are met.(Citation: StarBlizzard)(Citation: QR-cofense)
2608.profile: [profile]Hide Real Addresses, identified as T1665, is a Command and Control tactic technique used to hide infrastructure by manipulating network traffic to evade detection. This involves using proxies or VPNs to disguise IP addresses, filtering traffic to block defensive tools and user agents, and employing geo-fencing to avoid sandboxing. Adversaries also mask malicious domains and use trusted services like URL shorteners to redirect to C2 infrastructure, supported by resource development activities such as acquiring or compromising infrastructure. This technique is associated with groups like APT29 and Zirconium.[/profile]
2608.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Hide Real Addresses is a technique used to conceal the true source or destination of network communications, often by employing proxies, VPNs, or domain fronting to mask IP addresses and blend in with normal traffic. This method supports evasion and defense avoidance by bypassing geolocation-based security measures and conditional access policies. It is commonly associated with establishing and maintaining command and control infrastructure.

2609.name: Anti-Emulation Feature
2609.profile: [profile]Anti-Emulation Feature is a technique used to evade detection by security tools that rely on emulation or sandboxing. It is associated with the intrusion set Winnti. The technique involves malware incorporating checks for signs of a virtualized or monitored environment, such as specific processes, hardware artifacts, or user interaction patterns. If these emulation indicators are detected, the malware alters its behavior to appear benign or halts execution entirely, thereby avoiding analysis and bypassing automated defenses.
2609.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Anti-Emulation Feature is a technique used by adversaries to evade detection by security tools that use emulation or sandboxing for analysis. It involves malware incorporating checks for virtualized or emulated environments, such as looking for specific processes, registry keys, or hardware artifacts. If these indicators are present, the malicious code may alter its behavior, delay execution, or terminate to avoid revealing its true functionality within the analysis environment. This technique is often associated with groups like Patchwork, APT3, and OilRig.

2647.name: Commercial Cyber Espionage
2647.profile: [profile]Commercial Cyber Espionage is a technique (T1588) under the Resource Development tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. It involves adversaries acquiring capabilities, infrastructure, or information from third-party commercial entities to support their operations. This includes purchasing, stealing, or licensing software tools, exploits, and vulnerabilities, as well as gathering intelligence from commercial threat reports to understand their own exposure and adjust their tactics.[/profile]

Threat actors may use these commercially sourced tools for execution and post-compromise activities, monitor vulnerability databases to find weaknesses, and search threat vendor reports to gather intelligence on their own campaigns or those of other groups to inform and adapt their future operations.

2648.name: Intellectual Property Theft
2648.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may steal monetary resources from targets through extortion, social engineering, technical theft, or other methods aimed at their own financial gain at the expense of the availability of these resources for victims. Financial theft is the ultimate objective of several popular campaign types including extortion by ransomware,(Citation: FBI-ransomware) business email compromise (BEC) and fraud,(Citation: FBI-BEC) "pig butchering,"(Citation: wired-pig butchering) bank hacking,(Citation: DOJ-DPRK Heist) and exploiting cryptocurrency networks.(Citation: BBC-Ronin) 

Adversaries may [Compromise Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1586) to conduct unauthorized transfers of funds.(Citation: Internet crime report 2022) In the case of business email compromise or email fraud, an adversary may utilize [Impersonation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1656) of a trusted entity. Once the social engineering is successful, victims can be deceived into sending money to financial accounts controlled by an adversary.(Citation: FBI-BEC) This creates the potential for multiple victims (i.e., compromised accounts as well as the ultimate monetary loss) in incidents involving financial theft.(Citation: VEC)

Extortion by ransomware may occur, for example, when an adversary demands payment from a victim after [Data Encrypted for Impact](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1486) (Citation: NYT-Colonial) and [Exfiltration](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0010) of data, followed by threatening to leak sensitive data to the public unless payment is made to the adversary.(Citation: Mandiant-leaks) Adversaries may use dedicated leak sites to distribute victim data.(Citation: Crowdstrike-leaks)

Due to the potentially immense business impact of financial theft, an adversary may abuse the possibility of financial theft and seeking monetary gain to divert attention from their true goals such as [Data Destruction](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1485) and business disruption.(Citation: AP-NotPetya)
2648.profile: [profile]The entity is named "Financial Theft" with the MITRE ATT&CK ID T1657, categorized under the Impact tactic. It is a technique where adversaries steal monetary resources through methods like extortion via ransomware, business email compromise (BEC), and social engineering to deceive victims into transferring funds to adversary-controlled accounts. The technique involves compromising accounts for unauthorized transfers and may use data encryption and exfiltration to pressure victims for payment. Associated groups include FIN13, Scattered Spider, and APT17.
2648.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Intellectual Property Theft is a technique where adversaries steal proprietary data, such as trade secrets, source code, or blueprints, for strategic or financial advantage. This typically occurs after initial network access and involves the exfiltration of sensitive information, often using established command and control channels to covertly transfer the stolen data out of the victim's environment. The primary goal is to compromise a target's competitive edge or to monetize the stolen intellectual assets.

2653.name: Email Phishing
2653.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may send phishing messages to gain access to victim systems. All forms of phishing are electronically delivered social engineering. Phishing can be targeted, known as spearphishing. In spearphishing, a specific individual, company, or industry will be targeted by the adversary. More generally, adversaries can conduct non-targeted phishing, such as in mass malware spam campaigns.

Adversaries may send victims emails containing malicious attachments or links, typically to execute malicious code on victim systems. Phishing may also be conducted via third-party services, like social media platforms. Phishing may also involve social engineering techniques, such as posing as a trusted source, as well as evasive techniques such as removing or manipulating emails or metadata/headers from compromised accounts being abused to send messages (e.g., [Email Hiding Rules](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1564/008)).(Citation: Microsoft OAuth Spam 2022)(Citation: Palo Alto Unit 42 VBA Infostealer 2014) Another way to accomplish this is by [Email Spoofing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1672)(Citation: Proofpoint-spoof) the identity of the sender, which can be used to fool both the human recipient as well as automated security tools,(Citation: cyberproof-double-bounce) or by including the intended target as a party to an existing email thread that includes malicious files or links (i.e., "thread hijacking").(Citation: phishing-krebs)

Victims may also receive phishing messages that instruct them to call a phone number where they are directed to visit a malicious URL, download malware,(Citation: sygnia Luna Month)(Citation: CISA Remote Monitoring and Management Software) or install adversary-accessible remote management tools onto their computer (i.e., [User Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204)).(Citation: Unit42 Luna Moth)
2653.profile: [profile]Phishing, identified as MITRE ATT&CK T1566, is an Initial Access technique targeting multiple platforms. It involves sending emails with malicious attachments or links to execute code, often using social engineering by posing as a trusted source. Evasive methods include email spoofing, thread hijacking, and manipulating email headers or hiding rules from compromised accounts. The technique is used by groups like APT3, Sea Turtle, and Kimsuky.[/profile]
2653.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Email Phishing is a technique aligned with MITRE ATT&CK ID T1566 under the Initial Access tactic, targeting multiple platforms. It involves sending deceptive emails containing malicious attachments or links to execute code, often using social engineering by posing as a trusted source. Evasive methods include email spoofing, manipulating email headers, and hijacking existing email threads to enhance credibility and bypass security filters.

2654.name: Information Gathering
2654.profile: [profile]Information Gathering is a broad Reconnaissance tactic (TA0043) within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, encompassing techniques to collect data about a victim prior to attacks. It includes specific techniques such as gathering victim host (T1592), identity (T1589), network (T1590), and organization information (T1591), as well as Phishing for Information (T1598). These activities, used by groups like OilRig and APT3, involve methods like active scanning, elicitation via phishing, and harvesting data from open sources to profile targets and plan subsequent intrusion steps.[/profile]
2654.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Information Gathering is a broad reconnaissance activity within the Reconnaissance tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. It encompasses the systematic collection of data about a victim's hosts, networks, identity, and organization to inform follow-on attacks. This is achieved through various methods including active scanning, phishing for information, and querying open sources like social media, victim-owned websites, and technical databases to obtain details such as IP ranges, domain names, employee roles, and system configurations.

2656.name: Malicious Email Attachment
2656.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may send spearphishing emails with a malicious attachment in an attempt to gain access to victim systems. Spearphishing attachment is a specific variant of spearphishing. Spearphishing attachment is different from other forms of spearphishing in that it employs the use of malware attached to an email. All forms of spearphishing are electronically delivered social engineering targeted at a specific individual, company, or industry. In this scenario, adversaries attach a file to the spearphishing email and usually rely upon [User Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204) to gain execution.(Citation: Unit 42 DarkHydrus July 2018) Spearphishing may also involve social engineering techniques, such as posing as a trusted source.

There are many options for the attachment such as Microsoft Office documents, executables, PDFs, or archived files. Upon opening the attachment (and potentially clicking past protections), the adversary's payload exploits a vulnerability or directly executes on the user's system. The text of the spearphishing email usually tries to give a plausible reason why the file should be opened, and may explain how to bypass system protections in order to do so. The email may also contain instructions on how to decrypt an attachment, such as a zip file password, in order to evade email boundary defenses. Adversaries frequently manipulate file extensions and icons in order to make attached executables appear to be document files, or files exploiting one application appear to be a file for a different one.
2656.profile: [profile]Spearphishing Attachment (T1566.001) is an Initial Access technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, applicable across multiple platforms. It involves sending targeted emails with malicious attachments like Microsoft Office documents, executables, PDFs, or archived files. Execution typically relies on user interaction to open the file, which may exploit a vulnerability or directly run a payload. Adversaries employ social engineering to justify opening the file, often providing instructions to bypass protections or decrypt attachments to evade defenses, and may manipulate file extensions and icons for masquerading.[/profile]
2656.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Malicious Email Attachment is an Initial Access technique where adversaries send emails with malware-laden files to gain system access. It aligns with the spearphishing concept, specifically MITRE ATT&CK ID T1566.001 under the Initial Access tactic, primarily targeting Windows, macOS, and Linux platforms. The technique relies on user execution, employing social engineering to trick recipients into opening attachments like Microsoft Office documents, executables, PDFs, or archived files. To evade defenses, adversaries often manipulate file extensions and icons, provide decryption instructions for password-protected archives, and craft plausible email narratives to bypass security warnings.
