2667.name: sogu
2667.profile: [profile]Sogu is a malware attributed to the APT3 intrusion set. It maintains persistence by creating copies in specific directories, such as C:\Users\<user>\AppData\Roaming\Intel\<SOGU CLSID>\ and <drive>:\RECYCLER.BIN\<SOGU CLSID>\, with its payload files encoded in Base64. It is associated with or shares infrastructure patterns with other malware families like PlugX and FrozenHill.[/profile]
2667.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Sogu is a malware family also known as PlugX and FrozenHill. It is attributed to multiple APT groups including APT22, APT26, APT31, APT41, Aurora Panda, Calypso Group, DragonOK, Emissary Panda, Hellsing, Hurricane Panda, Leviathan, Mirage, Mustang Panda, Nettraveler, Nightshade Panda, Slime29, Samurai Panda, Stone Panda, UPS, and Violin Panda. Its key technical behaviors include maintaining persistence by installing files to specific paths like C:\Users\<user>\AppData\Roaming\Intel\<SOGU CLSID>\ and <drive>:\RECYCLER.BIN\<SOGU CLSID>\, where the filenames are encoded in Base64. It targets the Windows platform and has been associated with infrastructure involving domains like gougounu[.site.]

2668.name: malicious attachments
2668.profile: [profile]The entity "malicious attachments" is a general delivery mechanism, not a specific malware. It is used by intrusion set APT3 and by groups like Gold Cabin, Mummy Spider, and Mealybug in Emotet campaigns, often as weaponized Word documents. It is also a vector for malware families like AsyncRAT and Crackedcantil, with observed delivery via Discord CDN links. Target platforms are typically Windows systems.
2668.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Malicious attachments are a common malware delivery vector, not a specific malware family. They are frequently used by groups like Emotet (associated with Gold Cabin, Mummy Spider, and Mealybug) to distribute payloads, often via email with documents like malicious Word files. These attachments can also be spread through other channels, such as Discord, to deliver compressed archives containing malware.

2672.name: PIRPI.2015
2672.uncertain_mes:
Operation Double Tap
Mandiant
Written by: Ned Moran, Mike Scott, Mike Oppenheim, Joshua Homan
2672.profile: [profile]PIRPI.2015, also known as pirpi, is a malware variant attributed to the APT3 intrusion set and associated with the 'ups' group. It shares similarities with PIRPI.2014, including command structures and C2 communication methods, and features anti-disassembly techniques. The malware was discussed in the context of Operation Double Tap by Mandiant analysts. Target platform information is not specified in the provided data.[/profile]
2672.profile_without_enhance: [profile]PIRPI.2015 is a variant of the PIRPI malware family attributed to the APT3 intrusion set and associated with the UPS group. It shares command-and-control (C2) communication infrastructure similarities with its PIRPI.2014 variant and employs anti-disassembly techniques. Key technical behaviors include cookie field exfiltration, command execution, process list enumeration, file upload, download, and deletion, DLL injection, and in-memory execution. It leverages the CVE-2015-3113 vulnerability.

2673.name: PIRPI.2014
2673.uncertain_mes:
Operation Double Tap
Mandiant
Written by: Ned Moran, Mike Scott, Mike Oppenheim, Joshua Homan
2673.profile: [profile]PIRPI.2014, also known as pirpi, is a malware family attributed to the APT3 intrusion set. Key technical behaviors include the use of specific commands for anti-disassembly and establishing command and control (C2) communications. The malware is associated with the group referred to as 'ups' and shares significant similarities in its infrastructure and C2 protocols with a later variant identified as Pirpi.2015.
2673.profile_without_enhance: [profile]PIRPI.2014 is a variant of the PIRPI malware family, attributed to the APT3 intrusion set and associated with the UPS group. It employs anti-disassembly techniques and provides a command set for remote control. Key technical behaviors include cookie field exfiltration, command execution, process list enumeration, file upload, file copy and deletion, DLL injection, in-memory execution, and file download and execution. Its command-and-control (C2) communications infrastructure shows similarities to the PIRPI.2015 variant, indicating a consistent operational protocol. It is known to exploit the vulnerability CVE-2014-1776.[/profile]

2676.name: Exploiting zero-day vulnerabilities
2676.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may acquire information about vulnerabilities that can be used during targeting. A vulnerability is a weakness in computer hardware or software that can, potentially, be exploited by an adversary to cause unintended or unanticipated behavior to occur. Adversaries may find vulnerability information by searching open databases or gaining access to closed vulnerability databases.(Citation: National Vulnerability Database)

An adversary may monitor vulnerability disclosures/databases to understand the state of existing, as well as newly discovered, vulnerabilities. There is usually a delay between when a vulnerability is discovered and when it is made public. An adversary may target the systems of those known to conduct vulnerability research (including commercial vendors). Knowledge of a vulnerability may cause an adversary to search for an existing exploit (i.e. [Exploits](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1588/005)) or to attempt to develop one themselves (i.e. [Exploits](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1587/004)).
2676.profile: [profile]Exploiting zero-day vulnerabilities is a technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, identified as T1588.006 under the Reconnaissance tactic and applicable across multiple platforms. It involves adversaries acquiring information about undisclosed software or hardware weaknesses by monitoring vulnerability databases, including closed sources, or targeting vulnerability researchers to gain early access. This intelligence gathering enables them to search for or develop corresponding exploits for use in subsequent attack phases, as observed in groups like Sandworm Team and Volt Typhoon.
2676.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Exploiting zero-day vulnerabilities is a technique used by adversaries to take advantage of previously unknown software flaws before a patch is available, enabling them to execute adversary-controlled code. This technique can be applied across multiple phases of an attack, including for defense evasion (T1211) to bypass security software, for denial of service (T1499.004) by crashing systems, and for initial access or execution. Adversaries may acquire these exploits through purchase, theft, or development, often targeting systems where such research is conducted.

2677.name: Malicious Flash Files
2677.uncertain_mes:
Introduction
Zscaler’s ThreatLabz threat research team recently has spotted a new variant of the emerging X-FILES infostealer attack with enhanced features to exfiltrate sensitive information. X-FILES is a stealer that aims to steal sensitive information, including logins and financial data.
2677.profile: [profile]Malicious Flash Files, also known as X-FILES stealer, is an infostealer attributed to APT3. It aims to steal sensitive information like logins and financial data, with its variants featuring enhanced exfiltration capabilities. The malware is associated with the exploitation of Adobe Flash vulnerabilities, specifically CVE-2015-3113, and utilizes Shellcode in its operations. Its target platform is systems running Adobe Flash.[/profile]
2677.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Malicious Flash Files is a malware entity that leverages vulnerabilities like CVE-2015-3113, CVE-2015-5119, and CVE-2014-1776 in Adobe Flash for exploitation. It is associated with the threat group UPS and utilizes techniques such as ActionScript code reuse to execute malicious actions and evade detection. The malware is delivered via shellcode, often in conjunction with other malware, and targets systems through exploits in web browsers and common third-party software like Adobe Flash Player.[/profile]

2678.name: ActionScript code reuse
2678.profile: [profile]ActionScript code reuse is a technique used by adversaries like APT3, often involving malicious Flash files. It falls under the Defense Evasion tactic (T1620) and targets platforms that support Adobe Flash. The technique works by reusing legitimate ActionScript code within malicious Flash files to bypass security checks and execute payloads, leveraging the trusted nature of the reused code to evade detection. This method is associated with specific intrusion sets and malware families, highlighting its use in targeted attacks.
2678.profile_without_enhance: [profile]ActionScript Code Reuse is a technique where adversaries leverage existing, legitimate ActionScript code within Flash files to execute malicious actions, often to evade detection by blending with normal application behavior. This can involve reusing code snippets or libraries to perform unauthorized operations without introducing new, easily identifiable malicious code.

2679.name: hextointarray
2679.profile: [profile]The entity 'hextointarray' is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the provided context, it appears to be a specific encoding or data manipulation method. It is directly associated with the intrusion set APT3. The retrieved information suggests it may function as a form of data obfuscation, potentially related to converting hexadecimal data into an integer array to obscure command and control traffic, aligning with general adversary practices of encoding data to evade detection.
2679.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Hextointarray is a technique for data obfuscation, likely used within the Command and Control tactic. It functions by converting hexadecimal strings into integer arrays, altering the data's format to evade signature-based detection. This method is a specific implementation of standard data encoding schemes like hexadecimal or Base64, which are used to make C2 traffic content more difficult to identify. The technique may be employed by various threat groups known for using such encoding practices.

2680.name: ror 7 instruction
2680.profile: [profile]The entity 'ror 7 instruction' is a specific attack pattern. Based on retrieved context, this technique likely involves injecting malicious code into a running process by manipulating it via ptrace system calls, such as using `PTRACE_SETREGS` or `PTRACE_POKETEXT` to control execution flow and write arbitrary code into process memory. This method allows adversaries to evade detection by masking execution under a legitimate process and may enable privilege escalation or access to system resources. It is associated with the intrusion-set APT3.
2680.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "ror 7 instruction" is an attack-pattern. Based on retrieved context, this technique is a method of process injection, specifically using the ptrace system call to execute arbitrary code within a separate live process. The technical mechanics involve attaching to a target process and using ptrace calls like PTRACE_SETREGS or PTRACE_POKETEXT to modify its memory and registers, thereby redirecting execution to injected malicious code. This allows adversaries to evade process-based defenses and potentially gain elevated privileges by running code under the guise of a legitimate process.

2681.name: single-byte xor algorithm
2681.profile: [profile]The entity "single-byte xor algorithm" is a custom cryptographic protocol (T1024) used for obfuscating command and control traffic or data (T1560.003) under the Command and Control tactic. It operates by applying the XOR operation to plaintext with a fixed, single-byte key, resulting in a weak ciphertext that is often implemented within malware without external libraries. This simple, reversible scheme is susceptible to analysis and reverse engineering to discover the key. Associated intrusion sets include APT3.
2681.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity is a cryptographic technique, likely corresponding to the MITRE ATT&CK technique "Obfuscated Files or Information: Indicator Removal from Tools" (T1027.002) under the Defense Evasion tactic. It operates by applying an XOR (exclusive OR) operation with a single-byte key to plaintext data, producing a weak form of encryption or obfuscation. This simple algorithm is often implemented directly in malware for custom data encryption prior to exfiltration or to hide command and control traffic, making it susceptible to analysis and reverse engineering to discover the key.

2682.name: Unicode string creation
2682.profile: [profile]Unicode string creation is a technique used to disguise malicious file names or strings by leveraging non-printing Unicode characters, such as the right-to-left override (RTLO or RLO, U+202E). This causes subsequent text to be displayed in reverse, tricking users into executing a file they perceive as benign, like a document instead of a script. It is commonly employed in spearphishing and malware delivery campaigns, as seen with groups like APT3, and can also be used to obfuscate data in command and control traffic or within the Windows Registry.[/profile]
2682.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Unicode string creation is a technique used by adversaries to create strings using Unicode encoding to potentially evade detection or analysis. It is related to the MITRE ATT&CK technique "Right-to-Left Override" (T1036.002), which falls under the Defense Evasion tactic and is applicable to multiple platforms. Specifically, adversaries may abuse the non-printing right-to-left override (RTLO) character (U+202E) to reverse the display order of subsequent characters, allowing them to disguise malicious file names—like making an executable "March 25‮cod.scr" appear as "March 25 rcs.docx"—to trick users into executing them, commonly observed in spearphishing campaigns.

2683.name: module base address resolution
2683.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may dynamically establish connections to command and control infrastructure to evade common detections and remediations. This may be achieved by using malware that shares a common algorithm with the infrastructure the adversary uses to receive the malware's communications. These calculations can be used to dynamically adjust parameters such as the domain name, IP address, or port number the malware uses for command and control.

Adversaries may use dynamic resolution for the purpose of [Fallback Channels](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1008). When contact is lost with the primary command and control server malware may employ dynamic resolution as a means to reestablishing command and control.(Citation: Talos CCleanup 2017)(Citation: FireEye POSHSPY April 2017)(Citation: ESET Sednit 2017 Activity)
2683.profile: [profile]The entity "module base address resolution" is a technique for obfuscating API calls to evade static analysis. It operates by dynamically resolving the memory addresses of critical functions during runtime instead of storing them statically. This is commonly achieved using Windows API functions like `GetProcAddress()` and `LoadLibrary()`, often with function names represented as hashes or encrypted strings that are decoded on execution. The method conceals malicious intent by avoiding clear import address tables and static strings in the payload. It is associated with groups like Lazarus Group and Mustang Panda.[/profile]
2683.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Module base address resolution is a technique used by adversaries to evade static analysis by dynamically resolving the base addresses of loaded modules at runtime. This method avoids leaving static import address table (IAT) artifacts, making malware analysis more difficult. It is commonly implemented by using functions like GetProcAddress() and LoadLibrary() to manually look up and load API functions, often referencing them via obfuscated hashes instead of plain strings. This technique is associated with groups like Lazarus Group and Mustang Panda and is a sub-technique of Obfuscated Files or Information (T1027.007) under the Defense Evasion tactic, primarily targeting the Windows platform.

2684.name: Cookie field exfiltration
2684.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries can use stolen session cookies to authenticate to web applications and services. This technique bypasses some multi-factor authentication protocols since the session is already authenticated.(Citation: Pass The Cookie)

Authentication cookies are commonly used in web applications, including cloud-based services, after a user has authenticated to the service so credentials are not passed and re-authentication does not need to occur as frequently. Cookies are often valid for an extended period of time, even if the web application is not actively used. After the cookie is obtained through [Steal Web Session Cookie](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539) or [Web Cookies](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1606/001), the adversary may then import the cookie into a browser they control and is then able to use the site or application as the user for as long as the session cookie is active. Once logged into the site, an adversary can access sensitive information, read email, or perform actions that the victim account has permissions to perform.

There have been examples of malware targeting session cookies to bypass multi-factor authentication systems.(Citation: Unit 42 Mac Crypto Cookies January 2019)
2684.profile: [profile]The entity is a technique named "Web Session Cookie" with the MITRE ATT&CK ID T1550.004, categorized under the Defense Evasion tactic and applicable to multiple platforms including Windows, macOS, and Linux. This technique involves adversaries using stolen session cookies, obtained via methods like T1539, to authenticate to web applications and services, thereby bypassing multi-factor authentication. The stolen cookie is imported into a controlled browser, granting the adversary the victim's session privileges to access information and perform actions. Associated malware includes PIRPI.2014 and PIRPI.2015, and it has been used by groups like APT3 and Star Blizzard.
2684.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Cookie field exfiltration" is a data exfiltration technique. It involves stealing and transmitting specific fields from web session cookies, such as authentication tokens, to an adversary-controlled system. This method enables unauthorized access to web applications by bypassing multi-factor authentication, as the stolen cookie fields can be used to hijack authenticated sessions. The technique is executed after cookies are obtained, often via methods like stealing from browser storage or through adversary-in-the-middle attacks, and the data is typically exfiltrated over standard network protocols.

2685.name: Process creation
2685.profile: [profile]Process creation, identified as T1057 in the MITRE ATT&CK framework under the Discovery tactic for Windows, Linux, and Mac platforms, involves adversaries enumerating running processes to understand system software and shape follow-on actions. This is commonly performed using utilities like `tasklist` or `Get-Process` on Windows and the `ps` command or `/proc` enumeration on Unix-based systems. The technique is associated with groups like APT3 and is a fundamental step for situational awareness and target selection.
2685.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Process creation, identified as T1057, is a Discovery technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves adversaries enumerating running processes to understand the software landscape of a system and shape follow-on actions. This is commonly performed using utilities like `tasklist` or `Get-Process` on Windows and the `ps` command or enumeration of `/proc` on Unix-based systems, including ESXi hypervisors.

2686.name: Process list enumeration
2686.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may enumerate system and service logs to find useful data. These logs may highlight various types of valuable insights for an adversary, such as user authentication records ([Account Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1087)), security or vulnerable software ([Software Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1518)), or hosts within a compromised network ([Remote System Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1018)).

Host binaries may be leveraged to collect system logs. Examples include using `wevtutil.exe` or [PowerShell](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001) on Windows to access and/or export security event information.(Citation: WithSecure Lazarus-NoPineapple Threat Intel Report 2023)(Citation: Cadet Blizzard emerges as novel threat actor) In cloud environments, adversaries may leverage utilities such as the Azure VM Agent’s `CollectGuestLogs.exe` to collect security logs from cloud hosted infrastructure.(Citation: SIM Swapping and Abuse of the Microsoft Azure Serial Console)

Adversaries may also target centralized logging infrastructure such as SIEMs. Logs may also be bulk exported and sent to adversary-controlled infrastructure for offline analysis.

In addition to gaining a better understanding of the environment, adversaries may also monitor logs in real time to track incident response procedures. This may allow them to adjust their techniques in order to maintain persistence or evade defenses.(Citation: Permiso GUI-Vil 2023)
2686.profile: [profile]Process list enumeration, also known as log enumeration (T1654), is a Discovery technique used on Windows and cloud platforms. Adversaries enumerate system and service logs to gather insights like user accounts, software, and network hosts. They use host binaries like `wevtutil.exe` or PowerShell on Windows, and utilities like Azure VM Agent's `CollectGuestLogs.exe` in cloud environments, to access and export event logs. They may also target centralized logging infrastructure like SIEMs, bulk export logs for offline analysis, or monitor logs in real-time to track incident response. This technique has been associated with groups including Volt Typhoon, APT5, and Mustang Panda.[/profile]
2686.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Process list enumeration is a technique for discovering information about running processes on a system, typically mapped to MITRE ATT&CK ID T1057 (Process Discovery) under the Discovery tactic. It is applicable across Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. Adversaries execute this by using native system commands and APIs; common methods include using `tasklist` or `Get-Process` in Windows, the `ps` command or enumerating the `/proc` directory in Linux and macOS, and `esxcli system process list` on ESXi hosts. The gathered details, such as process names and IDs, help adversaries understand the software environment, identify security tools for evasion, and shape subsequent attack actions. Groups like Volt Typhoon, Lazarus, and MuddyWater have been observed using this technique.]

2687.name: Process termination
2687.profile: [profile]Process termination, known as T1489 in MITRE ATT&CK, falls under the Impact tactic and targets Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. This technique involves adversaries stopping or killing critical system processes or services to disrupt operations, cause denial-of-service, or hinder recovery. It is executed using commands like `taskkill` on Windows or `kill` and `pkill` on Unix-based systems. Associated malware includes PIRPI.2014 and PIRPI.2015, and it has been used by the intrusion set APT3.
2687.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Process termination is a technique where adversaries stop or kill running processes to disrupt operations, evade detection, or remove security software. This action can be executed using system commands or APIs, such as the `taskkill` command on Windows or the `kill` command on Unix-like systems, to terminate specific processes by name or process ID.

2688.name: File download and execution
2688.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may enumerate files and directories or may search in specific locations of a host or network share for certain information within a file system. Adversaries may use the information from [File and Directory Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1083) during automated discovery to shape follow-on behaviors, including whether or not the adversary fully infects the target and/or attempts specific actions. Many command shell utilities can be used to obtain this information. Examples include dir, tree, ls, find, and locate.(Citation: Windows Commands JPCERT) Custom tools may also be used to gather file and directory information and interact with the [Native API](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1106). Adversaries may also leverage a [Network Device CLI](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/008) on network devices to gather file and directory information (e.g. dir, show flash, and/or nvram).(Citation: US-CERT-TA18-106A) Some files and directories may require elevated or specific user permissions to access.
2688.profile: [profile]File and Directory Discovery, identified as T1083, is a Discovery tactic used across Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. Adversaries enumerate files and directories to gather information that shapes follow-on actions. This is commonly performed using command shell utilities like `dir`, `tree`, `ls`, `find`, and `locate`, or by leveraging a Network Device CLI with commands such as `show flash`. The technique is associated with numerous threat groups, including APT3, and has been used by malware families like PIRPI.
2688.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "File download and execution" is a common adversary behavior pattern. It involves downloading a file from an external source onto a compromised system and subsequently executing it to achieve code execution. This often utilizes utilities like `curl`, `wget`, `certutil`, or PowerShell commands such as `Invoke-WebRequest` or `IEX(New-Object Net.WebClient).downloadString()` for the transfer. The execution phase typically follows via user interaction, such as clicking a malicious link or opening a file, or through automated scripts. This technique supports initial access, lateral movement, and persistence.

2689.name: Malware termination
2689.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may develop malware and malware components that can be used during targeting. Building malicious software can include the development of payloads, droppers, post-compromise tools, backdoors (including backdoored images), packers, C2 protocols, and the creation of infected removable media. Adversaries may develop malware to support their operations, creating a means for maintaining control of remote machines, evading defenses, and executing post-compromise behaviors.(Citation: Mandiant APT1)(Citation: Kaspersky Sofacy)(Citation: ActiveMalwareEnergy)(Citation: FBI Flash FIN7 USB)

During malware development, adversaries may intentionally include indicators aligned with other known actors in order to mislead attribution by defenders.(Citation: Olympic Destroyer)(Citation: Risky Bulletin Threat actor impersonates FSB APT)(Citation: GamaCopy organization)

As with legitimate development efforts, different skill sets may be required for developing malware. The skills needed may be located in-house, or may need to be contracted out. Use of a contractor may be considered an extension of that adversary's malware development capabilities, provided the adversary plays a role in shaping requirements and maintains a degree of exclusivity to the malware.

Some aspects of malware development, such as C2 protocol development, may require adversaries to obtain additional infrastructure. For example, malware developed that will communicate with Twitter for C2, may require use of [Web Services](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1583/006).(Citation: FireEye APT29)
2689.profile: [profile]The entity "Malware termination" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the provided data, the core concept aligns with MITRE ATT&CK technique T1587.001: Develop Capabilities: Malware. This technique falls under the Resource Development tactic and applies to multiple platforms. It involves adversaries developing malicious software, including payloads, droppers, backdoors, and C2 protocols, to support operations. Development may involve in-house skills or contractors and can include false indicators for misattribution. Associated groups include APT29, FIN7, and Lazarus Group.[/profile]
2689.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Malware termination" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the provided context, it likely refers to actions adversaries take to stop or remove their own malware from a compromised system to evade detection and cleanup evidence. This can involve copying payloads to new locations and deleting original files to separate from initial execution events, hindering forensic analysis. It may also involve modifying malware to remove detection indicators if quarantined, then reusing the updated version.

2690.name: Sleep command
2690.profile: [profile]The entity "Sleep command" is a technique used by adversaries to delay malware execution, often for evasion. It involves using programmatic sleep commands or native system scheduling to introduce pauses, which can help avoid detection by automated analysis environments that may have time thresholds. This behavior is associated with the intrusion set APT3 and malware families PIRPI.2014 and PIRPI.2015, and it aligns with the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1678 (Delay Execution) under the Defense Evasion tactic, applicable across multiple platforms.
2690.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Sleep command" is a specific technique within the broader MITRE ATT&CK technique T1678, Delay Execution, under the Defense Evasion tactic. It operates across multiple platforms. This technique involves adversaries using programmatic sleep commands or native system scheduling to introduce delays in malware execution. This is primarily done to evade automated analysis environments, such as sandboxes, which may have time thresholds for execution, and to blend malicious activity with normal system timing to avoid detection.

2691.name: C2 configuration update
2691.profile: [profile]C2 configuration update is a technique used by adversaries to dynamically modify the command and control infrastructure of malware, such as PIRPI.2014 and PIRPI.2015, to evade detection and maintain persistence. This involves changing communication parameters, domains, or IP addresses used by the malware to connect to adversary-controlled servers. Associated with APT3, this activity is part of a broader strategy to hide infrastructure and sustain long-term access within a compromised network.[/profile]
2691.profile_without_enhance: [profile]C2 configuration update is a Command and Control technique where adversaries modify the settings of their command and control infrastructure to evade detection and maintain persistence. This involves dynamically altering server addresses, communication ports, or encryption keys within the malware's configuration files. Adversaries may use this method to rotate through compromised domains or IPs, switch protocols, or update malware modules, thereby bypassing static network defenses and prolonging their access to the victim network.

2692.name: In-memory execution
2692.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may attempt to access credential material stored in the process memory of the Local Security Authority Subsystem Service (LSASS). After a user logs on, the system generates and stores a variety of credential materials in LSASS process memory. These credential materials can be harvested by an administrative user or SYSTEM and used to conduct [Lateral Movement](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0008) using [Use Alternate Authentication Material](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1550). As well as in-memory techniques, the LSASS process memory can be dumped from the target host and analyzed on a local system. For example, on the target host use procdump: * procdump -ma lsass.exe lsass_dump Locally, mimikatz can be run using: * sekurlsa::Minidump lsassdump.dmp * sekurlsa::logonPasswords Built-in Windows tools such as `comsvcs.dll` can also be used: * rundll32.exe C:\Windows\System32\comsvcs.dll MiniDump PID lsass.dmp full(Citation: Volexity Exchange Marauder March 2021)(Citation: Symantec Attacks Against Government Sector) Similar to [Image File Execution Options Injection](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1546/012), the silent process exit mechanism can be abused to create a memory dump of `lsass.exe` through Windows Error Reporting (`WerFault.exe`).(Citation: Deep Instinct LSASS) Windows Security Support Provider (SSP) DLLs are loaded into LSASS process at system start. Once loaded into the LSA, SSP DLLs have access to encrypted and plaintext passwords that are stored in Windows, such as any logged-on user's Domain password or smart card PINs. The SSP configuration is stored in two Registry keys: HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa\Security Packages and HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa\OSConfig\Security Packages. An adversary may modify these Registry keys to add new SSPs, which will be loaded the next time the system boots, or when the AddSecurityPackage Windows API function is called.(Citation: Graeber 2014) The following SSPs can be used to access credentials: * Msv: Interactive logons, batch logons, and service logons are done through the MSV authentication package. * Wdigest: The Digest Authentication protocol is designed for use with Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) and Simple Authentication Security Layer (SASL) exchanges.(Citation: TechNet Blogs Credential Protection) * Kerberos: Preferred for mutual client-server domain authentication in Windows 2000 and later. * CredSSP: Provides SSO and Network Level Authentication for Remote Desktop Services.(Citation: TechNet Blogs Credential Protection)
2692.profile: [profile]LSASS Memory, identified as T1003.001 under the Credential Access tactic, targets Windows platforms. This technique involves accessing credential material stored within the Local Security Authority Subsystem Service (LSASS) process memory post-user logon. Adversaries harvest these credentials using tools like Mimikatz (e.g., sekurlsa::logonPasswords) or by dumping the LSASS process to a file with utilities such as Procdump (procdump -ma lsass.exe) or built-in Windows DLLs (e.g., comsvcs.dll via rundll32). The stolen credentials, including Kerberos tickets and hashes, are then used for lateral movement. Groups like APT3, APT28, and MuddyWater have employed this method.[/profile]
2692.profile_without_enhance: [profile]In-memory execution is a technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, categorized under Defense Evasion and Privilege Escalation (Tactic). It operates across Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. This technique involves executing malicious code directly within the memory space of a legitimate process to avoid detection by file-based security controls. Specific sub-techniques include proc memory injection, which manipulates a process's memory via the Linux `/proc/[pid]` filesystem to overwrite memory maps and execute crafted payloads, and Extra Window Memory (EWM) injection on Windows, which abuses registered window class memory to store and trigger a pointer to malicious code. This execution method masks activity under a legitimate process and can bypass defenses like Data Execution Prevention.

2693.name: DLL injection
2693.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may abuse dynamic-link library files (DLLs) in order to achieve persistence, escalate privileges, and evade defenses. DLLs are libraries that contain code and data that can be simultaneously utilized by multiple programs. While DLLs are not malicious by nature, they can be abused through mechanisms such as side-loading, hijacking search order, and phantom DLL hijacking.(Citation: unit 42)

Specific ways DLLs are abused by adversaries include:

### DLL Sideloading
Adversaries may execute their own malicious payloads by side-loading DLLs. Side-loading involves hijacking which DLL a program loads by planting and then invoking a legitimate application that executes their payload(s).

Side-loading positions both the victim application and malicious payload(s) alongside each other. Adversaries likely use side-loading as a means of masking actions they perform under a legitimate, trusted, and potentially elevated system or software process. Benign executables used to side-load payloads may not be flagged during delivery and/or execution. Adversary payloads may also be encrypted/packed or otherwise obfuscated until loaded into the memory of the trusted process.

Adversaries may also side-load other packages, such as BPLs (Borland Package Library).(Citation: kroll bpl)

Adversaries may chain DLL sideloading multiple times to fragment functionality hindering analysis. Adversaries using multiple DLL files can split the loader functions across different DLLs, with a main DLL loading the separated export functions. (Citation: Virus Bulletin) Spreading loader functions across multiple DLLs makes analysis harder, since all files must be collected to fully understand the malware’s behavior.  Another method implements a “loader-for-a-loader”, where a malicious DLL’s sole role is to load a second DLL (or a chain of DLLs) that contain the real payload. (Citation: Sophos)

### DLL Search Order Hijacking
Adversaries may execute their own malicious payloads by hijacking the search order that Windows uses to load DLLs. This search order is a sequence of special and standard search locations that a program checks when loading a DLL. An adversary can plant a trojan DLL in a directory that will be prioritized by the DLL search order over the location of a legitimate library. This will cause Windows to load the malicious DLL when it is called for by the victim program.(Citation: unit 42)

### DLL Redirection
Adversaries may directly modify the search order via DLL redirection, which after being enabled (in the Registry or via the creation of a redirection file) may cause a program to load a DLL from a different location.(Citation: Microsoft redirection)(Citation: Microsoft - manifests/assembly)

### Phantom DLL Hijacking
Adversaries may leverage phantom DLL hijacking by targeting references to non-existent DLL files. They may be able to load their own malicious DLL by planting it with the correct name in the location of the missing module.(Citation: Hexacorn DLL Hijacking)(Citation: Hijack DLLs CrowdStrike)

### DLL Substitution
Adversaries may target existing, valid DLL files and substitute them with their own malicious DLLs, planting them with the same name and in the same location as the valid DLL file.(Citation: Wietze Beukema DLL Hijacking)

Programs that fall victim to DLL hijacking may appear to behave normally because malicious DLLs may be configured to also load the legitimate DLLs they were meant to replace, evading defenses.

Remote DLL hijacking can occur when a program sets its current directory to a remote location, such as a Web share, before loading a DLL.(Citation: dll pre load owasp)(Citation: microsoft remote preloading)

If a valid DLL is configured to run at a higher privilege level, then the adversary-controlled DLL that is loaded will also be executed at the higher level. In this case, the technique could be used for privilege escalation.
2693.profile: [profile]DLL injection, identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1055.001, is a sub-technique of Process Injection under the Defense Evasion and Privilege Escalation tactics, primarily targeting Windows. It involves executing arbitrary code within the address space of a separate live process by loading a malicious dynamic-link library (DLL). Common methods include using Windows API calls like VirtualAllocEx, WriteProcessMemory, and CreateRemoteThread to write a DLL path into the target process and invoke LoadLibrary. Advanced variations such as reflective DLL injection or module stomping manually map and execute the DLL in memory to bypass relocation issues and evade detection by masking execution under a legitimate process. This technique is used by groups like Lazarus Group and Wizard Spider.
2693.profile_without_enhance: [profile]DLL injection, identified as MITRE ATT&CK T1055.001, is a sub-technique of Process Injection under the Defense Evasion and Privilege Escalation tactics for Windows. It involves executing arbitrary code within the address space of a separate live process by forcing it to load a malicious dynamic-link library. Common methods include using Windows API calls like `VirtualAllocEx`, `WriteProcessMemory`, and `CreateRemoteThread` to write a DLL path into the target process and invoke `LoadLibrary`. Variations such as reflective DLL injection and module stomping overcome relocation issues and help conceal the malicious code by leveraging legitimate DLLs on disk, allowing access to the host process's memory and resources while evading detection.

2694.name: File upload
2694.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may upload malware to third-party or adversary controlled infrastructure to make it accessible during targeting. Malicious software can include payloads, droppers, post-compromise tools, backdoors, and a variety of other malicious content. Adversaries may upload malware to support their operations, such as making a payload available to a victim network to enable [Ingress Tool Transfer](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1105) by placing it on an Internet accessible web server.

Malware may be placed on infrastructure that was previously purchased/rented by the adversary ([Acquire Infrastructure](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1583)) or was otherwise compromised by them ([Compromise Infrastructure](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1584)). Malware can also be staged on web services, such as GitHub or Pastebin; hosted on the InterPlanetary File System (IPFS), where decentralized content storage makes the removal of malicious files difficult; or saved on the blockchain as smart contracts, which are resilient against takedowns that would affect traditional infrastructure.(Citation: Volexity Ocean Lotus November 2020)(Citation: Talos IPFS 2022)(Citation: Guardio Etherhiding 2023)(Citation: Bleeping Computer Binance Smart Chain 2023)

Adversaries may upload backdoored files, such as software packages, application binaries, virtual machine images, or container images, to third-party software stores, package libraries, extension marketplaces, or repositories (ex: GitHub, CNET, AWS Community AMIs, Docker Hub, PyPi, NPM).(Citation: Datadog Security Labs Malicious PyPi Packages 2024) By chance encounter, victims may directly download/install these backdoored files via [User Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204). Masquerading, including typo-squatting legitimate software, may increase the chance of users mistakenly executing these files.
2694.profile: [profile]Upload Malware, designated as T1608.001 within the Resource Development tactic, involves adversaries staging malicious content on accessible infrastructure to enable subsequent operations. This includes placing payloads, droppers, or backdoors on adversary-controlled or compromised web servers, third-party services like GitHub or Pastebin, decentralized platforms such as IPFS, blockchain smart contracts, and software repositories like PyPI or Docker Hub to facilitate distribution and execution. Associated malware includes PIRPI.2014 and PIRPI.2015, and it is used by groups including APT3, Mustang Panda, and Fin7.[/profile]
2694.profile_without_enhance: [profile]File upload is a technique where adversaries transfer malicious files to a victim system to enable further actions. This can involve uploading malware or tools to adversary-controlled or compromised infrastructure, such as web servers, cloud storage, or software repositories like GitHub, Docker Hub, or PyPi, to stage payloads for operations like Ingress Tool Transfer. The uploaded files, which may be backdoored software packages, binaries, or scripts, are then accessed or executed on the target, often leveraging open network shares like a web server's root directory to place and trigger malicious content. This technique supports multiple tactics including Initial Access and Lateral Movement across various platforms.

2695.name: File listing
2695.profile: [profile]File listing is a Discovery technique where adversaries enumerate files and directories on a system to understand its layout and locate data of interest. This is commonly performed using native commands like `dir` on Windows or `ls` on Linux. The technique is associated with groups like APT3 and malware families such as PIRPI.2014 and PIRPI.2015, which use this capability for reconnaissance and to identify specific files for exfiltration or further malicious actions.
2695.profile_without_enhance: [profile]File listing is a Discovery technique where adversaries enumerate files and directories on a system to understand its contents and locate data of interest. This is often performed using native system commands like `dir` on Windows or `ls` on Linux and macOS. The activity supports follow-on actions such as data collection and exfiltration.

2696.name: File deletion
2696.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may delete files left behind by the actions of their intrusion activity. Malware, tools, or other non-native files dropped or created on a system by an adversary (ex: [Ingress Tool Transfer](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1105)) may leave traces to indicate to what was done within a network and how. Removal of these files can occur during an intrusion, or as part of a post-intrusion process to minimize the adversary's footprint. There are tools available from the host operating system to perform cleanup, but adversaries may use other tools as well.(Citation: Microsoft SDelete July 2016) Examples of built-in [Command and Scripting Interpreter](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059) functions include del on Windows, rm or unlink on Linux and macOS, and `rm` on ESXi.
2696.profile: [profile]File deletion, known as T1070.004 (Indicator Removal: File Deletion) under the Defense Evasion tactic, operates across Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. Adversaries use this technique to remove traces of intrusion, such as dropped malware or tools, by employing built-in command interpreters like `del` on Windows or `rm`/`unlink` on Unix-based systems, and may also utilize secure deletion tools like SDelete. It is associated with numerous threat groups including APT3, APT28, and Lazarus Group, and is linked to malware families like PIRPI.2014 and PIRPI.2015.[/profile]
2696.profile_without_enhance: [profile]File deletion, identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1070.004, falls under the Defense Evasion tactic and applies to Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves adversaries removing files like malware or tools to erase traces of intrusion, using native OS commands such as `del` on Windows or `rm`/`unlink` on Linux/macOS, as well as utilities like Windows Sysinternals SDelete. This is a post-intrusion cleanup action to minimize their forensic footprint.

2697.name: File copy and deletion
2697.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may delete files left behind by the actions of their intrusion activity. Malware, tools, or other non-native files dropped or created on a system by an adversary (ex: [Ingress Tool Transfer](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1105)) may leave traces to indicate to what was done within a network and how. Removal of these files can occur during an intrusion, or as part of a post-intrusion process to minimize the adversary's footprint. There are tools available from the host operating system to perform cleanup, but adversaries may use other tools as well.(Citation: Microsoft SDelete July 2016) Examples of built-in [Command and Scripting Interpreter](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059) functions include del on Windows, rm or unlink on Linux and macOS, and `rm` on ESXi.
2697.profile: [profile]File Deletion is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1070.004 under the Defense Evasion tactic, applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. It involves adversaries removing files like malware or tools to erase traces of intrusion, using native OS commands such as `del` on Windows, `rm` or `unlink` on Linux/macOS, and `rm` on ESXi, or tools like Windows Sysinternals SDelete. This cleanup minimizes their forensic footprint and is associated with groups like APT3 and malware like PIRPI.2014.[/profile]
2697.profile_without_enhance: [profile]File copy and deletion is a technique used by adversaries to manage their artifacts on a compromised system, primarily for defense evasion and covering their tracks. It involves copying malicious files to new locations to relocate them, often to blend in or establish persistence, and subsequently deleting the original or temporary files to remove forensic evidence. This process can utilize native OS commands like `copy` and `del` or dedicated tools to minimize the adversary's operational footprint.

2698.name: File download and save
2698.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may enumerate files and directories or may search in specific locations of a host or network share for certain information within a file system. Adversaries may use the information from [File and Directory Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1083) during automated discovery to shape follow-on behaviors, including whether or not the adversary fully infects the target and/or attempts specific actions. Many command shell utilities can be used to obtain this information. Examples include dir, tree, ls, find, and locate.(Citation: Windows Commands JPCERT) Custom tools may also be used to gather file and directory information and interact with the [Native API](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1106). Adversaries may also leverage a [Network Device CLI](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/008) on network devices to gather file and directory information (e.g. dir, show flash, and/or nvram).(Citation: US-CERT-TA18-106A) Some files and directories may require elevated or specific user permissions to access.
2698.profile: [profile]File and Directory Discovery, identified as T1083, is a Discovery tactic used across Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. Adversaries enumerate files and directories using command shell utilities like `dir`, `tree`, `ls`, `find`, `locate`, and network device commands such as `show flash` or `nvram` to gather information that shapes follow-on actions. This technique is associated with groups including APT3, APT28, and Lazarus Group, and has been used with malware like PIRPI.
2698.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "File download and save" is a technique where adversaries transfer tools or files from an external system into a compromised environment. This aligns with MITRE ATT&CK technique T1105, Ingress Tool Transfer, under the Command and Control tactic, applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. The technical mechanics involve using native utilities like `copy`, `certutil`, PowerShell's `Invoke-WebRequest` or `IEX(New-Object Net.WebClient).downloadString()` on Windows, and `curl`, `wget`, `scp`, or `rsync` on Linux/macOS to download files through command and control channels or protocols like FTP. Adversaries may also abuse installers like `yum` or `winget` and cloud sync services such as Dropbox for file transfer, often verifying file integrity with hashes post-download.

2699.name: Command execution
2699.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may abuse utilities that allow for command execution to bypass security restrictions that limit the use of command-line interpreters. Various Windows utilities may be used to execute commands, possibly without invoking [cmd](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0106). For example, [Forfiles](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0193), the Program Compatibility Assistant (`pcalua.exe`), components of the Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL), `Scriptrunner.exe`, as well as other utilities may invoke the execution of programs and commands from a [Command and Scripting Interpreter](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059), Run window, or via scripts.(Citation: VectorSec ForFiles Aug 2017)(Citation: Evi1cg Forfiles Nov 2017)(Citation: Secure Team - Scriptrunner.exe)(Citation: SS64)(Citation: Bleeping Computer - Scriptrunner.exe) Adversaries may also abuse the `ssh.exe` binary to execute malicious commands via the `ProxyCommand` and `LocalCommand` options, which can be invoked via the `-o` flag or by modifying the SSH config file.(Citation: Threat Actor Targets the Manufacturing industry with Lumma Stealer and Amadey Bot)

Adversaries may abuse these features for [Defense Evasion](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0005), specifically to perform arbitrary execution while subverting detections and/or mitigation controls (such as Group Policy) that limit/prevent the usage of [cmd](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0106) or file extensions more commonly associated with malicious payloads.
2699.profile: [profile]Indirect Command Execution is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1202 under the Defense Evasion tactic, primarily for Windows. It involves abusing trusted system utilities to execute commands without invoking the standard command-line interpreter (cmd.exe), thereby bypassing security restrictions and detections. Specific utilities include Forfiles, pcalua.exe, Windows Subsystem for Linux components, and Scriptrunner.exe. Adversaries also abuse ssh.exe via its ProxyCommand and LocalCommand options. This technique has been associated with groups like Lazarus Group and Redcurl, and malware such as PIRPI.2014 and PIRPI.2015.[/profile]
2699.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Command execution" is a foundational attack pattern within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, broadly categorized under the Execution tactic (TA0002). It involves an adversary's ability to run arbitrary commands, scripts, or binaries on a compromised system. This is frequently achieved by abusing built-in command and scripting interpreters like Windows Command Shell (cmd), PowerShell, Unix shells, or cross-platform interpreters such as Python. Adversaries may also leverage indirect methods, using utilities like Forfiles or ssh.exe to execute commands while evading security controls that monitor standard interpreters. The technique is platform-agnostic, applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS, and serves as a critical step for establishing control, lateral movement, and achieving broader campaign objectives.

2700.name: Working directory modification
2700.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may modify file or directory permissions/attributes to evade access control lists (ACLs) and access protected files.(Citation: Hybrid Analysis Icacls1 June 2018)(Citation: Hybrid Analysis Icacls2 May 2018) File and directory permissions are commonly managed by ACLs configured by the file or directory owner, or users with the appropriate permissions. File and directory ACL implementations vary by platform, but generally explicitly designate which users or groups can perform which actions (read, write, execute, etc.).

Modifications may include changing specific access rights, which may require taking ownership of a file or directory and/or elevated permissions depending on the file or directory’s existing permissions. This may enable malicious activity such as modifying, replacing, or deleting specific files or directories. Specific file and directory modifications may be a required step for many techniques, such as establishing Persistence via [Accessibility Features](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1546/008), [Boot or Logon Initialization Scripts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1037), [Unix Shell Configuration Modification](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1546/004), or tainting/hijacking other instrumental binary/configuration files via [Hijack Execution Flow](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1574).

Adversaries may also change permissions of symbolic links. For example, malware (particularly ransomware) may modify symbolic links and associated settings to enable access to files from local shortcuts with remote paths.(Citation: new_rust_based_ransomware)(Citation: bad_luck_blackcat)(Citation: falconoverwatch_blackcat_attack)(Citation: blackmatter_blackcat)(Citation: fsutil_behavior)
2700.profile: [profile]Working directory modification is a technique for evading access controls by altering file or directory permissions, often as a prerequisite for other techniques like persistence or hijack execution flow. The technical mechanics involve using platform-specific commands such as `icacls`, `cacls`, `takeown`, and `attrib` on Windows, or `chown` and `chmod` on Linux and macOS, to change access rights or ownership, and may include modifying permissions of symbolic links, particularly by ransomware. It is associated with groups like APT3 and malware like PIRPI.[/profile]
2700.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Working directory modification is a technique where adversaries alter the current working directory of a process to influence file operations and execution paths, often to evade detection or hijack legitimate processes. This technique is associated with the MITRE ATT&CK ID T1574.007 under the tactic of Privilege Escalation and Defense Evasion, primarily on Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. The technical mechanics involve changing environment variables or process parameters to redirect file reads, writes, or script executions to adversary-controlled locations, facilitating lateral movement or persistence by loading malicious DLLs or scripts from a tainted directory.

2701.name: IDA Pro disassembly trick
2701.profile: [profile]IDA Pro disassembly trick is a technique used to hinder static analysis by manipulating how disassemblers like IDA Pro interpret code. Adversaries may insert junk or dead code, such as No-Operation (NOP) instructions (e.g., the 0x90 opcode in x86 assembly), which forces analysts to step through non-functional segments, increasing analysis time and complexity. This method is distinct from simple binary padding as its primary goal is to obfuscate the malware's true functionality. It has been associated with groups like APT3.[/profile]
2701.profile_without_enhance: [profile]IDA Pro disassembly trick is a technique used to hinder static analysis by exploiting how disassemblers like IDA Pro interpret code. It involves inserting junk or dead code, such as No-Operation (NOP) instructions like the 0x90 opcode, into the binary. This forces analysts to step through non-functional code, increasing analysis time and complicating detection via static analysis. The technique is distinct from simple binary padding as its primary goal is to obfuscate the core functionality of the malware.

2702.name: conditional jump
2702.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may disable or modify conditional access policies to enable persistent access to compromised accounts. Conditional access policies are additional verifications used by identity providers and identity and access management systems to determine whether a user should be granted access to a resource.

For example, in Entra ID, Okta, and JumpCloud, users can be denied access to applications based on their IP address, device enrollment status, and use of multi-factor authentication.(Citation: Microsoft Conditional Access)(Citation: JumpCloud Conditional Access Policies)(Citation: Okta Conditional Access Policies) In some cases, identity providers may also support the use of risk-based metrics to deny sign-ins based on a variety of indicators. In AWS and GCP, IAM policies can contain `condition` attributes that verify arbitrary constraints such as the source IP, the date the request was made, and the nature of the resources or regions being requested.(Citation: AWS IAM Conditions)(Citation: GCP IAM Conditions) These measures help to prevent compromised credentials from resulting in unauthorized access to data or resources, as well as limit user permissions to only those required. 

By modifying conditional access policies, such as adding additional trusted IP ranges, removing [Multi-Factor Authentication](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1556/006) requirements, or allowing additional [Unused/Unsupported Cloud Regions](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1535), adversaries may be able to ensure persistent access to accounts and circumvent defensive measures.
2702.profile: [profile]Conditional Access Policies, identified as T1556.009, is a Credential Access technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework targeting cloud platforms like Entra ID, Okta, AWS, and GCP. Adversaries disable or modify these identity provider policies to ensure persistent access, specifically by adding trusted IP ranges, removing multi-factor authentication requirements, or allowing access from unsupported cloud regions. This activity has been associated with groups like Scattered Spider and Storm-0501.[/profile]
2702.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Conditional Jump is a software-based technique used for evasion and anti-analysis, not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. It operates by using conditional logic in code to alter execution flow based on environmental checks, such as detecting debuggers, virtual machines, or specific system configurations. This allows malicious code to behave differently or avoid execution in analysis environments, hindering detection and reverse engineering. The technique is distinct from higher-level policy manipulation like Conditional Access Policies (T1556.009).

2703.name: anti-debugging technique
2703.profile: [profile]The entity "anti-debugging technique" aligns with the MITRE ATT&CK technique Debugger Evasion (ID: T1622) under the Defense Evasion tactic, primarily for Windows and Linux platforms. It involves detecting debugger presence to alter malware behavior, using methods like the Native API `IsDebuggerPresent()` call or checking the `BeingDebugged` flag in Windows, and querying `/proc/self/status` for the `TracerPID` field in Linux. Adversaries, such as Mustang Panda, employ these checks to disengage or conceal core functions if a debugged environment is detected, and may also use Structured Exception Handling (SEH) to identify debuggers by throwing exceptions and monitoring process suspension.[/profile]
2703.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "anti-debugging technique" is a tactic used by adversaries to detect and evade debuggers, which are tools defenders use to analyze malware. This technique, which aligns with MITRE ATT&CK T1622 under the Defense Evasion tactic for Windows and Linux platforms, involves specific checks for debugging artifacts. These include using API calls like IsDebuggerPresent() on Windows, querying /proc/self/status on Linux, inspecting the Process Environment Block, leveraging Structured Exception Handling (SEH), and enumerating hardware breakpoints. Upon detecting a debugger, malware may alter its execution, disengage, or flood debug logs to avoid analysis.

2704.name: anti-disassembly technique
2704.profile: [profile]The entity is an anti-disassembly technique, a sub-technique of Obfuscated Files or Information (T1027). It falls under the Defense Evasion tactic and is applicable across multiple platforms. This technique involves modifying executable code to hinder static analysis by disassemblers and debuggers, making it difficult for security tools to examine the malware's true functionality. It is used by groups like APT3 and in malware such as PIRPI to protect malicious payloads from detection and analysis.
2704.profile_without_enhance: [profile]anti-disassembly technique is a Defense Evasion tactic used on Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves modifying executable code to hinder or mislead static analysis tools, such as disassemblers, by inserting misleading instructions, junk code, or manipulating the program's control flow. This technique is often employed alongside software packing to further obfuscate malware and evade signature-based detection.

2705.name: encoding algorithm
2705.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may encode data with a standard data encoding system to make the content of command and control traffic more difficult to detect. Command and control (C2) information can be encoded using a standard data encoding system that adheres to existing protocol specifications. Common data encoding schemes include ASCII, Unicode, hexadecimal, Base64, and MIME.(Citation: Wikipedia Binary-to-text Encoding)(Citation: Wikipedia Character Encoding) Some data encoding systems may also result in data compression, such as gzip.
2705.profile: [profile]Standard Encoding, identified as T1132.001 within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, is a Command and Control technique under the Exfiltration tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. It involves obfuscating C2 traffic by encoding data using established, protocol-compliant schemes such as ASCII, Unicode, hexadecimal, Base64, and MIME, which may also provide compression via systems like gzip. This technique is employed by groups including Hafnium, MuddyWater, and Lazarus Group.
2705.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "encoding algorithm" is a sub-technique of Data Encoding (T1132) within the Command and Control tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. It involves adversaries using specific computational procedures, such as Base64, ASCII, or Unicode, to transform command and control traffic, making it more difficult to detect. This technique adheres to or modifies standard protocol specifications to obfuscate network communications.

2706.name: state machine
2706.uncertain_mes:
An adversary may attempt to enumerate running virtual machines (VMs) after gaining access to a host or hypervisor. For example, adversaries may enumerate a list of VMs on an ESXi hypervisor using a [Hypervisor CLI](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/012) such as `esxcli` or `vim-cmd` (e.g. `esxcli vm process list or vim-cmd vmsvc/getallvms`).(Citation: Crowdstrike Hypervisor Jackpotting Pt 2 2021)(Citation: TrendMicro Play) Adversaries may also directly leverage a graphical user interface, such as VMware vCenter, in order to view virtual machines on a host. 

Adversaries may use the information from [Virtual Machine Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1673) during discovery to shape follow-on behaviors. Subsequently discovered VMs may be leveraged for follow-on activities such as [Service Stop](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1489) or [Data Encrypted for Impact](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1486).(Citation: Crowdstrike Hypervisor Jackpotting Pt 2 2021)
2706.profile: [profile]Virtual Machine Discovery is identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1673 under the Discovery tactic, applicable to Linux, Windows, and VMware ESXi platforms. The technique involves enumerating running virtual machines after compromising a host or hypervisor, using specific commands like `esxcli vm process list` or `vim-cmd vmsvc/getallvms` on ESXi systems, or accessing graphical interfaces like VMware vCenter. This discovery is used to inform subsequent malicious actions, such as service disruption or data encryption for impact, and has been associated with threat group UNC3886.[/profile]
2706.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "state machine" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the retrieved information, the term appears in the context of network protocols and denial-of-service attacks. Specifically, the OS Exhaustion Flood technique (T1499.001) exploits the stateful nature of protocols like TCP, where adversaries flood a target with packets (e.g., ACK floods) to exhaust the operating system's capacity to manage its connection state table. This computational exhaustion can cause the system to become sluggish or unresponsive, impairing service availability.

2707.name: reversible mathematical function
2707.uncertain_mes: An adversary may abuse Active Directory authentication encryption properties to gain access to credentials on Windows systems. The AllowReversiblePasswordEncryption property specifies whether reversible password encryption for an account is enabled or disabled. By default this property is disabled (instead storing user credentials as the output of one-way hashing functions) and should not be enabled unless legacy or other software require it.(Citation: store_pwd_rev_enc) If the property is enabled and/or a user changes their password after it is enabled, an adversary may be able to obtain the plaintext of passwords created/changed after the property was enabled. To decrypt the passwords, an adversary needs four components: 1. Encrypted password (G$RADIUSCHAP) from the Active Directory user-structure userParameters 2. 16 byte randomly-generated value (G$RADIUSCHAPKEY) also from userParameters 3. Global LSA secret (G$MSRADIUSCHAPKEY) 4. Static key hardcoded in the Remote Access Subauthentication DLL (RASSFM.DLL) With this information, an adversary may be able to reproduce the encryption key and subsequently decrypt the encrypted password value.(Citation: how_pwd_rev_enc_1)(Citation: how_pwd_rev_enc_2) An adversary may set this property at various scopes through Local Group Policy Editor, user properties, Fine-Grained Password Policy (FGPP), or via the ActiveDirectory [PowerShell](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001) module. For example, an adversary may implement and apply a FGPP to users or groups if the Domain Functional Level is set to "Windows Server 2008" or higher.(Citation: dump_pwd_dcsync) In PowerShell, an adversary may make associated changes to user settings using commands similar to Set-ADUser -AllowReversiblePasswordEncryption $true.
2707.profile: [profile]Reversible Encryption, designated as T1556.005 under the Credential Access tactic, targets Windows Active Directory. It exploits the 'AllowReversiblePasswordEncryption' property to store passwords with weak, reversible encryption instead of secure hashes. An adversary can decrypt these passwords by extracting specific components from the AD user structure and LSA secrets, such as the G$RADIUSCHAP value and the G$MSRADIUSCHAPKEY, and using a static key from RASSFM.DLL. The property can be enabled via PowerShell commands like `Set-ADUser -AllowReversiblePasswordEncryption $true`.
2707.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "reversible mathematical function" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on retrieved context, it is a general cryptographic concept where a mathematical operation can be reversed to obtain the original input. This is distinct from the specific ATT&CK technique T1556.005 "Reversible Encryption," which involves abusing Active Directory's `AllowReversiblePasswordEncryption` property to enable the storage of credentials in a decryptable format, allowing adversaries with specific components to recover plaintext passwords.

2708.name: Operation DoubleTap
2708.profile: [profile]Operation DoubleTap is a campaign associated with the APT3 intrusion set. It involves the use of Graphical User Interface (GUI) interaction, which is a deprecated technique now encompassed by Remote Services (T1021), where adversaries leverage remote interactive sessions like Remote Desktop Protocol (T1076) to execute files and search for information through mouse clicks or the Run command, bypassing command-line monitoring. The campaign also employs Screen Capture (T1113) to gather intelligence via native utilities or API calls such as CopyFromScreen, xwd, or screencapture. Additionally, Network Share Connection Removal (T1126) is used for operational cleanup by deleting connections with commands like `net use \\system\share /delete`.
2708.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Operation DoubleTap is a campaign name, not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on retrieved context, it is associated with techniques like Screen Capture (T1113), which adversaries use to gather information via tools like CopyFromScreen, xwd, or screencapture, and is linked to groups including APT28, FIN7, and MuddyWater.

2709.name: Operation ClandestineFox
2709.profile: [profile]Operation ClandestineFox is a campaign associated with the intrusion set APT3. It employs the T1113 Screen Capture technique, where adversaries capture desktop screens using native utilities or API calls like `CopyFromScreen`, `xwd`, or `screencapture` to gather information. The campaign also utilizes T1001.001 Junk Data, appending random characters to C2 protocols to hinder detection, and T1079 Multilayer Encryption, tunneling custom encryption within secure protocols like HTTPS for obfuscated command and control communications.
2709.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Operation ClandestineFox is a campaign entity, not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. The retrieved information describes associated technical methods, including screen capture (T1113) using utilities like `CopyFromScreen` or `screencapture`, command and control obfuscation via junk data insertion (T1001.001), and the use of multilayer encryption (T1079) such as tunneling custom encryption within HTTPS. These techniques are linked to groups like APT28, MuddyWater, and others.

2710.name: steganography
2710.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may use steganography techniques in order to prevent the detection of hidden information. Steganographic techniques can be used to hide data in digital media such as images, audio tracks, video clips, or text files. [Duqu](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0038) was an early example of malware that used steganography. It encrypted the gathered information from a victim's system and hid it within an image before exfiltrating the image to a C2 server.(Citation: Wikipedia Duqu) By the end of 2017, a threat group used Invoke-PSImage to hide [PowerShell](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001) commands in an image file (.png) and execute the code on a victim's system. In this particular case the [PowerShell](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001) code downloaded another obfuscated script to gather intelligence from the victim's machine and communicate it back to the adversary.(Citation: McAfee Malicious Doc Targets Pyeongchang Olympics)
2710.profile: [profile]Steganography is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1027.003, a sub-technique of Obfuscated Files or Information under the Defense Evasion tactic. It operates by hiding data within digital media like images, audio, video, or text files to prevent detection. A specific technical example is the use of the Invoke-PSImage tool to conceal PowerShell commands within a PNG image file for execution, as observed in a 2017 campaign. The technique is also referenced in the context of command and control (C1001.002) for hiding C2 traffic. Associated threat groups include APT29, APT3, Earth Lusca, and MuddyWater.[/profile]
2710.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Steganography, identified as T1027.003 and T1001.002, is a Defense Evasion and Command and Control technique used across multiple platforms. It involves hiding data within digital media like images, audio, or text files to prevent detection. For example, malware like Duqu has hidden encrypted stolen data in images for exfiltration, and tools like Invoke-PSImage have been used to conceal and execute PowerShell commands within PNG files. This method is also employed to obfuscate C2 traffic, making network communications less conspicuous.

2712.name: reusing delivery techniques
2712.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may attempt to make payloads difficult to discover and analyze by delivering files to victims as uncompiled code. Text-based source code files may subvert analysis and scrutiny from protections targeting executables/binaries. These payloads will need to be compiled before execution; typically via native utilities such as ilasm.exe(Citation: ATTACK IQ), csc.exe, or GCC/MinGW.(Citation: ClearSky MuddyWater Nov 2018)

Source code payloads may also be encrypted, encoded, and/or embedded within other files, such as those delivered as a [Phishing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566). Payloads may also be delivered in formats unrecognizable and inherently benign to the native OS (ex: EXEs on macOS/Linux) before later being (re)compiled into a proper executable binary with a bundled compiler and execution framework.(Citation: TrendMicro WindowsAppMac)
2712.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique "Compile After Delivery" (T1027.004), a Defense Evasion sub-technique. It operates on Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. Adversaries deliver payloads as uncompiled source code to bypass security tools scanning for binaries, requiring compilation on the victim system using native utilities like csc.exe, ilasm.exe, or GCC. Payloads may be obfuscated within other files or delivered in a benign format for the target OS before being compiled. Associated threat groups include Gamaredon Group, MuddyWater, Rocke, and Sea Turtle.
2712.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "reusing delivery techniques" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the provided context, it likely describes an adversary behavior of repeatedly employing known initial access or delivery methods, such as phishing or drive-by compromises, across different campaigns. This practice can increase operational efficiency for threat actors but may also leave consistent forensic artifacts. The retrieved information does not provide a specific MITRE ID, tactic, or platform, and the similar entity "compile after delivery" (T1027.004) describes a distinct technique for evading detection by delivering uncompiled code.
