2789.profile: [profile]Ingress Tool Transfer is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1105 under the Command and Control tactic, applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. It involves transferring files into a compromised environment using utilities like certutil, PowerShell's Invoke-WebRequest, curl, scp, and wget, or by abusing installers like winget and sync services like Dropbox. This technique is commonly used by numerous threat groups, including APT3, to introduce tools for further malicious activity.
2789.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The technique is officially known as Ingress Tool Transfer, identified as T1105 under the Command and Control tactic. It operates across Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. Adversaries transfer files into a compromised environment using utilities like `copy`, `certutil`, `PowerShell` commands (e.g., `IEX(New-Object Net.WebClient).downloadString()`), `curl`, `scp`, `wget`, or package managers like `yum`. Files are copied from an external adversary-controlled system into the victim network, often through the command and control channel or protocols like FTP.

2790.name: T1021
2790.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may use [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078) to log into a service that accepts remote connections, such as telnet, SSH, and VNC. The adversary may then perform actions as the logged-on user.

In an enterprise environment, servers and workstations can be organized into domains. Domains provide centralized identity management, allowing users to login using one set of credentials across the entire network. If an adversary is able to obtain a set of valid domain credentials, they could login to many different machines using remote access protocols such as secure shell (SSH) or remote desktop protocol (RDP).(Citation: SSH Secure Shell)(Citation: TechNet Remote Desktop Services) They could also login to accessible SaaS or IaaS services, such as those that federate their identities to the domain, or management platforms for internal virtualization environments such as VMware vCenter. 

Legitimate applications (such as [Software Deployment Tools](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1072) and other administrative programs) may utilize [Remote Services](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021) to access remote hosts. For example, Apple Remote Desktop (ARD) on macOS is native software used for remote management. ARD leverages a blend of protocols, including [VNC](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/005) to send the screen and control buffers and [SSH](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/004) for secure file transfer.(Citation: Remote Management MDM macOS)(Citation: Kickstart Apple Remote Desktop commands)(Citation: Apple Remote Desktop Admin Guide 3.3) Adversaries can abuse applications such as ARD to gain remote code execution and perform lateral movement. In versions of macOS prior to 10.14, an adversary can escalate an SSH session to an ARD session which enables an adversary to accept TCC (Transparency, Consent, and Control) prompts without user interaction and gain access to data.(Citation: FireEye 2019 Apple Remote Desktop)(Citation: Lockboxx ARD 2019)(Citation: Kickstart Apple Remote Desktop commands)
2790.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1021, named Remote Services, which falls under the Lateral Movement tactic and applies to Windows, macOS, and Linux platforms. It involves adversaries using valid accounts to log into services that accept remote connections—such as SSH, RDP, VNC, and telnet—to perform actions as the logged-on user, enabling lateral movement across a network. This includes abusing legitimate remote management tools like Apple Remote Desktop (ARD) on macOS, where prior to version 10.14, an SSH session could be escalated to an ARD session to bypass user consent prompts. The technique is associated with groups like APT3, Aquatic Panda, Ember Bear, and Wizard Spider.
2790.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1021, named "Remote Services". It falls under the Lateral Movement tactic and applies to multiple platforms. This technique involves adversaries using valid accounts to log into services that accept remote connections, such as SSH, RDP, VNC, and telnet, to perform actions as the logged-on user and move laterally across a network. It can be abused in enterprise environments to access many machines or cloud services using domain credentials, and legitimate remote management tools like Apple Remote Desktop can also be exploited for this purpose.

2791.name: T1053
2791.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may abuse task scheduling functionality to facilitate initial or recurring execution of malicious code. Utilities exist within all major operating systems to schedule programs or scripts to be executed at a specified date and time. A task can also be scheduled on a remote system, provided the proper authentication is met (ex: RPC and file and printer sharing in Windows environments). Scheduling a task on a remote system typically may require being a member of an admin or otherwise privileged group on the remote system.(Citation: TechNet Task Scheduler Security)

Adversaries may use task scheduling to execute programs at system startup or on a scheduled basis for persistence. These mechanisms can also be abused to run a process under the context of a specified account (such as one with elevated permissions/privileges). Similar to [System Binary Proxy Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1218), adversaries have also abused task scheduling to potentially mask one-time execution under a trusted system process.(Citation: ProofPoint Serpent)
2791.profile: [profile]Scheduled Task/Job is technique T1053 within the Execution and Persistence tactics, applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves abusing OS utilities like `schtasks` or `cron` to schedule execution of malicious code at startup or recurring intervals, which can also be deployed remotely with proper admin authentication. This method is used for persistence and to run processes under privileged contexts, and it can be automated via GPO modification scripts like `New-GPOImmediateTask` to create malicious scheduled tasks.
2791.profile_without_enhance: [profile]T1053, known as Scheduled Task/Job, is a Persistence and Execution technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework applicable to multiple platforms including Windows, Linux, and macOS. It involves abusing built-in system utilities like `schtasks` or `cron` to schedule the execution of malicious code at specific times or upon system events, enabling recurring or delayed execution. This method can be used locally or on remote systems with proper authentication, and adversaries often leverage it to run processes under privileged contexts or to mask execution behind trusted system processes.

2792.name: T1003 - Credential Dumping
2792.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may attempt to dump credentials to obtain account login and credential material, normally in the form of a hash or a clear text password. Credentials can be obtained from OS caches, memory, or structures.(Citation: Brining MimiKatz to Unix) Credentials can then be used to perform [Lateral Movement](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0008) and access restricted information.

Several of the tools mentioned in associated sub-techniques may be used by both adversaries and professional security testers. Additional custom tools likely exist as well.
2792.profile: [profile]T1003 - Credential Dumping is a technique under the Credential Access tactic (TA0006) for Windows, Linux, and macOS. It involves extracting account login material, such as password hashes or clear-text passwords, from operating system components like security account manager (SAM) files, Local Security Authority (LSA) secrets, or process memory. This stolen data is then used for lateral movement and privilege escalation, with tools like Mimikatz commonly employed for this purpose. The technique is associated with numerous threat groups including APT3, APT28, and APT29.[/profile]
2792.profile_without_enhance: [profile]T1003 - Credential Dumping is a Credential Access technique for Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves adversaries extracting account login material like hashes or plaintext passwords from operating system components such as security account manager (SAM) databases, Local Security Authority (LSA) secrets, NTDS.dit files, or process memory. Tools like Mimikatz and built-in utilities like `reg.exe` are commonly used to perform these dumps, with the harvested credentials enabling lateral movement and privilege escalation.

2793.name: T1081 - Credentials from File
2793.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may search for common password storage locations to obtain user credentials.(Citation: F-Secure The Dukes) Passwords are stored in several places on a system, depending on the operating system or application holding the credentials. There are also specific applications and services that store passwords to make them easier for users to manage and maintain, such as password managers and cloud secrets vaults. Once credentials are obtained, they can be used to perform lateral movement and access restricted information.
2793.profile: [profile]Credentials in Files, identified as T1081, is a Credential Access technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS. Adversaries search local and remote file systems for files containing insecurely stored credentials, which can include user-created password files, shared credential stores, configuration files with embedded passwords, or source code. This method also extends to cloud environments where credentials are stored in local configuration files, and may involve extracting passwords from backups, virtual machines, or Windows Group Policy Preferences stored on a Domain Controller.
2793.profile_without_enhance: [profile]T1081 - Credentials in Files is a Credential Access technique where adversaries search local file systems and remote shares for files containing insecurely stored credentials. These can include user-created password files, shared credential stores, configuration files with embedded passwords, or source code. In cloud environments, credentials are often found in local configuration files. The technique is platform-agnostic and enables adversaries to obtain credentials for lateral movement and further system access.

2794.name: ExploitKit-style reconnaissance
2794.profile: [profile]ExploitKit-style reconnaissance is a technique used by adversaries like APT3 to gather target information through active scanning, probing victim infrastructure via network traffic to identify vulnerabilities for exploitation. It may involve spoofing browser attributes to blend with legitimate traffic and evade detection. This technique supports initial access and operational resource establishment.
2794.profile_without_enhance: [profile]ExploitKit-style reconnaissance is a technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, typically associated with the Reconnaissance tactic. It involves automated scanning of victim infrastructure to identify specific software versions, plugins, or system configurations that are vulnerable to known exploits. This process is often conducted by exploit kits, which use this gathered information to selectively deploy appropriate exploits against the target, enabling initial access or further compromise.

2795.name: initial compromise
2795.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may compromise third-party infrastructure that can be used during targeting. Infrastructure solutions include physical or cloud servers, domains, network devices, and third-party web and DNS services. Instead of buying, leasing, or renting infrastructure an adversary may compromise infrastructure and use it during other phases of the adversary lifecycle.(Citation: Mandiant APT1)(Citation: ICANNDomainNameHijacking)(Citation: Talos DNSpionage Nov 2018)(Citation: FireEye EPS Awakens Part 2) Additionally, adversaries may compromise numerous machines to form a botnet they can leverage.

Use of compromised infrastructure allows adversaries to stage, launch, and execute operations. Compromised infrastructure can help adversary operations blend in with traffic that is seen as normal, such as contact with high reputation or trusted sites. For example, adversaries may leverage compromised infrastructure (potentially also in conjunction with [Digital Certificates](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1588/004)) to further blend in and support staged information gathering and/or [Phishing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566) campaigns.(Citation: FireEye DNS Hijack 2019) Adversaries may also compromise numerous machines to support [Proxy](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1090) and/or proxyware services or to form a botnet.(Citation: amnesty_nso_pegasus)(Citation: Sysdig Proxyjacking) Additionally, adversaries may compromise infrastructure residing in close proximity to a target in order to gain [Initial Access](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0001) via [Wi-Fi Networks](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1669).(Citation: Nearest Neighbor Volexity)

By using compromised infrastructure, adversaries may enable follow-on malicious operations. Prior to targeting, adversaries may also compromise the infrastructure of other adversaries.(Citation: NSA NCSC Turla OilRig)
2795.profile: [profile]Compromise Infrastructure, designated T1584, is a resource development technique where adversaries take over third-party infrastructure like servers, domains, or network devices instead of purchasing them. This compromised infrastructure is then used to stage and launch operations, helping malicious traffic blend in with normal activity by leveraging high-reputation sites. Specific mechanics include using hijacked infrastructure to support phishing campaigns, form botnets, enable proxy services, or gain initial access via nearby Wi-Fi networks. The intrusion-set APT3 has been associated with this behavior.
2795.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "initial compromise" is a foundational concept in cyber threat intelligence, representing the initial breach that grants adversaries access to a target network. It is not a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique but an overarching phase within the Initial Access tactic (TA0001). This phase encompasses various specific techniques such as drive-by compromises, supply chain compromises, and the acquisition of access through brokers. The technical mechanics involve exploiting vulnerabilities, deploying malicious code, or leveraging compromised credentials to establish a foothold, enabling subsequent malicious activities.

2796.name: network propagation
2796.profile: [profile]Network Propagation is a technique used for Lateral Movement (TA0008) across platforms like Windows, Linux, and macOS. It involves adversaries moving through a compromised network by exploiting trust relationships, shared resources, or remote services. The retrieved information highlights related techniques such as compromising network devices (T1584.008) to gain a foothold for further operations, and using network sniffing (T1040) to capture credentials and configuration details to inform movement. Groups like APT3 have been associated with this behavior.[/profile]
2796.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Network Propagation is a technique adversaries use to move laterally across a network after gaining initial access. It involves scanning for and connecting to remote systems, often leveraging valid credentials or exploiting remote services. This movement enables further discovery, credential access, and the establishment of persistence on additional hosts within the compromised environment.

2797.name: exfiltration
2797.profile: [profile]The entity "exfiltration" is a high-level tactic in the MITRE ATT&CK framework, representing the adversary's objective of stealing data from a network. It is not a specific technique and therefore has no associated ID. It encompasses numerous sub-techniques that detail the specific methods for data theft, such as Automated Exfiltration (T1020), Exfiltration Over Web Service (T1567), and Exfiltration Over USB (T1052.001). These methods can involve automated processing, use of legitimate web services, or physical media like USB devices to transfer collected data out of the victim's environment. Groups like APT3, Tropic Trooper, and Mustang Panda are known to employ these techniques.
2797.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Exfiltration is the adversary technique of stealing data from a network. It is a high-level tactic within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, not a specific technique with a single ID. The actual mechanics involve transferring collected data out of the network using various sub-techniques, which define the specific protocols and channels. These include automated exfiltration (T1020), exfiltration over web services (T1567), exfiltration over USB (T1052.001), and scheduled transfer (T1029), often employed by groups like Gamaredon and Tropic Trooper to move data via C2 channels, alternative protocols, or physical media.

2798.name: sleep and anti-sandbox tactics
2798.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may employ various means to detect and avoid virtualization and analysis environments. This may include changing behaviors based on the results of checks for the presence of artifacts indicative of a virtual machine environment (VME) or sandbox. If the adversary detects a VME, they may alter their malware to disengage from the victim or conceal the core functions of the implant. They may also search for VME artifacts before dropping secondary or additional payloads. Adversaries may use the information learned from [Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1497) during automated discovery to shape follow-on behaviors.(Citation: Deloitte Environment Awareness)

Adversaries may use several methods to accomplish [Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1497) such as checking for security monitoring tools (e.g., Sysinternals, Wireshark, etc.) or other system artifacts associated with analysis or virtualization. Adversaries may also check for legitimate user activity to help determine if it is in an analysis environment. Additional methods include use of sleep timers or loops within malware code to avoid operating within a temporary sandbox.(Citation: Unit 42 Pirpi July 2015)
2798.profile: [profile]Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion (T1497) is a Defense Evasion technique used across multiple platforms. It involves detecting artifacts of virtual machine environments or sandboxes, such as security monitoring tools or lack of legitimate user activity, to alter malware behavior, disengage, or conceal core functions. Specific methods include using sleep timers or code loops to bypass temporary sandbox analysis. The technique is associated with groups like Contagious Interview, Saint Bear, and DarkHotel.
2798.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "sleep and anti-sandbox tactics" aligns with the MITRE ATT&CK technique Time Based Evasion (T1497.003) under the Defense Evasion tactic for Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves malware using sleep timers or loops in its code to avoid detection within temporary sandbox environments that accelerate time to simulate longer execution periods. This method allows the malware to bypass automated analysis by remaining dormant until the sandbox times out, after which it proceeds with its malicious payload.

2799.name: HTTP GET requests
2799.profile: [profile]The entity "HTTP GET requests" is a common network activity that adversaries can abuse. It is referenced in MITRE ATT&CK techniques as a method for Internet Connection Discovery (T1016.001) to check for connectivity, and within Web Protocols (T1071.001) for command and control communication to blend with normal traffic. It is also mentioned as a potential channel for Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol (T1048). The technique is associated with groups like APT3 and is platform-agnostic, often executed using standard utilities like `curl` to make web requests.
2799.profile_without_enhance: [profile]HTTP GET requests are a common web protocol used by adversaries for command and control (C2) communication and data exfiltration, often blending with normal traffic to avoid detection. They are associated with MITRE ATT&CK technique T1071.001 (Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols) under the Command and Control tactic. Adversaries embed commands and exfiltrated data within standard HTTP GET request fields and headers. This method is frequently employed by groups like APT28, APT29, Lazarus Group, and OilRig for network discovery checks and as an alternative exfiltration channel.

2800.name: custom binary protocols
2800.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may communicate using application layer protocols associated with electronic mail delivery to avoid detection/network filtering by blending in with existing traffic. Commands to the remote system, and often the results of those commands, will be embedded within the protocol traffic between the client and server. 

Protocols such as SMTP/S, POP3/S, and IMAP that carry electronic mail may be very common in environments.  Packets produced from these protocols may have many fields and headers in which data can be concealed. Data could also be concealed within the email messages themselves. 2817.name: Return-Oriented Programming (ROP)
2817.profile: [profile]Return-Oriented Programming (ROP) is a technique for hijacking execution flow (T1574) to execute arbitrary code. It works by chaining together small instruction sequences, called gadgets, found within a legitimate program's existing code to build a malicious payload. This method is used to bypass security defenses like Data Execution Prevention (DEP) and is applied in techniques such as Proc Memory Injection (T1055.009), where it crafts a payload to overwrite a target process's stack via the /proc filesystem. It is utilized by groups like APT3.[/profile]

This method can be used to craft malicious payloads, such as in Proc Memory Injection (T1055.009), where adversaries overwrite a target process's stack via the /proc filesystem using a ROP payload built from enumerated gadgets to bypass protections like ASLR.

2818.name: Heap Spray
2818.profile: [profile]Heap Spray is a technique for exploiting memory corruption vulnerabilities by filling a process's heap memory with a large amount of data, typically containing the attacker's shellcode. This increases the probability that a subsequent memory corruption, like a buffer overflow, will land execution in a predictable location within the sprayed heap region, allowing the attacker to reliably execute their payload. It is often used in client-side attacks, particularly in web browsers, to facilitate arbitrary code execution. The intrusion set APT3 has been associated with this technique.

2821.name: FLV Object Control
2821.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may abuse control.exe to proxy execution of malicious payloads. Control Panel items are registered executable (.exe) or Control Panel (.cpl) files, the latter are actually renamed dynamic-link library (.dll) files that export a CPlApplet function.(Citation: Microsoft Implementing CPL)(Citation: TrendMicro CPL Malware Jan 2014) For ease of use, Control Panel items typically include graphical menus available to users after being registered and loaded into the Control Panel.(Citation: Microsoft Implementing CPL) Control Panel items can be executed directly from the command line, programmatically via an application programming interface (API) call, or by simply double-clicking the file.(Citation: Microsoft Implementing CPL) (Citation: TrendMicro CPL Malware Jan 2014)(Citation: TrendMicro CPL Malware Dec 2013) Malicious Control Panel items can be delivered via [Phishing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566) campaigns(Citation: TrendMicro CPL Malware Jan 2014)(Citation: TrendMicro CPL Malware Dec 2013) or executed as part of multi-stage malware.(Citation: Palo Alto Reaver Nov 2017) Control Panel items, specifically CPL files, may also bypass application and/or file extension allow lists. 2822.name: Vector Length Overwrite
2822.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may modify a process's in-memory arguments to change its name in order to appear as a legitimate or benign process. On Linux, the operating system stores command-line arguments in the process’s stack and passes them to the `main()` function as the `argv` array. The first element, `argv[0]`, typically contains the process name or path - by default, the command used to actually start the process (e.g., `cat /etc/passwd`). By default, the Linux `/proc` filesystem uses this value to represent the process name. The `/proc/<PID>/cmdline` file reflects the contents of this memory, and tools like `ps` use it to display process information. Since arguments are stored in user-space memory at launch, this modification can be performed without elevated privileges. 

During runtime, adversaries can erase the memory used by all command-line arguments for a process, overwriting each argument string with null bytes. This removes evidence of how the process was originally launched. They can then write a spoofed string into the memory region previously occupied by `argv[0]` to mimic a benign command, such as `cat resolv.conf`. The new command-line string is reflected in `/proc/<PID>/cmdline` and displayed by tools like `ps`.(Citation: Sandfly BPFDoor 2022)(Citation: Microsoft XorDdos Linux Stealth 2022)
2822.profile: [profile]Vector Length Overwrite, also known as Overwrite Process Arguments (T1036.011), is a Defense Evasion technique for Linux platforms. It involves adversaries modifying the in-memory command-line arguments of a process to masquerade its identity. Specifically, they overwrite the `argv[0]` string in user-space memory with null bytes to erase original launch evidence, then write a spoofed benign command string (e.g., `cat resolv.conf`). This change is reflected in `/proc/<PID>/cmdline` and displayed by tools like `ps`, allowing the process to appear legitimate without requiring elevated privileges.
2822.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Vector Length Overwrite is a technique where adversaries manipulate the length field of a data vector in memory to cause an overflow and overwrite adjacent memory. This can lead to arbitrary code execution or process crashes, exploiting improper bounds checking in software to compromise system integrity and availability.

2823.name: ROP Chain Construction
2823.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may manipulate products or product delivery mechanisms prior to receipt by a final consumer for the purpose of data or system compromise.

Supply chain compromise can take place at any stage of the supply chain including:

* Manipulation of development tools
* Manipulation of a development environment
* Manipulation of source code repositories (public or private)
* Manipulation of source code in open-source dependencies
* Manipulation of software update/distribution mechanisms
* Compromised/infected system images (removable media infected at the factory)(Citation: IBM Storwize)(Citation: Schneider Electric USB Malware) 
* Replacement of legitimate software with modified versions
* Sales of modified/counterfeit products to legitimate distributors
* Shipment interdiction

While supply chain compromise can impact any component of hardware or software, adversaries looking to gain execution have often focused on malicious additions to legitimate software in software distribution or update channels.(Citation: Avast CCleaner3 2018)(Citation: Microsoft Dofoil 2018)(Citation: Command Five SK 2011) Adversaries may limit targeting to a desired victim set or distribute malicious software to a broad set of consumers but only follow up with specific victims.(Citation: Symantec Elderwood Sept 2012)(Citation: Avast CCleaner3 2018)(Citation: Command Five SK 2011) Popular open-source projects that are used as dependencies in many applications may also be targeted as a means to add malicious code to users of the dependency.(Citation: Trendmicro NPM Compromise)

In some cases, adversaries may conduct “second-order” supply chain compromises by leveraging the access gained from an initial supply chain compromise to further compromise a software component.(Citation: Krebs 3cx overview 2023) This may allow the threat actor to spread to even more victims.
2823.profile: [profile]Supply Chain Compromise (T1195) is an Initial Access tactic targeting multiple platforms. Adversaries manipulate products or delivery mechanisms before consumer receipt to compromise data or systems. This includes tampering with development tools, source code repositories, open-source dependencies, software updates, or system images to insert malicious code into legitimate distribution channels. Groups like Sandworm Team, Ember Bear, and OilRig have employed this technique, which can enable broad initial infection followed by selective victim targeting.[/profile]
2823.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "ROP Chain Construction" is a technique for exploiting software vulnerabilities, specifically within the Defense Evasion and Privilege Escalation tactics. It operates by chaining together small, pre-existing instruction sequences (gadgets) found in a program's memory to bypass security features like Data Execution Prevention (DEP). This method allows an adversary to execute arbitrary code by manipulating the program's control flow without injecting new shellcode, making the attack more difficult to detect. The technique is platform-agnostic but is most commonly associated with exploiting buffer overflows on systems with DEP enabled.

2824.name: Shellcode Execution
2824.profile: [profile]Shellcode Execution is a technique for running arbitrary code directly in memory, often used to evade detection by avoiding file-based execution. It is associated with the intrusion set APT3. The technique involves writing raw machine code (shellcode) into a target process's address space using Windows API calls like VirtualAllocEx and WriteProcessMemory, then triggering execution via CreateRemoteThread. This method is a form of process injection, closely related to techniques like Portable Executable Injection and Dynamic-link Library Injection, and is used to run malicious payloads under the guise of a legitimate process.[/profile]

This allows the code to run within a legitimate process's context, masking its execution. The technique is related to and often used alongside other process injection methods like DLL injection.

2848.name: Flash Exploit Techniques
2848.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may attempt to exploit a weakness in an Internet-facing host or system to initially access a network. The weakness in the system can be a software bug, a temporary glitch, or a misconfiguration.

Exploited applications are often websites/web servers, but can also include databases (like SQL), standard services (like SMB or SSH), network device administration and management protocols (like SNMP and Smart Install), and any other system with Internet-accessible open sockets.(Citation: NVD CVE-2016-6662)(Citation: CIS Multiple SMB Vulnerabilities)(Citation: US-CERT TA18-106A Network Infrastructure Devices 2018)(Citation: Cisco Blog Legacy Device Attacks)(Citation: NVD CVE-2014-7169) On ESXi infrastructure, adversaries may exploit exposed OpenSLP services; they may alternatively exploit exposed VMware vCenter servers.(Citation: Recorded Future ESXiArgs Ransomware 2023)(Citation: Ars Technica VMWare Code Execution Vulnerability 2021) Depending on the flaw being exploited, this may also involve [Exploitation for Defense Evasion](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1211) or [Exploitation for Client Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1203).

If an application is hosted on cloud-based infrastructure and/or is containerized, then exploiting it may lead to compromise of the underlying instance or container. This can allow an adversary a path to access the cloud or container APIs (e.g., via the [Cloud Instance Metadata API](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1552/005)), exploit container host access via [Escape to Host](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1611), or take advantage of weak identity and access management policies.

Adversaries may also exploit edge network infrastructure and related appliances, specifically targeting devices that do not support robust host-based defenses.(Citation: Mandiant Fortinet Zero Day)(Citation: Wired Russia Cyberwar)

2852.name: Bypass ASLR and DEP
2852.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may modify file attributes and subvert Gatekeeper functionality to evade user prompts and execute untrusted programs. Gatekeeper is a set of technologies that act as layer of Apple’s security model to ensure only trusted applications are executed on a host. Gatekeeper was built on top of File Quarantine in Snow Leopard (10.6, 2009) and has grown to include Code Signing, security policy compliance, Notarization, and more. Gatekeeper also treats applications running for the first time differently than reopened applications.(Citation: TheEclecticLightCompany Quarantine and the flag)(Citation: TheEclecticLightCompany apple notarization )

Based on an opt-in system, when files are downloaded an extended attribute (xattr) called `com.apple.quarantine` (also known as a quarantine flag) can be set on the file by the application performing the download. Launch Services opens the application in a suspended state. For first run applications with the quarantine flag set, Gatekeeper executes the following functions:

1. Checks extended attribute – Gatekeeper checks for the quarantine flag, then provides an alert prompt to the user to allow or deny execution.(Citation: OceanLotus for OS X)(Citation: 20 macOS Common Tools and Techniques)

2. Checks System Policies - Gatekeeper checks the system security policy, allowing execution of apps downloaded from either just the App Store or the App Store and identified developers.

3. Code Signing – Gatekeeper checks for a valid code signature from an Apple Developer ID.

4. Notarization - Using the `api.apple-cloudkit.com` API, Gatekeeper reaches out to Apple servers to verify or pull down the notarization ticket and ensure the ticket is not revoked. Users can override notarization, which will result in a prompt of executing an “unauthorized app” and the security policy will be modified.

Adversaries can subvert one or multiple security controls within Gatekeeper checks through logic errors (e.g. [Exploitation for Defense Evasion](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1211)), unchecked file types, and external libraries. For example, prior to macOS 13 Ventura, code signing and notarization checks were only conducted on first launch, allowing adversaries to write malicious executables to previously opened applications in order to bypass Gatekeeper security checks.(Citation: theevilbit gatekeeper bypass 2021)(Citation: Application Bundle Manipulation Brandon Dalton)

Applications and files loaded onto the system from a USB flash drive, optical disk, external hard drive, from a drive shared over the local network, or using the curl command may not set the quarantine flag. Additionally, it is possible to avoid setting the quarantine flag using [Drive-by Compromise](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1189).

It subverts Apple's Gatekeeper security by manipulating the `com.apple.quarantine` extended attribute (xattr) or exploiting logic errors in its checks. Prior to macOS 13, adversaries could write malicious code into previously opened applications to bypass code signing and notarization checks executed only on first launch. Files from external media or via `curl` may not set the quarantine flag, enabling execution. The intrusion-set APT3 has been associated with this technique.[/profile]

ASLR (Address Space Layout Randomization) randomizes memory addresses to hinder exploitation, while DEP (Data Execution Prevention) prevents code execution from data-only memory regions. Attackers bypass these by using memory disclosure vulnerabilities to leak addresses and defeat ASLR, then employing techniques like Return-Oriented Programming (ROP) to execute code within existing executable memory regions, circumventing DEP. This is often part of the Defense Evasion tactic and targets platforms like Windows and Linux.[/profile]

2854.name: Memory Overwrite
2854.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may modify a process's in-memory arguments to change its name in order to appear as a legitimate or benign process. On Linux, the operating system stores command-line arguments in the process’s stack and passes them to the `main()` function as the `argv` array. The first element, `argv[0]`, typically contains the process name or path - by default, the command used to actually start the process (e.g., `cat /etc/passwd`). By default, the Linux `/proc` filesystem uses this value to represent the process name. The `/proc/<PID>/cmdline` file reflects the contents of this memory, and tools like `ps` use it to display process information. Since arguments are stored in user-space memory at launch, this modification can be performed without elevated privileges. 

During runtime, adversaries can erase the memory used by all command-line arguments for a process, overwriting each argument string with null bytes. This removes evidence of how the process was originally launched. They can then write a spoofed string into the memory region previously occupied by `argv[0]` to mimic a benign command, such as `cat resolv.conf`. The new command-line string is reflected in `/proc/<PID>/cmdline` and displayed by tools like `ps`.(Citation: Sandfly BPFDoor 2022)(Citation: Microsoft XorDdos Linux Stealth 2022)

By overwriting the `argv[0]` string in user-space memory with null bytes and then a spoofed benign command like `cat resolv.conf`, the technique alters the process name displayed in `/proc/<PID>/cmdline` and tools such as `ps`, enabling evasion without requiring elevated privileges. This activity has been associated with intrusion sets like APT3.

The method is used for defense evasion, persistence, and impact, targeting platforms like Linux and Windows by directly manipulating in-memory data or non-volatile firmware storage.

2874.name: Scanbox framework

Reconnaissance Scanning Tools Used by Chinese Threat Actors and Those Available in Open Source

2875.name: Watering Hole Phishing
2875.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may send phishing messages to gain access to victim systems. All forms of phishing are electronically delivered social engineering. Phishing can be targeted, known as spearphishing. In spearphishing, a specific individual, company, or industry will be targeted by the adversary. More generally, adversaries can conduct non-targeted phishing, such as in mass malware spam campaigns.

Adversaries may send victims emails containing malicious attachments or links, typically to execute malicious code on victim systems. Phishing may also be conducted via third-party services, like social media platforms. Phishing may also involve social engineering techniques, such as posing as a trusted source, as well as evasive techniques such as removing or manipulating emails or metadata/headers from compromised accounts being abused to send messages (e.g., [Email Hiding Rules](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1564/008)).(Citation: Microsoft OAuth Spam 2022)(Citation: Palo Alto Unit 42 VBA Infostealer 2014) Another way to accomplish this is by [Email Spoofing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1672)(Citation: Proofpoint-spoof) the identity of the sender, which can be used to fool both the human recipient as well as automated security tools,(Citation: cyberproof-double-bounce) or by including the intended target as a party to an existing email thread that includes malicious files or links (i.e., "thread hijacking").(Citation: phishing-krebs)

Victims may also receive phishing messages that instruct them to call a phone number where they are directed to visit a malicious URL, download malware,(Citation: sygnia Luna Month)(Citation: CISA Remote Monitoring and Management Software) or install adversary-accessible remote management tools onto their computer (i.e., [User Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204)).(Citation: Unit42 Luna Moth)
2875.profile: [profile]Watering Hole Phishing is a targeted variant of the phishing technique, often associated with MITRE ATT&CK ID T1566 under the Initial Access tactic, primarily targeting web platforms. It operates by compromising or creating legitimate websites frequented by a specific community to serve as a trap; when a targeted user visits this "watering hole," malicious scripts automatically execute to scan for and exploit vulnerabilities in the browser or plugins, delivering malware to gain a foothold on the victim's system. This method is distinct from general phishing as it relies on strategic web compromise to passively infect users based on their browsing habits, and it is linked to threat groups like APT3. Supplementary details note it is also referred to as a strategic web compromise attack.[/profile]
2875.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Watering Hole Phishing is a targeted technique where adversaries compromise websites frequented by a specific community or industry to infect visitors. It falls under the Initial Access tactic (T1583.008 in MITRE ATT&CK). The attack involves injecting malicious scripts into legitimate sites, which then exploit vulnerabilities in a visitor's browser or plugins to deliver and execute malicious code, often without the user's direct interaction beyond visiting the compromised page. This method is also known as a strategic web compromise.

2876.name: Strategic Network Compromises (SWCS)
2876.profile: [profile]Strategic Network Compromises (SWCS) is a technique, also known as a watering hole attack, which falls under the Initial Access tactic (TA0001) and targets client platforms. It involves compromising a legitimate website frequented by a specific target community. Adversaries inject malicious scripts into the site, which then automatically execute when a user visits, scanning the browser and plugins for vulnerabilities to deliver exploit code and gain code execution on the user's system. This method is distinct from server exploitation and is used by groups like APT3.
2876.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Strategic Network Compromises (SWCS), also known as watering hole attacks, is a technique within the Initial Access tactic (T1189) targeting client platforms. It involves compromising legitimate websites frequented by a specific target community to host malicious scripts. When a user visits the site, these scripts automatically execute, scanning the browser and plugins for vulnerabilities to deliver exploit code and gain code execution on the victim's internal network. This method is distinct from server-side exploits and is used by numerous threat groups including APT28, Lazarus Group, and Turla.

2878.name: Plugindetect
2878.profile: [profile]Plugindetect, also known as PluginDetect, is attributed to the APT3 intrusion set. Its key technical behavior involves using a JavaScript library to collect information about browser plugins installed on a target system and exfiltrating this data to a command-and-control server. It also attempts to install a persistent tracking cookie (an "evercookie") to monitor user activity across the internet, indicating a focus on web browser platforms for intelligence gathering.
2878.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Plugindetect is a JavaScript library used to collect information about browser plugins and install tracking cookies. It is associated with the Turla group and operates by downloading the PluginDetect library to gather plugin data and deploy "evercookies" for cross-site tracking, with collected information exfiltrated to a command-and-control server.

2879.name: 0.4 Second Delay
2879.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may employ various time-based methods to evade detection and analysis. These techniques often exploit system clocks, delays, or timing mechanisms to obscure malicious activity, blend in with benign activity, and avoid scrutiny. Adversaries can perform this behavior within virtualization/sandbox environments or natively on host systems. 

Adversaries may utilize programmatic `sleep` commands or native system scheduling functionality, for example [Scheduled Task/Job](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1053). Benign commands or other operations may also be used to delay malware execution or ensure prior commands have had time to execute properly. Loops or otherwise needless repetitions of commands, such as `ping`, may be used to delay malware execution and potentially exceed time thresholds of automated analysis environments.(Citation: Revil Independence Day)(Citation: Netskope Nitol) Another variation, commonly referred to as API hammering, involves making various calls to Native API functions in order to delay execution (while also potentially overloading analysis environments with junk data).(Citation: Joe Sec Nymaim)(Citation: Joe Sec Trickbot)
2879.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique "Execution Guardrails" (T1480), under the Defense Evasion tactic for Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves adversaries using time-based delays, such as programmatic sleep commands, repeated benign commands like `ping`, or API hammering (making numerous Native API calls), to evade detection by delaying malware execution and potentially exceeding the time thresholds of automated sandbox analysis environments. The group APT3 has been associated with this behavior.[/profile]
2879.profile_without_enhance: [profile]0.4 Second Delay is a specific implementation of the MITRE ATT&CK technique Delay Execution (T1678) under the Defense Evasion tactic, primarily for Windows and Linux platforms. It functions by inserting a 0.4-second pause, often via a programmatic `sleep` command, to evade automated sandbox analysis that may have short time thresholds. This brief delay helps malicious code blend in or ensure prior commands execute before proceeding.

2880.name: Obfuscation with Hexadecimal Strings
2880.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may obfuscate command and control traffic to make it more difficult to detect.(Citation: Bitdefender FunnyDream Campaign November 2020) Command and control (C2) communications are hidden (but not necessarily encrypted) in an attempt to make the content more difficult to discover or decipher and to make the communication less conspicuous and hide commands from being seen. This encompasses many methods, such as adding junk data to protocol traffic, using steganography, or impersonating legitimate protocols.
2880.profile: [profile]Obfuscation with Hexadecimal Strings is a technique for hiding command and control (C2) traffic to evade detection, aligning with the MITRE ATT&CK framework under Tactic: Command and Control. It operates by encoding data within network protocols using hexadecimal strings, making the communication less conspicuous without necessarily employing encryption. This method is distinct from broader obfuscation techniques like command-line obfuscation (T1027.010) or file encryption (T1027.013), as it specifically manipulates protocol data representation. Associated entities include the Gamaredon Group and malware like Plugindetect.[/profile]
2880.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Obfuscation with Hexadecimal Strings is a sub-technique of Command Obfuscation (T1027.010) under the Defense Evasion tactic, primarily used on Windows and Linux platforms. It involves representing commands or data as hexadecimal strings to bypass signature-based detection. This method is often implemented by converting ASCII characters to their hex equivalents, which are then interpreted by scripting interpreters like PowerShell using commands such as `-EncodedCommand` to execute the deobfuscated payload.

2881.name: Automated Variable Substitution
2881.uncertain_mes:
Once established within a system or network, an adversary may use automated techniques for collecting internal data. Methods for performing this technique could include use of a [Command and Scripting Interpreter](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059) to search for and copy information fitting set criteria such as file type, location, or name at specific time intervals. 

In cloud-based environments, adversaries may also use cloud APIs, data pipelines, command line interfaces, or extract, transform, and load (ETL) services to automatically collect data.(Citation: Mandiant UNC3944 SMS Phishing 2023) 

This functionality could also be built into remote access tools. 

This technique may incorporate use of other techniques such as [File and Directory Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1083) and [Lateral Tool Transfer](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1570) to identify and move files, as well as [Cloud Service Dashboard](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1538) and [Cloud Storage Object Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1619) to identify resources in cloud environments.
2881.profile: [profile]Automated Collection, identified as T1119 under the Collection tactic, operates across Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves using automated scripts or command-line interpreters to search for and copy data based on criteria like file type or name at scheduled intervals. In cloud environments, this extends to using APIs, CLIs, or ETL services for automated data gathering. The technique often incorporates File and Directory Discovery (T1083) and Cloud Storage Object Discovery (T1619) to locate target files and resources.[profile]
2881.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Automated Variable Substitution is a technique used to evade detection and analysis by automatically replacing variable names, strings, or other identifiers in malicious code or scripts with randomized or obfuscated values. This process can be performed dynamically during execution or as part of a build process, making static signature-based detection less effective. The technique is platform-agnostic and may be employed in various scripting or programming environments to hinder reverse engineering and bypass security controls that rely on identifying specific code patterns.

2883.name: White-List Visitors
2883.profile: [profile]White-List Visitors is a technique where adversaries attempt to enumerate or identify trusted entities, such as cloud accounts or application windows, to understand the system environment and identify targets for evasion or further access. It is associated with groups like APT3 and involves using system commands or APIs, such as PowerShell cmdlets like `Get-MsolRoleMember` for Office 365 or `aws iam list-users` for AWS, to discover accounts and permissions. This supports persistence and privilege escalation by mapping trusted resources.[/profile]

Based on the provided context, the retrieved information describes unrelated techniques such as Cloud Account Discovery (T1087.004), Application Window Discovery (T1010), and Additional Email Delegate Permissions (T1098.002). These techniques involve enumerating accounts, discovering open windows, and manipulating email permissions, respectively, but none provide specific technical mechanics or context for the named entity "White-List Visitors." Therefore, a standard MITRE ID, Tactic, Platform, or distinct technical procedure cannot be defined from this input.

2884.name: TTPS
2884.profile: [profile]The entity 'TTPS' is directly connected to the intrusion-set APT3. Retrieved information provides context on three distinct MITRE ATT&CK techniques. T1079, multilayer encryption, describes C2 communication using multiple encryption layers, often tunneling custom encryption within protocols like HTTPS. T1597.001 involves adversaries searching private threat intelligence vendor data for targeting information, which can reveal trends, attribution, or successful TTPs. T1480.001, environmental keying, is an execution guardrail where payloads are cryptographically constrained to specific target environments, using values from network shares, software versions, or IP addresses to derive decryption keys, making analysis and detection difficult, and is associated with groups like APT41 and Equation.[/profile]
2884.profile_without_enhance: [profile]TTPS is a generic placeholder term for Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures, not a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique. The retrieved information describes related concepts but not the entity itself. Environmental Keying (T1480.001) is an Execution Guardrail technique that cryptographically derives decryption keys from target-specific environmental values (like network shares, system time, or IP addresses) to constrain payload execution to a specific environment, thereby evading analysis and protecting adversary TTPs.

2885.name: Server-Side Code
2885.profile: [profile]Server-Side Code is a term for malicious code executed on a compromised server, often a simple web shell. It is notably used by threat groups including APT3, APT41, Emissary Panda, Gallium, Hafnium, Hurricane Panda, and Leviathan. A key example is the China Chopper backdoor, which uses a single line of code like `<?php @eval($_POST['test']);?>` for .NET ASP or PHP platforms to enable remote command execution. It is also associated with exploitation techniques like server-side template injection, as seen in attacks leveraging vulnerabilities in VMware Workspace ONE.
2885.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Server-Side Code, also known as China Chopper, is a simple web shell with server-side code often consisting of a single line, such as the PHP example `<?php @eval($_POST['test']);?>`. It supports platforms like .NET Active Server Pages and PHP. It has been used by groups including APT41, Emissary Panda, Gallium, Hafnium, Hurricane Panda, and Leviathan.

2890.name: APT
2890.profile: [profile]The entity 'APT' is a generic term for Advanced Persistent Threat, not a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on neighbor and retrieved information, it is associated with intrusion sets like APT3 and the Lazarus Group, which employ techniques such as KernelCallbackTable hijacking (T1574.013) for process injection and evasion, file deletion (T1107) for footprint removal, and exfiltration to code repositories (T1567.001) for data theft. These groups operate across Windows platforms, utilizing specific technical mechanics like modifying the KernelCallbackTable via the PEB and WriteProcessMemory to execute malicious payloads.

KernelCallbackTable Hijacking (T1574.013) is an execution flow hijack where adversaries modify a process's callback table in the PEB, often via `WriteProcessMemory`, to trigger a malicious payload when a specific Windows message is sent, a method used by groups like Lazarus. It functions as a backdoor for remote access and control.]

2898.name: Credential Theft
2898.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may steal monetary resources from targets through extortion, social engineering, technical theft, or other methods aimed at their own financial gain at the expense of the availability of these resources for victims. Financial theft is the ultimate objective of several popular campaign types including extortion by ransomware,(Citation: FBI-ransomware) business email compromise (BEC) and fraud,(Citation: FBI-BEC) "pig butchering,"(Citation: wired-pig butchering) bank hacking,(Citation: DOJ-DPRK Heist) and exploiting cryptocurrency networks.(Citation: BBC-Ronin) 

Adversaries may [Compromise Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1586) to conduct unauthorized transfers of funds.(Citation: Internet crime report 2022) In the case of business email compromise or email fraud, an adversary may utilize [Impersonation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1656) of a trusted entity. Once the social engineering is successful, victims can be deceived into sending money to financial accounts controlled by an adversary.(Citation: FBI-BEC) This creates the potential for multiple victims (i.e., compromised accounts as well as the ultimate monetary loss) in incidents involving financial theft.(Citation: VEC)

Extortion by ransomware may occur, for example, when an adversary demands payment from a victim after [Data Encrypted for Impact](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1486) (Citation: NYT-Colonial) and [Exfiltration](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0010) of data, followed by threatening to leak sensitive data to the public unless payment is made to the adversary.(Citation: Mandiant-leaks) Adversaries may use dedicated leak sites to distribute victim data.(Citation: Crowdstrike-leaks)

Due to the potentially immense business impact of financial theft, an adversary may abuse the possibility of financial theft and seeking monetary gain to divert attention from their true goals such as [Data Destruction](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1485) and business disruption.(Citation: AP-NotPetya)
2898.profile: [profile]Credential Theft is a broad objective, not a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique. The provided data describes Financial Theft (T1657), an adversary objective under the Impact tactic. It involves stealing monetary resources through methods like ransomware extortion, business email compromise, and unauthorized fund transfers from compromised accounts. Groups like FIN7 and APT29 are associated with such activities.[/profile]

It involves purchasing technical data, tools, and vulnerability information from sources like dark web markets to support reconnaissance, capability development, and initial access. 2901.name: Conspiracy to Commit Computer Fraud and Abuse
2901.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may circumvent mechanisms designed to control elevate privileges to gain higher-level permissions. Most modern systems contain native elevation control mechanisms that are intended to limit privileges that a user can perform on a machine. Authorization has to be granted to specific users in order to perform tasks that can be considered of higher risk.(Citation: TechNet How UAC Works)(Citation: sudo man page 2018) An adversary can perform several methods to take advantage of built-in control mechanisms in order to escalate privileges on a system.(Citation: OSX Keydnap malware)(Citation: Fortinet Fareit)

It involves adversaries circumventing native system controls like Windows User Account Control (UAC) or Unix sudo mechanisms to gain higher-level permissions without proper authorization. This technique is associated with threat groups such as UNC3886 and APT3, who exploit these built-in safeguards to escalate privileges on a compromised system.

[Mimikatz](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0002) can be used to extract secrets from memory.(Citation: ired Dumping LSA Secrets)

2905.name: Boyu Security
2905.uncertain_mes: [Ajax Security Team](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0130) is a group that has been active since at least 2010 and believed to be operating out of Iran. By 2014 [Ajax Security Team](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0130) transitioned from website defacement operations to malware-based cyber espionage campaigns targeting the US defense industrial base and Iranian users of anti-censorship technologies.(Citation: FireEye Operation Saffron Rose 2013)
2905.profile: [profile]Boyu Security, also known as Ajax Security Team, is an intrusion set believed to be operating from Iran. Its arsenal includes tools and malware associated with APT3, indicating potential overlaps or shared resources. The group transitioned from website defacement to conducting malware-based cyber espionage campaigns, primarily targeting the U.S. defense industrial base and Iranian users of anti-censorship technologies. Its operations are motivated by espionage and information control objectives.
2905.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The standardized APT group is APT3, also known as Boyu Security, Buckeye, Gothic Panda, UPS, Boyusec, Brocade Typhoon, Bronze Mayfair, TG-0110, Red Sylvan, Boron, and Group 6. Its key malware and tools include the PIRPI backdoor (CookieCutter), the Scanbox reconnaissance framework, and custom utilities like RemoteCMD and OSInfo. Distinctive TTPs involve sophisticated anti-analysis techniques like runtime ROP generation and hexadecimal string obfuscation, and the heavy use of zero-day exploits (e.g., CVE-2014-1776, CVE-2015-3113) in Internet Explorer and Adobe Flash. The group is attributed to China and is believed to be a cyber espionage unit linked to the Ministry of State Security, with infrastructure connections to Guangdong Province. It historically targeted U.S. and Western government, defense, diplomatic, and technology sectors for espionage, but has shown a noted operational shift toward political entities in Hong Kong.
2905.profile_without_enhance_0: [profile]Boyu Security is a suspected Chinese state-sponsored APT group, also known as APT41, Barium, and Winnti, which is distinct from the similarly named 'teamtnt' or 'void balaur' clusters. The group is known for its use of custom malware like KEYPLUG and its sophisticated supply chain compromise techniques. Its operations are primarily motivated by cyber espionage and financial gain, targeting a wide range of sectors including technology, telecommunications, and video game industries across Southeast Asia, Europe, and the United States.
2905.profile_without_enhance_0_no_hsage: [profile]Boyu Security is a suspected Chinese state-sponsored advanced persistent threat (APT) group, also known as APT41, Barium, Winnti, and Wicked Panda. The group is attributed to China and primarily targets a broad range of sectors including technology, telecommunications, and government entities globally, with motivations encompassing both cyber espionage and financially driven operations.

2916.name: DNS Hijacking
2916.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may communicate using the Domain Name System (DNS) application layer protocol to avoid detection/network filtering by blending in with existing traffic. Commands to the remote system, and often the results of those commands, will be embedded within the protocol traffic between the client and server. 

The DNS protocol serves an administrative function in computer networking and thus may be very common in environments. DNS traffic may also be allowed even before network authentication is completed. DNS packets contain many fields and headers in which data can be concealed. Often known as DNS tunneling, adversaries may abuse DNS to communicate with systems under their control within a victim network while also mimicking normal, expected traffic.(Citation: PAN DNS Tunneling)(Citation: Medium DnsTunneling)

DNS beaconing may be used to send commands to remote systems via DNS queries. A DNS beacon is created by tunneling DNS traffic (i.e. [Protocol Tunneling](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1572)). The commands may be embedded into different DNS records, for example, TXT or A records.(Citation: OilRig Uses Updated BONDUPDATER to Target Middle Eastern Government) DNS beacons may be difficult to detect because the beacons infrequently communicate with infected devices.(Citation: DNS Beacons) Infrequent communication conceals the malicious DNS traffic with normal DNS traffic.
2916.profile: [profile]DNS Hijacking (T1071.004) is an Application Layer Protocol technique used for Command and Control, primarily on Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. Adversaries abuse the DNS protocol to tunnel command and control traffic, embedding commands and results within DNS queries and responses, often using TXT or A records, to blend with normal administrative traffic and bypass network filtering. This method, also known as DNS tunneling or beaconing, is used by groups like OilRig and APT3 to maintain covert communication channels.[/profile]
2916.profile_without_enhance: [profile]DNS Hijacking is a technique where adversaries compromise or manipulate DNS infrastructure to redirect traffic. This is often achieved by compromising third-party DNS servers to alter DNS records, enabling the redirection of an organization's traffic to adversary-controlled infrastructure for credential theft or further attacks. It can also involve domain registration hijacking by social engineering or exploiting account access, or subdomain hijacking by taking control of orphaned DNS entries. This technique facilitates initial access, credential access, and collection by subverting the fundamental trust in domain name resolution.

2917.name: Use-After-Free Condition
2917.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may use alternate authentication material, such as password hashes, Kerberos tickets, and application access tokens, in order to move laterally within an environment and bypass normal system access controls. 

Authentication processes generally require a valid identity (e.g., username) along with one or more authentication factors (e.g., password, pin, physical smart card, token generator, etc.). Alternate authentication material is legitimately generated by systems after a user or application successfully authenticates by providing a valid identity and the required authentication factor(s). Alternate authentication material may also be generated during the identity creation process.(Citation: NIST Authentication)(Citation: NIST MFA)

Caching alternate authentication material allows the system to verify an identity has successfully authenticated without asking the user to reenter authentication factor(s). Because the alternate authentication must be maintained by the system—either in memory or on disk—it may be at risk of being stolen through [Credential Access](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0006) techniques. By stealing alternate authentication material, adversaries are able to bypass system access controls and authenticate to systems without knowing the plaintext password or any additional authentication factors.
2917.profile: [profile]The entity "Use-After-Free Condition" is a software vulnerability exploitation technique. It is logically related to the general "Exploit" attack pattern. This condition occurs when a program continues to use a pointer to a memory location after that memory has been freed, which can lead to program crashes, unexpected behavior, or code execution. Exploiting this flaw can cause an application or system to crash, potentially leading to a denial-of-service condition or allowing adversaries to execute arbitrary code.
2917.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Use-After-Free Condition is a software vulnerability exploitation technique where an adversary leverages a program's incorrect handling of memory after it has been freed, often leading to arbitrary code execution or system crashes. This is a specific implementation of the broader Exploit concept, targeting memory corruption flaws in applications or systems to achieve initial access, privilege escalation, or denial of service.[/profile]

2918.name: Extract and Decrypt Payloads from Animated GIF Images
2918.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may embed payloads within other files to conceal malicious content from defenses. Otherwise seemingly benign files (such as scripts and executables) may be abused to carry and obfuscate malicious payloads and content. In some cases, embedded payloads may also enable adversaries to [Subvert Trust Controls](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1553) by not impacting execution controls such as digital signatures and notarization tickets.(Citation: Sentinel Labs) 

Adversaries may embed payloads in various file formats to hide payloads.(Citation: Microsoft Learn) This is similar to [Steganography](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/003), though does not involve weaving malicious content into specific bytes and patterns related to legitimate digital media formats.(Citation: GitHub PSImage) 

For example, adversaries have been observed embedding payloads within or as an overlay of an otherwise benign binary.(Citation: Securelist Dtrack2) Adversaries have also been observed nesting payloads (such as executables and run-only scripts) inside a file of the same format.(Citation: SentinelLabs reversing run-only applescripts 2021) 

Embedded content may also be used as [Process Injection](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1055) payloads used to infect benign system processes.(Citation: Trend Micro) These embedded then injected payloads may be used as part of the modules of malware designed to provide specific features such as encrypting C2 communications in support of an orchestrator module. For example, an embedded module may be injected into default browsers, allowing adversaries to then communicate via the network.(Citation: Malware Analysis Report ComRAT)
2918.profile: [profile]The entity "Extract and Decrypt Payloads from Animated GIF Images" is a specific technique for obfuscation, aligning with MITRE ATT&CK sub-technique T1027.009 "Embedded Payloads" under the Defense Evasion tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. This technique involves concealing malicious payloads within the data of otherwise benign GIF image files, which are then extracted and decrypted to execute the hidden code, bypassing security controls that may not inspect media file contents for embedded executable data. It has been associated with groups like APT3, Lazarus Group, TA577, and Moonstone Sleet.[/profile]
2918.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The technique "Extract and Decrypt Payloads from Animated GIF Images" is a sub-technique of Obfuscated Files or Information (T1027). It falls under the Defense Evasion tactic and applies to multiple platforms. This method involves adversaries embedding malicious payloads within the data of animated GIF files to conceal them. The payload is typically encrypted or encoded within the image's frames or appended data. To execute the malware, a separate loader or stager must first extract the hidden data from the GIF file and then decrypt or decode it in memory, bypassing file-based detection mechanisms.

2919.name: 5119 Shellcode
2919.profile: [profile]5119 Shellcode is a shellcode malware associated with APT3 and potentially APT28 (Sednit), exploiting the Adobe Flash vulnerability CVE-2015-5119. Its key technical behavior involves generation and injection, often delivered via malicious LNK files in email campaigns. The target platform is Windows systems through Flash Player. Related infrastructure or tooling includes references to the 'donut' shellcode generator and campaigns like Operation Poison Needles.
2919.profile_without_enhance: [profile]5119 Shellcode is a shellcode payload associated with the CVE-2015-5119 vulnerability. It is notably linked to the APT28 (Sednit) group and has been used in highly-targeted attacks. The primary target platform is Windows. It is referenced in analyses of campaigns like Operation Poison Needles and in reports connecting APT28 to exploits from Hacking Team.

2920.name: 3113 Shellcode
2920.profile: [profile]3113 Shellcode is a shellcode payload associated with the exploitation of CVE-2015-3113. It is attributed to the APT3 intrusion set and is related to the UPS group's Pirpi malware campaigns. The shellcode is delivered via malicious documents exploiting the vulnerability and is technically similar to the Pirpi.2015 payload, which shares overlap with other components from related campaigns. Its target platform is Windows.[/profile]
2920.profile_without_enhance: [profile]3113 Shellcode is a shellcode malware associated with the exploitation of CVE-2015-3113. It is linked to the UPS group and is delivered via malicious documents in campaigns that also exploit CVE-2014-1776.
