Adversaries may also perform DLL substitution, replacing valid DLLs, or target phantom DLLs (non-existent references) to load malicious code. These methods allow execution within trusted processes, often enabling privilege escalation if the hijacked program runs at a higher privilege level.

3038.name: bypass integrity checks
3038.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may employ various system checks to detect and avoid virtualization and analysis environments. This may include changing behaviors based on the results of checks for the presence of artifacts indicative of a virtual machine environment (VME) or sandbox. If the adversary detects a VME, they may alter their malware to disengage from the victim or conceal the core functions of the implant. They may also search for VME artifacts before dropping secondary or additional payloads. Adversaries may use the information learned from [Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1497) during automated discovery to shape follow-on behaviors.(Citation: Deloitte Environment Awareness)

Specific checks will vary based on the target and/or adversary, but may involve behaviors such as [Windows Management Instrumentation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1047), [PowerShell](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001), [System Information Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1082), and [Query Registry](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1012) to obtain system information and search for VME artifacts. Adversaries may search for VME artifacts in memory, processes, file system, hardware, and/or the Registry. Adversaries may use scripting to automate these checks  into one script and then have the program exit if it determines the system to be a virtual environment. 

Checks could include generic system properties such as host/domain name and samples of network traffic. Adversaries may also check the network adapters addresses, CPU core count, and available memory/drive size. Once executed, malware may also use [File and Directory Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1083) to check if it was saved in a folder or file with unexpected or even analysis-related naming artifacts such as `malware`, `sample`, or `hash`.

Other common checks may enumerate services running that are unique to these applications, installed programs on the system, manufacturer/product fields for strings relating to virtual machine applications, and VME-specific hardware/processor instructions.(Citation: McAfee Virtual Jan 2017) In applications like VMWare, adversaries can also use a special I/O port to send commands and receive output. 
 
Hardware checks, such as the presence of the fan, temperature, and audio devices, could also be used to gather evidence that can be indicative a virtual environment. Adversaries may also query for specific readings from these devices.(Citation: Unit 42 OilRig Sept 2018)
3038.profile: [profile]System Checks, identified as T1497.001 within the Defense Evasion tactic, is a technique used on Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms to detect virtualization and analysis environments. Adversaries automate checks for VME artifacts in memory, processes, the file system, hardware, and the Registry using tools like WMI, PowerShell, and system information queries. Specific checks include examining network adapter addresses, CPU core count, available memory, drive size, and looking for analysis-related folder names like "malware" or "sample". If a virtual environment is detected, the malware may alter its behavior, disengage, or exit to evade analysis.[/profile]
3038.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Bypass Integrity Checks is a Defense Evasion technique where adversaries subvert mechanisms that verify the integrity of software, processes, or systems to execute unauthorized code. This can involve disabling security features, exploiting logic errors in checks, or manipulating files to avoid detection. The technique is used to evade defenses like Apple's Gatekeeper on macOS or Windows integrity controls, allowing malicious programs to run without user prompts or security validation.

3039.name: execute second executable
3039.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may inject portable executables (PE) into processes in order to evade process-based defenses as well as possibly elevate privileges. PE injection is a method of executing arbitrary code in the address space of a separate live process. PE injection is commonly performed by copying code (perhaps without a file on disk) into the virtual address space of the target process before invoking it via a new thread. The write can be performed with native Windows API calls such as VirtualAllocEx and WriteProcessMemory, then invoked with CreateRemoteThread or additional code (ex: shellcode). The displacement of the injected code does introduce the additional requirement for functionality to remap memory references. (Citation: Elastic Process Injection July 2017) Running code in the context of another process may allow access to the process's memory, system/network resources, and possibly elevated privileges. Execution via PE injection may also evade detection from security products since the execution is masked under a legitimate process.
3039.profile: [profile]Execute Second Executable is an alias for the technique Portable Executable Injection (T1055.002) under the Privilege Escalation tactic, primarily targeting Windows. It involves copying a PE file into a target process's memory using Windows API calls like VirtualAllocEx and WriteProcessMemory, then executing it via CreateRemoteThread to run code under a legitimate process's context, evading detection and potentially gaining higher privileges. The intrusion set APT29 has been associated with this technique.[/profile]
3039.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Execute Second Executable is a technique where an adversary runs a secondary, often malicious, program after an initial legitimate process or installer has been invoked. This can be achieved by exploiting weaknesses in file system permissions or installation routines, such as when installers unpack binaries into temporary directories with improper write restrictions, allowing an adversary to replace or place a second executable that is then executed, potentially with elevated privileges. It is related to persistence and privilege escalation tactics, often observed in groups like Mustang Panda.

3040.name: Decryption
3040.profile: [profile]The entity "Decryption" is a core action within adversary tradecraft, not a standalone MITRE ATT&CK technique. It is a functional component used across multiple techniques, including T1573.001 (Symmetric Cryptography) and T1480.001 (Environmental Keying). In these contexts, decryption is the process of converting ciphertext back to plaintext using a key. For symmetric cryptography, the same key is used for both encryption and decryption of C2 traffic. In environmental keying, the decryption key is derived from specific target system values, such as installed software or network configurations, to constrain payload execution to the intended victim and evade analysis. This action is associated with groups like APT29, APT41, and MuddyWater.[/profile]
3040.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Decryption, as a general concept, is not a distinct MITRE ATT&CK technique but a core cryptographic action used within many techniques. It is employed to reverse the encryption applied to data, commands, or payloads to make them functional. This process is central to techniques like Symmetric Cryptography (T1573.001) and Standard Cryptographic Protocol (T1032) for C2 protection, and Environmental Keying (T1480.001) for execution guardrails, where decryption keys are derived from specific target environment values to constrain malware execution and evade analysis.

3047.name: Infecting executables in .torrent files
3047.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may search local file systems and remote file shares for files containing insecurely stored credentials. These can be files created by users to store their own credentials, shared credential stores for a group of individuals, configuration files containing passwords for a system or service, or source code/binary files containing embedded passwords.

It is possible to extract passwords from backups or saved virtual machines through [OS Credential Dumping](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003).(Citation: CG 2014) Passwords may also be obtained from Group Policy Preferences stored on the Windows Domain Controller.(Citation: SRD GPP)

In cloud and/or containerized environments, authenticated user and service account credentials are often stored in local configuration and credential files.(Citation: Unit 42 Hildegard Malware) They may also be found as parameters to deployment commands in container logs.(Citation: Unit 42 Unsecured Docker Daemons) In some cases, these files can be copied and reused on another machine or the contents can be read and then used to authenticate without needing to copy any files.(Citation: Specter Ops - Cloud Credential Storage)
3047.profile: [profile]The entity "Infecting executables in .torrent files" is a technique for delivering malware by embedding malicious code within legitimate executable files distributed via torrents. 3065.name: SAML Token Forgery
3065.uncertain_mes: An adversary may forge SAML tokens with any permissions claims and lifetimes if they possess a valid SAML token-signing certificate.(Citation: Microsoft SolarWinds Steps) The default lifetime of a SAML token is one hour, but the validity period can be specified in the NotOnOrAfter value of the conditions ... element in a token. This value can be changed using the AccessTokenLifetime in a LifetimeTokenPolicy.(Citation: Microsoft SAML Token Lifetimes) Forged SAML tokens enable adversaries to authenticate across services that use SAML 2.0 as an SSO (single sign-on) mechanism.(Citation: Cyberark Golden SAML) An adversary may utilize [Private Keys](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1552/004) to compromise an organization's token-signing certificate to create forged SAML tokens. If the adversary has sufficient permissions to establish a new federation trust with their own Active Directory Federation Services (AD FS) server, they may instead generate their own trusted token-signing certificate.(Citation: Microsoft SolarWinds Customer Guidance) This differs from [Steal Application Access Token](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1528) and other similar behaviors in that the tokens are new and forged by the adversary, rather than stolen or intercepted from legitimate users. An adversary may gain administrative Entra ID privileges if a SAML token is forged which claims to represent a highly privileged account. This may lead to [Use Alternate Authentication Material](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1550), which may bypass multi-factor and other authentication protection mechanisms.(Citation: Microsoft SolarWinds Customer Guidance)
3065.profile: [profile]SAML Token Forgery is technique T1606.002 under the Defense Evasion tactic, targeting Windows, Azure AD, and SaaS platforms. It involves forging new SAML tokens for authentication by compromising a valid SAML token-signing certificate, such as by stealing private keys, or by generating a new trusted certificate after establishing a rogue AD FS federation trust. This allows adversaries to create tokens with arbitrary permissions and extended lifetimes, bypassing MFA to gain administrative access across SAML 2.0 SSO services, as observed with APT29. It is distinct from stealing existing tokens.[/profile]
3065.profile_without_enhance: [profile]SAML Token Forgery is a technique where adversaries forge new SAML tokens to bypass authentication. This technique, known as Golden SAML, requires possession of a valid SAML token-signing certificate, which can be stolen via Private Keys or generated by establishing a new federation trust with a malicious AD FS server. The forged tokens can contain arbitrary permissions and extended lifetimes, enabling adversaries to authenticate as any user across services using SAML 2.0 for SSO, potentially gaining administrative privileges in Entra ID and bypassing multi-factor authentication.

3066.name: Exploiting Public-Facing Applications
3066.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may attempt to exploit a weakness in an Internet-facing host or system to initially access a network. The weakness in the system can be a software bug, a temporary glitch, or a misconfiguration.

Exploited applications are often websites/web servers, but can also include databases (like SQL), standard services (like SMB or SSH), network device administration and management protocols (like SNMP and Smart Install), and any other system with Internet-accessible open sockets.(Citation: NVD CVE-2016-6662)(Citation: CIS Multiple SMB Vulnerabilities)(Citation: US-CERT TA18-106A Network Infrastructure Devices 2018)(Citation: Cisco Blog Legacy Device Attacks)(Citation: NVD CVE-2014-7169) On ESXi infrastructure, adversaries may exploit exposed OpenSLP services; they may alternatively exploit exposed VMware vCenter servers.(Citation: Recorded Future ESXiArgs Ransomware 2023)(Citation: Ars Technica VMWare Code Execution Vulnerability 2021) Depending on the flaw being exploited, this may also involve [Exploitation for Defense Evasion](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1211) or [Exploitation for Client Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1203).

If an application is hosted on cloud-based infrastructure and/or is containerized, then exploiting it may lead to compromise of the underlying instance or container. This can allow an adversary a path to access the cloud or container APIs (e.g., via the [Cloud Instance Metadata API](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1552/005)), exploit container host access via [Escape to Host](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1611), or take advantage of weak identity and access management policies.

Adversaries may also exploit edge network infrastructure and related appliances, specifically targeting devices that do not support robust host-based defenses.(Citation: Mandiant Fortinet Zero Day)(Citation: Wired Russia Cyberwar)

For websites and databases, the OWASP top 10 and CWE top 25 highlight the most common web-based vulnerabilities.(Citation: OWASP Top 10)(Citation: CWE top 25)
3066.profile: [profile]Exploit Public-Facing Application, identified as T1190, is an Initial Access tactic targeting systems with internet-accessible open sockets across multiple platforms. The technique exploits weaknesses like software bugs or misconfigurations in web servers, databases (e.g., SQL), standard services (e.g., SMB, SSH), and network management protocols (e.g., SNMP). It can extend to cloud and containerized infrastructure, potentially leading to compromise of underlying instances and access to cloud APIs. Common vulnerability sources include the OWASP Top 10 and CWE Top 25 lists.[/profile]
3066.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Exploiting Public-Facing Applications is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1190 under the Initial Access tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It involves targeting weaknesses such as software bugs, temporary glitches, or misconfigurations in internet-facing systems like web servers, databases (e.g., SQL), standard services (SMB, SSH), and network device management protocols (SNMP, Smart Install) to gain initial network access. Exploitation can extend to cloud or containerized applications, potentially leading to compromise of the underlying instance and access to cloud APIs, or targeting edge network infrastructure with weak host-based defenses. Common vulnerability sources include the OWASP Top 10 and CWE Top 25 lists for web applications and databases.

3067.name: External Remote Services
3067.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may leverage external-facing remote services to initially access and/or persist within a network. Remote services such as VPNs, Citrix, and other access mechanisms allow users to connect to internal enterprise network resources from external locations. There are often remote service gateways that manage connections and credential authentication for these services. Services such as [Windows Remote Management](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/006) and [VNC](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/005) can also be used externally.(Citation: MacOS VNC software for Remote Desktop)

Access to [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078) to use the service is often a requirement, which could be obtained through credential pharming or by obtaining the credentials from users after compromising the enterprise network.(Citation: Volexity Virtual Private Keylogging) Access to remote services may be used as a redundant or persistent access mechanism during an operation.

Access may also be gained through an exposed service that doesn’t require authentication. In containerized environments, this may include an exposed Docker API, Kubernetes API server, kubelet, or web application such as the Kubernetes dashboard.(Citation: Trend Micro Exposed Docker Server)(Citation: Unit 42 Hildegard Malware)

Adversaries may also establish persistence on network by configuring a Tor hidden service on a compromised system. Adversaries may utilize the tool `ShadowLink` to facilitate the installation and configuration of the Tor hidden service. Tor hidden service is then accessible via the Tor network because `ShadowLink` sets up a .onion address on the compromised system. `ShadowLink` may be used to forward any inbound connections to RDP, allowing the adversaries to have remote access.(Citation: The BadPilot campaign) Adversaries may get `ShadowLink` to persist on a system by masquerading it as an MS Defender application.(Citation: Russian threat actors dig in, prepare to seize on war fatigue)
3067.profile: [profile]External Remote Services is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1133 under the Initial Access tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It involves leveraging external-facing services like VPNs, Citrix, RDP, VNC, or exposed container APIs (e.g., Docker, Kubernetes) to gain network access, often requiring valid accounts obtained through credential theft. Persistence can be established by configuring Tor hidden services using tools like ShadowLink, which sets up a .onion address and can forward RDP connections while masquerading as legitimate software such as MS Defender.
3067.profile_without_enhance: [profile]External Remote Services, identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1133 under the Initial Access tactic, targets Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves adversaries leveraging external-facing services like VPNs, Citrix, RDP, VNC, and exposed container APIs (e.g., Docker, Kubernetes) to gain initial network access or persistence, often using valid accounts obtained through credential theft. Specific implementations include using the tool ShadowLink to configure a Tor hidden service for persistent RDP access, masquerading it as a legitimate application like MS Defender.

3068.name: Credential Misuse
3068.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may use credentials obtained from breach dumps of unrelated accounts to gain access to target accounts through credential overlap. Occasionally, large numbers of username and password pairs are dumped online when a website or service is compromised and the user account credentials accessed. The information may be useful to an adversary attempting to compromise accounts by taking advantage of the tendency for users to use the same passwords across personal and business accounts.

Credential stuffing is a risky option because it could cause numerous authentication failures and account lockouts, depending on the organization's login failure policies.

Typically, management services over commonly used ports are used when stuffing credentials. Commonly targeted services include the following:

* SSH (22/TCP)
* Telnet (23/TCP)
* FTP (21/TCP)
* NetBIOS / SMB / Samba (139/TCP & 445/TCP)
* LDAP (389/TCP)
* Kerberos (88/TCP)
* RDP / Terminal Services (3389/TCP)
* HTTP/HTTP Management Services (80/TCP & 443/TCP)
* MSSQL (1433/TCP)
* Oracle (1521/TCP)
* MySQL (3306/TCP)
* VNC (5900/TCP)

In addition to management services, adversaries may "target single sign-on (SSO) and cloud-based applications utilizing federated authentication protocols," as well as externally facing email applications, such as Office 365.(Citation: US-CERT TA18-068A 2018)
3068.profile: [profile]Credential Stuffing (T1110.004) is a Credential Access technique where adversaries use username/password pairs from unrelated breach dumps to access target accounts by exploiting password reuse. It typically targets management services on common ports like SSH (22), RDP (3389), and HTTP/HTTPS (80/443), as well as cloud applications and SSO systems, and is associated with groups like Chimera and APT29.
3068.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Credential Misuse is a technique where adversaries use stolen or compromised credentials to gain unauthorized access, escalate privileges, or move laterally within a network. This involves abusing obtained credentials, such as those from domain or local accounts, to authenticate to services and systems. The technique leverages password reuse across accounts and can follow credential dumping or stuffing to exploit valid logins for persistent access and evasion.

3069.name: Path Traversal
3069.uncertain_mes: **This technique has been deprecated. Please use [Path Interception by PATH Environment Variable](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1574/007), [Path Interception by Search Order Hijacking](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1574/008), and/or [Path Interception by Unquoted Path](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1574/009).** Path interception occurs when an executable is placed in a specific path so that it is executed by an application instead of the intended target. One example of this was the use of a copy of [cmd](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0106) in the current working directory of a vulnerable application that loads a CMD or BAT file with the CreateProcess function. (Citation: TechNet MS14-019) There are multiple distinct weaknesses or misconfigurations that adversaries may take advantage of when performing path interception: unquoted paths, path environment variable misconfigurations, and search order hijacking. The first vulnerability deals with full program paths, while the second and third occur when program paths are not specified. These techniques can be used for persistence if executables are called on a regular basis, as well as privilege escalation if intercepted executables are started by a higher privileged process. ### Unquoted Paths Service paths (stored in Windows Registry keys) (Citation: Microsoft Subkey) and shortcut paths are vulnerable to path interception if the path has one or more spaces and is not surrounded by quotation marks (e.g., C:\unsafe path with space\program.exe vs. "C:\safe path with space\program.exe"). (Citation: Baggett 2012) An adversary can place an executable in a higher level directory of the path, and Windows will resolve that executable instead of the intended executable. For example, if the path in a shortcut is C:\program files\myapp.exe, an adversary may create a program at C:\program.exe that will be run instead of the intended program. (Citation: SecurityBoulevard Unquoted Services APR 2018) (Citation: SploitSpren Windows Priv Jan 2018) ### PATH Environment Variable Misconfiguration The PATH environment variable contains a list of directories. Certain methods of executing a program (namely using cmd.exe or the command-line) rely solely on the PATH environment variable to determine the locations that are searched for a program when the path for the program is not given. If any directories are listed in the PATH environment variable before the Windows directory, %SystemRoot%\system32 (e.g., C:\Windows\system32), a program may be placed in the preceding directory that is named the same as a Windows program (such as cmd, PowerShell, or Python), which will be executed when that command is executed from a script or command-line. For example, if C:\example path precedes C:\Windows\system32 is in the PATH environment variable, a program that is named net.exe and placed in C:\example path will be called instead of the Windows system "net" when "net" is executed from the command-line. ### Search Order Hijacking Search order hijacking occurs when an adversary abuses the order in which Windows searches for programs that are not given a path. The search order differs depending on the method that is used to execute the program. (Citation: Microsoft CreateProcess) (Citation: Hill NT Shell) (Citation: Microsoft WinExec) However, it is common for Windows to search in the directory of the initiating program before searching through the Windows system directory. An adversary who finds a program vulnerable to search order hijacking (i.e., a program that does not specify the path to an executable) may take advantage of this vulnerability by creating a program named after the improperly specified program and placing it within the initiating program's directory. For example, "example.exe" runs "cmd.exe" with the command-line argument net user. An adversary may place a program called "net.exe" within the same directory as example.exe, "net.exe" will be run instead of the Windows system utility net. In addition, if an adversary places a program called "net.com" in the same directory as "net.exe", then cmd.exe /C net user will execute "net.com" instead of "net.exe" due to the order of executable extensions defined under PATHEXT. (Citation: MSDN Environment Property) Search order hijacking is also a common practice for hijacking DLL loads and is covered in [DLL Search Order Hijacking](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1038).
3069.profile: [profile]Path Interception, also known as T1034, is a deprecated technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework under the Defense Evasion tactic, primarily targeting Windows. It involves placing a malicious executable in a specific directory to be executed instead of the intended program by exploiting path resolution weaknesses. The technique manifests through three specific vulnerabilities: unquoted service or shortcut paths, where an executable like "C:\\program.exe" is placed to intercept a call to "C:\\program files\\myapp.exe"; PATH environment variable misconfiguration, where a directory listed before system folders allows a malicious "net.exe" to be run instead of the system utility; and search order hijacking, where a program like "net.exe" placed in the initiating program's directory is executed due to Windows' file search order. This method can be used for persistence and privilege escalation.[/profile]
3069.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Path Traversal, also known as Directory Traversal, is a technique where an adversary exploits insufficient input validation to access files and directories outside the intended web root or restricted directory. This is typically achieved by manipulating file paths using sequences like "../" (dot-dot-slash) or absolute paths in user-controlled input fields, such as URL parameters or file uploads, to navigate the file system. It is primarily used for initial access, discovery, and collection, allowing unauthorized reading, writing, or execution of files, and commonly affects web applications on multiple platforms.

3070.name: XML External Entity Injection (XXE)
3070.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may use an external proxy to act as an intermediary for network communications to a command and control server to avoid direct connections to their infrastructure. Many tools exist that enable traffic redirection through proxies or port redirection, including [HTRAN](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0040), ZXProxy, and ZXPortMap. (Citation: Trend Micro APT Attack Tools) Adversaries use these types of proxies to manage command and control communications, to provide resiliency in the face of connection loss, or to ride over existing trusted communications paths to avoid suspicion.

External connection proxies are used to mask the destination of C2 traffic and are typically implemented with port redirectors. Compromised systems outside of the victim environment may be used for these purposes, as well as purchased infrastructure such as cloud-based resources or virtual private servers. Proxies may be chosen based on the low likelihood that a connection to them from a compromised system would be investigated. Victim systems would communicate directly with the external proxy on the Internet and then the proxy would forward communications to the C2 server.
3070.profile: [profile]XML External Entity Injection (XXE) is a technique, but the provided data incorrectly describes it using information from MITRE ATT&CK ID T1090.002 "External Proxy." Based on the standard MITRE ATT&CK framework, XXE is a distinct technique for initial access, often on web platforms, where attackers exploit vulnerable XML processors to read files, execute code, or cause denial of service by injecting malicious external entity references. The retrieved and neighbor information is irrelevant to XXE and describes command and control proxy behaviors.[/profile]
3070.profile_without_enhance: [profile]XML External Entity Injection (XXE) is a technique, T1557.001, used in the Initial Access tactic, primarily targeting web applications. It exploits misconfigured XML parsers by injecting malicious external entity references within XML documents. When processed, these entities can force the application to disclose internal files, perform server-side request forgery (SSRF) to access internal systems, or cause denial-of-service. This vulnerability is often found in web services and document parsers that accept XML input.

3071.name: Arbitrary File Read
3071.profile: [profile]Arbitrary File Read is a technique where adversaries exploit vulnerabilities or misconfigurations to read files outside the intended directory, often targeting sensitive system or application files. This can be achieved through path traversal attacks (e.g., using sequences like `../`), exploiting insecure direct object references, or abusing functions in web applications that do not properly validate user input. The technique is associated with the APT29 intrusion set and is used for information discovery and credential access, such as reading configuration files containing passwords.
3071.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Arbitrary File Read is a technique adversaries use to access files on a system without proper authorization, often by exploiting vulnerabilities or misconfigurations in applications or operating systems. The technique can be used to read sensitive data, such as configuration files, credentials, or source code. It is commonly associated with the Credential Access tactic and can be performed on multiple platforms, including Windows, Linux, and macOS. Attackers may use specific commands or scripts to bypass access controls, such as reading files directly from a volume or exploiting web application flaws to read arbitrary files from the server's filesystem.

3072.name: Scanning
3072.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may scan victims for vulnerabilities that can be used during targeting. Vulnerability scans typically check if the configuration of a target host/application (ex: software and version) potentially aligns with the target of a specific exploit the adversary may seek to use.

These scans may also include more broad attempts to [Gather Victim Host Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1592) that can be used to identify more commonly known, exploitable vulnerabilities. Vulnerability scans typically harvest running software and version numbers via server banners, listening ports, or other network artifacts.(Citation: OWASP Vuln Scanning) Information from these scans may reveal opportunities for other forms of reconnaissance (ex: [Search Open Websites/Domains](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1593) or [Search Open Technical Databases](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1596)), establishing operational resources (ex: [Develop Capabilities](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1587) or [Obtain Capabilities](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1588)), and/or initial access (ex: [Exploit Public-Facing Application](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1190)).
3072.profile: [profile]Vulnerability Scanning, identified as T1595.002, is a reconnaissance technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, applicable across multiple platforms. It involves probing target hosts or applications to harvest configuration data like software versions and service banners from listening ports, specifically to identify potential vulnerabilities that align with available exploits. This activity, used by groups like APT29, can inform subsequent phases of an attack, including further reconnaissance or initial access via public-facing application exploits.[/profile]
3072.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Scanning is a broad reconnaissance technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, encompassing specific sub-techniques like Active Scanning (T1595). It falls under the Reconnaissance tactic and applies to multiple platforms. The technique involves adversaries actively probing victim infrastructure via network traffic to gather information, such as by using ICMP pings or scanning IP blocks to identify active hosts and network details. This gathered intelligence supports subsequent targeting activities like vulnerability identification and initial access planning.

3073.name: Persistent Access
3073.profile: [profile]Persistent Access is a deprecated technique (formerly T1108) under the Persistence tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. It involves maintaining network access by deploying multiple remote access tools with different C2 protocols or using credentialed access to external remote services like VPNs. This redundancy ensures that if one access method is detected and blocked, the adversary retains control, often leveraging valid accounts, web shells, or cloud infrastructure for resilient footholds.[/profile]
3073.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Persistent Access is a deprecated MITRE ATT&CK technique (ID: T1108) under the Persistence tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. It involves adversaries maintaining network access by deploying multiple, varied remote access tools with different command-and-control protocols or by establishing credentialed access to external remote services like VPNs. This redundancy ensures that if one access mechanism is detected or removed, others remain functional, allowing continued adversary presence.

3075.name: Anonymising Services
3075.profile: [profile]Anonymising Services is a technique used by adversaries to obscure their network infrastructure and activities. It involves leveraging third-party services like VPNs, proxy servers, Tor, or bulletproof hosting to hide the source of connections, making attribution and detection difficult. This technique supports multiple tactics, including Command and Control and Defense Evasion, and is used by groups such as APT29 to mask their operations across various platforms.[/profile]
3075.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Anonymising Services, identified as T1189 in the MITRE ATT&CK framework under the Initial Access tactic, primarily targets Windows, Linux, and Mac platforms. This technique involves adversaries using services like VPNs, Tor, or web proxies to obfuscate the source of malicious traffic, such as phishing links or drive-by compromises, making attribution and detection more difficult.

3078.name: Organisations Involved in COVID-19 Vaccine Development

3079.name: TLS
3079.profile: [profile]The entity "TLS" is a foundational protocol for secure communication, not a specific MITRE ATT&CK attack pattern. The retrieved information describes how adversaries abuse TLS-related mechanisms. This includes creating or installing self-signed digital certificates (T1587.003, T1608.003) to encrypt command and control traffic or enable adversary-in-the-middle attacks, and impersonating SSL/TLS handshakes (T1001.003) to disguise malicious traffic as legitimate encrypted sessions. The WellMess malware is a known user of such TLS-based obfuscation for its C2 channels.
3079.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "TLS" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique; it is a protocol. The retrieved information describes how adversaries misuse TLS, such as by creating self-signed SSL/TLS certificates to encrypt command and control traffic or enable adversary-in-the-middle attacks, and by impersonating TLS handshakes to disguise malicious traffic as legitimate encrypted communications.

3080.name: DNS
3080.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may communicate using the Domain Name System (DNS) application layer protocol to avoid detection/network filtering by blending in with existing traffic. Commands to the remote system, and often the results of those commands, will be embedded within the protocol traffic between the client and server. 

The DNS protocol serves an administrative function in computer networking and thus may be very common in environments. DNS traffic may also be allowed even before network authentication is completed. DNS packets contain many fields and headers in which data can be concealed. Often known as DNS tunneling, adversaries may abuse DNS to communicate with systems under their control within a victim network while also mimicking normal, expected traffic.(Citation: PAN DNS Tunneling)(Citation: Medium DnsTunneling)

DNS beaconing may be used to send commands to remote systems via DNS queries. A DNS beacon is created by tunneling DNS traffic (i.e. [Protocol Tunneling](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1572)). The commands may be embedded into different DNS records, for example, TXT or A records.(Citation: OilRig Uses Updated BONDUPDATER to Target Middle Eastern Government) DNS beacons may be difficult to detect because the beacons infrequently communicate with infected devices.(Citation: DNS Beacons) Infrequent communication conceals the malicious DNS traffic with normal DNS traffic.
3080.profile: [profile]DNS is the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1071.004 under the Command and Control tactic. It operates across Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. Adversaries abuse the DNS protocol for covert communication by embedding commands and exfiltrated data within DNS query and response traffic, a method known as DNS tunneling. Specific technical mechanics include using DNS beaconing, where commands are concealed within DNS record types like TXT or A records, and infrequent communication to blend with normal network traffic. The WellMess malware is associated with this technique. Threat actors such as OilRig, APT41, and FIN7 have been observed employing it.
3080.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "DNS" is the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1071.004 (Application Layer Protocol: DNS) under the Command and Control tactic for Windows, Linux, and macOS. It involves adversaries using the Domain Name System protocol to communicate with compromised systems, embedding commands and data within DNS traffic fields like TXT or A records to blend with normal administrative traffic and bypass network filtering, a method often called DNS tunneling or beaconing.

3081.name: Hard-coded TLS Certificates
3081.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may buy and/or steal SSL/TLS certificates that can be used during targeting. SSL/TLS certificates are designed to instill trust. They include information about the key, information about its owner's identity, and the digital signature of an entity that has verified the certificate's contents are correct. If the signature is valid, and the person examining the certificate trusts the signer, then they know they can use that key to communicate with its owner.

Adversaries may purchase or steal SSL/TLS certificates to further their operations, such as encrypting C2 traffic (ex: [Asymmetric Cryptography](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1573/002) with [Web Protocols](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1071/001)) or even enabling [Adversary-in-the-Middle](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1557) if the certificate is trusted or otherwise added to the root of trust (i.e. [Install Root Certificate](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1553/004)). The purchase of digital certificates may be done using a front organization or using information stolen from a previously compromised entity that allows the adversary to validate to a certificate provider as that entity. Adversaries may also steal certificate materials directly from a compromised third-party, including from certificate authorities.(Citation: DiginotarCompromise) Adversaries may register or hijack domains that they will later purchase an SSL/TLS certificate for.

Certificate authorities exist that allow adversaries to acquire SSL/TLS certificates, such as domain validation certificates, for free.(Citation: Let's Encrypt FAQ)

After obtaining a digital certificate, an adversary may then install that certificate (see [Install Digital Certificate](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1608/003)) on infrastructure under their control.
3081.profile: [profile]The entity is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1588.004, Digital Certificates, under the Resource Development tactic. It involves adversaries purchasing or stealing SSL/TLS certificates to enable operations like encrypting command and control traffic or facilitating adversary-in-the-middle attacks. Certificates may be acquired using front organizations, stolen validation data from compromised entities, or directly from compromised certificate authorities, including through free domain validation services. Associated threat groups include Sea Turtle, Lazarus Group, and Mustang Panda. The obtained certificates are subsequently installed on controlled infrastructure.
3081.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Hard-coded TLS Certificates is a technique where adversaries embed pre-defined Transport Layer Security certificates within malware or malicious tools. This practice establishes persistence and secure command and control channels by bypassing the need for external certificate validation during runtime. The technique is associated with the Resource Development tactic, primarily used on Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms, enabling malware to maintain covert, encrypted communications with attacker-controlled infrastructure.

3082.name: Linux Shell Command Execution
3082.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may abuse the Windows command shell for execution. The Windows command shell ([cmd](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0106)) is the primary command prompt on Windows systems. The Windows command prompt can be used to control almost any aspect of a system, with various permission levels required for different subsets of commands. The command prompt can be invoked remotely via [Remote Services](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021) such as [SSH](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/004).(Citation: SSH in Windows)

Batch files (ex: .bat or .cmd) also provide the shell with a list of sequential commands to run, as well as normal scripting operations such as conditionals and loops. Common uses of batch files include long or repetitive tasks, or the need to run the same set of commands on multiple systems.

Adversaries may leverage [cmd](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0106) to execute various commands and payloads. Common uses include [cmd](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0106) to execute a single command, or abusing [cmd](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0106) interactively with input and output forwarded over a command and control channel.
3082.profile: [profile]Linux Shell Command Execution is a technique where adversaries abuse Unix shell commands and scripts for execution on Linux, macOS, or ESXi systems. Unix shells (e.g., sh, bash, zsh) are the primary command prompt and can control every aspect of a system, with certain commands requiring elevated privileges. Adversaries may execute various commands or payloads interactively via command and control channels or during lateral movement with SSH, or they may leverage shell scripts to deliver and execute multiple commands for tasks like persistence. This technique is associated with groups like UNC3886, Volt Typhoon, and TeamTNT. The malware WellMail has been linked to its use.[/profile]
3082.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Linux Shell Command Execution is the adversary abuse of Unix shell commands and scripts for execution. This technique, identified as T1059.004 under the Execution tactic, primarily targets Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. Adversaries leverage various shells (e.g., sh, bash, zsh) to run commands or payloads interactively via command and control channels or during lateral movement with SSH. They also use shell scripts for delivering multiple commands, automating repetitive tasks, or establishing persistence by inserting malicious commands into shell configuration files like ~/.bash_profile or ~/.bashrc.

3083.name: Exfiltration over HTTP
3083.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may attempt to exfiltrate data over a USB connected physical device. In certain circumstances, such as an air-gapped network compromise, exfiltration could occur via a USB device introduced by a user. The USB device could be used as the final exfiltration point or to hop between otherwise disconnected systems.
3083.profile: [profile]Exfiltration over HTTP is a technique used for data theft, categorized under the Exfiltration tactic. It involves adversaries stealing data by transmitting it out of a network using the HTTP or HTTPS protocol, often to blend in with normal web traffic. This method can utilize common system utilities like curl or wget to send files to adversary-controlled web servers. The technique is distinct from exfiltration over USB (T1052.001) or Bluetooth and is associated with malware such as SoreFang.
3083.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Exfiltration over HTTP is a data theft technique (ID: T1048.001) within the Exfiltration tactic. It involves stealing data by transmitting it over the HTTP or HTTPS protocol, often using common utilities like curl or PowerShell. This method can blend with legitimate web traffic, especially if data is sent to common web services or cloud storage endpoints, and may leverage encryption via HTTPS for additional protection.

3085.name: Download Second Stage Malware
3085.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may develop malware and malware components that can be used during targeting. Building malicious software can include the development of payloads, droppers, post-compromise tools, backdoors (including backdoored images), packers, C2 protocols, and the creation of infected removable media. Adversaries may develop malware to support their operations, creating a means for maintaining control of remote machines, evading defenses, and executing post-compromise behaviors.(Citation: Mandiant APT1)(Citation: Kaspersky Sofacy)(Citation: ActiveMalwareEnergy)(Citation: FBI Flash FIN7 USB)

During malware development, adversaries may intentionally include indicators aligned with other known actors in order to mislead attribution by defenders.(Citation: Olympic Destroyer)(Citation: Risky Bulletin Threat actor impersonates FSB APT)(Citation: GamaCopy organization)

As with legitimate development efforts, different skill sets may be required for developing malware. The skills needed may be located in-house, or may need to be contracted out. Use of a contractor may be considered an extension of that adversary's malware development capabilities, provided the adversary plays a role in shaping requirements and maintains a degree of exclusivity to the malware.

Some aspects of malware development, such as C2 protocol development, may require adversaries to obtain additional infrastructure. For example, malware developed that will communicate with Twitter for C2, may require use of [Web Services](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1583/006).(Citation: FireEye APT29)
3085.profile: [profile]The entity "Download Second Stage Malware" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the provided context, it describes a post-compromise behavior where an adversary, after initial access, retrieves additional malicious payloads. This is a component of multi-stage attack chains, often involving command and control (C2) infrastructure to deliver more capable remote access tools (RATs) or other malware like SoreFang to the compromised host. This action supports objectives like maintaining persistence and executing further malicious activities.
3085.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The technique "Download Second Stage Malware" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the retrieved context, it describes a post-compromise action where an adversary, after initial access, transfers a more capable secondary payload onto the victim system. This is often facilitated by an initial loader or first-stage malware that calls back to a command and control server to receive instructions and retrieve the second-stage malware, enabling more advanced remote access and persistence. This behavior is a component of broader techniques like Ingress Tool Transfer (T1105) and is commonly associated with multi-stage command and control (T1104).[/profile]

3091.name: polymorphic compiler
3091.profile: [profile]Polymorphic Compiler is a tool used by the APT29 intrusion set. It is a C++ 11/14-based compiler that generates obfuscated code at compile time without external tools or compiler modifications. Its key technical behavior is introducing randomness to create polymorphic code, specifically through the encryption of string literals and the obfuscation of function calls using finite state machines. It is associated with the development of malware like AppleJeus, which is attributed to the Lazarus Group.

It is associated with the Lazarus Group and Mustang Panda, and employs techniques like polymorphic stack strings where all strings are constructed and decoded in the stack area to defeat compiler-level obfuscations.

3109.name: HTTP traffic
3109.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may use traffic signaling to hide open ports or other malicious functionality used for persistence or command and control. Traffic signaling involves the use of a magic value or sequence that must be sent to a system to trigger a special response, such as opening a closed port or executing a malicious task. This may take the form of sending a series of packets with certain characteristics before a port will be opened that the adversary can use for command and control. Usually this series of packets consists of attempted connections to a predefined sequence of closed ports (i.e. [Port Knocking](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1205/001)), but can involve unusual flags, specific strings, or other unique characteristics. After the sequence is completed, opening a port may be accomplished by the host-based firewall, but could also be implemented by custom software.

Adversaries may also communicate with an already open port, but the service listening on that port will only respond to commands or trigger other malicious functionality if passed the appropriate magic value(s).

The observation of the signal packets to trigger the communication can be conducted through different methods. One means, originally implemented by Cd00r (Citation: Hartrell cd00r 2002), is to use the libpcap libraries to sniff for the packets in question. Another method leverages raw sockets, which enables the malware to use ports that are already open for use by other programs.

On network devices, adversaries may use crafted packets to enable [Network Device Authentication](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1556/004) for standard services offered by the device such as telnet.  Such signaling may also be used to open a closed service port such as telnet, or to trigger module modification of malware implants on the device, adding, removing, or changing malicious capabilities.  Adversaries may use crafted packets to attempt to connect to one or more (open or closed) ports, but may also attempt to connect to a router interface, broadcast, and network address IP on the same port in order to achieve their goals and objectives.(Citation: Cisco Synful Knock Evolution)(Citation: Mandiant - Synful Knock)(Citation: Cisco Blog Legacy Device Attacks)  To enable this traffic signaling on embedded devices, adversaries must first achieve and leverage [Patch System Image](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1601/001) due to the monolithic nature of the architecture.

Adversaries may also use the Wake-on-LAN feature to turn on powered off systems. Wake-on-LAN is a hardware feature that allows a powered down system to be powered on, or woken up, by sending a magic packet to it. Once the system is powered on, it may become a target for lateral movement.(Citation: Bleeping Computer - Ryuk WoL)(Citation: AMD Magic Packet)
3109.profile: [profile]Traffic Signaling, identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1205 under the Defense Evasion tactic, operates across multiple platforms. It involves sending a specific sequence or "magic value" to trigger a hidden response, such as opening a closed port for command and control. This is commonly implemented through port knocking, where a predefined series of connection attempts to closed ports is made, or by sending crafted packets with unusual flags or strings to an open port. The technique can use libpcap libraries or raw sockets to sniff for the trigger packets and has been adapted for network devices, requiring a patched system image to enable. Associated groups include APT29, UNC3886, Mustang Panda, and Kimsuky.[/profile]
3109.profile_without_enhance: [profile]HTTP traffic, identified as T1071.001 (Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols) under the Command and Control tactic, is used by adversaries to blend malicious communications with normal network activity. This technique involves embedding command and control data within standard HTTP/S or WebSocket traffic, concealing it within common packet fields and headers to mimic legitimate web requests and evade detection.

3111.name: base64 decoding
3111.profile: [profile]The entity 'base64 decoding' is a specific implementation of the MITRE ATT&CK technique Data Encoding (T1132), falling under the sub-technique Standard Encoding (T1132.001) within the Command and Control tactic. It operates across multiple platforms. This technique involves adversaries using Base64, a standard binary-to-text encoding scheme, to obfuscate command and control traffic, making it more difficult to detect. The related group APT29 has been associated with this behavior.
3111.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Base64 Decoding is a sub-technique (T1132.001) of the Data Encoding technique within the Command and Control tactic. It operates across multiple platforms and involves adversaries decoding Base64-encoded data within command and control traffic to retrieve original payloads or commands, making malicious content appear as benign text-based data during transmission. This technique is commonly employed by threat groups like Hafnium, MuddyWater, and Lazarus Group.

3114.name: Supply Chain Compromise
3114.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may manipulate products or product delivery mechanisms prior to receipt by a final consumer for the purpose of data or system compromise.

Supply chain compromise can take place at any stage of the supply chain including:

* Manipulation of development tools
* Manipulation of a development environment
* Manipulation of source code repositories (public or private)
* Manipulation of source code in open-source dependencies
* Manipulation of software update/distribution mechanisms
* Compromised/infected system images (removable media infected at the factory)(Citation: IBM Storwize)(Citation: Schneider Electric USB Malware) 
* Replacement of legitimate software with modified versions
* Sales of modified/counterfeit products to legitimate distributors
* Shipment interdiction

While supply chain compromise can impact any component of hardware or software, adversaries looking to gain execution have often focused on malicious additions to legitimate software in software distribution or update channels.(Citation: Avast CCleaner3 2018)(Citation: Microsoft Dofoil 2018)(Citation: Command Five SK 2011) Adversaries may limit targeting to a desired victim set or distribute malicious software to a broad set of consumers but only follow up with specific victims.(Citation: Symantec Elderwood Sept 2012)(Citation: Avast CCleaner3 2018)(Citation: Command Five SK 2011) Popular open-source projects that are used as dependencies in many applications may also be targeted as a means to add malicious code to users of the dependency.(Citation: Trendmicro NPM Compromise)

In some cases, adversaries may conduct “second-order” supply chain compromises by leveraging the access gained from an initial supply chain compromise to further compromise a software component.(Citation: Krebs 3cx overview 2023) This may allow the threat actor to spread to even more victims.
3114.profile: [profile]Supply Chain Compromise is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1195 under the Initial Access tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It involves manipulating products or delivery mechanisms before consumer receipt to compromise systems. Key methods include tampering with development tools, source code repositories, open-source dependencies, and software update channels to insert malicious code. Adversaries may conduct broad distribution followed by selective targeting or execute "second-order" compromises by leveraging initial access to further infiltrate the supply chain. Associated groups include OilRig, APT29, Sandworm Team, and Ember Bear.[/profile]
3114.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Supply Chain Compromise is a MITRE ATT&CK technique with ID T1195, categorized under Initial Access. It involves adversaries manipulating products or their delivery mechanisms before they reach the end consumer to compromise data or systems. This can occur at multiple stages, including tampering with development tools, source code repositories, open-source dependencies, or software update channels. Attackers may also compromise hardware supply chains to insert backdoors into devices. The technique allows for broad distribution with selective follow-up on specific victims and is associated with groups like Sandworm Team and OilRig.

3115.name: Malicious RTF Files
3115.uncertain_mes:
An adversary may rely upon a user opening a malicious file in order to gain execution. Users may be subjected to social engineering to get them to open a file that will lead to code execution. This user action will typically be observed as follow-on behavior from [Spearphishing Attachment](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001). Adversaries may use several types of files that require a user to execute them, including .doc, .pdf, .xls, .rtf, .scr, .exe, .lnk, .pif, .cpl, .reg, and .iso.(Citation: Mandiant Trojanized Windows 10)

Adversaries may employ various forms of [Masquerading](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1036) and [Obfuscated Files or Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027) to increase the likelihood that a user will open and successfully execute a malicious file. These methods may include using a familiar naming convention and/or password protecting the file and supplying instructions to a user on how to open it.(Citation: Password Protected Word Docs) 

While [Malicious File](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002) frequently occurs shortly after Initial Access it may occur at other phases of an intrusion, such as when an adversary places a file in a shared directory or on a user's desktop hoping that a user will click on it. This activity may also be seen shortly after [Internal Spearphishing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1534).
3115.profile: [profile]Malicious RTF Files is a sub-technique of User Execution: Malicious File (T1204.002) under the Execution tactic, primarily targeting Windows platforms. It involves adversaries delivering malicious Rich Text Format files, often via spearphishing attachments, that rely on user interaction to open and execute. A specific technical mechanic involves adversaries altering the bytes of an RTF file to insert a template control word field containing a URL, which forces the retrieval and loading of a malicious payload when the document is opened. This method can bypass static detection and has been used by groups like APT29.
3115.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Malicious RTF Files is a technique where adversaries abuse the legitimate template control word within an RTF file to conceal and download malicious code. By altering the bytes of an existing .rtf file to insert a template control word field that includes a URL, adversaries can force the document to retrieve a malicious payload when opened, often delivered via phishing. This method can also enable forced authentication by injecting a credential-prompting URL. It is associated with groups like Gamaredon Group, Dragonfly, and APT28, and is a sub-technique of Template Injection (T1221) under the Defense Evasion tactic, primarily targeting Windows platforms.

It involves adversaries manipulating products or delivery mechanisms before consumer receipt to compromise systems. Specific mechanics include maliciously modifying development tools, source code repositories, open-source dependencies, software update channels, or system images, often to insert backdoors. 3116.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Cyber Kill Chain is a conceptual framework, not a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique, that outlines the stages of a cyber intrusion. The framework's phases include Reconnaissance, Weaponization, Delivery, Exploitation, Installation, Command and Control, and Actions on Objectives (or Operations Against Targets). It provides a structured model for analyzing and defending against attacks by mapping adversary activities from initial planning to achieving their final goal.[/profile]

3117.name: Weaponization
3117.profile: [profile]Weaponization is a phase within the Cyber Kill Chain framework where adversaries prepare a deliverable malicious payload. This involves developing capabilities (T1587) in-house, such as malware or exploits, or obtaining capabilities (T1588) through purchase, theft, or download. The process focuses on creating or acquiring the tools necessary for the subsequent delivery and exploitation phases of an attack.[/profile]
3117.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Weaponization is a stage within the Lockheed Martin Cyber Kill Chain framework, not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique, so it lacks a T-ID and associated tactic or platform. It involves adversaries building or obtaining malicious tools for use in an attack. This includes the in-house development of malware and exploits (as in T1587) or the procurement and theft of such capabilities (as in T1588), preparing them for delivery to a target.

3118.name: Delivery
3118.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may attempt to make payloads difficult to discover and analyze by delivering files to victims as uncompiled code. Text-based source code files may subvert analysis and scrutiny from protections targeting executables/binaries. These payloads will need to be compiled before execution; typically via native utilities such as ilasm.exe(Citation: ATTACK IQ), csc.exe, or GCC/MinGW.(Citation: ClearSky MuddyWater Nov 2018)

Source code payloads may also be encrypted, encoded, and/or embedded within other files, such as those delivered as a [Phishing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566). Payloads may also be delivered in formats unrecognizable and inherently benign to the native OS (ex: EXEs on macOS/Linux) before later being (re)compiled into a proper executable binary with a bundled compiler and execution framework.(Citation: TrendMicro WindowsAppMac)
3118.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique "Obfuscated Files or Information: Compile After Delivery" (T1027.004), categorized under Defense Evasion. It operates across Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. The technique involves delivering payloads as uncompiled source code (e.g., C#, C) to bypass security tools scanning for binaries, then compiling them on the victim system using native utilities like csc.exe, ilasm.exe, or GCC. Payloads may be further obfuscated through encryption or embedding within other files like phishing attachments. Associated threat groups include Gamaredon Group, MuddyWater, Rocke, and Sea Turtle.
3118.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Delivery is a stage in the Cyber Kill Chain framework, not a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique, and therefore lacks a T-ID and defined Tactic or Platform. It conceptually represents the method by which a weaponized payload is transmitted to a target victim's environment. This stage can encompass various technical mechanics, such as using phishing emails, drive-by compromises, or supply chain attacks to introduce malicious code.

3119.name: Installation
3119.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may abuse vSphere Installation Bundles (VIBs) to establish persistent access to ESXi hypervisors. VIBs are collections of files used for software distribution and virtual system management in VMware environments. Since ESXi uses an in-memory filesystem where changes made to most files are stored in RAM rather than in persistent storage, these modifications are lost after a reboot. However, VIBs can be used to create startup tasks, apply custom firewall rules, or deploy binaries that persist across reboots. Typically, administrators use VIBs for updates and system maintenance. VIBs can be broken down into three components:(Citation: VMware VIBs) * VIB payload: a `.vgz` archive containing the directories and files to be created and executed on boot when the VIBs are loaded. * Signature file: verifies the host acceptance level of a VIB, indicating what testing and validation has been done by VMware or its partners before publication of a VIB. By default, ESXi hosts require a minimum acceptance level of PartnerSupported for VIB installation, meaning the VIB is published by a trusted VMware partner. However, privileged users can change the default acceptance level using the `esxcli` command line interface. Additionally, VIBs are able to be installed regardless of acceptance level by using the esxcli software vib install --force command. * XML descriptor file: a configuration file containing associated VIB metadata, such as the name of the VIB and its dependencies. Adversaries may leverage malicious VIB packages to maintain persistent access to ESXi hypervisors, allowing system changes to be executed upon each bootup of ESXi – such as using `esxcli` to enable firewall rules for backdoor traffic, creating listeners on hard coded ports, and executing backdoors.(Citation: Google Cloud Threat Intelligence ESXi VIBs 2022) Adversaries may also masquerade their malicious VIB files as PartnerSupported by modifying the XML descriptor file.(Citation: Google Cloud Threat Intelligence ESXi VIBs 2022)
3119.profile: [profile]The entity "Installation" is specifically the MITRE ATT&CK technique "vSphere Installation Bundles (VIBs)" with ID T1505.006 under the Persistence tactic for the VMware ESXi platform. This technique involves abusing VIB packages, which are archives containing a payload, signature, and XML descriptor, to establish persistent access on ESXi hypervisors. Adversaries install malicious VIBs, often using the `esxcli software vib install --force` command to bypass acceptance levels, to execute backdoors, create listeners, or apply firewall rules that persist across reboots, as ESXi typically uses a non-persistent in-memory filesystem. Groups like UNC3886 have been associated with this activity.
3119.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Installation is a stage within the Cyber Kill Chain framework, not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique, and therefore lacks a T-ID. It follows the Exploitation stage and involves establishing a persistent foothold on a compromised system. This can be achieved through methods like deploying malicious vSphere Installation Bundles (VIBs) on ESXi hypervisors to create persistent startup tasks, or by abusing installer package scripts (e.g., macOS postinstall or Linux maintainer scripts) to execute malicious payloads with elevated permissions during legitimate software installation processes.

3120.name: Network Vulnerability Scanning
3120.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may scan victims for vulnerabilities that can be used during targeting. Vulnerability scans typically check if the configuration of a target host/application (ex: software and version) potentially aligns with the target of a specific exploit the adversary may seek to use.

These scans may also include more broad attempts to [Gather Victim Host Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1592) that can be used to identify more commonly known, exploitable vulnerabilities. Vulnerability scans typically harvest running software and version numbers via server banners, listening ports, or other network artifacts.(Citation: OWASP Vuln Scanning) Information from these scans may reveal opportunities for other forms of reconnaissance (ex: [Search Open Websites/Domains](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1593) or [Search Open Technical Databases](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1596)), establishing operational resources (ex: [Develop Capabilities](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1587) or [Obtain Capabilities](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1588)), and/or initial access (ex: [Exploit Public-Facing Application](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1190)).
3120.profile: [profile]Network Vulnerability Scanning, designated as T1595.002, is a reconnaissance technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, applicable across multiple platforms. It involves actively probing victim infrastructure to identify exploitable software and version misconfigurations by harvesting data from server banners, listening ports, and other network artifacts. This information is used to support subsequent operations like developing exploits or gaining initial access, and is employed by groups including APT29, APT41, and Sandworm Team.[/profile]
3120.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Network Vulnerability Scanning is a reconnaissance technique where adversaries probe victim infrastructure via network traffic to identify exploitable vulnerabilities. This active scanning method checks target host and application configurations, such as software versions, by harvesting information from server banners, listening ports, and other network artifacts. The gathered data can reveal opportunities for further reconnaissance, capability development, or initial access through exploits.

3121.name: Operations Against Targets
3121.profile: [profile]Operations Against Targets is a preparatory technique within the Cyber Kill Chain framework, representing the adversary's phase of executing their plan against selected victims. It follows initial reconnaissance and weaponization stages. The technique involves leveraging established infrastructure, such as compromised social media accounts for persona-based social engineering, or commandeered servers and virtual private servers to host malicious content for operations like phishing, drive-by compromises, and command and control, thereby obscuring the attacker's true origin.
3121.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Operations Against Targets is a conceptual stage within the Cyber Kill Chain framework, representing the final phase of an attack where adversaries achieve their primary goals, such as data exfiltration, destruction, or fraud. It is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique and therefore lacks a T-ID, tactic, or platform. The stage follows Command and Control and involves actions like data theft or system impact, as seen in campaigns by groups like APT29.

3128.name: anti-analysis techniques
3128.profile: [profile]The entity "anti-analysis techniques" is a broad category of adversary behaviors rather than a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique. It encompasses methods used to evade detection and hinder forensic analysis. Retrieved information provides examples of such techniques, including "indicator removal from tools" (T1027.005/T1066), where adversaries modify malware to avoid signature-based detection, and "timestomp" (T1099), which involves altering file timestamps to hide malicious activity. These techniques are employed by groups like APT29 to maintain persistence and avoid discovery by defensive systems.

3129.name: office testing persistence method
3129.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may clear artifacts associated with previously established persistence on a host system to remove evidence of their activity. This may involve various actions, such as removing services, deleting executables, [Modify Registry](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1112), [Plist File Modification](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1647), or other methods of cleanup to prevent defenders from collecting evidence of their persistent presence.(Citation: Cylance Dust Storm) Adversaries may also delete accounts previously created to maintain persistence (i.e. [Create Account](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1136)).(Citation: Talos - Cisco Attack 2022)

In some instances, artifacts of persistence may also be removed once an adversary’s persistence is executed in order to prevent errors with the new instance of the malware.(Citation: NCC Group Team9 June 2020)
3129.profile: [profile]Office Test, identified as T1137.002 within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, is a persistence technique under the Persistence tactic targeting the Windows platform. It operates by abusing the Microsoft Office "Office Test" Registry key, which allows an adversary to specify a malicious DLL that automatically executes whenever an Office application like Word or Excel is started. This key, not created by default during installation, can be added at paths such as HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Office test\Special\Perf. The technique has been associated with threat groups including APT28 (Sofacy Group).[/profile]
3129.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "office testing persistence method" aligns with the MITRE ATT&CK technique "Office Test" (ID: T1137.002) under the Persistence tactic, targeting Windows platforms. It involves abusing the Microsoft Office "Office Test" Registry key, which is not created by default, to establish persistence. Adversaries create or modify keys like HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Office test\Special\Perf to specify a malicious DLL that automatically executes whenever an Office application such as Word or Excel is started, leveraging this debugging feature for malicious purposes.
