3132.name: Malicious macro
3132.uncertain_mes:
An adversary may rely upon a user opening a malicious file in order to gain execution. Users may be subjected to social engineering to get them to open a file that will lead to code execution. This user action will typically be observed as follow-on behavior from [Spearphishing Attachment](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001). Adversaries may use several types of files that require a user to execute them, including .doc, .pdf, .xls, .rtf, .scr, .exe, .lnk, .pif, .cpl, .reg, and .iso.(Citation: Mandiant Trojanized Windows 10)

Adversaries may employ various forms of [Masquerading](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1036) and [Obfuscated Files or Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027) to increase the likelihood that a user will open and successfully execute a malicious file. These methods may include using a familiar naming convention and/or password protecting the file and supplying instructions to a user on how to open it.(Citation: Password Protected Word Docs) 

While [Malicious File](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002) frequently occurs shortly after Initial Access it may occur at other phases of an intrusion, such as when an adversary places a file in a shared directory or on a user's desktop hoping that a user will click on it. This activity may also be seen shortly after [Internal Spearphishing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1534).
3132.profile: [profile]Malicious File, identified as T1204.002 under the Execution tactic, primarily targets Windows platforms. This technique relies on a user opening a malicious file, such as .doc, .pdf, .xls, .scr, .exe, .lnk, or .iso, to execute adversary code. Execution is often triggered via social engineering, such as spearphishing attachments, or by placing files in shared directories. Adversaries increase success by masquerading files with familiar names or password-protecting them and providing opening instructions. It is associated with numerous threat groups including APT29, FIN7, and Lazarus Group.
3132.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Malicious macro is a technique where adversaries embed malicious Visual Basic for Applications (VBA) code within Microsoft Office documents (like .doc, .xls) to achieve execution when a user enables macros. This technique is often delivered via spearphishing attachments (T1566.001) and relies on social engineering to trick users into enabling content, which then executes payloads to establish initial access or persistence. It is commonly associated with groups like MuddyWater and is a subset of the User Execution tactic.

3133.name: Dynamic link library (DLL)
3133.profile: [profile]Dynamic link library (DLL) is a file format used by malware, as seen in attacks by APT29. It is employed by the Lazarus Group in campaigns like ImprudentCook, where legitimate libraries are maliciously modified for targeted attacks on South Korean enterprises. The Snake malware uses a malicious DLL file on compromised servers, while the ISFB banking trojan can download and inject DLLs from specified URLs into the explorer.exe process. Its use spans Windows platforms, often requiring a separate executable or trigger to run.[/profile]
3133.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Dynamic link library (DLL) is a file format that is often exploited by malware. It is used by threat groups like Lazarus Group and Gold Cabin, who employ malicious or trojanized DLLs in targeted attacks. These malicious DLLs are injected into processes like explorer.exe, are loaded from remote URLs, and can be triggered by other components, though specific initial access vectors are often unclear. The primary target platforms are Windows systems.

3134.name: Calling export functions by ordinal
3134.profile: [profile]Calling export functions by ordinal is a sub-technique of Defense Evasion, T1218.011 (Rundll32), within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, primarily targeting Windows. It involves executing DLL functions via rundll32.exe using their export ordinal numbers (e.g., `rundll32.exe file.dll,#1`) instead of named functions, which can obscure malicious code from analysis by bypassing checks for specific function names. This method is often used alongside other obfuscation or masquerading techniques to evade detection.[/profile]
3134.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Calling export functions by ordinal is a sub-technique of Defense Evasion (T1218.011) under the Windows platform, specifically within the context of abusing rundll32.exe. It involves executing DLL functions by specifying an ordinal number (e.g., rundll32.exe file.dll,#1) instead of a named function, which can obscure the malicious code being called. This method leverages Windows compatibility behavior where rundll32 checks for wide/Unicode (W) or ANSI (A) function name suffixes before loading the specified function, allowing adversaries to hide payloads among similarly named, benign exports.

3135.name: blank export name technique
3135.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may match or approximate the names of legitimate accounts to make newly created ones appear benign. This will typically occur during [Create Account](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1136), although accounts may also be renamed at a later date. This may also coincide with [Account Access Removal](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1531) if the actor first deletes an account before re-creating one with the same name.(Citation: Huntress MOVEit 2023)

Often, adversaries will attempt to masquerade as service accounts, such as those associated with legitimate software, data backups, or container cluster management.(Citation: Elastic CUBA Ransomware 2022)(Citation: Aquasec Kubernetes Attack 2023) They may also give accounts generic, trustworthy names, such as “admin”, “help”, or “root.”(Citation: Invictus IR Cloud Ransomware 2024) Sometimes adversaries may model account names off of those already existing in the system, as a follow-on behavior to [Account Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1087).  

Note that this is distinct from [Impersonation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1656), which describes impersonating specific trusted individuals or organizations, rather than user or service account names.
3135.profile: [profile]Masquerade Account Name, also known as T1036.010, is a Defense Evasion technique used on Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. Adversaries match or approximate the names of legitimate user or service accounts when creating or renaming accounts to appear benign, often targeting names like "admin" or "root" or modeling names after existing system accounts discovered through reconnaissance. This technique is associated with groups like APT29, APT3, Dragonfly, and Magic Hound.
3135.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity is an attack pattern named "blank export name technique." Based on the retrieved context, this technique involves manipulating the Server Name Indication (SNI) field in a TLS header by leaving it blank or using a different domain than the HTTP Host header to obfuscate the true destination of HTTPS traffic, often in conjunction with domain fronting to evade detection. This is a method of network traffic obfuscation.

3136.name: Exploiting IDA disassembler bug
3136.profile: [profile]The entity "Exploiting IDA disassembler bug" is a technique for defense evasion, likely aligned with MITRE ATT&CK. It involves exploiting a specific vulnerability or bug within the Interactive Disassembler (IDA) software to cause unintended behavior, hindering accurate static analysis of malware. This method can be used by groups like APT29 to obfuscate code functionality, making reverse engineering more difficult for analysts.
3136.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Exploiting IDA disassembler bug" is a technique where adversaries leverage a specific vulnerability in the IDA Pro disassembler software. This technique is used for defense evasion, specifically to hinder static analysis by security tools and analysts. By exploiting this bug, malicious code can be crafted to cause the disassembler to misinterpret or fail to correctly parse the executable's instructions, thereby obfuscating the true control flow and intent of the malware. This method directly targets the analysis phase to increase the complexity of reverse engineering efforts.

3156.name: Multi-Layer Encryption and Obfuscation
3156.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may obfuscate command and control traffic to make it more difficult to detect.(Citation: Bitdefender FunnyDream Campaign November 2020) Command and control (C2) communications are hidden (but not necessarily encrypted) in an attempt to make the content more difficult to discover or decipher and to make the communication less conspicuous and hide commands from being seen. This encompasses many methods, such as adding junk data to protocol traffic, using steganography, or impersonating legitimate protocols.
3156.profile: [profile]The entity aligns with MITRE ATT&CK technique T1001, Data Obfuscation, under the Command and Control tactic for multiple platforms. This technique hides C2 traffic to impede detection, not necessarily through encryption. Specific methods include adding junk data to protocol traffic, using steganography to conceal data within files, or impersonating legitimate protocols to make communications less conspicuous. The Gamaredon Group is associated with its use.[/profile]
3156.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Multi-Layer Encryption and Obfuscation is a technique for securing command and control (C2) communications, aligning with the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1079 under the Command and Control tactic. It operates by applying multiple, nested layers of encryption to C2 traffic, such as tunneling a custom encryption scheme within a standard protocol encryption like HTTPS or SMTPS. This method significantly increases the difficulty of detecting and analyzing the malicious network traffic.

3157.name: Encrypted Communication
3157.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may use an existing, legitimate external Web service as a means for sending commands to and receiving output from a compromised system over the Web service channel. Compromised systems may leverage popular websites and social media to host command and control (C2) instructions. Those infected systems can then send the output from those commands back over that Web service channel. The return traffic may occur in a variety of ways, depending on the Web service being utilized. For example, the return traffic may take the form of the compromised system posting a comment on a forum, issuing a pull request to development project, updating a document hosted on a Web service, or by sending a Tweet. 

Popular websites and social media acting as a mechanism for C2 may give a significant amount of cover due to the likelihood that hosts within a network are already communicating with them prior to a compromise. Using common services, such as those offered by Google or Twitter, makes it easier for adversaries to hide in expected noise. Web service providers commonly use SSL/TLS encryption, giving adversaries an added level of protection.
3157.profile: [profile]Encrypted Communication, identified as T1102.002 (Web Service: Bidirectional Communication) under the Command and Control tactic, operates across multiple platforms. This technique leverages legitimate, encrypted web services (like Google or Twitter using SSL/TLS) for bidirectional C2, where compromised systems send commands and receive output via channels such as posting forum comments, making pull requests, updating documents, or sending Tweets to blend with normal traffic. It is notably used by groups including APT29, APT28, Lazarus Group, and MuddyWater.[/profile]
3157.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Encrypted Communication is a technique for concealing command and control or exfiltration traffic by applying an encryption algorithm to the data, separate from any protocol-level encryption like TLS. This can involve symmetric (e.g., AES, RC4) or asymmetric (public-key) cryptographic algorithms, and adversaries may implement multiple layers of encryption, such as a custom scheme within HTTPS. The goal is to hide malicious communications from detection and network inspection, though implementations using hardcoded or poorly generated keys may be vulnerable to reverse engineering.

3158.name: Persistence Mechanisms
3158.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may clear artifacts associated with previously established persistence on a host system to remove evidence of their activity. This may involve various actions, such as removing services, deleting executables, [Modify Registry](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1112), [Plist File Modification](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1647), or other methods of cleanup to prevent defenders from collecting evidence of their persistent presence.(Citation: Cylance Dust Storm) Adversaries may also delete accounts previously created to maintain persistence (i.e. [Create Account](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1136)).(Citation: Talos - Cisco Attack 2022)

In some instances, artifacts of persistence may also be removed once an adversary’s persistence is executed in order to prevent errors with the new instance of the malware.(Citation: NCC Group Team9 June 2020)
3158.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique "Indicator Removal: Clear Persistence" (ID: T1070.009), categorized under the Defense Evasion tactic and applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. Its technical mechanism involves adversaries removing artifacts of their own previously established persistence, such as by deleting malicious services, executables, registry keys, plist files, or user accounts, to eliminate forensic evidence and avoid detection. The intrusion set APT29 has been associated with this behavior.
3158.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Persistence Mechanisms" is a broad attack-pattern category, not a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique with a T-ID. It encompasses various methods adversaries use to maintain long-term access to compromised systems. Related techniques include Office Application Startup (T1137) for persistence via Microsoft Office features, Pre-OS Boot (T1542) for persistence below the operating system level by modifying firmware or boot drivers, and Event Triggered Execution (T1546) for maintaining access by abusing system mechanisms that execute code based on specific events.

3159.name: Kerberos Pass-the-Ticket Attack
3159.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may “pass the ticket” using stolen Kerberos tickets to move laterally within an environment, bypassing normal system access controls. Pass the ticket (PtT) is a method of authenticating to a system using Kerberos tickets without having access to an account's password. Kerberos authentication can be used as the first step to lateral movement to a remote system.

When preforming PtT, valid Kerberos tickets for [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078) are captured by [OS Credential Dumping](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003). A user's service tickets or ticket granting ticket (TGT) may be obtained, depending on the level of access. A service ticket allows for access to a particular resource, whereas a TGT can be used to request service tickets from the Ticket Granting Service (TGS) to access any resource the user has privileges to access.(Citation: ADSecurity AD Kerberos Attacks)(Citation: GentilKiwi Pass the Ticket)

A [Silver Ticket](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1558/002) can be obtained for services that use Kerberos as an authentication mechanism and are used to generate tickets to access that particular resource and the system that hosts the resource (e.g., SharePoint).(Citation: ADSecurity AD Kerberos Attacks)

A [Golden Ticket](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1558/001) can be obtained for the domain using the Key Distribution Service account KRBTGT account NTLM hash, which enables generation of TGTs for any account in Active Directory.(Citation: Campbell 2014)

Adversaries may also create a valid Kerberos ticket using other user information, such as stolen password hashes or AES keys. For example, "overpassing the hash" involves using a NTLM password hash to authenticate as a user (i.e. [Pass the Hash](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1550/002)) while also using the password hash to create a valid Kerberos ticket.(Citation: Stealthbits Overpass-the-Hash)
3159.profile: [profile]Pass the Ticket (PtT), identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1550.003, is a lateral movement tactic used on Windows platforms. It involves authenticating to systems using stolen Kerberos tickets, such as Ticket Granting Tickets (TGTs) or service tickets, without requiring the account's plaintext password. These tickets are typically captured via credential dumping and can be forged into Golden or Silver Tickets using the KRBTGT hash or service account hashes, respectively, to bypass access controls and move within an Active Directory environment. It is associated with threat groups like APT29, APT32, and Bronze Butler.[profile]
3159.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Kerberos Pass-the-Ticket Attack, also known as Pass the Ticket (PtT) and identified as MITRE ATT&CK T1550.003, is a Lateral Movement technique used on Windows platforms. It involves authenticating to systems by reusing stolen Kerberos tickets, such as Ticket-Granting Tickets (TGTs) or service tickets, which are often captured via OS Credential Dumping. This bypasses the need for account passwords, enabling adversaries to access network resources. The technique is related to the creation of forged Silver and Golden Tickets and has been associated with threat groups like APT32, BRONZE BUTLER, and APT29.

3160.name: EFAX-Themed Emails
3160.profile: [profile]EFAX-Themed Emails is a technique where adversaries send spearphishing emails disguised as legitimate EFAX notifications to compromise targets. The retrieved information describes related but distinct techniques for post-compromise email manipulation, such as using inbox rules (T1564.008) to hide malicious emails, clearing mailbox data (T1070.008) to remove evidence, and general email collection (T1114). The direct neighbor link to APT29 suggests this group may employ this specific phishing lure.
3160.profile_without_enhance: [profile]EFAX-Themed Emails is a technique where adversaries use emails with an EFAX or fax-themed subject line and content as a lure for phishing attacks. This method is a sub-technique of Spearphishing Attachment (T1566.001) under the Initial Access tactic, primarily targeting Windows, macOS, and cloud platforms. The emails contain malicious attachments or links, exploiting the familiarity of fax communications to trick recipients into opening them, thereby deploying malware or harvesting credentials.

3168.name: Leveraging External Remote Services
3168.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may leverage external-facing remote services to initially access and/or persist within a network. Remote services such as VPNs, Citrix, and other access mechanisms allow users to connect to internal enterprise network resources from external locations. There are often remote service gateways that manage connections and credential authentication for these services. Services such as [Windows Remote Management](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/006) and [VNC](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/005) can also be used externally.(Citation: MacOS VNC software for Remote Desktop)

Access to [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078) to use the service is often a requirement, which could be obtained through credential pharming or by obtaining the credentials from users after compromising the enterprise network.(Citation: Volexity Virtual Private Keylogging) Access to remote services may be used as a redundant or persistent access mechanism during an operation.

Access may also be gained through an exposed service that doesn’t require authentication. In containerized environments, this may include an exposed Docker API, Kubernetes API server, kubelet, or web application such as the Kubernetes dashboard.(Citation: Trend Micro Exposed Docker Server)(Citation: Unit 42 Hildegard Malware)

Adversaries may also establish persistence on network by configuring a Tor hidden service on a compromised system. Adversaries may utilize the tool `ShadowLink` to facilitate the installation and configuration of the Tor hidden service. Tor hidden service is then accessible via the Tor network because `ShadowLink` sets up a .onion address on the compromised system. `ShadowLink` may be used to forward any inbound connections to RDP, allowing the adversaries to have remote access.(Citation: The BadPilot campaign) Adversaries may get `ShadowLink` to persist on a system by masquerading it as an MS Defender application.(Citation: Russian threat actors dig in, prepare to seize on war fatigue)
3168.profile: [profile]Leveraging External Remote Services is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1133 under the Initial Access tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It involves using externally accessible services like VPNs, Citrix, RDP, VNC, or exposed container APIs (e.g., Docker, Kubernetes) to gain initial network entry or maintain persistence. Access typically requires valid accounts, but can also exploit services without authentication. A specific implementation uses the tool ShadowLink to configure a Tor hidden service with a .onion address, forwarding RDP connections for persistent remote access while masquerading as a legitimate application like MS Defender. It is associated with numerous threat groups including APT29 and Volt Typhoon.
3168.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Leveraging External Remote Services is identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1133, falling under the Initial Access tactic and applicable across Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. This technique involves adversaries using external-facing services like VPNs, Citrix, RDP, or exposed APIs (e.g., Docker, Kubernetes) to gain initial network access, often requiring valid accounts obtained through credential theft. It can also be used for persistence, with methods including configuring Tor hidden services via tools like ShadowLink to forward RDP connections through a .onion address, providing redundant access channels.

3169.name: Domain Fronting
3169.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may take advantage of routing schemes in Content Delivery Networks (CDNs) and other services which host multiple domains to obfuscate the intended destination of HTTPS traffic or traffic tunneled through HTTPS. (Citation: Fifield Blocking Resistent Communication through domain fronting 2015) Domain fronting involves using different domain names in the SNI field of the TLS header and the Host field of the HTTP header. If both domains are served from the same CDN, then the CDN may route to the address specified in the HTTP header after unwrapping the TLS header. A variation of the the technique, "domainless" fronting, utilizes a SNI field that is left blank; this may allow the fronting to work even when the CDN attempts to validate that the SNI and HTTP Host fields match (if the blank SNI fields are ignored).

For example, if domain-x and domain-y are customers of the same CDN, it is possible to place domain-x in the TLS header and domain-y in the HTTP header. Traffic will appear to be going to domain-x, however the CDN may route it to domain-y.
3169.profile: [profile]Domain Fronting is a sub-technique of T1090.004, classified under the Command and Control tactic within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, applicable to multiple platforms. It exploits Content Delivery Network (CDN) routing by placing different domain names in the TLS header's SNI field and the HTTP header's Host field; if both domains share the same CDN, traffic is routed to the HTTP host, obfuscating its true destination. A "domainless" variation uses a blank SNI field to bypass validation. This technique has been used by groups like APT29 to evade detection.
3169.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Domain Fronting is a defense evasion technique, identified as T1090.004 in the MITRE ATT&CK framework, applicable to multiple platforms. It exploits Content Delivery Network (CDN) routing by placing a benign domain in the TLS header's Server Name Indication (SNI) field and a different, actual command-and-control domain in the HTTP Host header. When both domains are hosted on the same CDN, traffic is routed to the hidden Host header destination after TLS decryption, obfuscating the true endpoint. A "domainless" variation uses a blank SNI field to bypass validation checks.

3181.name: Port Forwarding (62304→3389, 62305→139, 62306→445)
3181.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may setup email forwarding rules to collect sensitive information. Adversaries may abuse email forwarding rules to monitor the activities of a victim, steal information, and further gain intelligence on the victim or the victim’s organization to use as part of further exploits or operations.(Citation: US-CERT TA18-068A 2018) Furthermore, email forwarding rules can allow adversaries to maintain persistent access to victim's emails even after compromised credentials are reset by administrators.(Citation: Pfammatter - Hidden Inbox Rules) Most email clients allow users to create inbox rules for various email functions, including forwarding to a different recipient. These rules may be created through a local email application, a web interface, or by command-line interface. Messages can be forwarded to internal or external recipients, and there are no restrictions limiting the extent of this rule. Administrators may also create forwarding rules for user accounts with the same considerations and outcomes.(Citation: Microsoft Tim McMichael Exchange Mail Forwarding 2)(Citation: Mac Forwarding Rules)

Any user or administrator within the organization (or adversary with valid credentials) can create rules to automatically forward all received messages to another recipient, forward emails to different locations based on the sender, and more. Adversaries may also hide the rule by making use of the Microsoft Messaging API (MAPI) to modify the rule properties, making it hidden and not visible from Outlook, OWA or most Exchange Administration tools.(Citation: Pfammatter - Hidden Inbox Rules)

In some environments, administrators may be able to enable email forwarding rules that operate organization-wide rather than on individual inboxes. For example, Microsoft Exchange supports transport rules that evaluate all mail an organization receives against user-specified conditions, then performs a user-specified action on mail that adheres to those conditions.(Citation: Microsoft Mail Flow Rules 2023) Adversaries that abuse such features may be able to enable forwarding on all or specific mail an organization receives.
3181.profile: [profile]The entity "Port Forwarding (62304→3389, 62305→139, 62306→445)" is a network-based technique for Command and Control, likely corresponding to MITRE ATT&CK ID T1572 (Protocol Tunneling). It operates on Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. The specific mechanics involve redirecting traffic from local ports (62304, 62305, 62306) to standard service ports (3389/RDP, 139/NetBIOS, 445/SMB) on a remote host, creating an encrypted tunnel to encapsulate protocols and bypass network defenses. This is associated with APT29 and Backdoor malware.
3181.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Port Forwarding (62304→3389, 62305→139, 62306→445)" is a specific network-based attack pattern. It functions by redirecting traffic from one network port to another, as exemplified by mapping external ports 62304, 62305, and 62306 to internal ports 3389 (RDP), 139 (NetBIOS), and 445 (SMB) respectively. This technique is commonly used for Defense Evasion and Command and Control, allowing adversaries to bypass network filtering, hide malicious services behind seemingly benign ports, and tunnel protocols to internal services for lateral movement or persistent access.

3182.name: Encrypted Proxy Connections
3182.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may use a connection proxy to direct network traffic between systems or act as an intermediary for network communications to a command and control server to avoid direct connections to their infrastructure. Many tools exist that enable traffic redirection through proxies or port redirection, including [HTRAN](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0040), ZXProxy, and ZXPortMap. (Citation: Trend Micro APT Attack Tools) Adversaries use these types of proxies to manage command and control communications, reduce the number of simultaneous outbound network connections, provide resiliency in the face of connection loss, or to ride over existing trusted communications paths between victims to avoid suspicion. Adversaries may chain together multiple proxies to further disguise the source of malicious traffic.

Adversaries can also take advantage of routing schemes in Content Delivery Networks (CDNs) to proxy command and control traffic.
3182.profile: [profile]Encrypted Proxy Connections is a Command and Control technique (T1090) under the Command and Control tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It involves using intermediary systems to relay and obscure C2 traffic, employing tools like HTRAN, ZXProxy, and ZXPortMap for redirection. Adversaries chain multiple proxies or abuse Content Delivery Network routing to disguise traffic sources, manage communications, and leverage trusted paths to avoid detection. Groups like APT29, Volt Typhoon, and Turla are associated with this method.[/profile]
3182.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Encrypted Proxy Connections is a technique for command and control, where adversaries use a proxy as an intermediary for network traffic and encrypt the communications channel to conceal C2 activity. This combines proxy use, such as tools like HTRAN, ZXProxy, or ZXPortMap for traffic redirection, with encryption algorithms to hide the traffic content. The method masks the true destination of C2 traffic and can leverage external or internal proxy systems to avoid direct connections and blend in with normal network paths.[/profile]

3183.name: Traffic Obfuscation
3183.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may use traffic signaling to hide open ports or other malicious functionality used for persistence or command and control. Traffic signaling involves the use of a magic value or sequence that must be sent to a system to trigger a special response, such as opening a closed port or executing a malicious task. This may take the form of sending a series of packets with certain characteristics before a port will be opened that the adversary can use for command and control. Usually this series of packets consists of attempted connections to a predefined sequence of closed ports (i.e. [Port Knocking](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1205/001)), but can involve unusual flags, specific strings, or other unique characteristics. After the sequence is completed, opening a port may be accomplished by the host-based firewall, but could also be implemented by custom software.

Adversaries may also communicate with an already open port, but the service listening on that port will only respond to commands or trigger other malicious functionality if passed the appropriate magic value(s).

The observation of the signal packets to trigger the communication can be conducted through different methods. One means, originally implemented by Cd00r (Citation: Hartrell cd00r 2002), is to use the libpcap libraries to sniff for the packets in question. Another method leverages raw sockets, which enables the malware to use ports that are already open for use by other programs.

On network devices, adversaries may use crafted packets to enable [Network Device Authentication](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1556/004) for standard services offered by the device such as telnet.  Such signaling may also be used to open a closed service port such as telnet, or to trigger module modification of malware implants on the device, adding, removing, or changing malicious capabilities.  Adversaries may use crafted packets to attempt to connect to one or more (open or closed) ports, but may also attempt to connect to a router interface, broadcast, and network address IP on the same port in order to achieve their goals and objectives.(Citation: Cisco Synful Knock Evolution)(Citation: Mandiant - Synful Knock)(Citation: Cisco Blog Legacy Device Attacks)  To enable this traffic signaling on embedded devices, adversaries must first achieve and leverage [Patch System Image](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1601/001) due to the monolithic nature of the architecture.

Adversaries may also use the Wake-on-LAN feature to turn on powered off systems. Wake-on-LAN is a hardware feature that allows a powered down system to be powered on, or woken up, by sending a magic packet to it. Once the system is powered on, it may become a target for lateral movement.(Citation: Bleeping Computer - Ryuk WoL)(Citation: AMD Magic Packet)
3183.profile: [profile]Traffic Signaling, identified as T1205 under the Defense Evasion tactic, operates on Linux, Windows, and Network platforms. It involves sending a specific sequence of packets, known as a magic value, to trigger a hidden response such as opening a closed port or activating malicious functionality. This can be implemented via port knocking on a predefined sequence of closed ports, using unusual packet flags or strings, or by communicating with an open port that only responds to the correct signal. Adversaries like APT29 may use this technique to conceal command and control channels, employing methods like libpcap sniffing or raw sockets to detect the trigger packets.
3183.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Traffic Obfuscation is a technique adversaries use to hide malicious network communications, making them harder to detect and analyze. It aligns with the Command and Control tactic and is applicable across multiple platforms. The technique involves concealing C2 traffic within legitimate protocols like HTTP/S or WebSockets by embedding commands in packet headers and fields. Methods include using multi-hop proxy chains, such as Tor Hidden Services, to disguise traffic sources and adding junk data to protocol traffic to obscure the content. The goal is to blend malicious activity with normal network traffic to evade security monitoring.[/profile]

3184.name: start.ps1
3184.profile: [profile]start.ps1 is a PowerShell script dropper attributed to APT29. It is used to deploy BlueSky ransomware, being Base64-encoded and DEFLATE-compressed, and is also associated with Cobalt Strike and BazarBackdoor payloads. Its key technical behavior is acting as an initial dropper for ransomware and other malware families, primarily targeting Windows platforms via PowerShell execution. Infrastructure includes the hosting URL hxxps://kmsauto[.]us/someone/start.ps1.
3184.profile_without_enhance: [profile]start.ps1 is a PowerShell script dropper. It is known for delivering BlueSky ransomware, with its initial dropper being Base64-encoded and DEFLATE-compressed. The script has been associated with threat groups including APT29, APT32, APT41, FIN6, FIN7, Mustang Panda, and UNC1878, and is linked to tools like Cobalt Strike and BazarBackdoor. Its primary target platform is Windows.

3186.name: RDP tunneling
3186.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may hijack a legitimate user’s remote desktop session to move laterally within an environment. Remote desktop is a common feature in operating systems. It allows a user to log into an interactive session with a system desktop graphical user interface on a remote system. Microsoft refers to its implementation of the Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) as Remote Desktop Services (RDS).(Citation: TechNet Remote Desktop Services)

Adversaries may perform RDP session hijacking which involves stealing a legitimate user's remote session. Typically, a user is notified when someone else is trying to steal their session. With System permissions and using Terminal Services Console, `c:\windows\system32\tscon.exe [session number to be stolen]`, an adversary can hijack a session without the need for credentials or prompts to the user.(Citation: RDP Hijacking Korznikov) This can be done remotely or locally and with active or disconnected sessions.(Citation: RDP Hijacking Medium) It can also lead to [Remote System Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1018) and Privilege Escalation by stealing a Domain Admin or higher privileged account session. All of this can be done by using native Windows commands, but it has also been added as a feature in red teaming tools.(Citation: Kali Redsnarf)
3186.profile: [profile]RDP Tunneling, also known as RDP Hijacking (MITRE ATT&CK ID T1563.002), is a Lateral Movement technique used on Windows platforms. It involves hijacking an existing Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) session by using the native Windows tool `tscon.exe` with System permissions to attach to a target session ID, allowing an adversary to assume control without credentials or user prompts, even over active or disconnected sessions. This method can facilitate privilege escalation and has been incorporated into red teaming tools. The intrusion set APT29 has been associated with this technique.[/profile]
3186.profile_without_enhance: [profile]RDP tunneling is a sub-technique of Protocol Tunneling (T1572) under the Command and Control tactic, primarily used on Windows platforms. It involves encapsulating the Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) within another protocol to conceal malicious traffic, bypass network filtering, and route RDP packets to otherwise unreachable systems. This technique enables adversaries to blend in with legitimate traffic and establish encrypted channels for lateral movement or persistent access.

3192.name: hiding network traffic
3192.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may use traffic signaling to hide open ports or other malicious functionality used for persistence or command and control. Traffic signaling involves the use of a magic value or sequence that must be sent to a system to trigger a special response, such as opening a closed port or executing a malicious task. This may take the form of sending a series of packets with certain characteristics before a port will be opened that the adversary can use for command and control. Usually this series of packets consists of attempted connections to a predefined sequence of closed ports (i.e. [Port Knocking](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1205/001)), but can involve unusual flags, specific strings, or other unique characteristics. After the sequence is completed, opening a port may be accomplished by the host-based firewall, but could also be implemented by custom software.

Adversaries may also communicate with an already open port, but the service listening on that port will only respond to commands or trigger other malicious functionality if passed the appropriate magic value(s).

The observation of the signal packets to trigger the communication can be conducted through different methods. One means, originally implemented by Cd00r (Citation: Hartrell cd00r 2002), is to use the libpcap libraries to sniff for the packets in question. Another method leverages raw sockets, which enables the malware to use ports that are already open for use by other programs.

On network devices, adversaries may use crafted packets to enable [Network Device Authentication](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1556/004) for standard services offered by the device such as telnet.  Such signaling may also be used to open a closed service port such as telnet, or to trigger module modification of malware implants on the device, adding, removing, or changing malicious capabilities.  Adversaries may use crafted packets to attempt to connect to one or more (open or closed) ports, but may also attempt to connect to a router interface, broadcast, and network address IP on the same port in order to achieve their goals and objectives.(Citation: Cisco Synful Knock Evolution)(Citation: Mandiant - Synful Knock)(Citation: Cisco Blog Legacy Device Attacks)  To enable this traffic signaling on embedded devices, adversaries must first achieve and leverage [Patch System Image](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1601/001) due to the monolithic nature of the architecture.

Adversaries may also use the Wake-on-LAN feature to turn on powered off systems. Wake-on-LAN is a hardware feature that allows a powered down system to be powered on, or woken up, by sending a magic packet to it. Once the system is powered on, it may become a target for lateral movement.(Citation: Bleeping Computer - Ryuk WoL)(Citation: AMD Magic Packet)
3192.profile: [profile]This entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique "Traffic Signaling," ID T1205, under the Defense Evasion tactic, applicable to Linux, Windows, and Network platforms. It involves sending a specific sequence or "magic" packet to a system to trigger a hidden response, such as opening a closed port for command and control. Common implementations include port knocking, where a predefined sequence of connection attempts to closed ports is used, or using crafted packets with unusual flags or strings. The technique can leverage libpcap for packet sniffing or raw sockets, and on network devices, it may require patching the system image to enable. It has been associated with groups like APT29, UNC3886, and Mustang Panda.
3192.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Hiding Network Traffic is a technique used for Defense Evasion and Command and Control, primarily on Network platforms. It involves manipulating network communications to conceal malicious activity and evade detection. This can be achieved by blending C2 traffic within common web protocols like HTTP/S, using proxies or VPNs to disguise source IPs, and filtering traffic to block security tool user agents or avoid geolocation-based blocks. Adversaries may also obfuscate data within protocol fields to make commands less conspicuous. The technique is associated with groups like APT29 and Zirconium.

3193.name: new persistence creation
3193.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may clear artifacts associated with previously established persistence on a host system to remove evidence of their activity. This may involve various actions, such as removing services, deleting executables, [Modify Registry](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1112), [Plist File Modification](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1647), or other methods of cleanup to prevent defenders from collecting evidence of their persistent presence.(Citation: Cylance Dust Storm) Adversaries may also delete accounts previously created to maintain persistence (i.e. [Create Account](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1136)).(Citation: Talos - Cisco Attack 2022)

In some instances, artifacts of persistence may also be removed once an adversary’s persistence is executed in order to prevent errors with the new instance of the malware.(Citation: NCC Group Team9 June 2020)
3193.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1070.009, named Clear Persistence, under the Defense Evasion tactic and applicable to multiple platforms. It involves adversaries removing artifacts from previously established persistence mechanisms to eliminate evidence of their activity. This cleanup can include actions like deleting services, executables, modifying the registry, altering plist files, or removing created accounts to prevent defenders from detecting their persistent presence. In some cases, these artifacts are cleared after a new malware instance executes to avoid operational errors. The intrusion set APT29 has been associated with this behavior.
3193.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "new persistence creation" is a general persistence tactic. It involves adversaries establishing mechanisms to maintain access across system restarts, such as by creating new services (T1050) that execute at startup via registry modification or service utilities, often with privilege escalation to SYSTEM. Related techniques include clearing old persistence artifacts (T1070.009), relocating malware (T1070.010), and creating accounts (T1136) for secondary access. The focus is on deploying fresh, often disguised, persistence methods while potentially cleaning up previous traces.

3194.name: CozyDuke Dropper
3194.uncertain_mes:
