3194.profile: [profile]CozyDuke Dropper, also known as CozyDuke, is a malware dropper attributed to the APT29 intrusion set. It serves as the initial stage to deploy the CozyDuke Implant payload and was active at least until Spring 2015. Its key behavior is functioning as a dropper to install further malicious components.[/profile]
3194.profile_without_enhance: [profile]CozyDuke Dropper is a malware dropper associated with the APT29 intrusion set. It is responsible for deploying the CozyDuke Implant and is part of the broader "Dukes" malware family, which includes variants like MiniDuke, CosmicDuke, and GeminiDuke. Its key activity was notably documented around Spring 2015, with its primary function being to deliver the final payload.[/profile]

3195.name: Office Monkeys Dropper
3195.profile: [profile]Office Monkeys Dropper is a malware dropper attributed to the APT29 intrusion set (also known as CozyBear, The Dukes, or CozyDuke). It is associated with the broader Cobalt Strike framework and is used in campaigns to deploy further payloads, often leveraging Microsoft Office documents as lures for initial infection. Its primary target platform is Windows systems, and it operates as part of sophisticated, state-sponsored espionage operations.[/profile]
3195.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Office Monkeys Dropper is a malware dropper. It is associated with the APT group known as APT29, also called CozyBear or The Dukes. This group is linked to broader clusters including Winnti and Cobalt Strike. The dropper is designed to target Microsoft Office environments, deploying further payloads via documents, as indicated by its name and its contextual association with other Office-based droppers like those used by Dridex and Emotet.

3196.name: CozyDuke Implant
3196.uncertain_mes:
THE DUKES
7 YEARS OF RUSSIAN
CYBERESPIONAGE
F-Secure Whitepaper
3196.profile: [profile]CozyDuke Implant, also known as CozyDuke, is a malware implant attributed to the APT29 intrusion set. It is part of the broader "Dukes" cyberespionage toolset, which includes other malware like MiniDuke, CosmicDuke, and GeminiDuke. The implant is used for initial infection and data theft, with its activity documented as recently as Spring 2015. It is deployed via a dedicated CozyDuke Dropper, and related tools like HammerDuke and GeminiDuke are used as secondary backdoors on systems already compromised by CozyDuke.[/profile]
3196.profile_without_enhance: [profile]CozyDuke Implant is a malware payload delivered by the CozyDuke Dropper, which is attributed to the APT29 intrusion set. It is part of the broader 'Dukes' malware family, which includes variants like MiniDuke, CosmicDuke, and GeminiDuke. Its key technical behavior is to be deployed as the final implant by its dropper, with known activity observed up to Spring 2015. Its target platform is Windows.[/profile]

3197.name: RAR SFX
3197.profile: [profile]RAR SFX, also known as a RAR self-extracting archive, is a file format leveraged by threat actors like APT29 for initial access. It is used to deliver embedded malicious payloads, such as downloaders or configuration files, often disguised within decoy documents or legitimate-looking executables. The technique involves executing macros to trigger the embedded RAR SFX, which then extracts and runs its contents. This method targets Windows platforms and is associated with malware families like Machete and Infy, utilizing domains and services like ngrok for command and control infrastructure.
3197.profile_without_enhance: [profile]RAR SFX, also known as a RAR Self-Extracting archive, is a malware delivery mechanism. It is used by groups like Machete and Infy to package and deploy malicious payloads. Key technical behaviors include embedding configuration data or downloader components within the archive, often executed via macros in malicious documents. The payloads target Windows platforms and may download additional modules from remote domains such as koliast[.]com or via ngrok services.

3198.name: Fake Flash Videos
3198.profile: [profile]Fake Flash Videos, also known as Fake Flash Player updates, is a malware entity attributed to APT29. It operates by creating malicious iframes from domains like lopiax[.]us to deliver fake Flash Player update recommendations, a tactic also associated with Magecart campaigns. Its infrastructure includes multiple fake installer domains such as update[.]flash-installer[.]com, flash[.]com[.]cm, and flash[.]co[.]cm, which are used in XSS attacks and are linked to the BIOPASS RAT's C&C server at 0x3s[.]com, indicating potential overlaps with APT41 operations. The primary target platforms are systems where users are tricked into installing malicious updates, typically via web browsers.
3198.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Fake Flash Videos, also known as a fake Flash Player update, is a malware entity attributed to groups like FIN6, Magecart, and APT41. Its key technical behavior involves creating an iframe from domains like lopiax[.]us to deliver a fake Flash Player update recommendation, often as part of XSS attacks or to distribute other malware like the BIOPASS RAT. It primarily targets users through web-based deception, utilizing associated fake installer domains such as update[.]flash-installer[.]com and flash[.]com[.]cm to facilitate its malicious activities.[/profile]

3199.name: 32-bit DLL (Screenshot)
3199.profile: [profile]32-bit DLL (Screenshot) is a component used by the APT29 intrusion set. Its technical behavior involves capturing screenshots via Windows GDI functions including CreateCompatibleBitmap, SelectObject, BitBlt, DeleteObject, StretchBlt, GetObjectW, GetDIBits, SaveDC, CreateDIBSection, DeleteDC, and RestoreDC. It also performs credential theft using functions like CryptUnprotectData, BCryptDecrypt, VaultOpenVault, VaultEnumerateItems, and VaultCloseVault, and can gather system information via DsRoleGetPrimaryDomainInformation and GetModuleFileNameExA.[/profile]
3199.profile_without_enhance: [profile]32-bit DLL (Screenshot) is a component associated with the Ducktail malware family. Its technical behavior involves capturing screenshots using Windows GDI functions such as CreateCompatibleBitmap, BitBlt, and GetDIBits. It also interacts with system credential storage via functions like CryptUnprotectData and VaultEnumerateItems. The malware targets Windows platforms and is linked to the Ducktail information-stealing campaign, which utilizes embedded libraries like SQLitePCLRaw and System.Security.Cryptography.ProtectedData.dll for data handling and encryption operations.

3200.name: 32-bit DLL (Multiple Primitives)
3200.profile: [profile]32-bit DLL (Multiple Primitives) is a malware component attributed to APT29. Its technical behavior involves being a 32-bit DLL module, as referenced in analyses of other malware like Gozi and Ducktail, where it is identified among unpacked samples and embedded libraries such as SQLitePCLRaw.core.dll and System.Security.Cryptography.ProtectedData.dll, indicating potential data handling or encryption routines.
3200.profile_without_enhance: [profile]32-bit DLL (Multiple Primitives) is a malware component referenced in analyses of the Ducktail and Gozi malware families. It appears as a 32-bit DLL module within unpacked samples, often associated with libraries for SQLite database interaction (e.g., SQLitePCLRaw.core.dll, e_sqlite3.dll) and system functions like cryptography (System.Security.Cryptography.ProtectedData.dll). Its technical behavior involves being embedded within larger malware payloads, indicating its role as a modular component for data handling or system interaction, primarily targeting Windows platforms through DLL loading mechanisms.

3203.name: VictimDecode
3203.profile: [profile]VictimDecode is a malware attributed to the APT29 intrusion set. It is associated with or shares victimology characteristics with the macamax, killav, and cuba malware families, the latter of which is linked to the 1937cn group. Its primary function involves victimology, indicating a focus on profiling or analyzing victim systems for targeted operations. Its target platforms are unspecified in the provided data.
3203.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Name: VictimDecode. Aliases: macamax, killav, cuba. Attributed Groups: 1937cn. Key TTPs/Technical Behaviors: Associated with victimology analysis. Target Platforms: Not specified. Infrastructure/Supplementary Info: No additional details provided.

3204.name: ChromeUpdate
3204.profile: [profile]ChromeUpdate, also known as Mac-Installer.InstallerAlert, is a malware binary functionally matching the ChromeUpdate sample with 86% similarity. It is attributed to the APT29 intrusion set. Its key technical behaviors include masquerading as a legitimate update binary and containing identical strings and functions to the ChromeUpdate malware. It primarily targets macOS platforms, distributed within InstallerAlert.app bundles. Supplementary infrastructure or tools include components referenced by Apple's FERRET rules.
3204.profile_without_enhance: [profile]ChromeUpdate, also known as Chrome Update, is a malware binary. It has been functionally matched to the Mac-Installer.InstallerAlert binary found in the InstallerAlert.app, sharing 86% similarity and identical strings and functions. This malware is associated with the threat groups Wagemole and The Gorgon Group. It is delivered through deceptive installers, such as update1.exe, and is designed to target macOS systems.

3213.name: Email Attachments
3213.profile: [profile]Email Attachments is a common initial access technique where adversaries send malicious files via email, often as part of spearphishing campaigns. The technique relies on user execution to open the attachment, which can deliver malware like remote access tools or ransomware. APT29 is a known user of this method. The primary technical mechanic involves delivering and executing a malicious payload through a file attached to a socially engineered email.[/profile]
3213.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Email Attachments is a technique within the Initial Access tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. It involves sending malicious files, such as executables, documents, or archives, directly within an email message to a victim. Execution typically requires the user to open the attachment, leveraging social engineering to bypass technical controls. This method is distinct from spearphishing links, which use URLs instead of attached files.

3214.name: Internal Network Propagation
3214.uncertain_mes: An adversary may deface systems internal to an organization in an attempt to intimidate or mislead users, thus discrediting the integrity of the systems. This may take the form of modifications to internal websites or server login messages, or directly to user systems with the replacement of the desktop wallpaper.(Citation: Novetta Blockbuster)(Citation: Varonis) Disturbing or offensive images may be used as a part of [Internal Defacement](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1491/001) in order to cause user discomfort, or to pressure compliance with accompanying messages. Since internally defacing systems exposes an adversary's presence, it often takes place after other intrusion goals have been accomplished.(Citation: Novetta Blockbuster Destructive Malware)
3214.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique "Internal Defacement" (ID: T1491.001) under the Impact tactic, targeting Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves an adversary modifying internal systems, such as internal websites, server login messages, or user desktop wallpapers, often using disturbing or offensive images to intimidate users, discredit system integrity, or pressure compliance. This activity typically occurs after primary intrusion goals are met to avoid early detection and has been associated with groups like Lazarus Group, Gamaredon Group, and BlackByte.[/profile]
3214.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Internal Network Propagation is a technique adversaries use to move laterally within a compromised network after gaining initial access. It involves leveraging compromised internal systems as proxies or pivots to manage command and control traffic, using tools like HTRAN, ZXProxy, or ZXPortMap for traffic redirection. This method helps conceal the true destination of communications, reduces outbound connections, and blends in by using trusted protocols like SMB. The tactic is primarily associated with Lateral Movement, targeting Windows, Linux, and Network platforms, and is used by groups like FIN13, Lazarus Group, and Volt Typhoon.

3215.name: Anti-Virus Evasion
3215.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may employ various means to detect and avoid debuggers. Debuggers are typically used by defenders to trace and/or analyze the execution of potential malware payloads.(Citation: ProcessHacker Github) Debugger evasion may include changing behaviors based on the results of the checks for the presence of artifacts indicative of a debugged environment. Similar to [Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1497), if the adversary detects a debugger, they may alter their malware to disengage from the victim or conceal the core functions of the implant. They may also search for debugger artifacts before dropping secondary or additional payloads. Specific checks will vary based on the target and/or adversary. On Windows, this may involve [Native API](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1106) function calls such as IsDebuggerPresent() and NtQueryInformationProcess(), or manually checking the BeingDebugged flag of the Process Environment Block (PEB). On Linux, this may involve querying `/proc/self/status` for the `TracerPID` field, which indicates whether or not the process is being traced by dynamic analysis tools.(Citation: Cado Security P2PInfect 2023)(Citation: Positive Technologies Hellhounds 2023) Other checks for debugging artifacts may also seek to enumerate hardware breakpoints, interrupt assembly opcodes, time checks, or measurements if exceptions are raised in the current process (assuming a present debugger would “swallow” or handle the potential error).(Citation: hasherezade debug)(Citation: AlKhaser Debug)(Citation: vxunderground debug) Malware may also leverage Structured Exception Handling (SEH) to detect debuggers by throwing an exception and detecting whether the process is suspended. SEH handles both hardware and software expectations, providing control over the exceptions including support for debugging. If a debugger is present, the program’s control will be transferred to the debugger, and the execution of the code will be suspended. If the debugger is not present, control will be transferred to the SEH handler, which will automatically handle the exception and allow the program’s execution to continue.(Citation: Apriorit) Adversaries may use the information learned from these debugger checks during automated discovery to shape follow-on behaviors. Debuggers can also be evaded by detaching the process or flooding debug logs with meaningless data via messages produced by looping [Native API](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1106) function calls such as OutputDebugStringW().(Citation: wardle evilquest partii)(Citation: Checkpoint Dridex Jan 2021)
3215.profile: [profile]The entity is Debugger Evasion, technique T1622 under the Defense Evasion tactic, applicable to Windows and Linux platforms. It involves detecting debuggers to alter malware behavior, using checks like Windows API calls (IsDebuggerPresent, NtQueryInformationProcess) to inspect the Process Environment Block, or querying Linux /proc/self/status for the TracerPID field. Other methods include examining hardware breakpoints, using Structured Exception Handling (SEH) to test for process suspension, or flooding debug logs with data via OutputDebugStringW to evade analysis. The intrusion set APT29 has been associated with this technique.[/profile]
3215.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Anti-Virus Evasion is a Defense Evasion technique where adversaries modify malware to bypass detection by antivirus software. This is often achieved by altering the malware's file signature after detection, using methods like software packing to create a new, undetected version. The technique is commonly executed on Windows and Linux platforms, enabling persistent malicious activity by evading signature-based security controls.

3216.name: WMI/WQL
3216.profile: [profile]The entity "WMI/WQL" aligns with MITRE ATT&CK technique T1047 (Windows Management Instrumentation) under the Execution tactic for Windows platforms. It involves adversaries abusing Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) and its query language (WQL) to execute malicious commands and payloads locally or remotely, often using tools like `wmic.exe` (now deprecated) or PowerShell. This provides a means for behaviors such as discovery and execution, as seen in groups like APT29. Supplementary use includes establishing persistence via WMI event subscriptions (T1546.003).
3216.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "WMI/WQL" is a technique for Execution (T1047) on Windows platforms, involving the abuse of Windows Management Instrumentation and its query language to interact with systems. It enables adversaries to execute commands and payloads locally or remotely via tools like wmic.exe or PowerShell, often for discovery or to perform actions like deleting shadow copies. The technique is associated with numerous threat groups including APT29, Lazarus Group, and MuddyWater.

3217.name: XOR Cipher
3217.profile: [profile]XOR Cipher is a basic symmetric encryption technique (T1024) used for Defense Evasion and Command and Control. It operates across multiple platforms. The technique works by applying an exclusive OR (XOR) operation to data with a fixed key, producing a weak ciphertext that can be easily reversed if the key is discovered. It is commonly implemented in custom cryptographic protocols or for compressing/encrypting data prior to exfiltration, as seen in activities by groups like APT29 and RocketKitten.
3217.profile_without_enhance: [profile]XOR Cipher, identified as a sub-technique for data obfuscation and command and control, is a simple symmetric encryption method where plaintext is combined with a key using the exclusive OR (XOR) operation. It is commonly implemented as a custom archival method (T1560.003) to compress or encrypt collected data prior to exfiltration, or as a weak custom cryptographic protocol (T1024) to hide C2 traffic. Adversaries like Lazarus Group and Mustang Panda use these custom XOR implementations, often without external libraries, to create a basic cipher that is vulnerable to analysis and reverse engineering.[/profile]

3218.name: RC4 Decrypts
3218.profile: [profile]RC4 Decrypts is a sub-technique (T1573.001) for Encrypted Channel under the Command and Control tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It involves adversaries using the RC4 symmetric encryption algorithm to conceal command and control or data exfiltration traffic, often by manually implementing the algorithm to encrypt and decrypt communications using a shared key, which may add an encryption layer atop standard protocols like HTTP or HTTPS. The technique is associated with groups like APT29, MuddyWater, and Lazarus Group.
3218.profile_without_enhance: [profile]RC4 Decrypts is a technique for decrypting data using the RC4 symmetric stream cipher. It is associated with the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1573.001 (Symmetric Cryptography) under the Command and Control tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. The technique involves adversaries using the RC4 algorithm with a shared key to decrypt command and control traffic or exfiltrated data that was previously encrypted, often implemented manually within malware to bypass protocol-level protections. This activity is linked to groups like APT28, Lazarus, and MuddyWater.

3219.name: URL Parses
3219.profile: [profile]The entity "URL Parses" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the provided context, it appears to be a foundational action for handling malicious links used in spearphishing. The related technique "Spearphishing Link" (T1598.003/T1566.002) involves sending messages with malicious URLs to harvest credentials or gain execution. Attackers like APT29 may use obfuscated URLs, clone legitimate login pages, or employ services like link shorteners to host these link targets and deceive victims into clicking.[/profile]
3219.profile_without_enhance: [profile]URL Parses is a technique where adversaries manipulate or exploit how URLs are interpreted to deceive victims and facilitate attacks like spearphishing. This involves obfuscating the true destination by abusing URL schema quirks, such as using integer-based hostname formats or inserting text before an "@" symbol (e.g., `hxxp://google.com@1157586937`) to mask malicious links. The technique supports the Initial Access tactic, often leveraging web platforms, by making phishing links appear legitimate or redirecting to cloned login pages or malware hosted on trusted domains like link shortening services.

3220.name: Collects Victim System Data
3220.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may search local system sources, such as file systems, configuration files, local databases, virtual machine files, or process memory, to find files of interest and sensitive data prior to Exfiltration.

Adversaries may do this using a [Command and Scripting Interpreter](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059), such as [cmd](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0106) as well as a [Network Device CLI](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/008), which have functionality to interact with the file system to gather information.(Citation: show_run_config_cmd_cisco) Adversaries may also use [Automated Collection](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1119) on the local system.
3220.profile: [profile]Data from Local System, identified as T1005 within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, falls under the Collection tactic and targets multiple platforms. This technique involves adversaries searching local system sources like file systems, configuration files, databases, virtual machine files, and process memory to find sensitive data prior to exfiltration. Execution is commonly performed using Command and Scripting Interpreters such as cmd or a Network Device CLI, which interact with the file system, and may also leverage Automated Collection. Numerous threat groups, including APT29, are associated with its use.[/profile]
3220.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Collects Victim System Data" is a reconnaissance technique where adversaries gather information about a victim's hosts for targeting. This includes administrative data like system names and IPs, and configuration details such as the operating system and language. Information is collected via methods like Active Scanning or Phishing for Information, and can also be obtained from online data sets or by analyzing User-Agent HTTP headers to tailor follow-on actions.

3221.name: Encrypts Collected Data
3221.uncertain_mes:
An adversary may compress and/or encrypt data that is collected prior to exfiltration. Compressing the data can help to obfuscate the collected data and minimize the amount of data sent over the network.(Citation: DOJ GRU Indictment Jul 2018) Encryption can be used to hide information that is being exfiltrated from detection or make exfiltration less conspicuous upon inspection by a defender.

Both compression and encryption are done prior to exfiltration, and can be performed using a utility, 3rd party library, or custom method.
3221.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique Archive Collected Data (T1560) under the Collection tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It involves compressing and/or encrypting collected data prior to exfiltration to obfuscate the content and reduce network footprint, using utilities, third-party libraries, or custom methods. Related sub-techniques include archive via custom method (T1560.003), and it is associated with groups like APT29, Lazarus Group, and Dragonfly.
3221.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Encrypts Collected Data is a sub-technique of Archive Collected Data (T1560) under the Collection tactic. It involves using encryption to hide collected data prior to exfiltration, making it less conspicuous and harder to detect during network inspection or forensic analysis. This can be performed using standard utilities, third-party libraries, or custom methods like XOR or stream ciphers, and is commonly employed by groups such as FIN6, Lazarus Group, and UNC3886 to protect stolen information.

3222.name: Sends Stolen Data
3222.profile: [profile]Sends Stolen Data is a technique used by adversaries to exfiltrate collected data from a compromised system. It is commonly associated with groups like APT29. The stolen data is typically transmitted over an existing command and control channel (T1041), where it is encoded into the normal communications protocol. Alternatively, exfiltration may occur over unencrypted, non-command and control protocols (T1048.003), such as HTTP or FTP, where data can be obfuscated within protocol headers. Prior to sending, adversaries often prepare the data through staging (T1074) or compression (T1002) to make it portable and minimize network detection.[/profile]
3222.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Sends Stolen Data is a technique within the Exfiltration tactic. It involves adversaries transmitting collected data from a compromised system to an external location they control. This can be achieved by exfiltrating the data over an existing, often encrypted, command and control (C2) channel, or by using other unencrypted network protocols like HTTP or FTP, sometimes with obfuscation such as base64 encoding. The data may be staged, compressed, or archived prior to transmission to minimize detection.

3223.name: Hides Functionality
3223.profile: [profile]Hides Functionality is a technique adversaries use to conceal malicious code or actions within legitimate processes or files, often by abusing shared modules or inserting junk code. This technique is associated with groups like APT29 and Mustang Panda. It involves loading executable shared objects or DLLs from arbitrary paths using functions like `dlopen` or `LoadLibrary` to modularize and hide payloads, or adding non-functional code like NOP instructions to obfuscate analysis and evade detection.
3223.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Hides Functionality is a technique where adversaries conceal malicious actions to evade detection. It aligns with the Defense Evasion tactic (T1564) and applies across multiple platforms. This involves using system features like hidden files or directories, virtualization to isolate malicious processes, and inserting non-functional junk code to obscure analysis. Groups like Mustang Panda and APT32 have employed these methods to hide their tools and activities from security monitoring.

3224.name: Keeps Code in Encrypted Blocks
3224.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may scan victim IP blocks to gather information that can be used during targeting. Public IP addresses may be allocated to organizations by block, or a range of sequential addresses.

Adversaries may scan IP blocks in order to [Gather Victim Network Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1590), such as which IP addresses are actively in use as well as more detailed information about hosts assigned these addresses. Scans may range from simple pings (ICMP requests and responses) to more nuanced scans that may reveal host software/versions via server banners or other network artifacts.(Citation: Botnet Scan) Information from these scans may reveal opportunities for other forms of reconnaissance (ex: [Search Open Websites/Domains](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1593) or [Search Open Technical Databases](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1596)), establishing operational resources (ex: [Develop Capabilities](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1587) or [Obtain Capabilities](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1588)), and/or initial access (ex: [External Remote Services](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1133)).
3224.profile: [profile]The entity "Keeps Code in Encrypted Blocks" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the provided context, it appears to be a custom or mislabeled concept. The retrieved information primarily describes the MITRE technique "Scan IP Blocks" (T1595.001), which is a reconnaissance tactic involving scanning sequential public IP address ranges using methods from simple ICMP pings to nuanced scans that reveal host software via banners. This activity is used to gather victim network information for further targeting. The neighbor and related content also mention APT29 and encrypted channels (T1573), but these are distinct from the core scanning behavior described.[/profile]
3224.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Keeps Code in Encrypted Blocks is a technique for obfuscating malicious code by storing it within encrypted data blocks, often within files like configuration or payload artifacts. The encryption aims to conceal static signatures, requiring decryption during execution to reveal the functional code. This method is related to sub-techniques like T1027.013 (Encrypted/Encoded File) and shares the objective of hindering detection through layered obfuscation.

3225.name: DLLMain
3225.profile: [profile]The entity 'DLLMain' is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the retrieved context, it is a critical function within a Windows Dynamic-link Library (DLL) that is automatically executed when the DLL is loaded into a process. This function is fundamental to several ATT&CK techniques that abuse DLL loading for malicious purposes. These include AppCert DLLs (T1182) for persistence and privilege escalation, DLL Side-Loading (T1073) to mask actions under trusted processes, and DLL Search Order Hijacking (T1038) for privilege escalation by placing a malicious DLL in a search path location prior to the legitimate one. The intrusion-set APT29 is linked to this entity.[/profile]
3225.profile_without_enhance: [profile]DLLMain is a process injection technique (T1055.001) within the Execution tactic for Windows. It operates by exploiting the standard entry point of a Dynamic-link Library (DLL), the DllMain function, which is automatically executed by the operating system when the DLL is loaded into a process. This allows malicious code within DllMain to run in the context of the host process, enabling execution, persistence, and evasion.

3226.name: ADB_Load
3226.profile: [profile]ADB_Load is a technique for persistence and privilege escalation, likely mapped to the MITRE ATT&CK framework under DLL Side-Loading (T1073) within the Persistence tactic for Windows platforms. It operates by exploiting a legitimate program's vulnerability to load a malicious DLL, often by placing the malicious DLL in a location Windows searches before the legitimate one, such as the current working directory. This allows adversaries to execute code under the guise of a trusted process. The technique is associated with the intrusion set APT29.
3226.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity 'ADB_Load' is a technique for persistence and privilege escalation, likely mapped to the MITRE ATT&CK framework. It operates by abusing the Android Debug Bridge (ADB) to load and execute malicious payloads on compromised devices. This method typically involves establishing a connection via ADB and using commands to sideload or execute unauthorized applications or code, allowing adversaries to maintain access and control.

3227.name: Encrypted Data Block
3227.uncertain_mes:
Data is encrypted before being exfiltrated in order to hide the information that is being exfiltrated from detection or to make the exfiltration less conspicuous upon inspection by a defender. The encryption is performed by a utility, programming library, or custom algorithm on the data itself and is considered separate from any encryption performed by the command and control or file transfer protocol. Common file archive formats that can encrypt files are RAR and zip.

Other exfiltration techniques likely apply as well to transfer the information out of the network, such as [Exfiltration Over C2 Channel](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1041) and [Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1048)
3227.profile: [profile]Encrypted Data Block, identified as T1022 in the MITRE ATT&CK framework, is a technique under the Exfiltration tactic used across Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves encrypting data with utilities, libraries, or custom algorithms like RAR or zip before exfiltration to evade detection, independent of any C2 channel encryption. This technique is often paired with other exfiltration methods such as Exfiltration Over C2 Channel (T1041) and has been associated with threat groups like APT29.
3227.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Encrypted Data Block is a sub-technique of Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol (T1048) under the Exfiltration tactic. It involves adversaries stealing data by exfiltrating it over a non-command and control network protocol after encrypting the data block itself. This separate encryption, performed using utilities, libraries, or custom algorithms like AES or RC4, aims to hide the exfiltrated content from detection, regardless of whether the underlying protocol (e.g., HTTP, FTP) is natively encrypted or not.

3228.name: Exported Function
3228.profile: [profile]Exported Function is a component of the broader MITRE ATT&CK technique Subverting Trust: SIP and Trust Provider Hijacking (T1553.003), which falls under the Defense Evasion tactic on Windows platforms. This technique involves adversaries hijacking Subject Interface Package (SIP) or trust provider components by redirecting registry keys like `Dll` and `FuncName` to point to a maliciously-crafted DLL containing a specific exported function. This malicious function can be designed to always return a known-good signature or a successful validation result (TRUE), thereby misleading signature validation checks performed by the WinVerifyTrust API to bypass security policies and allow malicious code to execute.
3228.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Exported Function is a sub-technique of SIP and Trust Provider Hijacking (T1553.003) under the Defense Evasion tactic, targeting Windows platforms. It involves adversaries modifying registry keys (e.g., Dll and FuncName values) to redirect the CryptSIPDllGetSignedDataMsg or CryptSIPDllVerifyIndirectData functions to a malicious DLL. This malicious DLL contains an exported function that returns a known good signature or a TRUE validation result, thereby bypassing signature validation checks and allowing unsigned or malicious code to appear legitimately signed. This method can also enable persistent code execution and be achieved via DLL search order hijacking without direct registry modification.

3229.name: Network Stealing Function
3229.profile: [profile]The entity "Network Stealing Function" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the provided context, it is associated with the intrusion set APT29. The retrieved information describes a technique for credential theft, where adversaries passively sniff network traffic to capture authentication material, especially from insecure protocols, by placing a network interface into promiscuous mode or using span ports. This activity supports subsequent lateral movement and defense evasion.
3229.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Network Stealing Function" is an attack-pattern. Based on the provided context, it is associated with the technique of Network Sniffing (MITRE ATT&CK ID T1040) under the Collection tactic. This technique involves passively capturing network traffic by placing a network interface into promiscuous mode or using span ports to monitor data in transit over wired or wireless connections. The captured data can include user credentials sent over unencrypted protocols, system configuration details, and other network characteristics like IP addresses and hostnames, which adversaries use for subsequent lateral movement or defense evasion.

3230.name: Data Stealing Function
3230.profile: [profile]Data Stealing Function is a technique used by adversaries like APT29 to collect and exfiltrate sensitive information. It involves gathering data, potentially staging it in a central location, and then transmitting it out of the network, often using existing command and control channels to blend the stolen data with normal traffic. The process may include compressing the data prior to exfiltration to reduce its size and evade detection.
3230.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Data Stealing Function is a technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, though it lacks a specific T-ID. It falls under the Collection tactic. The technique involves malware using dedicated functions or modules to systematically locate, gather, and package sensitive data from a compromised system. This process is distinct from general data access and is a preparatory step for exfiltration, as indicated by its association with techniques like Exfiltration Over C2 Channel (T1041).

3231.name: Randomly Assigned Naming
3231.profile: [profile]Randomly Assigned Naming is a technique for defense evasion, identified as T1036.005 (Masquerading: Match Legitimate Name or Location) within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, applicable to Windows and containerized platforms. It works by placing malicious files or registry keys in trusted directories (e.g., System32) or naming them to closely resemble legitimate system resources (e.g., svchost.exe) to evade detection. This technique is commonly used by groups like APT29, Carbanak, and MuddyWater.
3231.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Randomly Assigned Naming is a sub-technique of Defense Evasion (T1036) used on Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves adversaries naming malicious files, processes, or services with random or non-suspicious strings to avoid detection by static security rules. This technique is distinct from using legitimate names (Masquerading) and is employed by groups like APT29 and MuddyWater to blend malicious activity into normal system operations.

3235.uncertain_mes:

Gable is an open source obfuscation framework for GO which also includes a string encryption feature. It has been used in multiple GO based malware builds including RootTeam and Bandit Stealer.
String Obfuscation/Encryption
3235.profile: [profile]Bandit Stealer is a malware family written in Go and obfuscated using the Garble framework for string encryption. It is attributed to the APT29 intrusion set. Its key technical behavior involves the use of Golang Garble string decryption to hide its functionality. Target platforms are not specified, but it is part of a broader category of information-stealing malware.

August Stealer is delivered via fileless techniques using Word macros and PowerShell, often in campaigns attributed to threat actor TA530 targeting retail sector staff. PXA Stealer and Bandit Stealer are Python-based stealers, identified by their specific hash values. These tools primarily target Windows platforms to exfiltrate stolen data.

3236.name: Implant (WMI Anti-Virus)
3236.uncertain_mes:
Thrip: Espionage Group Hits Satellite, Telecoms, and Defense Companies
Symantec’s artificial-intelligence-based Targeted Attack Analytics uncovers new wide-ranging espionage operation.
3236.profile: [profile]Implant (WMI Anti-Virus), also known as wmi ghost, is attributed to the Thrip group (also associated with APT29). Its key technical behavior involves querying the Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) to check for the presence of installed Anti-Virus software; if AV is detected, it aborts the installation of its embedded keylogger component. The keylogger payload, named 'AdobePrintFr', is packed using Confuser-Ex. The malware targets Windows systems, gathering system information such as machine name, username, OS details, architecture, and local IP address via WMI queries.[/profile]
3236.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Implant (WMI Anti-Virus) is a malware that checks for the presence of Anti-Virus software via WMI queries to determine whether to proceed with its malicious payload installation. It is associated with the espionage group Thrip and shares similarities with the WMI Ghost malware. Its technical behavior involves using WMI to gather system information, including machine name, username, OS, architecture, and local IP address, and it conditionally deploys a keylogger resource named 'AdobePrintFr' if no AV is detected. The target platform is Windows systems.

3240.uncertain_mes:
[APT28](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0007) is a threat group that has been attributed to Russia's General Staff Main Intelligence Directorate (GRU) 85th Main Special Service Center (GTsSS) military unit 26165.(Citation: NSA/FBI Drovorub August 2020)(Citation: Cybersecurity Advisory GRU Brute Force Campaign July 2021) This group has been active since at least 2004.(Citation: DOJ GRU Indictment Jul 2018)(Citation: Ars Technica GRU indictment Jul 2018)(Citation: Crowdstrike DNC June 2016)(Citation: FireEye APT28)(Citation: SecureWorks TG-4127)(Citation: FireEye APT28 January 2017)(Citation: GRIZZLY STEPPE JAR)(Citation: Sofacy DealersChoice)(Citation: Palo Alto Sofacy 06-2018)(Citation: Symantec APT28 Oct 2018)(Citation: ESET Zebrocy May 2019)

[APT28](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0007) reportedly compromised the Hillary Clinton campaign, the Democratic National Committee, and the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee in 2016 in an attempt to interfere with the U.S. presidential election.(Citation: Crowdstrike DNC June 2016) In 2018, the US indicted five GRU Unit 26165 officers associated with [APT28](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0007) for cyber operations (including close-access operations) conducted between 2014 and 2018 against the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA), the US Anti-Doping Agency, a US nuclear facility, the Organization for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons (OPCW), the Spiez Swiss Chemicals Laboratory, and other organizations.(Citation: US District Court Indictment GRU Oct 2018) Some of these were conducted with the assistance of GRU Unit 74455, which is also referred to as [Sandworm Team](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0034).

Its primary motivation is espionage and political influence, with notable targets including government, political organizations, and critical infrastructure in the U.S. and allied nations, such as its compromise of the Democratic National Committee in 2016.

3245.name: Supply Chain Attack
3245.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may manipulate products or product delivery mechanisms prior to receipt by a final consumer for the purpose of data or system compromise.

Supply chain compromise can take place at any stage of the supply chain including:

* Manipulation of development tools
* Manipulation of a development environment
* Manipulation of source code repositories (public or private)
* Manipulation of source code in open-source dependencies
* Manipulation of software update/distribution mechanisms
* Compromised/infected system images (removable media infected at the factory)(Citation: IBM Storwize)(Citation: Schneider Electric USB Malware) 
* Replacement of legitimate software with modified versions
* Sales of modified/counterfeit products to legitimate distributors
* Shipment interdiction

While supply chain compromise can impact any component of hardware or software, adversaries looking to gain execution have often focused on malicious additions to legitimate software in software distribution or update channels.(Citation: Avast CCleaner3 2018)(Citation: Microsoft Dofoil 2018)(Citation: Command Five SK 2011) Adversaries may limit targeting to a desired victim set or distribute malicious software to a broad set of consumers but only follow up with specific victims.(Citation: Symantec Elderwood Sept 2012)(Citation: Avast CCleaner3 2018)(Citation: Command Five SK 2011) Popular open-source projects that are used as dependencies in many applications may also be targeted as a means to add malicious code to users of the dependency.(Citation: Trendmicro NPM Compromise)

In some cases, adversaries may conduct “second-order” supply chain compromises by leveraging the access gained from an initial supply chain compromise to further compromise a software component.(Citation: Krebs 3cx overview 2023) This may allow the threat actor to spread to even more victims.
3245.profile: [profile]Supply Chain Compromise, identified as T1195, is an Initial Access tactic applicable across multiple platforms. It involves adversaries manipulating products or delivery mechanisms before they reach the end user to compromise systems. Key technical mechanics include inserting malicious code into software distribution or update channels, tampering with source code in open-source dependencies, and compromising development tools or CI/CD pipelines. This technique enables broad or targeted initial access and can be leveraged for second-order compromises, as seen in campaigns by groups like APT41 and Sandworm Team.
3245.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Supply Chain Attack is a technique under MITRE ATT&CK ID T1195, primarily associated with the Initial Access tactic and applicable across multiple platforms. It involves compromising products or delivery mechanisms before they reach the end user to achieve system or data compromise. Specific technical mechanics include manipulating development tools, source code repositories, open-source dependencies, software update channels, or hardware components to insert malicious code. Adversaries may conduct broad distribution with selective follow-up attacks or execute second-order compromises to expand their reach.

3246.name: MFA Bypass
3246.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may modify file attributes and subvert Gatekeeper functionality to evade user prompts and execute untrusted programs. Gatekeeper is a set of technologies that act as layer of Apple’s security model to ensure only trusted applications are executed on a host. Gatekeeper was built on top of File Quarantine in Snow Leopard (10.6, 2009) and has grown to include Code Signing, security policy compliance, Notarization, and more. Gatekeeper also treats applications running for the first time differently than reopened applications.(Citation: TheEclecticLightCompany Quarantine and the flag)(Citation: TheEclecticLightCompany apple notarization )

Based on an opt-in system, when files are downloaded an extended attribute (xattr) called `com.apple.quarantine` (also known as a quarantine flag) can be set on the file by the application performing the download. Launch Services opens the application in a suspended state. For first run applications with the quarantine flag set, Gatekeeper executes the following functions:

1. Checks extended attribute – Gatekeeper checks for the quarantine flag, then provides an alert prompt to the user to allow or deny execution.(Citation: OceanLotus for OS X)(Citation: 20 macOS Common Tools and Techniques)

2. Checks System Policies - Gatekeeper checks the system security policy, allowing execution of apps downloaded from either just the App Store or the App Store and identified developers.

3. Code Signing – Gatekeeper checks for a valid code signature from an Apple Developer ID.

4. Notarization - Using the `api.apple-cloudkit.com` API, Gatekeeper reaches out to Apple servers to verify or pull down the notarization ticket and ensure the ticket is not revoked. Users can override notarization, which will result in a prompt of executing an “unauthorized app” and the security policy will be modified.

Adversaries can subvert one or multiple security controls within Gatekeeper checks through logic errors (e.g. [Exploitation for Defense Evasion](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1211)), unchecked file types, and external libraries. For example, prior to macOS 13 Ventura, code signing and notarization checks were only conducted on first launch, allowing adversaries to write malicious executables to previously opened applications in order to bypass Gatekeeper security checks.(Citation: theevilbit gatekeeper bypass 2021)(Citation: Application Bundle Manipulation Brandon Dalton)

Applications and files loaded onto the system from a USB flash drive, optical disk, external hard drive, from a drive shared over the local network, or using the curl command may not set the quarantine flag. Additionally, it is possible to avoid setting the quarantine flag using [Drive-by Compromise](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1189).
3246.profile: [profile]Gatekeeper Bypass, identified as T1553.001 under the Defense Evasion tactic for macOS, involves subverting Apple's Gatekeeper security controls to execute untrusted programs. Technical mechanics include exploiting logic errors, using unchecked file types or external libraries, and, prior to macOS 13, writing malicious code into previously opened applications to avoid code signing and notarization checks on first launch. Adversaries can also prevent the setting of the quarantine flag (com.apple.quarantine) by delivering files via physical media, network shares, or specific commands like curl.
3246.profile_without_enhance: [profile]MFA Bypass is a technique adversaries use to circumvent multi-factor authentication (MFA) controls. It is associated with the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1621 (Multi-Factor Authentication Request Generation) under the Initial Access tactic, primarily targeting cloud platforms. Technical mechanics involve generating repeated MFA push notifications or calls to cause "MFA fatigue," leading a user to accidentally approve access, or abusing self-service password reset flows to trigger such notifications. Adversaries may also disable MFA by modifying system files like the hosts file to redirect authentication traffic or by registering a new, adversary-controlled device to a compromised account to bypass future checks. Groups like Scattered Spider, LAPSUS$, and APT29 have employed these methods.

3266.name: Infect Target Hosts
3266.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may put in place resources that are referenced by a link that can be used during targeting. An adversary may rely upon a user clicking a malicious link in order to divulge information (including credentials) or to gain execution, as in [Malicious Link](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/001). Links can be used for spearphishing, such as sending an email accompanied by social engineering text to coax the user to actively click or copy and paste a URL into a browser. Prior to a phish for information (as in [Spearphishing Link](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1598/003)) or a phish to gain initial access to a system (as in [Spearphishing Link](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/002)), an adversary must set up the resources for a link target for the spearphishing link. 

Typically, the resources for a link target will be an HTML page that may include some client-side script such as [JavaScript](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/007) to decide what content to serve to the user. Adversaries may clone legitimate sites to serve as the link target, this can include cloning of login pages of legitimate web services or organization login pages in an effort to harvest credentials during [Spearphishing Link](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1598/003).(Citation: Malwarebytes Silent Librarian October 2020)(Citation: Proofpoint TA407 September 2019) Adversaries may also [Upload Malware](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1608/001) and have the link target point to malware for download/execution by the user.

Adversaries may purchase domains similar to legitimate domains (ex: homoglyphs, typosquatting, different top-level domain, etc.) during acquisition of infrastructure ([Domains](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1583/001)) to help facilitate [Malicious Link](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/001).

Links can be written by adversaries to mask the true destination in order to deceive victims by abusing the URL schema and increasing the effectiveness of phishing.(Citation: Kaspersky-masking)(Citation: mandiant-masking)

Adversaries may also use free or paid accounts on link shortening services and Platform-as-a-Service providers to host link targets while taking advantage of the widely trusted domains of those providers to avoid being blocked while redirecting victims to malicious pages.(Citation: Netskope GCP Redirection)(Citation: Netskope Cloud Phishing)(Citation: Intezer App Service Phishing)(Citation: Cofense-redirect) In addition, adversaries may serve a variety of malicious links through uniquely generated URIs/URLs (including one-time, single use links).(Citation: iOS URL Scheme)(Citation: URI)(Citation: URI Use)(Citation: URI Unique) Finally, adversaries may take advantage of the decentralized nature of the InterPlanetary File System (IPFS) to host link targets that are difficult to remove.(Citation: Talos IPFS 2022)
3266.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique "Link Target", identified as T1608.005 under the Resource Development tactic. It involves adversaries preparing resources for a malicious link, such as creating HTML pages with client-side scripts to serve content or harvest credentials, often by cloning legitimate login pages. They may use deceptive domains, link shortening services, or platforms like the InterPlanetary File System (IPFS) to host these targets and evade detection, facilitating spearphishing campaigns.
3266.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Infect Target Hosts is a preparatory technique within the Resource Development tactic, applicable across multiple platforms, where adversaries stage malicious content to compromise systems. This involves preparing operational environments, such as adversary-controlled websites for drive-by compromises or setting up malicious link targets for spearphishing, to deliver exploits or malware when visited by a victim. The technique includes uploading malicious scripts, using typosquatted domains, and leveraging trusted services to host deceptive content, facilitating initial access or credential harvesting.

3267.name: Establish Backdoor Access
3267.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may create and cultivate accounts with services that can be used during targeting. Adversaries can create accounts that can be used to build a persona to further operations. Persona development consists of the development of public information, presence, history and appropriate affiliations. This development could be applied to social media, website, or other publicly available information that could be referenced and scrutinized for legitimacy over the course of an operation using that persona or identity.(Citation: NEWSCASTER2014)(Citation: BlackHatRobinSage)

For operations incorporating social engineering, the utilization of an online persona may be important. These personas may be fictitious or impersonate real people. The persona may exist on a single site or across multiple sites (ex: Facebook, LinkedIn, Twitter, Google, GitHub, Docker Hub, etc.). Establishing a persona may require development of additional documentation to make them seem real. This could include filling out profile information, developing social networks, or incorporating photos.(Citation: NEWSCASTER2014)(Citation: BlackHatRobinSage)

Establishing accounts can also include the creation of accounts with email providers, which may be directly leveraged for [Phishing for Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1598) or [Phishing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566).(Citation: Mandiant APT1) In addition, establishing accounts may allow adversaries to abuse free services, such as registering for trial periods to [Acquire Infrastructure](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1583) for malicious purposes.(Citation: Free Trial PurpleUrchin)
3267.profile: [profile]Establish Accounts, also known as T1585, is a Resource Development technique used to build operational infrastructure across various platforms. Adversaries create and cultivate accounts on services like social media, email providers, and code repositories to develop fictitious or impersonated personas for social engineering, such as phishing, or to abuse free trials for malicious infrastructure. This technique is associated with groups including APT17, Kimsuky, and Fox Kitten.
3267.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Establish Backdoor Access is a technique for maintaining persistent, covert access to a compromised system, often by creating or exploiting alternative entry points. This can be achieved through methods like deploying web shells on servers, modifying system accessibility features (e.g., replacing utilman.exe with cmd.exe), or patching domain controller authentication processes (e.g., using a Skeleton Key). These backdoors provide adversaries with redundant access channels to ensure continued presence even if primary access is lost.

3268.name: Gather Host Information
3268.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may gather information about the victim's hosts that can be used during targeting. Information about hosts may include a variety of details, including administrative data (ex: name, assigned IP, functionality, etc.) as well as specifics regarding its configuration (ex: operating system, language, etc.).

Adversaries may gather this information in various ways, such as direct collection actions via [Active Scanning](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1595) or [Phishing for Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1598). Adversaries may also compromise sites then include malicious content designed to collect host information from visitors.(Citation: ATT ScanBox) Information about hosts may also be exposed to adversaries via online or other accessible data sets (ex: [Social Media](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1593/001) or [Search Victim-Owned Websites](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1594)). Gathering this information may reveal opportunities for other forms of reconnaissance (ex: [Search Open Websites/Domains](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1593) or [Search Open Technical Databases](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1596)), establishing operational resources (ex: [Develop Capabilities](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1587) or [Obtain Capabilities](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1588)), and/or initial access (ex: [Supply Chain Compromise](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195) or [External Remote Services](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1133)).

Adversaries may also gather victim host information via User-Agent HTTP headers, which are sent to a server to identify the application, operating system, vendor, and/or version of the requesting user agent. This can be used to inform the adversary’s follow-on action. For example, adversaries may check user agents for the requesting operating system, then only serve malware for target operating systems while ignoring others.(Citation: TrellixQakbot)
3268.profile: [profile]Gather Victim Host Information is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1592 under the Reconnaissance tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. It involves collecting details about a victim's hosts, such as administrative data (name, IP, functionality) and configuration specifics (operating system, language). This information can be gathered through methods like Active Scanning, Phishing for Information, compromising websites to deploy info-stealing content, or analyzing accessible datasets. A specific technical mechanic includes extracting host details from HTTP User-Agent headers to tailor follow-on actions, such as serving malware only to specific operating systems. The technique is associated with threat groups like Volt Typhoon.[/profile]
3268.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Gather Victim Host Information is a reconnaissance technique under MITRE ATT&CK ID T1592 within the Reconnaissance tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. It involves adversaries collecting details about victim hosts, including administrative data like names and IPs, and configuration specifics such as operating system and language. This can be achieved through direct actions like Active Scanning or Phishing for Information, by compromising websites to deploy information-gathering scripts, or by analyzing accessible datasets. A specific technical method includes extracting host details from User-Agent HTTP headers to tailor follow-on malicious payloads, as observed with groups like Volt Typhoon.

3269.name: Modular Attack Platform
3269.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may downgrade or use a version of system features that may be outdated, vulnerable, and/or does not support updated security controls. Downgrade attacks typically take advantage of a system’s backward compatibility to force it into less secure modes of operation. 

Adversaries may downgrade and use various less-secure versions of features of a system, such as [Command and Scripting Interpreter](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059)s or even network protocols that can be abused to enable [Adversary-in-the-Middle](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1557) or [Network Sniffing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1040).(Citation: Praetorian TLS Downgrade Attack 2014) For example, [PowerShell](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001) versions 5+ includes Script Block Logging (SBL), which can record executed script content. However, adversaries may attempt to execute a previous version of PowerShell that does not support SBL with the intent to [Impair Defenses](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1562) while running malicious scripts that may have otherwise been detected.(Citation: CrowdStrike BGH Ransomware 2021)(Citation: Mandiant BYOL 2018)(Citation: att_def_ps_logging)

Adversaries may similarly target network traffic to downgrade from an encrypted HTTPS connection to an unsecured HTTP connection that exposes network data in clear text.(Citation: Targeted SSL Stripping Attacks Are Real)(Citation: Crowdstrike Downgrade) On Windows systems, adversaries may downgrade the boot manager to a vulnerable version that bypasses Secure Boot, granting the ability to disable various operating system security mechanisms.(Citation: SafeBreach)
3269.profile: [profile]Downgrade Attack, identified as T1562.010 under the Defense Evasion tactic, targets Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms by exploiting backward compatibility to force systems into less secure modes. This technique involves executing outdated software versions, such as PowerShell prior to version 5 to bypass Script Block Logging, or downgrading network protocols from HTTPS to HTTP to enable traffic interception. It is also used to downgrade a system's boot manager to bypass Secure Boot. The intrusion set APT29 has been associated with this method.[/profile]
3269.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Modular Attack Platform" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the retrieved context, it is a concept describing a flexible, modular malware or attack framework. Such platforms use components like software extensions or automation scripts (e.g., AutoHotKey) to perform various malicious tasks, allowing adversaries to customize and update functionality. They may be distributed through compromised supply chains or by abusing trusted software ecosystems to establish persistent access.

3270.name: Droppers
3270.profile: [profile]Droppers is a class of malware designed to deploy other malicious payloads. It is associated with intrusion sets such as RocketKitten and APT29. This malware type is referenced in the context of other entities like Mandrake, Vultur, and Grimplant, where it functions as a component or delivery mechanism for those specific threats.[/profile]
3270.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Droppers are a type of malware designed to install or deploy other malicious payloads onto a target system. They are utilized by various threat groups, including those associated with the Darkmatter and Ricinus malware families. Specific dropper components and functionalities are observed in malware such as Mandrake, Vultur, and GrimPlant, indicating their role in complex attack chains to deliver final-stage threats like spyware or ransomware onto compromised devices.

3272.name: Self-Extracting RAR Archive
3272.profile: [profile]Self-Extracting RAR Archive is a file packaging and delivery mechanism. It is employed by APT29 and, as referenced, by groups such as Gamaredon Group (Operation Armageddon) and threat actors like Mummy Spider (using Emotet). Key technical behaviors include delivering password-protected archives containing malicious executables (e.g., service.exe, worm.exe) that are configured to execute automatically upon extraction. This method targets Windows platforms and is used to deploy other malware payloads like the Pteranodon module or HZ RAT.
3272.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Self-Extracting RAR Archive is a malware delivery and packaging method, not a distinct malware family. It is used as a container by various malware families, including Emotet (attributed to groups like Mummy Spider and Mealybug), which packages files like service.exe and worm.exe to execute automatically upon extraction. The Pteranodon malware, linked to the Gamaredon Group, also employs this method, often inside password-protected archives. Its primary target platform is Windows, facilitating initial infection and payload deployment through deceptive archive execution.

3273.name: Decoy PDF Document
3273.profile: [profile]Decoy PDF Document is a malicious file type used as a lure by multiple threat groups, including APT29, Ghostwriter, MirrorFace, and APT28. It functions as a decoy document, often impersonating legitimate files like a step-by-step instruction guide or a cryptocurrency wallet interface, to trick users into executing associated malware such as PicassoLoader, LodeInfo, or SedUploader.

3274.name: Decoy Flash Video
3274.profile: [profile]Decoy Flash Video is a malware entity attributed to APT29. It operates by presenting a fake video player dialog, often claiming a Flash Player update is required to lure victims into executing the malicious payload. This technique is used in conjunction with other malware like Kerrdown and Houdini, where decoy video files are opened to distract the user while the malicious payload runs in the background. The primary target platform is Windows systems.

The malware opens decoy documents or videos as a lure while executing background payloads like Hworm, and it targets Windows systems through fake video or movie client files, often using socially engineered themes such as adult content or movie downloads to entice execution.

3275.name: Email-Based Initial Infection
3275.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may employ various time-based methods to detect virtualization and analysis environments, particularly those that attempt to manipulate time mechanisms to simulate longer elapses of time. This may include enumerating time-based properties, such as uptime or the system clock. 

Adversaries may use calls like `GetTickCount` and `GetSystemTimeAsFileTime` to discover if they are operating within a virtual machine or sandbox, or may be able to identify a sandbox accelerating time by sampling and calculating the expected value for an environment's timestamp before and after execution of a sleep function.(Citation: ISACA Malware Tricks)
3275.profile: [profile]The entity "Email-Based Initial Infection" is a technique for Initial Access. It involves delivering malicious content via email to compromise a target system. This can be achieved through spearphishing attachments, links, or other social engineering lures embedded within emails. The intrusion-set APT29 has been associated with using this method. The technique leverages user interaction to execute code and establish a foothold.
3275.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Email-Based Initial Infection is a technique within the Initial Access tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. It describes the adversary's use of email to deliver malicious content or links as the initial infection vector. This includes sending spearphishing emails with malicious attachments or links to compromise a system, often leveraging social engineering to trick users into executing code or revealing credentials.

3276.name: Antivirus Evasion
3276.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may employ various means to detect and avoid debuggers. Debuggers are typically used by defenders to trace and/or analyze the execution of potential malware payloads.(Citation: ProcessHacker Github) Debugger evasion may include changing behaviors based on the results of the checks for the presence of artifacts indicative of a debugged environment. Similar to [Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1497), if the adversary detects a debugger, they may alter their malware to disengage from the victim or conceal the core functions of the implant. They may also search for debugger artifacts before dropping secondary or additional payloads. Specific checks will vary based on the target and/or adversary. On Windows, this may involve [Native API](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1106) function calls such as IsDebuggerPresent() and NtQueryInformationProcess(), or manually checking the BeingDebugged flag of the Process Environment Block (PEB). On Linux, this may involve querying `/proc/self/status` for the `TracerPID` field, which indicates whether or not the process is being traced by dynamic analysis tools.(Citation: Cado Security P2PInfect 2023)(Citation: Positive Technologies Hellhounds 2023) Other checks for debugging artifacts may also seek to enumerate hardware breakpoints, interrupt assembly opcodes, time checks, or measurements if exceptions are raised in the current process (assuming a present debugger would “swallow” or handle the potential error).(Citation: hasherezade debug)(Citation: AlKhaser Debug)(Citation: vxunderground debug) Malware may also leverage Structured Exception Handling (SEH) to detect debuggers by throwing an exception and detecting whether the process is suspended. SEH handles both hardware and software expectations, providing control over the exceptions including support for debugging. If a debugger is present, the program’s control will be transferred to the debugger, and the execution of the code will be suspended. If the debugger is not present, control will be transferred to the SEH handler, which will automatically handle the exception and allow the program’s execution to continue.(Citation: Apriorit) Adversaries may use the information learned from these debugger checks during automated discovery to shape follow-on behaviors. Debuggers can also be evaded by detaching the process or flooding debug logs with meaningless data via messages produced by looping [Native API](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1106) function calls such as OutputDebugStringW().(Citation: wardle evilquest partii)(Citation: Checkpoint Dridex Jan 2021)
3276.profile: [profile]The entity is Debugger Evasion (T1622), a Defense Evasion technique applicable to Linux and Windows. It involves detecting debugger presence to alter malware behavior or avoid analysis. Specific checks include Windows API calls like IsDebuggerPresent(), examining the PEB's BeingDebugged flag, querying Linux's /proc/self/status for TracerPID, using Structured Exception Handling (SEH), or enumerating hardware breakpoints. Upon detection, malware may disengage, conceal functions, or flood debug logs with data via OutputDebugStringW(). The group Mustang Panda has been associated with this technique.[/profile]
3276.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Antivirus Evasion, identified as T1497 in the MITRE ATT&CK framework, is a Defense Evasion technique applicable to multiple platforms. It involves methods to bypass or disable antivirus (AV) software, such as exploiting vulnerabilities in the AV software itself, hiding malicious files in folders excluded from AV scanning, or using polymorphic code to alter the malware's signature to avoid detection.

3277.name: Anti-Sandbox Detection
3277.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may employ various means to detect and avoid virtualization and analysis environments. This may include changing behaviors based on the results of checks for the presence of artifacts indicative of a virtual machine environment (VME) or sandbox. If the adversary detects a VME, they may alter their malware to disengage from the victim or conceal the core functions of the implant. They may also search for VME artifacts before dropping secondary or additional payloads. Adversaries may use the information learned from [Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1497) during automated discovery to shape follow-on behaviors.(Citation: Deloitte Environment Awareness)

Adversaries may use several methods to accomplish [Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1497) such as checking for security monitoring tools (e.g., Sysinternals, Wireshark, etc.) or other system artifacts associated with analysis or virtualization. Adversaries may also check for legitimate user activity to help determine if it is in an analysis environment. Additional methods include use of sleep timers or loops within malware code to avoid operating within a temporary sandbox.(Citation: Unit 42 Pirpi July 2015)
3277.profile: [profile]Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion is a Defense Evasion technique with MITRE ID T1497, applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves malware checking for artifacts of virtual machines or sandboxes, such as specific processes (e.g., Sysinternals, Wireshark), hardware attributes, or a lack of legitimate user activity, to alter its behavior, delay execution via sleep timers, or avoid deploying payloads. This technique is used by groups like APT29, Contagious Interview, Saint Bear, and DarkHotel to evade automated analysis environments.[/profile]
3277.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Anti-Sandbox Detection is a technique aligned with MITRE ATT&CK's Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion (T1497) under the Defense Evasion tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It involves malware checking for artifacts of virtual machines or sandboxes, such as security monitoring tools or a lack of legitimate user activity, and altering its behavior to disengage or delay execution using sleep timers to evade analysis environments.

3280.name: System Information Collection
3280.uncertain_mes: An adversary may attempt to get detailed information about the operating system and hardware, including version, patches, hotfixes, service packs, and architecture. Adversaries may use this information to shape follow-on behaviors, including whether or not the adversary fully infects the target and/or attempts specific actions. This behavior is distinct from [Local Storage Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1680) which is an adversary's discovery of local drive, disks and/or volumes. Tools such as [Systeminfo](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0096) can be used to gather detailed system information. If running with privileged access, a breakdown of system data can be gathered through the systemsetup configuration tool on macOS. Adversaries may leverage a [Network Device CLI](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/008) on network devices to gather detailed system information (e.g. show version).(Citation: US-CERT-TA18-106A) On ESXi servers, threat actors may gather system information from various esxcli utilities, such as `system hostname get` and `system version get`.(Citation: Crowdstrike Hypervisor Jackpotting Pt 2 2021)(Citation: Varonis) Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) cloud providers such as AWS, GCP, and Azure allow access to instance and virtual machine information via APIs. Successful authenticated API calls can return data such as the operating system platform and status of a particular instance or the model view of a virtual machine.(Citation: Amazon Describe Instance)(Citation: Google Instances Resource)(Citation: Microsoft Virutal Machine API) [System Information Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1082) combined with information gathered from other forms of discovery and reconnaissance can drive payload development and concealment.(Citation: OSX.FairyTale)(Citation: 20 macOS Common Tools and Techniques)
3280.profile: [profile]System Information Discovery is technique T1082 under the Discovery tactic, applicable to Windows, macOS, Linux, and cloud platforms. It involves adversaries collecting detailed OS and hardware data like version, patches, and architecture to inform follow-on actions. Specific mechanics include using tools like `systeminfo` on Windows, the `systemsetup` command on macOS, CLI commands like `show version` on network devices, `esxcli` utilities on ESXi, and cloud instance APIs from AWS, GCP, or Azure. It is distinct from local storage discovery and is used by numerous threat groups including APT29.
