3293.name: Command Execution Module
3293.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may abuse utilities that allow for command execution to bypass security restrictions that limit the use of command-line interpreters. Various Windows utilities may be used to execute commands, possibly without invoking [cmd](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0106). For example, [Forfiles](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0193), the Program Compatibility Assistant (`pcalua.exe`), components of the Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL), `Scriptrunner.exe`, as well as other utilities may invoke the execution of programs and commands from a [Command and Scripting Interpreter](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059), Run window, or via scripts.(Citation: VectorSec ForFiles Aug 2017)(Citation: Evi1cg Forfiles Nov 2017)(Citation: Secure Team - Scriptrunner.exe)(Citation: SS64)(Citation: Bleeping Computer - Scriptrunner.exe) Adversaries may also abuse the `ssh.exe` binary to execute malicious commands via the `ProxyCommand` and `LocalCommand` options, which can be invoked via the `-o` flag or by modifying the SSH config file.(Citation: Threat Actor Targets the Manufacturing industry with Lumma Stealer and Amadey Bot)

Adversaries may abuse these features for [Defense Evasion](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0005), specifically to perform arbitrary execution while subverting detections and/or mitigation controls (such as Group Policy) that limit/prevent the usage of [cmd](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0106) or file extensions more commonly associated with malicious payloads.
3293.profile: [profile]Indirect Command Execution, designated T1202, is a Defense Evasion technique for Windows platforms. It involves abusing trusted system utilities to execute commands while bypassing restrictions on standard interpreters like cmd.exe. Specific methods include using Forfiles, pcalua.exe, Windows Subsystem for Linux components, or Scriptrunner.exe to invoke programs. Adversaries may also misuse ssh.exe via its ProxyCommand or LocalCommand options. This technique has been associated with groups like Lazarus Group and Redcurl, and malware such as CozyDuke.
3293.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Command Execution Module" is a generic attack pattern for executing arbitrary commands, aligning with the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1059 (Command and Scripting Interpreter) under the Execution tactic, primarily on Windows platforms. It functions by leveraging system utilities or modules to run adversary-supplied commands, often to bypass security controls that restrict direct interpreter usage. Related context from similar techniques, such as Indirect Command Execution (T1202), indicates abuse of utilities like Forfiles, pcalua.exe, or SSH options (ProxyCommand, LocalCommand) to perform execution without invoking cmd.exe, serving as a Defense Evasion mechanism.

3294.name: Password Stealer Module
3294.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries with no prior knowledge of legitimate credentials within the system or environment may guess passwords to attempt access to accounts. Without knowledge of the password for an account, an adversary may opt to systematically guess the password using a repetitive or iterative mechanism. An adversary may guess login credentials without prior knowledge of system or environment passwords during an operation by using a list of common passwords. Password guessing may or may not take into account the target's policies on password complexity or use policies that may lock accounts out after a number of failed attempts.

Guessing passwords can be a risky option because it could cause numerous authentication failures and account lockouts, depending on the organization's login failure policies. (Citation: Cylance Cleaver)

Typically, management services over commonly used ports are used when guessing passwords. Commonly targeted services include the following:

* SSH (22/TCP)
* Telnet (23/TCP)
* FTP (21/TCP)
* NetBIOS / SMB / Samba (139/TCP & 445/TCP)
* LDAP (389/TCP)
* Kerberos (88/TCP)
* RDP / Terminal Services (3389/TCP)
* HTTP/HTTP Management Services (80/TCP & 443/TCP)
* MSSQL (1433/TCP)
* Oracle (1521/TCP)
* MySQL (3306/TCP)
* VNC (5900/TCP)
* SNMP (161/UDP and 162/TCP/UDP)

In addition to management services, adversaries may "target single sign-on (SSO) and cloud-based applications utilizing federated authentication protocols," as well as externally facing email applications, such as Office 365.(Citation: US-CERT TA18-068A 2018). Further, adversaries may abuse network device interfaces (such as `wlanAPI`) to brute force accessible wifi-router(s) via wireless authentication protocols.(Citation: Trend Micro Emotet 2020)

In default environments, LDAP and Kerberos connection attempts are less likely to trigger events over SMB, which creates Windows "logon failure" event ID 4625.
3294.profile: [profile]Password Guessing, identified as T1110.001 under the Credential Access tactic, is a technique where adversaries systematically attempt to access accounts by trying common passwords without prior knowledge of legitimate credentials. It targets a wide range of management services over standard ports like SSH (22/TCP), Telnet (23/TCP), SMB (445/TCP), and RDP (3389/TCP), as well as cloud applications and SSO systems. This method risks triggering authentication failures and account lockouts. Groups such as APT29 and APT28 have been associated with this technique, which is also used to brute-force master passwords for password managers.
3294.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Password Stealer Module is a credential access technique that extracts stored passwords from a victim's system. It operates by targeting specific storage locations, such as web browser credential databases (e.g., Chrome's `Login Data` file) or password manager vaults. The module often uses system functions like `CryptUnprotectData` to decrypt the credentials, leveraging the user's cached logon key. This allows adversaries to harvest plaintext passwords for reuse in further attacks.

3295.name: NTLM Stealer Module
3295.profile: [profile]NTLM Stealer Module is a technique for credential access, likely aligned with MITRE ATT&CK T1557.001 (LLMNR/NBT-NS Poisoning and SMB Relay) under the Collection tactic on Windows platforms. It operates by intercepting authentication materials, specifically NTLM hashes, often through network traffic spoofing via protocols like LLMNR/NBT-NS or by forcing SMB/WebDAV authentication from a victim to an adversary-controlled system. The stolen NTLMv1/v2 hashes can be relayed for lateral movement or cracked offline. This module is associated with malware like CozyDuke and groups such as Lazarus Group and Wizard Spider.[/profile]
3295.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "NTLM Stealer Module" is an attack pattern that aligns with the MITRE ATT&CK technique Forced Authentication (T1187) under the Credential Access tactic, primarily targeting Windows platforms. It operates by tricking a system into automatically sending user authentication hashes, specifically NTLM credentials, to an adversary-controlled server. This is commonly achieved through mechanisms like malicious document templates or crafted files (e.g., .SCF or .LNK files) that trigger SMB or WebDAV authentication requests when accessed. The intercepted NTLM hashes can then be relayed in attacks or cracked offline to obtain plaintext passwords.

3296.name: System Information Module
3296.uncertain_mes: An adversary may attempt to get detailed information about the operating system and hardware, including version, patches, hotfixes, service packs, and architecture. Adversaries may use this information to shape follow-on behaviors, including whether or not the adversary fully infects the target and/or attempts specific actions. This behavior is distinct from [Local Storage Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1680) which is an adversary's discovery of local drive, disks and/or volumes. Tools such as [Systeminfo](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0096) can be used to gather detailed system information. If running with privileged access, a breakdown of system data can be gathered through the systemsetup configuration tool on macOS. Adversaries may leverage a [Network Device CLI](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/008) on network devices to gather detailed system information (e.g. show version).(Citation: US-CERT-TA18-106A) On ESXi servers, threat actors may gather system information from various esxcli utilities, such as `system hostname get` and `system version get`.(Citation: Crowdstrike Hypervisor Jackpotting Pt 2 2021)(Citation: Varonis) Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) cloud providers such as AWS, GCP, and Azure allow access to instance and virtual machine information via APIs. Successful authenticated API calls can return data such as the operating system platform and status of a particular instance or the model view of a virtual machine.(Citation: Amazon Describe Instance)(Citation: Google Instances Resource)(Citation: Microsoft Virutal Machine API) [System Information Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1082) combined with information gathered from other forms of discovery and reconnaissance can drive payload development and concealment.(Citation: OSX.FairyTale)(Citation: 20 macOS Common Tools and Techniques)
3296.profile: [profile]System Information Discovery is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1082 under the Discovery tactic, applicable to Windows, macOS, Linux, Network, IaaS, and ESXi platforms. It involves adversaries gathering detailed OS and hardware data like version, patches, and architecture to inform follow-on actions. Specific technical mechanics include using the `systeminfo` command on Windows, the `systemsetup` tool on macOS, CLI commands like `show version` on network devices, esxcli utilities such as `system version get` on ESXi, and cloud instance APIs from AWS, GCP, and Azure. It is distinct from local storage discovery and is used by numerous threat groups including APT41, Lazarus Group, and FIN7.
3296.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "System Information Module" is a software component used for System Information Discovery, aligning with MITRE ATT&CK technique T1082 under the Discovery tactic on Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It operates by gathering detailed data about the operating system, hardware, version, patches, and architecture. This information is used to shape follow-on adversary actions, such as determining whether to fully infect a target or attempt specific exploits. Common methods include using tools like `systeminfo` on Windows, the `systemsetup` command on macOS, or `esxcli` utilities like `system hostname get` on ESXi servers.

3300.name: Encryption of Configuration
3300.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may compromise a network device’s encryption capability in order to bypass encryption that would otherwise protect data communications. (Citation: Cisco Synful Knock Evolution)

Encryption can be used to protect transmitted network traffic to maintain its confidentiality (protect against unauthorized disclosure) and integrity (protect against unauthorized changes). Encryption ciphers are used to convert a plaintext message to ciphertext and can be computationally intensive to decipher without the associated decryption key. Typically, longer keys increase the cost of cryptanalysis, or decryption without the key.

Adversaries can compromise and manipulate devices that perform encryption of network traffic. For example, through behaviors such as [Modify System Image](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1601), [Reduce Key Space](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1600/001), and [Disable Crypto Hardware](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1600/002), an adversary can negatively effect and/or eliminate a device’s ability to securely encrypt network traffic. This poses a greater risk of unauthorized disclosure and may help facilitate data manipulation, Credential Access, or Collection efforts. (Citation: Cisco Blog Legacy Device Attacks)
3300.profile: [profile]The entity "Encryption of Configuration" aligns with MITRE ATT&CK technique T1600, "Weaken Encryption," under the Defense Evasion tactic, targeting network devices. This technique involves compromising a device's encryption capability to bypass data protection, for instance by reducing the cryptographic key space or disabling dedicated hardware, thereby weakening or eliminating secure traffic encryption to facilitate unauthorized data access or manipulation.
3300.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Encryption of Configuration is a technique where adversaries encrypt configuration files to obfuscate malicious settings and evade detection. This involves applying encryption algorithms to configuration data, such as command-and-control (C2) parameters, making them unreadable without the decryption key. The encryption keys are often embedded within the malware binary or delivered separately, requiring reverse engineering to recover the plaintext configuration. This method enhances operational security by hiding critical attack details from static analysis tools.

3301.name: XML Configuration Storage
3301.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may store data in "fileless" formats to conceal malicious activity from defenses. Fileless storage can be broadly defined as any format other than a file. Common examples of non-volatile fileless storage in Windows systems include the Windows Registry, event logs, or WMI repository.(Citation: Microsoft Fileless)(Citation: SecureList Fileless) Shared memory directories on Linux systems (`/dev/shm`, `/run/shm`, `/var/run`, and `/var/lock`) and volatile directories on Network Devices (`/tmp` and `/volatile`) may also be considered fileless storage, as files written to these directories are mapped directly to RAM and not stored on the disk.(Citation: Elastic Binary Executed from Shared Memory Directory)(Citation: Akami Frog4Shell 2024)(Citation: Aquasec Muhstik Malware 2024)(Citation: Bitsight 7777 Botnet)(Citation: CISCO Nexus 900 Config).

Similar to fileless in-memory behaviors such as [Reflective Code Loading](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1620) and [Process Injection](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1055), fileless data storage may remain undetected by anti-virus and other endpoint security tools that can only access specific file formats from disk storage. Leveraging fileless storage may also allow adversaries to bypass the protections offered by read-only file systems in Linux.(Citation: Sysdig Fileless Malware 23022)

Adversaries may use fileless storage to conceal various types of stored data, including payloads/shellcode (potentially being used as part of [Persistence](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0003)) and collected data not yet exfiltrated from the victim (e.g., [Local Data Staging](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1074/001)). Adversaries also often encrypt, encode, splice, or otherwise obfuscate this fileless data when stored. 

Some forms of fileless storage activity may indirectly create artifacts in the file system, but in central and otherwise difficult to inspect formats such as the WMI (e.g., `%SystemRoot%\System32\Wbem\Repository`) or Registry (e.g., `%SystemRoot%\System32\Config`) physical files.(Citation: Microsoft Fileless)
3301.profile: [profile]XML Configuration Storage, also known as fileless storage (T1027.011), is a Defense Evasion technique used on Windows, Linux, and Network Device platforms. It involves storing malicious data in non-file formats like the Windows Registry, WMI repository, or Linux shared memory directories (/dev/shm) to evade detection by disk-based security tools. This method can conceal payloads or staged data, and adversaries like APT32 and Turla may further obfuscate the stored content.[/profile]
3301.profile_without_enhance: [profile]XML Configuration Storage is a technique where adversaries store malicious data or configurations within XML files to conceal their activity. This method can be used for persistence or data staging, leveraging the structured format of XML to hide payloads. The technique is related to data storage and manipulation, potentially falling under tactics like Persistence or Defense Evasion, and can be executed on platforms that process XML files, such as Windows systems using tools like msxsl.exe for script processing within these files.

3302.profile: [profile]Agent is a malware entity. Its aliases include 'ati-agent'. It is attributed to APT 29. Key technical behaviors involve using specific User-Agent strings for C2 communication, such as 'agent', 'gate', 'SenukeDR102', 'bDZOQP3', and 'EznTvkbq', and establishing persistence via Windows registry keys. Its target platform is Windows. It is related to the malware families CozyDuke and Agent NextGen.[/profile]

It is related to variants like Agent NextGen and is part of broader malware families including CozyDuke from the Dukes family. Key technical behaviors involve using specific file extensions and notes such as "you are stupid!.txt". It has been active since at least 2019, with updates into 2022, and is referenced in the context of other malware like hakbit, evilnum (as Core Agent), and ismagent (as QUADAGENT), the latter also linked to groups Greenbug and APT34. It is also mentioned in DarkRat C2 communications via a "User-Agent: agent" string.[/profile]

Its key technical behaviors involve using specific User-Agent strings for C2 communication, such as 'agent', 'gate', and 'SenukeDR102', and establishing persistence via Windows Registry keys. It targets Windows systems and shares connections with the CozyDuke and Agent malware families.[/profile]

3304.name: Registry Run Key
3304.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may achieve persistence by adding a program to a startup folder or referencing it with a Registry run key. Adding an entry to the "run keys" in the Registry or startup folder will cause the program referenced to be executed when a user logs in.(Citation: Microsoft Run Key) These programs will be executed under the context of the user and will have the account's associated permissions level. The following run keys are created by default on Windows systems: * HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run * HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunOnce * HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run * HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunOnce Run keys may exist under multiple hives.(Citation: Microsoft Wow6432Node 2018)(Citation: Malwarebytes Wow6432Node 2016) The HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunOnceEx is also available but is not created by default on Windows Vista and newer. Registry run key entries can reference programs directly or list them as a dependency.(Citation: Microsoft Run Key) For example, it is possible to load a DLL at logon using a "Depend" key with RunOnceEx: reg add HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunOnceEx\0001\Depend /v 1 /d "C:\temp\evil[.]dll" (Citation: Oddvar Moe RunOnceEx Mar 2018) Placing a program within a startup folder will also cause that program to execute when a user logs in. There is a startup folder location for individual user accounts as well as a system-wide startup folder that will be checked regardless of which user account logs in. The startup folder path for the current user is C:\Users\\[Username]\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup. The startup folder path for all users is C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\StartUp. The following Registry keys can be used to set startup folder items for persistence: * HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Explorer\User Shell Folders * HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Explorer\Shell Folders * HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Explorer\Shell Folders * HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Explorer\User Shell Folders The following Registry keys can control automatic startup of services during boot: * HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunServicesOnce * HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunServicesOnce * HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunServices * HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunServices Using policy settings to specify startup programs creates corresponding values in either of two Registry keys: * HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\Explorer\Run * HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\Explorer\Run Programs listed in the load value of the registry key HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Windows run automatically for the currently logged-on user. By default, the multistring BootExecute value of the registry key HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\System\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager is set to autocheck autochk *. This value causes Windows, at startup, to check the file-system integrity of the hard disks if the system has been shut down abnormally. Adversaries can add other programs or processes to this registry value which will automatically launch at boot. Adversaries can use these configuration locations to execute malware, such as remote access tools, to maintain persistence through system reboots. Adversaries may also use [Masquerading](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1036) to make the Registry entries look as if they are associated with legitimate programs.
3304.profile: [profile]Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1547.001 under the Persistence tactic for Windows. It achieves persistence by adding entries to specific Windows Registry keys or placing executables in startup folders, causing referenced programs to execute upon user logon. Default run keys include HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run and HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run. A specific example is using the RunOnceEx key with a "Depend" value to load a DLL, e.g., `reg add HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunOnceEx\0001\Depend /v 1 /d "C:\temp\evil.dll"`. This technique is used by numerous threat groups including APT28, Lazarus, and FIN7.[/profile]
3304.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Registry Run Keys is a persistence technique identified as T1547.001 within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, falling under the Privilege Escalation and Persistence tactics for the Windows platform. It works by adversaries adding entries to specific Windows Registry keys, such as HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run or HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run, which causes the referenced program or DLL to execute automatically upon user logon or system boot, providing sustained access.

3305.name: Scheduled Task
3305.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may abuse the Windows Task Scheduler to perform task scheduling for initial or recurring execution of malicious code. There are multiple ways to access the Task Scheduler in Windows. The [schtasks](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0111) utility can be run directly on the command line, or the Task Scheduler can be opened through the GUI within the Administrator Tools section of the Control Panel.(Citation: Stack Overflow) In some cases, adversaries have used a .NET wrapper for the Windows Task Scheduler, and alternatively, adversaries have used the Windows netapi32 library and [Windows Management Instrumentation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1047) (WMI) to create a scheduled task. Adversaries may also utilize the Powershell Cmdlet `Invoke-CimMethod`, which leverages WMI class `PS_ScheduledTask` to create a scheduled task via an XML path.(Citation: Red Canary - Atomic Red Team)

An adversary may use Windows Task Scheduler to execute programs at system startup or on a scheduled basis for persistence. The Windows Task Scheduler can also be abused to conduct remote Execution as part of Lateral Movement and/or to run a process under the context of a specified account (such as SYSTEM). Similar to [System Binary Proxy Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1218), adversaries have also abused the Windows Task Scheduler to potentially mask one-time execution under signed/trusted system processes.(Citation: ProofPoint Serpent)

Adversaries may also create "hidden" scheduled tasks (i.e. [Hide Artifacts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1564)) that may not be visible to defender tools and manual queries used to enumerate tasks. Specifically, an adversary may hide a task from `schtasks /query` and the Task Scheduler by deleting the associated Security Descriptor (SD) registry value (where deletion of this value must be completed using SYSTEM permissions).(Citation: SigmaHQ)(Citation: Tarrask scheduled task) Adversaries may also employ alternate methods to hide tasks, such as altering the metadata (e.g., `Index` value) within associated registry keys.(Citation: Defending Against Scheduled Task Attacks in Windows Environments)
3305.profile: [profile]Scheduled Task, also known as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1053.005, falls under the Execution and Persistence tactics primarily on Windows platforms. It involves abusing the Windows Task Scheduler via utilities like `schtasks`, .NET wrappers, WMI, or the PowerShell `Invoke-CimMethod` cmdlet to schedule malicious code for initial or recurring execution. This technique is used for persistence, lateral movement, and running processes under privileged contexts like SYSTEM, and adversaries can hide tasks by deleting the associated Security Descriptor registry value or altering registry key metadata. Associated threat groups include FIN7 and APT29, and malware like CozyDuke has utilized this method.
3305.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Scheduled Task is a technique (T1053) within the Execution and Persistence tactics, applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS. Adversaries abuse system task schedulers like the Windows Task Scheduler (via schtasks, WMI, or PowerShell's Invoke-CimMethod) or Linux's at command to execute malicious code at startup or on a recurring schedule for persistence, lateral movement, or privilege escalation. They may create hidden tasks by deleting Security Descriptor registry values or masquerading task names to evade detection.

3306.name: COM Hijacking
3306.profile: [profile]COM Hijacking, also known as Component Object Model Hijacking, is a persistence technique (T1546.015) within the Defense Evasion and Persistence tactics, targeting the Windows platform. It involves modifying Windows Registry entries to replace references to legitimate COM objects, causing malicious code to execute when the hijacked system component is invoked. Adversaries often target frequently used COM objects to maintain stealth, and variations may abuse Type Libraries to redirect functionality to remote scripts. The malware CozyDuke has been associated with this technique.[/profile]
3306.profile_without_enhance: [profile]COM Hijacking is a persistence technique (T1546.015) within the Execution tactic on Windows platforms. It involves modifying Windows Registry keys to replace references to legitimate Component Object Model (COM) objects, causing malicious code to execute when the hijacked system component is triggered. Adversaries may also abuse Type Libraries (TypeLibs) to redirect functionality to remote scripts, enabling stealthy payload execution while maintaining system stability to avoid detection.

3308.name: Cobalt Strike BEACON
3308.uncertain_mes:
[Cobalt Strike](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0154) is a commercial, full-featured, remote access tool that bills itself as “adversary simulation software designed to execute targeted attacks and emulate the post-exploitation actions of advanced threat actors”. Cobalt Strike’s interactive post-exploit capabilities cover the full range of ATT&CK tactics, all executed within a single, integrated system.(Citation: cobaltstrike manual)

In addition to its own capabilities, [Cobalt Strike](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0154) leverages the capabilities of other well-known tools such as Metasploit and [Mimikatz](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0002).(Citation: cobaltstrike manual)
3308.profile: [profile]Cobalt Strike BEACON, also known as cobalt strike, is a commercial remote access tool and adversary simulation software used for post-exploitation. It is leveraged by numerous threat groups including APT29, APT32, APT41, FIN6, FIN7, Mustang Panda, CopyKittens, DarkHydrus, Leviathan, and Aquatic Panda. Its key TTPs include emulating advanced threat actor actions, integrating capabilities from tools like Metasploit and Mimikatz, and utilizing configurable C2 profiles such as WordPress, Amazon, and WooCommerce for beacon activity. It targets various platforms and its infrastructure is associated with activity clusters like UNC2447, UNC1878, and UNC2452.[/profile]
3308.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Cobalt Strike BEACON, also known as Cobalt Strike, is a commercial penetration testing tool widely repurposed as malware. It is attributed to or used by numerous threat groups including APT29, APT32, APT41, FIN6, FIN7, Mustang Panda, and UNC1878. Its key technical behaviors involve beaconing for command and control using configurable profiles that can mimic legitimate traffic from services like Amazon, Bing, WordPress, and WooCommerce to evade detection. It primarily targets Windows platforms, with its infrastructure and supplementary activity often identified through specific beacon configurations and network signatures.

3309.name: Trojanized SolarWinds Orion
3309.profile: [profile]Name: Trojanized SolarWinds Orion. Aliases: SUNBURST. Attributed Groups: UNC2452, APT 29. Key TTPs/Technical Behaviors: A backdoor deployed via a trojanized, digitally-signed SolarWinds Orion software update (SolarWinds.Orion.Core.BusinessLayer.dll) in a supply chain compromise, communicating via HTTP to third-party servers. Target Platforms: SolarWinds Orion software framework. Infrastructure/Supplementary Info: Post-compromise activity was observed in related incidents.[/profile]
3309.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Trojanized SolarWinds Orion, also known as SUNBURST or sunburst, is a malware attributed to APT29 and UNC2452. It is delivered via a trojanized update to the SolarWinds Orion software framework, using a digitally-signed component (SolarWinds.Orion.Core.BusinessLayer.dll) as a backdoor that communicates via HTTP to third-party servers. It has a dormant period before establishing command and control, often beaconing to internal IP ranges. It is associated with the TEARDROP payload and primarily targets Windows environments as part of a supply-chain compromise.

3310.name: System Profiling
3310.profile: [profile]System Profiling is a technique adversaries use to gather detailed information about a target's operating system, hardware, and configuration, such as version, patches, architecture, and installed services. This discovery, often performed using commands like `systeminfo`, `sc query`, or `tasklist /svc`, helps shape follow-on attack behaviors, including payload development and target selection. It is associated with malware like SUNBURST and numerous threat groups including Turla, Lazarus, and FIN7.
3310.profile_without_enhance: [profile]System Profiling is a discovery technique where adversaries gather detailed information about a system's operating system, hardware, and configuration to inform follow-on actions. This can involve using commands like `systeminfo` on Windows or `systemsetup` on macOS to obtain version, architecture, patch levels, and service pack details. Adversaries may also query APIs in cloud environments or use network device CLIs to collect similar data, using this intelligence to tailor their attack payloads and evasion strategies.

3311.name: Reboot
3311.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may shutdown/reboot systems to interrupt access to, or aid in the destruction of, those systems. Operating systems may contain commands to initiate a shutdown/reboot of a machine or network device. In some cases, these commands may also be used to initiate a shutdown/reboot of a remote computer or network device via [Network Device CLI](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/008) (e.g. reload).(Citation: Microsoft Shutdown Oct 2017)(Citation: alert_TA18_106A) They may also include shutdown/reboot of a virtual machine via hypervisor / cloud consoles or command line tools. Shutting down or rebooting systems may disrupt access to computer resources for legitimate users while also impeding incident response/recovery. Adversaries may also use Windows API functions, such as `InitializeSystemShutdownExW` or `ExitWindowsEx`, to force a system to shut down or reboot.(Citation: CrowdStrike Blog)(Citation: Unit42 Agrius 2023) Alternatively, the `NtRaiseHardError`or `ZwRaiseHardError` Windows API functions with the `ResponseOption` parameter set to `OptionShutdownSystem` may deliver a “blue screen of death” (BSOD) to a system.(Citation: SonicWall)(Citation: NtRaiseHardError)(Citation: NotMe-BSOD) In order to leverage these API functions, an adversary may need to acquire `SeShutdownPrivilege` (e.g., via [Access Token Manipulation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1134)).(Citation: Unit42 Agrius 2023) In some cases, the system may not be able to boot again. Adversaries may attempt to shutdown/reboot a system after impacting it in other ways, such as [Disk Structure Wipe](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1561/002) or [Inhibit System Recovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1490), to hasten the intended effects on system availability.(Citation: Talos Nyetya June 2017)(Citation: Talos Olympic Destroyer 2018)
3311.profile: [profile]System Shutdown/Reboot is identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1529 under the Impact tactic for Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves using OS commands (e.g., `reload` for network devices), hypervisor tools, or specific Windows API functions like `InitializeSystemShutdownExW`, `ExitWindowsEx`, or `NtRaiseHardError` with the `OptionShutdownSystem` parameter to force a shutdown, reboot, or BSOD, often requiring `SeShutdownPrivilege`. This action disrupts access and can be combined with wipers to hasten destruction, as observed with groups like Lazarus Group and APT38. The malware SUNBURST has been associated with this technique.[/profile]
3311.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Reboot" aligns with the MITRE ATT&CK technique "System Shutdown/Reboot" (T1529) under the Impact tactic, applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. Adversaries use this technique to disrupt system availability by executing OS commands (e.g., `reload` for network devices), leveraging Windows API functions like `ExitWindowsEx` or `NtRaiseHardError` to force a reboot or cause a BSOD, often after acquiring `SeShutdownPrivilege`. It is commonly used following data destruction techniques to hasten impact and has been associated with groups like APT37 and Lazarus Group.

3312.name: Service Disabling
3312.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may disable security tools to avoid possible detection of their tools and activities. This can take the form of killing security software or event logging processes, deleting Registry keys so that tools do not start at run time, or other methods to interfere with security scanning or event reporting.
3312.profile: [profile]Service Disabling, also known as T1089 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Tools, is a Defense Evasion tactic used on Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. The technique involves adversaries killing security software or event logging processes, deleting Registry keys to prevent tools from starting at runtime, or using other methods to interfere with security scanning and event reporting to avoid detection. The malware SUNBURST has been associated with this behavior.[/profile]
3312.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Service Disabling, mapped to MITRE ATT&CK T1489 within the Impact tactic, targets Windows, Linux, and cloud platforms. This technique involves stopping or disabling system services to render them unavailable, often targeting critical services like MSExchangeIS to inhibit incident response or enable follow-on actions such as data destruction. Adversaries achieve this using commands like `sc stop`, `systemctl stop`, or cloud APIs such as AWS's `DisableAPIServiceAccess`.

3313.name: Masquerading
3313.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may attempt to manipulate features of their artifacts to make them appear legitimate or benign to users and/or security tools. Masquerading occurs when the name or location of an object, legitimate or malicious, is manipulated or abused for the sake of evading defenses and observation. This may include manipulating file metadata, tricking users into misidentifying the file type, and giving legitimate task or service names.

Renaming abusable system utilities to evade security monitoring is also a form of [Masquerading](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1036).(Citation: LOLBAS Main Site)
3313.profile: [profile]Masquerading is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1036 under the Defense Evasion tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It involves manipulating the name, location, or metadata of files and system utilities to appear legitimate, such as renaming malicious executables or abusing trusted service names to evade detection. This technique is commonly used by groups like APT28, Sandworm Team, and OilRig, and is related to behaviors like shortcut modification (T1023) and the sub-technique of masquerading account names (T1036.010).[/profile]
3313.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Masquerading is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1036 under the Defense Evasion tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. It involves manipulating object names, locations, or metadata to appear legitimate, such as renaming malicious files or system utilities, giving processes legitimate service names, or using shortcuts to disguise malicious targets. This technique is employed by numerous threat groups including APT28, Sandworm Team, and OilRig.

3314.name: Obfuscated Blocklists
3314.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may attempt to make an executable or file difficult to discover or analyze by encrypting, encoding, or otherwise obfuscating its contents on the system or in transit. This is common behavior that can be used across different platforms and the network to evade defenses. 

Payloads may be compressed, archived, or encrypted in order to avoid detection. These payloads may be used during Initial Access or later to mitigate detection. Sometimes a user's action may be required to open and [Deobfuscate/Decode Files or Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1140) for [User Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204). The user may also be required to input a password to open a password protected compressed/encrypted file that was provided by the adversary. (Citation: Volexity PowerDuke November 2016) Adversaries may also use compressed or archived scripts, such as JavaScript. 

Portions of files can also be encoded to hide the plain-text strings that would otherwise help defenders with discovery. (Citation: Linux/Cdorked.A We Live Security Analysis) Payloads may also be split into separate, seemingly benign files that only reveal malicious functionality when reassembled. (Citation: Carbon Black Obfuscation Sept 2016)

Adversaries may also abuse [Command Obfuscation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/010) to obscure commands executed from payloads or directly via [Command and Scripting Interpreter](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059). Environment variables, aliases, characters, and other platform/language specific semantics can be used to evade signature based detections and application control mechanisms. (Citation: FireEye Obfuscation June 2017) (Citation: FireEye Revoke-Obfuscation July 2017)(Citation: PaloAlto EncodedCommand March 2017)
3314.profile: [profile]Obfuscated Files or Information is MITRE technique T1027 under the Defense Evasion tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. It involves making files or executables difficult to analyze by encrypting, encoding, compressing, or archiving their contents. Specific mechanics include splitting payloads into benign-seeming files for later reassembly, using password-protected archives requiring user interaction, and encoding portions of files to hide plain-text strings. It is associated with malware like SUNBURST and groups including APT41, Sandworm Team, and Lazarus Group.
3314.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Obfuscated Blocklists is a technique used to evade detection by security tools that rely on static signatures or hash-based blocklists. Adversaries modify malware by adding non-functional, junk data (binary padding) to change the file's checksum and on-disk representation, thereby avoiding hash matches. This padding increases the file size, which can also bypass security tools with file size limitations. The technique is a sub-type of obfuscation aimed specifically at defeating blocklist mechanisms.

3315.name: Memory-only dropper
3315.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may attempt to access credential material stored in the process memory of the Local Security Authority Subsystem Service (LSASS). After a user logs on, the system generates and stores a variety of credential materials in LSASS process memory. These credential materials can be harvested by an administrative user or SYSTEM and used to conduct [Lateral Movement](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0008) using [Use Alternate Authentication Material](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1550). As well as in-memory techniques, the LSASS process memory can be dumped from the target host and analyzed on a local system. For example, on the target host use procdump: * procdump -ma lsass.exe lsass_dump Locally, mimikatz can be run using: * sekurlsa::Minidump lsassdump.dmp * sekurlsa::logonPasswords Built-in Windows tools such as `comsvcs.dll` can also be used: * rundll32.exe C:\Windows\System32\comsvcs.dll MiniDump PID lsass.dmp full(Citation: Volexity Exchange Marauder March 2021)(Citation: Symantec Attacks Against Government Sector) Similar to [Image File Execution Options Injection](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1546/012), the silent process exit mechanism can be abused to create a memory dump of `lsass.exe` through Windows Error Reporting (`WerFault.exe`).(Citation: Deep Instinct LSASS) Windows Security Support Provider (SSP) DLLs are loaded into LSASS process at system start. Once loaded into the LSA, SSP DLLs have access to encrypted and plaintext passwords that are stored in Windows, such as any logged-on user's Domain password or smart card PINs. The SSP configuration is stored in two Registry keys: HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa\Security Packages and HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa\OSConfig\Security Packages. An adversary may modify these Registry keys to add new SSPs, which will be loaded the next time the system boots, or when the AddSecurityPackage Windows API function is called.(Citation: Graeber 2014) The following SSPs can be used to access credentials: * Msv: Interactive logons, batch logons, and service logons are done through the MSV authentication package. * Wdigest: The Digest Authentication protocol is designed for use with Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) and Simple Authentication Security Layer (SASL) exchanges.(Citation: TechNet Blogs Credential Protection) * Kerberos: Preferred for mutual client-server domain authentication in Windows 2000 and later. * CredSSP: Provides SSO and Network Level Authentication for Remote Desktop Services.(Citation: TechNet Blogs Credential Protection)
3315.profile: [profile]Memory-only dropper is a technique for executing malicious code without writing to disk, often to evade file-based detection. It operates within the Credential Access tactic, primarily on Windows systems, by using in-memory execution methods. The technique is associated with the SUNBURST malware, which employed it to load its payload directly from memory, bypassing traditional file system scans. This approach leverages legitimate system processes or specially crafted code that resides solely in volatile memory, leaving minimal forensic artifacts on the host.
3315.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Memory-only dropper is a technique where malware payloads are delivered and executed directly in system memory without writing to disk, evading file-based detection. It often involves process injection or hollowing to run code within legitimate processes, leveraging tools like PowerShell or reflective DLL loading to fetch and execute payloads from remote sources into memory, leaving minimal forensic traces.

3316.name: SolarWinds.Orion.Core.BusinessLayer.dll
3316.profile: [profile]SolarWinds.Orion.Core.BusinessLayer.dll, also known as Sunburst, is a SolarWinds-signed plugin component of the Orion software framework. It is attributed to the intrusion sets APT29 and UNC2452. Its key technical behavior is acting as an obfuscated backdoor that communicates via HTTP to third-party servers. Its target platform is the SolarWinds Orion software framework.[/profile]
3316.profile_without_enhance: [profile]SolarWinds.Orion.Core.BusinessLayer.dll, also known as SUNBURST, is a malicious SolarWinds-signed plugin component of the Orion software framework. It is attributed to groups APT 29 and UNC2452. Its key behaviors include profiling the system and identifying forensic/antivirus tools via processes, services, and drivers for discovery. It features an obfuscated backdoor that communicates via HTTP to third-party servers, using techniques like masquerading as the OIP protocol for defense evasion. It also transfers and executes files and can disable system services. The malware targets the Windows platform.

3317.name: Masquerading as OIP protocol
3317.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may attempt to manipulate features of their artifacts to make them appear legitimate or benign to users and/or security tools. Masquerading occurs when the name or location of an object, legitimate or malicious, is manipulated or abused for the sake of evading defenses and observation. This may include manipulating file metadata, tricking users into misidentifying the file type, and giving legitimate task or service names.

Renaming abusable system utilities to evade security monitoring is also a form of [Masquerading](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1036).(Citation: LOLBAS Main Site)
3317.profile: [profile]Masquerading, designated as T1036, is a Defense Evasion technique where adversaries manipulate artifacts to appear legitimate. This involves altering file names, locations, or metadata, such as renaming malicious utilities or giving processes legitimate service names, to evade detection by users and security tools. It is associated with groups like APT28, Sandworm Team, and OilRig, and a related malware example is SolarWinds.Orion.Core.BusinessLayer.dll.
3317.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Masquerading as OIP protocol is a specific form of the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1036 (Masquerading) under the Defense Evasion tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It involves adversaries manipulating network traffic or artifacts to appear as legitimate OIP (Obfuscated IP or a similar proprietary) protocol communications. This technique is used to evade detection by security tools that might whitelist or not deeply inspect this specific protocol, blending malicious activity within seemingly benign network flows to bypass defenses.

3318.name: Transfer and execute files
3318.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may set files and directories to be hidden to evade detection mechanisms. To prevent normal users from accidentally changing special files on a system, most operating systems have the concept of a ‘hidden’ file. These files don’t show up when a user browses the file system with a GUI or when using normal commands on the command line. Users must explicitly ask to show the hidden files either via a series of Graphical User Interface (GUI) prompts or with command line switches (dir /a for Windows and ls –a for Linux and macOS). On Linux and Mac, users can mark specific files as hidden simply by putting a “.” as the first character in the file or folder name (Citation: Sofacy Komplex Trojan) (Citation: Antiquated Mac Malware). Files and folders that start with a period, ‘.’, are by default hidden from being viewed in the Finder application and standard command-line utilities like “ls”. Users must specifically change settings to have these files viewable. Files on macOS can also be marked with the UF_HIDDEN flag which prevents them from being seen in Finder.app, but still allows them to be seen in Terminal.app (Citation: WireLurker). On Windows, users can mark specific files as hidden by using the attrib.exe binary. Many applications create these hidden files and folders to store information so that it doesn’t clutter up the user’s workspace. For example, SSH utilities create a .ssh folder that’s hidden and contains the user’s known hosts and keys. Additionally, adversaries may name files in a manner that would allow the file to be hidden such as naming a file only a “space” character. Adversaries can use this to their advantage to hide files and folders anywhere on the system and evading a typical user or system analysis that does not incorporate investigation of hidden files.
3318.profile: [profile]The entity "Transfer and execute files" is a technique for moving and running files within a compromised environment. It involves using native tools like `copy`, `scp`, `curl`, or `ftp`, and file-sharing protocols such as SMB over Windows Admin Shares or via Remote Desktop Protocol connections. This supports lateral movement and staging of adversary tools after initial ingress. Associated malware includes SolarWinds.Orion.Core.BusinessLayer.dll, and related techniques are Ingress Tool Transfer (T1105) and Lateral Tool Transfer (T1570).[/profile]
3318.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Transfer and execute files" is a foundational technique for moving and running malicious code. It encompasses both Ingress Tool Transfer (T1105) for bringing tools into a network and Lateral Tool Transfer (T1570) for moving them internally. Adversaries use native utilities like `copy`, `certutil`, `PowerShell`, `curl`, `scp`, and `ftp`, or leverage protocols such as SMB, RDP, and web services like Dropbox. The technique supports execution via scheduled tasks or by abusing features like Windows BITS jobs for stealthy, persistent file operations.

3319.name: Profile the system
3319.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may gain persistence and elevate privileges by executing malicious content triggered by PowerShell profiles. A PowerShell profile (profile.ps1) is a script that runs when [PowerShell](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001) starts and can be used as a logon script to customize user environments. [PowerShell](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001) supports several profiles depending on the user or host program. For example, there can be different profiles for [PowerShell](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001) host programs such as the PowerShell console, PowerShell ISE or Visual Studio Code. An administrator can also configure a profile that applies to all users and host programs on the local computer. (Citation: Microsoft About Profiles) Adversaries may modify these profiles to include arbitrary commands, functions, modules, and/or [PowerShell](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001) drives to gain persistence. Every time a user opens a [PowerShell](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001) session the modified script will be executed unless the -NoProfile flag is used when it is launched. (Citation: ESET Turla PowerShell May 2019) An adversary may also be able to escalate privileges if a script in a PowerShell profile is loaded and executed by an account with higher privileges, such as a domain administrator. (Citation: Wits End and Shady PowerShell Profiles)
3319.profile: [profile]The technique "PowerShell Profile" is identified as MITRE ATT&CK T1546.013 under the Persistence tactic for Windows platforms. It involves adversaries modifying PowerShell profile scripts (e.g., profile.ps1) to execute arbitrary commands, functions, or modules each time a PowerShell session starts, unless the session is launched with the `-NoProfile` flag. This can be used to gain persistence and potentially escalate privileges if the profile is executed by a higher-privileged account, as observed in campaigns by the Turla group.
3319.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Profile the system is a discovery technique where adversaries gather detailed information about a target's operating system, hardware, and configuration to inform follow-on actions. This includes identifying OS version, patches, architecture, and installed services using commands like `systeminfo`, `sc query`, or cloud instance APIs. The gathered intelligence helps tailor payloads and select appropriate exploitation methods.

3320.name: Disable system services
3320.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may abuse system services or daemons to execute commands or programs. Adversaries can execute malicious content by interacting with or creating services either locally or remotely. Many services are set to run at boot, which can aid in achieving persistence ([Create or Modify System Process](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1543)), but adversaries can also abuse services for one-time or temporary execution.
3320.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique "System Services" with ID T1569, categorized under the Execution tactic and applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves adversaries abusing or creating system services or daemons to execute malicious commands or programs, either for one-time execution or to achieve persistence by leveraging services configured to run at boot. A related malware example is SolarWinds.Orion.Core.BusinessLayer.dll.[/profile]
3320.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Disable system services is a technique adversaries use to stop critical services, often as part of impact tactics like Service Stop (T1489) or Inhibit System Recovery (T1490). This action can render systems or specific applications (like MSExchangeIS) inaccessible to users, facilitate data destruction by halting processes that lock data stores, or disable recovery mechanisms. It is executed using commands like `sc stop` or `systemctl stop` to target services on Windows or Linux systems, respectively, and is employed by groups such as Sandworm Team and Lazarus Group.

3321.name: Identify forensic and antivirus tools via processes, services, drivers
3321.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may gather information about identities and roles within the victim organization that can be used during targeting. Information about business roles may reveal a variety of targetable details, including identifiable information for key personnel as well as what data/resources they have access to.

Adversaries may gather this information in various ways, such as direct elicitation via [Phishing for Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1598). Information about business roles may also be exposed to adversaries via online or other accessible data sets (ex: [Social Media](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1593/001) or [Search Victim-Owned Websites](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1594)).(Citation: ThreatPost Broadvoice Leak) Gathering this information may reveal opportunities for other forms of reconnaissance (ex: [Phishing for Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1598) or [Search Open Websites/Domains](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1593)), establishing operational resources (ex: [Establish Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1585) or [Compromise Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1586)), and/or initial access (ex: [Phishing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566)).
3321.profile: [profile]The entity "Identify forensic and antivirus tools via processes, services, drivers" is a technique for Security Software Discovery (T1518.001) under the Discovery tactic, applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves adversaries enumerating running processes, services, and installed drivers using native system utilities like `driverquery.exe` or `lsmod` to identify the presence and specifics of security software, antivirus, and forensic tools on a compromised host. This reconnaissance aids in evading defenses and planning subsequent actions. Associated malware includes SolarWinds.Orion.Core.BusinessLayer.dll, and related threat groups are Hexane, FIN7, LAPSUS$, and Volt Typhoon.
3321.profile_without_enhance: [profile]This technique, Identify forensic and antivirus tools via processes, services, drivers, is a sub-technique of Security Software Discovery (T1518.001) under the Discovery tactic. It operates on Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. Adversaries execute this by enumerating running processes, active services, and loaded drivers to detect the presence of security software like antivirus and forensic tools. This discovery is often performed using native system utilities such as `driverquery.exe` and `EnumDeviceDrivers()` on Windows or `lsmod` and `modinfo` on Linux/macOS, enabling the adversary to identify and subsequently evade or disable these defensive measures.

3340.name: Geolocating IP addresses
3340.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may gather the victim's IP addresses that can be used during targeting. Public IP addresses may be allocated to organizations by block, or a range of sequential addresses. Information about assigned IP addresses may include a variety of details, such as which IP addresses are in use. IP addresses may also enable an adversary to derive other details about a victim, such as organizational size, physical location(s), Internet service provider, and or where/how their publicly-facing infrastructure is hosted.

Adversaries may gather this information in various ways, such as direct collection actions via [Active Scanning](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1595) or [Phishing for Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1598). Information about assigned IP addresses may also be exposed to adversaries via online or other accessible data sets (ex: [Search Open Technical Databases](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1596)).(Citation: WHOIS)(Citation: DNS Dumpster)(Citation: Circl Passive DNS) Gathering this information may reveal opportunities for other forms of reconnaissance (ex: [Active Scanning](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1595) or [Search Open Websites/Domains](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1593)), establishing operational resources (ex: [Acquire Infrastructure](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1583) or [Compromise Infrastructure](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1584)), and/or initial access (ex: [External Remote Services](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1133)).
3340.profile: [profile]Geolocating IP addresses, identified as T1590.005 under the Reconnaissance tactic, is a technique adversaries use to gather a victim's public IP addresses for targeting. This information, which can reveal organizational size, physical location, ISP, and hosting infrastructure, is collected through methods like Active Scanning (T1595), Phishing for Information (T1598), or querying open technical databases such as WHOIS and DNS Dumpster. Groups like Hafnium, Andariel, and Magic Hound have employed this technique, which enables follow-on actions like further reconnaissance or establishing operational resources for initial access.
3340.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Geolocating IP addresses is a reconnaissance technique where adversaries determine the physical location of a victim's IP address to infer details like organizational size, ISP, and hosting infrastructure. This information, often gathered from public databases via techniques like Search Open Technical Databases, supports follow-on activities such as Active Scanning or infrastructure acquisition for initial access.

3341.name: Using multiple IP addresses per VPS provider
3341.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may gather the victim's IP addresses that can be used during targeting. Public IP addresses may be allocated to organizations by block, or a range of sequential addresses. Information about assigned IP addresses may include a variety of details, such as which IP addresses are in use. IP addresses may also enable an adversary to derive other details about a victim, such as organizational size, physical location(s), Internet service provider, and or where/how their publicly-facing infrastructure is hosted.

Adversaries may gather this information in various ways, such as direct collection actions via [Active Scanning](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1595) or [Phishing for Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1598). Information about assigned IP addresses may also be exposed to adversaries via online or other accessible data sets (ex: [Search Open Technical Databases](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1596)).(Citation: WHOIS)(Citation: DNS Dumpster)(Citation: Circl Passive DNS) Gathering this information may reveal opportunities for other forms of reconnaissance (ex: [Active Scanning](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1595) or [Search Open Websites/Domains](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1593)), establishing operational resources (ex: [Acquire Infrastructure](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1583) or [Compromise Infrastructure](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1584)), and/or initial access (ex: [External Remote Services](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1133)).
3341.profile: [profile]The entity "Using multiple IP addresses per VPS provider" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the provided context, it appears to be a specific operational security method for infrastructure acquisition and obfuscation. This technique involves adversaries renting multiple Virtual Private Servers (VPSs) from a single cloud provider and assigning distinct IP addresses to each, complicating attribution and blocking efforts by blending malicious traffic with legitimate provider infrastructure. This practice is associated with groups like APT29.
3341.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Using multiple IP addresses per VPS provider is a technique for establishing operational resources, likely within the Acquire Infrastructure tactic. It involves adversaries renting a Virtual Private Server (VPS) and then provisioning multiple, distinct IP addresses from that single provider. This method helps obscure malicious activity by distributing it across several IPs from a single, potentially trusted or anonymous cloud service, making attribution and blocking more difficult.

3343.name: Software supply chain compromise
3343.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may manipulate application software prior to receipt by a final consumer for the purpose of data or system compromise. Supply chain compromise of software can take place in a number of ways, including manipulation of the application source code, manipulation of the update/distribution mechanism for that software, or replacing compiled releases with a modified version.

Targeting may be specific to a desired victim set or may be distributed to a broad set of consumers but only move on to additional tactics on specific victims.(Citation: Avast CCleaner3 2018)(Citation: Command Five SK 2011)
3343.profile: [profile]The technique "Compromise Software Supply Chain" is formally identified as MITRE ATT&CK T1195.002 under the Initial Access tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. It involves adversaries manipulating application software before it reaches the end user to enable data or system compromise. Specific technical mechanics include tampering with the application source code, hijacking the software update or distribution mechanism, or directly replacing legitimate compiled releases with maliciously modified versions. This method has been employed by groups including APT41, Sandworm Team, and Dragonfly, and can involve either broad distribution with selective follow-on attacks or precise targeting of a specific victim set.
3343.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Software supply chain compromise, identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1195.002 under the Initial Access tactic, targets multiple platforms. This technique involves adversaries manipulating application software prior to consumer receipt to achieve system compromise. Specific technical mechanics include the manipulation of application source code, tampering with software update or distribution mechanisms, and replacing legitimate compiled releases with maliciously modified versions. Associated threat groups include Dragonfly, FIN7, APT41, and Sandworm Team.

3344.name: Legitimate credentials
3344.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may gather credentials that can be used during targeting. Account credentials gathered by adversaries may be those directly associated with the target victim organization or attempt to take advantage of the tendency for users to use the same passwords across personal and business accounts.

Adversaries may gather credentials from potential victims in various ways, such as direct elicitation via [Phishing for Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1598). Adversaries may also compromise sites then add malicious content designed to collect website authentication cookies from visitors.(Citation: ATT ScanBox) (Citation: Register Deloitte)(Citation: Register Uber)(Citation: Detectify Slack Tokens)(Citation: Forbes GitHub Creds)(Citation: GitHub truffleHog)(Citation: GitHub Gitrob)(Citation: CNET Leaks) Where multi-factor authentication (MFA) based on out-of-band communications is in use, adversaries may compromise a service provider to gain access to MFA codes and one-time passwords (OTP).(Citation: Okta Scatter Swine 2022)

Credential information may also be exposed to adversaries via leaks to online or other accessible data sets (ex: [Search Engines](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1593/002), breach dumps, code repositories, etc.). Adversaries may purchase credentials from dark web markets, such as Russian Market and 2easy, or through access to Telegram channels that distribute logs from infostealer malware.(Citation: Bleeping Computer 2easy 2021)(Citation: SecureWorks Infostealers 2023)(Citation: Bleeping Computer Stealer Logs 2023)

Gathering this information may reveal opportunities for other forms of reconnaissance (ex: [Search Open Websites/Domains](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1593) or [Phishing for Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1598)), establishing operational resources (ex: [Compromise Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1586)), and/or initial access (ex: [External Remote Services](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1133) or [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078)).
3344.profile: [profile]Legitimate Credentials is the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1589.001 under the Reconnaissance tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It involves adversaries gathering account credentials for future use, employing methods such as phishing, compromising websites to steal authentication cookies, purchasing credentials from dark web markets like Russian Market and 2easy, and harvesting leaked data from sources like breach dumps and code repositories. This activity is associated with groups including APT28, Leviathan, and Lapsus$.
3344.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Legitimate credentials" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the retrieved context, it refers to the adversary use of valid, non-compromised user credentials for initial access, persistence, privilege escalation, and lateral movement. This is a foundational concept for techniques like Valid Accounts (T1078), where adversaries leverage credentials obtained through theft, purchase, or social engineering to bypass normal authentication mechanisms and operate within a network.

3345.name: Remote access
3345.uncertain_mes:
An adversary may use legitimate remote access tools to establish an interactive command and control channel within a network. Remote access tools create a session between two trusted hosts through a graphical interface, a command line interaction, a protocol tunnel via development or management software, or hardware-level access such as KVM (Keyboard, Video, Mouse) over IP solutions. Desktop support software (usually graphical interface) and remote management software (typically command line interface) allow a user to control a computer remotely as if they are a local user inheriting the user or software permissions. This software is commonly used for troubleshooting, software installation, and system management.(Citation: Symantec Living off the Land)(Citation: CrowdStrike 2015 Global Threat Report)(Citation: CrySyS Blog TeamSpy) Adversaries may similarly abuse response features included in EDR and other defensive tools that enable remote access.

Remote access tools may be installed and used post-compromise as an alternate communications channel for redundant access or to establish an interactive remote desktop session with the target system. It may also be used as a malware component to establish a reverse connection or back-connect to a service or adversary-controlled system.

Installation of many remote access tools may also include persistence (e.g., the software's installation routine creates a [Windows Service](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1543/003)). Remote access modules/features may also exist as part of otherwise existing software (e.g., Google Chrome’s Remote Desktop).(Citation: Google Chrome Remote Desktop)(Citation: Chrome Remote Desktop)
3345.profile: [profile]Remote Access Tools, designated T1219 within the MITRE ATT&CK framework under the Command and Control tactic, is a technique for establishing interactive control over compromised systems. It involves abusing legitimate software like graphical desktop support tools, command-line remote management applications, or features within EDR tools to create sessions, often inheriting local user permissions. These tools can be installed post-compromise to provide redundant command and control channels, establish remote desktop sessions, or act as malware components for reverse connections, with their installation routines frequently creating persistence mechanisms like Windows Services.[/profile]
3345.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Remote access" is a broad concept, not a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on retrieved information, it relates to adversaries using legitimate tools or services to establish command and control or maintain persistent access. This includes software tools (like remote desktop or management software) and hardware devices (like KVM-over-IP) to create interactive sessions, often for lateral movement or redundant access. The activity is associated with groups like Carbanak, MuddyWater, and FIN7, and can involve protocols such as RDP, SSH, and VNC, or abuse of features in defensive tools like EDR.[/profile]

3346.name: Lateral Movement Using Different Credentials
3346.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may transfer tools or other files between systems in a compromised environment. Once brought into the victim environment (i.e., [Ingress Tool Transfer](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1105)) files may then be copied from one system to another to stage adversary tools or other files over the course of an operation.

Adversaries may copy files between internal victim systems to support lateral movement using inherent file sharing protocols such as file sharing over [SMB/Windows Admin Shares](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002) to connected network shares or with authenticated connections via [Remote Desktop Protocol](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/001).(Citation: Unit42 LockerGoga 2019)

Files can also be transferred using native or otherwise present tools on the victim system, such as scp, rsync, curl, sftp, and [ftp](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0095). In some cases, adversaries may be able to leverage [Web Service](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1102)s such as Dropbox or OneDrive to copy files from one machine to another via shared, automatically synced folders.(Citation: Dropbox Malware Sync)
3346.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique "Lateral Tool Transfer" (T1570) under the Lateral Movement tactic, primarily for Windows. It involves copying tools or files between systems within a compromised network to stage for operations, using protocols like SMB/Windows Admin Shares or RDP, or native tools such as scp, rsync, curl, sftp, and ftp. Adversaries may also leverage web services like Dropbox or OneDrive via shared, automatically synced folders. Groups like APT29, Wizard Spider, and Volt Typhoon have been associated with this technique.
3346.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Lateral Movement Using Different Credentials" is a technique for moving within a network by leveraging stolen or discovered account credentials to access remote systems. This involves using valid accounts, often obtained via credential dumping, to authenticate with remote services like SSH or RDP, enabling adversaries to perform actions as the logged-on user across the environment.

3347.name: LogonTracker module
3347.profile: [profile]The entity "LogonTracker module" is a component used by the APT29 intrusion set. It operates within the Windows platform, leveraging logon persistence mechanisms. The module likely functions by modifying Windows Registry keys associated with the Winlogon process, such as those under HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon\, to load and execute malicious code during user logon events, thereby establishing persistence on a compromised system.
3347.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The LogonTracker module is a persistence mechanism that operates by leveraging Windows logon scripts. It establishes persistence by adding a script path to the `HKCU\Environment\UserInitMprLogonScript` Registry key, ensuring the script executes automatically when a specific user logs into the system. This technique is associated with groups like Cobalt Group and APT28.

3348.name: Temporary File Replacement Technique
3348.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may abuse permission configurations that allow them to gain temporarily elevated access to cloud resources. Many cloud environments allow administrators to grant user or service accounts permission to request just-in-time access to roles, impersonate other accounts, pass roles onto resources and services, or otherwise gain short-term access to a set of privileges that may be distinct from their own. 

Just-in-time access is a mechanism for granting additional roles to cloud accounts in a granular, temporary manner. This allows accounts to operate with only the permissions they need on a daily basis, and to request additional permissions as necessary. Sometimes just-in-time access requests are configured to require manual approval, while other times the desired permissions are automatically granted.(Citation: Azure Just in Time Access 2023)

Account impersonation allows user or service accounts to temporarily act with the permissions of another account. For example, in GCP users with the `iam.serviceAccountTokenCreator` role can create temporary access tokens or sign arbitrary payloads with the permissions of a service account, while service accounts with domain-wide delegation permission are permitted to impersonate Google Workspace accounts.(Citation: Google Cloud Service Account Authentication Roles)(Citation: Hunters Domain Wide Delegation Google Workspace 2023)(Citation: Google Cloud Just in Time Access 2023)(Citation: Palo Alto Unit 42 Google Workspace Domain Wide Delegation 2023) In Exchange Online, the `ApplicationImpersonation` role allows a service account to use the permissions associated with specified user accounts.(Citation: Microsoft Impersonation and EWS in Exchange) 

Many cloud environments also include mechanisms for users to pass roles to resources that allow them to perform tasks and authenticate to other services. While the user that creates the resource does not directly assume the role they pass to it, they may still be able to take advantage of the role's access -- for example, by configuring the resource to perform certain actions with the permissions it has been granted. In AWS, users with the `PassRole` permission can allow a service they create to assume a given role, while in GCP, users with the `iam.serviceAccountUser` role can attach a service account to a resource.(Citation: AWS PassRole)(Citation: Google Cloud Service Account Authentication Roles)

While users require specific role assignments in order to use any of these features, cloud administrators may misconfigure permissions. This could result in escalation paths that allow adversaries to gain access to resources beyond what was originally intended.(Citation: Rhino Google Cloud Privilege Escalation)(Citation: Rhino Security Labs AWS Privilege Escalation)

**Note:** this technique is distinct from [Additional Cloud Roles](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1098/003), which involves assigning permanent roles to accounts rather than abusing existing permissions structures to gain temporarily elevated access to resources. However, adversaries that compromise a sufficiently privileged account may grant another account they control [Additional Cloud Roles](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1098/003) that would allow them to also abuse these features. This may also allow for greater stealth than would be had by directly using the highly privileged account, especially when logs do not clarify when role impersonation is taking place.(Citation: CrowdStrike StellarParticle January 2022)
3348.profile: [profile]Temporary File Replacement Technique is a technique where adversaries exploit weak file system permissions on directories used by legitimate processes, such as temporary folders created by installers, to replace authentic binaries with malicious ones. When the legitimate process, often running with elevated privileges, executes, it runs the adversary's file instead, leading to privilege escalation or persistence. This method leverages insecure default permissions on temporary directories to achieve execution.
3348.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Temporary File Replacement Technique" is a file manipulation method within the MITRE ATT&CK framework. It operates by exploiting weak permissions on temporary directories, often those created by installers in %TEMP%, to replace legitimate binaries with malicious ones during execution. This allows adversaries to achieve persistence or privilege escalation, as the malicious file inherits the higher permissions of the original process, such as SYSTEM. This technique is related to weaknesses in file system permissions and can be used to bypass user account controls.

3349.name: Scheduled Task Modification
3349.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may abuse the Windows Task Scheduler to perform task scheduling for initial or recurring execution of malicious code. There are multiple ways to access the Task Scheduler in Windows.
