The [schtasks](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0111) utility can be run directly on the command line, or the Task Scheduler can be opened through the GUI within the Administrator Tools section of the Control Panel.(Citation: Stack Overflow) In some cases, adversaries have used a .NET wrapper for the Windows Task Scheduler, and alternatively, adversaries have used the Windows netapi32 library and [Windows Management Instrumentation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1047) (WMI) to create a scheduled task. Adversaries may also utilize the Powershell Cmdlet `Invoke-CimMethod`, which leverages WMI class `PS_ScheduledTask` to create a scheduled task via an XML path.(Citation: Red Canary - Atomic Red Team)

An adversary may use Windows Task Scheduler to execute programs at system startup or on a scheduled basis for persistence. The Windows Task Scheduler can also be abused to conduct remote Execution as part of Lateral Movement and/or to run a process under the context of a specified account (such as SYSTEM). Similar to [System Binary Proxy Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1218), adversaries have also abused the Windows Task Scheduler to potentially mask one-time execution under signed/trusted system processes.(Citation: ProofPoint Serpent)

Adversaries may also create "hidden" scheduled tasks (i.e. [Hide Artifacts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1564)) that may not be visible to defender tools and manual queries used to enumerate tasks. Specifically, an adversary may hide a task from `schtasks /query` and the Task Scheduler by deleting the associated Security Descriptor (SD) registry value (where deletion of this value must be completed using SYSTEM permissions).(Citation: SigmaHQ)(Citation: Tarrask scheduled task) Adversaries may also employ alternate methods to hide tasks, such as altering the metadata (e.g., `Index` value) within associated registry keys.(Citation: Defending Against Scheduled Task Attacks in Windows Environments)
3349.profile: [profile]Scheduled Task Modification is a Windows-specific technique under ID T1053.005, primarily used for Persistence, Privilege Escalation, and Lateral Movement. It involves abusing the Windows Task Scheduler via utilities like schtasks.exe, .NET wrappers, WMI, or the PowerShell Cmdlet Invoke-CimMethod to create tasks for recurring or one-time execution of malicious code. Adversaries can hide tasks by deleting the associated Security Descriptor registry value or altering registry key metadata to evade detection. This technique is widely used by numerous threat groups, including APT29.[/profile]
3349.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Scheduled Task Modification is a technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, identified as T1053.005 under the Scheduled Task/Job sub-technique. It falls under the Persistence, Privilege Escalation, and Execution tactics, primarily targeting the Windows platform. This technique involves adversaries modifying existing legitimate scheduled tasks to change their execution properties, such as the associated program path or trigger times, to run malicious code. This allows for the maintenance of persistence, execution with elevated privileges, or lateral movement, often while evading detection by blending with normal system activity.

3350.name: Backdoor Removal
3350.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may delete or modify artifacts generated within systems to remove evidence of their presence or hinder defenses. Various artifacts may be created by an adversary or something that can be attributed to an adversary’s actions. Typically these artifacts are used as defensive indicators related to monitored events, such as strings from downloaded files, logs that are generated from user actions, and other data analyzed by defenders. Location, format, and type of artifact (such as command or login history) are often specific to each platform.

Removal of these indicators may interfere with event collection, reporting, or other processes used to detect intrusion activity. This may compromise the integrity of security solutions by causing notable events to go unreported. This activity may also impede forensic analysis and incident response, due to lack of sufficient data to determine what occurred.
3350.profile: [profile]The entity maps to MITRE ATT&CK technique T1070, Indicator Removal, under the Defense Evasion tactic and applicable across multiple platforms. This technique involves adversaries deleting or modifying artifacts like logs, command history, or downloaded file strings to erase evidence of their presence and hinder detection, event reporting, and forensic analysis. The intrusion set APT29 is linked to this behavior. Specific sub-techniques include file deletion using commands like `del` on Windows or `rm` on Linux, and removing network share connections with commands such as `net use \\system\share /delete`.[/profile]
3350.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Backdoor Removal is a post-compromise technique where adversaries delete or disable their own backdoors to erase evidence and hinder detection. This action is part of the Defense Evasion tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. The technique involves using system utilities like `del` on Windows or `rm` on Linux to delete malicious files, or employing commands to disable accounts or services used for persistence. It is often executed late in an intrusion to clean the footprint and can impede forensic analysis by removing key indicators of compromise.

3351.name: Unknown Binaries Execution
3351.profile: [profile]The entity "Unknown Binaries Execution" is a technique for running unverified or malicious code. It is associated with the intrusion set APT29. The execution can involve direct user actions, such as opening malicious documents from phishing, or automated methods like abusing the Windows Service Control Manager via tools like PsExec or sc.exe to run payloads. This technique is distinct from execution guardrails, which constrain payloads to specific target conditions.
3351.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity 'Unknown Binaries Execution' is an attack pattern for executing non-standard or unsigned binaries to evade detection. It is analogous to MITRE ATT&CK technique T1204 (User Execution) under the Execution tactic on Windows platforms. The technique relies on user actions, such as opening malicious documents or links delivered via phishing, to initiate code execution. This can involve deceiving users into enabling remote access tools, running malicious scripts, or manually executing malicious code, often as a follow-on behavior from initial access vectors.

3352.name: T1012 Query Registry
3352.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may interact with the Windows Registry to gather information about the system, configuration, and installed software.

The Registry contains a significant amount of information about the operating system, configuration, software, and security.(Citation: Wikipedia Windows Registry) Information can easily be queried using the [Reg](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0075) utility, though other means to access the Registry exist. Some of the information may help adversaries to further their operation within a network. Adversaries may use the information from [Query Registry](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1012) during automated discovery to shape follow-on behaviors, including whether or not the adversary fully infects the target and/or attempts specific actions.
3352.profile: [profile]Query Registry is technique T1012 under the Discovery tactic, targeting Windows platforms. It involves adversaries interacting with the Windows Registry to gather system, configuration, and software information, often using utilities like Reg.exe to query keys. This collected data is used during automated discovery to inform subsequent attack behaviors and decisions.
3352.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Query Registry is technique T1012 under the Discovery tactic, primarily targeting Windows. Adversaries interact with the Windows Registry to gather system, configuration, and software information, often using the built-in Reg utility. This collected intelligence is used during automated discovery to inform follow-on actions, such as whether to fully compromise a target. The technique is commonly employed by groups like APT41, Lazarus Group, and Volt Typhoon.

3353.name: T1027 Obfuscated Files or Information
3353.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may attempt to make an executable or file difficult to discover or analyze by encrypting, encoding, or otherwise obfuscating its contents on the system or in transit. This is common behavior that can be used across different platforms and the network to evade defenses. 

Payloads may be compressed, archived, or encrypted in order to avoid detection. These payloads may be used during Initial Access or later to mitigate detection. Sometimes a user's action may be required to open and [Deobfuscate/Decode Files or Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1140) for [User Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204). The user may also be required to input a password to open a password protected compressed/encrypted file that was provided by the adversary. (Citation: Volexity PowerDuke November 2016) Adversaries may also use compressed or archived scripts, such as JavaScript. 

Portions of files can also be encoded to hide the plain-text strings that would otherwise help defenders with discovery. (Citation: Linux/Cdorked.A We Live Security Analysis) Payloads may also be split into separate, seemingly benign files that only reveal malicious functionality when reassembled. (Citation: Carbon Black Obfuscation Sept 2016)

Adversaries may also abuse [Command Obfuscation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/010) to obscure commands executed from payloads or directly via [Command and Scripting Interpreter](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059). Environment variables, aliases, characters, and other platform/language specific semantics can be used to evade signature based detections and application control mechanisms. (Citation: FireEye Obfuscation June 2017) (Citation: FireEye Revoke-Obfuscation July 2017)(Citation: PaloAlto EncodedCommand March 2017)
3353.profile: [profile]Obfuscated Files or Information is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1027 under the Defense Evasion tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. It involves making files or executables difficult to detect or analyze by encrypting, encoding, compressing, or archiving their contents. Specific methods include splitting payloads into benign-seeming fragments for later reassembly, using password-protected archives requiring user interaction, and employing command obfuscation with environment variables or aliases to evade signature-based defenses.[/profile]
3353.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Obfuscated Files or Information, designated T1027, is a Defense Evasion technique applicable across multiple platforms. It involves encrypting, encoding, compressing, or archiving files to hinder detection and analysis. Specific methods include using password-protected archives, encoding file portions to hide strings, splitting payloads into benign-seeming fragments for later reassembly, and employing command obfuscation via environment variables or aliases. This technique is often paired with T1140 (Deobfuscate/Decode Files or Information) for execution.

3354.name: T1057 Process Discovery
3354.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may attempt to get information about running processes on a system. Information obtained could be used to gain an understanding of common software/applications running on systems within the network. Administrator or otherwise elevated access may provide better process details. Adversaries may use the information from [Process Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1057) during automated discovery to shape follow-on behaviors, including whether or not the adversary fully infects the target and/or attempts specific actions. In Windows environments, adversaries could obtain details on running processes using the [Tasklist](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0057) utility via [cmd](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0106) or Get-Process via [PowerShell](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001). Information about processes can also be extracted from the output of [Native API](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1106) calls such as CreateToolhelp32Snapshot. In Mac and Linux, this is accomplished with the ps command. Adversaries may also opt to enumerate processes via `/proc`. ESXi also supports use of the `ps` command, as well as `esxcli system process list`.(Citation: Sygnia ESXi Ransomware 2025)(Citation: Crowdstrike Hypervisor Jackpotting Pt 2 2021) On network devices, [Network Device CLI](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/008) commands such as `show processes` can be used to display current running processes.(Citation: US-CERT-TA18-106A)(Citation: show_processes_cisco_cmd)
3354.profile: [profile]Process Discovery, designated as T1057, is a Discovery tactic technique used across Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms to gather information about running processes. It involves executing commands like `tasklist` or `Get-Process` in Windows, `ps` or enumerating `/proc` on Linux/Mac, and `esxcli system process list` on ESXi hypervisors to understand system software and shape subsequent attack behaviors. The technique is employed by numerous threat groups including APT29, Volt Typhoon, and Lazarus Group.[/profile]
3354.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Process Discovery is technique T1057 under the Discovery tactic. It operates across Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. Adversaries enumerate running processes to understand the software environment and guide follow-on actions. Specific technical mechanics include using the Windows `tasklist` or PowerShell `Get-Process` commands, the `ps` command on Linux/macOS, enumeration via the `/proc` directory, the `esxcli system process list` command on ESXi, or native Windows API calls like `CreateToolhelp32Snapshot`.

3355.name: T1070.004 File Deletion
3355.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may delete files left behind by the actions of their intrusion activity. Malware, tools, or other non-native files dropped or created on a system by an adversary (ex: [Ingress Tool Transfer](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1105)) may leave traces to indicate to what was done within a network and how. Removal of these files can occur during an intrusion, or as part of a post-intrusion process to minimize the adversary's footprint. There are tools available from the host operating system to perform cleanup, but adversaries may use other tools as well.(Citation: Microsoft SDelete July 2016) Examples of built-in [Command and Scripting Interpreter](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059) functions include del on Windows, rm or unlink on Linux and macOS, and `rm` on ESXi.
3355.profile: [profile]T1070.004 File Deletion is a Defense Evasion technique under the MITRE ATT&CK framework, applicable across Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. It involves adversaries removing non-native files like malware or tools to erase traces of intrusion, using native OS commands such as `del` on Windows, `rm` or `unlink` on Linux/macOS, and `rm` on ESXi, or specialized tools like SDelete. This activity is commonly associated with groups including APT29, Lazarus Group, and Wizard Spider.[/profile]
3355.profile_without_enhance: [profile]T1070.004 File Deletion is an Indicator Removal technique under the Defense Evasion tactic targeting Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. It involves adversaries deleting files, such as malware or tools, left on a system to erase traces of intrusion. Common methods include using built-in OS commands like `del` on Windows, `rm` or `unlink` on Linux/macOS, and `rm` on ESXi, or employing tools like Windows Sysinternals SDelete for secure deletion. This cleanup minimizes the adversary's forensic footprint during or after an operation.

3356.name: T1071.001 Web Protocols
3356.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may communicate using application layer protocols associated with web traffic to avoid detection/network filtering by blending in with existing traffic. Commands to the remote system, and often the results of those commands, will be embedded within the protocol traffic between the client and server. 

Protocols such as HTTP/S(Citation: CrowdStrike Putter Panda) and WebSocket(Citation: Brazking-Websockets) that carry web traffic may be very common in environments. HTTP/S packets have many fields and headers in which data can be concealed. An adversary may abuse these protocols to communicate with systems under their control within a victim network while also mimicking normal, expected traffic.
3356.profile: [profile]T1071.001 Web Protocols is a Command and Control technique under the Command and Control tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It involves adversaries using common web traffic protocols like HTTP/S and WebSocket to blend malicious communications with normal network activity. Commands and exfiltrated data are concealed within standard protocol fields and headers, such as HTTP request/response headers, to evade detection and network filtering. This technique is widely adopted by numerous threat groups, including APT29, to mimic legitimate traffic within a victim environment.[/profile]
3356.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Web Protocols (T1071.001) is a Command and Control technique under the Command and Control tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It involves adversaries using common web traffic protocols like HTTP/S and WebSocket to blend malicious communications with normal network activity. Commands and exfiltrated data are concealed within standard protocol fields and headers, such as HTTP request/response headers, to evade detection and network filtering while mimicking legitimate traffic.

3357.name: T1071.004 Application Layer Protocol: DNS
3357.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may communicate using OSI application layer protocols to avoid detection/network filtering by blending in with existing traffic. Commands to the remote system, and often the results of those commands, will be embedded within the protocol traffic between the client and server. 

Adversaries may utilize many different protocols, including those used for web browsing, transferring files, electronic mail, DNS, or publishing/subscribing. For connections that occur internally within an enclave (such as those between a proxy or pivot node and other nodes), commonly used protocols are SMB, SSH, or RDP.(Citation: Mandiant APT29 Eye Spy Email Nov 22)
3357.profile: [profile]T1071.004 Application Layer Protocol: DNS is a Command and Control technique under the Command and Control tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It involves adversaries using the DNS protocol to blend with normal traffic, embedding commands and data within DNS queries and responses. This is often implemented as DNS tunneling or beaconing, where data is concealed in fields like TXT or A records, and communication is infrequent to evade detection. Groups such as APT29, OilRig, and FIN7 have been observed using this method.[/profile]
3357.profile_without_enhance: [profile]T1071.004 Application Layer Protocol: DNS is a Command and Control technique under the Exfiltration tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It involves adversaries using the Domain Name System protocol to covertly communicate with compromised systems, blending with legitimate administrative traffic to avoid detection. Commands and exfiltrated data are embedded within DNS packet fields and headers, such as TXT or A records, often through DNS tunneling or infrequent beaconing to mimic normal query patterns.

3358.name: T1083 File and Directory Discovery
3358.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may enumerate files and directories or may search in specific locations of a host or network share for certain information within a file system. Adversaries may use the information from [File and Directory Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1083) during automated discovery to shape follow-on behaviors, including whether or not the adversary fully infects the target and/or attempts specific actions. Many command shell utilities can be used to obtain this information. Examples include dir, tree, ls, find, and locate.(Citation: Windows Commands JPCERT) Custom tools may also be used to gather file and directory information and interact with the [Native API](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1106). Adversaries may also leverage a [Network Device CLI](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/008) on network devices to gather file and directory information (e.g. dir, show flash, and/or nvram).(Citation: US-CERT-TA18-106A) Some files and directories may require elevated or specific user permissions to access.
3358.profile: [profile]File and Directory Discovery, identified as T1083, is a Discovery tactic used across multiple platforms including Windows, Linux, and macOS. Adversaries enumerate files and directories to gather information that shapes follow-on actions, using command shell utilities like dir, tree, ls, find, and locate, or custom tools interacting with the Native API. The technique is also leveraged via Network Device CLI commands such as show flash and nvram. It is associated with numerous threat groups including APT29, Volt Typhoon, and Lazarus Group.
3358.profile_without_enhance: [profile]File and Directory Discovery, designated as T1083, is a Discovery tactic used across Windows, Linux, and Mac platforms. Adversaries enumerate files and directories to gather information that shapes follow-on actions, using command shell utilities like `dir`, `tree`, `ls`, `find`, and `locate`. The technique can also involve custom tools interacting with the Native API or leveraging a Network Device CLI on network devices with commands such as `show flash` or `nvram`.

3359.name: T1105 Ingress Tool Transfer
3359.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may transfer tools or other files from an external system into a compromised environment. Tools or files may be copied from an external adversary-controlled system to the victim network through the command and control channel or through alternate protocols such as [ftp](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0095). Once present, adversaries may also transfer/spread tools between victim devices within a compromised environment (i.e. [Lateral Tool Transfer](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1570)). On Windows, adversaries may use various utilities to download tools, such as `copy`, `finger`, [certutil](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0160), and [PowerShell](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001) commands such as IEX(New-Object Net.WebClient).downloadString() and Invoke-WebRequest. On Linux and macOS systems, a variety of utilities also exist, such as `curl`, `scp`, `sftp`, `tftp`, `rsync`, `finger`, and `wget`.(Citation: t1105_lolbas) A number of these tools, such as `wget`, `curl`, and `scp`, also exist on ESXi. After downloading a file, a threat actor may attempt to verify its integrity by checking its hash value (e.g., via `certutil -hashfile`).(Citation: Google Cloud Threat Intelligence COSCMICENERGY 2023) Adversaries may also abuse installers and package managers, such as `yum` or `winget`, to download tools to victim hosts. Adversaries have also abused file application features, such as the Windows `search-ms` protocol handler, to deliver malicious files to victims through remote file searches invoked by [User Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204) (typically after interacting with [Phishing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566) lures).(Citation: T1105: Trellix_search-ms) Files can also be transferred using various [Web Service](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1102)s as well as native or otherwise present tools on the victim system.(Citation: PTSecurity Cobalt Dec 2016) In some cases, adversaries may be able to leverage services that sync between a web-based and an on-premises client, such as Dropbox or OneDrive, to transfer files onto victim systems. For example, by compromising a cloud account and logging into the service's web portal, an adversary may be able to trigger an automatic syncing process that transfers the file onto the victim's machine.(Citation: Dropbox Malware Sync)
3359.profile: [profile]Ingress Tool Transfer is a Command and Control technique with the MITRE ATT&CK ID T1105, operating across Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves transferring tools into a compromised environment from an external system, often using utilities like certutil, PowerShell commands (e.g., IEX(New-Object Net.WebClient).downloadString()), curl, wget, or scp. Adversaries may also abuse package managers like yum or winget, leverage cloud sync services like Dropbox, or use the Windows search-ms protocol handler to facilitate the file transfer. This technique is commonly used by numerous threat groups, including APT29, to stage tools for further operations.[/profile]
3359.profile_without_enhance: [profile]T1105 Ingress Tool Transfer is a Command and Control technique used to transfer tools or files from an external adversary-controlled system into a compromised environment. Common utilities for this include Windows commands like `copy`, `certutil`, and PowerShell's `IEX(New-Object Net.WebClient).downloadString()`, as well as Linux/macOS/ESXi tools like `curl`, `scp`, `sftp`, `wget`, and `rsync`. Adversaries may also abuse installers like `yum` or `winget`, web services, or cloud syncing services like Dropbox to facilitate the file transfer into the victim network.

3360.name: T1132.001 Standard Encoding
3360.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may encode data with a standard data encoding system to make the content of command and control traffic more difficult to detect. Command and control (C2) information can be encoded using a standard data encoding system that adheres to existing protocol specifications. Common data encoding schemes include ASCII, Unicode, hexadecimal, Base64, and MIME.(Citation: Wikipedia Binary-to-text Encoding)(Citation: Wikipedia Character Encoding) Some data encoding systems may also result in data compression, such as gzip.
3360.profile: [profile]Standard Encoding is technique T1132.001 under the Command and Control tactic. It involves adversaries using common, protocol-compliant encoding schemes like ASCII, Unicode, hexadecimal, Base64, and MIME to obfuscate command and control traffic, making it more difficult to detect. Some implementations, such as gzip, may also compress data. This technique is associated with groups including APT29, Hafnium, MuddyWater, and Lazarus Group.[/profile]
3360.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Standard Encoding, identified as T1132.001, is an adversary technique within the Command and Control tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. It involves encoding command and control data using established, non-proprietary schemes like ASCII, Unicode, hexadecimal, Base64, or MIME to obfuscate traffic and evade detection. This method adheres to standard protocol specifications and may also provide data compression, as seen with gzip. Threat actors such as Hafnium, MuddyWater, and Lazarus Group have been associated with its use.

3361.name: T1195.002 Compromise Software Supply Chain
3361.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may manipulate application software prior to receipt by a final consumer for the purpose of data or system compromise. Supply chain compromise of software can take place in a number of ways, including manipulation of the application source code, manipulation of the update/distribution mechanism for that software, or replacing compiled releases with a modified version.

Targeting may be specific to a desired victim set or may be distributed to a broad set of consumers but only move on to additional tactics on specific victims.(Citation: Avast CCleaner3 2018)(Citation: Command Five SK 2011)
3361.profile: [profile]T1195.002 Compromise Software Supply Chain is a technique within the Initial Access tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. It involves manipulating application software before it reaches end-users to enable subsequent compromise. Specific methods include tampering with the application's source code, hijacking its software update or distribution mechanism, or directly replacing legitimate compiled releases with maliciously modified versions. This technique is associated with groups including APT41, Sandworm Team, and FIN7.
3361.profile_without_enhance: [profile]T1195.002 Compromise Software Supply Chain is a sub-technique of T1195 (Supply Chain Compromise) under the Initial Access tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. It involves adversaries manipulating application software before it reaches the end user to enable data or system compromise. Specific technical mechanics include the manipulation of application source code, tampering with software update or distribution mechanisms, or replacing legitimate compiled releases with maliciously modified versions. This technique has been associated with groups including Dragonfly, FIN7, APT41, and Sandworm Team.

3362.name: T1518 Software Discovery
3362.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may attempt to get a listing of software and software versions that are installed on a system or in a cloud environment. Adversaries may use the information from [Software Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1518) during automated discovery to shape follow-on behaviors, including whether or not the adversary fully infects the target and/or attempts specific actions.

Such software may be deployed widely across the environment for configuration management or security reasons, such as [Software Deployment Tools](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1072), and may allow adversaries broad access to infect devices or move laterally.

Adversaries may attempt to enumerate software for a variety of reasons, such as figuring out what security measures are present or if the compromised system has a version of software that is vulnerable to [Exploitation for Privilege Escalation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1068).
3362.profile: [profile]T1518 Software Discovery is a Discovery technique used to enumerate installed software and versions on a system or in a cloud environment. Adversaries use this information to assess security measures, identify vulnerable software for exploitation, and shape follow-on actions like lateral movement. The technique is employed by groups including APT29, SideWinder, and MuddyWater across Windows, Linux, and Mac platforms, and includes sub-techniques like T1518.001 for discovering security software specifically.[/profile]
3362.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Software Discovery, identified as T1518, is a Discovery tactic technique applicable to Windows, macOS, and Linux platforms. It involves adversaries enumerating installed software and versions on a system or in a cloud environment to inform follow-on actions, such as identifying security measures, finding vulnerable software for exploitation, or determining lateral movement opportunities. This can be performed using commands like `netsh`, `reg query`, `dir`, and `Tasklist`, and is associated with groups including MuddyWater, Volt Typhoon, and SideWinder.

3363.name: T1518.001 Security Software Discovery
3363.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may attempt to get a listing of security software, configurations, defensive tools, and sensors that are installed on a system or in a cloud environment. This may include things such as cloud monitoring agents and anti-virus. Adversaries may use the information from [Security Software Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1518/001) during automated discovery to shape follow-on behaviors, including whether or not the adversary fully infects the target and/or attempts specific actions. Example commands that can be used to obtain security software information are [netsh](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0108), reg query with [Reg](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0075), dir with [cmd](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0106), and [Tasklist](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0057), but other indicators of discovery behavior may be more specific to the type of software or security system the adversary is looking for. It is becoming more common to see macOS malware perform checks for LittleSnitch and KnockKnock software. Adversaries may also utilize the [Cloud API](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/009) to discover cloud-native security software installed on compute infrastructure, such as the AWS CloudWatch agent, Azure VM Agent, and Google Cloud Monitor agent. These agents may collect metrics and logs from the VM, which may be centrally aggregated in a cloud-based monitoring platform.
3363.profile: [profile]Security Software Discovery (T1518.001) is a Discovery technique used to identify security software, defensive tools, and monitoring agents installed on a system or in a cloud environment. It operates on Windows, macOS, Linux, and cloud platforms. Adversaries use commands like `netsh`, `reg query`, `dir`, and `Tasklist`, or cloud APIs to discover agents like AWS CloudWatch or Azure VM Agent, with macOS malware often checking for LittleSnitch and KnockKnock. This reconnaissance shapes follow-on attack decisions.
3363.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Security Software Discovery (T1518.001) is a Discovery tactic technique applicable to Windows, macOS, and cloud platforms. It involves adversaries enumerating installed security software, configurations, defensive tools, and sensors—such as antivirus, firewalls, and cloud monitoring agents (e.g., AWS CloudWatch, Azure VM Agent)—to inform follow-on actions. Discovery methods include commands like `netsh`, `reg query`, `dir`, and `tasklist`, with macOS malware often checking for LittleSnitch and KnockKnock. Adversaries may also use Cloud APIs for discovery in cloud environments.

3364.name: T1543.003 Windows Service
3364.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may create or modify Windows services to repeatedly execute malicious payloads as part of persistence. When Windows boots up, it starts programs or applications called services that perform background system functions.(Citation: TechNet Services) Windows service configuration information, including the file path to the service's executable or recovery programs/commands, is stored in the Windows Registry.

Adversaries may install a new service or modify an existing service to execute at startup in order to persist on a system. Service configurations can be set or modified using system utilities (such as sc.exe), by directly modifying the Registry, or by interacting directly with the Windows API. 

Adversaries may also use services to install and execute malicious drivers. For example, after dropping a driver file (ex: `.sys`) to disk, the payload can be loaded and registered via [Native API](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1106) functions such as `CreateServiceW()` (or manually via functions such as `ZwLoadDriver()` and `ZwSetValueKey()`), by creating the required service Registry values (i.e. [Modify Registry](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1112)), or by using command-line utilities such as `PnPUtil.exe`.(Citation: Symantec W.32 Stuxnet Dossier)(Citation: Crowdstrike DriveSlayer February 2022)(Citation: Unit42 AcidBox June 2020) Adversaries may leverage these drivers as [Rootkit](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1014)s to hide the presence of malicious activity on a system. Adversaries may also load a signed yet vulnerable driver onto a compromised machine (known as "Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver" (BYOVD)) as part of [Exploitation for Privilege Escalation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1068).(Citation: ESET InvisiMole June 2020)(Citation: Unit42 AcidBox June 2020)

Services may be created with administrator privileges but are executed under SYSTEM privileges, so an adversary may also use a service to escalate privileges. Adversaries may also directly start services through [Service Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1569/002).

To make detection analysis more challenging, malicious services may also incorporate [Masquerade Task or Service](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1036/004) (ex: using a service and/or payload name related to a legitimate OS or benign software component). Adversaries may also create ‘hidden’ services (i.e., [Hide Artifacts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1564)), for example by using the `sc sdset` command to set service permissions via the Service Descriptor Definition Language (SDDL). This may hide a Windows service from the view of standard service enumeration methods such as `Get-Service`, `sc query`, and `services.exe`.(Citation: SANS 1)(Citation: SANS 2)
3364.profile: [profile]Windows Service (T1543.003) is a Persistence technique for Windows platforms. It involves creating or modifying a service to execute a malicious payload at system startup, often using utilities like sc.exe, direct Registry modification, or Windows API calls. It can also be used to install and execute malicious drivers via functions like CreateServiceW() or tools like PnPUtil.exe, potentially for privilege escalation to SYSTEM or to deploy rootkits. Adversaries may hide these services using the `sc sdset` command with SDDL to evade standard enumeration.
3364.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Windows Service, identified as T1543.003, is a persistence and privilege escalation technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, applicable to the Windows platform. Adversaries create or modify Windows services to execute malicious payloads at system startup, often using utilities like sc.exe, direct Registry modification, or Windows API calls such as CreateServiceW(). This method can also be used to install and execute malicious drivers, potentially for rootkit functionality or BYOVD attacks. Services run with SYSTEM privileges, enabling privilege escalation, and may be hidden using commands like sc sdset to evade detection by standard enumeration tools.

3365.name: T1553.002 Code Signing
3365.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may create, acquire, or steal code signing materials to sign their malware or tools. Code signing provides a level of authenticity on a binary from the developer and a guarantee that the binary has not been tampered with. (Citation: Wikipedia Code Signing) The certificates used during an operation may be created, acquired, or stolen by the adversary. (Citation: Securelist Digital Certificates) (Citation: Symantec Digital Certificates) Unlike [Invalid Code Signature](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1036/001), this activity will result in a valid signature.

Code signing to verify software on first run can be used on modern Windows and macOS systems. It is not used on Linux due to the decentralized nature of the platform. (Citation: Wikipedia Code Signing)(Citation: EclecticLightChecksonEXECodeSigning)

Code signing certificates may be used to bypass security policies that require signed code to execute on a system.
3365.profile: [profile]T1553.002 Code Signing is a Defense Evasion technique where adversaries create, acquire, or steal code signing certificates to apply valid digital signatures to malware or tools, providing a false level of authenticity and bypassing security policies that require signed code to execute. It is applicable to Windows and macOS platforms, and is distinct from techniques using invalid signatures. Associated groups include APT29, Lazarus Group, and Wizard Spider.[/profile]
3365.profile_without_enhance: [profile]T1553.002 Code Signing is a Defense Evasion technique where adversaries create, acquire, or steal code signing certificates to digitally sign their malware, providing a valid signature that appears authentic and bypasses security policies requiring signed code. It is primarily used on Windows and macOS platforms, but not Linux. The technique is distinct from using invalid signatures, as it results in a legitimate-appearing certificate to increase trust and evade detection.

3366.name: T1568.002 Domain Generation Algorithms
3366.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may make use of Domain Generation Algorithms (DGAs) to dynamically identify a destination domain for command and control traffic rather than relying on a list of static IP addresses or domains. This has the advantage of making it much harder for defenders to block, track, or take over the command and control channel, as there potentially could be thousands of domains that malware can check for instructions.(Citation: Cybereason Dissecting DGAs)(Citation: Cisco Umbrella DGA)(Citation: Unit 42 DGA Feb 2019)

DGAs can take the form of apparently random or “gibberish” strings (ex: istgmxdejdnxuyla.ru) when they construct domain names by generating each letter. Alternatively, some DGAs employ whole words as the unit by concatenating words together instead of letters (ex: cityjulydish.net). Many DGAs are time-based, generating a different domain for each time period (hourly, daily, monthly, etc). Others incorporate a seed value as well to make predicting future domains more difficult for defenders.(Citation: Cybereason Dissecting DGAs)(Citation: Cisco Umbrella DGA)(Citation: Talos CCleanup 2017)(Citation: Akamai DGA Mitigation)

Adversaries may use DGAs for the purpose of [Fallback Channels](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1008). When contact is lost with the primary command and control server malware may employ a DGA as a means to reestablishing command and control.(Citation: Talos CCleanup 2017)(Citation: FireEye POSHSPY April 2017)(Citation: ESET Sednit 2017 Activity)
3366.profile: [profile]Domain Generation Algorithms (DGAs) is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1568.002 under the Command and Control tactic for Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It dynamically generates a large number of potential command and control domains, making blocking difficult. Technical mechanics include constructing domains from random strings (e.g., istgmxdejdnxuyla.ru) or concatenated words (e.g., cityjulydish.net), often using time-based seeds to produce different domains per period (hourly, daily). It is used by groups like APT41 and TA551 and can serve as a fallback channel to re-establish lost C2 connections.[/profile]
3366.profile_without_enhance: [profile]T1568.002 Domain Generation Algorithms is a Command and Control technique under the Command and Control tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It dynamically generates a large number of potential command and control domains using an algorithm, making static blocking difficult. The algorithm can create seemingly random strings (e.g., istgmxdejdnxuyla.ru) or concatenate words (e.g., cityjulydish.net), often using time-based seeds to produce different domains per period (hourly, daily). This method is also used to establish fallback channels if primary C2 is lost, and is associated with groups like APT41 and TA551.

3367.name: T1569.002 Service Execution
3367.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may abuse the Windows service control manager to execute malicious commands or payloads. The Windows service control manager (services.exe) is an interface to manage and manipulate services.(Citation: Microsoft Service Control Manager) The service control manager is accessible to users via GUI components as well as system utilities such as sc.exe and [Net](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0039). [PsExec](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0029) can also be used to execute commands or payloads via a temporary Windows service created through the service control manager API.(Citation: Russinovich Sysinternals) Tools such as [PsExec](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0029) and sc.exe can accept remote servers as arguments and may be used to conduct remote execution. Adversaries may leverage these mechanisms to execute malicious content. This can be done by either executing a new or modified service. This technique is the execution used in conjunction with [Windows Service](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1543/003) during service persistence or privilege escalation.
3367.profile: [profile]Service Execution, identified as T1569.002, is an Execution tactic technique for Windows platforms. It involves abusing the Windows Service Control Manager (services.exe) to run malicious commands or payloads. This is achieved by interacting with the manager via utilities like sc.exe and Net, or by using tools such as PsExec to create a temporary service through the API, which also enables remote execution. The technique is commonly used in conjunction with service persistence methods like Windows Service (T1543.003) and is associated with threat groups including APT29, APT41, and Wizard Spider.
3367.profile_without_enhance: [profile]T1569.002 Service Execution is a MITRE ATT&CK technique (ID: T1569.002) under the Execution tactic for the Windows platform. It involves abusing the Windows Service Control Manager (services.exe) to execute malicious commands or payloads, either by creating a new service or modifying an existing one. This is commonly performed using utilities like sc.exe, Net, or PsExec, which can also facilitate remote execution. The technique is frequently used in conjunction with service persistence methods like Windows Service (T1543.003) and has been associated with threat groups including APT41, FIN7, and Wizard Spider.

3368.name: T1584 Compromise Infrastructure
3368.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may compromise third-party infrastructure that can be used during targeting. Infrastructure solutions include physical or cloud servers, domains, network devices, and third-party web and DNS services. Instead of buying, leasing, or renting infrastructure an adversary may compromise infrastructure and use it during other phases of the adversary lifecycle.(Citation: Mandiant APT1)(Citation: ICANNDomainNameHijacking)(Citation: Talos DNSpionage Nov 2018)(Citation: FireEye EPS Awakens Part 2) Additionally, adversaries may compromise numerous machines to form a botnet they can leverage.

Use of compromised infrastructure allows adversaries to stage, launch, and execute operations. Compromised infrastructure can help adversary operations blend in with traffic that is seen as normal, such as contact with high reputation or trusted sites. For example, adversaries may leverage compromised infrastructure (potentially also in conjunction with [Digital Certificates](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1588/004)) to further blend in and support staged information gathering and/or [Phishing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566) campaigns.(Citation: FireEye DNS Hijack 2019) Adversaries may also compromise numerous machines to support [Proxy](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1090) and/or proxyware services or to form a botnet.(Citation: amnesty_nso_pegasus)(Citation: Sysdig Proxyjacking) Additionally, adversaries may compromise infrastructure residing in close proximity to a target in order to gain [Initial Access](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0001) via [Wi-Fi Networks](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1669).(Citation: Nearest Neighbor Volexity)

By using compromised infrastructure, adversaries may enable follow-on malicious operations. Prior to targeting, adversaries may also compromise the infrastructure of other adversaries.(Citation: NSA NCSC Turla OilRig)
3368.profile: [profile]Compromise Infrastructure is technique T1584 under the Resource Development tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It involves adversaries taking over third-party infrastructure like physical or cloud servers, domains, and network devices instead of acquiring them legitimately. This compromised infrastructure is used to stage, launch, and execute operations, helping blend malicious traffic with normal activity by leveraging high-reputation sites or forming botnets for proxy services. It can also involve compromising infrastructure near a target for Wi-Fi-based initial access or seizing other adversaries' infrastructure. The intrusion set APT29 has been associated with this technique.
3368.profile_without_enhance: [profile]T1584 Compromise Infrastructure is a Resource Development technique where adversaries compromise third-party infrastructure like physical or cloud servers, domains, network devices, and DNS services to use during targeting. This method allows operations to blend with normal traffic, supports phishing or proxy campaigns, and can involve forming botnets or hijacking infrastructure from other adversaries to stage and execute attacks.

3369.name: NOBELIUM
3369.uncertain_mes:
[APT29](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0016) is threat group that has been attributed to Russia's Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR).(Citation: White House Imposing Costs RU Gov April 2021)(Citation: UK Gov Malign RIS Activity April 2021) They have operated since at least 2008, often targeting government networks in Europe and NATO member countries, research institutes, and think tanks. [APT29](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0016) reportedly compromised the Democratic National Committee starting in the summer of 2015.(Citation: F-Secure The Dukes)(Citation: GRIZZLY STEPPE JAR)(Citation: Crowdstrike DNC June 2016)(Citation: UK Gov UK Exposes Russia SolarWinds April 2021)

In April 2021, the US and UK governments attributed the [SolarWinds Compromise](https://attack.mitre.org/campaigns/C0024) to the SVR; public statements included citations to [APT29](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0016), Cozy Bear, and The Dukes.(Citation: NSA Joint Advisory SVR SolarWinds April 2021)(Citation: UK NSCS Russia SolarWinds April 2021) Industry reporting also referred to the actors involved in this campaign as UNC2452, NOBELIUM, StellarParticle, Dark Halo, and SolarStorm.(Citation: FireEye SUNBURST Backdoor December 2020)(Citation: MSTIC NOBELIUM Mar 2021)(Citation: CrowdStrike SUNSPOT Implant January 2021)(Citation: Volexity SolarWinds)(Citation: Cybersecurity Advisory SVR TTP May 2021)(Citation: Unit 42 SolarStorm December 2020)
3369.profile: [profile]NOBELIUM, also known as APT29, Cozy Bear, The Dukes, Midnight Blizzard, and UNC2452, is a Russian state-sponsored threat group attributed to the Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR). Its arsenal includes custom malware like SUNBURST and SUNSPOT from the SolarWinds campaign. Key TTPs involve sophisticated supply-chain compromises and spear-phishing. The group primarily targets government networks in Europe and NATO countries, research institutes, and think tanks, with motivations centered on espionage and intelligence gathering for the Russian state.

Its key custom malware includes SUNBURST, GoldMax, WellMess, and the CozyDuke platform. Characteristic TTPs involve sophisticated supply chain compromise (notably in the SolarWinds incident), credential misuse, and advanced post-exploitation techniques. The group is attributed to Russia's Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR) and primarily conducts state-sponsored espionage targeting government, diplomatic, technology, and research sectors in North America and Europe.[/profile]

3371.name: GoldFinder
3371.uncertain_mes: [GoldFinder](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0597) is a custom HTTP tracer tool written in Go that logs the route a packet takes between a compromised network and a C2 server. It can be used to inform  threat actors of potential points of discovery or logging of their actions, including C2 related to other malware. [GoldFinder](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0597) was discovered in early 2021 during an investigation into the [SolarWinds Compromise](https://attack.mitre.org/campaigns/C0024) by [APT29](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0016).(Citation: MSTIC NOBELIUM Mar 2021)
3371.profile: [profile]GoldFinder, also known as SOLARFLARE, is a custom HTTP tracer tool written in Go that logs network routes between a compromised system and a command-and-control server to identify potential detection points. It is attributed to APT29 and was discovered in early 2021 during the SolarWinds compromise investigation. Key technical behaviors include environmental analysis as a stage 2 tool, often used in tandem with the SUNSHUTTLE/GoldMax malware. It primarily targets Windows platforms, specifically as a 64-bit executable.
3371.profile_without_enhance: [profile]GoldFinder, also known as SOLARFLARE, is a custom HTTP tracer tool written in Go that logs the route a packet takes between a compromised network and a C2 server. It is attributed to APT29 (NOBELIUM) and UNC2452, discovered during the SolarWinds compromise. It functions as a stage 2 environmental analysis tool, used in tandem with SUNSHUTTLE/GoldMax, and operates by making HTTP requests and handling redirections to conceal C2 traffic, utilizing hardcoded IP addresses for its infrastructure.

3372.name: Sibot
3372.uncertain_mes: [Sibot](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0589) is dual-purpose malware written in VBScript designed to achieve persistence on a compromised system as well as download and execute additional payloads. Microsoft discovered three [Sibot](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0589) variants in early 2021 during its investigation of [APT29](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0016) and the [SolarWinds Compromise](https://attack.mitre.org/campaigns/C0024).(Citation: MSTIC NOBELIUM Mar 2021)
3372.profile: [profile]Sibot is a dual-purpose VBScript malware designed for persistence and downloading/executing additional payloads. It is attributed to APT29 and was used during the SolarWinds compromise. Key technical behaviors include achieving persistence via scheduled tasks (e.g., variant AikCetnrll) and functioning as a trojan bot. It targets Windows systems, with three variants (A, B, C) identified. Infrastructure or supplementary details include detection via specific YARA rules and references in related malware like GoldMax.[/profile]
3372.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Sibot is a dual-purpose malware written in VBScript, also known as Variant B. It is attributed to the APT28 and APT29 intrusion sets, with Variant A also being a related variant of TONESHELL. Key technical behaviors include achieving persistence on a compromised system, downloading and executing additional payloads, and for Variant A, generating a victim ID from the tick count, username, and computer name. Target platforms include Windows, with a macOS variant distributed via DMG files and Mach-O executables. It was discovered in early 2021 during investigations into the SolarWinds compromise and APT29 activities.[/profile]

3375.name: SUNSHUTTLE
3375.profile: [profile]SUNSHUTTLE, also known as GoldMax, is a backdoor attributed to the threat groups APT29 and UNC2452. Its key technical behaviors include using the string "main.request_session_key" and employing a private key for communication, as indicated by the PEM header string. The malware is designed to target Windows platforms and operates by establishing command and control sessions to exfiltrate data. Infrastructure connections involve resolving backend server hostnames from specific URLs for coordination.
3375.profile_without_enhance: [profile]SUNSHUTTLE, also known as GOLDMAX, is a backdoor attributed to the UNC2452 threat group. Its key technical behaviors include using a string "main.request_session_key" and a private key block beginning with "LS0tLS1CRUdJTiBQUklWQVRFIEtFWS0tLS0tCk" for command and control communication. The malware is designed for Windows and Android platforms, as indicated by related decoy applications like SUNSPINNER, which is a Flutter-based GUI used to resolve backend server hostnames for potential C2 infrastructure.

The malware targets the Windows platform, with infrastructure and supplementary information linking it to activity groups like DEV-0832 and 'VSocCrypt' ransomware prevention alerts.

3377.name: second-stage script

The script is delivered via a de-obfuscated first-stage PowerShell script, as observed in Emotet campaigns, and it functions as a second instance within an attack chain, similar to patterns seen with Zeppelin malware.
