3506.name: Compromising Supply Chains
3506.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may manipulate products or product delivery mechanisms prior to receipt by a final consumer for the purpose of data or system compromise.

Supply chain compromise can take place at any stage of the supply chain including:

* Manipulation of development tools
* Manipulation of a development environment
* Manipulation of source code repositories (public or private)
* Manipulation of source code in open-source dependencies
* Manipulation of software update/distribution mechanisms
* Compromised/infected system images (removable media infected at the factory)(Citation: IBM Storwize)(Citation: Schneider Electric USB Malware) 
* Replacement of legitimate software with modified versions
* Sales of modified/counterfeit products to legitimate distributors
* Shipment interdiction

While supply chain compromise can impact any component of hardware or software, adversaries looking to gain execution have often focused on malicious additions to legitimate software in software distribution or update channels.(Citation: Avast CCleaner3 2018)(Citation: Microsoft Dofoil 2018)(Citation: Command Five SK 2011) Adversaries may limit targeting to a desired victim set or distribute malicious software to a broad set of consumers but only follow up with specific victims.(Citation: Symantec Elderwood Sept 2012)(Citation: Avast CCleaner3 2018)(Citation: Command Five SK 2011) Popular open-source projects that are used as dependencies in many applications may also be targeted as a means to add malicious code to users of the dependency.(Citation: Trendmicro NPM Compromise)

In some cases, adversaries may conduct “second-order” supply chain compromises by leveraging the access gained from an initial supply chain compromise to further compromise a software component.(Citation: Krebs 3cx overview 2023) This may allow the threat actor to spread to even more victims.
3506.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique Supply Chain Compromise (T1195) under the Initial Access tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It involves adversaries manipulating products or delivery mechanisms before consumer receipt to compromise systems. Specific mechanics include maliciously modifying development tools, source code repositories, open-source dependencies, and software update channels to insert backdoors. This technique can enable broad distribution with selective follow-on attacks and has been associated with groups like Sandworm Team and APT29.

Adversaries often focus on malicious additions to legitimate software in distribution channels, potentially targeting specific victims or broad sets, and may conduct second-order compromises to spread further. Associated groups include Sandworm Team, Ember Bear, and OilRig.

3507.name: Anti-VM Detection
3507.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may leverage [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078) to log directly into accessible cloud hosted compute infrastructure through cloud native methods. Many cloud providers offer interactive connections to virtual infrastructure that can be accessed through the [Cloud API](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/009), such as Azure Serial Console(Citation: Azure Serial Console), AWS EC2 Instance Connect(Citation: EC2 Instance Connect)(Citation: lucr-3: Getting SaaS-y in the cloud), and AWS System Manager.(Citation: AWS System Manager).

Methods of authentication for these connections can include passwords, application access tokens, or SSH keys. These cloud native methods may, by default, allow for privileged access on the host with SYSTEM or root level access. 

Adversaries may utilize these cloud native methods to directly access virtual infrastructure and pivot through an environment.(Citation: SIM Swapping and Abuse of the Microsoft Azure Serial Console) These connections typically provide direct console access to the VM rather than the execution of scripts (i.e., [Cloud Administration Command](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1651)).
3507.profile: [profile]The entity "Anti-VM Detection" is a technique for detecting and evading virtual machine or sandbox analysis environments, aligning with the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1497.001 under the Defense Evasion tactic for Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves executing system checks for artifacts like specific processes, files, hardware properties (e.g., fan, temperature sensors), registry keys, or network adapter configurations that indicate a virtualized environment. Adversaries may use tools like WMI, PowerShell, or scripting to automate these discovery checks and alter malicious behavior—such as halting execution or hiding core functions—if a virtual environment is detected. Groups including Gamaredon Group, OilRig, and Volt Typhoon have been associated with this activity.
3507.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Anti-VM Detection" aligns with the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1497.001, "System Checks," under the Defense Evasion tactic and is applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. This technique involves adversaries performing checks for artifacts indicative of a virtual machine or sandbox environment, such as querying system properties, hardware details, registry keys, running processes, and installed programs. If a virtual environment is detected, malware may alter its behavior, disengage, or conceal its core functions to evade analysis. Specific methods include using WMI, PowerShell, and checking for VME-specific hardware, services, or unusual file/folder names like "malware" or "sample."

3508.name: Encrypted C2 Communication
3508.uncertain_name: exfiltration over asymmetric encrypted non-c2 protocol
3508.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may steal data by exfiltrating it over an asymmetrically encrypted network protocol other than that of the existing command and control channel. The data may also be sent to an alternate network location from the main command and control server. 

Asymmetric encryption algorithms are those that use different keys on each end of the channel. Also known as public-key cryptography, this requires pairs of cryptographic keys that can encrypt/decrypt data from the corresponding key. Each end of the communication channels requires a private key (only in the procession of that entity) and the public key of the other entity. The public keys of each entity are exchanged before encrypted communications begin. 

Network protocols that use asymmetric encryption (such as HTTPS/TLS/SSL) often utilize symmetric encryption once keys are exchanged. Adversaries may opt to use these encrypted mechanisms that are baked into a protocol.
3508.profile: [profile]Exfiltration Over Asymmetric Encrypted Non-C2 Protocol (T1048.002) is a technique under the Exfiltration tactic. It involves stealing data by sending it over a separate, asymmetrically encrypted network channel distinct from the primary command and control (C2) channel, potentially to an alternate location. This method uses public-key cryptography, where each endpoint uses a private key and the other's public key, with keys exchanged before communication begins. Adversaries often leverage native protocol encryption mechanisms, such as HTTPS/TLS/SSL, which may subsequently use symmetric encryption. Associated groups include APT28, Curium, and Storm-1811.
3508.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Encrypted C2 Communication is a technique where adversaries encrypt command and control traffic to conceal it from detection, using algorithms like AES or RC4. This can involve implementing custom encryption within malware or using multiple layers of encryption, such as tunneling a custom scheme inside protocols like HTTPS. The method protects C2 communications but may be vulnerable if encryption keys are embedded within the malware.

3509.name: C2 Communication via HTTP
3509.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may use an existing, legitimate external Web service as a means for sending commands to and receiving output from a compromised system over the Web service channel. Compromised systems may leverage popular websites and social media to host command and control (C2) instructions. Those infected systems can then send the output from those commands back over that Web service channel. The return traffic may occur in a variety of ways, depending on the Web service being utilized. For example, the return traffic may take the form of the compromised system posting a comment on a forum, issuing a pull request to development project, updating a document hosted on a Web service, or by sending a Tweet. 

Popular websites and social media acting as a mechanism for C2 may give a significant amount of cover due to the likelihood that hosts within a network are already communicating with them prior to a compromise. Using common services, such as those offered by Google or Twitter, makes it easier for adversaries to hide in expected noise. Web service providers commonly use SSL/TLS encryption, giving adversaries an added level of protection.
3509.profile: [profile]C2 Communication via HTTP is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1102.002 under the Command and Control tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It involves adversaries using legitimate external web services like social media or cloud platforms (e.g., Google, Twitter) to send commands and receive output from a compromised system, leveraging the service's inherent SSL/TLS encryption for stealth. Return traffic can manifest as forum comments, pull requests, document updates, or tweets. Associated groups include APT29, Polonium, and MuddyWater.[/profile]
3509.profile_without_enhance: [profile]C2 Communication via HTTP is a technique within the Command and Control tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. It involves adversaries using the HTTP protocol to send commands to and receive data from compromised systems, blending malicious traffic with legitimate web traffic to evade detection. This method often employs standard HTTP requests and responses, potentially using encryption like HTTPS for additional protection.

3510.name: Register Domains Resembling Legitimate Organizations
3510.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may acquire domains that can be used during targeting. Domain names are the human readable names used to represent one or more IP addresses. They can be purchased or, in some cases, acquired for free.

Adversaries may use acquired domains for a variety of purposes, including for [Phishing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566), [Drive-by Compromise](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1189), and Command and Control.(Citation: CISA MSS Sep 2020) Adversaries may choose domains that are similar to legitimate domains, including through use of homoglyphs or use of a different top-level domain (TLD).(Citation: FireEye APT28)(Citation: PaypalScam) Typosquatting may be used to aid in delivery of payloads via [Drive-by Compromise](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1189). Adversaries may also use internationalized domain names (IDNs) and different character sets (e.g. Cyrillic, Greek, etc.) to execute "IDN homograph attacks," creating visually similar lookalike domains used to deliver malware to victim machines.(Citation: CISA IDN ST05-016)(Citation: tt_httrack_fake_domains)(Citation: tt_obliqueRAT)(Citation: httrack_unhcr)(Citation: lazgroup_idn_phishing)

Different URIs/URLs may also be dynamically generated to uniquely serve malicious content to victims (including one-time, single use domain names).(Citation: iOS URL Scheme)(Citation: URI)(Citation: URI Use)(Citation: URI Unique)

Adversaries may also acquire and repurpose expired domains, which may be potentially already allowlisted/trusted by defenders based on an existing reputation/history.(Citation: Categorisation_not_boundary)(Citation: Domain_Steal_CC)(Citation: Redirectors_Domain_Fronting)(Citation: bypass_webproxy_filtering)

Domain registrars each maintain a publicly viewable database that displays contact information for every registered domain. Private WHOIS services display alternative information, such as their own company data, rather than the owner of the domain. Adversaries may use such private WHOIS services to obscure information about who owns a purchased domain. Adversaries may further interrupt efforts to track their infrastructure by using varied registration information and purchasing domains with different domain registrars.(Citation: Mandiant APT1)

In addition to legitimately purchasing a domain, an adversary may register a new domain in a compromised environment. For example, in AWS environments, adversaries may leverage the Route53 domain service to register a domain and create hosted zones pointing to resources of the threat actor’s choosing.(Citation: Invictus IR DangerDev 2024)
3510.profile: [profile]The technique "Register Domains Resembling Legitimate Organizations" is identified as MITRE ATT&CK ID T1583.001 under the Resource Development tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. Adversaries acquire domains for use in phishing, drive-by compromises, or command and control. The core technical mechanics involve registering domains that are visually similar to legitimate ones through typosquatting, using different top-level domains (TLDs), homoglyphs, or internationalized domain names (IDNs) for homograph attacks. They may also repurpose expired domains to exploit existing trust, use private WHOIS services to obscure ownership, and dynamically generate unique, single-use domain names to evade detection. This technique is associated with numerous threat groups, including APT29.[/profile]
3510.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The technique "Register Domains Resembling Legitimate Organizations" is a sub-technique of Acquire Infrastructure: Domains (T1583.001) within the Resource Development tactic. It operates across multiple platforms. Adversaries purchase or acquire domains that visually mimic legitimate organizations to establish malicious infrastructure. This includes using homoglyphs, different top-level domains (TLDs), or internationalized domain names (IDNs) for homograph attacks, as well as employing typosquatting. The domains are often used for subsequent phases like Phishing or Command and Control, and adversaries may use private WHOIS services or varied registrar information to obscure ownership. Associated threat groups include APT28, Lazarus Group, and FIN7.[/profile]

3511.name: Hacking into Networks
3511.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may gain initial access to target systems by connecting to wireless networks. They may accomplish this by exploiting open Wi-Fi networks used by target devices or by accessing secured Wi-Fi networks — requiring [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078) — belonging to a target organization.(Citation: DOJ GRU Charges 2018)(Citation: Nearest Neighbor Volexity) Establishing a connection to a Wi-Fi access point requires a certain level of proximity to both discover and maintain a stable network connection. 

Adversaries may establish a wireless connection through various methods, such as by physically positioning themselves near a Wi-Fi network to conduct close access operations. To bypass the need for physical proximity, adversaries may attempt to remotely compromise nearby third-party systems that have both wired and wireless network connections available (i.e., dual-homed systems). These third-party compromised devices can then serve as a bridge to connect to a target’s Wi-Fi network.(Citation: Nearest Neighbor Volexity)

Once an initial wireless connection is achieved, adversaries may leverage this access for follow-on activities in the victim network or further targeting of specific devices on the network. Adversaries may perform [Network Sniffing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1040) or [Adversary-in-the-Middle](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1557) activities for [Credential Access](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0006) or [Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0007).
3511.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique known as "Wi-Fi Networks" (ID: T1669) under the Initial Access tactic. It involves adversaries connecting to target wireless networks to gain access. This can be achieved by exploiting open networks, using stolen credentials for secured networks, or physically positioning themselves within proximity. To bypass proximity requirements, they may remotely compromise dual-homed third-party devices to serve as a bridge to the target Wi-Fi. Once connected, this access enables follow-on activities like network sniffing or adversary-in-the-middle attacks. The technique is associated with groups like APT28, and a related sub-technique is Evil Twin (T1557.004), which involves deploying malicious access points.
3511.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Hacking into Networks" is a general concept rather than a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the retrieved context, it encompasses methods for gaining initial access via wireless networks. This includes exploiting open or secured Wi-Fi networks, sometimes requiring valid accounts or physical proximity. Adversaries may use compromised dual-homed systems as a bridge to target networks or deploy "Evil Twin" attacks by creating fraudulent Wi-Fi access points with spoofed SSIDs to trick devices into connecting. Once connected, this access enables follow-on activities like network sniffing or adversary-in-the-middle attacks for credential access and discovery.

3512.name: Stealing Credentials
3512.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may gather credentials that can be used during targeting. Account credentials gathered by adversaries may be those directly associated with the target victim organization or attempt to take advantage of the tendency for users to use the same passwords across personal and business accounts.

Adversaries may gather credentials from potential victims in various ways, such as direct elicitation via [Phishing for Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1598). Adversaries may also compromise sites then add malicious content designed to collect website authentication cookies from visitors.(Citation: ATT ScanBox) (Citation: Register Deloitte)(Citation: Register Uber)(Citation: Detectify Slack Tokens)(Citation: Forbes GitHub Creds)(Citation: GitHub truffleHog)(Citation: GitHub Gitrob)(Citation: CNET Leaks) Where multi-factor authentication (MFA) based on out-of-band communications is in use, adversaries may compromise a service provider to gain access to MFA codes and one-time passwords (OTP).(Citation: Okta Scatter Swine 2022)

Credential information may also be exposed to adversaries via leaks to online or other accessible data sets (ex: [Search Engines](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1593/002), breach dumps, code repositories, etc.). Adversaries may purchase credentials from dark web markets, such as Russian Market and 2easy, or through access to Telegram channels that distribute logs from infostealer malware.(Citation: Bleeping Computer 2easy 2021)(Citation: SecureWorks Infostealers 2023)(Citation: Bleeping Computer Stealer Logs 2023)

Gathering this information may reveal opportunities for other forms of reconnaissance (ex: [Search Open Websites/Domains](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1593) or [Phishing for Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1598)), establishing operational resources (ex: [Compromise Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1586)), and/or initial access (ex: [External Remote Services](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1133) or [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078)).
3512.profile: [profile]Stealing Credentials is a reconnaissance technique, identified as T1589.001, within the Credential Access tactic. It involves adversaries gathering account credentials through multiple methods including phishing, compromising websites to steal authentication cookies, purchasing credentials from dark web markets or Telegram channels, and exploiting credential leaks in online data sets, breach dumps, or code repositories. This activity is associated with groups like APT29, Chimera, and LAPSUS$.
3512.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Stealing Credentials is a broad adversary objective within the Credential Access tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. It encompasses various specific techniques for acquiring authentication materials. These include OS Credential Dumping (T1003) from memory or caches, extracting Credentials from Web Browsers (T1503) via files or process memory, and searching for Unsecured Credentials (T1552) in files, the registry, or configuration stores. Adversaries use tools like Mimikatz or custom scripts to obtain hashes or plaintext passwords, which are then used for lateral movement or persistent access.

3513.name: WMI Persistence
3513.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may clear artifacts associated with previously established persistence on a host system to remove evidence of their activity. This may involve various actions, such as removing services, deleting executables, [Modify Registry](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1112), [Plist File Modification](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1647), or other methods of cleanup to prevent defenders from collecting evidence of their persistent presence.(Citation: Cylance Dust Storm) Adversaries may also delete accounts previously created to maintain persistence (i.e. [Create Account](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1136)).(Citation: Talos - Cisco Attack 2022)

In some instances, artifacts of persistence may also be removed once an adversary’s persistence is executed in order to prevent errors with the new instance of the malware.(Citation: NCC Group Team9 June 2020)
3513.profile: [profile]WMI Persistence is a technique for maintaining access, typically mapped to MITRE ATT&CK ID T1546.003 under the Persistence tactic on Windows platforms. It works by creating Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) event subscriptions, which involve installing filters, providers, and consumers to trigger and execute malicious code automatically when specific system events occur, such as user logon or at a set time. The WMI Provider Host process (WmiPrvSe.exe) often executes this code, potentially with SYSTEM privileges. Adversaries may compile scripts into .mof files using tools like mofcomp.exe to deploy these subscriptions, and this technique has been used by groups including APT29.
3513.profile_without_enhance: [profile]WMI Persistence is a technique, likely aligned with MITRE ATT&CK T1546.003 (Event Triggered Execution: Windows Management Instrumentation Event Subscription), within the Persistence tactic for Windows platforms. It involves creating WMI event subscriptions (filters, consumers, bindings) to execute malicious code when specific system events occur, such as user logon or at a scheduled time. Adversaries may compile scripts into MOF files using tools like mofcomp.exe, with execution proxied by the WmiPrvSe.exe process, potentially granting SYSTEM privileges. This method is used by threat groups like APT29 and Turla.

3514.name: Event Log Clearing
3514.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may enumerate system and service logs to find useful data. These logs may highlight various types of valuable insights for an adversary, such as user authentication records ([Account Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1087)), security or vulnerable software ([Software Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1518)), or hosts within a compromised network ([Remote System Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1018)).

Host binaries may be leveraged to collect system logs. Examples include using `wevtutil.exe` or [PowerShell](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001) on Windows to access and/or export security event information.(Citation: WithSecure Lazarus-NoPineapple Threat Intel Report 2023)(Citation: Cadet Blizzard emerges as novel threat actor) In cloud environments, adversaries may leverage utilities such as the Azure VM Agent’s `CollectGuestLogs.exe` to collect security logs from cloud hosted infrastructure.(Citation: SIM Swapping and Abuse of the Microsoft Azure Serial Console)

Adversaries may also target centralized logging infrastructure such as SIEMs. Logs may also be bulk exported and sent to adversary-controlled infrastructure for offline analysis.

In addition to gaining a better understanding of the environment, adversaries may also monitor logs in real time to track incident response procedures. This may allow them to adjust their techniques in order to maintain persistence or evade defenses.(Citation: Permiso GUI-Vil 2023)
3514.profile: [profile]Event Log Clearing, also known as T1070.001, is a Defense Evasion technique used on Windows systems. Adversaries clear Windows Event Logs to hide intrusion activity, typically using administrator privileges to execute commands like `wevtutil cl system`, `wevtutil cl application`, and `wevtutil cl security`. Logs can also be cleared via PowerShell with `Remove-EventLog -LogName Security` or by directly deleting files in `C:\Windows\System32\winevt\logs\`. This technique is associated with groups like APT29, Hafnium, and Volt Typhoon.
3514.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Event Log Clearing, known as T1070.001 in the MITRE ATT&CK framework, is a Defense Evasion technique primarily targeting the Windows platform. It involves adversaries clearing Windows Event Logs to erase evidence of intrusion. With administrator privileges, this is commonly executed using the `wevtutil` utility with commands like `wevtutil cl system`, `wevtutil cl application`, and `wevtutil cl security`. Logs can also be cleared via PowerShell commands such as `Remove-EventLog` or by directly deleting the log files stored in `C:\Windows\System32\winevt\logs\`. This action hinders forensic analysis and incident response by removing records of malicious activity.

3515.name: File Timestamp Reset
3515.profile: [profile]File Timestamp Reset, also known as Timestomp (T1070.006), is a Defense Evasion technique. It operates by modifying file timestamps (modify, access, create, and change times) to hide new or altered files. On Windows, adversaries commonly alter the user-accessible `$STANDARD_INFORMATION` attribute via API calls, and may also modify the kernel-managed `$FILE_NAME` attribute ("double timestomping") to evade forensic detection that looks for discrepancies. On Linux/ESXi, commands like `touch -a -m -t` can be used. This technique is employed by groups like APT29 to blend malicious files with legitimate ones.
3515.profile_without_enhance: [profile]File Timestamp Reset, also known as Timestomp (T1070.006), is a Defense Evasion technique where adversaries modify file timestamps to hide new or altered files. This is achieved by altering the `$STANDARD_INFORMATION` attribute in Windows via API calls to mimic timestamps of legitimate files, or using commands like `touch` in Linux. The goal is to evade forensic detection by making malicious files appear inconspicuous and blend in with normal system files.

3528.name: MFA bypass
3528.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may modify file attributes and subvert Gatekeeper functionality to evade user prompts and execute untrusted programs. Gatekeeper is a set of technologies that act as layer of Apple’s security model to ensure only trusted applications are executed on a host. Gatekeeper was built on top of File Quarantine in Snow Leopard (10.6, 2009) and has grown to include Code Signing, security policy compliance, Notarization, and more. Gatekeeper also treats applications running for the first time differently than reopened applications.(Citation: TheEclecticLightCompany Quarantine and the flag)(Citation: TheEclecticLightCompany apple notarization )

Based on an opt-in system, when files are downloaded an extended attribute (xattr) called `com.apple.quarantine` (also known as a quarantine flag) can be set on the file by the application performing the download. Launch Services opens the application in a suspended state. For first run applications with the quarantine flag set, Gatekeeper executes the following functions:

1. Checks extended attribute – Gatekeeper checks for the quarantine flag, then provides an alert prompt to the user to allow or deny execution.(Citation: OceanLotus for OS X)(Citation: 20 macOS Common Tools and Techniques)

2. Checks System Policies - Gatekeeper checks the system security policy, allowing execution of apps downloaded from either just the App Store or the App Store and identified developers.

3. Code Signing – Gatekeeper checks for a valid code signature from an Apple Developer ID.

4. Notarization - Using the `api.apple-cloudkit.com` API, Gatekeeper reaches out to Apple servers to verify or pull down the notarization ticket and ensure the ticket is not revoked. Users can override notarization, which will result in a prompt of executing an “unauthorized app” and the security policy will be modified.

Adversaries can subvert one or multiple security controls within Gatekeeper checks through logic errors (e.g. [Exploitation for Defense Evasion](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1211)), unchecked file types, and external libraries. For example, prior to macOS 13 Ventura, code signing and notarization checks were only conducted on first launch, allowing adversaries to write malicious executables to previously opened applications in order to bypass Gatekeeper security checks.(Citation: theevilbit gatekeeper bypass 2021)(Citation: Application Bundle Manipulation Brandon Dalton)

Applications and files loaded onto the system from a USB flash drive, optical disk, external hard drive, from a drive shared over the local network, or using the curl command may not set the quarantine flag. Additionally, it is possible to avoid setting the quarantine flag using [Drive-by Compromise](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1189).
3528.profile: [profile]The entity "MFA bypass" is a technique for evading multi-factor authentication controls, though it lacks a specific MITRE ATT&CK ID. It operates under the Defense Evasion tactic and targets cloud platforms. Technical mechanics include disabling MFA via policy modification, redirecting authentication calls to localhost, or abusing self-enrollment to register adversary-controlled devices. The intrusion-set APT29 has been associated with related techniques such as device registration and multi-factor authentication request generation.
3528.profile_without_enhance: [profile]MFA Bypass is a technique adversaries use to circumvent multi-factor authentication (MFA) controls. Common methods include generating repeated push notifications to cause "MFA fatigue" and trick users into approving access, or registering a new adversary-controlled device to an existing account to bypass initial MFA requirements. Attackers may also modify or disable MFA mechanisms entirely after gaining initial access, such as by altering configuration files or abusing policy exclusions. This technique is often associated with groups like Scattered Spider, LAPSUS$, and APT29.

3533.name: Authentication Token Exploitation
3533.profile: [profile]Authentication Token Exploitation is a technique for credential access and defense evasion, primarily targeting Windows and cloud platforms. It involves stealing or forging authentication tokens, such as Kerberos tickets or OAuth access tokens, to bypass normal authentication and impersonate users or services. Adversaries may exploit vulnerabilities like MS14-068 to forge Kerberos tickets, use stolen OAuth tokens for long-term API access to cloud services like email, or manipulate Windows access tokens to escalate privileges from administrator to SYSTEM level. Groups like APT29 have been associated with such methods.[/profile]
3533.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Authentication Token Exploitation, identified as T1550.001 in the MITRE ATT&CK framework, falls under the Credential Access tactic and applies to Windows, Linux, and Cloud platforms. This technique involves adversaries stealing or forging authentication tokens, such as OAuth access tokens or Kerberos tickets, to bypass standard authentication and impersonate users or services. For example, stolen OAuth tokens can be used to make authorized API calls to cloud services like email, enabling long-term access and data exfiltration, while forged Kerberos tickets (e.g., via MS14-068) can grant unauthorized domain access. The exploitation negates multi-factor authentication and can be difficult to detect as it mimics legitimate API workflows.

3535.name: ActiveSync anomalies
3535.profile: [profile]ActiveSync anomalies is a technique likely associated with the Collection tactic, targeting mobile device management platforms. It involves exploiting irregularities in Microsoft Exchange ActiveSync protocols to facilitate unauthorized data access or exfiltration from mobile devices synchronized with an Exchange server. The intrusion set APT29 has been linked to this activity, indicating its use in targeted campaigns for email and data collection.
3535.profile_without_enhance: [profile]ActiveSync anomalies is a technique where adversaries manipulate Microsoft Exchange ActiveSync protocols to maintain persistence and exfiltrate data from mobile devices. This involves abusing the protocol to deploy malicious configuration profiles or rules that trigger actions like data synchronization to adversary-controlled servers when specific conditions, such as receiving a crafted email, are met. It primarily targets mobile platforms and email systems integrated with Exchange.

3536.name: Email data exfiltration
3536.profile: [profile]Email data exfiltration is a technique for data theft, categorized under the Exfiltration tactic. It involves adversaries stealing sensitive information by extracting data from email systems. This can be achieved by forwarding emails from a compromised account to an adversary-controlled address or by using automated scripts or command-line tools to export mailbox contents. Groups like APT29 have been associated with this method. To evade detection, exfiltrated email data is often compressed or encrypted before being transferred out of the network.
3536.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The technique 'Email data exfiltration' is a method for data theft, likely aligning with the Exfiltration tactic. It involves adversaries using email protocols to covertly export stolen data out of a network, often by embedding it within or attaching it to seemingly legitimate emails. This activity is related to clearing mailbox data post-exfiltration to remove evidence, such as using PowerShell commands like `Remove-MailboxExportRequest` on Exchange servers. The technique may also involve automating the exfiltration process and potentially archiving the data before transmission.

3537.name: Command-line actions
3537.profile: [profile]Command-line actions, corresponding to MITRE ATT&CK technique T1059 (Command and Scripting Interpreter), fall under the Execution tactic and span Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. This technique involves adversaries directly using system command-line interfaces like cmd, PowerShell, or bash to execute native commands or scripts for discovery, lateral movement, and payload deployment. As seen with APT29, it serves as a fundamental execution method, often following initial access and preceding data exfiltration or persistence activities.
3537.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Command-line actions, identified as T1059 in the MITRE ATT&CK framework, fall under the Execution tactic and are applicable across Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. This technique involves adversaries directly using command-line interfaces like cmd, PowerShell, or bash to execute commands and scripts for discovery, lateral movement, and other objectives. It serves as a foundational method for interactive control and can be leveraged through various interpreters or abused utilities to run malicious payloads and system commands.

3538.name: PowerShell
3538.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may abuse PowerShell commands and scripts for execution. PowerShell is a powerful interactive command-line interface and scripting environment included in the Windows operating system.(Citation: TechNet PowerShell) Adversaries can use PowerShell to perform a number of actions, including discovery of information and execution of code. Examples include the Start-Process cmdlet which can be used to run an executable and the Invoke-Command cmdlet which runs a command locally or on a remote computer (though administrator permissions are required to use PowerShell to connect to remote systems). PowerShell may also be used to download and run executables from the Internet, which can be executed from disk or in memory without touching disk. A number of PowerShell-based offensive testing tools are available, including [Empire](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0363), [PowerSploit](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0194), [PoshC2](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0378), and PSAttack.(Citation: Github PSAttack) PowerShell commands/scripts can also be executed without directly invoking the powershell.exe binary through interfaces to PowerShell's underlying System.Management.Automation assembly DLL exposed through the .NET framework and Windows Common Language Interface (CLI).(Citation: Sixdub PowerPick Jan 2016)(Citation: SilentBreak Offensive PS Dec 2015)(Citation: Microsoft PSfromCsharp APR 2014)
3538.profile: [profile]PowerShell, identified as T1059.001, is a Command and Scripting Interpreter technique within the Execution tactic, primarily targeting Windows. It involves abusing the built-in command-line interface to execute arbitrary code, using cmdlets like Start-Process and Invoke-Command to run processes locally or remotely. Adversaries can download and execute payloads directly in memory, bypassing disk, and leverage tools like Empire and PowerSploit. Execution can also occur without powershell.exe by calling the System.Management.Automation DLL, and it is widely used by groups including FIN7 and APT29.[/profile]

Adversaries abuse it for discovery and code execution using cmdlets like Start-Process and Invoke-Command, to download and run executables from the internet, often in-memory to avoid disk. Execution can also occur without powershell.exe by leveraging the System.Management.Automation DLL via .NET. It is associated with numerous threat groups and tools like Empire and PowerSploit.

This activity is associated with threat groups including Volt Typhoon, Mustang Panda, and Scattered Spider.

3540.name: AdFind
3540.profile: [profile]AdFind is a legitimate Active Directory reconnaissance tool that has been repurposed by multiple threat actors for malicious network discovery. It is notably used by APT29, as well as groups including APT10, APT32, Anunak, Gallium, and FIN7. Its primary function is to query and enumerate Active Directory environments, often serving as an initial step in a compromise chain, and it is frequently deployed alongside other tools like Cobalt Strike and Mimikatz in broader intrusion campaigns.[/profile]

Its key behavior is performing reconnaissance within Windows Active Directory environments to collect data on users, groups, and systems. 3541.name: sqlceip.exe

3547.name: Scheduled Task Creation
3547.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may abuse the Windows Task Scheduler to perform task scheduling for initial or recurring execution of malicious code. There are multiple ways to access the Task Scheduler in Windows. The [schtasks](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0111) utility can be run directly on the command line, or the Task Scheduler can be opened through the GUI within the Administrator Tools section of the Control Panel.(Citation: Stack Overflow) In some cases, adversaries have used a .NET wrapper for the Windows Task Scheduler, and alternatively, adversaries have used the Windows netapi32 library and [Windows Management Instrumentation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1047) (WMI) to create a scheduled task. Adversaries may also utilize the Powershell Cmdlet `Invoke-CimMethod`, which leverages WMI class `PS_ScheduledTask` to create a scheduled task via an XML path.(Citation: Red Canary - Atomic Red Team)

An adversary may use Windows Task Scheduler to execute programs at system startup or on a scheduled basis for persistence. The Windows Task Scheduler can also be abused to conduct remote Execution as part of Lateral Movement and/or to run a process under the context of a specified account (such as SYSTEM). Similar to [System Binary Proxy Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1218), adversaries have also abused the Windows Task Scheduler to potentially mask one-time execution under signed/trusted system processes.(Citation: ProofPoint Serpent)

Adversaries may also create "hidden" scheduled tasks (i.e. [Hide Artifacts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1564)) that may not be visible to defender tools and manual queries used to enumerate tasks. Specifically, an adversary may hide a task from `schtasks /query` and the Task Scheduler by deleting the associated Security Descriptor (SD) registry value (where deletion of this value must be completed using SYSTEM permissions).(Citation: SigmaHQ)(Citation: Tarrask scheduled task) Adversaries may also employ alternate methods to hide tasks, such as altering the metadata (e.g., `Index` value) within associated registry keys.(Citation: Defending Against Scheduled Task Attacks in Windows Environments)
3547.profile: [profile]Scheduled Task Creation, also known as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1053.005, is a persistence and execution tactic within the Windows platform. It involves abusing the Windows Task Scheduler via utilities like `schtasks.exe`, .NET wrappers, WMI, or the PowerShell `Invoke-CimMethod` cmdlet to schedule malicious code. Adversaries can create tasks to run at startup or on a recurring basis, and they may hide tasks by deleting the associated Security Descriptor registry value or altering registry key metadata to evade detection. This technique is commonly used by groups like APT29 and OilRig.[/profile]
3547.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Scheduled Task Creation is a technique aligned with MITRE ATT&CK ID T1053.005 under the Execution tactic, primarily for Windows platforms. It involves abusing the Windows Task Scheduler for initial or recurring execution of malicious code. This can be achieved via command-line utilities like `schtasks`, .NET wrappers, the netapi32 library, Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI), or the PowerShell `Invoke-CimMethod` cmdlet using the `PS_ScheduledTask` WMI class. The technique is used for persistence, lateral movement, and privilege execution, and adversaries may hide tasks by deleting the associated Security Descriptor registry value.

3579.name: Wiping logs
3579.profile: [profile]Wiping logs is a general technique adversaries use to hide intrusion activity by deleting system log data. It aligns with the MITRE ATT&CK tactic of Defense Evasion. Specific implementations include clearing Windows Event Logs using commands like `wevtutil cl security` or PowerShell's `Remove-EventLog`, and clearing Linux/Mac logs by deleting files in directories like `/var/log/`. Groups such as APT29 have been associated with related techniques like disabling cloud logs.[/profile]

The primary tactic is Defense Evasion. It is executed on multiple platforms including Windows, Linux, and macOS. Technical mechanics involve adversaries clearing or deleting system and application log files to hide intrusion evidence. On Windows, this can be done using commands like `wevtutil cl` or PowerShell's `Remove-EventLog`, or by directly deleting files in `C:\Windows\System32\winevt\logs\`. On Linux/macOS, logs under `/var/log/` such as `auth.log` or `messages` are targeted. Command history in Unix-like systems (e.g., `~/.bash_history`) can also be wiped using commands like `history -c` or by manipulating environment variables like `HISTFILE`.

3597.name: multi-stage infection chains
3597.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may create multiple stages for command and control that are employed under different conditions or for certain functions. Use of multiple stages may obfuscate the command and control channel to make detection more difficult.

Remote access tools will call back to the first-stage command and control server for instructions. The first stage may have automated capabilities to collect basic host information, update tools, and upload additional files. A second remote access tool (RAT) could be uploaded at that point to redirect the host to the second-stage command and control server. The second stage will likely be more fully featured and allow the adversary to interact with the system through a reverse shell and additional RAT features.

The different stages will likely be hosted separately with no overlapping infrastructure. The loader may also have backup first-stage callbacks or [Fallback Channels](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1008) in case the original first-stage communication path is discovered and blocked.

3601.profile: [profile]NativeZone is a disposable custom Cobalt Strike loader used by APT29 since at least 2021. It is a DLL downloader that primarily calls rundll32.exe to download and execute subsequent infection stages, which can be camouflaged within PDF documents. The malware is associated with the APT29 intrusion set and targets the Windows platform.
3601.profile_without_enhance: [profile]NativeZone downloader, also known as Nativezone, is a DLL downloader malware attributed to APT29. Its primary function is to call rundll32.exe to execute subsequent payloads, which are often camouflaged within PDF documents. It operates on the Windows platform and is part of a toolset used to deploy further stages of infection, such as Cobalt Strike loaders.

3602.name: KM.FileSystem.dll
3602.profile: [profile]KM.FileSystem.dll is a malicious DLL used as part of a poisoned installer targeting Ukrainian government security applications, where it is packaged in a zip file alongside legitimate components. It is associated with the intrusion set APT29 and is delivered via the Cobalt Strike Beacon v4 malware. Its primary target platform is Windows systems.
3602.profile_without_enhance: [profile]KM.FileSystem.dll is a malicious DLL used as a component alongside Cobalt Strike Beacon v4. It is deployed via a poisoned installer targeting Ukrainian government security applications, where it is packaged in a zip file with legitimate components. Its key technical behaviors include using API hash resolution to obfuscate function calls and XOR 0x2E decryption for data obfuscation. It targets Windows systems and is associated with groups attributed to Cobalt Strike, including APT29, APT32, APT41, FIN6, and FIN7.[/profile]

3606.name: XOR 0x2E decryption
3606.profile: [profile]XOR 0x2E decryption is a custom cryptographic technique, aligning with the MITRE ATT&CK sub-technique T1024 for Command and Control. It operates by applying the XOR (exclusive OR) bitwise operation with the static key 0x2E to ciphertext to recover plaintext. This method represents a weak, roll-your-own encryption scheme often implemented directly within malware without external libraries, as observed in tools like KM.FileSystem.dll used by groups such as APT29. Its simplicity makes it vulnerable to analysis and reverse engineering for key recovery.
3606.profile_without_enhance: [profile]XOR 0x2E decryption is a technique for data obfuscation, often used as a custom cryptographic method for compressing or encrypting collected data prior to exfiltration (T1560.003) or for hiding command and control traffic (T1024). The technical mechanic involves applying the exclusive OR (XOR) bitwise operation with the static key 0x2E (decimal 46) to decrypt ciphertext into plaintext. This implementation is a simple, weak symmetric cipher that adversaries may deploy in custom archival utilities or protocols without external library references, as observed in campaigns by groups like FIN6 and Lazarus Group.

3607.name: API hash resolution
3607.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may obfuscate then dynamically resolve API functions called by their malware in order to conceal malicious functionalities and impair defensive analysis. Malware commonly uses various [Native API](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1106) functions provided by the OS to perform various tasks such as those involving processes, files, and other system artifacts.

API functions called by malware may leave static artifacts such as strings in payload files. Defensive analysts may also uncover which functions a binary file may execute via an import address table (IAT) or other structures that help dynamically link calling code to the shared modules that provide functions.(Citation: Huntress API Hash)(Citation: IRED API Hashing)

To avoid static or other defensive analysis, adversaries may use dynamic API resolution to conceal malware characteristics and functionalities. Similar to [Software Packing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/002), dynamic API resolution may change file signatures and obfuscate malicious API function calls until they are resolved and invoked during runtime.

Various methods may be used to obfuscate malware calls to API functions. For example, hashes of function names are commonly stored in malware in lieu of literal strings. Malware can use these hashes (or other identifiers) to manually reproduce the linking and loading process using functions such as `GetProcAddress()` and `LoadLibrary()`. These hashes/identifiers can also be further obfuscated using encryption or other string manipulation tricks (requiring various forms of [Deobfuscate/Decode Files or Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1140) during execution).(Citation: BlackHat API Packers)(Citation: Drakonia HInvoke)(Citation: Huntress API Hash)
3607.profile: [profile]Dynamic API Resolution, also known as API Hash Resolution and identified as T1027.007 under the Defense Evasion tactic, is a technique used on Windows platforms to conceal malware functionality. It works by storing hashes of API function names instead of literal strings, then dynamically resolving these functions at runtime using calls like `GetProcAddress()` and `LoadLibrary()`. This process obfuscates the import address table and changes file signatures to evade static analysis, with the hashes often being further encrypted. It has been associated with groups like APT29, Lazarus Group, and Mustang Panda.[/profile]
3607.profile_without_enhance: [profile]API hash resolution is a sub-technique of Obfuscated Files or Information (T1027.007) under the Defense Evasion tactic, primarily for Windows. It works by storing hashes of Windows API function names within malware instead of literal strings. During execution, the malware dynamically resolves these hashes using functions like `GetProcAddress()` and `LoadLibrary()` to manually link and load the required API functions, thereby obfuscating the malware's intent and evading static analysis that looks for imported function names.

3608.name: LNK file execution
3608.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may smuggle commands to download malicious payloads past content filters by hiding them within otherwise seemingly benign windows shortcut files. Windows shortcut files (.LNK) include many metadata fields, including an icon location field (also known as the `IconEnvironmentDataBlock`) designed to specify the path to an icon file that is to be displayed for the LNK file within a host directory. 

Adversaries may abuse this LNK metadata to download malicious payloads. For example, adversaries have been observed using LNK files as phishing payloads to deliver malware. Once invoked (e.g., [Malicious File](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002)), payloads referenced via external URLs within the LNK icon location field may be downloaded. These files may also then be invoked by [Command and Scripting Interpreter](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059)/[System Binary Proxy Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1218) arguments within the target path field of the LNK.(Citation: Unprotect Shortcut)(Citation: Booby Trap Shortcut 2017)

LNK Icon Smuggling may also be utilized post compromise, such as malicious scripts executing an LNK on an infected host to download additional malicious payloads.
3608.profile: [profile]LNK Icon Smuggling, also known as T1027.012, is a Defense Evasion technique for Windows. It abuses the IconEnvironmentDataBlock metadata field within Windows shortcut (.LNK) files to embed external URLs that download malicious payloads when the LNK file is executed, often delivered via phishing. This method can bypass content filters and has been used by groups like Mustang Panda, Gamaredon Group, and Kimsuky.[/profile]
3608.profile_without_enhance: [profile]LNK file execution is a technique where adversaries abuse Windows shortcut (.LNK) files to execute malicious code, often delivered via phishing. The LNK file's target path field can contain commands or references to malicious scripts or executables, which are run when a user opens the file. This method is commonly used for initial access and execution, leveraging user interaction to trigger the payload.

3609.name: ASKOD
3609.profile: [profile]ASKOD is a custom command and control protocol (T1094) used for adversary communication, falling under the Command and Control tactic. It operates by eschewing standard application layer protocols, instead implementing a bespoke protocol that may mimic legitimate services or use raw sockets over TCP/IP. This technique is associated with the intrusion set APT29, which utilizes it to obscure its network traffic and evade detection. The protocol's design complicates analysis and monitoring efforts.[/profile]
3609.profile_without_enhance: [profile]ASKOD is a custom command and control protocol technique (MITRE ATT&CK ID T1094) used for Command and Control. It involves adversaries developing a unique communication protocol instead of using standard application layer protocols. This can be implemented by mimicking legitimate protocols or creating entirely new ones using raw sockets over standard network stacks like TCP/IP, making detection and analysis more difficult.

3610.name: Almaz-1K
3610.profile: [profile]Almaz-1K is a custom command and control protocol (T1094) used by adversaries like APT29. It operates within the Command and Control tactic, typically on Windows platforms. The technique involves adversaries developing and using a unique communication protocol, which may mimic legitimate protocols or utilize raw sockets, to encapsulate their command and control traffic instead of relying on standard application layer protocols. This custom implementation makes network traffic analysis and detection more difficult for defenders.
3610.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Almaz-1K is a custom command and control protocol technique (T1094) used in the Command and Control tactic. It operates across multiple platforms, including Windows. The technique involves adversaries developing a unique, custom protocol for communication, which can be implemented by mimicking well-known protocols or by creating entirely new protocols on top of standard network stacks like TCP/IP, instead of using existing application layer protocols.

3611.name: GraphicalComponent.dll
3611.profile: [profile] GraphicalComponent.dll, also known as ITW name GraphicalComponent.dll, is attributed to the APT29 intrusion set. It is a malicious DLL with a malicious export named VisualServiceComponent, using a C&C server at 139.99.167[.]177. It is associated with the DLL_stageless and CheckUpdteFrameJavaCurrentVersion malware families and targets the Windows platform.
3611.profile_without_enhance: [profile]GraphicalComponent.dll, also known as ITW Name GraphicalComponent.dll, is a malicious DLL associated with the APT29 intrusion set. Its key technical behaviors include being delivered via the DLL_stageless component using DLL side-loading and containing encrypted command-and-control configurations. It targets Windows platforms and has used C&C infrastructure including the IP 139.99.167[.]177 and the domain hanproud[.]com. A specific variant hash is SHA256 a4f1f09a2b9bc87de90891da6c0fca28e2f88fd67034648060cef9862af9a3bf.

3613.name: CheckUpdteFrameJavaCurrentVersion
3613.profile: [profile]CheckUpdteFrameJavaCurrentVersion is a malicious export function within a DLL (e.g., Java_SRE_runtime_update.dll) used to launch malware functionality, attributed to the APT29 intrusion set. Its key technical behavior includes checking the Java Runtime Environment version (1.6, 1.7, or 1.8) by executing javaw.exe with the -version parameter. It communicates with the command-and-control server hanproud[.]com.
3613.profile_without_enhance: [profile]CheckUpdteFrameJavaCurrentVersion, also known as the malicious export for the Java_SRE_runtime_update.dll ITW sample, is a malware component associated with the APT29 intrusion set and the Cobalt Strike framework. Its command-and-control infrastructure includes the domain hanproud[.]com. The malware is linked to other components like GraphicalComponent.dll and targets the Windows platform, with functionality that includes checking for specific Java Runtime Environment versions (1.6, 1.7, or 1.8).

3617.name: FIN7
3617.uncertain_mes: [FIN7](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0046) is a financially-motivated threat group that has been active since 2013. [FIN7](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0046) has targeted the retail, restaurant, hospitality, software, consulting, financial services, medical equipment, cloud services, media, food and beverage, transportation, pharmaceutical, and utilities industries in the United States. A portion of [FIN7](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0046) was operated out of a front company called Combi Security and often used point-of-sale malware for targeting efforts. Since 2020, [FIN7](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0046) shifted operations to big game hunting (BGH), including use of [REvil](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0496) ransomware and their own Ransomware-as-a-Service (RaaS), Darkside. FIN7 may be linked to the [Carbanak](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0008) Group, but multiple threat groups have been observed using [Carbanak](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0030), leading these groups to be tracked separately.(Citation: FireEye FIN7 March 2017)(Citation: FireEye FIN7 April 2017)(Citation: FireEye CARBANAK June 2017)(Citation: FireEye FIN7 Aug 2018)(Citation: CrowdStrike Carbon Spider August 2021)(Citation: Mandiant FIN7 Apr 2022)(Citation: BiZone Lizar May 2021)
3617.profile: [profile]FIN7, also known as Carbon Spider, Sangria Tempest, and ITG14, is a financially-motivated cybercrime group active since at least 2013. Its arsenal includes point-of-sale malware, the REvil ransomware, and its own Darkside Ransomware-as-a-Service platform. The group is known for sophisticated spear-phishing and big game hunting operations, having operated through a front company called Combi Security. While showing overlaps with the Carbanak group due to shared tooling, it is tracked separately. FIN7 primarily targets a wide range of industries in the United States, including retail, restaurant, hospitality, and financial services, with the core motivation of financial theft and extortion.
3617.profile_without_enhance: [profile]FIN7, also known as Carbanak, Carbon Spider, Sangria Tempest, and Anunak, is a financially motivated cybercriminal group believed to operate from Eastern Europe, primarily targeting financial institutions, retail, and hospitality sectors globally. Its key custom malware includes Carbanak, Bateleur, Halfbaked, and Pillowmint, often used to scrape payment card data from Point-of-Sale (POS) systems. The group employs sophisticated TTPs such as spear-phishing, RDP for lateral movement, fileless attacks, and dynamic detection evasion, frequently leveraging tools like Cobalt Strike. Its operations show overlaps with other criminal entities like Pinchy Spider, but it is distinct in its focus on large-scale financial theft and its use of a complex, evolving malware toolkit.[/profile]
3617.profile_without_enhance_0: [profile]FIN7, also known as Carbanak, Carbon Spider, Sangria Tempest, and Coreid, is a financially motivated cybercriminal group attributed to Russian-speaking actors. It is distinguished by its use of custom malware like Carbanak and Bateleur, and tools such as the Tinymet downloader, primarily targeting the retail, hospitality, and financial sectors in North America and Europe for large-scale data theft and payment card fraud.
3617.profile_without_enhance_0_no_hsage: [profile]FIN7, also known as Carbanak, Carbon Spider, Sangria Tempest, Coreid, and JokerStash, is a financially motivated cybercriminal group attributed to Russian-speaking actors. Its key malware includes the Carbanak backdoor, the Bateleur beacon, and the Tinymet downloader. The group primarily targets the retail, hospitality, and financial sectors, particularly in the United States and Europe, to conduct large-scale payment card theft and data breaches for monetary gain.
3617.profile_without_enhance_20: [profile]FIN7, also known as Carbanak, Carbon Spider, Sangria Tempest, and Anunak, is a financially motivated cybercriminal group believed to operate from Eastern Europe, primarily Russia and Ukraine. It is distinguished by its use of custom malware like the Carbanak backdoor, Lizar/Tirion RAT, JSSLoader, and tools such as Bateleur, Halfbaked, and Pillowmint for POS system targeting. Key TTPs include spear-phishing with malicious documents, extensive use of PowerShell for fileless execution, lateral movement via RDP, and DNS-based command and control. The group primarily targets the retail, hospitality, and financial sectors, especially in the United States and Europe, to steal payment card data and conduct large-scale financial fraud. Its operations show overlaps with other criminal entities and it has been known to recruit technical talent, including programmers and reverse engineers.[/profile]
3617.profile_without_enhance_20_no_hsage: [profile]FIN7, also known as Carbanak, Carbon Spider, Sangria Tempest, and JokerStash, is a financially motivated cybercriminal group attributed to Russian-speaking actors. Key TTPs involve spear-phishing with malicious documents (using OLE embedding), lateral movement, and techniques like fraudulent bank transaction manipulation for theft. 3618.name: Fileless Attack
3618.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may store data in "fileless" formats to conceal malicious activity from defenses. Fileless storage can be broadly defined as any format other than a file. Common examples of non-volatile fileless storage in Windows systems include the Windows Registry, event logs, or WMI repository.(Citation: Microsoft Fileless)(Citation: SecureList Fileless) Shared memory directories on Linux systems (`/dev/shm`, `/run/shm`, `/var/run`, and `/var/lock`) and volatile directories on Network Devices (`/tmp` and `/volatile`) may also be considered fileless storage, as files written to these directories are mapped directly to RAM and not stored on the disk.(Citation: Elastic Binary Executed from Shared Memory Directory)(Citation: Akami Frog4Shell 2024)(Citation: Aquasec Muhstik Malware 2024)(Citation: Bitsight 7777 Botnet)(Citation: CISCO Nexus 900 Config).

Similar to fileless in-memory behaviors such as [Reflective Code Loading](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1620) and [Process Injection](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1055), fileless data storage may remain undetected by anti-virus and other endpoint security tools that can only access specific file formats from disk storage. Leveraging fileless storage may also allow adversaries to bypass the protections offered by read-only file systems in Linux.(Citation: Sysdig Fileless Malware 23022)

Adversaries may use fileless storage to conceal various types of stored data, including payloads/shellcode (potentially being used as part of [Persistence](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0003)) and collected data not yet exfiltrated from the victim (e.g., [Local Data Staging](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1074/001)). Adversaries also often encrypt, encode, splice, or otherwise obfuscate this fileless data when stored. 

Some forms of fileless storage activity may indirectly create artifacts in the file system, but in central and otherwise difficult to inspect formats such as the WMI (e.g., `%SystemRoot%\System32\Wbem\Repository`) or Registry (e.g., `%SystemRoot%\System32\Config`) physical files.(Citation: Microsoft Fileless)
3618.profile: [profile]Fileless Storage, identified as T1027.011, is a Defense Evasion technique that operates across Windows, Linux, and Network Device platforms. It involves storing data like payloads or collected information in non-file system locations to avoid detection by disk-based security tools. Common storage mediums include the Windows Registry, WMI repository, event logs, and Linux shared memory directories such as `/dev/shm`. Adversaries, including groups like APT32 and Turla, often further obfuscate this stored data through encryption or encoding. While fileless, some activities may leave indirect artifacts in central system files.[/profile]
3618.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Fileless Attack is a technique where adversaries execute malicious code directly in memory without writing files to disk to evade detection. It leverages legitimate system tools like PowerShell, WMI, or macros to load and run payloads, often using process injection or reflective loading. This approach avoids traditional file-based antivirus scans and leaves minimal forensic artifacts, making it a common method for initial execution, persistence, and defense evasion across Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms.

3619.name: RTF Files
3619.uncertain_mes:
Introduction
Zscaler’s ThreatLabz threat research team recently has spotted a new variant of the emerging X-FILES infostealer attack with enhanced features to exfiltrate sensitive information. X-FILES is a stealer that aims to steal sensitive information, including logins and financial data.
3619.profile: [profile]RTF Files, also known as X-FILES stealer, is an infostealer malware attributed to the FIN7 group. Its key behaviors include stealing sensitive information like logins and financial data, and it is distributed via malicious RTF files. The malware's infrastructure involves hosting domains such as digital-ministry[.]ru, and it has been associated with Cobalt Strike payloads delivered through MSHTML exploits. Its primary target platform is Windows systems via document-based attacks.[/profile]
3619.profile_without_enhance: [profile]RTF Files is a file format (not a malware family itself) that is commonly exploited as an initial infection vector or delivery mechanism for malware. It is notably used by threat groups like Emotet (attributed to groups including Gold Cabin, Mummy Spider, and Mealybug) and in campaigns deploying Cobalt Strike (attributed to numerous APTs including APT29, APT32, FIN6, and Mustang Panda). These attacks involve weaponized RTF documents that host malicious scripts or exploits to download payloads like infostealers (e.g., X-FILES) or Cobalt Strike beacons from domains such as digital-ministry[.]ru.

3620.name: DOCX Files
3620.uncertain_mes:
Introduction
Zscaler’s ThreatLabz threat research team recently has spotted a new variant of the emerging X-FILES infostealer attack with enhanced features to exfiltrate sensitive information. X-FILES is a stealer that aims to steal sensitive information, including logins and financial data.
3620.profile: [profile]The entity is the X-FILES infostealer, also known as x-files stealer. It is attributed to the FIN7 intrusion set. Its key technical behavior is to exfiltrate sensitive information, including logins and financial data. It targets Windows systems, as indicated by its delivery through malicious .docx files, a method also associated with malware like QakBot and KOMPLEX in campaigns by groups such as Gold Cabin and APT28. Supplementary infrastructure involves the use of these weaponized document files for initial infection.[/profile]
3620.profile_without_enhance: [profile]DOCX Files is a file format commonly exploited as a delivery mechanism for malware. It is used by threat actors such as APT28 (in campaigns like KOMPLEX) and the group Gold Cabin (in Qakbot campaigns) to distribute malicious payloads. The files are often weaponized by embedding malicious macros or linking to external malicious executables, as seen in CMOON campaigns. The primary target platforms are Windows systems, where these documents are used in phishing attacks to initiate infection chains.
