3621.profile: [profile]The malware is known as LNK Files, also referred to as mocky lnk. It is attributed to the APT28 group. Its key technical behavior is acting as a downloader, often distributed via spam emails containing ZIP archives with malicious LNK files that masquerade as documents (e.g., Label.doc.lnk, InvoiceAug5.doc.lnk). This method is also employed by other malware families like TrickBot, QakBot, and RokRAT, which are linked to groups such as TA505, Wizard Spider, Gold Cabin, and APT37. The primary target platform is Windows systems.
3621.profile_without_enhance: [profile]LNK Files is a file format often weaponized as a downloader or initial access vector in malware campaigns. It is notably used by TrickBot (associated with groups like TA505, UNC1878, and Wizard Spider) distributed via spam emails with malicious ZIP attachments containing disguised .lnk files. The RokRAT malware is also distributed through LNK files, a method attributed to APT37 (ScarCruft/RedEyes). The format's abuse is a common technique for initial execution, as referenced in campaigns involving QakBot.

3622.name: Stealer DLL Variants
3622.profile: [profile]Stealer DLL Variants, also known as August Stealer, is attributed to the FIN7 intrusion set. Its key technical behaviors include fileless loading via Word macros and PowerShell, and it deploys both 32-bit and 64-bit DLL files as final payloads for data theft. The malware targets retail sector customer service and managerial staff. Infrastructure and supplementary information includes the use of specific SHA256 hashes for SantaStealer DLL variants and artifacts like 'twonelf-ld.ps1' and 'twonelf.exe' associated with Stealerium.
3622.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Stealer DLL Variants, also known as August Stealer, are malware variants deployed as DLL files, with both 32-bit and 64-bit versions observed. These variants are loaded via fileless techniques using Word macros and PowerShell, often in campaigns attributed to threat actor TA530. The malware functions as a stealer, targeting customer service and managerial staff at retail organizations.

3625.name: OLE Objects
3625.profile: [profile]OLE Objects is a deprecated technique, now replaced by T1559.001 (Component Object Model) and T1021.003 (Distributed Component Object Model). It was used for local code execution or remote execution via DCOM as part of lateral movement. Adversaries could abuse COM interfaces to invoke arbitrary execution and use DCOM to remotely execute shellcode or macros through applications like Microsoft Office. The technique is associated with intrusion sets like FIN7.[/profile]
3625.profile_without_enhance: [profile]OLE Objects is a technique (ID not specified in MITRE ATT&CK) used for execution, likely on Windows platforms. It involves embedding and activating Object Linking and Embedding (OLE) objects within documents to execute arbitrary code or commands. This method can be leveraged for initial access or persistence when a user opens a malicious document containing these manipulated objects.

3626.name: Base64 Decoding
3626.profile: [profile]Base64 Decoding is a sub-technique (T1132.001) under the Command and Control tactic, used by adversaries like FIN7 to make C2 traffic harder to detect. It involves decoding data that has been encoded using the Base64 binary-to-text standard, which adheres to existing protocol specifications to obfuscate the content of communications.
3626.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Base64 Decoding is a sub-technique of Data Encoding (T1132.001) within the Command and Control tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. It involves adversaries using the Base64 binary-to-text encoding scheme to obfuscate command and control traffic, making the content more difficult to detect by adhering to standard protocol specifications. This technique is employed by various threat groups including HAFNIUM, MuddyWater, and Lazarus Group.

3627.name: Hexadecimal Encoding
3627.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may encode data with a standard data encoding system to make the content of command and control traffic more difficult to detect. Command and control (C2) information can be encoded using a standard data encoding system that adheres to existing protocol specifications. Common data encoding schemes include ASCII, Unicode, hexadecimal, Base64, and MIME.(Citation: Wikipedia Binary-to-text Encoding)(Citation: Wikipedia Character Encoding) Some data encoding systems may also result in data compression, such as gzip.
3627.profile: [profile]Hexadecimal Encoding is a sub-technique (T1132.001) under the Command and Control tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. It involves converting binary data into a hexadecimal representation, using the standard 0-9 and A-F characters, to obfuscate command and control traffic and make it more difficult to detect. This technique is distinct from non-standard encoding and is used by threat actors including FIN7, MuddyWater, and Lazarus Group.
3627.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Hexadecimal Encoding is a sub-technique of Data Encoding (T1132.001) under the Command and Control tactic. It operates across multiple platforms, where adversaries convert binary data into a hexadecimal (base-16) text representation using characters 0-9 and A-F to adhere to protocol specifications and obfuscate C2 traffic, making detection more difficult. This is a standard encoding method used by groups like MuddyWater and Lazarus Group.

3628.name: Dynamic Detection Evasion
3628.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may employ various means to detect and avoid debuggers. Debuggers are typically used by defenders to trace and/or analyze the execution of potential malware payloads.(Citation: ProcessHacker Github) Debugger evasion may include changing behaviors based on the results of the checks for the presence of artifacts indicative of a debugged environment. Similar to [Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1497), if the adversary detects a debugger, they may alter their malware to disengage from the victim or conceal the core functions of the implant. They may also search for debugger artifacts before dropping secondary or additional payloads. Specific checks will vary based on the target and/or adversary. On Windows, this may involve [Native API](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1106) function calls such as IsDebuggerPresent() and NtQueryInformationProcess(), or manually checking the BeingDebugged flag of the Process Environment Block (PEB). On Linux, this may involve querying `/proc/self/status` for the `TracerPID` field, which indicates whether or not the process is being traced by dynamic analysis tools.(Citation: Cado Security P2PInfect 2023)(Citation: Positive Technologies Hellhounds 2023) Other checks for debugging artifacts may also seek to enumerate hardware breakpoints, interrupt assembly opcodes, time checks, or measurements if exceptions are raised in the current process (assuming a present debugger would “swallow” or handle the potential error).(Citation: hasherezade debug)(Citation: AlKhaser Debug)(Citation: vxunderground debug) Malware may also leverage Structured Exception Handling (SEH) to detect debuggers by throwing an exception and detecting whether the process is suspended. SEH handles both hardware and software expectations, providing control over the exceptions including support for debugging. If a debugger is present, the program’s control will be transferred to the debugger, and the execution of the code will be suspended. If the debugger is not present, control will be transferred to the SEH handler, which will automatically handle the exception and allow the program’s execution to continue.(Citation: Apriorit) Adversaries may use the information learned from these debugger checks during automated discovery to shape follow-on behaviors. Debuggers can also be evaded by detaching the process or flooding debug logs with meaningless data via messages produced by looping [Native API](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1106) function calls such as OutputDebugStringW().(Citation: wardle evilquest partii)(Citation: Checkpoint Dridex Jan 2021)
3628.profile: [profile]The technique Debugger Evasion, identified as T1622 under the Defense Evasion tactic, operates on Windows and Linux platforms. It involves malware checking for artifacts of a debugged environment to alter its behavior or halt execution. Specific mechanics include Windows API calls like IsDebuggerPresent(), inspecting the PEB's BeingDebugged flag, querying Linux's /proc/self/status for TracerPID, leveraging Structured Exception Handling (SEH) to detect process suspension, enumerating hardware breakpoints, or flooding debug logs via OutputDebugStringW(). The intrusion-set FIN7 has been associated with this technique.[/profile]
3628.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Dynamic Detection Evasion is a technique adversaries use to avoid detection by dynamically altering their malware's behavior, code, or signatures. This can involve techniques like environmental keying, where payloads are encrypted and only decrypted using keys derived from specific target system properties, preventing execution in analysis environments. It also includes modifying tools upon detection, such as changing file signatures after anti-virus quarantine, and dynamically adjusting network parameters like domain names for command and control to evade blocklists. This evasion operates across multiple platforms including Windows, Linux, and macOS, primarily supporting the Defense Evasion tactic.

3629.name: Scheduled Task Persistence
3629.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may abuse the Windows Task Scheduler to perform task scheduling for initial or recurring execution of malicious code. There are multiple ways to access the Task Scheduler in Windows. The [schtasks](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0111) utility can be run directly on the command line, or the Task Scheduler can be opened through the GUI within the Administrator Tools section of the Control Panel.(Citation: Stack Overflow) In some cases, adversaries have used a .NET wrapper for the Windows Task Scheduler, and alternatively, adversaries have used the Windows netapi32 library and [Windows Management Instrumentation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1047) (WMI) to create a scheduled task. Adversaries may also utilize the Powershell Cmdlet `Invoke-CimMethod`, which leverages WMI class `PS_ScheduledTask` to create a scheduled task via an XML path.(Citation: Red Canary - Atomic Red Team)

An adversary may use Windows Task Scheduler to execute programs at system startup or on a scheduled basis for persistence. The Windows Task Scheduler can also be abused to conduct remote Execution as part of Lateral Movement and/or to run a process under the context of a specified account (such as SYSTEM). Similar to [System Binary Proxy Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1218), adversaries have also abused the Windows Task Scheduler to potentially mask one-time execution under signed/trusted system processes.(Citation: ProofPoint Serpent)

Adversaries may also create "hidden" scheduled tasks (i.e. [Hide Artifacts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1564)) that may not be visible to defender tools and manual queries used to enumerate tasks. Specifically, an adversary may hide a task from `schtasks /query` and the Task Scheduler by deleting the associated Security Descriptor (SD) registry value (where deletion of this value must be completed using SYSTEM permissions).(Citation: SigmaHQ)(Citation: Tarrask scheduled task) Adversaries may also employ alternate methods to hide tasks, such as altering the metadata (e.g., `Index` value) within associated registry keys.(Citation: Defending Against Scheduled Task Attacks in Windows Environments)
3629.profile: [profile]Scheduled Task Persistence (T1053.005) is a Persistence technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework for the Windows platform. It involves abusing the Windows Task Scheduler to execute malicious code at system startup or on a recurring schedule. Technical mechanics include using the `schtasks` utility, .NET wrappers, WMI via `Invoke-CimMethod`, or the netapi32 library to create tasks. Adversaries can hide tasks by deleting the associated Security Descriptor registry value or altering registry key metadata to evade detection. This technique is also used for lateral movement and privilege execution, and is associated with numerous threat groups including FIN7.
3629.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Scheduled Task Persistence is the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1053.005 under the Persistence tactic, primarily for Windows. It involves abusing the Windows Task Scheduler to execute malicious code at system startup or on a recurring schedule for persistence. Technical mechanics include using the command-line utility schtasks, .NET wrappers, Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI), or the PowerShell Cmdlet `Invoke-CimMethod` with the `PS_ScheduledTask` WMI class to create tasks. Adversaries may also create hidden tasks by deleting the associated Security Descriptor registry value to evade detection by tools like `schtasks /query`.

3632.name: PowerShell Reflective DLL Injection
3632.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may abuse PowerShell commands and scripts for execution. PowerShell is a powerful interactive command-line interface and scripting environment included in the Windows operating system.(Citation: TechNet PowerShell) Adversaries can use PowerShell to perform a number of actions, including discovery of information and execution of code. Examples include the Start-Process cmdlet which can be used to run an executable and the Invoke-Command cmdlet which runs a command locally or on a remote computer (though administrator permissions are required to use PowerShell to connect to remote systems). PowerShell may also be used to download and run executables from the Internet, which can be executed from disk or in memory without touching disk. A number of PowerShell-based offensive testing tools are available, including [Empire](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0363), [PowerSploit](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0194), [PoshC2](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0378), and PSAttack.(Citation: Github PSAttack) PowerShell commands/scripts can also be executed without directly invoking the powershell.exe binary through interfaces to PowerShell's underlying System.Management.Automation assembly DLL exposed through the .NET framework and Windows Common Language Interface (CLI).(Citation: Sixdub PowerPick Jan 2016)(Citation: SilentBreak Offensive PS Dec 2015)(Citation: Microsoft PSfromCsharp APR 2014)
3632.profile: [profile]PowerShell Reflective DLL Injection is a technique where adversaries abuse PowerShell to load and execute DLLs directly in memory without writing to disk. This method leverages PowerShell's ability to call the `Assembly.Load()` method or similar functions to perform reflective DLL injection, loading malicious code into the current process's memory to evade detection. It is associated with groups like FIN7 and is a sub-technique of Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059.001) within the Execution tactic, primarily targeting Windows platforms.
3632.profile_without_enhance: [profile]PowerShell Reflective DLL Injection is a technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, aligning with the Defense Evasion and Privilege Escalation tactics on Windows platforms. It involves reflectively loading a malicious Dynamic-Link Library (DLL) directly into the memory of a running PowerShell process without writing the DLL to disk. This is achieved by using PowerShell to allocate memory within its own process, write the DLL's raw bytes, and then manually map and execute it, bypassing the standard Windows `LoadLibrary` API. This fileless method helps evade detection by process-based defenses and avoids leaving disk artifacts.

3633.name: DeflateStream Compression
3633.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may use compression to obfuscate their payloads or files. Compressed file formats such as ZIP, gzip, 7z, and RAR can compress and archive multiple files together to make it easier and faster to transfer files. In addition to compressing files, adversaries may also compress shellcode directly - for example, in order to store it in a Windows Registry key (i.e., [Fileless Storage](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/011)).(Citation: Trustwave Pillowmint June 2020)

In order to further evade detection, adversaries may combine multiple ZIP files into one archive. This process of concatenation creates an archive that appears to be a single archive but in fact contains the central directories of the embedded archives. Some ZIP readers, such as 7zip, may not be able to identify concatenated ZIP files and miss the presence of the malicious payload.(Citation: Perception Point)

File archives may be sent as one [Spearphishing Attachment](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001) through email. Adversaries have sent malicious payloads as archived files to encourage the user to interact with and extract the malicious payload onto their system (i.e., [Malicious File](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002)).(Citation: NTT Security Flagpro new December 2021) However, some file compression tools, such as 7zip, can be used to produce self-extracting archives. Adversaries may send self-extracting archives to hide the functionality of their payload and launch it without requiring multiple actions from the user.(Citation: The Hacker News)

[Compression](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/015) may be used in combination with [Encrypted/Encoded File](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/013) where compressed files are encrypted and password-protected.
3633.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique Compression, identified as T1027.015 under the Defense Evasion tactic for Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves using standard formats like ZIP, gzip, 7z, or RAR to obfuscate payloads and files, including compressing shellcode for storage in locations like the Windows Registry. Adversaries may concatenate multiple ZIP archives into one to evade detection by some readers and distribute payloads via spearphishing attachments or self-extracting archives. It is associated with groups like Gamaredon Group and FIN7 and can be combined with encryption.
3633.profile_without_enhance: [profile]DeflateStream Compression is a technique for data obfuscation and exfiltration preparation, likely aligning with MITRE ATT&CK Tactic Exfiltration. It involves using the .NET DeflateStream class or similar custom implementations to compress collected data, such as sensitive documents, prior to transfer. This compression makes the data more portable, minimizes network footprint, and can help obfuscate the payload. The method may be employed as a custom archival utility, distinct from common tools like ZIP or 7zip, to evade detection.

3637.name: Lizar
3637.uncertain_mes: [Lizar](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0681) is a modular remote access tool written using the .NET Framework that shares structural similarities to [Carbanak](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0030). It has likely been used by [FIN7](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0046) since at least February 2021.(Citation: BiZone Lizar May 2021)(Citation: Threatpost Lizar May 2021)(Citation: Gemini FIN7 Oct 2021)
3637.profile: [profile]Lizar, also known as lizar, is a modular .NET remote access tool structurally similar to Carbanak and attributed to the FIN7 group since at least February 2021. Its key technical behaviors include a toolkit architecture with a loader and plugins that combine into a bot component, and it functions as a client on infected systems. The target platform is systems running the .NET Framework. Supplementary information indicates it was discovered in February 2021 and its components interact as part of a broader toolkit.[/profile]
3637.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Lizar (alias lizar) is a modular .NET remote access tool (RAT) structurally similar to Carbanak, likely used by the FIN7 group since at least February 2021. Its toolkit architecture includes a loader and plugins that combine into a bot component.

3639.name: Carbanak
3639.uncertain_mes: [Carbanak](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0030) is a full-featured, remote backdoor used by a group of the same name ([Carbanak](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0008)). It is intended for espionage, data exfiltration, and providing remote access to infected machines. (Citation: Kaspersky Carbanak) (Citation: FireEye CARBANAK June 2017)
3639.profile: [profile]Carbanak, also known as Anunak, is a full-featured remote backdoor used for espionage and data exfiltration, attributed to the FIN7 group. Key technical behaviors include providing remote access to infected machines and utilizing associated tools like the Lizar client, Halfbaked, Bateleur, and Tinymet downloader. Its infrastructure involves SSL certificate detection and command-and-control beacons. The malware targets financial institutions and related sectors, with earlier activity linked to campaigns like Driftpin.
3639.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Carbanak, also known as CARBANAK, is a malware attributed to the FIN7 (Anunak) intrusion set. Its key technical behaviors include using RC2 encryption in CBC mode with PKCS#5 padding for command and control traffic, employing TCP tunneling, and utilizing VNC for remote desktop control. It performs file system management, file transfer, and compression for data staging and exfiltration, and specifically targets financial data through POS data theft and Outlook data theft. It operates on Windows platforms and is structurally related to the Lizar client and Halfbaked malware.[/profile]

3641.name: Data exfiltration
3641.profile: [profile]Data exfiltration is a technique (ID not specified) within the Exfiltration tactic. It involves the unauthorized transfer of data from a target network. The retrieved information details specific methods, including automated processing (T1020) and scheduling transfers (T1029) to blend with normal activity. Data is often compressed or encrypted (T1560) prior to transfer using utilities like clip.exe or custom methods. Exfiltration can occur over various channels, including C2, webhooks, Bluetooth, or USB devices. Associated groups include RocketKitten, FIN7, Gamaredon Group, and Lazarus Group.[/profile]
3641.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Data exfiltration is a high-level adversarial objective rather than a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique, falling under the Exfiltration tactic. It involves the unauthorized transfer of data from a victim's network, often using specific sub-techniques as transport mechanisms. These include Exfiltration Over C2 Channel (T1041), Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol (T1048), and Exfiltration Over Web Service (T1567). Prior to transfer, adversaries may compress or encrypt the data (T1560) to avoid detection, and the exfiltration itself can be automated (T1020) or scheduled (T1029) to blend with normal traffic.

3655.name: data retrieval
3655.profile: [profile]The entity "data retrieval" is a foundational cyber adversary technique for gathering information from a victim system, typically aligned with the Collection tactic. Its technical mechanics involve accessing and extracting specific data types, such as clipboard contents using commands like `clip.exe` or `Get-Clipboard` on Windows or `pbpaste` on macOS/Linux, often as a precursor to staging or exfiltration. This activity is associated with malware like the Lizar client and threat groups including APT38 and APT39.[/profile]
3655.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Data Retrieval is a technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, though it lacks a standard T-ID. It falls under the Collection tactic and operates across multiple platforms. The technique involves adversaries gathering specific data from a compromised system, such as clipboard contents using commands like `clip.exe` or `Get-Clipboard` on Windows or `pbpaste` on macOS/Linux. Retrieved data is often staged in a central location prior to exfiltration, a process sometimes linked to groups like Scattered Spider or Wizard Spider.

3656.name: Grabber
3656.profile: [profile]Grabber is a malware entity. It is associated with the Lizar client malware. The retrieved information does not directly describe Grabber's specific mechanics but references related adversary techniques. These include screen capture (T1113) using utilities like `CopyFromScreen`, `xwd`, or `screencapture`; input capture (T1056) for credential theft via methods like API hooking; and data exfiltration over USB (T1052.001). These techniques are employed by various threat groups such as APT28, MuddyWater, and Mustang Panda, indicating Grabber may operate in similar espionage or data theft campaigns.
3656.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Grabber is a technique for capturing user input to obtain credentials or collect information. It operates by intercepting user inputs, often transparently through methods like credential API hooking or by deceiving users into entering data into fake web portals. This technique is associated with threat groups such as Storm-1811, APT39, and APT42.

3657.name: Info
3657.profile: [profile]The entity "Info" is a broad concept, but based on the retrieved context, it aligns with reconnaissance techniques for gathering victim information. This includes searching victim-owned websites (T1594) and open websites/domains (T1593), which are tactics under Reconnaissance. These techniques involve manually browsing or using automated tools to find details like employee data, business operations, and hidden directories to enable further attacks like phishing or initial access. The malware "Lizar client" is a related tool.
3657.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Info is a reconnaissance technique (T1592) under the Reconnaissance tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. It involves gathering technical details about a target's infrastructure, such as hardware, software, network configurations, and security defenses, from public sources like search engines, social media, vendor sites, and network traffic. This collected data enables adversaries to identify vulnerabilities and plan subsequent attack stages.

3658.name: Jump to
3658.profile: [profile]The entity "Jump to" is a technique for establishing command and control, likely related to tunneling or proxy connections, as indicated by its association with the "Lizar client" malware. 3659.name: Kill
3659.profile: [profile]Kill is a technique adversaries use to disable security tools or eliminate competing malware processes, often by terminating security software or event logging processes to avoid detection. This action is commonly associated with the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1089, "Disable or Modify Tools," under the Defense Evasion tactic, applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves using commands or system utilities to stop processes, which can disrupt security scanning and event reporting. This behavior is observed in malware like Lizar client and in activities such as cryptocurrency mining, where it helps adversaries monopolize system resources.
3659.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Kill" is a technique adversaries use to terminate processes, often as part of the Defense Evasion tactic. It is commonly employed to disable security software, event logging, or competing malware processes to avoid detection and ensure resource availability for malicious activities like cryptocurrency mining. This action can be performed using system utilities or custom tools to interact with operating system APIs.

3660.name: List Processes
3660.profile: [profile]The entity "List Processes" is a specific implementation of the MITRE ATT&CK technique Process Discovery (T1057), under the Discovery tactic, applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. It involves obtaining information on running processes using commands like `tasklist` or `Get-Process` in Windows, `ps` or enumeration of `/proc` in Linux/macOS, and `ps` or `esxcli system process list` on ESXi. This information is used to understand the software environment and shape follow-on adversarial actions.
3660.profile_without_enhance: [profile]List Processes is a reconnaissance technique within the Discovery tactic, applicable across Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves querying the operating system to enumerate running processes, commonly using commands like `tasklist` or `Get-Process` on Windows, `ps` or examining `/proc` on Linux and macOS, and `esxcli system process list` on ESXi servers. This information helps adversaries understand the software landscape and identify targets for follow-on actions.

3661.name: Mimikatz (command)
3661.profile: [profile]Mimikatz (command) is a credential dumping tool used to extract passwords, hashes, and Kerberos tickets from Windows memory, primarily associated with the OS Credential Dumping technique (T1003). It operates on Windows platforms to facilitate credential access. The tool's specific mechanics include using the "lsadump" module to perform DCSync attacks against Active Directory and extracting credentials from the Security Account Manager (SAM) database. It is linked to malware like Lizar client and is utilized by numerous threat groups for lateral movement and privilege escalation.
3661.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Mimikatz (command) is a tool used for OS Credential Dumping (T1003), specifically targeting Windows platforms. It operates by extracting credential material from system memory, including the Security Account Manager (SAM) database and the Local Security Authority Subsystem Service (LSASS). The tool can also perform DCSync attacks to simulate domain controller replication and pull password hashes from Active Directory. This functionality enables adversaries to obtain hashed or cleartext passwords for lateral movement and privilege escalation.

3662.name: Network analysis
3662.profile: [profile]Network analysis is a reconnaissance technique, likely mapping to MITRE ATT&CK T1590 (Reconnaissance), used to gather information about a victim's network topology, including physical and logical arrangements, devices, and infrastructure details. This information can be collected via methods like active scanning or phishing and is used to identify opportunities for subsequent attacks, such as initial access or lateral movement.
3662.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Network analysis, corresponding to MITRE ATT&CK technique T1040 (Network Sniffing) under the Discovery tactic, involves adversaries passively capturing network traffic to gather information. This is achieved by placing a network interface into promiscuous mode or using span ports to monitor data in transit over wired or wireless connections, often to harvest credentials sent over unencrypted protocols or to understand network configuration details like services and hostnames for subsequent lateral movement.

3663.name: New session
3663.uncertain_mes:
When operating systems boot up, they can start programs or applications called services that perform background system functions. (Citation: TechNet Services) A service's configuration information, including the file path to the service's executable, is stored in the Windows Registry. 

Adversaries may install a new service that can be configured to execute at startup by using utilities to interact with services or by directly modifying the Registry. The service name may be disguised by using a name from a related operating system or benign software with [Masquerading](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1036). Services may be created with administrator privileges but are executed under SYSTEM privileges, so an adversary may also use a service to escalate privileges from administrator to SYSTEM. Adversaries may also directly start services through [Service Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1035).
3663.profile: [profile]This entity corresponds to the MITRE ATT&CK technique "Create or Modify System Process: Windows Service" (T1543.003) under the Persistence tactic, primarily for Windows. Adversaries install a new service by configuring its executable path in the Windows Registry or using service utilities, enabling execution at system startup. Services are often created with administrator privileges but run under SYSTEM, allowing privilege escalation. The service name may be disguised through masquerading to appear legitimate.
3663.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "New session" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the retrieved context, it is a foundational action for establishing authenticated access. This can involve creating a new logon session using stolen or forged credentials, such as via the `LogonUser` function to generate a new access token, or by establishing a new authenticated web session using stolen or forged session cookies. These new sessions allow adversaries to impersonate users, bypass multi-factor authentication, and access resources without needing the original credentials for each interaction.

3664.name: Rat
3664.profile: [profile]Rat is a Remote Access Tool (RAT) malware, often deployed in multi-stage command and control (C2) operations. In these operations, a first-stage RAT calls back to a server to collect host data and upload additional files, which can include a second, more fully-featured RAT to establish a reverse shell and provide persistent adversary interaction. The malware 'Lizar client' is a directly associated variant. This technique is commonly used by groups like APT3, APT41, MuddyWater, and Lazarus Group.
3664.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Rat is a remote access tool (RAT) used for command and control, often deployed in multi-stage campaigns. It typically operates by calling back to a first-stage command and control server to receive instructions, collect host information, and potentially upload a more fully-featured second-stage RAT, enabling adversary interaction through a reverse shell. This technique is associated with groups like APT3, APT41, MuddyWater, and Lazarus Group.

3665.name: Screenshot
3665.profile: [profile]Screenshot is a technique aligned with MITRE ATT&CK T1113 (Screen Capture) under the Collection tactic, primarily targeting Windows and macOS platforms. It involves adversaries capturing desktop images to gather information post-compromise, often using native utilities or API calls like CopyFromScreen, xwd, or screencapture. This behavior is associated with malware such as the Lizar client and numerous threat groups including APT28, MuddyWater, and Volt Typhoon.
3665.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Screenshot is a technique used for Collection under the Discovery tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It involves adversaries capturing images of the desktop to gather information during an operation. This can be achieved through native utilities or API calls like `CopyFromScreen`, `xwd`, or `screencapture`, or as a feature within remote access tools. The technique is associated with numerous threat groups including APT28, FIN7, and MuddyWater.

3666.name: Command Line
3666.profile: [profile]Command Line is a core technique (T1059) under Execution, used across Windows, Linux, and macOS. It involves adversaries using command-line interfaces to interact with a system and run malicious commands or scripts. This can be executed through native interpreters like cmd, PowerShell, or bash, or by abusing system utilities such as forfiles or ssh.exe to indirectly invoke commands for evasion. The technique is fundamental for activities like discovery, lateral movement, and payload execution, as seen with malware like Lizar client.
3666.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Command Line is a fundamental technique (T1059) within the Execution tactic, applicable across multiple platforms, that adversaries use to interact with a system's shell or command interpreter. It serves as the primary interface for executing native operating system commands to run software, control processes, and perform discovery. This technique is foundational, as command-line execution is leveraged by numerous other specific techniques for obfuscation, script interpretation, and remote service abuse.

3667.name: Executer
3667.profile: [profile]The entity "Executer" is a malware client named "Lizar client". It functions as a malware component. Its operational mechanics involve executing commands or programs by abusing system services or daemons, which can be done locally or remotely to run malicious content. This activity can support persistence by leveraging services set to run at boot. Additionally, it may hijack the operating system's execution flow to run its payloads, potentially for persistence, privilege escalation, or evasion of defenses like application control, by manipulating how the OS locates programs or libraries.[/profile]
3667.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Executer is a technique where adversaries abuse system services or daemons to execute commands or programs, interacting with or creating services locally or remotely for one-time or temporary execution. This method can also involve hijacking the operating system's execution flow to run malicious payloads by manipulating how programs or libraries are located, potentially for persistence, privilege escalation, or evasion of defenses.

3670.name: social-engineering efforts
3670.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may search social media for information about victims that can be used during targeting. Social media sites may contain various information about a victim organization, such as business announcements as well as information about the roles, locations, and interests of staff.

Adversaries may search in different social media sites depending on what information they seek to gather. Threat actors may passively harvest data from these sites, as well as use information gathered to create fake profiles/groups to elicit victim’s into revealing specific information (i.e. [Spearphishing Service](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1598/001)).(Citation: Cyware Social Media) Information from these sources may reveal opportunities for other forms of reconnaissance (ex: [Phishing for Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1598) or [Search Open Technical Databases](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1596)), establishing operational resources (ex: [Establish Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1585) or [Compromise Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1586)), and/or initial access (ex: [Spearphishing via Service](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/003)).
3670.profile: [profile]This entity is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1593.001, Social Media, under the Reconnaissance tactic and applicable to multiple platforms. It involves adversaries passively harvesting information from social media sites to gather data on victim organizations and staff, such as business announcements, roles, and interests. This collected intelligence can be used to create fake profiles for eliciting further information, enabling follow-on actions like spearphishing, account establishment, or initial access. The technique has been associated with groups including Contagious Interview, Exotic Lily, and Kimsuky.
3670.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Social-engineering efforts are a broad adversary tactic for eliciting sensitive information or gaining access. This technique involves psychological manipulation of targets through various electronic means, such as spearphishing via service (T1598.001), voice (T1598.004), or link (T1598.003). The core mechanics involve crafting targeted lures, often using information from prior reconnaissance, and posing as a trusted source to create urgency, rapport, or alarm to trick victims into divulging credentials or other actionable data.

3674.name: Visual Studio Project
3674.uncertain_mes: It has been 10 years since the discovery of Skimer, the first malware specifically designed to attack automated teller machines (ATMs). At the time, the learning curve for understanding its functionality was rather steep and analysis required specific knowledge of a manufacturer's ATM API functions and parameters, which were not publicly documented.
3674.profile: [profile]Visual Studio Project, also known as project alice, is a malware entity attributed to the FIN7 intrusion set. It is specifically designed to attack automated teller machines (ATMs) and requires deep knowledge of proprietary ATM API functions for analysis. Its technical behavior involves executing commands via Visual Studio Build Events during the compilation of provided project files, a technique also associated with malware families like dratzarus, comebacker, and dtrack used by groups such as Lazarus Group and Silent Chollima. The primary target platform is ATM systems.
3674.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Visual Studio Project is a malware entity. It is associated with the Lazarus Group and potentially Silent Chollima. Its key technical behavior involves the execution of malicious commands via Visual Studio Build Events during the project compilation process, often using a default Visual Studio MFC project or other programs as a cover. The target platform is Windows, as indicated by its abuse of the Visual Studio development environment.

3675.name: malicious code
3675.profile: [profile]The malware, known as Rovnix, is a bootkit that infects the Master Boot Record (MBR) and Volume Boot Record (VBR) by hooking the system's bootstrap code to load a malicious, unsigned driver. It is associated with the intrusion sets Turla and FIN7. Its key technical behavior involves a complex bootkit infection chain to establish persistence at the disk level, primarily targeting the Windows platform via the NTFS file system.[/profile]
3675.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The malware is known as Rovnix, a bootkit that infects the Master Boot Record (MBR) or Volume Boot Record (VBR). It operates by replacing the legitimate bootstrap code with its own malicious bootstrap code to gain execution control during system startup. Its primary target platform is Windows systems, specifically manipulating the NTFS file system.

3681.name: Dynamic Data Exchange (DDE)
3681.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may use Windows Dynamic Data Exchange (DDE) to execute arbitrary commands. DDE is a client-server protocol for one-time and/or continuous inter-process communication (IPC) between applications. Once a link is established, applications can autonomously exchange transactions consisting of strings, warm data links (notifications when a data item changes), hot data links (duplications of changes to a data item), and requests for command execution.

Object Linking and Embedding (OLE), or the ability to link data between documents, was originally implemented through DDE. Despite being superseded by [Component Object Model](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1559/001), DDE may be enabled in Windows 10 and most of Microsoft Office 2016 via Registry keys.(Citation: BleepingComputer DDE Disabled in Word Dec 2017)(Citation: Microsoft ADV170021 Dec 2017)(Citation: Microsoft DDE Advisory Nov 2017)

Microsoft Office documents can be poisoned with DDE commands, directly or through embedded files, and used to deliver execution via [Phishing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566) campaigns or hosted Web content, avoiding the use of Visual Basic for Applications (VBA) macros.(Citation: SensePost PS DDE May 2016)(Citation: Kettle CSV DDE Aug 2014)(Citation: Enigma Reviving DDE Jan 2018)(Citation: SensePost MacroLess DDE Oct 2017) Similarly, adversaries may infect payloads to execute applications and/or commands on a victim device by way of embedding DDE formulas within a CSV file intended to be opened through a Windows spreadsheet program.(Citation: OWASP CSV Injection)(Citation: CSV Excel Macro Injection )

DDE could also be leveraged by an adversary operating on a compromised machine who does not have direct access to a [Command and Scripting Interpreter](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059). DDE execution can be invoked remotely via [Remote Services](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021) such as [Distributed Component Object Model](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/003) (DCOM).(Citation: Fireeye Hunting COM June 2019)
3681.profile: [profile]Dynamic Data Exchange (DDE) is technique T1559.002 under the Execution tactic for Windows. It is a legacy Windows inter-process communication protocol that adversaries abuse to execute arbitrary commands by poisoning Microsoft Office documents or CSV files with embedded DDE formulas, enabling execution without Visual Basic for Applications macros. It can also be invoked remotely via Distributed Component Object Model (DCOM) for lateral movement and is used by groups like FIN7 and APT28.
3681.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Dynamic Data Exchange (DDE), identified as T1559.002, is an execution technique within the Windows platform. It is a client-server IPC protocol that adversaries abuse to run arbitrary commands by poisoning Microsoft Office documents or CSV files with DDE formulas, enabling execution without VBA macros. This method can also be invoked remotely via DCOM for lateral movement and is associated with groups like FIN7 and APT28.

3683.name: malicious documents
3683.profile: [profile]Malicious Documents, also known as griffon and ave maria, are attributed to the FIN7 intrusion set as well as groups like anthropoid spider, anunak, and the Lazarus Group. They serve as initial infection vectors, often delivering payloads like the one with the unpacked hash 032ccd6ae0a6e49ac93b7bd10c7d249f853fff3f5771a1fe3797f733f09db5a0. Their primary function is to deploy subsequent malware, such as Ave Maria, onto target systems.
3683.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The malware is known as malicious documents, which are used as initial attack vectors. It is associated with groups including FIN7, Anthropoid Spider (also known as Anunak), and the Lazarus Group. Key technical behaviors involve delivering initial payloads through these documents, with specific examples including the use of malicious files linked to hashes such as cec26d8629c5f223a120677a5c7fbd8d477f9a1b963f19d3f1195a7f94bc194b and ff58189452668d8c2829a0e9ba8a98a34482c4f2c5c363dc0671700ba58b7bee. Target platforms are typically Windows systems, as these documents often exploit vulnerabilities or macros to execute further malware like Ave Maria or Griffon. Infrastructure details are not specified beyond the document-based delivery method.

3684.name: tweaking code to evade detection
3684.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may exfiltrate data to a code repository rather than over their primary command and control channel. Code repositories are often accessible via an API (ex: https://api.github.com). Access to these APIs are often over HTTPS, which gives the adversary an additional level of protection.

Exfiltration to a code repository can also provide a significant amount of cover to the adversary if it is a popular service already used by hosts within the network.
3684.profile: [profile]The entity "tweaking code to evade detection" is a technique for Defense Evasion. It involves adversaries modifying malicious code, such as through polymorphism, to alter its runtime footprint with each execution, thereby evading signature-based detection tools like antivirus software. This can be combined with other obfuscation methods like software packing or command obfuscation. The intrusion-set FIN7 has been associated with this behavior.
3684.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "tweaking code to evade detection" is a technique for Defense Evasion. It involves modifying malicious software to alter its signature or runtime footprint, thereby bypassing signature-based detection systems like antivirus. This can be achieved through methods such as using polymorphic or metamorphic code that mutates with each execution, or by removing specific indicators from tools after detection to create an undetected version. The technique is often associated with sub-techniques like Polymorphic Code (T1027.014) and Indicator Removal from Tools (T1066).

3685.name: Initial intrusion
3685.profile: [profile]Initial Intrusion is a foundational attack phase not directly mapped to a specific MITRE ATT&CK ID. It represents the initial compromise of a system or network, often preceding more specific techniques. The intrusion-set FIN7 is associated with this phase. Technical mechanics for subsequent actions include deleting files (T1107) to remove forensic evidence, adding junk data to C2 traffic (T1001.001) to obfuscate communications, and compromising hardware in the supply chain (T1195.003) to implant persistent backdoors.[/profile]
3685.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Initial intrusion" is a general phase of an attack rather than a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique. It refers to the initial compromise stage where an adversary first gains access to a target network or system. Common methods for achieving this include exploiting software vulnerabilities, using stolen credentials, or deploying malware through phishing campaigns. This phase sets the stage for subsequent malicious activities like establishing persistence, moving laterally, and executing objectives.

3686.name: Establishing a foothold
3686.profile: [profile]Establishing a foothold is a foundational adversary objective, not a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique with a T-ID. It describes the initial act of gaining and maintaining access to a target network, often through purchased access from brokers or by creating new accounts. This persistent access enables subsequent malicious activities and is a prerequisite for groups like FIN7 to operate. The process may involve securing exclusive control of a compromised system to prevent interference from other threat actors.
3686.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Establishing a foothold is a foundational adversary objective, not a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique. It describes the initial phase of gaining and maintaining a presence within a compromised network. This can be achieved through various methods, such as purchasing access from initial access brokers, creating new accounts for persistence, or securing exclusive control of a system by patching vulnerabilities or removing competing malware to ensure unchallenged access.

3687.name: Escalating privileges
3687.profile: [profile]The entity "Escalating privileges" is a broad adversarial objective, not a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique with a designated ID. It is associated with the intrusion set FIN7. The retrieved information describes specific techniques for privilege escalation, such as abusing the deprecated macOS AuthorizationExecuteWithPrivileges API (T1548.004) to prompt users for credentials and execute code with root privileges, often by modifying legitimate programs or loading world-writable files. Another related technique is the general abuse of elevation control mechanisms (T1548). The core technical mechanic involves circumventing or exploiting native system controls to gain higher-level permissions.[/profile]
3687.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Escalating privileges is a core adversarial objective, not a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique. The provided data references specific techniques that achieve privilege escalation. For example, T1548.004, "Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism: Elevated Execution with Prompt," is a macOS technique where adversaries abuse the deprecated AuthorizationExecuteWithPrivileges API to prompt users for credentials, enabling execution of malicious code with root privileges without origin or integrity checks.

3688.name: Maintaining presence
3688.profile: [profile]Maintaining presence is a deprecated technique, with its functions now covered by Create Account (T1136), Web Shell (T1505.003), and External Remote Services (T1133). It involved adversaries using multiple remote access tools or credentialed services to retain network access if one mechanism was blocked. This could include deploying redundant command and control protocols, using valid accounts for external VPNs, or installing web shells on externally accessible servers to ensure persistent access. The intrusion set FIN7 has been associated with this behavior.[/profile]
3688.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Maintaining presence" is a deprecated attack pattern. Its core technique involves deploying multiple, diverse remote access tools, such as web shells or external VPN services, to ensure continuous network access if one method is discovered and blocked. This redundancy allows adversaries to retain control by using alternative command and control channels or valid accounts.

3689.name: Moving laterally
3689.profile: [profile]Moving laterally, also known as Lateral Movement (Tactic TA0008), is a post-compromise objective where adversaries pivot through a network using techniques like Pass the Hash (T1550.002). This involves using stolen password hashes to authenticate to remote systems without the plaintext password, bypassing normal access controls. The technique relies on prior credential access and is used by groups like FIN7 to expand their foothold within an environment.
3689.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Moving laterally is a technique where adversaries move within a network after initial compromise. It is often associated with the Lateral Movement tactic (TA0008) on Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. This movement is achieved by using stolen credentials or alternate authentication material, such as password hashes or Kerberos tickets, to authenticate to remote systems and bypass normal access controls, as demonstrated in techniques like Pass the Hash (T1550.002).

3690.name: Completing the mission
3690.profile: [profile]The entity "Completing the mission" is a technique used by adversaries like FIN7 to finalize an attack, often after achieving primary objectives like data theft or encryption. This phase involves actions to secure the intrusion, such as removing adversary-controlled accounts to inhibit legitimate user access and impede incident response. It is associated with the Impact tactic, targeting Windows, Linux, and potentially ESXi platforms, and involves specific commands like `Set-LocalUser` or `passwd` to lock or manipulate accounts.
3690.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Completing the mission" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the provided context, it appears to be a conceptual phase describing post-compromise actions. Related content describes adversaries performing final disruptive actions, such as using bootkits for deep persistence below the OS, establishing fallback communication channels to maintain C2, and removing account access (e.g., by deleting, locking, or changing credentials) to inhibit recovery, often as part of ransomware or destructive attacks.

3691.name: fileless malware
3691.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may store data in "fileless" formats to conceal malicious activity from defenses. Fileless storage can be broadly defined as any format other than a file. Common examples of non-volatile fileless storage in Windows systems include the Windows Registry, event logs, or WMI repository.(Citation: Microsoft Fileless)(Citation: SecureList Fileless) Shared memory directories on Linux systems (`/dev/shm`, `/run/shm`, `/var/run`, and `/var/lock`) and volatile directories on Network Devices (`/tmp` and `/volatile`) may also be considered fileless storage, as files written to these directories are mapped directly to RAM and not stored on the disk.(Citation: Elastic Binary Executed from Shared Memory Directory)(Citation: Akami Frog4Shell 2024)(Citation: Aquasec Muhstik Malware 2024)(Citation: Bitsight 7777 Botnet)(Citation: CISCO Nexus 900 Config).

Similar to fileless in-memory behaviors such as [Reflective Code Loading](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1620) and [Process Injection](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1055), fileless data storage may remain undetected by anti-virus and other endpoint security tools that can only access specific file formats from disk storage. Leveraging fileless storage may also allow adversaries to bypass the protections offered by read-only file systems in Linux.(Citation: Sysdig Fileless Malware 23022)

Adversaries may use fileless storage to conceal various types of stored data, including payloads/shellcode (potentially being used as part of [Persistence](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0003)) and collected data not yet exfiltrated from the victim (e.g., [Local Data Staging](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1074/001)). Adversaries also often encrypt, encode, splice, or otherwise obfuscate this fileless data when stored. 

Some forms of fileless storage activity may indirectly create artifacts in the file system, but in central and otherwise difficult to inspect formats such as the WMI (e.g., `%SystemRoot%\System32\Wbem\Repository`) or Registry (e.g., `%SystemRoot%\System32\Config`) physical files.(Citation: Microsoft Fileless)
3691.profile: [profile]The entity "Fileless Malware" is a technique for storing malicious data in non-file formats to evade detection, corresponding to MITRE ATT&CK ID T1027.011 under the Defense Evasion tactic, applicable to Windows, Linux, and Network Device platforms. It operates by storing payloads or staged data in memory-mapped locations like the Windows Registry, WMI repository, or Linux shared memory directories (e.g., /dev/shm), which are not written to disk, thereby bypassing traditional file-based security tools. Adversaries, including groups like APT32 and Turla, often further obfuscate this stored data. While artifacts may persist in system files like the Registry hives, the primary mechanism avoids standard file system scrutiny.[/profile]
3691.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Fileless malware is a technique where malicious code executes directly in system memory without writing files to disk, often to evade detection. It operates by loading payloads into volatile memory using methods like reflective code loading or process injection, leveraging system tools and legitimate processes for execution. This approach bypasses traditional file-based security controls and leaves minimal forensic artifacts, making it a stealthy method for initial access, execution, and persistence across Windows, Linux, and network device platforms.

3692.name: Visual Basic
3692.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may abuse Visual Basic (VB) for execution. VB is a programming language created by Microsoft with interoperability with many Windows technologies such as [Component Object Model](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1559/001) and the [Native API](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1106) through the Windows API. Although tagged as legacy with no planned future evolutions, VB is integrated and supported in the .NET Framework and cross-platform .NET Core.(Citation: VB .NET Mar 2020)(Citation: VB Microsoft)

Derivative languages based on VB have also been created, such as Visual Basic for Applications (VBA) and VBScript. VBA is an event-driven programming language built into Microsoft Office, as well as several third-party applications.(Citation: Microsoft VBA)(Citation: Wikipedia VBA) VBA enables documents to contain macros used to automate the execution of tasks and other functionality on the host. VBScript is a default scripting language on Windows hosts and can also be used in place of [JavaScript](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/007) on HTML Application (HTA) webpages served to Internet Explorer (though most modern browsers do not come with VBScript support).(Citation: Microsoft VBScript)

Adversaries may use VB payloads to execute malicious commands. Common malicious usage includes automating execution of behaviors with VBScript or embedding VBA content into [Spearphishing Attachment](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001) payloads (which may also involve [Mark-of-the-Web Bypass](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1553/005) to enable execution).(Citation: Default VBS macros Blocking )
3692.profile: [profile]Visual Basic is a Microsoft programming language used for execution, designated as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1059.005 under the Execution tactic primarily on Windows platforms. Adversaries abuse it by creating malicious payloads, commonly using VBScript to automate behaviors or embedding VBA macros into spearphishing attachments to run commands. It interoperates with Windows technologies like COM and the Native API, and its derivatives VBA and VBScript are often leveraged in malicious documents and scripts for initial access and code execution.
3692.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Visual Basic is a Microsoft programming language (MITRE ID T1059.005) used for Execution, primarily on Windows platforms. Adversaries abuse it for malicious execution via its derivatives, VBA and VBScript, to automate tasks, embed macros in spearphishing attachments, or run scripts. It interoperates with Windows technologies like COM and the Native API, and its compiled p-code can be hidden via VBA stomping to evade detection. It is also abused in living-off-the-land techniques, such as proxying execution via the PubPrn.vbs script.

3694.name: malicious Word attachments
3694.profile: [profile]Malicious Word attachments are a common malware delivery vector, used by groups like FIN7. They are frequently employed in campaigns by the Emotet malware, which is operated by groups such as Gold Cabin, Mummy Spider, and Mealybug, often in emails that may also contain benign PDF attachments to evade detection. This method is also associated with the distribution of other malware like AsyncRAT.
3694.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity 'malicious Word attachments' is a common malware delivery vector, not a distinct malware family. It is frequently used as an initial infection mechanism by established malware families such as Emotet, which has been attributed to groups including Gold Cabin, Mummy Spider, and Mealybug. The primary technical behavior involves embedding malicious macros or exploits within Microsoft Word documents, which are then distributed via email campaigns, sometimes alongside benign attachments like PDFs to evade detection. The target platform is Microsoft Windows systems via the Microsoft Office suite.

3695.name: multi-stage infection process
3695.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may create multiple stages for command and control that are employed under different conditions or for certain functions. Use of multiple stages may obfuscate the command and control channel to make detection more difficult.

Remote access tools will call back to the first-stage command and control server for instructions. The first stage may have automated capabilities to collect basic host information, update tools, and upload additional files. A second remote access tool (RAT) could be uploaded at that point to redirect the host to the second-stage command and control server. The second stage will likely be more fully featured and allow the adversary to interact with the system through a reverse shell and additional RAT features.

The different stages will likely be hosted separately with no overlapping infrastructure. The loader may also have backup first-stage callbacks or [Fallback Channels](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1008) in case the original first-stage communication path is discovered and blocked.
3695.profile: [profile]Multi-Stage Channels, also known as T1104, is a Command and Control technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework applicable to multiple platforms. It involves creating separate, non-overlapping C2 stages to obfuscate detection; a first-stage server provides automated instructions, collects host data, and can upload a second, more fully-featured Remote Access Tool (RAT) to redirect the host to a second-stage server for interactive adversary control, often incorporating fallback channels for resilience. It has been associated with groups like APT3, APT41, MuddyWater, and Lazarus Group.
3695.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Multi-Stage Infection Process is an adversary technique involving sequential execution phases to establish persistence and deliver payloads. It often begins with an initial dropper or downloader that retrieves and executes subsequent, more capable stages, such as a full remote access tool (RAT). This process can use techniques like Process Hollowing (T1055.012) to mask malicious code within legitimate processes and may involve tools like control.exe (T1218.002) to proxy execution. The multi-stage approach complicates detection by separating delivery, installation, and command-and-control functions across distinct components.

3699.name: malspam campaign
3699.profile: [profile]The entity "malspam campaign" is a malicious spam campaign, not a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique. It is associated with the intrusion set FIN7 and commonly employs the technique Spearphishing Attachment (T1193, Initial Access). This technique involves sending targeted emails with malicious attachments, such as documents or executables, that rely on user execution to deploy malware. Campaigns may use data obfuscation (T1001) to hide communications and often utilize purchased or repurposed malware (T1588.001) as their payload.[/profile]

3700.name: fake legal complaint

3702.name: JSSLoader RAT
3702.uncertain_mes: In 2020, CARBON SPIDER began conducting big game hunting (BGH) ransomware campaigns with PINCHY SPIDER’s REvil before introducing Darkside. The adversary later opened up Darkside to affiliates through a ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) program, allowing other actors to use the ransomware while paying CARBON SPIDER a portion of the received ransom.

It is delivered via phishing emails with malicious XLL or XLM Excel add-in attachments, targeting Windows platforms.

3703.name: Excel attachment
3703.profile: [profile]Excel attachment is a common initial infection vector, not a malware family itself. It is frequently used by groups like FIN7 and TA505, as well as by Gorgon Group in campaigns distributing Revenge RAT and XpertRAT. The malicious Excel files typically contain macros that download and execute secondary payloads, such as MSI files or KiXtart loaders, ultimately deploying malware like MirrorBlast onto Windows systems.
3703.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Excel attachment is a malware delivery method, not a distinct malware family itself. It is used by groups like TA505 and The Gorgon Group. The technique involves malicious Excel files, often containing macros, which download and execute secondary payloads such as MSI files or loaders like KiXtart. This method is associated with campaigns delivering malware like MirrorBlast, Revenge RAT, and XpertRAT, primarily targeting Windows systems through phishing emails.

3704.name: Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI)
3704.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may abuse Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) to execute malicious commands and payloads. WMI is designed for programmers and is the infrastructure for management data and operations on Windows systems.(Citation: WMI 1-3) WMI is an administration feature that provides a uniform environment to access Windows system components.

The WMI service enables both local and remote access, though the latter is facilitated by [Remote Services](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021) such as [Distributed Component Object Model](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/003) and [Windows Remote Management](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/006).(Citation: WMI 1-3) Remote WMI over DCOM operates using port 135, whereas WMI over WinRM operates over port 5985 when using HTTP and 5986 for HTTPS.(Citation: WMI 1-3) (Citation: Mandiant WMI)

An adversary can use WMI to interact with local and remote systems and use it as a means to execute various behaviors, such as gathering information for [Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0007) as well as [Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0002) of commands and payloads.(Citation: Mandiant WMI) For example, `wmic.exe` can be abused by an adversary to delete shadow copies with the command `wmic.exe Shadowcopy Delete` (i.e., [Inhibit System Recovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1490)).(Citation: WMI 6)

**Note:** `wmic.exe` is deprecated as of January of 2024, with the WMIC feature being “disabled by default” on Windows 11+. WMIC will be removed from subsequent Windows releases and replaced by [PowerShell](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001) as the primary WMI interface.(Citation: WMI 7,8) In addition to PowerShell and tools like `wbemtool.exe`, COM APIs can also be used to programmatically interact with WMI via C++, .NET, VBScript, etc.(Citation: WMI 7,8)
3704.profile: [profile]Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) is technique T1047 under the Execution tactic for Windows. It is a Windows administration infrastructure abused to execute commands and payloads locally or remotely, often via tools like the deprecated wmic.exe (e.g., using `wmic.exe Shadowcopy Delete`) or programmatically via PowerShell, COM APIs, or wbemtool.exe. Remote access is facilitated through DCOM on port 135 or WinRM on ports 5985/5986. It is commonly used by groups like FIN7 for discovery and execution.
3704.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1047 under the Execution tactic for Windows platforms. It is a Windows administration infrastructure abused to execute malicious commands and payloads locally and remotely, with remote access facilitated by services like DCOM (port 135) or WinRM (ports 5985/5986). Adversaries use tools like the deprecated `wmic.exe` (e.g., for commands like `wmic.exe Shadowcopy Delete`) or PowerShell to interact with WMI for execution and discovery. The technique is also leveraged for persistence via WMI Event Subscriptions (T1546.003), where compiled MOF files or scripts trigger malicious code on system events.

3705.name: Magecart
3705.profile: [profile]Magecart is a threat actor group, not a MITRE ATT&CK technique. It is associated with the intrusion-set FIN7. Magecart operations often involve techniques like Data from Cloud Storage (T1530), where they exploit misconfigured cloud storage such as publicly accessible Amazon S3 buckets to steal sensitive data like credit card information, and Credentials from Web Browsers (T1555.003/T1503), where they extract saved credentials from browser files or memory to facilitate further unauthorized access and credential reuse.
3705.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Magecart is a threat actor group, not a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique. The group is known for conducting digital skimming attacks, primarily targeting e-commerce websites to steal payment card data. Their operations often involve compromising third-party scripts or supply chain components, such as misconfigured cloud storage buckets (e.g., Amazon S3), to inject malicious JavaScript code that captures sensitive information entered by users on checkout pages. This activity is associated with techniques like Data from Cloud Storage (T1530) and Credentials from Web Browsers (T1555.003).

3707.name: Ryuk ransomware
3707.uncertain_mes: [Ryuk](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0446) is a ransomware designed to target enterprise environments that has been used in attacks since at least 2018. [Ryuk](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0446) shares code similarities with Hermes ransomware.(Citation: CrowdStrike Ryuk January 2019)(Citation: FireEye Ryuk and Trickbot January 2019)(Citation: FireEye FIN6 Apr 2019)
3707.profile: [profile]Ryuk is a ransomware targeting enterprise environments since at least 2018, sharing code similarities with Hermes ransomware. Its aliases include Ryuk. It is attributed to groups such as FIN6, Wizard Spider, Grim Spider, and UNC1878. Key technical behaviors involve persistence via registry modification (e.g., "HKEY_CURRENT_USER\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run" /v "svchos") and distribution often linked to TrickBot malware. It primarily targets Windows platforms and is associated with campaigns distributing other ransomware like Conti. Infrastructure and supplementary details note its use in targeted attacks with specific ransom notes.
3707.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Ryuk ransomware, also known as Ryuk, is a ransomware attributed to groups including FIN6, Grim Spider, UNC1878, and Wizard Spider. It is distributed by other malware like TrickBot and is linked to the later Conti ransomware. Its technical behaviors include persistence via a Windows Run registry key ("HKEY_CURRENT_USER\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run" /v "svchos") and the deployment of ransom notes. It primarily targets Windows platforms.

3708.uncertain_mes:
«Он не выходит на связь»: что известно о барнаульце, объявленном в розыск ФБР по обвинению в киберпреступлениях

3727.name: Bateleur
3727.uncertain_mes: Throughout 2020, CARBON SPIDER dramatically overhauled their operations. In April 2020, the adversary abruptly shifted from narrow campaigns focused entirely on companies operating point-of-sale (POS) devices to broad, indiscriminate operations that attempted to infect very many victims across all sectors.
3727.profile: [profile]Bateleur, also known as Carbanak, is a malware attributed to the FIN7 (CARBON SPIDER/Anunak) cybercriminal group. It operates as a backdoor and downloader, using SSL certificates for C2 beacons and communicating with command-and-control servers over HTTPS on ports like 443, with known infrastructure including IPs 195.133.48.65 and 185.154.53.65. It is associated with document droppers and the Tinymet downloader, and its campaigns have shifted from targeting point-of-sale systems to broader, indiscriminate infections across sectors.
3727.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Bateleur, also known as bateleur, is a malware attributed to the CARBON SPIDER (Anunak) group. Its key behaviors include command execution via WMI queries and PowerShell (WPowerShell Execution, APowerShell Execution), system information discovery, and establishing command and control (C2) communication over HTTPS. It uses HTTP POST requests for C2 traffic and is associated with financial data theft. The malware operates on Windows platforms, as indicated by techniques like WEXE Execution. Its infrastructure includes specific C2 servers such as 195.133.48[.]65:443 and 185.154.53[.]65:443.[/profile]

3728.name: Birddog
3728.profile: [profile]Birddog is a backdoor malware used since at least September 2017. It is attributed to the FIN7 intrusion set. Its key technical behaviors include functioning as a loader and establishing persistence by creating a registry key for automatic execution on system startup. The target platform is Windows systems. It is associated with the distribution of other malware like Carbanak.]

3730.name: Griffon
3730.uncertain_mes: [GRIFFON](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0417) is a JavaScript backdoor used by [FIN7](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0046). (Citation: SecureList Griffon May 2019)
3730.profile: [profile]Griffon, also known as GRIFFON, is a JavaScript backdoor attributed to the FIN7 cybercrime group. It establishes persistence via registry keys for automatic execution and communicates with command-and-control (C2) servers, with its infrastructure linked to a fake pentest company. The malware primarily targets Windows systems.

3731.name: Malicious Attachments
3731.profile: [profile]Malicious Attachments is a delivery mechanism used by threat groups like FIN7 and Turla. It involves distributing malware via email attachments, such as malicious Word documents, which can be accompanied by benign PDFs to evade detection, as seen with Emotet. These attachments are also distributed through platforms like Discord, where they are hosted as archive files (e.g., .rar) for download. The primary targets are typically Windows-based systems, leveraging social engineering to initiate infections.]

It is employed by groups like Gold Cabin (Mummy Spider/Mealybug) for distributing malware such as Emotet, often via emails containing both benign (e.g., PDFs) and malicious (e.g., Word documents) files. It is also utilized in campaigns like CrackedCantil, where malicious archives are hosted and distributed through channels like Discord CDN. The primary target platforms are Windows systems via user interaction with email attachments or downloaded files.

3732.name: Digital Certificates
3732.profile: [profile]Digital Certificates are a tool used by threat actors like the FIN7 intrusion set to sign malware, as seen with EternalPetya (linked to groups like Telebots and Sandworm), SolarMarker, and ClipBanker, enabling malicious code to appear legitimate and bypass security checks on target platforms.
3732.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Digital Certificates are not a malware family but a tool or resource used by malware. They can be used to sign malicious code, as seen with malware families like EternalPetya (attributed to groups like TeleBots or Sandworm) and SolarMarker, to make it appear legitimate and bypass security checks. This technique is a key TTP for enhancing malware persistence and evasion across various platforms.

3733.name: Custom Video Protocol
3733.profile: [profile]Custom Video Protocol is a custom video recording capability and protocol used by the FIN7 intrusion set. It is custom-written by FIN7 with no external library dependencies, contains Cyrillic comments in the code, and requires a bespoke video player unique to FIN7 for playback. It was recovered during multiple FIN7 intrusions and reverse-engineered by FireEye's FLARE team.

It is a bespoke protocol with no external library dependencies, contains Cyrillic comments in its code, and requires a unique video player for playback, indicating it was custom-written by the threat actor.

3734.name: Custom Video Player
3734.profile: [profile]Custom Video Player is a custom video recording capability used by the FIN7 intrusion set. It is a bespoke tool with a unique video player, contains Cyrillic comments in its code, and has no external library dependencies, indicating it was custom-written by the group.
