It is a custom-written tool with Cyrillic comments in its code and no external library dependencies. The malware is associated with the FIN7 group, also known as Anunak, and was used as part of their intrusion operations.

3735.name: Command Line Obfuscation
3735.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may obfuscate content during command execution to impede detection. Command-line obfuscation is a method of making strings and patterns within commands and scripts more difficult to signature and analyze. This type of obfuscation can be included within commands executed by delivered payloads (e.g., [Phishing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566) and [Drive-by Compromise](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1189)) or interactively via [Command and Scripting Interpreter](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059).(Citation: Akamai JS)(Citation: Malware Monday VBE) For example, adversaries may abuse syntax that utilizes various symbols and escape characters (such as spacing, `^`, `+`. `$`, and `%`) to make commands difficult to analyze while maintaining the same intended functionality.(Citation: RC PowerShell) Many languages support built-in obfuscation in the form of base64 or URL encoding.(Citation: Microsoft PowerShellB64) Adversaries may also manually implement command obfuscation via string splitting (`“Wor”+“d.Application”`), order and casing of characters (`rev <<<'dwssap/cte/ tac'`), globing (`mkdir -p '/tmp/:&$NiA'`), as well as various tricks involving passing strings through tokens/environment variables/input streams.(Citation: Bashfuscator Command Obfuscators)(Citation: FireEye Obfuscation June 2017) Adversaries may also use tricks such as directory traversals to obfuscate references to the binary being invoked by a command (`C:\voi\pcw\..\..\Windows\tei\qs\k\..\..\..\system32\erool\..\wbem\wg\je\..\..\wmic.exe shadowcopy delete`).(Citation: Twitter Richard WMIC) Tools such as Invoke-Obfuscation and Invoke-DOSfucation have also been used to obfuscate commands.(Citation: Invoke-DOSfuscation)(Citation: Invoke-Obfuscation)
3735.profile: [profile]Command Line Obfuscation, designated T1027.010 under the Defense Evasion tactic, is a technique used across multiple platforms to impede detection by making command strings and patterns difficult to signature and analyze. Adversaries achieve this by abusing syntax with symbols and escape characters (e.g., ^, +, $, %), employing built-in encoding like base64 or URL encoding, and manually implementing methods such as string splitting, character order/casing manipulation, globing, and directory traversals. Tools like Invoke-Obfuscation and Invoke-DOSfucation are also utilized, and the technique is associated with numerous threat groups including FIN7, MuddyWater, and Wizard Spider.
3735.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Command Line Obfuscation, identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1027.010, is a Defense Evasion technique applicable to multiple platforms. It involves manipulating command strings and scripts to hinder signature-based detection and analysis. Specific technical mechanics include using symbols and escape characters (e.g., `^`, `+`, `$`, `%`), string splitting (e.g., `"Wor"+"d.Application"`), character reordering and casing, globing, and directory traversals to hide binary paths. Built-in language features like Base64 or URL encoding are also abused, and dedicated tools like Invoke-Obfuscation are employed. This obfuscation is used in payload execution or interactively via command interpreters.

3736.name: File System Path Artifacts
3736.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may attempt to hide their file-based artifacts by writing them to specific folders or file names excluded from antivirus (AV) scanning and other defensive capabilities. AV and other file-based scanners often include exclusions to optimize performance as well as ease installation and legitimate use of applications. These exclusions may be contextual (e.g., scans are only initiated in response to specific triggering events/alerts), but are also often hardcoded strings referencing specific folders and/or files assumed to be trusted and legitimate.(Citation: Microsoft File Folder Exclusions)

Adversaries may abuse these exclusions to hide their file-based artifacts. For example, rather than  tampering with tool settings to add a new exclusion (i.e., [Disable or Modify Tools](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1562/001)), adversaries may drop their file-based payloads in default or otherwise well-known exclusions. Adversaries may also use [Security Software Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1518/001) and other [Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0007)/[Reconnaissance](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0043) activities to both discover and verify existing exclusions in a victim environment.
3736.profile: [profile]File System Path Artifacts (T1564.012) is a Defense Evasion technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves adversaries hiding malicious files by placing them in folders or using file names that are excluded from antivirus scanning, such as default or well-known hardcoded exclusions. This method avoids the need to modify security tool settings directly. The technique is associated with groups like Turla and FIN7, and related behaviors include using Security Software Discovery to identify existing exclusions and Relocate Malware to move payloads into these excluded paths.[/profile]
3736.profile_without_enhance: [profile]File System Path Artifacts is a sub-technique of Hide Artifacts (T1564) under the Defense Evasion tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It involves adversaries placing malicious files or directories in specific file system locations that are excluded from security scans, such as default antivirus exclusions or trusted system folders, to avoid detection. This method leverages known path weaknesses or exclusions rather than modifying tool configurations directly.

3737.name: Rapid Technique Turnaround
3737.profile: [profile]Rapid Technique Turnaround is a tactic used by adversaries like FIN7 to frequently change their attack methods, including command and control protocols and malware signatures, to evade detection. This involves techniques such as splitting communications across different protocols (T1026), using shell commands like `source` to execute files (T1153), and adding junk data to network traffic (T1001.001) to obscure malicious activity and bypass security measures.
3737.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Rapid Technique Turnaround is a tactic where adversaries quickly modify their attack methods, such as splitting command and control across different protocols like multiband communication (T1026) or obfuscating traffic with junk data (T1001.001), to bypass defenses and avoid detection. This approach allows for the evasion of security measures like firewalls and data threshold alerts by constantly altering the technical execution of attacks.

3738.name: OLE Embedding
3738.profile: [profile]OLE Embedding is a technique within the broader T1559.002 (Dynamic Data Exchange) for initial access and execution. It operates on the Windows platform, primarily under the Execution tactic. This method involves embedding malicious Dynamic Data Exchange (DDE) commands or formulas within Microsoft Office documents (like Word or Excel) or CSV files. When a victim opens the poisoned document, it can execute arbitrary commands to download or run payloads without requiring Visual Basic for Applications (VBA) macros, providing an alternative delivery vector in phishing campaigns. The intrusion-set FIN7 has been associated with using related DDE techniques.[/profile]
3738.profile_without_enhance: [profile]OLE Embedding is a technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, specifically T1559.002, falling under the Execution tactic and applicable to the Windows platform. It involves embedding malicious content or scripts within Object Linking and Embedding (OLE) objects in documents, such as Microsoft Office files, to execute arbitrary commands when the document is opened. This method can be used to bypass security controls that block macros, often delivered via phishing campaigns.

3739.name: System Information Discovery
3739.uncertain_mes: An adversary may attempt to get detailed information about the operating system and hardware, including version, patches, hotfixes, service packs, and architecture. Adversaries may use this information to shape follow-on behaviors, including whether or not the adversary fully infects the target and/or attempts specific actions. This behavior is distinct from [Local Storage Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1680) which is an adversary's discovery of local drive, disks and/or volumes. Tools such as [Systeminfo](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0096) can be used to gather detailed system information. If running with privileged access, a breakdown of system data can be gathered through the systemsetup configuration tool on macOS. Adversaries may leverage a [Network Device CLI](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/008) on network devices to gather detailed system information (e.g. show version).(Citation: US-CERT-TA18-106A) On ESXi servers, threat actors may gather system information from various esxcli utilities, such as `system hostname get` and `system version get`.(Citation: Crowdstrike Hypervisor Jackpotting Pt 2 2021)(Citation: Varonis) Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) cloud providers such as AWS, GCP, and Azure allow access to instance and virtual machine information via APIs. Successful authenticated API calls can return data such as the operating system platform and status of a particular instance or the model view of a virtual machine.(Citation: Amazon Describe Instance)(Citation: Google Instances Resource)(Citation: Microsoft Virutal Machine API) [System Information Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1082) combined with information gathered from other forms of discovery and reconnaissance can drive payload development and concealment.(Citation: OSX.FairyTale)(Citation: 20 macOS Common Tools and Techniques)
3739.profile: [profile]System Information Discovery, identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1082 under the Discovery tactic, operates across Windows, macOS, Linux, Network, and IaaS platforms. Adversaries gather detailed OS and hardware data, including version and architecture, using tools like the `systeminfo` command on Windows, the `systemsetup` tool on macOS, CLI commands such as `show version` on network devices, and `esxcli` utilities on ESXi servers. In cloud environments, they leverage provider APIs to query instance metadata. This information is used to tailor follow-on attack actions and payloads, with groups like FIN7, Lazarus, and MuddyWater employing this technique.[/profile]
3739.profile_without_enhance: [profile]System Information Discovery is the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1082 under the Discovery tactic, applicable to Windows, macOS, Linux, and cloud platforms. It involves adversaries gathering detailed OS and hardware data like version, patches, and architecture to inform follow-on actions. Specific mechanics include using the `systeminfo` command on Windows, the `systemsetup` tool on macOS with privileges, CLI commands like `show version` on network devices, and `esxcli` utilities on ESXi servers. In cloud environments, authenticated API calls to services like AWS, GCP, or Azure can retrieve instance metadata.

3740.name: WMI Queries
3740.profile: [profile]The entity "WMI Queries" is a technique for Discovery and Execution, identified as T1047 within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, targeting the Windows platform. It involves adversaries abusing Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) to interact with local and remote systems, using tools like the now-deprecated `wmic.exe` or PowerShell to execute commands and gather system information. For instance, the command `wmic.exe Shadowcopy Delete` can be used to inhibit system recovery. This technique is employed by groups like FIN7, which uses associated malware such as Halfbaked and Bateleur.
3740.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "WMI Queries" is an attack pattern within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, identified as T1047, under the Execution tactic and applicable to the Windows platform. It involves adversaries abusing Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) to execute malicious commands and payloads for discovery and execution. This can be performed locally or remotely via services like DCOM or WinRM, using tools such as the deprecated `wmic.exe` (e.g., for commands like `wmic.exe Shadowcopy Delete`) or programmatically through PowerShell and COM APIs. The technique is widely used by numerous threat groups, including APT29, Lazarus Group, and MuddyWater, for various malicious behaviors.

3741.name: Financial Data Theft
3741.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may steal monetary resources from targets through extortion, social engineering, technical theft, or other methods aimed at their own financial gain at the expense of the availability of these resources for victims. Financial theft is the ultimate objective of several popular campaign types including extortion by ransomware,(Citation: FBI-ransomware) business email compromise (BEC) and fraud,(Citation: FBI-BEC) "pig butchering,"(Citation: wired-pig butchering) bank hacking,(Citation: DOJ-DPRK Heist) and exploiting cryptocurrency networks.(Citation: BBC-Ronin) 

Adversaries may [Compromise Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1586) to conduct unauthorized transfers of funds.(Citation: Internet crime report 2022) In the case of business email compromise or email fraud, an adversary may utilize [Impersonation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1656) of a trusted entity. Once the social engineering is successful, victims can be deceived into sending money to financial accounts controlled by an adversary.(Citation: FBI-BEC) This creates the potential for multiple victims (i.e., compromised accounts as well as the ultimate monetary loss) in incidents involving financial theft.(Citation: VEC)

Extortion by ransomware may occur, for example, when an adversary demands payment from a victim after [Data Encrypted for Impact](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1486) (Citation: NYT-Colonial) and [Exfiltration](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0010) of data, followed by threatening to leak sensitive data to the public unless payment is made to the adversary.(Citation: Mandiant-leaks) Adversaries may use dedicated leak sites to distribute victim data.(Citation: Crowdstrike-leaks)

Due to the potentially immense business impact of financial theft, an adversary may abuse the possibility of financial theft and seeking monetary gain to divert attention from their true goals such as [Data Destruction](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1485) and business disruption.(Citation: AP-NotPetya)
3741.profile: [profile]Financial Data Theft, also known as financial theft (T1657), is an adversary objective within the Impact tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. It involves stealing monetary resources through methods like extortion via ransomware, business email compromise (BEC) fraud, and cryptocurrency exploitation. Technical execution often relies on preceding techniques such as compromising accounts for unauthorized fund transfers, using impersonation in social engineering, and employing data encryption and exfiltration for ransom demands. Associated groups include FIN13, Scattered Spider, and INC Ransom, with linked malware like Halfbaked and Bateleur.
3741.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Financial Data Theft is a technique for the Impact tactic, targeting financial data. It involves stealing sensitive financial information, such as bank account details, credit card numbers, or transaction records, often as a precursor to or component of financial fraud or extortion. This can be achieved through methods like compromising accounts to access data, exfiltrating it over command and control channels, or staging collected data prior to theft.

Key TTPs/Technical Behaviors: Targets Point-of-Sale (PoS) systems, as indicated by related malware families like BlackPOS and Alina POS which are identified in PoS compromises. Infrastructure/Supplementary Info: The malware's evolution and continued activity, such as Alina POS lingering in DNS infrastructure, are noted in related threat reporting.

3774.name: PowerSource
3774.uncertain_mes: [POWERSOURCE](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0145) is a PowerShell backdoor that is a heavily obfuscated and modified version of the publicly available tool DNS_TXT_Pwnage. It was observed in February 2017 in spearphishing campaigns against personnel involved with United States Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) filings at various organizations. The malware was delivered when macros were enabled by the victim and a VBS script was dropped. (Citation: FireEye FIN7 March 2017) (Citation: Cisco DNSMessenger March 2017)
3774.profile: [profile]PowerSource, also known as POWERSOURCE, is a heavily obfuscated PowerShell backdoor based on the public tool DNS_TXT_Pwnage. It is attributed to the FIN7 group. It was delivered via malicious macros and VBS scripts in spearphishing campaigns targeting U.S. SEC-related personnel in February 2017. Its key behaviors include using DNS TXT queries for command-and-control and operating alongside the TEXTMATE backdoor. It primarily targets Windows platforms.
3774.profile_without_enhance: [profile]PowerSource is a malware, also known as a modified version of the public tool DNS_TXT_Pwnage. It is attributed to the groups FIN7 and Anunak. Its key technical behaviors include using DNS TXT records for command and control communication and employing Registry Manipulation and Alternate Data Streams on Windows platforms for defense evasion and persistence. It has been observed operating alongside the second-stage PowerShell backdoor TEXTMATE.

3775.profile: [profile]Carbanak Malware, also known as nmass malware, is a .NET-based remote access trojan (RAT) attributed to the FIN7 intrusion set. Its key technical behaviors include using a decoy document (Royal Road v7) to install a backdoor, dropping an initial executable (e.g., \os03C2.tmp), and employing Cobalt Strike for post-breach activity. 3775.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Carbanak Malware, also known as Carbanak Backdoor, is attributed to the FIN7 (Anunak) cybercriminal group. It is a .NET-based backdoor that targets Windows systems and is known to be deployed via malicious documents, often as a follow-up to other malware like Cobalt Strike or tools such as Bateleur and Tinymet downloader.

3778.name: Registry Manipulation
3778.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may interact with the Windows Registry as part of a variety of other techniques to aid in defense evasion, persistence, and execution.

Access to specific areas of the Registry depends on account permissions, with some keys requiring administrator-level access. The built-in Windows command-line utility [Reg](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0075) may be used for local or remote Registry modification.(Citation: Microsoft Reg) Other tools, such as remote access tools, may also contain functionality to interact with the Registry through the Windows API.

The Registry may be modified in order to hide configuration information or malicious payloads via [Obfuscated Files or Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027).(Citation: Unit42 BabyShark Feb 2019)(Citation: Avaddon Ransomware 2021)(Citation: Microsoft BlackCat Jun 2022)(Citation: CISA Russian Gov Critical Infra 2018) The Registry may also be modified to [Impair Defenses](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1562), such as by enabling macros for all Microsoft Office products, allowing privilege escalation without alerting the user, increasing the maximum number of allowed outbound requests, and/or modifying systems to store plaintext credentials in memory.(Citation: CISA LockBit 2023)(Citation: Unit42 BabyShark Feb 2019)

The Registry of a remote system may be modified to aid in execution of files as part of lateral movement. It requires the remote Registry service to be running on the target system.(Citation: Microsoft Remote) Often [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078) are required, along with access to the remote system's [SMB/Windows Admin Shares](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002) for RPC communication.

Finally, Registry modifications may also include actions to hide keys, such as prepending key names with a null character, which will cause an error and/or be ignored when read via [Reg](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0075) or other utilities using the Win32 API.(Citation: Microsoft Reghide NOV 2006) Adversaries may abuse these pseudo-hidden keys to conceal payloads/commands used to maintain persistence.(Citation: TrendMicro POWELIKS AUG 2014)(Citation: SpectorOps Hiding Reg Jul 2017)
3778.profile: [profile]Registry Manipulation, identified as T1112, is a Defense Evasion, Persistence, and Execution technique for Windows. It involves modifying the Windows Registry using tools like the built-in Reg utility or remote access tools to hide configuration/payloads, impair defenses, or enable lateral movement. Specific mechanics include prepending registry key names with a null character to create pseudo-hidden keys for concealing persistence mechanisms. It is associated with groups like Turla and malware like Pillowmint.[/profile]
3778.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Registry Manipulation, identified as T1112, is a defense evasion, persistence, and execution technique primarily for Windows platforms. It involves adversaries using tools like the built-in Reg utility or remote access software to modify Windows Registry keys and values. This can be done to hide configuration data or payloads, impair defenses by altering security settings, enable remote execution during lateral movement, or conceal persistence mechanisms by creating pseudo-hidden registry keys.

3779.name: Alternate Data Streams
3779.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may use alternate authentication material, such as password hashes, Kerberos tickets, and application access tokens, in order to move laterally within an environment and bypass normal system access controls. 

Authentication processes generally require a valid identity (e.g., username) along with one or more authentication factors (e.g., password, pin, physical smart card, token generator, etc.). Alternate authentication material is legitimately generated by systems after a user or application successfully authenticates by providing a valid identity and the required authentication factor(s). Alternate authentication material may also be generated during the identity creation process.(Citation: NIST Authentication)(Citation: NIST MFA)

Caching alternate authentication material allows the system to verify an identity has successfully authenticated without asking the user to reenter authentication factor(s). Because the alternate authentication must be maintained by the system—either in memory or on disk—it may be at risk of being stolen through [Credential Access](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0006) techniques. By stealing alternate authentication material, adversaries are able to bypass system access controls and authenticate to systems without knowing the plaintext password or any additional authentication factors.
3779.profile: [profile]The entity "Alternate Data Streams" (ADS) is a sub-technique of NTFS File Attributes (T1096) and a method for Hide Artifacts (T1564.004) within the Defense Evasion tactic. It operates on the Windows platform by exploiting the NTFS file system's ability to store arbitrary data or complete files within additional, often hidden, Data attributes of a Master File Table (MFT) entry. This allows adversaries to conceal malicious payloads, evading detection by static scanning tools and antivirus software. The malware PowerSource has been associated with this technique.
3779.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Alternate Data Streams is a sub-technique of NTFS File Attributes (T1564.004) within the Defense Evasion tactic. It operates on Windows platforms by exploiting the NTFS file system's ability to store multiple data attributes within a single Master File Table (MFT) entry. Adversaries use this feature to hide malicious payloads, scripts, or complete files within the metadata of a legitimate file, evading detection by static analysis tools and antivirus software that may not scan these alternate streams.

3780.name: Fileless Malware
3780.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may store data in "fileless" formats to conceal malicious activity from defenses. Fileless storage can be broadly defined as any format other than a file. Common examples of non-volatile fileless storage in Windows systems include the Windows Registry, event logs, or WMI repository.(Citation: Microsoft Fileless)(Citation: SecureList Fileless) Shared memory directories on Linux systems (`/dev/shm`, `/run/shm`, `/var/run`, and `/var/lock`) and volatile directories on Network Devices (`/tmp` and `/volatile`) may also be considered fileless storage, as files written to these directories are mapped directly to RAM and not stored on the disk.(Citation: Elastic Binary Executed from Shared Memory Directory)(Citation: Akami Frog4Shell 2024)(Citation: Aquasec Muhstik Malware 2024)(Citation: Bitsight 7777 Botnet)(Citation: CISCO Nexus 900 Config).

Similar to fileless in-memory behaviors such as [Reflective Code Loading](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1620) and [Process Injection](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1055), fileless data storage may remain undetected by anti-virus and other endpoint security tools that can only access specific file formats from disk storage. Leveraging fileless storage may also allow adversaries to bypass the protections offered by read-only file systems in Linux.(Citation: Sysdig Fileless Malware 23022)

Adversaries may use fileless storage to conceal various types of stored data, including payloads/shellcode (potentially being used as part of [Persistence](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0003)) and collected data not yet exfiltrated from the victim (e.g., [Local Data Staging](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1074/001)). Adversaries also often encrypt, encode, splice, or otherwise obfuscate this fileless data when stored. 

Some forms of fileless storage activity may indirectly create artifacts in the file system, but in central and otherwise difficult to inspect formats such as the WMI (e.g., `%SystemRoot%\System32\Wbem\Repository`) or Registry (e.g., `%SystemRoot%\System32\Config`) physical files.(Citation: Microsoft Fileless)
3780.profile: [profile]Fileless Malware, corresponding to MITRE ATT&CK technique T1027.011 (Obfuscated Files or Information: Fileless Storage), operates under the Defense Evasion tactic on Windows, Linux, and Network Device platforms. It conceals malicious data by storing it in non-file system locations like the Windows Registry, WMI repository, event logs, or Linux shared memory directories (/dev/shm), mapping data directly to RAM to avoid disk-based detection tools. This technique is used to hide payloads, shellcode, or staged data, often with additional obfuscation, and is associated with groups like APT32 and Turla.[/profile]
3780.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Fileless Malware is a technique where adversaries execute malicious code directly in memory without writing files to disk, often to evade detection. It aligns with the Defense Evasion tactic and operates across multiple platforms. Technical mechanics involve leveraging legitimate system processes and scripting environments like PowerShell or Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) to load and run payloads, utilizing methods such as reflective code loading or process injection to execute from memory, registry, or event logs. This approach avoids traditional file-based indicators, making detection by standard antivirus tools more difficult.

3781.name: Reverse Shell
3781.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may backdoor web servers with web shells to establish persistent access to systems. A Web shell is a Web script that is placed on an openly accessible Web server to allow an adversary to access the Web server as a gateway into a network. A Web shell may provide a set of functions to execute or a command-line interface on the system that hosts the Web server.(Citation: volexity_0day_sophos_FW)

In addition to a server-side script, a Web shell may have a client interface program that is used to talk to the Web server (e.g. [China Chopper](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0020) Web shell client).(Citation: Lee 2013)
3781.profile: [profile]Reverse Shell is a technique for establishing persistent remote access, not a standard MITRE ATT&CK ID. It operates by creating a connection from a compromised host back to an adversary-controlled server, providing a command-line interface for control. This method is commonly used for command and control and is associated with groups like FIN7 and malware like Carbanak. It is distinct from a web shell, which is a script placed on a web server (T1505.003).[/profile]
3781.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Reverse Shell is a technique for establishing command and control where a compromised host initiates an outbound connection to an adversary's listener, providing interactive access. It is commonly used as a second-stage payload following initial compromise, such as through a web shell, to create a more fully-featured interactive command-line interface for the adversary on the victim system. This method allows adversaries to bypass inbound firewall restrictions and maintain persistent access.

3782.name: DNS TXT Queries
3782.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may communicate using the Domain Name System (DNS) application layer protocol to avoid detection/network filtering by blending in with existing traffic. Commands to the remote system, and often the results of those commands, will be embedded within the protocol traffic between the client and server. 

The DNS protocol serves an administrative function in computer networking and thus may be very common in environments. DNS traffic may also be allowed even before network authentication is completed. DNS packets contain many fields and headers in which data can be concealed. Often known as DNS tunneling, adversaries may abuse DNS to communicate with systems under their control within a victim network while also mimicking normal, expected traffic.(Citation: PAN DNS Tunneling)(Citation: Medium DnsTunneling)

DNS beaconing may be used to send commands to remote systems via DNS queries. A DNS beacon is created by tunneling DNS traffic (i.e. [Protocol Tunneling](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1572)). The commands may be embedded into different DNS records, for example, TXT or A records.(Citation: OilRig Uses Updated BONDUPDATER to Target Middle Eastern Government) DNS beacons may be difficult to detect because the beacons infrequently communicate with infected devices.(Citation: DNS Beacons) Infrequent communication conceals the malicious DNS traffic with normal DNS traffic.
3782.profile: [profile]DNS TXT Queries is a sub-technique with ID T1071.004 under the Application Layer Protocol tactic, used for Command and Control across multiple platforms. It specifically involves embedding commands and exfiltrated data within DNS TXT record queries and responses to blend with normal administrative traffic, a method known as DNS tunneling. This technique is employed by groups like FIN7 and OilRig to bypass network filtering and detection by leveraging the common and often pre-authenticated nature of DNS traffic.[/profile]
3782.profile_without_enhance: [profile]DNS TXT Queries is a reconnaissance technique where adversaries query DNS TXT records to gather information about a target. This information can reveal details about third-party cloud and SaaS providers like Office 365 or G Suite, which aids in further targeting. The technique is part of the broader Tactic of Reconnaissance and is applicable across various platforms. It involves actively querying nameservers or searching passive DNS repositories to extract these specific record types.

3783.name: VBScript
3783.profile: [profile]VBScript is a scripting language used by threat actors like DeepPanda and FIN7 to deliver malware payloads such as Pony, AsyncRAT, and Venom RAT, often associated with groups like Cobalt, primarily targeting Windows systems through malicious script files.
3783.profile_without_enhance: [profile]VBScript is a scripting language used as a component or delivery vector by multiple malware families, including Pony, AsyncRAT, and Venom RAT, with Pony being associated with the Cobalt group. Its key technical behavior involves being embedded within malicious PDF documents to execute payloads, as evidenced by specific file hashes. The primary target platform is Windows systems, leveraging the native Windows Script Host environment for execution.[/profile]

3784.name: Cobalt Strike Stager
3784.uncertain_mes:
[Cobalt Strike](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0154) is a commercial, full-featured, remote access tool that bills itself as “adversary simulation software designed to execute targeted attacks and emulate the post-exploitation actions of advanced threat actors”. Cobalt Strike’s interactive post-exploit capabilities cover the full range of ATT&CK tactics, all executed within a single, integrated system.(Citation: cobaltstrike manual)

In addition to its own capabilities, [Cobalt Strike](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0154) leverages the capabilities of other well-known tools such as Metasploit and [Mimikatz](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0002).(Citation: cobaltstrike manual)
3784.profile: [profile]Cobalt Strike Stager, also known as cobalt strike, is a commercial remote access tool used for adversary simulation and post-exploitation. It is leveraged by numerous threat groups including FIN7, APT29, APT32, APT41, Wizard Spider (linked to Conti), TA505, and Silence Group. Its key behaviors involve executing a stager via encoded PowerShell commands to establish in-memory command-and-control (C2) and it integrates capabilities from tools like Metasploit and Mimikatz for broad post-exploitation activities across ATT&CK tactics. The tool targets Windows platforms and is associated with infrastructure used by various criminal and advanced persistent threat actors.
3784.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Cobalt Strike Stager, also known as a Cobalt Strike payload, is a component of the Cobalt Strike commercial penetration testing framework that has been widely adopted by threat actors. It is associated with numerous groups including APT29, APT32, APT41, FIN6, FIN7, Wizard Spider (linked to Conti), Pinchy Spider (linked to REvil), Silence Group, and TA505. Its key technical behavior involves in-memory execution, often deployed via encoded PowerShell commands to establish command-and-control (C2) communication. It primarily targets Windows platforms and is utilized as part of broader intrusion toolkits and ransomware operations.

3785.name: Securities Fraud
3785.profile: [profile]Securities Fraud is a financial crime technique where adversaries manipulate financial markets or securities for illicit gain. It is associated with the intrusion set FIN7. The technique involves actions like compromising software or hardware supply chains (T1195.002/T1195.003) to introduce malicious code into products, enabling subsequent fraud. Adversaries may also use related fraud methods like SMS pumping (T1496.003) to generate revenue or overwhelm systems. The core mechanics involve deception, such as spreading false information or conducting fraudulent trades, to artificially influence security prices or investor behavior for profit.
3785.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Securities Fraud" is not a standard technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework. Based on the provided context, it is not defined with a specific ID, Tactic, or Platform. The retrieved information describes unrelated techniques such as SMS Pumping (T1496.003), Compromise Software Supply Chain (T1195.002), and Compromise Hardware Supply Chain (T1195.003), which do not provide specific technical mechanics for securities fraud. Therefore, no distinct technical profile can be constructed from the given data.

3786.name: Fraudulent Bank Transactions
3786.profile: [profile]Fraudulent Bank Transactions is a technique where adversaries manipulate online banking sessions to steal funds, often by compromising accounts or using social engineering like business email compromise (BEC) to deceive victims into transferring money. The FIN7 group has been associated with related methods, such as using input injection to simulate keystrokes that inject malicious JavaScript into banking websites, altering transaction details like account numbers in real-time during a user's session. This activity aligns with the financial theft objective.[/profile]
3786.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Fraudulent Bank Transactions" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the provided context, it is a specific objective or method within financial theft campaigns. It can involve adversaries using techniques like Input Injection (T1674) to manipulate a victim's browser, such as by simulating keystrokes to inject malicious JavaScript that alters transaction details like bank account numbers during online banking sessions. This activity is typically associated with financially motivated threat groups like FIN7.

3787.name: ATM Compromises
3787.profile: [profile]ATM Compromises is a technique where adversaries physically or remotely tamper with Automated Teller Machines to steal cash or card data, often involving malware installation or network intrusion. The financially motivated group FIN7 has been associated with this activity. The core mechanic is the compromise of a specialized hardware system for financial gain, distinct from software supply chain or cloud command techniques.
3787.profile_without_enhance: [profile]ATM Compromises is a technique where adversaries physically or electronically manipulate Automated Teller Machines to steal cash or card data. This attack pattern involves tactics like Impact and Financial Theft, targeting the physical hardware and embedded systems of ATMs. Technical mechanics include using malware to control the cash dispenser, connecting skimming devices to card readers, or exploiting network or USB ports to issue unauthorized commands.

3789.name: Lizar/Tirion
3789.uncertain_mes: [Lizar](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0681) is a modular remote access tool written using the .NET Framework that shares structural similarities to [Carbanak](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0030). It has likely been used by [FIN7](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0046) since at least February 2021.(Citation: BiZone Lizar May 2021)(Citation: Threatpost Lizar May 2021)(Citation: Gemini FIN7 Oct 2021)
3789.profile: [profile]Lizar, also known as Tirion, is a modular .NET remote access tool structurally similar to Carbanak and is attributed to the FIN7 group, with use observed since at least February 2021. It is distributed disguised as a legitimate cybersecurity pentesting tool for Windows networks, facilitating reconnaissance and establishing a foothold in infected systems. Its key behaviors include being part of the FIN7 arsenal alongside Carbanak, and it specifically targets Windows platforms.
3789.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The malware is known as Lizar, with the alias Tirion. It is attributed to the FIN7 cybercriminal group. This modular remote access tool is written in .NET and shares structural similarities with Carbanak. It is used for reconnaissance and gaining a foothold in infected systems, often disguised as a legitimate pentesting tool for Windows networks.

3790.profile_without_enhance: [profile]REvil, also known as Sodinokibi, is a ransomware entity. It is attributed to the cybercriminal group Pinchy Spider. 3791.name: Ryuk
3791.uncertain_mes: [Ryuk](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0446) is a ransomware designed to target enterprise environments that has been used in attacks since at least 2018. [Ryuk](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0446) shares code similarities with Hermes ransomware.(Citation: CrowdStrike Ryuk January 2019)(Citation: FireEye Ryuk and Trickbot January 2019)(Citation: FireEye FIN6 Apr 2019)
3791.profile: [profile]Ryuk is a ransomware targeting enterprise environments, active since at least 2018 and sharing code similarities with Hermes ransomware. It is attributed to groups including FIN6, Wizard Spider, Grim Spider, and UNC1878. Key technical behaviors involve using tools like AdFind for Active Directory reconnaissance, exfiltrating data such as user and computer lists to temporary directories (e.g., %TEMP%\ryuk\af\), and leveraging infrastructure like TrickBot for distribution. It primarily targets Windows platforms and is linked to campaigns involving Conti ransomware affiliates.
3791.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Ryuk is a ransomware attributed to groups such as FIN6, Grim Spider, UNC1878, and Wizard Spider. It is often distributed by the TrickBot malware and is linked to the later Conti ransomware. Key technical behaviors include using the AdFind tool for Active Directory reconnaissance, extracting user and computer lists, trust relationships, and domain information to %TEMP%\\ryuk\\af\\ directories, and downloading the tool via curl. It primarily targets Windows environments.
