3803.name: Exploiting Point-of-Sale Systems
3803.profile: [profile]The entity "Exploiting Point-of-Sale Systems" is a technique for initial access and execution, targeting the Windows platform within the Initial Access tactic. It involves compromising POS systems, often through memory-scraping malware to capture payment card data from system RAM, and is notably used by the intrusion set FIN7 for financial theft.
3803.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Exploiting Point-of-Sale Systems" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the provided context, it describes a method of compromising POS systems, likely for initial access or to execute malicious code. This activity is often associated with financially motivated threat groups targeting retail environments to steal payment card data. The technical mechanics involve exploiting vulnerabilities or misconfigurations in POS software or hardware to deploy malware or skimmers that intercept transaction data.

3804.name: Ransomware Attacks
3804.profile: [profile]Ransomware Attacks are a form of Data Encrypted for Impact (T1486) under the Impact tactic, targeting multiple platforms. The technique involves encrypting files, disk partitions, or virtual machines to render data inaccessible, demanding a ransom for decryption. Attackers may use worm-like propagation via techniques like Valid Accounts and SMB shares, and often employ preparatory actions such as Account Access Removal (T1531) to hinder recovery. Groups like FIN7 are known to use this method for financial theft (T1657).[/profile]
3804.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Ransomware Attacks is a broad category of attack patterns, not a single MITRE ATT&CK technique. It primarily aligns with the Impact tactic and involves encrypting data on target systems to render it inaccessible, demanding a ransom for decryption. Technical mechanics include encrypting common user files (Office documents, PDFs, images), critical system files, disk partitions, the MBR, and virtual machines on hypervisors like ESXi. Attackers may use worm-like propagation via techniques like Valid Accounts and SMB shares, and employ preparatory actions such as File and Directory Permissions Modification or Account Access Removal to hinder recovery before encryption.

3805.name: POS system infections
3805.profile: [profile]POS system infections is a technique used by adversaries like FIN7 to compromise Point-of-Sale environments. The primary tactic is Initial Access, though it may also involve Execution and Persistence. This technique typically targets Windows platforms. Adversaries achieve infection by delivering malicious payloads to shared network directories, tainting legitimate files to propagate malware when accessed by POS terminals. This lateral movement method can lead to broad system compromise and data theft, such as payment card information.
3805.profile_without_enhance: [profile]POS system infections target Point-of-Sale environments to steal payment card data. This technique, which can be mapped to the MITRE ATT&CK tactic of Credential Access, involves compromising the specialized software or hardware of retail systems. Adversaries achieve this by deploying memory-scraping malware to capture card details from process memory during transactions, often using techniques like binary infections or tainted shared content on network drives to spread the malware laterally across the retail network.

3806.name: Disinformation Tactics
3806.profile: [profile]Disinformation Tactics is a technique used by adversaries to manipulate information, often linked to groups like FIN7. It involves spreading false or misleading content to deceive targets, influence public opinion, or disrupt operations. This tactic can be employed across various platforms to achieve objectives such as undermining trust or enabling further malicious activities.
3806.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Disinformation Tactics is an attack-pattern. It is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the provided context, adversaries may add junk data, such as random or meaningless characters appended, prepended, or inserted between significant characters, to command and control traffic to hinder detection and analysis. This specific behavior is formally defined as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1001.001: Data Obfuscation - Junk Data.

3807.name: Website Phishing
3807.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may send phishing messages to gain access to victim systems. All forms of phishing are electronically delivered social engineering. Phishing can be targeted, known as spearphishing. In spearphishing, a specific individual, company, or industry will be targeted by the adversary. More generally, adversaries can conduct non-targeted phishing, such as in mass malware spam campaigns.

Adversaries may send victims emails containing malicious attachments or links, typically to execute malicious code on victim systems. Phishing may also be conducted via third-party services, like social media platforms. Phishing may also involve social engineering techniques, such as posing as a trusted source, as well as evasive techniques such as removing or manipulating emails or metadata/headers from compromised accounts being abused to send messages (e.g., [Email Hiding Rules](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1564/008)).(Citation: Microsoft OAuth Spam 2022)(Citation: Palo Alto Unit 42 VBA Infostealer 2014) Another way to accomplish this is by [Email Spoofing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1672)(Citation: Proofpoint-spoof) the identity of the sender, which can be used to fool both the human recipient as well as automated security tools,(Citation: cyberproof-double-bounce) or by including the intended target as a party to an existing email thread that includes malicious files or links (i.e., "thread hijacking").(Citation: phishing-krebs)

Victims may also receive phishing messages that instruct them to call a phone number where they are directed to visit a malicious URL, download malware,(Citation: sygnia Luna Month)(Citation: CISA Remote Monitoring and Management Software) or install adversary-accessible remote management tools onto their computer (i.e., [User Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204)).(Citation: Unit42 Luna Moth)
3807.profile: [profile]Website Phishing, also known as Phishing (T1566), is an Initial Access technique primarily used on Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves sending electronic messages, such as emails with malicious attachments or links, to trick victims into executing code or revealing credentials. Techniques include spearphishing for specific targets, using social engineering to pose as trusted sources, and employing evasive tactics like email spoofing or thread hijacking. Groups like FIN7 have been associated with this method.
3807.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Website Phishing" is a technique where adversaries create fraudulent websites to deceive victims into divulging sensitive information, such as credentials. It is a specific form of phishing, often delivered via malicious links in spearphishing emails (T1566.002) or used for information gathering (T1598). The technique involves cloning legitimate login portals, using obfuscated URLs, and may employ adversary-in-the-middle tools like EvilProxy to steal session cookies and bypass multi-factor authentication. It primarily targets user credentials through social engineering and web-based deception.

3808.name: Phishing Lure: Recruitment
3808.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may send phishing messages to gain access to victim systems. All forms of phishing are electronically delivered social engineering. Phishing can be targeted, known as spearphishing. In spearphishing, a specific individual, company, or industry will be targeted by the adversary. More generally, adversaries can conduct non-targeted phishing, such as in mass malware spam campaigns.

Adversaries may send victims emails containing malicious attachments or links, typically to execute malicious code on victim systems. Phishing may also be conducted via third-party services, like social media platforms. Phishing may also involve social engineering techniques, such as posing as a trusted source, as well as evasive techniques such as removing or manipulating emails or metadata/headers from compromised accounts being abused to send messages (e.g., [Email Hiding Rules](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1564/008)).(Citation: Microsoft OAuth Spam 2022)(Citation: Palo Alto Unit 42 VBA Infostealer 2014) Another way to accomplish this is by [Email Spoofing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1672)(Citation: Proofpoint-spoof) the identity of the sender, which can be used to fool both the human recipient as well as automated security tools,(Citation: cyberproof-double-bounce) or by including the intended target as a party to an existing email thread that includes malicious files or links (i.e., "thread hijacking").(Citation: phishing-krebs)

Victims may also receive phishing messages that instruct them to call a phone number where they are directed to visit a malicious URL, download malware,(Citation: sygnia Luna Month)(Citation: CISA Remote Monitoring and Management Software) or install adversary-accessible remote management tools onto their computer (i.e., [User Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204)).(Citation: Unit42 Luna Moth)
3808.profile: [profile]Phishing Lure: Recruitment is a sub-technique of Phishing (T1566) under the Initial Access tactic, targeting multiple platforms. It involves sending deceptive electronic messages, often emails, that pose as legitimate job recruitment opportunities to trick specific individuals or organizations. These messages contain malicious attachments or links designed to execute code on the victim's system, leveraging social engineering by impersonating a trusted source. The intrusion-set FIN7 has been associated with this activity.[/profile]
3808.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Phishing Lure: Recruitment is a specific social engineering technique within the broader phishing (T1566) and spearphishing tactics. It operates under the Initial Access tactic, primarily targeting Windows, macOS, and Linux platforms. The technique involves crafting deceptive communications, such as emails or social media messages, that impersonate a legitimate recruiter or company to offer fake job opportunities. This lure is designed to trick targets into opening malicious attachments, clicking on harmful links, or divulging sensitive personal and credential information, thereby enabling initial compromise or information gathering.

3809.name: Creating Fake Websites
3809.profile: [profile]Creating Fake Websites is a technique used in phishing campaigns, often as part of Spearphishing Link (T1598.003) to establish a Link Target (T1608.005). It involves adversaries cloning legitimate login portals or creating deceptive websites that closely mimic real ones to harvest credentials. These fake sites may be hosted on typosquatted domains or trusted cloud services. The technique is employed by groups like FIN7 to facilitate credential theft, often bypassing URL verification through obfuscation or by using adversary-in-the-middle phishing kits to capture session cookies and bypass multi-factor authentication.[/profile]
3809.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Creating Fake Websites is a technique used for credential harvesting, often as part of spearphishing campaigns. Adversaries create fraudulent websites that are clones of legitimate login portals, such as corporate or online services, to deceive victims into entering their credentials. These fake sites can be deployed using purchased domains that resemble real ones through typosquatting or homoglyphs, or hosted on trusted platforms like link-shortening services to avoid detection. The gathered information is then sent back to the adversary, enabling further compromise. This technique is commonly associated with groups like Silent Librarian and is a preparatory step for techniques like Spearphishing Link (T1598.003).

3810.name: Job Posting Deception
3810.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may abuse task scheduling functionality to facilitate initial or recurring execution of malicious code. Utilities exist within all major operating systems to schedule programs or scripts to be executed at a specified date and time. A task can also be scheduled on a remote system, provided the proper authentication is met (ex: RPC and file and printer sharing in Windows environments). Scheduling a task on a remote system typically may require being a member of an admin or otherwise privileged group on the remote system.(Citation: TechNet Task Scheduler Security)

Adversaries may use task scheduling to execute programs at system startup or on a scheduled basis for persistence. These mechanisms can also be abused to run a process under the context of a specified account (such as one with elevated permissions/privileges). Similar to [System Binary Proxy Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1218), adversaries have also abused task scheduling to potentially mask one-time execution under a trusted system process.(Citation: ProofPoint Serpent)
3810.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique Scheduled Task/Job (T1053), a Persistence and Execution tactic used across Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves abusing OS utilities like Windows Task Scheduler, cron, at, or launchd to schedule malicious code execution at specific times or system startup, enabling recurring execution. Tasks can be scheduled locally or, on Windows, remotely via RPC with proper authentication, often requiring admin privileges. This method can also be used to run processes under specific account contexts, including elevated ones, to mask execution. The intrusion set FIN7 has been associated with this technique.
3810.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Job Posting Deception is a technique where adversaries create fake job listings to lure and recruit individuals, often for malicious purposes like insider threats or to gather intelligence. This method is a form of social engineering and initial access, targeting human resources and recruitment platforms. The technical mechanics involve crafting legitimate-looking postings for high-demand roles to solicit applications, enabling the adversary to collect sensitive information from candidates or to establish contact with potential insiders. This tactic exploits trust in professional hiring processes.

3811.name: Map out compromised companies’ systems
3811.profile: [profile]The entity 'Map out compromised companies’ systems' is a reconnaissance activity, likely aligning with the MITRE ATT&CK technique System Network Connections Discovery (T1049) under the Discovery tactic. It involves adversaries using commands like netstat, net use, or net session on compromised systems to enumerate active network connections and sessions. This enables them to understand the network layout of a victim's environment, including cloud VPCs, to identify connected systems and services for further targeting. The intrusion set FIN7 is associated with this behavior.
3811.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Map out compromised companies’ systems" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the retrieved information, this activity aligns with the general post-compromise discovery phase. It involves adversaries gaining access to a system and then performing network discovery to understand the connected environment, including cloud-based Virtual Private Clouds (VPCs) or virtual networks. This reconnaissance is performed using standard system utilities and commands to list network connections and active sessions, enabling the adversary to identify other systems and services for potential lateral movement or further exploitation.

3812.name: Identify users and devices within the systems
3812.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may compromise third-party network devices that can be used during targeting. Network devices, such as small office/home office (SOHO) routers, may be compromised where the adversary's ultimate goal is not [Initial Access](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0001) to that environment, but rather to leverage these devices to support additional targeting.

Once an adversary has control, compromised network devices can be used to launch additional operations, such as hosting payloads for [Phishing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566) campaigns (i.e., [Link Target](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1608/005)) or enabling the required access to execute [Content Injection](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1659) operations. Adversaries may also be able to harvest reusable credentials (i.e., [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078)) from compromised network devices.

Adversaries often target Internet-facing edge devices and related network appliances that specifically do not support robust host-based defenses.(Citation: Mandiant Fortinet Zero Day)(Citation: Wired Russia Cyberwar)

Compromised network devices may be used to support subsequent [Command and Control](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0011) activity, such as [Hide Infrastructure](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1665) through an established [Proxy](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1090) and/or [Botnet](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1584/005) network.(Citation: Justice GRU 2024)
3812.profile: [profile]The entity "Identify users and devices within the systems" is a reconnaissance technique. Its technical mechanics involve using network device CLI commands, such as `show users` and `show ssh`, to enumerate users currently logged into network infrastructure devices. This activity supports the Discovery tactic by identifying active user sessions on compromised or targeted network hardware, aiding in follow-on targeting and lateral movement. The technique is associated with groups including FIN7.[/profile]
3812.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Identify users and devices within the systems" is a reconnaissance technique aligned with the MITRE ATT&CK framework, likely corresponding to System Owner/User Discovery (T1033) under the Discovery tactic. It operates across multiple platforms and involves enumerating active users and connected devices to profile the target environment. Technical mechanics include using commands like `whoami`, `w`, `who`, and `dscl . list /Users` on macOS/Linux, or `show users` and `show ssh` on network devices. This information aids in shaping follow-on adversarial actions such as credential attacks or lateral movement.

3813.name: Locate backup servers and files
3813.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may set files and directories to be hidden to evade detection mechanisms. To prevent normal users from accidentally changing special files on a system, most operating systems have the concept of a ‘hidden’ file. These files don’t show up when a user browses the file system with a GUI or when using normal commands on the command line. Users must explicitly ask to show the hidden files either via a series of Graphical User Interface (GUI) prompts or with command line switches (dir /a for Windows and ls –a for Linux and macOS). On Linux and Mac, users can mark specific files as hidden simply by putting a “.” as the first character in the file or folder name (Citation: Sofacy Komplex Trojan) (Citation: Antiquated Mac Malware). Files and folders that start with a period, ‘.’, are by default hidden from being viewed in the Finder application and standard command-line utilities like “ls”. Users must specifically change settings to have these files viewable. Files on macOS can also be marked with the UF_HIDDEN flag which prevents them from being seen in Finder.app, but still allows them to be seen in Terminal.app (Citation: WireLurker). On Windows, users can mark specific files as hidden by using the attrib.exe binary. Many applications create these hidden files and folders to store information so that it doesn’t clutter up the user’s workspace. For example, SSH utilities create a .ssh folder that’s hidden and contains the user’s known hosts and keys. Additionally, adversaries may name files in a manner that would allow the file to be hidden such as naming a file only a “space” character. Adversaries can use this to their advantage to hide files and folders anywhere on the system and evading a typical user or system analysis that does not incorporate investigation of hidden files.
3813.profile: [profile]The entity "Locate backup servers and files" is a Discovery technique where adversaries search for backup systems to shape follow-on attacks like data destruction. Technical mechanics involve using commands such as `dir`, `reg query`, or `tasklist` to discover specific backup software like Veeam, Acronis, or Dropbox. This activity is associated with groups including FIN7 and Wizard Spider. The provided uncertain ID T1564.001 and name "hidden files and directories" are not aligned with this technique's core function and are disregarded.[/profile]
3813.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Locate backup servers and files is a Discovery technique where adversaries search for backup software, configurations, and associated files to inform follow-on attacks like Data Destruction or Inhibit System Recovery. This involves using commands such as `dir`, `reg query`, or specific queries for software like Veeam or Acronis to identify backup catalogues, volume shadow copies, and backup file locations on local systems or network shares. The gathered intelligence enables targeted disruption of recovery mechanisms.

3814.name: Malware and Ransomware Infection Process
3814.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may develop malware and malware components that can be used during targeting. Building malicious software can include the development of payloads, droppers, post-compromise tools, backdoors (including backdoored images), packers, C2 protocols, and the creation of infected removable media. Adversaries may develop malware to support their operations, creating a means for maintaining control of remote machines, evading defenses, and executing post-compromise behaviors.(Citation: Mandiant APT1)(Citation: Kaspersky Sofacy)(Citation: ActiveMalwareEnergy)(Citation: FBI Flash FIN7 USB)

During malware development, adversaries may intentionally include indicators aligned with other known actors in order to mislead attribution by defenders.(Citation: Olympic Destroyer)(Citation: Risky Bulletin Threat actor impersonates FSB APT)(Citation: GamaCopy organization)

As with legitimate development efforts, different skill sets may be required for developing malware. The skills needed may be located in-house, or may need to be contracted out. Use of a contractor may be considered an extension of that adversary's malware development capabilities, provided the adversary plays a role in shaping requirements and maintains a degree of exclusivity to the malware.

Some aspects of malware development, such as C2 protocol development, may require adversaries to obtain additional infrastructure. For example, malware developed that will communicate with Twitter for C2, may require use of [Web Services](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1583/006).(Citation: FireEye APT29)
3814.profile: [profile]Malware and Ransomware Infection Process is a technique aligned with MITRE ATT&CK ID T1587.001 (Develop Capabilities: Malware) under the Resource Development tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. The technical process involves adversaries developing malicious software components like payloads, droppers, backdoors, and C2 protocols to maintain control, evade defenses, and execute post-compromise actions. This development can include intentionally embedding false indicators to mislead attribution and may require contracting specialized skills or obtaining additional infrastructure, such as web services for command and control. The technique is associated with numerous threat groups, including FIN7, APT29, and Lazarus Group.
3814.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Malware and Ransomware Infection Process" is a broad attack pattern not directly mapped to a single MITRE ATT&CK ID. It encompasses multiple techniques for deploying malicious software. Technical mechanics include copying malware to removable media to exploit Autorun features for initial access or lateral movement, and modifying or creating shortcuts to execute malicious payloads during system boot or user login to establish persistence. Adversaries may also relocate malware on a victim system to evade detection and remove forensic evidence.

3823.name: Pillowmint
3823.uncertain_mes: [Pillowmint](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0517) is a point-of-sale malware used by [FIN7](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0046) designed to capture credit card information.(Citation: Trustwave Pillowmint June 2020)
3823.profile: [profile]Pillowmint, also known as Monkey Thief, is a point-of-sale malware attributed to the FIN7 group. It is designed to capture credit card information from infected POS devices. The malware's operations were notably overhauled in 2020, shifting from targeted POS campaigns to broader, indiscriminate infection attempts across various sectors. Its primary target platform is point-of-sale systems.
3823.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Pillowmint, also known as pillowmint, is attributed to the cybercriminal group FIN7 (also referenced as CARBON SPIDER or anunak). Its key technical behaviors include logging its own activity for operational control, executing commands for system control, reading process memory for credential access, and manipulating the Windows Registry for persistence and defense evasion. It specifically targets Point-of-Sale (POS) systems to scrape payment card data from memory. The malware establishes persistence through registry key creation and has been associated with broad, indiscriminate infection campaigns across multiple sectors.

3824.name: Halfbaked
3824.uncertain_mes: [HALFBAKED](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0151) is a malware family consisting of multiple components intended to establish persistence in victim networks. (Citation: FireEye FIN7 April 2017)
3824.profile: [profile]Halfbaked is a malware family attributed to the FIN7 group, also known as Anunak. It functions as a backdoor designed to establish persistence and maintain a foothold in victim networks, primarily targeting financial information. Key technical behaviors include gathering system information via WMI queries, enumerating running processes, and collecting OS, processor, and BIOS details. It connects to specified command-and-control servers for remote access and data exfiltration.[/profile]
3824.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Halfbaked, also known as HALFBAKED, is a backdoor malware attributed to the FIN7 (Anunak) criminal group. Its key technical behaviors include gathering system information via WMI queries and enumerating running processes, and it establishes persistence through registry modifications. The malware primarily targets financial institutions to exfiltrate sensitive financial data, connecting to dedicated command and control (C2) servers. It is associated with the Carbanak malware family and utilizes infrastructure such as C2 servers for its operations.

3825.name: Memory Scraper
3825.profile: [profile]Memory Scraper, also known as pillowmint, is attributed to the FIN7 intrusion set. Its key technical behavior involves scraping credit card data from system memory, initiating this process after a 10-second sleep period. It is associated with the Anunak group and operates as a data theft tool targeting Windows systems.
3825.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Memory Scraper, also known as pillowmint, is attributed to the Anunak group. Its key technical behavior involves a dedicated thread for scraping credit card data from memory, which initiates after a 10-second sleep period. It functions as a process list updater and is capable of executing process commands. The malware targets Windows systems and is part of a suite of information-stealing tools designed to exfiltrate sensitive data from a victim's computer.

3826.name: shim database modification
3826.profile: [profile]Shim Database Modification is a persistence and privilege escalation technique (ID: T1546.011) within the Privilege Escalation and Persistence tactics, targeting the Windows platform. Adversaries, such as FIN7, modify the Application Compatibility Shim database to execute malicious code when specific programs run. This involves installing custom shims that can bypass User Account Control (UAC), inject DLLs, or disable security features like Data Execution Prevention by redirecting program execution through a malicious shim database. The technique leverages the Windows shim infrastructure to establish a persistent backdoor with elevated privileges.[/profile]
3826.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Shim Database Modification is a Windows-specific persistence and privilege escalation technique (likely T1546.011) within the Execution tactic. It involves adversaries modifying the Application Compatibility Shim database (.sdb files) to inject malicious code or redirect program execution. By altering custom databases stored in %WINDIR%\AppPatch\custom or the associated registry keys, attackers can force targeted applications to load malicious DLLs or bypass security controls like User Account Control each time the shimmed program runs.

3827.name: POS Malware Attack
3827.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may downgrade or use a version of system features that may be outdated, vulnerable, and/or does not support updated security controls. Downgrade attacks typically take advantage of a system’s backward compatibility to force it into less secure modes of operation. 

Adversaries may downgrade and use various less-secure versions of features of a system, such as [Command and Scripting Interpreter](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059)s or even network protocols that can be abused to enable [Adversary-in-the-Middle](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1557) or [Network Sniffing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1040).(Citation: Praetorian TLS Downgrade Attack 2014) For example, [PowerShell](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001) versions 5+ includes Script Block Logging (SBL), which can record executed script content. However, adversaries may attempt to execute a previous version of PowerShell that does not support SBL with the intent to [Impair Defenses](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1562) while running malicious scripts that may have otherwise been detected.(Citation: CrowdStrike BGH Ransomware 2021)(Citation: Mandiant BYOL 2018)(Citation: att_def_ps_logging)

Adversaries may similarly target network traffic to downgrade from an encrypted HTTPS connection to an unsecured HTTP connection that exposes network data in clear text.(Citation: Targeted SSL Stripping Attacks Are Real)(Citation: Crowdstrike Downgrade) On Windows systems, adversaries may downgrade the boot manager to a vulnerable version that bypasses Secure Boot, granting the ability to disable various operating system security mechanisms.(Citation: SafeBreach)
3827.profile: [profile]The entity is Downgrade Attack, identified as T1562.010 under the Impair Defenses tactic, primarily targeting Windows platforms. It exploits system backward compatibility to force less secure modes, such as executing older PowerShell versions to bypass Script Block Logging or downgrading HTTPS connections to unencrypted HTTP to enable network sniffing. Associated intrusion set FIN7 and malware Pillowmint are linked to this technique.
3827.profile_without_enhance: [profile]POS Malware Attack is a technique targeting Point-of-Sale (POS) systems, primarily within the Initial Access tactic. The technical mechanics involve deploying specialized malware designed to scrape payment card data from the memory of compromised POS terminals. This malware often operates by scanning process memory for track data, which is then exfiltrated. The attack pattern is distinct from general malware deployment, focusing on the specific hardware and software environment of retail payment systems.

3828.name: malicious shim database
3828.uncertain_mes:
An adversary may rely upon a user opening a malicious file in order to gain execution. Users may be subjected to social engineering to get them to open a file that will lead to code execution. This user action will typically be observed as follow-on behavior from [Spearphishing Attachment](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001). Adversaries may use several types of files that require a user to execute them, including .doc, .pdf, .xls, .rtf, .scr, .exe, .lnk, .pif, .cpl, .reg, and .iso.(Citation: Mandiant Trojanized Windows 10)

Adversaries may employ various forms of [Masquerading](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1036) and [Obfuscated Files or Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027) to increase the likelihood that a user will open and successfully execute a malicious file. These methods may include using a familiar naming convention and/or password protecting the file and supplying instructions to a user on how to open it.(Citation: Password Protected Word Docs) 

While [Malicious File](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002) frequently occurs shortly after Initial Access it may occur at other phases of an intrusion, such as when an adversary places a file in a shared directory or on a user's desktop hoping that a user will click on it. This activity may also be seen shortly after [Internal Spearphishing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1534).
3828.profile: [profile]Malicious Shim Database is a sub-technique of Application Shimming (T1546.011) under the Persistence tactic, targeting Windows. It involves adversaries installing a custom shim database (.sdb file) to hijack the Windows Application Compatibility Framework. When a program executes, the malicious shim uses hooking to redirect code, enabling actions like privilege escalation (e.g., UAC bypass via RedirectEXE), DLL injection (InjectDLL), or disabling security features (DisableNX, DisableSEH) without modifying the original application. Custom databases are stored in %WINDIR%\AppPatch\custom and require administrator privileges to install, as seen in FIN7 campaigns.[/profile]
3828.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Malicious Shim Database is a sub-technique of Application Shimming (T1546.011) under the Persistence tactic, targeting the Windows platform. It involves adversaries creating or modifying a custom Windows Application Compatibility Database (.sdb file) to inject malicious code. This malicious shim database is installed using tools like sdbinst.exe and leverages the legitimate shimming framework to hook and redirect application execution, enabling actions such as privilege escalation, bypassing User Account Control (UAC), disabling security features like Data Execution Prevention, and establishing persistent backdoors. Custom databases are typically stored in directories like %WINDIR%\AppPatch\custom and require administrator privileges to install.

3829.name: mapping injection technique
3829.profile: [profile]Mapping Injection Technique is a technique used by adversaries like FIN7 to manipulate network traffic by injecting malicious content into data-transfer channels, often from a man-in-the-middle or man-on-the-side position, to gain initial access or deliver additional payloads to victim systems. This method can involve compromising upstream channels such as internet service providers.[/profile]
3829.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "mapping injection technique" is a specific form of process injection. It operates by writing malicious code into the virtual address space of a target process, often using Windows API calls like VirtualAllocEx and WriteProcessMemory, and then executing it via a mechanism such as CreateRemoteThread. This allows the injected code to run within the context of a legitimate process, potentially evading detection and gaining access to that process's memory and privileges.

3830.name: logging its own activity
3830.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may employ various user activity checks to detect and avoid virtualization and analysis environments. This may include changing behaviors based on the results of checks for the presence of artifacts indicative of a virtual machine environment (VME) or sandbox. If the adversary detects a VME, they may alter their malware to disengage from the victim or conceal the core functions of the implant. They may also search for VME artifacts before dropping secondary or additional payloads. Adversaries may use the information learned from [Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1497) during automated discovery to shape follow-on behaviors.(Citation: Deloitte Environment Awareness)

Adversaries may search for user activity on the host based on variables such as the speed/frequency of mouse movements and clicks (Citation: Sans Virtual Jan 2016) , browser history, cache, bookmarks, or number of files in common directories such as home or the desktop. Other methods may rely on specific user interaction with the system before the malicious code is activated, such as waiting for a document to close before activating a macro (Citation: Unit 42 Sofacy Nov 2018) or waiting for a user to double click on an embedded image to activate.(Citation: FireEye FIN7 April 2017)
3830.profile: [profile]The entity "logging its own activity" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the provided context, it appears to be a misinterpretation or a specific implementation of the technique "User Activity Based Checks" (T1497.002) under the Defense Evasion tactic. This technique involves malware altering its behavior based on checks for user activity to evade detection, such as monitoring mouse movement speed/frequency, browser history, or waiting for specific user interactions like a document close or a double-click before activating malicious code. It is associated with groups like FIN7 and DarkHotel.
3830.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "logging its own activity" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the retrieved context, it describes an adversary's action to record their own malicious actions, which contrasts with techniques like Impair Defenses (T1562) that disable or clear logs (e.g., using `wevtutil cl` or `auditpol`). This self-logging could be used for operational control or debugging, creating a separate, adversarial record of events that persists even if system logs are tampered with or disabled.

3846.name: Process Memory Reading
3846.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may attempt to access credential material stored in the process memory of the Local Security Authority Subsystem Service (LSASS). After a user logs on, the system generates and stores a variety of credential materials in LSASS process memory. These credential materials can be harvested by an administrative user or SYSTEM and used to conduct [Lateral Movement](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0008) using [Use Alternate Authentication Material](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1550). As well as in-memory techniques, the LSASS process memory can be dumped from the target host and analyzed on a local system. For example, on the target host use procdump: * procdump -ma lsass.exe lsass_dump Locally, mimikatz can be run using: * sekurlsa::Minidump lsassdump.dmp * sekurlsa::logonPasswords Built-in Windows tools such as `comsvcs.dll` can also be used: * rundll32.exe C:\Windows\System32\comsvcs.dll MiniDump PID lsass.dmp full(Citation: Volexity Exchange Marauder March 2021)(Citation: Symantec Attacks Against Government Sector) Similar to [Image File Execution Options Injection](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1546/012), the silent process exit mechanism can be abused to create a memory dump of `lsass.exe` through Windows Error Reporting (`WerFault.exe`).(Citation: Deep Instinct LSASS) Windows Security Support Provider (SSP) DLLs are loaded into LSASS process at system start. Once loaded into the LSA, SSP DLLs have access to encrypted and plaintext passwords that are stored in Windows, such as any logged-on user's Domain password or smart card PINs. The SSP configuration is stored in two Registry keys: HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa\Security Packages and HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa\OSConfig\Security Packages. An adversary may modify these Registry keys to add new SSPs, which will be loaded the next time the system boots, or when the AddSecurityPackage Windows API function is called.(Citation: Graeber 2014) The following SSPs can be used to access credentials: * Msv: Interactive logons, batch logons, and service logons are done through the MSV authentication package. * Wdigest: The Digest Authentication protocol is designed for use with Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) and Simple Authentication Security Layer (SASL) exchanges.(Citation: TechNet Blogs Credential Protection) * Kerberos: Preferred for mutual client-server domain authentication in Windows 2000 and later. * CredSSP: Provides SSO and Network Level Authentication for Remote Desktop Services.(Citation: TechNet Blogs Credential Protection)
3846.profile: [profile]Process Memory Reading, also known as LSASS Memory (T1003.001), is a Credential Access technique targeting Windows platforms. It involves accessing or dumping the memory of the Local Security Authority Subsystem Service (LSASS.exe) to harvest stored credential materials like hashes and plaintext passwords. Specific execution methods include using tools like procdump (`procdump -ma lsass.exe`), Mimikatz modules (`sekurlsa::Minidump`), or built-in Windows utilities like `comsvcs.dll` via `rundll32.exe`. Adversaries may also abuse the silent process exit mechanism or modify Security Support Provider (SSP) Registry keys to load malicious DLLs into LSASS for credential theft, facilitating lateral movement.[/profile]
3846.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Process Memory Reading is a technique for credential access, likely mapped to the MITRE ATT&CK framework. It involves adversaries reading the memory of running processes to extract sensitive data like passwords, encryption keys, or authentication tokens. This is commonly performed on critical system processes such as LSASS on Windows or securityd on macOS to harvest cached credentials. Attackers may use tools like Mimikatz or built-in OS utilities (e.g., procdump, comsvcs.dll) to dump process memory for offline analysis, enabling lateral movement and privilege escalation.

3847.name: update process list
3847.profile: [profile]Update Process List is a technique used by adversaries to impair defenses by modifying or disabling system update mechanisms, hindering security patches and maintaining persistence. This tactic, part of Impair Defenses (T1562), typically targets Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. The technical mechanics involve altering update configurations, blocking update services, or tampering with update files to prevent the installation of patches that could remove malicious access. It is associated with malware like Halfbaked and Pillowmint.

3849.name: File Persistence
3849.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may clear artifacts associated with previously established persistence on a host system to remove evidence of their activity. This may involve various actions, such as removing services, deleting executables, [Modify Registry](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1112), [Plist File Modification](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1647), or other methods of cleanup to prevent defenders from collecting evidence of their persistent presence.(Citation: Cylance Dust Storm) Adversaries may also delete accounts previously created to maintain persistence (i.e. [Create Account](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1136)).(Citation: Talos - Cisco Attack 2022)

In some instances, artifacts of persistence may also be removed once an adversary’s persistence is executed in order to prevent errors with the new instance of the malware.(Citation: NCC Group Team9 June 2020)
3849.profile: [profile]File Persistence, also known as clear persistence (T1070.009), is a Defense Evasion technique where adversaries remove artifacts of previously established persistence to eliminate evidence. This involves actions like deleting executables, removing services, modifying the registry, or deleting accounts created for persistence, as seen with malware like Pillowmint. The goal is to clean the host system to prevent defenders from detecting the persistent presence or to avoid errors with new malware instances.
3849.profile_without_enhance: [profile]File Persistence is a technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, categorized under the Persistence (TA0003) tactic for the macOS and Linux platforms. It involves adversaries establishing persistence by adding malicious application paths to specific system property list (plist) files, such as `com.apple.loginwindow.[UUID].plist` within the `~/Library/Preferences/ByHost` directory, to ensure their payloads are automatically executed when a user logs back into the system.

3850.name: Cobalt Strike
3850.uncertain_mes:
[Cobalt Strike](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0154) is a commercial, full-featured, remote access tool that bills itself as “adversary simulation software designed to execute targeted attacks and emulate the post-exploitation actions of advanced threat actors”. Cobalt Strike’s interactive post-exploit capabilities cover the full range of ATT&CK tactics, all executed within a single, integrated system.(Citation: cobaltstrike manual)

In addition to its own capabilities, [Cobalt Strike](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0154) leverages the capabilities of other well-known tools such as Metasploit and [Mimikatz](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0002).(Citation: cobaltstrike manual)
3850.profile: [profile]Cobalt Strike is a commercial remote access tool and adversary simulation software used for post-exploitation activities, emulating advanced threat actors. It is also known by its standard name Cobalt Strike. It has been attributed to numerous groups including APT17, FIN7, APT29, APT32, APT41, FIN6, Mustang Panda, CopyKittens, DarkHydrus, Leviathan, Wizard Spider, and TA505. Its key technical behaviors include leveraging capabilities from tools like Metasploit and Mimikatz, covering the full range of ATT&CK tactics, and utilizing C2 servers with domains such as asureupdate.tech and akamaclouds.app. It targets various platforms through its integrated post-exploit system.[/profile]
3850.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Cobalt Strike is a commercial penetration testing framework, widely abused by threat actors as a post-exploitation tool. It is associated with numerous APT and criminal groups including APT29, APT32, APT41, FIN6, FIN7, Wizard Spider (linked to Conti), Pinchy Spider (linked to REvil), and TA2101 (linked to Maze). Its key TTPs involve providing a flexible command and control (C2) infrastructure, with observed C2 servers using domains like asureupdate.tech, akamaclouds.app, and azurestat.app. It primarily targets Windows platforms for lateral movement, persistence, and data exfiltration.

Its key technical behaviors include DNS beaconing for C2 communication and using HTTPS with specific configurations for data exfiltration via HTTP GET and POST requests to URIs like /cm and /submit.php. Its infrastructure is associated with domains such as wordst7512[.]net, dns[.]investsystemus[.]net, septcntr[.]com, dns[.]wellsystemte[.]net, dns[.]realeinvestment[.]net, bionetcloud[.]com, and dns[.]clearsystemwo[.]net.[/profile]

3853.name: Command and Control Techniques
3853.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may communicate using a custom command and control protocol instead of encapsulating commands/data in an existing [Application Layer Protocol](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1071). Implementations include mimicking well-known protocols or developing custom protocols (including raw sockets) on top of fundamental protocols provided by TCP/IP/another standard network stack.
3853.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique "Custom Command and Control Protocol" (T1094) under the Command and Control tactic. It operates across multiple platforms and involves adversaries designing bespoke communication protocols instead of using standard ones. Implementations include mimicking legitimate protocols or creating entirely new ones using raw sockets atop TCP/IP. The intrusion set FIN7 has been associated with this technique.[/profile]
3853.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Command and Control Techniques is a broad category of adversary behaviors within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, encompassing the tactic of Command and Control (TA0011). These techniques are used to establish and maintain communications with compromised systems. Specific methods include using custom command and control protocols (T1094) to mimic or create new protocols, employing steganography (T1001.002) to hide C2 traffic within digital files like images, and applying multilayer encryption (T1079) by tunneling custom encryption within standard protocols like HTTPS to obscure communications.

3855.name: DNS RRS Queries
3855.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may communicate using the Domain Name System (DNS) application layer protocol to avoid detection/network filtering by blending in with existing traffic. Commands to the remote system, and often the results of those commands, will be embedded within the protocol traffic between the client and server. 

The DNS protocol serves an administrative function in computer networking and thus may be very common in environments. DNS traffic may also be allowed even before network authentication is completed. DNS packets contain many fields and headers in which data can be concealed. Often known as DNS tunneling, adversaries may abuse DNS to communicate with systems under their control within a victim network while also mimicking normal, expected traffic.(Citation: PAN DNS Tunneling)(Citation: Medium DnsTunneling)

DNS beaconing may be used to send commands to remote systems via DNS queries. A DNS beacon is created by tunneling DNS traffic (i.e. [Protocol Tunneling](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1572)). The commands may be embedded into different DNS records, for example, TXT or A records.(Citation: OilRig Uses Updated BONDUPDATER to Target Middle Eastern Government) DNS beacons may be difficult to detect because the beacons infrequently communicate with infected devices.(Citation: DNS Beacons) Infrequent communication conceals the malicious DNS traffic with normal DNS traffic.
3855.profile: [profile]DNS RRS Queries is a technique identified as T1071.004 within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, falling under the Command and Control tactic and applicable to multiple platforms. It involves adversaries using the DNS application layer protocol to conceal command and control traffic by blending it with normal administrative DNS queries. This is achieved by embedding commands and exfiltrated data within various DNS record fields, such as TXT or A records, a method often referred to as DNS tunneling or beaconing. The technique is employed by groups like FIN7 and OilRig to evade network filtering and detection.[/profile]
3855.profile_without_enhance: [profile]DNS RRS Queries is a reconnaissance technique where adversaries query DNS Resource Record Sets (RRS) to gather targeting information. This involves actively querying a victim's DNS servers for specific record types, such as MX, TXT, SPF, or AXFR zone transfers, to discover details about subdomains, mail servers, third-party cloud services, and internal network addressing. The gathered data supports follow-on activities like active scanning, infrastructure acquisition, and initial access planning.

3856.name: PowerShell Script
3856.uncertain_mes: powershell_web_backdoor This is a very simple powershell web backdoor Usage: hxxp://127.0.0.1:9999/backdoor/?cmd=<Insert Your powershell compatible base64 encoded command here
3856.profile: [profile]PowerShell Script, also known as powershell_web_backdoor, is a simple web backdoor that executes commands via a web interface using a URL parameter like 'cmd' containing a Base64-encoded PowerShell command. It has been associated with intrusion sets OilRig, FIN7, and menuPass. Its key behavior involves command execution through HTTP GET requests to a specified listener, and it is referenced in the toolchains of other malware families like eugenloader and gootloader, which use obfuscated PowerShell scripts for persistence and loading subsequent stages. The target platform is Windows systems capable of running PowerShell.[profile]
3856.profile_without_enhance: [profile]PowerShell Script is a versatile scripting tool and malware component, not a specific malware family itself, but it is widely leveraged by threat actors for malicious purposes. It is used by groups such as OilRig (APT34) in components like ISMAgent, and by Storm-0249 in campaigns like GootLoader. Key malicious techniques include acting as a web backdoor, enabling persistence, loading further payloads, and facilitating command and control via methods like DNS TXT record logging to blend with normal traffic. Its primary target platform is Windows, where it executes to perform espionage and data exfiltration.[/profile]

3857.name: DNS TXT Logging Stage
3857.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may upload, install, or otherwise set up capabilities that can be used during targeting. To support their operations, an adversary may need to take capabilities they developed ([Develop Capabilities](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1587)) or obtained ([Obtain Capabilities](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1588)) and stage them on infrastructure under their control. These capabilities may be staged on infrastructure that was previously purchased/rented by the adversary ([Acquire Infrastructure](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1583)) or was otherwise compromised by them ([Compromise Infrastructure](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1584)). Capabilities may also be staged on web services, such as GitHub or Pastebin, or on Platform-as-a-Service (PaaS) offerings that enable users to easily provision applications.(Citation: Volexity Ocean Lotus November 2020)(Citation: Dragos Heroku Watering Hole)(Citation: Malwarebytes Heroku Skimmers)(Citation: Netskope GCP Redirection)(Citation: Netskope Cloud Phishing)

Staging of capabilities can aid the adversary in a number of initial access and post-compromise behaviors, including (but not limited to):

* Staging web resources necessary to conduct [Drive-by Compromise](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1189) when a user browses to a site.(Citation: FireEye CFR Watering Hole 2012)(Citation: Gallagher 2015)(Citation: ATT ScanBox)
* Staging web resources for a link target to be used with spearphishing.(Citation: Malwarebytes Silent Librarian October 2020)(Citation: Proofpoint TA407 September 2019)
* Uploading malware or tools to a location accessible to a victim network to enable [Ingress Tool Transfer](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1105).(Citation: Volexity Ocean Lotus November 2020)
* Installing a previously acquired SSL/TLS certificate to use to encrypt command and control traffic (ex: [Asymmetric Cryptography](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1573/002) with [Web Protocols](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1071/001)).(Citation: DigiCert Install SSL Cert)
3857.profile: [profile]The entity "DNS TXT Logging Stage" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the provided information, it appears to be a specific implementation of a staging capability (T1608) for command and control. The technique involves using DNS TXT records to host and stage malicious payloads or configuration data, which can then be retrieved by compromised systems. This method leverages the DNS protocol (T1071.004) for covert communication and is associated with malware like PowerShell Scripts. The primary tactic is Resource Development, with the platform being network-based systems.[/profile]
3857.profile_without_enhance: [profile]DNS TXT Logging Stage is a technique where adversaries use DNS TXT records as a covert channel for command and control (C2). It falls under the Command and Control tactic, specifically as a sub-technique of Application Layer Protocol (T1071.004), and operates across multiple platforms. The technique involves embedding commands or exfiltrated data into DNS TXT record queries and responses, allowing malware to communicate with attacker-controlled DNS servers. This method can blend with normal DNS traffic, making detection difficult, and is often used as part of multi-stage C2 channels or for data exfiltration.

3858.name: Encrypted Communication Channels
3858.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may use fallback or alternate communication channels if the primary channel is compromised or inaccessible in order to maintain reliable command and control and to avoid data transfer thresholds.
3858.profile: [profile]Encrypted Communication Channels, also known as Fallback Channels (T1008), is a Command and Control technique used to maintain reliable C2 by employing alternate or backup channels when the primary channel is compromised, blocked, or to avoid data transfer thresholds. It is used by groups including FIN7, APT41, Lazarus Group, OilRig, and UNC3886. This technique is distinct from general protocol encryption (T1573) and is a component of more complex multi-stage C2 architectures (T1104).[/profile]
3858.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Encrypted Communication Channels is a technique used in the Command and Control tactic. It involves adversaries employing encryption algorithms to conceal command and traffic, going beyond the inherent protections of standard secure protocols like HTTPS. This is done to hide C2 activity from network monitoring and defeat content-based detection. Implementations may be vulnerable if secret keys are embedded within malware samples or configuration files. The technique is related to concepts like multilayer encryption and fallback channels for maintaining reliable communication.

3860.name: Maintain Low Profile
3860.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may gain persistence and elevate privileges by executing malicious content triggered by PowerShell profiles. A PowerShell profile (profile.ps1) is a script that runs when [PowerShell](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001) starts and can be used as a logon script to customize user environments. [PowerShell](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001) supports several profiles depending on the user or host program. For example, there can be different profiles for [PowerShell](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001) host programs such as the PowerShell console, PowerShell ISE or Visual Studio Code. An administrator can also configure a profile that applies to all users and host programs on the local computer. (Citation: Microsoft About Profiles) Adversaries may modify these profiles to include arbitrary commands, functions, modules, and/or [PowerShell](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001) drives to gain persistence. Every time a user opens a [PowerShell](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001) session the modified script will be executed unless the -NoProfile flag is used when it is launched. (Citation: ESET Turla PowerShell May 2019) An adversary may also be able to escalate privileges if a script in a PowerShell profile is loaded and executed by an account with higher privileges, such as a domain administrator. (Citation: Wits End and Shady PowerShell Profiles)
3860.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique PowerShell Profile, ID T1546.013, under the Persistence tactic for Windows platforms. It involves adversaries modifying the `profile.ps1` script that runs automatically at PowerShell startup to execute arbitrary malicious commands, functions, or modules, thereby gaining persistence. Execution occurs each time a PowerShell session is launched unless the `-NoProfile` flag is used. This method can also lead to privilege escalation if a higher-privileged account loads the profile. The technique has been associated with groups like Turla and FIN7.[/profile]
3860.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Maintain Low Profile" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the provided context, it may refer to a general adversarial objective rather than a specific TTP. The retrieved information describes the technique "PowerShell Profile" (T1546.013), which is a persistence mechanism where adversaries modify PowerShell profile scripts (profile.ps1) to execute malicious commands automatically when PowerShell starts, unless the session is launched with the -NoProfile flag. This can also lead to privilege escalation if executed by a higher-privileged account.

3866.name: Large-Scale Data Exfiltration
3866.profile: [profile]Large-Scale Data Exfiltration is a technique for the Exfiltration tactic. It involves the automated processing and transfer of significant volumes of collected data, such as sensitive documents, out of a compromised network. This process often leverages other specific exfiltration sub-techniques like Exfiltration Over C2 Channel or Alternative Protocol to move the information. Adversaries, including groups like FIN7, may schedule these transfers or compress and encrypt the data prior to exfiltration to blend with normal traffic and avoid detection.
3866.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Large-Scale Data Exfiltration" is a data exfiltration technique. Prior to exfiltration, adversaries may compress or encrypt the collected data to obfuscate it and minimize network footprint. The technique can be scheduled to blend with normal traffic patterns.

3868.name: Stolen Credentials
3868.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may gather credentials that can be used during targeting. Account credentials gathered by adversaries may be those directly associated with the target victim organization or attempt to take advantage of the tendency for users to use the same passwords across personal and business accounts.

Adversaries may gather credentials from potential victims in various ways, such as direct elicitation via [Phishing for Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1598). Adversaries may also compromise sites then add malicious content designed to collect website authentication cookies from visitors.(Citation: ATT ScanBox) (Citation: Register Deloitte)(Citation: Register Uber)(Citation: Detectify Slack Tokens)(Citation: Forbes GitHub Creds)(Citation: GitHub truffleHog)(Citation: GitHub Gitrob)(Citation: CNET Leaks) Where multi-factor authentication (MFA) based on out-of-band communications is in use, adversaries may compromise a service provider to gain access to MFA codes and one-time passwords (OTP).(Citation: Okta Scatter Swine 2022)

Credential information may also be exposed to adversaries via leaks to online or other accessible data sets (ex: [Search Engines](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1593/002), breach dumps, code repositories, etc.). Adversaries may purchase credentials from dark web markets, such as Russian Market and 2easy, or through access to Telegram channels that distribute logs from infostealer malware.(Citation: Bleeping Computer 2easy 2021)(Citation: SecureWorks Infostealers 2023)(Citation: Bleeping Computer Stealer Logs 2023)

Gathering this information may reveal opportunities for other forms of reconnaissance (ex: [Search Open Websites/Domains](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1593) or [Phishing for Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1598)), establishing operational resources (ex: [Compromise Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1586)), and/or initial access (ex: [External Remote Services](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1133) or [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078)).
3868.profile: [profile]Stolen Credentials, identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1589.001, is a reconnaissance tactic used to gather account login information for future attacks. Adversaries obtain credentials through phishing, purchasing them from dark web markets like Russian Market or 2easy, harvesting them from infostealer malware logs on Telegram, or collecting them from compromised websites. These stolen credentials are then leveraged for subsequent actions, including initial access via Valid Accounts, as employed by groups like FIN7, APT28, and LAPSUS$.
3868.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Stolen Credentials" is a technique for initial access, where adversaries use credentials illicitly obtained from sources like phishing, breach dumps, or dark web markets to gain entry to systems. This technique, often associated with groups like APT28 and LAPSUS$, involves using these stolen usernames and passwords to authenticate to services such as SSH, RDP, or cloud applications, bypassing normal access controls.

3869.name: Domain Admin Accounts
3869.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may obtain and abuse credentials of a domain account as a means of gaining Initial Access, Persistence, Privilege Escalation, or Defense Evasion.(Citation: TechNet Credential Theft) Domain accounts are those managed by Active Directory Domain Services where access and permissions are configured across systems and services that are part of that domain. Domain accounts can cover users, administrators, and services.(Citation: Microsoft AD Accounts)

Adversaries may compromise domain accounts, some with a high level of privileges, through various means such as [OS Credential Dumping](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003) or password reuse, allowing access to privileged resources of the domain.
3869.profile: [profile]Domain Admin Accounts, also known as T1078.002 (Domain Accounts), is a technique within the Valid Accounts tactic used on Windows platforms. It involves adversaries obtaining and abusing credentials of domain accounts managed by Active Directory Domain Services to gain initial access, persistence, privilege escalation, or defense evasion. Compromise is achieved through methods like OS Credential Dumping or password reuse, granting access to privileged domain resources. The technique is associated with groups such as FIN7, Volt Typhoon, and Wizard Spider.
3869.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Domain Admin Accounts is a specific type of domain account within the Valid Accounts technique (T1078.002), used for Initial Access, Persistence, Privilege Escalation, and Defense Evasion. These accounts are managed by Active Directory Domain Services and provide extensive access and permissions across all systems and services in the domain. Adversaries compromise these high-privilege accounts through methods like OS Credential Dumping or password reuse, enabling access to privileged domain resources.

3870.name: PSEXEC_PSH
3870.profile: [profile]PSEXEC_PSH is a technique for remote command execution that combines PsExec and PowerShell. It leverages the Windows service control manager via PsExec to create a temporary service on a remote system, which is then used to execute PowerShell commands or scripts. This method allows adversaries to run arbitrary code on remote machines, often for lateral movement or payload deployment, and is associated with groups like FIN7. The technique falls under the Execution tactic (T1569.002) on the Windows platform.
3870.profile_without_enhance: [profile]PSEXEC_PSH is a technique for remote execution, aligning with the MITRE ATT&CK framework under T1569.002 (Service Execution) within the Execution tactic for Windows. It specifically refers to using the PsExec utility to create a temporary Windows service for command execution, but with the payload or commands delivered and executed via PowerShell. This method allows adversaries to run arbitrary code on remote systems by leveraging the service control manager to instantiate a PowerShell process, enabling fileless execution and potentially bypassing defenses that monitor for traditional command-line interpreters.

3871.name: RPC Service Controller Protocol
3871.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may impersonate legitimate protocols or web service traffic to disguise command and control activity and thwart analysis efforts. By impersonating legitimate protocols or web services, adversaries can make their command and control traffic blend in with legitimate network traffic.  

Adversaries may impersonate a fake SSL/TLS handshake to make it look like subsequent traffic is SSL/TLS encrypted, potentially interfering with some security tooling, or to make the traffic look like it is related with a trusted entity. 

Adversaries may also leverage legitimate protocols to impersonate expected web traffic or trusted services. For example, adversaries may manipulate HTTP headers, URI endpoints, SSL certificates, and transmitted data to disguise C2 communications or mimic legitimate services such as Gmail, Google Drive, and Yahoo Messenger.(Citation: ESET Okrum July 2019)(Citation: Malleable-C2-U42)
3871.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique "Protocol or Service Impersonation," identified as T1001.003 under the Command and Control tactic. It operates across multiple platforms where adversaries disguise C2 traffic by mimicking legitimate protocols or web services. This involves manipulating HTTP headers, URI endpoints, and SSL certificates to blend in with trusted traffic, such as impersonating fake SSL/TLS handshakes or services like Gmail. The technique has been associated with groups including Lazarus Group, Higaisa, and Mustang Panda.
3871.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "RPC Service Controller Protocol" is a technique for remote system interaction, likely within the T1021.002 "SMB/Windows Admin Shares" context. It enables adversaries with valid accounts to perform remote procedure calls (RPCs) over SMB, facilitating lateral movement and remote execution of binaries through methods like Scheduled Tasks, Service Execution, and Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI). This protocol is foundational for administrative functions on Windows networks.

3874.name: Non-Standard Traffic
3874.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may communicate using a protocol and port pairing that are typically not associated. For example, HTTPS over port 8088(Citation: Symantec Elfin Mar 2019) or port 587(Citation: Fortinet Agent Tesla April 2018) as opposed to the traditional port 443. Adversaries may make changes to the standard port used by a protocol to bypass filtering or muddle analysis/parsing of network data.

Adversaries may also make changes to victim systems to abuse non-standard ports. For example, Registry keys and other configuration settings can be used to modify protocol and port pairings.(Citation: change_rdp_port_conti)
3874.profile: [profile]Non-Standard Traffic, also known as Non-Standard Port (T1571), is a Command and Control technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework. It operates across Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. The technique involves adversaries using atypical protocol and port pairings, such as HTTPS over port 8088 instead of the standard port 443, to bypass network filtering and complicate traffic analysis. Attackers may also modify victim system settings, like Registry keys, to reconfigure services to use these non-standard ports. This method is associated with groups including FIN7, Lazarus Group, and Sandworm Team.[/profile]
3874.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Non-Standard Traffic is a Command and Control technique where adversaries use protocol and port pairings that deviate from expected standards, such as running HTTPS over port 8088 instead of 443, to bypass network filtering and evade detection. It serves as a foundational method for establishing persistent, low-profile channels for other malicious activities like data exfiltration.[/profile]
