Written by: James T. Bennett, Barry Vengerik
3877.profile: [profile]DriftPin, also known as Spy.Agent.ORM and Toshliph, is a malware previously associated with the CARBANAK backdoor and attributed to the groups Anunak and FIN7. It has been deployed in spear-phishing campaigns, notably by FIN7 in early 2016, as an initial payload targeting Russian and Eastern European banks. Its key behavior involves establishing persistence via Windows registry keys for automatic execution. The primary target platform is Microsoft Windows systems.
3877.profile_without_enhance: [profile]DriftPin, also known as Spy.Agent.ORM and Toshliph, is a malware attributed to the Carbanak cybercriminal gang and associated with the Anunak group. It functions as a first-stage trojan payload, sharing code similarities with the core Carbanak malware and has been deployed in spear-phishing campaigns, including by FIN7, targeting sectors like banking. Its target platform is Windows.

3878.name: Laziok
3878.profile: [profile]Laziok is a malware with an infection vector, attributed to the FIN7 cybercriminal group. Its activity infrastructure has overlapped with other malware like NETWIRE and DRIFTPIN in campaigns targeting financial entities.
3878.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Laziok, also known as laziok, is a malware entity associated with financial targeting. Its activity clusters have been linked to campaigns like DRIFTPIN, which share overlapping infrastructure with LAZIOK and NETWIRE, targeting similar financial entities. The malware's primary infection vector is unspecified, and while related to groups like Lazarus in broader threat landscapes, direct attribution in the provided data remains unclear. Key technical behaviors and specific target platforms are not detailed in the available information.

3879.name: Netwire
3879.uncertain_mes: [NETWIRE](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0198) is a publicly available, multiplatform remote administration tool (RAT) that has been used by criminal and APT groups since at least 2012.(Citation: FireEye APT33 Sept 2017)(Citation: McAfee Netwire Mar 2015)(Citation: FireEye APT33 Webinar Sept 2017)
3879.profile: [profile]Netwire is a publicly available, multiplatform remote administration tool (RAT) used as malware by criminal and APT groups since at least 2012. Aliases include NetWire RC. It has been attributed to groups including APT33, TA2541, SilverTerrier, The White Company, and FIN7. Key technical behaviors involve its use as a remote access tool for control and data exfiltration, with specific variants identified for Linux and Mac OS platforms. Target platforms are multiplatform, including Windows, Linux, and Mac OS. Supplementary infrastructure or related tools include connections to JSOutProx malware in campaigns by groups like Solar Spider.]
3879.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Netwire is a Remote Access Trojan (RAT) malware, also known as NetWire RC. It is attributed to cyber groups including APT33 and Solar Spider. Its key technical behaviors involve functioning as a multi-platform RAT with variants for Windows, Linux, and Mac OS. It is associated with the JSOutProx malware as part of a multi-stage infection chain. The FBI has conducted takedown operations against its infrastructure.

3880.name: RIG exploit kit
3880.profile: [profile]RIG exploit kit, also known as Rig Exploit Kit, is attributed to the FIN7 cybercrime group. It functions as a delivery platform, historically evolving to distribute payloads like the Neutrino exploit kit, the Cerber ransomware, and more recently the WastedLoader malware. Its key technical behavior involves exploiting vulnerabilities in web browsers to download and execute malicious payloads from compromised websites, with traffic often captured in network packet captures (PCAPs). Its primary target is Windows systems through web-based drive-by attacks.]
3880.profile_without_enhance: [profile]RIG exploit kit, also known as RIG Exploit Kit, is a cybercrime tool attributed to unknown groups. Its key technical behaviors include delivering payloads like the WastedLoader malware and information stealers, often distributed through password-protected archives. The kit targets web browsers and platforms via exploit-driven campaigns, leveraging traffic captured in PCAP files for analysis. Its infrastructure and evolution have been documented through various security analyses since at least 2016.

3881.name: 64-bit variants of the backdoor
3881.uncertain_mes: Just two weeks after reporting about the commercialization of the KINS banking Trojan, RSA reveals yet another weapon to be used in a cybercriminal’s arsenal.
3881.profile: [profile]The malware is known as "Hand of Thief" and its 64-bit variants. It is a backdoor used by the cybercriminal group FIN7. It is a weapon in a cybercriminal's arsenal, similar to the KINS banking Trojan. Its technical behavior involves being a 64-bit backdoor. The target platform is 64-bit systems. Supplementary information indicates it is part of a commercialized cybercrime toolkit.[/profile]
3881.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity is a 64-bit variant of a backdoor malware. It is referenced in the context of other malware families, including SLUB and Daxin, which are also described as 64-bit backdoors. The technical behavior for a related 64-bit variant involves loading a CLR assembly via the CLRCreateInstance Windows API call. No specific aliases, attributed groups, or target platforms are definitively provided in the input data.

3889.name: Desktop Video Capture
3889.uncertain_mes:
An adversary can leverage a computer's peripheral devices (e.g., integrated cameras or webcams) or applications (e.g., video call services) to capture video recordings for the purpose of gathering information. Images may also be captured from devices or applications, potentially in specified intervals, in lieu of video files.

Malware or scripts may be used to interact with the devices through an available API provided by the operating system or an application to capture video or images. Video or image files may be written to disk and exfiltrated later. This technique differs from [Screen Capture](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1113) due to use of specific devices or applications for video recording rather than capturing the victim's screen.

In macOS, there are a few different malware samples that record the user's webcam such as FruitFly and Proton. (Citation: objective-see 2017 review)
3889.profile: [profile]Desktop Video Capture is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1125 under the Collection tactic, applicable to Windows, macOS, and Linux platforms. It involves using malware or scripts to interact with peripheral devices like integrated webcams or video call applications via operating system or application APIs to capture video or still images, which are written to disk for later exfiltration. This technique is distinct from screen capture and has been associated with groups like SILENCE, FIN7, and Ember Bear.[/profile]
3889.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Desktop Video Capture is a technique for gathering information by recording video from a computer's desktop screen. It is distinct from capturing video from peripheral cameras. Adversaries may use native utilities or API calls like `CopyFromScreen`, `xwd`, or `screencapture` to take these captures, often through malware or remote access tools. The captured video files are typically saved to disk for later exfiltration.

3890.name: VNC
3890.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may use [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078) to remotely control machines using Virtual Network Computing (VNC).  VNC is a platform-independent desktop sharing system that uses the RFB (“remote framebuffer”) protocol to enable users to remotely control another computer’s display by relaying the screen, mouse, and keyboard inputs over the network.(Citation: The Remote Framebuffer Protocol)

VNC differs from [Remote Desktop Protocol](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/001) as VNC is screen-sharing software rather than resource-sharing software. By default, VNC uses the system's authentication, but it can be configured to use credentials specific to VNC.(Citation: MacOS VNC software for Remote Desktop)(Citation: VNC Authentication)

Adversaries may abuse VNC to perform malicious actions as the logged-on user such as opening documents, downloading files, and running arbitrary commands. An adversary could use VNC to remotely control and monitor a system to collect data and information to pivot to other systems within the network. Specific VNC libraries/implementations have also been susceptible to brute force attacks and memory usage exploitation.(Citation: Hijacking VNC)(Citation: macOS root VNC login without authentication)(Citation: VNC Vulnerabilities)(Citation: Offensive Security VNC Authentication Check)(Citation: Attacking VNC Servers PentestLab)(Citation: Havana authentication bug)
3890.profile: [profile]VNC, designated as T1021.005 under the Remote Services tactic, is a platform-independent technique for remote control using the RFB protocol to relay screen, keyboard, and mouse inputs. It differs from RDP as screen-sharing software and typically uses system authentication, though it can be configured with dedicated VNC credentials. Adversaries abuse it to perform actions as the logged-on user, such as executing commands and pivoting, and specific implementations have been vulnerable to brute-force attacks and memory exploitation. It has been associated with groups like Gamaredon Group and Fin7 and malware like Carbanak.
3890.profile_without_enhance: [profile]This entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique "Virtual Network Computing (VNC)" (ID: T1021.005) under the Remote Services tactic. It is a platform-independent desktop sharing system that uses the RFB protocol to relay screen, mouse, and keyboard inputs for remote control. Adversaries abuse VNC with valid accounts to perform actions as the logged-on user, such as executing commands and pivoting within a network. It differs from RDP as screen-sharing software and, while defaulting to system authentication, can use VNC-specific credentials. Specific VNC implementations have been susceptible to brute-force attacks and memory exploitation.

3891.name: HTTP Form Grabbing
3891.profile: [profile]HTTP Form Grabbing is a technique for credential theft, aligning with the Input Capture tactic (T1056). It specifically targets data submitted through web forms, such as login pages, by intercepting the HTTP POST request before it is encrypted and sent over the network. This allows adversaries to capture usernames, passwords, and other sensitive information in plaintext. The malware Carbanak is known to utilize this method for financial fraud.[/profile]
3891.profile_without_enhance: [profile]HTTP Form Grabbing is a technique within the broader Input Capture (T1056) tactic of Credential Access. It specifically targets web-based login forms to steal user credentials. Adversaries implement this by injecting malicious code, such as JavaScript, into compromised websites or by using man-in-the-middle proxies to intercept and log the data a user submits through HTTP POST requests. This stolen information is then typically exfiltrated to an attacker-controlled server, often using common web protocols like HTTP/S (T1071.001) to blend with normal traffic.

3892.name: File System Management
3892.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may use a hidden file system to conceal malicious activity from users and security tools. File systems provide a structure to store and access data from physical storage. Typically, a user engages with a file system through applications that allow them to access files and directories, which are an abstraction from their physical location (ex: disk sector). Standard file systems include FAT, NTFS, ext4, and APFS. File systems can also contain other structures, such as the Volume Boot Record (VBR) and Master File Table (MFT) in NTFS.(Citation: MalwareTech VFS Nov 2014)

Adversaries may use their own abstracted file system, separate from the standard file system present on the infected system. In doing so, adversaries can hide the presence of malicious components and file input/output from security tools. Hidden file systems, sometimes referred to as virtual file systems, can be implemented in numerous ways. One implementation would be to store a file system in reserved disk space unused by disk structures or standard file system partitions.(Citation: MalwareTech VFS Nov 2014)(Citation: FireEye Bootkits) Another implementation could be for an adversary to drop their own portable partition image as a file on top of the standard file system.(Citation: ESET ComRAT May 2020) Adversaries may also fragment files across the existing file system structure in non-standard ways.(Citation: Kaspersky Equation QA)
3892.profile: [profile]The technique "Hidden File System" is formally identified as MITRE ATT&CK T1564.005, a sub-technique of Hide Artifacts within the Defense Evasion tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It involves adversaries creating a separate, abstracted file system to conceal malicious components and file I/O from users and security tools. Specific implementations include storing a file system in reserved, unused disk space; dropping a portable partition image file onto the standard file system; or fragmenting files across the existing file system in non-standard ways, as observed in malware like Carbanak and groups like Equation and Strider.
3892.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "File System Management" is a technique where adversaries interact with and manipulate file systems to achieve objectives. This can involve direct access to logical volumes using tools like PowerShell's NinjaCopy to bypass standard file access controls and monitoring, reading and writing files by analyzing file system data structures. Adversaries may also abuse built-in utilities such as vssadmin, wbadmin, or esentutl to create shadow copies or backups of data from system volumes, facilitating data theft or evasion.

3893.name: TCP Tunneling
3893.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may tunnel network communications to and from a victim system within a separate protocol to avoid detection/network filtering and/or enable access to otherwise unreachable systems. Tunneling involves explicitly encapsulating a protocol within another. This behavior may conceal malicious traffic by blending in with existing traffic and/or provide an outer layer of encryption (similar to a VPN). Tunneling could also enable routing of network packets that would otherwise not reach their intended destination, such as SMB, RDP, or other traffic that would be filtered by network appliances or not routed over the Internet. 

There are various means to encapsulate a protocol within another protocol. For example, adversaries may perform SSH tunneling (also known as SSH port forwarding), which involves forwarding arbitrary data over an encrypted SSH tunnel.(Citation: SSH Tunneling)(Citation: Sygnia Abyss Locker 2025) 

[Protocol Tunneling](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1572) may also be abused by adversaries during [Dynamic Resolution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1568). Known as DNS over HTTPS (DoH), queries to resolve C2 infrastructure may be encapsulated within encrypted HTTPS packets.(Citation: BleepingComp Godlua JUL19) 

Adversaries may also leverage [Protocol Tunneling](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1572) in conjunction with [Proxy](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1090) and/or [Protocol or Service Impersonation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1001/003) to further conceal C2 communications and infrastructure.
3893.profile: [profile]TCP Tunneling is a specific implementation of the MITRE ATT&CK technique Protocol Tunneling (T1572) under the Command and Control tactic. It operates across multiple platforms by encapsulating malicious traffic within the TCP protocol to bypass network filtering and detection. This method forwards arbitrary data, such as SMB or RDP packets, within an encrypted outer layer, often using tools like SSH port forwarding to create a covert channel. It is associated with malware like Carbanak and used by threat groups including FIN7 and Oilrig to conceal C2 communications, sometimes in conjunction with proxy techniques.[/profile]
3893.profile_without_enhance: [profile]TCP Tunneling is a specific method of Protocol Tunneling (T1572) under the Command and Control tactic. It operates by encapsulating malicious network traffic within standard TCP packets to bypass network filtering and detection systems. This technique enables adversaries to route otherwise blocked traffic, such as for C2 communications, by blending it with legitimate TCP data streams, often using common ports like 22 (SSH) or 3389 (RDP) to appear as normal activity.

3894.name: HTTP Proxy
3894.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may use a connection proxy to direct network traffic between systems or act as an intermediary for network communications to a command and control server to avoid direct connections to their infrastructure. Many tools exist that enable traffic redirection through proxies or port redirection, including [HTRAN](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0040), ZXProxy, and ZXPortMap. (Citation: Trend Micro APT Attack Tools) Adversaries use these types of proxies to manage command and control communications, reduce the number of simultaneous outbound network connections, provide resiliency in the face of connection loss, or to ride over existing trusted communications paths between victims to avoid suspicion. Adversaries may chain together multiple proxies to further disguise the source of malicious traffic.

Adversaries can also take advantage of routing schemes in Content Delivery Networks (CDNs) to proxy command and control traffic.
3894.profile: [profile]HTTP Proxy is a network proxy technique (MITRE ATT&CK T1090) under the Command and Control tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It directs traffic between systems or to a C2 server via intermediary proxies to avoid direct connections, using tools like HTRAN, ZXProxy, and ZXPortMap for redirection. Adversaries chain multiple proxies or abuse Content Delivery Network (CDN) routing schemes to disguise traffic sources, as seen with groups like APT41 and Volt Typhoon.
3894.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "HTTP Proxy" is a specific implementation of the MITRE ATT&CK technique Proxy (T1090), falling under the Command and Control tactic. It operates across Windows, Linux, and Mac platforms. This technique involves using an HTTP proxy server as an intermediary to relay network traffic between a compromised system and an adversary's command and control infrastructure, thereby masking the true destination of malicious communications. Adversaries may chain multiple proxies or use common ports like TCP/80 to blend with normal web traffic and avoid detection.

3895.name: OS Subversion
3895.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may attempt to dump credentials to obtain account login and credential material, normally in the form of a hash or a clear text password. Credentials can be obtained from OS caches, memory, or structures.(Citation: Brining MimiKatz to Unix) Credentials can then be used to perform [Lateral Movement](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0008) and access restricted information.

Several of the tools mentioned in associated sub-techniques may be used by both adversaries and professional security testers. Additional custom tools likely exist as well.
3895.profile: [profile]OS Credential Dumping (T1003) is a Credential Access technique for Windows, Linux, and macOS. It involves extracting account login material like hashes or plaintext passwords from operating system components such as caches, memory, or security structures. For example, on older macOS systems, adversaries with root access can scan the memory of the `securityd` daemon to find encryption keys and decrypt the user's keychain, obtaining various stored passwords. This technique is used by groups like APT28 and Carbanak malware to facilitate lateral movement.
3895.profile_without_enhance: [profile]OS Subversion is a technique where adversaries compromise the integrity of an operating system's core functions. This can involve modifying or bypassing OS security mechanisms, such as exploiting vulnerabilities in system services like `securityd` on older macOS versions to decrypt cached keychain passwords from memory, thereby gaining unauthorized access to sensitive credentials. The technique targets the operating system platform to undermine its fundamental security controls.

3896.name: POS Data Theft
3896.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may steal monetary resources from targets through extortion, social engineering, technical theft, or other methods aimed at their own financial gain at the expense of the availability of these resources for victims. Financial theft is the ultimate objective of several popular campaign types including extortion by ransomware,(Citation: FBI-ransomware) business email compromise (BEC) and fraud,(Citation: FBI-BEC) "pig butchering,"(Citation: wired-pig butchering) bank hacking,(Citation: DOJ-DPRK Heist) and exploiting cryptocurrency networks.(Citation: BBC-Ronin) 

Adversaries may [Compromise Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1586) to conduct unauthorized transfers of funds.(Citation: Internet crime report 2022) In the case of business email compromise or email fraud, an adversary may utilize [Impersonation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1656) of a trusted entity. Once the social engineering is successful, victims can be deceived into sending money to financial accounts controlled by an adversary.(Citation: FBI-BEC) This creates the potential for multiple victims (i.e., compromised accounts as well as the ultimate monetary loss) in incidents involving financial theft.(Citation: VEC)

Extortion by ransomware may occur, for example, when an adversary demands payment from a victim after [Data Encrypted for Impact](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1486) (Citation: NYT-Colonial) and [Exfiltration](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0010) of data, followed by threatening to leak sensitive data to the public unless payment is made to the adversary.(Citation: Mandiant-leaks) Adversaries may use dedicated leak sites to distribute victim data.(Citation: Crowdstrike-leaks)

Due to the potentially immense business impact of financial theft, an adversary may abuse the possibility of financial theft and seeking monetary gain to divert attention from their true goals such as [Data Destruction](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1485) and business disruption.(Citation: AP-NotPetya)
3896.profile: [profile]POS Data Theft is a specific technique for Financial Theft (T1657) under the Impact tactic, targeting financial systems like Point-of-Sale (POS) terminals. It involves stealing payment card data, often by deploying malware like Carbanak to scrape memory from POS systems or by intercepting data during transaction processing. The stolen data, including track data and PINs, is then exfiltrated for monetization through card fraud.
3896.profile_without_enhance: [profile]POS Data Theft is a technique targeting financial data from Point-of-Sale systems, falling under the Collection tactic. It operates on Windows and POS-specific platforms. Adversaries deploy malware to scrape payment card data from the memory of running POS software, often using RAM scrapers. The stolen data, including track data from magnetic stripes, is then staged locally before exfiltration, typically over a command and control channel or via a USB device for air-gapped networks, to facilitate financial theft.

3897.profile: [profile]Outlook Data Theft is a technique for financial theft, targeting Windows and Microsoft 365 platforms within the Impact tactic. It involves stealing sensitive financial data directly from a user's local Microsoft Outlook client by accessing and exfiltrating offline data files such as .ost or .pst files, which are typically stored in the user's Documents or AppData directories. The malware Carbanak has been associated with this activity.
3897.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Outlook Data Theft is a technique for data collection, likely aligned with T1114.001 (Local Email Collection) under the Collection tactic on Windows platforms. It involves adversaries targeting and exfiltrating sensitive information from a user's local Microsoft Outlook data files, such as .ost or .pst files, which are typically stored in directories like `C:\Users\<username>\Documents\Outlook Files` or `C:\Users\<username>\AppData\Local\Microsoft\Outlook`.

3898.name: Pseudo-HTTP
3898.profile: [profile]Pseudo-HTTP is a technique for adversary command and control (C2) communication, aligning with MITRE ATT&CK Tactic Command and Control (ID: T1071.001). It operates by blending malicious traffic within legitimate web protocols, primarily HTTP/S. The technique conceals commands and data within standard HTTP packet fields and headers to mimic normal traffic and evade network detection. It is associated with malware like Carbanak and numerous threat groups including APT28 and Lazarus Group.
3898.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Pseudo-HTTP is a technique where adversaries communicate using application layer protocols associated with web traffic, such as HTTP/S, to blend in with normal traffic and avoid detection. Commands and their results are embedded within standard protocol traffic, often concealed within various HTTP/S packet fields and headers. This method allows adversaries to mimic expected web communications while maintaining control over compromised systems within a victim network.

3899.name: RC2 Implementation in CBC Mode with PKCS#5 Padding
3899.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may use binary padding to add junk data and change the on-disk representation of malware. This can be done without affecting the functionality or behavior of a binary, but can increase the size of the binary beyond what some security tools are capable of handling due to file size limitations. 

Binary padding effectively changes the checksum of the file and can also be used to avoid hash-based blocklists and static anti-virus signatures.(Citation: ESET OceanLotus) The padding used is commonly generated by a function to create junk data and then appended to the end or applied to sections of malware.(Citation: Securelist Malware Tricks April 2017) Increasing the file size may decrease the effectiveness of certain tools and detection capabilities that are not designed or configured to scan large files. This may also reduce the likelihood of being collected for analysis. Public file scanning services, such as VirusTotal, limits the maximum size of an uploaded file to be analyzed.(Citation: VirusTotal FAQ)
3899.profile: [profile]The entity "RC2 Implementation in CBC Mode with PKCS#5 Padding" is a custom cryptographic implementation. It functions as a specific encryption scheme, using the RC2 algorithm in Cipher Block Chaining (CBC) mode with PKCS#5 padding to obfuscate data, likely for command and control traffic or to protect payloads. This custom protocol can hide communications, and while analysis may reveal the algorithm, its bespoke nature complicates detection. It is associated with the Carbanak malware.
3899.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "RC2 Implementation in CBC Mode with PKCS#5 Padding" is a cryptographic technique, likely associated with the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1024 (Custom Cryptographic Protocol) under the Command and Control tactic. It functions as a specific encryption method where data is encrypted using the RC2 cipher in Cipher Block Chaining (CBC) mode, with PKCS#5 padding applied to ensure the plaintext fits the cipher's block size. This custom implementation can be used to obfuscate command and control traffic, and its use of a known but potentially weak or custom-configured algorithm may introduce vulnerabilities that allow for decryption or analysis if the key is discovered.

3900.name: PHP
3900.profile: [profile]PHP is a server-side scripting language, not a MITRE ATT&CK technique. The retrieved information describes how adversaries misuse PHP. For example, in shared webroot exploitation (T1051), an adversary can upload a PHP script to a web server's open network share, which executes when visited, potentially granting system privileges. PHP files are also used in masquerading (T1036.008), where malicious backdoors are renamed with benign extensions like .gif to evade detection. The Carbanak malware is known to utilize such PHP-based attacks.[/profile]
3900.profile_without_enhance: [profile]PHP is a server-side scripting language and platform, not a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique. Adversaries exploit PHP to execute malicious code on web servers, often for initial access or persistence. This can involve uploading PHP scripts disguised with benign file extensions (e.g., naming a backdoor `test.gif`) to bypass security checks, as seen in Masquerade File Type (T1036.008). PHP scripts can also be placed in a shared webroot directory (T1051) to be executed when visited, enabling lateral movement and remote code execution under the web server's permissions.

3901.name: BML
3901.profile: [profile]BML is a custom command and control protocol (T1094) used for communication, falling under the Command and Control tactic. It is employed by malware such as Carbanak. The protocol operates by mimicking well-known protocols or developing custom protocols on top of standard network stacks like TCP/IP, rather than encapsulating data within existing application layer protocols. This technique allows adversaries to evade detection by avoiding common protocol analysis methods.
3901.profile_without_enhance: [profile]BML is a custom command and control protocol technique (T1094) used in the Command and Control tactic. It operates across Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. Adversaries implement this by developing a unique protocol, which can involve mimicking legitimate protocols or using raw sockets built on top of standard network stacks like TCP/IP, to evade detection that relies on known application layer protocols.

3902.name: CGI
3902.profile: [profile]CGI is a technique where adversaries use web servers' Common Gateway Interface (CGI) for command and control, often by sending malicious HTTP requests to execute commands. It is associated with the Carbanak malware. The technique can be obfuscated by encoding C2 data with schemes like Base64 or MIME (T1132) or by adding junk characters to the traffic (T1001.001) to evade detection.[/profile]
3902.profile_without_enhance: [profile]CGI is a technique for command and control, where adversaries use Common Gateway Interface scripts on web servers to blend malicious communications with legitimate HTTP traffic. This method allows them to send commands and receive outputs through standard web requests, making their activity harder to distinguish from normal web server operations.

3906.name: Continuous Monitoring
3906.profile: [profile]Continuous Monitoring is a technique used by adversaries to persistently observe and gather information from a compromised system. It is associated with the malware Halfbaked, which may employ this behavior. The technique involves establishing long-term presence to track user activity, system changes, or network traffic, enabling ongoing data exfiltration and facilitating further malicious actions without immediate detection.
3906.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Continuous Monitoring is a technique where adversaries persistently observe a target environment to gather intelligence and maintain access. It is associated with the Discovery tactic and primarily targets Windows platforms. The technique can involve mechanisms like Image File Execution Options (IFEO) to attach debuggers or monitor processes, enabling persistence through continuous invocation when a specified program exits, as seen in registry modifications that launch a malicious executable like 'evil.exe' upon notepad.exe termination.

3907.name: File Management Capabilities
3907.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may upload, install, or otherwise set up capabilities that can be used during targeting. To support their operations, an adversary may need to take capabilities they developed ([Develop Capabilities](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1587)) or obtained ([Obtain Capabilities](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1588)) and stage them on infrastructure under their control. These capabilities may be staged on infrastructure that was previously purchased/rented by the adversary ([Acquire Infrastructure](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1583)) or was otherwise compromised by them ([Compromise Infrastructure](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1584)). Capabilities may also be staged on web services, such as GitHub or Pastebin, or on Platform-as-a-Service (PaaS) offerings that enable users to easily provision applications.(Citation: Volexity Ocean Lotus November 2020)(Citation: Dragos Heroku Watering Hole)(Citation: Malwarebytes Heroku Skimmers)(Citation: Netskope GCP Redirection)(Citation: Netskope Cloud Phishing)

Staging of capabilities can aid the adversary in a number of initial access and post-compromise behaviors, including (but not limited to):

* Staging web resources necessary to conduct [Drive-by Compromise](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1189) when a user browses to a site.(Citation: FireEye CFR Watering Hole 2012)(Citation: Gallagher 2015)(Citation: ATT ScanBox)
* Staging web resources for a link target to be used with spearphishing.(Citation: Malwarebytes Silent Librarian October 2020)(Citation: Proofpoint TA407 September 2019)
* Uploading malware or tools to a location accessible to a victim network to enable [Ingress Tool Transfer](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1105).(Citation: Volexity Ocean Lotus November 2020)
* Installing a previously acquired SSL/TLS certificate to use to encrypt command and control traffic (ex: [Asymmetric Cryptography](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1573/002) with [Web Protocols](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1071/001)).(Citation: DigiCert Install SSL Cert)
3907.profile: [profile]Stage Capabilities is a technique with the MITRE ATT&CK ID T1608, falling under the Resource Development tactic and applicable across multiple platforms. It involves adversaries uploading, installing, or setting up their developed or obtained tools on infrastructure they control, such as purchased servers, compromised systems, or web services like GitHub and Pastebin. This staging supports various attack phases, including preparing web resources for drive-by compromises or spearphishing links, uploading malware for later transfer into victim networks, and installing SSL/TLS certificates to encrypt command and control traffic. The malware Halfbaked has been associated with this behavior.[/profile]
3907.profile_without_enhance: [profile]File Management Capabilities is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the retrieved context, it appears to describe a general adversary capability for uploading, installing, and staging tools or malware on infrastructure under their control to support operations. This activity is preparatory and can aid in various subsequent behaviors like Drive-by Compromise or Ingress Tool Transfer. The capability itself is not a specific technique but a foundational action that enables other, more defined ATT&CK techniques.

3908.name: 34 Commands
3908.profile: [profile]34 Commands is a technique used by adversaries to execute malicious actions, as seen with the Halfbaked malware. It aligns with the MITRE ATT&CK framework under T1059 (Command and Scripting Interpreter) within the Execution tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. The technique involves abusing command-line interfaces like Unix Shell (T1059.004) to run arbitrary commands or scripts, often delivered via initial access payloads or remote services. Adversaries may impair command history logging (T1562.003) by manipulating environment variables such as HISTFILE or using PowerShell settings to hide their activities, thereby evading detection.
3908.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "34 Commands" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the retrieved information, it appears to be a non-standard reference, potentially to a specific set of commands. The related content describes the general technique of abusing command and scripting interpreters (T1059), which involves using built-in system interfaces like Unix Shell (T1059.004) or Windows Command Shell to execute arbitrary commands, scripts, or binaries for execution. Adversaries deliver these commands in payloads or through interactive shells, and may attempt to impair command history logging (T1562.003) on Linux, macOS, or Windows systems to hide their activity by manipulating environment variables or PowerShell settings.

3909.name: State
3909.profile: [profile]State is a technique associated with the malware Halfbaked. The retrieved context describes TCP state-exhaustion attacks, such as SYN floods and ACK floods, which exhaust a system's OS-imposed limits on concurrent TCP connections or overwhelm its state table with rogue packets, causing sluggishness or unresponsiveness. This is a denial-of-service mechanism targeting network services.
3909.profile_without_enhance: [profile]State is a technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, specifically identified as a sub-technique of T1499: Endpoint Denial of Service. It falls under the Impact tactic and primarily targets Network platforms. The technique involves TCP state-exhaustion attacks, such as SYN floods where excessive SYN packets are sent without completing the TCP handshake to exhaust a system's maximum concurrent connection limit, and ACK floods where non-existent connection ACK packets force the OS to exhaustively search its state table, consuming computational resources and causing sluggishness or unresponsiveness in the targeted service.

3910.name: LoadConfig
3910.profile: [profile]LoadConfig is a technique used by adversaries to maintain persistence or execute code during system boot. It is associated with the malware Halfbaked. The technique involves manipulating system configuration files or boot processes to automatically run malicious programs. For example, adversaries can hide code in files like rc.common on macOS, which executes on each reboot as root, or access network device configuration files to export settings for later use. This allows the malicious activity to restart with the system, ensuring continued access.
3910.profile_without_enhance: [profile]LoadConfig is a technique for persistence where adversaries manipulate system configuration files to automatically execute malicious code during boot or logon. It operates on macOS and Linux platforms and falls under the Privilege Escalation and Persistence tactics. Specifically, on macOS, adversaries can inject code into the /etc/rc.common shell script, which is executed as root during the boot process, to establish persistence. This method is considered deprecated in favor of launch agents but is still utilized in malware.

3911.name: Toshliph
3911.profile: [profile]Toshliph, also known as Win32/Toshliph or Win32/Spy.Agent.ORM, is a trojan attributed to the Carbanak (Anunak) criminal gang. It functions as a first-stage payload and shares code similarities with other Carbanak malware. A testing version of its binary was signed with a Blik certificate. It targets the Windows platform and is directly related to the DriftPin malware.
3911.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Toshliph, also known as Win32/Toshliph and Spy.Agent.ORM, is a malware associated with the Anunak group and the Carbanak gang. It is used as a first-stage payload in spear phishing campaigns, particularly targeting Russian and Eastern European banks, and is linked to the CARBANAK backdoor in these operations. The testing version of its binary was signed with a Blik certificate.[/profile]

3912.name: Run Process
3912.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may carry out malicious operations using a virtual instance to avoid detection. A wide variety of virtualization technologies exist that allow for the emulation of a computer or computing environment. By running malicious code inside of a virtual instance, adversaries can hide artifacts associated with their behavior from security tools that are unable to monitor activity inside the virtual instance.(Citation: CyberCX Akira Ransomware) Additionally, depending on the virtual networking implementation (ex: bridged adapter), network traffic generated by the virtual instance can be difficult to trace back to the compromised host as the IP address and hostname might not match known values.(Citation: SingHealth Breach Jan 2019)

Adversaries may utilize native support for virtualization (ex: Hyper-V), deploy lightweight emulators (ex: QEMU), or drop the necessary files to run a virtual instance (ex: VirtualBox binaries).(Citation: Securonix CronTrap 2024) After running a virtual instance, adversaries may create a shared folder between the guest and host with permissions that enable the virtual instance to interact with the host file system.(Citation: Sophos Ragnar May 2020)

Threat actors may also leverage temporary virtualized environments such as the Windows Sandbox, which supports the use of `.wsb` configuration files for defining execution parameters. For example, the `<MappedFolder>` property supports the creation of a shared folder, while the `<LogonCommand>` property allows the specification of a payload.(Citation: ESET MirrorFace 2025)(Citation: ITOCHU Hack the Sandbox)(Citation: ITOCHU Sandbox PPT)

In VMWare environments, adversaries may leverage the vCenter console to create new virtual machines. However, they may also create virtual machines directly on ESXi servers by running a valid `.vmx` file with the `/bin/vmx` utility. Adding this command to `/etc/rc.local.d/local.sh` (i.e., [RC Scripts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1037/004)) will cause the VM to persistently restart.(Citation: vNinja Rogue VMs 2024) Creating a VM this way prevents it from appearing in the vCenter console or in the output to the `vim-cmd vmsvc/getallvms` command on the ESXi server, thereby hiding it from typical administrative activities.(Citation: MITRE VMware Abuse 2024)
3912.profile: [profile]The entity "Run Process" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the provided data, the described behavior aligns with the MITRE technique "Run Virtual Instance" (T1564.006) under the Defense Evasion tactic, primarily targeting Windows, Linux, and ESXi platforms. The technique involves executing malicious code within a virtualized environment like Hyper-V, QEMU, or VirtualBox to hide artifacts from host-based security tools. Specific implementations include using Windows Sandbox `.wsb` configuration files with `<LogonCommand>` for payloads or creating hidden VMs on ESXi servers by executing a `.vmx` file with `/bin/vmx` and adding the command to `/etc/rc.local.d/local.sh` for persistence, which prevents the VM from appearing in standard administrative consoles. The intrusion-set FIN7 is associated with this behavior.[/profile]
3912.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Run Process is a foundational technique for executing code, often mapped to MITRE ATT&CK ID T1059 (Execution). It falls under the Execution tactic and operates across Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. The core technical mechanic involves adversaries using system utilities, command-line interpreters, or APIs to start new processes, which can be leveraged to run malicious payloads, scripts, or legitimate tools for further attack actions. This basic execution method is a prerequisite for many other, more sophisticated techniques like Process Injection.

3913.name: Browser Information Discovery
3913.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may enumerate information about browsers to learn more about compromised environments. Data saved by browsers (such as bookmarks, accounts, and browsing history) may reveal a variety of personal information about users (e.g., banking sites, relationships/interests, social media, etc.) as well as details about internal network resources such as servers, tools/dashboards, or other related infrastructure.(Citation: Kaspersky Autofill)

Browser information may also highlight additional targets after an adversary has access to valid credentials, especially [Credentials In Files](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1552/001) associated with logins cached by a browser.

Specific storage locations vary based on platform and/or application, but browser information is typically stored in local files and databases (e.g., `%APPDATA%/Google/Chrome`).(Citation: Chrome Roaming Profiles)
3913.profile: [profile]Browser Information Discovery is the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1217 under the Discovery tactic, applicable to Windows, macOS, and Linux platforms. It involves adversaries enumerating data saved by browsers, such as bookmarks, accounts, browsing history, and cached credentials, to gather personal user information and details about internal network resources. This information is typically stored in local files and databases, for example in the path `%APPDATA%/Google/Chrome`. The technique has been used by groups including Chimera, APT38, Fox Kitten, Scattered Spider, Moonstone Sleet, and Volt Typhoon.[/profile]
3913.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Browser Information Discovery is identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1217 under the Discovery tactic, applicable to Windows, macOS, and Linux platforms. It involves adversaries enumerating browser data like bookmarks, accounts, and browsing history stored in local files and databases, such as `%APPDATA%/Google/Chrome`, to gather personal information and details about internal network resources. This information can reveal credentials cached by the browser and highlight additional targets for follow-on actions.

3914.name: Post-Exploitation Tool
3914.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may buy, steal, or download software tools that can be used during targeting. Tools can be open or closed source, free or commercial. A tool can be used for malicious purposes by an adversary, but (unlike malware) were not intended to be used for those purposes (ex: [PsExec](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0029)). 

Adversaries may obtain tools to support their operations, including to support execution of post-compromise behaviors. Tools may also be leveraged for testing – for example, evaluating malware against commercial antivirus or endpoint detection and response (EDR) applications.(Citation: Forescout Conti Leaks 2022)(Citation: Sentinel Labs Top Tier Target 2025)

Tool acquisition may involve the procurement of commercial software licenses, including for red teaming tools such as Cobalt Strike. In addition to freely downloading or purchasing software, adversaries may steal software and/or software licenses from third-party entities (including other adversaries). Threat actors may also crack trial versions of software.(Citation: Recorded Future Beacon 2019)
3914.profile: [profile]The entity "Post-Exploitation Tool" is a general concept rather than a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the provided context, it relates to the acquisition of software tools (T1588.002 - Obtain Capability: Tool) for use after initial compromise. Adversaries obtain these tools, which are legitimate but repurposed for malicious post-exploitation activities like lateral movement or defense evasion, through purchasing, stealing, downloading, or cracking licenses, with examples including commercial red teaming frameworks. Groups like FIN7 and DeepPanda are associated with this behavior.[/profile]
3914.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Post-Exploitation Tool is a general term for any software utility, often legitimate, that adversaries acquire and use after initial compromise to facilitate malicious activities. These tools, which can be purchased, stolen, or downloaded, are not inherently malicious but are repurposed to support operations like lateral movement, data obfuscation, log clearing, and maintaining command and control channels. They are employed across various platforms to execute post-compromise behaviors, including transferring files between systems and exploiting vulnerabilities for persistence and defense evasion.[/profile]

3915.name: Video Commands
3915.uncertain_mes:
An adversary can leverage a computer's peripheral devices (e.g., integrated cameras or webcams) or applications (e.g., video call services) to capture video recordings for the purpose of gathering information. Images may also be captured from devices or applications, potentially in specified intervals, in lieu of video files.

Malware or scripts may be used to interact with the devices through an available API provided by the operating system or an application to capture video or images. Video or image files may be written to disk and exfiltrated later. This technique differs from [Screen Capture](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1113) due to use of specific devices or applications for video recording rather than capturing the victim's screen.

In macOS, there are a few different malware samples that record the user's webcam such as FruitFly and Proton. (Citation: objective-see 2017 review)
3915.profile: [profile]Video Capture, designated as T1125 under the Collection tactic, operates across Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves malware or scripts using operating system or application APIs to interact with peripheral devices like integrated cameras or webcams to record video or capture images, often at specified intervals. The captured files are written to disk for later exfiltration, distinguishing it from screen capture techniques. Groups like FIN7, SILENCE, and Ember Bear have been associated with this technique, and macOS malware samples such as FruitFly and Proton demonstrate its implementation.
3915.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Video Commands is a technique for gathering information by leveraging a computer's peripheral devices or applications to capture video recordings. Malware or scripts interact with devices through available APIs to record video, with files written to disk for later exfiltration. This differs from screen capture as it uses specific hardware like integrated cameras or software like video call services.

3917.name: Tunneling Commands
3917.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may tunnel network communications to and from a victim system within a separate protocol to avoid detection/network filtering and/or enable access to otherwise unreachable systems. Tunneling involves explicitly encapsulating a protocol within another. This behavior may conceal malicious traffic by blending in with existing traffic and/or provide an outer layer of encryption (similar to a VPN). Tunneling could also enable routing of network packets that would otherwise not reach their intended destination, such as SMB, RDP, or other traffic that would be filtered by network appliances or not routed over the Internet. 

There are various means to encapsulate a protocol within another protocol. For example, adversaries may perform SSH tunneling (also known as SSH port forwarding), which involves forwarding arbitrary data over an encrypted SSH tunnel.(Citation: SSH Tunneling)(Citation: Sygnia Abyss Locker 2025) 

[Protocol Tunneling](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1572) may also be abused by adversaries during [Dynamic Resolution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1568). Known as DNS over HTTPS (DoH), queries to resolve C2 infrastructure may be encapsulated within encrypted HTTPS packets.(Citation: BleepingComp Godlua JUL19) 

Adversaries may also leverage [Protocol Tunneling](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1572) in conjunction with [Proxy](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1090) and/or [Protocol or Service Impersonation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1001/003) to further conceal C2 communications and infrastructure.
3917.profile: [profile]Protocol Tunneling, identified as MITRE ATT&CK T1572, is a Command and Control tactic applicable across multiple platforms. It works by explicitly encapsulating one network protocol within another, such as performing SSH port forwarding or using DNS over HTTPS (DoH), to conceal malicious traffic, bypass network filtering, and route otherwise blocked protocols like SMB or RDP. This technique is often used in conjunction with proxy methods and is associated with threat groups including FIN7, Oilrig, and Scattered Spider.
3917.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Tunneling Commands is a technique for command and control (C2) where adversaries encapsulate malicious commands and data within the traffic of an allowed protocol to evade detection. This is achieved by performing protocol tunneling, such as SSH port forwarding or DNS over HTTPS (DoH), to forward arbitrary data through an encrypted channel. The method blends malicious communications with legitimate network traffic, often in conjunction with proxy or multilayer encryption techniques, to conceal C2 infrastructure and bypass network filtering.

3918.name: Shim Databases (SDB)
3918.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may leverage databases to mine valuable information. These databases may be hosted on-premises or in the cloud (both in platform-as-a-service and software-as-a-service environments). 

Examples of databases from which information may be collected include MySQL, PostgreSQL, MongoDB, Amazon Relational Database Service, Azure SQL Database, Google Firebase, and Snowflake. Databases may include a variety of information of interest to adversaries, such as usernames, hashed passwords, personally identifiable information, and financial data. Data collected from databases may be used for [Lateral Movement](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0008), [Command and Control](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0011), or [Exfiltration](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0010). Data exfiltrated from databases may also be used to extort victims or may be sold for profit.(Citation: Google Cloud Threat Intelligence UNC5537 Snowflake 2024)
3918.profile: [profile]The entity "Shim Databases (SDB)" is a technique for persistence and privilege escalation, formally known as Application Shimming (T1546.011) under the Persistence tactic on Windows. The technique involves installing a custom shim database (.sdb file) using the sdbinst.exe tool, which acts as a buffer between applications and the OS. When a targeted program executes, the shim database uses hooking to redirect code, enabling malicious acts like UAC bypass, DLL injection, or disabling security features such as Data Execution Prevention. Custom databases are stored in directories like %WINDIR%\AppPatch\custom and require administrator privileges to install, with the FIN7 group linked to its use.[/profile]
3918.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Shim Databases (SDB) is a component of the Windows Application Compatibility Framework, referenced in MITRE ATT&CK as part of technique T1546.011 (Application Shimming) under the Persistence tactic for Windows platforms. The .sdb file acts as a buffer, using hooking to redirect program code when executed. Adversaries with administrator privileges can install malicious custom shim databases to perform actions like privilege escalation, UAC bypass via RedirectEXE, DLL injection via InjectDLL, or disabling security features like Data Execution Prevention. These databases are stored in %WINDIR%\AppPatch\custom and corresponding registry keys.

3919.name: Power Admin PaExec
3919.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may impair a system's ability to hibernate, reboot, or shut down in order to extend access to infected machines. When a computer enters a dormant state, some or all software and hardware may cease to operate which can disrupt malicious activity.(Citation: Sleep, shut down, hibernate)

Adversaries may abuse system utilities and configuration settings to maintain access by preventing machines from entering a state, such as standby, that can terminate malicious activity.(Citation: Microsoft: Powercfg command-line options)(Citation: systemdsleep Linux)

For example, `powercfg` controls all configurable power system settings on a Windows system and can be abused to prevent an infected host from locking or shutting down.(Citation: Two New Monero Malware Attacks Target Windows and Android Users) Adversaries may also extend system lock screen timeout settings.(Citation: BATLOADER: The Evasive Downloader Malware) Other relevant settings, such as disk and hibernate timeout, can be similarly abused to keep the infected machine running even if no user is active.(Citation: CoinLoader: A Sophisticated Malware Loader Campaign)

Aware that some malware cannot survive system reboots, adversaries may entirely delete files used to invoke system shut down or reboot.(Citation: Condi-Botnet-binaries)
3919.profile: [profile]The entity "Power Admin PaExec" is a tool used for remote execution, likely aligning with MITRE ATT&CK technique T1569.002 (Service Execution) under the Execution tactic on Windows platforms. It functions as a legitimate system administration utility that adversaries abuse to execute commands or payloads on remote systems, often by leveraging administrative shares and valid credentials for lateral movement. The intrusion-set FIN7 has been associated with its use. This tool enables execution without dropping files by directly running commands through a service or process on a target machine.
3919.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Power Admin PaExec is a technique for remote execution, likely aligning with MITRE ATT&CK's T1569.002 (Service Execution) under the Execution tactic on Windows platforms. It involves using the legitimate PaExec utility to run commands or payloads on remote systems, often by leveraging administrative shares (like C$ or ADMIN$) and valid credentials for lateral movement. This tool can execute processes remotely without requiring interactive logon, making it a method for indirect command execution and evasion of security controls that monitor standard remote administration tools.

3921.name: AES-256
3921.profile: [profile]AES-256 is a symmetric encryption algorithm referenced in MITRE ATT&CK techniques T1573.001 (Encrypted Channel: Symmetric Cryptography) and T1048.001 (Exfiltration Over Symmetric Encrypted Non-C2 Protocol). It is used within the Command and Control and Exfiltration tactics. Adversaries employ it to manually encrypt C2 or exfiltration traffic, often layering it over standard protocols like HTTPS to conceal data. The malware Carbanak is associated with its use.[/profile]
3921.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity 'AES-256' is a specific implementation of the symmetric encryption algorithm referenced in MITRE ATT&CK techniques. It is used within the broader techniques T1573.001 (Encrypted Channel: Symmetric Cryptography) for command and control obfuscation and T1048.001 (Exfiltration Over Symmetric Encrypted Non-C2 Protocol) for data theft. The technical mechanism involves using a 256-bit key for both encryption and decryption, allowing adversaries to manually apply this strong encryption to network traffic, potentially creating multiple layers of encryption on top of standard protocols like HTTPS or HTTP.

3922.name: RSA Key Exchange
3922.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may reduce the level of effort required to decrypt data transmitted over the network by reducing the cipher strength of encrypted communications.(Citation: Cisco Synful Knock Evolution)

Adversaries can weaken the encryption software on a compromised network device by reducing the key size used by the software to convert plaintext to ciphertext (e.g., from hundreds or thousands of bytes to just a couple of bytes). As a result, adversaries dramatically reduce the amount of effort needed to decrypt the protected information without the key.

Adversaries may modify the key size used and other encryption parameters using specialized commands in a [Network Device CLI](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/008) introduced to the system through [Modify System Image](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1601) to change the configuration of the device. (Citation: Cisco Blog Legacy Device Attacks)
3922.profile: [profile]The entity "RSA Key Exchange" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the provided context, it is best described by the technique "Reduce Key Space" (T1600.001) under the Impact tactic, targeting Network Devices. This technique involves adversaries weakening encryption on a compromised network device by reducing the cryptographic key size, for example from hundreds of bytes to just a few, drastically lowering the effort required for decryption. Modification is typically performed using specialized commands in a Network Device CLI, often introduced via a modified system image. The malware Carbanak has been associated with this activity.
3922.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "RSA Key Exchange" is a network encryption technique, likely corresponding to MITRE ATT&CK technique T1573.002 (Asymmetric Cryptography) under the Command and Control tactic. It operates across multiple platforms and involves using the RSA algorithm to establish a secure communication channel. In this process, a sender encrypts a session key or data with the receiver's public key, which can only be decrypted with the corresponding private key. This method is fundamental for securing initial connections in protocols like SSL/TLS, ensuring that only the intended recipient can access the transmitted information. A related indicator is the "RSA Private Key," which is the critical secret component needed to decrypt such exchanges.

3923.name: Compression
3923.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may use compression to obfuscate their payloads or files. Compressed file formats such as ZIP, gzip, 7z, and RAR can compress and archive multiple files together to make it easier and faster to transfer files. In addition to compressing files, adversaries may also compress shellcode directly - for example, in order to store it in a Windows Registry key (i.e., [Fileless Storage](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/011)).(Citation: Trustwave Pillowmint June 2020)

In order to further evade detection, adversaries may combine multiple ZIP files into one archive. This process of concatenation creates an archive that appears to be a single archive but in fact contains the central directories of the embedded archives. Some ZIP readers, such as 7zip, may not be able to identify concatenated ZIP files and miss the presence of the malicious payload.(Citation: Perception Point)

File archives may be sent as one [Spearphishing Attachment](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001) through email. Adversaries have sent malicious payloads as archived files to encourage the user to interact with and extract the malicious payload onto their system (i.e., [Malicious File](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002)).(Citation: NTT Security Flagpro new December 2021) However, some file compression tools, such as 7zip, can be used to produce self-extracting archives. Adversaries may send self-extracting archives to hide the functionality of their payload and launch it without requiring multiple actions from the user.(Citation: The Hacker News)

[Compression](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/015) may be used in combination with [Encrypted/Encoded File](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/013) where compressed files are encrypted and password-protected.
3923.profile: [profile]Compression is a sub-technique of Obfuscated Files or Information (T1027.015) under the Defense Evasion tactic, primarily used on Windows platforms. It involves using common formats like ZIP, gzip, 7z, and RAR to obfuscate payloads or files, including compressing shellcode for storage in locations like the Windows Registry. For further evasion, adversaries may concatenate multiple ZIP files into a single archive that some readers cannot properly parse. This technique is often delivered via spearphishing attachments or as self-extracting archives to minimize user interaction and is frequently combined with encryption. Associated groups include Gamaredon Group and Turla, and it has been used with malware like Carbanak.[/profile]
3923.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Compression is identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1027.015 under the Defense Evasion tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. It involves adversaries using tools like ZIP, gzip, 7z, or RAR to obfuscate payloads and files, often to facilitate transfer and evade detection. Specific mechanics include compressing shellcode for fileless storage in the Windows Registry, concatenating multiple ZIP files into a single archive to bypass some readers, and creating self-extracting archives to minimize user interaction. This technique is frequently associated with groups like Gamaredon Group and Leviathan, and is used in combination with other evasion methods such as encryption.

3924.name: Message Chunking
3924.profile: [profile]Message Chunking is a technique for Exfiltration (T1030). It involves breaking data into fixed-size chunks or limiting packet sizes during transfer to avoid detection by network monitoring thresholds that trigger on large data transfers. This method is used by threat groups like APT28 and APT41. The malware Carbanak is associated with this technique.
3924.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Message Chunking is a technique for data exfiltration where adversaries transfer data in fixed-size chunks or limit packet sizes to stay below network monitoring thresholds, thereby avoiding detection. This method is used to circumvent alerts triggered by large data transfers.

3928.name: Protocol Evolution
3928.profile: [profile]Protocol Evolution is a command and control (C2) technique where adversaries modify their communication protocols to evade detection. It involves changing protocol versions, such as shifting between versions 3 and 4, or altering encryption methods and packet structures over time. This evolution is used by malware like Carbanak to maintain stealth and persistence by making network traffic appear legitimate or by bypassing signature-based security tools that rely on static protocol analysis.
3928.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Protocol Evolution is a technique within the Command and Control tactic, identified as T1071.001, targeting multiple platforms. It involves adversaries modifying their C2 communications to use different application layer protocols (such as HTTP, HTTPS, FTP, or SMTP) over time to blend with normal traffic and avoid static network-based detection. This evolution can include switching between standard and non-standard ports or altering protocol-specific fields and behaviors to bypass signature-based defenses.

3929.name: Version 3
3929.profile: [profile]The entity "Version 3" is likely a placeholder or generic name and cannot be definitively mapped to a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique ID or Tactic based on the provided data. The retrieved information describes a downgrade attack technique (T1562.010, Impair Defenses), where adversaries may execute a previous, less-secure version of a tool, such as using PowerShell version 2 or 3 to bypass Script Block Logging present in version 5+. This technique exploits backward compatibility to disable security controls. It is connected to the attack pattern "Protocol Evolution".
3929.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Version 3 is a command and control technique (Tactic: Command and Control) where adversaries modify communication protocols to evade detection, specifically by shifting to a new protocol version. This technique is related to Protocol Evolution, which involves changing versions or encryption within a protocol family. The primary technical mechanic is the alteration of the protocol version itself, such as malware updating its C2 channel to use "Version 3" of a custom protocol to bypass security signatures that monitor for older versions.[/profile]

3930.name: Activity Code
3930.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may employ various user activity checks to detect and avoid virtualization and analysis environments. This may include changing behaviors based on the results of checks for the presence of artifacts indicative of a virtual machine environment (VME) or sandbox. If the adversary detects a VME, they may alter their malware to disengage from the victim or conceal the core functions of the implant. They may also search for VME artifacts before dropping secondary or additional payloads. Adversaries may use the information learned from [Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1497) during automated discovery to shape follow-on behaviors.(Citation: Deloitte Environment Awareness)

Adversaries may search for user activity on the host based on variables such as the speed/frequency of mouse movements and clicks (Citation: Sans Virtual Jan 2016) , browser history, cache, bookmarks, or number of files in common directories such as home or the desktop. Other methods may rely on specific user interaction with the system before the malicious code is activated, such as waiting for a document to close before activating a macro (Citation: Unit 42 Sofacy Nov 2018) or waiting for a user to double click on an embedded image to activate.(Citation: FireEye FIN7 April 2017)
3930.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique "User Activity Based Checks" (ID: T1497.002), a sub-technique of Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion under the Defense Evasion tactic, primarily targeting Windows and Linux platforms. It operates by malware checking for indicators of a virtual or sandboxed environment, such as analyzing mouse movement speed, browser history, or file counts in common directories. The malware may also wait for specific user interactions, like a document closing or an image double-click, before activating its payload to avoid detection in automated analysis systems. Associated threat groups include FIN7 and DarkHotel.[/profile]
3930.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Activity Code is a technique where adversaries embed malicious code within legitimate documents or files, often using macros or scripts, to evade detection and execute unauthorized actions. It operates under the Defense Evasion tactic, primarily targeting Windows systems. The method involves hiding malicious activity by blending with normal user actions, such as waiting for specific interactions like document closures before activating payloads, thereby increasing stealth and persistence.

3931.name: Lie Dormant
3931.profile: [profile]Lie Dormant is a technique where adversaries impair a system's ability to hibernate, reboot, or shut down to maintain persistent access. They abuse system utilities and configuration settings, such as using the Windows `powercfg` command to prevent a host from locking or shutting down, or extending lock screen and disk timeout settings. Some adversaries may delete files required for system shutdown to ensure malware survives reboots. This technique is used by groups like FIN7 to keep infected machines active and extend malicious operations.
3931.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Lie Dormant is a technique adversaries use to extend access to infected machines by impairing a system's ability to hibernate, reboot, or shut down, as entering a dormant state can disrupt malicious activity. This is achieved by abusing system utilities and configuration settings, such as using the Windows `powercfg` command to prevent a host from locking or shutting down, or by extending system lock screen and disk timeout settings. In some cases, adversaries may delete files used to invoke a system reboot to ensure malware persistence.

3933.name: Attack Techniques
3933.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may downgrade or use a version of system features that may be outdated, vulnerable, and/or does not support updated security controls. Downgrade attacks typically take advantage of a system’s backward compatibility to force it into less secure modes of operation. 

Adversaries may downgrade and use various less-secure versions of features of a system, such as [Command and Scripting Interpreter](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059)s or even network protocols that can be abused to enable [Adversary-in-the-Middle](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1557) or [Network Sniffing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1040).(Citation: Praetorian TLS Downgrade Attack 2014) For example, [PowerShell](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001) versions 5+ includes Script Block Logging (SBL), which can record executed script content. However, adversaries may attempt to execute a previous version of PowerShell that does not support SBL with the intent to [Impair Defenses](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1562) while running malicious scripts that may have otherwise been detected.(Citation: CrowdStrike BGH Ransomware 2021)(Citation: Mandiant BYOL 2018)(Citation: att_def_ps_logging)

Adversaries may similarly target network traffic to downgrade from an encrypted HTTPS connection to an unsecured HTTP connection that exposes network data in clear text.(Citation: Targeted SSL Stripping Attacks Are Real)(Citation: Crowdstrike Downgrade) On Windows systems, adversaries may downgrade the boot manager to a vulnerable version that bypasses Secure Boot, granting the ability to disable various operating system security mechanisms.(Citation: SafeBreach)
3933.profile: [profile]Downgrade Attack, identified as T1562.010 under the Defense Evasion tactic, targets Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It exploits system backward compatibility to force less secure modes of operation, such as executing older PowerShell versions to bypass Script Block Logging or downgrading HTTPS connections to unencrypted HTTP to facilitate network sniffing. The technique is used by groups like FIN7 to impair security controls.[/profile]
3933.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Attack Techniques" is a generic placeholder lacking a specific MITRE ATT&CK mapping. Based on the retrieved information, it may broadly encompass various adversarial methods. These include downgrade attacks (T1562.010) to use less secure system features, reflection amplification (T1498.002) for network denial-of-service, adding junk data (T1001.001) to obscure command and control traffic, and exploiting software vulnerabilities (T1212) to gain access to credentials.

3934.name: Malware Obfuscation
3934.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may develop malware and malware components that can be used during targeting. Building malicious software can include the development of payloads, droppers, post-compromise tools, backdoors (including backdoored images), packers, C2 protocols, and the creation of infected removable media. Adversaries may develop malware to support their operations, creating a means for maintaining control of remote machines, evading defenses, and executing post-compromise behaviors.(Citation: Mandiant APT1)(Citation: Kaspersky Sofacy)(Citation: ActiveMalwareEnergy)(Citation: FBI Flash FIN7 USB)

During malware development, adversaries may intentionally include indicators aligned with other known actors in order to mislead attribution by defenders.(Citation: Olympic Destroyer)(Citation: Risky Bulletin Threat actor impersonates FSB APT)(Citation: GamaCopy organization)

As with legitimate development efforts, different skill sets may be required for developing malware. The skills needed may be located in-house, or may need to be contracted out. Use of a contractor may be considered an extension of that adversary's malware development capabilities, provided the adversary plays a role in shaping requirements and maintains a degree of exclusivity to the malware.

Some aspects of malware development, such as C2 protocol development, may require adversaries to obtain additional infrastructure. For example, malware developed that will communicate with Twitter for C2, may require use of [Web Services](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1583/006).(Citation: FireEye APT29)
3934.profile: [profile]Malware Obfuscation is a sub-technique of T1027 (Obfuscated Files or Information) within the Defense Evasion tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. It involves modifying malicious software to hinder detection and analysis, using methods such as encryption, encoding, and software packing to conceal payloads, strings, and command structures. This technique is employed by groups like FIN7 to evade signature-based defenses and complicate forensic investigations.[/profile]
3934.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Malware Obfuscation, corresponding to MITRE ATT&CK technique T1027 (Obfuscated Files or Information) under the Defense Evasion tactic for Windows, Linux, and macOS, involves making malicious files difficult to detect or analyze. This is achieved by encrypting, encoding, or compressing payloads, sometimes splitting them into benign-seeming components that only reveal malicious functionality when reassembled. The technique also includes obfuscating command strings within scripts or during execution to evade signature-based detection.

3936.name: Fileless Malware
3936.uncertain_mes:
A .NET rat targets Mongolia
A new document royal road v7 installs a backdoor in .NET. a first executable is dropped \os03C2.tmp. This exe has many similarities with older campaigns using by Operation LagTime or Tonto Team.
Document
The decoy document is a document about infection of covid19 in Russia send to the Mongolia Authorities. The document is fake signed A. Amarsaikhan.
3936.profile: [profile]Fileless Malware, also referenced as nmass malware, is a .NET-based Remote Access Trojan (RAT) attributed to the FIN7 intrusion set. It employs a fileless infection chain, often initiated via a malicious Royal Road v7 document that drops an initial executable (e.g., \os03C2.tmp) to install a backdoor. The malware uses decoy documents, such as one falsely about COVID-19 in Russia targeting Mongolian authorities with a fake signature from A. Amarsaikhan, and shares similarities with campaigns linked to Operation LagTime or Tonto Team. Its primary target platform is Windows systems.
3936.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Fileless Malware, also known as JS_POWMET, is a type of malware that employs a completely fileless infection chain to evade detection. It is associated with the criminal group Monty Spider. Its key technical behavior is executing malicious code directly in memory without writing files to disk, making forensic analysis difficult. It primarily targets Windows systems. This malware is often delivered through malicious documents, such as those using the Royal Road template, and can be part of campaigns like those attributed to Operation LagTime or Tonto Team.

3940.name: JScript
3940.profile: [profile]JScript is a scripting language used by threat actors like FIN7 and TA505 as a component or dropper within malware campaigns. It is employed in obfuscated scripts, such as in the MirrorBlast macro, and serves as a dropper module for malware like Astaroth. The language is also referenced in analyses of other malware, including Agent Tesla. Its primary role is in the execution and deployment stages of attacks, often on Windows platforms.
