Its key techniques include evaluating obfuscated content to trigger malicious actions and reading from files to bypass security controls. It primarily targets Windows platforms.

3941.name: Batch Script
3941.profile: [profile]Batch Script is a scripting language used by threat actors to automate malicious tasks. It is associated with groups including FIN7, Gold Rebellion, STAC5143, Storm-0506, Storm-0826, TA2101, UNC3973, UNC4393, APT41, Emissary Panda, Gallium, Hafnium, Hurricane Panda, Leviathan, APT10, APT32, and Anunak. Key technical behaviors involve using WScript to execute malicious scripts or decode payloads, as seen in malware families like TrickBot, Loki Password Stealer, and Kopiluwak, which utilize it to run obfuscated JavaScript or VBScript content for initial access and persistence on Windows platforms.[/profile]

3944.name: Obfuscation Techniques
3944.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may obfuscate command and control traffic to make it more difficult to detect.(Citation: Bitdefender FunnyDream Campaign November 2020) Command and control (C2) communications are hidden (but not necessarily encrypted) in an attempt to make the content more difficult to discover or decipher and to make the communication less conspicuous and hide commands from being seen. This encompasses many methods, such as adding junk data to protocol traffic, using steganography, or impersonating legitimate protocols.
3944.profile: [profile]Obfuscation Techniques, identified as T1001 under the Command and Control tactic, is a technique applicable across multiple platforms where adversaries hide C2 communications to evade detection. This is achieved by adding junk data to protocol traffic, employing steganography, or impersonating legitimate protocols to make the traffic less conspicuous and more difficult to decipher. The technique is associated with threat groups like Gamaredon Group and FIN7.
3944.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Obfuscation Techniques is a broad adversarial tactic to hide malicious artifacts and evade detection. It encompasses specific MITRE ATT&CK techniques like Data Obfuscation (T1001) for concealing C2 traffic, Command Obfuscation (T1027.010) for scripting, and Obfuscated Files or Information (T1027) for payloads. Technical mechanics include using encoding (e.g., Base64), string manipulation, junk data insertion, steganography, and impersonating legitimate protocols to obscure content across platforms.

3950.name: Runs WScript
3950.profile: [profile]The entity "Runs WScript" is a technique for executing malicious scripts. It is associated with the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1059.005, "Visual Basic," under the Execution tactic for Windows platforms. This technique involves using the Windows Script Host (wscript.exe or cscript.exe) to run Visual Basic Script (VBS) files, which can execute arbitrary commands or download and run further payloads. A specific example of its abuse is through the signed PubPrn.vbs script, where adversaries can set a parameter to reference a remote scriptlet file (.sct) to proxy execution and potentially bypass application controls, though this specific vector is blocked in later Windows versions.

3951.name: Reads from the File
3951.profile: [profile]The entity "Reads from the File" is a technique where an adversary accesses and reads data from files on a compromised system. This action is typically performed to gather sensitive information, such as credentials or configuration data, from local files or network shares. It is associated with the malware JScript and is conceptually related to techniques for data collection from shared drives and direct volume access, which also involve reading stored data to support adversary objectives.

This is achieved by using utilities that read file system data structures directly from the drive, allowing them to read files without triggering typical security mechanisms. Tools like `NinjaCopy` in PowerShell can perform these actions.

3952.name: Evaluates Content
3952.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may gain access and continuously communicate with victims by injecting malicious content into systems through online network traffic. Rather than luring victims to malicious payloads hosted on a compromised website (i.e., [Drive-by Target](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1608/004) followed by [Drive-by Compromise](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1189)), adversaries may initially access victims through compromised data-transfer channels where they can manipulate traffic and/or inject their own content. These compromised online network channels may also be used to deliver additional payloads (i.e., [Ingress Tool Transfer](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1105)) and other data to already compromised systems.(Citation: ESET MoustachedBouncer)

Adversaries may inject content to victim systems in various ways, including:

* From the middle, where the adversary is in-between legitimate online client-server communications (**Note:** this is similar but distinct from [Adversary-in-the-Middle](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1557), which describes AiTM activity solely within an enterprise environment) (Citation: Kaspersky Encyclopedia MiTM)
* From the side, where malicious content is injected and races to the client as a fake response to requests of a legitimate online server (Citation: Kaspersky ManOnTheSide)

Content injection is often the result of compromised upstream communication channels, for example at the level of an internet service provider (ISP) as is the case with "lawful interception."(Citation: Kaspersky ManOnTheSide)(Citation: ESET MoustachedBouncer)(Citation: EFF China GitHub Attack)
3952.profile: [profile]Content Injection, designated as T1659, is a technique within the Initial Access tactic, targeting network platforms. It involves adversaries manipulating or inserting malicious data into online network traffic channels to gain initial access or maintain communication with victims. This is achieved by compromising upstream data-transfer channels, such as at an ISP level, and can be executed "from the middle" by intercepting client-server communications or "from the side" by racing a malicious response to a client's legitimate request. The technique is associated with the threat group MoustachedBouncer and can facilitate follow-on actions like Ingress Tool Transfer.
3952.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Evaluates Content is a technique where adversaries assess the content of files, data, or communications to identify valuable information or trigger malicious actions. It is often a precursor to data theft or execution. This behavior can involve automated scanning of file contents, network traffic, or shared storage to locate specific data patterns, credentials, or system information that can be leveraged for further exploitation, such as in lateral movement or data exfiltration campaigns.

3960.name: DNS Queries
3960.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may communicate using the Domain Name System (DNS) application layer protocol to avoid detection/network filtering by blending in with existing traffic. Commands to the remote system, and often the results of those commands, will be embedded within the protocol traffic between the client and server. 

The DNS protocol serves an administrative function in computer networking and thus may be very common in environments. DNS traffic may also be allowed even before network authentication is completed. DNS packets contain many fields and headers in which data can be concealed. Often known as DNS tunneling, adversaries may abuse DNS to communicate with systems under their control within a victim network while also mimicking normal, expected traffic.(Citation: PAN DNS Tunneling)(Citation: Medium DnsTunneling)

DNS beaconing may be used to send commands to remote systems via DNS queries. A DNS beacon is created by tunneling DNS traffic (i.e. [Protocol Tunneling](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1572)). The commands may be embedded into different DNS records, for example, TXT or A records.(Citation: OilRig Uses Updated BONDUPDATER to Target Middle Eastern Government) DNS beacons may be difficult to detect because the beacons infrequently communicate with infected devices.(Citation: DNS Beacons) Infrequent communication conceals the malicious DNS traffic with normal DNS traffic.
3960.profile: [profile]The entity is the Application Layer Protocol: DNS technique, MITRE ATT&CK ID T1071.004, under the Command and Control tactic. It operates across multiple platforms. Adversaries abuse the DNS protocol to covertly communicate with compromised systems, embedding commands and data within DNS queries and responses to blend with normal traffic, a method known as DNS tunneling. Commands are often concealed within specific DNS record types like TXT or A records, and communication may be infrequent (DNS beaconing) to evade detection. This technique is associated with groups including FIN7, OilRig, and APT41.[/profile]
3960.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "DNS Queries" is a reconnaissance technique. Based on the retrieved information, it aligns with the MITRE ATT&CK technique "Gather Victim DNS Information" (T1590.002) under the Reconnaissance tactic. It operates across multiple platforms. The technique involves querying DNS servers to collect details such as registered name servers, subdomain addressing, and specific records (MX, TXT, SPF) that can reveal third-party services. Adversaries may also perform DNS zone transfers (AXFR queries) to extract all records from misconfigured servers, gathering data useful for further targeting and initial access.

3971.name: Bypass Behavioral Analysis
3971.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may modify file attributes and subvert Gatekeeper functionality to evade user prompts and execute untrusted programs. Gatekeeper is a set of technologies that act as layer of Apple’s security model to ensure only trusted applications are executed on a host. Gatekeeper was built on top of File Quarantine in Snow Leopard (10.6, 2009) and has grown to include Code Signing, security policy compliance, Notarization, and more. Gatekeeper also treats applications running for the first time differently than reopened applications.(Citation: TheEclecticLightCompany Quarantine and the flag)(Citation: TheEclecticLightCompany apple notarization )

Based on an opt-in system, when files are downloaded an extended attribute (xattr) called `com.apple.quarantine` (also known as a quarantine flag) can be set on the file by the application performing the download. Launch Services opens the application in a suspended state. For first run applications with the quarantine flag set, Gatekeeper executes the following functions:

1. Checks extended attribute – Gatekeeper checks for the quarantine flag, then provides an alert prompt to the user to allow or deny execution.(Citation: OceanLotus for OS X)(Citation: 20 macOS Common Tools and Techniques)

2. Checks System Policies - Gatekeeper checks the system security policy, allowing execution of apps downloaded from either just the App Store or the App Store and identified developers.

3. Code Signing – Gatekeeper checks for a valid code signature from an Apple Developer ID.

4. Notarization - Using the `api.apple-cloudkit.com` API, Gatekeeper reaches out to Apple servers to verify or pull down the notarization ticket and ensure the ticket is not revoked. Users can override notarization, which will result in a prompt of executing an “unauthorized app” and the security policy will be modified.

Adversaries can subvert one or multiple security controls within Gatekeeper checks through logic errors (e.g. [Exploitation for Defense Evasion](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1211)), unchecked file types, and external libraries. For example, prior to macOS 13 Ventura, code signing and notarization checks were only conducted on first launch, allowing adversaries to write malicious executables to previously opened applications in order to bypass Gatekeeper security checks.(Citation: theevilbit gatekeeper bypass 2021)(Citation: Application Bundle Manipulation Brandon Dalton)

Applications and files loaded onto the system from a USB flash drive, optical disk, external hard drive, from a drive shared over the local network, or using the curl command may not set the quarantine flag. Additionally, it is possible to avoid setting the quarantine flag using [Drive-by Compromise](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1189).
3971.profile: [profile]Gatekeeper Bypass, identified as T1553.001 under the Defense Evasion tactic for macOS, involves subverting Apple's Gatekeeper security controls to execute untrusted programs. Technical mechanics include removing the `com.apple.quarantine` extended attribute, exploiting logic errors, or writing malicious code into previously opened applications to avoid code signing and notarization checks, particularly effective prior to macOS 13. This technique has been associated with the intrusion set FIN7.
3971.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Bypass Behavioral Analysis" is a defense evasion technique. It involves adversaries modifying their malware's execution behavior to evade detection by security tools that monitor for suspicious system activities. This can be achieved through methods like delaying malicious actions, mimicking legitimate software patterns, or splitting malicious code across multiple processes to appear benign. The technique is platform-agnostic, targeting systems where behavioral monitoring is active.

3975.name: DNS Messaging Technique
3975.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may leverage chat and messaging applications, such as Microsoft Teams, Google Chat, and Slack, to mine valuable information.  

The following is a brief list of example information that may hold potential value to an adversary and may also be found on messaging applications: 

* Testing / development credentials (i.e., [Chat Messages](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1552/008)) 
* Source code snippets 
* Links to network shares and other internal resources 
* Proprietary data(Citation: Guardian Grand Theft Auto Leak 2022)
* Discussions about ongoing incident response efforts(Citation: SC Magazine Ragnar Locker 2021)(Citation: Microsoft DEV-0537)

In addition to exfiltrating data from messaging applications, adversaries may leverage data from chat messages in order to improve their targeting - for example, by learning more about an environment or evading ongoing incident response efforts.(Citation: Sentinel Labs NullBulge 2024)(Citation: Permiso Scattered Spider 2023)
3975.profile: [profile]The entity "DNS Messaging Technique" appears to be a misalignment; the provided Self Info and primary similar entity describe the MITRE technique T1213.005: Data from Information Repositories: Messaging Applications. This technique, under the Collection tactic, involves adversaries mining chat applications like Microsoft Teams, Slack, and Google Chat for valuable data such as source code snippets, internal resource links, proprietary data, and discussions on incident response to improve targeting and evasion. Groups like Scattered Spider, LAPSUS$, and Fox Kitten have been associated with this activity. The retrieved DNS-related entities are contextually irrelevant to this specific messaging application technique and are therefore discarded.[/profile]
3975.profile_without_enhance: [profile]DNS Messaging Technique is a Command and Control (C2) method where adversaries abuse the Domain Name System (DNS) application layer protocol to blend malicious traffic with normal network activity, often to bypass detection and filtering. This technique, which can be mapped to the MITRE ATT&CK framework as T1071.004 (Application Layer Protocol: DNS), falls under the Command and Control tactic and operates across multiple platforms. It works by tunneling C2 traffic through DNS queries and responses, embedding commands and exfiltrated data within various DNS record fields like TXT or A records. This communication can be infrequent to mimic legitimate DNS traffic and may involve adversaries setting up their own DNS servers for greater control over the C2 channel.

Adversaries may scan victims for vulnerabilities that can be used during targeting. Vulnerability scans typically check if the configuration of a target host/application (ex: software and version) potentially aligns with the target of a specific exploit the adversary may seek to use.

These scans may also include more broad attempts to [Gather Victim Host Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1592) that can be used to identify more commonly known, exploitable vulnerabilities. Vulnerability scans typically harvest running software and version numbers via server banners, listening ports, or other network artifacts.(Citation: OWASP Vuln Scanning) Information from these scans may reveal opportunities for other forms of reconnaissance (ex: [Search Open Websites/Domains](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1593) or [Search Open Technical Databases](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1596)), establishing operational resources (ex: [Develop Capabilities](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1587) or [Obtain Capabilities](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1588)), and/or initial access (ex: [Exploit Public-Facing Application](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1190)).
3979.profile: [profile]Evade Memory Scanning Solutions is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the provided context, it appears to be a technique for avoiding detection by security software that scans process memory. This can be achieved by injecting malicious code into a live process via methods like proc memory injection, which involves overwriting a target process's memory map through the `/proc/[pid]/maps` file using tools like `dd` to execute a payload. Another related method is VDSO hijacking, which redirects library calls to execute malicious code. These methods allow execution to be masked under a legitimate process, evading process-based defenses.[/profile]
3979.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Evade Memory Scanning Solutions is a technique within the Defense Evasion tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It involves manipulating or obfuscating malicious code in memory to avoid detection by security tools. Specific methods include injecting code into processes via the /proc filesystem (proc memory injection) or hijacking the virtual dynamic shared object (vdso) to redirect execution flow, masking activity under legitimate processes. The goal is to bypass process-based defenses and memory scans.

3985.name: Phishing Lure: Complaints
3985.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may send phishing messages to gain access to victim systems. All forms of phishing are electronically delivered social engineering. Phishing can be targeted, known as spearphishing. In spearphishing, a specific individual, company, or industry will be targeted by the adversary. More generally, adversaries can conduct non-targeted phishing, such as in mass malware spam campaigns.

Adversaries may send victims emails containing malicious attachments or links, typically to execute malicious code on victim systems. Phishing may also be conducted via third-party services, like social media platforms. Phishing may also involve social engineering techniques, such as posing as a trusted source, as well as evasive techniques such as removing or manipulating emails or metadata/headers from compromised accounts being abused to send messages (e.g., [Email Hiding Rules](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1564/008)).(Citation: Microsoft OAuth Spam 2022)(Citation: Palo Alto Unit 42 VBA Infostealer 2014) Another way to accomplish this is by [Email Spoofing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1672)(Citation: Proofpoint-spoof) the identity of the sender, which can be used to fool both the human recipient as well as automated security tools,(Citation: cyberproof-double-bounce) or by including the intended target as a party to an existing email thread that includes malicious files or links (i.e., "thread hijacking").(Citation: phishing-krebs)

Victims may also receive phishing messages that instruct them to call a phone number where they are directed to visit a malicious URL, download malware,(Citation: sygnia Luna Month)(Citation: CISA Remote Monitoring and Management Software) or install adversary-accessible remote management tools onto their computer (i.e., [User Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204)).(Citation: Unit42 Luna Moth)
3985.profile: [profile]Phishing Lure: Complaints is a specific social engineering technique within the broader Phishing (T1566) framework, falling under the Initial Access tactic and applicable across multiple platforms. It involves crafting deceptive messages that impersonate complaints or similar urgent communications to trick recipients into opening malicious attachments or clicking on links, thereby enabling the execution of code or credential theft. The intrusion-set FIN7 has been associated with this method, which leverages the psychological pressure of addressing a supposed grievance to increase the likelihood of user interaction and compromise.[/profile]
3985.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Phishing Lure: Complaints is a social engineering technique within the broader Phishing (T1566) and Phishing for Information (T1598) tactics. It operates on multiple platforms, including email and voice, by crafting messages that pose as official complaints or urgent notifications to create a sense of alarm and prompt the victim into clicking malicious links, opening attachments, or divulging sensitive credentials. This method leverages pretexts of urgency and authority to bypass user skepticism.

3997.name: malware obfuscation methods
3997.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may develop malware and malware components that can be used during targeting. Building malicious software can include the development of payloads, droppers, post-compromise tools, backdoors (including backdoored images), packers, C2 protocols, and the creation of infected removable media. Adversaries may develop malware to support their operations, creating a means for maintaining control of remote machines, evading defenses, and executing post-compromise behaviors.(Citation: Mandiant APT1)(Citation: Kaspersky Sofacy)(Citation: ActiveMalwareEnergy)(Citation: FBI Flash FIN7 USB)

During malware development, adversaries may intentionally include indicators aligned with other known actors in order to mislead attribution by defenders.(Citation: Olympic Destroyer)(Citation: Risky Bulletin Threat actor impersonates FSB APT)(Citation: GamaCopy organization)

As with legitimate development efforts, different skill sets may be required for developing malware. The skills needed may be located in-house, or may need to be contracted out. Use of a contractor may be considered an extension of that adversary's malware development capabilities, provided the adversary plays a role in shaping requirements and maintains a degree of exclusivity to the malware.

Some aspects of malware development, such as C2 protocol development, may require adversaries to obtain additional infrastructure. For example, malware developed that will communicate with Twitter for C2, may require use of [Web Services](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1583/006).(Citation: FireEye APT29)
3997.profile: [profile]The entity "malware obfuscation methods" aligns with the MITRE ATT&CK technique Obfuscated Files or Information (T1027) under the Defense Evasion tactic for multiple platforms. This technique involves encrypting, encoding, or otherwise obfuscating file contents to evade detection. Specific methods include using password-protected documents or archives, base64 encoding, splitting payloads, and applying redundant obfuscation layers to conceal malicious strings and impede static analysis.

The technique involves adversaries making malicious files or information difficult to detect or analyze by encrypting, encoding, or otherwise obfuscating their contents. This includes using compression or archiving, splitting payloads into benign-seeming components for later reassembly, and applying layered encoding like Base64. Specific methods can involve password-protected documents or self-extracting archives to conceal payloads until user execution triggers deobfuscation.

4006.name: Ransomware-as-a-Service (RaaS)
4006.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may reveal credentials of accounts that have disabled Kerberos preauthentication by [Password Cracking](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1110/002) Kerberos messages.(Citation: Harmj0y Roasting AS-REPs Jan 2017) 

Preauthentication offers protection against offline [Password Cracking](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1110/002). When enabled, a user requesting access to a resource initiates communication with the Domain Controller (DC) by sending an Authentication Server Request (AS-REQ) message with a timestamp that is encrypted with the hash of their password. If and only if the DC is able to successfully decrypt the timestamp with the hash of the user’s password, it will then send an Authentication Server Response (AS-REP) message that contains the Ticket Granting Ticket (TGT) to the user. Part of the AS-REP message is signed with the user’s password.(Citation: Microsoft Kerberos Preauth 2014)

For each account found without preauthentication, an adversary may send an AS-REQ message without the encrypted timestamp and receive an AS-REP message with TGT data which may be encrypted with an insecure algorithm such as RC4. The recovered encrypted data may be vulnerable to offline [Password Cracking](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1110/002) attacks similarly to [Kerberoasting](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1558/003) and expose plaintext credentials. (Citation: Harmj0y Roasting AS-REPs Jan 2017)(Citation: Stealthbits Cracking AS-REP Roasting Jun 2019) 

An account registered to a domain, with or without special privileges, can be abused to list all domain accounts that have preauthentication disabled by utilizing Windows tools like [PowerShell](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001) with an LDAP filter. Alternatively, the adversary may send an AS-REQ message for each user. If the DC responds without errors, the account does not require preauthentication and the AS-REP message will already contain the encrypted data. (Citation: Harmj0y Roasting AS-REPs Jan 2017)(Citation: Stealthbits Cracking AS-REP Roasting Jun 2019)

Cracked hashes may enable [Persistence](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0003), [Privilege Escalation](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0004), and [Lateral Movement](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0008) via access to [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078).(Citation: SANS Attacking Kerberos Nov 2014)
4006.profile: [profile]The technique is formally known as AS-REP Roasting with the MITRE ATT&CK ID T1558.004 under the Credential Access tactic for Windows platforms. It exploits Kerberos by sending an AS-REQ message to a Domain Controller for accounts with preauthentication disabled, which responds with an AS-REP containing TGT data encrypted with a potentially weak algorithm like RC4. This encrypted data can be captured and subjected to offline password cracking to recover plaintext credentials, enabling further persistence and lateral movement. The intrusion-set FIN7 has been associated with this technique.
4006.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Ransomware-as-a-Service (RaaS) is a business model, not a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique. It operates as a subscription-based platform where developers sell or lease ransomware tools to affiliates, who then execute attacks and share profits. This model lowers the barrier to entry for cybercriminals, enabling widespread ransomware campaigns. Affiliates often acquire initial network access through brokers, leveraging compromised systems or credentials to deploy the ransomware payload.

4007.name: Sekur
4007.profile: [profile]Sekur is a malware entity associated with the FIN7 intrusion set. It is deployed via custom PowerShell stager scripts, such as those installed by the Pillowmint tool to the %LOCALAPPDATA%\\Microsoft\\WindowsDefender\\ClearTemp.ps1 location. It is referenced in the context of PlugX malware operations, with specific SHA256 hashes provided for related samples. Its primary target platform is Microsoft Windows.[/profile]
4007.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Sekur is a malware entity, also known as Saker. It is associated with the Anunak group and potentially linked to APT22, APT26, APT31, APT41, Aurora Panda, Calypso Group, Dragonok, Emissary Panda, Hellsing, Hurricane Panda, Leviathan, Mirage, Mustang Panda, Nettraveler, Nightshade Panda, Slime29, Samurai Panda, Stone Panda, UPS, and Violin Panda. A key technical behavior involves a PowerShell stager being installed to a specific Windows Defender directory path. Its target platform is Windows, and it utilizes custom infrastructure indicated by specific SHA256 hashes.

4008.name: VB Flash
4008.profile: [profile]VB Flash is a first-stage implant and RAT (Remote Access Trojan) attributed to the FIN7 (CARBON SPIDER) intrusion set. It was later re-developed into JS Flash, which retained VB Flash's capabilities while adding new obfuscation methods, a new C2 protocol, and additional features. The malware has been used to target the U.S. hospitality sector.[/profile]
4008.profile_without_enhance: [profile]VB Flash is a first-stage implant and RAT, also known as Agent ORM or Toshliph. It is attributed to the CARBON SPIDER group (aka red menshen). Its key technical behaviors include being re-developed into a JavaScript version called JS Flash, which incorporates new obfuscation methods and a new C2 protocol while retaining VB Flash's original capabilities. It primarily targets the U.S. hospitality sector, including hotel chains.

4009.name: Harpy
4009.profile: [profile]Harpy is a malware attributed to the FIN7 intrusion set. It contacts a command-and-control (C2) server to deliver and execute a JavaScript system enumeration module. This module strongly resembles a PowerShell (PS) system enumeration module written for the Domenus suite, indicating a shared developer lineage with that tool.
4009.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Harpy is a malware that contacts its command-and-control server to deliver and execute a JavaScript system enumeration module. This module strongly resembles a PS system enumeration module written for the Domenus suite, indicating a shared developer. The malware has been used in campaigns associated with the Anunak group.

4010.name: PILLOWMINT
4010.uncertain_mes: [Pillowmint](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0517) is a point-of-sale malware used by [FIN7](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0046) designed to capture credit card information.(Citation: Trustwave Pillowmint June 2020)
4010.profile: [profile]PILLOWMINT, also known as pillowmint, is a point-of-sale malware attributed to the FIN7 group. It is designed to capture credit card information from infected systems. Its operations have been associated with broad, indiscriminate campaigns targeting various sectors, and it is referenced in the context of FIN7's activities under the moniker "Monkey Thief."
4010.profile_without_enhance: [profile]PILLOWMINT, also known as pillowmint, is a malware attributed to the criminal group FIN7, also referenced as CARBON SPIDER or Anunak. It is associated with broad, indiscriminate infection campaigns across all sectors, a shift from earlier narrow operations focused on point-of-sale (POS) devices. Its technical behavior includes establishing persistence via a Windows registry key for automatic execution on system startup. The target platform is Windows systems.

4011.name: JSS Loader
4011.uncertain_mes: [JSS Loader](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0648) is Remote Access Trojan (RAT) with .NET and C++ variants that has been used by [FIN7](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0046) since at least 2020.(Citation: eSentire FIN7 July 2021)(Citation: CrowdStrike Carbon Spider August 2021)
4011.profile: [profile]JSS Loader is a Remote Access Trojan (RAT) with .NET and C++ variants, attributed to the FIN7 group and in use since at least 2020. Its key technical behaviors include the ability to load additional executables, PowerShell, and JavaScript files. An observed infection chain involved downloading and executing a setup VBScript from the domain petshopbook.com. The malware targets Windows platforms and has been used in campaigns by groups like FIN7 and Anunak.[/profile]
4011.profile_without_enhance: [profile]JSS Loader is a Remote Access Trojan (RAT) attributed to the FIN7 group. It exists in both .NET and C++ variants and is capable of loading additional executables, PowerShell, and JavaScript files. A typical infection chain involves downloading and executing a setup VBScript from a remote server, such as the observed domain petshopbook.com. Its target platform is Windows.

4012.name: Domenus VBS
4012.profile: [profile]Domenus VBS is a backdoor written in VBScript, also known as Domenus JS when in JavaScript form. It is attributed to the FIN7 (aka CARBON SPIDER or ANUNAK) intrusion set. Key behaviors include enumerating system information, capturing screenshots and browser history, and downloading secondary payloads like JS, PEs, DLLs, and PS scripts from a C2 server. It establishes persistence via scheduled tasks and is delivered through opportunistic phishing campaigns alongside malware like Harpy and JSS Loader.
4012.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Domenus VBS is a backdoor written in VBScript, also known simply as Domenus. It is attributed to the CARBON SPIDER criminal group (also referenced as anunak). Its key behaviors include enumerating system information, capturing screenshots and browser history, and downloading secondary payloads like JS, PEs, DLLs, and PS scripts from a command-and-control server. It establishes persistence via a scheduled task and is delivered through phishing campaigns alongside other malware like Harpy, Leo VBS, JSS Loader, and Domenus JS.

4013.name: Domenus JS
4013.profile: [profile]Domenus JS is a JavaScript-based malware. It is attributed to the FIN7 cybercrime group. Key TTPs include phishing campaigns that leverage compromised and legitimate services such as WordPress installations, SharePoint services, web servers, and Google Docs to host its toolchain payloads. Its target platforms are web-based environments and systems susceptible to these delivery methods.
4013.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Domenus JS is a JavaScript-based malware, also known as Domenus VBS/JS. It is attributed to the Anunak cybercriminal group. Its key TTPs involve phishing campaigns that use compromised and legitimate services, such as WordPress installations, SharePoint services, web servers, and Google Docs, to host its toolchain payloads. It primarily targets web platforms and is associated with campaigns delivering other malware like REvil ransomware.

4014.name: Leo VBS
4014.profile: [profile]Leo VBS is a family of obfuscated VBScripts that downloads and executes a remote payload, specifically performing an HTTP GET request to a domain like alphalanding[.]com to retrieve and write a JSS Loader binary (e.g., as PaintHelper.exe) to the %TEMP% directory. It is attributed to the FIN7 intrusion set and has been associated with the Anunak group. Its primary target platform is Windows.[/profile]
4014.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Leo VBS is a family of obfuscated VBScripts used to download and execute remote payloads. It is also known as pillowmint and bateleur. It has been attributed to the Anunak group. Its key technical behaviors include performing HTTP GET requests to specific URLs, such as https://alphalanding.com/successfully/warranty.eml, and writing downloaded binaries like a JSS Loader to the %TEMP% directory as PaintHelper.exe. It targets Windows platforms.

4015.name: Sekur PS stager
4015.profile: [profile]Sekur PS stager, also known as a custom PowerShell RAT, is attributed to the FIN7 intrusion set and is installed via scripts like pillowmint. It is deployed as a PowerShell script, specifically to %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\WindowsDefender\ClearTemp.ps1, and is associated with second-stage VBS and third-stage PS1 payloads, indicating a multi-stage infection chain targeting Windows platforms. Its infrastructure and deployment are linked to campaigns targeting individuals seeking information on geopolitical events like the Ukraine crisis.
4015.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Sekur PS stager, also known as a custom PowerShell RAT, is a malware stager attributed to the Anunak group. It is installed via scripts like Pillowmint to a specific path, %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\WindowsDefender\ClearTemp.ps1. Its key behavior is acting as a PowerShell-based remote access trojan (RAT) stager. It primarily targets the Windows platform, leveraging PowerShell for execution and staging further payloads.

4016.name: KillACK PS backdoor
4016.profile: [profile]KillACK PS backdoor is a custom PowerShell backdoor. It is attributed to the FIN7 group (also known as CARBON SPIDER or Anunak). Its key technical behaviors include being executed via PowerShell and PowerShell ISE, profiling Active Directory with tools like ADFind, and sending host information to command-and-control (C2) servers such as againcome<.>com and besaintegration<.>com. It targets Windows platforms and is delivered via custom stagers like PS Sekur.
4016.profile_without_enhance: [profile]KillACK PS backdoor is a custom PowerShell backdoor used by the CARBON SPIDER group (also known as Anunak). It is executed via PowerShell or PowerShell ISE, sends host information to a command-and-control server (such as againcome<.>com or besaintegration<.>com), and is deployed alongside tools like the PS Sekur stager and the ADFind utility for profiling Active Directory environments.

4017.name: Cobalt Strike stagers
4017.uncertain_mes:
[Cobalt Strike](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0154) is a commercial, full-featured, remote access tool that bills itself as “adversary simulation software designed to execute targeted attacks and emulate the post-exploitation actions of advanced threat actors”. Cobalt Strike’s interactive post-exploit capabilities cover the full range of ATT&CK tactics, all executed within a single, integrated system.(Citation: cobaltstrike manual)

In addition to its own capabilities, [Cobalt Strike](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0154) leverages the capabilities of other well-known tools such as Metasploit and [Mimikatz](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0002).(Citation: cobaltstrike manual)
4017.profile: [profile]Cobalt Strike stagers, also known as Cobalt Strike, are commercial remote access tool components used for initial compromise and lateral movement. They are attributed to numerous threat groups including FIN7, FIN6, APT29, APT32, APT41, Mustang Panda, CopyKittens, DarkHydrus, Wizard Spider, and Leviathan. Key technical behaviors involve leveraging capabilities from tools like Metasploit and Mimikatz for post-exploitation activities across the full range of ATT&CK tactics. The target platform is primarily Windows, and its infrastructure has been observed with active stager URLs long after initial campaigns.
4017.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Cobalt Strike stagers are components of the Cobalt Strike framework, which is a penetration testing tool often repurposed for malicious use. They are associated with numerous threat groups including APT29, APT32, APT41, FIN6, FIN7, Wizard Spider (via Conti), and others like Mustang Panda and Winnti. These stagers are used for initial system compromise and lateral movement, often in conjunction with ransomware like LockerGoga and Ryuk. They typically target Windows platforms and operate through active command and control (C2) infrastructure, with some stager URLs remaining active for extended periods post-deployment.

4018.name: Cobalt Strike samples
4018.uncertain_mes:
[Cobalt Strike](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0154) is a commercial, full-featured, remote access tool that bills itself as “adversary simulation software designed to execute targeted attacks and emulate the post-exploitation actions of advanced threat actors”. Cobalt Strike’s interactive post-exploit capabilities cover the full range of ATT&CK tactics, all executed within a single, integrated system.(Citation: cobaltstrike manual)

In addition to its own capabilities, [Cobalt Strike](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0154) leverages the capabilities of other well-known tools such as Metasploit and [Mimikatz](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0002).(Citation: cobaltstrike manual)
4018.profile: [profile]Cobalt Strike is a commercial remote access tool used for adversary simulation and post-exploitation activities, leveraging capabilities from tools like Metasploit and Mimikatz. It is associated with groups including FIN7, APT29, APT32, APT41, FIN6, Mustang Panda, CopyKittens, DarkHydrus, Wizard Spider, and Anunak. Its key TTPs cover the full range of ATT&CK tactics, often deployed via PowerShell stagers and used in campaigns delivering malware like REvil and Sekur, with samples sharing configuration metadata across incidents. 4019.name: Plink
4019.profile: [profile]Plink is a malware tool associated with intrusion sets including RocketKitten, OilRig, and FIN7. It is frequently used alongside other utilities like Korplug/PlugX loaders, SecretsDump, FSCAN, and RAR compressors in operations attributed to various APT groups such as APT22, APT26, APT31, APT41, Emissary Panda, and Mustang Panda. Its primary function is to facilitate credential dumping and network scanning, often deployed on Windows systems as part of broader intrusion toolkits.[/profile]
4019.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Plink is a tool associated with multiple APT groups including APT22, APT26, APT31, APT41, Emissary Panda, Gallium, and Mustang Panda. It is used in conjunction with other tools like Korplug/PlugX loader, SecretsDump, FSCAN, and RAR compressor. A key technique is "Reverse RDP over SSH" (T1572), which tunnels RDP traffic through SSH for covert lateral movement and remote access, bypassing network security controls. Its target platform is Windows systems, as it facilitates remote administration and credential dumping in targeted attacks.

4020.name: GoToAssist
4020.profile: [profile]GoToAssist is a remote access tool (RAT) attributed to the financially motivated intrusion set FIN7. It is used for clandestine data exfiltration and remote system control, potentially leveraging Tor for covert network communications. Its deployment is associated with campaigns involving other malware families like Cuba, AsyncRAT, and Redrum.[/profile]
4020.profile_without_enhance: [profile]GoToAssist is a malware entity. It has been referenced in the context of the Cobalt Strike framework, which is associated with numerous APT and criminal groups including APT29, APT32, APT41, FIN6, FIN7, Mustang Panda, and Winnti. Its technical behavior may involve the potential use of Tor for clandestine data exfiltration. The target platform is not specified in the provided data.

4021.name: TightVNC
4021.profile: [profile]TightVNC is an open-source VNC (Virtual Network Computing) utility. It is customized and used as a tool by threat groups including RocketKitten and FIN7. Its key technical behavior is supporting a reverse VNC feature, allowing a compromised system to initiate a connection to an attacker's client. It consists of a server module (tvnserver.exe) and a client module (tvnviewer.exe). It has been distributed via other malware like the AppleSeed backdoor and is associated with tools like TinyNuke and Pebbledash.
4021.profile_without_enhance: [profile] TightVNC is an open-source VNC utility that can be customized by attackers for malicious use. It is characterized by its support for a reverse VNC feature, allowing connections to be initiated from the target. The malware consists of a server module (tvnserver.exe) and a client module (tvnviewer.exe). It has been distributed via other malware like the AppleSeed backdoor and is associated with tools like TinyNuke and HVNC.

4022.name: sleep.exe
4022.profile: [profile]sleep.exe is a malware component associated with the FIN7 intrusion set. Key technical behaviors include setting configurable sleep intervals (e.g., for 24 hours or 6 days) to evade detection and downloading/executing additional payloads via HTTP GET requests for files with a ".exe" extension. It has been observed alongside other malicious executables like GrooveMonitor.exe and juboot.exe in campaigns such as batchwiper.[/profile]
4022.profile_without_enhance: [profile]sleep.exe is a malware component, also known as SLEEP.EXE, associated with the Comment Crew APT group. It functions as a dropper or backdoor with commands to set sleep intervals (e.g., for 24 hours or 6 days) and reconnect, and it can download and execute .exe files via HTTP GET requests from a specified hostname. It targets Windows platforms and has been linked to campaigns like Helauto and Seasalt.

4036.name: Phishing Attachments
4036.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may send phishing messages to gain access to victim systems. All forms of phishing are electronically delivered social engineering. Phishing can be targeted, known as spearphishing. In spearphishing, a specific individual, company, or industry will be targeted by the adversary. More generally, adversaries can conduct non-targeted phishing, such as in mass malware spam campaigns.

Adversaries may send victims emails containing malicious attachments or links, typically to execute malicious code on victim systems. Phishing may also be conducted via third-party services, like social media platforms. Phishing may also involve social engineering techniques, such as posing as a trusted source, as well as evasive techniques such as removing or manipulating emails or metadata/headers from compromised accounts being abused to send messages (e.g., [Email Hiding Rules](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1564/008)).(Citation: Microsoft OAuth Spam 2022)(Citation: Palo Alto Unit 42 VBA Infostealer 2014) Another way to accomplish this is by [Email Spoofing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1672)(Citation: Proofpoint-spoof) the identity of the sender, which can be used to fool both the human recipient as well as automated security tools,(Citation: cyberproof-double-bounce) or by including the intended target as a party to an existing email thread that includes malicious files or links (i.e., "thread hijacking").(Citation: phishing-krebs)

Victims may also receive phishing messages that instruct them to call a phone number where they are directed to visit a malicious URL, download malware,(Citation: sygnia Luna Month)(Citation: CISA Remote Monitoring and Management Software) or install adversary-accessible remote management tools onto their computer (i.e., [User Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204)).(Citation: Unit42 Luna Moth)
4036.profile: [profile]Phishing Attachments is a sub-technique of Phishing (T1566) within the Initial Access tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It involves sending emails with malicious attachments, such as documents or executables, to trick victims into opening them, leading to code execution. This method often employs social engineering, like posing as a trusted source, and may use evasive tactics including email spoofing or thread hijacking to enhance delivery. The intrusion-set FIN7 is associated with this technique.[/profile]
4036.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Phishing Attachments is a sub-technique of Phishing (T1566) under the Initial Access tactic, targeting multiple platforms. It involves adversaries sending emails containing malicious attachments, such as documents or executables, to victims. The technique relies on social engineering to trick users into opening the attachments, which typically leads to the execution of malicious code on the victim's system, facilitating initial compromise.

4037.name: Spam Campaign
4037.profile: [profile]The entity "Spam Campaign" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique but a general adversarial activity often associated with the Initial Access tactic. It is commonly executed via email and can leverage compromised email accounts (T1586.002) to enhance trust and evade filters, or hijack cloud email services (T1496.004) for large-scale distribution. The intrusion-set FIN7 has been linked to such campaigns. The core technical mechanic involves sending bulk, malicious emails to deliver payloads or conduct phishing.[profile]
4037.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Spam Campaign is a technique aligned with MITRE ATT&CK's Tactic of Initial Access (T1566.001) and Platform: Windows, macOS, Linux. It involves adversaries sending large volumes of unsolicited emails, often leveraging compromised email accounts or hijacked cloud services like AWS SES to enhance legitimacy and bypass filters. The emails typically contain malicious links or attachments as a primary infection vector, and the scale of the campaign itself can be used to overwhelm targets or obscure malicious traffic.

4043.name: RDP
4043.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may hijack a legitimate user’s remote desktop session to move laterally within an environment. Remote desktop is a common feature in operating systems. It allows a user to log into an interactive session with a system desktop graphical user interface on a remote system. Microsoft refers to its implementation of the Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) as Remote Desktop Services (RDS).(Citation: TechNet Remote Desktop Services)

Adversaries may perform RDP session hijacking which involves stealing a legitimate user's remote session. Typically, a user is notified when someone else is trying to steal their session. With System permissions and using Terminal Services Console, `c:\windows\system32\tscon.exe [session number to be stolen]`, an adversary can hijack a session without the need for credentials or prompts to the user.(Citation: RDP Hijacking Korznikov) This can be done remotely or locally and with active or disconnected sessions.(Citation: RDP Hijacking Medium) It can also lead to [Remote System Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1018) and Privilege Escalation by stealing a Domain Admin or higher privileged account session. All of this can be done by using native Windows commands, but it has also been added as a feature in red teaming tools.(Citation: Kali Redsnarf)
4043.profile: [profile]RDP Hijacking, identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1563.002 under the Lateral Movement tactic for Windows platforms, involves stealing a legitimate user's active or disconnected Remote Desktop Protocol session. With SYSTEM permissions, adversaries use the native Windows command `tscon.exe` with a target session number to hijack the session without triggering user alerts or requiring credentials, facilitating privilege escalation and further network discovery. This technique has been utilized by groups like Axiom and is featured in red teaming tools such as RedSnarf.[/profile]
4043.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "RDP" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique name; the retrieved information describes techniques that use the Remote Desktop Protocol. The primary relevant technique is Remote Desktop Protocol (ID: T1021.001) under the Remote Services: Remote Desktop Protocol sub-technique, categorized under the Lateral Movement tactic on Windows platforms. It involves adversaries using valid accounts to log into remote systems via RDP to expand access, often after obtaining credentials through Credential Access techniques. Specific mechanics include using the native Windows command `tscon.exe` with system permissions to hijack existing RDP sessions without triggering user prompts, enabling lateral movement and privilege escalation. This behavior is associated with numerous threat groups, including APT41, FIN7, and Lazarus Group.

4044.name: SSH
4044.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may use [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078) to log into remote machines using Secure Shell (SSH). The adversary may then perform actions as the logged-on user.

SSH is a protocol that allows authorized users to open remote shells on other computers. Many Linux and macOS versions come with SSH installed by default, although typically disabled until the user enables it. On ESXi, SSH can be enabled either directly on the host (e.g., via `vim-cmd hostsvc/enable_ssh`) or via vCenter.(Citation: Sygnia ESXi Ransomware 2025)(Citation: TrendMicro ESXI Ransomware)(Citation: Sygnia Abyss Locker 2025) The SSH server can be configured to use standard password authentication or public-private keypairs in lieu of or in addition to a password. In this authentication scenario, the user’s public key must be in a special file on the computer running the server that lists which keypairs are allowed to login as that user (i.e., [SSH Authorized Keys](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1098/004)).
4044.profile: [profile]The entity SSH is the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1021.004 under the tactic Lateral Movement, applicable to Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. It involves using valid accounts to log into remote machines via the Secure Shell protocol to open remote shells and perform actions. The service may be enabled on ESXi hosts using commands like `vim-cmd hostsvc/enable_ssh` and supports authentication via passwords or public-private key pairs, where authorized keys are listed in a user-specific file. Associated groups include FIN7, Lazarus Group, and Scattered Spider.[/profile]
4044.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "SSH" aligns with the MITRE ATT&CK technique "Remote Services: SSH" (T1021.004) under the Lateral Movement tactic, primarily targeting Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. Adversaries use valid accounts to log into remote machines via the SSH protocol, which provides an encrypted tunnel for remote shell access. The service, often pre-installed but disabled by default, can be enabled on ESXi hosts using commands like `vim-cmd hostsvc/enable_ssh`. Authentication mechanisms include passwords or public-private key pairs, where authorized public keys are listed in files such as `~/.ssh/authorized_keys` or `/etc/ssh/keys-<username>/authorized_keys`. This technique is distinct from SSH Hijacking (T1563.001), which involves seizing existing sessions.

4045.name: PS
4045.profile: [profile]The entity "PS" is a standard Linux command-line utility used to display information about running processes, which adversaries can abuse for Discovery. Adversaries may use `ps` to list processes and identify targets for further action. Relatedly, the technique Overwrite Process Arguments (T1036.011) describes how adversaries can manipulate the `/proc/<PID>/cmdline` file and memory to spoof process names, making malicious processes appear benign when viewed with tools like `ps`. The intrusion set FIN7 has been associated with this type of activity.[/profile]
4045.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "PS" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique ID or name. Based on the retrieved information, it likely refers to the Linux `ps` command-line utility used to display information about running processes. Adversaries can manipulate process arguments in memory to hide malicious activity, as seen in techniques like Overwrite Process Arguments (T1036.011). When a process's `argv[0]` value is overwritten, tools like `ps` will display the spoofed command name, making the malicious process appear benign. This technique is used for defense evasion on Linux platforms.

4046.name: ADFind
4046.profile: [profile]ADFind is a tool used for Active Directory reconnaissance, aligning with MITRE ATT&CK technique T1087.002 (Domain Account Discovery) under the Discovery tactic on Windows platforms. It operates by querying Active Directory to enumerate domain accounts, groups, and objects, providing adversaries with detailed information about the network structure and user permissions. This tool is notably associated with the FIN7 intrusion set, which leverages it for initial access and privilege escalation within targeted environments.
4046.profile_without_enhance: [profile]ADFind is a tool used for Active Directory reconnaissance, aligning with MITRE ATT&CK technique T1087.002 (Domain Account Discovery) under the Discovery tactic on Windows platforms. It functions by querying Active Directory to enumerate domain accounts, groups, and their membership, often using LDAP queries to gather information that aids in identifying privileged accounts for lateral movement or privilege escalation. The tool has been associated with threat groups like Scattered Spider and FIN7.

4047.name: PowerShell ISE
4047.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may abuse PowerShell commands and scripts for execution. PowerShell is a powerful interactive command-line interface and scripting environment included in the Windows operating system.(Citation: TechNet PowerShell) Adversaries can use PowerShell to perform a number of actions, including discovery of information and execution of code. Examples include the Start-Process cmdlet which can be used to run an executable and the Invoke-Command cmdlet which runs a command locally or on a remote computer (though administrator permissions are required to use PowerShell to connect to remote systems). PowerShell may also be used to download and run executables from the Internet, which can be executed from disk or in memory without touching disk. A number of PowerShell-based offensive testing tools are available, including [Empire](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0363), [PowerSploit](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0194), [PoshC2](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0378), and PSAttack.(Citation: Github PSAttack) PowerShell commands/scripts can also be executed without directly invoking the powershell.exe binary through interfaces to PowerShell's underlying System.Management.Automation assembly DLL exposed through the .NET framework and Windows Common Language Interface (CLI).(Citation: Sixdub PowerPick Jan 2016)(Citation: SilentBreak Offensive PS Dec 2015)(Citation: Microsoft PSfromCsharp APR 2014)
4047.profile: [profile]PowerShell ISE is a host program for the Windows PowerShell scripting environment. As part of the Command and Scripting Interpreter technique (T1059.001) under the Execution tactic, it operates on the Windows platform. Adversaries can abuse it to run arbitrary scripts for discovery and code execution, using cmdlets like Start-Process and Invoke-Command. It is also specifically referenced as a host program that can load a malicious PowerShell profile (T1546.013) for persistence, where a modified profile.ps1 script executes automatically when the ISE session starts unless the -NoProfile flag is used.[/profile]
4047.profile_without_enhance: [profile]PowerShell ISE is a host program for the PowerShell scripting environment on Windows. It is referenced in MITRE ATT&CK sub-technique T1546.013 (Event Triggered Execution: PowerShell Profile) under the Persistence tactic. Adversaries can target the ISE-specific user profile to execute malicious scripts automatically when PowerShell ISE starts, providing a method for persistence. This technique is distinct from general PowerShell execution (T1059.001) and is specifically associated with the Turla threat group.

4048.name: CrackMapExec
4048.profile: [profile]CrackMapExec is a post-exploitation tool used for credential dumping (T1003) and password guessing (T1110.001) to facilitate credential access and lateral movement, particularly against services like SMB, SSH, and LDAP. It is commonly used by groups like FIN7 to automate attacks on Windows and Linux platforms by executing commands and extracting hashes from compromised systems.
4048.profile_without_enhance: [profile]CrackMapExec is a post-exploitation tool primarily used for credential access and lateral movement on Windows networks. It operates by leveraging obtained credentials to authenticate against network services, enabling actions like password spraying, credential dumping, and executing commands on remote systems. The tool is often associated with techniques such as OS Credential Dumping (T1003) and Password Guessing (T1110.001), targeting services like SMB, LDAP, and MSSQL to facilitate adversary operations.

4049.name: Kerberoasting
4049.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may abuse a valid Kerberos ticket-granting ticket (TGT) or sniff network traffic to obtain a ticket-granting service (TGS) ticket that may be vulnerable to [Brute Force](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1110).(Citation: Empire InvokeKerberoast Oct 2016)(Citation: AdSecurity Cracking Kerberos Dec 2015) 

Service principal names (SPNs) are used to uniquely identify each instance of a Windows service. To enable authentication, Kerberos requires that SPNs be associated with at least one service logon account (an account specifically tasked with running a service(Citation: Microsoft Detecting Kerberoasting Feb 2018)).(Citation: Microsoft SPN)(Citation: Microsoft SetSPN)(Citation: SANS Attacking Kerberos Nov 2014)(Citation: Harmj0y Kerberoast Nov 2016)

Adversaries possessing a valid Kerberos ticket-granting ticket (TGT) may request one or more Kerberos ticket-granting service (TGS) service tickets for any SPN from a domain controller (DC).(Citation: Empire InvokeKerberoast Oct 2016)(Citation: AdSecurity Cracking Kerberos Dec 2015) Portions of these tickets may be encrypted with the RC4 algorithm, meaning the Kerberos 5 TGS-REP etype 23 hash of the service account associated with the SPN is used as the private key and is thus vulnerable to offline [Brute Force](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1110) attacks that may expose plaintext credentials.(Citation: AdSecurity Cracking Kerberos Dec 2015)(Citation: Empire InvokeKerberoast Oct 2016) (Citation: Harmj0y Kerberoast Nov 2016)

This same behavior could be executed using service tickets captured from network traffic.(Citation: AdSecurity Cracking Kerberos Dec 2015)

Cracked hashes may enable [Persistence](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0003), [Privilege Escalation](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0004), and [Lateral Movement](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0008) via access to [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078).(Citation: SANS Attacking Kerberos Nov 2014)
4049.profile: [profile]Kerberoasting (T1558.003) is a Credential Access technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, operating on Windows platforms. It involves an adversary, possessing a valid Kerberos Ticket-Granting Ticket (TGT), requesting Ticket-Granting Service (TGS) tickets for Service Principal Names (SPNs) from a domain controller. The critical vulnerability lies in portions of these tickets being encrypted with the RC4 algorithm, where the Kerberos 5 TGS-REP etype 23 hash of the associated service account acts as the key, making the hash vulnerable to offline brute-force attacks to recover plaintext credentials. This attack can also be performed by sniffing service tickets from network traffic, and cracked credentials facilitate persistence, privilege escalation, and lateral movement. It is notably used by groups like FIN7.[/profile]
4049.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Kerberoasting, identified as T1558.003 within the Credential Access tactic, targets Windows platforms. It involves an adversary abusing a valid Kerberos Ticket-Granting Ticket (TGT) to request Ticket-Granting Service (TGS) tickets for Service Principal Names (SPNs) from a domain controller. Portions of these tickets, specifically the Kerberos 5 TGS-REP etype 23 hash, are often encrypted with the RC4 algorithm, making the service account's password hash vulnerable to offline brute-force attacks to recover plaintext credentials. This attack can also be performed using service tickets captured from network traffic, and cracked credentials facilitate persistence, privilege escalation, and lateral movement.

4050.name: Mimikatz
4050.profile: [profile]Mimikatz is a credential theft tool (Software ID: S0002) used in the Credential Access tactic on Windows platforms. Its technical mechanics include the 'lsadump' module, which can perform DCSync attacks to pull password hashes from Active Directory by abusing domain replication APIs, and it can extract Local Security Authority (LSA) secrets directly from system memory. It is associated with intrusion sets like FIN7 and is a common utility for dumping OS credentials.
4050.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Mimikatz is a credential dumping tool (software, not a MITRE technique ID) used on Windows platforms to extract credentials from system memory. It can dump LSA secrets from the HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SECURITY\Policy\Secrets registry or memory and includes the lsadump module for performing DCSync attacks against Active Directory to pull password hashes.

4051.name: PowerSploit
4051.profile: [profile]PowerSploit is a deprecated software entity (S0194) used for Execution and Post-Exploitation, primarily on the Windows platform. It is a PowerShell-based offensive framework containing modules for tasks like privilege escalation, credential dumping, and persistence. It is referenced by threat groups like FIN7 and is commonly used alongside other tools like Empire and Metasploit for post-compromise operations.
4051.profile_without_enhance: [profile]PowerSploit is a PowerShell-based post-exploitation framework used by adversaries for offensive operations. It is referenced under MITRE ATT&CK techniques T1059.001 (Command and Scripting Interpreter: PowerShell) and the deprecated T1064 (Scripting), indicating its use for execution and automating post-compromise tasks. The framework operates on Windows platforms and includes modules for various activities such as code execution, reconnaissance, and persistence, often allowing execution directly in memory to evade disk-based detection. It is cited alongside other tools like Empire and Metasploit in the context of adversary testing and operations.

4052.name: SessionGopher
4052.profile: [profile]SessionGopher is a tool used by the FIN7 intrusion set for credential access, specifically to steal web session cookies. It functions by using PowerShell to search a victim's computer for files containing saved session information from popular applications like PuTTY, WinSCP, FileZilla, and Microsoft Remote Desktop. The tool extracts these credentials, which often include plaintext passwords or session cookies, enabling adversaries to authenticate to services and bypass multi-factor authentication without needing the original user credentials.
4052.profile_without_enhance: [profile]SessionGopher is an attack pattern that aligns with the MITRE ATT&CK technique Steal Web Session Cookie (T1539) under the Credential Access tactic, targeting Windows platforms. It functions by extracting saved session information, including cookies and credentials, from various applications such as remote desktop clients (e.g., PuTTY, WinSCP, FileZilla) and web browsers by querying the Windows registry and file system. This enables adversaries to hijack authenticated sessions, potentially bypassing multi-factor authentication, and is associated with threat groups like APT42 and Scattered Spider.

4053.name: Self-Propagation
4053.profile: [profile]Self-Propagation is a technique used in the Lateral Movement tactic. It involves an adversary's malware or tool autonomously spreading within a compromised environment, often by exploiting network vulnerabilities or leveraging stolen credentials to move from one system to another. The intrusion set FIN7 has been associated with this behavior, which can enable rapid network-wide compromise and hinder defensive responses by overwhelming containment efforts.
4053.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Self-Propagation is a technique where malware or malicious code autonomously spreads within or across systems without requiring direct adversary interaction. This behavior is distinct from initial access and falls under the tactic of Lateral Movement. It operates across multiple platforms. The mechanism involves the malicious payload replicating itself, often by exploiting network shares, removable drives, or software vulnerabilities to infect new hosts. This capability enables the incident to expand its scope independently, hindering containment efforts.

4054.name: AMSI Hot-Patching
4054.profile: [profile]AMSI Hot-Patching is a technique, likely categorized under Defense Evasion (T1562) or Execution (T1574), for the Windows platform. It involves patching the in-memory functions of the Antimalware Scan Interface (AMSI) to bypass or disable its scanning capabilities, allowing malicious code to execute undetected. This method is used by groups like FIN7 to impair defenses and maintain persistence by hijacking the execution flow of legitimate software processes.
4054.profile_without_enhance: [profile]AMSI Hot-Patching is a technique used to impair defenses, specifically targeting the Antimalware Scan Interface (AMSI) on Windows platforms. It works by directly patching the memory of the AMSI.dll library to bypass its scanning functionality, often achieved by overwriting key function prologues with return instructions or redirecting execution flow to neutral code. This method allows malicious scripts or payloads to execute without being intercepted and analyzed by AMSI-aware security products.

4055.name: Network Enumeration
4055.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may enumerate system and service logs to find useful data. These logs may highlight various types of valuable insights for an adversary, such as user authentication records ([Account Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1087)), security or vulnerable software ([Software Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1518)), or hosts within a compromised network ([Remote System Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1018)).

Host binaries may be leveraged to collect system logs. Examples include using `wevtutil.exe` or [PowerShell](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001) on Windows to access and/or export security event information.(Citation: WithSecure Lazarus-NoPineapple Threat Intel Report 2023)(Citation: Cadet Blizzard emerges as novel threat actor) In cloud environments, adversaries may leverage utilities such as the Azure VM Agent’s `CollectGuestLogs.exe` to collect security logs from cloud hosted infrastructure.(Citation: SIM Swapping and Abuse of the Microsoft Azure Serial Console)

Adversaries may also target centralized logging infrastructure such as SIEMs. Logs may also be bulk exported and sent to adversary-controlled infrastructure for offline analysis.

In addition to gaining a better understanding of the environment, adversaries may also monitor logs in real time to track incident response procedures. This may allow them to adjust their techniques in order to maintain persistence or evade defenses.(Citation: Permiso GUI-Vil 2023)
4055.profile: [profile]Network Enumeration, also known as log enumeration (T1654), is a Discovery technique. Adversaries enumerate system, service, and security logs to gather intelligence, using host binaries like `wevtutil.exe` or PowerShell on Windows and utilities like Azure's `CollectGuestLogs.exe` in cloud environments. They target centralized logging infrastructure like SIEMs, bulk exporting logs for offline analysis to discover user accounts, software, and remote systems, and may monitor logs in real-time to track incident response. Groups like Volt Typhoon and FIN7 have been associated with this activity.
4055.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Network Enumeration is a Discovery technique (Tactic: TA0007) used to map a target network's structure and identify active systems. Adversaries perform this by actively scanning for hosts, open ports, and services using tools like ping sweeps, port scanners (e.g., Nmap), and commands such as `net view`. This reconnaissance reveals IP addresses, hostnames, and network topology, which is critical for planning subsequent lateral movement and targeting specific systems for exploitation.

4056.name: Hypervisor Jackpotting
4056.uncertain_mes:
**This technique has been deprecated and should no longer be used.**

A type-1 hypervisor is a software layer that sits between the guest operating systems and system's hardware. (Citation: Wikipedia Hypervisor) It presents a virtual running environment to an operating system. An example of a common hypervisor is Xen. (Citation: Wikipedia Xen) A type-1 hypervisor operates at a level below the operating system and could be designed with [Rootkit](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1014) functionality to hide its existence from the guest operating system. (Citation: Myers 2007) A malicious hypervisor of this nature could be used to persist on systems through interruption.
4056.profile: [profile]Hypervisor Jackpotting, a deprecated technique formerly under ID T1062, involves adversaries abusing hypervisor command-line interfaces (CLIs) like `esxcli` and `vim-cmd` on platforms such as ESXi to execute malicious commands. This enables actions such as listing, starting, and stopping virtual machines, configuring firewall rules, and facilitating further attacks like data encryption for impact, as observed in campaigns by groups like FIN7 and UNC3886.[/profile]
4056.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Hypervisor Jackpotting is a technique where adversaries abuse hypervisor command-line interfaces (CLIs) like `esxcli` and `vim-cmd` on ESXi systems to execute malicious commands for discovery and impact. This technique, related to T1059.012 (Hypervisor CLI), falls under the Execution tactic and targets virtualization platforms. Specific mechanics include using commands such as `esxcli vm process list` or `vim-cmd vmsvc/getallvms` to enumerate virtual machines, which can then be leveraged for follow-on actions like service disruption or data encryption. It has been associated with threat group UNC3886.

4057.name: Carbanak/Cobalt
4057.uncertain_mes: [Carbanak](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0030) is a full-featured, remote backdoor used by a group of the same name ([Carbanak](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0008)). It is intended for espionage, data exfiltration, and providing remote access to infected machines. (Citation: Kaspersky Carbanak) (Citation: FireEye CARBANAK June 2017)
4057.profile: [profile]Carbanak/Cobalt, also known as Carbanak, is a full-featured remote backdoor attributed to the FIN7 and Carbanak groups, used for espionage, data exfiltration, and remote access. Key technical behaviors include gathering victim information, constructing Command-and-Control URLs for communication, and employing obfuscation and delay functions. It is known to be used as a follow-up to breaches alongside tools like Cobalt Strike. The malware primarily targets financial institutions and other organizations for data theft and remote control operations.
4057.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Carbanak, also known as Cobalt, is a malware attributed to the financially motivated cybercrime group FIN7. It functions as a backdoor, gathering victim information and communicating with command-and-control servers via constructed URLs. The group is known to employ follow-up tools like Cobalt Strike for post-breach activities. Associated infrastructure and tools include Bateleur and Tinymet. Its primary targets are financial institutions.

4065.name: Malicious PDF File
4065.profile: [profile]Malicious PDF File, also known as BAE_HPC_SE.pdf and BAE_2020_JD_SSE.pdf, is attributed to the FIN7 and Lazarus Group intrusion sets. The malware specifically targets Windows systems through malicious PDF documents designed to exploit or masquerade as legitimate applications such as PDF readers.]

It serves as an initial infection vector, potentially leading to secondary payloads like neddnloader, and its infrastructure includes files such as InternalViewer2.exe.

4066.name: Malicious JPEG
4066.profile: [profile]Malicious JPEG is a technique used to hide malware components within publicly accessible image files, as seen in the Oski stealer which disguises DLL dependencies (e.g., sqlite3.dll, freebl3.dll) as JPEG files downloaded from its C&C server. This method is associated with the FIN7 intrusion set. The primary target platforms are Windows systems, leveraging image files as a delivery and obfuscation mechanism for malicious payloads.
