It is associated with the Oski Stealer, which downloads its dependencies by making seven specific requests to a C&C server for files disguised as JPEGs (e.g., 1.jpeg = sqlite3.dll, 2.jpeg = freebl3.dll, 3.jpeg = mozglue.dll, 4.jpeg = msvcp140.dll, 5.jpeg = nss3.dll, 6.jpeg = softokn3.dll, 7.jpeg = vcruntime140.dll). This technique of concealing payloads within image files is also referenced in the context of other malware like AsyncRAT and the unidentified '122' stealer.

4068.name: Bypass AppLocker Whitelisting
4068.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may modify file attributes and subvert Gatekeeper functionality to evade user prompts and execute untrusted programs. Gatekeeper is a set of technologies that act as layer of Apple’s security model to ensure only trusted applications are executed on a host. Gatekeeper was built on top of File Quarantine in Snow Leopard (10.6, 2009) and has grown to include Code Signing, security policy compliance, Notarization, and more. Gatekeeper also treats applications running for the first time differently than reopened applications.(Citation: TheEclecticLightCompany Quarantine and the flag)(Citation: TheEclecticLightCompany apple notarization )

Based on an opt-in system, when files are downloaded an extended attribute (xattr) called `com.apple.quarantine` (also known as a quarantine flag) can be set on the file by the application performing the download. Launch Services opens the application in a suspended state. For first run applications with the quarantine flag set, Gatekeeper executes the following functions:

1. Checks extended attribute – Gatekeeper checks for the quarantine flag, then provides an alert prompt to the user to allow or deny execution.(Citation: OceanLotus for OS X)(Citation: 20 macOS Common Tools and Techniques)

2. Checks System Policies - Gatekeeper checks the system security policy, allowing execution of apps downloaded from either just the App Store or the App Store and identified developers.

3. Code Signing – Gatekeeper checks for a valid code signature from an Apple Developer ID.

4. Notarization - Using the `api.apple-cloudkit.com` API, Gatekeeper reaches out to Apple servers to verify or pull down the notarization ticket and ensure the ticket is not revoked. Users can override notarization, which will result in a prompt of executing an “unauthorized app” and the security policy will be modified.

Adversaries can subvert one or multiple security controls within Gatekeeper checks through logic errors (e.g. [Exploitation for Defense Evasion](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1211)), unchecked file types, and external libraries. For example, prior to macOS 13 Ventura, code signing and notarization checks were only conducted on first launch, allowing adversaries to write malicious executables to previously opened applications in order to bypass Gatekeeper security checks.(Citation: theevilbit gatekeeper bypass 2021)(Citation: Application Bundle Manipulation Brandon Dalton)

Applications and files loaded onto the system from a USB flash drive, optical disk, external hard drive, from a drive shared over the local network, or using the curl command may not set the quarantine flag. Additionally, it is possible to avoid setting the quarantine flag using [Drive-by Compromise](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1189).
4068.profile: [profile]Bypass AppLocker Whitelisting, identified as T1553.001, is a Defense Evasion technique for the macOS platform. It involves subverting Apple's Gatekeeper security by exploiting logic errors, using unchecked file types, or manipulating the quarantine flag (`com.apple.quarantine` extended attribute) to execute untrusted programs without user prompts. Prior to macOS 13, adversaries could write malicious code into previously opened applications to bypass code signing and notarization checks. This technique has been associated with the intrusion set FIN7.[/profile]
4068.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Bypass AppLocker Whitelisting is a defense evasion technique (Tactic) for Windows (Platform). It involves subverting application whitelisting controls like AppLocker by abusing trusted, signed system binaries to proxy execution of malicious code. For example, adversaries can supply the legitimate Microsoft program CMSTP.exe with a malicious INF file to load and execute DLLs or scriptlets from remote servers, thereby bypassing AppLocker policies. Other methods include using trusted, signed Microsoft scripts to proxy execution of malicious files.

4072.name: Email Impersonating European Banking Federation
4072.profile: [profile]Email Impersonating European Banking Federation is a specific phishing technique, likely a sub-technique of T1656 (Impersonation) under the Initial Access tactic, used on Windows, macOS, and Linux platforms. The technique involves adversaries, such as the FIN7 group, crafting deceptive emails that falsely appear to originate from the trusted European Banking Federation to manipulate targets. This impersonation leverages established organizational trust to increase the success rate of phishing attempts, tricking recipients into divulging sensitive information or performing actions like transferring funds. The core mechanic is the abuse of email protocols and social engineering to bypass security through deception.[/profile]
4072.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Email Impersonating European Banking Federation is a specific spearphishing technique where adversaries craft emails to masquerade as the European Banking Federation, a trusted entity, to deceive targets. This falls under the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1566.001 (Spearphishing Attachment) or T1566.002 (Spearphishing Link), primarily within the Initial Access tactic. The mechanics involve using the impersonated identity to lend credibility, often with urgent or financial-themed language, to trick recipients into opening malicious attachments or clicking links, thereby compromising systems. This is a targeted application of broader impersonation (T1656) tactics.

4073.name: JScript Backdoor
4073.profile: [profile]JScript Backdoor, also known as Outlook Backdoor or Mosquito, is a JavaScript-based backdoor attributed to the FIN7 and Turla intrusion sets. It operates by downloading and executing malicious JavaScript files, such as through ieuinit.exe, and can utilize Google Apps Script for command and control (C2) communication. Its key behaviors include command execution via JavaScript (T1059.007) and potential privilege escalation using tools like Metasploit modules. The malware primarily targets Windows platforms and is associated with campaigns involving Cobalt Strike and other loaders like GootLoader.
4073.profile_without_enhance: [profile]JScript Backdoor, also known as the Mosquito JScript backdoor, is attributed to the Turla group. Its key technical behaviors include using JavaScript for command and scripting interpretation, specifically leveraging Google Apps Script as its command-and-control server. The malware targets systems where it can execute JavaScript, and it has been observed in operations involving the download of JavaScript files for backdoor functionality.

4074.name: VBA Scripts
4074.profile: [profile]VBA Scripts, also known as VBScript, are a scripting language and file type frequently weaponized by threat actors. They are attributed to the FIN7 intrusion set and are used by groups like Cobalt (associated with Pony) and Gold Cabin, Mummy Spider, and Mealybug (associated with Emotet). Key technical behaviors include the use of highly obfuscated macros embedded within documents like Excel files to execute malicious payloads. The target platform is primarily Windows systems, leveraging the native Windows Script Host. Infrastructure and supplementary information include the use of weaponized documents as initial infection vectors, with observed file hashes linked to malicious VBScript samples.[/profile]
4074.profile_without_enhance: [profile]VBA Scripts, also known as VBScript, are a scripting language and component used as a delivery mechanism or initial payload by various malware families. They are employed by threat groups including Gold Cabin, Mummy Spider, Mealybug (associated with Emotet), and Cobalt (associated with Pony). Key technical behaviors include the use of highly obfuscated VBA macros embedded within weaponized documents like Excel files to enable initial execution when macros are enabled. The target platform is primarily Microsoft Windows systems that support the execution of these scripts.

4075.name: Malicious VBA-Scripted Word Document
4075.profile: [profile]Malicious VBA-Scripted Word Document, also known as a malicious OLE document, is attributed to the FIN7 intrusion set. Its key technical behavior involves using an auto-executable malicious VBA Macro within a Microsoft Word document to deliver malware payloads such as Agent Tesla. The target platform is Microsoft Windows systems via Office documents. Infrastructure includes specific malicious document hashes used for distribution.
4075.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Malicious VBA-Scripted Word Document, also known as a malicious OLE document, is attributed to groups such as Sweed and UAC-0226. It operates by using auto-executable malicious VBA Macros embedded within Microsoft Word documents to deliver payloads like Agent Tesla and Saint Bot, facilitating initial infection and subsequent malicious activities on Windows platforms.

4076.name: INF File
4076.profile: [profile]INF File is a Windows configuration file format that can be weaponized for execution. Adversaries, such as the FIN7 intrusion set, supply malicious INF files to the legitimate CMSTP.exe utility to install infected service profiles. This technique, known as CMSTP (T1191), falls under the Defense Evasion and Execution tactics on Windows platforms. The INF file contains scripted commands that CMSTP.exe processes, enabling the loading and execution of malicious DLLs or COM scriptlets from remote servers, often bypassing application whitelisting and User Account Control due to CMSTP's trusted, signed status.[/profile]
4076.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "INF File" is a file format used in the context of the MITRE ATT&CK technique CMSTP (T1191) under the Defense Evasion tactic for Windows platforms. Specifically, adversaries supply the Microsoft Connection Manager Profile Installer (CMSTP.exe) with malicious INF files to execute arbitrary commands, load remote DLLs or COM scriptlets, and bypass security controls like AppLocker and User Account Control. This abuse leverages the legitimate, signed CMSTP.exe to run code from a crafted installation information file.

4078.name: JavaScript Backdoor
4078.profile: [profile]JavaScript Backdoor is a malware stager attributed to the FIN7 intrusion set. It is delivered via ieuinit.exe and executed as a scriptlet COM object (SCT) using regsvr32.exe for persistence through registry keys. 4078.profile_without_enhance: [profile]JavaScript Backdoor is a malware believed to be a stager for additional payloads, exhibiting functionality for persistence via registry key settings and being launched in an SCT (scriptlet COM object) called via regsvr32.exe. It is attributed to groups like Cobalt and Turla. The backdoor is implemented in JavaScript and is downloaded by other executables like ieuinit.exe.

4079.name: DLL File Disguised as Text
4079.profile: [profile]DLL File Disguised as Text is a technique attributed to the FIN7 intrusion set. It involves a malicious DLL file masquerading as a benign .dat file, such as "C:\ProgramData\desktop.dat". The DLL exports functions from the Perl Compatible Regular Expressions (PCRE) library to appear legitimate while containing decryption routines for malicious payloads. This technique is a form of defense evasion and is deployed on Windows platforms.
4079.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The malware 'DLL File Disguised as Text' is a component that disguises itself as a .dat file, specifically noted as 'C:\ProgramData\desktop.dat'. It exports numerous functions, primarily Perl Compatible Regular Expressions (PCRE) library functions, to masquerade as a benign file. This DLL also contains functionality to decrypt data. It has been associated with the Lazarus Group. Its key behaviors include file masquerading and data decryption, primarily targeting Windows platforms through deceptive file distribution.

4081.name: Remote Payload
4081.profile: [profile]Remote Payload is a generic term for malicious code injected into a remote process. It is associated with the FIN7 intrusion set and is referenced in the context of malware families like Zeus and Dridex, which allocate memory and write the payload into a remote svchost.exe process using NtAllocateVirtualMemory and ZwWriteVirtualMemory. It is also discussed in relation to Cobalt Strike payloads. Its target platform is Windows.
4081.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Remote Payload is a malicious payload referenced in the context of other malware families. It is associated with the technical behavior of being injected into a remote svchost.exe process, where memory is allocated and the payload is written using the Windows API calls NtAllocateVirtualMemory and ZwWriteVirtualMemory. This specific injection technique is documented in the context of the Zeus and Dridex malware families. Dridex is further linked to the groups Evil Corp, Indrik Spider, and TA505. The payload's target platform is Windows.

4082.name: Spoofed Internal Sender
4082.uncertain_mes: An adversary may deface systems internal to an organization in an attempt to intimidate or mislead users, thus discrediting the integrity of the systems. This may take the form of modifications to internal websites or server login messages, or directly to user systems with the replacement of the desktop wallpaper.(Citation: Novetta Blockbuster)(Citation: Varonis) Disturbing or offensive images may be used as a part of [Internal Defacement](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1491/001) in order to cause user discomfort, or to pressure compliance with accompanying messages. Since internally defacing systems exposes an adversary's presence, it often takes place after other intrusion goals have been accomplished.(Citation: Novetta Blockbuster Destructive Malware)
4082.profile: [profile]Spoofed Internal Sender is a technique where adversaries forge the sender identity in email headers, such as the FROM field, to appear as a trusted internal contact. This often exploits weak or absent email authentication policies like SPF, DKIM, and DMARC. A specific method involves abusing Microsoft 365's Direct Send functionality via internal devices like printers to send unauthenticated spoofed emails. This technique supports tactics like Initial Access and is used to enable phishing and impersonation within a compromised network.[/profile]
4082.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Spoofed Internal Sender is a technique where adversaries forge email headers, such as the FROM field, to impersonate a trusted sender within the same organization. This often exploits weak or absent email authentication policies like SPF, DKIM, and DMARC to bypass security checks. The technique is used to conduct phishing or internal spearphishing campaigns, increasing the likelihood of victim compliance by leveraging perceived internal trust. It can be executed by abusing functionalities like Microsoft 365's Direct Send from internal devices.

4083.name: Disable Scripts by Default
4083.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may establish persistence by modifying RC scripts, which are executed during a Unix-like system’s startup. These files allow system administrators to map and start custom services at startup for different run levels. RC scripts require root privileges to modify. Adversaries may establish persistence by adding a malicious binary path or shell commands to rc.local, rc.common, and other RC scripts specific to the Unix-like distribution.(Citation: IranThreats Kittens Dec 2017)(Citation: Intezer HiddenWasp Map 2019) Upon reboot, the system executes the script's contents as root, resulting in persistence. Adversary abuse of RC scripts is especially effective for lightweight Unix-like distributions using the root user as default, such as ESXi hypervisors, IoT, or embedded systems.(Citation: intezer-kaiji-malware) As ESXi servers store most system files in memory and therefore discard changes on shutdown, leveraging `/etc/rc.local.d/local.sh` is one of the few mechanisms for enabling persistence across reboots.(Citation: Juniper Networks ESXi Backdoor 2022) Several Unix-like systems have moved to Systemd and deprecated the use of RC scripts. This is now a deprecated mechanism in macOS in favor of Launchd.(Citation: Apple Developer Doco Archive Launchd)(Citation: Startup Items) This technique can be used on Mac OS X Panther v10.3 and earlier versions which still execute the RC scripts.(Citation: Methods of Mac Malware Persistence) To maintain backwards compatibility some systems, such as Ubuntu, will execute the RC scripts if they exist with the correct file permissions.(Citation: Ubuntu Manpage systemd rc)
4083.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique "Boot or Logon Initialization Scripts: RC Scripts" (T1037.004) under the Persistence tactic, targeting Unix-like platforms including Linux, macOS, and ESXi. Adversaries establish persistence by adding malicious commands or binary paths to RC scripts like `rc.local` or `/etc/rc.local.d/local.sh`, which execute with root privileges during system startup. This is particularly effective on systems using root by default, such as ESXi hypervisors and embedded devices, though it is deprecated in modern macOS and systems using Systemd. Groups like APT29, VELVET ANT, and UNC3886 have been associated with this technique.[/profile]
4083.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Disable Scripts by Default" is a defensive configuration technique, not a direct MITRE ATT&CK attack pattern. It describes a security measure where systems are configured to prevent the automatic execution of scripts, such as JavaScript in web browsers or macros in documents, to mitigate risks from techniques like Drive-by Compromise (T1189). This setting forces explicit user consent for script execution, disrupting common initial access and execution vectors used by adversaries to deliver malware without interaction.

4085.name: Phishing Lures
4085.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may send phishing messages to gain access to victim systems. All forms of phishing are electronically delivered social engineering. Phishing can be targeted, known as spearphishing. In spearphishing, a specific individual, company, or industry will be targeted by the adversary. More generally, adversaries can conduct non-targeted phishing, such as in mass malware spam campaigns.

Adversaries may send victims emails containing malicious attachments or links, typically to execute malicious code on victim systems. Phishing may also be conducted via third-party services, like social media platforms. Phishing may also involve social engineering techniques, such as posing as a trusted source, as well as evasive techniques such as removing or manipulating emails or metadata/headers from compromised accounts being abused to send messages (e.g., [Email Hiding Rules](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1564/008)).(Citation: Microsoft OAuth Spam 2022)(Citation: Palo Alto Unit 42 VBA Infostealer 2014) Another way to accomplish this is by [Email Spoofing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1672)(Citation: Proofpoint-spoof) the identity of the sender, which can be used to fool both the human recipient as well as automated security tools,(Citation: cyberproof-double-bounce) or by including the intended target as a party to an existing email thread that includes malicious files or links (i.e., "thread hijacking").(Citation: phishing-krebs)

Victims may also receive phishing messages that instruct them to call a phone number where they are directed to visit a malicious URL, download malware,(Citation: sygnia Luna Month)(Citation: CISA Remote Monitoring and Management Software) or install adversary-accessible remote management tools onto their computer (i.e., [User Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204)).(Citation: Unit42 Luna Moth)
4085.profile: [profile]Phishing, identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1566 under the Initial Access tactic, targets multiple platforms including Windows, macOS, and Linux. It involves sending electronic messages, such as emails with malicious attachments or links, to execute code on victim systems. This technique employs social engineering by posing as a trusted source and utilizes evasive methods like email spoofing and thread hijacking. It is associated with groups including APT17, FIN7, and Kimsuky.[/profile]
4085.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Phishing Lures is a component of broader phishing techniques (T1566, T1598) within the Initial Access tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It involves crafting deceptive messages to trick recipients into revealing sensitive information or executing malicious actions. These lures often employ social engineering, such as posing as a trusted source, and may use obfuscated URLs, QR codes ("quishing"), or adversary-in-the-middle phishing kits like EvilProxy to capture credentials and bypass multi-factor authentication. The content is tailored using reconnaissance data to increase believability and urgency.

4086.name: PowerShell Scripts
4086.uncertain_mes: powershell_web_backdoor This is a very simple powershell web backdoor Usage: hxxp://127.0.0.1:9999/backdoor/?cmd=<Insert Your powershell compatible base64 encoded command here
4086.profile: [profile]PowerShell Scripts, also known as powershell_web_backdoor, is a simple web backdoor that executes base64-encoded commands via a web parameter. It is associated with intrusion sets Turla, menuPass, OilRig, and FIN7. Its key technical behavior involves executing commands delivered through a web request to a specified URI parameter. It targets systems where PowerShell is available and is referenced in the context of other malware like Xenorat, Moonpeak, and Emotet, which use PowerShell scripts for payload download and execution with obfuscation.[/profile]
4086.profile_without_enhance: [profile]PowerShell Scripts, also known as powershell_web_backdoor, are leveraged by groups like Gold Cabin, Mummy Spider, and Mealybug in campaigns involving malware such as Emotet. Key TTPs include executing scripts to download payloads, often using multiple layers of obfuscation, and establishing command and control via DNS Tunneling to encapsulate traffic within DNS queries. The primary target platform is Windows, with scripts frequently embedded in macros or fetched from remote servers to deploy backdoors.

4089.name: GGLDR
4089.uncertain_mes:
Carbanak Group uses Google for malware command-and-control
0 min read

4091.name: 58d2a83f7778d5.36783181.vbs

4093.name: Anti-Analysis (Obfuscation)
4093.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may obfuscate command and control traffic to make it more difficult to detect.(Citation: Bitdefender FunnyDream Campaign November 2020) Command and control (C2) communications are hidden (but not necessarily encrypted) in an attempt to make the content more difficult to discover or decipher and to make the communication less conspicuous and hide commands from being seen. This encompasses many methods, such as adding junk data to protocol traffic, using steganography, or impersonating legitimate protocols.
4093.profile: [profile]Data Obfuscation is the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1001 under the Command and Control tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It specifically hides C2 traffic to evade detection by adding junk data to protocols, using steganography, or impersonating legitimate traffic, without necessarily employing encryption. The intrusion-set FIN7 has been associated with this technique.[/profile]
4093.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Anti-Analysis (Obfuscation)" is a general adversary technique to hinder detection and analysis, not a specific MITRE ATT&CK ID. It encompasses methods like obfuscating files or information (T1027) to hide payloads through encryption, encoding, or splitting, and command obfuscation (T1027.010) using syntax tricks, character manipulation, and tools like Invoke-Obfuscation to disguise scripts and commands during execution. These techniques are used across multiple platforms to evade defenses.

4094.name: Anti-Sandbox Capabilities
4094.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may employ various means to detect and avoid virtualization and analysis environments. This may include changing behaviors based on the results of checks for the presence of artifacts indicative of a virtual machine environment (VME) or sandbox. If the adversary detects a VME, they may alter their malware to disengage from the victim or conceal the core functions of the implant. They may also search for VME artifacts before dropping secondary or additional payloads. Adversaries may use the information learned from [Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1497) during automated discovery to shape follow-on behaviors.(Citation: Deloitte Environment Awareness)

Adversaries may use several methods to accomplish [Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1497) such as checking for security monitoring tools (e.g., Sysinternals, Wireshark, etc.) or other system artifacts associated with analysis or virtualization. Adversaries may also check for legitimate user activity to help determine if it is in an analysis environment. Additional methods include use of sleep timers or loops within malware code to avoid operating within a temporary sandbox.(Citation: Unit 42 Pirpi July 2015)
4094.profile: [profile]Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion, identified as T1497 under the Defense Evasion tactic, is a technique used across multiple platforms to detect and avoid analysis environments. It operates by checking for artifacts like security monitoring tools (e.g., Sysinternals, Wireshark), virtual machine indicators, or lack of legitimate user activity; upon detection, malware may alter its behavior, disengage, or employ sleep timers to evade temporary sandboxes. This technique is distinct from execution guardrails like Environmental Keying, which require a specific match to proceed, whereas sandbox evasion halts execution upon finding analysis artifacts. It has been associated with groups like FIN7, Contagious Interview, Saint Bear, and DarkHotel.[/profile]
4094.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Anti-Sandbox Capabilities" is a sub-technique of Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion (T1497) under the Defense Evasion tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It involves malware detecting and avoiding analysis environments by checking for artifacts like known security tools, virtual machine indicators, or a lack of legitimate user activity. Upon detection, it may alter its behavior, disengage, or use delays to evade automated sandboxes. This is distinct from execution guardrails, which check for specific target values to enable execution.

4095.name: Retrieve System Information
4095.uncertain_mes: An adversary may attempt to get detailed information about the operating system and hardware, including version, patches, hotfixes, service packs, and architecture. Adversaries may use this information to shape follow-on behaviors, including whether or not the adversary fully infects the target and/or attempts specific actions. This behavior is distinct from [Local Storage Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1680) which is an adversary's discovery of local drive, disks and/or volumes. Tools such as [Systeminfo](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0096) can be used to gather detailed system information. If running with privileged access, a breakdown of system data can be gathered through the systemsetup configuration tool on macOS. Adversaries may leverage a [Network Device CLI](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/008) on network devices to gather detailed system information (e.g. show version).(Citation: US-CERT-TA18-106A) On ESXi servers, threat actors may gather system information from various esxcli utilities, such as `system hostname get` and `system version get`.(Citation: Crowdstrike Hypervisor Jackpotting Pt 2 2021)(Citation: Varonis) Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) cloud providers such as AWS, GCP, and Azure allow access to instance and virtual machine information via APIs. Successful authenticated API calls can return data such as the operating system platform and status of a particular instance or the model view of a virtual machine.(Citation: Amazon Describe Instance)(Citation: Google Instances Resource)(Citation: Microsoft Virutal Machine API) [System Information Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1082) combined with information gathered from other forms of discovery and reconnaissance can drive payload development and concealment.(Citation: OSX.FairyTale)(Citation: 20 macOS Common Tools and Techniques)
4095.profile: [profile]System Information Discovery, designated T1082, is a Discovery tactic used across Windows, macOS, Linux, and cloud platforms. It involves gathering detailed OS and hardware data like version, patches, and architecture to inform follow-on actions. Specific techniques include using the `systeminfo` command on Windows, the `systemsetup` tool on macOS, CLI commands like `show version` on network devices, and `esxcli` utilities such as `system version get` on ESXi servers. Cloud instances can be queried via provider APIs. This information is often used for payload development and evasion, and is associated with groups like FIN7.
4095.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Retrieve System Information is a technique for gathering detailed OS and hardware data, including version, patches, and architecture, to inform follow-on actions. It is mapped to MITRE ATT&CK T1082 under the Discovery tactic for Windows, macOS, Linux, and cloud platforms. Technical execution involves tools like the `systeminfo` command, the macOS `systemsetup` utility, network device CLI commands (e.g., `show version`), and cloud instance APIs. This information is often combined with other discovery results for payload development and evasion.

4096.name: Process Enumeration
4096.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may enumerate system and service logs to find useful data. These logs may highlight various types of valuable insights for an adversary, such as user authentication records ([Account Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1087)), security or vulnerable software ([Software Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1518)), or hosts within a compromised network ([Remote System Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1018)).

Host binaries may be leveraged to collect system logs. Examples include using `wevtutil.exe` or [PowerShell](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001) on Windows to access and/or export security event information.(Citation: WithSecure Lazarus-NoPineapple Threat Intel Report 2023)(Citation: Cadet Blizzard emerges as novel threat actor) In cloud environments, adversaries may leverage utilities such as the Azure VM Agent’s `CollectGuestLogs.exe` to collect security logs from cloud hosted infrastructure.(Citation: SIM Swapping and Abuse of the Microsoft Azure Serial Console)

Adversaries may also target centralized logging infrastructure such as SIEMs. Logs may also be bulk exported and sent to adversary-controlled infrastructure for offline analysis.

In addition to gaining a better understanding of the environment, adversaries may also monitor logs in real time to track incident response procedures. This may allow them to adjust their techniques in order to maintain persistence or evade defenses.(Citation: Permiso GUI-Vil 2023)
4096.profile: [profile]Process Enumeration, also known as log enumeration (T1654), is a Discovery technique primarily for Windows and cloud platforms. It involves adversaries enumerating system and service logs to find data like user authentication records, security software details, or network hosts. Technical mechanics include using host binaries like `wevtutil.exe` or PowerShell on Windows, and utilities like Azure VM Agent's `CollectGuestLogs.exe` in cloud environments. Adversaries may also target centralized logging infrastructure like SIEMs, bulk export logs for offline analysis, or monitor logs in real-time to track incident response. Associated groups include Volt Typhoon, APT5, Mustang Panda, Ember Bear, and Aquatic Panda.[/profile]
4096.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Process Enumeration is a Discovery technique. It involves adversaries obtaining information about running processes on a system to understand the software environment and shape follow-on actions. In Windows, this can be done using commands like `tasklist` in cmd or `Get-Process` in PowerShell, or via Native API calls such as `CreateToolhelp32Snapshot`. On Linux and Mac systems, adversaries use the `ps` command or enumerate the `/proc` directory.

4097.name: Load Executables/DLLs
4097.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may establish persistence and/or elevate privileges by executing malicious content triggered by AppInit DLLs loaded into processes. Dynamic-link libraries (DLLs) that are specified in the AppInit_DLLs value in the Registry keys HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\Software\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Windows or HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\Software\Wow6432Node\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Windows are loaded by user32.dll into every process that loads user32.dll. In practice this is nearly every program, since user32.dll is a very common library. (Citation: Elastic Process Injection July 2017) Similar to Process Injection, these values can be abused to obtain elevated privileges by causing a malicious DLL to be loaded and run in the context of separate processes on the computer. (Citation: AppInit Registry) Malicious AppInit DLLs may also provide persistence by continuously being triggered by API activity. The AppInit DLL functionality is disabled in Windows 8 and later versions when secure boot is enabled. (Citation: AppInit Secure Boot)
4097.profile: [profile]AppInit DLLs, identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1546.010 under the Privilege Escalation and Persistence tactics for Windows, involves adversaries establishing persistence and elevating privileges by loading malicious DLLs via the AppInit_DLLs Registry keys. These DLLs are loaded by user32.dll into nearly every process, allowing malicious code to run in the context of separate processes. This functionality is disabled in Windows 8 and later when secure boot is enabled. The technique has been associated with groups like APT39 and FIN7.[/profile]
4097.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Load Executables/DLLs is a foundational technique for executing code, mapped to MITRE ATT&CK ID T1574.001 (Hijack Execution Flow) under the Persistence and Privilege Escalation tactics, primarily on Windows. It works by abusing the Windows DLL search order or application-specific loading mechanisms to load a malicious dynamic-link library. This includes methods like DLL search order hijacking, where a trojan DLL is placed in a directory searched before the legitimate one, and DLL side-loading, which exploits ambiguities in a program's manifest to load an unintended DLL. The technique enables adversaries to run their payload within the context of a trusted process, aiding in defense evasion and persistence.

4098.name: Screenshot Capture
4098.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may attempt to take screen captures of the desktop to gather information over the course of an operation. Screen capturing functionality may be included as a feature of a remote access tool used in post-compromise operations. Taking a screenshot is also typically possible through native utilities or API calls, such as CopyFromScreen, xwd, or screencapture.(Citation: CopyFromScreen .NET)(Citation: Antiquated Mac Malware)
4098.profile: [profile]Screen Capture, also known as T1113, is a collection technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework. It involves adversaries taking screenshots of the desktop to gather information, often using features of remote access tools, native utilities, or API calls such as CopyFromScreen, xwd, or screencapture. This technique is commonly used by groups like FIN7, APT28, and MuddyWater to visually exfiltrate data from compromised systems.[profile]
4098.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Screenshot Capture is the technique T1113 under the Collection tactic, applicable to Windows, macOS, and Linux. Adversaries capture screen images to gather information, often using features of remote access tools or native OS utilities and API calls like `CopyFromScreen`, `xwd`, or `screencapture`. The captured files are typically saved to disk for later exfiltration. This technique is distinct from video capture and has been associated with threat groups including APT28, APT39, Fin7, and MuddyWater.

4099.name: Self-Update/Uninstall
4099.profile: [profile]Self-Update/Uninstall is a technique where adversaries manipulate a software's own update or uninstall mechanism to maintain persistence or execute malicious code. It is associated with the intrusion set FIN7. The technique involves compromising the legitimate distribution channel of an application, allowing the adversary to push modified updates or removal routines to a victim's system, thereby enabling continued access or further malicious actions.
4099.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Self-Update/Uninstall" is a deprecated attack pattern. Based on the retrieved context, this technique is no longer in active use, and its specific MITRE ATT&CK ID, associated tactics, and technical mechanics are not provided in the available information.

4100.name: C2 Communication (HTTPS)
4100.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may use an existing, legitimate external Web service as a means for sending commands to and receiving output from a compromised system over the Web service channel. Compromised systems may leverage popular websites and social media to host command and control (C2) instructions. Those infected systems can then send the output from those commands back over that Web service channel. The return traffic may occur in a variety of ways, depending on the Web service being utilized. For example, the return traffic may take the form of the compromised system posting a comment on a forum, issuing a pull request to development project, updating a document hosted on a Web service, or by sending a Tweet. 

Popular websites and social media acting as a mechanism for C2 may give a significant amount of cover due to the likelihood that hosts within a network are already communicating with them prior to a compromise. Using common services, such as those offered by Google or Twitter, makes it easier for adversaries to hide in expected noise. Web service providers commonly use SSL/TLS encryption, giving adversaries an added level of protection.
4100.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique "Bidirectional Communication" (ID: T1102.002) under the Command and Control tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It involves using legitimate external web services like social media or cloud platforms for two-way C2, where commands are hosted and output is returned via mechanisms such as forum posts, document updates, or tweets. This provides cover by blending with normal traffic and often leverages inherent SSL/TLS encryption. Associated groups include FIN7, APT28, and Lazarus Group, and malware like Bateleur has been observed using it.[profile]
4100.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity is a Command and Control (C2) technique using the HTTPS protocol, aligning with the broader MITRE ATT&CK technique "Web Service" (T1102). It falls under the Command and Control tactic and operates across Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. This method involves adversaries establishing a covert communication channel with a compromised system by leveraging the encrypted HTTPS traffic of legitimate web services, which provides significant cover by blending with normal network noise and evading detection through standard encryption.

4101.name: Virtual Machine Detection
4101.uncertain_mes:
An adversary may attempt to enumerate running virtual machines (VMs) after gaining access to a host or hypervisor. For example, adversaries may enumerate a list of VMs on an ESXi hypervisor using a [Hypervisor CLI](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/012) such as `esxcli` or `vim-cmd` (e.g. `esxcli vm process list or vim-cmd vmsvc/getallvms`).(Citation: Crowdstrike Hypervisor Jackpotting Pt 2 2021)(Citation: TrendMicro Play) Adversaries may also directly leverage a graphical user interface, such as VMware vCenter, in order to view virtual machines on a host. 

Adversaries may use the information from [Virtual Machine Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1673) during discovery to shape follow-on behaviors. Subsequently discovered VMs may be leveraged for follow-on activities such as [Service Stop](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1489) or [Data Encrypted for Impact](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1486).(Citation: Crowdstrike Hypervisor Jackpotting Pt 2 2021)
4101.profile: [profile]Virtual Machine Discovery, identified as T1673 under the Discovery tactic for Linux, macOS, and Windows, involves adversaries enumerating running virtual machines after gaining host or hypervisor access. This is achieved by executing specific hypervisor CLI commands like `esxcli vm process list` or `vim-cmd vmsvc/getallvms` on ESXi systems or by using graphical interfaces like VMware vCenter. The gathered information on VMs is used to shape follow-on malicious activities, such as service disruption or data encryption for impact.[/profile]
4101.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Virtual Machine Detection is a technique adversaries use to identify virtualized environments to evade analysis. It aligns with MITRE ATT&CK technique T1497.001 (Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion) under the Defense Evasion tactic, applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS. Technical mechanics involve checking for artifacts like specific processes, services, registry keys, hardware properties (e.g., fan, temperature), manufacturer strings, or using special I/O ports in VMware. Scripts may automate these checks, causing malware to exit if a virtual machine is detected, thereby avoiding sandbox analysis.

4102.name: WEXE Execution
4102.profile: [profile]WEXE Execution is a technique used by adversaries to execute malicious code. It is associated with the FIN7 intrusion set and the Bateleur malware. The technique involves the execution of a Windows executable (WEXE) file, often initiated through user interaction such as clicking a malicious link delivered via spearphishing, which is a common follow-on behavior. This method facilitates initial code execution on a target system.
4102.profile_without_enhance: [profile]WEXE Execution is an attack pattern. The provided context suggests it is a technique for executing malicious code, likely by tricking a user into opening a malicious Windows Executable (.wexe) file, which is a form of User Execution (T1204). This technique operates on the Windows platform. The primary technical mechanic involves social engineering to induce a user to click on or open a malicious link or file, leading to the execution of the adversary's payload.

4103.name: APowerShell Execution
4103.profile: [profile]APowerShell Execution is a technique for executing malicious code using PowerShell, aligning with MITRE ATT&CK ID T1059.001 under the Execution tactic on Windows platforms. It involves running commands or scripts via the `powershell.exe` binary or its underlying .NET assembly, enabling actions like process creation, remote command execution, and in-memory payload execution without touching disk. This method is used by groups like FIN7 and malware such as Bateleur for post-compromise activities.[/profile]
4103.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "APowerShell Execution" is a technique for executing malicious code using PowerShell, aligning with MITRE ATT&CK ID T1059.001 under the Execution tactic for Windows platforms. It involves using PowerShell commands and scripts, such as Start-Process or Invoke-Command, to run executables locally or remotely, often downloading and executing payloads from the internet directly in memory to avoid disk detection. This method is widely abused by numerous threat groups, including FIN6, APT29, and Wizard Spider, for activities like discovery and code execution, and can be performed without invoking powershell.exe by leveraging PowerShell's underlying .NET assembly.

4104.name: WPowerShell Execution
4104.profile: [profile]WPowerShell Execution is a technique mapped to MITRE ATT&CK ID T1059.001 (Command and Scripting Interpreter: PowerShell) under the Execution tactic, primarily for Windows platforms. It involves adversaries using PowerShell commands and scripts to execute malicious code, often from memory to avoid disk-based detection, and can leverage cmdlets like `Start-Process` or `Invoke-Command` for local or remote execution. This technique is associated with groups like FIN7 and malware like Bateleur, and it can be delivered via methods such as malicious links requiring user interaction.[/profile]
4104.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "WPowerShell Execution" is a technique for executing malicious code using PowerShell. It aligns with the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1059.001 (Command and Scripting Interpreter: PowerShell) under the Execution tactic, primarily for Windows platforms. The technique involves using PowerShell commands and scripts, such as `Start-Process` or `Invoke-Command`, to run executables or arbitrary code, which can be executed directly from disk or entirely in memory to avoid detection. This method is widely abused by numerous threat groups for discovery and code execution, often by downloading payloads from the internet or leveraging PowerShell's underlying .NET interfaces without invoking the standard `powershell.exe` binary.

4107.name: Shamoon 2
4107.uncertain_mes: [Shamoon](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0140) is wiper malware that was first used by an Iranian group known as the "Cutting Sword of Justice" in 2012. Other versions known as Shamoon 2 and Shamoon 3 were observed in 2016 and 2018. [Shamoon](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0140) has also been seen leveraging [RawDisk](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0364) and Filerase to carry out data wiping tasks. Analysis has linked [Shamoon](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0140) with [Kwampirs](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0236) based on multiple shared artifacts and coding patterns.(Citation: Cylera Kwampirs 2022) The term Shamoon is sometimes used to refer to the group using the malware as well as the malware itself.(Citation: Palo Alto Shamoon Nov 2016)(Citation: Unit 42 Shamoon3 2018)(Citation: Symantec Shamoon 2012)(Citation: FireEye Shamoon Nov 2016)
4107.profile: [profile]Shamoon 2 is a version of the Shamoon wiper malware, observed in 2016. It is attributed to an Iranian group known as the "Cutting Sword of Justice". Its key behaviors include data wiping, often leveraging tools like RawDisk and Filerase. Analysis has linked it to Kwampirs malware based on shared artifacts and coding patterns, and both collect the same initial data (MAC address, system info, keyboard layout) for C2 communication. Its neighbor components include DistTrack, C2, wiper, and communication modules, and it is associated with the intrusion set RocketKitten. The term Shamoon can refer to both the malware and the group using it.[/profile]
4107.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Shamoon 2 is a destructive wiper malware, also known as DistTrack. It is attributed to groups including Magic Hound, Timberworm, and Cobalt Gipsy, and is linked to the intrusion set RocketKitten. Its key technical behaviors include data wiping using the EldoS RawDisk driver, worm-like propagation via SMB for lateral movement, and the use of XOR decryption for obfuscation. It establishes command and control channels, with components like a C2 framework and a communication module, and uses scheduled tasks for persistence. It primarily targets Windows platforms, with infrastructure involving specific IP addresses and domains for C2 communication.[/profile]

4108.profile: [profile]DistTrack, also known as W32.Disttrack and its variants (W32.Disttrack.B, W32.Disttrack!gen1, etc.), is a destructive malware family. It is related to the Shamoon malware and has been associated with groups like Magic Hound, Timberworm, and Cobalt Gipsy.
