It primarily targets Windows platforms and has been distributed in campaigns in the Middle East, particularly Saudi Arabia, with detection names including variants like W32.Disttrack.B and Trojan.Filerase.[/profile]

4109.name: Stonedrill
4109.uncertain_mes: [StoneDrill](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0380) is wiper malware discovered in destructive campaigns against both Middle Eastern and European targets in association with [APT33](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0064).(Citation: FireEye APT33 Sept 2017)(Citation: Kaspersky StoneDrill 2017)
4109.profile: [profile]StoneDrill is a wiper malware associated with APT33 and used in destructive campaigns against Middle Eastern and European targets. It shares technical code similarities and command and control (C&C) server naming schemes with the NewsBeef malware, and both are linked to the Charming Kitten group (also known as APT33 and Rocket Kitten). Its key behaviors include a strings decryption routine and a payload Winmain function for its destructive operations, primarily targeting Windows platforms.
4109.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Stonedrill is a malware linked to the Iranian group Charming Kitten. It shares technical code similarities and command and control (C&C) naming schemes with the NewsBeef malware. It is also associated with artifacts and coding patterns of the Shamoon wiper malware. Its target platform is Windows.[/profile]

4110.name: Credential harvesting
4110.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may use credentials obtained from breach dumps of unrelated accounts to gain access to target accounts through credential overlap. Occasionally, large numbers of username and password pairs are dumped online when a website or service is compromised and the user account credentials accessed. The information may be useful to an adversary attempting to compromise accounts by taking advantage of the tendency for users to use the same passwords across personal and business accounts.

Credential stuffing is a risky option because it could cause numerous authentication failures and account lockouts, depending on the organization's login failure policies.

Typically, management services over commonly used ports are used when stuffing credentials. Commonly targeted services include the following:

* SSH (22/TCP)
* Telnet (23/TCP)
* FTP (21/TCP)
* NetBIOS / SMB / Samba (139/TCP & 445/TCP)
* LDAP (389/TCP)
* Kerberos (88/TCP)
* RDP / Terminal Services (3389/TCP)
* HTTP/HTTP Management Services (80/TCP & 443/TCP)
* MSSQL (1433/TCP)
* Oracle (1521/TCP)
* MySQL (3306/TCP)
* VNC (5900/TCP)

In addition to management services, adversaries may "target single sign-on (SSO) and cloud-based applications utilizing federated authentication protocols," as well as externally facing email applications, such as Office 365.(Citation: US-CERT TA18-068A 2018)
4110.profile: [profile]Credential stuffing, identified as MITRE ATT&CK T1110.004 under the Credential Access tactic, involves using credentials from unrelated breach dumps to access target accounts by exploiting password reuse across services. It typically targets management services on common ports like SSH (22/TCP), FTP (21/TCP), RDP (3389/TCP), and HTTP/HTTPS (80/443/TCP), as well as cloud applications and SSO systems. This technique risks triggering authentication failures and account lockouts. The intrusion set RocketKitten has been associated with this activity.[/profile]
4110.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Credential harvesting is a technique within the Credential Access tactic, applicable across multiple platforms, where adversaries illicitly gather authentication materials like usernames and passwords. This is distinct from credential stuffing or dumping, and often involves targeting specific storage locations, such as reading encrypted credential stores from web browsers (e.g., Chrome's Login Data file) and using system APIs like CryptUnprotectData for decryption, or by hooking into credential APIs to intercept authentication calls.

4111.name: Hardcoded Credentials
4111.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may gather credentials that can be used during targeting. Account credentials gathered by adversaries may be those directly associated with the target victim organization or attempt to take advantage of the tendency for users to use the same passwords across personal and business accounts.

Adversaries may gather credentials from potential victims in various ways, such as direct elicitation via [Phishing for Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1598). Adversaries may also compromise sites then add malicious content designed to collect website authentication cookies from visitors.(Citation: ATT ScanBox) (Citation: Register Deloitte)(Citation: Register Uber)(Citation: Detectify Slack Tokens)(Citation: Forbes GitHub Creds)(Citation: GitHub truffleHog)(Citation: GitHub Gitrob)(Citation: CNET Leaks) Where multi-factor authentication (MFA) based on out-of-band communications is in use, adversaries may compromise a service provider to gain access to MFA codes and one-time passwords (OTP).(Citation: Okta Scatter Swine 2022)

Credential information may also be exposed to adversaries via leaks to online or other accessible data sets (ex: [Search Engines](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1593/002), breach dumps, code repositories, etc.). Adversaries may purchase credentials from dark web markets, such as Russian Market and 2easy, or through access to Telegram channels that distribute logs from infostealer malware.(Citation: Bleeping Computer 2easy 2021)(Citation: SecureWorks Infostealers 2023)(Citation: Bleeping Computer Stealer Logs 2023)

Gathering this information may reveal opportunities for other forms of reconnaissance (ex: [Search Open Websites/Domains](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1593) or [Phishing for Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1598)), establishing operational resources (ex: [Compromise Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1586)), and/or initial access (ex: [External Remote Services](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1133) or [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078)).
4111.profile: [profile]Hardcoded Credentials is a technique where adversaries embed static, plaintext passwords or other authentication secrets directly within source code, configuration files, or software binaries. This insecure practice allows unauthorized access to systems or services without requiring credential theft. The technique is associated with the intrusion-set RocketKitten and is often discovered through code analysis or by examining application artifacts for embedded authentication strings.
4111.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Hardcoded Credentials is a technique where adversaries embed authentication information like passwords or keys directly into source code or configuration files. This insecure practice allows unauthorized access to systems or services by extracting these plaintext credentials from the compromised software or its deployment artifacts. It is commonly associated with initial access and persistence tactics across various platforms.

4112.name: Scheduled Task/Job
4112.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may abuse task scheduling functionality to facilitate initial or recurring execution of malicious code. Utilities exist within all major operating systems to schedule programs or scripts to be executed at a specified date and time. A task can also be scheduled on a remote system, provided the proper authentication is met (ex: RPC and file and printer sharing in Windows environments). Scheduling a task on a remote system typically may require being a member of an admin or otherwise privileged group on the remote system.(Citation: TechNet Task Scheduler Security)

Adversaries may use task scheduling to execute programs at system startup or on a scheduled basis for persistence. These mechanisms can also be abused to run a process under the context of a specified account (such as one with elevated permissions/privileges). Similar to [System Binary Proxy Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1218), adversaries have also abused task scheduling to potentially mask one-time execution under a trusted system process.(Citation: ProofPoint Serpent)
4112.profile: [profile]Scheduled Task/Job is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1053 under the Execution and Persistence tactics, applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS. It involves abusing native OS utilities like Windows Task Scheduler (via schtasks, WMI, or PowerShell's Invoke-CimMethod), cron, at, or launchd to schedule malicious code execution at specific times or system startup for persistence, lateral movement, or privilege escalation. Tasks can be created remotely on Windows with proper admin authentication, and adversaries may hide tasks by deleting Security Descriptor registry values. Associated threat groups include OilRig and RocketKitten.[/profile]
4112.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Scheduled Task/Job is a MITRE ATT&CK technique with ID T1053 under the Execution and Persistence tactics, applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS. It involves abusing native OS scheduling utilities like Windows Task Scheduler (via schtasks, WMI, or PowerShell's Invoke-CimMethod), cron, at, or launchd to execute malicious code at specified times or on startup for persistence, lateral movement, or privilege escalation. Tasks can be scheduled remotely on Windows with proper admin authentication, and adversaries may hide tasks by deleting Security Descriptor registry values or altering metadata to evade detection.[/profile]

4113.name: Disabling UAC
4113.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may disable security tools to avoid possible detection of their tools and activities. This can take the form of killing security software or event logging processes, deleting Registry keys so that tools do not start at run time, or other methods to interfere with security scanning or event reporting.
4113.profile: [profile]Disabling UAC is a technique aligned with the MITRE ATT&CK ID T1548.002 under the Defense Evasion tactic for Windows platforms. It involves bypassing Windows User Account Control (UAC) mechanisms to elevate process privileges without user consent. Specific methods include exploiting auto-elevation in trusted processes like `eventvwr.exe` to execute malicious payloads, using tools like UACMe to leverage crafted DLLs and COM objects, or performing lateral movement with known administrator credentials where UAC protections do not apply across systems. It has been associated with groups like APT37 and APT38.[/profile]
4113.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Disabling UAC is a technique mapped to MITRE ATT&CK ID T1548.002 under the Defense Evasion tactic, targeting the Windows platform. It involves adversaries turning off or lowering Windows User Account Control settings to prevent prompts for administrator privileges, thereby allowing malicious processes to run with elevated permissions without user consent. This can be achieved by modifying registry keys, such as setting 'EnableLUA' to 0, or using tools and scripts to disable the UAC prompt entirely.

4114.name: Disabling WOW64 Redirection
4114.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may disable security tools to avoid possible detection of their tools and activities. This can take the form of killing security software or event logging processes, deleting Registry keys so that tools do not start at run time, or other methods to interfere with security scanning or event reporting.
4114.profile: [profile]Disabling WOW64 Redirection is a technique for defense evasion, likely targeting Windows platforms. It involves disabling the Windows on Windows 64 (WOW64) file system redirection mechanism, which allows 32-bit applications to run on 64-bit systems by redirecting file and registry calls to appropriate directories (e.g., System32 to SysWOW64). By disabling this, an adversary can directly access the native 64-bit system directories, potentially to place or execute malicious 64-bit binaries from paths a 32-bit process would normally be redirected from, thereby evading detection or ensuring correct payload execution. The technique has been associated with the RocketKitten intrusion set and Shamoon 2 malware.[/profile]
4114.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Disabling WOW64 Redirection is a technique used by adversaries to evade defenses by disabling the Windows on Windows 64 (WOW64) file system redirection. This allows a 64-bit process to directly access the 32-bit system directory (SysWOW64) instead of being redirected, enabling the loading of malicious 32-bit DLLs into a 64-bit context. This method can be used to bypass security controls and maintain persistence by exploiting the native Windows WOW64DisableWow64FsRedirection function.

4115.name: Time Manipulation
4115.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may abuse time providers to execute DLLs when the system boots. The Windows Time service (W32Time) enables time synchronization across and within domains.(Citation: Microsoft W32Time Feb 2018) W32Time time providers are responsible for retrieving time stamps from hardware/network resources and outputting these values to other network clients.(Citation: Microsoft TimeProvider)

Time providers are implemented as dynamic-link libraries (DLLs) that are registered in the subkeys of `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\System\CurrentControlSet\Services\W32Time\TimeProviders\`.(Citation: Microsoft TimeProvider) The time provider manager, directed by the service control manager, loads and starts time providers listed and enabled under this key at system startup and/or whenever parameters are changed.(Citation: Microsoft TimeProvider)

Adversaries may abuse this architecture to establish persistence, specifically by creating a new arbitrarily named subkey  pointing to a malicious DLL in the `DllName` value. Administrator privileges are required for time provider registration, though execution will run in context of the Local Service account.(Citation: Github W32Time Oct 2017)
4115.profile: [profile]Time Providers, identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1547.003, is a persistence tactic for Windows. It involves abusing the Windows Time service (W32Time) architecture by creating a new subkey under `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\System\CurrentControlSet\Services\W32Time\TimeProviders\` that points to a malicious DLL via the `DllName` value. This malicious provider, which requires administrator privileges to register, is then loaded and executed in the Local Service account context at system startup to maintain access.[/profile]
4115.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Time Manipulation is a technique adversaries use to interfere with system time functions, often to evade detection, disrupt operations, or enable other malicious activities. This can involve tampering with the system clock, timestamps on files, or time-based security mechanisms. The primary tactic is Defense Evasion, and it is applicable across multiple platforms including Windows, Linux, and macOS. Technical mechanics include altering system time settings via commands or registry edits to bypass time-based locks, invalidate log entries, or trigger delayed payloads. It is distinct from persistence techniques like Time Providers (T1547.003) and discovery techniques like System Time Discovery (T1124).[/profile]

4116.name: Hardcoded Information
4116.profile: [profile]Hardcoded Information is a technique where adversaries embed sensitive data like credentials or encryption keys directly within malware or software code. This eliminates the need for external communication to fetch this data, simplifying deployment but making the information easily discoverable if the code is analyzed. The intrusion-set RocketKitten has been associated with using this technique. The method is distinct from standard encoding or data obfuscation techniques like junk data or reversible encryption, which focus on hiding data in transit or storage.
4116.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Hardcoded Information is a technique where adversaries embed sensitive data like passwords, keys, or configuration details directly within malware source code or executables. This practice bypasses external authentication mechanisms and provides persistent access. The embedded data can include credentials, IP addresses, or cryptographic keys, allowing malware to function without needing to retrieve this information from an external server, which can simplify deployment and increase stealth.

4122.name: Data Wipe
4122.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may wipe or corrupt raw disk data on specific systems or in large numbers in a network to interrupt availability to system and network resources. With direct write access to a disk, adversaries may attempt to overwrite portions of disk data. Adversaries may opt to wipe arbitrary portions of disk data and/or wipe disk structures like the master boot record (MBR). A complete wipe of all disk sectors may be attempted.

To maximize impact on the target organization in operations where network-wide availability interruption is the goal, malware used for wiping disks may have worm-like features to propagate across a network by leveraging additional techniques like [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078), [OS Credential Dumping](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003), and [SMB/Windows Admin Shares](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002).(Citation: Novetta Blockbuster Destructive Malware)

On network devices, adversaries may wipe configuration files and other data from the device using [Network Device CLI](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/008) commands such as `erase`.(Citation: erase_cmd_cisco)
4122.profile: [profile]Data Wipe, identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1561, is an Impact tactic technique targeting Windows, Linux, and Network platforms to disrupt availability. It involves overwriting raw disk data, which can include arbitrary portions, critical structures like the master boot record (MBR), or all disk sectors. Adversaries may gain direct write access to the disk, sometimes using third-party drivers, or on network devices, use CLI commands like `erase`. Malware implementing this, such as Shamoon 2, may propagate using worm-like features and auxiliary techniques like Valid Accounts to maximize network-wide impact.
4122.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Data Wipe is a technique within the Impact tactic, targeting multiple platforms to interrupt availability. It involves adversaries wiping or corrupting raw disk data to render it irrecoverable. This can include overwriting arbitrary portions of disk data, specific structures like the master boot record (MBR), or performing a complete sector wipe. Attackers may use direct disk access, leverage tools like the RawDisk driver, or employ network device commands such as `erase`. The technique is distinct from file-level data destruction as it targets disk sections and may be deployed with worm-like features for network propagation.

4123.name: C2 component
4123.uncertain_mes: Nimbo-C2 is yet another (simple and lightweight) C2 framework.
4123.profile: [profile]Nimbo-C2, also referred to as nimbo-c2, is a simple and lightweight C2 (Command and Control) framework. It is associated with the Shamoon 2 malware and is utilized by unknown groups. The framework's infrastructure includes components for submitting data, such as a screenshotter submitting images to a C2 server via a URL like hxxp[:]//109[.]107.173.72/screenshot/%serial%.[/profile]
4123.profile_without_enhance: [profile]C2 component is a malware entity that functions as a command and control (C2) framework. It is associated with Shamoon 2 (DistTrack) wiper malware, sharing its C2 communication protocols which collect system data like MAC address and keyboard layout. Related entities include the nimbo-c2 framework, the wasabiseed screenshotter component that submits images to a C2 server, the 9002 RAT used by groups like aurora panda and apt31, and privateloader which uses specific dead drop resolvers and C2 addresses. It primarily targets Windows platforms.

4125.name: XOR Decryption
4125.profile: [profile]XOR Decryption is a technique adversaries use to obfuscate data, often for command and control or prior to exfiltration, by applying the exclusive-or (XOR) operation with a fixed key. This method produces a weak ciphertext that is simple to implement without external libraries. It is associated with malware like Shamoon 2 and is referenced in techniques for custom cryptographic protocols (T1024) and custom archival methods (T1560.003), where reverse engineering can often reveal the algorithm and key.[/profile]
4125.profile_without_enhance: [profile]XOR Decryption, identified as a sub-technique of Obfuscated Files or Information (T1027), falls under the Defense Evasion tactic. It is a weak symmetric encryption method where plaintext data is combined with a key using the exclusive OR (XOR) operation to produce ciphertext, often implemented in custom malware to hide command and control traffic or archive collected data prior to exfiltration. Analysis and reverse engineering of samples can frequently reveal the simple algorithm and key.

4128.name: wiper component
4128.uncertain_mes: [Wiper](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0041) is a family of destructive malware used in March 2013 during breaches of South Korean banks and media companies. (Citation: Dell Wiper)
4128.profile: [profile]The malware, referred to as Wiper or a wiper component, is a family of destructive malware. It is a component of the Shamoon malware family, as indicated by a debug path string "C:\Shamoon\ArabianGulf\wiper\release\wiper.pdb" found in the Disttrack threat. It has been used in attacks against South Korean banks and media companies. Its primary function is data destruction to hinder recovery and cover attacker tracks, as seen in its role as a final-stage module in threats like Industroyer.[/profile]
4128.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The malware is a wiper component, an alias for DistTrack and a component of the Shamoon 2 malware family. It has been attributed to the RocketKitten intrusion set, also known as Shamoon, Magic Hound, Timberworm, and Cobalt Gipsy. Its key technical behavior is data wiping, and it is associated with components like RawDisk and Filerase. It primarily targets Windows platforms, and its development path on a developer's system was indicated by a debug string: C:\Shamoon\ArabianGulf\wiper\release\wiper.pdb.[/profile]

4129.name: communication component
4129.profile: [profile]Name: Communication Component. Aliases: Not specified. Attributed Groups: Not specified. Key TTPs/Technical Behaviors: Serves as a communication mechanism for malware families like Shamoon 2; similar to components in Mandrake that use Android intents for inter-component communication, and to communication protocols in Keymarble and Vawtrak. Target Platforms: Likely cross-platform, associated with Windows malware (Shamoon) and Android (Mandrake). Infrastructure/Supplementary Info: Functions as a module enabling command and control or internal data exchange within a malware ecosystem.[/profile]
4129.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Communication Component is a malware component. It is associated with Shamoon 2 (DistTrack) wiper malware and the RocketKitten intrusion set. Its key technical behaviors include inter-component communication via Android intents, registering for custom events to create communication channels, and it shares C2 communication protocols with Kwampirs malware for collecting system data like MAC address and keyboard layout. It targets Windows platforms.

4131.name: Anti-Debugging
4131.profile: [profile]The entity is mapped to the MITRE ATT&CK technique Debugger Evasion, ID T1622, under the Defense Evasion tactic. It primarily targets Windows and Linux platforms. The technique involves detecting debuggers to alter malware behavior, using checks like Windows API calls IsDebuggerPresent() and NtQueryInformationProcess(), inspecting the PEB's BeingDebugged flag, or on Linux querying /proc/self/status for the TracerPID field. Other methods include checking for hardware breakpoints, using time checks, or leveraging Structured Exception Handling (SEH) to see if an exception transfers control to a debugger. Adversaries may also evade by detaching from the debugger or flooding debug logs. It is associated with malware like Shamoon and groups like Mustang Panda.
4131.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Anti-Debugging is a Defense Evasion technique (T1622) used by adversaries to detect and avoid debuggers, which are analysis tools. It works by checking for artifacts of a debugged environment, such as calling Windows API functions like IsDebuggerPresent() or querying the Linux /proc/self/status file. If a debugger is detected, malware may alter its behavior, disengage, or conceal its core functions to evade analysis.

4133.name: pkcs12
4133.profile: [profile]PKCS12 is a wiper module used by the Shamoon malware (also known as Disttrack), which is attributed to groups including Shamoon, Magic Hound, Timberworm, and Cobalt Gipsy. It is deployed as a binary resource within the malware. The PKCS12 format is also referenced in command-line operations for certificate and private key extraction by threat actors like APT41, Emissary Panda, Gallium, Hafnium, Hurricane Panda, and Leviathan, as seen in tools such as ChinaChopper. Its primary target platform is Windows systems.
4133.profile_without_enhance: [profile]PKCS12 is a wiper module associated with the Shamoon (also known as Disttrack) malware family, also linked to groups like Magic Hound, Timberworm, and Cobalt Gipsy. It is deployed as a payload resource within the malware's architecture, specifically identified in files such as 'PKCS12112.bin'. Its primary function is destructive data wiping. The name PKCS12 is also referenced in the context of certificate and private key extraction using OpenSSL commands, as seen in tooling related to threat groups like APT41.[/profile]

4143.name: 硬编码Windows Active Directory凭证
4143.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may achieve persistence by adding a Registry key to the Active Setup of the local machine. Active Setup is a Windows mechanism that is used to execute programs when a user logs in. The value stored in the Registry key will be executed after a user logs into the computer.(Citation: Klein Active Setup 2010) These programs will be executed under the context of the user and will have the account's associated permissions level. Adversaries may abuse Active Setup by creating a key under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Active Setup\Installed Components\ and setting a malicious value for StubPath. This value will serve as the program that will be executed when a user logs into the computer.(Citation: Mandiant Glyer APT 2010)(Citation: Citizenlab Packrat 2015)(Citation: FireEye CFR Watering Hole 2012)(Citation: SECURELIST Bright Star 2015)(Citation: paloalto Tropic Trooper 2016) Adversaries can abuse these components to execute malware, such as remote access tools, to maintain persistence through system reboots. Adversaries may also use [Masquerading](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1036) to make the Registry entries look as if they are associated with legitimate programs.
4143.profile: [profile]Active Setup is a persistence technique (MITRE ATT&CK T1547.014) under the Boot or Logon Autostart Execution tactic for Windows. It works by creating a malicious Registry key under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Active Setup\Installed Components\ and setting a program path in the StubPath value, which is then executed when a user logs into the system. This mechanism can be used to run malware like remote access tools and maintain persistence across reboots, often while masquerading as legitimate software.[/profile]
4143.profile_without_enhance: [profile]硬编码Windows Active Directory凭证 is a technique where adversaries embed Windows Active Directory credentials directly into malicious software or scripts. This allows the software to authenticate to the domain without requiring interactive logon or storing credentials externally. The hardcoded credentials, such as usernames and passwords, are compiled into the binary or script, enabling persistence and lateral movement within the network. This method bypasses some credential access controls and can be used to maintain access or execute commands with the permissions of the embedded account.

4144.name: Targeted Attack
4144.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may downgrade or use a version of system features that may be outdated, vulnerable, and/or does not support updated security controls. Downgrade attacks typically take advantage of a system’s backward compatibility to force it into less secure modes of operation. 

Adversaries may downgrade and use various less-secure versions of features of a system, such as [Command and Scripting Interpreter](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059)s or even network protocols that can be abused to enable [Adversary-in-the-Middle](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1557) or [Network Sniffing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1040).(Citation: Praetorian TLS Downgrade Attack 2014) For example, [PowerShell](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001) versions 5+ includes Script Block Logging (SBL), which can record executed script content. However, adversaries may attempt to execute a previous version of PowerShell that does not support SBL with the intent to [Impair Defenses](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1562) while running malicious scripts that may have otherwise been detected.(Citation: CrowdStrike BGH Ransomware 2021)(Citation: Mandiant BYOL 2018)(Citation: att_def_ps_logging)

Adversaries may similarly target network traffic to downgrade from an encrypted HTTPS connection to an unsecured HTTP connection that exposes network data in clear text.(Citation: Targeted SSL Stripping Attacks Are Real)(Citation: Crowdstrike Downgrade) On Windows systems, adversaries may downgrade the boot manager to a vulnerable version that bypasses Secure Boot, granting the ability to disable various operating system security mechanisms.(Citation: SafeBreach)
4144.profile: [profile]Downgrade Attack, identified as T1562.010 under the Impair Defenses tactic, operates on Windows and other platforms by exploiting system backward compatibility to force less secure modes. This technique specifically involves executing older versions of software, such as PowerShell versions prior to 5 that lack Script Block Logging, to run malicious scripts without detection. It also includes downgrading network connections from HTTPS to unencrypted HTTP to expose data and manipulating the Windows boot manager to bypass Secure Boot and disable OS security mechanisms. The intrusion set RocketKitten has been associated with this method.
4144.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Targeted Attack" is a generic term not directly mapped to a specific MITRE ATT&CK ID or Tactic. Based on retrieved context, it can involve techniques like Endpoint Denial of Service (T1499) to degrade service availability by exhausting application resources (T1499.003), or Exploitation for Credential Access (T1212) to leverage software vulnerabilities like Kerberos forgery (MS14-068) or replay attacks to obtain or bypass authentication. These actions are conducted by specific threat groups, such as Sandworm Team or UNC3886, to achieve objectives like disruption or unauthorized access.

4145.name: Political Espionage
4145.profile: [profile]Political Espionage is a technique for gathering intelligence to inform national decision-making, often conducted by state-sponsored groups. It is linked to the intrusion set RocketKitten. The technique can involve using software deployment tools like SCCM or AWS Systems Manager for lateral movement and remote code execution across enterprise networks, as observed with groups including APT32 and Sandworm Team. Adversaries may also monitor threat intelligence reports about their own campaigns to alter their behavior and avoid detection.
4145.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Political Espionage is a technique where adversaries conduct espionage to collect intelligence on political entities, parties, or figures. This activity is often associated with state-sponsored groups and involves persistent campaigns to gather sensitive information for strategic advantage. The technique is related to groups like Sandworm Team and Ember Bear, who have been linked to operations targeting political organizations and using methods such as external website defacement to spread propaganda or discredit targets.

4147.profile: [profile]Ghole, also known as WoolGoldfish, is a malware attributed to the RocketKitten intrusion set. It is associated with the Operation WOOLEN-GOLDFISH campaign, which involves phishing activities. The malware's technical behaviors include an export function for data exfiltration. Its target platform is Windows, as indicated by its use of registry keys for persistence. Infrastructure connections include the use of Core Impact Pro, suggesting exploitation capabilities.
4147.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Ghole is a malware variant attributed to the Rocket Kitten (APT35) intrusion set, directly connected to the WoolGoldfish malware. It operates by using decoy documents for initial infection and drops an executable file named os03C2.tmp. The malware communicates with C&C servers using specific URI patterns like 'index.php?c=%s&r=%x' and employs techniques to cover its tracks to evade detection. Its infrastructure involves C&C servers and IP addresses, and it is associated with campaigns such as Operation WOOLEN-GOLDFISH and the GHOLE Campaign.[/profile]

4148.name: Core Impact Pro
4148.uncertain_mes: In 2019, Unit 42 researchers documented cloud-targeted malware used by the Rocke Group to conduct cryptojacking attacks to mine for Monero. Since then, cybersecurity companies have had the malware on their radar, which hampered Rocke Group’s cryptojacking operation. In response, the threat actors updated the malware.
4148.profile: [profile]Core Impact Pro, also known as pro-ocean, is a penetration testing framework. It has been repurposed for malicious use, with a modified version linked to the Woolen-GoldFish campaign attributed to the Rocket Kitten APT35 group. The malware is associated with the Rocke Group, which used a cloud-targeted variant for cryptojacking to mine Monero, prompting subsequent updates to evade detection. Its primary function is to facilitate network penetration and insider threat simulations, often operating on Windows platforms.
4148.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Core Impact Pro is a penetration testing framework developed by Core Security, which has been repurposed for malicious use. It is also known as a modified version of Core Impact. It has been used in the Woolen-GoldFish campaign, which is attributed to the Rocket Kitten (also known as APT35) intrusion set. Its key technical behavior involves being utilized as a post-compromise tool, likely for exploitation and network penetration, following initial infection by malware like Ghole. The primary target platform is Windows systems.

4149.name: Malicious Microsoft Office Macro
4149.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may abuse the Microsoft Office "Office Test" Registry key to obtain persistence on a compromised system. An Office Test Registry location exists that allows a user to specify an arbitrary DLL that will be executed every time an Office application is started. This Registry key is thought to be used by Microsoft to load DLLs for testing and debugging purposes while developing Office applications. This Registry key is not created by default during an Office installation.(Citation: Hexacorn Office Test)(Citation: Palo Alto Office Test Sofacy) There exist user and global Registry keys for the Office Test feature, such as: * HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Office test\Special\Perf * HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\Software\Microsoft\Office test\Special\Perf Adversaries may add this Registry key and specify a malicious DLL that will be executed whenever an Office application, such as Word or Excel, is started.
4149.profile: [profile]Malicious Microsoft Office Macro, also known as "Office Test" (T1137.002), is a persistence technique within the Defense Evasion and Persistence tactics targeting Windows. It works by abusing the non-default Microsoft Office "Office Test" Registry key (e.g., HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Office test\Special\Perf) to specify a malicious DLL that automatically executes whenever an Office application like Word or Excel starts. This method has been associated with threat groups such as APT28 and RocketKitten.
4149.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Malicious Microsoft Office Macro is a user execution technique (T1204.002) within the Initial Access and Execution tactics, targeting the Windows platform. It involves adversaries embedding malicious Visual Basic for Applications (VBA) code within Office documents (e.g., .doc, .xls) to gain execution when a user enables macros. Attackers often employ social engineering, such as spearphishing, to lure victims into opening these files and may use obfuscation methods like VBA Stomping (T1564.007) to hide malicious p-code within the document's module streams, bypassing static analysis. This technique is widely used by numerous threat groups, including APT28, APT29, and Lazarus Group.

4150.name: Cwoolger
4150.profile: [profile]Cwoolger, also known as CWoolger Keylogger, is attributed to the RocketKitten intrusion set. It functions as a keylogger, with recent activities documented under the alias Wool3n.H4t. Its technical behaviors include initial compromise and keylogging capabilities, primarily targeting Windows platforms. The malware is related to the Wrapper/gholee malware family, and its activities are discussed in the context of the Woolger report, which details its operations and possible attribution to RocketKitten.[/profile]
4150.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Cwoolger, also known as CWoolger, is a keylogger malware. It is associated with the Rocket Kitten intrusion set and is technically related to the Woolger malware family. Its key technical behavior is capturing user keystrokes to steal credentials. For command and control and data exfiltration, it utilizes an FTP server, specifically connecting to infrastructure like wool3n.h4t.[/profile]

4159.name: Asset Discovery
4159.profile: [profile]Asset Discovery is a Discovery technique (T1580) within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, applicable to IaaS platforms. It involves adversaries enumerating cloud service resources, such as storage instances, databases, and virtual machines, to map the environment. This is often performed using native cloud APIs or command-line interfaces to identify available assets and services, aiding in follow-on targeting and lateral movement. The intrusion set RocketKitten has been associated with this behavior.[/profile]
4159.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Asset Discovery is a technique within the Discovery tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. It involves adversaries enumerating resources like systems, devices, or network infrastructure to map the target environment, often using built-in commands or APIs. This reconnaissance shapes follow-on actions, such as lateral movement or targeting specific assets.

4160.name: Steal Credentials
4160.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may gather credentials that can be used during targeting. Account credentials gathered by adversaries may be those directly associated with the target victim organization or attempt to take advantage of the tendency for users to use the same passwords across personal and business accounts.

Adversaries may gather credentials from potential victims in various ways, such as direct elicitation via [Phishing for Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1598). Adversaries may also compromise sites then add malicious content designed to collect website authentication cookies from visitors.(Citation: ATT ScanBox) (Citation: Register Deloitte)(Citation: Register Uber)(Citation: Detectify Slack Tokens)(Citation: Forbes GitHub Creds)(Citation: GitHub truffleHog)(Citation: GitHub Gitrob)(Citation: CNET Leaks) Where multi-factor authentication (MFA) based on out-of-band communications is in use, adversaries may compromise a service provider to gain access to MFA codes and one-time passwords (OTP).(Citation: Okta Scatter Swine 2022)

Credential information may also be exposed to adversaries via leaks to online or other accessible data sets (ex: [Search Engines](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1593/002), breach dumps, code repositories, etc.). Adversaries may purchase credentials from dark web markets, such as Russian Market and 2easy, or through access to Telegram channels that distribute logs from infostealer malware.(Citation: Bleeping Computer 2easy 2021)(Citation: SecureWorks Infostealers 2023)(Citation: Bleeping Computer Stealer Logs 2023)

Gathering this information may reveal opportunities for other forms of reconnaissance (ex: [Search Open Websites/Domains](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1593) or [Phishing for Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1598)), establishing operational resources (ex: [Compromise Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1586)), and/or initial access (ex: [External Remote Services](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1133) or [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078)).
4160.profile: [profile]Steal Credentials, designated as T1589.001 within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, is a technique under the Reconnaissance tactic applicable to multiple platforms. It involves adversaries gathering account credentials through various methods including phishing, compromising websites to collect authentication cookies, purchasing logs from infostealer malware on dark web markets, and exploiting credential leaks from public data sets like code repositories or breach dumps. This activity is associated with groups such as APT28, LAPSUS$, and Leviathan.
4160.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Steal Credentials is a broad adversary objective, not a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique. It encompasses various methods for obtaining authentication materials, including searching for insecurely stored credentials in plaintext files, the Windows Registry, or memory. Adversaries may also steal web session cookies or application access tokens to bypass multi-factor authentication and gain unauthorized access to systems and resources. This activity is foundational for initial access and lateral movement.

4161.name: Malware Download
4161.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may develop malware and malware components that can be used during targeting. Building malicious software can include the development of payloads, droppers, post-compromise tools, backdoors (including backdoored images), packers, C2 protocols, and the creation of infected removable media. Adversaries may develop malware to support their operations, creating a means for maintaining control of remote machines, evading defenses, and executing post-compromise behaviors.(Citation: Mandiant APT1)(Citation: Kaspersky Sofacy)(Citation: ActiveMalwareEnergy)(Citation: FBI Flash FIN7 USB)

During malware development, adversaries may intentionally include indicators aligned with other known actors in order to mislead attribution by defenders.(Citation: Olympic Destroyer)(Citation: Risky Bulletin Threat actor impersonates FSB APT)(Citation: GamaCopy organization)

As with legitimate development efforts, different skill sets may be required for developing malware. The skills needed may be located in-house, or may need to be contracted out. Use of a contractor may be considered an extension of that adversary's malware development capabilities, provided the adversary plays a role in shaping requirements and maintains a degree of exclusivity to the malware.

Some aspects of malware development, such as C2 protocol development, may require adversaries to obtain additional infrastructure. For example, malware developed that will communicate with Twitter for C2, may require use of [Web Services](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1583/006).(Citation: FireEye APT29)
4161.profile: [profile]Malware Download is a technique where adversaries acquire malicious software to support their operations, corresponding to MITRE ATT&CK ID T1588.001 under the Resource Development tactic. This involves obtaining payloads, droppers, backdoors, and C2 protocols by downloading free malware from the internet, purchasing it from criminal marketplaces or Malware-as-a-Service (MaaS) providers, or stealing and repurposing it from other adversaries. This technique provides a means for maintaining control, evading defenses, and executing post-compromise behaviors without requiring in-house development.
4161.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Malware Download is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the provided context, it describes the adversary action of acquiring malicious software from external sources. This can involve downloading free malware from the internet, purchasing it from criminal marketplaces (Malware-as-a-Service), or stealing and repurposing malware from other entities. The acquired malware, which includes payloads, droppers, and C2 protocols, is used to support operations by enabling control of systems, evading defenses, and executing post-compromise activities.

4162.name: Account Takeover
4162.profile: [profile]Account Takeover is a technique where adversaries compromise and assume control of legitimate user or system accounts. It is often facilitated by initial access via credential theft or phishing, and is linked to groups like RocketKitten. The technique enables persistent access and privilege escalation within a target environment, allowing adversaries to conduct further malicious activities while evading detection by operating under trusted identities.
4162.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Account Takeover is a technique where adversaries gain unauthorized control of a legitimate user account, often as a follow-on behavior after Account Discovery (T1087). It is associated with the Persistence, Privilege Escalation, and Initial Access tactics, primarily affecting Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. The technical mechanics involve using compromised credentials to access systems, potentially leading to actions like data theft or lateral movement. This technique is frequently employed by groups such as Scattered Spider and is a precursor to other malicious activities like Account Manipulation (T1098).

4163.name: tspy_woolerg
4163.profile: [profile]Tspy_Woolerg, also known as Woolerg, is attributed to the RocketKitten intrusion set. It functions as a keylogger, capturing sensitive user input. Its technical behaviors include creating a registry key for persistence to ensure automatic execution on system startup. The malware primarily targets the Windows platform.]
4163.profile_without_enhance: [profile]tspy_woolerg is a keylogger malware. It is related to the Keylogger malware family, which is associated with intrusion sets including Lazarus, RocketKitten, APT3, OilRig, and APT28. A key technical behavior involves the use of an 'Encryption Layer' technique, applying multiple layers of encryption to command and control (C2) communications to obfuscate traffic.[/profile]

4164.name: Relatively Simple Tools
4164.profile: [profile]Relatively Simple Tools is a malware entity attributed to the RocketKitten intrusion set. Its key technical behaviors include using relatively simple code structures and basic anti-analysis checks, such as environment detection mechanisms that can be bypassed with simple patching or evasion scripts. It targets various platforms, as indicated by its low barrier to analysis and association with tools used by modern cybercriminals for efficient impact.
4164.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Relatively Simple Tools is a malware entity associated with the APT28 group, as referenced in the 'oldbait' report. Its key technical behavior involves a relatively simple code structure, which is noted for achieving significant impact despite its lack of depth and sophistication. The malware demonstrates basic anti-analysis mechanisms, such as checks for reverse engineering environments, but these can be bypassed with simple binary patching, sandbox evasion scripts, or debugger cloaking tools, indicating a low barrier to analysis.

4165.name: Publicly Available Tools
4165.profile: [profile]Publicly Available Tools, also known as open source tools, are utilized by intrusion sets like RocketKitten for malicious purposes. These tools, which include publicly available RATs and modified tools, are employed for activities such as persistence and remote access, as referenced in the context of tools like datper and poortry.
4165.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Publicly Available Tools is a category of malware that includes open-source or publicly accessible remote access tools (RATs) and modified utilities. It is associated with groups like Tick, which have been observed using such tools, including datper. These tools are often employed for persistence and remote access, with techniques like injecting shellcode into processes such as svchost.exe. The target platforms are typically Windows systems, leveraging these readily available tools for malicious activities.

4169.name: Personal Cloud Services (Gmail, Google Drive, Yahoo!)

4170.name: Exploiting Home Perimeter Vulnerabilities
4170.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may acquire information about vulnerabilities that can be used during targeting. A vulnerability is a weakness in computer hardware or software that can, potentially, be exploited by an adversary to cause unintended or unanticipated behavior to occur. Adversaries may find vulnerability information by searching open databases or gaining access to closed vulnerability databases.(Citation: National Vulnerability Database)

An adversary may monitor vulnerability disclosures/databases to understand the state of existing, as well as newly discovered, vulnerabilities. There is usually a delay between when a vulnerability is discovered and when it is made public. An adversary may target the systems of those known to conduct vulnerability research (including commercial vendors). Knowledge of a vulnerability may cause an adversary to search for an existing exploit (i.e. [Exploits](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1588/005)) or to attempt to develop one themselves (i.e. [Exploits](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1587/004)).
4170.profile: [profile]Exploiting Home Perimeter Vulnerabilities is a technique with the ID T1588.006, aligned with the Reconnaissance tactic. It involves adversaries acquiring information about vulnerabilities in hardware or software that can be exploited to cause unintended behavior. This is achieved by searching open databases like the National Vulnerability Database, monitoring vulnerability disclosures, or targeting systems of known vulnerability researchers to understand existing or newly discovered weaknesses. This intelligence gathering can lead to searching for or developing specific exploits. Associated groups include Sandworm Team, Storm-0501, and Volt Typhoon.[/profile]
4170.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Exploiting Home Perimeter Vulnerabilities is a technique where adversaries target weaknesses in internet-facing systems within home networks to gain initial access. This involves identifying and leveraging software bugs, misconfigurations, or unpatched vulnerabilities in devices like routers, IoT appliances, or personal servers. The activity is closely related to the standard MITRE ATT&CK technique Exploit Public-Facing Application (T1190) under the Initial Access tactic, applicable to multiple platforms including network devices and cloud instances.

4171.name: Device Infection via Personal Endpoints
4171.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may register a device to an adversary-controlled account. Devices may be registered in a multifactor authentication (MFA) system, which handles authentication to the network, or in a device management system, which handles device access and compliance.

MFA systems, such as Duo or Okta, allow users to associate devices with their accounts in order to complete MFA requirements. An adversary that compromises a user’s credentials may enroll a new device in order to bypass initial MFA requirements and gain persistent access to a network.(Citation: CISA MFA PrintNightmare)(Citation: DarkReading FireEye SolarWinds) In some cases, the MFA self-enrollment process may require only a username and password to enroll the account's first device or to enroll a device to an inactive account. (Citation: Mandiant APT29 Microsoft 365 2022)

Similarly, an adversary with existing access to a network may register a device or a virtual machine to Entra ID and/or its device management system, Microsoft Intune, in order to access sensitive data or resources while bypassing conditional access policies.(Citation: AADInternals - Device Registration)(Citation: AADInternals - Conditional Access Bypass)(Citation: Microsoft DEV-0537)(Citation: Expel Atlas Lion 2025)

Devices registered in Entra ID may be able to conduct [Internal Spearphishing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1534) campaigns via intra-organizational emails, which are less likely to be treated as suspicious by the email client.(Citation: Microsoft - Device Registration) Additionally, an adversary may be able to perform a [Service Exhaustion Flood](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1499/002) on an Entra ID tenant by registering a large number of devices.(Citation: AADInternals - BPRT)
4171.profile: [profile]Device Infection via Personal Endpoints is a technique aligned with MITRE ATT&CK ID T1098.005, under the Persistence tactic, targeting Windows, Azure AD, and MFA platforms. It involves an adversary registering a new device to a compromised user account within an MFA system like Duo or Okta, or a device management system like Microsoft Intune, to bypass initial MFA requirements and conditional access policies, thereby gaining persistent network access. This method can also enable internal spearphishing or be used to perform service exhaustion floods in Entra ID tenants. The intrusion set RocketKitten has been associated with this behavior.[/profile]
4171.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Device Infection via Personal Endpoints" is a technique for Initial Access, where adversaries use a victim's personal mobile device (like a smartphone) connected via USB to a corporate system to deliver malware. This exploits the system automatically mounting the device as a drive, potentially leveraging Autorun features to execute malicious code from the mobile device onto the PC, bypassing network-based defenses.

4179.name: 建立信任/收集信息
4179.profile: [profile]The entity "建立信任/收集信息" is a reconnaissance technique aligned with MITRE ATT&CK. It involves adversaries gathering information to establish trust or collect intelligence for targeting. Specific sub-techniques include gathering victim identity information (T1589) such as personal data and credentials via phishing or probing authentication services, identifying business relationships (T1591.002) like third-party vendors through social media or victim websites, and discovering network trust dependencies (T1590.003) such as managed service provider access via open databases. This information enables further reconnaissance, resource establishment, and initial access vectors like trusted relationships or supply chain compromise.[/profile]
4179.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "建立信任/收集信息" is a reconnaissance technique. Based on retrieved information, it aligns with the broader MITRE ATT&CK tactic of Reconnaissance (TA0043). The technique involves gathering specific victim information to enable further attacks. This includes collecting details on network trust dependencies (T1590.003), such as third-party service providers with network access; business relationships (T1591.002), like suppliers and contractors; and victim identity information (T1589), including personal data, credentials, and MFA configurations. Information is gathered through methods like phishing for information, searching open technical databases, social media, and victim-owned websites, or via active scanning of authentication services. This collected intelligence can reveal opportunities for subsequent reconnaissance, resource establishment, and initial access operations.

4181.name: Fake Trend Micro Housecall Installer
4181.profile: [profile]Fake Trend Micro Housecall Installer, also known as holcus installer (adware), is an adware installer associated with malvertising campaigns labeled "Made in China." It is attributed to the RocketKitten intrusion set. The malware operates by masquerading as a legitimate Trend Micro Housecall installer to deceive users, and it is delivered through malicious installers. Its primary target platform is Windows systems.
4181.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Fake Trend Micro Housecall Installer is a malicious installer. 4184.name: Encryption Layer
4184.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may compromise a network device’s encryption capability in order to bypass encryption that would otherwise protect data communications. (Citation: Cisco Synful Knock Evolution)

Encryption can be used to protect transmitted network traffic to maintain its confidentiality (protect against unauthorized disclosure) and integrity (protect against unauthorized changes). Encryption ciphers are used to convert a plaintext message to ciphertext and can be computationally intensive to decipher without the associated decryption key. Typically, longer keys increase the cost of cryptanalysis, or decryption without the key.

Adversaries can compromise and manipulate devices that perform encryption of network traffic. For example, through behaviors such as [Modify System Image](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1601), [Reduce Key Space](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1600/001), and [Disable Crypto Hardware](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1600/002), an adversary can negatively effect and/or eliminate a device’s ability to securely encrypt network traffic. This poses a greater risk of unauthorized disclosure and may help facilitate data manipulation, Credential Access, or Collection efforts. (Citation: Cisco Blog Legacy Device Attacks)
4184.profile: [profile]The entity "Encryption Layer" aligns with MITRE ATT&CK technique T1600, "Weaken Encryption," under the Impact tactic for Network platforms. This technique involves compromising a network device's encryption capability to bypass data protection. Specific mechanics include manipulating the device through sub-techniques like Reduce Key Space (T1600.001) or Disable Crypto Hardware (T1600.002), which can eliminate secure encryption to facilitate unauthorized data disclosure or credential access. The malware tspy_woolerg is associated with this behavior.[/profile]
4184.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Encryption Layer is a technique where adversaries apply multiple layers of encryption to command and control (C2) communications, typically by tunneling a custom encryption scheme within a standard protocol encryption like HTTPS or SMTPS. This method enhances the obfuscation of malicious traffic, making detection and analysis more difficult by blending encrypted payloads within common, encrypted network protocols.

4190.name: Fake Login Pages
4190.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may add login items to execute upon user login to gain persistence or escalate privileges. Login items are applications, documents, folders, or server connections that are automatically launched when a user logs in.(Citation: Open Login Items Apple) Login items can be added via a shared file list or Service Management Framework.(Citation: Adding Login Items) Shared file list login items can be set using scripting languages such as [AppleScript](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/002), whereas the Service Management Framework uses the API call SMLoginItemSetEnabled. Login items installed using the Service Management Framework leverage launchd, are not visible in the System Preferences, and can only be removed by the application that created them.(Citation: Adding Login Items)(Citation: SMLoginItemSetEnabled Schroeder 2013) Login items created using a shared file list are visible in System Preferences, can hide the application when it launches, and are executed through LaunchServices, not launchd, to open applications, documents, or URLs without using Finder.(Citation: Launch Services Apple Developer) Users and applications use login items to configure their user environment to launch commonly used services or applications, such as email, chat, and music applications. Adversaries can utilize [AppleScript](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/002) and [Native API](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1106) calls to create a login item to spawn malicious executables.(Citation: ELC Running at startup) Prior to version 10.5 on macOS, adversaries can add login items by using [AppleScript](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/002) to send an Apple events to the “System Events” process, which has an AppleScript dictionary for manipulating login items.(Citation: Login Items AE) Adversaries can use a command such as tell application “System Events” to make login item at end with properties /path/to/executable.(Citation: Startup Items Eclectic)(Citation: hexed osx.dok analysis 2019)(Citation: Add List Remove Login Items Apple Script) This command adds the path of the malicious executable to the login item file list located in ~/Library/Application Support/com.apple.backgroundtaskmanagementagent/backgrounditems.btm.(Citation: Startup Items Eclectic) Adversaries can also use login items to launch executables that can be used to control the victim system remotely or as a means to gain privilege escalation by prompting for user credentials.(Citation: objsee mac malware 2017)(Citation: CheckPoint Dok)(Citation: objsee netwire backdoor 2019)
4190.profile: [profile]The entity "Fake Login Pages" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on retrieved context, it is a resource or method used within other techniques, specifically for credential harvesting. It is referenced in techniques like Link Target (T1608.005) and Spearphishing Link (T1598.003), where adversaries clone legitimate login portals to create deceptive web pages. These fake pages are hosted to trick victims into entering their credentials, which are then captured by the adversary. This activity supports the Initial Access and Credential Access tactics, primarily targeting users via web services.[/profile]
4190.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Fake Login Pages is a technique used to steal credentials by presenting fraudulent interfaces that mimic legitimate login portals. It is associated with the MITRE ATT&CK ID T1608.005 (Link Target) under Resource Development and T1598.003 (Spearphishing Link) under Reconnaissance, primarily targeting web platforms. The technical mechanics involve adversaries cloning legitimate login pages, often using phishing kits like EvilProxy to perform adversary-in-the-middle attacks, which capture credentials and session cookies to potentially bypass multi-factor authentication. This technique is frequently employed in spearphishing campaigns to harvest sensitive information.

4191.name: Phishing via Phone Calls
4191.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may send phishing messages to gain access to victim systems. All forms of phishing are electronically delivered social engineering. Phishing can be targeted, known as spearphishing. In spearphishing, a specific individual, company, or industry will be targeted by the adversary. More generally, adversaries can conduct non-targeted phishing, such as in mass malware spam campaigns.

Adversaries may send victims emails containing malicious attachments or links, typically to execute malicious code on victim systems. Phishing may also be conducted via third-party services, like social media platforms. Phishing may also involve social engineering techniques, such as posing as a trusted source, as well as evasive techniques such as removing or manipulating emails or metadata/headers from compromised accounts being abused to send messages (e.g., [Email Hiding Rules](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1564/008)).(Citation: Microsoft OAuth Spam 2022)(Citation: Palo Alto Unit 42 VBA Infostealer 2014) Another way to accomplish this is by [Email Spoofing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1672)(Citation: Proofpoint-spoof) the identity of the sender, which can be used to fool both the human recipient as well as automated security tools,(Citation: cyberproof-double-bounce) or by including the intended target as a party to an existing email thread that includes malicious files or links (i.e., "thread hijacking").(Citation: phishing-krebs)

Victims may also receive phishing messages that instruct them to call a phone number where they are directed to visit a malicious URL, download malware,(Citation: sygnia Luna Month)(Citation: CISA Remote Monitoring and Management Software) or install adversary-accessible remote management tools onto their computer (i.e., [User Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204)).(Citation: Unit42 Luna Moth)
4191.profile: [profile]Phishing via Phone Calls, also known as Spearphishing Voice (T1566.004), is an Initial Access technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, applicable across multiple platforms. It involves adversaries using voice communications, such as phone calls, to manipulate users into performing actions that grant system access. The technical mechanics typically involve sending a phishing message that instructs the victim to call a provided number; during the call, the adversary directs the user to visit a malicious URL, download malware, or install adversary-accessible remote management tools, relying on User Execution for compromise. This method often employs social engineering, such as impersonating a trusted entity like technical support, and may be combined with Multi-Factor Authentication Request Generation to bypass security.[/profile]
4191.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Phishing via Phone Calls is a technique aligned with MITRE ATT&CK ID T1566.004 (Spearphishing: Voice), falling under the Initial Access tactic and applicable to multiple platforms. This method, often called vishing, involves adversaries using phone calls to manipulate victims into performing actions that compromise security, such as calling a provided number to visit a malicious URL, download malware, or install remote management tools, frequently employing social engineering by impersonating trusted entities like technical support to create urgency.

4192.name: Cloud Account Takeover
4192.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may attempt to get a listing of cloud accounts. Cloud accounts are those created and configured by an organization for use by users, remote support, services, or for administration of resources within a cloud service provider or SaaS application. With authenticated access there are several tools that can be used to find accounts. The Get-MsolRoleMember PowerShell cmdlet can be used to obtain account names given a role or permissions group in Office 365.(Citation: Microsoft msolrolemember)(Citation: GitHub Raindance) The Azure CLI (AZ CLI) also provides an interface to obtain user accounts with authenticated access to a domain. The command az ad user list will list all users within a domain.(Citation: Microsoft AZ CLI)(Citation: Black Hills Red Teaming MS AD Azure, 2018) The AWS command aws iam list-users may be used to obtain a list of users in the current account while aws iam list-roles can obtain IAM roles that have a specified path prefix.(Citation: AWS List Roles)(Citation: AWS List Users) In GCP, gcloud iam service-accounts list and gcloud projects get-iam-policy may be used to obtain a listing of service accounts and users in a project.(Citation: Google Cloud - IAM Servie Accounts List API)
4192.profile: [profile]Cloud Account Takeover is a technique aligned with MITRE ATT&CK ID T1087.004 under the Discovery tactic, targeting cloud platforms like AWS, Azure, and GCP. It involves adversaries using authenticated access and specific commands to enumerate cloud accounts, such as `aws iam list-users` in AWS, `az ad user list` in Azure, or `gcloud iam service-accounts list` in GCP, to identify user and service accounts for follow-on targeting. This activity is associated with groups like Storm-0501 and APT29.
4192.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Cloud Account Takeover is a technique where adversaries gain unauthorized control over legitimate cloud accounts (T1078.004). This provides initial access, persistence, and a platform for privilege escalation. Attackers may compromise accounts via phishing or credential theft, then add persistent adversary-controlled credentials (T1098.001), such as SSH keys in AWS/GCP or app passwords in Azure to bypass MFA. They can also create new, stealthy cloud accounts (T1136.003) to maintain access. Compromised accounts, especially high-privileged or federated ones, enable lateral movement, data exfiltration to adversary-controlled cloud accounts (T1537), and potential pivots to on-premises environments.

4193.name: Facebook Messages
4193.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may directly collect unsecured credentials stored or passed through user communication services. Credentials may be sent and stored in user chat communication applications such as email, chat services like Slack or Teams, collaboration tools like Jira or Trello, and any other services that support user communication. Users may share various forms of credentials (such as usernames and passwords, API keys, or authentication tokens) on private or public corporate internal communications channels.

Rather than accessing the stored chat logs (i.e., [Credentials In Files](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1552/001)), adversaries may directly access credentials within these services on the user endpoint, through servers hosting the services, or through administrator portals for cloud hosted services. Adversaries may also compromise integration tools like Slack Workflows to automatically search through messages to extract user credentials. These credentials may then be abused to perform follow-on activities such as lateral movement or privilege escalation (Citation: Slack Security Risks).
4193.profile: [profile]Chat Messages is the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1552.008 under the Credential Access tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It involves adversaries directly collecting unsecured credentials from active user communication services like Slack, Teams, or email, rather than from stored log files. Credentials such as passwords, API keys, or tokens are harvested by accessing the services on user endpoints, servers, or cloud admin portals, or by compromising integration tools like Slack Workflows to automatically search and extract them from messages for follow-on activities like lateral movement.[/profile]
4193.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Facebook Messages is a technique aligned with MITRE ATT&CK ID T1552.008 (Chat Messages) under the Credential Access tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It involves adversaries directly collecting unsecured credentials, such as usernames, passwords, API keys, or authentication tokens, that are stored or transmitted through the Facebook Messages service. This can be achieved by accessing the service on the user endpoint, through hosting servers, or via administrator portals for cloud-hosted instances, potentially using compromised integration tools to automatically search and extract credentials from messages for follow-on activities like lateral movement.
