4201.name: GUID Randomization
4201.profile: [profile]GUID Randomization is a sub-technique of SIP and Trust Provider Hijacking (T1553.003) under the Defense Evasion tactic, primarily affecting Windows platforms. It involves adversaries modifying the globally unique identifier (GUID) registry entries associated with Subject Interface Packages (SIPs) or trust providers to redirect validation functions to malicious DLLs. This allows them to spoof digital signature checks, making malicious code appear legitimately signed to bypass security policies and application controls, and can provide persistent execution. The intrusion-set RocketKitten is linked to this activity.
4201.profile_without_enhance: [profile]GUID Randomization is a sub-technique of SIP and Trust Provider Hijacking (T1553.003) under the Defense Evasion tactic, targeting the Windows platform. It involves adversaries modifying the Globally Unique Identifier (GUID) registry keys associated with Subject Interface Packages (SIPs) or trust providers in the Windows Cryptography architecture. By redirecting the `Dll` and `FuncName` values for these components to malicious or repurposed DLLs, attackers can spoof digital signature validation. This allows malicious code to be misclassified as legitimately signed, bypassing application control tools and security policies that rely on Authenticode verification.

4202.name: Infection Vectors
4202.profile: [profile]Infection Vectors is a broad category of adversary techniques for gaining initial access to a system. A specific technique is Replication Through Removable Media (T1091), used for Initial Access and Lateral Movement. This tactic involves copying malware to removable drives or mobile devices, often exploiting Autorun features or disguising malware as legitimate files to execute when the media is connected to a target system, such as a PC via USB. The intrusion set RocketKitten is known to utilize related methods.[/profile]
4202.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Infection Vectors is a general concept, not a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique. The retrieved information describes related techniques like Replication through Removable Media (T1091), which involves copying malware to removable drives and exploiting Autorun features, including via USB-connected mobile devices, for initial access or lateral movement.

4203.name: Be Vigilant
4203.profile: [profile]Be Vigilant is a technique used by adversaries to avoid leaving command history traces in Unix-like systems. This is achieved by manipulating the HISTCONTROL environment variable, which controls what is saved by the history command. By setting HISTCONTROL to "ignorespace" or "ignoreboth", any command preceded by a space will not be recorded in the user's bash history file (~/.bash_history), allowing for stealthier terminal operations. This technique has been associated with the intrusion set RocketKitten.
4203.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Be Vigilant is a technique where adversaries prepend a space to terminal commands to avoid logging. On Linux and macOS systems, this exploits the HISTCONTROL environment variable when set to "ignorespace" or "ignoreboth", causing commands starting with a space to be omitted from the bash history file (~/.bash_history). This allows adversaries to operate without leaving command traces in the user's history upon logout.

4204.name: Information Sharing
4204.profile: [profile]Information Sharing is a technique used by adversaries to exchange collected data, often for operational coordination or to support further attacks. It is associated with the intrusion set RocketKitten. This technique involves the transfer of intelligence between compromised systems or to external command and control infrastructure, enabling persistent threat activities and collaborative malicious operations.
4204.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Information Sharing is a technique where adversaries exchange collected data, often using established communication channels or protocols to coordinate actions or exfiltrate intelligence. This activity is part of the Collection tactic and can occur across multiple platforms. Technical mechanics involve using shared network drives, collaboration platforms like SharePoint or Slack, and cloud storage services to pool information from compromised systems. Adversaries leverage these repositories to centralize data such as credentials, network diagrams, and technical documentation for later use in campaigns or lateral movement.

4205.name: Malicious Links
4205.profile: [profile]Malicious Links is a technique used by threat actors like RocketKitten for initial access, often delivered via phishing emails containing links to malicious documents. It is associated with groups including Lazarus Group, APT29, APT32, APT41, and others, and serves as a delivery mechanism for malware such as Cobalt Strike and AsyncRAT by directing victims to malicious domains or infrastructure.
4205.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Malicious Links is a malware delivery mechanism, not a distinct malware family itself. Its primary alias is 'malicious domains'. It is attributed to the Lazarus Group and is used by a wide range of APT groups including APT29, APT32, APT41, and FIN7, among others. Its key behavior is facilitating initial access through phishing emails containing links to malicious documents or payloads. It targets general users and operates across common platforms via web browsers. Its infrastructure consists of the malicious domains and URLs used in these campaigns.

4206.name: Password Reset Attempts
4206.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries with no prior knowledge of legitimate credentials within the system or environment may guess passwords to attempt access to accounts. Without knowledge of the password for an account, an adversary may opt to systematically guess the password using a repetitive or iterative mechanism. An adversary may guess login credentials without prior knowledge of system or environment passwords during an operation by using a list of common passwords. Password guessing may or may not take into account the target's policies on password complexity or use policies that may lock accounts out after a number of failed attempts.

Guessing passwords can be a risky option because it could cause numerous authentication failures and account lockouts, depending on the organization's login failure policies. (Citation: Cylance Cleaver)

Typically, management services over commonly used ports are used when guessing passwords. Commonly targeted services include the following:

* SSH (22/TCP)
* Telnet (23/TCP)
* FTP (21/TCP)
* NetBIOS / SMB / Samba (139/TCP & 445/TCP)
* LDAP (389/TCP)
* Kerberos (88/TCP)
* RDP / Terminal Services (3389/TCP)
* HTTP/HTTP Management Services (80/TCP & 443/TCP)
* MSSQL (1433/TCP)
* Oracle (1521/TCP)
* MySQL (3306/TCP)
* VNC (5900/TCP)
* SNMP (161/UDP and 162/TCP/UDP)

In addition to management services, adversaries may "target single sign-on (SSO) and cloud-based applications utilizing federated authentication protocols," as well as externally facing email applications, such as Office 365.(Citation: US-CERT TA18-068A 2018). Further, adversaries may abuse network device interfaces (such as `wlanAPI`) to brute force accessible wifi-router(s) via wireless authentication protocols.(Citation: Trend Micro Emotet 2020)

In default environments, LDAP and Kerberos connection attempts are less likely to trigger events over SMB, which creates Windows "logon failure" event ID 4625.
4206.profile: [profile]Password Guessing, identified as T1110.001 under the Credential Access tactic, operates across multiple platforms including Windows, Linux, and cloud environments. It involves adversaries systematically attempting to authenticate using repetitive guesses or common password lists against services like SSH, SMB, LDAP, Kerberos, RDP, and cloud applications. This technique risks triggering account lockouts but may avoid detection by targeting protocols like LDAP and Kerberos, which generate fewer conspicuous failure events than SMB. It is associated with groups like APT29 and APT28.[/profile]
4206.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Password Reset Attempts is a technique where adversaries abuse self-service password reset (SSPR) mechanisms to bypass multi-factor authentication (MFA) and gain account access. When configured for SSPR, these systems can automatically generate MFA push notifications or codes; adversaries lacking credentials can trigger these requests to bombard a user, potentially leading to "MFA fatigue" where the user accidentally accepts the reset, granting the adversary control. This method is used by groups like Scattered Spider and Lapsus$ to circumvent authentication controls.

4209.name: 2FA (Two-Factor Authentication)
4209.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may disable or modify multi-factor authentication (MFA) mechanisms to enable persistent access to compromised accounts.

Once adversaries have gained access to a network by either compromising an account lacking MFA or by employing an MFA bypass method such as [Multi-Factor Authentication Request Generation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1621), adversaries may leverage their access to modify or completely disable MFA defenses. This can be accomplished by abusing legitimate features, such as excluding users from Azure AD Conditional Access Policies, registering a new yet vulnerable/adversary-controlled MFA method, or by manually patching MFA programs and configuration files to bypass expected functionality.(Citation: Mandiant APT42)(Citation: Azure AD Conditional Access Exclusions)

For example, modifying the Windows hosts file (`C:\windows\system32\drivers\etc\hosts`) to redirect MFA calls to localhost instead of an MFA server may cause the MFA process to fail. If a "fail open" policy is in place, any otherwise successful authentication attempt may be granted access without enforcing MFA. (Citation: Russians Exploit Default MFA Protocol - CISA March 2022) 

Depending on the scope, goals, and privileges of the adversary, MFA defenses may be disabled for individual accounts or for all accounts tied to a larger group, such as all domain accounts in a victim's network environment.(Citation: Russians Exploit Default MFA Protocol - CISA March 2022)
4209.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique "Modify Authentication Process: Multi-Factor Authentication", identified as T1556.006 under the Credential Access tactic for Windows, Azure AD, and SaaS platforms. Its technical mechanics involve adversaries who have already gained network access disabling or modifying MFA to maintain persistence. This is achieved by abusing legitimate features like excluding users from Azure AD Conditional Access Policies, registering a new adversary-controlled MFA method, or patching configuration files; a specific example is modifying the Windows hosts file to redirect MFA calls to localhost, potentially exploiting a "fail open" policy. The threat actor Scattered Spider has been associated with this technique.[/profile]
4209.profile_without_enhance: [profile]2FA (Two-Factor Authentication) is a security control, not a specific adversary technique. The retrieved information describes related adversary techniques for bypassing or subverting MFA. These include Multi-Factor Authentication Request Generation (T1621), where adversaries generate push notifications to cause "MFA fatigue," and Multi-Factor Authentication Interception (T1111), which involves capturing hardware token codes or SMS messages. Adversaries may also disable MFA mechanisms (T1556.006) after initial access. The primary technical mechanics involve abusing notification systems, using keyloggers, or modifying configuration files to circumvent the additional authentication factor.

4210.name: Man-in-the-middle attack
4210.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may attempt to position themselves between two or more networked devices using an adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) technique to support follow-on behaviors such as [Network Sniffing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1040), [Transmitted Data Manipulation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1565/002), or replay attacks ([Exploitation for Credential Access](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1212)). By abusing features of common networking protocols that can determine the flow of network traffic (e.g. ARP, DNS, LLMNR, etc.), adversaries may force a device to communicate through an adversary controlled system so they can collect information or perform additional actions.(Citation: Rapid7 MiTM Basics)

For example, adversaries may manipulate victim DNS settings to enable other malicious activities such as preventing/redirecting users from accessing legitimate sites and/or pushing additional malware.(Citation: ttint_rat)(Citation: dns_changer_trojans)(Citation: ad_blocker_with_miner) Adversaries may also manipulate DNS and leverage their position in order to intercept user credentials, including access tokens ([Steal Application Access Token](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1528)) and session cookies ([Steal Web Session Cookie](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539)).(Citation: volexity_0day_sophos_FW)(Citation: Token tactics) [Downgrade Attack](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1562/010)s can also be used to establish an AiTM position, such as by negotiating a less secure, deprecated, or weaker version of communication protocol (SSL/TLS) or encryption algorithm.(Citation: mitm_tls_downgrade_att)(Citation: taxonomy_downgrade_att_tls)(Citation: tlseminar_downgrade_att)

Adversaries may also leverage the AiTM position to attempt to monitor and/or modify traffic, such as in [Transmitted Data Manipulation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1565/002). Adversaries can setup a position similar to AiTM to prevent traffic from flowing to the appropriate destination, potentially to [Impair Defenses](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1562) and/or in support of a [Network Denial of Service](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1498).
4210.profile: [profile]Adversary-in-the-Middle (AiTM) is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1557 under the Collection tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It works by positioning an adversary-controlled system between networked devices, achieved by abusing protocols like ARP, DNS, or LLMNR to redirect traffic. This enables follow-on actions such as network sniffing, credential interception (including access tokens and session cookies), and transmitted data manipulation. Adversaries may also use downgrade attacks on protocols like SSL/TLS to establish this position. Groups like Kimsuky, Sea Turtle, and Mustang Panda have been associated with this technique.
4210.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Man-in-the-middle attack is a foundational network attack technique where an adversary secretly intercepts and potentially alters communications between two parties who believe they are directly communicating. It is not a specific MITRE ATT&CK ID but underpins techniques like Adversary-in-the-Middle (T1557). Attackers achieve this by abusing protocols like ARP, DNS, or LLMNR to reroute traffic through a controlled system, enabling credential theft, data manipulation, or session hijacking. Downgrade attacks on protocols like SSL/TLS can also be used to establish this position.

4211.name: Man-in-the-browser attack
4211.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may attempt to position themselves between two or more networked devices using an adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) technique to support follow-on behaviors such as [Network Sniffing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1040), [Transmitted Data Manipulation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1565/002), or replay attacks ([Exploitation for Credential Access](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1212)). By abusing features of common networking protocols that can determine the flow of network traffic (e.g. ARP, DNS, LLMNR, etc.), adversaries may force a device to communicate through an adversary controlled system so they can collect information or perform additional actions.(Citation: Rapid7 MiTM Basics)

For example, adversaries may manipulate victim DNS settings to enable other malicious activities such as preventing/redirecting users from accessing legitimate sites and/or pushing additional malware.(Citation: ttint_rat)(Citation: dns_changer_trojans)(Citation: ad_blocker_with_miner) Adversaries may also manipulate DNS and leverage their position in order to intercept user credentials, including access tokens ([Steal Application Access Token](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1528)) and session cookies ([Steal Web Session Cookie](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539)).(Citation: volexity_0day_sophos_FW)(Citation: Token tactics) [Downgrade Attack](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1562/010)s can also be used to establish an AiTM position, such as by negotiating a less secure, deprecated, or weaker version of communication protocol (SSL/TLS) or encryption algorithm.(Citation: mitm_tls_downgrade_att)(Citation: taxonomy_downgrade_att_tls)(Citation: tlseminar_downgrade_att)

Adversaries may also leverage the AiTM position to attempt to monitor and/or modify traffic, such as in [Transmitted Data Manipulation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1565/002). Adversaries can setup a position similar to AiTM to prevent traffic from flowing to the appropriate destination, potentially to [Impair Defenses](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1562) and/or in support of a [Network Denial of Service](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1498).
4211.profile: [profile]Man-in-the-browser attack is a specific form of adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM), aligning with MITRE technique T1557 under the Collection tactic, primarily targeting Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It operates by injecting malicious code, such as a browser extension or plugin, into a user's web browser. This allows adversaries to stealthily intercept, monitor, and manipulate web traffic and transactions between the user and websites, enabling activities like credential theft, session cookie hijacking, and data manipulation without the user's knowledge. It is distinct from network-level AiTM as it directly compromises the client browser software. The intrusion-set RocketKitten has been associated with this technique.[/profile]
4211.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Man-in-the-browser attack is a specific form of browser session hijacking (T1185) under the Collection tactic, targeting Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It works by injecting malicious software, such as a browser extension, into a user's web browser. This allows the adversary to inherit the user's authenticated sessions, cookies, and SSL certificates, enabling them to silently intercept, monitor, and manipulate web transactions (like modifying form submissions or redirecting funds) without the user's knowledge, often bypassing multi-factor authentication.

4212.name: SIM card registration
4212.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may register a device to an adversary-controlled account. Devices may be registered in a multifactor authentication (MFA) system, which handles authentication to the network, or in a device management system, which handles device access and compliance.

MFA systems, such as Duo or Okta, allow users to associate devices with their accounts in order to complete MFA requirements. An adversary that compromises a user’s credentials may enroll a new device in order to bypass initial MFA requirements and gain persistent access to a network.(Citation: CISA MFA PrintNightmare)(Citation: DarkReading FireEye SolarWinds) In some cases, the MFA self-enrollment process may require only a username and password to enroll the account's first device or to enroll a device to an inactive account. (Citation: Mandiant APT29 Microsoft 365 2022)

Similarly, an adversary with existing access to a network may register a device or a virtual machine to Entra ID and/or its device management system, Microsoft Intune, in order to access sensitive data or resources while bypassing conditional access policies.(Citation: AADInternals - Device Registration)(Citation: AADInternals - Conditional Access Bypass)(Citation: Microsoft DEV-0537)(Citation: Expel Atlas Lion 2025)

Devices registered in Entra ID may be able to conduct [Internal Spearphishing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1534) campaigns via intra-organizational emails, which are less likely to be treated as suspicious by the email client.(Citation: Microsoft - Device Registration) Additionally, an adversary may be able to perform a [Service Exhaustion Flood](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1499/002) on an Entra ID tenant by registering a large number of devices.(Citation: AADInternals - BPRT)
4212.profile: [profile]SIM card registration, also known as Device Registration (MITRE ATT&CK T1098.005), is a persistence technique within the Initial Access tactic, primarily targeting Windows, Azure AD, and MFA platforms. It involves an adversary registering a new device, such as a phone or virtual machine, to a compromised user account within an MFA system (like Duo or Okta) or a device management system (like Microsoft Intune). This action bypasses initial MFA requirements and conditional access policies, granting persistent network access. The technique can also enable internal spearphishing and has been associated with threat groups like APT29.
4212.profile_without_enhance: [profile]SIM card registration is a technique where adversaries register a SIM card to an adversary-controlled account to bypass multi-factor authentication (MFA) and gain persistent network access. This can involve enrolling a new device in an MFA system using only compromised credentials, particularly for an account's first device or an inactive account. Registered devices may then bypass conditional access policies, access sensitive resources, conduct internal spearphishing, or enable service exhaustion floods by registering numerous devices to a tenant.

4213.name: Voicemail exploitation
4213.profile: [profile]Voicemail exploitation is a technique used by adversaries like RocketKitten to gain unauthorized access or information by targeting vulnerabilities in voicemail systems. This method typically involves exploiting weak or default authentication mechanisms, such as predictable PINs or lack of account lockouts, to access voicemail boxes remotely. The primary goal is often credential access or initial intrusion, potentially enabling further lateral movement or data exfiltration within a network. It operates on telephony and network platforms, leveraging misconfigurations rather than complex software vulnerabilities.[/profile]
4213.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Voicemail exploitation is a technique where adversaries target vulnerabilities in voicemail systems, often to gain unauthorized access, collect credentials, or achieve lateral movement. This method involves exploiting software bugs or misconfigurations in voicemail applications or their underlying services to execute adversary-controlled code, potentially leading to credential theft, privilege escalation, or denial of service. It is commonly associated with tactics like credential access, privilege escalation, and lateral movement, and can impact platforms such as telephony and unified communication systems.

4214.name: Real-time login attempts
4214.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may add login items to execute upon user login to gain persistence or escalate privileges. Login items are applications, documents, folders, or server connections that are automatically launched when a user logs in.(Citation: Open Login Items Apple) Login items can be added via a shared file list or Service Management Framework.(Citation: Adding Login Items) Shared file list login items can be set using scripting languages such as [AppleScript](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/002), whereas the Service Management Framework uses the API call SMLoginItemSetEnabled. Login items installed using the Service Management Framework leverage launchd, are not visible in the System Preferences, and can only be removed by the application that created them.(Citation: Adding Login Items)(Citation: SMLoginItemSetEnabled Schroeder 2013) Login items created using a shared file list are visible in System Preferences, can hide the application when it launches, and are executed through LaunchServices, not launchd, to open applications, documents, or URLs without using Finder.(Citation: Launch Services Apple Developer) Users and applications use login items to configure their user environment to launch commonly used services or applications, such as email, chat, and music applications. Adversaries can utilize [AppleScript](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/002) and [Native API](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1106) calls to create a login item to spawn malicious executables.(Citation: ELC Running at startup) Prior to version 10.5 on macOS, adversaries can add login items by using [AppleScript](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/002) to send an Apple events to the “System Events” process, which has an AppleScript dictionary for manipulating login items.(Citation: Login Items AE) Adversaries can use a command such as tell application “System Events” to make login item at end with properties /path/to/executable.(Citation: Startup Items Eclectic)(Citation: hexed osx.dok analysis 2019)(Citation: Add List Remove Login Items Apple Script) This command adds the path of the malicious executable to the login item file list located in ~/Library/Application Support/com.apple.backgroundtaskmanagementagent/backgrounditems.btm.(Citation: Startup Items Eclectic) Adversaries can also use login items to launch executables that can be used to control the victim system remotely or as a means to gain privilege escalation by prompting for user credentials.(Citation: objsee mac malware 2017)(Citation: CheckPoint Dok)(Citation: objsee netwire backdoor 2019)
4214.profile: [profile]The entity "login items" corresponds to MITRE ATT&CK technique T1547.015, categorized under Persistence and Privilege Escalation tactics for macOS. This technique involves adding applications, documents, or executables to launch automatically upon user login. Adversaries can implement this via a shared file list, using AppleScript commands like `tell application “System Events” to make login item at end with properties /path/to/executable`, which modifies files such as `~/Library/Application Support/com.apple.backgroundtaskmanagementagent/backgrounditems.btm` or plists like `com.apple.loginitems.plist`. Alternatively, using the Service Management Framework API `SMLoginItemSetEnabled` creates hidden login items managed by `launchd` that are not visible in System Preferences and are removable only by the creating application. The intrusion-set RocketKitten has been associated with this method.
4214.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Real-time login attempts is a technique where adversaries continuously attempt to log into accounts, often to guess passwords or bombard users with multi-factor authentication (MFA) requests to cause "MFA fatigue" and gain unauthorized access. This activity targets services like SSH, Telnet, FTP, SMB, LDAP, Kerberos, RDP, HTTP/S, and various database and management ports. It is associated with initial access and credential access tactics, and can be used in campaigns by groups like APT29, APT28, Scattered Spider, and LAPSUS$ to bypass security controls.

4215.name: Malware campaigns
4215.uncertain_mes:
A .NET rat targets Mongolia
A new document royal road v7 installs a backdoor in .NET. a first executable is dropped \os03C2.tmp. This exe has many similarities with older campaigns using by Operation LagTime or Tonto Team.
Document
The decoy document is a document about infection of covid19 in Russia send to the Mongolia Authorities. The document is fake signed A. Amarsaikhan.
4215.profile: [profile]The entity is a malware campaign using a .NET RAT (Remote Access Trojan) referred to as 'nmass malware'. It employs a malicious document created with Royal Road v7 as a decoy, which is a fake document about COVID-19 in Russia sent to Mongolian authorities and falsely signed 'A. Amarsaikhan'. The campaign drops an initial executable (os03C2.tmp) and shares similarities with older campaigns attributed to Operation LagTime or Tonto Team. The intrusion-set RocketKitten is a directly connected neighbor. The target is Mongolia.
4215.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Malware campaigns are malicious operations that distribute various malware families, such as nmass (a .NET RAT targeting Mongolia via decoy documents), AzorUlt (historically linked to Crimson malware and The Gorgon Group), JasperLoader (distributed via malicious spam), and Dreambot (distributed via exploit kits). These campaigns employ tactics like using fake documents, malicious spam, and exploit kits to infect systems.

4216.name: Android app
4216.uncertain_mes: Amidst the coronavirus/COVID-19 pandemic, attackers continue to seek ways to exploit the public's fears to victimize online users.
4216.profile: [profile]The malware is referred to as 'coronavirus android worm', an Android application exploiting pandemic fears. It is attributed to the RocketKitten intrusion set. Key technical behaviors include sending SMS messages via accessibility services, downloading and playing MP3 files, setting files as ringtones, launching and extracting data from the Metamask app, and dropping/installing additional APK payloads like NFSkate. Its target platform is Android, and it was distributed outside official app stores.
4216.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Android app is a malicious application, also known as badpatch, attributed to the Molerats group. It is not available on the official Android store. Its key behaviors include sending SMS messages via accessibility services, downloading and playing MP3 files, setting ringtones, launching and extracting recovery phrases from the Metamask app, and installing and running the NFSkate APK file. It targets the Android platform.

4218.name: Fake 2FA Authentication Page
4218.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may abuse Microsoft Outlook's Home Page feature to obtain persistence on a compromised system. Outlook Home Page is a legacy feature used to customize the presentation of Outlook folders. This feature allows for an internal or external URL to be loaded and presented whenever a folder is opened. A malicious HTML page can be crafted that will execute code when loaded by Outlook Home Page.(Citation: SensePost Outlook Home Page)

Once malicious home pages have been added to the user’s mailbox, they will be loaded when Outlook is started. Malicious Home Pages will execute when the right Outlook folder is loaded/reloaded.(Citation: SensePost Outlook Home Page)
4218.profile: [profile]Fake 2FA Authentication Page is a technique for credential access, likely targeting web platforms. It operates by presenting a fraudulent two-factor authentication page to a user, mimicking a legitimate service's interface to intercept the second authentication factor, such as a one-time code, after the initial credentials have been captured. This method is used by groups like RocketKitten to bypass multi-factor authentication controls.[/profile]
4218.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Fake 2FA Authentication Page is a technique for credential access, likely operating on web platforms. It involves adversaries creating a fraudulent two-factor authentication (2FA) page, often mimicking legitimate services like VPN portals, to intercept user credentials and secondary authentication codes. This method is a specific implementation of GUI Input Capture (T1056.002) or Web Portal Capture (T1056.003), where the fake page is presented to users, typically through phishing or by compromising a legitimate external service login portal.

It involves adversaries creating a fraudulent Google Drive login portal, often delivered via spearphishing links, to harvest user credentials. This method directly captures credentials entered by victims into the spoofed web form, which are then transmitted to the attacker. The stolen credentials are then transmitted to the attacker for unauthorized access.

4221.name: Google Docs
4221.profile: [profile]Google Docs is a cloud storage service that adversaries can abuse for data exfiltration (T1567.002), providing cover by blending into legitimate network traffic. It is also referenced as a component of Google Workspace, which adversaries may target for remote email collection (T1114.002) and to enumerate user accounts via the directory service (T1087.003). The intrusion set RocketKitten is a known user of related techniques.
4221.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Google Docs" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on retrieved context, it is referenced as an example of a cloud storage service. Specifically, it is mentioned within the technique "Exfiltration to Cloud Storage" (T1567.002), where adversaries may use services like Google Docs to exfiltrate data, leveraging the legitimate network traffic of such services for cover. It is also referenced in the context of targeting Google Workspace for email collection (T1114.002) and enumerating user accounts. The technical mechanics involve using the service's APIs or web interfaces for data storage, retrieval, and user directory access, often with stolen credentials.

4234.name: PHP mail scripts
4234.uncertain_mes:
Key Findings
- This research focuses on the ‘Mail-O’ malware used against the FSB and other Russian government organizations, detailed in the May 2021 FSB NKTsKI and Rostelecom-Solar report.
- Early armchair commentary presumed that given the targets, this attack would undoubtedly be the work of a Western government, Five Eyes, or the United States.
- Our analysis disproves that hypothesis.
4234.profile: [profile]The malware is known as Mail-O, also referred to as PHP mail scripts. It has been attributed to the RocketKitten intrusion set. Its key technical behavior involves using PHP-based mailer scripts, such as PHPMailer, for email delivery, potentially leveraging services like SendGrid. The primary targets are Russian government organizations, including the FSB. Infrastructure includes compromised mail servers and web scripts used as command-and-control points, such as hxxp://mail[.]namusoft[.]kr/jsp/user/eam/board[.]jsp.[/profile]
4234.profile_without_enhance: [profile]PHP mail scripts are malware components used for sending malicious emails. They are associated with the PHPMailer library and have been utilized by groups like Kimsuky, Lazarus Group, and Silent Chollima. Key technical behaviors include using scripts like mailer.php and sender.py to send emails, often leveraging services like SendGrid for delivery. The malware targets email communication infrastructure to facilitate broader campaigns, as seen in operations involving second-stage C2 servers hosted on compromised domains.

4236.name: Thamar Reservoir
4236.uncertain_mes:
View Only
Feb 27, 2017 09:11 AM
Recent attacks involving the destructive malware Shamoon (W32.Disttrack.B) were launched by attackers conducting a much wider campaign in the Middle East. While the attackers have compromised multiple targets in the region, only selected targets in Saudi Arabia were infected with Shamoon.
4236.profile: [profile]Thamar Reservoir, also known as Rocket Kitten, Timberworm, Temp.Beanie, and Operation Woolen Goldfish, is an intrusion set believed to be linked to Iranian state interests. It is associated with the destructive Shamoon malware and has shown overlaps with groups like RocketKitten and Charming Kitten. The group's operations have primarily targeted sectors in Saudi Arabia and Israel, with a focus on academic and institutional entities, often employing phishing campaigns for initial access as part of broader regional cyber espionage activities.
4236.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The intrusion set is most likely the Iranian state-sponsored group widely standardized as APT35, also known as Charming Kitten, Phosphorus, Rocket Kitten, and Thamar Reservoir. Its key custom malware includes Woolger (also known as WoolGoldfish), Ghole, Sima, and Firemalv. Primary TTPs involve sophisticated spear-phishing with malicious Office macros and credential harvesting via fake login pages, including two-factor authentication phishing. Believed to be linked to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, the group primarily targets the Middle East, with a strong focus on Israel and Saudi Arabia, as well as government, military, academic, and media sectors in Europe and North America, motivated by geopolitical intelligence collection.[/profile]

4240.name: Master Boot Record (MBR) destruction
4240.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may destroy data and files on specific systems or in large numbers on a network to interrupt availability to systems, services, and network resources. Data destruction is likely to render stored data irrecoverable by forensic techniques through overwriting files or data on local and remote drives.(Citation: Symantec Shamoon 2012)(Citation: FireEye Shamoon Nov 2016)(Citation: Palo Alto Shamoon Nov 2016)(Citation: Kaspersky StoneDrill 2017)(Citation: Unit 42 Shamoon3 2018)(Citation: Talos Olympic Destroyer 2018) Common operating system file deletion commands such as del and rm often only remove pointers to files without wiping the contents of the files themselves, making the files recoverable by proper forensic methodology. This behavior is distinct from [Disk Content Wipe](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1561/001) and [Disk Structure Wipe](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1561/002) because individual files are destroyed rather than sections of a storage disk or the disk's logical structure. Adversaries may attempt to overwrite files and directories with randomly generated data to make it irrecoverable.(Citation: Kaspersky StoneDrill 2017)(Citation: Unit 42 Shamoon3 2018) In some cases politically oriented image files have been used to overwrite data.(Citation: FireEye Shamoon Nov 2016)(Citation: Palo Alto Shamoon Nov 2016)(Citation: Kaspersky StoneDrill 2017) To maximize impact on the target organization in operations where network-wide availability interruption is the goal, malware designed for destroying data may have worm-like features to propagate across a network by leveraging additional techniques like [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078), [OS Credential Dumping](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003), and [SMB/Windows Admin Shares](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002).(Citation: Symantec Shamoon 2012)(Citation: FireEye Shamoon Nov 2016)(Citation: Palo Alto Shamoon Nov 2016)(Citation: Kaspersky StoneDrill 2017)(Citation: Talos Olympic Destroyer 2018). In cloud environments, adversaries may leverage access to delete cloud storage objects, machine images, database instances, and other infrastructure crucial to operations to damage an organization or their customers.(Citation: Data Destruction - Threat Post)(Citation: DOJ - Cisco Insider) Similarly, they may delete virtual machines from on-prem virtualized environments.
4240.profile: [profile]Master Boot Record (MBR) destruction is a specific data destruction technique, mapped to MITRE ATT&CK ID T1487 under the Impact tactic for Windows platforms. It works by overwriting the master boot record or partition table on a hard drive, which contains critical data like the initial boot loader code. This corruption renders the system unable to boot an operating system, making it unavailable. The technique is distinct from general file deletion and is associated with malware like Shamoon, which may use worm-like propagation to maximize disruption across a network.[/profile]
4240.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Master Boot Record (MBR) destruction is a specific technique for Disk Structure Wipe (MITRE ID T1487) under the Impact tactic, primarily targeting Windows systems. The technique works by overwriting or corrupting the master boot record, the first sector of a hard drive containing the boot loader and partition table, which renders the system unable to boot the operating system. This is distinct from file deletion and is often employed by destructive malware like Shamoon to maximize disruption by targeting critical systems.

4241.name: Data erasure
4241.profile: [profile]Data erasure is a technique within the Impact tactic, mapped to MITRE ATT&CK ID T1487. It targets Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. This technique involves adversaries using commands like `del` or `rm` to delete files, but these often only remove file pointers, leaving data recoverable. To ensure irrecoverability, adversaries may overwrite files with random data or specific image files. Malware like Shamoon has employed this technique, sometimes incorporating worm-like features to propagate across a network and maximize destructive impact by leveraging credentials and network shares for wider data destruction.
4241.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Data erasure is a technique where adversaries delete or overwrite files to render data irrecoverable, often using commands like `del` or `rm` that remove file pointers but may leave recoverable data, or by overwriting with random data or specific image files to ensure destruction. It is distinct from disk wiping and can be combined with worm-like propagation using valid accounts and credential dumping for network-wide impact. In cloud environments, this includes deleting storage objects, machine images, and database instances.

4242.name: malicious macros
4242.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may abuse Microsoft Office templates to obtain persistence on a compromised system. Microsoft Office contains templates that are part of common Office applications and are used to customize styles. The base templates within the application are used each time an application starts. (Citation: Microsoft Change Normal Template) Office Visual Basic for Applications (VBA) macros (Citation: MSDN VBA in Office) can be inserted into the base template and used to execute code when the respective Office application starts in order to obtain persistence. Examples for both Word and Excel have been discovered and published. By default, Word has a Normal.dotm template created that can be modified to include a malicious macro. Excel does not have a template file created by default, but one can be added that will automatically be loaded.(Citation: enigma0x3 normal.dotm)(Citation: Hexacorn Office Template Macros) Shared templates may also be stored and pulled from remote locations.(Citation: GlobalDotName Jun 2019) Word Normal.dotm location:
C:\Users\<username>\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Templates\Normal.dotm Excel Personal.xlsb location:
C:\Users\<username>\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Excel\XLSTART\PERSONAL.XLSB Adversaries may also change the location of the base template to point to their own by hijacking the application's search order, e.g. Word 2016 will first look for Normal.dotm under C:\Program Files (x86)\Microsoft Office\root\Office16\, or by modifying the GlobalDotName registry key. By modifying the GlobalDotName registry key an adversary can specify an arbitrary location, file name, and file extension to use for the template that will be loaded on application startup. To abuse GlobalDotName, adversaries may first need to register the template as a trusted document or place it in a trusted location.(Citation: GlobalDotName Jun 2019) An adversary may need to enable macros to execute unrestricted depending on the system or enterprise security policy on use of macros.
4242.profile: [profile]Office Template Macros is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1137.001 under the Persistence tactic for Windows. It involves inserting malicious VBA macros into base Office templates like Word's Normal.dotm or Excel's Personal.xlsb, which execute code when the respective application starts. Persistence can also be achieved by modifying the GlobalDotName registry key to point to a malicious template in a custom location. The MuddyWater group has been associated with this technique.
4242.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Malicious Macros, corresponding to MITRE ATT&CK technique T1204.002 (User Execution: Malicious File), is an Initial Access and Execution tactic primarily targeting the Windows platform. It involves adversaries embedding malicious Visual Basic for Applications (VBA) code within Microsoft Office documents (e.g., .doc, .xls) to gain execution when a user is socially engineered into opening the file and enabling macros. The technique is often delivered via spearphishing attachments and may employ obfuscation methods like VBA Stomping, where the malicious p-code is executed while the source code is replaced with benign data to evade static analysis.

4243.name: PowerShell commands
4243.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may abuse PowerShell commands and scripts for execution. PowerShell is a powerful interactive command-line interface and scripting environment included in the Windows operating system.(Citation: TechNet PowerShell) Adversaries can use PowerShell to perform a number of actions, including discovery of information and execution of code. Examples include the Start-Process cmdlet which can be used to run an executable and the Invoke-Command cmdlet which runs a command locally or on a remote computer (though administrator permissions are required to use PowerShell to connect to remote systems). PowerShell may also be used to download and run executables from the Internet, which can be executed from disk or in memory without touching disk. A number of PowerShell-based offensive testing tools are available, including [Empire](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0363), [PowerSploit](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0194), [PoshC2](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0378), and PSAttack.(Citation: Github PSAttack) PowerShell commands/scripts can also be executed without directly invoking the powershell.exe binary through interfaces to PowerShell's underlying System.Management.Automation assembly DLL exposed through the .NET framework and Windows Common Language Interface (CLI).(Citation: Sixdub PowerPick Jan 2016)(Citation: SilentBreak Offensive PS Dec 2015)(Citation: Microsoft PSfromCsharp APR 2014)
4243.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1059.001, named "Command and Scripting Interpreter: PowerShell", under the Execution tactic for the Windows platform. It involves adversaries abusing PowerShell's command-line interface and scripting environment to execute malicious actions, such as running code via cmdlets like Start-Process and Invoke-Command, downloading and executing payloads from the internet (potentially in-memory), and leveraging offensive frameworks like Empire and PowerSploit. Execution can also occur without invoking powershell.exe directly by using the underlying System.Management.Automation assembly through the .NET framework.[/profile]
4243.profile_without_enhance: [profile]PowerShell commands, identified as T1059.001 within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, fall under the Execution tactic and target the Windows platform. This technique involves adversaries abusing the PowerShell environment to execute malicious commands and scripts, enabling actions like code execution, information discovery, and fileless attacks. Specific cmdlets such as `Start-Process` and `Invoke-Command` are commonly used, and execution can occur without invoking `powershell.exe` directly by leveraging the underlying `System.Management.Automation` assembly. It is widely associated with numerous threat groups and offensive tools like Empire and PowerSploit.

4255.name: Malicious macro activation
4255.uncertain_mes:
An adversary may rely upon a user opening a malicious file in order to gain execution. Users may be subjected to social engineering to get them to open a file that will lead to code execution. This user action will typically be observed as follow-on behavior from [Spearphishing Attachment](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001). Adversaries may use several types of files that require a user to execute them, including .doc, .pdf, .xls, .rtf, .scr, .exe, .lnk, .pif, .cpl, .reg, and .iso.(Citation: Mandiant Trojanized Windows 10)

Adversaries may employ various forms of [Masquerading](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1036) and [Obfuscated Files or Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027) to increase the likelihood that a user will open and successfully execute a malicious file. These methods may include using a familiar naming convention and/or password protecting the file and supplying instructions to a user on how to open it.(Citation: Password Protected Word Docs) 

While [Malicious File](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002) frequently occurs shortly after Initial Access it may occur at other phases of an intrusion, such as when an adversary places a file in a shared directory or on a user's desktop hoping that a user will click on it. This activity may also be seen shortly after [Internal Spearphishing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1534).
4255.profile: [profile]Malicious File, designated as T1204.002 within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, is an execution technique under the Initial Access tactic primarily targeting Windows platforms. It involves an adversary relying on a user to manually open a malicious file to execute code, often delivered via spearphishing attachments. The technique leverages social engineering and employs file types like .doc, .pdf, .xls, .exe, .lnk, and .iso, frequently using masquerading tactics such as familiar naming conventions or password protection with instructions to increase success rates. It is associated with numerous threat groups including RocketKitten, APT28, and Lazarus Group.
4255.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Malicious macro activation is a technique where adversaries embed and execute malicious Visual Basic for Applications (VBA) code within Microsoft Office documents (like .doc, .xls) to gain execution. This often follows spearphishing and requires user interaction to enable macros, bypassing security restrictions. The malicious code can then download or execute payloads, establish persistence, or perform other malicious actions.

4258.name: PowerShell macros
4258.uncertain_mes: powershell_web_backdoor This is a very simple powershell web backdoor Usage: hxxp://127.0.0.1:9999/backdoor/?cmd=<Insert Your powershell compatible base64 encoded command here
4258.profile: [profile]PowerShell macros, also known as powershell_web_backdoor, is a simple web backdoor that executes base64-encoded PowerShell commands via an HTTP GET request to a specified URL parameter (e.g., hxxp://127.0.0.1:9999/backdoor/?cmd=). It is associated with the RocketKitten intrusion set. Its key behavior involves leveraging PowerShell for command execution, often delivered or enabled through document macros, as referenced in campaigns like Emotet. The malware targets Windows platforms and operates as a web-based backdoor for remote control.[/profile]
4258.profile_without_enhance: [profile]PowerShell macros is a technique, not a distinct malware family, used by malware like Emotet to execute a base64-encoded PowerShell script for persistence via document macros. It is associated with groups such as Gold Cabin, Mummy Spider, and Mealybug. Key technical behaviors include using the PowerShell command-line switch "-nop" and "-enc" to run encoded scripts. The primary target platform is Windows, exploiting Microsoft Office environments where macros are enabled. This technique is a common initial infection vector for delivering further payloads.

4260.name: Shamoon-related files
4260.uncertain_mes: [Shamoon](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0140) is wiper malware that was first used by an Iranian group known as the "Cutting Sword of Justice" in 2012. Other versions known as Shamoon 2 and Shamoon 3 were observed in 2016 and 2018. [Shamoon](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0140) has also been seen leveraging [RawDisk](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0364) and Filerase to carry out data wiping tasks. Analysis has linked [Shamoon](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0140) with [Kwampirs](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0236) based on multiple shared artifacts and coding patterns.(Citation: Cylera Kwampirs 2022) The term Shamoon is sometimes used to refer to the group using the malware as well as the malware itself.(Citation: Palo Alto Shamoon Nov 2016)(Citation: Unit 42 Shamoon3 2018)(Citation: Symantec Shamoon 2012)(Citation: FireEye Shamoon Nov 2016)
4260.profile: [profile]Shamoon is a wiper malware, also known as Shamoon 2 and Shamoon 3, first used in 2012. It is attributed to the Iranian group "Cutting Sword of Justice" and has been linked to RocketKitten. Its key TTPs include leveraging RawDisk and Filerase for destructive data wiping tasks, and it shares artifacts and coding patterns with Kwampirs. It primarily targets Windows platforms for destructive attacks against hard disk data.
4260.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Shamoon-related files are associated with the Shamoon malware family, also known as DistTrack, a wiper first used in 2012 by the Iranian group "Cutting Sword of Justice" and later linked to intrusion sets like OilRig and Timberworm. Key technical behaviors include leveraging RawDisk and Filerase for data wiping tasks and sharing artifacts and coding patterns with related malware like Kwampirs, Stonedrill, and ZeroCleare. It primarily targets Windows platforms and has been associated with campaigns and versions such as Shamoon 2 and Shamoon 3.[/profile]

4263.name: VirtualAlloc
4263.profile: [profile]VirtualAlloc is a core Windows API function (not a MITRE ATT&CK technique ID) used for Process Injection (T1055) on the Windows platform. It operates by allocating memory within a target process, often with permissions like PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE, enabling adversaries to write and then execute malicious code in that process's address space. This technique is fundamental to many injection sub-techniques and is associated with groups like RocketKitten.
4263.profile_without_enhance: [profile]VirtualAlloc is a Windows API function used for memory allocation, falling under the Defense Evasion tactic. It operates on the Windows platform, enabling adversaries to allocate memory within a process's virtual address space. This function is a core mechanism for various process injection techniques, such as VDSO hijacking and Extra Window Memory injection, where it is used to allocate regions for malicious code before execution is redirected. Its use helps avoid detection by bypassing common API monitoring for functions like WriteProcessMemory.

4264.name: Memset
4264.profile: [profile]Memset is a technique used by adversaries to fill memory with data, often to obscure malicious code or operations. The intrusion-set RocketKitten has been associated with this technique. It functions by allocating and writing data to memory regions, which can hinder analysis and detection by making malicious payloads less conspicuous or by corrupting memory to disrupt system functionality. This method is related to broader obfuscation and impact tactics within the MITRE ATT&CK framework.
4264.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity 'Memset' is not a standard technique in the MITRE ATT&CK framework. Based on the provided context, it appears to be a specific implementation or variant of data obfuscation. The retrieved information describes the technique of adding junk or meaningless data to protocols or code to hinder detection and analysis, making traffic decoding and static analysis more difficult. This aligns with the general concept of data obfuscation for command and control or malware functionality.

4265.name: CreateThread
4265.profile: [profile]CreateThread is a technique used for process injection and execution, often associated with the RocketKitten intrusion-set. It involves creating a new thread within a legitimate process to run malicious code, enabling adversaries to evade detection by operating under the guise of a trusted process. This method is commonly used to execute payloads, maintain persistence, and perform privilege escalation by leveraging the host process's memory space and permissions.
4265.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "CreateThread" is a core Windows API function, not a distinct MITRE ATT&CK technique. It is a fundamental system call used to create a new thread of execution within a process. This function is ubiquitously leveraged by adversaries across various techniques, such as Process Injection (T1055) and Thread Execution Hijacking (T1055.003), to run malicious code within the context of a legitimate process. Its primary technical mechanics involve allocating memory in a target process, writing shellcode, and then using CreateThread to execute that code in the new thread, enabling stealth and persistence.

4266.name: DWORD XOR
4266.profile: [profile]DWORD XOR is a custom cryptographic technique used by adversaries to obfuscate data, such as for command and control traffic (T1024) or for archiving collected data prior to exfiltration (T1560.003). It functions by applying a simple XOR operation with a fixed key, producing a weak ciphertext that can be reversed through analysis. This method has been employed by groups including RocketKitten, Lazarus Group, and UNC3886 to hinder detection and analysis.
4266.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "DWORD XOR" is a custom cryptographic technique used for data obfuscation. It functions as a simple encryption method where data is XORed with a fixed key, producing a weak ciphertext. This technique is employed to hide data, such as during archival prior to exfiltration (T1560.003) or to obfuscate command and control traffic (T1024), making analysis more difficult. It is associated with threat groups including Lazarus Group and APT28.

4267.name: invoke-expression (iex)
4267.profile: [profile]The entity "Invoke-Expression (IEX)" is a PowerShell cmdlet used for code execution, aligning with MITRE ATT&CK technique T1059.001 (Command and Scripting Interpreter: PowerShell) under the Execution tactic on Windows. It works by taking a string input and executing it as a PowerShell command, enabling adversaries to run scripts directly in memory. This method is commonly used to download and execute remote payloads, such as with the command `IEX(New-Object Net.WebClient).downloadString()`, facilitating tool transfer and in-memory execution without writing to disk. The intrusion-set RocketKitten has been associated with its use.[/profile]
4267.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Invoke-Expression (IEX) is a PowerShell cmdlet used for execution, corresponding to MITRE ATT&CK technique T1059.001 (Command and Scripting Interpreter: PowerShell) under the Execution tactic on Windows. It directly executes PowerShell commands or scripts provided as strings, enabling adversaries to run code in memory without writing to disk, often used to download and execute payloads from remote sources via commands like `IEX(New-Object Net.WebClient).downloadString()`. This technique is commonly leveraged by threat actors for lateral tool transfer and remote code execution.

4268.name: UrldownloadtofileA
4268.profile: [profile]UrldownloadtofileA is a technique for downloading files to a specified location on disk, typically used during initial access or execution. It is commonly implemented via the `UrlDownloadToFileA` function in Windows APIs or through PowerShell commands like `Invoke-WebRequest`. This method allows adversaries to retrieve and save additional payloads, such as malware, directly from a remote server to the victim's system, facilitating further stages of an attack. The RocketKitten intrusion-set has been associated with this behavior.
4268.profile_without_enhance: [profile]UrldownloadtofileA is a technique for downloading files from the internet to a local system, commonly used for malware delivery. It operates within the Execution tactic on Windows platforms. The technique typically functions by using the `URLDownloadToFile` Windows API function, which allows a process to retrieve a file from a specified URL and save it to a designated location on disk. This behavior is often observed in malicious scripts or payloads to stage tools or additional malware components.
