4270.name: data deletion
4270.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may delete files left behind by the actions of their intrusion activity. Malware, tools, or other non-native files dropped or created on a system by an adversary (ex: [Ingress Tool Transfer](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1105)) may leave traces to indicate to what was done within a network and how. Removal of these files can occur during an intrusion, or as part of a post-intrusion process to minimize the adversary's footprint. There are tools available from the host operating system to perform cleanup, but adversaries may use other tools as well.(Citation: Microsoft SDelete July 2016) Examples of built-in [Command and Scripting Interpreter](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059) functions include del on Windows, rm or unlink on Linux and macOS, and `rm` on ESXi.
4270.profile: [profile]The technique is MITRE ATT&CK File Deletion (T1070.004), a Defense Evasion tactic used on Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. It involves adversaries removing traces of their activity by deleting non-native files, tools, or malware left on a system. This is commonly performed using built-in command interpreters like `del` on Windows or `rm` and `unlink` on Unix-based systems, as well as tools like Windows Sysinternals SDelete. The technique is associated with numerous threat groups, including APT29, Lazarus Group, and Wizard Spider, and is exemplified by malware like Shamoon, which uses such deletion for data destruction.[/profile]
4270.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Data Deletion, mapped to MITRE ATT&CK technique T1485, falls under the Impact tactic and targets Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. This technique involves adversaries destroying data to render it irrecoverable, often by overwriting files with random data or specific images, going beyond simple file pointer removal. It can be executed using native OS commands like `del` or `rm`, secure deletion tools like SDelete, or by manipulating cloud storage lifecycle policies to trigger bulk object destruction. This action is frequently associated with ransomware and destructive attacks by groups like APT38 and Sandworm Team.

4271.name: network protection
4271.profile: [profile]Network Protection is a defensive security concept, not a MITRE ATT&CK attack pattern. It encompasses strategies and tools like firewalls, intrusion detection/prevention systems (IDS/IPS), and segmentation to monitor, control, and secure network traffic against unauthorized access and malicious activities. The intrusion set RocketKitten is noted as a neighbor entity, indicating it may be an actor that defenders aim to protect networks against using these measures.[/profile]
4271.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "network protection" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the retrieved information, it is a broad defensive concept, not an adversarial attack pattern. The provided similar entities describe various attack techniques targeting or leveraging networks, such as compromising network devices (T1584.008), sniffing traffic (T1040), discovering network topology (T1590.004), and conducting denial-of-service floods (T1498.001). These techniques fall under tactics like Initial Access, Credential Access, Discovery, and Impact. The content-related entities describe exfiltration methods (T1567, T1567.001) and a deprecated command and control technique (T1026), which are not directly defining for "network protection."

4272.name: network security
4272.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may gather information about the victim's network security appliances that can be used during targeting. Information about network security appliances may include a variety of details, such as the existence and specifics of deployed firewalls, content filters, and proxies/bastion hosts. Adversaries may also target information about victim network-based intrusion detection systems (NIDS) or other appliances related to defensive cybersecurity operations.

Adversaries may gather this information in various ways, such as direct collection actions via [Active Scanning](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1595) or [Phishing for Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1598).(Citation: Nmap Firewalls NIDS) Information about network security appliances may also be exposed to adversaries via online or other accessible data sets (ex: [Search Victim-Owned Websites](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1594)). Gathering this information may reveal opportunities for other forms of reconnaissance (ex: [Search Open Technical Databases](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1596) or [Search Open Websites/Domains](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1593)), establishing operational resources (ex: [Develop Capabilities](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1587) or [Obtain Capabilities](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1588)), and/or initial access (ex: [External Remote Services](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1133)).
4272.profile: [profile]Network Security Appliances, identified as T1590.006 under the Reconnaissance tactic, involves adversaries gathering intelligence on a victim's defensive infrastructure. This includes identifying specific details of deployed firewalls, proxies, content filters, and network intrusion detection systems (NIDS). Information is collected via methods like Active Scanning, Phishing for Information, or by searching victim-owned websites and open datasets to inform subsequent attack stages. The group Volt Typhoon has been associated with this technique.[/profile]
4272.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "network security" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the retrieved information, the closest related technique is "Gather Victim Network Information: Network Security Appliances" (T1590.006). This reconnaissance technique involves adversaries collecting details about a victim's defensive infrastructure, such as firewalls, intrusion detection systems (NIDS), content filters, and proxy hosts. Information gathering methods include active scanning, phishing for information, and searching victim-owned websites. This intelligence can enable follow-on actions like further reconnaissance, capability development, or initial access.

4273.name: Full Version of Shamoon
4273.uncertain_mes: [Shamoon](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0140) is wiper malware that was first used by an Iranian group known as the "Cutting Sword of Justice" in 2012. Other versions known as Shamoon 2 and Shamoon 3 were observed in 2016 and 2018. [Shamoon](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0140) has also been seen leveraging [RawDisk](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0364) and Filerase to carry out data wiping tasks. Analysis has linked [Shamoon](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0140) with [Kwampirs](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0236) based on multiple shared artifacts and coding patterns.(Citation: Cylera Kwampirs 2022) The term Shamoon is sometimes used to refer to the group using the malware as well as the malware itself.(Citation: Palo Alto Shamoon Nov 2016)(Citation: Unit 42 Shamoon3 2018)(Citation: Symantec Shamoon 2012)(Citation: FireEye Shamoon Nov 2016)
4273.profile: [profile]Shamoon, also known as the Full Version of Shamoon, Shamoon 2, and Shamoon 3, is a wiper malware first used in 2012 by the Iranian group "Cutting Sword of Justice." Its key technical behaviors include leveraging RawDisk and Filerase drivers to perform destructive data wiping tasks. Analysis has linked it to Kwampirs malware through shared artifacts and coding patterns. It primarily targets platforms in the Middle East, with campaigns facilitated by groups like Timberworm. The term Shamoon can refer to both the malware and the group using it.
4273.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The malware is known as the Full Version of Shamoon, an alias for Shamoon. It is a wiper malware attributed to the Iranian group "Cutting Sword of Justice" and linked to Timberworm. Key technical behaviors include leveraging RawDisk and Filerase for data wiping tasks and sharing artifacts and coding patterns with Kwampirs. It primarily targets systems in the Middle East and has been used in destructive attack campaigns, with observed versions including Shamoon 2 and Shamoon 3.

4274.name: PaExec
4274.profile: [profile]PaExec is a redistributable version of the legitimate Sysinternals tool PsExec used for lateral movement, often renamed by attackers to connect to remote servers and execute commands or additional tools. It is attributed to the RocketKitten intrusion set and is commonly leveraged by a wide range of threat actors including APT29, APT32, APT41, FIN6, FIN7, Mustang Panda, and others. Its key behavior is remote service creation and execution (T1570), primarily targeting Windows platforms.
4274.profile_without_enhance: [profile]PaExec is a redistributable version of the legitimate Sysinternals PsExec tool, used for lateral movement by executing commands on remote systems. It has been employed by numerous threat groups including APT29, APT32, APT41, FIN6, FIN7, Mustang Panda, and Winnti. Its key behavior is creating and starting a service remotely to facilitate lateral transfer, commonly observed in cyberattacks targeting Windows platforms.

4275.name: Malicious Macro
4275.uncertain_mes:
An adversary may rely upon a user opening a malicious file in order to gain execution. Users may be subjected to social engineering to get them to open a file that will lead to code execution. This user action will typically be observed as follow-on behavior from [Spearphishing Attachment](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001). Adversaries may use several types of files that require a user to execute them, including .doc, .pdf, .xls, .rtf, .scr, .exe, .lnk, .pif, .cpl, .reg, and .iso.(Citation: Mandiant Trojanized Windows 10)

Adversaries may employ various forms of [Masquerading](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1036) and [Obfuscated Files or Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027) to increase the likelihood that a user will open and successfully execute a malicious file. These methods may include using a familiar naming convention and/or password protecting the file and supplying instructions to a user on how to open it.(Citation: Password Protected Word Docs) 

While [Malicious File](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002) frequently occurs shortly after Initial Access it may occur at other phases of an intrusion, such as when an adversary places a file in a shared directory or on a user's desktop hoping that a user will click on it. This activity may also be seen shortly after [Internal Spearphishing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1534).
4275.profile: [profile]Malicious File, designated as T1204.002 under the Execution tactic, primarily targets Windows platforms. This technique relies on user interaction to open a malicious file, such as .doc, .pdf, .xls, .exe, .lnk, or .iso, often delivered via spearphishing. Adversaries employ masquerading and obfuscation, like using familiar file names or password protection with instructions, to increase success. The malicious file may be placed in shared directories or on desktops to trigger execution, commonly associated with groups like OilRig and RocketKitten.
4275.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Malicious Macro is a technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, specifically ID T1204.002 under the Initial Access tactic, primarily targeting the Windows platform. It involves adversaries embedding malicious Visual Basic for Applications (VBA) code within Microsoft Office documents (e.g., .doc, .xls) to gain execution when a user enables macros. This often follows spearphishing and employs masquerading and obfuscation to evade detection, leveraging the trusted nature of Office files to bypass security controls and execute payloads.

4276.name: Office Macros
4276.profile: [profile]Office Macros is a technique used for initial access and execution, notably by the RocketKitten intrusion set. It involves embedding malicious code within Microsoft Office documents, such as Excel, to deliver payloads when macros are enabled. The technique has been widely used, with security recommendations advising organizations to block macros from the internet by default to mitigate this threat.
4276.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Office Macros is a technique or malware delivery vector, not a specific malware family, often used to deliver malicious payloads via Microsoft Office documents. It is associated with groups like Lazarus Group. Key technical behaviors include exploiting Microsoft Office's macro functionality to execute malicious code, typically delivered via email attachments or downloaded documents, targeting Windows platforms primarily. Infrastructure and supplementary information highlight that Microsoft has changed default settings to block macros from the internet, with security recommendations to enforce policies controlling macro behavior in office files.

4277.name: NetScan
4277.profile: [profile]NetScan is a network scanning utility. It is associated with the intrusion set RocketKitten. Key technical behaviors include the ability to change its default language to Russian upon installation, as indicated by output containing Cyrillic characters. It is referenced in the context of other tools like Trigona and Mimikatz, which are linked to various APT groups, but NetScan itself is directly attributed to RocketKitten. Its primary function is network reconnaissance.
4277.profile_without_enhance: [profile]NetScan is a network scanning utility. It has been used by threat groups including APT10, APT32, Anunak, and Gallium. A notable technical behavior is its configurable default language, which can be set to Russian upon installation, with observed output containing Cyrillic characters. This tool is associated with broader campaigns like InvisibleFerret and has been recovered in contexts alongside tools like Mimikatz and the ransomware Trigona.

4278.name: Samdump
4278.profile: [profile]Samdump is a post-exploitation tool, specifically the CQHashDumpv2 component of the CQTools penetration testing toolkit, used to dump password hashes in pwdump format. It is executed via the command-line argument `--samdump`, often by other malware like Shadowpad. It is attributed to the intrusion set RocketKitten and has been used by various APT groups, including APT22, APT26, APT31, APT41, Aurora Panda, Calypso Group, Dragonok, Emissary Panda, Hellsing, Hurricane Panda, Leviathan, Mirage, Mustang Panda, Nettraveler, Nightshade Panda, Slime29, Samurai Panda, Stone Panda, UPS, Violin Panda, and Wizard Spider.
4278.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Samdump is a post-exploitation tool, specifically the CQHashDumpv2 component of the CQTools penetration testing toolkit. It is used to dump password hashes in pwdump format. The tool has been leveraged by malware families like Shadowpad and PlugX, which are associated with various APT groups including APT22, APT26, APT31, APT41, Aurora Panda, Calypso Group, Dragonok, Emissary Panda, Hellsing, Hurricane Panda, Leviathan, Mirage, Mustang Panda, Nettraveler, Nightshade Panda, Slime29, Samurai Panda, Stone Panda, UPS, and Violin Panda. Its key technical behavior involves executing with the `--samdump` argument to extract system credentials.

4279.name: Rar
4279.profile: [profile]Rar is a malware family associated with the RocketKitten intrusion set. It is referenced in operations by APT32 (OceanLotus) where a RAR archive was used to deliver the Kerrdown downloader. The StrongPity APT group (also known as Promethium) has used compromised domains to host malicious RAR installers for software like WinRAR. The ISFB banking trojan (Ursnif) campaign by the Gold Cabin group also used RAR archives to distribute modules. Key behaviors include using RAR archives as a delivery mechanism for various malware payloads, targeting Windows systems, and leveraging compromised infrastructure for hosting.
4279.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Rar is a malware family associated with the APT32 group, as indicated by its use in the Kerrdown campaign where it was delivered via a RAR archive. It is also linked to the Gold Cabin group through Ursnif modules distributed in files like cook32.rar and stilak32.rar. The StrongPity group (also known as Promethium) has used Rar in operations, distributing trojanized WinRAR installers from domains like ralrab[.]com. Its key behaviors include being delivered in compressed archive formats to deploy other malware payloads, targeting Windows platforms primarily through executable installers and archived modules.

4280.name: Living off the Land
4280.profile: [profile]Living off the Land is a strategic approach, not a single MITRE ATT&CK technique, where adversaries abuse legitimate system tools and processes to evade detection. This technique is associated with the intrusion-set RocketKitten. It involves executing malicious actions through trusted binaries like SyncAppvPublishingServer.vbs to proxy PowerShell commands or using legitimate remote desktop software for command and control, thereby blending in with normal administrative activity.[/profile]
4280.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Living off the Land is a strategic approach, not a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique with a T-ID. It describes adversaries using legitimate, pre-installed system tools and software (like PowerShell, wscript.exe, or remote desktop applications such as VNC or TeamViewer) to perform malicious activities. This methodology enables execution, persistence, and lateral movement while evading detection by blending in with normal administrative traffic and bypassing application allowlists. It is commonly employed across various platforms by numerous threat groups to obscure their operations within a target environment.

4281.name: Coordinated Takedown Events
4281.profile: [profile]Coordinated Takedown Events is a technique where adversaries compromise multiple third-party systems to form or acquire a botnet, a network of systems instructed to perform coordinated tasks. This can be achieved by building a botnet through compromise, taking over an existing botnet, or leasing one from a service. With control of a botnet, adversaries can conduct large-scale follow-on activities such as Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attacks or phishing campaigns, as seen with groups like RocketKitten.[/profile]
4281.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Coordinated Takedown Events is a technique where adversaries compromise or acquire numerous third-party systems to form a botnet, a network that can be instructed to perform coordinated, large-scale tasks. This botnet can be built from scratch by compromising systems, taken over from existing networks, or leased from booter/stresser services, often utilizing end-of-life devices. The botnet is then used to conduct follow-on activities such as large-scale phishing campaigns or Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attacks.

4285.name: Reverse RDP over SSH
4285.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may hijack a legitimate user’s remote desktop session to move laterally within an environment. Remote desktop is a common feature in operating systems. It allows a user to log into an interactive session with a system desktop graphical user interface on a remote system. Microsoft refers to its implementation of the Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) as Remote Desktop Services (RDS).(Citation: TechNet Remote Desktop Services)

Adversaries may perform RDP session hijacking which involves stealing a legitimate user's remote session. Typically, a user is notified when someone else is trying to steal their session. With System permissions and using Terminal Services Console, `c:\windows\system32\tscon.exe [session number to be stolen]`, an adversary can hijack a session without the need for credentials or prompts to the user.(Citation: RDP Hijacking Korznikov) This can be done remotely or locally and with active or disconnected sessions.(Citation: RDP Hijacking Medium) It can also lead to [Remote System Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1018) and Privilege Escalation by stealing a Domain Admin or higher privileged account session. All of this can be done by using native Windows commands, but it has also been added as a feature in red teaming tools.(Citation: Kali Redsnarf)
4285.profile: [profile]Reverse RDP over SSH is a technique aligned with MITRE ATT&CK T1563.002 (Remote Service Session Hijacking: RDP Hijacking) under the Lateral Movement tactic, primarily targeting Windows platforms. It involves hijacking an existing Remote Desktop Protocol session, often using the native Windows tool tscon.exe with system permissions to steal a session without credentials or user prompts. This technique can be performed remotely or locally on active or disconnected sessions, potentially enabling privilege escalation by hijacking high-privilege accounts. The method is distinct from standard RDP use as it exploits established sessions rather than creating new ones.
4285.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Reverse RDP over SSH is a technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, categorized under Tactic TA0011 (Lateral Movement) and Technique T1572 (Protocol Tunneling). It operates by encapsulating Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) traffic within an encrypted Secure Shell (SSH) tunnel. This method is used to bypass network security controls that might filter or block standard RDP ports, enabling covert remote access and lateral movement across systems by forwarding the RDP session through the established SSH connection.

Affiliations

4287.name: Destructive Wiper Attacks
4287.profile: [profile]Destructive Wiper Attacks is a class of attack patterns focused on rendering systems inoperable. It aligns with the MITRE ATT&CK technique Disk Wipe (T1561) under the Impact tactic, primarily targeting Windows platforms. The core technical mechanic involves overwriting arbitrary portions of disk content or critical structures like the master boot record (MBR) with random data, often using direct disk access via tools like the RawDisk driver. To maximize disruption, these attacks may propagate across networks using worm-like features, leveraging techniques such as Valid Accounts and OS Credential Dumping, and have been associated with groups like Lazarus and Gamaredon.
4287.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Destructive Wiper Attacks is a technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, aligning with the sub-technique Disk Content Wipe (T1561.001) under the Impact tactic, primarily targeting Windows platforms. It involves adversaries overwriting arbitrary portions of a storage device's raw disk content with random data to render data irrecoverable, often using direct hardware access or third-party drivers like RawDisk. To maximize disruption, associated malware may propagate across networks using worm-like features and techniques such as Valid Accounts and OS Credential Dumping.

4288.name: Network Reconnaissance
4288.profile: [profile]Network Reconnaissance is a technique within the Reconnaissance tactic, applicable across multiple platforms, where adversaries gather information about a target's network infrastructure. This includes identifying network topology, devices, security appliances, and shared resources through methods like active scanning, network sniffing, and querying network shares to inform subsequent attack stages. The intrusion-set Greenbug is linked to this activity.
4288.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Network Reconnaissance is a technique within the Reconnaissance tactic, applicable across multiple platforms, where adversaries gather information about a target's network infrastructure. This involves probing for details such as network topology, device configurations, and security appliances through methods like active scanning or analyzing accessible data sets. The collected intelligence, including IP addresses, hostnames, and service versions, is used to identify vulnerabilities and plan subsequent attack stages like initial access or lateral movement.

4289.name: Persistent Remote Access
4289.uncertain_mes:
An adversary may use legitimate remote access tools to establish an interactive command and control channel within a network. Remote access tools create a session between two trusted hosts through a graphical interface, a command line interaction, a protocol tunnel via development or management software, or hardware-level access such as KVM (Keyboard, Video, Mouse) over IP solutions. Desktop support software (usually graphical interface) and remote management software (typically command line interface) allow a user to control a computer remotely as if they are a local user inheriting the user or software permissions. This software is commonly used for troubleshooting, software installation, and system management.(Citation: Symantec Living off the Land)(Citation: CrowdStrike 2015 Global Threat Report)(Citation: CrySyS Blog TeamSpy) Adversaries may similarly abuse response features included in EDR and other defensive tools that enable remote access.

Remote access tools may be installed and used post-compromise as an alternate communications channel for redundant access or to establish an interactive remote desktop session with the target system. It may also be used as a malware component to establish a reverse connection or back-connect to a service or adversary-controlled system.

Installation of many remote access tools may also include persistence (e.g., the software's installation routine creates a [Windows Service](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1543/003)). Remote access modules/features may also exist as part of otherwise existing software (e.g., Google Chrome’s Remote Desktop).(Citation: Google Chrome Remote Desktop)(Citation: Chrome Remote Desktop)
4289.profile: [profile]The entity is a technique known as Remote Access Tools, with the MITRE ATT&CK ID T1219 under the Command and Control tactic, applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves adversaries using legitimate software like desktop support or remote management tools to establish an interactive command and control channel, creating a session through graphical or command-line interfaces, protocol tunnels, or hardware-level KVM over IP. This allows remote control as a local user, often installed post-compromise for redundant access or as a malware component for reverse connections, with installation routines potentially creating persistence mechanisms like Windows Services. It is associated with groups including Carbanak, MuddyWater, and FIN7.[/profile]
4289.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Persistent Remote Access is a technique for maintaining long-term, interactive control over a compromised system, often as part of the Persistence tactic. It is achieved by establishing redundant channels such as legitimate remote access tools (RDP, VNC, SSH), external remote services (VPNs, Citrix), or by creating new accounts. Adversaries deploy these mechanisms to ensure continuous access even if primary methods are detected, using tools that may include built-in persistence features like Windows Services or hardware-based solutions like KVM over IP devices.

4291.name: Vishing
4291.profile: [profile]Vishing, also known as Spearphishing Voice, corresponds to MITRE ATT&CK techniques T1566.004 and T1598.004 under the Initial Access and Collection tactics, primarily targeting users. This technique involves adversaries using phone calls or voice communications to manipulate victims into divulging sensitive credentials or information, or into performing actions like downloading malware or accepting multi-factor authentication prompts, often by spoofing caller ID and impersonating a trusted entity. It has been employed by groups such as Scattered Spider, LAPSUS$, and Storm-1811.
4291.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Vishing, also known as Spearphishing Voice, is a social engineering technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, identified as T1566.004 (Initial Access) and T1598.004 (Reconnaissance). It operates across multiple platforms, primarily targeting human interaction via phone calls. The technique involves adversaries, often impersonating trusted entities like technical support or business partners, using voice communications to trick victims into divulging sensitive credentials, accepting multi-factor authentication prompts, or performing actions like downloading malware or visiting malicious URLs. This can be executed manually, through call centers, or via automated robocalls, with phone number spoofing commonly used to enhance the deception. Groups such as Scattered Spider, LAPSUS$, and Storm-1811 have employed this method, and recent trends indicate the use of AI-generated audio to make vishing campaigns more convincing and scalable.

4292.name: Keylogger
4292.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may log user keystrokes to intercept credentials as the user types them. Keylogging is likely to be used to acquire credentials for new access opportunities when [OS Credential Dumping](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003) efforts are not effective, and may require an adversary to intercept keystrokes on a system for a substantial period of time before credentials can be successfully captured. In order to increase the likelihood of capturing credentials quickly, an adversary may also perform actions such as clearing browser cookies to force users to reauthenticate to systems.(Citation: Talos Kimsuky Nov 2021)

Keylogging is the most prevalent type of input capture, with many different ways of intercepting keystrokes.(Citation: Adventures of a Keystroke) Some methods include:

* Hooking API callbacks used for processing keystrokes. Unlike [Credential API Hooking](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1056/004), this focuses solely on API functions intended for processing keystroke data.
* Reading raw keystroke data from the hardware buffer.
* Windows Registry modifications.
* Custom drivers.
* [Modify System Image](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1601) may provide adversaries with hooks into the operating system of network devices to read raw keystrokes for login sessions.(Citation: Cisco Blog Legacy Device Attacks)
4292.profile: [profile]Keylogger is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1056.001 under the Credential Access tactic, primarily for Windows. It captures keystrokes to intercept credentials, often when credential dumping fails, and may involve clearing browser cookies to force re-authentication. Specific technical methods include hooking keystroke-processing API callbacks, reading raw data from the hardware buffer, modifying the Windows Registry, deploying custom drivers, or altering system images on network devices. It is associated with groups like APT28 and Lazarus and linked to malware such as Cwoolger Keylogger.
4292.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Keylogger is identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1056.001 (Input Capture: Keylogging) within the Credential Access tactic, primarily targeting Windows platforms. It works by intercepting user keystrokes to capture credentials, often employing methods like hooking API callbacks for keystroke processing, reading raw data from the hardware buffer, or making Windows Registry modifications. This technique is commonly used when credential dumping fails and may involve clearing browser cookies to force re-authentication. It is also leveraged to bypass multi-factor authentication by capturing passwords for hardware tokens like smart cards. Numerous threat groups, including APT28, Lazarus Group, and Kimsuky, utilize keyloggers.

4293.name: Download File
4293.profile: [profile]Download File is a technique (T1105) within the Command and Control tactic, applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS. It involves transferring tools or other files into a compromised environment from an external adversary-controlled system. Common utilities for this include `certutil`, PowerShell commands like `IEX(New-Object Net.WebClient).downloadString()`, `curl`, `wget`, `scp`, and `ftp`. Adversaries may also abuse installers like `winget` or cloud sync services such as Dropbox. This technique is used by groups like RocketKitten and is associated with malware such as Cwoolger Keylogger.[/profile]

It involves transferring tools or files into a compromised environment from an external system using command and control channels or utilities like `certutil`, PowerShell's `Invoke-WebRequest`, `curl`, `wget`, or `scp`. Adversaries may also abuse installers like `winget` or cloud sync services such as Dropbox to facilitate the file transfer, often verifying file integrity with checks like `certutil -hashfile`.

4294.name: TTPs
4294.profile: [profile]The entity "TTPs" is a generic term for Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures used in cyber attacks. It is directly associated with the intrusion set RocketKitten. Specific techniques related to TTPs include multilayer encryption (T1079) for command and control, where adversaries tunnel custom encryption within protocols like HTTPS, and environmental keying (T1480.001), a form of execution guardrail used by groups like APT41 and Equation to cryptographically constrain malware execution to specific target environments, making analysis and detection difficult.

For example, Environmental Keying (T1480.001) is an Execution Guardrail technique where malware uses cryptography to derive decryption keys from target-specific environmental values (like network shares, system time, or IP addresses) to constrain execution to intended victims and evade analysis. Similarly, Multilayer Encryption (T1079) involves tunneling custom encryption within protocols like HTTPS for C2, and Searching Private Threat Intel Vendor Data (T1597.001) is a reconnaissance technique. 4295.name: IP Theft
4295.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may steal monetary resources from targets through extortion, social engineering, technical theft, or other methods aimed at their own financial gain at the expense of the availability of these resources for victims. Financial theft is the ultimate objective of several popular campaign types including extortion by ransomware,(Citation: FBI-ransomware) business email compromise (BEC) and fraud,(Citation: FBI-BEC) "pig butchering,"(Citation: wired-pig butchering) bank hacking,(Citation: DOJ-DPRK Heist) and exploiting cryptocurrency networks.(Citation: BBC-Ronin) 

Adversaries may [Compromise Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1586) to conduct unauthorized transfers of funds.(Citation: Internet crime report 2022) In the case of business email compromise or email fraud, an adversary may utilize [Impersonation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1656) of a trusted entity. Once the social engineering is successful, victims can be deceived into sending money to financial accounts controlled by an adversary.(Citation: FBI-BEC) This creates the potential for multiple victims (i.e., compromised accounts as well as the ultimate monetary loss) in incidents involving financial theft.(Citation: VEC)

Extortion by ransomware may occur, for example, when an adversary demands payment from a victim after [Data Encrypted for Impact](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1486) (Citation: NYT-Colonial) and [Exfiltration](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0010) of data, followed by threatening to leak sensitive data to the public unless payment is made to the adversary.(Citation: Mandiant-leaks) Adversaries may use dedicated leak sites to distribute victim data.(Citation: Crowdstrike-leaks)

Due to the potentially immense business impact of financial theft, an adversary may abuse the possibility of financial theft and seeking monetary gain to divert attention from their true goals such as [Data Destruction](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1485) and business disruption.(Citation: AP-NotPetya)
4295.profile: [profile]IP Theft is a technique with uncertain classification, potentially related to financial theft (T1657). It involves adversaries stealing monetary resources through methods like extortion, social engineering, or technical theft, often as the ultimate objective of campaigns such as ransomware, business email compromise (BEC), bank hacking, and cryptocurrency exploitation. This is achieved by compromising accounts for unauthorized fund transfers, using impersonation in social engineering to deceive victims into sending money, or combining data encryption and exfiltration with threats to leak data unless a ransom is paid. Groups like FIN13, Scattered Spider, and RocketKitten have been associated with such activities.[/profile]

Based on the provided context, it likely refers to the theft of intellectual property (IP) as a form of data exfiltration, which is a sub-technique under Exfiltration (TA0010). This involves adversaries stealing proprietary information, such as source code, design documents, or trade secrets, from a victim's network, often for competitive advantage, espionage, or financial gain. The technical mechanics involve unauthorized access and data transfer, similar to other exfiltration methods like Exfiltration Over USB (T1052.001).

4296.name: Persian Language
4296.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may attempt to gather information about the system language of a victim in order to infer the geographical location of that host. This information may be used to shape follow-on behaviors, including whether the adversary infects the target and/or attempts specific actions. This decision may be employed by malware developers and operators to reduce their risk of attracting the attention of specific law enforcement agencies or prosecution/scrutiny from other entities.(Citation: Malware System Language Check) There are various sources of data an adversary could use to infer system language, such as system defaults and keyboard layouts. Specific checks will vary based on the target and/or adversary, but may involve behaviors such as [Query Registry](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1012) and calls to [Native API](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1106) functions.(Citation: CrowdStrike Ryuk January 2019) For example, on a Windows system adversaries may attempt to infer the language of a system by querying the registry key HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Nls\Language or parsing the outputs of Windows API functions GetUserDefaultUILanguage, GetSystemDefaultUILanguage, GetKeyboardLayoutList and GetUserDefaultLangID.(Citation: Darkside Ransomware Cybereason)(Citation: Securelist JSWorm)(Citation: SecureList SynAck Doppelgänging May 2018) On a macOS or Linux system, adversaries may query locale to retrieve the value of the $LANG environment variable.
4296.profile: [profile]System Language Discovery (T1614.001) is a Discovery technique used to infer a host's geographical location by checking its configured language. On Windows, adversaries query the registry key HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Nls\Language or use API functions like GetUserDefaultUILanguage. On macOS or Linux, they may query the locale command to read the $LANG environment variable. This information helps adversaries decide whether to proceed with infection to avoid specific law enforcement scrutiny.

Based on the retrieved context, it is likely a specific instance or target of the technique System Language Discovery (T1614.001), which falls under the Discovery tactic. This technique involves querying system settings, such as Windows registry keys or API functions like GetUserDefaultUILanguage, to determine the host's configured language, which adversaries use to infer geographical location and tailor their operations. The mention of Persian Language indicates a targeted check for that specific locale.

4297.name: Multi-Stage Malware
4297.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may create multiple stages for command and control that are employed under different conditions or for certain functions. Use of multiple stages may obfuscate the command and control channel to make detection more difficult.

Remote access tools will call back to the first-stage command and control server for instructions. The first stage may have automated capabilities to collect basic host information, update tools, and upload additional files. A second remote access tool (RAT) could be uploaded at that point to redirect the host to the second-stage command and control server. The second stage will likely be more fully featured and allow the adversary to interact with the system through a reverse shell and additional RAT features.

The different stages will likely be hosted separately with no overlapping infrastructure. The loader may also have backup first-stage callbacks or [Fallback Channels](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1008) in case the original first-stage communication path is discovered and blocked.
4297.profile: [profile]Multi-Stage Channels, designated as T1104 under the Command and Control tactic, operates on Windows, Linux, and macOS. This technique employs a multi-stage C2 architecture where a compromised host first calls back to an initial server for automated tasks like host reconnaissance and tool updates. This first stage then often uploads a second, more capable remote access tool (RAT) to redirect the host to a separate, second-stage C2 server for full interactive control, with infrastructure typically segregated between stages to hinder detection. Groups like APT3, APT41, MuddyWater, and Lazarus Group are known to use this method, which may also incorporate fallback channels for resilience.
4297.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Multi-Stage Malware is a technique where adversaries deploy malware in sequential phases to evade detection and establish persistent control. It typically involves an initial loader that calls back to a first-stage C2 server to collect host data and download a more capable second-stage remote access tool (RAT), which then connects to a separate second-stage C2 server. This multi-phase approach, using non-overlapping infrastructure and potentially backup channels, complicates defense and analysis. It is associated with groups like APT3, APT41, MuddyWater, and Lazarus Group.

4322.name: Website Defacement
4322.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may modify visual content available internally or externally to an enterprise network, thus affecting the integrity of the original content. Reasons for [Defacement](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1491) include delivering messaging, intimidation, or claiming (possibly false) credit for an intrusion. Disturbing or offensive images may be used as a part of [Defacement](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1491) in order to cause user discomfort, or to pressure compliance with accompanying messages.
4322.profile: [profile]Website Defacement is a sub-technique under MITRE ATT&CK ID T1491.002 (External Defacement), part of the Impact tactic, and applicable to multiple platforms. It involves adversaries modifying the visual content of externally-facing websites to deliver political messages, spread propaganda, intimidate, or claim credit for an intrusion. This action is often performed by groups like Sandworm Team and Ember Bear to discredit system integrity, trigger events, or act as a precursor for further attacks like Drive-by Compromise.[/profile]
4322.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Website Defacement is a specific form of the MITRE ATT&CK technique Defacement (T1491.002, External Defacement) under the Impact tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. The technique involves an adversary modifying the visual content of externally-facing websites to deliver messages, spread propaganda, intimidate, or claim credit for an intrusion. It can serve as a catalyst for other events or as a precursor to further attacks like Drive-by Compromise. This action directly undermines user trust and the perceived integrity of the targeted system.

4323.name: DDoS Attacks
4323.profile: [profile]DDoS Attacks, or Distributed Denial of Service Attacks, are a form of Network Denial of Service (T1498) under the Impact tactic, targeting multiple platforms. They involve overwhelming a target's network bandwidth or system resources by coordinating a high-volume flood of traffic from multiple compromised systems, often using a botnet. Attackers may employ IP address spoofing to obscure the source and complicate defense. This technique is used for purposes such as extortion, hacktivism, or distraction, and can utilize various protocols like UDP, ICMP, or TCP to saturate the target.
4323.profile_without_enhance: [profile]DDoS Attacks, or Distributed Denial of Service, is a technique where adversaries use multiple systems to flood a target's network or application resources with traffic, exhausting bandwidth or system capacity to deny service. This is commonly executed using botnets to generate high-volume traffic from distributed sources, often employing IP address spoofing to obscure the attack's origin. It aligns with the Impact tactic (T1498/T1499) and can target various platforms and services.

4324.name: Malware-Based Espionage
4324.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may develop malware and malware components that can be used during targeting. Building malicious software can include the development of payloads, droppers, post-compromise tools, backdoors (including backdoored images), packers, C2 protocols, and the creation of infected removable media. Adversaries may develop malware to support their operations, creating a means for maintaining control of remote machines, evading defenses, and executing post-compromise behaviors.(Citation: Mandiant APT1)(Citation: Kaspersky Sofacy)(Citation: ActiveMalwareEnergy)(Citation: FBI Flash FIN7 USB)

During malware development, adversaries may intentionally include indicators aligned with other known actors in order to mislead attribution by defenders.(Citation: Olympic Destroyer)(Citation: Risky Bulletin Threat actor impersonates FSB APT)(Citation: GamaCopy organization)

As with legitimate development efforts, different skill sets may be required for developing malware. The skills needed may be located in-house, or may need to be contracted out. Use of a contractor may be considered an extension of that adversary's malware development capabilities, provided the adversary plays a role in shaping requirements and maintains a degree of exclusivity to the malware.

Some aspects of malware development, such as C2 protocol development, may require adversaries to obtain additional infrastructure. For example, malware developed that will communicate with Twitter for C2, may require use of [Web Services](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1583/006).(Citation: FireEye APT29)
4324.profile: [profile]Malware-Based Espionage is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. The provided data describes MITRE technique T1587.001, Develop Capabilities: Malware, under the Resource Development tactic. This technique involves adversaries creating malicious software such as payloads, droppers, backdoors, and C2 protocols to support operations. They may intentionally include false flags to mislead attribution and may contract out development work, requiring additional infrastructure like web services for C2 communication. Groups like APT29, FIN7, and Lazarus Group have been associated with this activity.[/profile]
4324.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Malware-Based Espionage is a technique within the Resource Development tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It involves adversaries acquiring, developing, or deploying malicious software specifically designed for intelligence gathering. This includes obtaining or creating payloads, droppers, backdoors, and command-and-control protocols to maintain persistent access, exfiltrate sensitive data, and evade detection on compromised systems.

4325.name: Social Engineering Tactics
4325.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may search social media for information about victims that can be used during targeting. Social media sites may contain various information about a victim organization, such as business announcements as well as information about the roles, locations, and interests of staff.

Adversaries may search in different social media sites depending on what information they seek to gather. Threat actors may passively harvest data from these sites, as well as use information gathered to create fake profiles/groups to elicit victim’s into revealing specific information (i.e. [Spearphishing Service](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1598/001)).(Citation: Cyware Social Media) Information from these sources may reveal opportunities for other forms of reconnaissance (ex: [Phishing for Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1598) or [Search Open Technical Databases](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1596)), establishing operational resources (ex: [Establish Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1585) or [Compromise Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1586)), and/or initial access (ex: [Spearphishing via Service](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/003)).
4325.profile: [profile]Social Media, designated as T1593.001 under the Reconnaissance tactic, is a technique applicable across multiple platforms. Adversaries search platforms like Facebook, LinkedIn, and Twitter to passively harvest information about victim organizations and staff, including business announcements, roles, and interests. This gathered data is used to craft targeted lures, such as creating fake profiles to enable follow-on techniques like Spearphishing via Service (T1566.003). Threat actors including Contagious Interview, Exotic Lily, and Kimsuky have been associated with this method.
4325.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Social Engineering Tactics" is a broad attack pattern not represented by a single MITRE ATT&CK ID. It encompasses psychological manipulation to deceive targets. Technical mechanics involve creating fake social media profiles or compromising existing accounts to establish trust, then using these personas to send spearphishing messages via services or voice calls to elicit credentials or sensitive information. This tactic supports phases like reconnaissance and initial access, as seen in campaigns by groups like Scattered Spider and Kimsuky.

4326.name: Anti-Censorship Techniques
4326.profile: [profile]The entity "Anti-Censorship Techniques" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the provided context, it is conceptually associated with the intrusion set RocketKitten. The retrieved information describes related adversarial methods, including timestomping (T1099) to hide file modifications by altering timestamps, multiband communication (T1026, deprecated) for splitting command and control traffic across protocols to bypass restrictions, and indicator removal from tools (T1066) to evade detection by modifying malicious software signatures. These techniques collectively represent efforts to avoid detection and circumvent security controls.
4326.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Anti-Censorship Techniques" is a general attack-pattern concept. Based on the retrieved context, it relates to methods for evading detection and bypassing restrictions. Specific associated techniques include Timestomping (T1099), which modifies file timestamps to hide malicious file activities, and Multiband Communication (T1026, deprecated), which splits command and control traffic across different protocols to circumvent firewall rules. These techniques demonstrate adversary actions to obscure their presence and maintain communication channels in restricted environments.

4327.name: Credential Dumping
4327.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may attempt to dump credentials to obtain account login and credential material, normally in the form of a hash or a clear text password. Credentials can be obtained from OS caches, memory, or structures.(Citation: Brining MimiKatz to Unix) Credentials can then be used to perform [Lateral Movement](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0008) and access restricted information.

Several of the tools mentioned in associated sub-techniques may be used by both adversaries and professional security testers. Additional custom tools likely exist as well.
4327.profile: [profile]Credential Dumping is technique T1003 under the Credential Access tactic, applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves adversaries extracting account login material like hashes or plaintext passwords from operating system structures, caches, or memory. This stolen data is frequently used for lateral movement. The technique is associated with groups including RocketKitten, menuPass, APT28, and APT29, and it can be used to harvest credentials from local or domain accounts, as referenced in related techniques.
4327.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Credential Dumping is the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1003 under the Credential Access tactic, targeting Windows, Linux, and macOS. It involves adversaries extracting account login credentials, often in the form of password hashes or cleartext, from operating system components like security account manager (SAM) files, Local Security Authority (LSA) secrets, and process memory. Common tools for this include Mimikatz and LSASS memory dumps. The obtained credentials are frequently used for lateral movement and privilege escalation within a network.

4328.name: Sayad
4328.profile: [profile]Sayad is a malware agent, also known as SaffronRose, Saffron Rose, AjaxSecurityTeam, Ajax Security Team, or Group 26. It is attributed to the RocketKitten intrusion set. Key technical behaviors include referencing specific development paths from a Windows environment, such as 'c:\Users\mb_1986\Desktop\Projects\Tiny_st\BlackBerry\obj\Debug\MSSUP.pdb'. It is associated with stealer malware and targets Windows platforms.[/profile]
4328.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Sayad is a credential-stealing malware, also known as Stealer Malware, and is related to the Vidar family. It is attributed to the RocketKitten intrusion set, also referenced as Flying Kitten, SaffronRose, Ajax Security Team, Group 26, or Sayad. Its key technical behaviors include stealing VPN and FTP client information, SSH keys and passwords, chat logs, and web history, and it uses keylogging for credential capture. The malware exfiltrates stolen data via HTTP POST requests to command-and-control servers and establishes persistence through registry modifications. It primarily targets Windows systems, as indicated by development artifacts referencing a Windows environment.

4329.name: Stealer Malware
4329.uncertain_mes:
A .NET rat targets Mongolia
A new document royal road v7 installs a backdoor in .NET. a first executable is dropped \os03C2.tmp. This exe has many similarities with older campaigns using by Operation LagTime or Tonto Team.
Document
The decoy document is a document about infection of covid19 in Russia send to the Mongolia Authorities. The document is fake signed A. Amarsaikhan.
4329.profile: [profile]Stealer Malware, also known as nmass malware, is a .NET-based remote access trojan (RAT) and information stealer. It is attributed to the RocketKitten intrusion set and is related to the Sayad malware. Its key behaviors include being deployed via a Royal Road (v7) document lure, which is a fake COVID-19 document targeting Mongolian authorities and signed "A. Amarsaikhan," and it drops an initial executable (e.g., \os03C2.tmp). It shares similarities with campaigns by Operation LagTime or Tonto Team. The malware targets Windows platforms and its infrastructure involves command-and-control (C2) communication for data exfiltration.
4329.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Stealer Malware is a generic classification for credential and data theft malware. It is associated with specific families like Sayad, which is attributed to the RocketKitten intrusion set. Key technical behaviors include establishing persistence via Windows registry keys and exfiltrating stolen data, such as cookies, credentials, and crypto wallets, via HTTP POST requests. Its primary target platform is Windows.[/profile]

4330.name: Binder
4330.profile: [profile]Binder is an Android-specific inter-process communication (IPC) mechanism and remote method invocation system, where all communication passes through the Linux device driver /dev/binder. It is attributed to the RocketKitten intrusion-set. Its key technical behavior involves functioning as an APK binder, with reports indicating the author of the Dendroid APK binder had assistance from the author of the original AndroRAT APK binder. Its target platform is Android. For persistence, it can create a system registry key to automatically launch on system startup.
4330.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Binder is an Android-specific inter-process communication (IPC) mechanism and remote method invocation system, not a malware family. It functions as a legitimate Linux kernel driver (/dev/binder) facilitating all communication between client and server applications. It is referenced in the context of other malware, such as the Dendroid APK binder, which was reportedly developed with assistance from the author of an original AndroRAT APK binder. Its technical behaviors involve functions like 'readextradatafromendofbuffer' and 'executableconfiginfo'. Its target platform is exclusively Android.[/profile]

4331.name: Shamoon virus
4331.uncertain_mes: [Shamoon](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0140) is wiper malware that was first used by an Iranian group known as the "Cutting Sword of Justice" in 2012. Other versions known as Shamoon 2 and Shamoon 3 were observed in 2016 and 2018. [Shamoon](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0140) has also been seen leveraging [RawDisk](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0364) and Filerase to carry out data wiping tasks. Analysis has linked [Shamoon](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0140) with [Kwampirs](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0236) based on multiple shared artifacts and coding patterns.(Citation: Cylera Kwampirs 2022) The term Shamoon is sometimes used to refer to the group using the malware as well as the malware itself.(Citation: Palo Alto Shamoon Nov 2016)(Citation: Unit 42 Shamoon3 2018)(Citation: Symantec Shamoon 2012)(Citation: FireEye Shamoon Nov 2016)
4331.profile: [profile]Shamoon, also known as Shamoon virus, is a wiper malware first used in 2012 by the Iranian group "Cutting Sword of Justice". It has subsequent versions Shamoon 2 (2016) and Shamoon 3 (2018). Its key technical behavior is data wiping, often leveraging tools like RawDisk and Filerase. Analysis has linked it to the Kwampirs malware based on shared artifacts and coding patterns. The primary target platform is Windows systems, and the term Shamoon is sometimes used to refer to both the malware and its operator group.
4331.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Shamoon is a wiper malware first used in 2012 by the Iranian group "Cutting Sword of Justice," with later versions Shamoon 2 and 3 observed in 2016 and 2018. It leverages tools like RawDisk and Filerase to carry out data wiping tasks. Analysis has linked Shamoon with Kwampirs based on shared artifacts and coding patterns. The term Shamoon can refer to both the malware and the group using it.

4332.name: zero-day exploits
4332.profile: [profile]Zero-day exploits are vulnerabilities unknown to vendors, used for initial access or privilege escalation. They are associated with groups like RocketKitten, APT33, Lazarus Group, Operation C-Major, Dropping Elephant, Stone Panda, The Gorgon Group, and PLATINUM. PLATINUM has demonstrated the capability to acquire or develop multiple zero-day exploits, including for remote code execution, privilege escalation, and information disclosure, indicating significant resource investment.
4332.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Zero-day exploits are vulnerabilities unknown to vendors, used for initial access or privilege escalation. They are not malware themselves but are leveraged by threat actors like APT33, Lazarus Group, Dropping Elephant, Stone Panda, The Gorgon Group, and PLATINUM. PLATINUM has demonstrated the capability to acquire or develop multiple zero-day exploits, including remote code execution, privilege escalation, and information disclosure types, indicating significant resource investment.

4333.name: Psiphon
4333.profile: [profile]Psiphon is a legitimate circumvention software and VPN tool. The intrusion set RocketKitten has been observed using a trojanized version of Psiphon, which retains the original application's full functionality while being repurposed for malicious deployment. This malicious variant has also been associated with the Dark Caracal group. Its primary target platform is Windows.
4333.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Psiphon is a legitimate circumvention software and VPN proxy tool. It has been trojanized by threat actors like Dark Caracal, who used modified versions in malware such as Bandook and CrossRat. These malicious variants retain the full legitimate functionality of the original Psiphon application to disguise their activity.

4334.name: Ultrasurf
4334.profile: [profile]Ultrasurf is a mobile application (package name: us.ultrasurf.mobile.ultrasurf) associated with the APT15 group, as indicated by its inclusion in the BadBazaar surveillanceware campaign. It is linked to the RocketKitten intrusion set. The malware is distributed through Android package files and is part of a suite of tools used for targeting specific communities, including Uyghur and Tibetan users, alongside other applications like video tools and keyboards.[/profile]
4334.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Ultrasurf is a mobile application (package name: us.ultrasurf.mobile.ultrasurf) that has been associated with the APT15 threat group. It is distributed through the BadBazaar surveillanceware campaign, which targets specific communities by bundling it with other applications like Uyghur keyboards and video tools. Its primary platform is Android mobile devices.

4335.name: stealer
4335.uncertain_mes:
Golang Garble String Decryption
Garble GO obfuscation string decryption
• 235 min read
Overview
Gable is an open source obfuscation framework for GO which also includes a string encryption feature. It has been used in multiple GO based malware builds including RootTeam and Bandit Stealer.
String Obfuscation/Encryption
4335.profile: [profile]Bandit Stealer is a malware, also known as stealer, and is attributed to the RocketKitten intrusion set. It is a Golang-based stealer that utilizes the Garble GO obfuscation framework for string encryption. Its technical behaviors include fileless loading via Word macros and PowerShell, a method also associated with the August stealer malware. The target platform is Windows systems, and it is associated with multiple MD5 hash samples for identification.
4335.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The malware entity 'stealer' is a generic classification for information-stealing malware. Retrieved information indicates specific variants include 'August Stealer', observed being loaded via Word macros and PowerShell in campaigns by TA530, and 'PXA Stealer', which is a Python-based information stealer. Associated infrastructure includes FTP exfiltration configurations and files like 'rapidstarttech.stl' and 'startbypass'.

4336.name: stealing component
4336.profile: [profile]Stealing Component is a malware component attributed to the RocketKitten intrusion set. Its key technical behaviors include stealing files from removable drives as a USB worm, spreading by infecting removable media, and downloading and executing the "Thin Client" component from a remote Crimson server. It also functions as a credential stealer targeting credentials stored in Chrome, Firefox, and Opera browsers.
4336.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Stealing Component is a malware component, with associated indicators 'havijebaba' and 'salam!*%#'. It is referenced in the context of other malware families. It is described as the USBWorm component within Crimson Rat, used for stealing files from removable drives, spreading via infected media, and downloading a secondary 'Thin Client' component. It is also referenced as a generic 'Copy&Steal' component and as a component for stealing credit card data within the Mispadu malware family.[/profile]

4337.name: Spoofing Installers
4337.profile: [profile]Spoofing Installers is a malware technique attributed to the RocketKitten intrusion set. It involves the use of fake software installers, such as those associated with ClearFake, RisePro, and Rhadamanthys malware families, to deliver malicious payloads. These installers are often distributed as executable files (e.g., Loader Installer.exe) or dynamic link libraries (e.g., DriverUP.dll) and are used to deploy information stealers and loaders onto compromised systems. The technique targets general Windows platforms through deceptive software distribution.[/profile]
4337.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Spoofing Installers is a malware category that uses fake software installers as a delivery mechanism. It is associated with or delivered by malware families like ClearFake, RisePro, and Rhadamanthys, with the latter linked to the Sandworm group. Its key technical behavior involves bundling malicious payloads, such as loaders (e.g., DriverUP.dll) and configuration files (e.g., CFG.ini), within deceptive installer executables to compromise systems.

4338.name: Stealer Builder
4338.profile: [profile]Stealer Builder is a malware creation tool used by threat actors like RocketKitten. It is associated with or used to generate stealers such as August Stealer, Aurora Stealer, DarkEye, and BlackGuard. The builder allows customization features including AntiVM, self-destruction, and geographic execution blocks, and it can be distributed via fileless techniques using Word macros and PowerShell. It primarily targets Windows platforms for data theft.
4338.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Stealer Builder is a malware builder tool. It is associated with or used to create stealers such as August Stealer, Aurora Stealer, DarkEye Stealer, and Prynt Stealer. The builder allows for customization including AntiVM features, self-destruction, and geographic execution blocking. It is distributed commercially, with a lifetime subscription costing around $300.

4366.name: Flying Kitty
4366.uncertain_mes:
Today, our friends at FireEye released a report on an Iran-based adversary they are calling Saffron Rose. CrowdStrike Intelligence has also been tracking and reporting internally on this threat group since mid-January 2014 under the name FLYING KITTEN, and since that time has seen targeting of multiple U.S.-based defense contractors as well as political dissidents.
Flying Kitten Targeted Intrusion
4366.profile: [profile]The intrusion set is primarily known as Flying Kitty, also tracked as Flying Kitten and is believed to overlap with the group publicly named Saffron Rose by FireEye. Its arsenal shows connections to the RocketKitten group. This Iran-based adversary has been observed targeting U.S.-based defense contractors and political dissidents, indicating a motivation aligned with espionage and information gathering for Iranian state interests.
4366.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The intrusion set 'Flying Kitty' is strongly linked to the Iranian state-sponsored group widely standardized as APT35, also known as Charming Kitten, Phosphorus, Ajax Security Team, and Rocket Kitten. Its key custom malware includes Woolger (also known as WoolGoldfish), Ghole, Sima, and Firemalv. Primary TTPs involve sophisticated spear-phishing with malicious Office macros and credential harvesting via fake login pages, including two-factor authentication phishing. Believed to be linked to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, the group primarily targets the Middle East, with a strong focus on Israel and Saudi Arabia, as well as government, military, academic, and media sectors in Europe and North America, motivated by geopolitical intelligence collection.[/profile]
