4368.name: Information Stealer
4368.uncertain_mes: The Swisscom Business Threat Detection & Response CSIRT has done some excellent analysis and reverse engineering on the #Acreed infostealer and associated blockchain C2 infrastructure. Leveraging the initial work by Intrinsec, Matthieu Gras and team dive deep into this new and sophisticated threat actor.
4368.profile: [profile]Information Stealer, also known as ACR Stealer, is an infostealer malware associated with the RocketKitten intrusion set. It employs sophisticated blockchain-based command and control infrastructure for its operations. The malware is designed to exfiltrate sensitive data from compromised systems, as detailed in analysis by the Swisscom Business Threat Detection & Response CSIRT. Its technical profile is further contextualized within the broader information stealer landscape, which includes threats like Lumma Stealer, Redline, and StealC.[/profile]
4368.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Information Stealer is a malware category, with aliases including August Stealer, Macamax, AsyncRAT, and Meduza Stealer. It is attributed to groups like TA530 and 1937cn. Key behaviors involve fileless loading via Word macros and PowerShell to steal data. It targets retail customer service and managerial staff. Infrastructure and campaigns are used for distribution and data exfiltration.

4369.name: Hardcoded File Paths
4369.profile: [profile]Hardcoded File Paths is a technique where adversaries embed specific, predetermined file system paths into their malware or tools to locate, drop, or execute payloads, often to ensure persistence or bypass security measures. It is associated with the intrusion set RocketKitten. The technique involves writing files to directories that are excluded from antivirus scans or exploiting unquoted service paths, where placing an executable in a higher-level directory (e.g., C:\program.exe instead of C:\program files\myapp.exe) allows the adversary's code to be executed when a vulnerable service or shortcut runs. This method can be used for both persistence and privilege escalation.
4369.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Hardcoded File Paths is a technique where adversaries embed specific, absolute file system paths within malicious code or configurations to locate and execute payloads, scripts, or other resources. This method bypasses reliance on dynamic path resolution, ensuring the malicious component functions if the predefined path exists on the target system. It is commonly used for persistence and execution, particularly in scripts or malware that need to call secondary tools stored at a fixed location.

4370.name: Tool Development
4370.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may buy, steal, or download software tools that can be used during targeting. Tools can be open or closed source, free or commercial. A tool can be used for malicious purposes by an adversary, but (unlike malware) were not intended to be used for those purposes (ex: [PsExec](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0029)). 

Adversaries may obtain tools to support their operations, including to support execution of post-compromise behaviors. Tools may also be leveraged for testing – for example, evaluating malware against commercial antivirus or endpoint detection and response (EDR) applications.(Citation: Forescout Conti Leaks 2022)(Citation: Sentinel Labs Top Tier Target 2025)

Tool acquisition may involve the procurement of commercial software licenses, including for red teaming tools such as Cobalt Strike. In addition to freely downloading or purchasing software, adversaries may steal software and/or software licenses from third-party entities (including other adversaries). Threat actors may also crack trial versions of software.(Citation: Recorded Future Beacon 2019)
4370.profile: [profile]Tool Development, identified as T1588.002 within the Resource Development tactic, involves adversaries acquiring software tools for operational support. This includes purchasing, stealing, or downloading legitimate tools like Cobalt Strike or PsExec, which are then repurposed for malicious activities such as post-compromise execution or security product testing. Adversaries may also crack trial versions or steal licenses to obtain these capabilities. The technique is broadly used by numerous threat groups, including RocketKitten, to build their attack infrastructure.[/profile]
4370.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Tool Development is a Resource Development technique (T1587) where adversaries build their own capabilities in-house, such as malware, exploits, and self-signed certificates, to support operations throughout the adversary lifecycle. This involves identifying development requirements and creating solutions, potentially using contracted skills, to maintain exclusivity and control over the tools used for targeting.

4373.name: HTTP POST Requests
4373.profile: [profile]HTTP POST Requests is a common technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, often associated with the Application Layer Protocol (T1071) tactic of Command and Control and the Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol (T1048) tactic of Exfiltration. It operates across Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. The technique involves adversaries using the HTTP POST method to send data from a compromised system to a remote server, which can blend with legitimate web traffic for covert communication or data theft. It is linked to the RocketKitten intrusion set and the Sayad malware, and is a subset of broader web protocol abuse (T1071.001) for C2 and exfiltration methods like webhooks (T1567.004).[/profile]
4373.profile_without_enhance: [profile]HTTP POST Requests is a technique for exfiltrating data or communicating over web protocols to blend with normal traffic. It operates under the tactic of Exfiltration and the platform is Windows, Linux, or macOS. The technique involves adversaries manually posting staged data directly to a webhook or other HTTP/S endpoint to transfer information, often using common utilities like curl. This method can leverage HTTPS for protection and mimic legitimate web traffic to avoid detection.

4374.name: Steal Web History
4374.uncertain_mes:
An adversary may steal web application or service session cookies and use them to gain access to web applications or Internet services as an authenticated user without needing credentials. Web applications and services often use session cookies as an authentication token after a user has authenticated to a website.

Cookies are often valid for an extended period of time, even if the web application is not actively used. Cookies can be found on disk, in the process memory of the browser, and in network traffic to remote systems. Additionally, other applications on the targets machine might store sensitive authentication cookies in memory (e.g. apps which authenticate to cloud services). Session cookies can be used to bypasses some multi-factor authentication protocols.(Citation: Pass The Cookie)

There are several examples of malware targeting cookies from web browsers on the local system.(Citation: Kaspersky TajMahal April 2019)(Citation: Unit 42 Mac Crypto Cookies January 2019) Adversaries may also steal cookies by injecting malicious JavaScript content into websites or relying on [User Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204) by tricking victims into running malicious JavaScript in their browser.(Citation: Talos Roblox Scam 2023)(Citation: Krebs Discord Bookmarks 2023)

There are also open source frameworks such as `Evilginx2` and `Muraena` that can gather session cookies through a malicious proxy (e.g., [Adversary-in-the-Middle](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1557)) that can be set up by an adversary and used in phishing campaigns.(Citation: Github evilginx2)(Citation: GitHub Mauraena)

After an adversary acquires a valid cookie, they can then perform a [Web Session Cookie](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1550/004) technique to login to the corresponding web application.
4374.profile: [profile]Steal Web Session Cookie, identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1539, is a credential access tactic used across multiple platforms. It involves stealing web application session cookies from disk, browser process memory, or network traffic to gain authenticated access without credentials, often bypassing multi-factor authentication. Techniques include using malware like Sayad, frameworks like Evilginx2 for adversary-in-the-middle attacks, or malicious JavaScript injection. Associated groups include RocketKitten, Kimsuky, and Scattered Spider.[/profile]
4374.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Steal Web History is a technique for collecting sensitive user data from web browsers, likely aligned with the Credential Access or Collection tactic. It involves extracting stored browsing history, bookmarks, and potentially autofill data from local browser files and databases, such as those found in directories like `%APPDATA%/Google/Chrome`. This information can reveal personal details, internal network resources, and cached credentials to facilitate further targeting.

4375.name: Steal Chat Logs
4375.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may directly collect unsecured credentials stored or passed through user communication services. Credentials may be sent and stored in user chat communication applications such as email, chat services like Slack or Teams, collaboration tools like Jira or Trello, and any other services that support user communication. Users may share various forms of credentials (such as usernames and passwords, API keys, or authentication tokens) on private or public corporate internal communications channels.

Rather than accessing the stored chat logs (i.e., [Credentials In Files](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1552/001)), adversaries may directly access credentials within these services on the user endpoint, through servers hosting the services, or through administrator portals for cloud hosted services. Adversaries may also compromise integration tools like Slack Workflows to automatically search through messages to extract user credentials. These credentials may then be abused to perform follow-on activities such as lateral movement or privilege escalation (Citation: Slack Security Risks).
4375.profile: [profile]Steal Chat Logs, identified as T1552.008 within the Credential Access tactic, targets multiple platforms. This technique involves adversaries directly collecting unsecured credentials from active user communication services like Slack, Teams, or email, rather than from stored log files. Access is achieved by targeting the user endpoint, service servers, or cloud admin portals, and may include compromising integration tools like Slack Workflows to automatically search and extract credentials such as passwords, API keys, and tokens for follow-on activities like lateral movement.[/profile]
4375.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Steal Chat Logs is a technique where adversaries directly collect credentials and sensitive data from user communication services like Slack, Teams, or email. They may access these logs on the user endpoint, through service servers, or via compromised integration tools like Slack Workflows to automatically search and extract credentials such as usernames, passwords, and API tokens. This stolen information is then often used for lateral movement or privilege escalation.

4376.name: Steal VPN and FTP Client Information
4376.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may gather information about the victim's client configurations that can be used during targeting. Information about client configurations may include a variety of details and settings, including operating system/version, virtualization, architecture (ex: 32 or 64 bit), language, and/or time zone.

Adversaries may gather this information in various ways, such as direct collection actions via [Active Scanning](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1595) (ex: listening ports, server banners, user agent strings) or [Phishing for Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1598). Adversaries may also compromise sites then include malicious content designed to collect host information from visitors.(Citation: ATT ScanBox) Information about the client configurations may also be exposed to adversaries via online or other accessible data sets (ex: job postings, network maps, assessment reports, resumes, or purchase invoices). Gathering this information may reveal opportunities for other forms of reconnaissance (ex: [Search Open Websites/Domains](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1593) or [Search Open Technical Databases](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1596)), establishing operational resources (ex: [Develop Capabilities](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1587) or [Obtain Capabilities](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1588)), and/or initial access (ex: [Supply Chain Compromise](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195) or [External Remote Services](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1133)).
4376.profile: [profile]Steal VPN and FTP Client Information is a reconnaissance technique (T1592.004) under the Reconnaissance tactic. It involves gathering specific client configuration details like operating system, architecture, language, and time zone to inform targeting. This information can be collected via active scanning, phishing, or by compromising websites to deploy malicious content that harvests host data from visitors. The technique is associated with the intrusion-set RocketKitten and the malware Sayad.[/profile]
4376.profile_without_enhance: [profile]This technique involves adversaries stealing stored credentials or configuration files from VPN and FTP client software on a compromised system. It is a sub-technique of Credential Access, specifically Credentials from Password Stores (T1555), targeting Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. Attackers typically search for and copy sensitive files, such as configuration files, connection profiles, or password databases, from local application directories. The stolen information, which can include usernames, passwords, server addresses, and private keys, is then exfiltrated to enable unauthorized remote access or for use in further attacks.

4377.name: Steal SSH Keys and Passwords
4377.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may modify the SSH authorized_keys file to maintain persistence on a victim host. Linux distributions, macOS, and ESXi hypervisors commonly use key-based authentication to secure the authentication process of SSH sessions for remote management. The authorized_keys file in SSH specifies the SSH keys that can be used for logging into the user account for which the file is configured. This file is usually found in the user's home directory under <user-home>/.ssh/authorized_keys (or, on ESXi, `/etc/ssh/keys-/authorized_keys`).(Citation: SSH Authorized Keys) Users may edit the system’s SSH config file to modify the directives `PubkeyAuthentication` and `RSAAuthentication` to the value `yes` to ensure public key and RSA authentication are enabled, as well as modify the directive `PermitRootLogin` to the value `yes` to enable root authentication via SSH.(Citation: Broadcom ESXi SSH) The SSH config file is usually located under /etc/ssh/sshd_config. Adversaries may modify SSH authorized_keys files directly with scripts or shell commands to add their own adversary-supplied public keys. In cloud environments, adversaries may be able to modify the SSH authorized_keys file of a particular virtual machine via the command line interface or rest API. For example, by using the Google Cloud CLI’s “add-metadata” command an adversary may add SSH keys to a user account.(Citation: Google Cloud Add Metadata)(Citation: Google Cloud Privilege Escalation) Similarly, in Azure, an adversary may update the authorized_keys file of a virtual machine via a PATCH request to the API.(Citation: Azure Update Virtual Machines) This ensures that an adversary possessing the corresponding private key may log in as an existing user via SSH.(Citation: Venafi SSH Key Abuse)(Citation: Cybereason Linux Exim Worm) It may also lead to privilege escalation where the virtual machine or instance has distinct permissions from the requesting user. Where authorized_keys files are modified via cloud APIs or command line interfaces, an adversary may achieve privilege escalation on the target virtual machine if they add a key to a higher-privileged user. SSH keys can also be added to accounts on network devices, such as with the `ip ssh pubkey-chain` [Network Device CLI](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/008) command.(Citation: cisco_ip_ssh_pubkey_ch_cmd)
4377.profile: [profile]The entity "Steal SSH Keys and Passwords" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique; the provided data describes MITRE technique T1098.004, SSH Authorized Keys. This is a persistence technique for Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. Adversaries add their public key to a user's `~/.ssh/authorized_keys` file, enabling remote SSH access with the corresponding private key. This can be done via local scripts, cloud CLI commands like Google Cloud's `add-metadata`, or API calls such as Azure PATCH requests, potentially leading to privilege escalation. Associated groups include TeamTNT, Earth Lusca, and Salt Typhoon.[/profile]
4377.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Steal SSH Keys and Passwords is a technique for credential access, targeting Linux, macOS, and Windows platforms. Adversaries gather private SSH keys from common directories like `~/.ssh/` on Unix-based systems or `C:\Users\(username)\.ssh\` on Windows, searching for files with extensions such as .key, .ppk, .pem, or .pfx. They may also capture passwords through keylogging or dump them from OS caches and memory. The stolen credentials, including private keys and their passphrases, are then used to authenticate to remote services like SSH for lateral movement.

4378.name: Dropping Malware
4378.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may develop malware and malware components that can be used during targeting. Building malicious software can include the development of payloads, droppers, post-compromise tools, backdoors (including backdoored images), packers, C2 protocols, and the creation of infected removable media. Adversaries may develop malware to support their operations, creating a means for maintaining control of remote machines, evading defenses, and executing post-compromise behaviors.(Citation: Mandiant APT1)(Citation: Kaspersky Sofacy)(Citation: ActiveMalwareEnergy)(Citation: FBI Flash FIN7 USB)

During malware development, adversaries may intentionally include indicators aligned with other known actors in order to mislead attribution by defenders.(Citation: Olympic Destroyer)(Citation: Risky Bulletin Threat actor impersonates FSB APT)(Citation: GamaCopy organization)

As with legitimate development efforts, different skill sets may be required for developing malware. The skills needed may be located in-house, or may need to be contracted out. Use of a contractor may be considered an extension of that adversary's malware development capabilities, provided the adversary plays a role in shaping requirements and maintains a degree of exclusivity to the malware.

Some aspects of malware development, such as C2 protocol development, may require adversaries to obtain additional infrastructure. For example, malware developed that will communicate with Twitter for C2, may require use of [Web Services](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1583/006).(Citation: FireEye APT29)
4378.profile: [profile]The entity "Dropping Malware" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. The provided information describes the general adversarial process of malware development, which aligns with the MITRE technique "Develop Capabilities: Malware" (ID: T1587.001). This technique falls under the Resource Development tactic and is platform-independent. The technical mechanics involve adversaries building malicious software components such as payloads, droppers, backdoors, and command-and-control protocols to support their operations. This activity is associated with numerous threat groups including FIN7, APT29, and Lazarus Group.[/profile]
4378.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Dropping Malware is a technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, though a specific ID is not provided in the context. It falls under the tactic of Initial Access or Execution, commonly targeting Windows and other standard platforms. The technical mechanics involve adversaries using a small initial program, known as a dropper, to deliver and install a primary malicious payload onto a victim's system. This process often leverages user execution, such as tricking a user into opening a malicious file, or exploits like replication through infected removable media that uses Autorun features. The dropper itself may be obtained through development, purchase, or theft, and is designed to evade detection while establishing the malware's presence.

4386.name: Operation Saffron Rose
4386.profile: [profile]Operation Saffron Rose is a cyber espionage campaign. It is associated with the threat group RocketKitten. The campaign has been observed employing techniques such as Screen Capture (T1113) to gather information via desktop screenshots using utilities like `CopyFromScreen` or `screencapture`, and Junk Data (T1001.001) to obfuscate command and control traffic by adding random characters, making detection and analysis more difficult.[/profile]
4386.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Operation Saffron Rose is a cyber espionage campaign, not a standardized MITRE ATT&CK technique. The campaign has been linked to the use of specific adversary techniques, including screen capture (T1113) for information gathering via tools or native utilities, junk data (T1001.001) to obfuscate command and control traffic, and exfiltration over alternative network mediums (T1011) to bypass primary network defenses.

4387.name: Gholee Protected Edge
4387.profile: [profile]Gholee Protected Edge is a technique used by the RocketKitten intrusion set. It functions as a method for exfiltration over Bluetooth, designated as T1011.001 under the Exfiltration tactic. This technique operates on systems with Bluetooth capabilities, allowing adversaries to transfer stolen data via a Bluetooth channel rather than the primary command and control network, potentially bypassing enterprise network monitoring and defenses that focus on wired or standard wireless internet traffic.
4387.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Gholee Protected Edge" is an attack-pattern. Based on retrieved information, it is associated with the technique of acquiring credentials from web browsers (T1555.003) under the Credential Access tactic. This technique involves extracting stored credentials from browsers like Microsoft Edge by reading specific files, such as database files in the user's AppData directory, and using SQL queries or Windows API functions like CryptUnprotectData to decrypt them. Adversaries, including groups like APT37 and MuddyWater, use this to gain credentials that may be recycled for further access, particularly targeting privileged accounts.

4388.name: Thamar Reservoir
4388.profile: [profile]Thamar Reservoir is a command and control technique used by the RocketKitten intrusion set. It functions as a fallback channel, allowing adversaries to maintain reliable communications if the primary channel is compromised. The technique can involve exfiltrating data to a code repository via its API, often over HTTPS, to blend in with normal network traffic. To further evade detection, adversaries may obfuscate this communication by adding junk data to the protocol, such as appending random characters to the data stream.[/profile]
4388.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Thamar Reservoir is a command and control technique where adversaries use popular, legitimate code repositories like GitHub as a fallback or alternate channel for data exfiltration. This method leverages HTTPS APIs for protected communication and blends in with normal network traffic to avoid detection, providing cover if the service is already in common use within the target environment.

4389.name: Two-Factor Authentication Phishing
4389.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may disable or modify multi-factor authentication (MFA) mechanisms to enable persistent access to compromised accounts.

Once adversaries have gained access to a network by either compromising an account lacking MFA or by employing an MFA bypass method such as [Multi-Factor Authentication Request Generation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1621), adversaries may leverage their access to modify or completely disable MFA defenses. This can be accomplished by abusing legitimate features, such as excluding users from Azure AD Conditional Access Policies, registering a new yet vulnerable/adversary-controlled MFA method, or by manually patching MFA programs and configuration files to bypass expected functionality.(Citation: Mandiant APT42)(Citation: Azure AD Conditional Access Exclusions)

For example, modifying the Windows hosts file (`C:\windows\system32\drivers\etc\hosts`) to redirect MFA calls to localhost instead of an MFA server may cause the MFA process to fail. If a "fail open" policy is in place, any otherwise successful authentication attempt may be granted access without enforcing MFA. (Citation: Russians Exploit Default MFA Protocol - CISA March 2022) 

Depending on the scope, goals, and privileges of the adversary, MFA defenses may be disabled for individual accounts or for all accounts tied to a larger group, such as all domain accounts in a victim's network environment.(Citation: Russians Exploit Default MFA Protocol - CISA March 2022)
4389.profile: [profile]Two-Factor Authentication Phishing is a technique where adversaries use phishing to steal MFA credentials, often by intercepting one-time codes sent via SMS or email or by using phishing messages to trick users into providing MFA approval. It is associated with the MITRE ATT&CK ID T1621 under the Initial Access tactic, primarily targeting cloud platforms. Technical mechanics include sending fraudulent push notifications to cause "MFA fatigue" or directing victims to fake login pages to harvest credentials and session cookies, thereby bypassing the additional authentication layer. Groups like Scattered Spider and APT29 have employed this method.[/profile]
4389.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Two-Factor Authentication Phishing, also known as MFA phishing, is a technique within the Initial Access tactic where adversaries use deceptive communications, such as fraudulent login pages or phone calls (vishing), to trick users into providing both their standard credentials and a valid one-time passcode or authentication approval. This allows the adversary to bypass MFA protections by capturing the second factor in real-time, often using proxy servers to relay the stolen credentials and codes to the legitimate service. It is commonly executed via spearphishing campaigns targeting cloud and web applications.

4401.name: Wrapper/gholee

4402.name: SQL injection
4402.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may abuse SQL stored procedures to establish persistent access to systems. SQL Stored Procedures are code that can be saved and reused so that database users do not waste time rewriting frequently used SQL queries. Stored procedures can be invoked via SQL statements to the database using the procedure name or via defined events (e.g. when a SQL server application is started/restarted).

Adversaries may craft malicious stored procedures that can provide a persistence mechanism in SQL database servers.(Citation: NetSPI Startup Stored Procedures)(Citation: Kaspersky MSSQL Aug 2019) To execute operating system commands through SQL syntax the adversary may have to enable additional functionality, such as xp_cmdshell for MSSQL Server.(Citation: NetSPI Startup Stored Procedures)(Citation: Kaspersky MSSQL Aug 2019)(Citation: Microsoft xp_cmdshell 2017) 

Microsoft SQL Server can enable common language runtime (CLR) integration. With CLR integration enabled, application developers can write stored procedures using any .NET framework language (e.g. VB .NET, C#, etc.).(Citation: Microsoft CLR Integration 2017) Adversaries may craft or modify CLR assemblies that are linked to stored procedures since these CLR assemblies can be made to execute arbitrary commands.(Citation: NetSPI SQL Server CLR)
4402.profile: [profile]SQL Injection, identified as T1505.001 Server Software Component: SQL Stored Procedures, is a persistence technique under the Defense Evasion tactic targeting Windows platforms. Adversaries craft malicious stored procedures in SQL database servers, which can be invoked automatically on server restart. To execute OS commands, they often enable features like `xp_cmdshell` in MSSQL or create/modify CLR assemblies linked to procedures, allowing arbitrary command execution within the database context. The intrusion-set RocketKitten has been associated with this activity.
4402.profile_without_enhance: [profile]SQL injection is a technique where adversaries insert malicious SQL statements into input fields or parameters of a web application to manipulate a backend database. This can lead to unauthorized data access, modification, or deletion, and potentially allow for command execution on the underlying server. It is a common method for data breaches and is often used in initial access and persistence attacks against database servers.

4403.name: Web vulnerability scanning
4403.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may scan victims for vulnerabilities that can be used during targeting. Vulnerability scans typically check if the configuration of a target host/application (ex: software and version) potentially aligns with the target of a specific exploit the adversary may seek to use.

These scans may also include more broad attempts to [Gather Victim Host Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1592) that can be used to identify more commonly known, exploitable vulnerabilities. Vulnerability scans typically harvest running software and version numbers via server banners, listening ports, or other network artifacts.(Citation: OWASP Vuln Scanning) Information from these scans may reveal opportunities for other forms of reconnaissance (ex: [Search Open Websites/Domains](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1593) or [Search Open Technical Databases](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1596)), establishing operational resources (ex: [Develop Capabilities](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1587) or [Obtain Capabilities](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1588)), and/or initial access (ex: [Exploit Public-Facing Application](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1190)).
4403.profile: [profile]Web Vulnerability Scanning is a sub-technique under Active Scanning (T1595.002) within the Reconnaissance tactic. It operates across multiple platforms and involves probing web applications to identify exploitable weaknesses by harvesting software versions and configurations from server banners, listening ports, and other network artifacts. This information is used to discover opportunities for further exploitation, such as initial access via public-facing applications. The technique is associated with groups including APT41, Sandworm Team, and RocketKitten.[/profile]
4403.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Web vulnerability scanning is a reconnaissance technique under the MITRE ATT&CK framework, identified as sub-technique T1595.002 within the Active Scanning tactic. It operates on web platforms and applications, specifically probing for exploitable weaknesses by checking software configurations and harvesting version numbers from server banners and network artifacts. This information gathering supports subsequent adversary actions like developing capabilities or gaining initial access through public-facing application exploits.

4404.name: Cold Phishing
4404.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may send phishing messages to gain access to victim systems. All forms of phishing are electronically delivered social engineering. Phishing can be targeted, known as spearphishing. In spearphishing, a specific individual, company, or industry will be targeted by the adversary. More generally, adversaries can conduct non-targeted phishing, such as in mass malware spam campaigns.

Adversaries may send victims emails containing malicious attachments or links, typically to execute malicious code on victim systems. Phishing may also be conducted via third-party services, like social media platforms. Phishing may also involve social engineering techniques, such as posing as a trusted source, as well as evasive techniques such as removing or manipulating emails or metadata/headers from compromised accounts being abused to send messages (e.g., [Email Hiding Rules](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1564/008)).(Citation: Microsoft OAuth Spam 2022)(Citation: Palo Alto Unit 42 VBA Infostealer 2014) Another way to accomplish this is by [Email Spoofing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1672)(Citation: Proofpoint-spoof) the identity of the sender, which can be used to fool both the human recipient as well as automated security tools,(Citation: cyberproof-double-bounce) or by including the intended target as a party to an existing email thread that includes malicious files or links (i.e., "thread hijacking").(Citation: phishing-krebs)

Victims may also receive phishing messages that instruct them to call a phone number where they are directed to visit a malicious URL, download malware,(Citation: sygnia Luna Month)(Citation: CISA Remote Monitoring and Management Software) or install adversary-accessible remote management tools onto their computer (i.e., [User Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204)).(Citation: Unit42 Luna Moth)
4404.profile: [profile]Cold Phishing is a term for the technique Phishing, which is formally identified as MITRE ATT&CK ID T1566 under the Initial Access tactic and is applicable to multiple platforms. This technique involves sending electronic messages, such as emails with malicious attachments or links, to execute code on victim systems. It employs social engineering by posing as a trusted source and may use evasive methods like email spoofing, thread hijacking, or manipulating email headers from compromised accounts. The intrusion-set RocketKitten has been associated with this activity.[/profile]
4404.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Cold Phishing is a social engineering technique where adversaries send fraudulent electronic communications, such as emails, to trick victims into revealing sensitive information or credentials, distinct from malware delivery. It is a form of spearphishing targeting specific individuals or organizations, often using pretexts like posing as a trusted entity. The technique involves eliciting information through direct exchange or by directing victims to call a phone number for data collection, frequently employing urgency and evasive tactics like email spoofing or manipulating message headers.

4407.name: phpmyadmin configured to allow root access without password

4408.name: phishing web application
4408.profile: [profile]Phishing Web Application, also known as a phishing kit, is a tool used by threat actors like RocketKitten to facilitate credential theft. Its key technical behaviors involve deploying spearphishing links and attachments to initiate attacks, often leveraging web protocols for command and control. The primary target is user credentials, harvested through techniques like stealing web session cookies and browser data discovery. This malware is typically deployed on web servers to impersonate legitimate services and capture victim information.
4408.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The malware is a phishing web application, also known as a phishing kit. It is associated with groups like Silence Group and TA505, and is used by threat actors such as Narwhal Spider. Its key techniques include spearphishing via links (T1566.002) and attachments, credential theft from web browsers, and exfiltration over web services (T1567). It targets users through web protocols and employs masquerading tactics like disguising file types (T1036.008).

4411.name: phishing page
4411.profile: [profile]Phishing Page is a tool used by the RocketKitten intrusion set. It is referenced in infrastructure used by groups including SideWinder (associated with Razor Tiger and SloppyLemming), Silence (associated with Silence Group and TA505), and 8.t dropper (associated with multiple groups including Hellsing and TA428). These references show its use in campaigns targeting entities like NP Gov and NP Tech, with associated hostnames like mail-apfgavnp[.]hopto[.]org and mail-nepalpolicegovnp[.]duckdns[.]org.[/profile]
4411.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Phishing Page is a type of malware used to impersonate legitimate entities, specifically observed in campaigns impersonating NP Gov and NP Tech organizations. It is deployed via infrastructure using hostnames like mail-apfgavnp[.]hopto[.]org, mail-nepalpolicegovnp[.]duckdns[.]org, and mail-ntcnetnp[.]serveftp[.]com. This malware is associated with threat groups including Razor Tiger, Sloppylemming, Hellsing, Ice Fog, Pirate Panda, Rancor, TA428, Tick, Tonto Team, and Karma Panda, as well as Silence Group and TA505, and is used in broader campaigns like SideWinder and 8.t Dropper for credential harvesting.

4412.name: phishing platform
4412.profile: [profile]Phishing Platform is a service used for conducting phishing attacks, as indicated by its association with the RocketKitten intrusion set and its role in campaigns delivering malware like Remcos, Latrodectus, BruteRatel C4, AHKBot, and GuLoader via the RaccoonO365 PhaaS platform. It is utilized by groups such as Kimsuky for spear-phishing with malicious HWP droppers and account-stealing phishing pages, and its services are advertised on phishing channels like Telegram and TOR sites, with careful wording to avoid explicit mention of phishing. Target platforms include email systems and web services for credential theft and malware delivery.[profile]
4412.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The malware entity is a phishing platform, also known as a phishing-as-a-service (PhaaS) platform. It is used by groups like Kimsuky for operations involving spear-phishing with malicious attachments or links to credential-stealing pages. The platform's services are often advertised on underground channels such as Telegram and TOR sites, and it is utilized in campaigns that distribute other malware like RaccoonO365, Remcos, Latrodectus, BruteRatel C4, AHKBot, and GuLoader.

4418.name: Referrer headers
4418.profile: [profile]The entity "Referrer headers" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the provided context, it is a component of web protocols (T1071.001) used by adversaries for communication. Specifically, adversaries may conceal command and control data within the Referer header field of HTTP/S packets to mimic normal web traffic and avoid detection. This method is employed by numerous threat groups, including APT28, Lazarus Group, and MuddyWater, to blend malicious communications with legitimate network activity.
4418.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Referrer headers, a technique for defense evasion (tactic), involves adversaries manipulating the HTTP Referer header to conceal the origin of malicious web requests. This can be used to bypass security controls that track request sources, making malicious traffic appear to come from a trusted or benign site within the network.

4420.name: Havij
4420.profile: [profile]Havij is an automated SQL injection tool with a graphical user interface, used for web vulnerability scanning and exploitation. It is attributed to the RocketKitten intrusion set and is noted for its Iranian origin. The tool is commonly used for automated SQL injection and vulnerability assessments against web applications and databases, as referenced in profiles of other tools like Matryoshka RAT and MPKBot.
4420.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Havij is an automatic SQL injection tool with a graphical user interface, freely distributed by the Iranian security company ITSecTeam. It is used for automated SQL injection attacks and web vulnerability assessments. The tool has been associated with groups including Rocket Kitten and Magic Hound, and is commonly referenced alongside other exploitation tools like SQLMap, Acunetix, Netsparker, and the WSO web shell.

4421.name: Acunetix
4421.profile: [profile]Acunetix is a web vulnerability scanner. It is used by intrusion sets such as RocketKitten and Unit 29155 for reconnaissance, specifically to identify open ports, services, and vulnerabilities in target networks [T1595.002]. Its target platform is web applications and networks.
4421.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Acunetix is a web vulnerability scanner used for legitimate security testing but can be leveraged by threat actors for malicious reconnaissance. Specifically, it has been used by Unit 29155 cyber actors to identify open ports, services, and vulnerabilities on target networks as part of their reconnaissance phase [T1595.002]. Its primary target platform is web applications and associated network infrastructure.

4424.name: Creative Phishing
4424.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may send phishing messages to gain access to victim systems. All forms of phishing are electronically delivered social engineering. Phishing can be targeted, known as spearphishing. In spearphishing, a specific individual, company, or industry will be targeted by the adversary. More generally, adversaries can conduct non-targeted phishing, such as in mass malware spam campaigns.

Adversaries may send victims emails containing malicious attachments or links, typically to execute malicious code on victim systems. Phishing may also be conducted via third-party services, like social media platforms. Phishing may also involve social engineering techniques, such as posing as a trusted source, as well as evasive techniques such as removing or manipulating emails or metadata/headers from compromised accounts being abused to send messages (e.g., [Email Hiding Rules](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1564/008)).(Citation: Microsoft OAuth Spam 2022)(Citation: Palo Alto Unit 42 VBA Infostealer 2014) Another way to accomplish this is by [Email Spoofing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1672)(Citation: Proofpoint-spoof) the identity of the sender, which can be used to fool both the human recipient as well as automated security tools,(Citation: cyberproof-double-bounce) or by including the intended target as a party to an existing email thread that includes malicious files or links (i.e., "thread hijacking").(Citation: phishing-krebs)

Victims may also receive phishing messages that instruct them to call a phone number where they are directed to visit a malicious URL, download malware,(Citation: sygnia Luna Month)(Citation: CISA Remote Monitoring and Management Software) or install adversary-accessible remote management tools onto their computer (i.e., [User Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204)).(Citation: Unit42 Luna Moth)
4424.profile: [profile]Phishing, also known as T1566, is an Initial Access tactic used across multiple platforms. It involves sending electronic messages, such as emails with malicious attachments or links, to trick victims into executing code, often via User Execution. Techniques include spearphishing specific targets, using third-party services like social media, and employing evasive methods like email spoofing, thread hijacking, or manipulating email headers from compromised accounts. It is distinct from T1598 (Phishing for Information), which aims to gather data. Associated groups include RocketKitten, Sea Turtle, and Kimsuky.
4424.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Creative Phishing is a social engineering attack pattern where adversaries craft deceptive messages to gain access or information. It operates under the Initial Access tactic, typically targeting Windows, macOS, and Linux platforms. The technique involves sending emails with malicious attachments or links, often using spoofed sender identities or hijacking existing email threads to appear legitimate. It can also be conducted via phone calls (vishing) where victims are directed to call a number to divulge credentials or download malware, employing urgent pretexts and impersonation of trusted entities to bypass security.

4425.name: Simple Custom Malware
4425.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may develop malware and malware components that can be used during targeting. Building malicious software can include the development of payloads, droppers, post-compromise tools, backdoors (including backdoored images), packers, C2 protocols, and the creation of infected removable media. Adversaries may develop malware to support their operations, creating a means for maintaining control of remote machines, evading defenses, and executing post-compromise behaviors.(Citation: Mandiant APT1)(Citation: Kaspersky Sofacy)(Citation: ActiveMalwareEnergy)(Citation: FBI Flash FIN7 USB)

During malware development, adversaries may intentionally include indicators aligned with other known actors in order to mislead attribution by defenders.(Citation: Olympic Destroyer)(Citation: Risky Bulletin Threat actor impersonates FSB APT)(Citation: GamaCopy organization)

As with legitimate development efforts, different skill sets may be required for developing malware. The skills needed may be located in-house, or may need to be contracted out. Use of a contractor may be considered an extension of that adversary's malware development capabilities, provided the adversary plays a role in shaping requirements and maintains a degree of exclusivity to the malware.

Some aspects of malware development, such as C2 protocol development, may require adversaries to obtain additional infrastructure. For example, malware developed that will communicate with Twitter for C2, may require use of [Web Services](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1583/006).(Citation: FireEye APT29)
4425.profile: [profile]The entity "Simple Custom Malware" aligns with MITRE ATT&CK technique T1587.001 (Develop Capabilities: Malware), under the Resource Development tactic for multiple platforms. This involves adversaries building malicious software, including payloads, droppers, backdoors, and custom command and control protocols, to support their operations. The development process can incorporate false indicators for misattribution and may utilize contracted skills or require supporting infrastructure like web services. The intrusion-set RocketKitten is a directly connected group associated with this activity.[/profile]
4425.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Simple Custom Malware is a technique where adversaries develop tailored malicious software to support their operations. This involves creating payloads, droppers, backdoors, and command-and-control protocols. The malware is often designed to evade defenses and maintain control over compromised systems, and may be uploaded to adversary-controlled or third-party infrastructure for deployment. Development can be done in-house or through contractors, and adversaries may intentionally include false indicators to mislead attribution.

4439.name: Remote Access
4439.uncertain_mes:
An adversary may use legitimate remote access tools to establish an interactive command and control channel within a network. Remote access tools create a session between two trusted hosts through a graphical interface, a command line interaction, a protocol tunnel via development or management software, or hardware-level access such as KVM (Keyboard, Video, Mouse) over IP solutions. Desktop support software (usually graphical interface) and remote management software (typically command line interface) allow a user to control a computer remotely as if they are a local user inheriting the user or software permissions. This software is commonly used for troubleshooting, software installation, and system management.(Citation: Symantec Living off the Land)(Citation: CrowdStrike 2015 Global Threat Report)(Citation: CrySyS Blog TeamSpy) Adversaries may similarly abuse response features included in EDR and other defensive tools that enable remote access.

Remote access tools may be installed and used post-compromise as an alternate communications channel for redundant access or to establish an interactive remote desktop session with the target system. It may also be used as a malware component to establish a reverse connection or back-connect to a service or adversary-controlled system.

Installation of many remote access tools may also include persistence (e.g., the software's installation routine creates a [Windows Service](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1543/003)). Remote access modules/features may also exist as part of otherwise existing software (e.g., Google Chrome’s Remote Desktop).(Citation: Google Chrome Remote Desktop)(Citation: Chrome Remote Desktop)
4439.profile: [profile]Remote Access Tools, identified as T1219 within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, is a Command and Control technique used across Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves the abuse of legitimate software like desktop support or remote management tools to establish interactive sessions, creating graphical or command-line channels that inherit user permissions for control. These tools are often installed post-compromise to provide redundant access, can be embedded within malware for reverse connections, and their installation routines may create persistence mechanisms like Windows services. Associated threat groups include Carbanak, MuddyWater, and FIN7.[/profile]
4439.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Remote Access" is a general concept, not a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on retrieved data, it encompasses the adversarial use of legitimate tools and services to establish interactive command and control. This includes software tools (like remote desktop or management software) and hardware (like KVM-over-IP devices) to create sessions, often post-compromise, for persistent control, lateral movement, and redundant access, frequently abusing features in administrative or defensive software. Associated MITRE techniques include Remote Access Software (T1219), Remote Services (T1021), and External Remote Services (T1133).

4443.profile: [profile]wsc.vbs is a VBScript malware component associated with the Rocket Kitten group, responsible for installing persistence by creating a "WinDefender" shortcut in the startup folder using a Notepad icon and enabling keylogging via the SetWindowsHookExW API. It is directly connected to WoolGoldfish and Woolger malware families.
4443.profile_without_enhance: [profile]wsc.vbs, also known as Woolger, is a malware attributed to the Rocket Kitten intrusion set. It is a VBS script that installs persistence by creating a startup folder shortcut named "WinDefender" with a Notepad icon and enables keylogging via the SetWindowsHookExW API. It operates within an infrastructure using FTP for data transfer and communicates with C&C servers. The malware is directly connected to the WoolGoldfish and Ghole variants and primarily targets Windows systems.[/profile]

4444.profile: [profile]WoolGoldfish malware, also known as nmass malware, is a .NET-based remote access trojan (RAT) that targets Mongolia. It is attributed to the RocketKitten intrusion set and shares similarities with older campaigns by Operation LagTime or Tonto Team. Key technical behaviors include being delivered via a Royal Road v7 document lure about COVID-19 in Russia, which drops an initial executable (os03C2.tmp) to install a backdoor. Its target platform is Windows, leveraging .NET frameworks. Related malware includes Ghole and wsc.vbs, and it uses decoy documents fake-signed by A. Amarsaikhan for initial compromise.[/profile]
4444.profile_without_enhance: [profile]WoolGoldfish is a malware, also known as Woolger, attributed to the RocketKitten group. Its key TTPs include using the SetWindowsHookExW API for keylogging, the SetTimer API for timer-based execution, and Persistence via Startup Folder by creating a "WinDefender" shortcut. It exfiltrates data via FTP Upload to a C&C server (singlehop as32475) using a custom Uploadtocnc function. The target platform is Windows, and it is related to the Ghole malware and the wsc.vbs persistence installer.

4445.name: Macro Exploitation
4445.profile: [profile]Macro Exploitation is a technique where adversaries embed malicious code within documents (like Microsoft Office files) that support macros, exploiting the trust in these legitimate applications to execute code when a user opens the file. This method is commonly used for initial execution, often delivered via spearphishing, and is associated with groups like RocketKitten. It falls under the Execution tactic and primarily targets Windows and macOS platforms, leveraging the user's action to enable arbitrary code execution.
4445.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Macro Exploitation is a technique where adversaries embed malicious macros within documents, such as Microsoft Office files, to execute arbitrary code when a user enables the content. It falls under the Execution tactic and targets Windows, macOS, and Linux platforms. The attack typically involves social engineering to trick users into opening a document and enabling macros, which then runs payloads for initial access or further compromise. This method is commonly delivered via spearphishing attachments.

4446.name: Cover Their Tracks
4446.profile: [profile]Cover Their Tracks is a technique where adversaries hide artifacts of their activity to evade detection. They may abuse built-in operating system features to conceal files, directories, or user accounts, or create isolated environments like virtual machines to avoid security tools. This behavior is associated with the RocketKitten intrusion set and the Ghole malware, aligning with the broader MITRE ATT&CK technique "Hide Artifacts" (T1564) under the Defense Evasion tactic.[/profile]
4446.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Cover Their Tracks is a technique where adversaries attempt to hide artifacts associated with their malicious activities to evade detection. This can involve abusing operating system features designed to conceal files, directories, or user accounts. Adversaries may also create isolated computing environments, such as through virtualization, to hide their actions from common security tools.

4447.name: Operation Woolen-Goldfish
4447.profile: [profile]Operation Woolen-Goldfish is a campaign name, not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. The provided neighbor info links it to the RocketKitten intrusion-set. Retrieved info contains unrelated ATT&CK techniques (T1061, T1113, T1001.001) describing general adversary behaviors like GUI interaction, screen capture, and data obfuscation for C2, but these are not specific to this campaign. The profile is therefore based solely on the link to the RocketKitten threat group.[/profile]
4447.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Operation Woolen-Goldfish is a technique for which standard MITRE ATT&CK details are not available. Based on retrieved information, it is associated with the deprecated technique Graphical User Interface (T1061), which involves interacting with a system's GUI via remote sessions like Remote Desktop Protocol to search for information and execute files. It is also linked to Screen Capture (T1113), where adversaries use tools or native utilities like `CopyFromScreen` to take screenshots, and to Junk Data (T1001.001), which involves adding meaningless characters to command and control traffic to hinder detection.

4460.name: SetWindowsHookExW API
4460.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may interact with the native OS application programming interface (API) to execute behaviors. Native APIs provide a controlled means of calling low-level OS services within the kernel, such as those involving hardware/devices, memory, and processes.(Citation: NT API Windows)(Citation: Linux Kernel API) These native APIs are leveraged by the OS during system boot (when other system components are not yet initialized) as well as carrying out tasks and requests during routine operations. Adversaries may abuse these OS API functions as a means of executing behaviors. Similar to [Command and Scripting Interpreter](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059), the native API and its hierarchy of interfaces provide mechanisms to interact with and utilize various components of a victimized system. Native API functions (such as NtCreateProcess) may be directed invoked via system calls / syscalls, but these features are also often exposed to user-mode applications via interfaces and libraries.(Citation: OutFlank System Calls)(Citation: CyberBit System Calls)(Citation: MDSec System Calls) For example, functions such as the Windows API CreateProcess() or GNU fork() will allow programs and scripts to start other processes.(Citation: Microsoft CreateProcess)(Citation: GNU Fork) This may allow API callers to execute a binary, run a CLI command, load modules, etc. as thousands of similar API functions exist for various system operations.(Citation: Microsoft Win32)(Citation: LIBC)(Citation: GLIBC) Higher level software frameworks, such as Microsoft .NET and macOS Cocoa, are also available to interact with native APIs. These frameworks typically provide language wrappers/abstractions to API functionalities and are designed for ease-of-use/portability of code.(Citation: Microsoft NET)(Citation: Apple Core Services)(Citation: MACOS Cocoa)(Citation: macOS Foundation) Adversaries may use assembly to directly or in-directly invoke syscalls in an attempt to subvert defensive sensors and detection signatures such as user mode API-hooks.(Citation: Redops Syscalls) Adversaries may also attempt to tamper with sensors and defensive tools associated with API monitoring, such as unhooking monitored functions via [Disable or Modify Tools](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1562/001).
4460.profile: [profile]SetWindowsHookExW API is a specific Windows Native API function used for Hooking (T1179) within the Execution tactic on Windows platforms. It allows adversaries to install hook procedures that intercept and execute code in response to system events like keystrokes or messages, enabling behaviors such as credential theft via Credential API Hooking (T1056.004) and providing persistence. Malware like WoolGoldfish may abuse this API to load malicious code into other processes, masking execution and accessing process memory. Adversaries may also use it to subvert API-hook based detection by directly invoking syscalls.[/profile]
4460.profile_without_enhance: [profile]SetWindowsHookExW API is a specific Windows API function used for Hooking (T1179) under the Execution tactic on Windows platforms. It installs an application-defined hook procedure into a hook chain, enabling adversaries to intercept and monitor system events like keystrokes and mouse inputs. This technique is commonly abused to inject malicious code into another process's context for stealthy execution, persistence, and credential access by capturing authentication data from API calls.

4462.name: Uploadtocnc Function
4462.profile: [profile]The entity "Uploadtocnc Function" is a specific function within the WoolGoldfish malware, used for data exfiltration. Its primary technical mechanic involves uploading stolen data to a cloud storage service, such as Dropbox or Google Docs, to blend exfiltration traffic with legitimate network communications and avoid detection by command and control channel monitoring.[/profile]

4463.name: FTP Upload
4463.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may upload malware to third-party or adversary controlled infrastructure to make it accessible during targeting. Malicious software can include payloads, droppers, post-compromise tools, backdoors, and a variety of other malicious content. Adversaries may upload malware to support their operations, such as making a payload available to a victim network to enable [Ingress Tool Transfer](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1105) by placing it on an Internet accessible web server.

Malware may be placed on infrastructure that was previously purchased/rented by the adversary ([Acquire Infrastructure](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1583)) or was otherwise compromised by them ([Compromise Infrastructure](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1584)). Malware can also be staged on web services, such as GitHub or Pastebin; hosted on the InterPlanetary File System (IPFS), where decentralized content storage makes the removal of malicious files difficult; or saved on the blockchain as smart contracts, which are resilient against takedowns that would affect traditional infrastructure.(Citation: Volexity Ocean Lotus November 2020)(Citation: Talos IPFS 2022)(Citation: Guardio Etherhiding 2023)(Citation: Bleeping Computer Binance Smart Chain 2023)

Adversaries may upload backdoored files, such as software packages, application binaries, virtual machine images, or container images, to third-party software stores, package libraries, extension marketplaces, or repositories (ex: GitHub, CNET, AWS Community AMIs, Docker Hub, PyPi, NPM).(Citation: Datadog Security Labs Malicious PyPi Packages 2024) By chance encounter, victims may directly download/install these backdoored files via [User Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204). Masquerading, including typo-squatting legitimate software, may increase the chance of users mistakenly executing these files.
4463.profile: [profile]FTP Upload is a technique for data exfiltration or tool transfer, identified as T1048.001 under the Exfiltration tactic. It operates across multiple platforms, leveraging the FTP protocol to covertly steal data or stage malicious tools by blending file transfers with normal network traffic, often using common utilities like the FTP command-line client. This method is distinct from general upload techniques as it specifically utilizes the FTP application layer protocol.

4464.name: Persistence via Startup Folder
4464.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may achieve persistence by adding a program to a startup folder or referencing it with a Registry run key. Adding an entry to the "run keys" in the Registry or startup folder will cause the program referenced to be executed when a user logs in.(Citation: Microsoft Run Key) These programs will be executed under the context of the user and will have the account's associated permissions level. The following run keys are created by default on Windows systems: * HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run * HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunOnce * HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run * HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunOnce Run keys may exist under multiple hives.(Citation: Microsoft Wow6432Node 2018)(Citation: Malwarebytes Wow6432Node 2016) The HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunOnceEx is also available but is not created by default on Windows Vista and newer. Registry run key entries can reference programs directly or list them as a dependency.(Citation: Microsoft Run Key) For example, it is possible to load a DLL at logon using a "Depend" key with RunOnceEx: reg add HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunOnceEx\0001\Depend /v 1 /d "C:\temp\evil[.]dll" (Citation: Oddvar Moe RunOnceEx Mar 2018) Placing a program within a startup folder will also cause that program to execute when a user logs in. There is a startup folder location for individual user accounts as well as a system-wide startup folder that will be checked regardless of which user account logs in. The startup folder path for the current user is C:\Users\\[Username]\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup. The startup folder path for all users is C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\StartUp. The following Registry keys can be used to set startup folder items for persistence: * HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Explorer\User Shell Folders * HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Explorer\Shell Folders * HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Explorer\Shell Folders * HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Explorer\User Shell Folders The following Registry keys can control automatic startup of services during boot: * HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunServicesOnce * HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunServicesOnce * HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunServices * HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunServices Using policy settings to specify startup programs creates corresponding values in either of two Registry keys: * HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\Explorer\Run * HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\Explorer\Run Programs listed in the load value of the registry key HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Windows run automatically for the currently logged-on user. By default, the multistring BootExecute value of the registry key HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\System\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager is set to autocheck autochk *. This value causes Windows, at startup, to check the file-system integrity of the hard disks if the system has been shut down abnormally. Adversaries can add other programs or processes to this registry value which will automatically launch at boot. Adversaries can use these configuration locations to execute malware, such as remote access tools, to maintain persistence through system reboots. Adversaries may also use [Masquerading](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1036) to make the Registry entries look as if they are associated with legitimate programs.
4464.profile: [profile]Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder, identified as MITRE ATT&CK T1547.001, is a Persistence technique for Windows platforms. It achieves persistence by adding malicious programs to startup folders or referencing them via Registry run keys, causing automatic execution upon user logon. Key paths include the per-user startup folder (C:\Users\[Username]\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup) and the all-users folder (C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\StartUp). Primary Registry keys leveraged are HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run and HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run, among others like RunOnce and RunOnceEx, which can reference executables or DLLs directly. Adversaries often use Masquerading to disguise these entries as legitimate.[/profile]
4464.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Persistence via Startup Folder is a technique for establishing persistence on Windows systems, aligning with the MITRE ATT&CK ID T1547.001 under the Persistence tactic. It operates by placing a malicious executable or shortcut within specific startup folders, causing it to execute automatically upon user login. The primary paths are C:\Users\[Username]\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup for the current user and C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\StartUp for all users. Execution occurs under the context of the logged-in user with their associated permissions, maintaining access through system reboots.

4476.name: menuPass
4476.uncertain_mes:
[menuPass](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0045) is a threat group that has been active since at least 2006. Individual members of [menuPass](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0045) are known to have acted in association with the Chinese Ministry of State Security's (MSS) Tianjin State Security Bureau and worked for the Huaying Haitai Science and Technology Development Company.(Citation: DOJ APT10 Dec 2018)(Citation: District Court of NY APT10 Indictment December 2018)

[menuPass](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0045) has targeted healthcare, defense, aerospace, finance, maritime, biotechnology, energy, and government sectors globally, with an emphasis on Japanese organizations. In 2016 and 2017, the group is known to have targeted managed IT service providers (MSPs), manufacturing and mining companies, and a university.(Citation: Palo Alto menuPass Feb 2017)(Citation: Crowdstrike CrowdCast Oct 2013)(Citation: FireEye Poison Ivy)(Citation: PWC Cloud Hopper April 2017)(Citation: FireEye APT10 April 2017)(Citation: DOJ APT10 Dec 2018)(Citation: District Court of NY APT10 Indictment December 2018)
4476.profile: [profile]menuPass, also known as APT10, Stone Panda, Bronze Riverside, Red Apollo, Potassium, Cicada, Hogfish, and CVNX, is a Chinese state-sponsored threat group active since at least 2006, with members linked to the Ministry of State Security's Tianjin State Security Bureau and the Huaying Haitai Science and Technology Development Company. Its arsenal includes the use and modification of tools like Impacket, Mimikatz, pwdump, PowerSploit, and Csvde, employing techniques such as base64 and XOR obfuscation, file compression with TAR/RAR, and encryption before exfiltration. The group has globally targeted sectors including healthcare, defense, aerospace, finance, maritime, biotechnology, energy, and government, with a particular emphasis on Japanese organizations and managed IT service providers.[/profile]
4476.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The most likely standardized APT group name is APT10, also known as menuPass, Stone Panda, Cloud Hopper, POTASSIUM, Bronze Riverside, Red Apollo, and Hogfish. Key TTPs involve spear-phishing with malicious Office macros, credential compromise from web browsers, memory obfuscation, and strategic supply-chain attacks against Managed Service Providers, while leveraging open-source tools like Impacket, Mimikatz, and PowerSploit. The group is a Chinese state-sponsored cyber espionage actor, attributed to contractors for China's Ministry of State Security and believed to be linked to its Tianjin Bureau. 4477.name: Redleaves
4477.uncertain_mes: [RedLeaves](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0153) is a malware family used by [menuPass](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0045). The code overlaps with [PlugX](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0013) and may be based upon the open source tool Trochilus. (Citation: PWC Cloud Hopper Technical Annex April 2017) (Citation: FireEye APT10 April 2017)
4477.profile: [profile]RedLeaves is a malware family used by the menuPass group (also known as Stone Panda). Its code overlaps with PlugX and may be based on the open-source RAT Trochilus. Key technical behaviors include being loaded and decoded by a loader within a legitimate application, then injecting itself into a process like Internet Explorer to run. It has been observed since 2016 in targeted email attachments for information leakage operations.
4477.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Redleaves, also known as a variant of Himawari, is a malware attributed to the Stone Panda (APT31, Gallium) intrusion set. It is a second-stage backdoor based on the open-source Trochilus RAT, sharing structural similarities with droppers for retooled Gh0st RAT and adopting capabilities from PlugX. Its technical behaviors include process injection (e.g., into Internet Explorer) for stealth, lateral movement, and data exfiltration via custom command-and-control infrastructure using specific URL patterns. It employs obfuscation techniques like XOR encryption (with keys 0x40 and 0x9D) and base64 encoding for communication. The malware primarily targets Windows systems and has been used in cyberespionage campaigns since at least 2016.[/profile]
