4480.name: Exploit (Office Macro)
4480.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may abuse the Microsoft Office "Office Test" Registry key to obtain persistence on a compromised system. An Office Test Registry location exists that allows a user to specify an arbitrary DLL that will be executed every time an Office application is started. This Registry key is thought to be used by Microsoft to load DLLs for testing and debugging purposes while developing Office applications. This Registry key is not created by default during an Office installation.(Citation: Hexacorn Office Test)(Citation: Palo Alto Office Test Sofacy) There exist user and global Registry keys for the Office Test feature, such as: * HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Office test\Special\Perf * HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\Software\Microsoft\Office test\Special\Perf Adversaries may add this Registry key and specify a malicious DLL that will be executed whenever an Office application, such as Word or Excel, is started.
4480.profile: [profile]Office Test, identified as T1137.002 within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, is a persistence technique under the Persistence tactic targeting the Windows platform. It involves abusing the Microsoft Office "Office Test" Registry key, which is not created by default, to specify a malicious DLL that automatically executes each time an Office application like Word or Excel starts. This mechanism is exploited by adversaries such as APT28 and menuPass to maintain access to compromised systems.
4480.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Exploit (Office Macro) is a technique within the broader T1203: Exploitation for Client Execution, falling under the Execution tactic and targeting Windows platforms. It involves adversaries embedding malicious Visual Basic for Applications (VBA) macros within Microsoft Office documents (like Word or Excel files) delivered via phishing. Execution requires the user to open the document and enable macros, which then runs arbitrary code to compromise the system. This method is commonly used by threat groups such as APT28, MuddyWater, and APT29.

4481.name: process hollowing
4481.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may inject malicious code into suspended and hollowed processes in order to evade process-based defenses. Process hollowing is a method of executing arbitrary code in the address space of a separate live process. Process hollowing is commonly performed by creating a process in a suspended state then unmapping/hollowing its memory, which can then be replaced with malicious code. A victim process can be created with native Windows API calls such as CreateProcess, which includes a flag to suspend the processes primary thread. At this point the process can be unmapped using APIs calls such as ZwUnmapViewOfSection or NtUnmapViewOfSection before being written to, realigned to the injected code, and resumed via VirtualAllocEx, WriteProcessMemory, SetThreadContext, then ResumeThread respectively.(Citation: Leitch Hollowing)(Citation: Elastic Process Injection July 2017) This is very similar to [Thread Local Storage](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1055/005) but creates a new process rather than targeting an existing process. This behavior will likely not result in elevated privileges since the injected process was spawned from (and thus inherits the security context) of the injecting process. However, execution via process hollowing may also evade detection from security products since the execution is masked under a legitimate process.
4481.profile: [profile]Process Hollowing, identified as MITRE ATT&CK T1055.012 under the Defense Evasion tactic for Windows, is a process injection technique where a legitimate process is created in a suspended state. Its memory is then unmapped using APIs like `ZwUnmapViewOfSection` and replaced with malicious code via `VirtualAllocEx` and `WriteProcessMemory` before the thread is resumed with `SetThreadContext` and `ResumeThread`. This masks execution under a legitimate process to evade detection, though it typically does not elevate privileges as it inherits the security context of the injector. It has been used by groups including Gorgon Group, Patchwork, and menuPass.
4481.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Process Hollowing (T1055.012) is a Defense Evasion technique for Windows where a legitimate process is created in a suspended state. Its memory is then unmapped using APIs like `NtUnmapViewOfSection` and replaced with malicious code via `VirtualAllocEx` and `WriteProcessMemory`. Execution is resumed with `SetThreadContext` and `ResumeThread`, masking the malicious activity under the guise of a legitimate process to evade detection.

4482.name: mutex creation
4482.profile: [profile]The entity is mapped to MITRE ATT&CK technique T1480.002 (Mutex Creation) under the Execution tactic, applicable to Windows and Linux platforms. Adversaries create unique system mutexes to verify if a system is already compromised by their malware, preventing multiple instances; in Linux, this involves acquiring a lock on a mutex file. Mutex names can be hard-coded or algorithmically generated. The intrusion set menuPass is associated with this technique.
4482.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "mutex creation" aligns with the MITRE ATT&CK technique "Mutex: Mutex" (ID: T1480.002) under the Defense Evasion tactic, applicable to Windows and Linux platforms. It involves adversaries creating a unique system mutex or attempting to lock a mutex file to synchronize processes and verify if a system is already compromised, thereby preventing multiple instances of the same malware from running. Mutex names can be hard-coded or dynamically generated using predictable algorithms.

4483.name: HTTP communication
4483.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may use an existing, legitimate external Web service as a means for sending commands to and receiving output from a compromised system over the Web service channel. Compromised systems may leverage popular websites and social media to host command and control (C2) instructions. Those infected systems can then send the output from those commands back over that Web service channel. The return traffic may occur in a variety of ways, depending on the Web service being utilized. For example, the return traffic may take the form of the compromised system posting a comment on a forum, issuing a pull request to development project, updating a document hosted on a Web service, or by sending a Tweet. 

Popular websites and social media acting as a mechanism for C2 may give a significant amount of cover due to the likelihood that hosts within a network are already communicating with them prior to a compromise. Using common services, such as those offered by Google or Twitter, makes it easier for adversaries to hide in expected noise. Web service providers commonly use SSL/TLS encryption, giving adversaries an added level of protection.
4483.profile: [profile]HTTP communication, designated as T1102.002 under the Command and Control tactic, operates across various platforms by leveraging legitimate external web services for bidirectional command and control. This technique uses channels like social media posts, forum comments, or document updates on services such as Google or Twitter to both send instructions to and receive output from a compromised system, blending into normal encrypted HTTPS traffic to evade detection. It is associated with groups including APT28, Lazarus Group, and MuddyWater. The related intrusion-set menuPass is also noted.[/profile]
4483.profile_without_enhance: [profile]HTTP communication, identified as T1071.001 (Web Protocols) under the Command and Control tactic, operates on Windows, Linux, and macOS. Adversaries use standard HTTP/S traffic to conceal command and control (C2) communications, embedding commands and exfiltrated data within the numerous fields and headers of web packets to blend with normal network traffic and bypass detection. This technique is widely employed by groups like APT28, Lazarus, and Turla.

4485.name: Take screenshots
4485.profile: [profile]Take screenshots, corresponding to MITRE ATT&CK technique T1113 under the Collection tactic, is a method adversaries use to gather information by capturing the contents of a victim's display. This can be achieved through native utilities or API calls like `CopyFromScreen`, `xwd`, or `screencapture`, and is often a feature of remote access tools. The intrusion-set menuPass has been associated with this activity.
4485.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Take screenshots" is a technique for information collection, aligning with MITRE ATT&CK ID T1113 under the Collection tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It involves capturing the contents of a user's display, often using native OS utilities or API calls such as `CopyFromScreen`, `xwd`, or `screencapture`, or as a feature within a remote access tool. This activity is commonly employed by threat actors like APT28, FIN7, and MuddyWater to gather visual data during post-compromise operations.

4486.name: Collect browser usernames and passwords
4486.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may abuse internet browser extensions to establish persistent access to victim systems. Browser extensions or plugins are small programs that can add functionality to and customize aspects of internet browsers. They can be installed directly via a local file or custom URL or through a browser's app store - an official online platform where users can browse, install, and manage extensions for a specific web browser. Extensions generally inherit the web browser's permissions previously granted.(Citation: Wikipedia Browser Extension)(Citation: Chrome Extensions Definition) Malicious extensions can be installed into a browser through malicious app store downloads masquerading as legitimate extensions, through social engineering, or by an adversary that has already compromised a system. Security can be limited on browser app stores, so it may not be difficult for malicious extensions to defeat automated scanners.(Citation: Malicious Chrome Extension Numbers) Depending on the browser, adversaries may also manipulate an extension's update url to install updates from an adversary-controlled server or manipulate the mobile configuration file to silently install additional extensions. Adversaries may abuse how chromium-based browsers load extensions by modifying or replacing the Preferences and/or Secure Preferences files to silently install malicious extensions. When the browser is not running, adversaries can alter these files, ensuring the extension is loaded, granted desired permissions, and will persist in browser sessions. This method does not require user consent and extensions are silently loaded in the background from disk or from the browser's trusted store.(Citation: Pulsedive) Previous to macOS 11, adversaries could silently install browser extensions via the command line using the profiles tool to install malicious .mobileconfig files. In macOS 11+, the use of the profiles tool can no longer install configuration profiles; however, .mobileconfig files can be planted and installed with user interaction.(Citation: xorrior chrome extensions macOS) Once the extension is installed, it can browse to websites in the background, steal all information that a user enters into a browser (including credentials), and be used as an installer for a RAT for persistence.(Citation: Chrome Extension Crypto Miner)(Citation: ICEBRG Chrome Extensions)(Citation: Banker Google Chrome Extension Steals Creds)(Citation: Catch All Chrome Extension) There have also been instances of botnets using a persistent backdoor through malicious Chrome extensions for [Command and Control](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0011).(Citation: Stantinko Botnet)(Citation: Chrome Extension C2 Malware) Adversaries may also use browser extensions to modify browser permissions and components, privacy settings, and other security controls for [Defense Evasion](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0005).(Citation: Browers FriarFox)(Citation: Browser Adrozek)
4486.profile: [profile]The entity "Collect browser usernames and passwords" is a specific technique under the broader MITRE ATT&CK technique "Credentials from Web Browsers" (T1555.003), falling under the Credential Access tactic and applicable to multiple platforms including Windows. It involves extracting saved login data from browser storage, such as by reading encrypted credential database files like Chrome's "Login Data" and using system functions like CryptUnprotectData to decrypt them, enabling adversaries to steal authentication details for reuse. The intrusion-set menuPass has been associated with related browser-focused activities.]
4486.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Collect browser usernames and passwords is a technique aligned with MITRE ATT&CK T1555.003 (Credentials from Web Browsers) under the Credential Access tactic, primarily targeting Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves extracting saved credentials from browser-specific files, such as reading the Chrome 'Login Data' database and using the Windows API CryptUnprotectData for decryption, or searching browser process memory for credential patterns. This enables adversaries to steal authentication details for websites and potentially gain further access.

4487.name: Collect extended system information
4487.uncertain_mes: An adversary may attempt to get detailed information about the operating system and hardware, including version, patches, hotfixes, service packs, and architecture. Adversaries may use this information to shape follow-on behaviors, including whether or not the adversary fully infects the target and/or attempts specific actions. This behavior is distinct from [Local Storage Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1680) which is an adversary's discovery of local drive, disks and/or volumes. Tools such as [Systeminfo](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0096) can be used to gather detailed system information. If running with privileged access, a breakdown of system data can be gathered through the systemsetup configuration tool on macOS. Adversaries may leverage a [Network Device CLI](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/008) on network devices to gather detailed system information (e.g. show version).(Citation: US-CERT-TA18-106A) On ESXi servers, threat actors may gather system information from various esxcli utilities, such as `system hostname get` and `system version get`.(Citation: Crowdstrike Hypervisor Jackpotting Pt 2 2021)(Citation: Varonis) Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) cloud providers such as AWS, GCP, and Azure allow access to instance and virtual machine information via APIs. Successful authenticated API calls can return data such as the operating system platform and status of a particular instance or the model view of a virtual machine.(Citation: Amazon Describe Instance)(Citation: Google Instances Resource)(Citation: Microsoft Virutal Machine API) [System Information Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1082) combined with information gathered from other forms of discovery and reconnaissance can drive payload development and concealment.(Citation: OSX.FairyTale)(Citation: 20 macOS Common Tools and Techniques)
4487.profile: [profile]System Information Discovery, identified as T1082, is a Discovery tactic used across Windows, macOS, Linux, Network, IaaS, and ESXi platforms. It involves gathering detailed OS and hardware data like version, patches, and architecture using tools such as `systeminfo` on Windows, the `systemsetup` command on macOS, CLI commands like `show version` on network devices, `esxcli` utilities on ESXi, and cloud provider APIs. This information is used to shape subsequent attack actions and payload development, and is associated with numerous threat groups including Lazarus Group and APT41.
4487.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Collect extended system information" is a Discovery technique. It involves adversaries gathering detailed operating system and hardware data, including version, patches, architecture, and service packs, to inform subsequent attack actions. This can be achieved using tools like `systeminfo` on Windows, the `systemsetup` tool on macOS with privileged access, or CLI commands like `show version` on network devices. On ESXi servers, actors may use esxcli commands such as `system hostname get`. Cloud instance metadata can also be collected via provider APIs. This information aids in tailoring payloads and evasion strategies.

4488.name: Send, receive, execute commands from C2 server
4488.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may buy, lease, rent, or obtain physical servers that can be used during targeting. Use of servers allows an adversary to stage, launch, and execute an operation. During post-compromise activity, adversaries may utilize servers for various tasks, such as watering hole operations in [Drive-by Compromise](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1189), enabling [Phishing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566) operations, or facilitating [Command and Control](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0011). Instead of compromising a third-party [Server](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1584/004) or renting a [Virtual Private Server](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1583/003), adversaries may opt to configure and run their own servers in support of operations. Free trial periods of cloud servers may also be abused.(Citation: Free Trial PurpleUrchin)(Citation: Freejacked) 

Adversaries may only need a lightweight setup if most of their activities will take place using online infrastructure. Or, they may need to build extensive infrastructure if they want to test, communicate, and control other aspects of their activities on their own systems.(Citation: NYTStuxnet)
4488.profile: [profile]The entity "Send, receive, execute commands from C2 server" is a core Command and Control activity, not a distinct MITRE ATT&CK technique. It describes the fundamental behavior of malware establishing a communication channel with an adversary-controlled server to receive instructions, send data, and execute remote commands. This activity is central to techniques like Application Layer Protocol (T1071) and can utilize various channels, including Web Services (T1102) or specialized protocols like MQTT (T1071.005), to blend with legitimate traffic for stealth. The intrusion-set menuPass is associated with this behavior.[/profile]
4488.profile_without_enhance: [profile]This technique, known as "Send, receive, execute commands from C2 server," is a core Command and Control (TA0011) activity. It involves a compromised host establishing a communication channel with an adversary-controlled server to receive directives, send back data, and execute issued commands. This bidirectional interaction can be implemented over various application layer protocols, including common web services or specialized publish/subscribe protocols like MQTT, to blend with legitimate traffic.

4489.name: monitoring
4489.profile: [profile]The entity 'monitoring' is a general concept, not a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the retrieved context, it is referenced as a security function that adversaries actively seek to bypass. For instance, the technique 'direct volume access' (T1006) is used to circumvent file system monitoring controls on Windows by allowing programs to read and write files directly to a drive's logical volume, analyzing file system data structures to avoid detection by standard monitoring tools.
4489.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity 'monitoring' is a generic term and does not correspond to a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique ID. Based on the retrieved context, it is associated with adversary actions to bypass security tools. Related techniques include Direct Volume Access (T1006), which allows reading/writing files directly from a drive to bypass file system monitoring using tools like NinjaCopy or built-in utilities like vssadmin. Other associated behaviors are adding Junk Data (T1001.001) to C2 traffic to hinder detection and performing Internet Connection Discovery (T1016.001) to check for connectivity before establishing C2. These techniques are used by groups like Scattered Spider, Volt Typhoon, and APT28.

4490.name: blocking
4490.uncertain_mes: An adversary may attempt to block indicators or events typically captured by sensors from being gathered and analyzed. This could include maliciously redirecting(Citation: Microsoft Lamin Sept 2017) or even disabling host-based sensors, such as Event Tracing for Windows (ETW)(Citation: Microsoft About Event Tracing 2018), by tampering settings that control the collection and flow of event telemetry.(Citation: Medium Event Tracing Tampering 2018) These settings may be stored on the system in configuration files and/or in the Registry as well as being accessible via administrative utilities such as [PowerShell](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001) or [Windows Management Instrumentation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1047). For example, adversaries may modify the `File` value in HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\EventLog\Security to hide their malicious actions in a new or different .evtx log file. This action does not require a system reboot and takes effect immediately.(Citation: disable_win_evt_logging) ETW interruption can be achieved multiple ways, however most directly by defining conditions using the [PowerShell](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001) Set-EtwTraceProvider cmdlet or by interfacing directly with the Registry to make alterations. In the case of network-based reporting of indicators, an adversary may block traffic associated with reporting to prevent central analysis. This may be accomplished by many means, such as stopping a local process responsible for forwarding telemetry and/or creating a host-based firewall rule to block traffic to specific hosts responsible for aggregating events, such as security information and event management (SIEM) products. In Linux environments, adversaries may disable or reconfigure log processing tools such as syslog or nxlog to inhibit detection and monitoring capabilities to facilitate follow on behaviors. (Citation: LemonDuck) ESXi also leverages syslog, which can be reconfigured via commands such as `esxcli system syslog config set` and `esxcli system syslog config reload`.(Citation: Google Cloud Threat Intelligence ESXi VIBs 2022)(Citation: Broadcom Configuring syslog on ESXi)
4490.profile: [profile]Indicator Blocking, designated as T1562.006 under the Defense Evasion tactic, targets Windows and Linux platforms. It involves tampering with system settings to block or redirect sensor data, preventing event collection and analysis. Techniques include modifying Windows Registry values like HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\EventLog\Security to redirect logs, using PowerShell's Set-EtwTraceProvider to disable Event Tracing for Windows (ETW), and reconfiguring Linux syslog or ESXi logging via commands like esxcli system syslog config set. Adversaries may also stop telemetry processes or create host firewall rules to block traffic to security monitoring systems like SIEMs. This technique has been associated with groups like APT41 and APT5.
4490.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity 'blocking' is a technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, identified as T1562.001 'Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Tools', under the Defense Evasion tactic for Windows platforms. It involves adversaries actively preventing the collection of security telemetry by tampering with or disabling host-based sensors like Event Tracing for Windows (ETW). This is achieved by maliciously altering system settings stored in configuration files or the Windows Registry, often using administrative utilities such as PowerShell or Windows Management Instrumentation to execute commands that interrupt data flow. The technique can also extend to blocking network-based reporting by stopping local telemetry processes or creating host firewall rules to prevent event forwarding to central analysis systems like SIEMs.

4491.name: search activity
4491.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may employ various user activity checks to detect and avoid virtualization and analysis environments. This may include changing behaviors based on the results of checks for the presence of artifacts indicative of a virtual machine environment (VME) or sandbox. If the adversary detects a VME, they may alter their malware to disengage from the victim or conceal the core functions of the implant. They may also search for VME artifacts before dropping secondary or additional payloads. Adversaries may use the information learned from [Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1497) during automated discovery to shape follow-on behaviors.(Citation: Deloitte Environment Awareness)

Adversaries may search for user activity on the host based on variables such as the speed/frequency of mouse movements and clicks (Citation: Sans Virtual Jan 2016) , browser history, cache, bookmarks, or number of files in common directories such as home or the desktop. Other methods may rely on specific user interaction with the system before the malicious code is activated, such as waiting for a document to close before activating a macro (Citation: Unit 42 Sofacy Nov 2018) or waiting for a user to double click on an embedded image to activate.(Citation: FireEye FIN7 April 2017)
4491.profile: [profile]User Activity Based Checks (T1497.002) is a Defense Evasion technique for Windows, macOS, and Linux. It involves malware checking for signs of user interaction, such as mouse movement speed, browser history, or file counts in common directories, to detect sandboxes or virtual environments. It may also wait for specific user actions, like closing a document or double-clicking an image, before activating its malicious payload. Groups like DarkHotel and FIN7 have been associated with this technique.[/profile]
4491.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "search activity" is a reconnaissance technique where adversaries gather information about victims to enable future targeting. This activity involves querying various sources such as search engines, open websites, victim-owned websites, and closed sources to collect data like employee details, network information, or operational intelligence. The gathered information can then be used to shape subsequent attack phases, including establishing resources or gaining initial access.

4492.name: damage assessment
4492.profile: [profile]Damage Assessment is a post-compromise activity where adversaries evaluate the impact and success of their intrusion. It is associated with the intrusion set menuPass. This process involves analyzing compromised systems to determine the extent of data accessed, exfiltrated, or altered, and to assess whether operational objectives were met, often to inform subsequent actions or cover tracks.[/profile]

Based on the provided context, it appears to be a concept related to adversary actions following an attack. The retrieved information describes techniques adversaries use to cause denial of service or resource exhaustion, such as bandwidth hijacking (T1496.002) to leverage victim network resources, adding junk data to C2 traffic (T1001.001) to hinder analysis, and exploiting application vulnerabilities (T1499.004) to crash systems. These actions can be part of an adversary's process to evaluate the impact and effectiveness of their attacks, though the specific technical mechanics for "damage assessment" itself are not detailed in the provided data.

4494.name: Obfuscation (XOR 0x40)
4494.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may obfuscate command and control traffic to make it more difficult to detect.(Citation: Bitdefender FunnyDream Campaign November 2020) Command and control (C2) communications are hidden (but not necessarily encrypted) in an attempt to make the content more difficult to discover or decipher and to make the communication less conspicuous and hide commands from being seen. This encompasses many methods, such as adding junk data to protocol traffic, using steganography, or impersonating legitimate protocols.
4494.profile: [profile]Obfuscation (XOR 0x40) is a specific data obfuscation technique (T1001) under the Command and Control tactic, used to hide C2 traffic by applying a simple XOR cipher with the key 0x40. This method transforms plaintext into a weak ciphertext without strong encryption, making the communication less conspicuous. It is associated with malware like Redleaves and ptl.aym and has been used by groups such as Gamaredon Group. The technique is a subset of broader obfuscation and custom cryptographic protocol methods.[/profile]
4494.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Obfuscation (XOR 0x40) is a specific data obfuscation technique where adversaries apply an XOR operation with the key 0x40 to data, such as files or network traffic, to hide its contents. This method is a simple form of encryption or encoding used to evade signature-based detection by making the data appear as non-plaintext. It is commonly employed to obfuscate collected data prior to exfiltration or to conceal command and control communications, representing a weak, custom cryptographic implementation.

4500.name: Hogfish
4500.uncertain_mes:
[menuPass](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0045) is a threat group that has been active since at least 2006. Individual members of [menuPass](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0045) are known to have acted in association with the Chinese Ministry of State Security's (MSS) Tianjin State Security Bureau and worked for the Huaying Haitai Science and Technology Development Company.(Citation: DOJ APT10 Dec 2018)(Citation: District Court of NY APT10 Indictment December 2018)

[menuPass](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0045) has targeted healthcare, defense, aerospace, finance, maritime, biotechnology, energy, and government sectors globally, with an emphasis on Japanese organizations. In 2016 and 2017, the group is known to have targeted managed IT service providers (MSPs), manufacturing and mining companies, and a university.(Citation: Palo Alto menuPass Feb 2017)(Citation: Crowdstrike CrowdCast Oct 2013)(Citation: FireEye Poison Ivy)(Citation: PWC Cloud Hopper April 2017)(Citation: FireEye APT10 April 2017)(Citation: DOJ APT10 Dec 2018)(Citation: District Court of NY APT10 Indictment December 2018)
4500.profile: [profile]Hogfish, also known as menuPass, APT10, BRONZE RIVERSIDE, RED APOLLO, POTASSIUM, STONE PANDA, CVNX, and CICADA, is a cyber espionage group active since at least 2006. It has been attributed to actors associated with the Chinese Ministry of State Security's Tianjin State Security Bureau and the Huaying Haitai Science and Technology Development Company. The group's known TTPs include using tools like csvde.exe to export Active Directory data. It has globally targeted sectors such as healthcare, defense, aerospace, finance, maritime, biotechnology, energy, and government, with a particular emphasis on Japanese organizations and managed IT service providers. Its primary motivation is believed to be state-sponsored intelligence gathering.
4500.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The most likely standardized APT group name is APT10, also known as menuPass, Stone Panda, Cloud Hopper, POTASSIUM, Bronze Riverside, Hogfish, Red Apollo, and CVNX. Key TTPs involve spear-phishing, credential compromise, file compression and encryption before exfiltration, and sophisticated supply-chain attacks via managed IT service providers. The group is a Chinese state-sponsored cyber espionage actor, attributed to contractors for China's Ministry of State Security. 4506.name: koadic
4506.uncertain_mes:
Hunting Koadic Pt. 2 - JARM Fingerprinting
A year ago, I looked into Koadic C2, a post-exploitation tool used by APTs and Pentesters alike.
At the time, I was able to fingerprint all non-fronted Koadic C2 servers across the internet, due to mismatches in it’s 404 page, where it fails to make the server look like a benign Apache web server.
4506.profile: [profile]Koadic, also known as Koadic C2, is a post-exploitation tool used by APT groups like APT28 (MenuPass) and Stone Panda. It operates as a command and control (C2) framework, where its servers can be fingerprinted due to mismatches in its 404 error page that fail to properly mimic a benign Apache web server. It executes shell commands via %COMSPEC%, using parent processes like rundll32.exe, regsvr32.exe, and wmic.exe, and can be configured to run over HTTPS. Its primary target platform is Windows.[/profile]
4506.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Koadic, a post-exploitation tool and command-and-control (C2) framework, is used by APT groups like APT28 and Stone Panda, as well as pentesters. Its key technical behaviors include executing shell commands via %COMSPEC% using parent processes like rundll32.exe, regsvr32.exe, and wmic.exe, and directing output to temporary files. The framework can be configured to run C2 servers over HTTPS, and its non-fronted servers can be fingerprinted via JARM due to identifiable mismatches in their 404 error pages, which fail to properly mimic a benign Apache web server.

4519.name: Custom Tools
4519.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may use a custom cryptographic protocol or algorithm to hide command and control traffic. A simple scheme, such as XOR-ing the plaintext with a fixed key, will produce a very weak ciphertext.

Custom encryption schemes may vary in sophistication. Analysis and reverse engineering of malware samples may be enough to discover the algorithm and encryption key used.

Some adversaries may also attempt to implement their own version of a well-known cryptographic algorithm instead of using a known implementation library, which may lead to unintentional errors. (Citation: F-Secure Cosmicduke)
4519.profile: [profile]Custom Cryptographic Protocol, also known as T1024, is a Command and Control technique under the Exfiltration tactic. It operates across Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. Adversaries implement custom encryption algorithms, such as simple XOR operations with a fixed key, to obfuscate C2 traffic. These bespoke schemes can vary in sophistication and may include flawed re-implementations of known algorithms. The technique is used by groups like menuPass, and analysis or reverse engineering of malware can often reveal the encryption key and algorithm.[/profile]
4519.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Custom Tools" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique; it is a general concept. Based on the retrieved context, custom tools are adversary-developed software used for various malicious purposes. These purposes include implementing custom cryptographic protocols (like XOR-based ciphers) for command and control, creating custom archival methods for data compression and encryption prior to exfiltration, and performing specific offensive actions such as credential dumping where standard tools may be insufficient or detectable.

4520.name: Anonymization
4520.profile: [profile]Anonymization is a technique used by adversaries to obfuscate collected data prior to exfiltration, often to evade detection. This is achieved by compressing and/or encrypting the data using utilities like 7zip, RAR, or ZIP, third-party libraries, or custom methods such as XOR encryption or custom compression algorithms. The intrusion-set menuPass has been associated with this behavior. The technique facilitates data portability and minimizes network footprint during the exfiltration process.[/profile]
4520.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Anonymization is a technique used by adversaries to obfuscate collected data prior to exfiltration, primarily to evade detection and minimize network footprint. This is achieved by compressing data using common utilities like 7zip, RAR, or ZIP, or by employing encryption, including custom methods like XOR or stream ciphers. These actions are performed separately from the exfiltration channel.

4521.name: RC4 Encryption
4521.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may compromise a network device’s encryption capability in order to bypass encryption that would otherwise protect data communications. (Citation: Cisco Synful Knock Evolution)

Encryption can be used to protect transmitted network traffic to maintain its confidentiality (protect against unauthorized disclosure) and integrity (protect against unauthorized changes). Encryption ciphers are used to convert a plaintext message to ciphertext and can be computationally intensive to decipher without the associated decryption key. Typically, longer keys increase the cost of cryptanalysis, or decryption without the key.

Adversaries can compromise and manipulate devices that perform encryption of network traffic. For example, through behaviors such as [Modify System Image](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1601), [Reduce Key Space](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1600/001), and [Disable Crypto Hardware](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1600/002), an adversary can negatively effect and/or eliminate a device’s ability to securely encrypt network traffic. This poses a greater risk of unauthorized disclosure and may help facilitate data manipulation, Credential Access, or Collection efforts. (Citation: Cisco Blog Legacy Device Attacks)
4521.profile: [profile]RC4 Encryption is a symmetric encryption algorithm, referenced under MITRE ATT&CK ID T1573.001 for Encrypted Channel, applicable across multiple platforms. It uses the same key for both encryption and decryption of data. Adversaries employ RC4 to obfuscate command and control traffic or to exfiltrate data over non-C2 protocols, often implementing it manually to add a custom encryption layer atop standard protocols. It is a known cipher listed alongside AES and DES for these purposes.
4521.profile_without_enhance: [profile]RC4 Encryption is a symmetric encryption algorithm (T1573.001) used in the Command and Control tactic. It operates across multiple platforms, including Windows, Linux, and macOS. Technically, adversaries employ this known algorithm to manually encrypt C2 or exfiltration traffic, often adding a custom encryption layer atop standard protocols like HTTPS or HTTP. It is a shared-key cipher, requiring pre-arranged key exchange, and is commonly implemented alongside other algorithms like AES or within multi-layer encryption schemes.

4523.name: In-Memory Module Loading
4523.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may attempt to access credential material stored in the process memory of the Local Security Authority Subsystem Service (LSASS). After a user logs on, the system generates and stores a variety of credential materials in LSASS process memory. These credential materials can be harvested by an administrative user or SYSTEM and used to conduct [Lateral Movement](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0008) using [Use Alternate Authentication Material](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1550). As well as in-memory techniques, the LSASS process memory can be dumped from the target host and analyzed on a local system. For example, on the target host use procdump: * procdump -ma lsass.exe lsass_dump Locally, mimikatz can be run using: * sekurlsa::Minidump lsassdump.dmp * sekurlsa::logonPasswords Built-in Windows tools such as `comsvcs.dll` can also be used: * rundll32.exe C:\Windows\System32\comsvcs.dll MiniDump PID lsass.dmp full(Citation: Volexity Exchange Marauder March 2021)(Citation: Symantec Attacks Against Government Sector) Similar to [Image File Execution Options Injection](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1546/012), the silent process exit mechanism can be abused to create a memory dump of `lsass.exe` through Windows Error Reporting (`WerFault.exe`).(Citation: Deep Instinct LSASS) Windows Security Support Provider (SSP) DLLs are loaded into LSASS process at system start. Once loaded into the LSA, SSP DLLs have access to encrypted and plaintext passwords that are stored in Windows, such as any logged-on user's Domain password or smart card PINs. The SSP configuration is stored in two Registry keys: HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa\Security Packages and HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa\OSConfig\Security Packages. An adversary may modify these Registry keys to add new SSPs, which will be loaded the next time the system boots, or when the AddSecurityPackage Windows API function is called.(Citation: Graeber 2014) The following SSPs can be used to access credentials: * Msv: Interactive logons, batch logons, and service logons are done through the MSV authentication package. * Wdigest: The Digest Authentication protocol is designed for use with Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) and Simple Authentication Security Layer (SASL) exchanges.(Citation: TechNet Blogs Credential Protection) * Kerberos: Preferred for mutual client-server domain authentication in Windows 2000 and later. * CredSSP: Provides SSO and Network Level Authentication for Remote Desktop Services.(Citation: TechNet Blogs Credential Protection)
4523.profile: [profile]The entity "In-Memory Module Loading" is a technique for executing arbitrary code by loading modules directly into a process's memory, bypassing disk-based defenses. It is associated with the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1620, Reflective Code Loading, under the Defense Evasion tactic and is platform-agnostic. The technical mechanism involves allocating and executing payloads, such as compiled binaries or shellcode, directly within a process's own memory space using functions like `Assembly.Load()` in PowerShell or similar reflective loaders. This method conceals execution under a legitimate process and avoids file artifacts, with payloads often remaining encrypted until runtime. Groups like Lazarus, Gamaredon, FIN7, and Kimsuky have been observed using this technique.[/profile]
4523.profile_without_enhance: [profile]In-Memory Module Loading is a technique where adversaries load malicious code directly into a process's memory without creating a file on disk, often to evade detection. This can be achieved by using functions like `LoadLibrary` on Windows or `dlopen` on Linux/macOS to load shared modules from arbitrary paths, or through reflective loading that allocates and executes payloads directly within the process's own memory space, such as via PowerShell's `Assembly.Load()` method. This method masks execution under legitimate processes and avoids disk artifacts.

4524.name: MD5 Mid-8 Bytes Usage
4524.profile: [profile]MD5 Mid-8 Bytes Usage is a technique for generating unique identifiers or encryption keys by extracting the middle 8 bytes (characters 9-24) from a 32-character MD5 hash. This method is used by malware families like bkdr_chches and bkdr_anel to create lightweight, deterministic keys for operations such as data encryption or command and control communication, avoiding the use of full cryptographic libraries.[/profile]
4524.profile_without_enhance: [profile]MD5 Mid-8 Bytes Usage is a technique for generating unique identifiers, likely for evasion or tracking, by using only the middle 8 bytes (characters 9-24) of a 32-character MD5 hash. This creates a shorter, less predictable string compared to the full hash. The method is referenced in the context of custom data archival methods, such as encryption with XOR or stream ciphers, used by groups like Lazarus Group and FIN6.

4526.name: Behavioral Monitoring
4526.profile: [profile]Behavioral Monitoring is a defensive technique, not an attack pattern. It involves analyzing system and user activities to detect anomalies and potential threats. These techniques are employed by groups like Scattered Spider, Volt Typhoon, and APT28 to circumvent security controls.[/profile]
4526.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Behavioral Monitoring is a technique where adversaries monitor user and system behaviors to gather intelligence or identify patterns for malicious purposes. 4527.name: Application Controls
4527.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may undermine security controls that will either warn users of untrusted activity or prevent execution of untrusted programs. Operating systems and security products may contain mechanisms to identify programs or websites as possessing some level of trust. Examples of such features would include a program being allowed to run because it is signed by a valid code signing certificate, a program prompting the user with a warning because it has an attribute set from being downloaded from the Internet, or getting an indication that you are about to connect to an untrusted site.

Adversaries may attempt to subvert these trust mechanisms. The method adversaries use will depend on the specific mechanism they seek to subvert. Adversaries may conduct [File and Directory Permissions Modification](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1222) or [Modify Registry](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1112) in support of subverting these controls.(Citation: SpectorOps Subverting Trust Sept 2017) Adversaries may also create or steal code signing certificates to acquire trust on target systems.(Citation: Securelist Digital Certificates)(Citation: Symantec Digital Certificates)
4527.profile: [profile]Application Controls, also known as Subvert Trust Controls (T1553) under the Defense Evasion tactic, targets Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. This technique undermines security mechanisms that warn users or block untrusted programs, such as code signing validation or Mark-of-the-Web attributes. Adversaries may subvert these controls by modifying file permissions or registry keys, or by creating or stealing code signing certificates to gain illicit trust on a system. The intrusion set menuPass has been associated with this behavior.
4527.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Application Controls is a defense technique, not an adversary attack pattern. It refers to security measures that manage the execution of software, such as whitelisting or blacklisting applications, to prevent unauthorized or malicious code from running. The retrieved information discusses adversary techniques to subvert these controls, including modifying file permissions or registry settings to bypass trust mechanisms, and altering code signing policies to allow unsigned code execution. These subversion methods are detailed in techniques like Subvert Trust Controls (T1553) and Code Signing Policy Modification (T1553.006).

4528.name: Email Gateway Monitoring
4528.profile: [profile]Email Gateway Monitoring is a technique used by adversaries to covertly monitor email traffic for sensitive information. The intrusion-set menuPass has been observed using this method. Adversaries may compromise an email gateway to intercept, collect, or forward emails, allowing them to gather intelligence, including trade secrets, personal data, or incident response details, which can be used to adjust their attack techniques and evade detection. This activity is often a precursor to data exfiltration or further network compromise.
4528.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Email Gateway Monitoring is a technique where adversaries monitor email traffic passing through an organization's email gateway to collect sensitive information. This involves intercepting and analyzing emails to gather intelligence, which can include trade secrets, personal data, or details of incident response operations. This activity supports the Collection tactic and is applicable to platforms with email services.

4529.name: Zero-Day Attack Monitoring
4529.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may downgrade or use a version of system features that may be outdated, vulnerable, and/or does not support updated security controls. Downgrade attacks typically take advantage of a system’s backward compatibility to force it into less secure modes of operation. 

Adversaries may downgrade and use various less-secure versions of features of a system, such as [Command and Scripting Interpreter](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059)s or even network protocols that can be abused to enable [Adversary-in-the-Middle](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1557) or [Network Sniffing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1040).(Citation: Praetorian TLS Downgrade Attack 2014) For example, [PowerShell](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001) versions 5+ includes Script Block Logging (SBL), which can record executed script content. However, adversaries may attempt to execute a previous version of PowerShell that does not support SBL with the intent to [Impair Defenses](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1562) while running malicious scripts that may have otherwise been detected.(Citation: CrowdStrike BGH Ransomware 2021)(Citation: Mandiant BYOL 2018)(Citation: att_def_ps_logging)

Adversaries may similarly target network traffic to downgrade from an encrypted HTTPS connection to an unsecured HTTP connection that exposes network data in clear text.(Citation: Targeted SSL Stripping Attacks Are Real)(Citation: Crowdstrike Downgrade) On Windows systems, adversaries may downgrade the boot manager to a vulnerable version that bypasses Secure Boot, granting the ability to disable various operating system security mechanisms.(Citation: SafeBreach)
4529.profile: [profile]Downgrade Attack, identified as T1562.010 under the Defense Evasion tactic, targets multiple platforms including Windows. It exploits backward compatibility to force systems into less secure modes, such as executing older PowerShell versions lacking Script Block Logging to evade detection, downgrading HTTPS to HTTP to expose cleartext data, or reverting a Windows boot manager to bypass Secure Boot. The intrusion-set menuPass has been associated with this technique.
4529.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Zero-Day Attack Monitoring is a security practice, not a MITRE ATT&CK technique. It involves detecting and analyzing exploitation attempts targeting unknown vulnerabilities (zero-days) before patches are available. This process is critical for early threat detection and is often associated with defensive evasion techniques like T1211 (Exploitation for Defense Evasion), where adversaries exploit vulnerabilities to bypass security software.

4536.name: Operation Cloud Hopper
4536.profile: [profile]Operation Cloud Hopper is a cyber espionage campaign, not a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique. It is attributed to the intrusion set menuPass (APT10). The campaign primarily targeted managed IT service providers to gain access to their clients' data. Its technical mechanics involved data staging within cloud environments prior to exfiltration, often to cloud storage services, to blend with legitimate traffic and evade detection. The operation leveraged compromised cloud accounts and infrastructure to facilitate its activities.
4536.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Operation Cloud Hopper is a cyber espionage campaign, not a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique. It primarily targets managed IT service providers (MSPs) to gain access to their clients' cloud environments. The campaign involves using valid accounts to access cloud services and APIs, staging collected data within compromised cloud instances, and exfiltrating data to cloud storage. This approach leverages trusted relationships for broad, stealthy access across multiple victim networks.

4537.name: Cloud Funnel Operation
4537.profile: [profile]Cloud Funnel Operation is a technique used by adversaries like menuPass to compromise and leverage cloud accounts for operational support. It involves obtaining cloud credentials through methods like phishing or password spraying, then using those accounts to access cloud services and APIs for activities such as data exfiltration to cloud storage (T1567.002), tool hosting, or acquiring serverless infrastructure. The technique exploits trusted cloud service relationships and allows adversaries to operate with significant cover by blending into normal cloud traffic.[/profile]
4537.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Cloud Funnel Operation" is a cloud-focused attack pattern. It involves adversaries compromising cloud accounts to acquire and leverage cloud infrastructure for malicious operations. Compromised accounts are used to access services like cloud storage (e.g., AWS S3, Dropbox) for data exfiltration or to host tools, and to provision infrastructure such as virtual private servers. Attackers obtain these accounts through methods like credential phishing, password spraying, or stealing application tokens, often targeting privileged accounts to exploit trusted relationships with service providers.

4538.name: Intellectual Property and Sensitive Data Theft
4538.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may steal monetary resources from targets through extortion, social engineering, technical theft, or other methods aimed at their own financial gain at the expense of the availability of these resources for victims. Financial theft is the ultimate objective of several popular campaign types including extortion by ransomware,(Citation: FBI-ransomware) business email compromise (BEC) and fraud,(Citation: FBI-BEC) "pig butchering,"(Citation: wired-pig butchering) bank hacking,(Citation: DOJ-DPRK Heist) and exploiting cryptocurrency networks.(Citation: BBC-Ronin) 

Adversaries may [Compromise Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1586) to conduct unauthorized transfers of funds.(Citation: Internet crime report 2022) In the case of business email compromise or email fraud, an adversary may utilize [Impersonation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1656) of a trusted entity. Once the social engineering is successful, victims can be deceived into sending money to financial accounts controlled by an adversary.(Citation: FBI-BEC) This creates the potential for multiple victims (i.e., compromised accounts as well as the ultimate monetary loss) in incidents involving financial theft.(Citation: VEC)

Extortion by ransomware may occur, for example, when an adversary demands payment from a victim after [Data Encrypted for Impact](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1486) (Citation: NYT-Colonial) and [Exfiltration](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0010) of data, followed by threatening to leak sensitive data to the public unless payment is made to the adversary.(Citation: Mandiant-leaks) Adversaries may use dedicated leak sites to distribute victim data.(Citation: Crowdstrike-leaks)

Due to the potentially immense business impact of financial theft, an adversary may abuse the possibility of financial theft and seeking monetary gain to divert attention from their true goals such as [Data Destruction](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1485) and business disruption.(Citation: AP-NotPetya)
4538.profile: [profile]The entity is a financial theft attack pattern, identified as T1657, which falls under the Impact tactic and targets multiple platforms. It involves stealing monetary resources through methods like extortion via ransomware, business email compromise, or direct bank hacking. Adversaries may compromise accounts to conduct unauthorized fund transfers, use impersonation in social engineering to deceive victims into sending money, or demand payment after encrypting and exfiltrating data, threatening to leak it if unpaid. Associated groups include FIN13, Scattered Spider, and Inc Ransom.
4538.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Intellectual Property and Sensitive Data Theft is a cyber adversary objective focused on the theft of proprietary information and confidential data. The technical mechanics involve collecting sensitive data from systems, which may include using techniques like Email Collection to gather trade secrets from user inboxes. Prior to exfiltration, adversaries often stage and compress the collected data using utilities like 7zip or RAR to minimize network footprint. This activity is commonly associated with the Exfiltration tactic and can be performed across various platforms.

4539.name: Domain Registration
4539.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may register a device to an adversary-controlled account. Devices may be registered in a multifactor authentication (MFA) system, which handles authentication to the network, or in a device management system, which handles device access and compliance.

MFA systems, such as Duo or Okta, allow users to associate devices with their accounts in order to complete MFA requirements. An adversary that compromises a user’s credentials may enroll a new device in order to bypass initial MFA requirements and gain persistent access to a network.(Citation: CISA MFA PrintNightmare)(Citation: DarkReading FireEye SolarWinds) In some cases, the MFA self-enrollment process may require only a username and password to enroll the account's first device or to enroll a device to an inactive account. (Citation: Mandiant APT29 Microsoft 365 2022)

Similarly, an adversary with existing access to a network may register a device or a virtual machine to Entra ID and/or its device management system, Microsoft Intune, in order to access sensitive data or resources while bypassing conditional access policies.(Citation: AADInternals - Device Registration)(Citation: AADInternals - Conditional Access Bypass)(Citation: Microsoft DEV-0537)(Citation: Expel Atlas Lion 2025)

Devices registered in Entra ID may be able to conduct [Internal Spearphishing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1534) campaigns via intra-organizational emails, which are less likely to be treated as suspicious by the email client.(Citation: Microsoft - Device Registration) Additionally, an adversary may be able to perform a [Service Exhaustion Flood](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1499/002) on an Entra ID tenant by registering a large number of devices.(Citation: AADInternals - BPRT)
4539.profile: [profile]Device Registration, identified as MITRE technique T1098.005 under the Persistence tactic, targets Windows Azure Active Directory and Office 365 platforms. It involves an adversary enrolling a new device or virtual machine into a compromised user's MFA system (like Duo or Okta) or a device management system (like Microsoft Intune) using stolen credentials, thereby bypassing initial MFA and conditional access policies to gain persistent network access. This technique has been associated with APT29 and can facilitate internal spearphishing or service exhaustion floods in Entra ID.
4539.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Domain Registration is identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1583.001 under Resource Development. It involves adversaries acquiring domain names for use in operations such as Phishing, Drive-by Compromise, and Command and Control. Technical mechanics include purchasing or acquiring domains, often using typosquatting, homoglyphs, or different top-level domains to create lookalike domains, and employing private WHOIS services to obscure ownership. Domains can be dynamically generated for unique, one-time use or repurposed from expired domains to leverage existing trust. This technique supports establishing infrastructure for subsequent attack phases.

4540.name: Infrastructure Management
4540.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may manipulate network traffic in order to hide and evade detection of their C2 infrastructure. This can be accomplished by identifying and filtering traffic from defensive tools,(Citation: TA571) masking malicious domains to obfuscate the true destination from both automated scanning tools and security researchers,(Citation: Schema-abuse)(Citation: Facad1ng)(Citation: Browser-updates) and otherwise hiding malicious artifacts to delay discovery and prolong the effectiveness of adversary infrastructure that could otherwise be identified, blocked, or taken down entirely.

C2 networks may include the use of [Proxy](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1090) or VPNs to disguise IP addresses, which can allow adversaries to blend in with normal network traffic and bypass conditional access policies or anti-abuse protections. For example, an adversary may use a virtual private cloud to spoof their IP address to closer align with a victim's IP address ranges. This may also bypass security measures relying on geolocation of the source IP address.(Citation: sysdig)(Citation: Orange Residential Proxies)

Adversaries may also attempt to filter network traffic in order to evade defensive tools in numerous ways, including blocking/redirecting common incident responder or security appliance user agents.(Citation: mod_rewrite)(Citation: SocGholish-update) Filtering traffic based on IP and geo-fencing may also avoid automated sandboxing or researcher activity (i.e., [Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1497)).(Citation: TA571)(Citation: mod_rewrite)

Hiding C2 infrastructure may also be supported by [Resource Development](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0042) activities such as [Acquire Infrastructure](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1583) and [Compromise Infrastructure](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1584). For example, using widely trusted hosting services or domains such as prominent URL shortening providers or marketing services for C2 networks may enable adversaries to present benign content that later redirects victims to malicious web pages or infrastructure once specific conditions are met.(Citation: StarBlizzard)(Citation: QR-cofense)
4540.profile: [profile]Hide Infrastructure, identified as T1665 within the Resource Development tactic, involves manipulating network traffic to conceal command and control (C2) infrastructure. Techniques include using proxies or VPNs to disguise IP addresses, filtering traffic to block defensive tool user agents or specific IP ranges, and employing geo-fencing to evade sandboxes. Adversaries also mask malicious domains, for instance by using trusted URL shorteners that redirect to malicious endpoints, to blend in with normal traffic and delay detection. This activity is often supported by acquiring or compromising infrastructure.
4540.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Infrastructure Management is a Resource Development technique (T1583) used by adversaries to acquire, lease, rent, or obtain infrastructure such as physical/cloud servers, domains, and third-party web services for staging and executing operations. This includes utilizing free trials, residential proxy services, and botnets to blend in with normal traffic and obscure attribution. The technique is employed by groups like Sea Turtle, Kimsuky, and Sandworm Team.

4541.name: Malware Development
4541.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may develop malware and malware components that can be used during targeting. Building malicious software can include the development of payloads, droppers, post-compromise tools, backdoors (including backdoored images), packers, C2 protocols, and the creation of infected removable media. Adversaries may develop malware to support their operations, creating a means for maintaining control of remote machines, evading defenses, and executing post-compromise behaviors.(Citation: Mandiant APT1)(Citation: Kaspersky Sofacy)(Citation: ActiveMalwareEnergy)(Citation: FBI Flash FIN7 USB)

During malware development, adversaries may intentionally include indicators aligned with other known actors in order to mislead attribution by defenders.(Citation: Olympic Destroyer)(Citation: Risky Bulletin Threat actor impersonates FSB APT)(Citation: GamaCopy organization)

As with legitimate development efforts, different skill sets may be required for developing malware. The skills needed may be located in-house, or may need to be contracted out. Use of a contractor may be considered an extension of that adversary's malware development capabilities, provided the adversary plays a role in shaping requirements and maintains a degree of exclusivity to the malware.

Some aspects of malware development, such as C2 protocol development, may require adversaries to obtain additional infrastructure. For example, malware developed that will communicate with Twitter for C2, may require use of [Web Services](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1583/006).(Citation: FireEye APT29)
4541.profile: [profile]Malware Development is a technique under MITRE ATT&CK ID T1587.001, categorized within the Resource Development tactic. It involves the in-house or contracted creation of malicious software components such as payloads, droppers, post-compromise tools, backdoors, packers, and custom command and control (C2) protocols. A distinct technical mechanic includes adversaries intentionally incorporating false-flag indicators during development to mislead attribution. This activity is associated with numerous threat groups including APT29, Lazarus Group, and FIN7, and may require supporting infrastructure like web services for C2 functionality.[/profile]
4541.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Malware Development is a sub-technique (T1587.001) under the Resource Development tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. It involves the in-house or contracted creation of malicious software components such as payloads, droppers, post-compromise tools, backdoors, packers, and custom command and control (C2) protocols to support adversary operations. During development, adversaries may intentionally embed false flags to mislead attribution and may require additional infrastructure, like web services, for specialized functions such as C2 protocol implementation.

4542.name: Target Operations
4542.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may put in place resources that are referenced by a link that can be used during targeting. An adversary may rely upon a user clicking a malicious link in order to divulge information (including credentials) or to gain execution, as in [Malicious Link](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/001). Links can be used for spearphishing, such as sending an email accompanied by social engineering text to coax the user to actively click or copy and paste a URL into a browser. Prior to a phish for information (as in [Spearphishing Link](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1598/003)) or a phish to gain initial access to a system (as in [Spearphishing Link](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/002)), an adversary must set up the resources for a link target for the spearphishing link. 

Typically, the resources for a link target will be an HTML page that may include some client-side script such as [JavaScript](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/007) to decide what content to serve to the user. Adversaries may clone legitimate sites to serve as the link target, this can include cloning of login pages of legitimate web services or organization login pages in an effort to harvest credentials during [Spearphishing Link](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1598/003).(Citation: Malwarebytes Silent Librarian October 2020)(Citation: Proofpoint TA407 September 2019) Adversaries may also [Upload Malware](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1608/001) and have the link target point to malware for download/execution by the user.

Adversaries may purchase domains similar to legitimate domains (ex: homoglyphs, typosquatting, different top-level domain, etc.) during acquisition of infrastructure ([Domains](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1583/001)) to help facilitate [Malicious Link](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/001).

Links can be written by adversaries to mask the true destination in order to deceive victims by abusing the URL schema and increasing the effectiveness of phishing.(Citation: Kaspersky-masking)(Citation: mandiant-masking)

Adversaries may also use free or paid accounts on link shortening services and Platform-as-a-Service providers to host link targets while taking advantage of the widely trusted domains of those providers to avoid being blocked while redirecting victims to malicious pages.(Citation: Netskope GCP Redirection)(Citation: Netskope Cloud Phishing)(Citation: Intezer App Service Phishing)(Citation: Cofense-redirect) In addition, adversaries may serve a variety of malicious links through uniquely generated URIs/URLs (including one-time, single use links).(Citation: iOS URL Scheme)(Citation: URI)(Citation: URI Use)(Citation: URI Unique) Finally, adversaries may take advantage of the decentralized nature of the InterPlanetary File System (IPFS) to host link targets that are difficult to remove.(Citation: Talos IPFS 2022)
4542.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique "Link Target" (ID T1608.005) under the Resource Development tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. It involves adversaries preparing the resources a malicious link points to, such as cloning legitimate login pages to harvest credentials, uploading malware for execution, or using deceptive domains acquired through typosquatting. They may host these targets on trusted services like link shorteners or decentralized systems like IPFS to evade blocking and removal, and they can mask the true destination URL to increase phishing effectiveness.
4542.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Target Operations is a preparatory technique where adversaries compromise third-party infrastructure like servers, virtual private servers, or network devices to use as staging grounds for subsequent attacks. This compromised infrastructure can then be leveraged to host malicious content for phishing campaigns, enabling techniques like Spearphishing Link or Drive-by Compromise, or to support command and control activities.

4544.name: Compromises of MSPs
4544.profile: [profile]Compromises of MSPs is a technique where adversaries target Managed Service Providers (MSPs) to gain initial access and leverage their trusted administrative access and tools for lateral movement into client networks. This is often conducted by intrusion sets like menuPass. The technique exploits the trusted relationship between MSPs and their customers, allowing adversaries to use the MSP's infrastructure and credentials to move across multiple client environments from a single, powerful entry point.

4545.profile: [profile]Poison Ivy, also known as Pivy Rat variant, is a Remote Access Tool (RAT) used by intrusion sets including APT17 and menuPass, as well as groups like Gallium. It was deployed in campaigns such as Operation Soft Cell to target telecommunications providers and exfiltrate Caller Detail Records. 4549.name: keylogging
4549.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may log user keystrokes to intercept credentials as the user types them. Keylogging is likely to be used to acquire credentials for new access opportunities when [OS Credential Dumping](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003) efforts are not effective, and may require an adversary to intercept keystrokes on a system for a substantial period of time before credentials can be successfully captured. In order to increase the likelihood of capturing credentials quickly, an adversary may also perform actions such as clearing browser cookies to force users to reauthenticate to systems.(Citation: Talos Kimsuky Nov 2021)

Keylogging is the most prevalent type of input capture, with many different ways of intercepting keystrokes.(Citation: Adventures of a Keystroke) Some methods include:

* Hooking API callbacks used for processing keystrokes. Unlike [Credential API Hooking](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1056/004), this focuses solely on API functions intended for processing keystroke data.
* Reading raw keystroke data from the hardware buffer.
* Windows Registry modifications.
* Custom drivers.
* [Modify System Image](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1601) may provide adversaries with hooks into the operating system of network devices to read raw keystrokes for login sessions.(Citation: Cisco Blog Legacy Device Attacks)
4549.profile: [profile]Keylogging, identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1056.001 under the Credential Access tactic, primarily targets Windows and Linux platforms. It captures keystrokes to intercept credentials, often when OS credential dumping fails, and may involve clearing browser cookies to force reauthentication. Specific technical methods include hooking API callbacks for keystroke processing, reading raw data from the hardware buffer, modifying the Windows Registry, deploying custom drivers, or altering system images on network devices. The malware Poison Ivy is known to use this technique, which is associated with numerous threat groups including APT28, Lazarus Group, and Kimsuky.[profile]
