It involves logging user keystrokes to intercept credentials, often used when credential dumping fails. Technical methods include hooking API callbacks for keystroke processing, reading raw data from the hardware buffer, modifying the Windows Registry, deploying custom drivers, or altering system images on network devices to capture login sessions. Associated threat groups include APT28, Lazarus Group, and Kimsuky.

4550.name: screen capture
4550.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may attempt to take screen captures of the desktop to gather information over the course of an operation. Screen capturing functionality may be included as a feature of a remote access tool used in post-compromise operations. Taking a screenshot is also typically possible through native utilities or API calls, such as CopyFromScreen, xwd, or screencapture.(Citation: CopyFromScreen .NET)(Citation: Antiquated Mac Malware)
4550.profile: [profile]Screen Capture is identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1113 under the Collection tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It involves adversaries capturing desktop screenshots to gather information, often using features of remote access tools or native utilities and API calls like CopyFromScreen, xwd, or screencapture. The malware Poison Ivy is associated with this technique, and it has been used by numerous threat groups including APT28, FIN7, and MuddyWater.[/profile]
4550.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Screen Capture is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1113 under the Collection tactic, applicable to Windows, macOS, and Linux. Adversaries take screenshots of the desktop to gather information, often using features of remote access tools or native utilities and API calls such as CopyFromScreen, xwd, or screencapture. Associated threat groups include Winter Vivern, Gamaredon Group, Dragonfly, MuddyWater, FIN7, and APT28.

4551.name: video capture
4551.uncertain_mes:
An adversary can leverage a computer's peripheral devices (e.g., integrated cameras or webcams) or applications (e.g., video call services) to capture video recordings for the purpose of gathering information. Images may also be captured from devices or applications, potentially in specified intervals, in lieu of video files.

Malware or scripts may be used to interact with the devices through an available API provided by the operating system or an application to capture video or images. Video or image files may be written to disk and exfiltrated later. This technique differs from [Screen Capture](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1113) due to use of specific devices or applications for video recording rather than capturing the victim's screen.

In macOS, there are a few different malware samples that record the user's webcam such as FruitFly and Proton. (Citation: objective-see 2017 review)
4551.profile: [profile]Video Capture is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1125 under the Collection tactic for macOS and Windows platforms. It involves using malware or scripts to interact with a system's peripheral devices like integrated cameras or applications such as video call services via available operating system or application APIs to record video or capture images, which are then written to disk for later exfiltration. This technique is distinct from screen capture and has been used by groups including Silence, FIN7, and Ember Bear, with malware like Poison Ivy potentially employing it.
4551.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Video Capture is a MITRE ATT&CK technique with ID T1125 under the Collection tactic, applicable to multiple platforms including macOS. It involves adversaries using malware or scripts to interact with peripheral devices like integrated cameras or applications such as video call services via operating system APIs to record video or capture images, which are then written to disk for later exfiltration. This technique is distinct from screen capture as it targets specific hardware or software for recording, with known malware examples like FruitFly and Proton targeting macOS webcams.

4552.name: file transfer
4552.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may communicate using application layer protocols associated with transferring files to avoid detection/network filtering by blending in with existing traffic. Commands to the remote system, and often the results of those commands, will be embedded within the protocol traffic between the client and server. 

Protocols such as SMB(Citation: US-CERT TA18-074A), FTP(Citation: ESET Machete July 2019), FTPS, and TFTP that transfer files may be very common in environments.  Packets produced from these protocols may have many fields and headers in which data can be concealed. Data could also be concealed within the transferred files. An adversary may abuse these protocols to communicate with systems under their control within a victim network while also mimicking normal, expected traffic.
4552.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique "File Transfer Protocols" (T1071.002) under the Command and Control tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It involves adversaries using common application-layer file transfer protocols like SMB, FTP, FTPS, and TFTP to blend malicious communications with normal network traffic. Commands and their results are embedded within the protocol's packet fields, headers, or within the transferred files themselves to evade detection. Associated malware includes Poison Ivy, and it has been used by groups such as SILVERTERRIER, APT41, Dragonfly, and Kimsuky.[/profile]
4552.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "file transfer" is a generic concept for moving data, not a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique. The retrieved information describes related techniques like Ingress Tool Transfer (T1105) and Lateral Tool Transfer (T1570), which involve moving files into and within a network using protocols like SMB, FTP, or tools like scp, curl, and certutil. These actions are typically associated with the Command and Control or Lateral Movement tactics and can occur across Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. The core mechanic is the abuse of legitimate file transfer mechanisms to deploy tools or exfiltrate data.

4553.name: password stealing
4553.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries with no prior knowledge of legitimate credentials within the system or environment may guess passwords to attempt access to accounts. Without knowledge of the password for an account, an adversary may opt to systematically guess the password using a repetitive or iterative mechanism. An adversary may guess login credentials without prior knowledge of system or environment passwords during an operation by using a list of common passwords. Password guessing may or may not take into account the target's policies on password complexity or use policies that may lock accounts out after a number of failed attempts.

Guessing passwords can be a risky option because it could cause numerous authentication failures and account lockouts, depending on the organization's login failure policies. (Citation: Cylance Cleaver)

Typically, management services over commonly used ports are used when guessing passwords. Commonly targeted services include the following:

* SSH (22/TCP)
* Telnet (23/TCP)
* FTP (21/TCP)
* NetBIOS / SMB / Samba (139/TCP & 445/TCP)
* LDAP (389/TCP)
* Kerberos (88/TCP)
* RDP / Terminal Services (3389/TCP)
* HTTP/HTTP Management Services (80/TCP & 443/TCP)
* MSSQL (1433/TCP)
* Oracle (1521/TCP)
* MySQL (3306/TCP)
* VNC (5900/TCP)
* SNMP (161/UDP and 162/TCP/UDP)

In addition to management services, adversaries may "target single sign-on (SSO) and cloud-based applications utilizing federated authentication protocols," as well as externally facing email applications, such as Office 365.(Citation: US-CERT TA18-068A 2018). Further, adversaries may abuse network device interfaces (such as `wlanAPI`) to brute force accessible wifi-router(s) via wireless authentication protocols.(Citation: Trend Micro Emotet 2020)

In default environments, LDAP and Kerberos connection attempts are less likely to trigger events over SMB, which creates Windows "logon failure" event ID 4625.
4553.profile: [profile]Password Guessing, identified as MITRE ATT&CK T1110.001 under the Credential Access tactic, is a technique where adversaries systematically attempt to access accounts by repetitively trying common passwords without prior knowledge of valid credentials. It targets a wide range of management services over common ports like SSH (22/TCP), Telnet (23/TCP), FTP (21/TCP), SMB (445/TCP), RDP (3389/TCP), and cloud applications, with LDAP and Kerberos attempts being less likely to trigger specific Windows logon failure alerts compared to SMB. This method risks triggering account lockouts and is associated with threat groups like APT29 and APT28.[/profile]
4553.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Password stealing, also known as credential theft, is a technique within the Credential Access tactic. It involves adversaries acquiring passwords or other authentication material from various sources. This can be achieved by extracting plaintext credentials from memory, reading encrypted credential stores from password managers or web browsers (like Chrome's login data file), or intercepting credentials as they are entered or validated, such as by registering a malicious password filter DLL. Stolen credentials are then used to gain unauthorized access to systems and services.

4554.name: system administration
4554.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may abuse ESXi administration services to execute commands on guest machines hosted within an ESXi virtual environment. Persistent background services on ESXi-hosted VMs, such as the VMware Tools Daemon Service, allow for remote management from the ESXi server. The tools daemon service runs as `vmtoolsd.exe` on Windows guest operating systems, `vmware-tools-daemon` on macOS, and `vmtoolsd ` on Linux.(Citation: Broadcom VMware Tools Services) 

Adversaries may leverage a variety of tools to execute commands on ESXi-hosted VMs – for example, by using the vSphere Web Services SDK to programmatically execute commands and scripts via APIs such as `StartProgramInGuest`, `ListProcessesInGuest`,  `ListFileInGuest`, and `InitiateFileTransferFromGuest`.(Citation: Google Cloud Threat Intelligence VMWare ESXi Zero-Day 2023)(Citation: Broadcom Running Guest OS Operations) This may enable follow-on behaviors on the guest VMs, such as [File and Directory Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1083), [Data from Local System](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1005), or [OS Credential Dumping](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003).
4554.profile: [profile]System Administration, identified as T1675, falls under the Execution tactic and targets ESXi platforms. Adversaries abuse ESXi administration services to execute commands on guest virtual machines by leveraging the VMware Tools Daemon Service (vmtoolsd/vmtoolsd.exe) or programmatically using the vSphere Web Services SDK APIs like StartProgramInGuest and InitiateFileTransferFromGuest. This technique facilitates follow-on discovery and data exfiltration activities on the compromised guest VMs. It has been associated with threat group UNC3886 and malware like Poison Ivy.[/profile]

4555.name: traffic relaying
4555.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may use traffic signaling to hide open ports or other malicious functionality used for persistence or command and control. Traffic signaling involves the use of a magic value or sequence that must be sent to a system to trigger a special response, such as opening a closed port or executing a malicious task. This may take the form of sending a series of packets with certain characteristics before a port will be opened that the adversary can use for command and control. Usually this series of packets consists of attempted connections to a predefined sequence of closed ports (i.e. [Port Knocking](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1205/001)), but can involve unusual flags, specific strings, or other unique characteristics. After the sequence is completed, opening a port may be accomplished by the host-based firewall, but could also be implemented by custom software.

Adversaries may also communicate with an already open port, but the service listening on that port will only respond to commands or trigger other malicious functionality if passed the appropriate magic value(s).

The observation of the signal packets to trigger the communication can be conducted through different methods. One means, originally implemented by Cd00r (Citation: Hartrell cd00r 2002), is to use the libpcap libraries to sniff for the packets in question. Another method leverages raw sockets, which enables the malware to use ports that are already open for use by other programs.

On network devices, adversaries may use crafted packets to enable [Network Device Authentication](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1556/004) for standard services offered by the device such as telnet.  Such signaling may also be used to open a closed service port such as telnet, or to trigger module modification of malware implants on the device, adding, removing, or changing malicious capabilities.  Adversaries may use crafted packets to attempt to connect to one or more (open or closed) ports, but may also attempt to connect to a router interface, broadcast, and network address IP on the same port in order to achieve their goals and objectives.(Citation: Cisco Synful Knock Evolution)(Citation: Mandiant - Synful Knock)(Citation: Cisco Blog Legacy Device Attacks)  To enable this traffic signaling on embedded devices, adversaries must first achieve and leverage [Patch System Image](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1601/001) due to the monolithic nature of the architecture.

Adversaries may also use the Wake-on-LAN feature to turn on powered off systems. Wake-on-LAN is a hardware feature that allows a powered down system to be powered on, or woken up, by sending a magic packet to it. Once the system is powered on, it may become a target for lateral movement.(Citation: Bleeping Computer - Ryuk WoL)(Citation: AMD Magic Packet)
4555.profile: [profile]Traffic Signaling is formally identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1205 under the Command and Control tactic, applicable to Linux, Windows, and Network platforms. It involves sending a specific "magic" sequence, such as a predefined series of connection attempts to closed ports (Port Knocking), packets with unusual flags, or specific strings, to trigger a hidden response like opening a firewall port or executing malicious code. Implementation methods include using libpcap to sniff for the trigger packets or leveraging raw sockets. This technique has been associated with malware like Poison Ivy and threat groups including Kimsuky, UNC3886, and Mustang Panda.
4555.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Traffic relaying, not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique, is a method used to obscure malicious communications by routing traffic through intermediate systems. It can be implemented using multi-hop proxy chains to disguise the traffic's original source and may leverage common web protocols like HTTP/S to blend in with normal network activity, often in conjunction with other techniques like adversary-in-the-middle attacks.

4559.name: launcher code
4559.profile: [profile]The malware entity is a launcher code component, known by the alias 'pocodown' and used by the intrusion-set 'menuPass' (also referenced as APT28). Its key technical behavior involves launching payloads and wiper components, with analyzed samples showing specific time and date triggers. It is associated with the protection of its code from reverse engineering, having switched from .NET Confuser to Reactor for obfuscation. The target platforms include systems running .NET applications, such as those in financial contexts like ATMs (as seen with Ploutus) and potentially critical infrastructure, as indicated by its relation to Industroyer and the Electrum group.[/profile]
4559.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The malware 'launcher code' is a modular component used to deploy payloads, including data wipers, and is associated with the APT group APT28. It is implemented as a .NET executable, such as 'Diebold.exe', and employs code obfuscation tools like Reactor to hinder reverse engineering. This launcher is specifically designed to execute at predetermined times and targets critical infrastructure systems, as evidenced by its use in the Industroyer campaign attributed to the Electrum threat group.

4562.name: Pivy server
4562.profile: [profile]Pivy server is a malware, also known as PIVY. It is attributed to the intrusion set menuPass (also known as Stone Panda). Key technical behaviors include side-loading into legitimate applications like a Samsung tool for execution, decrypting and loading a payload blob from disk, and achieving persistence via a rogue scheduled task. Its command and control infrastructure has used domains such as dick[.]ccfchrist[.]com, trout[.]belowto[.]com, and sakai[.]unhamj[.]com.

4563.name: Camellia-256
4563.profile: [profile]Camellia-256 is a symmetric block cipher algorithm, analogous to AES-256, used for encryption. It is employed by malware like Poison Ivy to obfuscate command and control (C2) communications and to encrypt collected data prior to exfiltration, implementing the techniques of symmetric cryptography for C2 (T1573.001) and archive via custom method (T1560.003). Its use is a specific instance of adversaries applying custom or known symmetric encryption to conceal malicious traffic and payloads.
4563.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Camellia-256 is a symmetric block cipher algorithm, analogous to AES-256, used for encryption. It can be employed by adversaries to conceal command and control traffic (T1573.001) or to encrypt data prior to exfiltration (T1560.003), providing a layer of obfuscation independent of any communication protocol. Known threat actors like Lazarus Group, Mustang Panda, and MuddyWater have utilized symmetric cryptography in their operations.

4564.name: lznt1
4564.profile: [profile]The entity 'lznt1' is a custom compression algorithm, specifically a variant of the LZNT1 algorithm, used by adversaries to compress data prior to exfiltration. It is a sub-technique of Archive via Custom Method (T1560.003) within the Exfiltration tactic. This method is employed to make collected data portable and minimize network footprint, often implemented without external library references to evade detection. The malware Poison Ivy is known to utilize this compression technique in its operations.[/profile]
4564.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "lznt1" is a data compression algorithm, not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. It is referenced in the context of data compression for exfiltration (T1002) and custom archiving methods (T1560.003). Specifically, adversaries may use custom implementations of compression algorithms like LZNT1 to compress collected data, making it portable and minimizing network footprint, often as part of a broader data collection and exfiltration process.

4566.name: Challenge-Response Authentication
4566.profile: [profile]Challenge-Response Authentication is a security protocol where a system verifies an entity by issuing a challenge that requires a specific, secret-based response. The Poison Ivy malware is known to utilize this mechanism to authenticate its command and control communications, allowing it to securely establish a connection with an infected host by proving knowledge of a shared secret without transmitting the secret itself over the network. This technique falls under the Credential Access tactic, enabling persistent and stealthy remote access.
4566.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Challenge-Response Authentication" is a core security protocol, not a specific adversarial technique, and therefore does not have a corresponding MITRE ATT&CK ID or Tactic. It is a fundamental mechanism used by legitimate systems where a claimant proves identity by correctly responding to a verifier's challenge, often using cryptographic methods. The retrieved information discusses related adversarial techniques that abuse authentication processes, such as patching authentication packages or forcing SMB authentication to steal credentials, but these describe exploitation of authentication systems rather than defining the protocol itself.

4571.name: password dumping
4571.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may attempt to dump credentials to obtain account login and credential material, normally in the form of a hash or a clear text password. Credentials can be obtained from OS caches, memory, or structures.(Citation: Brining MimiKatz to Unix) Credentials can then be used to perform [Lateral Movement](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0008) and access restricted information.

Several of the tools mentioned in associated sub-techniques may be used by both adversaries and professional security testers. Additional custom tools likely exist as well.
4571.profile: [profile]OS Credential Dumping, identified as T1003 under the Credential Access tactic, targets Windows, Linux, and Mac platforms. It involves extracting account login material like hashes or plaintext passwords from operating system components such as caches, memory, or security structures. The obtained credentials are subsequently used for lateral movement within a network. This technique is employed by various threat groups, including menuPass, and utilizes tools common to both adversaries and security professionals.
4571.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Password Dumping is a technique aligned with MITRE ATT&CK's OS Credential Dumping (T1003) under the Credential Access tactic, applicable to Windows, Linux, and Mac platforms. It involves extracting account credentials, often as hashes or plaintext passwords, from operating system components like security account manager (SAM) databases, Local Security Authority (LSA) secrets, or process memory. Tools such as Mimikatz are commonly used for this purpose, and the obtained credentials enable lateral movement and further system access.

4572.name: file and registry search
4572.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may enumerate files and directories or may search in specific locations of a host or network share for certain information within a file system. Adversaries may use the information from [File and Directory Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1083) during automated discovery to shape follow-on behaviors, including whether or not the adversary fully infects the target and/or attempts specific actions. Many command shell utilities can be used to obtain this information. Examples include dir, tree, ls, find, and locate.(Citation: Windows Commands JPCERT) Custom tools may also be used to gather file and directory information and interact with the [Native API](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1106). Adversaries may also leverage a [Network Device CLI](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/008) on network devices to gather file and directory information (e.g. dir, show flash, and/or nvram).(Citation: US-CERT-TA18-106A) Some files and directories may require elevated or specific user permissions to access.
4572.profile: [profile]File and Directory Discovery, identified as T1083, is a Discovery tactic technique used across Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves adversaries enumerating files and directories to gather information about the system, often using built-in command utilities like `dir`, `ls`, `find`, and `tree`, or custom tools that interact with the Native API. This reconnaissance can shape subsequent attack behaviors, and execution may also occur through a Network Device CLI using commands such as `show flash`. The technique is associated with numerous threat groups, including menuPass, APT28, and Lazarus Group.[profile]
4572.profile_without_enhance: [profile]File and Registry Search is a Discovery technique where adversaries enumerate files, directories, and the Windows Registry to gather system information. It involves using command-line utilities like `dir`, `tree`, `ls`, `find`, and `locate` for file system discovery and the `reg query` command to search Registry hives (e.g., `HKLM /f password /t REG_SZ /s`) for insecurely stored credentials or configuration data. This activity supports follow-on actions by revealing system details, installed software, and potential weaknesses.

4586.name: strategic cyberattacks
4586.profile: [profile]Strategic cyberattacks, often referred to as strategic web compromises or watering hole attacks, are a targeted campaign method. They involve compromising websites frequented by a specific community, such as a government sector or industry, with the goal of infecting a particular user or set of users based on a shared interest. This technique is executed through drive-by compromises, where adversaries stage malicious content on these sites to exploit visitors' browsers, often without requiring additional user interaction beyond visiting the page. The intrusion set menuPass is associated with this activity.[/profile]
4586.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "strategic cyberattacks" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the retrieved context, it is described as a targeted campaign type, often referred to as a strategic web compromise or watering hole attack. This involves compromising websites frequented by a specific community (e.g., government, industry, region) to infect visitors through drive-by compromise techniques. The goal is to compromise a specific user or set of users based on a shared interest, leveraging malicious scripts or iFrames injected into legitimate or adversary-controlled sites.

It is associated with the intrusion-set menuPass and is referenced as a component or feature within other malware families like PlugX and ZxShell, the latter indicating its inclusion as an added feature in version 3.2. Its technical behavior involves network traffic manipulation for potential man-in-the-middle attacks, with target platforms being Windows systems where such network spoofing tools are deployed.

4618.name: ARP spoofing tool
4618.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may buy, steal, or download software tools that can be used during targeting. Tools can be open or closed source, free or commercial. A tool can be used for malicious purposes by an adversary, but (unlike malware) were not intended to be used for those purposes (ex: [PsExec](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0029)). 

Adversaries may obtain tools to support their operations, including to support execution of post-compromise behaviors. Tools may also be leveraged for testing – for example, evaluating malware against commercial antivirus or endpoint detection and response (EDR) applications.(Citation: Forescout Conti Leaks 2022)(Citation: Sentinel Labs Top Tier Target 2025)

Tool acquisition may involve the procurement of commercial software licenses, including for red teaming tools such as Cobalt Strike. In addition to freely downloading or purchasing software, adversaries may steal software and/or software licenses from third-party entities (including other adversaries). Threat actors may also crack trial versions of software.(Citation: Recorded Future Beacon 2019)
4618.profile: [profile]ARP spoofing tool is a software utility used to conduct ARP cache poisoning, which maps to MITRE ATT&CK technique T1557.002 under the tactic Credential Access, targeting Network platforms. The tool works by sending falsified Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) messages, typically gratuitous replies or faster responses to ARP requests, to associate the adversary's MAC address with the IP address of a legitimate network device. This creates a man-in-the-middle position, enabling the interception and potential collection of network traffic, such as unencrypted credentials, and can facilitate follow-on actions like network sniffing or data manipulation. The intrusion-set menuPass is associated with its use.[/profile]
4618.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "ARP spoofing tool" is a software tool used to execute ARP cache poisoning, which corresponds to MITRE ATT&CK technique T1557.002 under the Collection tactic, applicable to Linux, macOS, and Windows platforms. The technical mechanics involve sending falsified ARP replies, either by responding faster than a legitimate device to a broadcast ARP request or by sending gratuitous ARP announcements, to maliciously associate the adversary's MAC address with a target IP address. This stateless protocol lacks authentication, allowing adversaries to poison network device caches, intercept traffic, and position themselves for man-in-the-middle attacks to collect credentials from insecure protocols.

It operates across multiple platforms. These tools, which can be legitimately obtained software like PsExec or Cobalt Strike, are used to create network tunnels or forward traffic from a compromised system to enable remote access, lateral movement, and command and control, often bypassing network defenses. It functions by encapsulating traffic within another protocol, such as using SSH tunneling to forward arbitrary data through an encrypted channel, allowing adversaries to conceal malicious communications and access otherwise unreachable systems. This tool supports operations like persistent access and evasion of network filtering.

4623.name: spear-phishing campaign
4623.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may send phishing messages to gain access to victim systems. All forms of phishing are electronically delivered social engineering. Phishing can be targeted, known as spearphishing. In spearphishing, a specific individual, company, or industry will be targeted by the adversary. More generally, adversaries can conduct non-targeted phishing, such as in mass malware spam campaigns.

Adversaries may send victims emails containing malicious attachments or links, typically to execute malicious code on victim systems. Phishing may also be conducted via third-party services, like social media platforms. Phishing may also involve social engineering techniques, such as posing as a trusted source, as well as evasive techniques such as removing or manipulating emails or metadata/headers from compromised accounts being abused to send messages (e.g., [Email Hiding Rules](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1564/008)).(Citation: Microsoft OAuth Spam 2022)(Citation: Palo Alto Unit 42 VBA Infostealer 2014) Another way to accomplish this is by [Email Spoofing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1672)(Citation: Proofpoint-spoof) the identity of the sender, which can be used to fool both the human recipient as well as automated security tools,(Citation: cyberproof-double-bounce) or by including the intended target as a party to an existing email thread that includes malicious files or links (i.e., "thread hijacking").(Citation: phishing-krebs)

Victims may also receive phishing messages that instruct them to call a phone number where they are directed to visit a malicious URL, download malware,(Citation: sygnia Luna Month)(Citation: CISA Remote Monitoring and Management Software) or install adversary-accessible remote management tools onto their computer (i.e., [User Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204)).(Citation: Unit42 Luna Moth)
4623.profile: [profile]Spear-phishing campaign is a targeted social engineering attack, corresponding to MITRE ATT&CK technique T1566 under the Initial Access tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It involves sending tailored electronic messages, often via email or third-party services, to specific individuals or organizations. These messages contain malicious attachments or links designed to trick the victim into executing code, often employing evasive techniques like email spoofing or thread hijacking to appear legitimate. The intrusion-set MenuPass has been associated with this technique.[/profile]
4623.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Spear-phishing campaign is a targeted social engineering attack (T1566.002, part of Phishing) under the Initial Access tactic, targeting multiple platforms. It involves sending tailored electronic messages, such as emails with malicious attachments or links, to specific individuals, companies, or industries to gain access or elicit sensitive information. Techniques include posing as a trusted source, using email spoofing, thread hijacking, or employing third-party services like social media to bypass enterprise security. Adversaries may use obfuscated URLs, tracking pixels, or phishing kits like EvilProxy to capture credentials and session cookies, often leveraging prior reconnaissance for persuasive lures.

4624.profile: [profile]Trochilus RAT (Trochilus Rat) is a remote access trojan attributed to groups including APT31, Gallium, and Stone Panda. It is deployed via structured droppers, shares technical similarities and code modifications with retooled versions of other RATs like Gh0st RAT and 9002 RAT, and has been used in cyberespionage campaigns targeting the gambling sector.[/profile]

Its key technical behaviors include being deployed via droppers that share a structure with those used for modified versions of Gh0st RAT and 9002 RAT, indicating shared development or tooling. It is related to or shares characteristics with malware families like RedLeaves and Himawari. Its primary target platform is Windows systems.[/profile]

4625.name: quasar
4625.profile: [profile]Quasar, also known as Quasar RAT, is a remote access trojan attributed to the Stone Panda intrusion set. 4647.name: SIGINT capabilities
4647.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may upload, install, or otherwise set up capabilities that can be used during targeting. To support their operations, an adversary may need to take capabilities they developed ([Develop Capabilities](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1587)) or obtained ([Obtain Capabilities](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1588)) and stage them on infrastructure under their control. These capabilities may be staged on infrastructure that was previously purchased/rented by the adversary ([Acquire Infrastructure](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1583)) or was otherwise compromised by them ([Compromise Infrastructure](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1584)). Capabilities may also be staged on web services, such as GitHub or Pastebin, or on Platform-as-a-Service (PaaS) offerings that enable users to easily provision applications.(Citation: Volexity Ocean Lotus November 2020)(Citation: Dragos Heroku Watering Hole)(Citation: Malwarebytes Heroku Skimmers)(Citation: Netskope GCP Redirection)(Citation: Netskope Cloud Phishing)

Staging of capabilities can aid the adversary in a number of initial access and post-compromise behaviors, including (but not limited to):

* Staging web resources necessary to conduct [Drive-by Compromise](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1189) when a user browses to a site.(Citation: FireEye CFR Watering Hole 2012)(Citation: Gallagher 2015)(Citation: ATT ScanBox)
* Staging web resources for a link target to be used with spearphishing.(Citation: Malwarebytes Silent Librarian October 2020)(Citation: Proofpoint TA407 September 2019)
* Uploading malware or tools to a location accessible to a victim network to enable [Ingress Tool Transfer](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1105).(Citation: Volexity Ocean Lotus November 2020)
* Installing a previously acquired SSL/TLS certificate to use to encrypt command and control traffic (ex: [Asymmetric Cryptography](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1573/002) with [Web Protocols](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1071/001)).(Citation: DigiCert Install SSL Cert)
4647.profile: [profile]SIGINT capabilities is a preparatory technique where adversaries stage operational tools and resources on controlled infrastructure. This involves uploading malware, exploits, or web resources to compromised, purchased, or public infrastructure like cloud platforms (e.g., Heroku, GitHub) to enable subsequent attacks such as drive-by compromises, spearphishing link targets, or tool transfers. It is part of the broader adversary lifecycle, following capability development or acquisition.[/profile]
4647.profile_without_enhance: [profile]SIGINT capabilities is a technique for gathering intelligence by intercepting signals, such as communications, using specialized infrastructure like satellite dishes. This capability supports the adversary lifecycle by enabling the collection of sensitive information from target environments, which can be used to inform and enable subsequent attack stages.

4655.name: targeting supply chains
4655.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may manipulate products or product delivery mechanisms prior to receipt by a final consumer for the purpose of data or system compromise.

Supply chain compromise can take place at any stage of the supply chain including:

* Manipulation of development tools
* Manipulation of a development environment
* Manipulation of source code repositories (public or private)
* Manipulation of source code in open-source dependencies
* Manipulation of software update/distribution mechanisms
* Compromised/infected system images (removable media infected at the factory)(Citation: IBM Storwize)(Citation: Schneider Electric USB Malware) 
* Replacement of legitimate software with modified versions
* Sales of modified/counterfeit products to legitimate distributors
* Shipment interdiction

While supply chain compromise can impact any component of hardware or software, adversaries looking to gain execution have often focused on malicious additions to legitimate software in software distribution or update channels.(Citation: Avast CCleaner3 2018)(Citation: Microsoft Dofoil 2018)(Citation: Command Five SK 2011) Adversaries may limit targeting to a desired victim set or distribute malicious software to a broad set of consumers but only follow up with specific victims.(Citation: Symantec Elderwood Sept 2012)(Citation: Avast CCleaner3 2018)(Citation: Command Five SK 2011) Popular open-source projects that are used as dependencies in many applications may also be targeted as a means to add malicious code to users of the dependency.(Citation: Trendmicro NPM Compromise)

In some cases, adversaries may conduct “second-order” supply chain compromises by leveraging the access gained from an initial supply chain compromise to further compromise a software component.(Citation: Krebs 3cx overview 2023) This may allow the threat actor to spread to even more victims.
4655.profile: [profile]Supply Chain Compromise, identified as T1195, is an Initial Access tactic applicable to multiple platforms. It involves manipulating products or delivery mechanisms before consumer receipt to compromise data or systems. Specific methods include tampering with development tools, environments, source code repositories, open-source dependencies, software update channels, system images, or through shipment interdiction. Adversaries often focus on malicious additions to legitimate software in distribution channels and may conduct "second-order" compromises to expand access. Groups like Sandworm Team, Ember Bear, and OilRig have been associated with this technique.[/profile]
4655.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "targeting supply chains" aligns with the MITRE ATT&CK technique Supply Chain Compromise (T1195) under the Initial Access tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. This involves adversaries manipulating products or delivery mechanisms before consumer receipt to compromise data or systems. Specific methods include tampering with development tools, source code repositories, software updates, or hardware components, and may involve broad distribution with selective follow-up on specific victims or leveraging initial compromises for second-order attacks. Related groups include Sandworm Team, Dragonfly, and APT41.

4656.name: targeting upstream vendors
4656.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may search private data from threat intelligence vendors for information that can be used during targeting. Threat intelligence vendors may offer paid feeds or portals that offer more data than what is publicly reported. Although sensitive details (such as customer names and other identifiers) may be redacted, this information may contain trends regarding breaches such as target industries, attribution claims, and successful TTPs/countermeasures.(Citation: D3Secutrity CTI Feeds)

Adversaries may search in private threat intelligence vendor data to gather actionable information. If a threat actor is searching for information on their own activities, that falls under [Search Threat Vendor Data](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1681). Information reported by vendors may also reveal opportunities other forms of reconnaissance (ex: [Search Open Websites/Domains](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1593)), establishing operational resources (ex: [Develop Capabilities](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1587) or [Obtain Capabilities](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1588)), and/or initial access (ex: [Exploit Public-Facing Application](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1190) or [External Remote Services](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1133)).
4656.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique "Gather Victim Host Information: Threat Intel Vendors" (ID: T1597.001), a sub-technique under the Reconnaissance tactic. It involves adversaries searching private, often paid, data feeds or portals from commercial threat intelligence vendors to gather actionable targeting information such as breach trends, target industries, attribution claims, and successful TTPs, which can inform follow-on operations like reconnaissance, capability development, or initial access. The intrusion-set menuPass is associated with this technique.
4656.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "targeting upstream vendors" is a reconnaissance technique where adversaries gather intelligence from software or service providers in a supply chain to facilitate downstream attacks. This involves searching private data from threat intelligence vendors for trends on breaches, target industries, and successful TTPs, which can inform subsequent actions like developing capabilities or initial access. It is related to broader supply chain compromise methods where adversaries manipulate software prior to consumer receipt. The technique leverages vulnerabilities and vendor data to identify and exploit weaknesses in the supply chain for targeted operations.

4658.name: Watering Holes
4658.profile: [profile]Watering Holes, designated as T1584.004 in the MITRE ATT&CK framework under the Resource Development tactic, involves adversaries compromising third-party web servers. The technique stages malicious code on these servers to infect visitors, often through drive-by compromises, as part of initial access operations. It is utilized by groups like menuPass to target users browsing to the compromised sites.
4658.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Watering Holes is a technique for initial access, identified as T1189 in the MITRE ATT&CK framework under the Initial Access tactic, applicable to multiple platforms including Windows, macOS, and Linux. This technique involves compromising or strategically creating websites that are likely to be visited by a specific target group. When victims browse to these compromised sites, malicious code is executed to exploit vulnerabilities in their web browsers or applications, facilitating system compromise. This method is often supported by staging malicious web resources on compromised infrastructure, such as third-party servers, to host the attack payload.

4659.name: Zero-day Exploits
4659.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may develop exploits that can be used during targeting. An exploit takes advantage of a bug or vulnerability in order to cause unintended or unanticipated behavior to occur on computer hardware or software. Rather than finding/modifying exploits from online or purchasing them from exploit vendors, an adversary may develop their own exploits.(Citation: NYTStuxnet) Adversaries may use information acquired via [Vulnerabilities](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1588/006) to focus exploit development efforts. As part of the exploit development process, adversaries may uncover exploitable vulnerabilities through methods such as fuzzing and patch analysis.(Citation: Irongeek Sims BSides 2017)

As with legitimate development efforts, different skill sets may be required for developing exploits. The skills needed may be located in-house, or may need to be contracted out. Use of a contractor may be considered an extension of that adversary's exploit development capabilities, provided the adversary plays a role in shaping requirements and maintains an initial degree of exclusivity to the exploit.

Adversaries may use exploits during various phases of the adversary lifecycle (i.e. [Exploit Public-Facing Application](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1190), [Exploitation for Client Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1203), [Exploitation for Privilege Escalation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1068), [Exploitation for Defense Evasion](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1211), [Exploitation for Credential Access](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1212), [Exploitation of Remote Services](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1210), and [Application or System Exploitation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1499/004)).
4659.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique "Develop Capabilities: Exploits," identified as T1587.004 within the Resource Development tactic. It operates across multiple platforms and involves adversaries developing their own exploits, as opposed to acquiring them, using methods like fuzzing and patch analysis to uncover vulnerabilities. This capability is used to support various subsequent attack phases, including initial access and privilege escalation, and has been associated with groups like UNC3886, Volt Typhoon, and Leviathan.[/profile]
4659.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Zero-day Exploits is a technique where adversaries leverage previously unknown vulnerabilities (zero-days) to cause unintended behavior in software or hardware, bypassing defenses due to the lack of available patches. These exploits are developed in-house, acquired, or modified and are used across multiple attack phases including initial access, privilege escalation, and defense evasion, as seen in campaigns by groups like UNC3886 and Volt Typhoon. The technical mechanics involve targeting unpatched bugs to execute adversary-controlled code, often requiring skills in vulnerability research like fuzzing or patch analysis.

4666.uncertain_mes: [gh0st RAT](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0032) is a remote access tool (RAT). The source code is public and it has been used by multiple groups.(Citation: FireEye Hacking Team)(Citation: Arbor Musical Chairs Feb 2018)(Citation: Nccgroup Gh0st April 2018)

4675.name: manual network and host enumeration
4675.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may enumerate system and service logs to find useful data. These logs may highlight various types of valuable insights for an adversary, such as user authentication records ([Account Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1087)), security or vulnerable software ([Software Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1518)), or hosts within a compromised network ([Remote System Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1018)).

Host binaries may be leveraged to collect system logs. Examples include using `wevtutil.exe` or [PowerShell](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001) on Windows to access and/or export security event information.(Citation: WithSecure Lazarus-NoPineapple Threat Intel Report 2023)(Citation: Cadet Blizzard emerges as novel threat actor) In cloud environments, adversaries may leverage utilities such as the Azure VM Agent’s `CollectGuestLogs.exe` to collect security logs from cloud hosted infrastructure.(Citation: SIM Swapping and Abuse of the Microsoft Azure Serial Console)

Adversaries may also target centralized logging infrastructure such as SIEMs. Logs may also be bulk exported and sent to adversary-controlled infrastructure for offline analysis.

In addition to gaining a better understanding of the environment, adversaries may also monitor logs in real time to track incident response procedures. This may allow them to adjust their techniques in order to maintain persistence or evade defenses.(Citation: Permiso GUI-Vil 2023)
4675.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique Log Enumeration (T1654), categorized under Discovery. It involves adversaries enumerating system, service, and security logs to gather intelligence. Specific technical mechanics include using host binaries like `wevtutil.exe` or PowerShell on Windows, and utilities like Azure VM Agent's `CollectGuestLogs.exe` in cloud environments, to access and export event logs. Adversaries may also target centralized logging infrastructure like SIEMs, bulk export logs for offline analysis, or monitor logs in real-time to track incident response. This technique is associated with groups including Volt Typhoon, APT5, and Mustang Panda.[/profile]
4675.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "manual network and host enumeration" is an attack pattern, though it lacks a standard MITRE ATT&CK ID. It falls under the Discovery tactic and can be executed on multiple platforms. The technique involves adversaries manually using native system utilities and commands to discover remote systems and gather host information within a compromised network. This can include using tools like Ping, `net view`, or examining local network configuration files such as ARP cache and host files to map the environment.

4699.name: Flash exploit
4699.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may attempt to exploit a weakness in an Internet-facing host or system to initially access a network. The weakness in the system can be a software bug, a temporary glitch, or a misconfiguration.

Exploited applications are often websites/web servers, but can also include databases (like SQL), standard services (like SMB or SSH), network device administration and management protocols (like SNMP and Smart Install), and any other system with Internet-accessible open sockets.(Citation: NVD CVE-2016-6662)(Citation: CIS Multiple SMB Vulnerabilities)(Citation: US-CERT TA18-106A Network Infrastructure Devices 2018)(Citation: Cisco Blog Legacy Device Attacks)(Citation: NVD CVE-2014-7169) On ESXi infrastructure, adversaries may exploit exposed OpenSLP services; they may alternatively exploit exposed VMware vCenter servers.(Citation: Recorded Future ESXiArgs Ransomware 2023)(Citation: Ars Technica VMWare Code Execution Vulnerability 2021) Depending on the flaw being exploited, this may also involve [Exploitation for Defense Evasion](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1211) or [Exploitation for Client Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1203).

If an application is hosted on cloud-based infrastructure and/or is containerized, then exploiting it may lead to compromise of the underlying instance or container. This can allow an adversary a path to access the cloud or container APIs (e.g., via the [Cloud Instance Metadata API](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1552/005)), exploit container host access via [Escape to Host](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1611), or take advantage of weak identity and access management policies.

Adversaries may also exploit edge network infrastructure and related appliances, specifically targeting devices that do not support robust host-based defenses.(Citation: Mandiant Fortinet Zero Day)(Citation: Wired Russia Cyberwar)

For websites and databases, the OWASP top 10 and CWE top 25 highlight the most common web-based vulnerabilities.(Citation: OWASP Top 10)(Citation: CWE top 25)
4699.profile: [profile]Flash exploit is a specific instance of the MITRE ATT&CK technique Exploitation for Client Execution (T1203) under the Initial Access tactic, targeting platforms like Windows and macOS. It involves adversaries exploiting vulnerabilities in common third-party applications such as Adobe Flash, often delivered via malicious documents like Microsoft Office files, to execute arbitrary code on a victim's system. This method is used by groups like APT28 and Lazarus Group to gain initial access.

It involves exploiting vulnerabilities in the Adobe Flash Player, a common third-party application, to execute arbitrary code. These exploits are often delivered via malicious files, such as objects embedded within Microsoft Office documents, requiring user interaction to open the file and trigger the exploit.

4702.name: Single-byte XOR encoding
4702.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may encode data with a standard data encoding system to make the content of command and control traffic more difficult to detect. Command and control (C2) information can be encoded using a standard data encoding system that adheres to existing protocol specifications. Common data encoding schemes include ASCII, Unicode, hexadecimal, Base64, and MIME.(Citation: Wikipedia Binary-to-text Encoding)(Citation: Wikipedia Character Encoding) Some data encoding systems may also result in data compression, such as gzip.
4702.profile: [profile]Single-byte XOR encoding, also known as standard encoding (T1132.001), is a Command and Control tactic used across multiple platforms. It involves encoding C2 traffic using common, protocol-compliant schemes like ASCII, Unicode, hexadecimal, Base64, and MIME to obfuscate content and evade detection, with groups like menuPass, Lazarus Group, and APT33 employing this technique.
4702.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Single-byte XOR encoding is a sub-technique of Data Encoding (T1132) within the Command and Control tactic. It operates across multiple platforms by applying a simple XOR cipher, where each byte of data is bitwise XORed with a single, static key value (e.g., 0xAA). This process transforms plaintext into obfuscated ciphertext to evade signature-based detection in network traffic or files. It is a lightweight, non-standard obfuscation method distinct from common encodings like Base64.

4711.name: dual persistence locations
4711.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may clear artifacts associated with previously established persistence on a host system to remove evidence of their activity. This may involve various actions, such as removing services, deleting executables, [Modify Registry](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1112), [Plist File Modification](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1647), or other methods of cleanup to prevent defenders from collecting evidence of their persistent presence.(Citation: Cylance Dust Storm) Adversaries may also delete accounts previously created to maintain persistence (i.e. [Create Account](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1136)).(Citation: Talos - Cisco Attack 2022)

In some instances, artifacts of persistence may also be removed once an adversary’s persistence is executed in order to prevent errors with the new instance of the malware.(Citation: NCC Group Team9 June 2020)
4711.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique "Clear Persistence" (ID: T1070.009), a Defense Evasion tactic. It operates on Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms by removing artifacts from previously established persistence mechanisms to eliminate evidence. This includes actions like deleting malicious services or executables, removing registry keys, modifying plist files, or deleting created user accounts. The intrusion set menuPass has been associated with this behavior.
4711.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "dual persistence locations" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the provided context, it appears to be a persistence method where adversaries establish redundant persistence mechanisms in multiple system locations. This can involve modifying property list (plist) files on macOS, creating accounts, or deploying network logon scripts to ensure continued access if one method is discovered and removed.

4712.name: using startup folders
4712.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may use startup items automatically executed at boot initialization to establish persistence. Startup items execute during the final phase of the boot process and contain shell scripts or other executable files along with configuration information used by the system to determine the execution order for all startup items.(Citation: Startup Items) This is technically a deprecated technology (superseded by [Launch Daemon](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1543/004)), and thus the appropriate folder, /Library/StartupItems isn’t guaranteed to exist on the system by default, but does appear to exist by default on macOS Sierra. A startup item is a directory whose executable and configuration property list (plist), StartupParameters.plist, reside in the top-level directory. An adversary can create the appropriate folders/files in the StartupItems directory to register their own persistence mechanism.(Citation: Methods of Mac Malware Persistence) Additionally, since StartupItems run during the bootup phase of macOS, they will run as the elevated root user.
4712.profile: [profile]Using Startup Folders, also known as T1037.005, is a persistence technique within the Boot or Logon Initialization Scripts tactic for macOS. It involves placing shell scripts or executables within the `/Library/StartupItems` directory, which is a deprecated macOS mechanism. A valid startup item is a directory containing an executable and a `StartupParameters.plist` configuration file. Items in this folder execute automatically during the final boot phase and run with root privileges, providing a high level of persistence and potential privilege escalation. The intrusion-set menuPass has been associated with this technique.
4712.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Using Startup Folders is a persistence technique (T1547.001) within the Persistence tactic on Windows. It works by placing a malicious executable or shortcut within specific system directories, such as C:\Users\[Username]\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup for the current user or C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\StartUp for all users, causing the referenced program to execute automatically upon user login.

4714.name: watering hole attack
4714.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may downgrade or use a version of system features that may be outdated, vulnerable, and/or does not support updated security controls. Downgrade attacks typically take advantage of a system’s backward compatibility to force it into less secure modes of operation. 

Adversaries may downgrade and use various less-secure versions of features of a system, such as [Command and Scripting Interpreter](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059)s or even network protocols that can be abused to enable [Adversary-in-the-Middle](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1557) or [Network Sniffing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1040).(Citation: Praetorian TLS Downgrade Attack 2014) For example, [PowerShell](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001) versions 5+ includes Script Block Logging (SBL), which can record executed script content. However, adversaries may attempt to execute a previous version of PowerShell that does not support SBL with the intent to [Impair Defenses](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1562) while running malicious scripts that may have otherwise been detected.(Citation: CrowdStrike BGH Ransomware 2021)(Citation: Mandiant BYOL 2018)(Citation: att_def_ps_logging)

Adversaries may similarly target network traffic to downgrade from an encrypted HTTPS connection to an unsecured HTTP connection that exposes network data in clear text.(Citation: Targeted SSL Stripping Attacks Are Real)(Citation: Crowdstrike Downgrade) On Windows systems, adversaries may downgrade the boot manager to a vulnerable version that bypasses Secure Boot, granting the ability to disable various operating system security mechanisms.(Citation: SafeBreach)
4714.profile: [profile]The entity "watering hole attack" is a technique where adversaries compromise websites frequented by a specific target community to stage exploits, such as injecting malicious JavaScript, for drive-by compromise. This is often used to profile and exploit visitors' web browsers. The associated group menuPass has been linked to this activity. The provided input incorrectly associates it with the downgrade attack technique (T1562.010), which is a distinct method for impairing defenses by forcing systems into less secure modes of operation.
4714.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity 'watering hole attack' is a technique aligned with MITRE ATT&CK ID T1608.004 (Drive-by Target) under the Resource Development tactic. It involves compromising websites frequented by a specific target community, such as a particular industry or government sector, to stage malicious content like JavaScript. This content is designed to exploit visitors' web browsers, often without requiring user interaction, to facilitate initial access. The technique is used by groups like Dragonfly and APT32, and it is a form of strategic web compromise where adversaries prepare the operational environment to infect systems during normal browsing.

4723.name: design
4723.profile: [profile]The entity "design" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. 4730.name: servicedll
4730.profile: [profile]Servicedll is a malware component attributed to APT17 and menuPass, functioning as a service DLL (ServiceDll) that registers via RegSetValueEx and operates within Svchost processes (Svchost\netsvcs). It implements standard service control handlers (ServiceMain, ServiceHandler for CONTROL_STOP, PAUSE, CONTINUE, etc.) for execution and persistence on Windows systems.[/profile]

It establishes persistence by creating and configuring Windows services via registry modifications, such as RegSetValueEx(ServiceDll) under SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services, and interacts with the service control manager through OpenSCManager and CreateService. The target platform is Windows, leveraging the Svchost process for execution.

4731.name: second-stage implant
4731.profile: [profile]Second-stage implant is a malware component deployed after an initial compromise. It is used by groups such as Vanilla Tempest, Stone Panda, and Molerats. Its primary function is to establish persistent, deeper access on compromised systems.

4738.name: stolen administrative credentials
4738.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may gather credentials that can be used during targeting. Account credentials gathered by adversaries may be those directly associated with the target victim organization or attempt to take advantage of the tendency for users to use the same passwords across personal and business accounts.

Adversaries may gather credentials from potential victims in various ways, such as direct elicitation via [Phishing for Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1598). Adversaries may also compromise sites then add malicious content designed to collect website authentication cookies from visitors.(Citation: ATT ScanBox) (Citation: Register Deloitte)(Citation: Register Uber)(Citation: Detectify Slack Tokens)(Citation: Forbes GitHub Creds)(Citation: GitHub truffleHog)(Citation: GitHub Gitrob)(Citation: CNET Leaks) Where multi-factor authentication (MFA) based on out-of-band communications is in use, adversaries may compromise a service provider to gain access to MFA codes and one-time passwords (OTP).(Citation: Okta Scatter Swine 2022)

Credential information may also be exposed to adversaries via leaks to online or other accessible data sets (ex: [Search Engines](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1593/002), breach dumps, code repositories, etc.). Adversaries may purchase credentials from dark web markets, such as Russian Market and 2easy, or through access to Telegram channels that distribute logs from infostealer malware.(Citation: Bleeping Computer 2easy 2021)(Citation: SecureWorks Infostealers 2023)(Citation: Bleeping Computer Stealer Logs 2023)

Gathering this information may reveal opportunities for other forms of reconnaissance (ex: [Search Open Websites/Domains](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1593) or [Phishing for Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1598)), establishing operational resources (ex: [Compromise Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1586)), and/or initial access (ex: [External Remote Services](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1133) or [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078)).
4738.profile: [profile]Stolen Administrative Credentials, identified as T1589.001, is a reconnaissance technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework targeting multiple platforms. Adversaries gather credentials through methods like phishing, compromising websites to steal authentication cookies, purchasing logs from infostealer malware on dark web markets, or exploiting credential leaks from public data sets and code repositories. This activity supports subsequent operations including initial access via Valid Accounts and is associated with groups such as APT28, Leviathan, and LAPSUS$.
4738.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "stolen administrative credentials" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the provided context, it refers to the use of compromised administrative-level credentials for unauthorized access. This is a core component of the Valid Accounts technique (T1078) and is used for Initial Access, Persistence, Privilege Escalation, and Lateral Movement. Credentials can be stolen via phishing, credential dumping from memory or files, or purchased from dark web markets. Once obtained, adversaries use these stolen credentials to log into services like VPNs, external remote services, or internal systems, often bypassing normal access controls.

4741.name: PowerSploit
4741.profile: [profile]PowerSploit is a post-exploitation framework and collection of PowerShell modules used for reconnaissance, privilege escalation, and lateral movement on Windows systems. It has been used by threat actors including menuPass, Turla, and APT17, who have employed its PowerView module for network discovery. Key technical behaviors include loading scripts via PowerShell's IEX command to download and execute modules from remote sources, and its functions support activities like SMB scanning, service abuse, and credential access.[profile]
4741.profile_without_enhance: [profile]PowerSploit is a post-exploitation framework written in PowerShell. It is used by threat actors, including APT17, for reconnaissance and lateral movement within Windows domains, as seen in Winnti campaigns. Its primary target platform is Microsoft Windows environments.

4742.name: plugx/sogu
4742.uncertain_mes: [PlugX](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0013) is a remote access tool (RAT) with modular plugins that has been used by multiple threat groups.(Citation: Lastline PlugX Analysis)(Citation: FireEye Clandestine Fox Part 2)(Citation: New DragonOK)(Citation: Dell TG-3390)
4742.profile: [profile]PlugX, also known as SOGU, KORPLUG, and DestroyRAT, is a modular remote access trojan (RAT) and backdoor first identified in 2012. It is attributed to numerous Chinese-speaking threat groups, including APT41, Mustang Panda, menuPass, and DragonOK. Its key behaviors include using legitimate signed executables to load malicious code, supporting commands for file exfiltration, keylogging, remote shell, and file transfers, and being extensible via plugins. It primarily targets Windows platforms and has been in continuous development since at least 2008.[/profile]
