It is based on an open-source Remote Access Trojan (RAT) framework. The primary target platform is Microsoft Windows systems.

4745.name: DLL sideloading
4745.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may abuse dynamic-link library files (DLLs) in order to achieve persistence, escalate privileges, and evade defenses. DLLs are libraries that contain code and data that can be simultaneously utilized by multiple programs. While DLLs are not malicious by nature, they can be abused through mechanisms such as side-loading, hijacking search order, and phantom DLL hijacking.(Citation: unit 42)

Specific ways DLLs are abused by adversaries include:

### DLL Sideloading
Adversaries may execute their own malicious payloads by side-loading DLLs. Side-loading involves hijacking which DLL a program loads by planting and then invoking a legitimate application that executes their payload(s).

Side-loading positions both the victim application and malicious payload(s) alongside each other. Adversaries likely use side-loading as a means of masking actions they perform under a legitimate, trusted, and potentially elevated system or software process. Benign executables used to side-load payloads may not be flagged during delivery and/or execution. Adversary payloads may also be encrypted/packed or otherwise obfuscated until loaded into the memory of the trusted process.

Adversaries may also side-load other packages, such as BPLs (Borland Package Library).(Citation: kroll bpl)

Adversaries may chain DLL sideloading multiple times to fragment functionality hindering analysis. Adversaries using multiple DLL files can split the loader functions across different DLLs, with a main DLL loading the separated export functions. (Citation: Virus Bulletin) Spreading loader functions across multiple DLLs makes analysis harder, since all files must be collected to fully understand the malware’s behavior.  Another method implements a “loader-for-a-loader”, where a malicious DLL’s sole role is to load a second DLL (or a chain of DLLs) that contain the real payload. (Citation: Sophos)

### DLL Search Order Hijacking
Adversaries may execute their own malicious payloads by hijacking the search order that Windows uses to load DLLs. This search order is a sequence of special and standard search locations that a program checks when loading a DLL. An adversary can plant a trojan DLL in a directory that will be prioritized by the DLL search order over the location of a legitimate library. This will cause Windows to load the malicious DLL when it is called for by the victim program.(Citation: unit 42)

### DLL Redirection
Adversaries may directly modify the search order via DLL redirection, which after being enabled (in the Registry or via the creation of a redirection file) may cause a program to load a DLL from a different location.(Citation: Microsoft redirection)(Citation: Microsoft - manifests/assembly)

### Phantom DLL Hijacking
Adversaries may leverage phantom DLL hijacking by targeting references to non-existent DLL files. They may be able to load their own malicious DLL by planting it with the correct name in the location of the missing module.(Citation: Hexacorn DLL Hijacking)(Citation: Hijack DLLs CrowdStrike)

### DLL Substitution
Adversaries may target existing, valid DLL files and substitute them with their own malicious DLLs, planting them with the same name and in the same location as the valid DLL file.(Citation: Wietze Beukema DLL Hijacking)

Programs that fall victim to DLL hijacking may appear to behave normally because malicious DLLs may be configured to also load the legitimate DLLs they were meant to replace, evading defenses.

Remote DLL hijacking can occur when a program sets its current directory to a remote location, such as a Web share, before loading a DLL.(Citation: dll pre load owasp)(Citation: microsoft remote preloading)

If a valid DLL is configured to run at a higher privilege level, then the adversary-controlled DLL that is loaded will also be executed at the higher level. In this case, the technique could be used for privilege escalation.
4745.profile: [profile]DLL Sideloading (T1574.001) is a Defense Evasion and Persistence technique primarily used on Windows. It involves placing a malicious DLL alongside a legitimate executable that, when invoked, loads the malicious DLL instead of or in addition to the intended library, thereby executing the adversary's payload under the guise of a trusted process. This technique can be chained multiple times to fragment functionality and hinder analysis, and adversaries may also side-load other package types like Borland Package Libraries (BPLs). It is associated with groups including menuPass, Lazarus Group, and APT41.
4745.profile_without_enhance: [profile]DLL Sideloading is a technique where adversaries execute malicious payloads by hijacking the DLL loading process of a legitimate application. The adversary plants a malicious DLL alongside a trusted executable, and when the application is invoked, it loads the adversary's DLL instead of or in addition to the legitimate one. This technique masks malicious actions under a trusted process, often for persistence, privilege escalation, or defense evasion. Payloads may be encrypted or obfuscated until loaded, and adversaries may chain multiple sideloading events to fragment functionality and hinder analysis.

4746.name: user impersonation
4746.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may impersonate a trusted person or organization in order to persuade and trick a target into performing some action on their behalf. For example, adversaries may communicate with victims (via [Phishing for Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1598), [Phishing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566), or [Internal Spearphishing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1534)) while impersonating a known sender such as an executive, colleague, or third-party vendor. Established trust can then be leveraged to accomplish an adversary’s ultimate goals, possibly against multiple victims. 
 
In many cases of business email compromise or email fraud campaigns, adversaries use impersonation to defraud victims -- deceiving them into sending money or divulging information that ultimately enables [Financial Theft](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1657).

Adversaries will often also use social engineering techniques such as manipulative and persuasive language in email subject lines and body text such as `payment`, `request`, or `urgent` to push the victim to act quickly before malicious activity is detected. These campaigns are often specifically targeted against people who, due to job roles and/or accesses, can carry out the adversary’s goal.   
 
Impersonation is typically preceded by reconnaissance techniques such as [Gather Victim Identity Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1589) and [Gather Victim Org Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1591) as well as acquiring infrastructure such as email domains (i.e. [Domains](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1583/001)) to substantiate their false identity.(Citation: CrowdStrike-BEC)
 
There is the potential for multiple victims in campaigns involving impersonation. For example, an adversary may [Compromise Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1586) targeting one organization which can then be used to support impersonation against other entities.(Citation: VEC)
4746.profile: [profile]User Impersonation (T1656) is a social engineering technique within the Initial Access tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It involves adversaries posing as a trusted person or organization, such as an executive or vendor, to deceive a target into performing actions like sending money or divulging information. This is often executed via phishing emails containing urgent language like "payment" or "request" to pressure victims, and is typically preceded by reconnaissance to gather identity and organizational information to substantiate the false identity. The technique is associated with groups like Kimsuky, APT41, and Scattered Spider.[/profile]
4746.profile_without_enhance: [profile]User Impersonation is a technique where adversaries impersonate trusted individuals or entities to deceive targets into performing actions like sending money or divulging information. It is often facilitated through social engineering via phishing emails that use urgent language and is preceded by reconnaissance to gather victim identity and organizational details. This technique is associated with groups like Kimsuky, APT41, and Scattered Spider.

4747.name: credential compromise
4747.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may use credentials obtained from breach dumps of unrelated accounts to gain access to target accounts through credential overlap. Occasionally, large numbers of username and password pairs are dumped online when a website or service is compromised and the user account credentials accessed. The information may be useful to an adversary attempting to compromise accounts by taking advantage of the tendency for users to use the same passwords across personal and business accounts.

Credential stuffing is a risky option because it could cause numerous authentication failures and account lockouts, depending on the organization's login failure policies.

Typically, management services over commonly used ports are used when stuffing credentials. Commonly targeted services include the following:

* SSH (22/TCP)
* Telnet (23/TCP)
* FTP (21/TCP)
* NetBIOS / SMB / Samba (139/TCP & 445/TCP)
* LDAP (389/TCP)
* Kerberos (88/TCP)
* RDP / Terminal Services (3389/TCP)
* HTTP/HTTP Management Services (80/TCP & 443/TCP)
* MSSQL (1433/TCP)
* Oracle (1521/TCP)
* MySQL (3306/TCP)
* VNC (5900/TCP)

In addition to management services, adversaries may "target single sign-on (SSO) and cloud-based applications utilizing federated authentication protocols," as well as externally facing email applications, such as Office 365.(Citation: US-CERT TA18-068A 2018)
4747.profile: [profile]Credential Stuffing is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1110.004 under the Credential Access tactic. It involves using credentials from unrelated breach dumps to access target accounts by exploiting password reuse. Attackers automate login attempts against management services on common ports like SSH (22/TCP), RDP (3389/TCP), and HTTP/S (80/443/TCP), as well as against cloud applications and SSO systems. This method risks triggering account lockouts due to authentication failures. The intrusion-set menuPass has been associated with this technique.[/profile]
4747.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Credential Compromise is a broad attack pattern where adversaries illicitly obtain account login and credential material, such as passwords or hashes, to gain unauthorized access. This encompasses techniques like OS Credential Dumping (T1003) from system memory and structures, extracting stored credentials from the Windows Credential Manager (T1555.004), and leveraging compromised credentials from breach dumps for credential stuffing (T1110.004) against services like SSH, RDP, and web applications. The gathered credentials are primarily used for initial access, lateral movement, and privilege escalation within a target environment.

4748.name: RC4 cipher communications
4748.profile: [profile]RC4 cipher communications is a technique used by adversaries to conceal command and control or exfiltration traffic by implementing the RC4 symmetric encryption algorithm within a network protocol. This method involves manually sharing a key to encrypt and decrypt data, which can be applied to protocols not typically encrypted, like HTTP, or layered within already encrypted channels like HTTPS. It is associated with groups such as menuPass, MuddyWater, and APT28.[/profile]
4748.profile_without_enhance: [profile]RC4 cipher communications is a technique where adversaries use the RC4 symmetric encryption algorithm to obfuscate command and control or data exfiltration traffic, often implementing it manually within a protocol to add an extra layer of encryption beyond any inherent protocol security.

4750.name: System Enumeration
4750.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may enumerate system and service logs to find useful data. These logs may highlight various types of valuable insights for an adversary, such as user authentication records ([Account Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1087)), security or vulnerable software ([Software Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1518)), or hosts within a compromised network ([Remote System Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1018)).

Host binaries may be leveraged to collect system logs. Examples include using `wevtutil.exe` or [PowerShell](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001) on Windows to access and/or export security event information.(Citation: WithSecure Lazarus-NoPineapple Threat Intel Report 2023)(Citation: Cadet Blizzard emerges as novel threat actor) In cloud environments, adversaries may leverage utilities such as the Azure VM Agent’s `CollectGuestLogs.exe` to collect security logs from cloud hosted infrastructure.(Citation: SIM Swapping and Abuse of the Microsoft Azure Serial Console)

Adversaries may also target centralized logging infrastructure such as SIEMs. Logs may also be bulk exported and sent to adversary-controlled infrastructure for offline analysis.

In addition to gaining a better understanding of the environment, adversaries may also monitor logs in real time to track incident response procedures. This may allow them to adjust their techniques in order to maintain persistence or evade defenses.(Citation: Permiso GUI-Vil 2023)
4750.profile: [profile]System Enumeration, also known as log enumeration and mapped to MITRE ATT&CK ID T1654 under the Discovery tactic, involves adversaries enumerating system and service logs to gather intelligence. This is performed on platforms like Windows and cloud environments using host binaries such as `wevtutil.exe` or PowerShell to access security event logs, or utilities like Azure VM Agent's `CollectGuestLogs.exe`. Adversaries may target centralized logging infrastructure like SIEMs, bulk export logs to offline analysis, and monitor logs in real-time to track incident response and adjust their tactics. The technique has been associated with groups including Volt Typhoon, APT5, and Mustang Panda.
4750.profile_without_enhance: [profile]System Enumeration is a Discovery technique where adversaries gather detailed information about a target operating system and hardware, including version, patches, architecture, and services. This is often performed using native commands and tools like `systeminfo` or `sc query` to understand the environment's configuration and identify potential vulnerabilities or security software for follow-on actions.

4751.name: Command Window Spawning
4751.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may use hidden windows to conceal malicious activity from the plain sight of users. In some cases, windows that would typically be displayed when an application carries out an operation can be hidden. This may be utilized by system administrators to avoid disrupting user work environments when carrying out administrative tasks. Adversaries may abuse these functionalities to hide otherwise visible windows from users so as not to alert the user to adversary activity on the system.(Citation: Antiquated Mac Malware) On macOS, the configurations for how applications run are listed in property list (plist) files. One of the tags in these files can be apple.awt.UIElement, which allows for Java applications to prevent the application's icon from appearing in the Dock. A common use for this is when applications run in the system tray, but don't also want to show up in the Dock. Similarly, on Windows there are a variety of features in scripting languages, such as [PowerShell](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001), Jscript, and [Visual Basic](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/005) to make windows hidden. One example of this is powershell.exe -WindowStyle Hidden.(Citation: PowerShell About 2019) The Windows Registry can also be edited to hide application windows from the current user. For example, by setting the `WindowPosition` subkey in the `HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Console\%SystemRoot%_System32_WindowsPowerShell_v1.0_PowerShell.exe` Registry key to a maximum value, PowerShell windows will open off screen and be hidden.(Citation: Cantoris Computing) In addition, Windows supports the `CreateDesktop()` API that can create a hidden desktop window with its own corresponding explorer.exe process.(Citation: Hidden VNC)(Citation: Anatomy of an hVNC Attack) All applications running on the hidden desktop window, such as a hidden VNC (hVNC) session,(Citation: Hidden VNC) will be invisible to other desktops windows. Adversaries may also leverage cmd.exe(Citation: Cybereason - Hidden Malicious Remote Access) as a parent process, and then utilize a LOLBin, such as DeviceCredentialDeployment.exe,(Citation: LOLBAS Project GitHub Device Cred Dep)(Citation: SecureList BlueNoroff Device Cred Dev) to hide windows.
4751.profile: [profile]Command Window Spawning is a technique within MITRE ATT&CK ID T1564.003 (Hidden Window), categorized under Defense Evasion and operating on Windows and macOS platforms. It involves concealing malicious activity by hiding windows from user view, using methods such as the PowerShell command `-WindowStyle Hidden`, editing the Windows Registry to position windows off-screen, leveraging the `CreateDesktop()` API to create a hidden desktop, or on macOS, setting the `apple.awt.UIElement` tag in plist files to hide application icons. This technique is employed by groups including Gamaredon Group, FIN7, and APT28 to avoid detection during operations.[/profile]
4751.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Command Window Spawning is a technique where adversaries launch commands from a parent process that creates a new, often hidden, command-line window to execute malicious code, evading detection by separating the execution context. This is typically associated with Defense Evasion tactics on Windows platforms, utilizing system utilities or scripting to spawn processes like cmd.exe or powershell.exe with hidden window styles to conceal activity.

4752.name: File System Enumeration
4752.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may enumerate system and service logs to find useful data. These logs may highlight various types of valuable insights for an adversary, such as user authentication records ([Account Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1087)), security or vulnerable software ([Software Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1518)), or hosts within a compromised network ([Remote System Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1018)).

Host binaries may be leveraged to collect system logs. Examples include using `wevtutil.exe` or [PowerShell](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001) on Windows to access and/or export security event information.(Citation: WithSecure Lazarus-NoPineapple Threat Intel Report 2023)(Citation: Cadet Blizzard emerges as novel threat actor) In cloud environments, adversaries may leverage utilities such as the Azure VM Agent’s `CollectGuestLogs.exe` to collect security logs from cloud hosted infrastructure.(Citation: SIM Swapping and Abuse of the Microsoft Azure Serial Console)

Adversaries may also target centralized logging infrastructure such as SIEMs. Logs may also be bulk exported and sent to adversary-controlled infrastructure for offline analysis.

In addition to gaining a better understanding of the environment, adversaries may also monitor logs in real time to track incident response procedures. This may allow them to adjust their techniques in order to maintain persistence or evade defenses.(Citation: Permiso GUI-Vil 2023)
4752.profile: [profile]File System Enumeration, also known as log enumeration (T1654), is a Discovery technique used to gather valuable system intelligence. Adversaries collect logs using host binaries like `wevtutil.exe` or PowerShell on Windows, and tools like Azure VM Agent's `CollectGuestLogs.exe` in cloud environments, to extract data on user accounts, software, and network hosts. They may also target centralized logging infrastructure like SIEMs, exporting logs for offline analysis or monitoring them in real-time to track defensive responses. This technique is associated with groups like Volt Typhoon and menuPass.[/profile]
4752.profile_without_enhance: [profile]File System Enumeration is a technique mapped to MITRE ATT&CK ID T1083 under the Discovery tactic, applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves adversaries using commands and utilities to survey and catalog directory contents, file metadata, and directory structures to understand the environment and locate valuable data. This can be performed via native system binaries like `dir` or `ls`, and may target specific directories such as user profiles or network shares to identify sensitive files for exfiltration.

4753.name: Network Traffic Compression and Encryption
4753.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may use compression to obfuscate their payloads or files. Compressed file formats such as ZIP, gzip, 7z, and RAR can compress and archive multiple files together to make it easier and faster to transfer files. In addition to compressing files, adversaries may also compress shellcode directly - for example, in order to store it in a Windows Registry key (i.e., [Fileless Storage](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/011)).(Citation: Trustwave Pillowmint June 2020)

In order to further evade detection, adversaries may combine multiple ZIP files into one archive. This process of concatenation creates an archive that appears to be a single archive but in fact contains the central directories of the embedded archives. Some ZIP readers, such as 7zip, may not be able to identify concatenated ZIP files and miss the presence of the malicious payload.(Citation: Perception Point)

File archives may be sent as one [Spearphishing Attachment](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001) through email. Adversaries have sent malicious payloads as archived files to encourage the user to interact with and extract the malicious payload onto their system (i.e., [Malicious File](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002)).(Citation: NTT Security Flagpro new December 2021) However, some file compression tools, such as 7zip, can be used to produce self-extracting archives. Adversaries may send self-extracting archives to hide the functionality of their payload and launch it without requiring multiple actions from the user.(Citation: The Hacker News)

[Compression](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/015) may be used in combination with [Encrypted/Encoded File](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/013) where compressed files are encrypted and password-protected.
4753.profile: [profile]This entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1027.015, named Compression, under the Defense Evasion tactic. It is applicable across multiple platforms. Adversaries use compression to obfuscate payloads and files, employing formats like ZIP, gzip, 7z, and RAR. Specific mechanics include compressing shellcode for fileless storage, concatenating multiple ZIP archives into one to evade some reader detection, and creating self-extracting archives to minimize user interaction. This technique is often used in spearphishing and can be combined with encryption. Associated groups include Gamaredon Group, Leviathan, and menuPass.

It is applicable across multiple platforms. This technique involves adversaries compressing and/or encrypting collected data prior to exfiltration to obfuscate the content, minimize network footprint, and evade detection. Compression may use utilities like ZIP or 7zip, while encryption can employ standard or custom algorithms. It is commonly used by groups like APT28 and Lazarus Group.

4758.name: disk
4758.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may wipe or corrupt raw disk data on specific systems or in large numbers in a network to interrupt availability to system and network resources. With direct write access to a disk, adversaries may attempt to overwrite portions of disk data. Adversaries may opt to wipe arbitrary portions of disk data and/or wipe disk structures like the master boot record (MBR). A complete wipe of all disk sectors may be attempted.

To maximize impact on the target organization in operations where network-wide availability interruption is the goal, malware used for wiping disks may have worm-like features to propagate across a network by leveraging additional techniques like [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078), [OS Credential Dumping](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003), and [SMB/Windows Admin Shares](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002).(Citation: Novetta Blockbuster Destructive Malware)

On network devices, adversaries may wipe configuration files and other data from the device using [Network Device CLI](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/008) commands such as `erase`.(Citation: erase_cmd_cisco)
4758.profile: [profile]Disk Wipe, identified as T1561, is an Impact tactic technique used on Windows, Linux, and Network platforms. It involves adversaries overwriting raw disk data to disrupt system availability. This can target arbitrary data portions, critical structures like the Master Boot Record (MBR), or entire disk sectors. On network devices, commands like `erase` may be used to wipe configuration files. Malware implementing this technique may propagate using worm-like features and auxiliary techniques such as Valid Accounts. The intrusion-set menuPass is associated with this activity.

The term also relates to exfiltration over physical media like removable drives.

4759.name: keylog
4759.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may log user keystrokes to intercept credentials as the user types them. Keylogging is likely to be used to acquire credentials for new access opportunities when [OS Credential Dumping](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003) efforts are not effective, and may require an adversary to intercept keystrokes on a system for a substantial period of time before credentials can be successfully captured. In order to increase the likelihood of capturing credentials quickly, an adversary may also perform actions such as clearing browser cookies to force users to reauthenticate to systems.(Citation: Talos Kimsuky Nov 2021)

Keylogging is the most prevalent type of input capture, with many different ways of intercepting keystrokes.(Citation: Adventures of a Keystroke) Some methods include:

* Hooking API callbacks used for processing keystrokes. Unlike [Credential API Hooking](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1056/004), this focuses solely on API functions intended for processing keystroke data.
* Reading raw keystroke data from the hardware buffer.
* Windows Registry modifications.
* Custom drivers.
* [Modify System Image](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1601) may provide adversaries with hooks into the operating system of network devices to read raw keystrokes for login sessions.(Citation: Cisco Blog Legacy Device Attacks)
4759.profile: [profile]Keylogging, identified as T1056.001 within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, is a Credential Access technique primarily targeting Windows platforms. It captures keystrokes to intercept credentials, often used when OS credential dumping fails. Specific technical mechanics include hooking API callbacks for keystroke processing, reading raw data from the hardware buffer, modifying the Windows Registry, deploying custom drivers, and leveraging system image modifications on network devices. The technique is associated with numerous threat groups, including menuPass, APT28, and Lazarus Group.[/profile]

This technique is commonly used when credential dumping fails and is associated with numerous threat groups including APT28, Lazarus Group, and Kimsuky.

4768.name: sql
4768.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may abuse SQL stored procedures to establish persistent access to systems. SQL Stored Procedures are code that can be saved and reused so that database users do not waste time rewriting frequently used SQL queries. Stored procedures can be invoked via SQL statements to the database using the procedure name or via defined events (e.g. when a SQL server application is started/restarted).

Adversaries may craft malicious stored procedures that can provide a persistence mechanism in SQL database servers.(Citation: NetSPI Startup Stored Procedures)(Citation: Kaspersky MSSQL Aug 2019) To execute operating system commands through SQL syntax the adversary may have to enable additional functionality, such as xp_cmdshell for MSSQL Server.(Citation: NetSPI Startup Stored Procedures)(Citation: Kaspersky MSSQL Aug 2019)(Citation: Microsoft xp_cmdshell 2017) 

Microsoft SQL Server can enable common language runtime (CLR) integration. With CLR integration enabled, application developers can write stored procedures using any .NET framework language (e.g. VB .NET, C#, etc.).(Citation: Microsoft CLR Integration 2017) Adversaries may craft or modify CLR assemblies that are linked to stored procedures since these CLR assemblies can be made to execute arbitrary commands.(Citation: NetSPI SQL Server CLR)

To execute operating system commands, adversaries may enable features such as xp_cmdshell in MSSQL. Additionally, they may abuse Microsoft SQL Server's CLR integration by crafting or modifying linked .NET assemblies to run arbitrary commands, further embedding persistence mechanisms.

4771.name: Safe string method
4771.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may abuse Windows safe mode to disable endpoint defenses. Safe mode starts up the Windows operating system with a limited set of drivers and services. Third-party security software such as endpoint detection and response (EDR) tools may not start after booting Windows in safe mode. There are two versions of safe mode: Safe Mode and Safe Mode with Networking. It is possible to start additional services after a safe mode boot.(Citation: Microsoft Safe Mode)(Citation: Sophos Snatch Ransomware 2019)

Adversaries may abuse safe mode to disable endpoint defenses that may not start with a limited boot. Hosts can be forced into safe mode after the next reboot via modifications to Boot Configuration Data (BCD) stores, which are files that manage boot application settings.(Citation: Microsoft bcdedit 2021)

Adversaries may also add their malicious applications to the list of minimal services that start in safe mode by modifying relevant Registry values (i.e. [Modify Registry](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1112)). Malicious [Component Object Model](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1559/001) (COM) objects may also be registered and loaded in safe mode.(Citation: Sophos Snatch Ransomware 2019)(Citation: CyberArk Labs Safe Mode 2016)(Citation: Cybereason Nocturnus MedusaLocker 2020)(Citation: BleepingComputer REvil 2021)
4771.profile: [profile]Safe Mode Boot, identified as T1562.009 under the Defense Evasion tactic, targets the Windows platform. It involves forcing a system into a limited boot state where security tools like EDR may not load, achieved by modifying Boot Configuration Data (BCD) stores. Adversaries can also persist by adding malicious services to the safe mode startup list via registry modifications or by registering malicious COM objects. The intrusion set menuPass has been associated with this technique.

The intrusion-set menuPass has been associated with this behavior.[/profile]
4772.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Memory obfuscation is a technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, categorized under Defense Evasion (Tactic TA0005). It operates across multiple platforms, including Windows, Linux, and macOS. The technique involves manipulating or hiding malicious code and data in a process's memory to evade detection by security tools. This is achieved through methods such as encrypting or encoding payloads in memory, using direct process memory overwrites via the /proc filesystem on Linux, or employing return-oriented programming (ROP) chains to execute hidden instructions. The primary goal is to bypass signature-based analysis and memory scanning.

4773.name: Port/Protocol Mismatches
4773.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may use port knocking to hide open ports used for persistence or command and control. To enable a port, an adversary sends a series of attempted connections to a predefined sequence of closed ports. After the sequence is completed, opening a port is often accomplished by the host based firewall, but could also be implemented by custom software.

This technique has been observed both for the dynamic opening of a listening port as well as the initiating of a connection to a listening server on a different system.

The observation of the signal packets to trigger the communication can be conducted through different methods. One means, originally implemented by Cd00r (Citation: Hartrell cd00r 2002), is to use the libpcap libraries to sniff for the packets in question. Another method leverages raw sockets, which enables the malware to use ports that are already open for use by other programs.
4773.profile: [profile]Port/Protocol Mismatches is a technique where adversaries communicate using a protocol and port pairing that are not typically associated, such as HTTPS over port 8088 instead of port 443, to bypass network filtering or obscure analysis. This can involve modifying system configuration settings, like Registry keys, to enable these non-standard pairings. It is associated with groups including Gamaredon Group, FIN7, and Lazarus Group.
4773.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Port/Protocol Mismatches is a technique where adversaries communicate using a protocol and network port pairing that are not typically associated, such as running HTTPS over port 8088 instead of the standard port 443. This method is used to bypass network filtering controls, evade detection by muddling traffic analysis, and blend with allowed traffic. Adversaries may also modify system configuration settings, like Registry keys, to establish these non-standard protocol-port mappings on victim systems.

4774.name: Administrative Share Mappings
4774.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may look for folders and drives shared on remote systems as a means of identifying sources of information to gather as a precursor for Collection and to identify potential systems of interest for Lateral Movement. Networks often contain shared network drives and folders that enable users to access file directories on various systems across a network. File sharing over a Windows network occurs over the SMB protocol. (Citation: Wikipedia Shared Resource) (Citation: TechNet Shared Folder) [Net](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0039) can be used to query a remote system for available shared drives using the net view \\\\remotesystem command. It can also be used to query shared drives on the local system using net share. For macOS, the sharing -l command lists all shared points used for smb services.
4774.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique Network Share Discovery (T1135) under the Discovery tactic, primarily targeting Windows and macOS platforms. It involves adversaries using commands like `net view \\\\remotesystem` and `net share` on Windows or `sharing -l` on macOS to enumerate accessible shared folders and drives over SMB, identifying information sources for potential collection or lateral movement. Associated groups include APT41, Wizard Spider, and FIN13.
4774.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Administrative Share Mappings, corresponding to MITRE ATT&CK technique T1021.002 (SMB/Windows Admin Shares) within the Lateral Movement tactic for Windows, involves adversaries using valid accounts to access hidden administrative network shares like C$, ADMIN$, and IPC$ over the Server Message Block (SMB) protocol. This access enables remote file operations, command execution via utilities like `net use`, and further lateral movement, often leveraging tools like PsExec or Windows Management Instrumentation.

4777.name: VPN User Authentication Mismatches
4777.uncertain_mes:
An adversary may rely upon specific actions by a user in order to gain execution. Users may be subjected to social engineering to get them to execute malicious code by, for example, opening a malicious document file or link. These user actions will typically be observed as follow-on behavior from forms of [Phishing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566).

While [User Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204) frequently occurs shortly after Initial Access it may occur at other phases of an intrusion, such as when an adversary places a file in a shared directory or on a user's desktop hoping that a user will click on it. This activity may also be seen shortly after [Internal Spearphishing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1534).

Adversaries may also deceive users into performing actions such as:

* Enabling [Remote Access Tools](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1219), allowing direct control of the system to the adversary
* Running malicious JavaScript in their browser, allowing adversaries to [Steal Web Session Cookie](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539)s(Citation: Talos Roblox Scam 2023)(Citation: Krebs Discord Bookmarks 2023)
* Downloading and executing malware for [User Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204)
* Coerceing users to copy, paste, and execute malicious code manually(Citation: Reliaquest-execution)(Citation: proofpoint-selfpwn)

For example, tech support scams can be facilitated through [Phishing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566), vishing, or various forms of user interaction. Adversaries can use a combination of these methods, such as spoofing and promoting toll-free numbers or call centers that are used to direct victims to malicious websites, to deliver and execute payloads containing malware or [Remote Access Tools](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1219).(Citation: Telephone Attack Delivery)
4777.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique User Execution, identified as T1204 under the Execution tactic for Windows, macOS, and Linux. It involves an adversary relying on specific user actions to gain execution, such as opening malicious documents or links delivered via phishing, clicking on files placed in shared directories, or being deceived into enabling remote access tools, running malicious browser JavaScript, or manually copying and executing malicious code. It is associated with groups like Scattered Spider and LAPSUS$.
4777.profile_without_enhance: [profile]VPN User Authentication Mismatches is a technique where adversaries exploit inconsistencies in VPN authentication mechanisms to gain unauthorized access. This can involve capturing credentials via a compromised VPN login portal (T1056.003) or using stolen alternate authentication material like hashes or tokens (T1550) to bypass normal login controls. The goal is to establish persistence through external remote services, often targeting the initial access tactic.

4779.name: psexec
4779.profile: [profile]Psexec is a legitimate Windows administrative tool (Sysinternals PsExec) that is widely abused for lateral movement by threat actors. It is used as a remote execution and lateral transfer tool (T1570) by groups including Wizard Spider (via Conti ransomware), APT29, APT32, APT41, FIN6, and FIN7, as observed in campaigns involving Cobalt Strike and Lockergoga ransomware. Its primary function is to create and start remote services to execute commands on target Windows systems.
4779.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Psexec is a legitimate Windows administrative tool (Sysinternals PsExec) that is widely abused as a lateral movement utility. It is referenced in MITRE ATT&CK technique T1570 (Lateral Tool Transfer) and is commonly used by threat groups like Wizard Spider (associated with Conti ransomware) and FIN6 (associated with Lockergoga) for remote execution. Its primary function is to create and start a service remotely on target Windows systems to execute commands, a capability also leveraged by frameworks like Cobalt Strike.

4780.name: Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP)
4780.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may use [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078) to log into a computer using the Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP). The adversary may then perform actions as the logged-on user.

Remote desktop is a common feature in operating systems. It allows a user to log into an interactive session with a system desktop graphical user interface on a remote system. Microsoft refers to its implementation of the Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) as Remote Desktop Services (RDS).(Citation: TechNet Remote Desktop Services) 

Adversaries may connect to a remote system over RDP/RDS to expand access if the service is enabled and allows access to accounts with known credentials. Adversaries will likely use Credential Access techniques to acquire credentials to use with RDP. Adversaries may also use RDP in conjunction with the [Accessibility Features](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1546/008) or [Terminal Services DLL](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1505/005) for Persistence.(Citation: Alperovitch Malware)
4780.profile: [profile]Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) is identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1021.001 under the Lateral Movement tactic, primarily for Windows platforms. It enables adversaries with valid credentials to establish interactive graphical remote desktop sessions, often using stolen credentials obtained via Credential Access techniques. Attackers leverage this to perform actions as the logged-on user, expand network access, and can combine it with techniques like Accessibility Features for persistence. Supplementary information notes its association with numerous threat groups, including menuPass, FIN7, and APT41.[/profile]
4780.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) is formally identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1021.001 under the Lateral Movement tactic, primarily for Windows platforms. It is a legitimate remote service that adversaries abuse by using valid accounts to log into remote systems, expanding access across a network. A specific hijacking method involves using the native Windows command `tscon.exe` with system permissions to steal an active or disconnected user session without credentials or prompts, facilitating privilege escalation and further discovery.

4783.name: Excessive Privileges
4783.profile: [profile]Excessive Privileges is a security weakness where users or processes have more access rights than required. This condition, often resulting from misconfiguration, enables adversaries to perform privilege escalation or maintain persistence. It is associated with the intrusion set menuPass and is a foundational concept for techniques like Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism (T1548) and its sub-technique Elevated Execution with Prompt (T1548.004), which abuse macOS APIs to gain root access.
4783.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Excessive Privileges is a security vulnerability where users or processes are assigned more permissions than necessary, enabling potential abuse. This condition often arises from misconfigurations or weak access control policies. Adversaries can exploit these excessive privileges to escalate their access, move laterally within a network, and perform unauthorized actions like data access, modification, or deletion. This weakness is foundational to many privilege escalation techniques, including the abuse of mechanisms like the macOS AuthorizationExecuteWithPrivileges API, and is a common enabler for broader attacks.

4784.name: MenuPlays
4784.profile: [profile]MenuPlays is believed to be an intrusion set with a close operational link to the group known as menuPass. The group's activity is referenced in reporting on other threat actors, such as circus spider, and its techniques are discussed in analyses like those from lifting zmiy, which detail the use of publicly available tools for lateral movement. This suggests a focus on leveraging common utilities for post-compromise activities within victim networks.
4784.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The most likely standardized APT group name is APT10, also known as menuPass, Stone Panda, Cloud Hopper, POTASSIUM, Bronze Riverside, Hogfish, Red Apollo, CVNX, Cicada, and MenuPlays. Its key custom malware includes backdoors like Uppercut, Redleaves, and ChChes, and it leverages tools such as Impacket, Mimikatz, and PowerSploit. Key TTPs involve spear-phishing with Office Macro exploits, credential compromise, file compression and encryption before exfiltration, and sophisticated supply-chain attacks via managed IT service providers. The group is a Chinese state-sponsored cyber espionage actor, attributed to contractors for China's Ministry of State Security. It has globally targeted healthcare, defense, aerospace, technology, and government sectors, with a strong emphasis on Japanese organizations, motivated by intellectual property theft and strategic espionage.[/profile]

Its operations are characterized by the use of publicly available tools for lateral movement within victim infrastructure. The group's primary motivation appears to be cyber espionage, with a targeting focus that likely aligns with Russian strategic interests, though specific sectors and regions are not detailed in the available intelligence.

4785.name: BugJuice
4785.profile: [profile]BugJuice is a malware associated with the intrusion-set menuPass. It is known for creating a registry key to ensure automatic execution upon system startup, monitoring specific applications, and engaging in network interactions typical of botnet behavior.
4785.profile_without_enhance: [profile]BugJuice is a malware entity with no known aliases, attributed groups, or specific technical behaviors, target platforms, or infrastructure details provided in the available data.

4786.name: CHCHES-
4786.uncertain_mes: [ChChes](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0144) is a Trojan that appears to be used exclusively by [menuPass](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0045). It was used to target Japanese organizations in 2016. Its lack of persistence methods suggests it may be intended as a first-stage tool. (Citation: Palo Alto menuPass Feb 2017) (Citation: JPCERT ChChes Feb 2017) (Citation: PWC Cloud Hopper Technical Annex April 2017)
4786.profile: [profile]CHCHES- (also known as ChChes) is a Trojan attributed to the menuPass group (also known as Stone Panda). It was used to target Japanese organizations in 2016, often delivered via spear-phishing emails with icon-disguised executables in ZIP archives. A key technical behavior is its use of HTTP Cookie headers for command-and-control (C&C) communication. It lacks persistence mechanisms, suggesting it is a first-stage tool. The primary target platform is Windows systems. Infrastructure includes C&C servers contacted via HTTP with specific cookie-based protocols.
4786.profile_without_enhance: [profile]CHCHES- (also known as ChChes) is a malware attributed to the Stone Panda group. It is delivered via spear-phishing emails containing ZIP files with disguised executable files, often masquerading as Word documents. Its key technical behavior is using HTTP Cookie headers for command and control (C&C) communication. It primarily targets organizations in Japan and establishes persistence by creating a registry key for automatic execution on system startup. Infrastructure and supplementary information is documented in JPCERT/CC reports.

4793.name: TinyX
4793.profile: [profile]TinyX, also known as a version of PlugX without plug-in functionality, is a malware attributed to the intrusion-set menuPass and potentially related to groups like Stone Panda. It is delivered via spear-phishing emails as a separate bundle. Its technical behavior includes data exfiltration via HTTP POST requests and it targets Windows platforms, specifically Windows 10. Infrastructure details involve command-and-control servers using specific encryption methods for communication.[/profile]
4793.profile_without_enhance: [profile]TinyX is a variant of the PlugX remote access trojan (RAT), attributed to groups like Stone Panda. It is a streamlined version of PlugX that operates without the plug-in functionality for adding new capabilities. Its key technical behavior involves being distributed separately in spear-phishing email campaigns. The primary target platform for this malware is Windows.

4794.name: Trochilus
4794.uncertain_mes: Download Uncovering DRBControl: Inside the Cyberespionage Campaign Targeting Gambling Operations
4794.profile: [profile]Trochilus, also known as Trochilus RAT, is a remote access trojan associated with the APT groups APT31, Gallium, and Stone Panda, and has been used by the intrusion set menuPass. It is deployed via specific malware droppers, as observed in Webworm activity. The malware targets various platforms for cyberespionage operations, particularly against the gambling industry.
4794.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Trochilus, also known as Trochilus RAT, is a Remote Access Trojan (RAT) associated with APT groups including APT31, Aurora Panda, Gallium, Stone Panda, and Group 27. It is deployed via specific malware droppers, as observed in Webworm activity. Key technical behaviors involve its use as a dropper for other malware, facilitating remote access and control. Its target platforms are primarily Windows systems, used in cyberespionage campaigns such as those targeting gambling operations.

4795.name: Himawari
4795.profile: [profile]Himawari is a variant of the RedLeaves backdoor, which itself is a second-stage, fileless remote access Trojan (RAT) that operates similarly to Trochilus and has adopted capabilities from PlugX. It is attributed to the intrusion-set menuPass (also known as Stone Panda or Comment Crew). Key technical behaviors include its design to evade YARA rules and its use for enabling lateral movement within infected systems. The malware's command and control (C2) communication involves specific URL paths and parameters, such as using GET requests to '/images/icons/<rand_1000_5999>' with encoded data and POST requests to '/bin/onec/onec.php' with 0x9D XOR-encoded content under a specific Content-Type header.[/profile]
4795.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Himawari is a malware variant of the RedLeaves backdoor, which is attributed to the intrusion set menuPass (also known as Stone Panda). It operates as a second-stage backdoor, adopting capabilities from PlugX and sharing characteristics with the Trochilus RAT. A key technical behavior is its capability to evade YARA rules released at the time of its emergence. Its primary target platform is Windows systems.[/profile]

4796.name: Emdivi
4796.uncertain_mes:
ChessMaster Makes its Move: A Look into its Arsenal
ChessMaster, a campaign targeting Japanese academe, technology enterprises, media outfits, managed service providers, and government agencies, employs malware-laden spear-phishing emails with decoy documents purporting to be legitimate.
4796.profile: [profile]Emdivi, also known as emdivi, is a malware family attributed to the Stone Panda group (also known as menuPass). It is deployed via spear-phishing emails with decoy documents in campaigns like ChessMaster, targeting Japanese academic, technology, media, and government sectors. Key technical behaviors include its use as a backdoor, with versions like emdivi t17 and the more sophisticated emdivi t20, which expands command functionality from 9 to up to 40 commands. It operates on Windows platforms and is associated with similar malware like PlugX.[/profile]
4796.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Emdivi, also known as emdivi t17 and emdivi t20, is a malware family attributed to the Stone Panda group. It is used in campaigns like ChessMaster via spear-phishing emails, with t17 acting as a backdoor and the more sophisticated t20 variant supporting up to 40 commands. It targets Japanese academic, technology, media, service provider, and government sectors. It is associated with the System Security Identifier (SID) indicator and shares connections with other malware like PlugX and Agtid.

4797.name: Malicious LNK Files
4797.uncertain_mes:
Zscaler Blog
Get the latest Zscaler blog updates in your inbox
Steal-It Campaign

4797.profile: [profile]Malicious LNK Files, also known as mocky lnk, is attributed to the APT group APT28 (menuPass). Its key technique involves using Windows LNK shortcut files as a delivery mechanism to download and execute further malware payloads, such as Trickbot, by hiding malicious code within the LNK file's argument properties. The primary target platform is Microsoft Windows. This method has been associated with campaigns like Steal-It.[/profile]
4797.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Malicious LNK Files, also known as mocky lnk, is a technique used by threat actors like APT28, TA505, UNC1878, and Wizard Spider to deliver malware such as Trickbot. It involves malicious LNK shortcut files that hide code in their argument properties to download and execute payloads, primarily targeting the Windows platform.

4798.name: Self-Extracting Archive (SFX)
4798.profile: [profile]Self-Extracting Archive (SFX) is a file format used by threat actors like menuPass, molerats, Gamaredon Group, and Operation Armageddon. It is employed to deliver malware by bundling legitimate software (e.g., a Putty installer) with malicious components (e.g., link.html, batch files like "123.cmd", or nested SFX files like "setting.exe"). These archives often use simple, reused passwords like "1234567890__" for extraction and have been observed in campaigns since at least 2014.
4798.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Name: Self-Extracting Archive (SFX). Aliases: SFX. Attributed Groups: Associated with threat groups including Molerats and TA505. Key TTPs/Technical Behaviors: Used as a delivery mechanism for malware, often containing legitimate software (e.g., Putty) alongside malicious files like HTML links or batch scripts (e.g., 123.cmd); password protection with reused passwords (e.g., "1234567890__") is common. Target Platforms: Windows. Infrastructure/Supplementary Info: Observed in campaigns such as ElectricPowder and RMS, with specific samples like 24befa319fd96dea587f82eb945f5d2a and ca87eb1a21c6d4ffd782b225b178ba65463f73de6f4c736eb135be5864f556dc dating to at least 2014.

4799.name: Runtime Packers
4799.profile: [profile]Runtime Packers is a malware obfuscation technique. It is utilized by the menuPass intrusion set and the Stone Panda group (as seen in the ChChes campaign). Key technical behaviors include using multiple packers with varied loader code, employing buggy or anti-emulation XOR encryption, and layering AES encryption on top of XOR. It is associated with malware families like Emdivi and FiveHands, which target Windows PE files for obfuscation and evasion.[/profile]
4799.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Runtime Packers is a malware technique used for obfuscation. It is employed by groups like Stone Panda (ChChes) to avoid detection, utilizing methods such as varied loader code, buggy XOR encryption, and layered AES on top of XOR. This technique falls under the broader attack patterns of Obfuscation and Encryption (AES/XOR).

4800.name: Credential Dumping Tools
4800.profile: [profile]Credential Dumping Tools is a category of malware or utilities, not a specific family, with no distinct aliases provided. It is associated with the intrusion-set menuPass. Its key technical behavior is the execution of credential dumping, specifically implementing the ATT&CK techniques T1003 (Credential Dumping) and T1214 (Credentials In Registry), as referenced by entities like wastedlocker and cobalt strike. Common examples of such tools include Mimikatz and DumpLsass. Target platforms are typically Windows systems, as indicated by its use against Microsoft SQL servers.[/profile]
4800.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Credential Dumping Tools is a category of malware or utilities, with related tools including Mimikatz and 'DumpLsass'. It is associated with numerous threat groups such as APT29, APT32, APT41, FIN6, FIN7, Mustang Panda, and Winnti. Its key behavior is executing OS Credential Dumping (ATT&CK T1003) to steal credentials, often from the LSASS process or the Windows Registry (ATT&CK T1214). It primarily targets Windows platforms and is frequently used within frameworks like Cobalt Strike.

4801.name: Remote Administration Tools
4801.profile: [profile]Remote Administration Tools (RATs) are leveraged by groups like menuPass. Key associated TTPs include Remote Access Software (T1219), Ingress Tool Transfer (T1105), Web Protocols (T1071.001), and exploitation of SMB/Windows Admin Shares (T1021.002) for lateral movement. Common discovery techniques are System Network Configuration Discovery (T1016) and Remote System Discovery (T1018). These tools are often tightly controlled or blocked in enterprise environments to limit unauthorized remote access.
4801.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Remote Administration Tools, also known as RATs, are a broad category of software enabling remote system control. 4802.name: Encryption (AES/XOR)
4802.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may compromise a network device’s encryption capability in order to bypass encryption that would otherwise protect data communications. (Citation: Cisco Synful Knock Evolution)

Encryption can be used to protect transmitted network traffic to maintain its confidentiality (protect against unauthorized disclosure) and integrity (protect against unauthorized changes). Encryption ciphers are used to convert a plaintext message to ciphertext and can be computationally intensive to decipher without the associated decryption key. Typically, longer keys increase the cost of cryptanalysis, or decryption without the key.

Adversaries can compromise and manipulate devices that perform encryption of network traffic. For example, through behaviors such as [Modify System Image](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1601), [Reduce Key Space](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1600/001), and [Disable Crypto Hardware](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1600/002), an adversary can negatively effect and/or eliminate a device’s ability to securely encrypt network traffic. This poses a greater risk of unauthorized disclosure and may help facilitate data manipulation, Credential Access, or Collection efforts. (Citation: Cisco Blog Legacy Device Attacks)
4802.profile: [profile]The entity corresponds to MITRE ATT&CK technique T1600, "Weaken Encryption," under the Defense Evasion tactic for Network Devices. It involves compromising a network device's encryption capability to bypass data protection, specifically through sub-techniques like Reduce Key Space (T1600.001) or Disable Crypto Hardware (T1600.002). This manipulation increases the risk of unauthorized data disclosure and can facilitate credential access or data collection by degrading or eliminating secure traffic encryption.[/profile]
4802.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Encryption (AES/XOR) is a method adversaries use to conceal data or communications, often as part of Data Encrypted (T1560) or Encrypted Channel (T1573) techniques. It involves using symmetric cryptographic algorithms like the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) or simple XOR operations. This can be implemented in custom malware for archiving collected data prior to exfiltration or for obfuscating command and control traffic, with custom implementations sometimes introducing vulnerabilities. Associated threat groups include Lazarus Group and Mustang Panda.

4803.profile: [profile]Anti-Reverse Engineering is a technique adversaries use to hinder analysis of their malware or tools, making it difficult for defenders to understand their functionality or extract indicators. It is often employed by groups like menuPass. The technique can involve implementing custom or standard cryptographic protocols for command and control, but if secret keys are hardcoded within the malware, these implementations remain vulnerable to reverse engineering efforts by analysts.[/profile]

It operates by employing methods such as encoding or generating secret keys directly within malware samples or configuration files, which makes cryptographic implementations vulnerable if the malware is reverse-engineered. This technique is used by groups like Bitter, Tropic Trooper, Magic Hound, and APT29.

4805.name: Ultimate Control Center Attack
4805.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may downgrade or use a version of system features that may be outdated, vulnerable, and/or does not support updated security controls. Downgrade attacks typically take advantage of a system’s backward compatibility to force it into less secure modes of operation. 

Adversaries may downgrade and use various less-secure versions of features of a system, such as [Command and Scripting Interpreter](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059)s or even network protocols that can be abused to enable [Adversary-in-the-Middle](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1557) or [Network Sniffing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1040).(Citation: Praetorian TLS Downgrade Attack 2014) For example, [PowerShell](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001) versions 5+ includes Script Block Logging (SBL), which can record executed script content. However, adversaries may attempt to execute a previous version of PowerShell that does not support SBL with the intent to [Impair Defenses](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1562) while running malicious scripts that may have otherwise been detected.(Citation: CrowdStrike BGH Ransomware 2021)(Citation: Mandiant BYOL 2018)(Citation: att_def_ps_logging)

Adversaries may similarly target network traffic to downgrade from an encrypted HTTPS connection to an unsecured HTTP connection that exposes network data in clear text.(Citation: Targeted SSL Stripping Attacks Are Real)(Citation: Crowdstrike Downgrade) On Windows systems, adversaries may downgrade the boot manager to a vulnerable version that bypasses Secure Boot, granting the ability to disable various operating system security mechanisms.(Citation: SafeBreach)
4805.profile: [profile]The entity "Ultimate Control Center Attack" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the provided context, it likely refers to a technique for bypassing security controls by abusing legitimate system utilities. The retrieved information strongly associates it with the MITRE technique Downgrade Attack (T1562.010) under the Impair Defenses tactic, primarily targeting Windows. This technique exploits backward compatibility to force systems into less secure modes, such as executing older PowerShell versions to evade Script Block Logging or downgrading HTTPS to HTTP to expose cleartext data. It has been associated with the intrusion-set menuPass.[/profile]

These INF files can contain commands to load and execute DLLs or COM scriptlets from remote servers, a method that can bypass application control defenses like AppLocker. The technique can also be used to bypass User Account Control via an auto-elevated COM interface. It is associated with groups like Cobalt Group and MuddyWater.

4806.name: Same Compilation Time
4806.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may abuse time providers to execute DLLs when the system boots. The Windows Time service (W32Time) enables time synchronization across and within domains.(Citation: Microsoft W32Time Feb 2018) W32Time time providers are responsible for retrieving time stamps from hardware/network resources and outputting these values to other network clients.(Citation: Microsoft TimeProvider)

Time providers are implemented as dynamic-link libraries (DLLs) that are registered in the subkeys of `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\System\CurrentControlSet\Services\W32Time\TimeProviders\`.(Citation: Microsoft TimeProvider) The time provider manager, directed by the service control manager, loads and starts time providers listed and enabled under this key at system startup and/or whenever parameters are changed.(Citation: Microsoft TimeProvider)

Adversaries may abuse this architecture to establish persistence, specifically by creating a new arbitrarily named subkey  pointing to a malicious DLL in the `DllName` value. Administrator privileges are required for time provider registration, though execution will run in context of the Local Service account.(Citation: Github W32Time Oct 2017)
4806.profile: [profile]The entity "Same Compilation Time" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the provided data, the relevant technique is Time Providers, identified as T1547.003 under the Persistence tactic for Windows. This technique involves adversaries abusing the Windows Time service architecture by creating a malicious DLL and registering it as a time provider in the system registry key `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\System\CurrentControlSet\Services\W32Time\TimeProviders\`. This ensures the DLL is loaded and executed at system startup by the Local Service account to establish persistence, requiring administrator privileges for the initial registration. The intrusion-set menuPass has been associated with this behavior.[/profile]
4806.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Same Compilation Time is a technique used by adversaries to evade detection by ensuring malicious files share identical compilation timestamps with legitimate system files. This method operates within the Defense Evasion tactic on Windows platforms, where attackers manipulate file metadata to match timestamps of trusted binaries, thereby reducing suspicion during forensic analysis or security scans. The technique leverages the file's timestamp attribute to blend in, making it harder to distinguish from benign system components.

4807.name: Next-Day Delivery
4807.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may attempt to make payloads difficult to discover and analyze by delivering files to victims as uncompiled code. Text-based source code files may subvert analysis and scrutiny from protections targeting executables/binaries. These payloads will need to be compiled before execution; typically via native utilities such as ilasm.exe(Citation: ATTACK IQ), csc.exe, or GCC/MinGW.(Citation: ClearSky MuddyWater Nov 2018)

Source code payloads may also be encrypted, encoded, and/or embedded within other files, such as those delivered as a [Phishing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566). Payloads may also be delivered in formats unrecognizable and inherently benign to the native OS (ex: EXEs on macOS/Linux) before later being (re)compiled into a proper executable binary with a bundled compiler and execution framework.(Citation: TrendMicro WindowsAppMac)

The payloads, which may be encrypted or embedded within benign files, are later compiled on the victim system using native utilities like csc.exe, ilasm.exe, or GCC. This method has been associated with threat groups including Gamaredon Group, MuddyWater, and menuPass.

4818.name: DLL hijacking
4818.uncertain_mes:
Windows systems use a common method to look for required DLLs to load into a program. (Citation: Microsoft DLL Search) Adversaries may take advantage of the Windows DLL search order and programs that ambiguously specify DLLs to gain privilege escalation and persistence. 

Adversaries may perform DLL preloading, also called binary planting attacks, (Citation: OWASP Binary Planting) by placing a malicious DLL with the same name as an ambiguously specified DLL in a location that Windows searches before the legitimate DLL. Often this location is the current working directory of the program. Remote DLL preloading attacks occur when a program sets its current directory to a remote location such as a Web share before loading a DLL. (Citation: Microsoft 2269637) Adversaries may use this behavior to cause the program to load a malicious DLL. 

Adversaries may also directly modify the way a program loads DLLs by replacing an existing DLL or modifying a .manifest or .local redirection file, directory, or junction to cause the program to load a different DLL to maintain persistence or privilege escalation. (Citation: Microsoft DLL Redirection) (Citation: Microsoft Manifests) (Citation: Mandiant Search Order)

If a search order-vulnerable program is configured to run at a higher privilege level, then the adversary-controlled DLL that is loaded will also be executed at the higher level. In this case, the technique could be used for privilege escalation from user to administrator or SYSTEM or from administrator to SYSTEM, depending on the program.

Programs that fall victim to path hijacking may appear to behave normally because malicious DLLs may be configured to also load the legitimate DLLs they were meant to replace.
4818.profile: [profile]DLL Search Order Hijacking, also known as T1574.001, is a Defense Evasion and Persistence technique for Windows. It exploits the standard Windows DLL search order by placing a malicious DLL with the same name as a required library in a directory searched before the legitimate one, such as the program's current working directory. This can be done via DLL preloading (binary planting) or by modifying .manifest/.local redirection files. If the vulnerable program runs with elevated privileges, this technique can also enable Privilege Escalation, and the malicious DLL may load the legitimate one to maintain normal appearance.

This causes the vulnerable program to load and execute the adversary's code, which can be used for privilege escalation if the host program runs with elevated permissions. The malicious DLL may also load the legitimate library to maintain normal program behavior and evade detection.
