4857.name: DNS Tunneling
4857.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may tunnel network communications to and from a victim system within a separate protocol to avoid detection/network filtering and/or enable access to otherwise unreachable systems. Tunneling involves explicitly encapsulating a protocol within another. This behavior may conceal malicious traffic by blending in with existing traffic and/or provide an outer layer of encryption (similar to a VPN). Tunneling could also enable routing of network packets that would otherwise not reach their intended destination, such as SMB, RDP, or other traffic that would be filtered by network appliances or not routed over the Internet. 

There are various means to encapsulate a protocol within another protocol. For example, adversaries may perform SSH tunneling (also known as SSH port forwarding), which involves forwarding arbitrary data over an encrypted SSH tunnel.(Citation: SSH Tunneling)(Citation: Sygnia Abyss Locker 2025) 

[Protocol Tunneling](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1572) may also be abused by adversaries during [Dynamic Resolution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1568). Known as DNS over HTTPS (DoH), queries to resolve C2 infrastructure may be encapsulated within encrypted HTTPS packets.(Citation: BleepingComp Godlua JUL19) 

Adversaries may also leverage [Protocol Tunneling](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1572) in conjunction with [Proxy](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1090) and/or [Protocol or Service Impersonation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1001/003) to further conceal C2 communications and infrastructure.
4857.profile: [profile]DNS Tunneling is a specific method of Protocol Tunneling (T1572) under the Command and Control tactic, used to evade network filtering by encapsulating malicious data within DNS queries and responses. It abuses the DNS protocol (T1071.004) to establish a covert channel, often embedding commands and exfiltrated data in DNS record fields like TXT or A records. This technique is employed by malware such as Helminth and Oopsie Trojan and is associated with threat groups like OilRig, enabling C2 communication that blends with legitimate, frequent DNS traffic.[/profile]
4857.profile_without_enhance: [profile]DNS Tunneling is a Command and Control technique (T1071.004) under the Command and Control tactic, operating on Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves encapsulating malicious traffic within the DNS protocol to avoid detection by blending with normal administrative traffic. Adversaries embed commands and data into DNS query and response fields, such as TXT or A records, to establish a covert channel with compromised systems, often using it for infrequent beaconing to further conceal activity.

4858.name: Mersenne Twister
4858.profile: [profile]Mersenne Twister is a pseudorandom number generator (PRNG) algorithm. It is used by adversaries like the OilRig intrusion set to generate junk data for protocol obfuscation in command and control channels, appending or prepending random characters to hinder traffic analysis and detection. It is also employed in custom data archival methods, such as implementing stream ciphers for encryption without external libraries prior to data exfiltration.
4858.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Mersenne Twister" is not a standard technique in the MITRE ATT&CK framework. Based on the provided context, it is referenced as a custom method for data obfuscation or encryption prior to exfiltration, specifically as a type of stream cipher. This technique is associated with groups like Lazarus Group and is used to make analysis of command and control traffic or archived data more difficult by implementing a well-known pseudorandom number generation algorithm without external libraries.

4869.name: Shell Command Execution
4869.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may abuse the Windows command shell for execution. The Windows command shell ([cmd](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0106)) is the primary command prompt on Windows systems. The Windows command prompt can be used to control almost any aspect of a system, with various permission levels required for different subsets of commands. The command prompt can be invoked remotely via [Remote Services](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021) such as [SSH](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/004).(Citation: SSH in Windows)

Batch files (ex: .bat or .cmd) also provide the shell with a list of sequential commands to run, as well as normal scripting operations such as conditionals and loops. Common uses of batch files include long or repetitive tasks, or the need to run the same set of commands on multiple systems.

Adversaries may leverage [cmd](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0106) to execute various commands and payloads. Common uses include [cmd](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0106) to execute a single command, or abusing [cmd](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0106) interactively with input and output forwarded over a command and control channel.
4869.profile: [profile]Shell Command Execution, identified as T1059 in the MITRE ATT&CK framework, is an Execution tactic technique applicable across Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves adversaries abusing command-line interpreters like cmd.exe or Unix shells (e.g., bash, sh) to run arbitrary commands, scripts, or payloads. This can be performed interactively via a command and control channel, through batch files (.bat/.cmd), or invoked remotely via services like SSH. The technique provides extensive system control and is commonly used by numerous threat groups for direct code execution and lateral movement.[/profile]
4869.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Shell Command Execution is a foundational technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, broadly categorized under the Execution tactic (TA0002) and applicable across multiple platforms. It involves the direct execution of operating system shell commands, such as through cmd.exe on Windows or sh/bash on Unix-like systems, to control a system, run payloads, or perform tasks. Adversaries commonly use this for immediate command execution, running scripts, or establishing interactive shells, often as part of initial access or lateral movement via remote services.

4870.name: Download
4870.profile: [profile]Download is a technique used to acquire malicious software from external sources. It involves adversaries obtaining malware such as payloads, droppers, or backdoors by purchasing, stealing, or downloading it from the internet, criminal marketplaces, or third-party entities. This supports operations by providing tools for maintaining control, evading defenses, and executing post-compromise behaviors.
4870.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Download" is a general technique for obtaining malicious files or tools. It is associated with MITRE ATT&CK ID T1105 and falls under the Command and Control tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. The technique involves transferring files from an external system to a compromised host, often using standard protocols like HTTP, HTTPS, FTP, or SMB. This can be used to deliver additional payloads, post-exploitation tools, or command-and-control utilities. Adversaries may acquire malware through purchase, theft, or download from the internet, including from criminal marketplaces. Specific methods include abusing Windows LNK file icon location metadata to smuggle download commands and exfiltrating data to code repositories via their APIs.

4871.name: Upload
4871.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may upload malware to third-party or adversary controlled infrastructure to make it accessible during targeting. Malicious software can include payloads, droppers, post-compromise tools, backdoors, and a variety of other malicious content. Adversaries may upload malware to support their operations, such as making a payload available to a victim network to enable [Ingress Tool Transfer](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1105) by placing it on an Internet accessible web server.

Malware may be placed on infrastructure that was previously purchased/rented by the adversary ([Acquire Infrastructure](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1583)) or was otherwise compromised by them ([Compromise Infrastructure](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1584)). Malware can also be staged on web services, such as GitHub or Pastebin; hosted on the InterPlanetary File System (IPFS), where decentralized content storage makes the removal of malicious files difficult; or saved on the blockchain as smart contracts, which are resilient against takedowns that would affect traditional infrastructure.(Citation: Volexity Ocean Lotus November 2020)(Citation: Talos IPFS 2022)(Citation: Guardio Etherhiding 2023)(Citation: Bleeping Computer Binance Smart Chain 2023)

Adversaries may upload backdoored files, such as software packages, application binaries, virtual machine images, or container images, to third-party software stores, package libraries, extension marketplaces, or repositories (ex: GitHub, CNET, AWS Community AMIs, Docker Hub, PyPi, NPM).(Citation: Datadog Security Labs Malicious PyPi Packages 2024) By chance encounter, victims may directly download/install these backdoored files via [User Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204). Masquerading, including typo-squatting legitimate software, may increase the chance of users mistakenly executing these files.
4871.profile: [profile]Upload Malware, designated as T1608.001, is a Resource Development technique. It involves staging malicious content like payloads, droppers, or backdoored software packages on accessible infrastructure. This includes adversary-controlled web servers, compromised hosts, or third-party services such as GitHub, Pastebin, PyPi, NPM, decentralized storage (IPFS), or blockchain smart contracts to facilitate resilient distribution and enable follow-on actions like Ingress Tool Transfer. It is associated with groups including Mustang Panda, FIN7, and TA505.[/profile]
4871.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Upload" is a generic attack pattern not directly mapped to a specific MITRE ATT&CK ID. Based on retrieved context, it encompasses techniques like uploading malware (T1608.001) or tools (T1608.002) to adversary-controlled or third-party infrastructure, such as web servers, cloud storage, or code repositories, to stage them for operations like Ingress Tool Transfer. This facilitates later deployment or exfiltration. The technical mechanics involve placing malicious or dual-use files on accessible services, including GitHub, Pastebin, IPFS, or package libraries like PyPi and Docker Hub.

4874.name: Trust Relationship Exploitation
4874.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may breach or otherwise leverage organizations who have access to intended victims. Access through trusted third party relationship abuses an existing connection that may not be protected or receives less scrutiny than standard mechanisms of gaining access to a network.

Organizations often grant elevated access to second or third-party external providers in order to allow them to manage internal systems as well as cloud-based environments. Some examples of these relationships include IT services contractors, managed security providers, infrastructure contractors (e.g. HVAC, elevators, physical security). The third-party provider's access may be intended to be limited to the infrastructure being maintained, but may exist on the same network as the rest of the enterprise. As such, [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078) used by the other party for access to internal network systems may be compromised and used.(Citation: CISA IT Service Providers)

In Office 365 environments, organizations may grant Microsoft partners or resellers delegated administrator permissions. By compromising a partner or reseller account, an adversary may be able to leverage existing delegated administrator relationships or send new delegated administrator offers to clients in order to gain administrative control over the victim tenant.(Citation: Office 365 Delegated Administration)
4874.profile: [profile]Trusted Relationship, designated as T1199 under the Initial Access tactic, targets Windows, Azure AD, and Office 365 platforms. This technique involves compromising third-party organizations like IT service providers or Microsoft partners to gain access to a victim's network, often by abusing their existing valid accounts or delegated administrator permissions in cloud environments such as Office 365. Groups including Hafnium, APT28, and APT29 have been observed using this method.
4874.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Trust Relationship Exploitation, mapped to MITRE ATT&CK T1199 under the Initial Access tactic, targets multiple platforms by compromising trusted third-party relationships to gain network access. Adversaries breach organizations like IT service providers or cloud resellers that have existing, often less-scrutinized, access to a victim's environment. For example, in Office 365, they may compromise a partner account to abuse delegated administrator permissions and gain administrative control over a client tenant. This technique leverages the valid accounts of the trusted entity as a primary vector for initial intrusion.

4876.name: evasion testing
4876.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may employ various means to detect and avoid debuggers. Debuggers are typically used by defenders to trace and/or analyze the execution of potential malware payloads.(Citation: ProcessHacker Github) Debugger evasion may include changing behaviors based on the results of the checks for the presence of artifacts indicative of a debugged environment. Similar to [Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1497), if the adversary detects a debugger, they may alter their malware to disengage from the victim or conceal the core functions of the implant. They may also search for debugger artifacts before dropping secondary or additional payloads. Specific checks will vary based on the target and/or adversary. On Windows, this may involve [Native API](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1106) function calls such as IsDebuggerPresent() and NtQueryInformationProcess(), or manually checking the BeingDebugged flag of the Process Environment Block (PEB). On Linux, this may involve querying `/proc/self/status` for the `TracerPID` field, which indicates whether or not the process is being traced by dynamic analysis tools.(Citation: Cado Security P2PInfect 2023)(Citation: Positive Technologies Hellhounds 2023) Other checks for debugging artifacts may also seek to enumerate hardware breakpoints, interrupt assembly opcodes, time checks, or measurements if exceptions are raised in the current process (assuming a present debugger would “swallow” or handle the potential error).(Citation: hasherezade debug)(Citation: AlKhaser Debug)(Citation: vxunderground debug) Malware may also leverage Structured Exception Handling (SEH) to detect debuggers by throwing an exception and detecting whether the process is suspended. SEH handles both hardware and software expectations, providing control over the exceptions including support for debugging. If a debugger is present, the program’s control will be transferred to the debugger, and the execution of the code will be suspended. If the debugger is not present, control will be transferred to the SEH handler, which will automatically handle the exception and allow the program’s execution to continue.(Citation: Apriorit) Adversaries may use the information learned from these debugger checks during automated discovery to shape follow-on behaviors. Debuggers can also be evaded by detaching the process or flooding debug logs with meaningless data via messages produced by looping [Native API](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1106) function calls such as OutputDebugStringW().(Citation: wardle evilquest partii)(Citation: Checkpoint Dridex Jan 2021)
4876.profile: [profile]Debugger Evasion is a defense evasion technique (T1622) used on Windows and Linux platforms. It involves detecting debugger presence to alter malware behavior, using methods like Windows API calls (IsDebuggerPresent, NtQueryInformationProcess), checking the PEB's BeingDebugged flag, querying Linux's /proc/self/status for TracerPID, leveraging Structured Exception Handling (SEH), or flooding debug logs with OutputDebugStringW. The intrusion-set OilRig has been associated with this activity.[/profile]
4876.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Evasion Testing is a defense evasion technique where adversaries test their malware against security tools like antivirus or EDR to identify detection signatures or behavioral triggers before deployment. This involves submitting samples to services like VirusTotal or using local sandboxes to analyze detection rates, allowing them to modify the malware to avoid detection, such as by altering code or using obfuscation, thereby enhancing its stealth and persistence in target environments.

This behavior may conceal malicious traffic by blending in with existing traffic and/or provide an outer layer of encryption (similar to a VPN). Tunneling could also enable routing of network packets that would otherwise not reach their intended destination, such as SMB, RDP, or other traffic that would be filtered by network appliances or not routed over the Internet. 

There are various means to encapsulate a protocol within another protocol. For example, adversaries may perform SSH tunneling (also known as SSH port forwarding), which involves forwarding arbitrary data over an encrypted SSH tunnel.(Citation: SSH Tunneling)(Citation: Sygnia Abyss Locker 2025) 

[Protocol Tunneling](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1572) may also be abused by adversaries during [Dynamic Resolution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1568). Known as DNS over HTTPS (DoH), queries to resolve C2 infrastructure may be encapsulated within encrypted HTTPS packets.(Citation: BleepingComp Godlua JUL19) 

Adversaries may also leverage [Protocol Tunneling](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1572) in conjunction with [Proxy](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1090) and/or [Protocol or Service Impersonation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1001/003) to further conceal C2 communications and infrastructure.
4877.profile: [profile]Protocol Tunneling (T1572) is a Command and Control technique under the Exfiltration tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. This method can conceal C2 traffic by blending it with normal traffic or adding an encryption layer, and is often used in conjunction with proxy techniques. The intrusion set OilRig has been associated with this technique.[/profile]
4877.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "custom DNS tunneling protocols" is a specific implementation of the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1071.004 (DNS) under the Command and Control tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It involves adversaries creating and using bespoke, non-standard protocols that operate over DNS ports to encapsulate and exfiltrate data or command-and-control traffic. This method explicitly tunnels arbitrary data within the DNS protocol, often encoding it within DNS query and response fields like TXT or A records, to evade network detection by blending with legitimate DNS traffic. It is a subset of the broader Protocol Tunneling (T1572) and Custom Command and Control Protocol (T1094) techniques.

4878.name: command and control (C2)
4878.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may communicate using a custom command and control protocol instead of encapsulating commands/data in an existing [Application Layer Protocol](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1071). Implementations include mimicking well-known protocols or developing custom protocols (including raw sockets) on top of fundamental protocols provided by TCP/IP/another standard network stack.
4878.profile: [profile]Custom Command and Control Protocol, identified as T1094 under the Command and Control tactic, operates across multiple platforms. This technique involves adversaries developing or mimicking custom communication protocols, often using raw sockets built on TCP/IP, to avoid detection by blending with or bypassing standard application-layer protocol analysis. The intrusion-set OilRig has been associated with its use. Supplementary methods to obscure this C2 traffic include data obfuscation, one-way communication, and data encoding.
4878.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Command and Control (C2) refers to the adversary technique of maintaining communication with compromised systems to remotely direct them. As a core tactic within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, it falls under the Command and Control tactic (TA0011) and applies across multiple platforms. The technical mechanics involve establishing covert channels, often using custom protocols, standard application layer protocols, or web services, to send instructions and exfiltrate data. Adversaries frequently employ obfuscation methods like data encoding or steganography to hide this traffic within legitimate network activity, making detection difficult.

4879.name: web shells
4879.profile: [profile]Web shells are malicious scripts enabling remote access to compromised web servers, often used for persistent command and control (C2). They are associated with intrusion sets like OilRig, Lazarus Group, and Gallium. Specific variants include 'Redhat', 'WSO', 'Venus', and 'Code Hunters' web shells, with known authentication such as the password '1234qwer' for Redhat and 'venus' for Venus. These shells facilitate activities like process injection and are deployed on web servers to establish redundant C2 infrastructure.[/profile]
4879.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Web shells are a class of malware providing backdoor access to compromised web servers. Common aliases or specific variants include 'Redhat', 'WSO', 'Venus', and 'Code Hunters' web shells. They have been used by groups such as Lazarus Group and Gallium. Key technical behaviors include being inserted to secure redundant access and abusing servers as command-and-control (C&C) infrastructure, with specific login passwords like '1234qwer' and 'venus' observed for certain variants. The primary target platform is web servers.

4880.name: backdoors
4880.uncertain_mes:

4880.profile: [profile]YiBackdoor is a newly identified malware family with links to the IcedID and Latrodectus malware. It is a backdoor, and its uncertain name suggests potential aliases. It has been associated with the intrusion sets OilRig, Turla, and DeepPanda. Its technical behavior includes backdoor capabilities for remote access and control. The target platform is unspecified. Supplementary information indicates it may be designed as a stealthy implant to avoid detection by not listening on ports or pinging a C2 server directly, similar to passive backdoors.]
4880.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Backdoors is a broad category of malware. It is known by aliases including AzorUlt, BPFDoor, and Daxin. It has been attributed to groups such as The Gorgon Group, Red Menshen, and unknown actors. Key technical behaviors include providing remote access and command execution, with specific variants like BPFDoor employing stealth techniques such as avoiding open ports to evade detection. Target platforms are typically Windows systems. Supplementary infrastructure may involve command-and-control servers for data exfiltration.

4881.name: persistent access
4881.profile: [profile]The entity "persistent access" is a general adversarial objective to maintain long-term presence within a compromised network, not a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique. This objective is achieved by employing redundant mechanisms such as using multiple remote access tools with different command and control protocols, establishing credentialed access via external remote services like VPNs, deploying web shells on externally accessible servers, and creating backup accounts. These methods ensure adversaries retain access even if one mechanism is discovered or removed, as observed in activities linked to groups like OilRig.[/profile]
4881.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "persistent access" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on retrieved context, it is a high-level concept describing an adversary's objective to maintain long-term footholds in a compromised environment. This is achieved through redundant mechanisms such as deploying multiple remote access tools with different C2 protocols, establishing credentialed access via external remote services like VPNs, creating backdoor accounts, planting web shells, and leveraging cloud infrastructure. The goal is to ensure continued network access even if one primary access vector is discovered and removed.

4882.name: Remote Desktop
4882.profile: [profile]Remote Desktop is a legitimate protocol for remote system access, but it is frequently exploited by threat actors for malicious purposes. It is used by intrusion sets like OilRig. The protocol is referenced in the context of malware tools such as mimikatz and HyperBro, and is specifically abused by the ColdRoot RAT, which creates a 'REMOTEDESKTOPTHREAD' to capture and stream screen content to an attacker. Its primary target is Windows-based systems.[/profile]
4882.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The malware named 'Remote Desktop' is a capability or module within other malware families, such as ColdRoot RAT, which spawns a dedicated 'REMOTEDESKTOPTHREAD' to capture and stream screen content from the victim's desktop to a remote attacker. It is associated with or utilized by groups including APT10, APT32, Anunak, Gallium, and Emissary Panda, and its primary function is to enable unauthorized remote access and surveillance.

4883.name: PuTTY
4883.profile: [profile]PuTTY is a legitimate SSH and telnet client, but its name is abused by threat actors for malicious infrastructure and tools. It is associated with the intrusion set OilRig. Observed malicious infrastructure includes domains like puttyy[.]org, puttysystems[.]com, and updaterputty[.]com, and a file hash (SHA256: 0b85ad058aa224d0b66ac7fdc4f3b71145aede462068cc9708ec2cee7c5717d4). Related technical behaviors from other campaigns include command output compression with Zlib and functions for screen control, proxy connections, and MySQL database interaction. Target platforms are primarily Windows systems.
4883.profile_without_enhance: [profile]PuTTY is a legitimate SSH and telnet client, but its name is abused by malicious actors for malware distribution and infrastructure spoofing. Associated infrastructure includes domains like puttyy[.]org, puttysystems[.]com, and updaterputty[.]com, which are linked to the Broomstick malware. A related SHA256 hash (0b85ad058aa224d0b66ac7fdc4f3b71145aede462068cc9708ec2cee7c5717d4) is also identified. In a separate context, the Winnti malware, attributed to APT17, uses functions like screen_send_input and tcpproxy_open_connection, and compresses command output with Zlib for exfiltration.

4884.name: credential dumping
4884.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may attempt to dump credentials to obtain account login and credential material, normally in the form of a hash or a clear text password. Credentials can be obtained from OS caches, memory, or structures.(Citation: Brining MimiKatz to Unix) Credentials can then be used to perform [Lateral Movement](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0008) and access restricted information.

Several of the tools mentioned in associated sub-techniques may be used by both adversaries and professional security testers. Additional custom tools likely exist as well.
4884.profile: [profile]OS Credential Dumping, identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1003 under the Credential Access tactic, targets Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. This technique involves adversaries extracting account login material like hashes or plaintext passwords from operating system components such as security account manager (SAM) files, Local Security Authority (LSA) secrets, and process memory, often using tools like Mimikatz. The stolen credentials are subsequently used for lateral movement and privilege escalation, as evidenced by its association with threat groups like OilRig, APT28, and APT29.[/profile]
4884.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Credential Dumping is a technique where adversaries extract account login and credential material, often in hash or plaintext form, from operating system components like memory, caches, or security structures. This activity, mapped to MITRE ATT&CK ID T1003 under the Credential Access tactic, primarily targets Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. The extracted credentials are then used for lateral movement and to access restricted information, with tools like Mimikatz commonly employed for this purpose.

4885.name: Phishing websites
4885.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may send phishing messages to gain access to victim systems. All forms of phishing are electronically delivered social engineering. Phishing can be targeted, known as spearphishing. In spearphishing, a specific individual, company, or industry will be targeted by the adversary. More generally, adversaries can conduct non-targeted phishing, such as in mass malware spam campaigns.

Adversaries may send victims emails containing malicious attachments or links, typically to execute malicious code on victim systems. Phishing may also be conducted via third-party services, like social media platforms. Phishing may also involve social engineering techniques, such as posing as a trusted source, as well as evasive techniques such as removing or manipulating emails or metadata/headers from compromised accounts being abused to send messages (e.g., [Email Hiding Rules](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1564/008)).(Citation: Microsoft OAuth Spam 2022)(Citation: Palo Alto Unit 42 VBA Infostealer 2014) Another way to accomplish this is by [Email Spoofing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1672)(Citation: Proofpoint-spoof) the identity of the sender, which can be used to fool both the human recipient as well as automated security tools,(Citation: cyberproof-double-bounce) or by including the intended target as a party to an existing email thread that includes malicious files or links (i.e., "thread hijacking").(Citation: phishing-krebs)

Victims may also receive phishing messages that instruct them to call a phone number where they are directed to visit a malicious URL, download malware,(Citation: sygnia Luna Month)(Citation: CISA Remote Monitoring and Management Software) or install adversary-accessible remote management tools onto their computer (i.e., [User Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204)).(Citation: Unit42 Luna Moth)
4885.profile: [profile]Phishing, identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1566 under the Initial Access tactic, is an electronically delivered social engineering attack targeting various platforms. It involves sending messages, often via email or social media, containing malicious attachments or links to execute code on victim systems. Techniques include spearphishing specific targets, email spoofing, thread hijacking, and using evasive methods like manipulating email headers. The intrusion-set OilRig is associated with this technique.[/profile]
4885.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Phishing Websites is a technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, categorized under Initial Access (Tactic TA0001) and often associated with T1566 (Phishing). It operates across multiple platforms. The technical mechanics involve adversaries creating fraudulent websites that mimic legitimate login portals or services to harvest credentials or deliver malware. These sites are often reached via malicious links in spearphishing campaigns and may use deceptive domain names (typosquatting) or be hosted on compromised infrastructure. The technique is a core component of credential harvesting and facilitates initial compromise.

4894.profile: [profile]TwoFace Webshell, also known as TwoFace Payload Shell, is a webshell malware associated with the OilRig intrusion set. It functions as a backdoor, allowing authenticated command execution on compromised web servers. The malware is part of a broader toolset that includes the IntrudingDivisor malware and is related to the Reshell backdoor family.[/profile]
4894.profile_without_enhance: [profile]TwoFace Webshell, also known as TwoFace Payload Shell or TwoFace++ Loader, is a webshell malware with a direct connection to IntrudingDivisor. It is attributed to the intrusion set OilRig and operates on web servers. Its key technical behaviors include command injection via HTTP cookies and HTTP POST requests to achieve remote code execution, and it can leverage vulnerabilities such as those involving the Exchange Trusted Subsystem Group.[profile]

4895.name: IntrudingDivisor
4895.profile: [profile]IntrudingDivisor, also known as IntrudingDivisor Webshell, is attributed to the intrusion set OilRig. Its key technical behavior is functioning as a webshell, with a direct connection to the TwoFace webshell malware. The target platform is web servers, as indicated by its webshell nature.[/profile]
4895.profile_without_enhance: [profile]IntrudingDivisor, also known as IntrudingDivisor Webshell, is a webshell. It is attributed to or associated with groups including APT27, APT34, OilRig, Turla, and UNC215. Its technical behavior includes functioning as a webshell for command execution on compromised systems. The target platform is web servers. It is directly related to the TwoFace Webshell malware.

4896.name: mimikatz
4896.uncertain_mes: Trigona ransomware is a relatively new strain that security researchers first discovered in late October 2022. By analyzing Trigona ransomware binaries and ransom notes obtained from VirusTotal, as well as information from Unit 42 incident response, we determined that Trigona was very active during December 2022, with at least 15 potential victims being compromised.
4896.profile: [profile]Mimikatz is a credential dumping tool used to extract passwords, hashes, and Kerberos tickets from Windows memory. It is associated with groups like OilRig and is often leveraged in post-exploitation for lateral movement. Key techniques include using modules like sekurlsa for LSASS memory access and performing pass-the-hash attacks. It primarily targets Windows platforms and is commonly integrated into other malware or attack frameworks for credential theft and privilege escalation.
4896.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Mimikatz is a post-exploitation credential dumping tool, also known as sekurlsa. It is used by groups including APT10, APT32, Anunak, and Gallium. Its key technical behaviors include extracting logon passwords and Kerberos tickets via modules like sekurlsa::logonpasswords and sekurlsa::tickets /export, and it can perform pass-the-hash attacks. It primarily targets Windows platforms to facilitate lateral movement and privilege escalation, and is often integrated into other malware or executed via PowerShell scripts.

4897.name: Remexi
4897.uncertain_mes: [Remexi](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0375) is a Windows-based Trojan that was developed in the C programming language.(Citation: Securelist Remexi Jan 2019)
4897.profile: [profile]Remexi, also known as remexi, is a Windows-based Trojan developed in C. It is attributed to the APT groups APT39 (OilRig) and Chafer. Its key technical behaviors include being used in long-standing cyber-espionage campaigns, primarily targeting foreign diplomatic entities based in Iran, and it functions as an improved version in domestic cyber-espionage operations. The target platform is Windows.
4897.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Remexi, also known as remexi, is a Windows-based Trojan attributed to the APT groups APT39 and Chafer. Developed in the C programming language, it has been used in long-standing cyber-espionage campaigns, notably targeting foreign diplomatic entities in Iran. Its key behaviors include functioning as a backdoor for espionage operations, with specific TTPs detailed in a MITRE ATT&CK matrix. The malware is designed for the Windows platform and has been associated with domestic cyber-espionage activities, indicating a focus on intelligence gathering.

4909.name: HTTP Protocol
4909.profile: [profile]The entity "HTTP Protocol" is not a MITRE ATT&CK technique itself but a foundational network protocol. It is commonly abused by adversaries as a channel for command and control (C2) and data exfiltration to blend with normal web traffic and bypass network filtering. Specifically, it is used within techniques like Application Layer Protocol (T1071.001) for C2 communications and Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol (T1048) for data theft. Threat groups such as OilRig leverage HTTP to conceal malicious traffic within standard web requests.
4909.profile_without_enhance: [profile]HTTP Protocol is a standard application layer protocol (T1071.001) under the Command and Control tactic. It is used by adversaries to blend malicious communications with normal web traffic, embedding commands and data within standard HTTP/S packets and their numerous headers and fields to avoid detection. This technique is commonly employed for C2 and data exfiltration, as seen in its use by groups like APT28 and Lazarus Group.

4910.name: Non-standard Port
4910.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may communicate using a protocol and port pairing that are typically not associated. For example, HTTPS over port 8088(Citation: Symantec Elfin Mar 2019) or port 587(Citation: Fortinet Agent Tesla April 2018) as opposed to the traditional port 443. Adversaries may make changes to the standard port used by a protocol to bypass filtering or muddle analysis/parsing of network data.

Adversaries may also make changes to victim systems to abuse non-standard ports. For example, Registry keys and other configuration settings can be used to modify protocol and port pairings.(Citation: change_rdp_port_conti)
4910.profile: [profile]Non-Standard Port (T1571) is a Command and Control tactic applicable to multiple platforms, where adversaries communicate using atypical protocol and port pairings to bypass filtering and evade detection. Specific examples include running HTTPS over port 8088 or 587 instead of the standard port 443. Adversaries may also modify victim system configurations, such as Registry keys, to enable the abuse of these non-standard ports for C2 channels. This technique has been associated with groups including OilRig, FIN7, and Lazarus Group.
4910.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Non-standard Port, designated as T1571 under the Command and Control tactic, is a technique where adversaries communicate using protocol and port pairings that deviate from standard associations, such as running HTTPS over port 8088 instead of port 443, to bypass network filtering and complicate traffic analysis. This can involve modifying victim system configurations, like Registry keys, to enable these non-standard pairings. It is employed by numerous threat groups including APT32, Lazarus Group, and Sandworm Team.

4911.name: Domain Admins Enumeration
4911.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may enumerate system and service logs to find useful data. These logs may highlight various types of valuable insights for an adversary, such as user authentication records ([Account Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1087)), security or vulnerable software ([Software Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1518)), or hosts within a compromised network ([Remote System Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1018)).

Host binaries may be leveraged to collect system logs. Examples include using `wevtutil.exe` or [PowerShell](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001) on Windows to access and/or export security event information.(Citation: WithSecure Lazarus-NoPineapple Threat Intel Report 2023)(Citation: Cadet Blizzard emerges as novel threat actor) In cloud environments, adversaries may leverage utilities such as the Azure VM Agent’s `CollectGuestLogs.exe` to collect security logs from cloud hosted infrastructure.(Citation: SIM Swapping and Abuse of the Microsoft Azure Serial Console)

Adversaries may also target centralized logging infrastructure such as SIEMs. Logs may also be bulk exported and sent to adversary-controlled infrastructure for offline analysis.

In addition to gaining a better understanding of the environment, adversaries may also monitor logs in real time to track incident response procedures. This may allow them to adjust their techniques in order to maintain persistence or evade defenses.(Citation: Permiso GUI-Vil 2023)
4911.profile: [profile]The entity is a technique for enumerating Domain Admins, which is a specific form of Account Discovery (T1087.002) under the Discovery tactic, primarily targeting Windows platforms. Adversaries use commands like `net group "Domain Admins" /domain` or PowerShell cmdlets such as `Get-ADGroupMember` to list members of the privileged Domain Admins group. This activity is associated with intrusion sets like OilRig and Volt Typhoon to identify high-value targets for privilege escalation and lateral movement.
4911.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Domain Admins Enumeration is a technique for discovering domain-level groups with elevated permissions, specifically targeting the Domain Admins group to identify privileged users. The technical mechanics involve using commands like `net group /domain` on Windows, `dscacheutil -q group` on macOS, or `ldapsearch` on Linux to list these groups, and PowerShell cmdlets such as `Get-ADGroupMember` for Active Directory enumeration. This technique is part of the Discovery tactic within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, primarily on Windows platforms, and is used by groups like Volt Typhoon and Mustang Panda.

4912.name: Data Encryption for Impact
4912.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may encrypt data on target systems or on large numbers of systems in a network to interrupt availability to system and network resources. They can attempt to render stored data inaccessible by encrypting files or data on local and remote drives and withholding access to a decryption key. This may be done in order to extract monetary compensation from a victim in exchange for decryption or a decryption key (ransomware) or to render data permanently inaccessible in cases where the key is not saved or transmitted.(Citation: US-CERT Ransomware 2016)(Citation: FireEye WannaCry 2017)(Citation: US-CERT NotPetya 2017)(Citation: US-CERT SamSam 2018)

In the case of ransomware, it is typical that common user files like Office documents, PDFs, images, videos, audio, text, and source code files will be encrypted (and often renamed and/or tagged with specific file markers). Adversaries may need to first employ other behaviors, such as [File and Directory Permissions Modification](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1222) or [System Shutdown/Reboot](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1529), in order to unlock and/or gain access to manipulate these files.(Citation: CarbonBlack Conti July 2020) In some cases, adversaries may encrypt critical system files, disk partitions, and the MBR.(Citation: US-CERT NotPetya 2017) Adversaries may also encrypt virtual machines hosted on ESXi or other hypervisors.(Citation: Crowdstrike Hypervisor Jackpotting Pt 2 2021) 

To maximize impact on the target organization, malware designed for encrypting data may have worm-like features to propagate across a network by leveraging other attack techniques like [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078), [OS Credential Dumping](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003), and [SMB/Windows Admin Shares](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002).(Citation: FireEye WannaCry 2017)(Citation: US-CERT NotPetya 2017) Encryption malware may also leverage [Internal Defacement](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1491/001), such as changing victim wallpapers or ESXi server login messages, or otherwise intimidate victims by sending ransom notes or other messages to connected printers (known as "print bombing").(Citation: NHS Digital Egregor Nov 2020)(Citation: Varonis)

In cloud environments, storage objects within compromised accounts may also be encrypted.(Citation: Rhino S3 Ransomware Part 1) For example, in AWS environments, adversaries may leverage services such as AWS’s Server-Side Encryption with Customer Provided Keys (SSE-C) to encrypt data.(Citation: Halcyon AWS Ransomware 2025)
4912.profile: [profile]Data Encryption for Impact, identified as T1486, is an Impact tactic technique targeting Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves encrypting files on local and remote drives, including critical system files, disk partitions, the MBR, and virtual machines on hypervisors like ESXi, to render data inaccessible. To maximize impact, malware may propagate via network shares using techniques like Valid Accounts and OS Credential Dumping, and may employ internal defacement or "print bombing" to intimidate victims. In cloud environments, adversaries can encrypt storage objects using services like AWS's Server-Side Encryption with Customer Provided Keys (SSE-C).
4912.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Data Encryption for Impact is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1486 under the Impact tactic, targeting Windows, Linux, and macOS. It involves adversaries encrypting data on target systems to disrupt availability, often for ransomware. Technical mechanics include encrypting common user files, critical system files, disk partitions, the MBR, and virtual machines on hypervisors like ESXi. To maximize impact, malware may employ worm-like propagation using techniques like Valid Accounts and SMB shares, and may use internal defacement or "print bombing" for intimidation. In cloud environments, adversaries can encrypt storage objects using services like AWS SSE-C.

4913.name: Maintaining Persistent Access
4913.profile: [profile]The entity "Maintaining Persistent Access" is a deprecated MITRE ATT&CK technique. It is superseded by specific techniques like Create Account (T1136), Web Shell (T1505.003), and External Remote Services (T1133). The core concept involves adversaries using multiple redundant access mechanisms, such as different remote access tools, valid accounts for external services like VPNs, or cloud-based infrastructure, to ensure they retain network access if one method is discovered and removed. This behavior is associated with groups like OilRig.[/profile]
4913.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Maintaining Persistent Access" is a deprecated MITRE ATT&CK technique. It is superseded by specific techniques such as Create Account (T1136), Web Shell (T1505.003), and External Remote Services (T1133). The core concept involves adversaries using multiple redundant access mechanisms, like different remote access tools or valid accounts for external services, to ensure they retain network access if one method is discovered and blocked. This persistence is a high-level objective across various platforms, achieved through the establishment of alternate, resilient command and control channels or credentialed footholds.

4914.name: Intermittent Access
4914.profile: [profile]Intermittent Access is a deprecated technique, now represented by standard MITRE techniques like Create Account (T1136), Web Shell (T1505.003), and External Remote Services (T1133). It describes an adversary's strategy to maintain persistent network footholds by employing multiple, diverse remote access mechanisms, such as different command and control tools or valid accounts for external services like VPNs. This redundancy ensures that if one access vector is discovered and blocked, the adversary retains operational access through an alternate channel, as historically used by groups like OilRig.[/profile]
4914.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Intermittent Access is a technique used to maintain persistent access to a compromised network by employing multiple, varied remote access mechanisms, such as different remote access tools with distinct command and control protocols or credentialed access via external remote services like VPNs. This redundancy ensures that if one access method is detected and blocked, the adversary retains network access through an alternate channel, potentially using web shells or cloud-based infrastructure.

4915.name: Hiding Artifacts
4915.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may attempt to hide artifacts associated with their behaviors to evade detection. Operating systems may have features to hide various artifacts, such as important system files and administrative task execution, to avoid disrupting user work environments and prevent users from changing files or features on the system. Adversaries may abuse these features to hide artifacts such as files, directories, user accounts, or other system activity to evade detection.(Citation: Sofacy Komplex Trojan)(Citation: Cybereason OSX Pirrit)(Citation: MalwareBytes ADS July 2015)

Adversaries may also attempt to hide artifacts associated with malicious behavior by creating computing regions that are isolated from common security instrumentation, such as through the use of virtualization technology.(Citation: Sophos Ragnar May 2020)
4915.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique "Hide Artifacts" (T1564) under the Defense Evasion tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It involves adversaries abusing built-in operating system features, such as file and directory hiding mechanisms or administrative task concealment, to obscure malicious files, directories, user accounts, or other activity. A supplementary method is the use of virtualization to create isolated computing regions that evade common security instrumentation. The intrusion set OilRig has been associated with this behavior.[/profile]
4915.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Hiding Artifacts is a technique aligned with the MITRE ATT&CK ID T1564 under the Defense Evasion tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. It involves adversaries abusing built-in operating system features, such as those for hiding system files or administrative tasks, to conceal malicious files, directories, user accounts, or system activity. This evasion can also extend to creating isolated computing regions using virtualization to avoid security instrumentation.

4916.name: Authentication Bypass
4916.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may modify file attributes and subvert Gatekeeper functionality to evade user prompts and execute untrusted programs. Gatekeeper is a set of technologies that act as layer of Apple’s security model to ensure only trusted applications are executed on a host. Gatekeeper was built on top of File Quarantine in Snow Leopard (10.6, 2009) and has grown to include Code Signing, security policy compliance, Notarization, and more. Gatekeeper also treats applications running for the first time differently than reopened applications.(Citation: TheEclecticLightCompany Quarantine and the flag)(Citation: TheEclecticLightCompany apple notarization )

Based on an opt-in system, when files are downloaded an extended attribute (xattr) called `com.apple.quarantine` (also known as a quarantine flag) can be set on the file by the application performing the download. Launch Services opens the application in a suspended state. For first run applications with the quarantine flag set, Gatekeeper executes the following functions:

1. Checks extended attribute – Gatekeeper checks for the quarantine flag, then provides an alert prompt to the user to allow or deny execution.(Citation: OceanLotus for OS X)(Citation: 20 macOS Common Tools and Techniques)

2. Checks System Policies - Gatekeeper checks the system security policy, allowing execution of apps downloaded from either just the App Store or the App Store and identified developers.

3. Code Signing – Gatekeeper checks for a valid code signature from an Apple Developer ID.

4. Notarization - Using the `api.apple-cloudkit.com` API, Gatekeeper reaches out to Apple servers to verify or pull down the notarization ticket and ensure the ticket is not revoked. Users can override notarization, which will result in a prompt of executing an “unauthorized app” and the security policy will be modified.

Adversaries can subvert one or multiple security controls within Gatekeeper checks through logic errors (e.g. [Exploitation for Defense Evasion](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1211)), unchecked file types, and external libraries. For example, prior to macOS 13 Ventura, code signing and notarization checks were only conducted on first launch, allowing adversaries to write malicious executables to previously opened applications in order to bypass Gatekeeper security checks.(Citation: theevilbit gatekeeper bypass 2021)(Citation: Application Bundle Manipulation Brandon Dalton)

Applications and files loaded onto the system from a USB flash drive, optical disk, external hard drive, from a drive shared over the local network, or using the curl command may not set the quarantine flag. Additionally, it is possible to avoid setting the quarantine flag using [Drive-by Compromise](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1189).
4916.profile: [profile]Gatekeeper Bypass is identified as MITRE technique T1553.001 under the Defense Evasion tactic for macOS. It involves subverting Apple's Gatekeeper security by manipulating file attributes like the `com.apple.quarantine` extended attribute or exploiting logic errors, such as writing malicious code into previously opened applications to avoid code signing and notarization checks on first launch. This allows execution of untrusted programs without user prompts. The intrusion-set OilRig has been associated with this technique.[/profile]
4916.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Authentication Bypass is a technique for evading authentication mechanisms to gain unauthorized access. It falls under the Defense Evasion tactic and can target multiple platforms. The technique involves subverting security controls, such as patching a domain controller's LSASS process to accept a master password (like Skeleton Key malware) or modifying Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM) on Unix systems to accept adversary-supplied credentials. It can also involve leveraging stolen alternate authentication material like password hashes or Kerberos tickets to authenticate without a valid account.

4918.name: 3DES Encryption
4918.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may compromise a network device’s encryption capability in order to bypass encryption that would otherwise protect data communications. (Citation: Cisco Synful Knock Evolution)

Encryption can be used to protect transmitted network traffic to maintain its confidentiality (protect against unauthorized disclosure) and integrity (protect against unauthorized changes). Encryption ciphers are used to convert a plaintext message to ciphertext and can be computationally intensive to decipher without the associated decryption key. Typically, longer keys increase the cost of cryptanalysis, or decryption without the key.

Adversaries can compromise and manipulate devices that perform encryption of network traffic. For example, through behaviors such as [Modify System Image](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1601), [Reduce Key Space](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1600/001), and [Disable Crypto Hardware](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1600/002), an adversary can negatively effect and/or eliminate a device’s ability to securely encrypt network traffic. This poses a greater risk of unauthorized disclosure and may help facilitate data manipulation, Credential Access, or Collection efforts. (Citation: Cisco Blog Legacy Device Attacks)
4918.profile: [profile]3DES Encryption is a symmetric encryption algorithm, referenced as a specific example within MITRE ATT&CK sub-technique T1573.001 (Symmetric Cryptography) under the Command and Control tactic. It operates on network platforms. The algorithm uses the same key for both encryption and decryption of data, and adversaries may employ it to obfuscate command and control or exfiltration traffic, potentially layering it within other encrypted protocols. It is a known cryptographic standard mentioned in the context of various threat groups' tooling.
4918.profile_without_enhance: [profile]3DES Encryption is a symmetric encryption algorithm used to conceal command and control traffic, referenced within MITRE ATT&CK sub-technique T1573.001. It functions as a shared-key cipher for encrypting plaintext and decrypting ciphertext. This algorithm is commonly employed by adversaries to obfuscate network communications, often implemented within custom encryption schemes or as part of multilayer encryption strategies for data exfiltration over non-C2 protocols.

4919.name: HTTP Cookie Command Injection
4919.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries can use stolen session cookies to authenticate to web applications and services. This technique bypasses some multi-factor authentication protocols since the session is already authenticated.(Citation: Pass The Cookie)

Authentication cookies are commonly used in web applications, including cloud-based services, after a user has authenticated to the service so credentials are not passed and re-authentication does not need to occur as frequently. Cookies are often valid for an extended period of time, even if the web application is not actively used. After the cookie is obtained through [Steal Web Session Cookie](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539) or [Web Cookies](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1606/001), the adversary may then import the cookie into a browser they control and is then able to use the site or application as the user for as long as the session cookie is active. Once logged into the site, an adversary can access sensitive information, read email, or perform actions that the victim account has permissions to perform.

There have been examples of malware targeting session cookies to bypass multi-factor authentication systems.(Citation: Unit 42 Mac Crypto Cookies January 2019)
4919.profile: [profile]HTTP Cookie Command Injection is a technique where adversaries inject malicious commands into HTTP cookies to execute unauthorized actions on a web server or application. This method involves manipulating cookie values to contain and trigger command execution, often as part of a broader attack chain. The technique can be used to bypass security controls, gain initial access, or achieve persistence by exploiting how web applications process cookie data. Associated malware like TwoFace Webshell and intrusion sets such as OilRig have been linked to its use.
4919.profile_without_enhance: [profile]HTTP Cookie Command Injection is a technique where adversaries inject malicious commands into HTTP cookies to execute arbitrary code on a web server. This attack exploits the server-side processing of cookie values, often through improper input validation, allowing the adversary to achieve remote code execution. The method is specific to web platforms and can be used for initial access or persistence by manipulating a standard web protocol component.

4920.name: HTTP POST Command Injection
4920.profile: [profile]HTTP POST Command Injection is a technique where adversaries inject malicious commands into HTTP POST request parameters to execute arbitrary code on a web server. It is associated with the OilRig intrusion set and the TwoFace Webshell malware. The technique exploits web application input validation flaws, allowing attackers to submit crafted POST data that the server processes as system commands, facilitating initial access or persistence. It leverages standard web protocols for communication and potential data exfiltration.[/profile]
4920.profile_without_enhance: [profile]HTTP POST Command Injection is a technique where adversaries inject malicious commands into the data of an HTTP POST request to execute arbitrary code on a vulnerable web server. This attack exploits insufficient input validation or sanitization in web applications, allowing the attacker to submit crafted POST parameters that are interpreted as system commands by the server's backend. It is commonly used for initial access, execution, and persistence, operating primarily on web server platforms.

4922.name: sekurlsa
4922.profile: [profile]Sekurlsa is a module of the Mimikatz credential-dumping tool, used to extract passwords, hashes, and Kerberos tickets from the LSASS process memory. It is employed by threat actors, including groups like APT10, APT32, Anunak, and Gallium, for post-exploitation credential access. Key commands include sekurlsa::logonpasswords for harvesting credentials and sekurlsa::tickets /export for stealing Kerberos tickets, often executed with elevated privileges via token::elevate. It targets Windows platforms and is commonly used in conjunction with other Mimikatz modules like lsadump for lateral movement and persistence.
4922.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Sekurlsa, also known as Mimikatz, is a credential dumping tool used by groups like APT10, APT32, Anunak, Gallium, and OilRig. Its key technical behaviors include extracting passwords, authentication tokens, and Kerberos tickets from Windows memory using specific commands like `sekurlsa::logonpasswords`, `sekurlsa::pth` for pass-the-hash attacks, and `sekurlsa::tickets /export`. It primarily targets Windows platforms to facilitate lateral movement and credential access, often being packaged in DLL formats for integration into other malware.[/profile]

4924.name: Clayslide
4924.profile: [profile]Clayslide, also known as Helminth, is a malware attributed to the OilRig intrusion set. Its delivery mechanism involves documents, as seen in the "New Clayslide Delivery Document" associated with Alma Communicator. For persistence, it creates a registry key to automatically launch a copy on system startup. It also performs monitoring of specific applications on the infected system. The malware targets the Windows platform.[/profile]
4924.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Clayslide is a malware family attributed to the OilRig intrusion set (APT34). It is used to deliver other malware, such as the Helminth backdoor, via malicious documents. Related variants include officeservicesstatus.vbs and officeservicesstatus, which target Windows systems, communicate with C2 infrastructure using specific URIs and HTTP headers, and exfiltrate data using Base64URL encoding.[/profile]

4925.name: Helminth

4925.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Helminth, also known as Clayslide, is a malware attributed to the OilRig intrusion set (APT34). 4927.name: update.vbs
4927.profile: [profile]The malware "update.vbs" is attributed to the intrusion set OilRig. It is delivered via a ZIP file downloaded from a domain like 360scanner[.]store and extracted to a %TEMP% directory, after which the VBScript is executed by wscript. 4928.name: fireeye.vbs
4928.profile: [profile]FireEye.vbs is a VBScript-based malware, with aliases including fireeyse.vbs and firaeeye.vbs. It is attributed to the APT group OilRig (also known as APT34). Key technical behaviors involve using cmd.exe or isoburn.exe to execute commands and mount a .iso file from the AppData\\Local directory, and using regsvr32.exe or PowerISO8.exe for execution. It targets the Windows platform. Its infrastructure includes specific URLs for command and control, and it is part of a malware family timeline that includes variants like komisova.vbs, update.vbs, and upd.vbs.
4928.profile_without_enhance: [profile]fireeye.vbs, also known as fireeyse.vbs and firaeeye.vbs, is attributed to the OilRig intrusion set (also known as APT34). Key technical behaviors include creating a copy of itself in the Startup folder with a filename like devopt(random 2 digit).exe for persistence, accessing system directories like Documents and Downloads, and being executed via cmd.exe or isoburn.exe to mount .iso files from AppData\Local. It uses a mutex like e4d6a6ec-320d-48ee-b6b2-fa24f03760d4. It is part of a variant chain including komisova.vbs, sharing infrastructure like specific URLs during transition phases.[/profile]

4937.name: weak passwords
4937.profile: [profile]The entity "weak passwords" is not a direct MITRE ATT&CK technique but a vulnerability condition enabling techniques like Credential Access T1110.001 Password Guessing. Attackers like OilRig systematically guess weak passwords using common lists against services including SSH, Telnet, FTP, SMB, LDAP, Kerberos, RDP, HTTP/S, databases, VNC, and SNMP, often targeting SSO, cloud apps, and wireless routers. This approach risks triggering authentication failures and account lockouts depending on organizational policies.
4937.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "weak passwords" is a foundational security vulnerability rather than a distinct MITRE ATT&CK technique. It represents the use of easily guessable or default credentials, often exploited through techniques like Password Guessing (T1110.001) or Brute Force (T1110). Adversaries leverage weak passwords to gain initial access, often targeting common management services such as SSH (22/TCP), Telnet (23/TCP), FTP (21/TCP), SMB (445/TCP), and RDP (3389/TCP). This weakness is a primary enabler for credential-based attacks and is frequently targeted by groups like APT29 and APT28.

4939.name: Base64 encoding
4939.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may encode data with a standard data encoding system to make the content of command and control traffic more difficult to detect. Command and control (C2) information can be encoded using a standard data encoding system that adheres to existing protocol specifications. Common data encoding schemes include ASCII, Unicode, hexadecimal, Base64, and MIME.(Citation: Wikipedia Binary-to-text Encoding)(Citation: Wikipedia Character Encoding) Some data encoding systems may also result in data compression, such as gzip.
4939.profile: [profile]Base64 Encoding, known as T1132.001 within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, is a sub-technique of Data Encoding under the Command and Control tactic. It operates across multiple platforms and involves adversaries using the standard Base64 binary-to-text encoding scheme to obfuscate command and control traffic, adhering to common protocol specifications to evade detection. This technique is associated with groups like OilRig, Hafnium, and MuddyWater.[/profile]
4939.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Base64 encoding is a specific instance of the standard encoding technique (T1132.001) within the Command and Control tactic. It is a common binary-to-text encoding scheme used by adversaries to obfuscate the content of C2 traffic, making it more difficult to detect by adhering to a widely recognized protocol specification. This technique is employed by groups such as Hafnium, MuddyWater, and Lazarus Group.[/profile]

4940.name: Hexadecimal encoding
4940.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may encode data with a standard data encoding system to make the content of command and control traffic more difficult to detect. Command and control (C2) information can be encoded using a standard data encoding system that adheres to existing protocol specifications. Common data encoding schemes include ASCII, Unicode, hexadecimal, Base64, and MIME.(Citation: Wikipedia Binary-to-text Encoding)(Citation: Wikipedia Character Encoding) Some data encoding systems may also result in data compression, such as gzip.
4940.profile: [profile]The entity "Hexadecimal encoding" is a sub-technique of Data Encoding, specifically identified as T1132.001 within the MITRE ATT&CK framework. It falls under the Command and Control tactic and is applicable across multiple platforms. This technique involves adversaries using standard, protocol-compliant encoding schemes like hexadecimal, ASCII, Unicode, Base64, or MIME to obfuscate command and control traffic, making it more difficult to detect. It is distinct from non-standard encoding (T1132.002) and is associated with threat groups including OilRig, MuddyWater, and Lazarus Group.
4940.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Hexadecimal encoding is a sub-technique of Data Encoding (T1132.001) under the Command and Control tactic. It operates across multiple platforms, including Windows, Linux, and macOS. This technique involves converting binary data into a hexadecimal (base-16) text representation, using characters 0-9 and A-F, to obfuscate command and control traffic and evade simple detection mechanisms. It is a standard, widely recognized encoding scheme often employed by threat groups like Hafnium, MuddyWater, and Lazarus Group.[/profile]

4941.name: Code Obfuscation
4941.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may obfuscate command and control traffic to make it more difficult to detect.(Citation: Bitdefender FunnyDream Campaign November 2020) Command and control (C2) communications are hidden (but not necessarily encrypted) in an attempt to make the content more difficult to discover or decipher and to make the communication less conspicuous and hide commands from being seen. This encompasses many methods, such as adding junk data to protocol traffic, using steganography, or impersonating legitimate protocols.
4941.profile: [profile]Code Obfuscation, likely aligned with MITRE ATT&CK T1027 (Obfuscated Files or Information), falls under the Defense Evasion tactic and applies to multiple platforms. This technique involves making files or information difficult to analyze by encrypting, encoding, or otherwise hiding their contents. Specific methods include using compression, splitting payloads into benign-seeming segments, and employing built-in language features like Base64 encoding to obscure strings and commands. The related group Gamaredon Group has been associated with such obfuscation practices.
4941.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Code Obfuscation" is a technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, identified as T1027 under the Defense Evasion tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. It involves adversaries making executables or files difficult to discover or analyze by encrypting, encoding, or otherwise obfuscating their contents. This includes methods like compressing or archiving payloads, splitting payloads into benign-seeming files for later reassembly, and encoding portions of files to hide plain-text strings, all aimed at evading signature-based detection and hindering analysis.

4942.name: Function Renaming
4942.profile: [profile]Function Renaming is a sub-technique of Masquerading (T1036.003) within the Defense Evasion tactic, applicable to Windows and other platforms. It involves adversaries renaming legitimate system utilities or tools (e.g., copying and renaming rundll32.exe) to bypass security monitoring and controls that are triggered by specific binary names or execution from non-standard paths, as observed in groups like APT38 and Lazarus Group.[/profile]
4942.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Function Renaming is a sub-technique of Masquerading (T1036.003) under the Defense Evasion tactic, primarily for Windows. It involves adversaries renaming legitimate system utilities or tools (e.g., `rundll32.exe`) to bypass security monitoring and controls that trigger on known malicious filenames or standard execution paths. This technique is used by groups like APT38 and Lazarus Group to abuse trusted binaries without detection.

4943.name: Command Modification
4943.profile: [profile]Command Modification, identified as T1650, is a Defense Evasion technique. It involves adversaries altering legitimate system commands or command parameters to bypass security controls, hide malicious activity, or subvert intended command functionality. This can be achieved by modifying environment variables, command aliases, or configuration files that dictate command behavior. The intrusion set OilRig has been associated with this technique.
4943.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Command Modification is a technique where adversaries alter legitimate system commands or their execution parameters to evade detection and maintain persistence. It operates within the Execution tactic, primarily affecting Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. This involves changing command syntax, arguments, or targets, such as editing shortcut paths or modifying environment variables like `HISTFILE` to impair logging, allowing malicious activity to blend with normal operations.

4944.name: Decoy Content Modification
4944.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may gain access and continuously communicate with victims by injecting malicious content into systems through online network traffic. Rather than luring victims to malicious payloads hosted on a compromised website (i.e., [Drive-by Target](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1608/004) followed by [Drive-by Compromise](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1189)), adversaries may initially access victims through compromised data-transfer channels where they can manipulate traffic and/or inject their own content. These compromised online network channels may also be used to deliver additional payloads (i.e., [Ingress Tool Transfer](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1105)) and other data to already compromised systems.(Citation: ESET MoustachedBouncer)

Adversaries may inject content to victim systems in various ways, including:

* From the middle, where the adversary is in-between legitimate online client-server communications (**Note:** this is similar but distinct from [Adversary-in-the-Middle](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1557), which describes AiTM activity solely within an enterprise environment) (Citation: Kaspersky Encyclopedia MiTM)
* From the side, where malicious content is injected and races to the client as a fake response to requests of a legitimate online server (Citation: Kaspersky ManOnTheSide)

Content injection is often the result of compromised upstream communication channels, for example at the level of an internet service provider (ISP) as is the case with "lawful interception."(Citation: Kaspersky ManOnTheSide)(Citation: ESET MoustachedBouncer)(Citation: EFF China GitHub Attack)
4944.profile: [profile]The technique is officially known as Content Injection with MITRE ID T1659, operating under the Initial Access tactic. It involves adversaries manipulating online network traffic to inject malicious content into victim systems, often through compromised upstream channels like an ISP. This can be executed 'from the middle' by intercepting client-server communications or 'from the side' by racing a malicious response to a legitimate request. The technique is distinct from enterprise-focused Adversary-in-the-Middle and is associated with groups like MoustachedBouncer and OilRig.
4944.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Decoy Content Modification is a technique where adversaries alter the content of decoy files or systems to mislead defenders and evade detection. This involves modifying the content of honeypots, canary files, or other deceptive assets to make them appear normal or to plant false indicators, thereby undermining security monitoring and incident response efforts. It is a sub-technique of Data Manipulation (T1565) and is primarily used to impair defensive operations.

4945.name: Malware Payload Removal
4945.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may develop malware and malware components that can be used during targeting. Building malicious software can include the development of payloads, droppers, post-compromise tools, backdoors (including backdoored images), packers, C2 protocols, and the creation of infected removable media. Adversaries may develop malware to support their operations, creating a means for maintaining control of remote machines, evading defenses, and executing post-compromise behaviors.(Citation: Mandiant APT1)(Citation: Kaspersky Sofacy)(Citation: ActiveMalwareEnergy)(Citation: FBI Flash FIN7 USB)

During malware development, adversaries may intentionally include indicators aligned with other known actors in order to mislead attribution by defenders.(Citation: Olympic Destroyer)(Citation: Risky Bulletin Threat actor impersonates FSB APT)(Citation: GamaCopy organization)

As with legitimate development efforts, different skill sets may be required for developing malware. The skills needed may be located in-house, or may need to be contracted out. Use of a contractor may be considered an extension of that adversary's malware development capabilities, provided the adversary plays a role in shaping requirements and maintains a degree of exclusivity to the malware.

Some aspects of malware development, such as C2 protocol development, may require adversaries to obtain additional infrastructure. For example, malware developed that will communicate with Twitter for C2, may require use of [Web Services](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1583/006).(Citation: FireEye APT29)
4945.profile: [profile]Malware Payload Removal is a technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, identified as T1070.010 (Relocate Malware) under the Defense Evasion tactic, applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves adversaries copying and moving malicious payloads to new locations on a compromised system to remove forensic evidence, evade detection, and hinder analysis. This is often done by renaming files to blend in, targeting specific directories for persistence, and can be combined with file deletion to clean up initial delivery artifacts, thereby separating the payload from earlier attack stages that may have triggered alerts.[/profile]
4945.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Malware Payload Removal is a technique within the broader Tactic of Defense Evasion, specifically mapped to MITRE ATT&CK ID T1070.004 (File Deletion). It operates across Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. The technical mechanics involve adversaries using native OS commands like `del` on Windows or `rm` and `unlink` on Linux/macOS to delete malicious files, tools, or other non-native artifacts dropped during an intrusion. This action is performed to remove forensic evidence, minimize their footprint, and hinder defensive analysis and incident response.

4946.name: Modify worksheet names
4946.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may gather employee names that can be used during targeting. Employee names be used to derive email addresses as well as to help guide other reconnaissance efforts and/or craft more-believable lures.

Adversaries may easily gather employee names, since they may be readily available and exposed via online or other accessible data sets (ex: [Social Media](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1593/001) or [Search Victim-Owned Websites](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1594)).(Citation: OPM Leak) Gathering this information may reveal opportunities for other forms of reconnaissance (ex: [Search Open Websites/Domains](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1593) or [Phishing for Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1598)), establishing operational resources (ex: [Compromise Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1586)), and/or initial access (ex: [Phishing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566) or [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078)).

This technique involves adversaries collecting employee names from publicly accessible sources like social media or victim-owned websites to derive email addresses, guide further reconnaissance, and craft more believable phishing lures for initial access or account compromise.
