4947.name: Add obfuscation strings
4947.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may abuse Microsoft Office add-ins to obtain persistence on a compromised system. Office add-ins can be used to add functionality to Office programs. (Citation: Microsoft Office Add-ins) There are different types of add-ins that can be used by the various Office products; including Word/Excel add-in Libraries (WLL/XLL), VBA add-ins, Office Component Object Model (COM) add-ins, automation add-ins, VBA Editor (VBE), Visual Studio Tools for Office (VSTO) add-ins, and Outlook add-ins. 4947.profile: [profile]Add obfuscation strings, identified as T1027.010 (Command Obfuscation) under the Defense Evasion tactic, operates on Windows, Linux, and macOS. This technique involves manipulating command syntax to hinder detection, using methods like string concatenation (e.g., "Wor"+"d.Application"), escape characters (^, +, $, %), base64 encoding, and directory traversal (e.g., C:\voi\pcw\..\..\Windows\system32\wmic.exe). This can be implemented through string concatenation (e.g., `"Wor"+"d.Application"`), use of escape characters, or encoding schemes like Base64 within command-line interpreters.

4948.name: Function name obfuscation
4948.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may obfuscate command and control traffic to make it more difficult to detect.(Citation: Bitdefender FunnyDream Campaign November 2020) Command and control (C2) communications are hidden (but not necessarily encrypted) in an attempt to make the content more difficult to discover or decipher and to make the communication less conspicuous and hide commands from being seen. This encompasses many methods, such as adding junk data to protocol traffic, using steganography, or impersonating legitimate protocols.

It specifically involves renaming functions within code or scripts to use benign, misleading, or random names, making malicious logic harder to identify during static analysis. This technique is distinct from broader data or command obfuscation, focusing on the manipulation of function identifiers to evade signature-based detection. It has been used by groups like OilRig.[/profile]

4976.name: Malicious PowerShell/Batch scripts
4976.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may abuse PowerShell commands and scripts for execution. PowerShell is a powerful interactive command-line interface and scripting environment included in the Windows operating system.(Citation: TechNet PowerShell) Adversaries can use PowerShell to perform a number of actions, including discovery of information and execution of code. Examples include the Start-Process cmdlet which can be used to run an executable and the Invoke-Command cmdlet which runs a command locally or on a remote computer (though administrator permissions are required to use PowerShell to connect to remote systems). PowerShell may also be used to download and run executables from the Internet, which can be executed from disk or in memory without touching disk. A number of PowerShell-based offensive testing tools are available, including [Empire](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0363), [PowerSploit](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0194), [PoshC2](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0378), and PSAttack.(Citation: Github PSAttack) PowerShell commands/scripts can also be executed without directly invoking the powershell.exe binary through interfaces to PowerShell's underlying System.Management.Automation assembly DLL exposed through the .NET framework and Windows Common Language Interface (CLI).(Citation: Sixdub PowerPick Jan 2016)(Citation: SilentBreak Offensive PS Dec 2015)(Citation: Microsoft PSfromCsharp APR 2014)
4976.profile: [profile]This entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1059.001, named Command and Scripting Interpreter: PowerShell, under the Execution tactic primarily for Windows. It involves abusing PowerShell's command-line interface and scripting environment for actions like code execution and discovery, using cmdlets such as Start-Process to run executables and Invoke-Command for local or remote command execution. Adversaries can download and run executables from the internet, executing them from disk or entirely in memory, and can bypass direct invocation of powershell.exe by leveraging the underlying System.Management.Automation assembly through .NET. It is associated with numerous threat groups, including OilRig.[/profile]
4976.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Malicious PowerShell/Batch scripts is a deprecated technique (T1064) under Execution. It involves adversaries using command-line batch scripts or PowerShell on Windows to automate and speed up operations, often bypassing manual processes. Scripts can be embedded in documents like macros to execute upon opening, facilitating actions such as downloading and running executables from the internet, potentially in memory without touching disk. This method leverages native Windows scripting environments for post-compromise activities and defense evasion.

4977.name: Living-off-the-land tactics
4977.profile: [profile]Living-off-the-land tactics is a broad adversary approach, not a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique with a T-ID. It involves using legitimate, pre-installed system tools and software (like remote desktop software or command-line utilities) to perform malicious activities such as discovery, lateral movement, and command and control, thereby blending in with normal administrative traffic to evade detection. This tactic is employed by groups like OilRig to operate stealthily within a target environment.[/profile]
4977.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Living-off-the-land tactics is a strategic approach where adversaries abuse legitimate, pre-installed system tools and software (like PowerShell, WMI, or remote desktop applications) to blend in with normal administrative activity, thereby evading detection by security controls. This technique falls under the Defense Evasion and Execution tactics and is applicable across Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. Its core technical mechanic involves using trusted binaries and processes for malicious purposes, such as lateral movement, data exfiltration, and command execution, without deploying custom malware.

4978.name: Overwrite MBR
4978.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may modify a process's in-memory arguments to change its name in order to appear as a legitimate or benign process. On Linux, the operating system stores command-line arguments in the process’s stack and passes them to the `main()` function as the `argv` array. The first element, `argv[0]`, typically contains the process name or path - by default, the command used to actually start the process (e.g., `cat /etc/passwd`). By default, the Linux `/proc` filesystem uses this value to represent the process name. The `/proc/<PID>/cmdline` file reflects the contents of this memory, and tools like `ps` use it to display process information. Since arguments are stored in user-space memory at launch, this modification can be performed without elevated privileges. 

During runtime, adversaries can erase the memory used by all command-line arguments for a process, overwriting each argument string with null bytes. This removes evidence of how the process was originally launched. They can then write a spoofed string into the memory region previously occupied by `argv[0]` to mimic a benign command, such as `cat resolv.conf`. The new command-line string is reflected in `/proc/<PID>/cmdline` and displayed by tools like `ps`.(Citation: Sandfly BPFDoor 2022)(Citation: Microsoft XorDdos Linux Stealth 2022)
4978.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique "Overwrite Process Arguments" (ID: T1036.011), a Defense Evasion tactic for Linux platforms. It works by adversaries overwriting the in-memory command-line arguments (argv[0]) of a running process with null bytes to erase its launch history, then writing a spoofed benign command string (e.g., 'cat resolv.conf') into that memory. This manipulation, which requires no elevated privileges, alters the process name displayed in `/proc/<PID>/cmdline` and tools like `ps` to appear legitimate. The intrusion set OilRig has been associated with this technique.
4978.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Overwrite MBR" is a technique where an adversary with raw access to the boot drive modifies the Master Boot Record (MBR), the first disk sector loaded by the BIOS during system startup. By overwriting this area, the adversary can divert execution from the legitimate boot loader to malicious code, enabling persistence or disruption before the operating system loads. This technique is often associated with bootkit malware and can be used for disk wiping to interrupt system availability.

4979.name: Disk Partition Damage
4979.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may wipe or corrupt raw disk data on specific systems or in large numbers in a network to interrupt availability to system and network resources. With direct write access to a disk, adversaries may attempt to overwrite portions of disk data. Adversaries may opt to wipe arbitrary portions of disk data and/or wipe disk structures like the master boot record (MBR). A complete wipe of all disk sectors may be attempted.

To maximize impact on the target organization in operations where network-wide availability interruption is the goal, malware used for wiping disks may have worm-like features to propagate across a network by leveraging additional techniques like [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078), [OS Credential Dumping](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003), and [SMB/Windows Admin Shares](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002).(Citation: Novetta Blockbuster Destructive Malware)

On network devices, adversaries may wipe configuration files and other data from the device using [Network Device CLI](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/008) commands such as `erase`.(Citation: erase_cmd_cisco)
4979.profile: [profile]Disk Partition Damage is a technique aligned with MITRE ATT&CK ID T1561 under the Impact tactic, targeting Windows, Linux, and Network platforms. It involves adversaries corrupting or overwriting critical disk structures like the master boot record (MBR) or partition table to render systems unbootable, thereby interrupting availability. This can be executed in isolation or combined with broader disk content wipes, and on network devices, may use CLI commands such as `format`. The intrusion-set OilRig has been associated with this technique.[/profile]
4979.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Disk Partition Damage is a technique aligned with MITRE ATT&CK ID T1561.002 (Disk Structure Wipe) under the Impact tactic, targeting Windows, Linux, and Network platforms. It specifically involves overwriting critical disk structures like the master boot record (MBR) or partition table to render a system unbootable, thereby interrupting availability. This is often performed with direct write access to the disk and may be combined with broader disk content wipes for greater destructive effect.

4980.name: Denial of Access
4980.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may perform Endpoint Denial of Service (DoS) attacks to degrade or block the availability of services to users. Endpoint DoS can be performed by exhausting the system resources those services are hosted on or exploiting the system to cause a persistent crash condition. Example services include websites, email services, DNS, and web-based applications. Adversaries have been observed conducting DoS attacks for political purposes(Citation: FireEye OpPoisonedHandover February 2016) and to support other malicious activities, including distraction(Citation: FSISAC FraudNetDoS September 2012), hacktivism, and extortion.(Citation: Symantec DDoS October 2014)

An Endpoint DoS denies the availability of a service without saturating the network used to provide access to the service. Adversaries can target various layers of the application stack that is hosted on the system used to provide the service. These layers include the Operating Systems (OS), server applications such as web servers, DNS servers, databases, and the (typically web-based) applications that sit on top of them. Attacking each layer requires different techniques that take advantage of bottlenecks that are unique to the respective components. A DoS attack may be generated by a single system or multiple systems spread across the internet, which is commonly referred to as a distributed DoS (DDoS).

To perform DoS attacks against endpoint resources, several aspects apply to multiple methods, including IP address spoofing and botnets.

Adversaries may use the original IP address of an attacking system, or spoof the source IP address to make the attack traffic more difficult to trace back to the attacking system or to enable reflection. This can increase the difficulty defenders have in defending against the attack by reducing or eliminating the effectiveness of filtering by the source address on network defense devices.

Botnets are commonly used to conduct DDoS attacks against networks and services. Large botnets can generate a significant amount of traffic from systems spread across the global internet. Adversaries may have the resources to build out and control their own botnet infrastructure or may rent time on an existing botnet to conduct an attack. In some of the worst cases for DDoS, so many systems are used to generate requests that each one only needs to send out a small amount of traffic to produce enough volume to exhaust the target's resources. In such circumstances, distinguishing DDoS traffic from legitimate clients becomes exceedingly difficult. Botnets have been used in some of the most high-profile DDoS attacks, such as the 2012 series of incidents that targeted major US banks.(Citation: USNYAG IranianBotnet March 2016)

In cases where traffic manipulation is used, there may be points in the global network (such as high traffic gateway routers) where packets can be altered and cause legitimate clients to execute code that directs network packets toward a target in high volume. This type of capability was previously used for the purposes of web censorship where client HTTP traffic was modified to include a reference to JavaScript that generated the DDoS code to overwhelm target web servers.(Citation: ArsTechnica Great Firewall of China)

For attacks attempting to saturate the providing network, see [Network Denial of Service](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1498).
4980.profile: [profile]Endpoint Denial of Service, identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1499 under the Impact tactic, targets Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It degrades or blocks service availability by exhausting host system resources like CPU, memory, or disk, or by exploiting software vulnerabilities to cause persistent crashes, without necessarily saturating the network. This can involve targeting specific application layers, using IP spoofing for obfuscation, and leveraging botnets for distributed attacks (DDoS). The Sandworm Team is a known user of this technique.[/profile]
4980.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Denial of Access is a technique within the Impact tactic, targeting Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves adversaries degrading or blocking service availability by exhausting system resources or exploiting vulnerabilities to cause persistent crashes. This can target various layers of the application stack, including operating systems, server applications like web or DNS servers, and the applications themselves. Attacks may use IP address spoofing or botnets to generate traffic, making the malicious activity harder to trace and filter.

4981.name: Degradation
4981.profile: [profile]Degradation is a command and control technique where adversaries intentionally reduce the quality or speed of a communication channel to evade detection by network monitoring tools. This method, used by groups like OilRig, involves manipulating protocol performance to blend malicious traffic with legitimate network noise, thereby avoiding thresholds and signature-based analysis.[/profile]

It involves splitting communications between different protocols, such as using one protocol for inbound command and control and another for outbound data. This method aims to bypass firewall restrictions or avoid data threshold alerts on any single communication channel.

4982.name: Disruption
4982.profile: [profile]Disruption is a tactic within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, representing the adversary's objective to interrupt the availability of systems, services, or data. It is associated with techniques such as Disabling Security Tools (T1089) and Disable or Modify Cloud Logs (T1562.008), which adversaries like APT29 and OilRig may employ to hinder defensive monitoring and operations. This tactic is platform-agnostic, applicable across enterprise networks and cloud environments, and is often a precursor or component of impactful attacks like ransomware and data destruction.

This pattern includes specific techniques such as Disabling Security Tools (T1089), which involves killing processes or deleting registry keys to stop security software, and Disable or Modify Cloud Logs (T1562.008), where adversaries with sufficient permissions tamper with AWS CloudTrail or Office 365 auditing to avoid detection. The ultimate objective of these disruptive actions can be to enable further malicious activities like Financial Theft (T1657), which involves extortion, unauthorized fund transfers, or data encryption for ransom.

4983.name: Deception
4983.profile: [profile]The entity "Deception" is a high-level concept, not a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the provided neighbor and retrieved information, it is associated with the intrusion set OilRig and relates to adversary techniques for evasion and misrepresentation. Relevant ATT&CK techniques include Masquerading (T1036), where adversaries manipulate file names, metadata, or locations to appear legitimate, and Defacement (T1491), involving the modification of visual content for intimidation or messaging. The technical mechanics involve abusing system utilities, renaming files, and altering web content to evade detection and mislead users or security systems.[/profile]
4983.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique Deception, which is a broad tactic rather than a specific technique ID. It encompasses various procedures where adversaries manipulate perceptions to achieve their goals. This can involve adding junk data to network traffic to obscure command and control, manipulating file names and metadata to masquerade as legitimate software, or altering visual content on systems for defacement and psychological impact. These actions are employed by numerous threat groups, including APT28, Sandworm Team, and OilRig, to evade detection and mislead defenders.

4985.name: Exploit Vulnerable Driver
4985.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may modify or add LSASS drivers to obtain persistence on compromised systems. The Windows security subsystem is a set of components that manage and enforce the security policy for a computer or domain. The Local Security Authority (LSA) is the main component responsible for local security policy and user authentication. The LSA includes multiple dynamic link libraries (DLLs) associated with various other security functions, all of which run in the context of the LSA Subsystem Service (LSASS) lsass.exe process.(Citation: Microsoft Security Subsystem)

Adversaries may target LSASS drivers to obtain persistence. By either replacing or adding illegitimate drivers (e.g., [Hijack Execution Flow](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1574)), an adversary can use LSA operations to continuously execute malicious payloads.
4985.profile: [profile]Exploit Vulnerable Driver, also known as T1068 sub-technique, is part of the Privilege Escalation tactic on Windows. It involves adversaries bringing a signed but vulnerable driver onto a compromised system, often via tool transfer, to exploit its flaw and execute arbitrary code with kernel-mode privileges, a method known as Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver (BYOVD). This technique is used by groups like OilRig to bypass security controls and elevate access.

4986.name: DSE bypass
4986.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may modify file attributes and subvert Gatekeeper functionality to evade user prompts and execute untrusted programs. Gatekeeper is a set of technologies that act as layer of Apple’s security model to ensure only trusted applications are executed on a host. Gatekeeper was built on top of File Quarantine in Snow Leopard (10.6, 2009) and has grown to include Code Signing, security policy compliance, Notarization, and more. Gatekeeper also treats applications running for the first time differently than reopened applications.(Citation: TheEclecticLightCompany Quarantine and the flag)(Citation: TheEclecticLightCompany apple notarization )

Based on an opt-in system, when files are downloaded an extended attribute (xattr) called `com.apple.quarantine` (also known as a quarantine flag) can be set on the file by the application performing the download. Launch Services opens the application in a suspended state. For first run applications with the quarantine flag set, Gatekeeper executes the following functions:

1. Checks extended attribute – Gatekeeper checks for the quarantine flag, then provides an alert prompt to the user to allow or deny execution.(Citation: OceanLotus for OS X)(Citation: 20 macOS Common Tools and Techniques)

2. Checks System Policies - Gatekeeper checks the system security policy, allowing execution of apps downloaded from either just the App Store or the App Store and identified developers.

3. Code Signing – Gatekeeper checks for a valid code signature from an Apple Developer ID.

4. Notarization - Using the `api.apple-cloudkit.com` API, Gatekeeper reaches out to Apple servers to verify or pull down the notarization ticket and ensure the ticket is not revoked. Users can override notarization, which will result in a prompt of executing an “unauthorized app” and the security policy will be modified.

Adversaries can subvert one or multiple security controls within Gatekeeper checks through logic errors (e.g. [Exploitation for Defense Evasion](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1211)), unchecked file types, and external libraries. For example, prior to macOS 13 Ventura, code signing and notarization checks were only conducted on first launch, allowing adversaries to write malicious executables to previously opened applications in order to bypass Gatekeeper security checks.(Citation: theevilbit gatekeeper bypass 2021)(Citation: Application Bundle Manipulation Brandon Dalton)

Applications and files loaded onto the system from a USB flash drive, optical disk, external hard drive, from a drive shared over the local network, or using the curl command may not set the quarantine flag. Additionally, it is possible to avoid setting the quarantine flag using [Drive-by Compromise](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1189).
4986.profile: [profile]DSE bypass, also known as Gatekeeper bypass (T1553.001), is a Defense Evasion technique targeting macOS. It subverts Apple's Gatekeeper security by exploiting logic errors, unchecked file types, or external libraries to execute untrusted code. A specific method involves writing malicious executables to previously opened applications, as prior to macOS 13 Ventura, code signing and notarization checks only occurred on first launch. Adversaries can also avoid setting the quarantine flag by delivering files via physical media, network shares, or curl commands. The intrusion-set OilRig has been associated with this technique.
4986.profile_without_enhance: [profile]DSE bypass is a technique for evading Driver Signature Enforcement (DSE) on Windows, a security control that ensures only valid, signed drivers can be loaded. Adversaries may modify kernel memory variables, such as `g_CiOptions`, to disable DSE checks, often by exploiting a signed but vulnerable driver to gain the necessary kernel access. This policy modification can also be achieved via commands like `bcdedit.exe -set TESTSIGNING ON` or through registry changes, potentially requiring a system reboot to take effect.

4998.name: Cyber-based Weapons
4998.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may employ various time-based methods to detect virtualization and analysis environments, particularly those that attempt to manipulate time mechanisms to simulate longer elapses of time. This may include enumerating time-based properties, such as uptime or the system clock. 

Adversaries may use calls like `GetTickCount` and `GetSystemTimeAsFileTime` to discover if they are operating within a virtual machine or sandbox, or may be able to identify a sandbox accelerating time by sampling and calculating the expected value for an environment's timestamp before and after execution of a sleep function.(Citation: ISACA Malware Tricks)

It involves adversaries using system calls like GetTickCount and GetSystemTimeAsFileTime to measure elapsed time, detecting if they are in a virtual machine or sandbox by identifying discrepancies such as accelerated time simulations. The intrusion-set OilRig has been associated with this technique.

5000.name: Destruction
5000.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may destroy data and files on specific systems or in large numbers on a network to interrupt availability to systems, services, and network resources. Data destruction is likely to render stored data irrecoverable by forensic techniques through overwriting files or data on local and remote drives.(Citation: Symantec Shamoon 2012)(Citation: FireEye Shamoon Nov 2016)(Citation: Palo Alto Shamoon Nov 2016)(Citation: Kaspersky StoneDrill 2017)(Citation: Unit 42 Shamoon3 2018)(Citation: Talos Olympic Destroyer 2018) Common operating system file deletion commands such as del and rm often only remove pointers to files without wiping the contents of the files themselves, making the files recoverable by proper forensic methodology. This behavior is distinct from [Disk Content Wipe](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1561/001) and [Disk Structure Wipe](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1561/002) because individual files are destroyed rather than sections of a storage disk or the disk's logical structure. Adversaries may attempt to overwrite files and directories with randomly generated data to make it irrecoverable.(Citation: Kaspersky StoneDrill 2017)(Citation: Unit 42 Shamoon3 2018) In some cases politically oriented image files have been used to overwrite data.(Citation: FireEye Shamoon Nov 2016)(Citation: Palo Alto Shamoon Nov 2016)(Citation: Kaspersky StoneDrill 2017) To maximize impact on the target organization in operations where network-wide availability interruption is the goal, malware designed for destroying data may have worm-like features to propagate across a network by leveraging additional techniques like [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078), [OS Credential Dumping](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003), and [SMB/Windows Admin Shares](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002).(Citation: Symantec Shamoon 2012)(Citation: FireEye Shamoon Nov 2016)(Citation: Palo Alto Shamoon Nov 2016)(Citation: Kaspersky StoneDrill 2017)(Citation: Talos Olympic Destroyer 2018). In cloud environments, adversaries may leverage access to delete cloud storage objects, machine images, database instances, and other infrastructure crucial to operations to damage an organization or their customers.(Citation: Data Destruction - Threat Post)(Citation: DOJ - Cisco Insider) Similarly, they may delete virtual machines from on-prem virtualized environments.
5000.profile: [profile]Data Destruction, identified as T1485, is an Impact tactic executed on Windows, Linux, and cloud platforms. It aims to render files irrecoverable by overwriting them with random data or specific image files, going beyond simple deletion with commands like 'del' or 'rm'. Malware implementing this technique may propagate using worm-like features and leverage cloud API access to delete storage objects and virtual infrastructure. Associated threat groups include APT38, Sandworm Team, and LAPSUS$.[/profile]

5011.name: Domain Squatting

The intrusion-set OilRig has been associated with this behavior.

Acquired domains are used for malicious activities such as Phishing and Drive-by Compromise, with adversaries often obscuring ownership through private WHOIS services and varied registrars.

5044.name: Webshell
5044.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may backdoor web servers with web shells to establish persistent access to systems. A Web shell is a Web script that is placed on an openly accessible Web server to allow an adversary to access the Web server as a gateway into a network. A Web shell may provide a set of functions to execute or a command-line interface on the system that hosts the Web server.(Citation: volexity_0day_sophos_FW)

In addition to a server-side script, a Web shell may have a client interface program that is used to talk to the Web server (e.g. [China Chopper](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0020) Web shell client).(Citation: Lee 2013)
5044.profile: [profile]Webshell is a technique identified as T1505.003 (Server Software Component: Web Shell) within the Persistence tactic, primarily targeting Web Servers. It involves placing a malicious web script on an accessible server to provide a persistent gateway into a network, often offering functions or a command-line interface for remote execution. The China Chopper client is a notable example used to interact with such shells. This method is employed by numerous threat groups, including OilRig, and can serve as redundant access if primary methods are compromised.[/profile]

It involves placing a malicious web script on an openly accessible server, which then acts as a gateway into the network, often providing a command-line interface or specific functions for remote execution; common implementations include client interface programs like China Chopper.

5045.profile: [profile]Credential Harvesters, also known as credential harvesting malware, is a tool attributed to intrusion sets like OilRig. Its key technical behavior involves crafting exact replicas of legitimate websites to deceive users into inputting their credentials, thereby stealing login information. This malware primarily targets web-based platforms to facilitate credential theft for subsequent malicious activities like data exfiltration or further network compromise.

5047.name: Spoofed websites

It involves creating fraudulent websites that closely mimic legitimate ones, such as login portals, to deceive victims into entering sensitive information. Adversaries may use typosquatted domains, clone legitimate sites, and host these pages on compromised or purchased infrastructure. This method supports spearphishing links and credential harvesting, enabling attackers to steal credentials and session cookies to bypass security measures like multi-factor authentication.

It works by extending IIS functionality, often as a DLL exporting a RegisterModule function or a .NET application, to gain unrestricted access to all incoming and outgoing HTTP requests and responses, enabling traffic observation, modification, or command execution. This technique has been associated with the intrusion set OilRig.[/profile]

These modules enable traffic observation, modification, command execution, or proxying of C2 traffic by extending server functionality.

5060.name: HTTP POST
5060.profile: [profile]HTTP POST is a specific method within the broader MITRE ATT&CK technique T1071.001 (Web Protocols) under the Command and Control tactic. It operates across Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. This technique involves adversaries embedding command and control communications or exfiltrated data within the body of standard HTTP POST requests to blend with normal web traffic. As illustrated by its use in exfiltration over alternative protocols (T1048) and webhooks (T1567.004), it is commonly employed by groups like OilRig and Turla to evade detection by mimicking legitimate HTTPS traffic to services like Discord or cloud platforms.

It operates on multiple platforms, including Linux, macOS, and Windows. The technique involves adversaries embedding commands and data within the body of HTTP POST requests to communicate with compromised systems. This method blends with normal web traffic, as HTTP/S is common in most environments, allowing adversaries to avoid detection by network filtering while mimicking legitimate traffic.

5081.name: Stack Memory Corruption
5081.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may overwrite or corrupt the flash memory contents of system BIOS or other firmware in devices attached to a system in order to render them inoperable or unable to boot, thus denying the availability to use the devices and/or the system.(Citation: Symantec Chernobyl W95.CIH) Firmware is software that is loaded and executed from non-volatile memory on hardware devices in order to initialize and manage device functionality. These devices may include the motherboard, hard drive, or video cards.

In general, adversaries may manipulate, overwrite, or corrupt firmware in order to deny the use of the system or devices. For example, corruption of firmware responsible for loading the operating system for network devices may render the network devices inoperable.(Citation: dhs_threat_to_net_devices)(Citation: cisa_malware_orgs_ukraine) Depending on the device, this attack may also result in [Data Destruction](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1485).
5081.profile: [profile]Stack Memory Corruption is a technique where adversaries exploit software vulnerabilities to corrupt the stack memory of a process, potentially causing a crash or denial of service. This can be achieved by overwriting memory contents, such as return addresses or local variables, through inputs that exceed buffer bounds. The technique is linked to the vulnerability CVE-2017-11882. It can lead to application instability, system crashes, and may be used to achieve code execution or facilitate other attacks like data destruction or firmware corruption.[/profile]
5081.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Stack Memory Corruption is a technique where adversaries exploit software vulnerabilities to corrupt the stack memory of a running application, often leading to a crash or denial of service. This can be achieved by triggering a specific vulnerability, such as CVE-2017-11882, to overwrite critical memory addresses and disrupt normal program execution, potentially causing the application or system to become unavailable.

5082.name: PowerShell command
5082.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may abuse PowerShell commands and scripts for execution. PowerShell is a powerful interactive command-line interface and scripting environment included in the Windows operating system.(Citation: TechNet PowerShell) Adversaries can use PowerShell to perform a number of actions, including discovery of information and execution of code. Examples include the Start-Process cmdlet which can be used to run an executable and the Invoke-Command cmdlet which runs a command locally or on a remote computer (though administrator permissions are required to use PowerShell to connect to remote systems). PowerShell may also be used to download and run executables from the Internet, which can be executed from disk or in memory without touching disk. A number of PowerShell-based offensive testing tools are available, including [Empire](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0363), [PowerSploit](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0194), [PoshC2](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0378), and PSAttack.(Citation: Github PSAttack) PowerShell commands/scripts can also be executed without directly invoking the powershell.exe binary through interfaces to PowerShell's underlying System.Management.Automation assembly DLL exposed through the .NET framework and Windows Common Language Interface (CLI).(Citation: Sixdub PowerPick Jan 2016)(Citation: SilentBreak Offensive PS Dec 2015)(Citation: Microsoft PSfromCsharp APR 2014)
5082.profile: [profile]This entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1059.001, named Command and Scripting Interpreter: PowerShell, primarily used for Execution on Windows platforms. It involves adversaries abusing the PowerShell environment to execute commands and scripts for actions like discovery and code execution, using cmdlets such as Start-Process to run executables and Invoke-Command for local or remote command execution. PowerShell can download and run executables from the internet, executing them from disk or in memory, and commands can be run without directly invoking powershell.exe via the System.Management.Automation assembly through .NET. It is associated with numerous threat groups, including OilRig.[/profile]
5082.profile_without_enhance: [profile]PowerShell Command is a sub-technique under T1059.001 (Command and Scripting Interpreter: PowerShell) within the Execution tactic, targeting Windows. It involves adversaries using the PowerShell environment to execute malicious commands and scripts, such as running executables with Start-Process, executing code remotely with Invoke-Command, or downloading and running payloads from the internet, often directly in memory. Execution can occur without invoking powershell.exe by leveraging the System.Management.Automation assembly, and it is associated with numerous threat groups and tools like Empire and PowerSploit.

5083.name: Persistence (Scheduled Task)
5083.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may abuse the Windows Task Scheduler to perform task scheduling for initial or recurring execution of malicious code. There are multiple ways to access the Task Scheduler in Windows. The [schtasks](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0111) utility can be run directly on the command line, or the Task Scheduler can be opened through the GUI within the Administrator Tools section of the Control Panel.(Citation: Stack Overflow) In some cases, adversaries have used a .NET wrapper for the Windows Task Scheduler, and alternatively, adversaries have used the Windows netapi32 library and [Windows Management Instrumentation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1047) (WMI) to create a scheduled task. Adversaries may also utilize the Powershell Cmdlet `Invoke-CimMethod`, which leverages WMI class `PS_ScheduledTask` to create a scheduled task via an XML path.(Citation: Red Canary - Atomic Red Team)

An adversary may use Windows Task Scheduler to execute programs at system startup or on a scheduled basis for persistence. The Windows Task Scheduler can also be abused to conduct remote Execution as part of Lateral Movement and/or to run a process under the context of a specified account (such as SYSTEM). Similar to [System Binary Proxy Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1218), adversaries have also abused the Windows Task Scheduler to potentially mask one-time execution under signed/trusted system processes.(Citation: ProofPoint Serpent)

Adversaries may also create "hidden" scheduled tasks (i.e. [Hide Artifacts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1564)) that may not be visible to defender tools and manual queries used to enumerate tasks. Specifically, an adversary may hide a task from `schtasks /query` and the Task Scheduler by deleting the associated Security Descriptor (SD) registry value (where deletion of this value must be completed using SYSTEM permissions).(Citation: SigmaHQ)(Citation: Tarrask scheduled task) Adversaries may also employ alternate methods to hide tasks, such as altering the metadata (e.g., `Index` value) within associated registry keys.(Citation: Defending Against Scheduled Task Attacks in Windows Environments)
5083.profile: [profile]Scheduled Task/Job: Windows Task Scheduler is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1053.005 under the Persistence tactic for Windows. Adversaries abuse it via command-line `schtasks`, GUI, .NET wrappers, netapi32, WMI, or PowerShell's `Invoke-CimMethod` with the `PS_ScheduledTask` class to schedule malicious code execution. Tasks can be hidden by deleting the Security Descriptor registry value or altering registry key metadata to evade detection. The technique is also used for lateral movement and privilege execution, and is associated with numerous threat groups including OilRig.
5083.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Persistence (Scheduled Task) is a technique for maintaining access, corresponding to MITRE ATT&CK ID T1053.005 under the Persistence tactic, primarily for Windows. It involves abusing the Windows Task Scheduler to execute malicious code at system startup or on a recurring schedule. Adversaries use utilities like `schtasks`, .NET wrappers, WMI, or the PowerShell `Invoke-CimMethod` cmdlet to create tasks. Tasks can be hidden from queries by deleting the Security Descriptor registry value or altering registry key metadata. This method is also used for lateral movement and to run processes under privileged accounts like SYSTEM.

5084.name: Data Encoding (Base64)
5084.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may encode data to make the content of command and control traffic more difficult to detect. Command and control (C2) information can be encoded using a standard data encoding system. Use of data encoding may adhere to existing protocol specifications and includes use of ASCII, Unicode, Base64, MIME, or other binary-to-text and character encoding systems.(Citation: Wikipedia Binary-to-text Encoding) (Citation: Wikipedia Character Encoding) Some data encoding systems may also result in data compression, such as gzip.
5084.profile: [profile]Data Encoding (Base64) is a Command and Control technique (T1132.001) under the Command and Control tactic. It works by adversaries encoding C2 traffic using standard, protocol-compliant schemes like Base64, ASCII, or Unicode to obfuscate content and evade detection, with some schemes like gzip also providing compression. The intrusion-set OilRig has been associated with related data theft techniques.[/profile]
5084.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Data Encoding (Base64) is a sub-technique (T1132.001) within the Command and Control tactic. It operates across multiple platforms, where adversaries use the standard Base64 binary-to-text encoding scheme to obfuscate command and control traffic, making it more difficult to detect. This technique adheres to existing protocol specifications and is commonly employed by threat groups like Hafnium, MuddyWater, and Lazarus Group.

Its key behaviors include executing PowerShell commands from remote URLs to download and run malicious .NET binaries, which are delivered in a gzip-compressed and encoded format, and performing anti-antivirus and UAC bypass activities. It primarily targets Windows platforms via script execution. Its infrastructure includes domains like go0gIe.com for command and control.

5088.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The malware is named hupdatecheckers.ps1, with the alias hupdatecheckers.base. It is associated with the Turla group. 5089.name: dupdatecheckers.ps1

5090.name: DGA
5090.profile: [profile]Domain Generation Algorithms (DGA), identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1568.002, is a Command and Control tactic used across multiple platforms. It dynamically generates a large number of potential command and control domains, often using time-based seeds or concatenating random letters or words (e.g., istgmxdejdnxuyla.ru), to evade blocking and tracking by defenders. This technique is employed by groups like OilRig, APT41, and TA551, and can serve as a resilient fallback channel when primary C2 is lost.[/profile]
5090.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Domain Generation Algorithms (DGA), identified as T1568.002 within the Command and Control tactic, is a technique where adversaries dynamically generate destination domains for C2 traffic to evade static blocklists. DGAs create numerous domains, often appearing as random strings (e.g., istgmxdejdnxuyla.ru) or concatenated words (e.g., cityjulydish.net), frequently using time-based or seeded algorithms to produce different domains per period (hourly, daily). This method is also employed as a fallback mechanism to reestablish lost C2 connections, making tracking and takeover significantly harder for defenders. Associated groups include APT41 and TA551.

5091.name: PowerShell script
5091.uncertain_mes: powershell_web_backdoor This is a very simple powershell web backdoor Usage: hxxp://127.0.0.1:9999/backdoor/?cmd=<Insert Your powershell compatible base64 encoded command here
5091.profile: [profile]The entity is a PowerShell script known as 'powershell_web_backdoor', a simple web backdoor that executes commands via a URL parameter (e.g., hxxp://127.0.0.1:9999/backdoor/?cmd=) where the command is base64-encoded. It is associated with the intrusion set OilRig. Its key technical behavior involves using web-based command execution. The target platform is Windows, leveraging PowerShell. Infrastructure involves a web server for command and control.[/profile]
5091.profile_without_enhance: [profile]PowerShell script is a broad category of malicious scripts leveraging the Windows PowerShell environment. Its aliases include powershell_web_backdoor, and it is associated with groups like apothecary spider (Storm-1113) and Storm-0249. Key technical behaviors involve executing arbitrary commands or payloads via PowerShell (Execution T1059.1), often using obfuscation and Script Block Logging evasion, and employing proxy techniques (T1090) for command and control traffic redirection. It primarily targets Windows platforms and is used as a loader or backdoor in multi-stage campaigns, such as those involving GootLoader, to download and deploy further malware.

5092.name: ISMDoor
5092.uncertain_mes:
Iranian Threat Agent Greenbug has been registering domains similar to those of Israeli High-Tech and Cyber Security Companies.
On 15 October 2017 a sample of ISMdoor was submitted to VirusTotal from Iraq. The sample name was WmiPrv.tmp (f5ef3b060fb476253f9a7638f82940d9) and it had the following PDB string:
C:\Users\Void\Desktop\v 10.0.194\x64\Release\swchost.pdb
5092.profile: [profile]ISMDoor, also known as ISMdoor, is a malware tool attributed to the Iranian threat actor Greenbug and also used by the intrusion set OilRig (APT34). It employs a DNS tunneling protocol for command and control, similar to the related tool ISMAgent. A sample submitted in 2017 from Iraq used the filename WmiPrv.tmp. Its primary targets are Israeli high-tech and cyber security companies.
5092.profile_without_enhance: [profile] ISMDoor, also known as ismdoor, is a malware attributed to the Iranian threat group Greenbug. It is a backdoor that uses DNS tunneling for command and control (C2) communication, as evidenced by a sample named WmiPrv.tmp with a specific PDB path. The malware has been used in targeted attacks against Israeli high-tech and security companies, with infrastructure involving domains mimicking these targets. Its operational use has also been noted in connection with the OilRig group's ISMAgent tool, which shares similar DNS tunneling protocols.

5093.name: licensecheck.vbs
5093.profile: [profile]Licensecheck.vbs is a Visual Basic Script malware attributed to the OilRig intrusion set. It is associated with the 'hazy tiger' group and shares infrastructure or code overlaps with other malware families including miyarat, bdarkrat, and orpcbackdoor, as indicated by common detection rule references and file hashes. Its primary target platform is Windows systems, leveraging script-based execution for initial compromise and persistence.[/profile]
5093.profile_without_enhance: [profile]LicenseCheck.vbs is a VBScript-based malware attributed to the threat actor Hazy Tiger. It shares code and infrastructure with other malware families like Miyarat, BDarkRat, and OrpcBackdoor, as indicated by common detection rule references and file hashes. Its primary technical behavior involves using specific string patterns in its code, such as the push instruction for a buffer. The malware targets Windows platforms.

5094.name: officeservicesstatus.vbs
5094.profile: [profile]officeservicesstatus.vbs is a malware script associated with the OilRig intrusion set. It is linked to the Clayslide malware family. Its key behaviors include enumerating system services using the EnumServicesStatusA function, specifically checking for services like VMware tools and VMware snapshot provider, and enumerating Windows drivers via EnumDeviceDrivers and GetDeviceDriverBaseName. It targets the Windows platform for information gathering and reconnaissance.
5094.profile_without_enhance: [profile]officeservicesstatus.vbs, also known as Clayslide or Helminth, is a malware attributed to the OilRig intrusion set. It is delivered via malicious documents and establishes persistence by creating a Windows registry key for automatic startup. The malware monitors specific applications on the system. Its primary target platform is Windows.[/profile]

5095.name: officeservicesstatus
5095.profile: [profile]Officeservicesstatus is a malware associated with the OilRig intrusion set and is related to the Clayslide malware. It communicates with command-and-control (C2) infrastructure using specific URIs and API endpoints, including paths like '/api/v2/status' and domains such as service.office247.tech. Its C2 communication involves crafted HTTP headers, including 'Accept', 'Referer', and 'Cookie' headers, and it uses Base64URL encoding for data exfiltration. The malware targets Windows platforms and leverages cloud service gateways for its infrastructure.[/profile]
5095.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Officeservicesstatus, also known as officeservicesstatus.vbs, is a malware component associated with the Clayslide (Helminth) malware family attributed to the OilRig intrusion set. It is delivered via documents like "alma communicator" and establishes persistence by creating a Windows registry key for automatic startup. Its primary target platform is Windows, where it monitors specific applications on the infected system.[/profile]

5096.name: trojan
5096.uncertain_mes: [Trojan.Karagany](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0094) is a modular remote access tool used for recon and linked to [Dragonfly](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0035). The source code for [Trojan.Karagany](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0094) originated from Dream Loader malware which was leaked in 2010 and sold on underground forums. (Citation: Symantec Dragonfly)(Citation: Secureworks Karagany July 2019)(Citation: Dragos DYMALLOY )
5096.profile: [profile]The malware is known as Trojan.Karagany, a modular remote access tool (RAT) used for reconnaissance. Its source code originated from the leaked Dream Loader malware. It is attributed to the Dragonfly intrusion set. Key technical behaviors include remote access capabilities for intelligence gathering. It primarily targets Windows platforms. The malware has been linked to infrastructure and activities associated with the Dragonfly group.
5096.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The malware is a generic Trojan. It is associated with the Lazarus Group and uses DNS Tunneling (T1071.004) to encapsulate malicious traffic within DNS queries and responses for covert command and control. It also uses the HTTP Protocol (T1071.001) to blend malicious communications with normal web traffic for C2 and data exfiltration. It primarily targets the Windows platform, as indicated by aliases such as Trojan/Win.Agent, Trojan/Win.LazarLoader, and Trojan/Win32.Agent.

5097.name: Embedding Payload in Macro
5097.profile: [profile]Embedding Payload in Macro is a technique for Initial Access, likely T1566.001, primarily targeting Windows via Microsoft Office. It involves adversaries concealing malicious code within the VBA code of a macro-enabled Office document (e.g., .docm). When a user enables macros, the embedded payload is executed, often to download or run additional malware. The intrusion-set OilRig has been associated with this method. Related evasion techniques include using stripped or embedded payloads to hinder analysis.
5097.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Embedding Payload in Macro is a technique for hiding malicious code within a macro-enabled document, typically Microsoft Office files. It is used in the Initial Access tactic, primarily on Windows platforms. The technique works by placing a payload, such as a script or executable, inside the document's macro code, which is then executed when the user enables macros. This method can evade static detection and is often delivered via phishing.

5098.name: Base64 String Concatenation
5098.profile: [profile]Base64 String Concatenation is a sub-technique of Data Encoding (T1132.001) within the Command and Control tactic. It involves adversaries splitting a Base64-encoded payload into multiple substrings, which are then concatenated within the malicious script or command line. This method, used by groups like OilRig, obfuscates the full encoded string to potentially evade signature-based detection, as the complete payload is only assembled at runtime before being decoded and executed.[/profile]
5098.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Base64 String Concatenation" is a technique for command and control traffic obfuscation, aligning with the MITRE ATT&CK sub-technique T1132.001 (Data Encoding: Standard Encoding) under the Command and Control tactic. It operates by splitting a malicious payload into multiple Base64-encoded strings, which are then concatenated at runtime to reconstruct the original executable or script, bypassing static detection that scans for complete, single Base64 blobs. This method is used by groups like APT33 and Lazarus to evade signature-based defenses.

5099.name: Multi-Cell Payload Extraction
5099.profile: [profile]Multi-Cell Payload Extraction is a technique used by the intrusion set OilRig. It involves splitting a malicious payload into multiple parts, often stored in separate cells of a spreadsheet document, to evade detection by security tools that scan for complete, known malicious signatures. The technique requires a loader or stager to recombine and execute the extracted payload fragments, facilitating initial access or execution on the target system.
5099.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Multi-Cell Payload Extraction is a technique for data exfiltration, operating within the Exfiltration tactic. It functions by splitting a payload into multiple smaller segments, which are then hidden within different, seemingly benign files or data streams. These segments are transmitted separately, often over distinct network mediums or channels, to evade detection by security tools that monitor for large, single data transfers. The payload is later reassembled at the adversary's destination.

5100.name: Helminth Script Access
5100.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may use Windows logon scripts automatically executed at logon initialization to establish persistence. Windows allows logon scripts to be run whenever a specific user or group of users log into a system.(Citation: TechNet Logon Scripts) This is done via adding a path to a script to the HKCU\Environment\UserInitMprLogonScript Registry key.(Citation: Hexacorn Logon Scripts) Adversaries may use these scripts to maintain persistence on a single system. Depending on the access configuration of the logon scripts, either local credentials or an administrator account may be necessary.
5100.profile: [profile]Helminth Script Access, also known as Windows Logon Script (MITRE ATT&CK T1037.001), is a Persistence technique for Windows. It operates by adding a script path to the HKCU\Environment\UserInitMprLogonScript Registry key, causing the script to execute automatically when a specific user or group logs into the system. This method is used by groups like APT28 and Cobalt Group to maintain access on a single host, potentially requiring local or administrative credentials.
5100.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Helminth Script Access is a technique where adversaries exploit web shells to maintain persistent access to compromised systems. This method involves placing a malicious script on a web server, which then acts as a gateway, providing functions or a command-line interface for remote control. It serves as a form of redundant access, ensuring adversaries retain entry even if primary methods are detected, and is commonly used by groups like Cobalt Group and APT28 across various platforms.

5110.name: Unauthenticated Access to Malicious Files
5110.uncertain_mes:
An adversary may rely upon a user opening a malicious file in order to gain execution. Users may be subjected to social engineering to get them to open a file that will lead to code execution. This user action will typically be observed as follow-on behavior from [Spearphishing Attachment](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001). Adversaries may use several types of files that require a user to execute them, including .doc, .pdf, .xls, .rtf, .scr, .exe, .lnk, .pif, .cpl, .reg, and .iso.(Citation: Mandiant Trojanized Windows 10)

Adversaries may employ various forms of [Masquerading](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1036) and [Obfuscated Files or Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027) to increase the likelihood that a user will open and successfully execute a malicious file. These methods may include using a familiar naming convention and/or password protecting the file and supplying instructions to a user on how to open it.(Citation: Password Protected Word Docs) 

While [Malicious File](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002) frequently occurs shortly after Initial Access it may occur at other phases of an intrusion, such as when an adversary places a file in a shared directory or on a user's desktop hoping that a user will click on it. This activity may also be seen shortly after [Internal Spearphishing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1534).
5110.profile: [profile]The entity "Malicious File" is the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1204.002 under the Execution tactic, primarily for Windows platforms. It involves an adversary relying on a user to open a malicious file to gain execution, often delivered via social engineering like spearphishing attachments. Common file types include .doc, .pdf, .xls, .scr, .exe, .lnk, and .iso. Adversaries may increase success by using familiar naming conventions, password-protecting files, or placing them in shared directories. This technique is associated with numerous threat groups, including OilRig, APT28, and Lazarus Group.[profile]
5110.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Unauthenticated Access to Malicious Files is a user execution technique where adversaries rely on users opening malicious files, such as .doc, .pdf, .exe, or .lnk files, often delivered via spearphishing attachments. This action leads to code execution, bypassing initial access controls. Adversaries frequently use masquerading and obfuscation to increase success rates. The technique is associated with numerous threat groups, including APT29, FIN7, and Lazarus Group.

5111.name: MySQL Databases
5111.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may leverage databases to mine valuable information. These databases may be hosted on-premises or in the cloud (both in platform-as-a-service and software-as-a-service environments). 

Examples of databases from which information may be collected include MySQL, PostgreSQL, MongoDB, Amazon Relational Database Service, Azure SQL Database, Google Firebase, and Snowflake. Databases may include a variety of information of interest to adversaries, such as usernames, hashed passwords, personally identifiable information, and financial data. Data collected from databases may be used for [Lateral Movement](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0008), [Command and Control](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0011), or [Exfiltration](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0010). Data exfiltrated from databases may also be used to extort victims or may be sold for profit.(Citation: Google Cloud Threat Intelligence UNC5537 Snowflake 2024)
5111.profile: [profile]MySQL Databases is a sub-technique under Data from Information Repositories (T1213.006) within the Collection tactic, targeting platforms including cloud and on-premises systems. Adversaries specifically target MySQL databases to mine valuable information such as usernames, hashed passwords, personally identifiable information, and financial data. This collected data can be used for subsequent actions like Lateral Movement, Command and Control, or Exfiltration, and has been associated with groups including Sandworm Team, Turla, and FIN6.
5111.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "MySQL Databases" is a sub-technique of Data from Information Repositories, specifically T1213.006, under the Collection tactic. It targets platforms including on-premises and cloud-based MySQL database systems. Adversaries target these databases to mine valuable information such as usernames, hashed passwords, personally identifiable information, and financial data. This collected data can be used for subsequent objectives like Lateral Movement, Command and Control, or Exfiltration, and has been associated with groups including Sandworm Team, Turla, FIN6, and Sea Turtle.

5112.name: Application Brute Force Attacks
5112.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may use brute force techniques to gain access to accounts when passwords are unknown or when password hashes are obtained.(Citation: TrendMicro Pawn Storm Dec 2020) Without knowledge of the password for an account or set of accounts, an adversary may systematically guess the password using a repetitive or iterative mechanism.(Citation: Dragos Crashoverride 2018) Brute forcing passwords can take place via interaction with a service that will check the validity of those credentials or offline against previously acquired credential data, such as password hashes.

Brute forcing credentials may take place at various points during a breach. For example, adversaries may attempt to brute force access to [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078) within a victim environment leveraging knowledge gathered from other post-compromise behaviors such as [OS Credential Dumping](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003), [Account Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1087), or [Password Policy Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1201). Adversaries may also combine brute forcing activity with behaviors such as [External Remote Services](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1133) as part of Initial Access. 

If an adversary guesses the correct password but fails to login to a compromised account due to location-based conditional access policies, they may change their infrastructure until they match the victim’s location and therefore bypass those policies.(Citation: ReliaQuest Health Care Social Engineering Campaign 2024)
5112.profile: [profile]Brute Force, identified as T1110, is a Credential Access technique applicable to multiple platforms. It involves systematically guessing passwords through repetitive interaction with an authentication service or offline against acquired password hashes. This activity can be combined with other techniques like External Remote Services for initial access or used post-compromise with data from OS Credential Dumping. Adversaries, including groups like OilRig, may also bypass location-based access controls by changing their infrastructure to match the victim's geography.
5112.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Application Brute Force Attacks is a technique where adversaries systematically guess passwords to gain unauthorized access to accounts, often targeting application login interfaces. It aligns with the Credential Access tactic (T1110) and can be performed online against a live service or offline using acquired password hashes. Attackers may use iterative mechanisms with common or custom wordlists, and this activity is often combined with reconnaissance like Password Policy Discovery to increase success rates and avoid account lockouts.

5113.name: Domain Generation Algorithm (DGA)
5113.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may make use of Domain Generation Algorithms (DGAs) to dynamically identify a destination domain for command and control traffic rather than relying on a list of static IP addresses or domains. This has the advantage of making it much harder for defenders to block, track, or take over the command and control channel, as there potentially could be thousands of domains that malware can check for instructions.(Citation: Cybereason Dissecting DGAs)(Citation: Cisco Umbrella DGA)(Citation: Unit 42 DGA Feb 2019)

DGAs can take the form of apparently random or “gibberish” strings (ex: istgmxdejdnxuyla.ru) when they construct domain names by generating each letter. Alternatively, some DGAs employ whole words as the unit by concatenating words together instead of letters (ex: cityjulydish.net). Many DGAs are time-based, generating a different domain for each time period (hourly, daily, monthly, etc). Others incorporate a seed value as well to make predicting future domains more difficult for defenders.(Citation: Cybereason Dissecting DGAs)(Citation: Cisco Umbrella DGA)(Citation: Talos CCleanup 2017)(Citation: Akamai DGA Mitigation)

Adversaries may use DGAs for the purpose of [Fallback Channels](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1008). When contact is lost with the primary command and control server malware may employ a DGA as a means to reestablishing command and control.(Citation: Talos CCleanup 2017)(Citation: FireEye POSHSPY April 2017)(Citation: ESET Sednit 2017 Activity)
5113.profile: [profile]Domain Generation Algorithm (DGA) is technique T1568.002 under the Command and Control tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It dynamically generates a large number of potential command and control domains algorithmically, using methods like creating random letter strings (e.g., istgmxdejdnxuyla.ru) or concatenating words (e.g., cityjulydish.net). These algorithms are often time-based or use a seed value to produce different domains per period (hourly, daily), making blocking and tracking extremely difficult. DGAs are also used to establish fallback channels when primary C2 is lost. Associated threat groups include APT41 and TA551, and it is used by malware like BondUpdater.[/profile]
5113.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Domain Generation Algorithm (DGA) is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1568.002 under the Command and Control tactic for Windows, Linux, and macOS. It dynamically generates a large number of potential command and control domains using algorithms, often based on time or a seed, to create seemingly random strings (e.g., istgmxdejdnxuyla.ru) or concatenated words (e.g., cityjulydish.net). This makes blocking or tracking C2 infrastructure difficult and is commonly used as a fallback channel. Associated groups include APT41 and TA551.

5114.name: DNS Exfiltration
5114.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may communicate using the Domain Name System (DNS) application layer protocol to avoid detection/network filtering by blending in with existing traffic. Commands to the remote system, and often the results of those commands, will be embedded within the protocol traffic between the client and server. 

The DNS protocol serves an administrative function in computer networking and thus may be very common in environments. DNS traffic may also be allowed even before network authentication is completed. DNS packets contain many fields and headers in which data can be concealed. Often known as DNS tunneling, adversaries may abuse DNS to communicate with systems under their control within a victim network while also mimicking normal, expected traffic.(Citation: PAN DNS Tunneling)(Citation: Medium DnsTunneling)

DNS beaconing may be used to send commands to remote systems via DNS queries. A DNS beacon is created by tunneling DNS traffic (i.e. [Protocol Tunneling](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1572)). The commands may be embedded into different DNS records, for example, TXT or A records.(Citation: OilRig Uses Updated BONDUPDATER to Target Middle Eastern Government) DNS beacons may be difficult to detect because the beacons infrequently communicate with infected devices.(Citation: DNS Beacons) Infrequent communication conceals the malicious DNS traffic with normal DNS traffic.
5114.profile: [profile]DNS Exfiltration, identified as T1048.001, is a technique within the Exfiltration tactic used across multiple platforms. It involves stealing data by tunneling it out of a network within DNS protocol traffic, often using DNS queries and responses. Adversaries embed stolen data into various DNS record types, such as TXT or A records, to blend with normal administrative traffic and bypass network filtering. This method is distinct from DNS-based command and control and is associated with groups like OilRig.
5114.profile_without_enhance: [profile]DNS Exfiltration, identified as T1048.001 within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, is an Exfiltration technique applicable to multiple platforms. It involves stealing data by encoding it into DNS queries, often using subdomains or specific record types like TXT, to covertly transmit information to an adversary-controlled DNS server, thereby bypassing network monitoring that may not inspect DNS traffic for data leakage. This method is a specific application of the broader Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol (T1048).

5115.name: RDP Exfiltration
5115.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may hijack a legitimate user’s remote desktop session to move laterally within an environment. Remote desktop is a common feature in operating systems. It allows a user to log into an interactive session with a system desktop graphical user interface on a remote system. Microsoft refers to its implementation of the Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) as Remote Desktop Services (RDS).(Citation: TechNet Remote Desktop Services)

Adversaries may perform RDP session hijacking which involves stealing a legitimate user's remote session. Typically, a user is notified when someone else is trying to steal their session. With System permissions and using Terminal Services Console, `c:\windows\system32\tscon.exe [session number to be stolen]`, an adversary can hijack a session without the need for credentials or prompts to the user.(Citation: RDP Hijacking Korznikov) This can be done remotely or locally and with active or disconnected sessions.(Citation: RDP Hijacking Medium) It can also lead to [Remote System Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1018) and Privilege Escalation by stealing a Domain Admin or higher privileged account session. All of this can be done by using native Windows commands, but it has also been added as a feature in red teaming tools.(Citation: Kali Redsnarf)
5115.profile: [profile]RDP Exfiltration is a technique for data theft, identified as T1048.003 under the Exfiltration tactic. It operates on Windows platforms by leveraging the Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) to transfer stolen data out of a network. The technique specifically uses the native RDP client (`mstsc.exe`) with specific command-line parameters, such as `/v:[target IP] /restrictedAdmin`, to establish an authenticated session for covert data transfer, often blending with legitimate administrative traffic. This method has been used by groups like OilRig.[/profile]
5115.profile_without_enhance: [profile]RDP Exfiltration is a data exfiltration technique where adversaries use the Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) as a covert channel to transfer stolen data out of a network. It operates under the Exfiltration tactic and primarily targets Windows platforms. The technique involves establishing an RDP connection to an external server controlled by the adversary, then using that session to upload collected files, often by copying data to the remote desktop or using the session for direct transfer. This method can blend with legitimate administrative traffic and may be facilitated by modifying firewall rules to allow RDP connections on non-standard ports.

5116.name: RAR Compression
5116.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may use compression to obfuscate their payloads or files. Compressed file formats such as ZIP, gzip, 7z, and RAR can compress and archive multiple files together to make it easier and faster to transfer files. In addition to compressing files, adversaries may also compress shellcode directly - for example, in order to store it in a Windows Registry key (i.e., [Fileless Storage](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/011)).(Citation: Trustwave Pillowmint June 2020)

In order to further evade detection, adversaries may combine multiple ZIP files into one archive. This process of concatenation creates an archive that appears to be a single archive but in fact contains the central directories of the embedded archives. Some ZIP readers, such as 7zip, may not be able to identify concatenated ZIP files and miss the presence of the malicious payload.(Citation: Perception Point)

File archives may be sent as one [Spearphishing Attachment](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001) through email. Adversaries have sent malicious payloads as archived files to encourage the user to interact with and extract the malicious payload onto their system (i.e., [Malicious File](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002)).(Citation: NTT Security Flagpro new December 2021) However, some file compression tools, such as 7zip, can be used to produce self-extracting archives. Adversaries may send self-extracting archives to hide the functionality of their payload and launch it without requiring multiple actions from the user.(Citation: The Hacker News)

[Compression](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/015) may be used in combination with [Encrypted/Encoded File](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/013) where compressed files are encrypted and password-protected.
5116.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique Compression, ID T1027.015, under the Defense Evasion tactic, applicable to multiple platforms.
