5389.name: Disguised as Microsoft's net command
5389.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may reveal credentials of accounts that have disabled Kerberos preauthentication by [Password Cracking](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1110/002) Kerberos messages.(Citation: Harmj0y Roasting AS-REPs Jan 2017) 

Preauthentication offers protection against offline [Password Cracking](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1110/002). When enabled, a user requesting access to a resource initiates communication with the Domain Controller (DC) by sending an Authentication Server Request (AS-REQ) message with a timestamp that is encrypted with the hash of their password. If and only if the DC is able to successfully decrypt the timestamp with the hash of the user’s password, it will then send an Authentication Server Response (AS-REP) message that contains the Ticket Granting Ticket (TGT) to the user. Part of the AS-REP message is signed with the user’s password.(Citation: Microsoft Kerberos Preauth 2014)

For each account found without preauthentication, an adversary may send an AS-REQ message without the encrypted timestamp and receive an AS-REP message with TGT data which may be encrypted with an insecure algorithm such as RC4. The recovered encrypted data may be vulnerable to offline [Password Cracking](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1110/002) attacks similarly to [Kerberoasting](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1558/003) and expose plaintext credentials. (Citation: Harmj0y Roasting AS-REPs Jan 2017)(Citation: Stealthbits Cracking AS-REP Roasting Jun 2019) 

An account registered to a domain, with or without special privileges, can be abused to list all domain accounts that have preauthentication disabled by utilizing Windows tools like [PowerShell](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001) with an LDAP filter. Alternatively, the adversary may send an AS-REQ message for each user. If the DC responds without errors, the account does not require preauthentication and the AS-REP message will already contain the encrypted data. (Citation: Harmj0y Roasting AS-REPs Jan 2017)(Citation: Stealthbits Cracking AS-REP Roasting Jun 2019)

Cracked hashes may enable [Persistence](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0003), [Privilege Escalation](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0004), and [Lateral Movement](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0008) via access to [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078).(Citation: SANS Attacking Kerberos Nov 2014)
5389.profile: [profile]The technique is officially known as AS-REP Roasting with the MITRE ATT&CK ID T1558.004, falling under the Credential Access tactic and targeting Windows platforms. It exploits accounts with Kerberos preauthentication disabled, allowing an adversary to send an AS-REQ message without an encrypted timestamp. The Domain Controller responds with an AS-REP containing Ticket Granting Ticket (TGT) data, which is often encrypted with a weak algorithm like RC4, making the recovered hash vulnerable to offline password cracking. Attackers can identify vulnerable accounts using tools like PowerShell with LDAP filters or by sending probe AS-REQ messages. This technique is associated with groups like APT17.
5389.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Disguised as Microsoft's net command" is a technique for Defense Evasion, operating on Windows platforms. It involves adversaries disguising malicious commands or binaries by naming them "net.exe" or placing them in directories where the legitimate Windows net command is expected to execute, thereby tricking users or systems and bypassing security controls. This method is a form of Masquerading to facilitate indirect command execution.

5390.name: Bootkit
5390.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may use bootkits to persist on systems. A bootkit is a malware variant that modifies the boot sectors of a hard drive, allowing malicious code to execute before a computer's operating system has loaded. Bootkits reside at a layer below the operating system and may make it difficult to perform full remediation unless an organization suspects one was used and can act accordingly.

In BIOS systems, a bootkit may modify the Master Boot Record (MBR) and/or Volume Boot Record (VBR).(Citation: Mandiant M Trends 2016) The MBR is the section of disk that is first loaded after completing hardware initialization by the BIOS. It is the location of the boot loader. An adversary who has raw access to the boot drive may overwrite this area, diverting execution during startup from the normal boot loader to adversary code.(Citation: Lau 2011)

The MBR passes control of the boot process to the VBR. Similar to the case of MBR, an adversary who has raw access to the boot drive may overwrite the VBR to divert execution during startup to adversary code.

In UEFI (Unified Extensible Firmware Interface) systems, a bootkit may instead create or modify files in the EFI system partition (ESP). The ESP is a partition on data storage used by devices containing UEFI that allows the system to boot the OS and other utilities used by the system. An adversary can use the newly created or patched files in the ESP to run malicious kernel code.(Citation: Microsoft Security)(Citation: welivesecurity)
5390.profile: [profile]Bootkit, identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1542.003 under the Persistence tactic, operates on Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It is a malware variant that achieves persistence by modifying the boot process below the operating system. In BIOS systems, it overwrites the Master Boot Record (MBR) or Volume Boot Record (VBR) to divert execution to malicious code during startup. In UEFI systems, it creates or modifies files within the EFI System Partition (ESP) to run malicious kernel code, making detection and remediation difficult. Associated threat groups include APT41, APT28, and Lazarus Group.[/profile]
5390.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Bootkit, identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1542.003, is a persistence tactic used on Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It is a malware variant that operates below the operating system by modifying boot sectors. In BIOS systems, it achieves persistence by overwriting the Master Boot Record (MBR) or Volume Boot Record (VBR) to divert system startup execution to adversary code. In UEFI systems, it may create or modify files within the EFI System Partition (ESP) to run malicious kernel code, making detection and remediation difficult.

5392.name: Boot phase infection
5392.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may abuse netbooting to load an unauthorized network device operating system from a Trivial File Transfer Protocol (TFTP) server. TFTP boot (netbooting) is commonly used by network administrators to load configuration-controlled network device images from a centralized management server. Netbooting is one option in the boot sequence and can be used to centralize, manage, and control device images.

Adversaries may manipulate the configuration on the network device specifying use of a malicious TFTP server, which may be used in conjunction with [Modify System Image](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1601) to load a modified image on device startup or reset. The unauthorized image allows adversaries to modify device configuration, add malicious capabilities to the device, and introduce backdoors to maintain control of the network device while minimizing detection through use of a standard functionality. This technique is similar to [ROMMONkit](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1542/004) and may result in the network device running a modified image. (Citation: Cisco Blog Legacy Device Attacks)
5392.profile: [profile]Boot phase infection, also known as TFTP Boot (MITRE ATT&CK ID T1542.005), is a Defense Evasion and Persistence technique targeting network device platforms. It works by adversaries manipulating a device's boot configuration to specify a malicious Trivial File Transfer Protocol (TFTP) server, forcing the device to load an unauthorized or modified operating system image upon startup or reset. This allows for backdoor installation and configuration changes while blending with legitimate network management traffic, similar to the ROMMONkit technique.
5392.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Boot phase infection is a persistence technique where adversaries compromise the system boot process to execute malicious code before the operating system loads. This can involve modifying low-level components like the Master Boot Record (MBR), Volume Boot Record (VBR), or files in the EFI system partition (ESP) on UEFI systems. By infecting these boot sectors or firmware, malware gains execution during hardware initialization, establishing a deep and stealthy persistence layer that is difficult to detect and remediate with standard OS-level defenses.

5393.name: MBR注入
5393.profile: [profile]MBR注入 is a technique aligned with MITRE ATT&CK ID T1542.003 (Bootkit) under the Persistence tactic, targeting Windows systems. It involves adversaries with raw disk access overwriting the Master Boot Record (MBR) to divert system startup execution from the legitimate boot loader to malicious code, enabling pre-OS execution and deep persistence. This method is used by groups like APT17 and can be part of bootkit malware, making remediation challenging as it operates below the OS level.
5393.profile_without_enhance: [profile]MBR注入 is a technique where adversaries overwrite the Master Boot Record (MBR) on a disk to divert system execution during startup to malicious code before the operating system loads, enabling persistence and bootkit deployment. This requires raw access to the boot drive and operates at a layer below the OS, making detection and remediation difficult. It is related to bootkits and can also be used in disk-wiping attacks to corrupt critical disk structures.

5394.name: 动态链接库自动运行
5394.profile: [profile]The entity "动态链接库自动运行" aligns with MITRE ATT&CK technique T1547.001 "Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder" under the Persistence tactic for Windows. It involves adversaries achieving persistence by adding a malicious DLL path to specific registry keys like AppCertDLLs, which causes the DLL to be automatically loaded into the memory space of every process that calls common API functions such as CreateProcess. This method allows the malicious code to run under the context of various trusted system processes.
5394.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "动态链接库自动运行" (Dynamic-link Library Autorun) is a persistence technique where malicious DLLs are automatically loaded by the operating system. This aligns with the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1547.010, "Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder," under the Persistence tactic for Windows platforms. It specifically abuses the AppCertDLLs Registry key (HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\System\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager), causing a specified DLL to be loaded into every process that calls common API functions like CreateProcess or WinExec. This provides both persistence and potential privilege escalation by executing code within the context of various legitimate processes.

5395.name: MBR Modification
5395.profile: [profile]MBR Modification is a technique where adversaries overwrite the Master Boot Record (MBR) on a hard drive to divert system startup execution to malicious code before the operating system loads, establishing persistence or rendering the system unbootable. It is associated with bootkits and disk-wiping malware, and has been used by groups like APT17. This technique operates at a layer below the OS, making remediation difficult.
5395.profile_without_enhance: [profile]MBR Modification is a technique where adversaries overwrite the Master Boot Record (MBR) on a hard drive to divert system execution during startup to malicious code before the operating system loads, enabling persistence or destructive actions like disk structure wipes. This requires raw access to the boot drive and is a core component of bootkit malware.

5396.name: Persistence via Startup
5396.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may clear artifacts associated with previously established persistence on a host system to remove evidence of their activity. This may involve various actions, such as removing services, deleting executables, [Modify Registry](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1112), [Plist File Modification](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1647), or other methods of cleanup to prevent defenders from collecting evidence of their persistent presence.(Citation: Cylance Dust Storm) Adversaries may also delete accounts previously created to maintain persistence (i.e. [Create Account](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1136)).(Citation: Talos - Cisco Attack 2022)

In some instances, artifacts of persistence may also be removed once an adversary’s persistence is executed in order to prevent errors with the new instance of the malware.(Citation: NCC Group Team9 June 2020)
5396.profile: [profile]The entity "Persistence via Startup" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the provided context, it likely refers to the established technique "Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder" (T1547.001) within the Persistence tactic on Windows. This technique works by adding a program path to specific Windows Registry run keys (e.g., HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run) or by placing a shortcut or executable in a user or system-wide Startup folder, causing the referenced program to execute automatically upon user login. The intrusion set APT17 is associated with this method.
5396.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Persistence via Startup is a technique categorized under Persistence (Tactic TA0003) in the MITRE ATT&CK framework, primarily targeting Windows and macOS platforms. It involves establishing persistence by placing malicious executables or scripts in system startup folders or referencing them via Registry run keys, such as HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run, to ensure automatic execution upon user login or system boot. On macOS, adversaries may abuse the deprecated /Library/StartupItems directory, creating folders with an executable and a StartupParameters.plist file to run code with root privileges during the boot process.

5397.name: Sector Injection
5397.profile: [profile]Sector Injection is a technique for executing arbitrary code by injecting it into the memory space of a separate, legitimate process to evade detection and potentially gain elevated privileges. It is associated with the intrusion set APT17 and operates on Windows platforms, falling under the Defense Evasion tactic. The method involves using native Windows API calls to write malicious code into a target process's memory and then executing it, often leveraging functionalities like Portable Executable (PE) injection or Asynchronous Procedure Call (APC) injection as specific sub-techniques.
5397.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Sector Injection is a technique where adversaries inject malicious code into the disk sectors of removable media, such as USB drives. This method allows the malicious code to execute automatically when the media is accessed by a victim's system, facilitating initial access or the execution of further payloads. The technique operates at a low level, targeting the storage device's structure to evade higher-level security measures and user awareness.

5398.name: Memory Offset Calculation
5398.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may perform calculations on addresses returned in DNS results to determine which port and IP address to use for command and control, rather than relying on a predetermined port number or the actual returned IP address. A IP and/or port number calculation can be used to bypass egress filtering on a C2 channel.(Citation: Meyers Numbered Panda)

One implementation of [DNS Calculation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1568/003) is to take the first three octets of an IP address in a DNS response and use those values to calculate the port for command and control traffic.(Citation: Meyers Numbered Panda)(Citation: Moran 2014)(Citation: Rapid7G20Espionage)
5398.profile: [profile]DNS Calculation, also known as T1568.003, is a Command and Control technique under the Exfiltration tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It involves adversaries performing calculations on addresses from DNS query results to dynamically determine the IP address and port for C2 traffic, bypassing static egress filtering. A specific implementation uses the first three octets of a returned IP address to calculate the port number. This technique has been associated with APT12.[/profile]
5398.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Memory Offset Calculation is a technique where adversaries compute specific memory addresses or offsets to locate and manipulate critical data or code within a process's address space, often to evade defenses like ASLR. This involves analyzing a process's memory mappings, such as those exposed via the /proc filesystem (e.g., `/proc/[pid]/maps`), to enumerate stack locations and find usable instruction gadgets for constructing a payload. The technique can be used to overwrite memory regions, such as a stack, to execute arbitrary code within the context of a legitimate process, potentially allowing access to that process's memory and resources while masking malicious activity.

5399.name: Modify Registry
5399.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may interact with the Windows Registry as part of a variety of other techniques to aid in defense evasion, persistence, and execution.

Access to specific areas of the Registry depends on account permissions, with some keys requiring administrator-level access. The built-in Windows command-line utility [Reg](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0075) may be used for local or remote Registry modification.(Citation: Microsoft Reg) Other tools, such as remote access tools, may also contain functionality to interact with the Registry through the Windows API.

The Registry may be modified in order to hide configuration information or malicious payloads via [Obfuscated Files or Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027).(Citation: Unit42 BabyShark Feb 2019)(Citation: Avaddon Ransomware 2021)(Citation: Microsoft BlackCat Jun 2022)(Citation: CISA Russian Gov Critical Infra 2018) The Registry may also be modified to [Impair Defenses](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1562), such as by enabling macros for all Microsoft Office products, allowing privilege escalation without alerting the user, increasing the maximum number of allowed outbound requests, and/or modifying systems to store plaintext credentials in memory.(Citation: CISA LockBit 2023)(Citation: Unit42 BabyShark Feb 2019)

The Registry of a remote system may be modified to aid in execution of files as part of lateral movement. It requires the remote Registry service to be running on the target system.(Citation: Microsoft Remote) Often [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078) are required, along with access to the remote system's [SMB/Windows Admin Shares](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002) for RPC communication.

Finally, Registry modifications may also include actions to hide keys, such as prepending key names with a null character, which will cause an error and/or be ignored when read via [Reg](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0075) or other utilities using the Win32 API.(Citation: Microsoft Reghide NOV 2006) Adversaries may abuse these pseudo-hidden keys to conceal payloads/commands used to maintain persistence.(Citation: TrendMicro POWELIKS AUG 2014)(Citation: SpectorOps Hiding Reg Jul 2017)
5399.profile: [profile]Modify Registry is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1112 under the Defense Evasion tactic for Windows. It involves adversaries altering the Windows Registry using utilities like Reg.exe or remote access tools to hide configuration data, impair defenses by enabling macros or disabling security features, and establish persistence by creating or modifying keys, including pseudo-hidden keys prefixed with null characters. This technique can also facilitate lateral movement if the remote Registry service is running and proper authentication is available.[/profile]
5399.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Modify Registry is a Windows-specific technique (T1112) used for defense evasion, persistence, and execution. Adversaries interact with the Windows Registry using utilities like Reg.exe or remote access tools to alter configuration data. This can involve hiding malicious payloads, impairing defenses by enabling macros or disabling security settings, enabling lateral movement via remote registry modification, or establishing persistence by creating or modifying service entries and file associations. The technique is employed by numerous threat groups including APT41, Wizard Spider, and Volt Typhoon.

5410.name: In-Memory Payload Execution
5410.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may attempt to access credential material stored in the process memory of the Local Security Authority Subsystem Service (LSASS). After a user logs on, the system generates and stores a variety of credential materials in LSASS process memory. These credential materials can be harvested by an administrative user or SYSTEM and used to conduct [Lateral Movement](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0008) using [Use Alternate Authentication Material](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1550). As well as in-memory techniques, the LSASS process memory can be dumped from the target host and analyzed on a local system. For example, on the target host use procdump: * procdump -ma lsass.exe lsass_dump Locally, mimikatz can be run using: * sekurlsa::Minidump lsassdump.dmp * sekurlsa::logonPasswords Built-in Windows tools such as `comsvcs.dll` can also be used: * rundll32.exe C:\Windows\System32\comsvcs.dll MiniDump PID lsass.dmp full(Citation: Volexity Exchange Marauder March 2021)(Citation: Symantec Attacks Against Government Sector) Similar to [Image File Execution Options Injection](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1546/012), the silent process exit mechanism can be abused to create a memory dump of `lsass.exe` through Windows Error Reporting (`WerFault.exe`).(Citation: Deep Instinct LSASS) Windows Security Support Provider (SSP) DLLs are loaded into LSASS process at system start. Once loaded into the LSA, SSP DLLs have access to encrypted and plaintext passwords that are stored in Windows, such as any logged-on user's Domain password or smart card PINs. The SSP configuration is stored in two Registry keys: HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa\Security Packages and HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa\OSConfig\Security Packages. An adversary may modify these Registry keys to add new SSPs, which will be loaded the next time the system boots, or when the AddSecurityPackage Windows API function is called.(Citation: Graeber 2014) The following SSPs can be used to access credentials: * Msv: Interactive logons, batch logons, and service logons are done through the MSV authentication package. * Wdigest: The Digest Authentication protocol is designed for use with Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) and Simple Authentication Security Layer (SASL) exchanges.(Citation: TechNet Blogs Credential Protection) * Kerberos: Preferred for mutual client-server domain authentication in Windows 2000 and later. * CredSSP: Provides SSO and Network Level Authentication for Remote Desktop Services.(Citation: TechNet Blogs Credential Protection)
5410.profile: [profile]The entity is LSASS Memory, identified as T1003.001 under the Credential Access tactic for Windows. This technique involves harvesting credential material from the Local Security Authority Subsystem Service (LSASS) process memory. Specific technical mechanics include using tools like procdump with the command `procdump -ma lsass.exe lsass_dump`, leveraging mimikatz modules such as `sekurlsa::Minidump` and `sekurlsa::logonPasswords`, or abusing built-in Windows utilities like `comsvcs.dll` via `rundll32.exe` to dump the LSASS process. Adversaries may also abuse the silent process exit mechanism or modify Security Support Provider (SSP) Registry keys to load malicious DLLs for credential access.
5410.profile_without_enhance: [profile]In-Memory Payload Execution is a technique within the Defense Evasion tactic, applicable to multiple platforms, where adversaries execute malicious code directly within a process's memory to avoid detection. This is achieved by loading payloads, such as position-independent shellcode or raw binaries, into the process's own address space without creating files on disk. Methods include reflective loading, using functions like `Assembly.Load()` in PowerShell, and injection via process memory spaces like the /proc filesystem or Extra Window Memory, which can bypass defenses like data execution prevention and evade process-based monitoring.

5411.name: 4-Byte XOR
5411.profile: [profile]4-Byte XOR is a custom cryptographic technique used by adversaries like APT17 for data obfuscation. It functions as a weak encryption method where data is XOR-ed with a fixed 4-byte key, often implemented in custom archival or command and control protocols to evade detection. This technique is associated with data obfuscation and weak cipher creation, as referenced in related methods like custom cryptographic protocol and custom archival.[/profile]
5411.profile_without_enhance: [profile]4-Byte XOR is a custom cryptographic technique adversaries use to obfuscate data, often for command and control (C2) or prior to exfiltration. It functions by applying an XOR operation to plaintext data using a fixed 4-byte key, producing a weak but simple ciphertext. This method is implemented in custom malware to avoid external library references, as seen in techniques like Custom Cryptographic Protocol (T1024) and Archive via Custom Method (T1560.003). Its use is associated with groups including Lazarus Group and FIN6.

5412.name: Diskless Payload
5412.profile: [profile]Diskless Payload is a technique for executing malicious code directly in memory without writing files to disk, often to evade detection. It is associated with intrusion set APT17. The technique involves adversaries embedding a second-stage payload into the extended attributes (xattrs) of a legitimate file on macOS or Linux. Using commands like `xattr -p` or `getfattr`, a loader retrieves and decodes this hidden payload for execution, leaving the original file's hash unchanged to bypass security tools.
5412.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Diskless Payload is a technique where adversaries embed malicious code within system metadata, such as extended attributes (xattrs) on macOS and Linux, to evade detection. On macOS, a payload can be embedded using the `xattr` command into a custom attribute of a legitimate file, while a separate loader retrieves it with `xattr -p`, decodes, and executes it. On Linux, `setfattr` can write a payload into the `user.` namespace, with a loader using `getfattr --only-values` to extract and execute it. This method allows the primary file content and its hash to remain unchanged, bypassing security tools that do not inspect these attributes.

5413.name: POST Request
5413.profile: [profile]The entity "POST Request" is a fundamental network technique, not a distinct MITRE ATT&CK technique itself. It is a core HTTP method used within various ATT&CK techniques for communication. In the provided context, it is associated with the APT17 intrusion set and is a mechanism for techniques like exfiltration over webhooks (T1567.004) or to code repositories (T1567.001), where adversaries send stolen data via HTTPS POST requests to blend with normal traffic or leverage trusted services.
5413.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "POST Request" is a fundamental web protocol technique, not a distinct MITRE ATT&CK technique. It is a standard HTTP method used within various ATT&CK techniques for data transmission. In adversarial contexts, POST requests are commonly employed for activities like data exfiltration, such as in Exfiltration Over Webhook (T1567.004), where adversaries manually post stolen data to a webhook URL, or Exfiltration to Code Repository (T1567.001), using API calls. They are also used in credential-based attacks, like in attempts to bypass multi-factor authentication by generating automated login or password reset requests sent to users.

5414.name: Base64 Stub Data
5414.profile: [profile]Base64 Stub Data is a sub-technique of Data Encoding (T1132.001) under the Command and Control tactic, primarily used on Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves adversaries embedding malicious payloads or commands within Base64-encoded strings, which are then decoded and executed in memory to evade signature-based detection. This technique is commonly employed by groups like APT17 to obfuscate their activities during operations.
5414.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Base64 Stub Data is a sub-technique of Data Encoding (T1132.001) within the Command and Control tactic. It involves adversaries using Base64 encoding to obfuscate malicious payloads or commands within seemingly benign data stubs, making network traffic analysis and detection more difficult. This technique is commonly employed by groups like Hafnium, MuddyWater, and Lazarus Group to hide their activities.

5415.name: Static String "lynx"
5415.profile: [profile]Static String "lynx" is a technique where adversaries embed the specific string "lynx" within malware or tools, likely as a command, configuration value, or identifier. This string is associated with the intrusion set APT17 and is used in the context of dynamic API resolution, a method to obfuscate and resolve operating system functions at runtime to evade detection. The technique involves using such static strings as part of obfuscated payloads or to trigger specific malicious behaviors.[/profile]
5415.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Static String "lynx" is a technique where adversaries use the static string "lynx" within malware or commands, often as a hardcoded identifier, user-agent, or command parameter, to blend with legitimate traffic or automate malicious activities. This technique is associated with browser fingerprinting (T1036.012) and can be used alongside dynamic API resolution (T1027.007) to evade detection.

5416.name: Incremental Hexadecimal URI
5416.profile: [profile]Incremental Hexadecimal URI is a technique used by adversaries like APT17 to encode command and control traffic using hexadecimal encoding, making it more difficult to detect. This method involves generating unique, dynamically changing URIs or URLs to serve malicious content, often using one-time or single-use domain names as part of infrastructure acquisition and obfuscation strategies.[/profile]

Based on the retrieved context, it likely refers to a method where adversaries dynamically generate unique URIs or URLs, potentially using hexadecimal encoding, to serve malicious content or for command and control, making detection more difficult. This behavior is associated with techniques like Data Encoding (T1132) and Acquire Infrastructure: Domains (T1583.001).

5417.name: Strategic Network Attacks
5417.profile: [profile]Strategic Network Attacks is a technique used by adversaries to degrade or block the availability of targeted network resources by exhausting network bandwidth. This is performed as a Network Denial of Service (DoS), often using a high volume of traffic from single or distributed systems (DDoS), potentially employing botnets and IP address spoofing to obscure the attack source and increase impact, as observed with groups like APT28.[/profile]
5417.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Strategic Network Attacks is a technique where adversaries compromise third-party network devices like SOHO routers not for initial access to that environment, but to leverage them for subsequent operations. Once compromised, these devices can be used to host payloads for phishing campaigns, enable content injection, harvest reusable credentials, or support command and control by acting as proxies or within a botnet. Adversaries often target internet-facing edge devices lacking robust host-based defenses.

5418.name: In-Memory Payload Delivery
5418.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may attempt to make payloads difficult to discover and analyze by delivering files to victims as uncompiled code. Text-based source code files may subvert analysis and scrutiny from protections targeting executables/binaries. These payloads will need to be compiled before execution; typically via native utilities such as ilasm.exe(Citation: ATTACK IQ), csc.exe, or GCC/MinGW.(Citation: ClearSky MuddyWater Nov 2018)

Source code payloads may also be encrypted, encoded, and/or embedded within other files, such as those delivered as a [Phishing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566). Payloads may also be delivered in formats unrecognizable and inherently benign to the native OS (ex: EXEs on macOS/Linux) before later being (re)compiled into a proper executable binary with a bundled compiler and execution framework.(Citation: TrendMicro WindowsAppMac)
5418.profile: [profile]The entity "In-Memory Payload Delivery" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the provided data, it is closely related to the technique "Compile After Delivery" (T1027.004), a sub-technique of Obfuscated Files or Information under the Defense Evasion tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. This technique involves delivering payloads as uncompiled source code (e.g., C#, C) to evade detection by security tools targeting binaries. The payloads are later compiled on the victim system using native utilities like csc.exe, ilasm.exe, or GCC/MinGW. Associated threat groups include MuddyWater and Gamaredon Group.[/profile]
5418.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "In-Memory Payload Delivery" is a technique where adversaries directly inject and execute malicious code within a process's memory space, bypassing traditional file-based detection. It aligns with the Defense Evasion tactic (Tactic TA0005) and is applicable to multiple platforms. This is achieved by writing payloads into the memory of a legitimate process, often using functions like `WriteProcessMemory`, and then triggering execution via mechanisms like thread creation or asynchronous procedure calls, allowing the malicious code to run without writing a file to disk.

5419.name: Multiple Nested Obfuscation
5419.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may obfuscate command and control traffic to make it more difficult to detect.(Citation: Bitdefender FunnyDream Campaign November 2020) Command and control (C2) communications are hidden (but not necessarily encrypted) in an attempt to make the content more difficult to discover or decipher and to make the communication less conspicuous and hide commands from being seen. This encompasses many methods, such as adding junk data to protocol traffic, using steganography, or impersonating legitimate protocols.
5419.profile: [profile]Multiple Nested Obfuscation is a technique for hiding command and control (C2) traffic, likely aligning with MITRE ATT&CK T1001 (Data Obfuscation) under the Command and Control tactic. It operates by applying multiple layers of obfuscation, such as embedding custom encryption within standard protocol encryption like HTTPS, to make network communications more difficult to detect and analyze. This method is distinct from simple command or file obfuscation, focusing specifically on layered obfuscation of C2 channel content.[/profile]
5419.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Multiple Nested Obfuscation is an attack pattern where adversaries apply multiple, layered obfuscation techniques to files, commands, or network traffic to evade detection and hinder analysis. This can involve combining methods like encoding (e.g., base64), string manipulation (e.g., splitting and concatenation), and embedding obfuscated content within encrypted protocols, effectively creating a compounded barrier for defensive tools. It is a sub-technique of general obfuscation (T1027) used across various platforms.

5420.name: Side Operation
5420.uncertain_mes:
Programs may specify DLLs that are loaded at runtime. Programs that improperly or vaguely specify a required DLL may be open to a vulnerability in which an unintended DLL is loaded. Side-loading vulnerabilities specifically occur when Windows Side-by-Side (WinSxS) manifests (Citation: MSDN Manifests) are not explicit enough about characteristics of the DLL to be loaded. Adversaries may take advantage of a legitimate program that is vulnerable to side-loading to load a malicious DLL. (Citation: Stewart 2014)

Adversaries likely use this technique as a means of masking actions they perform under a legitimate, trusted system or software process.
5420.profile: [profile]The entity is DLL Side-Loading, also known as T1574.002, a Defense Evasion technique for Windows. It works by placing a malicious DLL in the same directory as a legitimate, vulnerable application; when the application is invoked, it loads the malicious DLL instead of the intended one due to the Windows DLL search order, allowing adversaries to execute code under a trusted process. The APT17 group has been associated with this technique.
5420.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Side Operation" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the retrieved information, it is strongly associated with the technique DLL Side-Loading (T1574.002). This technique falls under the Defense Evasion tactic on Windows platforms. It works by placing a malicious DLL in the same directory as a legitimate, vulnerable executable. When the legitimate program is invoked, it follows the standard DLL search order and loads the adversary's malicious payload from the local directory instead of the intended, trusted library, thereby executing code under the guise of a trusted process.

5427.name: Sunshop Campaign Variant
5427.profile: [profile]Sunshop Campaign Variant, also known as Sunshop Group, is a malware variant associated with the APT17 intrusion set. It functions as a DLL backdoor and is related to the Derusbi malware family. Its command and control infrastructure has been linked to domains such as materialplies.com and news.colourtinctem.com, which are part of Campaign Alpha, and it has also utilized SoftEther VPN for operations.

It operates as a backdoor for malicious activities. Its target platform is Windows, as indicated by the DLL file format. Infrastructure connections include domains like materialplies.com and news.colourtinctem.com, which are related to its command and control servers.

5428.profile: [profile]Diskless 9002 Payload, also known as 9002 RAT, is a diskless variant of a remote access trojan. It has been associated with groups including aurora panda, apt31, and group 27. Its key technical behaviors involve execution via malicious PowerShell scripts or Java payloads like PhotoShow.jar, often delivered through embedded .LNK files. It communicates with command-and-control servers such as mx[.]i26[.]org and uses a hardcoded identifier "\\x28\\x02\\x13\\x20". The target platform is Windows, leveraging its scripting and execution environments.

It communicates with command-and-control servers like mx[.]i26[.]org and uses a hardcoded identifier "\\x28\\x02\\x13\\x20". Its target platform is Windows.

5436.name: Supply Chain Attacks
5436.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may manipulate products or product delivery mechanisms prior to receipt by a final consumer for the purpose of data or system compromise.

Supply chain compromise can take place at any stage of the supply chain including:

* Manipulation of development tools
* Manipulation of a development environment
* Manipulation of source code repositories (public or private)
* Manipulation of source code in open-source dependencies
* Manipulation of software update/distribution mechanisms
* Compromised/infected system images (removable media infected at the factory)(Citation: IBM Storwize)(Citation: Schneider Electric USB Malware) 
* Replacement of legitimate software with modified versions
* Sales of modified/counterfeit products to legitimate distributors
* Shipment interdiction

While supply chain compromise can impact any component of hardware or software, adversaries looking to gain execution have often focused on malicious additions to legitimate software in software distribution or update channels.(Citation: Avast CCleaner3 2018)(Citation: Microsoft Dofoil 2018)(Citation: Command Five SK 2011) Adversaries may limit targeting to a desired victim set or distribute malicious software to a broad set of consumers but only follow up with specific victims.(Citation: Symantec Elderwood Sept 2012)(Citation: Avast CCleaner3 2018)(Citation: Command Five SK 2011) Popular open-source projects that are used as dependencies in many applications may also be targeted as a means to add malicious code to users of the dependency.(Citation: Trendmicro NPM Compromise)

In some cases, adversaries may conduct “second-order” supply chain compromises by leveraging the access gained from an initial supply chain compromise to further compromise a software component.(Citation: Krebs 3cx overview 2023) This may allow the threat actor to spread to even more victims.
5436.profile: [profile]Supply Chain Compromise is identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1195 under the Initial Access tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. This technique involves adversaries manipulating products or delivery mechanisms before they reach the end user to compromise systems or data. Specific mechanics include tampering with development tools, source code repositories, open-source dependencies, and software update channels to insert malicious code. Attackers may conduct broad distribution followed by selective targeting of specific victims or execute "second-order" compromises by leveraging initial access to infiltrate further software components. Associated threat groups include Sandworm Team, Ember Bear, and OilRig.[profile]
5436.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Supply Chain Attacks correspond to MITRE ATT&CK technique T1195 under the Initial Access tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. This technique involves adversaries compromising products or delivery mechanisms before they reach the end user to gain system access. Specific mechanics include manipulating development tools, source code repositories, software update channels, or open-source dependencies to insert malicious code. A notable tactic is "second-order" compromise, where initial access is used to further taint software components, expanding the attack's reach.

5437.name: Bookworm Trojan
5437.uncertain_mes: [BOOKWORM](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S1226) is a modular trojan known to be leveraged by [Mustang Panda](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0129) and was first observed utilized in 2015.  [BOOKWORM](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S1226) was later updated in late 2021 and the fall of 2022 to launch shellcode represented as UUID parameters. (Citation: Broadcom)(Citation: Unit42 Bookworm Nov2015)(Citation: Palo Alto Networks, Unit 42)

It employs DLL side-loading, executes shellcode represented as UUID parameters, and can load additional modules directly from its command and control server. The malware primarily targets Windows systems and has been deployed in attacks focusing on Thailand.[/profile]

5438.name: ShadowPad
5438.uncertain_mes: [ShadowPad](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0596) is a modular backdoor that was first identified in a supply chain compromise of the NetSarang software in mid-July 2017. The malware was originally thought to be exclusively used by [APT41](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0096), but has since been observed to be used by various Chinese threat activity groups. (Citation: Recorded Future RedEcho Feb 2021)(Citation: Securelist ShadowPad Aug 2017)(Citation: Kaspersky ShadowPad Aug 2017)

5439.name: BeEF
5439.profile: [profile]BeEF is a web browser exploitation framework primarily used for client-side attacks, often associated with APT17. It functions by injecting a JavaScript hook into vulnerable web pages to control compromised browsers, enabling activities like keystroke logging, network reconnaissance, and further exploitation. The framework is platform-agnostic, targeting any system with a compatible web browser, and is commonly deployed in phishing campaigns or via compromised websites to establish persistent control over victim machines.[/profile]
5439.profile_without_enhance: [profile]BeEF is a browser exploitation framework used for penetration testing and red teaming. It hooks web browsers to launch client-side attacks, enabling actions like keylogging, social engineering, and network reconnaissance. 5440.name: NetWire
5440.uncertain_mes: [NETWIRE](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0198) is a publicly available, multiplatform remote administration tool (RAT) that has been used by criminal and APT groups since at least 2012.(Citation: FireEye APT33 Sept 2017)(Citation: McAfee Netwire Mar 2015)(Citation: FireEye APT33 Webinar Sept 2017)

5442.name: PassCV
5442.profile: [profile]PassCV is a cyber espionage group believed to be linked to or part of a broader Chinese state-aligned threat cluster, also known as APT41, Winnti Group, BARIUM, Wicked Panda, and GREF. It shows significant overlaps with APT17. The group's arsenal includes the Winnti backdoor. Its operations are primarily motivated by espionage, targeting a wide range of sectors and regions to support Chinese strategic interests.
5442.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The intrusion set is most widely known as APT17, also known as Axiom, Aurora Panda, Hidden Lynx, Group 72, Dogfish, Heart Typhoon, and Tailgater Team, with the alias PassCV also used in some reporting. Its key malware includes the custom HDRoot bootkit, the Hikit rootkit, and the DeputyDog backdoor. Key TTPs involve sophisticated social engineering via cultivated Microsoft TechNet profiles and exploitation of zero-day vulnerabilities (e.g., CVE-2012-1889, CVE-2013-3893). The group is attributed to China and primarily targets high-tech, aerospace, legal, software, and electronics sectors in the United States, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, and Southeast Asia for cyber espionage to gather political, economic, and military intelligence.

The group's operations are attributed to Chinese state-sponsored interests, primarily targeting intellectual property and sensitive data from various global sectors. Its activities show overlaps with other clusters under the APT41 umbrella, indicating a shared mission and toolset within a larger, coordinated cyber espionage apparatus.

5443.name: Axiom
5443.uncertain_mes: [Axiom](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0001) is a suspected Chinese cyber espionage group that has targeted the aerospace, defense, government, manufacturing, and media sectors since at least 2008. Some reporting suggests a degree of overlap between [Axiom](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0001) and [Winnti Group](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0044) but the two groups appear to be distinct based on differences in reporting on TTPs and targeting.(Citation: Kaspersky Winnti April 2013)(Citation: Kaspersky Winnti June 2015)(Citation: Novetta Winnti April 2015)
5443.profile: [profile]Axiom, also known as APT17, Aurora Panda, Group 72, and Hidden Lynx, is a suspected Chinese cyber espionage group. Its arsenal includes the use of exploits for vulnerabilities like CVE-2014-0322 and CVE-2012-4792, spear phishing for initial access, and remote administration tools like RDP for persistence. The group is attributed to China and has targeted sectors including aerospace, defense, government, manufacturing, and media since at least 2008, primarily for espionage purposes. Some reporting indicates potential overlaps with groups like Winnti, but Axiom is generally considered distinct based on its TTPs and victimology.

Key TTPs involve spear-phishing, exploitation of zero-day vulnerabilities (e.g., CVE-2012-1889, CVE-2013-3893), the use of remote administration tools like RDP, and privilege escalation via compromised accounts. [APT41](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0096) overlaps at least partially with public reporting on groups including BARIUM and [Winnti Group](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0044).(Citation: FireEye APT41 Aug 2019)(Citation: Group IB APT 41 June 2021)

Its key TTPs include targeting a diverse set of industries such as healthcare, telecom, technology, and finance across 14 countries. The group is attributed to China and shows overlaps with other reported clusters like APT17. Its primary motivations are espionage and financial gain, distinguishing it through this dual mission focus.

5447.name: Winnti Group
5447.uncertain_mes: [Winnti Group](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0044) is a threat group with Chinese origins that has been active since at least 2010. The group has heavily targeted the gaming industry, but it has also expanded the scope of its targeting.(Citation: Kaspersky Winnti April 2013)(Citation: Kaspersky Winnti June 2015)(Citation: Novetta Winnti April 2015) Some reporting suggests a number of other groups, including [Axiom](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0001), [APT17](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0025), and [Ke3chang](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0004), are closely linked to [Winnti Group](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0044).(Citation: 401 TRG Winnti Umbrella May 2018)
5447.profile: [profile]The Winnti Group, also known as Blackfly, is a Chinese-origin threat group active since at least 2010. It is known for using the Winnti backdoor and other malware, employing stolen certificates to sign its tools and using rootkits to modify server functionality. The group is believed to be closely linked to or share overlaps with other clusters such as APT17, Axiom, and Ke3chang. It has heavily targeted the gaming industry and has expanded to other sectors, including universities in Hong Kong. Its operations are primarily motivated by cyber espionage and intellectual property theft.

Its key malware includes the Winnti backdoor, rootkits for modifying server functionality, and tools like ff.exe, often signed with stolen certificates. Key TTPs involve supply chain attacks and targeting specific server processes. The group is attributed to China and primarily targets high-tech, aerospace, and academic sectors globally, including in Hong Kong, for cyber espionage and intellectual property theft, showing overlaps with clusters like APT17.

5448.name: HDROOT
5448.uncertain_mes: Some time ago while tracking Winnti group activity we came across a suspicious 64-bit sample. It was a standalone utility with the name HDD Rootkit for planting a bootkit on a computer. Once installed the bootkit infects the operating system with a backdoor at the early booting stage. The principles of this bootkit’s work, named HDRoot, have been described in the first part of our article.
5448.profile: [profile]HDROOT, also known as HDRoot or HDD Rootkit, is a bootkit attributed to APT17. It is a standalone utility that infects the operating system with a backdoor at the early booting stage. Detected as Hacktool, Rootkit, and Trojan.Boot variants, it is associated with backdoors like Backdoor.Win64.Winnti and downloaders such as Trojan.Win32.Agentb.aemr, primarily targeting Windows systems. The specific payload delivered by the bootkit can vary.[/profile]

It targets Windows platforms (32-bit and 64-bit) and is detected under various verdicts like Hacktool, Rootkit, and Trojan.Boot.

It is a standalone utility, often named hall32.exe, that installs a persistent bootkit to infect the operating system with a backdoor during the early boot stage. The installer targets the hard drive, using commands to modify bootmgr.exe for persistence. Associated malware includes backdoors like Backdoor.Win64.Winnti and downloaders, and it is detected under various verdicts including Hacktool, Rootkit, and Trojan.Boot for both 32-bit and 64-bit Windows systems.

It targets Windows platforms (32-bit and 64-bit) and is associated with downloaders like bootmgr.exe.

5451.name: Main DLL
5451.profile: [profile]Main DLL is a component of the Rover backdoor, which is attributed to the APT17 intrusion set. It is executed by a downloader Trojan after retrieving files including WindowsSecurityService3.exe (the 'Rover' main module) and various supporting DLLs like OpenAL32.dll and opencv_world300.dll. The backdoor's core functionality remains identical across different library versions. It is a Windows-targeted malware.[/profile]

It is associated with the 'Rover' malware family, where it serves as the main module (WindowsSecurityService3.exe) and functions identically across different library versions. It is also referenced in relation to 'eyservice' (hodll.dll) and 'microcin' (installer shellcode and DLL), indicating potential DLL hijacking or modular use within these contexts. Its attributed groups include '未知' and 'nazar'. Target platforms are Windows-based systems.

5452.name: Dynamic Link Library
5452.profile: [profile]Dynamic Link Library (DLL) is a legitimate Windows file format, but it is frequently abused by threat actors like APT17 for malicious purposes. It is used as a component in malware such as Stuxnet, where it masquerades as a Siemens SCADA module (s7otbldx.dll), and in the SolarWinds Sunburst backdoor (SolarWinds.Orion.Core.BusinessLayer.dll). The Lazarus Group has also employed maliciously modified DLLs in attacks against South Korean enterprises. Key malicious behaviors include exploiting RPC vulnerabilities for worm distribution and serving as a core component in supply chain attacks. The primary target platform is Microsoft Windows.
5452.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Dynamic Link Library is a generic file format for Windows libraries, not a specific malware family. It is referenced in the context of various malware campaigns. The Stuxnet worm used a fake Siemens SCADA dynamic link library named s7otbldx.dll. The SolarWinds Sunburst backdoor was delivered via a trojanized Dynamic Link Library named SolarWinds.Orion.Core.BusinessLayer.dll, attributed to APT29 (UNC2452). In the ImprudentCook campaign, maliciously modified Dynamic Link Library files were used in attacks attributed to the Lazarus Group. Its primary target platform is Microsoft Windows.

Its key technical behaviors include functioning as a remote shell for command execution, downloading and uploading files, creating processes, and self-deletion. It communicates with a hardcoded C&C server (media-seoengine[.]com) using authorized and encrypted communication. Target platforms are unspecified, but it is used in campaigns against Russian opposition. Infrastructure involves compromised LinkedIn profiles for initial access.

Its capabilities include downloading/uploading files, creating processes, and self-deletion. It is also mentioned as a feature of other malware like Quasar RAT, which is associated with groups including APT33, Dropping Elephant, Stone Panda, and The Gorgon Group.

5454.name: Network Driver
5454.profile: [profile]Network Driver is a kernel-mode component, specifically a miniport adapter driver, which operates at the lowest level of the network driver stack to bypass host-based security monitoring like personal firewalls and traffic inspection software. It is attributed to the APT17 intrusion set and is used by malware families including Win32/Gapz and Rovnix to facilitate covert communication. Its primary target platform is the Windows operating system, where it enables direct network packet communication for malicious payloads.
5454.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Network Driver is a malware component that operates at the kernel level, specifically implementing a custom TCP/IP stack as a miniport adapter driver. This low-level network driver position allows it to bypass host-based security software, such as personal firewalls and network-traffic-monitoring tools, by communicating directly with the network adapter. It is associated with the Win32/Gapz malware family and is utilized to evade detection on infected Windows systems.

5455.name: Server-Side Derusbi
5455.uncertain_mes: [Derusbi](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0021) is malware used by multiple Chinese APT groups.(Citation: Novetta-Axiom)(Citation: ThreatConnect Anthem) Both Windows and Linux variants have been observed.(Citation: Fidelis Turbo)
5455.profile: [profile]Server-Side Derusbi, also known as Derusbi, is a malware used by multiple Chinese APT groups, including APT41 and the Winnti Group. It has both Windows and Linux variants and functions as a malware loader. A key technical behavior involves a Python-based fetch-and-execute mechanism, where it continuously contacts a command-and-control server (e.g., hxxps://luke.compeyson.eu[.]org/runservice/api/public_result.php) to retrieve and dynamically run payloads until instructed to stop.
5455.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Server-Side Derusbi, also known as Derusbi, is a malware loader used by multiple advanced persistent threat groups, including the Winnti Group. Its key technical behavior involves a fetch-and-execute mechanism, where it contacts a command-and-control server (e.g., hxxps://luke.compeyson.eu[.]org/runservice/api/public_result.php) to retrieve and dynamically execute Python code payloads, continuing this operation until the server instructs it to stop. The malware targets Windows systems as part of broader intrusion campaigns.

5456.name: XOR-Encrypted Form
5456.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may employ an encryption algorithm to conceal command and control traffic rather than relying on any inherent protections provided by a communication protocol. Despite the use of a secure algorithm, these implementations may be vulnerable to reverse engineering if secret keys are encoded and/or generated within malware samples/configuration files.
5456.profile: [profile]The entity aligns with MITRE ATT&CK technique T1573.002, Encrypted Channel: Symmetric Cryptography, under the Command and Control tactic for Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves using XOR or other symmetric algorithms with a static key embedded in the malware to obfuscate C2 traffic. This custom implementation, while providing obfuscation, is often vulnerable to reverse engineering to recover the key. Groups like APT17, APT29, and Magic Hound have employed this method.
5456.profile_without_enhance: [profile]XOR-Encrypted Form is a sub-technique of Obfuscated Files or Information (T1027) under the Defense Evasion tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. It involves using the XOR (exclusive OR) bitwise operation with a static key to encrypt or obfuscate file content, such as payloads or configuration data, to hinder static analysis and detection. This method is a simple, custom cryptographic implementation often used for data archiving prior to exfiltration (T1560.003) and to conceal command and control traffic (T1024).

5457.name: Listening Mode
5457.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may abuse Windows safe mode to disable endpoint defenses. Safe mode starts up the Windows operating system with a limited set of drivers and services. Third-party security software such as endpoint detection and response (EDR) tools may not start after booting Windows in safe mode. There are two versions of safe mode: Safe Mode and Safe Mode with Networking. It is possible to start additional services after a safe mode boot.(Citation: Microsoft Safe Mode)(Citation: Sophos Snatch Ransomware 2019)

Adversaries may abuse safe mode to disable endpoint defenses that may not start with a limited boot. Hosts can be forced into safe mode after the next reboot via modifications to Boot Configuration Data (BCD) stores, which are files that manage boot application settings.(Citation: Microsoft bcdedit 2021)

Adversaries may also add their malicious applications to the list of minimal services that start in safe mode by modifying relevant Registry values (i.e. [Modify Registry](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1112)). Malicious [Component Object Model](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1559/001) (COM) objects may also be registered and loaded in safe mode.(Citation: Sophos Snatch Ransomware 2019)(Citation: CyberArk Labs Safe Mode 2016)(Citation: Cybereason Nocturnus MedusaLocker 2020)(Citation: BleepingComputer REvil 2021)
5457.profile: [profile]The entity "Listening Mode" appears to be incorrectly named; the provided data describes the MITRE ATT&CK technique "Safe Mode Boot" (ID: T1562.009), a Defense Evasion tactic for Windows. This technique involves forcing a system into Windows Safe Mode, which loads a minimal set of drivers and services, to prevent security software like EDR from starting. Adversaries achieve this by modifying the Boot Configuration Data (BCD) store to trigger safe mode on reboot and may add malicious services to the safe mode startup list via registry modifications or by registering malicious COM objects.
5457.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Listening Mode is a technique for network-based command and control where a compromised host establishes a persistent backdoor by opening a listening port and awaiting incoming connections from an adversary, rather than actively reaching out. This allows the malware to remain dormant and stealthy, only becoming active when contacted, which can bypass egress filtering and detection systems that look for outbound beaconing.

5458.name: Hooking (IRP_MJ_DIRECTORY_CONTROL - Network)
5458.uncertain_mes:
Windows processes often leverage application programming interface (API) functions to perform tasks that require reusable system resources. Windows API functions are typically stored in dynamic-link libraries (DLLs) as exported functions. 

Hooking involves redirecting calls to these functions and can be implemented via:

* **Hooks procedures**, which intercept and execute designated code in response to events such as messages, keystrokes, and mouse inputs. (Citation: Microsoft Hook Overview) (Citation: Elastic Process Injection July 2017)
* **Import address table (IAT) hooking**, which use modifications to a process’s IAT, where pointers to imported API functions are stored. (Citation: Elastic Process Injection July 2017) (Citation: Adlice Software IAT Hooks Oct 2014) (Citation: MWRInfoSecurity Dynamic Hooking 2015)
* **Inline hooking**, which overwrites the first bytes in an API function to redirect code flow. (Citation: Elastic Process Injection July 2017) (Citation: HighTech Bridge Inline Hooking Sept 2011) (Citation: MWRInfoSecurity Dynamic Hooking 2015)

Similar to [Process Injection](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1055), adversaries may use hooking to load and execute malicious code within the context of another process, masking the execution while also allowing access to the process's memory and possibly elevated privileges. Installing hooking mechanisms may also provide Persistence via continuous invocation when the functions are called through normal use.

Malicious hooking mechanisms may also capture API calls that include parameters that reveal user authentication credentials for Credential Access. (Citation: Microsoft TrojanSpy:Win32/Ursnif.gen!I Sept 2017)

Hooking is commonly utilized by [Rootkit](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1014)s to conceal files, processes, Registry keys, and other objects in order to hide malware and associated behaviors. (Citation: Symantec Windows Rootkits)
5458.profile: [profile]Hooking (IRP_MJ_DIRECTORY_CONTROL - Network) is a technique for intercepting and redirecting function calls, specifically targeting network-related I/O request packets (IRPs) in Windows. It is used for Defense Evasion and Persistence on Windows platforms. The technical mechanism involves hooking the IRP_MJ_DIRECTORY_CONTROL dispatch routine to filter or manipulate network file system operations, allowing adversaries to hide malicious files or directories from network enumeration. This method is distinct from standard API hooking and is often employed by rootkits. The intrusion set APT17 has been associated with this activity.[/profile]
5458.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Hooking (IRP_MJ_DIRECTORY_CONTROL - Network)" is a specific hooking technique targeting the Windows kernel's IRP_MJ_DIRECTORY_CONTROL I/O request packet function, which handles directory control operations for network file systems. This technique falls under the Defense Evasion tactic on the Windows platform. By intercepting this function via inline hooking or IAT hooking, adversaries can redirect or filter system calls related to network directory queries, such as enumerating shared folders or discovering network resources, to conceal malicious files, directories, or network shares from detection and facilitate lateral movement.

5459.uncertain_mes:

5459.profile: [profile]Hooking (IRP_MJ_DIRECTORY_CONTROL - File) is a technique for intercepting and redirecting Windows API function calls, typically implemented via hook procedures, Import Address Table (IAT) hooking, or inline hooking. It is used to load and execute malicious code within another process's context for defense evasion and privilege escalation, to capture API parameters for credential access, and by rootkits to conceal objects. This allows adversaries to filter or hide files and directories from system queries, commonly used by rootkits to conceal malicious artifacts. The hook can be implemented via inline hooking or IAT hooking to redirect the normal code flow of the function.

5460.name: Network Sniffing
5460.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may passively sniff network traffic to capture information about an environment, including authentication material passed over the network. Network sniffing refers to using the network interface on a system to monitor or capture information sent over a wired or wireless connection. An adversary may place a network interface into promiscuous mode to passively access data in transit over the network, or use span ports to capture a larger amount of data.

Data captured via this technique may include user credentials, especially those sent over an insecure, unencrypted protocol. Techniques for name service resolution poisoning, such as [LLMNR/NBT-NS Poisoning and SMB Relay](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1557/001), can also be used to capture credentials to websites, proxies, and internal systems by redirecting traffic to an adversary.

Network sniffing may reveal configuration details, such as running services, version numbers, and other network characteristics (e.g. IP addresses, hostnames, VLAN IDs) necessary for subsequent [Lateral Movement](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0008) and/or [Defense Evasion](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0005) activities. Adversaries may likely also utilize network sniffing during [Adversary-in-the-Middle](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1557) (AiTM) to passively gain additional knowledge about the environment.

In cloud-based environments, adversaries may still be able to use traffic mirroring services to sniff network traffic from virtual machines. For example, AWS Traffic Mirroring, GCP Packet Mirroring, and Azure vTap allow users to define specified instances to collect traffic from and specified targets to send collected traffic to.(Citation: AWS Traffic Mirroring)(Citation: GCP Packet Mirroring)(Citation: Azure Virtual Network TAP) Often, much of this traffic will be in cleartext due to the use of TLS termination at the load balancer level to reduce the strain of encrypting and decrypting traffic.(Citation: Rhino Security Labs AWS VPC Traffic Mirroring)(Citation: SpecterOps AWS Traffic Mirroring) The adversary can then use exfiltration techniques such as Transfer Data to Cloud Account in order to access the sniffed traffic.(Citation: Rhino Security Labs AWS VPC Traffic Mirroring)

On network devices, adversaries may perform network captures using [Network Device CLI](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/008) commands such as `monitor capture`.(Citation: US-CERT-TA18-106A)(Citation: capture_embedded_packet_on_software)
5460.profile: [profile]Network Sniffing is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1040 under the Collection tactic, applicable to Linux, Windows, and macOS platforms. It involves passively capturing network traffic by placing a network interface into promiscuous mode or using span ports to monitor data in transit. This technique can harvest unencrypted credentials and reveal network configuration details like IP addresses and services. In cloud environments, adversaries abuse traffic mirroring services (AWS, GCP, Azure) to capture cleartext traffic, often due to TLS termination at load balancers. On network devices, commands like `monitor capture` are used for packet capture. It is associated with groups including APT28, APT33, and Sandworm Team.[/profile]
5460.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Network Sniffing is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1040 under the Discovery tactic, applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, IaaS, and Network platforms. It involves passively capturing network traffic by placing a network interface into promiscuous mode or using span ports to monitor data in transit. This technique harvests unencrypted credentials and reveals system configuration details like IP addresses and services. In cloud environments, adversaries abuse native traffic mirroring services (e.g., AWS Traffic Mirroring) to collect cleartext traffic, often facilitated by TLS termination at load balancers. On network devices, captures can be performed using CLI commands like `monitor capture`.

5461.name: Data Redirection
5461.profile: [profile]Data Redirection is a technique where adversaries use proxies or port redirection tools like HTRAN, ZXProxy, or ZXPortMap to direct network traffic between systems, acting as an intermediary for command and control communications. This method avoids direct connections to adversary infrastructure, reduces simultaneous outbound connections, and can leverage trusted internal paths or external resources to evade detection. It is associated with groups such as APT17 and is related to broader proxy techniques like Proxy (T1090), Internal Proxy (T1090.001), and External Proxy (T1090.002).
5461.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Data Redirection is a technique where adversaries use proxies or port redirection tools to manage command and control traffic, avoiding direct connections to their infrastructure. This can involve internal proxies within a compromised environment or external proxies to mask the destination of C2 communications, often using tools like HTRAN, ZXProxy, or ZXPortMap to redirect traffic and evade detection.

5462.name: Process Execution
5462.profile: [profile]Process Execution is a foundational technique for running code on a system. As a core execution method, it is not assigned a specific MITRE ATT&CK ID. It occurs across all platforms and supports the Execution tactic. The technique involves the direct launching of processes, often through command-line interfaces or system APIs. It is a prerequisite for more advanced techniques like Process Injection, which adversaries such as APT17 use to mask malicious activity within legitimate processes.
5462.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Process Execution is a foundational technique (T1106) within the Execution tactic, applicable across Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves adversaries running malicious code or commands on a compromised system, often by leveraging native OS APIs or system utilities. This technique serves as a core mechanism for achieving initial code execution, which can then be followed by other behaviors like persistence or lateral movement. It is frequently a prerequisite for more complex sub-techniques such as Process Injection (T1055) or abuse of System Services (T1569).

5471.name: Internet Connection Sharing Service
5471.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may check for Internet connectivity on compromised systems. This may be performed during automated discovery and can be accomplished in numerous ways such as using [Ping](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0097), tracert, and GET requests to websites, or performing initial speed testing to confirm bandwidth. Adversaries may use the results and responses from these requests to determine if the system is capable of communicating with their C2 servers before attempting to connect to them. The results may also be used to identify routes, redirectors, and proxy servers.
5471.profile: [profile]The technique is officially known as Internet Connection Discovery (T1016.001) under the Discovery tactic for Windows, Linux, and macOS. It involves adversaries checking for Internet connectivity on compromised systems using tools like Ping, tracert, and GET requests to websites, or by performing speed tests. This reconnaissance is used to verify the system's capability to communicate with command and control servers and to identify potential network routes, redirectors, or proxy servers before establishing a connection. Groups such as APT29, Volt Typhoon, and Turla have been associated with this behavior.
5471.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Internet Connection Sharing Service" is a Windows service that adversaries may abuse for persistence or lateral movement. It can be manipulated via utilities like `sc.exe` or direct Registry modification to execute malicious payloads at startup, often under SYSTEM privileges. This technique is categorized under Windows service manipulation (T1543.003) within the Persistence tactic, primarily targeting Windows platforms.

5474.name: Disables Antivirus
5474.profile: [profile]Disables Antivirus, corresponding to MITRE ATT&CK technique T1562.001 (Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Tools), is a defense evasion tactic used across Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. Adversaries achieve this by killing security software processes, modifying or deleting registry keys and configuration files (e.g., to tamper with Sysmon logging in `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\WMI\Autologger\EventLog-Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon-Operational`), or disabling updates. They may also abuse legitimate drivers or tools, like GMER, to shut down hidden antivirus processes, or add directories to exclusion lists to hide malicious files, as seen in groups like FIN6, Wizard Spider, and Turla.
5474.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Disables Antivirus" is a technique for defense evasion, where adversaries modify or disable antivirus and other security tools to avoid detection. This can involve killing security processes, tampering with registry keys or configuration files to impair tool functionality, or adding directories to exclusion lists to hide malicious files. Specific methods include using legitimate drivers or tools like GMER to shut down hidden processes, altering Sysmon logging settings, or exploiting vulnerabilities in the security software itself.

The target platform is Windows-based systems where the security software is deployed.[/profile]

5480.name: HDROOT Infections

It functions as a bootkit that modifies the Master Boot Record (MBR) or Volume Boot Record (VBR) of a hard drive, enabling execution of adversary code during the system boot process below the operating system layer, which complicates detection and remediation efforts. This method ensures the malware remains active from startup.[/profile]

5493.name: Operation Ephemeral Hydra
5493.profile: [profile]Operation Ephemeral Hydra is a technique for compromising third-party servers, including Virtual Private Servers (VPS), to establish infrastructure for staging, launching, and executing operations. This supports tactics like Resource Development and Defense Evasion, as adversaries can use these compromised servers for command and control or to revert cloud instances to remove evidence. It is associated with groups like APT17, Turla, and Volt Typhoon.
