Associated threat groups include Turla and Volt Typhoon.

5494.name: Direct Memory Injection
5494.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may inject malicious code into process via Extra Window Memory (EWM) in order to evade process-based defenses as well as possibly elevate privileges. EWM injection is a method of executing arbitrary code in the address space of a separate live process. Before creating a window, graphical Windows-based processes must prescribe to or register a windows class, which stipulate appearance and behavior (via windows procedures, which are functions that handle input/output of data).(Citation: Microsoft Window Classes) Registration of new windows classes can include a request for up to 40 bytes of EWM to be appended to the allocated memory of each instance of that class. This EWM is intended to store data specific to that window and has specific application programming interface (API) functions to set and get its value. (Citation: Microsoft GetWindowLong function) (Citation: Microsoft SetWindowLong function) Although small, the EWM is large enough to store a 32-bit pointer and is often used to point to a windows procedure. Malware may possibly utilize this memory location in part of an attack chain that includes writing code to shared sections of the process’s memory, placing a pointer to the code in EWM, then invoking execution by returning execution control to the address in the process’s EWM. Execution granted through EWM injection may allow access to both the target process's memory and possibly elevated privileges. Writing payloads to shared sections also avoids the use of highly monitored API calls such as WriteProcessMemory and CreateRemoteThread.(Citation: Elastic Process Injection July 2017) More sophisticated malware samples may also potentially bypass protection mechanisms such as data execution prevention (DEP) by triggering a combination of windows procedures and other system functions that will rewrite the malicious payload inside an executable portion of the target process. (Citation: MalwareTech Power Loader Aug 2013) (Citation: WeLiveSecurity Gapz and Redyms Mar 2013) Running code in the context of another process may allow access to the process's memory, system/network resources, and possibly elevated privileges. Execution via EWM injection may also evade detection from security products since the execution is masked under a legitimate process.
5494.profile: [profile]Extra Window Memory Injection, also known as T1055.011, is a Defense Evasion and Privilege Escalation technique for Windows. It exploits up to 40 bytes of Extra Window Memory (EWM) allocated for a window class. Attackers write malicious code to a shared memory section, place a pointer to it in the EWM, and then redirect execution to that pointer, evading monitoring of APIs like WriteProcessMemory and CreateRemoteThread. This method can also be used to bypass Data Execution Prevention (DEP). The intrusion set APT17 has been associated with this technique.[/profile]
5494.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Direct Memory Injection is a process injection technique where adversaries write malicious code directly into the memory space of a target process to execute arbitrary code, evading defenses and potentially gaining elevated privileges. It operates within the Defense Evasion and Privilege Escalation tactics, primarily on Windows platforms. The method typically involves using Windows API calls like `VirtualAllocEx` and `WriteProcessMemory` to allocate and write code, then `CreateRemoteThread` to trigger execution within the legitimate process's context, masking malicious activity.

5495.name: Non-Persistent Payload
5495.profile: [profile]Non-Persistent Payload is a malware payload type. It is attributed to the intrusion set APT17. It is referenced as a stage or final component in other malware families, such as VPNFilter (Stage 3) and SideWinder. Its key technical behavior is its non-persistent nature, meaning it does not survive system reboots. Target platforms are unspecified.[/profile]

This payload is non-persistent, indicating it is designed to execute in memory without leaving a lasting trace on the infected system, and is deployed by droppers like 8.t or within multi-stage malware such as VPNFilter.

5496.name: HydraQ/MCRAT
5496.uncertain_mes: [Hydraq](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0203) is a data-theft trojan first used by [Elderwood](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0066) in the 2009 Google intrusion known as Operation Aurora, though variations of this trojan have been used in more recent campaigns by other Chinese actors, possibly including [APT17](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0025).(Citation: MicroFocus 9002 Aug 2016)(Citation: Symantec Elderwood Sept 2012)(Citation: Symantec Trojan.Hydraq Jan 2010)(Citation: ASERT Seven Pointed Dagger Aug 2015)(Citation: FireEye DeputyDog 9002 November 2013)(Citation: ProofPoint GoT 9002 Aug 2017)(Citation: FireEye Sunshop Campaign May 2013)(Citation: PaloAlto 3102 Sept 2015)
5496.profile: [profile]HydraQ, also known as MCRAT and Trojan.APT.9002, is a data-theft trojan historically attributed to the Elderwood group and used in Operation Aurora. It has also been associated with APT17 and Axiom. The malware is a plug-in-based bot, and its infrastructure has been deployed alongside tools like Htran. It primarily targets Windows platforms for cyber espionage purposes.
5496.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The malware is known as HydraQ/MCRAT, also referred to as Trojan.APT.9002 and 9002 rat. It is associated with threat groups Aurora Panda, APT31, and Group 27. 5507.name: watering hole intrusion techniques
5507.profile: [profile]Watering hole intrusion techniques align with MITRE ATT&CK technique T1189 "Drive-by Compromise" under the Initial Access tactic, primarily targeting Windows, Linux, and macOS. This technique involves compromising websites frequented by a specific target community to exploit client-side software vulnerabilities. Attackers, such as APT17, inject malicious scripts or iFrames into these sites; when a user visits, scripts automatically execute to find and exploit vulnerable browser or plugin versions, often requiring user interaction like enabling scripts. Successful exploitation grants the adversary code execution on the victim's system, facilitating further network access.

This tactic falls under Initial Access. The technique involves compromising a website frequented by a specific target community (e.g., a particular industry or government sector) to host malicious code. When a user from the target group visits the site, scripts automatically execute to scan for and exploit vulnerabilities in the user's browser or plugins, potentially leading to code execution on the client system. This approach is used by numerous threat groups, including APT28, APT32, Lazarus Group, and Turla.

5508.name: stealing digital certificates
5508.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may buy and/or steal SSL/TLS certificates that can be used during targeting. SSL/TLS certificates are designed to instill trust. They include information about the key, information about its owner's identity, and the digital signature of an entity that has verified the certificate's contents are correct. If the signature is valid, and the person examining the certificate trusts the signer, then they know they can use that key to communicate with its owner.

Adversaries may purchase or steal SSL/TLS certificates to further their operations, such as encrypting C2 traffic (ex: [Asymmetric Cryptography](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1573/002) with [Web Protocols](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1071/001)) or even enabling [Adversary-in-the-Middle](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1557) if the certificate is trusted or otherwise added to the root of trust (i.e. [Install Root Certificate](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1553/004)). The purchase of digital certificates may be done using a front organization or using information stolen from a previously compromised entity that allows the adversary to validate to a certificate provider as that entity. Adversaries may also steal certificate materials directly from a compromised third-party, including from certificate authorities.(Citation: DiginotarCompromise) Adversaries may register or hijack domains that they will later purchase an SSL/TLS certificate for.

Certificate authorities exist that allow adversaries to acquire SSL/TLS certificates, such as domain validation certificates, for free.(Citation: Let's Encrypt FAQ)

After obtaining a digital certificate, an adversary may then install that certificate (see [Install Digital Certificate](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1608/003)) on infrastructure under their control.
5508.profile: [profile]Stealing Digital Certificates is a technique under MITRE ATT&CK ID T1588.004, categorized under Resource Development. It involves adversaries purchasing or stealing SSL/TLS certificates to enable operations like encrypting command and control traffic or facilitating adversary-in-the-middle attacks. Certificates can be acquired through front organizations, by using stolen validation information, by directly compromising certificate authorities, or by using free services like Let's Encrypt. Groups such as Sea Turtle, Lazarus Group, and UNC3886 have been associated with this activity. The obtained certificates are subsequently installed on controlled infrastructure.[/profile]
5508.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Stealing Digital Certificates is a technique adversaries use to acquire SSL/TLS or authentication certificates for malicious purposes. This can involve stealing certificates directly from compromised systems, such as from encrypted storage in the Windows Registry, misplaced files, or via crypto APIs from the certificate store. Stolen certificates can be used to encrypt command and control traffic, lend credibility to phishing sites, enable adversary-in-the-middle attacks, or be used as authentication material for lateral movement and persistence, effectively acting as valid accounts for the certificate's duration.

5510.name: target identification and general reconnaissance activities
5510.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may put in place resources that are referenced by a link that can be used during targeting. An adversary may rely upon a user clicking a malicious link in order to divulge information (including credentials) or to gain execution, as in [Malicious Link](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/001). Links can be used for spearphishing, such as sending an email accompanied by social engineering text to coax the user to actively click or copy and paste a URL into a browser. Prior to a phish for information (as in [Spearphishing Link](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1598/003)) or a phish to gain initial access to a system (as in [Spearphishing Link](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/002)), an adversary must set up the resources for a link target for the spearphishing link. 

Typically, the resources for a link target will be an HTML page that may include some client-side script such as [JavaScript](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/007) to decide what content to serve to the user. Adversaries may clone legitimate sites to serve as the link target, this can include cloning of login pages of legitimate web services or organization login pages in an effort to harvest credentials during [Spearphishing Link](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1598/003).(Citation: Malwarebytes Silent Librarian October 2020)(Citation: Proofpoint TA407 September 2019) Adversaries may also [Upload Malware](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1608/001) and have the link target point to malware for download/execution by the user.

Adversaries may purchase domains similar to legitimate domains (ex: homoglyphs, typosquatting, different top-level domain, etc.) during acquisition of infrastructure ([Domains](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1583/001)) to help facilitate [Malicious Link](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/001).

Links can be written by adversaries to mask the true destination in order to deceive victims by abusing the URL schema and increasing the effectiveness of phishing.(Citation: Kaspersky-masking)(Citation: mandiant-masking)

Adversaries may also use free or paid accounts on link shortening services and Platform-as-a-Service providers to host link targets while taking advantage of the widely trusted domains of those providers to avoid being blocked while redirecting victims to malicious pages.(Citation: Netskope GCP Redirection)(Citation: Netskope Cloud Phishing)(Citation: Intezer App Service Phishing)(Citation: Cofense-redirect) In addition, adversaries may serve a variety of malicious links through uniquely generated URIs/URLs (including one-time, single use links).(Citation: iOS URL Scheme)(Citation: URI)(Citation: URI Use)(Citation: URI Unique) Finally, adversaries may take advantage of the decentralized nature of the InterPlanetary File System (IPFS) to host link targets that are difficult to remove.(Citation: Talos IPFS 2022)
5510.profile: [profile]Link Target (T1608.005) is a Resource Development technique where adversaries establish infrastructure for malicious links used in spearphishing. This involves creating HTML pages, often with client-side scripts, to host credential harvesting clones of legitimate sites or to serve malware. Adversaries may use deceptive domains, URL masking, link shortening services, Platform-as-a-Service providers, or the InterPlanetary File System (IPFS) to host resilient and evasive link targets, as employed by groups like Silent Librarian, FIN7, and LuminousMoth.

5525.name: evasion techniques
5525.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may employ various means to detect and avoid debuggers. Debuggers are typically used by defenders to trace and/or analyze the execution of potential malware payloads.(Citation: ProcessHacker Github) Debugger evasion may include changing behaviors based on the results of the checks for the presence of artifacts indicative of a debugged environment. Similar to [Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1497), if the adversary detects a debugger, they may alter their malware to disengage from the victim or conceal the core functions of the implant. They may also search for debugger artifacts before dropping secondary or additional payloads. Specific checks will vary based on the target and/or adversary. On Windows, this may involve [Native API](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1106) function calls such as IsDebuggerPresent() and NtQueryInformationProcess(), or manually checking the BeingDebugged flag of the Process Environment Block (PEB). On Linux, this may involve querying `/proc/self/status` for the `TracerPID` field, which indicates whether or not the process is being traced by dynamic analysis tools.(Citation: Cado Security P2PInfect 2023)(Citation: Positive Technologies Hellhounds 2023) Other checks for debugging artifacts may also seek to enumerate hardware breakpoints, interrupt assembly opcodes, time checks, or measurements if exceptions are raised in the current process (assuming a present debugger would “swallow” or handle the potential error).(Citation: hasherezade debug)(Citation: AlKhaser Debug)(Citation: vxunderground debug) Malware may also leverage Structured Exception Handling (SEH) to detect debuggers by throwing an exception and detecting whether the process is suspended. SEH handles both hardware and software expectations, providing control over the exceptions including support for debugging. If a debugger is present, the program’s control will be transferred to the debugger, and the execution of the code will be suspended. If the debugger is not present, control will be transferred to the SEH handler, which will automatically handle the exception and allow the program’s execution to continue.(Citation: Apriorit) Adversaries may use the information learned from these debugger checks during automated discovery to shape follow-on behaviors. Debuggers can also be evaded by detaching the process or flooding debug logs with meaningless data via messages produced by looping [Native API](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1106) function calls such as OutputDebugStringW().(Citation: wardle evilquest partii)(Citation: Checkpoint Dridex Jan 2021)
5525.profile: [profile]Debugger Evasion is a Defense Evasion technique (MITRE ATT&CK T1622) applicable to Windows and Linux platforms. It involves detecting debugger presence to alter malware behavior, using checks like Windows API calls (IsDebuggerPresent, NtQueryInformationProcess), inspecting the PEB's BeingDebugged flag, or querying Linux's /proc/self/status for TracerPID. Other methods include leveraging Structured Exception Handling (SEH) to test for process suspension or flooding debug logs with OutputDebugStringW calls. The technique is used by groups like Mustang Panda and APT17.[/profile]
5525.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "evasion techniques" is a broad category of adversary behaviors for avoiding detection and analysis, not a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the retrieved context, it encompasses methods like checking for debuggers using APIs such as `IsDebuggerPresent()` or querying `/proc/self/status`, detecting virtual machine or sandbox artifacts, and modifying malicious tools to remove detected indicators like file signatures. These techniques are employed by groups such as Mustang Panda, APT28, and OilRig to bypass security controls and analysis environments.

Based on the retrieved information, it is associated with specific techniques for evading detection on Linux systems. Technique T1036.011, "Overwrite Process Arguments," describes adversaries overwriting a process's in-memory `argv[0]` with null bytes and then a spoofed benign command string (e.g., `cat resolv.conf`) to manipulate its appearance in `/proc/<PID>/cmdline` and tools like `ps`.

5549.name: Code Signing Abuse
5549.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may create, acquire, or steal code signing materials to sign their malware or tools. Code signing provides a level of authenticity on a binary from the developer and a guarantee that the binary has not been tampered with. (Citation: Wikipedia Code Signing) The certificates used during an operation may be created, acquired, or stolen by the adversary. (Citation: Securelist Digital Certificates) (Citation: Symantec Digital Certificates) Unlike [Invalid Code Signature](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1036/001), this activity will result in a valid signature.

Code signing to verify software on first run can be used on modern Windows and macOS systems. It is not used on Linux due to the decentralized nature of the platform. (Citation: Wikipedia Code Signing)(Citation: EclecticLightChecksonEXECodeSigning)

Code signing certificates may be used to bypass security policies that require signed code to execute on a system.
5549.profile: [profile]Code Signing Abuse, identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1553.002 under the Defense Evasion tactic, primarily targets Windows and macOS platforms. Adversaries create, acquire, or steal legitimate code signing certificates to digitally sign their malware, producing a valid signature that bypasses security policies requiring signed code for execution. This technique is distinct from using invalid signatures and is leveraged by numerous threat groups including Lazarus Group, FIN7, and Wizard Spider to enhance the perceived legitimacy of their tools.
5549.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Code Signing Abuse is a technique where adversaries misuse code signing to lend malicious software a false appearance of legitimacy. It aligns with the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1553.002 (Sub-technique of Subvert Trust Controls) under the Defense Evasion tactic and primarily targets Windows and macOS platforms. The core mechanics involve adversaries creating, stealing, or purchasing valid code signing certificates to digitally sign their malware, thereby bypassing security policies that require signed code to execute and increasing the likelihood of evading detection by users and security tools. This activity is distinct from using invalid signatures and is a common practice among numerous threat groups.

These scans may also include more broad attempts to [Gather Victim Host Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1592) that can be used to identify more commonly known, exploitable vulnerabilities. Vulnerability scans typically harvest running software and version numbers via server banners, listening ports, or other network artifacts.(Citation: OWASP Vuln Scanning) Information from these scans may reveal opportunities for other forms of reconnaissance (ex: [Search Open Websites/Domains](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1593) or [Search Open Technical Databases](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1596)), establishing operational resources (ex: [Develop Capabilities](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1587) or [Obtain Capabilities](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1588)), and/or initial access (ex: [Exploit Public-Facing Application](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1190)).

The retrieved information on exploitation techniques (T1211, T1499.004, T1190) describes distinct, subsequent actions for defense evasion, denial-of-service, or initial access and should not be conflated with the scanning activity. 5559.name: Bypass Authentication
5559.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may modify file attributes and subvert Gatekeeper functionality to evade user prompts and execute untrusted programs. Gatekeeper is a set of technologies that act as layer of Apple’s security model to ensure only trusted applications are executed on a host. Gatekeeper was built on top of File Quarantine in Snow Leopard (10.6, 2009) and has grown to include Code Signing, security policy compliance, Notarization, and more. Gatekeeper also treats applications running for the first time differently than reopened applications.(Citation: TheEclecticLightCompany Quarantine and the flag)(Citation: TheEclecticLightCompany apple notarization )

Based on an opt-in system, when files are downloaded an extended attribute (xattr) called `com.apple.quarantine` (also known as a quarantine flag) can be set on the file by the application performing the download. Launch Services opens the application in a suspended state. For first run applications with the quarantine flag set, Gatekeeper executes the following functions:

1. Checks extended attribute – Gatekeeper checks for the quarantine flag, then provides an alert prompt to the user to allow or deny execution.(Citation: OceanLotus for OS X)(Citation: 20 macOS Common Tools and Techniques)

2. Checks System Policies - Gatekeeper checks the system security policy, allowing execution of apps downloaded from either just the App Store or the App Store and identified developers.

3. Code Signing – Gatekeeper checks for a valid code signature from an Apple Developer ID.

4. Notarization - Using the `api.apple-cloudkit.com` API, Gatekeeper reaches out to Apple servers to verify or pull down the notarization ticket and ensure the ticket is not revoked. Users can override notarization, which will result in a prompt of executing an “unauthorized app” and the security policy will be modified.

Adversaries can subvert one or multiple security controls within Gatekeeper checks through logic errors (e.g. [Exploitation for Defense Evasion](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1211)), unchecked file types, and external libraries. For example, prior to macOS 13 Ventura, code signing and notarization checks were only conducted on first launch, allowing adversaries to write malicious executables to previously opened applications in order to bypass Gatekeeper security checks.(Citation: theevilbit gatekeeper bypass 2021)(Citation: Application Bundle Manipulation Brandon Dalton)

Applications and files loaded onto the system from a USB flash drive, optical disk, external hard drive, from a drive shared over the local network, or using the curl command may not set the quarantine flag. Additionally, it is possible to avoid setting the quarantine flag using [Drive-by Compromise](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1189).
5559.profile: [profile]Gatekeeper Bypass, identified as T1553.001 under the Defense Evasion tactic for macOS, involves subverting Apple's Gatekeeper security controls to execute untrusted programs. Adversaries bypass user prompts and checks by manipulating file attributes, exploiting logic errors, or targeting unchecked file types. Specific methods include removing the 'com.apple.quarantine' extended attribute, writing malicious executables into previously opened applications to avoid code signing and notarization checks on first launch (prior to macOS 13), or delivering files via methods like USB drives or curl that do not set the quarantine flag initially.[/profile]
5559.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Bypass Authentication is a technique used in the Defense Evasion tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. It involves circumventing standard authentication mechanisms to gain unauthorized access without valid credentials. This can be achieved by exploiting logic errors in security checks, modifying authentication packages or PAM modules to accept adversary-supplied values, or stealing and reusing alternate authentication material like password hashes or Kerberos tickets. Specific methods include patching domain controller processes (e.g., Skeleton Key malware) or forcing systems to automatically transmit credential hashes via protocols like SMB.

5560.name: Data from Local System
5560.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may search local system sources, such as file systems, configuration files, local databases, virtual machine files, or process memory, to find files of interest and sensitive data prior to Exfiltration.

Adversaries may do this using a [Command and Scripting Interpreter](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059), such as [cmd](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0106) as well as a [Network Device CLI](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/008), which have functionality to interact with the file system to gather information.(Citation: show_run_config_cmd_cisco) Adversaries may also use [Automated Collection](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1119) on the local system.
5560.profile: [profile]Data from Local System is technique T1005 under the Collection tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. Adversaries search local sources like file systems, configuration files, databases, virtual machine files, and process memory to find sensitive data before exfiltration. This is commonly executed using command-line interpreters like cmd or a Network Device CLI, which interact with the file system, and may involve automated collection scripts. It is a precursor to staging data locally and is associated with numerous threat groups including APT28, Lazarus Group, and FIN7.
5560.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Data from Local System, identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1005 under the Collection tactic, targets Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. This technique involves adversaries searching local system sources like file systems, configuration files, local databases, virtual machine files, and process memory to find sensitive data for exfiltration. Execution is commonly performed using command-line interpreters like cmd or bash, or through automated collection scripts, to interact with and gather data from these local repositories.

5561.name: File and Directory Discovery
5561.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may enumerate files and directories or may search in specific locations of a host or network share for certain information within a file system. Adversaries may use the information from [File and Directory Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1083) during automated discovery to shape follow-on behaviors, including whether or not the adversary fully infects the target and/or attempts specific actions. Many command shell utilities can be used to obtain this information. Examples include dir, tree, ls, find, and locate.(Citation: Windows Commands JPCERT) Custom tools may also be used to gather file and directory information and interact with the [Native API](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1106). Adversaries may also leverage a [Network Device CLI](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/008) on network devices to gather file and directory information (e.g. dir, show flash, and/or nvram).(Citation: US-CERT-TA18-106A) Some files and directories may require elevated or specific user permissions to access.
5561.profile: [profile]File and Directory Discovery (T1083) is a Discovery tactic technique used across Windows, Linux, and Mac platforms. It involves adversaries enumerating files and directories on a host or network share using common command shell utilities like `dir`, `tree`, `ls`, `find`, and `locate`, or custom tools interacting with the Native API. It is also performed via Network Device CLI commands such as `show flash` or `nvram`. The gathered information shapes follow-on attack behaviors and is associated with numerous threat groups including APT28, Lazarus Group, and Volt Typhoon.[/profile]
5561.profile_without_enhance: [profile]File and Directory Discovery is technique T1083 under the Discovery tactic, applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves adversaries enumerating files and directories to gather information about a system's file system, often using common command shell utilities like `dir`, `tree`, `ls`, `find`, and `locate`. This reconnaissance can be performed via a Network Device CLI with commands such as `show flash` or `nvram` and is used to inform subsequent malicious actions.

5565.name: Cookie and HTTP header authentication-aware web shells
5565.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries can use stolen session cookies to authenticate to web applications and services. This technique bypasses some multi-factor authentication protocols since the session is already authenticated.(Citation: Pass The Cookie)

Authentication cookies are commonly used in web applications, including cloud-based services, after a user has authenticated to the service so credentials are not passed and re-authentication does not need to occur as frequently. Cookies are often valid for an extended period of time, even if the web application is not actively used. After the cookie is obtained through [Steal Web Session Cookie](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539) or [Web Cookies](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1606/001), the adversary may then import the cookie into a browser they control and is then able to use the site or application as the user for as long as the session cookie is active. Once logged into the site, an adversary can access sensitive information, read email, or perform actions that the victim account has permissions to perform.

There have been examples of malware targeting session cookies to bypass multi-factor authentication systems.(Citation: Unit 42 Mac Crypto Cookies January 2019)
5565.profile: [profile]The entity "Cookie and HTTP header authentication-aware web shells" is a technique for maintaining access to compromised web servers. It aligns with MITRE ATT&CK technique T1505.003 (Web Shell) under the Persistence tactic, primarily targeting Web Servers. This method involves deploying a web shell script on a server that is specifically designed to recognize and utilize stolen session cookies or forged HTTP authentication headers for authentication, allowing adversaries to bypass standard credential checks and maintain persistent, authenticated access to the web application or service. The intrusion-set DeepPanda has been associated with this activity.
5565.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Cookie and HTTP header authentication-aware web shells, aligned with MITRE ATT&CK technique T1505.003 under the Persistence tactic, target web platforms. These specialized web shells are designed to extract and utilize authentication tokens, such as session cookies or HTTP headers, from incoming requests to the server. This allows the shell to operate within the context of an authenticated user session, effectively bypassing standard authentication mechanisms and maintaining covert, persistent access to the compromised web server.

5566.name: gain a persistent foothold
5566.profile: [profile]The entity "gain a persistent foothold" is a high-level adversary objective, not a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique with a T-ID. It is associated with the intrusion-set DeepPanda. The objective is achieved through various techniques to maintain long-term access, such as acquiring existing system access from brokers (T1650), creating new accounts (T1136), and employing exclusive control measures like patching vulnerabilities or removing competing malware to ensure sole, undetected persistence on a compromised network.
5566.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "gain a persistent foothold" is a general adversarial objective, not a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique with a standard ID. Based on related content, it describes the goal of maintaining long-term access to a compromised system. This can be achieved through various specific techniques, such as acquiring existing access from broker networks, creating new accounts, or hindering other threat actors to maintain exclusive control. The overarching purpose is to establish a reliable base for later stages of an attack.

5567.name: Kernel-Mode Driver
5567.profile: [profile]Kernel-Mode Driver is a malicious driver utilized by threat actors like DeepPanda, GhostEmperor, PurpleFox, and TrickBot-associated groups (TA505, UNC1878, Wizard Spider). Its key technical behavior is to gain kernel-mode execution privileges, often exploiting signed or revoked certificates to bypass Kernel-Mode Code Signing (KMCS) enforcement on Windows. It enables arbitrary code execution in kernel space for persistence and evasion, as seen with components like RwDrv.sys.
5567.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Kernel-Mode Driver is a malicious software component, also referenced by aliases such as RwDrv.sys. It is attributed to groups including TA505, UNC1878, and Wizard Spider. Key TTPs involve abusing Windows kernel-mode code signing (KMCS) mechanisms to load drivers signed by revoked certificates, enabling privilege escalation and direct access to system memory and process address spaces. It targets the Windows operating system platform, specifically exploiting performance and backward compatibility features to execute unsigned or improperly signed kernel-mode drivers on 64-bit systems.

5568.name: Remote Access Tool (RAT)
5568.uncertain_mes:
An adversary may use legitimate remote access tools to establish an interactive command and control channel within a network. Remote access tools create a session between two trusted hosts through a graphical interface, a command line interaction, a protocol tunnel via development or management software, or hardware-level access such as KVM (Keyboard, Video, Mouse) over IP solutions. Desktop support software (usually graphical interface) and remote management software (typically command line interface) allow a user to control a computer remotely as if they are a local user inheriting the user or software permissions. This software is commonly used for troubleshooting, software installation, and system management.(Citation: Symantec Living off the Land)(Citation: CrowdStrike 2015 Global Threat Report)(Citation: CrySyS Blog TeamSpy) Adversaries may similarly abuse response features included in EDR and other defensive tools that enable remote access.

Remote access tools may be installed and used post-compromise as an alternate communications channel for redundant access or to establish an interactive remote desktop session with the target system. It may also be used as a malware component to establish a reverse connection or back-connect to a service or adversary-controlled system.

Installation of many remote access tools may also include persistence (e.g., the software's installation routine creates a [Windows Service](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1543/003)). Remote access modules/features may also exist as part of otherwise existing software (e.g., Google Chrome’s Remote Desktop).(Citation: Google Chrome Remote Desktop)(Citation: Chrome Remote Desktop)
5568.profile: [profile]Remote Access Tool (RAT) maps to MITRE ATT&CK technique T1219 under the Command and Control tactic, applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves adversaries using legitimate remote administration software like TeamViewer, AnyDesk, or Chrome Remote Desktop to establish interactive C2 channels, often granting local user-level control for remote system management. These tools can be installed post-compromise to create persistent backdoors, sometimes via Windows Services, and are used by groups like Carbanak and MuddyWater for redundant access and lateral movement within a network.
5568.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Remote Access Tool (RAT)" aligns with MITRE ATT&CK technique T1219 (Remote Access Software) under the Command and Control tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It involves using legitimate remote access software to establish an interactive command and control channel, often creating a session that allows control of a computer as if a local user. These tools can be installed post-compromise for persistent access, may include features for redundant communication, and are frequently used by threat actors like Carbanak and MuddyWater to support lateral movement and maintain presence.

5569.name: Initial Access
5569.profile: [profile]Initial Access is the MITRE ATT&CK tactic (TA0001) encompassing techniques adversaries use to gain their first foothold within a network. This includes methods like purchasing access from brokers, using stolen application tokens to bypass authentication, or deploying remote access tools to establish command and control. Groups such as DeepPanda and Turla employ this tactic, often utilizing malware like malicious DLLs to establish persistence after initial entry.[/profile]
5569.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Initial Access is not a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique but a high-level tactic (TA0001) encompassing various methods to gain the first foothold in a network. Based on retrieved information, this includes purchasing compromised access from brokers (T1650), using stolen application tokens (T1527) to bypass authentication, establishing remote access via legitimate tools (T1219), and creating or abusing local accounts (T1078.003, T1136) for persistent entry. The goal is to establish any form of initial presence, often leveraging external services, credentials, or backdoors.

5570.name: Data Obfuscation
5570.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may obfuscate command and control traffic to make it more difficult to detect.(Citation: Bitdefender FunnyDream Campaign November 2020) Command and control (C2) communications are hidden (but not necessarily encrypted) in an attempt to make the content more difficult to discover or decipher and to make the communication less conspicuous and hide commands from being seen. This encompasses many methods, such as adding junk data to protocol traffic, using steganography, or impersonating legitimate protocols.
5570.profile: [profile]Data Obfuscation, identified as T1001 under the Command and Control tactic, is a technique where adversaries hide C2 communications to evade detection, though not necessarily through encryption. Specific methods include adding junk data to protocol traffic, using steganography, or impersonating legitimate protocols. It has been associated with groups like Gamaredon.[/profile]
5570.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Data Obfuscation is a technique for hiding malicious data or commands to evade detection. It is not a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique but is a core concept within several. It can be applied to data at rest or in transit, such as through command-line obfuscation using syntax tricks, string splitting, and encoding (e.g., base64) to make analysis difficult, or by compressing and encrypting collected data prior to exfiltration to conceal its content. This practice is commonly used by threat actors during post-exploitation activities.[/profile]

5571.name: Log Cleardown
5571.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may enumerate system and service logs to find useful data. These logs may highlight various types of valuable insights for an adversary, such as user authentication records ([Account Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1087)), security or vulnerable software ([Software Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1518)), or hosts within a compromised network ([Remote System Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1018)).

Host binaries may be leveraged to collect system logs. Examples include using `wevtutil.exe` or [PowerShell](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001) on Windows to access and/or export security event information.(Citation: WithSecure Lazarus-NoPineapple Threat Intel Report 2023)(Citation: Cadet Blizzard emerges as novel threat actor) In cloud environments, adversaries may leverage utilities such as the Azure VM Agent’s `CollectGuestLogs.exe` to collect security logs from cloud hosted infrastructure.(Citation: SIM Swapping and Abuse of the Microsoft Azure Serial Console)

Adversaries may also target centralized logging infrastructure such as SIEMs. Logs may also be bulk exported and sent to adversary-controlled infrastructure for offline analysis.

In addition to gaining a better understanding of the environment, adversaries may also monitor logs in real time to track incident response procedures. This may allow them to adjust their techniques in order to maintain persistence or evade defenses.(Citation: Permiso GUI-Vil 2023)
5571.profile: [profile]The entity "Log Cleardown" is likely a reference to the MITRE ATT&CK technique "Indicator Removal: Clear Windows Event Logs" (T1070.001), falling under the Defense Evasion tactic on Windows platforms. This technique involves adversaries clearing Windows Event Logs to hide intrusion evidence, often using administrator privileges to execute commands like `wevtutil cl security` or PowerShell's `Remove-EventLog`. It is associated with threat groups including Volt Typhoon, APT38, and Aquatic Panda.
5571.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Log Cleardown is a technique for clearing system logs to hide intrusion evidence, aligning with MITRE ATT&CK sub-techniques T1070.001 (Clear Windows Event Logs) and T1070.002 (Clear Linux or Mac System Logs) under the Defense Evasion tactic for platforms including Windows, Linux, and macOS. Technical mechanics involve using utilities like `wevtutil cl` on Windows to clear System, Application, or Security logs, or deleting files in `C:\Windows\System32\winevt\logs\`, and on Linux/macOS, targeting log files in directories like `/var/log/`. This is often performed using post-exploitation tools.[/profile]

5572.name: Heartbeat/Keep-Alive
5572.profile: [profile]Heartbeat/Keep-Alive is a post-exploitation technique used by groups like DeepPanda to maintain command and control (C2) communication. It involves sending periodic signals from a compromised system to an adversary's server to confirm the system is still active and connected to the internet, ensuring the C2 channel remains open for ongoing malicious activity.
5572.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Heartbeat/Keep-Alive is a technique used to maintain a connection with a command and control (C2) server, ensuring the compromised system remains accessible for further instructions. It is often implemented by malware or post-exploitation tools to send regular, small packets of data, preventing the connection from timing out and allowing adversaries to persistently manage the infected host.[/profile]

5573.name: Anti-Debugging Technique
5573.profile: [profile]Anti-Debugging Technique is a Defense Evasion technique. It involves malware checking for artifacts of a debugged environment to alter its behavior or evade analysis. Specific mechanics include using Windows API calls like `IsDebuggerPresent()` or checking the `BeingDebugged` flag in the PEB, querying `/proc/self/status` on Linux for the `TracerPID` field, or leveraging Structured Exception Handling (SEH) to detect if a debugger handles an exception. It is associated with groups like Mustang Panda.
5573.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Anti-Debugging Technique" aligns with MITRE ATT&CK technique Debugger Evasion (T1622) under the Defense Evasion tactic. It involves detecting and avoiding debuggers to hinder analysis. Specific technical mechanics include using API calls like IsDebuggerPresent() on Windows, querying /proc/self/status on Linux, checking the PEB's BeingDebugged flag, leveraging Structured Exception Handling (SEH), and flooding debug logs with data via OutputDebugStringW() to evade detection.

5574.name: NSI Hook
5574.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may use a Login Hook to establish persistence executed upon user logon. A login hook is a plist file that points to a specific script to execute with root privileges upon user logon. The plist file is located in the /Library/Preferences/com.apple.loginwindow.plist file and can be modified using the defaults command-line utility. This behavior is the same for logout hooks where a script can be executed upon user logout. All hooks require administrator permissions to modify or create hooks.(Citation: Login Scripts Apple Dev)(Citation: LoginWindowScripts Apple Dev) Adversaries can add or insert a path to a malicious script in the com.apple.loginwindow.plist file, using the LoginHook or LogoutHook key-value pair. The malicious script is executed upon the next user login. If a login hook already exists, adversaries can add additional commands to an existing login hook. There can be only one login and logout hook on a system at a time.(Citation: S1 macOs Persistence)(Citation: Wardle Persistence Chapter) **Note:** Login hooks were deprecated in 10.11 version of macOS in favor of [Launch Daemon](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1543/004) and [Launch Agent](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1543/001)
5574.profile: [profile]Login Hook, designated as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1037.002 under the Boot or Logon Initialization Scripts tactic, is a macOS persistence mechanism. Adversaries with administrator privileges modify the /Library/Preferences/com.apple.loginwindow.plist file using the `defaults` utility, inserting a path to a malicious script via the `LoginHook` or `LogoutHook` key to execute it with root privileges upon user logon or logout. This technique was deprecated in macOS 10.11 in favor of Launch Daemon and Launch Agent methods.[/profile]
5574.profile_without_enhance: [profile]NSI Hook is a macOS-specific persistence technique, analogous to MITRE ATT&CK's Login Hook (T1037.002) under the Persistence tactic. It operates by modifying the system's loginwindow plist file, specifically the /Library/Preferences/com.apple.loginwindow.plist, using the defaults command-line utility to insert a path to a malicious script via the LoginHook key-value pair. This script then executes with root privileges upon subsequent user logins, requiring administrator permissions to implement.

5575.name: TCP Hooking
5575.uncertain_mes:
Windows processes often leverage application programming interface (API) functions to perform tasks that require reusable system resources. Windows API functions are typically stored in dynamic-link libraries (DLLs) as exported functions. 

Hooking involves redirecting calls to these functions and can be implemented via:

* **Hooks procedures**, which intercept and execute designated code in response to events such as messages, keystrokes, and mouse inputs. (Citation: Microsoft Hook Overview) (Citation: Elastic Process Injection July 2017)
* **Import address table (IAT) hooking**, which use modifications to a process’s IAT, where pointers to imported API functions are stored. (Citation: Elastic Process Injection July 2017) (Citation: Adlice Software IAT Hooks Oct 2014) (Citation: MWRInfoSecurity Dynamic Hooking 2015)
* **Inline hooking**, which overwrites the first bytes in an API function to redirect code flow. (Citation: Elastic Process Injection July 2017) (Citation: HighTech Bridge Inline Hooking Sept 2011) (Citation: MWRInfoSecurity Dynamic Hooking 2015)

Similar to [Process Injection](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1055), adversaries may use hooking to load and execute malicious code within the context of another process, masking the execution while also allowing access to the process's memory and possibly elevated privileges. Installing hooking mechanisms may also provide Persistence via continuous invocation when the functions are called through normal use.

Malicious hooking mechanisms may also capture API calls that include parameters that reveal user authentication credentials for Credential Access. (Citation: Microsoft TrojanSpy:Win32/Ursnif.gen!I Sept 2017)

Hooking is commonly utilized by [Rootkit](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1014)s to conceal files, processes, Registry keys, and other objects in order to hide malware and associated behaviors. (Citation: Symantec Windows Rootkits)
5575.profile: [profile]TCP Hooking is a technique aligned with MITRE ATT&CK ID T1179 under the Defense Evasion tactic, primarily targeting Windows. It involves intercepting and redirecting TCP-related API calls through methods like hook procedures, Import Address Table (IAT) hooking, or inline hooking to execute malicious code within a legitimate process, thereby masking activity, enabling persistence, and facilitating credential theft by capturing authentication parameters from network API calls. The intrusion-set DeepPanda has been associated with its use.[/profile]
5575.profile_without_enhance: [profile]TCP Hooking is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the context, it is a specific application of the general Hooking technique (T1179) to TCP network functions. It likely involves intercepting or redirecting TCP API calls or socket operations, such as `connect`, `send`, or `recv`, to manipulate network traffic, hide malicious connections, or exfiltrate data. This can be implemented via inline hooking or IAT hooking within a process, allowing adversaries to mask command and control activity or credential theft by monitoring network-related function parameters.

5576.name: Network Stack Hook
5576.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may use a Login Hook to establish persistence executed upon user logon. A login hook is a plist file that points to a specific script to execute with root privileges upon user logon. The plist file is located in the /Library/Preferences/com.apple.loginwindow.plist file and can be modified using the defaults command-line utility. This behavior is the same for logout hooks where a script can be executed upon user logout. All hooks require administrator permissions to modify or create hooks.(Citation: Login Scripts Apple Dev)(Citation: LoginWindowScripts Apple Dev) Adversaries can add or insert a path to a malicious script in the com.apple.loginwindow.plist file, using the LoginHook or LogoutHook key-value pair. The malicious script is executed upon the next user login. If a login hook already exists, adversaries can add additional commands to an existing login hook. There can be only one login and logout hook on a system at a time.(Citation: S1 macOs Persistence)(Citation: Wardle Persistence Chapter) **Note:** Login hooks were deprecated in 10.11 version of macOS in favor of [Launch Daemon](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1543/004) and [Launch Agent](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1543/001)
5576.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique Login Hook (T1037.002) under the Persistence tactic for macOS. It involves adversaries modifying the plist file at /Library/Preferences/com.apple.loginwindow.plist using the defaults command-line utility to insert a LoginHook or LogoutHook key-value pair pointing to a malicious script, which executes with root privileges upon the next user logon or logout. 5576.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Network Stack Hook is a technique where adversaries attach filters to a network socket to monitor traffic and trigger malicious actions, such as activating a backdoor for persistence or command and control. With elevated permissions, they use libraries like `libpcap` or `WinPcap` and functions like `pcap_setfilter` or `setsockopt` with `SO_ATTACH_FILTER` to install a filter on a raw socket. This filter inspects incoming packets; when a packet matching specific criteria is received, it can trigger the execution of a payload, like a reverse shell, making detection difficult due to low resource usage and passive network monitoring.

5577.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Kernel Call Table Hooking is a technique where adversaries redirect calls to kernel-level system functions by modifying the kernel call table, often to conceal malicious activity. This is a form of kernel-mode rootkit behavior used for Defense Evasion and Persistence, primarily on Windows and Linux platforms. The technique involves overwriting function pointers in the system call table to intercept and potentially alter the behavior of operating system routines, allowing malware to hide processes, files, and network activity.

5596.name: Code Published by Edward Sun
5596.uncertain_mes: Data exfiltration is a technique used by malicious actors to carry out an unauthorized data transfer from a computer resource. Data exfiltration can be done remotely or locally and can be difficult to detect from normal network traffic.
5596.profile: [profile]The entity is a malware known as 'Code Published by Edward Sun' with the alias 'rising sun'. It is associated with the 'operation sharpshooter' group. Its primary function is data exfiltration, which involves unauthorized data transfers that can be executed remotely or locally and are difficult to distinguish from normal network traffic. The target platforms are unspecified. Infrastructure details include a potential link to a domain registration in Hong Kong under the name 'edward davis' with contact information such as the email 'ddggcc@189.cn' and phone number '+86.2029171680'.
5596.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Code Published by Edward Sun is a malware entity associated with the individual Edward Sun. It is linked to the 'rising sun' malware family, which is used for data exfiltration and has been associated with Operation Sharpshooter. The malware's infrastructure may involve domains registered to 'edward davis' in Hong Kong, with connections to groups including APT23, APT41, APT17, Dagger Panda, Earth Lusca, Tonto Team, and Wet Panda.[/profile]

5597.name: Code Modification
5597.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may modify code signing policies to enable execution of unsigned or self-signed code. Code signing provides a level of authenticity on a program from a developer and a guarantee that the program has not been tampered with. Security controls can include enforcement mechanisms to ensure that only valid, signed code can be run on an operating system. Some of these security controls may be enabled by default, such as Driver Signature Enforcement (DSE) on Windows or System Integrity Protection (SIP) on macOS.(Citation: Microsoft DSE June 2017)(Citation: Apple Disable SIP) Other such controls may be disabled by default but are configurable through application controls, such as only allowing signed Dynamic-Link Libraries (DLLs) to execute on a system. Since it can be useful for developers to modify default signature enforcement policies during the development and testing of applications, disabling of these features may be possible with elevated permissions.(Citation: Microsoft Unsigned Driver Apr 2017)(Citation: Apple Disable SIP) Adversaries may modify code signing policies in a number of ways, including through use of command-line or GUI utilities, [Modify Registry](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1112), rebooting the computer in a debug/recovery mode, or by altering the value of variables in kernel memory.(Citation: Microsoft TESTSIGNING Feb 2021)(Citation: Apple Disable SIP)(Citation: FireEye HIKIT Rootkit Part 2)(Citation: GitHub Turla Driver Loader) Examples of commands that can modify the code signing policy of a system include bcdedit.exe -set TESTSIGNING ON on Windows and csrutil disable on macOS.(Citation: Microsoft TESTSIGNING Feb 2021)(Citation: Apple Disable SIP) Depending on the implementation, successful modification of a signing policy may require reboot of the compromised system. Additionally, some implementations can introduce visible artifacts for the user (ex: a watermark in the corner of the screen stating the system is in Test Mode). Adversaries may attempt to remove such artifacts.(Citation: F-Secure BlackEnergy 2014) To gain access to kernel memory to modify variables related to signature checks, such as modifying g_CiOptions to disable Driver Signature Enforcement, adversaries may conduct [Exploitation for Privilege Escalation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1068) using a signed, but vulnerable driver.(Citation: Unit42 AcidBox June 2020)(Citation: GitHub Turla Driver Loader)
5597.profile: [profile]Code Signing Policy Modification, identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1553.006 under the Defense Evasion tactic, primarily targets Windows and macOS platforms. This technique involves adversaries altering system policies to bypass security controls that enforce code signature validation, enabling the execution of unsigned or self-signed code. Specific technical mechanics include using commands like `bcdedit.exe -set TESTSIGNING ON` on Windows or `csrutil disable` on macOS, modifying the Windows Registry, booting into debug/recovery modes, or directly manipulating kernel memory variables such as `g_CiOptions` to disable Driver Signature Enforcement, often requiring system reboot and sometimes leaving visible artifacts like a "Test Mode" watermark. It has been associated with groups like APT39 and Turla.[/profile]
5597.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Code Modification is a technique where adversaries alter legitimate code to achieve malicious objectives, such as bypassing security controls or enabling persistence. This can involve modifying scripts, binaries, or configuration files to change their intended behavior. The technique is associated with the Defense Evasion tactic, as it is used to subvert trust mechanisms and avoid detection by altering the code's signature or execution logic.

5598.name: Tool Repurposing
5598.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may buy, steal, or download software tools that can be used during targeting. Tools can be open or closed source, free or commercial. A tool can be used for malicious purposes by an adversary, but (unlike malware) were not intended to be used for those purposes (ex: [PsExec](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0029)). 

Adversaries may obtain tools to support their operations, including to support execution of post-compromise behaviors. Tools may also be leveraged for testing – for example, evaluating malware against commercial antivirus or endpoint detection and response (EDR) applications.(Citation: Forescout Conti Leaks 2022)(Citation: Sentinel Labs Top Tier Target 2025)

Tool acquisition may involve the procurement of commercial software licenses, including for red teaming tools such as Cobalt Strike. In addition to freely downloading or purchasing software, adversaries may steal software and/or software licenses from third-party entities (including other adversaries). Threat actors may also crack trial versions of software.(Citation: Recorded Future Beacon 2019)
5598.profile: [profile]Tool Repurposing, identified as T1588.002 within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, falls under the Resource Development tactic and is platform-agnostic. This technique involves adversaries acquiring legitimate software tools through purchase, theft, or download, which are then weaponized for malicious purposes despite not being inherently malicious. Examples include using tools like PsExec or red teaming software such as Cobalt Strike. Adversaries may obtain these tools to support post-compromise execution, testing against security software, or by cracking trial versions, with procurement methods including stealing licenses from other entities.
5598.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Tool Repurposing is a technique where adversaries use legitimate, non-malicious software tools for malicious purposes during targeting. These tools, such as PsExec, are acquired, uploaded to accessible infrastructure, and transferred into victim networks to support post-compromise execution and lateral movement. The technique involves leveraging inherent system utilities or web services for file transfer and may include modifying tools to evade detection by removing identifiable indicators.

5608.name: Extortion
5608.profile: [profile]Extortion is a financial theft technique (T1657) under the Impact tactic. It involves coercing victims into providing payment, often through ransomware operations where adversaries encrypt or exfiltrate data and then threaten to leak it unless a ransom is paid. This technique is associated with groups like DeepPanda and is frequently linked to data encryption and exfiltration activities to enable the extortion demands.
5608.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Extortion, designated T1657 within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, is an adversary objective under the Impact tactic. It is a technique used to coerce victims into providing payment, often by threatening to leak stolen data unless a ransom is paid. This tactic is commonly executed following data exfiltration and encryption, with adversaries using dedicated leak sites to distribute victim information to increase pressure. It is frequently associated with ransomware campaigns and groups like FIN13, Scattered Spider, and Akira.

5609.name: Fraud
5609.profile: [profile]Fraud is a technique used by adversaries for financial theft, often as the objective of campaigns like business email compromise (BEC) and ransomware extortion. It involves tactics such as compromising accounts to conduct unauthorized fund transfers, using impersonation to deceive victims into sending money to adversary-controlled accounts, and leveraging extortion after data encryption and exfiltration. This technique is associated with groups like DeepPanda and can serve to divert attention from other malicious goals like data destruction.
5609.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity 'Fraud' is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique; it is a broad concept. Based on the retrieved context, it is associated with the financial theft objective (T1657) within the Impact tactic. This involves adversaries using methods like extortion (e.g., ransomware), social engineering (e.g., business email compromise), and technical theft to steal monetary resources or deceive victims into transferring funds, often through compromised accounts or impersonation.

5610.name: Identity theft
5610.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may steal monetary resources from targets through extortion, social engineering, technical theft, or other methods aimed at their own financial gain at the expense of the availability of these resources for victims. Financial theft is the ultimate objective of several popular campaign types including extortion by ransomware,(Citation: FBI-ransomware) business email compromise (BEC) and fraud,(Citation: FBI-BEC) "pig butchering,"(Citation: wired-pig butchering) bank hacking,(Citation: DOJ-DPRK Heist) and exploiting cryptocurrency networks.(Citation: BBC-Ronin) 

Adversaries may [Compromise Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1586) to conduct unauthorized transfers of funds.(Citation: Internet crime report 2022) In the case of business email compromise or email fraud, an adversary may utilize [Impersonation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1656) of a trusted entity. Once the social engineering is successful, victims can be deceived into sending money to financial accounts controlled by an adversary.(Citation: FBI-BEC) This creates the potential for multiple victims (i.e., compromised accounts as well as the ultimate monetary loss) in incidents involving financial theft.(Citation: VEC)

Extortion by ransomware may occur, for example, when an adversary demands payment from a victim after [Data Encrypted for Impact](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1486) (Citation: NYT-Colonial) and [Exfiltration](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0010) of data, followed by threatening to leak sensitive data to the public unless payment is made to the adversary.(Citation: Mandiant-leaks) Adversaries may use dedicated leak sites to distribute victim data.(Citation: Crowdstrike-leaks)

Due to the potentially immense business impact of financial theft, an adversary may abuse the possibility of financial theft and seeking monetary gain to divert attention from their true goals such as [Data Destruction](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1485) and business disruption.(Citation: AP-NotPetya)
5610.profile: [profile]Financial Theft, designated as T1657 within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, is an Impact tactic executed across multiple platforms. The technique involves adversaries stealing monetary resources through methods like extortion via ransomware, business email compromise (BEC) fraud, and cryptocurrency exploitation. This is achieved by compromising accounts to conduct unauthorized fund transfers, utilizing impersonation in social engineering to deceive victims into sending money, and using dedicated leak sites to threaten data exposure for ransom. Associated groups include FIN13, Scattered Spider, and Akira.[/profile]
5610.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Identity theft is not a formally defined MITRE ATT&CK technique; it is a high-level adversarial objective. The retrieved information describes it as the theft of personal or financial identity information for fraudulent gain, often achieved through techniques like Impersonation (T1656) and Financial Theft (T1657). Common mechanics include social engineering, business email compromise, and credential theft to conduct unauthorized transactions or assume a victim's identity.

It involves creating and submitting fraudulent documents, such as falsified damage reports or medical bills, to insurance providers. This method can be used for financial gain, money laundering, or to fund other malicious operations, often relying on social engineering to support the false claims and avoid detection during the claims process.

5613.name: Create fake patients
5613.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may create an account to maintain access to victim systems.(Citation: Symantec WastedLocker June 2020) With a sufficient level of access, creating such accounts may be used to establish secondary credentialed access that do not require persistent remote access tools to be deployed on the system.

Accounts may be created on the local system or within a domain or cloud tenant. In cloud environments, adversaries may create accounts that only have access to specific services, which can reduce the chance of detection.
5613.profile: [profile]The entity aligns with the MITRE ATT&CK technique "Create Account" (T1136) under the Persistence tactic, applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves adversaries creating local, domain, or cloud accounts to establish secondary credentialed access, often using specific permissions to reduce detection. The technique is associated with groups like Scattered Spider, Indrik Spider, and Salt Typhoon, and can involve masquerading account names to appear benign, such as mimicking existing service accounts.[/profile]
5613.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Create fake patients is a technique used in social engineering or fraud, likely within the Initial Access or Persistence tactics, to establish illegitimate identities within a system, such as a healthcare database. This involves generating fabricated patient records or accounts, potentially to blend in with legitimate activity, masquerade as normal users, or create a foothold for further malicious actions. The method is analogous to creating fraudulent accounts in other domains to bypass security controls.

5614.name: Access internal systems
5614.uncertain_mes: An adversary may deface systems internal to an organization in an attempt to intimidate or mislead users, thus discrediting the integrity of the systems. This may take the form of modifications to internal websites or server login messages, or directly to user systems with the replacement of the desktop wallpaper.(Citation: Novetta Blockbuster)(Citation: Varonis) Disturbing or offensive images may be used as a part of [Internal Defacement](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1491/001) in order to cause user discomfort, or to pressure compliance with accompanying messages. Since internally defacing systems exposes an adversary's presence, it often takes place after other intrusion goals have been accomplished.(Citation: Novetta Blockbuster Destructive Malware)
5614.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1491.001, Internal Defacement, under the Impact tactic for multiple platforms. It involves adversaries modifying internal systems like websites, server login messages, or desktop wallpapers, often using disturbing images to intimidate users, discredit system integrity, and pressure compliance. This activity typically occurs after primary intrusion goals are met, as it reveals the adversary's presence, and has been associated with groups like Lazarus Group, Gamaredon Group, and BlackByte.
5614.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Access internal systems is a foundational action rather than a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique, typically falling under the Initial Access or Lateral Movement tactics. It involves adversaries gaining entry to internal network systems, often through methods like exploiting external-facing services, using stolen credentials for valid accounts, or deploying malware via phishing. Once inside, they may establish persistence, move laterally using tools like internal proxies, and access sensitive internal resources such as SharePoint repositories for information gathering. This access enables further malicious activities, including internal spearphishing to compromise additional users.

5615.name: Steal Social Security numbers
5615.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may search social media for information about victims that can be used during targeting. Social media sites may contain various information about a victim organization, such as business announcements as well as information about the roles, locations, and interests of staff.

Adversaries may search in different social media sites depending on what information they seek to gather. Threat actors may passively harvest data from these sites, as well as use information gathered to create fake profiles/groups to elicit victim’s into revealing specific information (i.e. [Spearphishing Service](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1598/001)).(Citation: Cyware Social Media) Information from these sources may reveal opportunities for other forms of reconnaissance (ex: [Phishing for Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1598) or [Search Open Technical Databases](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1596)), establishing operational resources (ex: [Establish Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1585) or [Compromise Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1586)), and/or initial access (ex: [Spearphishing via Service](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/003)).
5615.profile: [profile]The entity "Steal Social Security numbers" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the provided context, the core technique described is "Search Social Media," which aligns with MITRE ATT&CK ID T1593.001 under the Reconnaissance tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. The technical mechanics involve adversaries passively harvesting data from social media sites to gather information about victim organizations and staff, which can then be used to create fake profiles or groups for elicitation, such as in spearphishing. The intrusion-set DeepPanda is a connected actor, and groups like Contagious Interview, Exotic Lily, and Kimsuky are associated with this behavior.
5615.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Steal Social Security numbers is a specific objective rather than a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the retrieved context, this action is a high-value goal within data theft. It can be achieved through various technical mechanics, including social engineering to deceive users into executing malicious actions, exfiltrating stolen data over existing command and control channels, or deploying malicious browser extensions to harvest credentials and sensitive information entered by the victim. This objective is often pursued by groups like Scattered Spider and Kimsuky.

5616.name: Steal health care information
5616.profile: [profile]Steal health care information is a technique where adversaries target and exfiltrate Protected Health Information (PHI) and other sensitive data from healthcare systems. This activity is associated with the intrusion-set DeepPanda. The theft can be executed through methods like exfiltration over a command and control channel or by using brute force attacks to gain access to accounts containing this data. The stolen information is highly valuable and may be used for fraud, extortion, or sold on illicit markets.
5616.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Steal health care information" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. 5618.name: Web Application Framework Vulnerability
5618.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may scan victims for vulnerabilities that can be used during targeting. Vulnerability scans typically check if the configuration of a target host/application (ex: software and version) potentially aligns with the target of a specific exploit the adversary may seek to use.

These scans may also include more broad attempts to [Gather Victim Host Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1592) that can be used to identify more commonly known, exploitable vulnerabilities. Vulnerability scans typically harvest running software and version numbers via server banners, listening ports, or other network artifacts.(Citation: OWASP Vuln Scanning) Information from these scans may reveal opportunities for other forms of reconnaissance (ex: [Search Open Websites/Domains](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1593) or [Search Open Technical Databases](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1596)), establishing operational resources (ex: [Develop Capabilities](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1587) or [Obtain Capabilities](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1588)), and/or initial access (ex: [Exploit Public-Facing Application](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1190)).
5618.profile: [profile]Web Application Framework Vulnerability is a sub-technique of Vulnerability Scanning (T1595.002) within the Reconnaissance tactic, targeting web platforms. It involves scanning victims to identify exploitable flaws in frameworks like Django or Spring by checking server banners, software versions, and listening ports. This activity, used by groups like APT41 and Sandworm Team, harvests configuration data to align with specific exploits for initial access.
5618.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Web Application Framework Vulnerability" is a technique where adversaries exploit known or unknown security flaws within web application frameworks (like Django, Spring, or Ruby on Rails) to gain unauthorized access or control. This technique falls under the Initial Access tactic, specifically aligning with MITRE ATT&CK technique T1190 (Exploit Public-Facing Application), and primarily targets web servers and applications. Exploitation mechanics involve targeting specific framework components, such as template engines or serialization libraries, to execute arbitrary code, bypass authentication, or achieve remote command execution, often leading to the deployment of a web shell for persistent access. This method is distinct from general vulnerability scanning, which is a precursor activity to identify such flaws.

5619.name: Code Signing Infrastructure Abuse
5619.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may create, acquire, or steal code signing materials to sign their malware or tools. Code signing provides a level of authenticity on a binary from the developer and a guarantee that the binary has not been tampered with. (Citation: Wikipedia Code Signing) The certificates used during an operation may be created, acquired, or stolen by the adversary. (Citation: Securelist Digital Certificates) (Citation: Symantec Digital Certificates) Unlike [Invalid Code Signature](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1036/001), this activity will result in a valid signature.

Code signing to verify software on first run can be used on modern Windows and macOS systems. It is not used on Linux due to the decentralized nature of the platform. (Citation: Wikipedia Code Signing)(Citation: EclecticLightChecksonEXECodeSigning)

Code signing certificates may be used to bypass security policies that require signed code to execute on a system.
5619.profile: [profile]Code Signing Infrastructure Abuse, identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1553.002 under the Defense Evasion tactic, primarily targets Windows and macOS platforms. This technique involves adversaries creating, acquiring, or stealing code signing certificates to generate valid digital signatures for their malware or tools, thereby bypassing security policies that require signed code to execute. The valid signature allows malicious binaries to masquerade as legitimate software, enhancing their ability to evade detection and application whitelisting controls. Associated threat groups include Lazarus Group, APT41, and Wizard Spider.[/profile]
5619.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Code Signing Infrastructure Abuse is a technique where adversaries compromise, misuse, or acquire the infrastructure responsible for generating and managing digital code signing certificates. This allows them to illegitimately sign malware and tools, providing a false appearance of authenticity to bypass security policies that require signed code to execute. The technique is associated with the Defense Evasion tactic and primarily impacts Windows and macOS platforms, enabling the deployment of trusted malicious binaries.

5620.uncertain_mes:

5620.profile: [profile]The malware, referred to as 'nmass malware' or 'Custom Backdoor Malware', is a .NET-based remote access trojan (RAT) that targets Mongolia. It is delivered via a Royal Road v7 document containing a decoy about COVID-19 infections in Russia, falsely signed by A. Amarsaikhan. The initial executable is dropped as 'os03C2.tmp'. Its technical behavior shows similarities to older campaigns associated with Operation LagTime or Tonto Team. The intrusion-set DeepPanda is a directly connected neighbor, though attribution remains uncertain. The malware's primary function is to establish a backdoor on infected systems.

It is associated with the nmass malware, a .NET RAT that targets Mongolia via decoy documents, and shares similarities with campaigns by Operation LagTime or Tonto Team.
