These references link it to groups like APT33, Lazarus Group, Operation C-Major, Dropping Elephant, Stone Panda, and The Gorgon Group.

5621.name: Exploiting Systems via RDP
5621.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may hijack a legitimate user’s remote desktop session to move laterally within an environment. Remote desktop is a common feature in operating systems. It allows a user to log into an interactive session with a system desktop graphical user interface on a remote system. Microsoft refers to its implementation of the Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) as Remote Desktop Services (RDS).(Citation: TechNet Remote Desktop Services)

Adversaries may perform RDP session hijacking which involves stealing a legitimate user's remote session. Typically, a user is notified when someone else is trying to steal their session. With System permissions and using Terminal Services Console, `c:\windows\system32\tscon.exe [session number to be stolen]`, an adversary can hijack a session without the need for credentials or prompts to the user.(Citation: RDP Hijacking Korznikov) This can be done remotely or locally and with active or disconnected sessions.(Citation: RDP Hijacking Medium) It can also lead to [Remote System Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1018) and Privilege Escalation by stealing a Domain Admin or higher privileged account session. All of this can be done by using native Windows commands, but it has also been added as a feature in red teaming tools.(Citation: Kali Redsnarf)
5621.profile: [profile]Exploiting Systems via RDP, also known as RDP Hijacking (MITRE ATT&CK T1563.002), is a Lateral Movement technique. It operates on Windows platforms by hijacking an existing Remote Desktop Protocol session. With SYSTEM permissions, an adversary can use the native Windows command `tscon.exe` to steal an active or disconnected user session without needing credentials or generating user prompts, enabling privilege escalation and further discovery. The intrusion-set Axiom has been associated with this technique.[/profile]
5621.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Exploiting Systems via RDP aligns with MITRE ATT&CK technique T1021.001 (Remote Desktop Protocol) under the Lateral Movement tactic for Windows. Adversaries use valid accounts to log into remote systems via RDP to expand access, often leveraging credentials obtained through credential access. The technique can be used with tools like tscon.exe for session hijacking without user prompts when executed with SYSTEM permissions, and it is commonly associated with persistence methods like modifying the Terminal Services DLL (termsrv.dll).

5622.name: Malicious Proxy Tools
5622.uncertain_mes:
By Jungsoo An, Wayne Lee and Vanja Svajcer.
- Cisco Talos discovered a new, stealthy espionage campaign that has likely persisted since at least March 2021. The observed activity affects an Islamic non-profit organization using backdoors for a previously unreported malware family we have named “Zardoor.”
5622.profile: [profile]Malicious Proxy Tools, also known as venom proxy, is a proxy/tunneling tool set. It is attributed to the intrusion set DeepPanda. Its key technical behaviors include enabling connection proxying (T1090) and facilitating network traffic redirection or manipulation, often to capture credentials or payment data. It targets general computing platforms, with supplementary infrastructure noting its use in espionage campaigns and its association with other proxy tool sets like ELECTRICFISH and FASTCash.
5622.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Malicious Proxy Tools, also known as proxy/tunneling tool sets, are associated with groups like Lazarus Group and Scully Spider. Key technical behaviors include redirecting and manipulating network traffic to capture credentials or payment data, and functioning as a component within Remote Access Trojans (RATs) and broader tool sets for espionage and financial attacks. These tools target multiple platforms, including Android. They are used in campaigns for stealthy espionage and financial operations, often as part of a larger malware ecosystem.

5623.name: Time/Date Mangling
5623.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may abuse time providers to execute DLLs when the system boots. The Windows Time service (W32Time) enables time synchronization across and within domains.(Citation: Microsoft W32Time Feb 2018) W32Time time providers are responsible for retrieving time stamps from hardware/network resources and outputting these values to other network clients.(Citation: Microsoft TimeProvider)

Time providers are implemented as dynamic-link libraries (DLLs) that are registered in the subkeys of `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\System\CurrentControlSet\Services\W32Time\TimeProviders\`.(Citation: Microsoft TimeProvider) The time provider manager, directed by the service control manager, loads and starts time providers listed and enabled under this key at system startup and/or whenever parameters are changed.(Citation: Microsoft TimeProvider)

Adversaries may abuse this architecture to establish persistence, specifically by creating a new arbitrarily named subkey  pointing to a malicious DLL in the `DllName` value. Administrator privileges are required for time provider registration, though execution will run in context of the Local Service account.(Citation: Github W32Time Oct 2017)
5623.profile: [profile]Time Providers, designated as T1547.003, is a persistence technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework for Windows platforms. It involves abusing the Windows Time service (W32Time) architecture by registering a malicious DLL as a time provider. This is achieved by creating a new subkey under `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\System\CurrentControlSet\Services\W32Time\TimeProviders\` with the path to the DLL specified in the `DllName` value, requiring administrator privileges for registration but executing in the Local Service account context upon system startup.
5623.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Time/Date Mangling is a technique where adversaries manipulate file timestamps to hide their activities. This can involve using commands like `timestomp` or `SetFileTime` to alter the creation, modification, or last accessed times of files, often setting them to match legitimate system files. This obfuscation aids in evading forensic detection and timeline analysis.

5624.name: Exploiting Compromised Credentials
5624.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may gather credentials that can be used during targeting. Account credentials gathered by adversaries may be those directly associated with the target victim organization or attempt to take advantage of the tendency for users to use the same passwords across personal and business accounts.

Adversaries may gather credentials from potential victims in various ways, such as direct elicitation via [Phishing for Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1598). Adversaries may also compromise sites then add malicious content designed to collect website authentication cookies from visitors.(Citation: ATT ScanBox) (Citation: Register Deloitte)(Citation: Register Uber)(Citation: Detectify Slack Tokens)(Citation: Forbes GitHub Creds)(Citation: GitHub truffleHog)(Citation: GitHub Gitrob)(Citation: CNET Leaks) Where multi-factor authentication (MFA) based on out-of-band communications is in use, adversaries may compromise a service provider to gain access to MFA codes and one-time passwords (OTP).(Citation: Okta Scatter Swine 2022)

Credential information may also be exposed to adversaries via leaks to online or other accessible data sets (ex: [Search Engines](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1593/002), breach dumps, code repositories, etc.). Adversaries may purchase credentials from dark web markets, such as Russian Market and 2easy, or through access to Telegram channels that distribute logs from infostealer malware.(Citation: Bleeping Computer 2easy 2021)(Citation: SecureWorks Infostealers 2023)(Citation: Bleeping Computer Stealer Logs 2023)

Gathering this information may reveal opportunities for other forms of reconnaissance (ex: [Search Open Websites/Domains](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1593) or [Phishing for Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1598)), establishing operational resources (ex: [Compromise Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1586)), and/or initial access (ex: [External Remote Services](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1133) or [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078)).
5624.profile: [profile]The entity "Exploiting Compromised Credentials" aligns with the MITRE ATT&CK technique Credentials (T1589.001) under the Reconnaissance tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. This technique involves adversaries gathering account credentials through methods such as phishing, purchasing from dark web markets like Russian Market and 2easy, harvesting from infostealer malware logs on Telegram, or extracting authentication cookies and MFA codes from compromised websites and service providers. Credentials are also sourced from public data leaks on search engines, breach dumps, and code repositories. This reconnaissance enables subsequent attacks like initial access via Valid Accounts. Associated threat groups include APT28, LAPSUS$, and Chimera.[/profile]
5624.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Exploiting Compromised Credentials is a technique where adversaries abuse stolen or discovered credentials to gain initial access, persistence, privilege escalation, or defense evasion. This involves using legitimate account access, such as Valid Accounts (T1078), to bypass security controls, access remote services like VPNs or Outlook Web Access, and pivot across systems. Adversaries may target inactive user accounts or leverage password reuse across networks to move laterally and escalate privileges, often without deploying malware to evade detection.

5626.name: Directory Traversal Vulnerability

Vulnerability scans typically harvest running software and version numbers via server banners, listening ports, or other network artifacts.(Citation: OWASP Vuln Scanning) Information from these scans may reveal opportunities for other forms of reconnaissance (ex: [Search Open Websites/Domains](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1593) or [Search Open Technical Databases](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1596)), establishing operational resources (ex: [Develop Capabilities](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1587) or [Obtain Capabilities](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1588)), and/or initial access (ex: [Exploit Public-Facing Application](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1190)).

It is primarily a platform-agnostic vulnerability but is commonly exploited on web servers.

5631.name: network reconnaissance
5631.profile: [profile]Network Reconnaissance, known as T1590 in the MITRE ATT&CK framework, is a Reconnaissance tactic used across multiple platforms to gather information about a victim's network infrastructure. This technique involves probing for details such as IP addresses, domain names, network topology, and security appliance configurations through methods like active scanning, DNS queries, and sniffing network traffic. It is a foundational activity for threat actors like DeepPanda to inform subsequent attack stages.
5631.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Network Reconnaissance is a technique under the Reconnaissance tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. It involves adversaries gathering information about a victim's network infrastructure to inform subsequent targeting. This can be achieved through direct actions like Active Scanning (T1595) to probe for details or by collecting data from online sources. The gathered intelligence, which includes specifics on network topology (T1590.004), devices, and security appliances (T1590.006), is used to identify opportunities for further reconnaissance, establish operational resources, or plan initial access.

5632.name: pass-the-hash
5632.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may “pass the hash” using stolen password hashes to move laterally within an environment, bypassing normal system access controls. Pass the hash (PtH) is a method of authenticating as a user without having access to the user's cleartext password. This method bypasses standard authentication steps that require a cleartext password, moving directly into the portion of the authentication that uses the password hash.

When performing PtH, valid password hashes for the account being used are captured using a [Credential Access](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0006) technique. Captured hashes are used with PtH to authenticate as that user. Once authenticated, PtH may be used to perform actions on local or remote systems.

Adversaries may also use stolen password hashes to "overpass the hash." Similar to PtH, this involves using a password hash to authenticate as a user but also uses the password hash to create a valid Kerberos ticket. This ticket can then be used to perform [Pass the Ticket](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1550/003) attacks.(Citation: Stealthbits Overpass-the-Hash)
5632.profile: [profile]Pass the Hash (PtH) is formally identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1550.002 under the Lateral Movement tactic, primarily targeting Windows platforms. It authenticates as a user using captured password hashes, bypassing the need for cleartext passwords. The technique directly uses the hash in the authentication process, often after credential dumping, to perform actions on local or remote systems. A related variant, "overpass the hash," uses the hash to also create a Kerberos ticket for Pass the Ticket attacks. Groups like APT28, APT41, and Wizard Spider have employed this method.[/profile]

This technique bypasses standard authentication steps, enabling actions on local or remote systems. 5633.name: Installing web shell
5633.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may backdoor web servers with web shells to establish persistent access to systems. A Web shell is a Web script that is placed on an openly accessible Web server to allow an adversary to access the Web server as a gateway into a network. A Web shell may provide a set of functions to execute or a command-line interface on the system that hosts the Web server.(Citation: volexity_0day_sophos_FW)

In addition to a server-side script, a Web shell may have a client interface program that is used to talk to the Web server (e.g. [China Chopper](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0020) Web shell client).(Citation: Lee 2013)
5633.profile: [profile]Web Shell (T1505.003) is a Persistence technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves placing a malicious web script on an openly accessible web server, which provides adversaries with a gateway into the network, often offering a command-line interface or set of executable functions. This script can be paired with a client-side program, such as China Chopper, for remote interaction. The technique is used by numerous threat groups, including APT28, APT29, and Hafnium, to maintain persistent access to compromised web servers.
5633.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Installing web shell is a technique where adversaries deploy a web script onto a publicly accessible web server to establish persistent access. This web shell acts as a backdoor, providing functions or a command-line interface on the host system, often accompanied by a client program like China Chopper for remote interaction. It is used for persistence and redundant access, commonly associated with groups like Hafnium and APT28. The technique involves placing the malicious script in server directories to enable remote command execution and maintain a foothold within the network.

5634.name: Registering DLL with IIS
5634.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may install malicious components that run on Internet Information Services (IIS) web servers to establish persistence. IIS provides several mechanisms to extend the functionality of the web servers. For example, Internet Server Application Programming Interface (ISAPI) extensions and filters can be installed to examine and/or modify incoming and outgoing IIS web requests. Extensions and filters are deployed as DLL files that export three functions: Get{Extension/Filter}Version, Http{Extension/Filter}Proc, and (optionally) Terminate{Extension/Filter}. IIS modules may also be installed to extend IIS web servers.(Citation: Microsoft ISAPI Extension Overview 2017)(Citation: Microsoft ISAPI Filter Overview 2017)(Citation: IIS Backdoor 2011)(Citation: Trustwave IIS Module 2013) Adversaries may install malicious ISAPI extensions and filters to observe and/or modify traffic, execute commands on compromised machines, or proxy command and control traffic. ISAPI extensions and filters may have access to all IIS web requests and responses. For example, an adversary may abuse these mechanisms to modify HTTP responses in order to distribute malicious commands/content to previously comprised hosts.(Citation: Microsoft ISAPI Filter Overview 2017)(Citation: Microsoft ISAPI Extension Overview 2017)(Citation: Microsoft ISAPI Extension All Incoming 2017)(Citation: Dell TG-3390)(Citation: Trustwave IIS Module 2013)(Citation: MMPC ISAPI Filter 2012) Adversaries may also install malicious IIS modules to observe and/or modify traffic. IIS 7.0 introduced modules that provide the same unrestricted access to HTTP requests and responses as ISAPI extensions and filters. IIS modules can be written as a DLL that exports RegisterModule, or as a .NET application that interfaces with ASP.NET APIs to access IIS HTTP requests.(Citation: Microsoft IIS Modules Overview 2007)(Citation: Trustwave IIS Module 2013)(Citation: ESET IIS Malware 2021)
5634.profile: [profile]Registering DLL with IIS is a persistence technique (T1505.004) under the Defense Evasion and Persistence tactics, targeting Windows IIS web servers. Adversaries install malicious DLLs as ISAPI extensions or filters, which export functions like GetExtensionVersion and HttpExtensionProc, or as IIS modules exporting RegisterModule. These components gain unrestricted access to all incoming and outgoing HTTP requests, enabling traffic observation/modification, command execution, and C2 proxying. The intrusion-set DeepPanda has been associated with this activity.[/profile]
5634.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Registering DLL with IIS is a persistence technique (T1505.004) under the Persistence tactic, targeting Windows platforms. It involves installing a malicious DLL as an ISAPI extension or filter, or as an IIS module, on an Internet Information Services web server. The malicious component, which must export specific functions like GetExtensionVersion and HttpExtensionProc for ISAPI, gains unrestricted access to all incoming and outgoing HTTP requests and responses, enabling traffic observation, modification, command execution, or acting as a command and control proxy.

5635.name: Modifying files
5635.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may attempt to steal Kerberos tickets stored in credential cache files (or ccache). These files are used for short term storage of a user's active session credentials. The ccache file is created upon user authentication and allows for access to multiple services without the user having to re-enter credentials. The /etc/krb5.conf configuration file and the KRB5CCNAME environment variable are used to set the storage location for ccache entries. On Linux, credentials are typically stored in the `/tmp` directory with a naming format of `krb5cc_%UID%` or `krb5.ccache`. On macOS, ccache entries are stored by default in memory with an `API:{uuid}` naming scheme. Typically, users interact with ticket storage using kinit, which obtains a Ticket-Granting-Ticket (TGT) for the principal; klist, which lists obtained tickets currently held in the credentials cache; and other built-in binaries.(Citation: Kerberos GNU/Linux)(Citation: Binary Defense Kerberos Linux) Adversaries can collect tickets from ccache files stored on disk and authenticate as the current user without their password to perform [Pass the Ticket](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1550/003) attacks. Adversaries can also use these tickets to impersonate legitimate users with elevated privileges to perform [Privilege Escalation](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0004). Tools like Kekeo can also be used by adversaries to convert ccache files to Windows format for further [Lateral Movement](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0008). On macOS, adversaries may use open-source tools or the Kerberos framework to interact with ccache files and extract TGTs or Service Tickets via lower-level APIs.(Citation: SpectorOps Bifrost Kerberos macOS 2019)(Citation: Linux Kerberos Tickets)(Citation: Brining MimiKatz to Unix)(Citation: Kekeo)
5635.profile: [profile]Steal Kerberos Tickets (T1558.005) is a Credential Access technique targeting Linux and macOS platforms. Adversaries steal Kerberos tickets from credential cache (ccache) files, which are created upon user authentication and store active session credentials. These files are located via the `/etc/krb5.conf` configuration file or the `KRB5CCNAME` environment variable, with Linux typically storing them in `/tmp` as `krb5cc_%UID%` and macOS storing them in memory. Stolen tickets enable Pass the Ticket attacks for lateral movement and privilege escalation without the user's password, and tools like Kekeo can convert these files for use on Windows systems.[/profile]
5635.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Modifying files is a foundational adversarial action without a specific MITRE ATT&CK ID. It is a technique within the Defense Evasion and Persistence tactics, applicable across all platforms. The core technical mechanic involves altering file contents, attributes, or permissions to achieve objectives such as establishing persistence, evading detection, or manipulating data. This can include editing configuration files like macOS plist files to execute malicious code on startup, changing file attributes to hide them, or tampering with stored data to impact business processes or decision-making.

5637.name: Leveraging RDP backdoor
5637.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may hijack a legitimate user’s remote desktop session to move laterally within an environment. Remote desktop is a common feature in operating systems. It allows a user to log into an interactive session with a system desktop graphical user interface on a remote system. Microsoft refers to its implementation of the Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) as Remote Desktop Services (RDS).(Citation: TechNet Remote Desktop Services)

Adversaries may perform RDP session hijacking which involves stealing a legitimate user's remote session. Typically, a user is notified when someone else is trying to steal their session. With System permissions and using Terminal Services Console, `c:\windows\system32\tscon.exe [session number to be stolen]`, an adversary can hijack a session without the need for credentials or prompts to the user.(Citation: RDP Hijacking Korznikov) This can be done remotely or locally and with active or disconnected sessions.(Citation: RDP Hijacking Medium) It can also lead to [Remote System Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1018) and Privilege Escalation by stealing a Domain Admin or higher privileged account session. All of this can be done by using native Windows commands, but it has also been added as a feature in red teaming tools.(Citation: Kali Redsnarf)
5637.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique "RDP Hijacking" (T1563.002) under the Lateral Movement tactic for Windows platforms. It involves adversaries with System permissions using the native Windows command `tscon.exe` to steal an existing, active, or disconnected Remote Desktop Protocol session without needing credentials or triggering user notifications, enabling lateral movement and potential privilege escalation. This technique has been used by groups like Axiom and is featured in red teaming tools.
5637.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Leveraging RDP backdoor" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the provided context, it likely refers to a method of persistence or unauthorized access using the Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP). This can involve techniques like RDP session hijacking, where an adversary with System permissions uses the native Windows command `tscon.exe` to steal an active or disconnected user session without needing credentials or triggering user prompts. This action facilitates lateral movement and can lead to privilege escalation, particularly by hijacking high-privilege account sessions.

5638.name: Traditional trojans signaling to target IP
5638.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may use traffic signaling to hide open ports or other malicious functionality used for persistence or command and control. Traffic signaling involves the use of a magic value or sequence that must be sent to a system to trigger a special response, such as opening a closed port or executing a malicious task. This may take the form of sending a series of packets with certain characteristics before a port will be opened that the adversary can use for command and control. Usually this series of packets consists of attempted connections to a predefined sequence of closed ports (i.e. [Port Knocking](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1205/001)), but can involve unusual flags, specific strings, or other unique characteristics. After the sequence is completed, opening a port may be accomplished by the host-based firewall, but could also be implemented by custom software.

Adversaries may also communicate with an already open port, but the service listening on that port will only respond to commands or trigger other malicious functionality if passed the appropriate magic value(s).

The observation of the signal packets to trigger the communication can be conducted through different methods. One means, originally implemented by Cd00r (Citation: Hartrell cd00r 2002), is to use the libpcap libraries to sniff for the packets in question. Another method leverages raw sockets, which enables the malware to use ports that are already open for use by other programs.

On network devices, adversaries may use crafted packets to enable [Network Device Authentication](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1556/004) for standard services offered by the device such as telnet.  Such signaling may also be used to open a closed service port such as telnet, or to trigger module modification of malware implants on the device, adding, removing, or changing malicious capabilities.  Adversaries may use crafted packets to attempt to connect to one or more (open or closed) ports, but may also attempt to connect to a router interface, broadcast, and network address IP on the same port in order to achieve their goals and objectives.(Citation: Cisco Synful Knock Evolution)(Citation: Mandiant - Synful Knock)(Citation: Cisco Blog Legacy Device Attacks)  To enable this traffic signaling on embedded devices, adversaries must first achieve and leverage [Patch System Image](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1601/001) due to the monolithic nature of the architecture.

Adversaries may also use the Wake-on-LAN feature to turn on powered off systems. Wake-on-LAN is a hardware feature that allows a powered down system to be powered on, or woken up, by sending a magic packet to it. Once the system is powered on, it may become a target for lateral movement.(Citation: Bleeping Computer - Ryuk WoL)(Citation: AMD Magic Packet)
5638.profile: [profile]Traffic Signaling is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1205 under the Command and Control tactic, applicable to Linux, Windows, and Network platforms. It involves sending a specific "magic" sequence of packets to a system to trigger a hidden response, such as opening a closed command and control port. This sequence often consists of connection attempts to a predefined order of closed ports (Port Knocking) or uses packets with unusual flags or strings. The listening malware, using methods like libpcap or raw sockets, detects this correct signal to activate. The technique is used by groups like Kimsuky, UNC3886, and Mustang Panda.[/profile]
5638.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Traditional Trojans Signaling to Target IP is a technique aligned with MITRE ATT&CK's T1205 (Traffic Signaling) under the Command and Control tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. It involves a Trojan using a specific "magic" sequence of packets, such as connections to a predefined order of closed ports (port knocking), sent to a target IP address to trigger a hidden response, like opening a command and control channel. This signaling can be implemented using libpcap for packet sniffing or raw sockets to monitor for the correct sequence, effectively hiding malicious ports and functionality from standard detection.

5641.name: checking handshake packets
5641.profile: [profile]The entity "checking handshake packets" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on retrieved context, it relates to network protocol analysis. Adversaries may inspect or manipulate TCP handshake packets, such as in SYN flood attacks (T1499.001) where excessive SYN packets are sent without completing the handshake to exhaust a system's connection resources, or in ACK floods that force an OS to search non-existent connections. This activity can be part of denial-of-service campaigns or used to disguise malicious traffic by impersonating legitimate SSL/TLS handshakes (T1001.003). The intrusion set DeepPanda is a connected neighbor in the graph.[/profile]
5641.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity 'checking handshake packets' is a technique where adversaries inspect or analyze network handshake packets, such as those from TCP or SSL/TLS protocols, to gather information or potentially disguise malicious traffic. This activity is often associated with network reconnaissance or evasion tactics. The technique is linked to broader adversarial methods like protocol or service impersonation, where fake SSL/TLS handshakes can be used to blend command and control traffic with legitimate network activity, thereby interfering with security tools. It is employed by threat groups including Lazarus Group, Higaisa, and Mustang Panda.

5643.name: Sticky Keys Backdoor
5643.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may search for private key certificate files on compromised systems for insecurely stored credentials. Private cryptographic keys and certificates are used for authentication, encryption/decryption, and digital signatures.(Citation: Wikipedia Public Key Crypto) Common key and certificate file extensions include: .key, .pgp, .gpg, .ppk., .p12, .pem, .pfx, .cer, .p7b, .asc. Adversaries may also look in common key directories, such as ~/.ssh for SSH keys on * nix-based systems or C:\Users\(username)\.ssh\ on Windows. Adversary tools may also search compromised systems for file extensions relating to cryptographic keys and certificates.(Citation: Kaspersky Careto)(Citation: Palo Alto Prince of Persia) When a device is registered to Entra ID, a device key and a transport key are generated and used to verify the device’s identity.(Citation: Microsoft Primary Refresh Token) An adversary with access to the device may be able to export the keys in order to impersonate the device.(Citation: AADInternals Azure AD Device Identities) On network devices, private keys may be exported via [Network Device CLI](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/008) commands such as `crypto pki export`.(Citation: cisco_deploy_rsa_keys) Some private keys require a password or passphrase for operation, so an adversary may also use [Input Capture](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1056) for keylogging or attempt to [Brute Force](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1110) the passphrase off-line. These private keys can be used to authenticate to [Remote Services](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021) like SSH or for use in decrypting other collected files such as email.
5643.profile: [profile]Sticky Keys Backdoor is a persistence and privilege escalation technique (T1546.008) under the Privilege Escalation tactic, targeting Windows. It exploits Windows accessibility features, such as sethc.exe (triggered by pressing Shift five times) or utilman.exe (triggered by Windows+U), which execute before user login. Adversaries establish a backdoor by either replacing the legitimate binary with a malicious one like cmd.exe or, on modern systems, using the Image File Execution Options Injection debugger method via Registry modification (e.g., setting a debugger for utilman.exe). This allows execution of arbitrary commands with SYSTEM privileges from the logon screen or over Remote Desktop Protocol, enabling unauthenticated access. Groups like APT3, DeepPanda, and APT29 have used this method.[/profile]
5643.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Sticky Keys Backdoor is a persistence and privilege escalation technique (ID: T1546.008) under the Defense Evasion and Privilege Escalation tactics for Windows. It exploits Windows accessibility features like sethc.exe (triggered by pressing Shift five times) or utilman.exe (Windows+U) to gain unauthenticated, SYSTEM-level access from the logon screen. Adversaries achieve this by either replacing the original binary (e.g., with cmd.exe) or, on modern systems, using Image File Execution Options Injection to set a debugger like cmd.exe, which executes when the feature's key combination is pressed, often via Remote Desktop Protocol.

5663.name: dynamic link library (DLL) sideloading
5663.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may inject dynamic-link libraries (DLLs) into processes in order to evade process-based defenses as well as possibly elevate privileges. DLL injection is a method of executing arbitrary code in the address space of a separate live process. DLL injection is commonly performed by writing the path to a DLL in the virtual address space of the target process before loading the DLL by invoking a new thread. The write can be performed with native Windows API calls such as VirtualAllocEx and WriteProcessMemory, then invoked with CreateRemoteThread (which calls the LoadLibrary API responsible for loading the DLL). (Citation: Elastic Process Injection July 2017) Variations of this method such as reflective DLL injection (writing a self-mapping DLL into a process) and memory module (map DLL when writing into process) overcome the address relocation issue as well as the additional APIs to invoke execution (since these methods load and execute the files in memory by manually preforming the function of LoadLibrary).(Citation: Elastic HuntingNMemory June 2017)(Citation: Elastic Process Injection July 2017) Another variation of this method, often referred to as Module Stomping/Overloading or DLL Hollowing, may be leveraged to conceal injected code within a process. This method involves loading a legitimate DLL into a remote process then manually overwriting the module's AddressOfEntryPoint before starting a new thread in the target process.(Citation: Module Stomping for Shellcode Injection) This variation allows attackers to hide malicious injected code by potentially backing its execution with a legitimate DLL file on disk.(Citation: Hiding Malicious Code with Module Stomping) Running code in the context of another process may allow access to the process's memory, system/network resources, and possibly elevated privileges. Execution via DLL injection may also evade detection from security products since the execution is masked under a legitimate process.
5663.profile: [profile]Dynamic Link Library (DLL) Sideloading, identified as T1574.002, is a Defense Evasion and Persistence technique for Windows. It involves placing a malicious DLL in the same directory as a legitimate, trusted executable. When the application is launched, it loads the malicious DLL from its local directory instead of the legitimate system library, thereby executing the adversary's payload under the guise of a trusted process. This method can be chained across multiple DLLs to fragment functionality and hinder analysis. It is associated with threat groups like Lazarus and BackdoorDiplomacy.[/profile]
5663.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Dynamic Link Library (DLL) Sideloading, identified as T1574.002 within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, is a Defense Evasion and Persistence technique primarily for Windows platforms. It involves an adversary planting a malicious DLL in the same directory as a legitimate, trusted executable; when the application is run, it loads the malicious DLL instead of or alongside the intended library from a standard system location. This method masks malicious actions under a trusted process, potentially evading detection. Adversaries may chain multiple sideloading events or use the malicious DLL to load further payloads, complicating analysis.

5664.name: malicious code placement
5664.uncertain_mes:
An adversary may rely upon a user opening a malicious file in order to gain execution. Users may be subjected to social engineering to get them to open a file that will lead to code execution. This user action will typically be observed as follow-on behavior from [Spearphishing Attachment](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001). Adversaries may use several types of files that require a user to execute them, including .doc, .pdf, .xls, .rtf, .scr, .exe, .lnk, .pif, .cpl, .reg, and .iso.(Citation: Mandiant Trojanized Windows 10)

Adversaries may employ various forms of [Masquerading](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1036) and [Obfuscated Files or Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027) to increase the likelihood that a user will open and successfully execute a malicious file. These methods may include using a familiar naming convention and/or password protecting the file and supplying instructions to a user on how to open it.(Citation: Password Protected Word Docs) 

While [Malicious File](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002) frequently occurs shortly after Initial Access it may occur at other phases of an intrusion, such as when an adversary places a file in a shared directory or on a user's desktop hoping that a user will click on it. This activity may also be seen shortly after [Internal Spearphishing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1534).
5664.profile: [profile]Malicious File, designated as T1204.002 under the Execution tactic, primarily targets Windows platforms. This technique relies on user interaction to open a malicious file, often delivered via spearphishing, to execute adversary code. Common file types include .doc, .pdf, .xls, .exe, .lnk, and .iso. Adversaries frequently employ masquerading, such as using familiar naming conventions, and obfuscation, like password-protecting files with instructions, to increase success. While common after initial access, it can also occur later, such as by placing a file in a shared directory. It is associated with numerous threat groups, including APT29, Lazarus Group, and FIN7.
5664.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Malicious Code Placement is a technique where adversaries position harmful code in locations where users or systems may inadvertently execute it. This can involve placing malicious files in shared directories or on user desktops, or uploading backdoored software packages, libraries, or virtual machine images to public repositories like PyPI, NPM, or Docker Hub. The goal is to bypass initial access controls by relying on user actions such as downloading, installing, or running these resources, which then leads to the execution of the adversary's payload.

5683.name: 517vpnconnected
5683.profile: [profile]517vpnconnected is a malware attributed to the DeepPanda intrusion set. Its key technical behavior involves scanning for and identifying VPN-related services and configurations, including OpenVPN, Cisco IOS SSL VPN, and WireGuard, through network traffic analysis and pattern matching in HTTP responses and TLS certificates. The malware targets network infrastructure to detect and potentially exploit VPN endpoints.[/profile]
5683.profile_without_enhance: [profile]517vpnconnected is a malware entity. Retrieved information suggests it may be associated with or share characteristics with the 'darkside' and 'smokedham' malware families, as these entities contain detection logic for VPN-related strings and services (including OpenVPN, Cisco IOS SSL VPN, and WireGuard) in their content. No specific attributed groups, key TTPs, or target platforms are detailed in the provided data.

5684.name: us-vpn2
5684.profile: [profile]us-vpn2 is a malware entity associated with the intrusion set DeepPanda. It is linked to infrastructure such as the domain vpn2.smi1egate[.]com. The malware appears in campaigns alongside other threats like SNAPPYBEE and DEMODEX, which are attributed to the group Earth Estries, and shares infrastructure with SoftEther VPN-based operations. Its technical indicators include a certificate thumbprint (2A89C5FD0C23B8AF622F0E91939B486E9DB7FAEF) and connections to IPs like 192.95.36[.]61.
5684.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The malware 'us-vpn2' is referenced in infrastructure data alongside 'hemigate' and 'snappybee' in Campaign Alpha, which is attributed to the group Earth Estries. It is also associated with the 'ghost rat' backdoor, which connects to the domain vpn2.smi1egate[.]com and is linked to multiple groups including Emissary Panda and Lazarus Group. Its key technical behavior involves using the domain vpn2.smi1egate[.]com for command and control.

5685.name: cyberespionage
5685.profile: [profile]The entity 'cyberespionage' is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the provided context, it is a high-level objective or campaign theme associated with intrusion sets like DeepPanda. Related technical procedures include adversaries conducting reconnaissance on threat intelligence reports about their own activity (T1681), acquiring malware and exploits from third parties (T1588), and exfiltrating stolen data through command and control channels (T1041).
5685.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity 'cyberespionage' is a high-level concept, not a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the retrieved information, it encompasses adversary activities like monitoring threat intelligence about their own operations (as described in T1681: search threat vendor data) and acquiring tools from third parties (T1588: obtain capabilities). A core technical component of cyberespionage campaigns is the exfiltration of stolen data, often conducted over established command and control channels (T1041: exfiltration over c2 channel).

5688.name: Scanbox Framework
5688.uncertain_mes:
Reconnaissance Scanning Tools Used by Chinese Threat Actors and Those Available in Open Source
China has its own ecosystem of scanning tools, whether for good or ill.
5688.profile: [profile]Scanbox Framework, also known as scanbox, is a JavaScript-based web reconnaissance and exploitation framework used to profile victims and deliver further malware, often in watering hole attacks. It is assessed as being shared privately among multiple China-based threat actors and has been associated with the Leviathan group. Its technical behaviors include sending host data via HTTP POST requests and using specific plugin data and keep-alive mechanisms for initial victim contact and data exfiltration.[/profile]
5688.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Scanbox Framework, also known as ScanBox, is a JavaScript-based web reconnaissance and exploitation framework used to profile victims and deliver further malware, often in watering hole attacks. It is assessed as being shared privately among multiple China-based threat actors, with links to the Leviathan group. The framework targets web platforms to conduct reconnaissance.

5689.name: Citrix VPN Backdoor
5689.profile: [profile]Citrix VPN Backdoor is a threat targeting Citrix NetScaler VPN gateways by exploiting the CVE-2019-19781 vulnerability. It is attributed to the intrusion set DeepPanda. Key technical behaviors include exploiting the public-facing Citrix application (T1190), transferring tools to internal hosts (T1105), and using SoftEther VPN for command and control (T1665). Its execution involves DLL side-loading (T1574.001) to deploy a backdoor. The primary target platform is Citrix NetScaler Gateway infrastructure.
5689.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Citrix VPN Backdoor is a malware that exploits the Citrix CVE-2019-19781 flaw to compromise NetScaler VPN gateways. Its key technical behaviors include exploiting public-facing applications (T1190), transferring tools to internal hosts (T1105), using SoftEther VPN for command and control (T1665), and executing via DLL side-loading (T1574.001). It has been deployed by actors like Earth Estries, and in some incidents, compromised servers were patched by attackers to maintain exclusive backdoor access.

5698.name: Typosquatting
5698.profile: [profile]Typosquatting is a technique used within the Initial Access tactic, primarily on Windows, macOS, and Linux platforms. It involves adversaries registering domain names that are visually similar to legitimate ones, often through homoglyphs, different top-level domains, or common misspellings. This method is used to facilitate delivery of malicious content via phishing or drive-by compromise attacks, tricking users into interacting with fraudulent sites or links. The intrusion-set DeepPanda has been associated with this technique.
5698.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Typosquatting is a technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, specifically categorized under Resource Development (T1583.001) and Initial Access. It operates by adversaries acquiring or creating domain names, software libraries, or other resources that closely resemble legitimate ones through the use of homoglyphs, different top-level domains, or common misspellings. This method is used to facilitate other techniques such as Spearphishing Link, Drive-by Compromise, and Malicious Link by deceiving users into interacting with malicious infrastructure, believing it to be trusted. It is employed by numerous threat groups including APT28, Lazarus Group, and Fin7.

5699.name: Social Engineering Lures
5699.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may search social media for information about victims that can be used during targeting. Social media sites may contain various information about a victim organization, such as business announcements as well as information about the roles, locations, and interests of staff.

Adversaries may search in different social media sites depending on what information they seek to gather. Threat actors may passively harvest data from these sites, as well as use information gathered to create fake profiles/groups to elicit victim’s into revealing specific information (i.e. [Spearphishing Service](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1598/001)).(Citation: Cyware Social Media) Information from these sources may reveal opportunities for other forms of reconnaissance (ex: [Phishing for Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1598) or [Search Open Technical Databases](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1596)), establishing operational resources (ex: [Establish Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1585) or [Compromise Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1586)), and/or initial access (ex: [Spearphishing via Service](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/003)).
5699.profile: [profile]Social Media, identified as T1593.001 under the Reconnaissance tactic, is a technique used across various platforms. Adversaries search social media sites to passively harvest information about victim organizations and staff, such as roles and business announcements. This gathered data is then used to craft targeted lures, including creating fake profiles or groups to elicit specific information from victims, enabling further reconnaissance or initial access operations like spearphishing. The intrusion-set DeepPanda has been associated with this technique.[/profile]
5699.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Social Engineering Lures is a technique within the Reconnaissance tactic, applicable across multiple platforms, where adversaries craft deceptive messages or pretexts to elicit sensitive information from targets. This involves using information gathered from prior reconnaissance, such as from social media or victim-owned websites, to create highly persuasive and believable scenarios. These lures are often delivered via spearphishing services, links, or voice communications to trick individuals into divulging credentials or other actionable data.

5701.name: Turla
5701.uncertain_mes: [Turla](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0010) is a cyber espionage threat group that has been attributed to Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB).  They have compromised victims in over 50 countries since at least 2004, spanning a range of industries including government, embassies, military, education, research and pharmaceutical companies. [Turla](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0010) is known for conducting watering hole and spearphishing campaigns, and leveraging in-house tools and malware, such as [Uroburos](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0022).(Citation: Kaspersky Turla)(Citation: ESET Gazer Aug 2017)(Citation: CrowdStrike VENOMOUS BEAR)(Citation: ESET Turla Mosquito Jan 2018)(Citation: Joint Cybersecurity Advisory AA23-129A Snake Malware May 2023)

Key TTPs include spearphishing, watering hole attacks, and sophisticated persistence mechanisms like registry-based payload storage. The group has targeted government, military, diplomatic, education, and research sectors in over 50 countries, primarily for intelligence gathering and strategic espionage.

5756.name: Linux Targeting
5756.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may abuse the [at](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0110) utility to perform task scheduling for initial, recurring, or future execution of malicious code. The [at](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0110) command within Linux operating systems enables administrators to schedule tasks.(Citation: Kifarunix - Task Scheduling in Linux) An adversary may use [at](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0110) in Linux environments to execute programs at system startup or on a scheduled basis for persistence. [at](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0110) can also be abused to conduct remote Execution as part of Lateral Movement and or to run a process under the context of a specified account. Adversaries may also abuse [at](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0110) to break out of restricted environments by using a task to spawn an interactive system shell or to run system commands. Similarly, [at](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0110) may also be used for [Privilege Escalation](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0004) if the binary is allowed to run as superuser via sudo.(Citation: GTFObins at)
5756.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique "at (linux)", ID T1053.001, under the Execution tactic for Linux platforms. It involves abusing the native `at` command to schedule tasks for malicious code execution, which can be used for persistence, lateral movement, or privilege escalation, especially if the binary is permitted to run via `sudo`. The intrusion set Turla is associated with this technique.[/profile]
5756.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Linux Targeting is a technique used by adversaries to focus malicious activities on Linux-based systems. It involves tailoring attack tools, payloads, and procedures specifically for the Linux environment, often leveraging native utilities like `at` for scheduling, `chmod`/`chown` for permission modification, or `auditctl` to disable logging. This targeting is a prerequisite step in broader campaigns, enabling follow-on behaviors such as persistence, privilege escalation, and lateral movement within Linux infrastructures.

5757.name: Hidden Network Communication
5757.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may use an existing, legitimate external Web service as a means for sending commands to and receiving output from a compromised system over the Web service channel. Compromised systems may leverage popular websites and social media to host command and control (C2) instructions. Those infected systems can then send the output from those commands back over that Web service channel. The return traffic may occur in a variety of ways, depending on the Web service being utilized. For example, the return traffic may take the form of the compromised system posting a comment on a forum, issuing a pull request to development project, updating a document hosted on a Web service, or by sending a Tweet. 

Popular websites and social media acting as a mechanism for C2 may give a significant amount of cover due to the likelihood that hosts within a network are already communicating with them prior to a compromise. Using common services, such as those offered by Google or Twitter, makes it easier for adversaries to hide in expected noise. Web service providers commonly use SSL/TLS encryption, giving adversaries an added level of protection.
5757.profile: [profile]Hidden Network Communication, identified as T1102.002 within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, falls under the Command and Control tactic and applies to multiple platforms. This technique involves adversaries using legitimate external web services like social media or cloud platforms (e.g., Google, Twitter) for bidirectional command and control. Commands are sent to a compromised system, and output is returned via the same channel through actions such as posting forum comments, making pull requests, updating documents, or sending Tweets, leveraging SSL/TLS encryption and common traffic for stealth. The intrusion-set Turla is associated with this method.
5757.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Hidden Network Communication is a technique for concealing C2 traffic. It can involve using legitimate web services like Google or Twitter to blend in with normal traffic, leveraging their SSL/TLS encryption for added stealth. This method avoids detection by hiding communications within expected network noise, making it difficult for security tools to distinguish malicious activity from regular user traffic.

5759.profile: [profile]Agent.BTZ, also known as Agent.btz, is a worm attributed to the Turla intrusion set. It primarily spreads via removable USB drives and was used to infect U.S. military networks in 2008. Its key behavior is its self-propagation mechanism through portable media.[/profile]

5760.name: Snake Rootkit
5760.uncertain_mes: Since January 2020, the CrowdStrike® Falcon OverWatchTM managed threat hunting team has observed an escalation in hands-on-keyboard activity. The COVID-19 pandemic has fundamentally shifted the way businesses are working, and adversaries are taking full advantage of businesses that fail to adapt their security postures in response.
5760.profile: [profile]Snake Rootkit, also known as Uroburos, is attributed to the Turla intrusion set. It is a highly complex espionage rootkit that provides backdoor access and hides from defenders, with technical analyses detailing its sophisticated capabilities. The malware targets businesses, with observed escalations in hands-on-keyboard activity since early 2020, exploiting shifts in security postures during the COVID-19 pandemic.
5760.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Snake Rootkit, also known as Snake, Uroburos, and Turla, is attributed to the Turla group. It is a highly complex espionage rootkit that provides backdoor access, hides from defenders, and performs hands-on-keyboard activity for data exfiltration. It primarily targets Windows systems, as indicated by its association with the Turla/Uroburos campaign and technical analyses of the Snake rootkit.

5765.name: UPX Packed Binary
5765.profile: [profile]UPX Packed Binary is a packer used to compress and obfuscate executable files, notably employed by the Turla intrusion set. It is commonly used to pack malware binaries, such as in the cases of perfctl, BitRAT, and SupremeBot, where the UPX header is sometimes removed to hinder analysis and prevent easy unpacking with standard UPX tools. Its target platforms include Linux (ELF binaries) and Windows systems.[profile]
5765.profile_without_enhance: [profile]UPX Packed Binary is a packer/compressor used to obfuscate malicious executables. It is associated with malware families like BitRAT and SupremeBot. Its key technical behavior involves compressing binaries, and its header is sometimes removed to hinder analysis and unpacking using standard UPX tools. The target platform is primarily Windows, but it is also used on Linux ELF binaries. Infrastructure or supplementary information includes its use in delivering payloads like 'checklist.php'.

5767.name: Public Key Data Encryption
5767.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may compromise a network device’s encryption capability in order to bypass encryption that would otherwise protect data communications. (Citation: Cisco Synful Knock Evolution)

Encryption can be used to protect transmitted network traffic to maintain its confidentiality (protect against unauthorized disclosure) and integrity (protect against unauthorized changes). Encryption ciphers are used to convert a plaintext message to ciphertext and can be computationally intensive to decipher without the associated decryption key. Typically, longer keys increase the cost of cryptanalysis, or decryption without the key.

Adversaries can compromise and manipulate devices that perform encryption of network traffic. For example, through behaviors such as [Modify System Image](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1601), [Reduce Key Space](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1600/001), and [Disable Crypto Hardware](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1600/002), an adversary can negatively effect and/or eliminate a device’s ability to securely encrypt network traffic. This poses a greater risk of unauthorized disclosure and may help facilitate data manipulation, Credential Access, or Collection efforts. (Citation: Cisco Blog Legacy Device Attacks)
5767.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique "Weaken Encryption" (T1600) under the Defense Evasion tactic, targeting network devices. It involves compromising a device's encryption capability to bypass data protection, for example by reducing the cryptographic key space or disabling dedicated hardware through CLI commands after modifying the system image, as observed in campaigns by groups like Turla. This weakens confidentiality and integrity to facilitate further data access or manipulation.[/profile]

5778.name: Random Installation Directories
5778.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may abuse vSphere Installation Bundles (VIBs) to establish persistent access to ESXi hypervisors. VIBs are collections of files used for software distribution and virtual system management in VMware environments. Since ESXi uses an in-memory filesystem where changes made to most files are stored in RAM rather than in persistent storage, these modifications are lost after a reboot. However, VIBs can be used to create startup tasks, apply custom firewall rules, or deploy binaries that persist across reboots. Typically, administrators use VIBs for updates and system maintenance. VIBs can be broken down into three components:(Citation: VMware VIBs) * VIB payload: a `.vgz` archive containing the directories and files to be created and executed on boot when the VIBs are loaded. * Signature file: verifies the host acceptance level of a VIB, indicating what testing and validation has been done by VMware or its partners before publication of a VIB. By default, ESXi hosts require a minimum acceptance level of PartnerSupported for VIB installation, meaning the VIB is published by a trusted VMware partner. However, privileged users can change the default acceptance level using the `esxcli` command line interface. Additionally, VIBs are able to be installed regardless of acceptance level by using the esxcli software vib install --force command. * XML descriptor file: a configuration file containing associated VIB metadata, such as the name of the VIB and its dependencies. Adversaries may leverage malicious VIB packages to maintain persistent access to ESXi hypervisors, allowing system changes to be executed upon each bootup of ESXi – such as using `esxcli` to enable firewall rules for backdoor traffic, creating listeners on hard coded ports, and executing backdoors.(Citation: Google Cloud Threat Intelligence ESXi VIBs 2022) Adversaries may also masquerade their malicious VIB files as PartnerSupported by modifying the XML descriptor file.(Citation: Google Cloud Threat Intelligence ESXi VIBs 2022)
5778.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique "vSphere Installation Bundles (VIBs)" with ID T1505.006 under the Persistence tactic for the VMware ESXi platform. Adversaries abuse VIB packages to install persistent components on ESXi hypervisors, as ESXi's in-memory filesystem typically loses changes after a reboot. A VIB payload is a .vgz archive executed on boot, and adversaries can force installation bypassing acceptance levels using the `esxcli software vib install --force` command. Malicious VIBs can create startup tasks, deploy backdoors, or modify firewall rules, and their XML descriptor can be altered to masquerade as trusted PartnerSupported packages. The intrusion set Turla has been associated with this technique.
5778.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Random Installation Directories is a technique where adversaries install malicious software in non-standard or random directories to evade detection and complicate removal. This method bypasses security tools that monitor common installation paths and can be used for persistence. It often involves using trusted system utilities like InstallUtil to execute the payload from the chosen directory.

5791.name: IDT Hooks
5791.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may achieve persistence by leveraging Python’s startup mechanisms, including path configuration (`.pth`) files and the `sitecustomize.py` or `usercustomize.py` modules. These files are automatically processed during the initialization of the Python interpreter, allowing for the execution of arbitrary code whenever Python is invoked.(Citation: Volexity GlobalProtect CVE 2024)

Path configuration files are designed to extend Python’s module search paths through the use of import statements. If a `.pth` file is placed in Python's `site-packages` or `dist-packages` directories, any lines beginning with `import` will be executed automatically on Python invocation.(Citation: DFIR Python Persistence 2025) Similarly, if `sitecustomize.py` or `usercustomize.py` is present in the Python path, these files will be imported during interpreter startup, and any code they contain will be executed.(Citation: Python Site Configuration Hook)

Adversaries may abuse these mechanisms to establish persistence on systems where Python is widely used (e.g., for automation or scripting in production environments).
5791.profile: [profile]IDT Hooks, also known as Python Startup Hooks (T1546.018), is a Persistence technique for Linux and Windows platforms. It works by placing a `.pth` file containing `import` statements, or a `sitecustomize.py` or `usercustomize.py` module, into Python's site-packages or dist-packages directories, causing the embedded code to execute automatically upon Python interpreter startup. The intrusion-set Turla has been associated with this method.[/profile]
5791.profile_without_enhance: [profile]IDT Hooks is a technique for achieving persistence and credential access by intercepting and redirecting calls to Windows API functions. It can be implemented through hook procedures, Import Address Table (IAT) hooking, or inline hooking, where the first bytes of an API function are overwritten to redirect code flow. This allows adversaries to execute malicious code within the context of legitimate processes, often to capture authentication credentials from API call parameters or to conceal malware activities like a rootkit.

5798.name: Raw data fingerprint
5798.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may attempt to blend in with legitimate traffic by spoofing browser and system attributes like operating system, system language, platform, user-agent string, resolution, time zone, etc.  The HTTP User-Agent request header is a string that lets servers and network peers identify the application, operating system, vendor, and/or version of the requesting user agent.(Citation: Mozilla User Agent)

Adversaries may gather this information through [System Information Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1082) or by users navigating to adversary-controlled websites, and then use that information to craft their web traffic to evade defenses.(Citation: Gummy Browsers: Targeted Browser Spoofing against State-of-the-Art Fingerprinting Techniques)
5798.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique "Masquerading: Browser Fingerprint Spoofing" (T1036.012) under the Defense Evasion tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It involves adversaries spoofing browser and system attributes like the User-Agent string, operating system, platform, and time zone to blend web traffic with legitimate traffic and evade detection. This data can be gathered via System Information Discovery or by luring users to malicious sites. The intrusion-set Turla has been associated with this technique.[/profile]
5798.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Raw data fingerprint is a technique where adversaries analyze raw, unprocessed data from a system to create a unique identifier or profile of that system, often for evasion or identification purposes. This can involve examining low-level system attributes or data streams that are not typically sanitized or randomized, allowing the adversary to distinguish or spoof specific devices or environments to blend with legitimate traffic or target further actions.

5799.name: relocations
5799.profile: [profile]The entity 'relocations' is a technique for hijacking execution flow, aligning with MITRE ATT&CK ID T1574 under the Persistence tactic for Windows. It operates by manipulating how the operating system locates and loads programs or libraries, such as by poisoning directories or the Windows Registry to redirect to malicious payloads. This method is used by groups like Turla for persistence, privilege escalation, and defense evasion.[/profile]
5799.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity 'relocations' is an attack pattern within the MITRE ATT&CK framework. It is related to the technique of Hijack Execution Flow (T1574) under the Persistence and Privilege Escalation tactics. This technique involves adversaries manipulating how an operating system locates and loads programs or libraries, such as by poisoning trusted directories or registry paths, to execute malicious payloads instead of legitimate code.

5802.name: HTTP 1.1
5802.profile: [profile]HTTP 1.1 is a specific implementation of the Application Layer Protocol (T1071.001) within the Command and Control tactic. It is used by adversaries like Turla to blend malicious communications with normal web traffic by concealing commands and data within standard HTTP packet headers and fields. This technique can also be repurposed for Exfiltration Over Unencrypted Non-C2 Protocol (T1048.003) to steal data without encryption.
