This method is also used for data exfiltration over unencrypted channels and can be combined with techniques like Domain Fronting to further obfuscate the traffic's final destination.

5803.name: LogonUserAs()
5803.profile: [profile]LogonUserAs() is a function used within the technique Make and Impersonate Token (T1134.003) under the Privilege Escalation tactic. It operates on Windows platforms to create a new logon session and access token for a user when adversaries have credentials but the user is not logged on, enabling them to impersonate that user and bypass access controls. This function is distinct from stealing existing tokens and has been associated with groups like Turla.
5803.profile_without_enhance: [profile]LogonUserAs() is a function used within the broader technique of Make and Impersonate Token (T1134.003) under the Privilege Escalation tactic on Windows platforms. It allows an adversary to create a new logon session and access token for a user by providing credentials, such as a username and password, even if that user is not currently logged on. This newly generated token can then be assigned to a thread using functions like SetThreadToken to impersonate the user, bypass access controls, and escalate privileges.

5804.name: Task Execution
5804.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may abuse the Windows Task Scheduler to perform task scheduling for initial or recurring execution of malicious code. There are multiple ways to access the Task Scheduler in Windows. The [schtasks](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0111) utility can be run directly on the command line, or the Task Scheduler can be opened through the GUI within the Administrator Tools section of the Control Panel.(Citation: Stack Overflow) In some cases, adversaries have used a .NET wrapper for the Windows Task Scheduler, and alternatively, adversaries have used the Windows netapi32 library and [Windows Management Instrumentation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1047) (WMI) to create a scheduled task. Adversaries may also utilize the Powershell Cmdlet `Invoke-CimMethod`, which leverages WMI class `PS_ScheduledTask` to create a scheduled task via an XML path.(Citation: Red Canary - Atomic Red Team)

An adversary may use Windows Task Scheduler to execute programs at system startup or on a scheduled basis for persistence. The Windows Task Scheduler can also be abused to conduct remote Execution as part of Lateral Movement and/or to run a process under the context of a specified account (such as SYSTEM). Similar to [System Binary Proxy Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1218), adversaries have also abused the Windows Task Scheduler to potentially mask one-time execution under signed/trusted system processes.(Citation: ProofPoint Serpent)

Adversaries may also create "hidden" scheduled tasks (i.e. [Hide Artifacts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1564)) that may not be visible to defender tools and manual queries used to enumerate tasks. Specifically, an adversary may hide a task from `schtasks /query` and the Task Scheduler by deleting the associated Security Descriptor (SD) registry value (where deletion of this value must be completed using SYSTEM permissions).(Citation: SigmaHQ)(Citation: Tarrask scheduled task) Adversaries may also employ alternate methods to hide tasks, such as altering the metadata (e.g., `Index` value) within associated registry keys.(Citation: Defending Against Scheduled Task Attacks in Windows Environments)
5804.profile: [profile]Scheduled Task (T1053.005) is a Privilege Escalation, Persistence, and Execution technique for Windows. It abuses the Windows Task Scheduler via utilities like `schtasks.exe`, the GUI, a .NET wrapper, WMI (using `Invoke-CimMethod` with the `PS_ScheduledTask` class), or the `netapi32` library. It can be used for remote execution, running processes as SYSTEM, and hiding tasks by deleting the Security Descriptor registry value or altering registry key metadata to evade detection.[/profile]
5804.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Task Execution is a broad technique for running adversary-controlled code on a system. It aligns with the Execution tactic (TA0002) and is applicable across multiple platforms. The provided context highlights specific sub-techniques like Scheduled Task/Job (T1053), which involves abusing OS utilities such as Windows Task Scheduler (`schtasks`), the `at` command, or WMI to schedule and execute programs at specified times for persistence, lateral movement, or privilege escalation. Adversaries may also hide these tasks by manipulating registry values to evade detection.

5805.name: CreateProcess()
5805.profile: [profile]CreateProcess() is a core Windows API function for spawning new processes. It is notably abused in techniques like Parent PID Spoofing (T1134.004), where adversaries use its parameter to explicitly set a spoofed parent process identifier (PPID) for evasion or privilege escalation. It is also leveraged for persistence via AppCert DLLs (T1182), where malicious DLLs registered in a specific Registry key are loaded into any process that calls this API. The intrusion set Turla has been associated with its use.
5805.profile_without_enhance: [profile]CreateProcess() is a fundamental Windows API function (not a distinct MITRE ATT&CK technique) used to create new processes. It is leveraged within multiple techniques, including AppCert DLLs (T1182) for persistence via DLL injection into processes that call this API, and Parent PID Spoofing (T1134.004) for defense evasion and privilege escalation by explicitly setting a spoofed parent process identifier during process creation. Its primary technical mechanics involve spawning executable modules with specified parameters, enabling control over process attributes and inheritance.

5806.name: Memory Allocation
5806.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may attempt to access credential material stored in the process memory of the Local Security Authority Subsystem Service (LSASS). After a user logs on, the system generates and stores a variety of credential materials in LSASS process memory. These credential materials can be harvested by an administrative user or SYSTEM and used to conduct [Lateral Movement](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0008) using [Use Alternate Authentication Material](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1550). As well as in-memory techniques, the LSASS process memory can be dumped from the target host and analyzed on a local system. For example, on the target host use procdump: * procdump -ma lsass.exe lsass_dump Locally, mimikatz can be run using: * sekurlsa::Minidump lsassdump.dmp * sekurlsa::logonPasswords Built-in Windows tools such as `comsvcs.dll` can also be used: * rundll32.exe C:\Windows\System32\comsvcs.dll MiniDump PID lsass.dmp full(Citation: Volexity Exchange Marauder March 2021)(Citation: Symantec Attacks Against Government Sector) Similar to [Image File Execution Options Injection](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1546/012), the silent process exit mechanism can be abused to create a memory dump of `lsass.exe` through Windows Error Reporting (`WerFault.exe`).(Citation: Deep Instinct LSASS) Windows Security Support Provider (SSP) DLLs are loaded into LSASS process at system start. Once loaded into the LSA, SSP DLLs have access to encrypted and plaintext passwords that are stored in Windows, such as any logged-on user's Domain password or smart card PINs. The SSP configuration is stored in two Registry keys: HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa\Security Packages and HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa\OSConfig\Security Packages. An adversary may modify these Registry keys to add new SSPs, which will be loaded the next time the system boots, or when the AddSecurityPackage Windows API function is called.(Citation: Graeber 2014) The following SSPs can be used to access credentials: * Msv: Interactive logons, batch logons, and service logons are done through the MSV authentication package. * Wdigest: The Digest Authentication protocol is designed for use with Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) and Simple Authentication Security Layer (SASL) exchanges.(Citation: TechNet Blogs Credential Protection) * Kerberos: Preferred for mutual client-server domain authentication in Windows 2000 and later. * CredSSP: Provides SSO and Network Level Authentication for Remote Desktop Services.(Citation: TechNet Blogs Credential Protection)
5806.profile: [profile]LSASS Memory, identified as T1003.001 under the Credential Access tactic for Windows, involves harvesting credentials from the Local Security Authority Subsystem Service process. Technical mechanics include dumping LSASS memory using tools like `procdump -ma lsass.exe` or `rundll32.exe comsvcs.dll MiniDump`, and in-memory extraction via Mimikatz modules like `sekurlsa::logonPasswords`. Adversaries can also abuse the silent process exit mechanism or modify Security Support Provider (SSP) Registry keys to load malicious DLLs for credential access. This technique is widely used by groups like APT28, Turla, and MuddyWater.[/profile]
5806.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Memory Allocation is a foundational system technique, not a distinct MITRE ATT&CK technique. It describes the process by which programs request and manage memory from the operating system, typically through APIs like `VirtualAlloc` or `malloc`. This core function is ubiquitously used by legitimate software and is a prerequisite for many adversarial techniques, such as process injection (e.g., T1055) where allocated memory is used to host malicious code. While benign, its misuse is a common step in broader attack chains for execution and evasion.

5807.name: Read Data
5807.profile: [profile]Read Data is a technique used by adversaries to access and collect information from a system. It is associated with the intrusion set Turla. The technique involves adversaries searching for and reading files of interest from compromised systems, often from network shared drives or other accessible locations, using common command-line utilities or scripts to gather the data prior to potential exfiltration.
5807.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Read Data is a foundational adversary technique for collecting information from local system sources, often as a precursor to exfiltration. It involves accessing and reading data from files, directories, or system resources, using native OS commands or utilities. This technique is commonly associated with the Collection tactic and spans multiple platforms like Windows, Linux, and macOS. The retrieved information indicates it is a broad category that enables follow-on actions like Data Staged (T1074) or Data from Network Shared Drive (T1039), and is leveraged by various threat groups including APT28 and Gamaredon Group.

5808.name: Connect to Pipe/IP Address
5808.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may gather the victim's IP addresses that can be used during targeting. Public IP addresses may be allocated to organizations by block, or a range of sequential addresses. Information about assigned IP addresses may include a variety of details, such as which IP addresses are in use. IP addresses may also enable an adversary to derive other details about a victim, such as organizational size, physical location(s), Internet service provider, and or where/how their publicly-facing infrastructure is hosted.

Adversaries may gather this information in various ways, such as direct collection actions via [Active Scanning](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1595) or [Phishing for Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1598). Information about assigned IP addresses may also be exposed to adversaries via online or other accessible data sets (ex: [Search Open Technical Databases](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1596)).(Citation: WHOIS)(Citation: DNS Dumpster)(Citation: Circl Passive DNS) Gathering this information may reveal opportunities for other forms of reconnaissance (ex: [Active Scanning](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1595) or [Search Open Websites/Domains](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1593)), establishing operational resources (ex: [Acquire Infrastructure](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1583) or [Compromise Infrastructure](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1584)), and/or initial access (ex: [External Remote Services](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1133)).
5808.profile: [profile]The entity "Connect to Pipe/IP Address" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the provided data, it appears to be a misinterpretation or mislabeling of the technique "Gather Victim Network Information: IP Addresses" (T1590.005) under the Reconnaissance tactic. This technique involves adversaries collecting a victim's public IP address blocks through methods like Active Scanning, Phishing for Information, or querying open technical databases (e.g., WHOIS, DNS Dumpster) to infer organizational details and plan subsequent attacks. The intrusion-set Turla is associated with this activity.
5808.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Connect to Pipe/IP Address" is a command and control technique. It involves adversaries establishing a connection to a remote pipe or IP address to facilitate communication with compromised systems. This method is part of the Command and Control tactic and is applicable across multiple platforms. The technique enables persistent remote access and data exfiltration by using specific network endpoints for covert communication channels.

5809.name: Initialize Communication
5809.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may use an existing, legitimate external Web service as a means for sending commands to and receiving output from a compromised system over the Web service channel. Compromised systems may leverage popular websites and social media to host command and control (C2) instructions. Those infected systems can then send the output from those commands back over that Web service channel. The return traffic may occur in a variety of ways, depending on the Web service being utilized. For example, the return traffic may take the form of the compromised system posting a comment on a forum, issuing a pull request to development project, updating a document hosted on a Web service, or by sending a Tweet. 

Popular websites and social media acting as a mechanism for C2 may give a significant amount of cover due to the likelihood that hosts within a network are already communicating with them prior to a compromise. Using common services, such as those offered by Google or Twitter, makes it easier for adversaries to hide in expected noise. Web service providers commonly use SSL/TLS encryption, giving adversaries an added level of protection.
5809.profile: [profile]Initialize Communication is the technique T1102.002, a sub-technique of Web Service within the Command and Control tactic. It operates across Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms by using legitimate external web services like social media sites or forums for bidirectional command and control. Compromised systems receive instructions from and send command output back through these channels, using methods such as posting comments, issuing pull requests, updating documents, or sending tweets to blend with normal traffic and leverage inherent SSL/TLS encryption. This technique is notably used by intrusion sets including Turla, APT28, and Lazarus Group.[profile]
5809.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Initialize Communication is a technique within the Command and Control tactic. It involves adversaries establishing the initial command and control (C2) channel with a compromised system. This foundational step enables subsequent malicious activities by creating a communication pathway, often using common protocols or services to blend with normal network traffic and avoid detection. The technique focuses on the initial handshake or connection setup before any data exfiltration or command execution occurs.

5813.name: Cryptographic keys
5813.profile: [profile]Cryptographic keys are digital keys used for encryption and decryption, as referenced in relation to the Turla intrusion set and the Equation Group's EquationDrug malware, which employs 3×1024-bit encryption keys, and are also utilized to decrypt Cobalt Strike traffic extracted from process memory, with associations to various APT groups including APT29, APT32, APT41, and others such as FIN6, FIN7, and Mustang Panda.

The retrieved information indicates these keys are used in high-profile cyber operations. For instance, cryptographic keys are extracted from process memory to decrypt Cobalt Strike traffic, a tool associated with groups like APT29, APT32, APT41, FIN6, FIN7, and Mustang Panda. Additionally, the EquationDrug malware, linked to the Equation Group, utilizes binaries with embedded 1024-bit encryption keys. This context highlights cryptographic keys as a target for theft and a component in malware like EquationDrug to secure communications and payloads.

5824.name: Execution Subsystem
5824.profile: [profile]Execution Subsystem is a malware component attributed to the Turla intrusion set. It is referenced in the context of other malware families like CaddyWiper, which is linked to APT28 and Sandworm, and Ave Maria, associated with groups like Anthropoid Spider and Anunak. Its technical behavior involves manipulating Windows registry keys, specifically within the Windows Messaging Subsystem profiles, to establish persistence or facilitate malicious execution flows on Windows platforms. This component is part of broader malware operations, including ransomware like CashRansomware, indicating its role in initial execution phases across various campaigns targeting Windows systems.[profile]

This malware is linked to threat groups including Anthropoid Spider and Anunak. It targets the Windows platform.

5825.name: Autorun Manager

5826.name: RSA+BZIP2 Compression
5826.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may use compression to obfuscate their payloads or files. Compressed file formats such as ZIP, gzip, 7z, and RAR can compress and archive multiple files together to make it easier and faster to transfer files. In addition to compressing files, adversaries may also compress shellcode directly - for example, in order to store it in a Windows Registry key (i.e., [Fileless Storage](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/011)).(Citation: Trustwave Pillowmint June 2020)

In order to further evade detection, adversaries may combine multiple ZIP files into one archive. This process of concatenation creates an archive that appears to be a single archive but in fact contains the central directories of the embedded archives. Some ZIP readers, such as 7zip, may not be able to identify concatenated ZIP files and miss the presence of the malicious payload.(Citation: Perception Point)

File archives may be sent as one [Spearphishing Attachment](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001) through email. Adversaries have sent malicious payloads as archived files to encourage the user to interact with and extract the malicious payload onto their system (i.e., [Malicious File](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002)).(Citation: NTT Security Flagpro new December 2021) However, some file compression tools, such as 7zip, can be used to produce self-extracting archives. Adversaries may send self-extracting archives to hide the functionality of their payload and launch it without requiring multiple actions from the user.(Citation: The Hacker News)

[Compression](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/015) may be used in combination with [Encrypted/Encoded File](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/013) where compressed files are encrypted and password-protected.
5826.profile: [profile]The entity "RSA+BZIP2 Compression" is a specific implementation of the MITRE ATT&CK technique Compression (T1027.015) under the Defense Evasion tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. This technique involves using the RSA algorithm for encryption and the BZIP2 algorithm for compression to obfuscate payloads or files, making them harder to detect and analyze. It is associated with threat groups including Gamaredon Group and Turla. The method can be used to store compressed shellcode in locations like the Windows Registry and is often combined with other techniques like data encryption for layered obfuscation.
5826.profile_without_enhance: [profile]RSA+BZIP2 Compression is a specific technique for data obfuscation and exfiltration, aligning with the MITRE ATT&CK tactic of Defense Evasion and potentially Exfiltration. It operates by using the BZIP2 algorithm to compress collected data, making it portable and minimizing network footprint, and may further employ RSA encryption for securing the compressed archive. This combination of compression and encryption is used to evade detection during transfer, with the technique applicable across multiple platforms where these libraries or utilities are available.

5827.name: Privileged Process Protection
5827.profile: [profile]Privileged Process Protection is a defensive technique, not an attack pattern, and does not have a corresponding MITRE ATT&CK ID or Tactic. It is a security mechanism designed to protect high-integrity processes from code injection or tampering by other processes, thereby mitigating techniques like Process Injection (T1055) and Process Hollowing (T1093). The intrusion-set Turla is a known entity that employs such injection techniques, which this protection aims to counter.
5827.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Privileged Process Protection is a security feature, not a MITRE ATT&CK attack pattern. The retrieved information describes adversarial techniques like Process Injection (T1055), Process Hollowing (T1093), and Process Doppelgänging (T1055.013), which involve executing code within legitimate processes to evade detection and potentially gain privileged access. These techniques work by creating or hijacking a process, unmapping its memory, and replacing it with malicious code, often using specific API calls or transactional file operations to avoid security monitoring.

5828.name: Standard Window Inject
5828.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may encode data with a standard data encoding system to make the content of command and control traffic more difficult to detect. Command and control (C2) information can be encoded using a standard data encoding system that adheres to existing protocol specifications. Common data encoding schemes include ASCII, Unicode, hexadecimal, Base64, and MIME.(Citation: Wikipedia Binary-to-text Encoding)(Citation: Wikipedia Character Encoding) Some data encoding systems may also result in data compression, such as gzip.
5828.profile: [profile]Standard Window Inject is a process injection technique (T1055.011) under the Defense Evasion and Privilege Escalation tactics, targeting Windows. It exploits the Extra Window Memory (EWM) allocated during window class registration, which can store a 32-bit pointer. Attackers write malicious code to shared memory sections, place a pointer to it in the EWM, and then redirect execution to that address, thereby running code within a legitimate process's context to evade detection and potentially gain elevated privileges while avoiding monitored APIs like WriteProcessMemory and CreateRemoteThread.
5828.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Standard Window Inject is a process injection technique (T1055) within the Execution tactic, targeting the Windows platform. It operates by exploiting the Windows GUI subsystem, where a malicious payload is written to a shared memory section. A pointer to this code is then stored in the 40 bytes of Extra Window Memory (EWM) allocated for a window class instance. Execution is invoked by redirecting control to this pointer, effectively running code within a legitimate process's address space to evade detection and potentially gain elevated privileges, while avoiding highly monitored APIs like WriteProcessMemory and CreateRemoteThread.

5829.name: Kernel Injector Subsystem
5829.profile: [profile]The entity "Kernel Injector Subsystem" is a technique for achieving persistence and evasion, associated with the Turla intrusion set. It operates by loading malicious code into the kernel space, such as through Loadable Kernel Modules (LKMs) on Linux or kernel extensions (kext) on macOS, granting it the highest operating system privileges (Ring 0). This allows it to hide files, processes, and network activity, tamper with logs, and provide backdoor access. The method is a form of kernel-mode rootkit execution, distinct from user-space process injection techniques like Portable Executable injection.[/profile]
5829.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Kernel Injector Subsystem is a technique for executing code within the kernel space of an operating system, often to evade detection and gain high-privilege persistence. It operates by loading malicious kernel modules or extensions, such as Linux Loadable Kernel Modules (LKMs) or macOS kernel extensions (kexts), which run with Ring 0 privileges. This allows adversaries to hide files, processes, and network activity, tamper with logs, and create backdoors. The method is platform-specific, leveraging OS mechanisms like `kextload` on macOS, and is a sophisticated form of kernel-mode rootkit.

5830.name: WhiteBear Components

Its technical behaviors include a binary loader and system injection, with a known sample compiled using MSVC 2010. The platform targets Windows systems, as indicated by its PE EXE file type.[/profile]
5830.profile_without_enhance: [profile]WhiteBear Components is a malware platform attributed to the Turla group. It implements an elaborate set of messaging and injection components to support full presence on victim hosts, including a binary loader. The platform is designed for Windows systems, as indicated by its PE EXE file type and compilation with MSVC 2010.

The payload is distributed in the form of JavaScript files with specific SHA256 hashes such as 781c63cf4981fa6aff002188307b278fac9785ca66f0b6dfcf68adbe7512e491, often alongside MSI and DLL payloads in coordinated campaigns targeting Windows systems.
5833.profile_without_enhance: [profile]JavaScript payload is a component used by multiple malware families, including IcedID (attributed to groups like Gold Cabin and Lunar Spider) and Latrodectus, as indicated by shared SHA256 hashes for JavaScript payloads. It serves as a delivery or execution mechanism within broader infection chains, often associated with MSI and DLL payloads. 5836.name: Operation Yankee Shotgun
5836.profile: [profile]Operation Yankee Shotgun is a campaign attributed to the Turla intrusion set. Its activities involve screen capture for information gathering, using native utilities or remote access tools. The campaign also employs data obfuscation, such as adding junk data to command and control traffic to hinder detection, and may attempt to masquerade scheduled tasks or services by using names similar to legitimate ones to evade security measures.
5836.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Operation Yankee Shotgun is a campaign name, not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the provided context, it is associated with the screen capture technique (T1113), which involves adversaries taking screenshots of the desktop to gather information. This can be done using remote access tools, native utilities, or API calls like `CopyFromScreen`, `xwd`, or `screencapture`. The campaign has been linked to multiple threat groups, including APT28, FIN7, and Lazarus Group.

5837.name: rogue program
5837.uncertain_mes: Research by: Aviran Hazum, Alex Shamshur, Raman Ladutska, Ohad Mana, Israel Wernik
5837.profile: [profile]The malware, known as 'rogue program' or simply 'rogue', is attributed to the Turla intrusion set. It is a malicious program that attempts to evade anti-virus protections by potentially abusing code-signing mechanisms. It is associated with fake browser update campaigns, such as the RogueRaticate example, and has been distributed historically through affiliate programs like "Traffic converter" that push rogue antivirus solutions. The primary target platform is Windows.[/profile]
5837.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The malware, known as "rogue program," is associated with or shares characteristics with entities named "rogue" and "RogueRaticate." It is referenced in the context of the HermeticWiper malware, where it may have used code-signing to evade anti-virus protections. It is also linked to distribution through affiliate programs, such as a "Traffic converter" program that disseminated rogue antivirus solutions, indicating a potential history of being bundled with other malware or deceptive software campaigns.

5839.name: Evercookie
5839.profile: [profile]Evercookie is a persistent tracking mechanism. Its implementation is based on publicly available GitHub code, as seen in the Turla group's LightNeuron malware, where it is used to set a unique MD5 value in a user's browser. It is attributed to the intrusion set Turla. A key technical behavior is its use of multiple browser storage mechanisms to resist deletion, creating a resilient identifier. Its primary target platform is web browsers, functioning as a client-side script for tracking and identification purposes.
5839.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Evercookie, also known as an evercookie, is a persistent tracking script that stores a unique identifier, such as an MD5 value, in a user's browser using multiple storage mechanisms to resist deletion. It is implemented based on publicly available code from GitHub. Its key technical behavior involves setting a persistent cookie to track users across sessions. The primary target platform is web browsers. It has been associated with the Turla group in the context of the LightNeuron malware, which uses it for tracking purposes.

5840.name: Creating Cookies in Multiple Storage Locations
5840.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may forge web cookies that can be used to gain access to web applications or Internet services. Web applications and services (hosted in cloud SaaS environments or on-premise servers) often use session cookies to authenticate and authorize user access.

Adversaries may generate these cookies in order to gain access to web resources. This differs from [Steal Web Session Cookie](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539) and other similar behaviors in that the cookies are new and forged by the adversary, rather than stolen or intercepted from legitimate users. Most common web applications have standardized and documented cookie values that can be generated using provided tools or interfaces.(Citation: Pass The Cookie) The generation of web cookies often requires secret values, such as passwords, [Private Keys](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1552/004), or other cryptographic seed values.

Once forged, adversaries may use these web cookies to access resources ([Web Session Cookie](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1550/004)), which may bypass multi-factor and other authentication protection mechanisms.(Citation: Volexity SolarWinds)(Citation: Pass The Cookie)(Citation: Unit 42 Mac Crypto Cookies January 2019)
5840.profile: [profile]Creating Cookies in Multiple Storage Locations is a technique identified as T1606.001 under the Credential Access tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It involves adversaries forging new web session cookies to gain unauthorized access to applications, differing from stealing existing cookies. This forgery typically requires obtaining secret values like passwords or private keys to generate standardized cookie values, which can then be used to bypass multi-factor authentication, as observed in campaigns by groups like Turla. The forged cookies are subsequently employed in Web Session Cookie (T1550.004) attacks for resource access.
5840.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Creating Cookies in Multiple Storage Locations is a technique where adversaries forge web cookies to gain unauthorized access to web applications or services, differing from stealing existing cookies. This involves generating new, valid session cookies, often requiring secret values like passwords or private keys, and storing these forged credentials in various non-standard or multiple locations to evade detection. The forged cookies can then be used in a Web Session Cookie attack to bypass multi-factor authentication and access resources as an authenticated user.

5841.name: Browser Fingerprinting
5841.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may abuse internet browser extensions to establish persistent access to victim systems. Browser extensions or plugins are small programs that can add functionality to and customize aspects of internet browsers. They can be installed directly via a local file or custom URL or through a browser's app store - an official online platform where users can browse, install, and manage extensions for a specific web browser. Extensions generally inherit the web browser's permissions previously granted.(Citation: Wikipedia Browser Extension)(Citation: Chrome Extensions Definition) Malicious extensions can be installed into a browser through malicious app store downloads masquerading as legitimate extensions, through social engineering, or by an adversary that has already compromised a system. Security can be limited on browser app stores, so it may not be difficult for malicious extensions to defeat automated scanners.(Citation: Malicious Chrome Extension Numbers) Depending on the browser, adversaries may also manipulate an extension's update url to install updates from an adversary-controlled server or manipulate the mobile configuration file to silently install additional extensions. Adversaries may abuse how chromium-based browsers load extensions by modifying or replacing the Preferences and/or Secure Preferences files to silently install malicious extensions. When the browser is not running, adversaries can alter these files, ensuring the extension is loaded, granted desired permissions, and will persist in browser sessions. This method does not require user consent and extensions are silently loaded in the background from disk or from the browser's trusted store.(Citation: Pulsedive) Previous to macOS 11, adversaries could silently install browser extensions via the command line using the profiles tool to install malicious .mobileconfig files. In macOS 11+, the use of the profiles tool can no longer install configuration profiles; however, .mobileconfig files can be planted and installed with user interaction.(Citation: xorrior chrome extensions macOS) Once the extension is installed, it can browse to websites in the background, steal all information that a user enters into a browser (including credentials), and be used as an installer for a RAT for persistence.(Citation: Chrome Extension Crypto Miner)(Citation: ICEBRG Chrome Extensions)(Citation: Banker Google Chrome Extension Steals Creds)(Citation: Catch All Chrome Extension) There have also been instances of botnets using a persistent backdoor through malicious Chrome extensions for [Command and Control](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0011).(Citation: Stantinko Botnet)(Citation: Chrome Extension C2 Malware) Adversaries may also use browser extensions to modify browser permissions and components, privacy settings, and other security controls for [Defense Evasion](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0005).(Citation: Browers FriarFox)(Citation: Browser Adrozek)
5841.profile: [profile]Browser Fingerprinting is a technique adversaries use to blend in with legitimate web traffic by spoofing browser and system attributes like the user-agent string, operating system, platform, and time zone. This technique, which can be mapped to Impersonation: Browser Fingerprinting (T1036.012) under the Defense Evasion tactic, operates across multiple platforms. The technical mechanics involve gathering system information or luring users to adversary-controlled sites to collect fingerprinting data, then crafting subsequent web traffic to mimic a legitimate user's browser profile, thereby evading detection mechanisms that rely on these attributes for identification.
5841.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Browser Fingerprinting is a reconnaissance technique where adversaries gather unique browser and system attributes such as the User-Agent string, operating system, language, resolution, and time zone to identify and track users. This information, often collected via websites or System Information Discovery, can be used to craft tailored web traffic for evasion or to profile targets for further attacks. It is associated with the active scanning technique T1595 and is a form of browser information discovery.

5842.name: Strategic Web Compromise
5842.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may compromise third-party infrastructure that can be used during targeting. Infrastructure solutions include physical or cloud servers, domains, network devices, and third-party web and DNS services. Instead of buying, leasing, or renting infrastructure an adversary may compromise infrastructure and use it during other phases of the adversary lifecycle.(Citation: Mandiant APT1)(Citation: ICANNDomainNameHijacking)(Citation: Talos DNSpionage Nov 2018)(Citation: FireEye EPS Awakens Part 2) Additionally, adversaries may compromise numerous machines to form a botnet they can leverage.

Use of compromised infrastructure allows adversaries to stage, launch, and execute operations. Compromised infrastructure can help adversary operations blend in with traffic that is seen as normal, such as contact with high reputation or trusted sites. For example, adversaries may leverage compromised infrastructure (potentially also in conjunction with [Digital Certificates](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1588/004)) to further blend in and support staged information gathering and/or [Phishing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566) campaigns.(Citation: FireEye DNS Hijack 2019) Adversaries may also compromise numerous machines to support [Proxy](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1090) and/or proxyware services or to form a botnet.(Citation: amnesty_nso_pegasus)(Citation: Sysdig Proxyjacking) Additionally, adversaries may compromise infrastructure residing in close proximity to a target in order to gain [Initial Access](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0001) via [Wi-Fi Networks](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1669).(Citation: Nearest Neighbor Volexity)

By using compromised infrastructure, adversaries may enable follow-on malicious operations. Prior to targeting, adversaries may also compromise the infrastructure of other adversaries.(Citation: NSA NCSC Turla OilRig)
5842.profile: [profile]Strategic Web Compromise, also known as a watering hole attack, is a technique where adversaries compromise legitimate websites frequented by a specific target community. This technique is used in the Resource Development tactic (T1584) and involves staging malicious content, such as JavaScript, on the compromised web server. The goal is to exploit visitors' browsers (Drive-by Compromise, T1189) to gain initial access, often by profiling the browser first to ensure vulnerability. This method leverages the trust associated with the legitimate site to blend malicious activity with normal traffic.[/profile]
5842.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Strategic Web Compromise, also known as a watering hole attack, is a technique within the Initial Access tactic (T1189) targeting web browsers. It involves compromising or creating a website frequented by a specific target community, such as a particular industry or government sector. The adversary stages malicious content, like JavaScript, on the site to exploit vulnerabilities in a visitor's browser or plugins, often delivering the exploit automatically without requiring extra user interaction beyond browsing to the page. This method is a targeted form of Drive-by Compromise, blending malicious activity with normal web traffic to infect specific users.

The retrieved information describes adversaries registering for or compromising legitimate third-party web services like Google or Twitter to use them for command and control, exfiltration, or phishing, blending malicious traffic with normal activity to avoid detection.

No specific technical mechanics for an attack pattern named "Web Analytics" are present in the input.

5844.name: Strategic Cyber-Attack (SWC)
5844.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may downgrade or use a version of system features that may be outdated, vulnerable, and/or does not support updated security controls. Downgrade attacks typically take advantage of a system’s backward compatibility to force it into less secure modes of operation. 

Adversaries may downgrade and use various less-secure versions of features of a system, such as [Command and Scripting Interpreter](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059)s or even network protocols that can be abused to enable [Adversary-in-the-Middle](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1557) or [Network Sniffing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1040).(Citation: Praetorian TLS Downgrade Attack 2014) For example, [PowerShell](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001) versions 5+ includes Script Block Logging (SBL), which can record executed script content. However, adversaries may attempt to execute a previous version of PowerShell that does not support SBL with the intent to [Impair Defenses](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1562) while running malicious scripts that may have otherwise been detected.(Citation: CrowdStrike BGH Ransomware 2021)(Citation: Mandiant BYOL 2018)(Citation: att_def_ps_logging)

Adversaries may similarly target network traffic to downgrade from an encrypted HTTPS connection to an unsecured HTTP connection that exposes network data in clear text.(Citation: Targeted SSL Stripping Attacks Are Real)(Citation: Crowdstrike Downgrade) On Windows systems, adversaries may downgrade the boot manager to a vulnerable version that bypasses Secure Boot, granting the ability to disable various operating system security mechanisms.(Citation: SafeBreach)
5844.profile: [profile]Downgrade Attack, identified as T1562.010 under the Impair Defenses tactic, targets Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It exploits system backward compatibility to force less secure operational modes, such as executing older PowerShell versions to bypass Script Block Logging or downgrading HTTPS connections to unencrypted HTTP to expose network traffic. This technique is used by groups like Turla to evade security controls and facilitate activities like adversary-in-the-middle attacks.[/profile]
5844.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Strategic Cyber-Attack (SWC) is a targeted campaign technique, also known as a watering hole attack, within the Initial Access tactic. It involves compromising specific websites frequented by a particular community, industry, or region to exploit visitors' web browsers. The adversary stages malicious content, such as injected scripts, on these sites to deliver exploits automatically when a targeted user visits, often without requiring additional interaction, thereby gaining access to internal network systems.

5845.name: Deception Techniques
5845.profile: [profile]Deception Techniques is a broad adversarial tactic for evading defenses and misleading users, often associated with groups like Turla. It encompasses specific techniques such as Masquerading (T1036), which manipulates file names, locations, and metadata to make malicious artifacts appear legitimate. This tactic is executed across multiple platforms and involves actions like renaming system utilities or spoofing file types to bypass security monitoring.
5845.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Deception Techniques" is a broad attack-pattern. The retrieved information describes specific techniques like Masquerading (T1036), which is a sub-technique under Defense Evasion. Masquerading involves manipulating file names, locations, or metadata to make malicious objects appear legitimate, such as by renaming system utilities to evade monitoring. Other retrieved techniques like "business relationships" (T1591.002) and "identify business tempo" (T1591.003) are unrelated reconnaissance methods and are not part of this entity's core technical mechanics, which are focused on deceptive practices to avoid detection.

5846.name: Linux
5846.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may abuse the [at](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0110) utility to perform task scheduling for initial, recurring, or future execution of malicious code. The [at](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0110) command within Linux operating systems enables administrators to schedule tasks.(Citation: Kifarunix - Task Scheduling in Linux) An adversary may use [at](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0110) in Linux environments to execute programs at system startup or on a scheduled basis for persistence. [at](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0110) can also be abused to conduct remote Execution as part of Lateral Movement and or to run a process under the context of a specified account. Adversaries may also abuse [at](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0110) to break out of restricted environments by using a task to spawn an interactive system shell or to run system commands. Similarly, [at](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0110) may also be used for [Privilege Escalation](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0004) if the binary is allowed to run as superuser via sudo.(Citation: GTFObins at)
5846.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique "at (linux)" with ID T1053.001, categorized under Execution and Persistence tactics for Linux platforms. It involves abusing the native `at` command to schedule tasks for executing malicious code at system startup, specific times, or on a recurring basis. This can facilitate persistence, lateral movement, privilege escalation via sudo, or breaking out of restricted environments by spawning shells. The intrusion set Turla has been associated with this technique.
5846.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity 'Linux' is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK attack pattern; it is an operating system platform. The retrieved information describes various techniques that adversaries may employ on Linux systems. These include abusing the 'at' utility for task scheduling (T1053.001), clearing system logs (T1070.002), disabling the audit system (T1562.012), modifying file permissions (T1222.002), dumping password files for offline cracking (T1003.008), and using local job scheduling methods like cron for persistence and execution (T1168).

5847.name: Trojanizing Software
5847.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may gather information about the victim's host software that can be used during targeting. Information about installed software may include a variety of details such as types and versions on specific hosts, as well as the presence of additional components that might be indicative of added defensive protections (ex: antivirus, SIEMs, etc.).

Adversaries may gather this information in various ways, such as direct collection actions via [Active Scanning](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1595) (ex: listening ports, server banners, user agent strings) or [Phishing for Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1598). Adversaries may also compromise sites then include malicious content designed to collect host information from visitors.(Citation: ATT ScanBox) Information about the installed software may also be exposed to adversaries via online or other accessible data sets (ex: job postings, network maps, assessment reports, resumes, or purchase invoices). Additionally, adversaries may analyze metadata from victim-owned files (e.g., PDFs, DOCs, images, and sound files hosted on victim-owned websites) to extract information about the software and hardware used to create or process those files. Metadata may reveal software versions, configurations, or timestamps that indicate outdated or vulnerable software. This information can be cross-referenced with known CVEs to identify potential vectors for exploitation in future operations.(Citation: Outpost24)

Gathering this information may reveal opportunities for other forms of reconnaissance (ex: [Search Open Websites/Domains](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1593) or [Search Open Technical Databases](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1596)), establishing operational resources (ex: [Develop Capabilities](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1587) or [Obtain Capabilities](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1588)), and/or for initial access (ex: [Supply Chain Compromise](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195) or [External Remote Services](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1133)).
5847.profile: [profile]The entity "Trojanizing Software" is a technique for compromising software supply chains, corresponding to MITRE ATT&CK ID T1195.002 under the Initial Access tactic, targeting multiple platforms. It involves manipulating application source code, update mechanisms, or compiled releases prior to distribution to end consumers. This method can be broadly distributed or specifically targeted, enabling adversaries like Sandworm Team to gain initial access by delivering malicious versions of legitimate software to victims.
5847.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Trojanizing Software is a technique within the broader Supply Chain Compromise (T1195.002) tactic. It involves manipulating legitimate software or its update mechanisms prior to distribution to end users, thereby inserting malicious code. This method allows adversaries to gain initial access by exploiting the trust in the software's source, often distributing the trojanized application broadly but activating payloads only on specific, targeted victims.

5851.name: Spear-Phishing Campaign
5851.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may send phishing messages to gain access to victim systems. All forms of phishing are electronically delivered social engineering. Phishing can be targeted, known as spearphishing. In spearphishing, a specific individual, company, or industry will be targeted by the adversary. More generally, adversaries can conduct non-targeted phishing, such as in mass malware spam campaigns.

Adversaries may send victims emails containing malicious attachments or links, typically to execute malicious code on victim systems. Phishing may also be conducted via third-party services, like social media platforms. Phishing may also involve social engineering techniques, such as posing as a trusted source, as well as evasive techniques such as removing or manipulating emails or metadata/headers from compromised accounts being abused to send messages (e.g., [Email Hiding Rules](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1564/008)).(Citation: Microsoft OAuth Spam 2022)(Citation: Palo Alto Unit 42 VBA Infostealer 2014) Another way to accomplish this is by [Email Spoofing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1672)(Citation: Proofpoint-spoof) the identity of the sender, which can be used to fool both the human recipient as well as automated security tools,(Citation: cyberproof-double-bounce) or by including the intended target as a party to an existing email thread that includes malicious files or links (i.e., "thread hijacking").(Citation: phishing-krebs)

Victims may also receive phishing messages that instruct them to call a phone number where they are directed to visit a malicious URL, download malware,(Citation: sygnia Luna Month)(Citation: CISA Remote Monitoring and Management Software) or install adversary-accessible remote management tools onto their computer (i.e., [User Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204)).(Citation: Unit42 Luna Moth)
5851.profile: [profile]Spear-Phishing Campaign is a targeted form of Phishing, corresponding to MITRE ATT&CK ID T1566 under the Initial Access tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It involves sending tailored electronic messages, such as emails with malicious attachments or links, to specific individuals or organizations to execute malicious code. Techniques include posing as a trusted source, email spoofing, thread hijacking, and using third-party services or social media to bypass enterprise security. The intrusion-set Turla has been associated with this technique.[/profile]
5851.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Spear-Phishing Campaign is a targeted social engineering technique, categorized under the MITRE ATT&CK framework as a form of Spearphishing (T1566) within the Initial Access tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It involves sending tailored electronic messages, such as emails with malicious attachments or links, to specific individuals or organizations to trick them into executing code or divulging credentials. The campaign often employs sophisticated lures, email spoofing, and may use third-party services or QR codes to evade detection, with the ultimate goal of gaining an initial foothold in a victim's environment.

5852.name: AddSecurityPackage API
5852.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may interact with the native OS application programming interface (API) to execute behaviors. Native APIs provide a controlled means of calling low-level OS services within the kernel, such as those involving hardware/devices, memory, and processes.(Citation: NT API Windows)(Citation: Linux Kernel API) These native APIs are leveraged by the OS during system boot (when other system components are not yet initialized) as well as carrying out tasks and requests during routine operations. Adversaries may abuse these OS API functions as a means of executing behaviors. Similar to [Command and Scripting Interpreter](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059), the native API and its hierarchy of interfaces provide mechanisms to interact with and utilize various components of a victimized system. Native API functions (such as NtCreateProcess) may be directed invoked via system calls / syscalls, but these features are also often exposed to user-mode applications via interfaces and libraries.(Citation: OutFlank System Calls)(Citation: CyberBit System Calls)(Citation: MDSec System Calls) For example, functions such as the Windows API CreateProcess() or GNU fork() will allow programs and scripts to start other processes.(Citation: Microsoft CreateProcess)(Citation: GNU Fork) This may allow API callers to execute a binary, run a CLI command, load modules, etc. as thousands of similar API functions exist for various system operations.(Citation: Microsoft Win32)(Citation: LIBC)(Citation: GLIBC) Higher level software frameworks, such as Microsoft .NET and macOS Cocoa, are also available to interact with native APIs. These frameworks typically provide language wrappers/abstractions to API functionalities and are designed for ease-of-use/portability of code.(Citation: Microsoft NET)(Citation: Apple Core Services)(Citation: MACOS Cocoa)(Citation: macOS Foundation) Adversaries may use assembly to directly or in-directly invoke syscalls in an attempt to subvert defensive sensors and detection signatures such as user mode API-hooks.(Citation: Redops Syscalls) Adversaries may also attempt to tamper with sensors and defensive tools associated with API monitoring, such as unhooking monitored functions via [Disable or Modify Tools](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1562/001).
5852.profile: [profile]AddSecurityPackage API is a specific Windows Native API function (T1106) used for Defense Evasion and Persistence, primarily on Windows platforms. It is called to dynamically load a new Security Support Provider (SSP) DLL into the Local Security Authority (LSA) process without requiring a system reboot, enabling adversaries to inject malicious code to harvest credentials. This technique is referenced in relation to the Security Support Provider (T1547.005) persistence method and has been associated with groups like Turla.
5852.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The AddSecurityPackage API is a Windows Native API function used within the Boot or Logon Autostart Execution tactic. It is specifically employed to dynamically load a Security Support Provider (SSP) DLL into the Local Security Authority (LSA) process without requiring a system reboot. This allows adversaries to inject malicious SSPs to harvest encrypted or plaintext credentials, such as domain passwords or smart card PINs, by calling this API after modifying the related SSP configuration Registry keys.

Adversaries may abuse these OS API functions as a means of executing behaviors. 5853.profile: [profile]The entity "DeviceIoControl API" is a specific Windows Native API function, aligning with the broader MITRE ATT&CK technique "Native API" (T1106) under the Execution tactic for Windows platforms. It provides a controlled interface for user-mode applications to send control codes directly to device drivers, enabling low-level hardware and system operations. Adversaries, including groups like Turla, may abuse this function to execute malicious driver commands or perform direct hardware manipulation, often to bypass higher-level security monitoring. This technique is part of a common pattern of leveraging OS APIs for stealthy execution.
5853.profile_without_enhance: [profile]DeviceIoControl API is a Windows Native API function used for low-level hardware and device communication. It is associated with the MITRE ATT&CK technique Native API (T1106) under the Execution tactic on Windows platforms. Adversaries abuse this API to send control codes directly to device drivers, enabling privileged operations like reading physical memory, interacting with storage volumes, or bypassing security software by communicating with kernel-mode components. This direct hardware access allows execution of malicious behaviors with elevated permissions.

5854.name: Function Ordinals with Gaps
5854.profile: [profile]Function Ordinals with Gaps is a technique used by adversaries like Turla to evade static analysis and detection. It involves deliberately leaving gaps or using non-sequential numbers for function ordinals within a DLL's export table, which can break automated parsing tools and complicate reverse engineering efforts. This method helps malicious code blend in or avoid signature-based detection by obscuring its true import structure.
5854.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Function Ordinals with Gaps is a technique for defense evasion and discovery, primarily on Windows platforms. It involves malware calling Windows API functions not by name but by their ordinal numbers, which are integer identifiers, and intentionally skipping or leaving gaps in the sequence of these calls. This unusual pattern of API usage is designed to evade static analysis and signature-based detection tools that look for standard API call sequences, making the malicious code harder to identify and analyze.
