5861.name: Remsec
5861.uncertain_mes: [Remsec](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0125) is a modular backdoor that has been used by [Strider](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0041) and appears to have been designed primarily for espionage purposes. Many of its modules are written in Lua. (Citation: Symantec Strider Blog)
5861.profile: [profile]Remsec, also known as ProjectSauron, is a modular backdoor attributed to the Strider (Turla) group, designed for espionage. Its key technical behaviors include using Lua-written modules for stealthy operations, and it targets various platforms for data exfiltration and surveillance. Infrastructure details are limited, but it is associated with advanced persistent threat activities.
5861.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Remsec is a malware attributed to the ProjectSauron group. Its modules have been documented by Symantec.

5862.name: Use non-hidden file name as base
5862.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may use a hidden file system to conceal malicious activity from users and security tools. File systems provide a structure to store and access data from physical storage. Typically, a user engages with a file system through applications that allow them to access files and directories, which are an abstraction from their physical location (ex: disk sector). Standard file systems include FAT, NTFS, ext4, and APFS. File systems can also contain other structures, such as the Volume Boot Record (VBR) and Master File Table (MFT) in NTFS.(Citation: MalwareTech VFS Nov 2014)

Adversaries may use their own abstracted file system, separate from the standard file system present on the infected system. In doing so, adversaries can hide the presence of malicious components and file input/output from security tools. Hidden file systems, sometimes referred to as virtual file systems, can be implemented in numerous ways. One implementation would be to store a file system in reserved disk space unused by disk structures or standard file system partitions.(Citation: MalwareTech VFS Nov 2014)(Citation: FireEye Bootkits) Another implementation could be for an adversary to drop their own portable partition image as a file on top of the standard file system.(Citation: ESET ComRAT May 2020) Adversaries may also fragment files across the existing file system structure in non-standard ways.(Citation: Kaspersky Equation QA)
5862.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique "Hidden File System" (ID: T1564.005) under the Defense Evasion tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It involves adversaries creating a separate, abstracted file system to conceal malicious components and file operations from users and security tools. Specific technical implementations include storing a file system in reserved, unused disk space, dropping a portable partition image file onto the standard file system, or fragmenting files across the existing file structure in non-standard ways. This technique has been associated with groups like Equation and Strider.
5862.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Use non-hidden file name as base" is a sub-technique of Defense Evasion. It involves adversaries using the name of a legitimate, non-hidden file as the base for naming a malicious file, often appending or prepending characters to create a deceptive filename that appears normal to users and may bypass basic security checks. This technique exploits the visual similarity to benign files to avoid detection.

5863.name: Fetch DLL names from system directory
5863.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may gather employee names that can be used during targeting. Employee names be used to derive email addresses as well as to help guide other reconnaissance efforts and/or craft more-believable lures.

Adversaries may easily gather employee names, since they may be readily available and exposed via online or other accessible data sets (ex: [Social Media](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1593/001) or [Search Victim-Owned Websites](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1594)).(Citation: OPM Leak) Gathering this information may reveal opportunities for other forms of reconnaissance (ex: [Search Open Websites/Domains](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1593) or [Phishing for Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1598)), establishing operational resources (ex: [Compromise Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1586)), and/or initial access (ex: [Phishing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566) or [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078)).
5863.profile: [profile]Fetch DLL names from system directory is a Discovery technique. Its technical mechanics involve enumerating DLL files within the system directory, often using command-line utilities like `dir` or `ls` to perform file and directory discovery. This reconnaissance activity is used to identify potential targets for follow-on actions such as DLL hijacking or side-loading. The intrusion-set Turla has been associated with this behavior.
5863.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Fetch DLL names from system directory is a technique aligned with MITRE ATT&CK's File and Directory Discovery (T1083) under the Discovery tactic, primarily on Windows platforms. It involves adversaries enumerating the system directory (e.g., using commands like `dir` or `ls`) to identify Dynamic Link Library (DLL) files. This reconnaissance is often a precursor to DLL hijacking or side-loading attacks, where the gathered names are used to plant malicious DLLs that exploit search order vulnerabilities for persistence, privilege escalation, or defense evasion.

5864.name: Avoid folders with 'Avast' in name
5864.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may match or approximate the names of legitimate accounts to make newly created ones appear benign. This will typically occur during [Create Account](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1136), although accounts may also be renamed at a later date. This may also coincide with [Account Access Removal](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1531) if the actor first deletes an account before re-creating one with the same name.(Citation: Huntress MOVEit 2023)

Often, adversaries will attempt to masquerade as service accounts, such as those associated with legitimate software, data backups, or container cluster management.(Citation: Elastic CUBA Ransomware 2022)(Citation: Aquasec Kubernetes Attack 2023) They may also give accounts generic, trustworthy names, such as “admin”, “help”, or “root.”(Citation: Invictus IR Cloud Ransomware 2024) Sometimes adversaries may model account names off of those already existing in the system, as a follow-on behavior to [Account Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1087).  

Note that this is distinct from [Impersonation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1656), which describes impersonating specific trusted individuals or organizations, rather than user or service account names.
5864.profile: [profile]The entity "Avoid folders with 'Avast' in name" is a sub-technique of Masquerading (T1036.005) under the Defense Evasion tactic, primarily for Windows. It involves adversaries placing malicious files or directories in paths excluded from antivirus scanning, specifically targeting folders containing the string "Avast" to abuse hardcoded trust in security software directories. This behavior has been associated with the Turla intrusion set. The technique exploits default AV exclusions to hide artifacts and evade detection.
5864.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The technique "Avoid folders with 'Avast' in name" is a sub-technique of Defense Evasion, specifically T1564.012: File and Directory Permissions Modification - File/Path Exclusions. It operates on Windows platforms and involves adversaries placing malicious files or payloads within directories whose names contain the string "Avast". This exploits hardcoded exclusions in antivirus software, which often skip scanning trusted vendor folders like those associated with Avast to optimize performance, thereby evading detection. This behavior is a specific application of hiding artifacts in excluded locations to bypass security scans.

5865.name: Truncate file name at extension
5865.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may abuse a double extension in the filename as a means of masquerading the true file type. A file name may include a secondary file type extension that may cause only the first extension to be displayed (ex: File.txt.exe may render in some views as just File.txt). However, the second extension is the true file type that determines how the file is opened and executed. The real file extension may be hidden by the operating system in the file browser (ex: explorer.exe), as well as in any software configured using or similar to the system’s policies.(Citation: PCMag DoubleExtension)(Citation: SOCPrime DoubleExtension) Adversaries may abuse double extensions to attempt to conceal dangerous file types of payloads. A very common usage involves tricking a user into opening what they think is a benign file type but is actually executable code. Such files often pose as email attachments and allow an adversary to gain [Initial Access](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0001) into a user’s system via [Spearphishing Attachment](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001) then [User Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204). For example, an executable file attachment named Evil.txt.exe may display as Evil.txt to a user. The user may then view it as a benign text file and open it, inadvertently executing the hidden malware.(Citation: SOCPrime DoubleExtension) Common file types, such as text files (.txt, .doc, etc.) and image files (.jpg, .gif, etc.) are typically used as the first extension to appear benign. Executable extensions commonly regarded as dangerous, such as .exe, .lnk, .hta, and .scr, often appear as the second extension and true file type.
5865.profile: [profile]The technique "Double File Extension" (MITRE ATT&CK T1036.007) is a Defense Evasion tactic used on Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves appending a secondary, often benign-looking file extension (like .txt or .jpg) before the true, executable extension (such as .exe or .scr), causing some system views to display only the first extension and trick users into executing malicious code. This method is commonly employed in spearphishing campaigns by groups like Mustang Panda and Kimsuky to gain initial access.
5865.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Truncate file name at extension is a Masquerading technique (likely a sub-technique of T1036) used for Defense Evasion. It operates by manipulating how a file's name is displayed, often by exploiting how operating systems or applications handle long filenames or extensions. The core mechanic involves creating a filename where the true, malicious extension is hidden because the displayed portion is truncated, for instance, showing "Document.pdf" when the actual file is "Document.pdf.exe". This tricks users into opening what appears to be a benign file type, leading to execution of the hidden payload, commonly as part of spearphishing campaigns.

5866.name: hiding malicious traffic as legitimate traffic
5866.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may use traffic signaling to hide open ports or other malicious functionality used for persistence or command and control. Traffic signaling involves the use of a magic value or sequence that must be sent to a system to trigger a special response, such as opening a closed port or executing a malicious task. This may take the form of sending a series of packets with certain characteristics before a port will be opened that the adversary can use for command and control. Usually this series of packets consists of attempted connections to a predefined sequence of closed ports (i.e. [Port Knocking](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1205/001)), but can involve unusual flags, specific strings, or other unique characteristics. After the sequence is completed, opening a port may be accomplished by the host-based firewall, but could also be implemented by custom software.

Adversaries may also communicate with an already open port, but the service listening on that port will only respond to commands or trigger other malicious functionality if passed the appropriate magic value(s).

The observation of the signal packets to trigger the communication can be conducted through different methods. One means, originally implemented by Cd00r (Citation: Hartrell cd00r 2002), is to use the libpcap libraries to sniff for the packets in question. Another method leverages raw sockets, which enables the malware to use ports that are already open for use by other programs.

On network devices, adversaries may use crafted packets to enable [Network Device Authentication](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1556/004) for standard services offered by the device such as telnet.  Such signaling may also be used to open a closed service port such as telnet, or to trigger module modification of malware implants on the device, adding, removing, or changing malicious capabilities.  Adversaries may use crafted packets to attempt to connect to one or more (open or closed) ports, but may also attempt to connect to a router interface, broadcast, and network address IP on the same port in order to achieve their goals and objectives.(Citation: Cisco Synful Knock Evolution)(Citation: Mandiant - Synful Knock)(Citation: Cisco Blog Legacy Device Attacks)  To enable this traffic signaling on embedded devices, adversaries must first achieve and leverage [Patch System Image](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1601/001) due to the monolithic nature of the architecture.

Adversaries may also use the Wake-on-LAN feature to turn on powered off systems. Wake-on-LAN is a hardware feature that allows a powered down system to be powered on, or woken up, by sending a magic packet to it. Once the system is powered on, it may become a target for lateral movement.(Citation: Bleeping Computer - Ryuk WoL)(Citation: AMD Magic Packet)
5866.profile: [profile]Traffic Signaling, identified as T1205 under the Defense Evasion tactic, operates on multiple platforms. It hides malicious ports or functionality by requiring a specific "magic" packet sequence to trigger a response, such as opening a closed port. This often involves sending connection attempts to a predefined sequence of closed ports (Port Knocking) or using packets with unusual flags or strings. The listening service, implemented via libpcap sniffing or raw sockets, only activates upon receiving the correct signal. This technique is associated with groups like Turla, Kimsuky, UNC3886, and Mustang Panda.[/profile]
5866.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "hiding malicious traffic as legitimate traffic" is a technique for concealing command and control or data exfiltration within normal network flows. This is achieved by mimicking legitimate protocols or services, such as manipulating HTTP headers and SSL certificates to impersonate trusted entities like Gmail, thereby blending malicious communications with benign web traffic to evade detection.

5867.name: Data Exfiltration via get.urls
5867.profile: [profile]Data Exfiltration via get.urls is a technique for data theft, likely aligned with the Exfiltration tactic. It involves using the `get.urls` command or utility to extract and transfer collected data from a compromised system. The retrieved information suggests this method may be part of an automated exfiltration process, potentially used by groups like Turla, and could involve staging data to remote locations or text storage sites before final transfer.
5867.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Data Exfiltration via get.urls is a technique for automated data theft, likely corresponding to T1020 (Automated Exfiltration) within the Exfiltration tactic. It operates across multiple platforms by using the `get.urls` command or utility to programmatically gather and stage collected data from remote locations for subsequent transfer. This method facilitates the automated processing and preparation of data prior to exfiltration over other channels.

5868.name: Local Man-in-the-Middle Attack
5868.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may attempt to position themselves between two or more networked devices using an adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) technique to support follow-on behaviors such as [Network Sniffing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1040), [Transmitted Data Manipulation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1565/002), or replay attacks ([Exploitation for Credential Access](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1212)). By abusing features of common networking protocols that can determine the flow of network traffic (e.g. ARP, DNS, LLMNR, etc.), adversaries may force a device to communicate through an adversary controlled system so they can collect information or perform additional actions.(Citation: Rapid7 MiTM Basics)

For example, adversaries may manipulate victim DNS settings to enable other malicious activities such as preventing/redirecting users from accessing legitimate sites and/or pushing additional malware.(Citation: ttint_rat)(Citation: dns_changer_trojans)(Citation: ad_blocker_with_miner) Adversaries may also manipulate DNS and leverage their position in order to intercept user credentials, including access tokens ([Steal Application Access Token](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1528)) and session cookies ([Steal Web Session Cookie](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539)).(Citation: volexity_0day_sophos_FW)(Citation: Token tactics) [Downgrade Attack](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1562/010)s can also be used to establish an AiTM position, such as by negotiating a less secure, deprecated, or weaker version of communication protocol (SSL/TLS) or encryption algorithm.(Citation: mitm_tls_downgrade_att)(Citation: taxonomy_downgrade_att_tls)(Citation: tlseminar_downgrade_att)

Adversaries may also leverage the AiTM position to attempt to monitor and/or modify traffic, such as in [Transmitted Data Manipulation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1565/002). Adversaries can setup a position similar to AiTM to prevent traffic from flowing to the appropriate destination, potentially to [Impair Defenses](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1562) and/or in support of a [Network Denial of Service](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1498).
5868.profile: [profile]Adversary-in-the-Middle (AiTM), identified as T1557 under the Collection tactic, operates on network platforms. It works by abusing protocols like ARP, DNS, or LLMNR to redirect traffic through an adversary-controlled system, enabling network sniffing, credential interception (including tokens and cookies), and data manipulation. Techniques include manipulating victim DNS settings and using downgrade attacks on SSL/TLS to establish the intermediary position. The intrusion-set Turla has been associated with this technique.[/profile]
5868.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Local Man-in-the-Middle Attack is a technique where an adversary positions a controlled system between two or more networked devices on a local network to intercept or manipulate communications. This is achieved by abusing network protocol features like ARP, DNS, or LLMNR to redirect traffic. The primary tactic is Credential Access, with the technique operating on Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It enables follow-on actions such as network sniffing, credential interception, and transmitted data manipulation.

5869.name: Stealth Techniques
5869.profile: [profile]Stealth Techniques is a general concept encompassing multiple specific MITRE ATT&CK techniques for evasion. These include Process Tree Breaking (T1036.009), which on Linux involves using fork() calls or daemon syscalls to detach a malicious process from its parent and hide its origin. It also involves Steganography (T1001.002) to conceal C2 traffic within other files and general methods to Hide Artifacts (T1564) by abusing OS features or virtualization. The intrusion set Turla is associated with these stealth methods.[/profile]
5869.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Stealth Techniques" is a broad attack pattern category. Retrieved information details specific sub-techniques. T1036.009, "Break Process Trees", is an Evasion technique for Linux/Unix platforms. It works by using API calls like `fork()` twice and exiting the parent process, making the grandchild process an orphan adopted by PID 1 (`init`), thereby severing its link to the original malicious process tree and evading parent-child relationship detection. Another method is using the `daemon` syscall to detach and run in the background.

5870.name: Web Service
5870.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may use an existing, legitimate external Web service as a means for relaying data to/from a compromised system. Popular websites, cloud services, and social media acting as a mechanism for C2 may give a significant amount of cover due to the likelihood that hosts within a network are already communicating with them prior to a compromise. Using common services, such as those offered by Google, Microsoft, or Twitter, makes it easier for adversaries to hide in expected noise.(Citation: Broadcom BirdyClient Microsoft Graph API 2024) Web service providers commonly use SSL/TLS encryption, giving adversaries an added level of protection.

Use of Web services may also protect back-end C2 infrastructure from discovery through malware binary analysis while also enabling operational resiliency (since this infrastructure may be dynamically changed).
5870.profile: [profile]Web Service, identified as T1102 under the Command and Control tactic, operates across multiple platforms by using legitimate external web services like Google, Microsoft, or Twitter to relay data to and from compromised systems. This technique provides cover by blending with normal network traffic and leverages the inherent SSL/TLS encryption of these services to protect communications and obscure backend infrastructure. It is associated with groups including Turla, Gamaredon Group, and FIN6.
5870.profile_without_enhance: [profile]This entity aligns with MITRE ATT&CK technique T1102, named Web Service, under the Command and Control tactic for multiple platforms. It involves adversaries using legitimate external web services like Google, Microsoft, or Twitter to relay command and control data to and from compromised systems. This provides cover by blending with normal network traffic, leverages existing SSL/TLS encryption for protection, and can obscure backend infrastructure from analysis.

5871.name: impersonation techniques
5871.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may impersonate a trusted person or organization in order to persuade and trick a target into performing some action on their behalf. For example, adversaries may communicate with victims (via [Phishing for Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1598), [Phishing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566), or [Internal Spearphishing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1534)) while impersonating a known sender such as an executive, colleague, or third-party vendor. Established trust can then be leveraged to accomplish an adversary’s ultimate goals, possibly against multiple victims. 
 
In many cases of business email compromise or email fraud campaigns, adversaries use impersonation to defraud victims -- deceiving them into sending money or divulging information that ultimately enables [Financial Theft](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1657).

Adversaries will often also use social engineering techniques such as manipulative and persuasive language in email subject lines and body text such as `payment`, `request`, or `urgent` to push the victim to act quickly before malicious activity is detected. These campaigns are often specifically targeted against people who, due to job roles and/or accesses, can carry out the adversary’s goal.   
 
Impersonation is typically preceded by reconnaissance techniques such as [Gather Victim Identity Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1589) and [Gather Victim Org Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1591) as well as acquiring infrastructure such as email domains (i.e. [Domains](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1583/001)) to substantiate their false identity.(Citation: CrowdStrike-BEC)
 
There is the potential for multiple victims in campaigns involving impersonation. For example, an adversary may [Compromise Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1586) targeting one organization which can then be used to support impersonation against other entities.(Citation: VEC)
5871.profile: [profile]Impersonation, known as T1656, is a social engineering technique within the Initial Access tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. It involves adversaries posing as a trusted person or organization, such as an executive or vendor, to deceive targets into actions like sending money or divulging information. This is often executed via phishing emails using urgent language like "payment" or "request" and is typically preceded by reconnaissance to gather victim identity and organizational details to substantiate the false persona.
5871.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "impersonation techniques" is a broad category of adversarial actions, not a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique. It encompasses various methods for assuming a false identity. This includes social engineering impersonation of trusted persons or organizations via phishing to deceive targets into actions like financial theft, often using urgent language like "payment" or "request" in emails. It also covers technical impersonation such as Token Impersonation/Theft (T1134.001), which involves duplicating a user's existing token using functions like `DuplicateToken` and `ImpersonateLoggedOnUser` to escalate privileges and bypass access controls.

5887.name: Browser Pseudo-Number Generation Alteration
5887.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may abuse internet browser extensions to establish persistent access to victim systems. Browser extensions or plugins are small programs that can add functionality to and customize aspects of internet browsers. They can be installed directly via a local file or custom URL or through a browser's app store - an official online platform where users can browse, install, and manage extensions for a specific web browser. Extensions generally inherit the web browser's permissions previously granted.(Citation: Wikipedia Browser Extension)(Citation: Chrome Extensions Definition) Malicious extensions can be installed into a browser through malicious app store downloads masquerading as legitimate extensions, through social engineering, or by an adversary that has already compromised a system. Security can be limited on browser app stores, so it may not be difficult for malicious extensions to defeat automated scanners.(Citation: Malicious Chrome Extension Numbers) Depending on the browser, adversaries may also manipulate an extension's update url to install updates from an adversary-controlled server or manipulate the mobile configuration file to silently install additional extensions. Adversaries may abuse how chromium-based browsers load extensions by modifying or replacing the Preferences and/or Secure Preferences files to silently install malicious extensions. When the browser is not running, adversaries can alter these files, ensuring the extension is loaded, granted desired permissions, and will persist in browser sessions. This method does not require user consent and extensions are silently loaded in the background from disk or from the browser's trusted store.(Citation: Pulsedive) Previous to macOS 11, adversaries could silently install browser extensions via the command line using the profiles tool to install malicious .mobileconfig files. In macOS 11+, the use of the profiles tool can no longer install configuration profiles; however, .mobileconfig files can be planted and installed with user interaction.(Citation: xorrior chrome extensions macOS) Once the extension is installed, it can browse to websites in the background, steal all information that a user enters into a browser (including credentials), and be used as an installer for a RAT for persistence.(Citation: Chrome Extension Crypto Miner)(Citation: ICEBRG Chrome Extensions)(Citation: Banker Google Chrome Extension Steals Creds)(Citation: Catch All Chrome Extension) There have also been instances of botnets using a persistent backdoor through malicious Chrome extensions for [Command and Control](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0011).(Citation: Stantinko Botnet)(Citation: Chrome Extension C2 Malware) Adversaries may also use browser extensions to modify browser permissions and components, privacy settings, and other security controls for [Defense Evasion](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0005).(Citation: Browers FriarFox)(Citation: Browser Adrozek)
5887.profile: [profile]Browser Pseudo-Number Generation Alteration is a technique for Defense Evasion, operating on Windows, macOS, and Linux platforms. It involves manipulating the browser's pseudo-random number generator (PRNG) to alter the generation of cryptographic nonces or session identifiers, thereby weakening security mechanisms that rely on these values for authentication or encryption. This manipulation can be achieved by injecting malicious code into the browser process, often via extensions or compromised libraries, to influence the entropy source or seed values used by the PRNG.
5887.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Browser Pseudo-Number Generation Alteration is a technique where adversaries manipulate a browser's pseudo-random number generator (PRNG) to compromise cryptographic security, such as weakening TLS/SSL session keys. This falls under the Defense Evasion tactic (TA0005) and impacts Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. The technical mechanics involve altering the browser's internal state or seeding process to generate predictable or weak cryptographic nonces and keys, enabling adversaries to decrypt secure communications or forge digital certificates. This method directly targets the foundational security of web sessions.

This method allows adversaries to exfiltrate data or receive instructions through standard HTTP/S channels.

5900.name: Infection Vector
5900.profile: [profile]Infection Vector is a technique used for Initial Access, where adversaries deliver malicious content to systems. This can occur through methods like Replication Through Removable Media (T1091), where malware is copied to USB drives or mobile devices to exploit Autorun features when connected. Malvertising (T1583.008) involves purchasing online ads to distribute malware, often by impersonating legitimate brands to trick users into clicking. The intrusion-set Turla has been associated with using such vectors. The technique primarily targets Windows and potentially other platforms via removable media.[/profile]

5903.name: Referer头伪装
5903.profile: [profile]The technique "Referer头伪装" (Referer Header Spoofing) involves an adversary modifying the HTTP Referer header in web requests to conceal the true origin of traffic or to bypass security controls that rely on Referer validation. This can be used to blend malicious requests with legitimate traffic from trusted sites, potentially evading detection or access restrictions. The intrusion set Turla has been associated with employing this technique. It aligns with the general tactic of Defense Evasion by obfuscating command and control or attack initiation points.]

It involves an adversary manipulating the HTTP Referer header to make malicious web requests appear as if they originate from a trusted or legitimate source within the same domain. This spoofing can bypass security controls like Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) tokens or other referer-based validation mechanisms, allowing unauthorized actions.

5904.name: TLS配置
5904.profile: [profile]TLS Configuration is a technique used to establish secure communication channels, often for encrypting command and control (C2) traffic. Adversaries, such as the Turla intrusion set, may install SSL/TLS certificates—either obtained or self-signed—on controlled infrastructure like web or email servers. This enables encrypted C2 using protocols like HTTPS, potentially employing multilayer encryption by tunneling custom schemes within standard TLS, to evade detection and lend credibility to malicious sites.[/profile]

The activity supports techniques like encrypted C2 and can be part of broader resource development or defense evasion efforts.

5905.name: 伪装策略
5905.profile: [profile]伪装策略 is a technique where adversaries manipulate the name, location, or metadata of files and processes to appear legitimate, evading detection. This includes renaming malicious files, abusing system utility names, and spoofing file types to mislead users and security tools. The technique is associated with intrusion sets like Turla and is broadly used by numerous threat groups for defense evasion.

5906.name: 文件同步
5906.profile: [profile]文件同步 is a technique used by adversaries to transfer tools or files between compromised systems within a network, supporting lateral movement. It can be executed using inherent file sharing protocols like SMB/Windows Admin Shares or authenticated connections via Remote Desktop Protocol. Adversaries may also leverage native tools such as scp, rsync, curl, sftp, or ftp, and in some cases utilize cloud storage services like Dropbox or OneDrive via automatically synced folders. This technique is associated with groups like Turla, Wizard Spider, and Volt Typhoon.

This technique is commonly employed by groups like Turla, MuddyWater, and Lazarus Group.

5909.name: 持久化
5909.profile: [profile]The entity "持久化" (Persistence) is a core adversary tactic, not a specific technique, focused on maintaining their foothold on a system. It is associated with the Turla intrusion set. Specific techniques under this tactic include abusing screensavers (T1546.002) by modifying Windows Registry settings like `SCRNSAVE.exe` to point to a malicious executable, enabling it to run after a period of user inactivity. Other related methods involve abusing system services (T1569) for execution and clearing persistence artifacts (T1070.009) to remove evidence.

5910.name: 模仿微软官方组件
5910.profile: [profile]模仿微软官方组件 is a technique where adversaries disguise malicious components to appear as legitimate Microsoft software. It aligns with MITRE ATT&CK technique T1036 (Masquerading) under the Defense Evasion tactic, primarily targeting Windows platforms. The method involves modifying or replacing legitimate system components, such as through COM hijacking (T1122) or abusing the Office Test Registry key (T1137.002), to execute malicious code when trusted processes or applications like Microsoft Office are launched. This provides persistence and evades detection by blending with normal system operations, as observed in campaigns by groups like APT28.
5910.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "模仿微软官方组件" (Imitate Microsoft Official Components) is a persistence technique where adversaries disguise malicious code as legitimate Microsoft components, such as through COM hijacking or abusing the Office Test Registry key. In COM hijacking, adversaries alter Windows Registry references to replace legitimate system components, causing their code to execute when the system component is invoked. Similarly, adversaries can abuse the Office Test Registry key by adding a malicious DLL that runs automatically whenever Microsoft Office applications like Word or Excel are launched. This technique leverages trusted Microsoft interfaces to maintain stealth and persistence on compromised systems.

5912.name: 暴力破解

This activity is often conducted in conjunction with initial access methods like External Remote Services or post-compromise behaviors such as OS Credential Dumping. The intrusion-set Turla is associated with this technique. Commonly targeted services include SSH, Telnet, FTP, SMB, LDAP, Kerberos, RDP, HTTP/S, and various database and management ports.

5916.name: XOR Key
5916.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may reduce the level of effort required to decrypt data transmitted over the network by reducing the cipher strength of encrypted communications.(Citation: Cisco Synful Knock Evolution)

Adversaries can weaken the encryption software on a compromised network device by reducing the key size used by the software to convert plaintext to ciphertext (e.g., from hundreds or thousands of bytes to just a couple of bytes). As a result, adversaries dramatically reduce the amount of effort needed to decrypt the protected information without the key.

Adversaries may modify the key size used and other encryption parameters using specialized commands in a [Network Device CLI](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/008) introduced to the system through [Modify System Image](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1601) to change the configuration of the device. (Citation: Cisco Blog Legacy Device Attacks)
5916.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique "Reduce Key Space" (ID: T1600.001), a Defense Evasion tactic targeting Network Devices. It involves weakening encryption on a compromised network device by reducing the cipher's key size, for example from hundreds of bytes to just a couple, dramatically easing decryption efforts without the key. This modification is typically performed via specialized commands in a Network Device CLI introduced through a modified system image. The intrusion-set Turla has been associated with this activity.
5916.profile_without_enhance: [profile]XOR Key is a simple cryptographic technique (T1024) used for Defense Evasion and Command and Control. It operates across Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. The core mechanic involves applying an exclusive OR (XOR) operation to data, such as plaintext or an archive, using a fixed key to produce a weak ciphertext, often as part of a custom protocol or encryption scheme for hiding C2 traffic or preparing data for exfiltration. This method is notably used by groups like Lazarus Group and FIN6.

It has been used by the intrusion set Turla (aka LuckyMouse or Emissary Panda). Its key technical behavior is polymorphic encoding, which changes the decoder stub with each iteration to evade signature-based detection. 5925.name: Second-Stage Backdoor
5925.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may upload, install, or otherwise set up capabilities that can be used during targeting. To support their operations, an adversary may need to take capabilities they developed ([Develop Capabilities](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1587)) or obtained ([Obtain Capabilities](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1588)) and stage them on infrastructure under their control. These capabilities may be staged on infrastructure that was previously purchased/rented by the adversary ([Acquire Infrastructure](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1583)) or was otherwise compromised by them ([Compromise Infrastructure](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1584)). Capabilities may also be staged on web services, such as GitHub or Pastebin, or on Platform-as-a-Service (PaaS) offerings that enable users to easily provision applications.(Citation: Volexity Ocean Lotus November 2020)(Citation: Dragos Heroku Watering Hole)(Citation: Malwarebytes Heroku Skimmers)(Citation: Netskope GCP Redirection)(Citation: Netskope Cloud Phishing)

Staging of capabilities can aid the adversary in a number of initial access and post-compromise behaviors, including (but not limited to):

* Staging web resources necessary to conduct [Drive-by Compromise](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1189) when a user browses to a site.(Citation: FireEye CFR Watering Hole 2012)(Citation: Gallagher 2015)(Citation: ATT ScanBox)
* Staging web resources for a link target to be used with spearphishing.(Citation: Malwarebytes Silent Librarian October 2020)(Citation: Proofpoint TA407 September 2019)
* Uploading malware or tools to a location accessible to a victim network to enable [Ingress Tool Transfer](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1105).(Citation: Volexity Ocean Lotus November 2020)
* Installing a previously acquired SSL/TLS certificate to use to encrypt command and control traffic (ex: [Asymmetric Cryptography](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1573/002) with [Web Protocols](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1071/001)).(Citation: DigiCert Install SSL Cert)
5925.profile: [profile]The entity "Second-Stage Backdoor" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the provided context, it likely refers to a component of the multi-stage command and control technique (T1104). This technique involves adversaries deploying a second, more capable remote access tool (RAT) after an initial callback. The second stage is hosted on separate infrastructure to obfuscate the C2 channel and provides enhanced functionality like a reverse shell for full system interaction, following the initial data collection and tool upload from the first stage. It is associated with groups like APT41 and MuddyWater.[/profile]
5925.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Second-Stage Backdoor is a technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, aligning with the concept of Multi-Stage Channels (T1104) under the Command and Control tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. This technique involves deploying a secondary, more fully-featured remote access tool (RAT) after an initial compromise. The first-stage malware typically calls back for instructions and may upload this second-stage backdoor, which then redirects communication to a separate, dedicated command and control server to provide enhanced interactive access like a reverse shell, thereby obfuscating the C2 channel for persistence and evasion.

5948.name: Fork and Hide
5948.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may manipulate network traffic in order to hide and evade detection of their C2 infrastructure. This can be accomplished by identifying and filtering traffic from defensive tools,(Citation: TA571) masking malicious domains to obfuscate the true destination from both automated scanning tools and security researchers,(Citation: Schema-abuse)(Citation: Facad1ng)(Citation: Browser-updates) and otherwise hiding malicious artifacts to delay discovery and prolong the effectiveness of adversary infrastructure that could otherwise be identified, blocked, or taken down entirely.

C2 networks may include the use of [Proxy](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1090) or VPNs to disguise IP addresses, which can allow adversaries to blend in with normal network traffic and bypass conditional access policies or anti-abuse protections. For example, an adversary may use a virtual private cloud to spoof their IP address to closer align with a victim's IP address ranges. This may also bypass security measures relying on geolocation of the source IP address.(Citation: sysdig)(Citation: Orange Residential Proxies)

Adversaries may also attempt to filter network traffic in order to evade defensive tools in numerous ways, including blocking/redirecting common incident responder or security appliance user agents.(Citation: mod_rewrite)(Citation: SocGholish-update) Filtering traffic based on IP and geo-fencing may also avoid automated sandboxing or researcher activity (i.e., [Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1497)).(Citation: TA571)(Citation: mod_rewrite)

Hiding C2 infrastructure may also be supported by [Resource Development](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0042) activities such as [Acquire Infrastructure](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1583) and [Compromise Infrastructure](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1584). For example, using widely trusted hosting services or domains such as prominent URL shortening providers or marketing services for C2 networks may enable adversaries to present benign content that later redirects victims to malicious web pages or infrastructure once specific conditions are met.(Citation: StarBlizzard)(Citation: QR-cofense)
5948.profile: [profile]Fork and Hide is a technique for hiding C2 infrastructure, aligning with the MITRE ATT&CK ID T1665 under the Command and Control tactic. It operates across multiple platforms by manipulating network traffic to evade detection. Specific methods include filtering traffic from defensive tools, blocking or redirecting common security user agents, and using IP/geo-fencing to avoid sandboxes. Adversaries may also disguise infrastructure by using proxies or VPNs to blend IP addresses with normal traffic, spoofing addresses to match victim ranges, and leveraging trusted hosting services that redirect to malicious pages after meeting specific conditions. This technique is associated with groups like APT29 and Zirconium.
5948.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Fork and Hide is a macOS-specific technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, categorized under the Defense Evasion tactic (T1564.009). It involves abusing the deprecated resource fork feature to conceal malicious executables or data. Adversaries attach a resource fork containing obfuscated or encrypted code to a benign file, then execute the hidden payload by moving it to an executable location and invoking it, effectively evading detection by security tools that do not inspect these legacy file structures.

6003.name: Remote Management
6003.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may use [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078) to interact with remote systems using Windows Remote Management (WinRM). The adversary may then perform actions as the logged-on user.

WinRM is the name of both a Windows service and a protocol that allows a user to interact with a remote system (e.g., run an executable, modify the Registry, modify services).(Citation: Microsoft WinRM) It may be called with the `winrm` command or by any number of programs such as PowerShell.(Citation: Jacobsen 2014) WinRM  can be used as a method of remotely interacting with [Windows Management Instrumentation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1047).(Citation: MSDN WMI)
6003.profile: [profile]Windows Remote Management (WinRM) is a sub-technique (T1021.006) under the Remote Services tactic (TA0008) for Lateral Movement, targeting Windows platforms. It involves adversaries using valid accounts to interact with remote systems via the WinRM protocol and service, which can be invoked with the `winrm` command or through programs like PowerShell to execute commands, modify the registry, or manage services, and it can serve as a method for remote interaction with Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI). Associated threat groups include FIN13, Chimera, and Wizard Spider.[/profile]
6003.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Remote Management is a technique (T1021) within the Lateral Movement tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It involves adversaries using Valid Accounts to log into services that accept remote connections, such as SSH, RDP, VNC, and telnet, to perform actions as the logged-on user. This includes leveraging specific protocols like Windows Remote Management (WinRM), which can be invoked via the `winrm` command or PowerShell to interact with remote systems and services like Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI).

6006.name: Multi-Stage Infection
6006.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may create multiple stages for command and control that are employed under different conditions or for certain functions. Use of multiple stages may obfuscate the command and control channel to make detection more difficult.

Remote access tools will call back to the first-stage command and control server for instructions. The first stage may have automated capabilities to collect basic host information, update tools, and upload additional files. A second remote access tool (RAT) could be uploaded at that point to redirect the host to the second-stage command and control server. The second stage will likely be more fully featured and allow the adversary to interact with the system through a reverse shell and additional RAT features.

The different stages will likely be hosted separately with no overlapping infrastructure. The loader may also have backup first-stage callbacks or [Fallback Channels](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1008) in case the original first-stage communication path is discovered and blocked.
6006.profile: [profile]Multi-Stage Channels is identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1104 under the Command and Control tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It involves creating separate, non-overlapping command and control stages to obfuscate detection. Typically, a first-stage C2 server provides automated instructions, collects host data, and uploads a second-stage remote access tool (RAT). This second stage then redirects to a more fully-featured C2 server, enabling interactive adversary access via a reverse shell. The technique may also incorporate fallback channels for resilience and has been associated with groups like APT41 and Lazarus.[/profile]
6006.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Multi-Stage Infection is a technique where adversaries deploy malware in sequential phases to evade detection and establish persistence. Initial stages often involve lightweight loaders or droppers that gather basic system information and download more sophisticated payloads, such as fully-featured remote access tools (RATs), from separate, distinct infrastructure. This approach complicates defense by separating delivery mechanisms from final malicious capabilities, as seen in campaigns using Control Panel items (.cpl files) as execution payloads in multi-stage attacks.

6007.name: Loader/Injector
6007.uncertain_mes:
Cutting Edge, Part 3: Investigating Ivanti Connect Secure VPN Exploitation and Persistence Attempts
Mandiant
Written by: Matt Lin, Robert Wallace, Austin Larsen, Ryan Gandrud, Jacob Thompson, Ashley Pearson, Ashley Frazer
6007.profile: [profile]The malware is known as Loader/Injector, with an alias Kubo Injector. It is attributed to the Turla intrusion set. Its key technical behavior involves a two-stage .NET-based injection process: a first-stage .NET PE ("Loader") and a second-stage .NET PE ("Injector") are stored in specific Windows Registry keys (e.g., HKCU\Software\[username]+'1' and HKCU\Software\[username]), and a PowerShell command is used to sequentially load and execute them to deploy final payloads. Its target platform is Windows, and it has been used in exploitation and persistence attempts against Ivanti Connect Secure VPN infrastructure.
6007.profile_without_enhance: [profile]This malware, generically named 'Loader/Injector', is referenced by aliases such as 'kubo injector', 'lowkey', and 'skip-2.0'. It is attributed to the APT41 group. Its key technical behavior involves a multi-stage injection process, where a first-stage .NET loader binary and a second-stage .NET injector binary are stored in specific Windows Registry keys (e.g., HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\[username] and [username]+'1') and executed sequentially via PowerShell to deploy final payloads like Cobalt Strike. It targets the Windows platform.

6008.name: Zagruzchik
6008.profile: [profile]Zagruzchik is a malware component whose name means "boot loader" in Russian. It is attributed to the Turla intrusion set. Its technical behaviors include being referenced as a Trojan-Dropper within the Epic Turla Operation and using Russian language artifacts like Codepage 1251. It primarily targets the Windows platform, as indicated by its Win32-based dropper variants like Trojan-Dropper.Win32.Turla.d.[/profile]
6008.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Zagruzchik is a malware whose name means "boot loader" in Russian. It is associated with the Turla group and has been observed in the Epic Turla Operation. Technical aliases for its components include Trojan-Dropper.Win32.Turla.d, Trojan.Win32.Agent.iber, and Trojan.Win32.Agent.ibgm. It targets the Windows platform.

6010.name: Microsoft Tools
6010.profile: [profile]Microsoft Tools is a malware family also known as gasket, danderspritz, and poortry, attributed to the Turla intrusion set. Its key behaviors include masquerading as legitimate Microsoft services and processes like MicrosoftTeamConnect, WindowsHealthSubSystem, and WindowsSoftwareManager for command and control, and abusing legitimate Microsoft programs such as Attestation signing to load malicious, Microsoft-signed drivers to evade detection. It primarily targets the Windows platform, modifying registry keys like those under Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run for persistence.[/profile]
6010.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Microsoft Tools is a malware entity that leverages legitimate Microsoft-signed binaries and processes, such as Attestation signing, to evade detection by loading malicious drivers with valid Microsoft certificates. It establishes persistence by modifying Windows Registry keys, including Software\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\winlogon (targeting Shell and Userinit values) and Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run[OnceEx], to execute its components. The malware uses command and control infrastructure and is associated with groups like gasket, danderspritz, and poortry, primarily targeting the Windows operating system.

6011.name: Doc File Enumeration
6011.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may enumerate system and service logs to find useful data. These logs may highlight various types of valuable insights for an adversary, such as user authentication records ([Account Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1087)), security or vulnerable software ([Software Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1518)), or hosts within a compromised network ([Remote System Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1018)).

Host binaries may be leveraged to collect system logs. Examples include using `wevtutil.exe` or [PowerShell](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001) on Windows to access and/or export security event information.(Citation: WithSecure Lazarus-NoPineapple Threat Intel Report 2023)(Citation: Cadet Blizzard emerges as novel threat actor) In cloud environments, adversaries may leverage utilities such as the Azure VM Agent’s `CollectGuestLogs.exe` to collect security logs from cloud hosted infrastructure.(Citation: SIM Swapping and Abuse of the Microsoft Azure Serial Console)

Adversaries may also target centralized logging infrastructure such as SIEMs. Logs may also be bulk exported and sent to adversary-controlled infrastructure for offline analysis.

In addition to gaining a better understanding of the environment, adversaries may also monitor logs in real time to track incident response procedures. This may allow them to adjust their techniques in order to maintain persistence or evade defenses.(Citation: Permiso GUI-Vil 2023)
6011.profile: [profile]The entity is a MITRE ATT&CK technique for Discovery, specifically Log Enumeration (T1654). It involves adversaries enumerating system and service logs to gather intelligence, using tools like `wevtutil.exe` or PowerShell on Windows, or utilities like Azure VM Agent's `CollectGuestLogs.exe` in cloud environments. They may target centralized logging infrastructure like SIEMs, export logs for offline analysis, and monitor logs in real-time to track incident response and adjust their tactics. This technique is associated with groups including Volt Typhoon, APT5, Mustang Panda, Ember Bear, and Aquatic Panda.[/profile]
6011.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Doc File Enumeration is a technique for File and Directory Discovery (T1083) within the Discovery tactic, primarily on Windows systems. It involves adversaries using command shell utilities or scripts to systematically list and search for specific document files (e.g., .doc, .pdf) on a host or network share to locate sensitive information or shape follow-on actions.

6012.name: NATO Email Search
6012.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may use search engines to collect information about victims that can be used during targeting. Search engine services typical crawl online sites to index context and may provide users with specialized syntax to search for specific keywords or specific types of content (i.e. filetypes).(Citation: SecurityTrails Google Hacking)(Citation: ExploitDB GoogleHacking)

Adversaries may craft various search engine queries depending on what information they seek to gather. Threat actors may use search engines to harvest general information about victims, as well as use specialized queries to look for spillages/leaks of sensitive information such as network details or credentials. Information from these sources may reveal opportunities for other forms of reconnaissance (ex: [Phishing for Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1598) or [Search Open Technical Databases](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1596)), establishing operational resources (ex: [Establish Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1585) or [Compromise Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1586)), and/or initial access (ex: [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078) or [Phishing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566)).
6012.profile: [profile]NATO Email Search is a reconnaissance technique where adversaries use search engines to gather victim information for targeting. It aligns with MITRE ATT&CK ID T1593.002 under the Reconnaissance tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. Attackers craft specialized search queries, including advanced syntax like specific filetypes or keywords, to harvest general victim data, discover network details, or find leaked credentials. This collected intelligence can enable follow-on actions such as phishing, credential compromise, or initial access. The intrusion-set Turla has been associated with this method.[/profile]
6012.profile_without_enhance: [profile]NATO Email Search is a reconnaissance technique where adversaries use search engines to gather email addresses and account information about NATO-affiliated personnel. This technique aligns with the MITRE ATT&CK framework under T1593.002 (Search Engines) within the Reconnaissance tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. Adversaries craft specialized search queries to harvest email addresses from publicly accessible data sets, which can then be used for subsequent operations like phishing or credential compromise.

6013.name: System Admin Privileges
6013.uncertain_mes: Windows systems have hidden network shares that are accessible only to administrators and provide the ability for remote file copy and other administrative functions. Example network shares include C$, ADMIN$, and IPC$. Adversaries may use this technique in conjunction with administrator-level [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078) to remotely access a networked system over server message block (SMB) (Citation: Wikipedia SMB) to interact with systems using remote procedure calls (RPCs), (Citation: TechNet RPC) transfer files, and run transferred binaries through remote Execution. Example execution techniques that rely on authenticated sessions over SMB/RPC are [Scheduled Task/Job](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1053), [Service Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1035), and [Windows Management Instrumentation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1047). Adversaries can also use NTLM hashes to access administrator shares on systems with [Pass the Hash](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1075) and certain configuration and patch levels. (Citation: Microsoft Admin Shares) The [Net](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0039) utility can be used to connect to Windows admin shares on remote systems using net use commands with valid credentials. (Citation: Technet Net Use)
6013.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique SMB/Windows Admin Shares (T1021.002) under the Lateral Movement tactic, targeting Windows platforms. It involves adversaries using valid administrator accounts or NTLM hashes to remotely access hidden administrative shares (e.g., C$, ADMIN$) over Server Message Block (SMB) protocol. This access enables file transfers, remote execution via utilities like `net use`, and interaction with services like Scheduled Tasks or WMI for lateral movement, as used by groups including Turla.
6013.profile_without_enhance: [profile]System Admin Privileges is a technique where adversaries leverage administrative-level access to perform malicious actions. It is associated with the Valid Accounts technique (T1078) under the Privilege Escalation and Defense Evasion tactics, primarily on Windows platforms. Adversaries use these elevated privileges to remotely access systems via protocols like SMB to interact with admin shares (e.g., C$, ADMIN$), execute commands through utilities like `net use`, and perform remote execution via methods such as Scheduled Tasks or Windows Management Instrumentation. This access can also be used to discover local administrator groups using commands like `net localgroup`.

6014.name: Hardcoded Command Encryption
6014.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may compromise a network device’s encryption capability in order to bypass encryption that would otherwise protect data communications. (Citation: Cisco Synful Knock Evolution)

Encryption can be used to protect transmitted network traffic to maintain its confidentiality (protect against unauthorized disclosure) and integrity (protect against unauthorized changes). Encryption ciphers are used to convert a plaintext message to ciphertext and can be computationally intensive to decipher without the associated decryption key. Typically, longer keys increase the cost of cryptanalysis, or decryption without the key.

Adversaries can compromise and manipulate devices that perform encryption of network traffic. For example, through behaviors such as [Modify System Image](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1601), [Reduce Key Space](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1600/001), and [Disable Crypto Hardware](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1600/002), an adversary can negatively effect and/or eliminate a device’s ability to securely encrypt network traffic. This poses a greater risk of unauthorized disclosure and may help facilitate data manipulation, Credential Access, or Collection efforts. (Citation: Cisco Blog Legacy Device Attacks)
6014.profile: [profile]Hardcoded Command Encryption is a technique where adversaries embed a fixed encryption or decryption key directly within malware or command scripts, bypassing the need for secure key exchange. This practice, often associated with weak or custom cryptographic protocols, simplifies command and control (C2) obfuscation but creates a static, recoverable signature for defenders. It is commonly used to conceal malicious commands and scripts, facilitating execution while evading detection through simple encryption.
6014.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Hardcoded Command Encryption is a technique where adversaries embed a fixed encryption key or algorithm directly within malware or scripts to obfuscate commands and control traffic. This method uses symmetric encryption, such as AES or XOR with a static key, to conceal communications. The encryption scheme is often custom or a known algorithm with the secret key compiled into the code, making it vulnerable to extraction through reverse engineering. This facilitates command obfuscation and hinders detection of malicious network activity.

6020.name: Browser/Email Process Injection
6020.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may inject code into processes in order to evade process-based defenses as well as possibly elevate privileges. Process injection is a method of executing arbitrary code in the address space of a separate live process. Running code in the context of another process may allow access to the process's memory, system/network resources, and possibly elevated privileges. Execution via process injection may also evade detection from security products since the execution is masked under a legitimate process. 

There are many different ways to inject code into a process, many of which abuse legitimate functionalities. These implementations exist for every major OS but are typically platform specific. 

More sophisticated samples may perform multiple process injections to segment modules and further evade detection, utilizing named pipes or other inter-process communication (IPC) mechanisms as a communication channel.

Adversaries, such as Turla, create a unique system mutex associated with their malware; if the mutex is present, the malware may exit to avoid multiple infections. 6034.name: Target Email
6034.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may put in place resources that are referenced by a link that can be used during targeting. An adversary may rely upon a user clicking a malicious link in order to divulge information (including credentials) or to gain execution, as in [Malicious Link](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/001). Links can be used for spearphishing, such as sending an email accompanied by social engineering text to coax the user to actively click or copy and paste a URL into a browser. Prior to a phish for information (as in [Spearphishing Link](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1598/003)) or a phish to gain initial access to a system (as in [Spearphishing Link](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/002)), an adversary must set up the resources for a link target for the spearphishing link. 

Typically, the resources for a link target will be an HTML page that may include some client-side script such as [JavaScript](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/007) to decide what content to serve to the user. Adversaries may clone legitimate sites to serve as the link target, this can include cloning of login pages of legitimate web services or organization login pages in an effort to harvest credentials during [Spearphishing Link](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1598/003).(Citation: Malwarebytes Silent Librarian October 2020)(Citation: Proofpoint TA407 September 2019) Adversaries may also [Upload Malware](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1608/001) and have the link target point to malware for download/execution by the user.

Adversaries may purchase domains similar to legitimate domains (ex: homoglyphs, typosquatting, different top-level domain, etc.) during acquisition of infrastructure ([Domains](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1583/001)) to help facilitate [Malicious Link](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/001).

Links can be written by adversaries to mask the true destination in order to deceive victims by abusing the URL schema and increasing the effectiveness of phishing.(Citation: Kaspersky-masking)(Citation: mandiant-masking)

Adversaries may also use free or paid accounts on link shortening services and Platform-as-a-Service providers to host link targets while taking advantage of the widely trusted domains of those providers to avoid being blocked while redirecting victims to malicious pages.(Citation: Netskope GCP Redirection)(Citation: Netskope Cloud Phishing)(Citation: Intezer App Service Phishing)(Citation: Cofense-redirect) In addition, adversaries may serve a variety of malicious links through uniquely generated URIs/URLs (including one-time, single use links).(Citation: iOS URL Scheme)(Citation: URI)(Citation: URI Use)(Citation: URI Unique) Finally, adversaries may take advantage of the decentralized nature of the InterPlanetary File System (IPFS) to host link targets that are difficult to remove.(Citation: Talos IPFS 2022)

Adversaries may attempt to blend in with legitimate traffic by spoofing browser and system attributes like operating system, system language, platform, user-agent string, resolution, time zone, etc.  The HTTP User-Agent request header is a string that lets servers and network peers identify the application, operating system, vendor, and/or version of the requesting user agent.(Citation: Mozilla User Agent)

Adversaries may gather this information through [System Information Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1082) or by users navigating to adversary-controlled websites, and then use that information to craft their web traffic to evade defenses.(Citation: Gummy Browsers: Targeted Browser Spoofing against State-of-the-Art Fingerprinting Techniques)
6042.profile: [profile]The entity "Smtp network fingerprint" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the provided context, it likely refers to the practice of adversaries using SMTP traffic to blend in with legitimate network activity, potentially as part of command and control or data exfiltration. This involves mimicking normal email protocol attributes to evade detection, a method associated with groups like Turla. The technical mechanics involve crafting network packets to resemble standard SMTP traffic on common ports like TCP/25, thereby disguising malicious communications within expected electronic mail delivery channels.[/profile]
6042.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "Smtp network fingerprint" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the retrieved context, it likely refers to the adversary practice of gathering or analyzing SMTP protocol attributes and server characteristics to profile a network. This information, which can include banner details and configuration specifics, is used for reconnaissance to understand the target environment and potentially evade detection by blending malicious traffic with legitimate email protocols.

6043.name: Virtual file system
6043.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may use a hidden file system to conceal malicious activity from users and security tools. File systems provide a structure to store and access data from physical storage. Typically, a user engages with a file system through applications that allow them to access files and directories, which are an abstraction from their physical location (ex: disk sector). Standard file systems include FAT, NTFS, ext4, and APFS. File systems can also contain other structures, such as the Volume Boot Record (VBR) and Master File Table (MFT) in NTFS.(Citation: MalwareTech VFS Nov 2014)

Adversaries may use their own abstracted file system, separate from the standard file system present on the infected system. In doing so, adversaries can hide the presence of malicious components and file input/output from security tools. Hidden file systems, sometimes referred to as virtual file systems, can be implemented in numerous ways. One implementation would be to store a file system in reserved disk space unused by disk structures or standard file system partitions.(Citation: MalwareTech VFS Nov 2014)(Citation: FireEye Bootkits) Another implementation could be for an adversary to drop their own portable partition image as a file on top of the standard file system.(Citation: ESET ComRAT May 2020) Adversaries may also fragment files across the existing file system structure in non-standard ways.(Citation: Kaspersky Equation QA)
6043.profile: [profile]Virtual File System, also known as Hidden File System, is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1564.005 under the Defense Evasion tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It involves adversaries implementing a separate, abstracted file system to conceal malicious components and file I/O from users and security tools. Specific technical implementations include storing a file system in reserved, unused disk space; dropping a portable partition image as a file on the standard file system; or fragmenting files across the existing file structure in non-standard ways. This technique has been associated with threat groups like Equation and Strider.[/profile]
6043.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Virtual File System is a technique for defense evasion, identified as T1564.005 within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves adversaries implementing an abstracted, hidden file system separate from the host's standard one to conceal malicious components and file I/O from security tools. Specific implementations include storing a file system in reserved, unused disk sectors, dropping a portable partition image file onto the standard file system, or fragmenting files non-standardly across the existing disk structure. This technique has been used by threat groups like Equation and Strider.

Its primary target platform is Windows, leveraging named pipes for inter-process communication and data theft.

6049.name: Remote Thread Execution
6049.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may inject malicious code into hijacked processes in order to evade process-based defenses as well as possibly elevate privileges. Thread Execution Hijacking is a method of executing arbitrary code in the address space of a separate live process. Thread Execution Hijacking is commonly performed by suspending an existing process then unmapping/hollowing its memory, which can then be replaced with malicious code or the path to a DLL. A handle to an existing victim process is first created with native Windows API calls such as OpenThread. At this point the process can be suspended then written to, realigned to the injected code, and resumed via SuspendThread , VirtualAllocEx, WriteProcessMemory, SetThreadContext, then ResumeThread respectively.(Citation: Elastic Process Injection July 2017) This is very similar to [Process Hollowing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1055/012) but targets an existing process rather than creating a process in a suspended state. Running code in the context of another process may allow access to the process's memory, system/network resources, and possibly elevated privileges. Execution via Thread Execution Hijacking may also evade detection from security products since the execution is masked under a legitimate process.
6049.profile: [profile]Thread Execution Hijacking, designated as T1055.003 under the MITRE ATT&CK framework, is a Defense Evasion and Privilege Escalation technique for Windows. It involves injecting code into a live process by first creating a handle with OpenThread, suspending the thread with SuspendThread, hollowing its memory, writing malicious code via VirtualAllocEx and WriteProcessMemory, redirecting execution with SetThreadContext, and finally resuming the thread with ResumeThread. This method, distinct from Process Hollowing as it targets an already running process, allows adversaries to mask execution under a legitimate process to evade detection and potentially gain elevated privileges. The intrusion-set Turla has been associated with this technique.[/profile]
6049.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Remote Thread Execution is a process injection technique where adversaries execute code in the context of a remote process's thread to evade defenses and potentially gain elevated privileges. It operates within the Defense Evasion and Privilege Escalation tactics, primarily on the Windows platform. The technique involves using Windows API calls like OpenThread to obtain a handle, suspending the thread with SuspendThread, writing malicious code or a DLL path into the process memory using VirtualAllocEx and WriteProcessMemory, redirecting the thread context with SetThreadContext, and then resuming execution via ResumeThread. This allows the malicious code to run masked under a legitimate remote process.
