6051.name: Enable Debug Privilege
6051.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may exploit software vulnerabilities in an attempt to elevate privileges. Exploitation of a software vulnerability occurs when an adversary takes advantage of a programming error in a program, service, or within the operating system software or kernel itself to execute adversary-controlled code. Security constructs such as permission levels will often hinder access to information and use of certain techniques, so adversaries will likely need to perform privilege escalation to include use of software exploitation to circumvent those restrictions.

When initially gaining access to a system, an adversary may be operating within a lower privileged process which will prevent them from accessing certain resources on the system. Vulnerabilities may exist, usually in operating system components and software commonly running at higher permissions, that can be exploited to gain higher levels of access on the system. This could enable someone to move from unprivileged or user level permissions to SYSTEM or root permissions depending on the component that is vulnerable. This could also enable an adversary to move from a virtualized environment, such as within a virtual machine or container, onto the underlying host. This may be a necessary step for an adversary compromising an endpoint system that has been properly configured and limits other privilege escalation methods.

Adversaries may bring a signed vulnerable driver onto a compromised machine so that they can exploit the vulnerability to execute code in kernel mode. This process is sometimes referred to as Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver (BYOVD).(Citation: ESET InvisiMole June 2020)(Citation: Unit42 AcidBox June 2020) Adversaries may include the vulnerable driver with files delivered during Initial Access or download it to a compromised system via [Ingress Tool Transfer](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1105) or [Lateral Tool Transfer](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1570).
6051.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique "Exploitation for Privilege Escalation" (T1068) under the Privilege Escalation tactic, primarily for Windows and Linux platforms. It involves exploiting software vulnerabilities, such as programming errors in OS components or high-privilege software, to execute adversary-controlled code and elevate permissions from user to SYSTEM/root. A specific method is Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver (BYOVD), where a signed but vulnerable driver is introduced to the system and exploited to run code in kernel mode. This technique is used by groups like Turla, APT28, and APT29 to bypass security controls when other escalation methods are limited.[/profile]
6051.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Enable Debug Privilege is a Windows-specific technique within the Privilege Escalation tactic. It involves a process using the `SeDebugPrivilege` token to gain the necessary access rights for debugging and manipulating other processes, which is a critical step for activities like code injection and memory dumping to elevate privileges or evade detection.

6052.name: Resource Extraction
6052.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may abuse resource forks to hide malicious code or executables to evade detection and bypass security applications. A resource fork provides applications a structured way to store resources such as thumbnail images, menu definitions, icons, dialog boxes, and code.(Citation: macOS Hierarchical File System Overview) Usage of a resource fork is identifiable when displaying a file’s extended attributes, using ls -l@ or xattr -l commands. Resource forks have been deprecated and replaced with the application bundle structure. Non-localized resources are placed at the top level directory of an application bundle, while localized resources are placed in the /Resources folder.(Citation: Resource and Data Forks)(Citation: ELC Extended Attributes) Adversaries can use resource forks to hide malicious data that may otherwise be stored directly in files. Adversaries can execute content with an attached resource fork, at a specified offset, that is moved to an executable location then invoked. Resource fork content may also be obfuscated/encrypted until execution.(Citation: sentinellabs resource named fork 2020)(Citation: tau bundlore erika noerenberg 2020)
6052.profile: [profile]Resource Forking, identified as T1564.009 within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, is a Defense Evasion technique primarily for macOS. It involves abusing the deprecated resource fork file structure to conceal malicious code or executables within a file's extended attributes, evading detection. The hidden content can be executed by moving it to a specified offset in an executable location, and it may be obfuscated or encrypted until runtime. The Turla intrusion-set has been associated with this method.
6052.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Resource Extraction is a technique where adversaries gather data from compromised systems, often as part of the Collection tactic. The technical mechanics involve automated processing to aggregate sensitive documents and other information after initial gathering. This automated exfiltration is frequently paired with other methods like Exfiltration Over C2 Channel to transfer the data out of the network.

6053.name: File Section Appending
6053.profile: [profile]File Section Appending is a sub-technique of Masquerading (T1036.005) under the Defense Evasion tactic, applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves appending data to a file, such as adding a space or other characters to the end of a filename, to manipulate how the operating system interprets the file type and potentially bypass security controls or trick users into execution. The intrusion-set Turla has been associated with related file obfuscation methods.
6053.profile_without_enhance: [profile]File Section Appending is a Defense Evasion technique where adversaries append malicious code to the end of a legitimate file's sections, such as the overlay of a Portable Executable (PE), to avoid altering the file's checksum and evade signature-based detection. This method allows the original program to execute normally while the appended malicious payload is also run, effectively hiding the malware within a trusted file structure.

6054.name: DLL Injection
6054.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may abuse dynamic-link library files (DLLs) in order to achieve persistence, escalate privileges, and evade defenses. DLLs are libraries that contain code and data that can be simultaneously utilized by multiple programs. While DLLs are not malicious by nature, they can be abused through mechanisms such as side-loading, hijacking search order, and phantom DLL hijacking.(Citation: unit 42)

Specific ways DLLs are abused by adversaries include:

### DLL Sideloading
Adversaries may execute their own malicious payloads by side-loading DLLs. Side-loading involves hijacking which DLL a program loads by planting and then invoking a legitimate application that executes their payload(s).

Side-loading positions both the victim application and malicious payload(s) alongside each other. Adversaries likely use side-loading as a means of masking actions they perform under a legitimate, trusted, and potentially elevated system or software process. Benign executables used to side-load payloads may not be flagged during delivery and/or execution. Adversary payloads may also be encrypted/packed or otherwise obfuscated until loaded into the memory of the trusted process.

Adversaries may also side-load other packages, such as BPLs (Borland Package Library).(Citation: kroll bpl)

Adversaries may chain DLL sideloading multiple times to fragment functionality hindering analysis. Adversaries using multiple DLL files can split the loader functions across different DLLs, with a main DLL loading the separated export functions. (Citation: Virus Bulletin) Spreading loader functions across multiple DLLs makes analysis harder, since all files must be collected to fully understand the malware’s behavior.  Another method implements a “loader-for-a-loader”, where a malicious DLL’s sole role is to load a second DLL (or a chain of DLLs) that contain the real payload. (Citation: Sophos)

### DLL Search Order Hijacking
Adversaries may execute their own malicious payloads by hijacking the search order that Windows uses to load DLLs. This search order is a sequence of special and standard search locations that a program checks when loading a DLL. An adversary can plant a trojan DLL in a directory that will be prioritized by the DLL search order over the location of a legitimate library. This will cause Windows to load the malicious DLL when it is called for by the victim program.(Citation: unit 42)

### DLL Redirection
Adversaries may directly modify the search order via DLL redirection, which after being enabled (in the Registry or via the creation of a redirection file) may cause a program to load a DLL from a different location.(Citation: Microsoft redirection)(Citation: Microsoft - manifests/assembly)

### Phantom DLL Hijacking
Adversaries may leverage phantom DLL hijacking by targeting references to non-existent DLL files. They may be able to load their own malicious DLL by planting it with the correct name in the location of the missing module.(Citation: Hexacorn DLL Hijacking)(Citation: Hijack DLLs CrowdStrike)

### DLL Substitution
Adversaries may target existing, valid DLL files and substitute them with their own malicious DLLs, planting them with the same name and in the same location as the valid DLL file.(Citation: Wietze Beukema DLL Hijacking)

Programs that fall victim to DLL hijacking may appear to behave normally because malicious DLLs may be configured to also load the legitimate DLLs they were meant to replace, evading defenses.

Remote DLL hijacking can occur when a program sets its current directory to a remote location, such as a Web share, before loading a DLL.(Citation: dll pre load owasp)(Citation: microsoft remote preloading)

If a valid DLL is configured to run at a higher privilege level, then the adversary-controlled DLL that is loaded will also be executed at the higher level. In this case, the technique could be used for privilege escalation.
6054.profile: [profile]DLL Injection is a sub-technique of Process Injection (T1055.001) within the Defense Evasion and Privilege Escalation tactics, primarily targeting Windows. It involves writing a malicious DLL's path into a target process's memory using APIs like VirtualAllocEx and WriteProcessMemory, then forcing its execution via CreateRemoteThread to invoke LoadLibrary. Variations include reflective injection and module stomping to conceal code by overwriting a legitimate DLL's entry point. This allows adversaries to run arbitrary code within a trusted process's context, evading detection and potentially gaining elevated privileges. It is used by groups like Turla and Lazarus Group.
6054.profile_without_enhance: [profile]DLL Injection, identified as MITRE ATT&CK T1055.001, is a Defense Evasion and Privilege Escalation technique for Windows. It executes arbitrary code by injecting a Dynamic-link Library into a separate live process's address space. Common implementation involves writing a DLL path into the target process's memory using APIs like VirtualAllocEx and WriteProcessMemory, then invoking it with CreateRemoteThread to call LoadLibrary. Variations include reflective DLL injection and Module Stomping to bypass relocation and hide malicious code. Execution under a legitimate process's context allows access to its memory and resources while evading detection.

6066.name: Rijndael
6066.profile: [profile]Rijndael is the symmetric encryption algorithm standardized as AES (Advanced Encryption Standard). It is used by adversaries to encrypt command and control traffic, as seen in technique T1573.001, to conceal communications from detection. The algorithm is employed by groups like Turla, APT28, and Lazarus Group to protect their C2 channels, though implementations can be vulnerable if encryption keys are embedded within the malware.
6066.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Rijndael is a symmetric encryption algorithm, which is the formal name for the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES). It is used by adversaries to conceal command and control traffic or data prior to exfiltration, implementing a known cryptographic protocol to avoid reliance on inherent communication channel protections. The algorithm uses the same key for both encryption and decryption, and its custom implementation in malware can sometimes be reverse-engineered if secret keys are embedded within the code or configuration files.

6067.name: BYOI
6067.profile: [profile]BYOI (Bring Your Own Infrastructure) is a technique where adversaries deploy and control their own dedicated infrastructure, such as servers or domains, to support malicious operations like command and control, rather than compromising or abusing existing victim or third-party services. This approach provides greater control, resilience, and stealth, making attribution and disruption more difficult for defenders. It is commonly associated with sophisticated threat groups like Turla.[/profile]
6067.profile_without_enhance: [profile]BYOI (Bring Your Own Infrastructure) is a technique where adversaries use their own infrastructure, such as domains, servers, or cloud services, to support their operations, rather than relying on compromised victim assets. This approach helps adversaries evade detection by security tools that monitor for suspicious activity from known malicious infrastructure. It is commonly used in various phases of an attack, including command and control, data exfiltration, and initial access.

It targets Windows platforms and is associated with other Turla malware like turlarpc and agent.btz, which incorporate its code for process injection.

6069.profile: [profile].NET injector, also known as kubo injector, is a .NET-based malware used by groups including Turla. 6080.name: Identify Users of Interest
6080.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may use hidden users to hide the presence of user accounts they create or modify. Administrators may want to hide users when there are many user accounts on a given system or if they want to hide their administrative or other management accounts from other users. In macOS, adversaries can create or modify a user to be hidden through manipulating plist files, folder attributes, and user attributes. To prevent a user from being shown on the login screen and in System Preferences, adversaries can set the userID to be under 500 and set the key value Hide500Users to TRUE in the /Library/Preferences/com.apple.loginwindow plist file.(Citation: Cybereason OSX Pirrit) Every user has a userID associated with it. When the Hide500Users key value is set to TRUE, users with a userID under 500 do not appear on the login screen and in System Preferences. Using the command line, adversaries can use the dscl utility to create hidden user accounts by setting the IsHidden attribute to 1. Adversaries can also hide a user’s home folder by changing the chflags to hidden.(Citation: Apple Support Hide a User Account) Adversaries may similarly hide user accounts in Windows. Adversaries can set the HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon\SpecialAccounts\UserList Registry key value to 0 for a specific user to prevent that user from being listed on the logon screen.(Citation: FireEye SMOKEDHAM June 2021)(Citation: US-CERT TA18-074A) On Linux systems, adversaries may hide user accounts from the login screen, also referred to as the greeter. The method an adversary may use depends on which Display Manager the distribution is currently using. For example, on an Ubuntu system using the GNOME Display Manger (GDM), accounts may be hidden from the greeter using the gsettings command (ex: sudo -u gdm gsettings set org.gnome.login-screen disable-user-list true).(Citation: Hide GDM User Accounts) Display Managers are not anchored to specific distributions and may be changed by a user or adversary.
6080.profile: [profile]The entity "Identify Users of Interest" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the provided data, the core technique described is "Hidden Users" (T1564.002), a Defense Evasion sub-technique. It operates on macOS, Windows, and Linux platforms. Technical mechanics involve manipulating system attributes to hide accounts: on macOS by setting the `Hide500Users` key to TRUE in a plist or using `dscl` to set the `IsHidden` attribute to 1; on Windows by setting a specific Registry key value to 0; and on Linux by using commands like `gsettings` with GNOME Display Manager. The related group Turla is associated with this behavior.[/profile]
6080.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Identify Users of Interest is a reconnaissance technique where adversaries gather information about specific individuals within a target organization to enable further targeting. This involves identifying key personnel, their roles, and access levels, often through methods like phishing for information, searching social media, or examining victim-owned websites. The gathered intelligence can be used to shape subsequent attacks, including establishing or compromising accounts and conducting spear-phishing campaigns.

6081.name: Attempting to Spread Evercookies Between Browsers
6081.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may acquire credentials from web browsers by reading files specific to the target browser.(Citation: Talos Olympic Destroyer 2018) Web browsers commonly save credentials such as website usernames and passwords so that they do not need to be entered manually in the future. Web browsers typically store the credentials in an encrypted format within a credential store; however, methods exist to extract plaintext credentials from web browsers. For example, on Windows systems, encrypted credentials may be obtained from Google Chrome by reading a database file, AppData\Local\Google\Chrome\User Data\Default\Login Data and executing a SQL query: SELECT action_url, username_value, password_value FROM logins;. The plaintext password can then be obtained by passing the encrypted credentials to the Windows API function CryptUnprotectData, which uses the victim’s cached logon credentials as the decryption key.(Citation: Microsoft CryptUnprotectData April 2018) Adversaries have executed similar procedures for common web browsers such as FireFox, Safari, Edge, etc.(Citation: Proofpoint Vega Credential Stealer May 2018)(Citation: FireEye HawkEye Malware July 2017) Windows stores Internet Explorer and Microsoft Edge credentials in Credential Lockers managed by the [Windows Credential Manager](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/004). Adversaries may also acquire credentials by searching web browser process memory for patterns that commonly match credentials.(Citation: GitHub Mimikittenz July 2016) After acquiring credentials from web browsers, adversaries may attempt to recycle the credentials across different systems and/or accounts in order to expand access. This can result in significantly furthering an adversary's objective in cases where credentials gained from web browsers overlap with privileged accounts (e.g. domain administrator).
6081.profile: [profile]The entity "Attempting to Spread Evercookies Between Browsers" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique. Based on the provided context, the core technique described is Credentials from Web Browsers (T1555.003), a Credential Access tactic primarily for Windows. Technical mechanics involve reading browser-specific files, such as Chrome's `Login Data` database, and using SQL queries to extract encrypted credentials, which are then decrypted via the Windows `CryptUnprotectData` API using the victim's cached logon key. This technique is also performed on other browsers like Firefox and Safari, and adversaries may search browser process memory for credential patterns. The intrusion-set Turla is associated with this behavior.[/profile]
6081.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Attempting to Spread Evercookies Between Browsers is a technique for Persistence. The technique's resilience comes from its ability to respawn a deleted cookie from one of these other storage mechanisms. The retrieved information primarily details credential theft from browsers (T1555.003) and browser information discovery (T1217), which are related but distinct techniques for credential access and discovery, not the specific persistence mechanism of evercookies.

6082.name: Recreating Deleted Cookies
6082.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may forge web cookies that can be used to gain access to web applications or Internet services. Web applications and services (hosted in cloud SaaS environments or on-premise servers) often use session cookies to authenticate and authorize user access.

Adversaries may generate these cookies in order to gain access to web resources. This differs from [Steal Web Session Cookie](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539) and other similar behaviors in that the cookies are new and forged by the adversary, rather than stolen or intercepted from legitimate users. Most common web applications have standardized and documented cookie values that can be generated using provided tools or interfaces.(Citation: Pass The Cookie) The generation of web cookies often requires secret values, such as passwords, [Private Keys](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1552/004), or other cryptographic seed values.

Once forged, adversaries may use these web cookies to access resources ([Web Session Cookie](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1550/004)), which may bypass multi-factor and other authentication protection mechanisms.(Citation: Volexity SolarWinds)(Citation: Pass The Cookie)(Citation: Unit 42 Mac Crypto Cookies January 2019)
6082.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique "Web Cookies" (ID: T1606.001) under the tactic Defense Evasion, applicable to multiple platforms. It involves adversaries forging new web session cookies to gain unauthorized access to web applications or services, differing from stealing existing cookies. This forgery requires secret values like passwords or private keys and leverages standardized cookie formats and documented tools. Once created, these forged cookies can be used to authenticate to resources, potentially bypassing multi-factor authentication mechanisms. The intrusion set Turla has been associated with this technique.

This method bypasses authentication by reusing valid session tokens, allowing access as the authenticated user without credentials. It is related to the broader tactic of credential access and leverages the persistence of session state in browser storage or system memory.

6085.name: Infecting Removable Storage Devices
6085.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may compromise third-party network devices that can be used during targeting. Network devices, such as small office/home office (SOHO) routers, may be compromised where the adversary's ultimate goal is not [Initial Access](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0001) to that environment, but rather to leverage these devices to support additional targeting.

Once an adversary has control, compromised network devices can be used to launch additional operations, such as hosting payloads for [Phishing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566) campaigns (i.e., [Link Target](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1608/005)) or enabling the required access to execute [Content Injection](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1659) operations. Adversaries may also be able to harvest reusable credentials (i.e., [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078)) from compromised network devices.

Adversaries often target Internet-facing edge devices and related network appliances that specifically do not support robust host-based defenses.(Citation: Mandiant Fortinet Zero Day)(Citation: Wired Russia Cyberwar)

Compromised network devices may be used to support subsequent [Command and Control](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0011) activity, such as [Hide Infrastructure](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1665) through an established [Proxy](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1090) and/or [Botnet](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1584/005) network.(Citation: Justice GRU 2024)

These techniques are employed by groups such as Turla to obstruct post-compromise investigations and maintain persistence.

6087.name: Targeting Filter
6087.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may register malicious password filter dynamic link libraries (DLLs) into the authentication process to acquire user credentials as they are validated. 

Windows password filters are password policy enforcement mechanisms for both domain and local accounts. Filters are implemented as DLLs containing a method to validate potential passwords against password policies. Filter DLLs can be positioned on local computers for local accounts and/or domain controllers for domain accounts. Before registering new passwords in the Security Accounts Manager (SAM), the Local Security Authority (LSA) requests validation from each registered filter. Any potential changes cannot take effect until every registered filter acknowledges validation. 

Adversaries can register malicious password filters to harvest credentials from local computers and/or entire domains. To perform proper validation, filters must receive plain-text credentials from the LSA. A malicious password filter would receive these plain-text credentials every time a password request is made.(Citation: Carnal Ownage Password Filters Sept 2013)
6087.profile: [profile]Password Filter DLL (T1556.002) is a Credential Access technique for Windows platforms. Adversaries register a malicious dynamic link library (DLL) as a password filter with the Local Security Authority (LSA). This forces the LSA to send plain-text credentials to the filter for validation during any password change or set request, enabling credential harvesting from local systems or entire domains. The intrusion-set Turla has been associated with this technique.
6087.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Targeting Filter is a technique for credential access, likely on Windows platforms. It involves adversaries registering a malicious password filter dynamic link library (DLL) into the authentication process. This malicious DLL, positioned on local computers or domain controllers, receives plain-text credentials from the Local Security Authority (LSA) for validation every time a password change is requested, enabling credential harvesting from the entire domain.

6096.name: Search %appdata% subtree
6096.uncertain_mes:

6096.profile: [profile]Search %appdata% subtree is a technique for Discovery, targeting Windows. It involves adversaries searching the %appdata% directory and its subfolders on a compromised system to locate and collect sensitive user data, such as email client files (e.g., Outlook .ost or .pst files stored in `C:\Users\<username>\AppData\Local\Microsoft\Outlook`), browser credentials, or application configuration files. This local filesystem search enables information gathering from a specific, user-accessible path to support further exploitation. The intrusion-set Turla has been associated with this behavior.
6096.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Search %appdata% subtree is a technique used for Discovery, likely on Windows platforms. It involves enumerating files and directories within the user's AppData folder (e.g., C:\Users\<username>\AppData) to locate sensitive information or specific application data, such as Outlook email storage files (.ost, .pst) or Office template files (e.g., Normal.dotm), which can be leveraged for data collection or persistence.

6097.name: installing backdoors
6097.profile: [profile]The entity "installing backdoors" is a technique for maintaining persistence and control after initial access, often associated with groups like Turla. It involves deploying malicious software or hardware modifications to create covert entry points into compromised systems. This can be achieved through methods such as manipulating hardware supply chains to insert undetectable backdoors into devices, compromising software libraries to trick users into installing backdoored packages, or acquiring and deploying specialized malware from criminal marketplaces. The technique enables adversaries to evade defenses and execute further malicious activities remotely.[profile]
6097.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Installing Backdoors is a technique where adversaries establish persistent, covert access to compromised systems. This involves deploying malicious software or modifying legitimate components to create hidden entry points, enabling ongoing control, data exfiltration, and evasion of security measures. It is often facilitated through supply chain compromises, malicious software libraries, or the acquisition of specialized malware.

6098.name: trick users
6098.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may use hidden users to hide the presence of user accounts they create or modify. Administrators may want to hide users when there are many user accounts on a given system or if they want to hide their administrative or other management accounts from other users. In macOS, adversaries can create or modify a user to be hidden through manipulating plist files, folder attributes, and user attributes. To prevent a user from being shown on the login screen and in System Preferences, adversaries can set the userID to be under 500 and set the key value Hide500Users to TRUE in the /Library/Preferences/com.apple.loginwindow plist file.(Citation: Cybereason OSX Pirrit) Every user has a userID associated with it. When the Hide500Users key value is set to TRUE, users with a userID under 500 do not appear on the login screen and in System Preferences. Using the command line, adversaries can use the dscl utility to create hidden user accounts by setting the IsHidden attribute to 1. Adversaries can also hide a user’s home folder by changing the chflags to hidden.(Citation: Apple Support Hide a User Account) Adversaries may similarly hide user accounts in Windows. Adversaries can set the HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon\SpecialAccounts\UserList Registry key value to 0 for a specific user to prevent that user from being listed on the logon screen.(Citation: FireEye SMOKEDHAM June 2021)(Citation: US-CERT TA18-074A) On Linux systems, adversaries may hide user accounts from the login screen, also referred to as the greeter. The method an adversary may use depends on which Display Manager the distribution is currently using. For example, on an Ubuntu system using the GNOME Display Manger (GDM), accounts may be hidden from the greeter using the gsettings command (ex: sudo -u gdm gsettings set org.gnome.login-screen disable-user-list true).(Citation: Hide GDM User Accounts) Display Managers are not anchored to specific distributions and may be changed by a user or adversary.
6098.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique "Hidden Users" (ID: T1564.002) under the Defense Evasion tactic, applicable to macOS, Windows, and Linux platforms. It involves hiding created or modified user accounts from system login interfaces to avoid detection. Specific technical mechanics include on macOS setting the `Hide500Users` plist key to TRUE or using the `dscl` utility to set the `IsHidden` attribute to 1; on Windows modifying the `SpecialAccounts\UserList` Registry key value to 0; and on Linux using commands like `gsettings` for the GNOME Display Manager to disable the user list. The intrusion set Turla is associated with this technique.[/profile]
6098.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "trick users" is a general adversarial behavior not formally mapped to a specific MITRE ATT&CK ID. It encompasses techniques where adversaries deceive users to enable malicious actions, such as credential theft or execution of harmful code. This can involve mimicking legitimate system prompts for credential input capture, as seen in GUI Input Capture (T1056.002), or manipulating file appearances, like appending a space to a filename (T1151), to disguise executables and trick users into launching them. The tactic is typically Initial Access or Execution, targeting user interaction across multiple platforms.

6099.profile: [profile]Hidden Users, identified as T1564.002 under the Defense Evasion tactic, operates on macOS, Windows, and Linux platforms. The technique involves manipulating system attributes to conceal user accounts from standard interfaces. On macOS, adversaries use the `dscl` utility to set the `IsHidden` attribute to `1` or modify the `/Library/Preferences/com.apple.loginwindow` plist to hide accounts with a userID under 500. In Windows, they set the `HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon\SpecialAccounts\UserList` Registry key value to `0` for a target user. On Linux systems like Ubuntu with GNOME, the `gsettings` command can disable the user list on the login greeter. This method is used by groups like Turla to maintain persistence and avoid detection.[profile]
6099.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "deceiving users" is a technique aligned with the MITRE ATT&CK framework, likely under the tactic of Credential Access. It involves adversaries mimicking legitimate system or application prompts to trick users into providing sensitive information such as credentials. This can be achieved through spoofed graphical user interface (GUI) dialog boxes, like fake authentication requests for software installers or malware removal tools, using scripting languages such as AppleScript, PowerShell, or Unix shell scripts. The method relies on social engineering to capture input under the guise of a genuine service, often paired with monitoring user activity to time these deceptive prompts effectively.

6100.name: BGP Hijack
6100.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may execute their own malicious payloads by hijacking the way operating systems run programs. Hijacking execution flow can be for the purposes of persistence, since this hijacked execution may reoccur over time. Adversaries may also use these mechanisms to elevate privileges or evade defenses, such as application control or other restrictions on execution.

There are many ways an adversary may hijack the flow of execution, including by manipulating how the operating system locates programs to be executed. How the operating system locates libraries to be used by a program can also be intercepted. Locations where the operating system looks for programs/resources, such as file directories and in the case of Windows the Registry, could also be poisoned to include malicious payloads.
6100.profile: [profile]The entity "BGP Hijack" is not a standard MITRE ATT&CK technique; the provided data primarily describes the MITRE technique "Hijack Execution Flow" (T1574). This technique is used for persistence, privilege escalation, and defense evasion by manipulating how an operating system locates and loads programs or libraries, such as through poisoning directories or the Windows Registry. The intrusion-set Turla is associated with this behavior. The retrieved information on DNS server compromise (T1584.002) and protocol obfuscation (T1001.001) is not directly relevant to the core execution flow hijack mechanics described for T1574.
6100.profile_without_enhance: [profile]BGP Hijack is a network technique where adversaries manipulate the Border Gateway Protocol to redirect internet traffic by announcing illegitimate network routes. This can be used to intercept, monitor, or modify data in transit, facilitating man-in-the-middle attacks, data collection, or credential theft. The method involves compromising or spoofing a BGP peer to broadcast false routing information, causing other autonomous systems to send traffic through the adversary's controlled infrastructure.

6101.name: Command and Control (C&C) server
6101.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may communicate using a custom command and control protocol instead of encapsulating commands/data in an existing [Application Layer Protocol](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1071). Implementations include mimicking well-known protocols or developing custom protocols (including raw sockets) on top of fundamental protocols provided by TCP/IP/another standard network stack.
6101.profile: [profile]The entity "custom command and control protocol" is likely MITRE ATT&CK technique T1094 under the Command and Control tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It involves adversaries creating or mimicking custom C2 protocols, using raw sockets or building on TCP/IP, to avoid detection by not encapsulating data within standard application layer protocols. The intrusion-set Turla is a known user of this technique.
6101.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Command and Control (C&C) server is a core infrastructure component used by adversaries to maintain communications with compromised systems within a victim network. It falls under the Command and Control tactic (TA0011) and is a sub-technique of Acquire Infrastructure (T1583). The server acts as a central hub for receiving exfiltrated data and sending commands, which can be executed via scripting interpreters like PowerShell. Adversaries often use custom protocols or abuse legitimate web services like social media for stealthy bidirectional communication to these servers, which they may acquire by renting, buying, or configuring their own physical or DNS servers.

6108.name: JavaScript backdoor
6108.profile: [profile]The malware is known as JavaScript backdoor. It is attributed to the Turla intrusion set. Its key technical behaviors include acting as a stager for additional payloads, using registry keys for persistence, and being launched in a scriptlet COM object (SCT) via regsvr32.exe. The target platform is Windows.
6108.profile_without_enhance: [profile]JavaScript backdoor, also known as a JS backdoor, is attributed to groups including Cobalt and potentially Turla. It functions as a stager for additional payloads, achieving persistence by setting registry keys and being launched within a scriptlet COM object (SCT) via regsvr32.exe. The backdoor downloads further JavaScript files from a specified URL to the target system, which is a Windows platform.

6110.name: Mosquit
6110.profile: [profile]Mosquit is a malware entity attributed to the Turla intrusion set. 6111.name: MacOS installer
6111.profile: [profile]The entity, known as MacOS installer or holcus installer (adware), is associated with malvertising campaigns described as "Made in China." It is attributed to the Turla intrusion set and has been linked to operations by the Lazarus Group, as indicated by its presence in malware like iconicstealer and 3cx backdoor. Its key technical behavior involves being distributed as a Mach-O 64-bit executable for macOS, often disguised within installer applications, and it may use code-signing with identifiers like com.coverpage.bluedome.caglayan.desktop.installer. The primary target platform is macOS.[/profile]
6111.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The malware is a macOS installer, with observed file hashes including 5407cda7d3a75e7b1e030b1f33337a56f293578ffa8b3ae19c671051ed314290 and e6bbc33815b9f20b0cf832d7401dd893fbc467c800728b5891336706da0dbcec. The installer is a Mach-O 64-bit executable (x86_64) and has been observed with the bundle identifier com.coverpage.bluedome.caglayan.desktop.installer, indicating potential masquerading tactics. Its primary target platform is macOS.

6112.name: Staging
6112.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may stage collected data in a central location or directory on the local system prior to Exfiltration. Data may be kept in separate files or combined into one file through techniques such as [Archive Collected Data](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1560). Interactive command shells may be used, and common functionality within [cmd](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0106) and bash may be used to copy data into a staging location.

Adversaries may also stage collected data in various available formats/locations of a system, including local storage databases/repositories or the Windows Registry.(Citation: Prevailion DarkWatchman 2021)
6112.profile: [profile]Local Data Staging is technique T1074.001 within the Collection tactic. It involves adversaries centralizing collected data on a compromised local system before exfiltration, using command shells like cmd or bash to copy files to a staging directory. Data can be kept separate or combined via archiving and may also be staged in local databases or the Windows Registry, as observed with groups like Turla. This preparation minimizes exfiltration connections and evades detection.[profile]
6112.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Staging, also known as Data Staged (T1074), is a Collection tactic technique used across Windows, Linux, and macOS. It involves adversaries consolidating collected data into a central location, such as a specific directory, cloud instance, or even the Windows Registry, prior to exfiltration. This consolidation can use command shells like cmd or bash to copy files and may involve combining data into archives to minimize C2 connections and evade detection.

6114.name: Virtual File Systems
6114.uncertain_mes:
An adversary may attempt to enumerate running virtual machines (VMs) after gaining access to a host or hypervisor. For example, adversaries may enumerate a list of VMs on an ESXi hypervisor using a [Hypervisor CLI](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/012) such as `esxcli` or `vim-cmd` (e.g. `esxcli vm process list or vim-cmd vmsvc/getallvms`).(Citation: Crowdstrike Hypervisor Jackpotting Pt 2 2021)(Citation: TrendMicro Play) Adversaries may also directly leverage a graphical user interface, such as VMware vCenter, in order to view virtual machines on a host. 

Adversaries may use the information from [Virtual Machine Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1673) during discovery to shape follow-on behaviors. Subsequently discovered VMs may be leveraged for follow-on activities such as [Service Stop](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1489) or [Data Encrypted for Impact](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1486).(Citation: Crowdstrike Hypervisor Jackpotting Pt 2 2021)
6114.profile: [profile]Virtual Machine Discovery is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1673 under the Discovery tactic, applicable to IaaS platforms. It involves enumerating running VMs on a compromised host or hypervisor, using specific commands like `esxcli vm process list` or `vim-cmd vmsvc/getallvms` on ESXi, or accessing graphical interfaces like VMware vCenter. This information is used to shape follow-on attacks such as Service Stop or Data Encrypted for Impact, as observed with groups like UNC3886.
6114.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Virtual File Systems is a technique within MITRE ATT&CK, specifically ID T1564.005, categorized under Defense Evasion. It operates across multiple platforms. Adversaries implement their own abstracted or hidden file systems, separate from the standard OS file system, to conceal malicious components and file I/O from security tools. This can be achieved by storing a file system in unused disk sectors, dropping a portable partition image file, or fragmenting files in non-standard ways across the existing disk structure.

6115.name: Reductor RAT
6115.profile: [profile]Reductor RAT, also known as 'Reductor', is attributed to the Turla intrusion set. Its key technical behaviors include typical RAT functions like file upload/download/execution, and it uniquely manipulates digital certificates while marking outbound TLS traffic with encrypted host-specific identifiers derived from hardware and software. It targets systems via TLS communication. Infrastructure and supplementary information indicate it was discovered through modules containing a '.pdb' path clue.]
6115.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Reductor RAT, also known by its internal module name 'Reductor', is a Remote Access Trojan (RAT) that performs typical functions like file upload, download, and execution. Its key technical behavior is the manipulation of digital certificates and the marking of outbound TLS traffic by embedding unique, encrypted host-based identifiers into the TLS handshake's "client random" field. This sophisticated technique is used for traffic identification and fingerprinting.

6119.name: HTTP GET
6119.profile: [profile]HTTP GET is a specific implementation of the Application Layer Protocol (T1071.001) for command and control and exfiltration (T1048). It operates within the Command and Control tactic on Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. Adversaries embed commands and stolen data within the standard fields and headers of HTTP GET requests to blend with normal web traffic, often using common utilities like `curl`. This method allows communication with and data theft from compromised systems while evading network filtering. The intrusion set Turla is known to employ this technique.
6119.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "HTTP GET" is a specific technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, identified as sub-technique T1071.001 under the Application Layer Protocol tactic. It operates across Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. Adversaries use the standard HTTP GET request method to blend command and control or data exfiltration traffic with normal web traffic, concealing malicious data within common HTTP packet fields and headers to avoid detection. This method is commonly employed by numerous threat groups, including APT28, Lazarus Group, and MuddyWater, for covert communication.

6120.name: Commander Backdoor
6120.profile: [profile]Commander Backdoor is a malware backdoor attributed to the Turla intrusion set. It functions as the main backdoor component within the Mosquito malware framework, involving setup, encryption, logging, and command-and-control server communications. It is associated with operations targeting Total Commander software installations, as seen in BlackGuard's attempted file collection from its directories.
6120.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Commander Backdoor, also known as Commander, is a main backdoor component used by the Turla threat group. Its technical behaviors include setup, encryption, logging, and command-and-control server communications. The malware is part of a larger toolset that includes an installer, crypter, and launcher (DebugParser). It has been observed in operations involving the Mosquito malware family.

6121.name: PowerStallion
6121.uncertain_mes: [PowerStallion](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0393) is a lightweight [PowerShell](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001) backdoor used by [Turla](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0010), possibly as a recovery access tool to install other backdoors.(Citation: ESET Turla PowerShell May 2019)
6121.profile: [profile]PowerStallion, also known as powerstallion, is a lightweight PowerShell backdoor attributed to the Turla group. It uses Microsoft OneDrive as a command and control (C&C) server, with hardcoded credentials in the script, and functions as a recovery access tool to install other backdoors. Its primary target platform is Windows via PowerShell execution.

Its key technical behaviors include using Microsoft OneDrive as its command and control (C2) server, with hardcoded credentials embedded in the script. 6123.name: Spearphishing Campaigns
6123.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may send spearphishing messages via third-party services to elicit sensitive information that can be used during targeting. Spearphishing for information is an attempt to trick targets into divulging information, frequently credentials or other actionable information. Spearphishing for information frequently involves social engineering techniques, such as posing as a source with a reason to collect information (ex: [Establish Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1585) or [Compromise Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1586)) and/or sending multiple, seemingly urgent messages.

All forms of spearphishing are electronically delivered social engineering targeted at a specific individual, company, or industry. In this scenario, adversaries send messages through various social media services, personal webmail, and other non-enterprise controlled services.(Citation: ThreatPost Social Media Phishing) These services are more likely to have a less-strict security policy than an enterprise. As with most kinds of spearphishing, the goal is to generate rapport with the target or get the target's interest in some way. Adversaries may create fake social media accounts and message employees for potential job opportunities. Doing so allows a plausible reason for asking about services, policies, and information about their environment. Adversaries may also use information from previous reconnaissance efforts (ex: [Social Media](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1593/001) or [Search Victim-Owned Websites](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1594)) to craft persuasive and believable lures.
6123.profile: [profile]Spearphishing via Service, identified as T1598.001 under the Reconnaissance tactic, targets multiple platforms. This technique involves adversaries sending targeted messages through third-party services like social media or personal webmail to elicit sensitive information, often by posing as a legitimate source or creating fake accounts to build rapport and craft believable lures based on prior reconnaissance. The intrusion-set Turla has been associated with this method.[/profile]
6123.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Spearphishing Campaigns is a broad category of targeted social engineering attacks, not a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique ID. It encompasses electronically delivered lures aimed at specific individuals, companies, or industries to gain initial access. The core mechanics involve sending tailored messages via email or other services, which contain malicious attachments (like Office documents or executables) or links to compromised websites, often relying on user interaction (User Execution) to trigger the payload. These campaigns frequently employ impersonation and urgency to increase effectiveness and may use obfuscation techniques like manipulated file extensions or URL tricks to evade detection.

6125.name: AES加密
6125.profile: [profile]The entity "AES加密" maps to the MITRE ATT&CK technique Symmetric Cryptography (T1573.001) under the Command and Control tactic. It is a platform-agnostic technique where adversaries use symmetric encryption algorithms, such as AES, to conceal C2 or exfiltration traffic. The technical mechanics involve using the same shared key for both encryption and decryption of data, which can be applied manually within non-encrypted protocols like HTTP or layered within already-encrypted channels like HTTPS. It is associated with groups including Turla, APT28, and Lazarus Group.[/profile]
6125.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "AES加密" maps to the MITRE ATT&CK technique "Symmetric Cryptography" (ID: T1573.001) under the Command and Control tactic. It is a platform-agnostic technique where adversaries use symmetric encryption algorithms like AES to conceal command and control traffic. The technical mechanics involve using the same key for both encryption and decryption of the communication channel, which can be implemented manually within protocols that are not natively encrypted, such as HTTP, to obfuscate the traffic.

6126.name: 通信策略
6126.profile: [profile]通信策略 is a technique for maintaining command and control (C2) resilience, analogous to the deprecated MITRE ATT&CK technique Multiband Communication (T1026). It involves splitting adversary communications across different protocols or channels, such as using one for inbound commands and another for outbound data exfiltration. This approach can help bypass firewall restrictions and avoid triggering data threshold alerts on any single communication stream, as employed by groups like Turla. The primary tactic is Command and Control.[/profile]
6126.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "通信策略" (Communication Strategy) is a general concept rather than a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique. It encompasses various methods for establishing and maintaining command and control (C2). Related techniques include Fallback Channels (T1008), where adversaries use alternate communication paths if the primary is lost, and Multilayer Encryption (T1079), which involves nesting custom encryption within standard protocol encryption like HTTPS. These methods aim to ensure reliable, stealthy C2 and evade detection by avoiding data thresholds or bypassing network defenses.

6127.name: 自身更新
6127.profile: [profile]自身更新 is a technique where adversaries modify their own malicious tools or software to evade detection after initial discovery. This involves identifying the specific indicator (like a file signature) that triggered defensive systems, then altering or removing that indicator to create an updated, undetected version for reuse. The intrusion-set Turla has been associated with this behavior.
6127.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "自身更新" (Self-Update) is an attack pattern where adversaries modify their own malicious tools or malware to evade detection after initial discovery. This is achieved by identifying and removing the specific indicator, such as a file signature, that triggered defensive systems, then deploying the updated, undetected version. This technique is analogous to MITRE ATT&CK techniques like Indicator Removal from Tools (T1027.005/T1066), allowing for persistent reuse of malicious code.

6128.name: 横向移动
6128.profile: [profile]横向移动 is a Chinese term for the MITRE ATT&CK tactic of Lateral Movement (TA0008), which involves techniques adversaries use to progressively move through a network to access and control remote systems. This tactic is not a specific technique but a category encompassing various methods like Remote Services, Pass the Hash, and Exploitation of Remote Services, primarily targeting enterprise networks. The intrusion set Turla is known to employ lateral movement techniques in their operations.[/profile]
6128.profile_without_enhance: [profile]横向移动 is a technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, though a specific ID is not provided in the context. It falls under the tactic of Lateral Movement and is applicable across multiple platforms. The technique involves adversaries moving through a network after initial access, using methods like exfiltration over alternative network mediums (e.g., WiFi, cellular, or Bluetooth) to bypass primary network defenses. This can include splitting communications between different protocols to avoid detection thresholds. The goal is to maintain presence and access different parts of the network for further malicious activity.

6129.name: 下载文件
6129.profile: [profile]The entity '下载文件' (Download File) is a technique used by adversaries to transfer malicious files from a remote system to a local one. It is associated with the Turla intrusion set. The technique involves using commands or scripts to retrieve files, often as part of a broader intrusion chain for staging or execution. Related techniques include data exfiltration to code repositories, collection from network shared drives, and automated exfiltration processes, indicating its role in the data collection and exfiltration phases of an attack.
6129.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "下载文件" (Download File) is a technique used by adversaries to transfer malicious files from a remote server to a compromised local system. It is often a component of broader attack chains, such as initial access or execution, where tools or payloads are retrieved. The technique can be implemented using various command-line utilities or scripting, and it may be associated with groups like Gamaredon Group. It is a foundational action for malware deployment and data staging.

6130.name: POST请求和响应结构
6130.profile: [profile]The entity "POST请求和响应结构" (POST Request and Response Structure) is a technique used for data exfiltration, aligning with the Exfiltration tactic. It operates by adversaries manually posting staged data directly to a webhook URL or leveraging automated webhook integrations with SaaS services to push data over HTTPS. This method can blend with normal traffic when using common services like Discord or Slack. The technique is associated with groups like Turla and is related to other exfiltration methods such as Exfiltration Over Webhook (T1567.004) and Exfiltration to Code Repository (T1567.001).[/profile]
6130.profile_without_enhance: [profile]POST请求和响应结构 is a technique that involves manipulating the structure of HTTP POST requests and responses. This method is used within the Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol tactic, specifically as a sub-technique of Exfiltration Over Web Service (T1567). It operates on platforms including Linux, Windows, and macOS. The technique focuses on altering the standard format of these web transactions, such as embedding exfiltrated data within specific fields or parameters of a POST request or its corresponding server response, to covertly transfer information while blending with legitimate web traffic.

6131.name: 钓鱼文档
6131.profile: [profile]The entity "钓鱼文档" (Spearphishing Attachment) is a technique where adversaries send malicious email attachments to execute code on a victim's system. It is used in the Initial Access tactic (TA0001) across Windows, macOS, and Linux platforms. The technique involves crafting emails with attached files, such as documents or archives, that exploit applications or user execution to run malicious payloads. It is associated with groups like Turla. Supplementary information notes that adversaries may use this method to deliver tools for follow-on actions like credential dumping (T1003) or to facilitate data exfiltration to cloud services (T1567.002).[/profile]
6131.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity '钓鱼文档' (Phishing Attachment) is a technique where adversaries send emails with malicious attachments to execute code on a victim's system. It is mapped to MITRE ATT&CK technique T1566.001 under the Initial Access tactic, targeting Windows, macOS, and Linux platforms. The technique involves delivering attachments like Microsoft Office documents or PDFs that, when opened, exploit vulnerabilities or use social engineering to trick users into enabling macros or executing embedded scripts, leading to the installation of malware or credential theft.

6134.name: 伪装Microsoft Exchange/IIS服务
6134.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may install malicious components that run on Internet Information Services (IIS) web servers to establish persistence. IIS provides several mechanisms to extend the functionality of the web servers. For example, Internet Server Application Programming Interface (ISAPI) extensions and filters can be installed to examine and/or modify incoming and outgoing IIS web requests. Extensions and filters are deployed as DLL files that export three functions: Get{Extension/Filter}Version, Http{Extension/Filter}Proc, and (optionally) Terminate{Extension/Filter}. IIS modules may also be installed to extend IIS web servers.(Citation: Microsoft ISAPI Extension Overview 2017)(Citation: Microsoft ISAPI Filter Overview 2017)(Citation: IIS Backdoor 2011)(Citation: Trustwave IIS Module 2013) Adversaries may install malicious ISAPI extensions and filters to observe and/or modify traffic, execute commands on compromised machines, or proxy command and control traffic. ISAPI extensions and filters may have access to all IIS web requests and responses. For example, an adversary may abuse these mechanisms to modify HTTP responses in order to distribute malicious commands/content to previously comprised hosts.(Citation: Microsoft ISAPI Filter Overview 2017)(Citation: Microsoft ISAPI Extension Overview 2017)(Citation: Microsoft ISAPI Extension All Incoming 2017)(Citation: Dell TG-3390)(Citation: Trustwave IIS Module 2013)(Citation: MMPC ISAPI Filter 2012) Adversaries may also install malicious IIS modules to observe and/or modify traffic. IIS 7.0 introduced modules that provide the same unrestricted access to HTTP requests and responses as ISAPI extensions and filters. IIS modules can be written as a DLL that exports RegisterModule, or as a .NET application that interfaces with ASP.NET APIs to access IIS HTTP requests.(Citation: Microsoft IIS Modules Overview 2007)(Citation: Trustwave IIS Module 2013)(Citation: ESET IIS Malware 2021)
6134.profile: [profile]伪装Microsoft Exchange/IIS服务 is a persistence technique mapped to MITRE ATT&CK ID T1505.004 (Server Software Component: IIS Components) under the Persistence tactic, targeting Windows platforms. It involves installing malicious ISAPI extensions, filters, or IIS modules as DLLs that export specific functions like GetExtensionVersion and HttpExtensionProc to intercept and manipulate all incoming and outgoing IIS web traffic, enabling command execution or traffic modification. The intrusion-set Turla has been associated with this activity.[/profile]
6134.profile_without_enhance: [profile]The entity "伪装Microsoft Exchange/IIS服务" is a technique where adversaries masquerade malicious components as legitimate Microsoft Exchange or Internet Information Services (IIS) processes to evade detection. This involves installing malicious ISAPI extensions, filters, or IIS modules—deployed as DLL files—to gain persistence and unrestricted access to web traffic on compromised servers, enabling traffic observation/modification, command execution, or proxying of command and control communications.

6136.name: 修改文件时间戳
6136.profile: [profile]The entity "修改文件时间戳" aligns with the MITRE ATT&CK technique Timestomping (T1070.006) under the Defense Evasion tactic, primarily for Windows and Linux platforms. This technique involves modifying file timestamps (modify, access, create, change) to hide malicious files by making them blend with legitimate ones. In Windows, adversaries commonly alter the user-accessible `$STANDARD_INFORMATION` attribute via API calls, and may perform "double timestomping" on both `$SI` and kernel-level `$FILE_NAME` attributes to evade forensic detection. In Linux/ESXi, commands like `touch -a -m -t <timestamp> <filename>` are used. It is frequently employed alongside Masquerading (T1036) and has been associated with groups including Turla, APT28, and APT29.
6136.profile_without_enhance: [profile]修改文件时间戳 corresponds to MITRE ATT&CK technique Timestomp (T1070.006), a Defense Evasion tactic used on Windows, Linux, and ESXi platforms. The technique modifies file timestamps (modify, access, create, change) to hide malicious activity by making files blend with legitimate ones. On Windows, adversaries commonly alter the user-accessible `$STANDARD_INFORMATION` attribute via API calls, and may also modify the kernel-level `$FILE_NAME` attribute for "double timestomping" to evade forensic detection. On Linux/ESXi, commands like `touch -a -m -t <timestamp> <filename>` are used. It is frequently employed by groups like APT28, APT29, and Lazarus Group.

6145.name: SystemTime Structure
6145.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may corrupt or wipe the disk data structures on a hard drive necessary to boot a system; targeting specific critical systems or in large numbers in a network to interrupt availability to system and network resources. 

Adversaries may attempt to render the system unable to boot by overwriting critical data located in structures such as the master boot record (MBR) or partition table.(Citation: Symantec Shamoon 2012)(Citation: FireEye Shamoon Nov 2016)(Citation: Palo Alto Shamoon Nov 2016)(Citation: Kaspersky StoneDrill 2017)(Citation: Unit 42 Shamoon3 2018) The data contained in disk structures may include the initial executable code for loading an operating system or the location of the file system partitions on disk. If this information is not present, the computer will not be able to load an operating system during the boot process, leaving the computer unavailable. [Disk Structure Wipe](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1561/002) may be performed in isolation, or along with [Disk Content Wipe](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1561/001) if all sectors of a disk are wiped.

On a network devices, adversaries may reformat the file system using [Network Device CLI](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/008) commands such as `format`.(Citation: format_cmd_cisco)

To maximize impact on the target organization, malware designed for destroying disk structures may have worm-like features to propagate across a network by leveraging other techniques like [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078), [OS Credential Dumping](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003), and [SMB/Windows Admin Shares](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002).(Citation: Symantec Shamoon 2012)(Citation: FireEye Shamoon Nov 2016)(Citation: Palo Alto Shamoon Nov 2016)(Citation: Kaspersky StoneDrill 2017)
6145.profile: [profile]Disk Structure Wipe, identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1561.002 under the Impact tactic, primarily targets Windows and Network Device platforms. It works by corrupting critical disk boot structures like the Master Boot Record (MBR) or partition table to render a system unbootable, thereby interrupting availability. This can be executed using commands like `format` on network devices. The technique is often associated with groups like APT38 and Sandworm Team and may be combined with full disk wiping or feature worm-like propagation using credentials and network shares.
6145.profile_without_enhance: [profile]SystemTime Structure is a technique where adversaries manipulate the system's time settings to disrupt operations, evade detection, or trigger time-based malware. This can involve changing the system clock or time zone via OS utilities or APIs, which may cause failures in time-sensitive applications, security logs, and scheduled tasks. It is often used to bypass time-based security checks or to execute payloads at a specific future time.

6151.name: intercepted traffic
6151.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may use traffic signaling to hide open ports or other malicious functionality used for persistence or command and control. Traffic signaling involves the use of a magic value or sequence that must be sent to a system to trigger a special response, such as opening a closed port or executing a malicious task. This may take the form of sending a series of packets with certain characteristics before a port will be opened that the adversary can use for command and control. Usually this series of packets consists of attempted connections to a predefined sequence of closed ports (i.e. [Port Knocking](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1205/001)), but can involve unusual flags, specific strings, or other unique characteristics. After the sequence is completed, opening a port may be accomplished by the host-based firewall, but could also be implemented by custom software.

Adversaries may also communicate with an already open port, but the service listening on that port will only respond to commands or trigger other malicious functionality if passed the appropriate magic value(s).

The observation of the signal packets to trigger the communication can be conducted through different methods. One means, originally implemented by Cd00r (Citation: Hartrell cd00r 2002), is to use the libpcap libraries to sniff for the packets in question. Another method leverages raw sockets, which enables the malware to use ports that are already open for use by other programs.

On network devices, adversaries may use crafted packets to enable [Network Device Authentication](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1556/004) for standard services offered by the device such as telnet.  Such signaling may also be used to open a closed service port such as telnet, or to trigger module modification of malware implants on the device, adding, removing, or changing malicious capabilities.  Adversaries may use crafted packets to attempt to connect to one or more (open or closed) ports, but may also attempt to connect to a router interface, broadcast, and network address IP on the same port in order to achieve their goals and objectives.(Citation: Cisco Synful Knock Evolution)(Citation: Mandiant - Synful Knock)(Citation: Cisco Blog Legacy Device Attacks)  To enable this traffic signaling on embedded devices, adversaries must first achieve and leverage [Patch System Image](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1601/001) due to the monolithic nature of the architecture.

Adversaries may also use the Wake-on-LAN feature to turn on powered off systems. Wake-on-LAN is a hardware feature that allows a powered down system to be powered on, or woken up, by sending a magic packet to it. Once the system is powered on, it may become a target for lateral movement.(Citation: Bleeping Computer - Ryuk WoL)(Citation: AMD Magic Packet)
6151.profile: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique Traffic Signaling, ID T1205, under the Defense Evasion tactic and applicable to Linux, Windows, and Network platforms. It involves sending a specific "magic" sequence of packets—such as connection attempts to a predefined order of closed ports (Port Knocking), packets with unusual flags, or specific strings—to a target system to trigger a hidden response like opening a closed command and control port or executing a malicious task. Implementation can use libpcap for packet sniffing or raw sockets, and on network devices, it may require patching the system image first. The intrusion set Turla has been associated with this technique.[/profile]
6151.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Intercepted Traffic is a technique where adversaries capture or redirect network communications to steal data or enable further attacks. It is often associated with the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1040 (Network Sniffing) under the Collection tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. Technical mechanics involve using tools like Wireshark or tcpdump to passively capture packets, or employing Adversary-in-the-Middle (AiTM) methods to actively redirect traffic through compromised systems. This technique is frequently used in conjunction with traffic duplication and can target web protocols to blend malicious communications with normal traffic, facilitating credential theft and data exfiltration.

6154.name: First-Stage Backdoor
6154.uncertain_mes:
Adversaries may upload, install, or otherwise set up capabilities that can be used during targeting. To support their operations, an adversary may need to take capabilities they developed ([Develop Capabilities](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1587)) or obtained ([Obtain Capabilities](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1588)) and stage them on infrastructure under their control. These capabilities may be staged on infrastructure that was previously purchased/rented by the adversary ([Acquire Infrastructure](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1583)) or was otherwise compromised by them ([Compromise Infrastructure](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1584)). Capabilities may also be staged on web services, such as GitHub or Pastebin, or on Platform-as-a-Service (PaaS) offerings that enable users to easily provision applications.(Citation: Volexity Ocean Lotus November 2020)(Citation: Dragos Heroku Watering Hole)(Citation: Malwarebytes Heroku Skimmers)(Citation: Netskope GCP Redirection)(Citation: Netskope Cloud Phishing)

Staging of capabilities can aid the adversary in a number of initial access and post-compromise behaviors, including (but not limited to):

* Staging web resources necessary to conduct [Drive-by Compromise](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1189) when a user browses to a site.(Citation: FireEye CFR Watering Hole 2012)(Citation: Gallagher 2015)(Citation: ATT ScanBox)
* Staging web resources for a link target to be used with spearphishing.(Citation: Malwarebytes Silent Librarian October 2020)(Citation: Proofpoint TA407 September 2019)
* Uploading malware or tools to a location accessible to a victim network to enable [Ingress Tool Transfer](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1105).(Citation: Volexity Ocean Lotus November 2020)
* Installing a previously acquired SSL/TLS certificate to use to encrypt command and control traffic (ex: [Asymmetric Cryptography](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1573/002) with [Web Protocols](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1071/001)).(Citation: DigiCert Install SSL Cert)
6154.profile: [profile]First-Stage Backdoor is a technique aligned with the MITRE ATT&CK framework, likely corresponding to T1608 (Stage Capabilities) under the Resource Development tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. It involves adversaries uploading, installing, or setting up capabilities—such as malware, tools, or web resources—on infrastructure under their control, including compromised systems, purchased infrastructure, or web services like GitHub and PaaS offerings. This staging supports various operations, including enabling drive-by compromises, spearphishing link targets, facilitating ingress tool transfer, and deploying SSL/TLS certificates for encrypted command and control. The technique is associated with groups like Mustang Panda and Turla, and it aids in obfuscating multi-stage C2 channels by separating infrastructure for initial callbacks and subsequent, more feature-rich stages.[/profile]
6154.profile_without_enhance: [profile]First-Stage Backdoor is a technique mapped to T1104 (Multi-Stage Channels) under the Command and Control tactic. It operates by deploying an initial, lightweight backdoor that calls back to a first-stage command and control server. This first stage typically has automated capabilities to collect basic host information, update tools, and upload additional files, such as a more fully-featured second-stage remote access tool (RAT). The stages are often hosted on separate infrastructure to obfuscate the C2 channel, and the loader may include backup callbacks or fallback channels.

6155.name: Custom Cryptography
6155.uncertain_mes: Adversaries may employ a known symmetric encryption algorithm to conceal command and control traffic rather than relying on any inherent protections provided by a communication protocol. Symmetric encryption algorithms use the same key for plaintext encryption and ciphertext decryption. Common symmetric encryption algorithms include AES, DES, 3DES, Blowfish, and RC4.
6155.profile: [profile]Custom Cryptography, also known as Symmetric Cryptography, aligns with MITRE ATT&CK technique T1573.001 under the Command and Control tactic, applicable to multiple platforms. It involves using known symmetric encryption algorithms like AES, DES, 3DES, Blowfish, or RC4 with a shared key to encrypt C2 traffic, bypassing protocol protections. This technique is employed by groups including Turla, APT28, Lazarus Group, and Volt Typhoon. Related methods include custom cryptographic protocols (T1024) for obfuscation and custom archival (T1560.003) for data preparation, but T1573.001 specifically uses established symmetric algorithms.[/profile]
6155.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Custom Cryptography is a technique for obfuscating data or C2 traffic using non-standard algorithms. It is analogous to MITRE ATT&CK techniques like T1024 (Custom Cryptographic Protocol) and T1560.003 (Archive via Custom Method). The technical mechanics involve adversaries implementing their own encryption schemes, such as simple XOR operations with a fixed key or custom implementations of known algorithms like stream ciphers, often without using external libraries. This practice can introduce errors and its security varies, but the custom code can be discovered through malware analysis and reverse engineering.

6156.name: Krypton
6156.uncertain_mes: [Turla](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0010) is a cyber espionage threat group that has been attributed to Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB).  They have compromised victims in over 50 countries since at least 2004, spanning a range of industries including government, embassies, military, education, research and pharmaceutical companies. [Turla](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0010) is known for conducting watering hole and spearphishing campaigns, and leveraging in-house tools and malware, such as [Uroburos](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0022).(Citation: Kaspersky Turla)(Citation: ESET Gazer Aug 2017)(Citation: CrowdStrike VENOMOUS BEAR)(Citation: ESET Turla Mosquito Jan 2018)(Citation: Joint Cybersecurity Advisory AA23-129A Snake Malware May 2023)
6156.profile: [profile]Turla, also known as Krypton, Snake, UAC-0024, Venomous Bear, Waterbug, and Uroburos, is a cyber espionage group attributed to Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB). It is known for its custom Uroburos malware and for conducting watering hole and spearphishing campaigns. The group has compromised victims in over 50 countries since at least 2004, primarily targeting government, military, diplomatic, education, and research sectors. Its operations have included the hostile takeover of another threat group's infrastructure to attack a Middle Eastern government.

Its distinctive TTPs include hijacking satellite internet connections for command and control and compromising other threat actors' infrastructure, as evidenced by its hostile takeover of an OilRig attack platform. Distinctive TTPs involve compromising other threat actors to repurpose their tools, storing encrypted payloads in the Windows Registry, and leveraging hijacked satellite internet connections for command and control. The group is attributed to Russian intelligence and primarily targets government, diplomatic, military, and research sectors across Europe, Central Asia, and the Middle East, motivated by long-term strategic intelligence collection.

6159.name: Venomous Bear
6159.uncertain_mes: [Turla](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0010) is a cyber espionage threat group that has been attributed to Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB).  They have compromised victims in over 50 countries since at least 2004, spanning a range of industries including government, embassies, military, education, research and pharmaceutical companies. [Turla](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0010) is known for conducting watering hole and spearphishing campaigns, and leveraging in-house tools and malware, such as [Uroburos](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0022).(Citation: Kaspersky Turla)(Citation: ESET Gazer Aug 2017)(Citation: CrowdStrike VENOMOUS BEAR)(Citation: ESET Turla Mosquito Jan 2018)(Citation: Joint Cybersecurity Advisory AA23-129A Snake Malware May 2023)
6159.profile: [profile]Venomous Bear, also known as Turla, Snake, Uroburos, Waterbug, and Secret Blizzard, is a sophisticated cyber espionage group attributed to Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB). Its arsenal prominently features custom malware like Uroburos. The group is known for conducting watering hole and spearphishing campaigns to compromise targets. It has operated since at least 2004, with victims in over 50 countries across government, military, diplomatic, education, and pharmaceutical sectors, primarily for intelligence gathering and espionage purposes.
6159.profile_without_enhance: [profile]Venomous Bear, also known as Turla, Snake, Uroburos, Waterbug, and Secret Blizzard, is a sophisticated cyber espionage group attributed to Russian intelligence services. Its key custom malware includes the Snake/Uroburos rootkit, Gazer, Carbon/ComRAT, Kopiluwak, and LightNeuron. Distinctive TTPs involve hijacking satellite internet connections for command and control and compromising other threat actors' infrastructure for operational cover. The group primarily targets government, diplomatic, military, and research sectors in Europe, Central Asia, and the Middle East, motivated by long-term strategic intelligence collection.
6159.profile_without_enhance_0: [profile]Venomous Bear, also known as Zombie Spider, is a distinct intrusion set. It has been observed developing a wider toolset since at least 2017, indicating an increased operational tempo. While the profile lacks specific malware or TTP details, its naming convention (e.g., "Spider" aliases) and activity timeline show overlaps with other groups like Twisted Spider (TA2101) and Cozy Bear, suggesting a potential nexus within broader Russian-aligned cyber operations. Its primary targets and motivations remain unspecified.
6159.profile_without_enhance_0_no_hsage: [profile]Venomous Bear, also known as Zombie Spider, is an intrusion set believed to be linked to or overlapping with the Russian-affiliated group COZY BEAR. Its primary motivation is suspected espionage, aligning with the strategic intelligence-gathering objectives commonly associated with its attributed origin.
